units.tr: Since this is done with your kind permission, I come to you, most distinguished gentlemen. For it is fitting that I render to you, after God, the first account of the leisure which your generosity towards our Academy has given us. Generosity whose praise is all the more illustrious because its examples among the men of your Order are the more remarkable. The Kings of France rejoice to call Paris their firstborn daughter. Yet nothing outstanding is found in that in comparison with the greatness of so great a majesty. Your glory in this respect is rarer, since those who are the Rectors of the City are the same men who are greeted as Curators of the Academy. Undoubtedly heroic was the spirit of the Fathers, by which they dared to put their hand to raising a work of such magnitude. Nonetheless the virtue of the Sons is no less, for no calamities of the most difficult times, when the Republic itself lay almost crushed, could frighten them from the steadfast defence of it. By God's standing, through the provident care of the illustrious City Senate, this seminary of the Fatherland and the Church stood firm amid the ruins of all things. Indeed you have acted so generously that, as if forgetful of the recent disaster, it may seem to have returned to its own strength and recovered its former honour. If from this recent memory of past things it is right to conceive hope for the future, nothing should ever be despaired of for the Academy, as long as your will towards it remains the same and lasts forever. Thus, most distinguished gentlemen, this [Academy] was handed down by the Fathers to your City.

units.tr: ...that it is established they have lived, yet they hasten on regardless. So mad is this fever that everyone rushes headlong into the very thing from which the footprints of very many, if they had any sense, ought to have frightened them off. And you, then, who read these Exercitationes: let someone say, do you dare to promise yourself a fortune different from the one that most who long to write have experienced? I would be a fool and far too dull if any such thought had ever entered my mind. In this kind of study, what praise I might win if self-love had persuaded me most strongly! Yet it has not blinded me so completely that I could not foresee, as I have long been unable to help foreseeing, that the subject of my writing should not have been chosen by one who did not intend it to be easy, since the mere look of it would be disapproved by most of those who nowadays want to hear more subtle things.

units.la: Tanta nimirum existit hisce diebus nominis Cartefiani existimatio, ut famæ prodigus videri queat, neque prudenter fatis suis rebus consulere, quisquis non satius habet mutam secum excolere Philosophiam, quam mutire quicquam Viri Nobilis meditationibus non consonum: prorsus ut Avorum ætate nemo salutatus erat Philosophus, cujus non omnis ad Ariftotelis modulum composita erat sapientia. Sic, personis mutatis, eadem sæpe numero agitur fabula. Et profectò, fi quantum habet compendiosæ viæ ad comparandam sibi eruditionis haud vulgaris gloriam, tantum id haberet integri animi ac generosæ mentis, ad serviendum scenæ in hoc orbe Cartesiano cum cæteris me componerem, qui non adeò forsan sum somnolenti ingenii, ut non facile mihi foret inter primos ad Galli cantum surgere. At verò antiquior mihi semper habita fuit candoris conscientia, quæ haud sinit virum bonum, publicum præcipuè Doctorem, illa ceu vera profiteri, quorum certitudinem non efficaciter animo persuasit immotum rectæ rationis dictamen; cui uni sacramentum dixit quisqunque Philosophus est verè liber. Quod itaque de se alibi Cartesius, de me ipso hic dicam: „Cum ille homo (Aristotelem is innuit; Ipsum ego) tam felix extiterit, ut, quæcunque olim sive cogitans „sive incogitans scriptitavit, hodie à plerisque pro oraculis „habeantur, nihil magis optarem, quam ut à veritate non „recedendo ejus vestigia in omnibus sequi possem. Certè à Viri decretis nusquam abscedere intendi, nisi sic ad veritatem propius accedere mihi viderer. Eâ per omnia usus sum philosophandi libertate, ut quæ ab aliis verè dicta, non quia ab aliis dicta, sed quia vera, ratione confirmare; quæ ab aliis falsò dicta, non quia ab aliis dicta, sed quia falsa, ratione infirmare, laboraverim. Exulant mihi humana Nomina; qui solis Dei Oraculis hanc habeo reverentiam, ut mea iis submittam philosophemata. Istud Philosophi, hoc Christiani esse arbitror: quantoque digniorem hic præ illo sustinet personam, tanto religiosius illi cavendum censeo, ne quid suis ideis unquam vel minimum detrahat Fidei simplicitati, quæ unica hujus existit gloria. Si quid hac parte erro, lubens erro, qui sic philosophari laudi mihi duco. Ridebunt mea hæc, sat scio, primi omnium illi quorum spinosa meditamenta Sacram lucem refugiunt, quia ei inimica. Sed & isti sciant, tantum à me abesse, ut talium vel sperem favorem vel metuam censuram, ut si meorum quicquam illis placiturum scirem, id vel ideo suspectum haberem quam maximè;· quippe qui abominor toto pectore impietatem, quæ in medio orbe Christiano palam profiteri non veretur Philosophiam gentilem plane atque omnis religionis expertem. Interim neque ignoro, munia toto cœlo diversa esse demonstrare, atque dictare; quorum illud Philosophiæ, hoc Theologiæ est proprium. Indè quoties Fidei capita illustrandis Rationis conclusionibus adduxi, eâ adduxi cautelâ, ut sui utriusque disciplinæ salvi manent limites. Peperit olim infelix alterius hujus cum altera confusio chimæram illam monstrificam Philosophiæ dicam, an Theologiæ, Scholasticæ; in qua cum Aristotele divisum habebat
units.tr: Indeed, so great is the reputation of the name of Descartes in these days that a man may seem a spendthrift with his good name, and not prudent in managing his own affairs, if he does not think it better to cultivate philosophy silently by himself than to utter anything not in harmony with the meditations of a Noble Man. Just as in our grandfathers' time no one was greeted as a philosopher unless all his wisdom was shaped to the measure of Aristotle, so now, with the persons changed, the same play is often performed. And indeed, if I had as much integrity of spirit and generosity of mind as I have of the short road to win for myself the glory of no common learning, I would join the rest in serving the stage of this Cartesian world. I am not perhaps so sluggish of wit that I could not easily be among the first to rise at the cock's crow of France. But the conscience of candour, which has always been held more important by me, does not allow a good man, and above all a public teacher, to profess as true those things whose certainty the unmoved dictate of right reason has not effectively persuaded his mind. To this alone, he says, whoever is truly a free philosopher has sworn an oath. So what Descartes has said of himself elsewhere, I shall say here of myself: "Since that man (he means Aristotle; I mean myself) has been so fortunate that whatever he once wrote, whether thinking or not thinking, is now held by many as oracles, I would wish nothing more than that, by not departing from the truth, I might follow his footsteps in all things. Certainly I have never intended to depart from that man's decisions, unless I seemed to myself to come closer to the truth thereby. I have used such freedom of philosophising in all things that what others have said truly, not because others said it but because it is true, I have labored to confirm by reason; and what others have said falsely, not because others said it but because it is false, I have labored to refute by reason. Human names are banished for me. I, who hold this reverence for the oracles of God alone, submit my philosophical opinions to them. This, I think, is the philosopher's way, and this the Christian's. And the more worthy the person he bears here than that one, the more religiously I think I must take care that he never takes away the least thing from the simplicity of faith by his ideas, which is its sole glory." If I err in this respect, I err gladly, since I count it a credit to me to philosophise in this way. I know well that my writings will be laughed at first of all by those whose thorny meditations shun the sacred light because it is hostile to them. But let them also know that I am so far from hoping for the favour or fearing the censure of such men that, if I knew any of my writings would please them, I would for that very reason hold it in the highest suspicion. For I abhor impiety with my whole heart, which in the midst of the Christian world does not hesitate to profess openly a pagan philosophy, utterly devoid of all religion. Meanwhile I am not unaware that the duties of philosophy and theology are as far apart as heaven from earth: to demonstrate belongs to the one, to dictate to the other. Hence, whenever I have brought the articles of faith forward to illustrate them with conclusions of reason, I have done so with the caution that the boundaries of each discipline remain intact. The unhappy confusion of the one with the other once gave birth to that monstrous chimera of Scholastic philosophy (or theology, call it what you will), in which it had divided itself with Aristotle.

units.la: imperium Divina Pagina. Explodunt cam jure merito qui fapientiæ sublimioris & non-vulgaris studia præ sese hodiè ferunt. Interim Scholasticæ illi novam ipsi substituunt composituram Theologiæ, conditæ ubique idearum Cartesianarum condimento : ipso licet Cartesio improbante, neque uno loco, confusaneam doctrinam. Itaque per hos Philosopho licet in Christi scholam irrumpere impune, ejusque tunicæ latè qui splendeat pannum affuere ; docente vero Philosopho, ne hiscere quidem Christo fas est. Sed jam dudum immemor mei videri potero, qui apologiam quasi parare incipio operi, quo nullius me venari velle applausum, ab initio monui. Quo ergo tandem instituto id prelo commiserim, roganti dicam, non penes me fuisse non committere. Cum primùm, Academicæ Juventutis exercendæ gratiâ, has Exercitationes mente concepi, nihil sanè minus cogitavi, quam eas omnium oculis aliquandò fore subjiciendas. Quæ Auditorum votis suos debebant natales officio functas putabam intra Academiæ nostræ parietes, indeque omnem de eis cogitationem planè seposueram. Neque etiam hodiè consilium mutassem, nisi quosdam, qui in impetranda à me earundem editione frustrà fuerant, id agitare intellexissem non semel, ut in unum collectæ alibi me inscio typis excuderentur. Quando itaque vidi prelo me amplius arcere non posse charras, quæ in plurium versantes manibus ex mea exiverant potestate, lambere nonnihil ipse volui meos fœtus, potius quam ut in conspectum prodirent toti rubentes, quales olim diversissimis occupationibus, quas benè multas postulat quotidiani muneris ratio, distracta mens variis temporibus pepererat. Sic mecum inibam consilia: at quorum mox pœnituit vehementer. Frustrà enim ritè recensendis cogitationibus, tumultuariâ operâ in chartam quondam conjectis, me accinxi, qui tantum pacis cum aliis negotiis habere non potui, ut sæpè subito eas resumere vix permiserit. ferit in tanta otii penuria festinans prelum. Hinc emendare minimè licuit disparilem nonnihil conceptuum, diffusorum modo, modo contractorum magis seriem; multo minus dissimilem sibi hic illic orationis atque verborum texturam. Succinctæ magis sunt Cogitationes de Deo; quarum dedi duntaxat quoddam quasi compendium: cui apud pium Lectorem nihil detrahent quidam mei, plerique aliorum versiculi, quibus, pro eo quo ex divina contemplatione affectus erat modo, indulsit nonnunquam animus. Laxiores ferè sunt subnexæ Dissertationes, quarum totum argumentum quandoquidem est controversiosum, in tractandis rebus litigiosis veniam facilè merebitur forma styli disputatrix. Non te pluribus morabor, Lector, si id unum me æquè ac te fuerim serio obtestatus, ut eâ semper animi pietate ac reverentiâ ad meditandas, quas nobis Deus manifestas fecit, Divinas perfectiones accedamus, ne unquam ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς hisce nostris evanescamus, inveniendi aliquando incexcusabiles; quales inveniemur sine dubio, nisi quod cognovimus glorificaverimus summum Numen. Hoc age, atque Vale!
units.tr: the authority of Divine Scripture. Those who today profess a higher and uncommon wisdom rightly reject it. Meanwhile, those Scholastics substitute for it a new compound of theology, seasoned throughout with Cartesian ideas, a confused doctrine, although Descartes himself disapproves of it in more than one place. Thus, through these men, it is permitted to break into Christ's school with impunity, and they have sewn on a patch that shines brightly on his tunic. But with the Philosopher as teacher, it is not even permitted for Christ to open his mouth. Yet I may seem to have long since forgotten myself, since I now begin to prepare, as it were, an apology for the work, though at the outset I stated that I did not wish to seek anyone's applause. To the one asking with what purpose I finally committed it to the press, I will say that it was not in my power not to commit it. When I first conceived these Exercises for the training of the academic youth, I thought of nothing less than that they would one day be placed before everyone's eyes. I supposed that they, having served the wishes of the students, had completed their birth within the walls of our Academy, and so I had wholly set aside any thought of them. Nor would I even have changed my plan today, had I not learned more than once that certain men, who had failed to obtain from me permission to publish them, were working to have them gathered into one collection and printed elsewhere without my knowledge. Since I saw that I could no longer keep these papers from the press, which had passed out of my control and into the hands of many, I wished to lick my offspring into some shape myself, rather than have them come into the light all blushing, as they were once born of a mind divided among very many different occupations, which the demands of my daily duty require in abundance, at various times. I made these plans for myself, but I soon regretted them greatly. For in vain did I set myself to properly arrange these thoughts, which I had earlier thrown onto paper in a hurried effort, since I could not spare enough peace from my other business to take them up again without being hindered. In such a shortage of leisure, the press was hurrying. Hence I was scarcely able to correct the somewhat uneven sequence of ideas, now spread out, now more compressed, and much less the texture of style and wording, which is in places quite unlike itself. The Thoughts on God are more condensed; I have given only a kind of summary of them. Some of my own words, and most of those of others, which my mind at times indulged in as its mood was stirred by the divine contemplation, will detract nothing from them in the eyes of the pious reader. The appended Dissertations are rather looser, and since their whole subject is controversial, the disputatious form of style will easily earn pardon in dealing with contested matters. I will not detain you further, reader, except to earnestly beseech you, as I beseech myself, that we always approach with such piety and reverence the divine perfections, which God has made manifest to us, to meditate on them, so that we never become futile in our reasonings [ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς], and are not found at last without excuse; and we will surely be found so, unless we glorify the highest Deity as we have come to know him. Attend to this, and farewell!

units.tr: By the light of nature, do you wish to know the nature of the Deity easily, fully and solidly? Turn over what FRISIUS, grants you in his Meletemata. You will find much that delights. For every line breathes the subtle genius and subtle mind of the man, whether he shows what is true or refutes the false and harmful dogmas that the ancients taught and the new sophists stoutly defend with voice and hand. Often you will see (if you seek to turn the remaining pages) signs of a free and noble spirit. He approves and rejects nothing merely because of what names have esteemed. Let that be fitting for a slavish herd! Reason alone and divine faith bend him. To place the rods of wise judgment upon such a man will be the task of that posterity which speaks late and of the one whom fame will carry above the orbs of heaven.

units.la: Applaudunt Docti, Studiosaque densa corona Plaudit, beatam se videns fœtu novo.
units.tr: The learned applaud, and the dense crowd of students cheers, seeing itself blessed with the new offspring.

units.la: Ominor hoc fatum (nec sim tibi vanus Aruspex) Elucubratæ & eruditæ paginæ.
units.tr: I foretell this fate for these learned and laboriously composed pages (may I not be a vain soothsayer to you).

units.la: Nec satis: in reliquum diffundet se labor orbem. Spe vanidâ vel circuitionibus
units.tr: Nor is that enough: the labour will spread itself through the rest of the world, by vain hope or by roundabout means

units.la: Non avidum fallet Lectorem, sed melioris Veri replebit corda succo, sanguine:
units.tr: it will not deceive the eager reader, but will fill hearts with the juice and blood of a better truth;

units.la: Doctior ut redeat, maturior Orbis Epoptes, Dei, Sui, Soli, Poli Consultior.
units.tr: so that the reader returns more learned, a more mature initiate of the world, better informed about God, himself, the sun and the heavens.
To an Old Friend
L. M. Q. sang this.
A. BOSCHMAN, V.D.M.

units.la: EXERCITATIO PRIMA PRÆLIMINARIS, DE THEOLOGIA NATURALI.
units.tr: FIRST PRELIMINARY EXERCISE, ON NATURAL THEOLOGY.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Theologiæ Naturalis studium præ aliis homine dignum. II. Menti humanæ in statu unionis difficillimum. III. Periculi quoque plenum; ideoque tractandum reverenter. IV. Naturalis de Deo notitia maximè practica est. V. Minimè tamen ad æternam beatitatem sufficiens. VI. Non confundenda cum Fidei revelatione. VII. Interim hujus illi habenda ratio. VIII. Naturalis Theologia Revelatæ utilissima. IX. Ejus certitudo summa, si ritè tradatur.
units.tr: I. The study of Natural Theology is more worthy of a human being than any other. II. It is most difficult for the human mind in its state of union with the body. III. It is also full of danger, and so must be handled reverently. IV. The natural knowledge of God is above all practical. V. Yet it is by no means sufficient for eternal blessedness. VI. It must not be confused with the revelation of faith. VII. Meanwhile, it must be given its due place. VIII. Natural Theology is most useful for Revealed Theology. IX. Its certainty is very great, if it is rightly taught.

units.la: Ti rebus omnibus, ita imprimis ratione gaudentibus, is quo feruntur ad consequendum sibi maximam quam possunt sui perfectionem, congenitus est impetus. Partem ejus haud minimam absolvit in homine quâ is omnis natura scire desiderat cupiditas. Hanc itaque nisi pro viribus satiare laboret, quanto hac parte existit negligentior, tanto magis indignis modis infra suam sortem semet ipsum abjice-
units.tr: In all things, and above all in those that enjoy reason, there is an innate impulse by which they strive towards the greatest perfection of themselves that they can reach. A very large part of this impulse in a human being is the desire to know everything about nature. So whoever does not labour, as far as his powers allow, to satisfy this desire, the more negligent he is in this respect, the more he debases himself in ways unworthy of his station, and must be regarded as

units.la: Note: the initial word "Ti" is the large woodcut initial "U" of "Cum" or similar; the first word reads as printed "Ti rebus" with the initial letter unreadable [?]. re habendus est. Summam nimirum humanæ mentis absolutionem optimo jure dixeris rerum scientiam; quando quo longius in ea animus progreditur, eo plus quasi rationis possidere videri quodammodo potest. Quod quamvis in omni cognitionis genere existat verissimum, verius tamen est nuspiam, quam ubi mens erigitur ad contemplationem earum rerum, quarum cognoscendarum illi uni concessa sunt adminicula. Excellit hac parte præ omni alia quæ de Summo Numine philosophatur sapientia: in qua si felici mediatione datum fuerit attingere verum, majus utique ex hac quam alia quavis philosophatione & operæ & temporis feremus pretium. Nulla etenim existit contemplatio & utilior, & sublimior pariter ac nobis ipsis dignior, quam quæ Dei, indeque etiam Nostri, nobis pandit cognitionem; quâ unâ supremum sapientiæ humanæ apicem absolvi, jure merito dictum passim fuit atque creditum. Corpora qualicunque modo cognoscere etiam brutis animantibus indulsit natura; at verò Spirituum, nominatim Summi Numinis, notitia rerum ratione pollentium peculium est. Istæ quippe solæ aptæ natæ sunt illam, cujus gestant imaginem, contemplari Divinitatem: quâ meditatione supra semet ipsam, & quicquid caducum est atque terrenum, elevata mens, aditum sibi parat (quousque cum naturæ viribus invenire mortalibus datum est) ad veram illam & minimè simulatam Philosophiam, quam Mentis nostræ cum Deo assimilationem scitè dixit Plato.
units.tr: (the first words of this line are the continuation of the preceding unit) ...as such. Certainly the highest perfection of the human mind may rightly be called the knowledge of things; for the further the mind advances in it, the more it may seem in some sense to possess reason. This is most true in every kind of knowledge, but nowhere is it more true than where the mind is raised to contemplate those things for which it alone has been granted the means of knowing. In this respect, the wisdom that philosophises about the Supreme Deity surpasses every other. If by a happy mediation we are granted to attain truth in it, we shall surely gain from this philosophy more worth for our labour and time than from any other. For there is no contemplation more useful, more sublime, and at the same time more worthy of ourselves, than that which opens to us the knowledge of God, and thereby of ourselves; by this alone, it has been commonly said and believed, the highest peak of human wisdom is reached. Nature has allowed animals to know bodies in some manner, but the knowledge of spirits, especially of the Supreme Deity, is the peculiar possession of beings who are endowed with reason. For these alone are fitted by birth to contemplate the Divinity, whose image they bear. By this meditation the mind, raised above itself and above all that is perishable and earthly, opens for itself a way (as far as mortals are granted to find it with the powers of nature) to that true and wholly unfeigned Philosophy, which Plato aptly called the assimilation of our mind to God.

units.la: Interim, quum quod pulchrum est non soleat idem esse facile, nihil mirabimur, si arduum sit tantum negotium nobis homuncionibus, qui constamus mente non tantum, sed & corpore; atque illâ quidem tam arctè huic associatâ „ ut ipsa omnium „ difficillimè ad illa attendat, quæ nec sensibus, nec quidem „ imaginationi sunt præsentia: sive quia talem, ex eo quod „ corpori conjuncta sit, habeat naturam; sive quia in primis „ annis, cum tantum circa sensus & imaginationes occupareturi „ majorem de ipsis, quam de cæteris rebus cogitandi usum & „ facilitatem acquisivit: uti alibi de hisce rectè philosophatur Cartefius. Tantum quas ipse disjunctivè narrat causas difficultatis cognoscendi res spirituales, ego conjungere malim utramque. que. Quicquid sit, experitur in sese quilibet nostrum, pertinacioris meditationis circa res tam immensum à sensu remotas, in hoc rerum statu, adeo parum esse patientem hominis animum, ut merito credendum sit, claram distinctamque earundem scientiam isti servari seculo, quo ipse corporis vinculis solutus, & existens ἐσόπτρῳ liberiori contemplatione ista coram intuebitur, quæ nunc in speculo duntaxat videt & quasi in ænigmate. Quæ quisquis ut oportet attenderit, cum Seneca, non mirabitur, tam tarde eme, quæ tam alte jacent. Ut sæpè animum subeat mirari, quâ ratione quibusdam hodiè rerum immaterialium, maximè Dei, contemplatio tantæ dicatur & facilitatis & evidentiæ. Certè quotquot sic instituunt, eos meras cogitationes esse oportet: saltem non vulgares viros, quibus adeò facile sit hominem exuere; isti scilicet se assuefacere, quod & mentis cum corpore unioni, & tam longæ atque à teneris stabilitæ consuetudini plane adversatur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, since what is beautiful is usually not easily attained, we shall not wonder if this task is hard for us poor mortals, who consist not only of mind but also of body; and the mind is so closely joined to the body "that it attends most poorly of all to those things which are present neither to the senses nor even to the imagination; either because it has such a nature from being joined to the body, or because in its early years, when it was occupied only with the senses and imaginings, it acquired a greater use and facility in thinking about these than about other things," as Descartes rightly philosophises elsewhere on these matters. Yet I would rather join both causes which he states as alternatives of the difficulty of knowing spiritual things. Whatever the case, each of us experiences in himself that, in this state of things, the human mind is so little able to bear a persistent meditation on things so immense and so remote from the senses, that it is rightly believed that a clear and distinct knowledge of them is reserved for that age in which, freed from the bonds of the body and existing in a mirror [ἐσόπτρῳ], it will behold these things face to face in a freer contemplation, which now it sees only in a mirror and as in a riddle. Whoever attends to these things as he ought will, with Seneca, not wonder that things lying so deep are learned so slowly. Often it comes into one's mind to wonder by what reasoning the contemplation of immaterial things, above all of God, is said by some today to be so easy and so evident. Certainly all who proceed in this way must be mere thinkers, at least not ordinary men, for whom it is so easy to strip off the human being; for they must accustom themselves to this, which is plainly opposed both to the union of mind with body and to the long and, from youth, firmly established habit.

units.la: At parum foret, si difficillima tantum, nisi simul solliciti timoris plenissima esset, hæc philosophatio. Quæ enim mens creata tantum sibi tribuat, neque suæ sibi imbecillitatis adeò hic existat conscia, ut non sæpius metuat vertiginem pati ex altissimarum ac nimium supra se positarum rerum cogitatione? At-qui quicunque hic labitur, tanto graviore lapsu ruit, quanto fastigium, ex quo decidit, est sublimius. Non enim in maximis erratur, nisi maximè: neque ullus levis esse potest error de Deo, de quo etiam vera dicere periculosum est. Quapropter qui nullis deviis plurimùm hic falli cupit, ante omnia hanc sibi hic legem figat, ita reverenter scrutandam Majestatem, ne opprimatur à gloria. Præclarè in hanc rem Seneca „ Nunquam „nos verecundiores esse debemus quam cum de Diis (Deo) agi-„tur. Si intramus templa compositi, si ad sacrificium accessu„ri vultum submittimus, togam adducimus, si in omne ar-„gumentum modestiæ fingimur; quanto hoc magis facere de-„bemus, cum de Deorum (Dei) natura disputamus, nequid „temerè, nequid impudenter, aut ignorantes affirmemus aut „scientes mentiamur.
units.tr: But this philosophy would be only very difficult, and not also full of anxious fear, if it were not so. For what created mind attributes so much to itself, or is so little aware of its own weakness, as not to fear often to suffer a giddiness from thinking of the highest things and things placed too far above it? Yet whoever slips here falls with a heavier fall, the higher the summit from which he tumbles. For one is not mistaken in great matters unless greatly; and no error can be slight concerning God, concerning whom it is dangerous even to speak what is true. Therefore, whoever wishes to avoid being greatly deceived here, above all should set this rule for himself, to search the Majesty so reverently that he is not overwhelmed by its glory. Seneca says excellently on this matter: "We ought never to be more reverent than when we treat of the gods (God). If we enter temples in a composed manner, if we lower our face when we are about to approach a sacrifice, if we bring a toga, if we feign modesty in every matter; how much more must we do this when we discuss the nature of the gods (God), so that we affirm nothing rashly or shamelessly, either affirming in ignorance or lying knowingly."

units.la: Neque tantum impingunt, qui indignas de Ente supremo suâ mente fovent cogitationes; etiam isti devotionis rei existunt quam maximè, qui quem Deum Optimum intelligunt & Maximum, eundem tamen tanquam talem minimè sibi venerandum proponunt. Damnanda profectò hac parte est temeritas (quid ni impietas? ) plurimorum Scholasticorum, nobilissimam hanc Philosophiæ partem suis profusissimæ audaciæ conceptibus non tantum fœdè polluentium, verum etiam illam totam re ipsâ enervantium; dum, cæterùm securi, satis habent aliquid otiosè de Deo speculari & garrire. Quasi de perfectissimo Numine quicquam cogitare fas sit, quod non singulari pietatis affectu animum commoveat! Gravissima certè Apostoli querela est de Gentilibus, quos vanos factos pronunciat & infatuatos in suis ratiocinationibus, quod, quem noverant Deum, non tamen ut Deum glorificaverint. Ut ipsa suâ naturâ tota practica sit hæc notitia: adeò quidem, ut nisi sit talis, universa Philosophia Moralis re verâ nulla sit; quippe quæ omnis quanta est, unicè pendet à practica notitia Dei, tanquam independentis Monarchæ ac supremi Legislatoris, in Regno naturæ rationalibus, & rationaliter à se pendentibus, creaturis jura dantis. Ex quo uno omnia honesti ac turpis discrimina, nec non quæ vis morum præcepta, petenda sunt.
units.tr: Nor do those merely stumble who harbour unworthy thoughts of the Supreme Being in their mind; those also are most of all guilty of irreverence who, though they understand God to be the Best and the Greatest, nevertheless do not set him before themselves as one to be venerated as such. Indeed, in this respect the rashness (why not say impiety?) of many Scholastics is to be condemned, who foully pollute this most noble part of philosophy with their most lavish conceptions of boldness, and in fact weaken it entirely; while, otherwise secure, they are content to speculate and chatter somewhat idly about God. As if it were permitted to think anything about the most perfect Deity that does not move the mind with a singular affection of piety! Certainly the Apostle's complaint about the Gentiles is most grave, whom he declares to have become vain and darkened in their reasonings, because, when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God. So entirely practical is this knowledge by its very nature: indeed, unless it were such, all Moral Philosophy would in truth be nothing; for all of it, in its whole extent, depends solely on the practical knowledge of God, as an independent Monarch and supreme Lawgiver, who gives laws in the kingdom of nature to rational creatures, which depend on him in a rational way. From this one source all distinctions between honourable and base, and also all the precepts of morality, must be sought.

units.la: Non tamen ita practicam volumus, quasi simul salutaris sit & ad æternam beatitatem ducens hæc ex naturæ lumine hausta de Deo meditatio. Absit! Sic qui sentit, nondum gratiosam Evangelici Fœderis dispensationem intelligit, nec quantum Christiani debeamus gloriosissimi Servatoris meritis: quibus solis aditus patet ad Deum, tanquam benignum remuneratorem eorum qui ipsum quærunt; quibusque indignissimis modis nimium detrahunt, quotquot hac parte naturam gratiæ vel minimum æquare nituntur. Ad ἀναπολογισμὸν saltem sufficiunt istæ, non quid possit, sed quid debeat officii præstare suo Creatori, hominem docentes rationis scintillæ: quarum tamen lumen, fateor, merito nullum fere videbitur illis, quos longè lucidiores illustrarunt melioris Justitiæ Solis radii. Quos qui non satisattendit, ecquid mirum, illum, dum ducem sequi mavult corruptæ rationis ignes fatuos, à veri via aberrare, in transversum agi, atque illas sæpè nectere fallaci ratiocinio consequentias, quæ veritati Revelatæ exist unt inimicæ, & periculosissimæ in rebus fidei sequelæ. Pleræque certè quæ & nunc & quondam Christianam Ecclesiam infestarunt hæreses, non ex aliis seminibus ortum suum habuerunt, quam ex cœlestis doctrinæ cum pseudoTheologiæ Naturalis dogmatibus mixtura: ob quam insipidam χρέαν jam olim Ecclesiæ Doctores dixerunt Philosophos Hæreticorum Patriarchas, ipsamque Philosophiam Hæresium quarumvis condimentum.
units.tr: Yet we do not wish it to be understood in such a way that this meditation on God, drawn from the light of nature, is at the same time saving and leads to eternal blessedness. Far from it! Whoever thinks so does not yet understand the gracious dispensation of the Gospel covenant, nor how much we Christians owe to the merits of our most glorious Saviour, through which alone access is open to God as a kind benefactor of those who seek him; and those who strive in this respect to equal nature with grace at all, however little, detract from him in the most unworthy ways. These considerations are sufficient at least for an apologia; they teach not what man can do, but what duty he ought to render to his Creator, by the sparks of reason; yet their light, I confess, will rightly seem almost nothing to those whom the rays of the much brighter Sun of a better Righteousness have illumined. Whoever does not attend to these things sufficiently, what wonder is it that, while he prefers to follow as his guide the will-o'-the-wisps of corrupted reason, he wanders from the way of truth, is driven off course, and often ties together by false reasoning consequences which are hostile to revealed truth and most dangerous results in matters of faith. Indeed, most of the heresies which have troubled the Christian Church both now and formerly did not have their origin from other seeds than from the mixture of heavenly doctrine with the dogmas of a spurious Natural Theology; on account of this insipid [χρείαν] usage, the teachers of the Church long ago called the Philosophers the patriarchs of heretics, and Philosophy itself the seasoning of whatever heresies.

units.la: Hos scopulos absque naufragio is solum præternavigabit incolumis, qui nec ab una parte confundit disciplinas distinctissimas, nec ab altera parte sic securus hic philosophatur, quasi nulla existat, cujus aliqua sit Philosopho habenda ratio, revelatæ religionis veritas. Dixi, non confundendas disciplinas; quippe quæ tantum distant, quantum à Ratione differt Revelatio, quantum à πίστις Scire differt τὸ Credere Etenim (ut sileam hujus generis quæ alia huc adduci possent bene multa) nullas format Naturalis Theologia conclusiones, quam quæ ex principiis naturâ notis demonstrantur; nullas alias Theologia Revelata, quâ talis, quam quæ auctoritate Divinâ excipiendæ proponuntur piâ fidei simplicitate. Quæ quisquis cogitat, mirabitur, tantam differitatem non rectius observasse doctissimum Amefium, ut peritissimum Theologiæ Naturalis mystam, ita oppugnatorem ejusdem acerrimum.
units.tr: These rocks will be passed safely only by the one who neither confuses two utterly distinct disciplines nor, on the other side, philosophizes so carelessly as if there were no truth of revealed religion that the philosopher ought to take into account. I said the disciplines must not be confused, since they differ as far as Revelation differs from Reason, and as knowing differs from believing [πίστις]. For (to pass over many other things of this kind that could be brought forward) natural theology forms no conclusions except those demonstrated from principles known by nature, and revealed theology, as such, has no propositions except those put forward by divine authority to be received in pious simplicity of faith. Anyone who considers this will be surprised that the very learned Amesius, who was a most skilled initiate of natural theology, did not observe so clear a distinction, and was yet its most bitter opponent.

units.la: Nos, fidem Christianam supponentes, ita quidem prudenti viro in hisce de Deo meditationibus versandum censemus, ut altero quidem oculo ducem sequatur rationem, altero interim semper respiciat & veneretur fidem. Neque frustrà Revelationem hic suspicit Philosophus: ea enim frequenter istas suppeditat pulcherrimos de Divinis perfectionibus conceptus formandi occasiones, absque quibus fuisset sæpè, ut nunquam forte cogitassemus de elegantissimis veritatibus, quas nunc nostra ratio, fide elevata altius, in ipsis naturæ principiis latere, satis aperte videt. Ut, si uspiam, hic certè philosophandum fuerit, Fide Magistra, Ratione Ministra. Quam qui fastidiosè nimis improbant methodum, vera gloriæ animalia, nescio quam idearum innatarum suppellestilem importunè crepantes, vix satis Christiani axiomate se præstant dignos; quatenus in cæcæ rationis tenebris palpare malunt, quam istis gradibus, quos divina monstrat. strat bonitas, initi ad maximum nostrorum de Deo philosophematum perfectionem. Isti sunt, inter primos, qui se & alios abducunt δ᾽ ἀ τὴς φιλοσοφίας χαὶ κοινῆς αἰτιάτης ; quos cavendos, graviter adeo monet alibi gentium Doctor.
units.tr: We, presupposing the Christian faith, judge that a prudent man engaged in these meditations on God ought to proceed in such a way that with one eye reason leads the way, while with the other he always looks to and reveres faith. Nor does the philosopher look to Revelation in vain: for it often supplies occasions for forming the most beautiful concepts of the divine perfections, without which we would perhaps often never have thought of the most elegant truths which our reason, raised higher by faith, now sees quite plainly to lie hidden in the very principles of nature. If philosophy is to be practised anywhere, it surely must be practised here: faith as mistress, reason as servant. Those who too disdainfully reject this method, creatures of vain glory that they are, noisily clattering some stock of innate ideas, hardly show themselves worthy of this Christian maxim, inasmuch as they prefer to grope in the shadows of blind reason rather than to enter, by those steps which divine goodness shows, upon the highest perfection of our philosophy about God. They are, above all, the ones who lead themselves and others astray "through philosophy and empty deceit" [δι᾽ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καὶ κενῆς ἀπάτης], whom the Teacher of the Gentiles elsewhere warns so seriously to beware of.

units.la: Ex adverso in eandem de rebus maximis veritatem confentiens cum Christiana Religione Naturalis Theologia, non tan-tum plurimos Christianorum errores circa verum Dei cultum efficacissimè refutare apta nata est, verum etiam, si quà alia, hac imprimis viâ inchoanda Gentilium ad saniorem de Deo sen-sum conversio; quatenus hæc reos convincens vanæ superstitionis, istis eos evolvit præjudiciis, quibus imbutiavitis erroribus mordicus adhærent, nec meliori sapientiæ revelatæ faciunt locum. Ut jam nihil dicam de stabilimento, quod Christianæ fidei accedit ex mirabili rationis & revelationis hac parte harmo-nia, alteriusque cum altera consensu. Non quod istis fulcimentis ipsa indigeat cœlestis doctrina, per se quàvis demonstratione immensum certior; sed quod infirmos nostros ac sæpè fluctuantes, eheu! nimium animos, ipsum rectæ rationis suffragium haud parum confirmare queat in immoto veritatis cœlitùs patefactæ assensu.
units.tr: On the other hand, natural theology, agreeing in the same truth about the greatest matters with the Christian religion, is fitted not only to refute very effectively the many errors of Christians concerning the true worship of God, but also, if any other way, is chiefly the way by which the conversion of the Gentiles to a saner sense of God should begin: since it convicts them of vain superstition and unfolds for them those prejudices with which they are steeped, and to which they cling stubbornly in their errors, and so makes no room for the better wisdom of revelation. I say nothing yet of the support that the Christian faith gains from the wonderful harmony between reason and revelation in this respect, and from the agreement of the one with the other. Not that the heavenly doctrine itself needs these props, being in itself far more certain than any demonstration; but that the right judgment of reason can greatly strengthen our weak and often wavering minds, alas too much so, in an unshaken assent to the truth revealed from heaven.

units.la: Istis legibus, non aliis, hic philosophari decretum est nobis; qui deducere conabimur alias veritates ex aliis, tantum ut ipsa rerum series, atque illis convenicns cogitationum connexio, postulabit. Quam methodum quia neglexerunt multi, omnia ad rigidiora systematis præcepta nimium cogentes, plurimum detraxerunt nobilissimæ disciplinæ & splendoris, & certitudinis. Hanc equidem tantam hic promittere ausim, ut mathematicæ demonstrationi nullà parte quicquam cedat. Cujus rei daturus experimentum in animum primùm induxeram, more Geome-trico, necessariis præmissis Definitionibus, Postulatis, atque Axiomatibus, continuâ serie per Theoremata omnia deducere. Verum mutavi consilium, quando attendi, plerosque, rebus geometricis minus assuetos, istius modi demonstrandi fore im-patientes. Non tamen, si cui id volupe fuerit, nostra intelligenti arduum erit in istum ordinem hæc redigere. Sed jam du-dum Præsaminis abundè est. Ad rem ipsam! Utinam verò Spirituum Pater adspiret Spiritu suo nostro huic defefe, Spiritu primo ac perfectissimo, labori! Imo, Dæ,
units.tr: By these laws, and no others, we have resolved to philosophize here: we shall try to deduce some truths from others, only so far as the very order of things and the connection of thoughts agreeing with them will require. Many have neglected this method, forcing everything too rigidly into the strict precepts of a system, and so have greatly detracted from the splendour and certainty of this most noble discipline. I would venture to promise here so much that in no part will it yield to mathematical demonstration. To give proof of this I had at first intended, in the geometrical manner, to set out the necessary definitions, postulates and axioms beforehand and to deduce everything in a continuous series of theorems. But I changed my plan when I considered that most people, less accustomed to geometrical matters, would be impatient of this kind of demonstration. Still, if anyone should wish it, it will not be difficult for an intelligent reader to reduce these things to that order. But enough of preliminaries for now. To the matter itself! Would that the Father of spirits would breathe on this our labour with his own Spirit, the first and most perfect Spirit! Yes, grant it!

units.la: Da, Pater, augustam menti conscendere sedem! Da fontem lustrare boni! Da luce repertâ In Te conspicuos animi defigere visus! Disjice terrena nebulas & pondera molis; Atque Tuo splendore mica! Tu namque serenum: Tu requies tranquilla piis: Te cernere finis, Principium, vector, dux, semita, terminus idem.
units.tr: Grant, Father, that I may climb to your august seat! Grant that I may cleanse the fountain of the good! Grant that, with the light once found, I may fix the eyes of my soul, clear-sighted, upon You! Scatter the clouds and the weight of the earthly mass; and shine with your splendour! For You are the calm light, You the tranquil rest of the pious: to see You is the end, the beginning, the guide, the way, the path, and the same is the goal.

units.la: EXERCITATIO SECUNDA, DE DEI EXISTENTIA, ejusque per naturae lumen cognos- cendae modis.
units.tr: SECOND EXERCITATION, ON THE EXISTENCE OF GOD, AND THE WAYS OF KNOWING HIM BY THE LIGHT OF NATURE.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Artissimus inter notitiam Dei & Nostri nexus. II. Non, An sit Deus, disputandum; Quod sit, tamen demonstrandum. III. Demonstratio pro Existentia Numinis à rerum obviarum dependentia sumpta. IV. Multiplex, quae ex ea fluit pro eadem veritate, argumentandi ratio. V. Vis demonstrationis à gemina Cartesii exceptione vindicata. VI. Famosum Hujus ab Idea Dei petitum argumentum ad examen revocatum. VII. Alterum ab eadem Idea sumptum argumentum expensum. VIII. Tertia Cartesii demonstratio excussa. IX. Ex origine mentis humanae, Deum esse probatur. X. Solâ admiratione, in quam
units.tr: I. The very close bond between the knowledge of God and of ourselves. II. That we must not dispute whether God exists, but we must still demonstrate that he does. III. A demonstration of God's existence drawn from the dependence of the things we see around us. IV. The many modes of argument that flow from it for the same truth. V. The force of the demonstration vindicated from Descartes' twofold exception. VI. The famous argument taken from the idea of God is brought back for examination. VII. The other argument taken from the same idea is weighed. VIII. Descartes' third demonstration is examined. IX. From the origin of the human mind, it is proved that God exists. X. It is taught that the same thing is instilled into the mind by wonder alone, into which the contemplation of the universe carries us away.

units.la: abripit Universi contemplatio, idem animo insinuari, docetur. XI. Innata menti de Existentia Dei persuasio explicatur. XII. Eam dari, ex Legis Naturalis conscientia evincitur. XIII. Demonstrationum omnium summa brevis & utilitas proponitur.
units.tr: XI. The persuasion of God's existence, innate in the mind, is explained. XII. That it is given is shown from the conscience of the natural law. XIII. A brief summary and the usefulness of all the demonstrations is set forth.

units.la: {a}Am arcta Dei inter & Nostri notitiam intercedit cognatio, tamque nulla accurata alterius sine altero haberi potest scientia, ut quisquis ordine de Spiritu philosophari instituit, mox is in bivio dubius haereat, utrum absolutissimam archetypi perfectionem, num admirandam ectypi pulchritudinem, prius meditari oporteat. Nemo enim in tantis ingenioli angustiis rite Deum cogitet, nisi qui se satis diligenter cogitaverit ante; formaturus scilicet qualescunque pro modulo de incomprehensibili Numine notiones, ex analogia illorum quae ipse in se ipso deprehendit. At neque ullus in distinctam sui notitiam devenerit, qui nescierit principium sui; a quo res haec omnis altius deducenda venit. Ut quidem ista contemplationis series creatae mentis imbecillitati fit accommodatior; haec vero & ipsi naturae rei convenientior, & Ente primo dignior. Quamobrem & nos faciemus a Iove principium: ita tamen, ut nonnulla quandoque simus assumturi, ad instar Postulatorum, ut loquuntur Mathematici, quae Mentis nostrae existentiam & quaedam ejusdem attributa supponent, alibi demonstranda.
units.tr: {a}There is a close kinship between the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves, and so no accurate knowledge of the one can be had without the other. Whoever sets out to reason about spiritual things in order must soon hesitate at a fork in the road, and ask whether he ought first to meditate on the most absolute perfection of the archetype or on the admirable beauty of the ectype. For no one in such narrow limits of his little mind would rightly think of God unless he had first thought about himself with sufficient care, since he must form, as best his measure allows, notions of the incomprehensible Godhead from the analogy of those things he finds within himself. Yet no one will arrive at a distinct knowledge of himself who has not known his own beginning, from which this whole matter must be derived more deeply. This order of contemplation is indeed better suited to the weakness of the created mind, but the other order is more fitting to the very nature of the thing and more worthy of the First Being. For this reason we too shall make Jove the beginning, yet in such a way that at times we shall assume some things, by way of postulates, as the mathematicians say, which presuppose the existence of our mind and certain of its attributes, to be demonstrated elsewhere.

units.la: II. Non lubet in limine disquirere, An sit Deus? quae in aliis thematibus primas tenere solet disceptatio. Nec enim fas esse arbitror, in Problema dialecticum convertere veritatis per se notae Axioma; quod uti omni luce exstitit clarius, omni explicatione notius, ita creaturae cuivis rationali non tam anxie est probandum, quam nudé potius supponendum. Etenim quis neget poenis potius compescendum esse, quam rationibus refellendum, si quis adeo nullam rationis rationem habeat, ut ipsam quoque primam rationem ejuret. Attamen ne hoc ipsum frustrà nos dixisse grunniat Atheorum furor, ante omnia clarè detegenda erit ferrea spirituum istorum fortium contumacia; quá, quam ipsi secum tremente animo sentiunt atque exhor-rescunt veritatis vim, ore tenus nihilominus negare malunt, quam se agnoscere tales, quales etiam inviti quotidie sese deprehendunt, pendentes nimirum ex independenti supremæ cujusdam causæ influxu & arbitrio. Hujus teterrimi hominum generis vesaniam si argumentis ex naturæ lumine ductis manifestam fecerimus, confutatum eâdem operâ dederimus Faustum Senensem, aliosque qui cum illo omnem naturalem Dei notitiam solùm non penitus expungunt: quæ imprimis ferenda neutiquam est perversa impietas in homine, qui ipse nullam fermè aliam quam ex corruptæ rationis lumine haustam profitetur Theologiam.
units.tr: II. I do not care to inquire at the threshold, Whether God exists? which is the dispute that usually holds the first place in other treatises. For I do not think it right to turn into a dialectical problem an axiom known of itself through truth; which, as it stands clearer than all light and better known than any explanation, is less to be proved anxiously to any rational creature than simply to be presupposed. Indeed, who would not deny that such a person should be restrained by punishments rather than refuted by arguments, if he had so little reason that he would even renounce the first principle of reason? Nevertheless, lest the rage of the atheists grunt that we have spoken in vain, first the iron obstinacy of those strong spirits must be clearly exposed. They deny the force of truth with their mouths, though in their trembling hearts they feel it and shudder at it, preferring not to acknowledge themselves as they are, as they discover themselves daily even against their will, namely dependent on the influence and will of some independent supreme cause. If we make the madness of this most loathsome kind of men plain by arguments drawn from the light of nature, we shall at the same time have refuted Faustus Socinus of Siena and others who, along with him, do not wholly expunge all natural knowledge of God. Above all, that perverse impiety must by no means be tolerated in a man who professes almost no theology other than one drawn from the light of corrupted reason.
III.

units.la: Istis, omnibusque simul aliis <bl>τῶ ἀξιοπίστω</bl> quomodocunque litantibus, occurrimus nos unâ hac demonstratione prorsus Achillea. Quodcunque existit finitum & imperfectum (sive sensibus id obvium sit, sive intellectui duntaxat: ipsum se v. c. cogitet Atheus, si detur) hoc omne vel à se est, vel ab alio. Illud si eligas, id vel erit à se, uti loquuntur, positivè, id est, tanquam à causa effectrice sui ipsius; vel negativè, quatenus usque adeo ad existendum sibi sufficit, ut nullius plane causæ sit indigum. Prius citra manifestam repugnantiam dici nequit, cum producere supponat fuisse, produci involvat non-fuisse. Quapropter si quid fuerit causa sui, fuisset id, nec tamen fuisset; dependens foret, & independens; se ipso prius simul esset, & posterius: verbo, idem foret, & tamen multis modis à se diversum. Quid? quod unumquodque tendat in sui perfectionem quantum potest: ut, si quid sibi suam dedisset essentiam, non limitatam illam quam possidet sed omnibus numeris absolutam potius eam in se contulisset. At neque dici potest posterius; quum, quod independens est, id finitæ perfectionis esse non posse, infrà firmissimè simus demonstraturi. Nequit itaque res finita qualicunque modo à se esse: quapropter restat, ut sit producta ab alio quo à se distincto. De isto vero eadem redibit quæstio. Si à se esse admittas, utique, ut dixi, imperfectum id esse non potest: ut jam re ipsa sic pervenerimus ad causam primam undiquaque perfectam; quae ipsa Deus est. Sin & istud à superiori rursum principio fluxisse contendas, atque hoc itidem ab alio, licebit quidem seriem causarum concipere bene longam, infinitam autem statuere ratio neutiquam permittit. Etenim ubi una eademque res diverso respectu causa simul est & effectum, istic qualis est ordo in descensu per effecta, talis idem est in ascensu per causas. Jam vero effectorum seriem finitam esse, res ipsa clamat; ergo & causarum. Adde, augeri indies causarum numerum, quoties nova effecta procedunt à causis, quae ipsae nuper effecta ultima duntaxat erant, non causae. Atqui id infinitati adversatur è diametro; quae, uti est quid maximum, ita omne sui incrementum, non minus quam ipsos fines, prorsus respuit. Cogitur ergo, quisquis evidenti rationisJumini palam contradicere non vult, in omni rerum ab aliis pendentium subordinatione subsistere tandem in aliquo principio, quod quemadmodum est causa causarum, ita à nullo pendens sibi sufficit plenissimè ad exsistendum. Ast hoc ipsum Deus est; cujus existentia erat demonstranda.
units.tr: Against these men, and against all others who in whatever way offer sacrifice to the credible [τῶ ἀξιοπίστω], we meet them with this one demonstration, which is altogether Achillean. Whatever exists finite and imperfect (whether it be obvious to the senses or to the intellect alone: let the atheist himself, if there is such a thing, think of himself) all of it is either from itself or from another. If you choose the first, then it will be from itself, as they say, either positively, that is, as from an efficient cause of itself, or negatively, in so far as it is so sufficient for existing that it has no need of any cause at all. The former cannot be said without a manifest contradiction, since to produce supposes that it has existed, and to be produced involves not having existed. Therefore if anything were the cause of itself, it would have been and yet would not have been; it would be dependent and independent; it would be prior and posterior to itself at the same time; in a word, it would be the same thing and yet different from itself in many ways. What more? Every thing strives toward its own perfection as far as it can, so that if something had given itself its own essence, it would have conferred upon itself not the limited essence it possesses, but one absolute in every respect. Yet neither can it be said to be posterior, since we shall most firmly demonstrate below that what is independent cannot be of finite perfection. Therefore a finite thing cannot in any way be from itself; it remains, then, that it is produced by another distinct from itself. But concerning that other, the same question returns. If you admit that it is from itself, then, as I said, it cannot be imperfect; and so in fact we have arrived at a first cause perfect in every respect, which is God himself. But if you contend that this too has flowed again from a higher principle, and that this in turn from another, one may indeed conceive a series of causes quite long, but reason by no means permits us to posit it as infinite. For where one and the same thing is at once a cause and an effect in different respects, the order of the descent through effects is the same as the order of the ascent through causes. Now the very thing cries out that the series of effects is finite; therefore so is the series of causes. Add that the number of causes grows daily whenever new effects proceed from causes which themselves were only lately the last effects and not causes. But this is diametrically opposed to infinity, which, being something greatest, utterly rejects every increase of itself, no less than its own limits. Therefore whoever does not wish to contradict openly the evident light of reason is compelled to rest, in the ordering of all things dependent on others, at last upon some principle which, as it is the cause of causes, so, depending on nothing, is fully sufficient for existing. But this very thing is God; whose existence was to be demonstrated.
IV.

units.la: Atque hoc unum argumentum nobis hic erit instar omnium: tum, quod per se sit longè efficacissimum, nullam relinquens evasionis rimam; tum, quod quae aliae adferuntur pro adstruenda summi Numinis existentia rationes, huic fere debeant certitudinis suae fundamenta. Caeterum, intelligenti minimè arduum erit ex hac pharetra complures depromere sagittas Atheismum confodientes. V. G. Occurrat res quaepiam contingens; ea, cum ex se & per se non magis apta nata sit exsistere quam non-existere, utique à causa quadam processit, per quam sit potius, quam non-sit: eaque vel necessaria erit, vel contingens. Si hoc, redit eadem difficultas. Quumque, per ante dicta, nullarum causarum, adeoque nec contingentium, ordo infinitus dari queat, nunquam quis se hic expediet, qui non velit subsistere in causa absolutae necessitatis in existendo; quae Deus solus est, ut infrà docebitur. Pari modo, ex rebus possibilibus inferre licebit primam aliquam potentiam; ex mutabilibus, principium quodpiam immutabile; ex finitis, causam quandam infinitam; ex temporariis ens aliquod quod ante tempus fuit sine tempore. Verum ista jam tractare pro meritis non finit præfixa brevitas: quæ eadem vetat urgere pulcherrimas rationes, quæ pro confirmanda eadem hac prima veritate peti possunt ab admiranda dispositione, ordine, ac varietate rerum naturalium; nec non ab earundem constanti tendentia, & quidem citra ullam ejus in se conscientiam, in suos fines; item ab appetitu summi boni voluntati finitæ ingenito; aliaque id genus plura, de quibus videndi scriptores, qui toti de hisce disseruerunt fusius.
units.tr: This one argument will serve here in place of all the others. It is by far the most effective in itself, leaving no crack for escape, and nearly all the other reasons brought forward to establish the existence of the supreme Deity draw their certainty from it. Moreover, it will not be difficult for an intelligent reader to draw from this quiver several arrows that pierce Atheism. For example, let some contingent thing present itself. Since it is by its own nature no more fit to exist than not to exist, it must have proceeded from some cause, through which it is rather than is not. That cause will either be necessary or contingent. If it is contingent, the same difficulty returns. And since, by what was said above, an infinite series of causes, and therefore of contingent causes, cannot be granted, no one who does not wish to stop at a cause of absolute necessity in existing will ever extricate himself. That cause is God alone, as will be taught below. In the same way, from possible things we may infer some first power; from changeable things, some unchangeable principle; from finite things, some infinite cause; from temporal things, some being that existed before time, without time. But the brevity I have set myself does not allow me to treat these matters as they deserve, nor does it allow me to press the most beautiful arguments that can be drawn, to confirm this same first truth, from the admirable arrangement, order and variety of natural things; nor from their constant tendency toward their ends, and that without any consciousness of it in themselves; likewise from the desire for the highest good, which is innate in the finite will; and many other arguments of this kind. On these, let readers consult the writers who have treated them at length in whole books.

units.la: Et ista quidem arma sunt, quibus victrix religio felicissimè hactenus Atheismum triumphavit: ut eorum, qui illis, etiam Scripturarum calculo probatis, qualicunque modo quicquam detrahere nituntur, merito prudentioribus suspecta sint consilia, nec admittenda quibus causa Dei ut sarta tecta maneat cordi est. Quapropter minimè ferenda hac parte prævaricatio quorundam, mirâ temeritate istæc omnia amoventium, quo solidioribus, scilicet! suis ab Idea quapiam Dei petitis demonstrationibus faciant locum. Neque enim censent hi, „ desu„mendum esse argumentum ex eo, quod videamus in sen„sibilibus esse ordinem, sive successionem quandam causarum „efficientium: tum, quia Deum existere multo evidentius esse „putant, quam ullas res sensibiles; tum etiam, quia per istam „causarum successionem non videntur alio possedevenire, quam „ad imperfectionem sui intellectus agnoscendam, quod nem„pe non possint comprehendere, quomodo infinitæ tales cau-„sæ sibi mutuo ab æterno ita successerunt, ut nulla fuerit pri-„ma. Nam certè ex eo quod istud non possunt comprehen„dere, non sequitur, aliquam primam esse debere, &c. Sileo nunc quæ ista involvunt Scepticismi fundamenta; gravius est', quod causam Atheismi immane quantum juvent. Frustrà tamen. Nam, ut verbo dicam, non ideo infinitam causarum successionem negamus, quod eam non possimus comprehendere (quamvis & ideò neganda foret iis, qui, cum Cartesio, nullam aliam normam habent eorum quæ affirmare & negare debent, quam propriam perceptionem); sed quod illam à parte rei manifestam, nec unam, involvere contradictionem firmissimè doceat recta ratio: uti ostendimus. Sic quidem longè falsissimum est posterius. At simul & experientiæ adversum, & miris modis in auctoritatem Sacram contumeliosum, exististprius. prius. Si namque Deum existere multò evidentius fit , quam ullas res sensibiles , mirum profectò est , adeo hanc subtilitatem vel nescivisse, vel neglexisse, Apostolum gentium, quando tanta cum emphasi urget & inculcat , invisibilia Dei , aeternam videlicet potentiam & NB. Divinitatem , mente perpensa pervideri jam inde à mundo condito ex iis quae fecit. An verò qui sic instituit etiam habendus est putasse , Deum existere multò evidentius esse , quam ullas res sensibiles ? Ita qui putat , eum simul putare necessum est , Spiritum S. in hisce similibusque ratiociniis usum fuisse termino medio , qui multò minus erat evidens quam ipsa conclusio demonstranda. Quod uti palam arguit defectum judicii , & modum argumentandi absurdissimum , ita quam istiusmodi cogitata benè conveniant cum debita Scripturarum reverentia , viderint isti qui neminem ante Agamemnona fortem vixisse sibi persuadere audent.
units.tr: These are indeed the weapons with which the victorious religion has so far most happily triumphed over Atheism. Hence, those who try in any way to take anything away from these weapons, even though they have been approved by the testimony of Scripture, are rightly regarded with suspicion by the more prudent, and their plans are not to be admitted, since they care that the cause of God remain whole and intact. For this reason, the transgression of certain men, who with astonishing rashness remove all these things so that, forsooth, they may make room for more solid demonstrations drawn from some idea of God, is in no way to be tolerated. For these men do not think that "the argument must be drawn from the fact that we see an order, or a certain succession of efficient causes, in sensible things; partly because they think that God's existence is much more evident than any sensible things; partly also because, through this succession of causes, they seem to arrive at nothing except the recognition of the imperfection of our intellect, namely that we cannot comprehend how such infinite causes have succeeded one another from eternity in mutual order, so that there was no first one. For certainly, from the fact that we cannot comprehend this, it does not follow that there must be some first cause, etc." I pass over for now what these assertions contain as foundations of Scepticism; what is more serious is that they greatly help the cause of Atheism. Yet they do so in vain. For, to put it in a word, we do not deny an infinite succession of causes because we cannot comprehend it (although on that ground it would have to be denied by those who, with Descartes, have no other norm of what they ought to affirm and deny than their own perception); rather, right reason teaches most firmly that such a succession, in reality, is manifest and not one, and involves a contradiction, as we have shown. So the latter view is by far the falsest. At the same time it is both contrary to experience and, in wonderful ways, insulting to the sacred authority of Scripture. For if God's existence is much more evident than any sensible things, it is truly amazing that the Apostle of the Gentiles either did not know or neglected this subtlety, when he urges and impresses with such emphasis that the invisible things of God, namely his eternal power and divinity, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, from the creation of the world. Or should we rather consider that the one who argued in this way also thought that God's existence is much more evident than any sensible things? Whoever thinks so must also think that the Holy Spirit, in these and similar reasonings, used a middle term far less evident than the conclusion to be demonstrated. As this plainly shows a lack of judgment and an utterly absurd method of arguing, so let those who dare to persuade themselves that no one lived before Agamemnon, the brave, see for themselves how well such thoughts agree with the due reverence owed to the Scriptures.

units.la: Imprimis verò non possunt non displicere conatus ejusmodi, quibus argumentorum ab omni aevo receptorum vim eludere conantur , si quinam hic nobis pro auro substituantur carbones, diligentius attendamus. Expendi volunt ante omnia Ideam quandam entis summè perfecti , quam sibi innatam ajunt; tum etiam causam quaerunt, non à qua olim sint producti tanquam homines mente constantes & corpore , sed à qua tempore praesenti tanquam merae mentes conserventur. Ita opinantur sé longè felicius, absque ulla aut rerum sensibilium existentia, aut causarum subordinatione , demonstrationes pro existentia summi Numinis instruere posse. Operae pretium erit , ob rei momentum , atque agitatas hodiè de ea controversias , ista excutere ; sed paucis , ne ab instituto nimium digrediamur. Sic ferè ex idea inferunt : Quaecunque attributa in clara alicujus rei idea continentur , ea ex vero ipsi illi rei à parte sui tribui possunt. Pergunt: At verò in entis summè perfecti clara idea inter caeteras perfectiones continetur necessaria existentia. Ex quibus concludunt : Potest ergò haec illi ex vero tribui ; consequenter , Deus quoque reipsa existit necessariò. Praeterèo quae de innatis rerum Idcis hic supponuntur; item, de Dei idea in nobis clara & distincta; quae saltem Atheo concessa non sunt. Sed de illis alibi. Nunc id in quo cardo rei vertitur quanti momomenti sit in re præsenti, examinasse tribus verbis sufficit. Quæcunque, ajunt, in clara idea alicujus rei continentur, ea ex vero rei illi à parte sui possunt tribui. Claudicat verò ista propositio; quippe quæ tunc demum vera est, quando constat ideam, quam de re quapiam habemus, ipsi rei extra mentem existenti per omnia esse similem. Neque ad istam conformitatem evincendam quicquam juvat quæ ideæ illi ab his auctoribus tribuitur claritas; quamdiu enim certi non sunt, & Deum existere, & cum minimè fallacem esse, ne quidem secundum propriam methodum iis constare potest, omnia quæ clarè percipiuntur esse vera. Itaque totum quod hic inferri poterat tantum hoc est: In cujus idea involvitur necessaria existentia, etiam, si quæ res isti ideæ similis existat extra mentem, de ea ex vero necessaria existentia potest affirmari. Quod si subsumas: Ast in idea Dei involvitur necessaria existentia; manifestum est nihil aliud legitimâ sequelâ inferri posse, quam hoc: Ergo, si quæ res ideæ Dei similis existat extra mentem, de ea ex vero necessaria existentia potest affirmari. Vides? Non jam categoricè doces, Deum existere, quod negat Atheus; sed tantum concludis hypotheticè, Deum, si existat ideæ similis, existere necessariò. Verum hoc totum utraque manu lubens dabit Atheus, nec quicquam ideò à sua opinione recedere necesse habebit, quatenus conditio, nondum demonstrata, nihil ponit in esse, ut vulgò dicunt. En argumentum apodicticum; quod ne leviter quidem adversarium ferit!
units.tr: Above all, if we look more carefully at what sort of things are substituted here for gold, such attempts cannot fail to displease, by which they try to elude the force of arguments received in every age. They first want an idea of a supremely perfect being to be weighed, which they say is innate in us. They also seek a cause, not by which we were once produced as beings constant in mind and body, but by which we are now preserved as mere minds. Thus they think they can construct demonstrations for the existence of the supreme Deity far more happily, without any existence of sensible things or any subordination of causes. Because of the importance of the matter, and the controversies on it stirred up today, it will be worth while to examine these claims; but briefly, lest we digress too far from our plan. They infer roughly as follows from the idea: whatever attributes are contained in the clear idea of some thing can truly be attributed to that very thing in its own reality. They go on: but in the clear idea of a supremely perfect being, necessary existence is contained among the other perfections. From these premises they conclude: therefore this can truly be attributed to him; consequently God also really exists necessarily. Furthermore, what is here assumed about innate ideas of things, and likewise about the clear and distinct idea of God in us, is not conceded, at least not by the Atheist. But of those matters elsewhere. Now it is enough to have examined in a few words how much weight the point on which the whole matter turns carries in the present case. "Whatever," they say, "is contained in the clear idea of some thing can truly be attributed to that thing in its own reality." But this proposition limps; for it is true only when it is established that the idea we have of some thing is in every respect similar to the thing existing outside the mind. Nor does the clarity these authors ascribe to that idea help to prove this conformity; for as long as they are not certain that God exists and is by no means deceptive, they cannot, even by their own method, agree that everything clearly perceived is true. Hence all that could be inferred here is this: whatever thing's idea involves necessary existence, if some thing similar to that idea exists outside the mind, necessary existence can truly be affirmed of that thing. But if you add the minor premise: but necessary existence is involved in the idea of God; it is clear that nothing else can be legitimately inferred than this: therefore, if some thing similar to the idea of God exists outside the mind, necessary existence can truly be affirmed of it. Do you see? You are not yet teaching categorically that God exists, which the Atheist denies; you are only concluding hypothetically that God, if he exists as similar to the idea, exists necessarily. Yet the Atheist will gladly grant all this with both hands, and he will not need to give up any of his opinion on that account, since a condition not yet demonstrated posits nothing in being, as people commonly say. Behold, an apodictic argument, which does not even lightly touch the adversary!

units.la: Verum demonstrationum fertilior est ista Dei Idea, quam ut hac unâ omnis ejus latitudo sit exhausta. Audiamus alium, quo ex illa inferunt, modum! Quælibet, ajunt, ex nostris ideis requirit causam, in qua vel formaliter vel eminenter continentur perfectiones, quæ in idea repræsentantur. Habemus autem ideam Dei, tanquam entis infinitè perfecti. Ergò aliqua ejus causa erit, in se vel formaliter vel eminenter perfectiones illas continens, quæ in idea tali repræsentantur. In nullo verò finito infinitæ perfectiones existunt. Ergò datur aliquod infinitè perfectum, in quo omnes illæ perfectiones continentur, quodque sit illius ideæ causa: proindè existit Deus. Ad quæ notandum verbo, vim nostram concipiendi non posse esse ipsâ mente majorem ; quare , cum hæc finita sit, etiam illa talis erit. Unde conficitur , non posse mentem nostram finitam clara aliquâ ideâ sibi positivè repræsentare perfectiones infinitas, tanquam tales. Cognosci tamen, fateor, pro modulo infinitè perfectum ; verum non aliter , quam perfectiones finitas multiplicando , iisque omnes limites ac imperfectiones detrahendo , ac denique judicando, id majus esse, quam quod à finita mente comprehendi queat. Quæ omnia cum à mente nostra satis commodè fieri possint , ideæ infiniti entis causam aliquam extra mentem quærere nil est necesse ; nedum ut ea statuatur infinita. Hæc nunc paucis : de quibus deindè suis locis plura. Quicquid sit , plane ac plenè negabit Atheus , quemquam habere infinitarum perfectionum positivè menti repræsentatarum tanquam talium claram ideam. Quod sufficiet illi , ad declinandam omnem, si quæ sit, hujus ratiocinii vim. Ut nec hæc ex idea illatio efficax sit ad Atheum convincendum.
units.tr: Yet this idea of God is too fertile in arguments to be exhausted by this one alone. Let us hear another way in which they infer it from the idea. Every idea of ours, they say, requires a cause in which the perfections represented in the idea are contained either formally or eminently. We have the idea of God as of a being infinitely perfect. Therefore there will be some cause of it that contains in itself, either formally or eminently, the perfections represented in such an idea. But no finite thing contains infinite perfections. Therefore there exists something infinitely perfect, in which all those perfections are contained, and which is the cause of that idea; hence God exists. On this we should note in passing that our power of conceiving cannot be greater than the mind itself; therefore, since the mind is finite, its power is also finite. From this it follows that our finite mind cannot represent to itself positively, by any clear idea, infinite perfections as such. I grant, however, that it knows the infinitely perfect, after its own manner; but only by multiplying finite perfections, stripping them of all limits and imperfections, and finally judging that the being is greater than what a finite mind can comprehend. Since all these things can be done quite easily by our mind, there is no need to seek some cause outside the mind for the idea of an infinite being, much less to posit that cause as infinite. So much for now briefly; more on these matters in their proper places. Be that as it may, the Atheist will flatly and fully deny that anyone has a clear idea of infinite perfections positively represented to the mind as such. That will be enough for him to escape the whole force of this reasoning, whatever it may be. So this inference from the idea is not effective for convincing the Atheist either.
VIII. Descartes' Third Demonstration is examined.

units.la: Denique , ut ostendat Cartesius , se in demonstranda existentia primi Entis causarum subordinatione nil indigere , ipse, missâ causâ sui efficiente, conservantem duntaxat hic attendi vult. Unde hanc instituit argumentationem. Non possum existere, quin conserver, quamdiu existo. At me ipsum conservandi vim non habeo; quapropter ab alio conservor. Is verò à quo conservor , necessariò in se habet id omne quod in me est ; quumque in me existat infinitarum perfectionum perceptio , utique eadem quoque erit in causa me conservante. Verum hæc habere nequit perceptionem perfectionum quas in se non continet : quapropter cum talem perceptionem omninò habeat, etiam ea in se continebit perfectiones ipsas , quarum habet perceptionem, id est, infinitas: atque ita Deus erit. Verum , quid si quis regerat , illum qui te conservat, ipsum iterum ab alio conservari , non tamen infinitè perfecto : atque hunc alium iterum conservari ab alio, tertio, quarto, quinto, &c. neque adeo unquam perveniendum esse ad primam causam in ista conservantium successione. Certè de conservantibus causis idem dici potest , quod de producentibus : cumque in harum serie primam aliquam necessariò admittendam non esse, putes tu , cur magis alter credat , in conservantium ordine
units.tr: Finally, to show that in demonstrating the existence of the first Being he needs nothing from the subordination of causes, Descartes sets aside efficient cause of himself and wishes here to consider only the conserving cause. Hence he sets up this argument: I cannot exist unless I am conserved for as long as I exist. But I do not have the power to conserve myself; therefore I am conserved by another. And that by which I am conserved necessarily has in itself all that is in me; and since the perception of infinite perfections exists in me, the same must surely be in the cause that conserves me. But this cause cannot have a perception of perfections that it does not contain in itself; therefore, since it altogether has such a perception, it will also contain in itself the very perfections of which it has a perception, that is, infinite ones; and thus it will be God. But what if someone should reply that he who conserves you is himself conserved again by another, not by an infinitely perfect being; and this other again by a third, fourth, fifth, and so on, and that we never arrive at a first cause in this succession of conservers? Certainly what is said of producing causes can also be said of conserving causes; and since you think there is no need to admit some first cause in the series of these causes, why should another believe otherwise about the order of conservers?

units.la: { } Scilicet ad. VIII. ne dari aliquod primum ? Tenuè est , quod admiscetur de infinitarum perfectionum perceptione , quæ in nulla causa nos conservante esse queat , nisi in ea quæ illas perfectiones actu possideat ; jam enim ex antè dictis intelligitur , hanc qualemcunque infinitarum perfectionum perceptionem , prout in mente nostra existit , esse posse ab ipsa mente finita , atque ita etiam potuisse existere in causa nos conservante ; sive hæc illam ideam ipsa confecerit , sive à sui causa conservante iterum acceperit. Ut nullum re verâ etiam hujus argumenti robur sit ad Atheum feliciter refellendum. Itaque, ut absolvam, quandoquidem liquet, & nullas justas rationes adserre Recentiores quibus doceatur, recedendum esse ab antiqua Divinæ existentiæ demonstratione ex causarum subordinatione necessariò finita, & eos loco illius alia haud adducere, quibus Atheismus solidè queat debellari, meritò methodus talis cuilibet, universum rei pondus rite expendenti, erit suspecta ; eique præseretur longissimè via hactenus tutò trita, quam qui sequitur non facilè errat , uti frequenter solent, qui, calcati tramitis fastidio, per avia & derupta novos sibi ad sapientiam aditus parare laborant : quorum profectò conatus dubii magis sunt eventus, quam ut illi tantarum rerum momenta committat vir prudens.
units.tr: Namely, to VIII.: that there is some first [cause]? What is mixed in about the perception of infinite perfections is weak, since it could exist in no cause conserving us except one that actually possesses those perfections. For it is already clear from what was said above that this perception of infinite perfections, however it exists in our mind, can come from the finite mind itself, and so could also have existed in the cause conserving us, whether that cause produced the idea itself or received it again from its own conserving cause. So in truth there is no strength even in this argument for successfully refuting the Atheist.
