Therefore, to finish: since it is clear that the more recent writers have offered no just reasons for abandoning the ancient demonstration of God's existence from the necessary subordination of finite causes, and have brought forward no other arguments by which Atheism could be solidly overthrown, such a method will rightly be suspect to anyone who weighs the whole matter properly; and the path hitherto safely trodden is far preferable to it. Whoever follows that path does not easily go astray, whereas those who, weary of the beaten track, labour to make for themselves new approaches to wisdom through trackless and broken ground often do otherwise. The outcome of their efforts is surely too doubtful for a prudent man to entrust to them the weight of such great matters.

units.la: Sic paucis, quantum fieri potuit, instruximus, ac simul vindicavimus, palmarium pro demonstranda & facilè, & evidenter, & firmiter, primi Entis existentia argumentum. Inquam, pro ea firmiter demonstranda, sic ut pertinaci Atheorum impietati os obturetur. Cæterùm enim piæ menti, & quæ rationi cedere paratior est quam sunt ista hominum portenta, nec aliæ desunt viæ ac modi, quibus de prima hac veritate reddatur certior certo. Ipsa se solam in se ipsa si satis diligenter attendat, inveniet, quæcunque non plane præsracta esse cupit, quo convincatur efficacissimè. Aliquam se sui agnoscere debere originem, docent eam abunde suæ imperfectiones & multiplex sufficientiæ defectus. At qualem illam? Non certe formari potuit à causa corporea ex corporeis elementis : talia respuit prorsus nobilissimæ substantiæ longissima à re omni materiali distantia. At simul indivisibilis rerum rationalium natura, ex substantia rei cujuspiam spiritualis decisam esse & pro-
units.tr: Thus, briefly and as far as could be done, we have set out and at the same time vindicated the chief argument for demonstrating the existence of the first Being easily, evidently, and firmly. I say firmly demonstrated, so that the stubborn impiety of the Atheists is stopped. Moreover, for a pious mind, one more ready to yield to reason than are those monsters of men, there are no lack of other ways and methods by which this first truth can be made more certain than certain. If the mind attends to itself carefully enough, it will find, whatever it wishes not to be plainly foretold, the means by which it is most effectively convinced. That it must acknowledge some origin of its own, its imperfections and its manifold deficiencies in sufficiency abundantly teach. But what origin? It certainly could not have been formed by a corporeal cause out of corporeal elements; the utterly noble substance, most remote from all material reality, rejects such things altogether. Yet at the same time the indivisible nature of rational things, cut off from the substance of some spiritual thing and...

units.la: IX. Ex origine mentis humanæ, Deum esse probatur. & progenitam, evidenter negat. Itaque quid superest aliud, quam ut ipse spiritus noster ex se, per saltum quasi & immediatè, nos ducat ad illum agnoscendum spirituum Patrem, qui potentiæ suæ vi ex nihilo existere jusserit rem tantis ornatam naturæ dotibus, quantis nulla alia contemplationi nostræ obvia? Id verò stupendum Creationis opus, transitumque rei pulcherrimæ ex nihilo ad istum perfectionis statum quem possidet, nemo ritè cogitaverit, qui non ilicò simul intellexerit, nullam virtutis finitæ causam tanto negotio sufficere: atque adeò animæ rationalis originem altiùs deducendam esse, à causa quadam spirituali infinitis modis & gradibus spiritu quovis finito potentiore, atque ideò perfectiore; qualis id ipsum Numen est, cujus existentiam adftrucbamus. Quamvis autem hæc per se satis solida fit cogitatio, atque æquo animo satisfacere abundè apta, quando tamen cum homine res est, qui agitur studio contradicendi, quinque nihil metuit quasvis veritates in dubium vocare in salsissimæ suæ hypothesèos gratiam, non eam habet convictionis vim, ut illà contra Atheum primò utendum videatur. Is quippe haud pauca excipiet, & circa animæ nostræ naturam immaterialem; & circa opus creationis incomprehensibile, quæ non minùs illi negabuntur, quam ipsa Dei existentia. Dum itaque per ista nos latius diffundere cogemur, à proposita demonstratione nimium abducemur; nobisque ipsis affumptorum postulatorum satis ardua erit contra negantem probatio, quamdiu & mentis nostræ naturam, & originem ejusdem, non rectius ex ipsa Dei cognitione habemus perspectam. Quapropter etiamnum inhærendum arbitror nostræ demonstrationi, petitæ à causarum subordinatione; cui & idcirco primas merito dedimus.
units.tr: IX. From the origin of the human mind, it is proved that God exists. and begotten, clearly denies it. What remains, then, but that our spirit itself, from itself, as it were by a leap and immediately, should lead us to acknowledge that Father of spirits, who by the power of his might ordered a thing adorned with such endowments of nature, than which none other is open to our contemplation, to exist out of nothing? No one who has rightly thought about this stupendous work of creation, and about the passage of a most beautiful thing from nothing to that state of perfection which it possesses, could fail to see at once that no finite power is sufficient for so great an undertaking. Hence the origin of the rational soul must be traced back higher, to some spiritual cause that is more powerful than any finite spirit in infinite ways and degrees, and therefore more perfect; such is that very Deity whose existence we are establishing. Although this thought is in itself quite solid and well suited to satisfy a calm mind, yet when the matter concerns a man who is driven by a zeal for contradiction, and who fears nothing in calling into doubt any truths whatever for the sake of his most salt-laden hypothesis, it does not have such force of conviction that it seems right to use it first against the Atheist. He will certainly except many things, both concerning the immaterial nature of our soul and concerning the incomprehensible work of creation, and these will be denied him no less than the very existence of God. So while we are compelled to spread ourselves more widely over these matters, we shall be drawn too far away from the proposed demonstration; and the proof of the postulates we have assumed will be quite difficult against one who denies them, as long as we do not have a more correct knowledge both of the nature of our mind and of its origin from the very knowledge of God. Therefore I think we should still cling to our demonstration, drawn from the subordination of causes, to which for this reason we rightly gave the first place.

units.la: Verum non disputando tantùm elucescit hæc veritas. Certè quisquis longâ impietatis consuetudine non penitus animum obfirmavit, fi vel leviter inspicere voluerit tantum opus, quantum fe oculis ubique manifestat, sentiet, fi quod res est sateri velit, admiratione se convictum de eo, quod rationibus sibi persuaderi non sinebat; esse videlicet Numen, quod modis imperscrutabilibus fecerit hæc omnia pondere, mensurâ, numero. Quis Cælum suspiciat, fornicatum illud mundi tectum, latiffimè simul & æqualissimè huic terræ punêto circumvolutatum, miramiráque actionis acrimoniâ defluviis suis intima telluris adyta penetrans? Quis scintillantes cœlorum oculos Sydera, illustrissima mundi luminaria, tot miraculis quot radiis plena, immenso campo indiga, propter tot suas ambitiones & varia, certa nihilominus suisque definita periodis, itinera? Quis Terræ sine pondere molem, & bases seipsis stabilitas, ac libratas quasi ad funiculi mensuram? Quis Elementa, disparia illa surgentis mundi primordia, atque ultima omnis naturæ sublunaris, post variam metamorphosin, pugnam, ac cladem, diverticula? Quis Meteora, admiranda illa mundi spectacula, quæ in orbe terrarum perpetuam dant tempestatum vicissitudinem? Quis speciosum mundi antiquarium, Gemmas, pretiosa naturæ cimelia, & sparsa quasi per terrenum globum sydera? Quis nata ad innumera hominis commoda Metalla, collectum gremio terræ atque reconditum ærarium mundi opulentissimum. Quis terram, ceu tessellatum pavimentum, picturatam Plantis, amœnissimo mundi viridario, tam innumerâ sobole, nullisque aëris injuriis interruptâ serie, tot seculis propagato? Quis Bruta, prolificum mundi vivarium, tam diverso partu, pastu opere, nullis artificum industriis imitando, varium? Quis denique, qui quasi universis hisce præest, Hominem, illud pulchritudinis passim sparsæ compendium, usuarium mundi colonum & incolam locupletissimum? Quis sexcenta maxima minimarum etiam naturarum miracula; quæ quia videmus quotidiè, attendimus minùs. Quis, inquam, qui ad ista, uti oportet, altius introspicienda animum adjicit, quiique, quod sapientis est, non tam insolita quam magna potius mirari consuevit, non tanto obruatur de tantis rebus admirationis stupore, ut nusquam exitum inveniat, nisi in sapientissimo Numine, provido hujus Universi structore simul & custode. Ut re verâ nemo tanti operis elaboratissimum artificium, mirissimam structuram, venustissimum ornatum, sapientissimum ordinem, satis intelligat, qui non intelligat pariter, hanc publicam naturæ domum sanctissimè consecratam esse in visibile invisibilis Majestatis monumentum, divinâ omnipræsentiâ, undiquaque se obviam exhibente, sanctificatum in Templum basilicum; cui pro ara, humanus animus; pro dedicandis muneribus, naturæ opes;
units.tr: Yet this truth is made clear not by argument alone. Certainly, whoever has not hardened his mind thoroughly through a long habit of impiety, if he is willing to look even briefly at the great work that shows itself to the eyes everywhere, will feel, if he is willing to say what is true, that he is overcome with wonder at what he would not let himself be persuaded of by reasons: namely, that there is a Deity who by inscrutable means has made all these things by weight, measure and number. Who can look up at the heavens, that vaulted roof of the world, which turns about this earth as a point, at once most widely and most evenly, and by its wondrous force penetrates with its streams the inmost recesses of the earth? Who can look at the sparkling eyes of the heavens, the stars, the most brilliant lights of the world, so full of miracles as they are of rays, needing an immense field for their many circuits, and yet their routes, though various, are certain and fixed by their own periods? Who can look at the mass of the earth without weight, and its foundations, which stand by themselves and are poised as if by a plumb line? Who can look at the elements, those dissimilar first principles of the rising world, and at the extremes of all sublunary nature, which after their varied change, conflict and collapse, turn aside? Who can look at the meteors, those wondrous spectacles of the world, which give the earth its constant alternation of weather? Who can look at the splendid storehouse of the world, the gems, the precious treasures of nature, and the stars scattered as it were over the globe? Who can look at the metals, born for countless human uses, the richest treasury of the world, gathered and hidden in the bosom of the earth? Who can look at the earth, like a tessellated pavement, painted with plants, the most pleasant garden of the world, propagated through so many ages by such an uninterrupted line of offspring, undisturbed by any injuries of the air? Who can look at the beasts, the fruitful aviary of the world, varied in their diverse births, food and works, which no skill of craftsmen can imitate? Who, finally, presides over all these things, and sees in man, that epitome of beauty scattered everywhere, the most abundant user and inhabitant of the world? Who considers the countless great and even the smallest miracles of nature, which we pay less attention to because we see them every day? Who, I say, applies his mind to examining these things more deeply, as one ought to do, and who is accustomed, as is the mark of a wise man, to wonder not so much at the unusual as at the great, and is not so overwhelmed with the stupor of admiration at such great things that he finds no way out except in the most wise Deity, the provident maker and at the same time keeper of this Universe? Indeed, no one can truly understand the most elaborate craftsmanship, the most wonderful structure, the most lovely ornament and the most wise order of so great a work, unless he understands equally that this public house of nature has been most holily consecrated as a visible monument of the invisible Majesty, sanctified as a basilica-temple by the divine omnipresence which shows itself to us on every side; in which the human mind serves as the altar, the riches of nature as the gifts to be dedicated,

units.la: C opes, pro perpetuo liturgo, ipse homo, qui non tantum in ipsius Templi specie externa hæreat, sed ad interiora penetrando immortale Numen in tanta rerum utilitate Optimum, in tanta amplitudine Maximum, in tanto decore Pulcherrimum, in tanta varietate Ditissimum, in tanta earundem perpetuitate Constantissimum, investiget, miretur, agnoscat, colat, & adoret. Ut inter tot mira mirorum omnium mirissimum sit, reperiri posse homines, qui eo usque infra sensum omnem & rationem se abjiciunt, ut augustissimum hoc Dei Optimi Maximi opificium, nullo artificis captu pervestigabile, nescio cui spontaneo corpusculorum concursui, & fortuitæ particularum minimarum cohærentiæ, tribuere ausint. Quam ridiculæ suæ stultitiæ hæreditatem magna ex parte Epicurus reliquisse videtur quibusdam nostræ ætatis Philosophis, mundum vorticosum solo mechanico materiæ motu formatum ita introducentibus, ut in tota ejus adornatione nulla fermè, saltem oppidò rara, Creatoris mentio. At verò si scelus sit de creaturis agere, & opificem omittere, ut Socrates jam olim censuit, & merito, nulla Atheismo porta latior aperiri potest, quam hac philosophandi ratione; quâ imprimis mens à meditatione opificis sic abducitur, ut in contemplando opificio evanescat. Magis placet ista Regii Vatis altius animum elevans pia admiratio: Jehova, Domine noster, quam magnificum nomen tuum in universa terra! Quando aspicio cælos tuos, opus digitorum tuorum; Lunam & stellas quas statuisti: Quid mortalis, quod memor sis ejus; aut filius hominis, quod visites eum? Præfecisti eum operibus manuum tuarum; omnia posuisti sub pedibus ejus, &c. Jehova, Domine noster, quam magnificum nomen tuum in universa terra! Quod si nihilominus quis ferreus nec demonstrationis efficacia victum, nec admirationis stupore motum se fateatur, tamen etiam clausos cæco furore oculos sic perstringit splendidissimum hoc veritatis jubar, ut suâ coruscatione totam replea animam, atque invitam quoque sentire faciat, quam inique laborat opprimere, Numinis notitiam: adeo quovis probationis genere efficaciora hac parte ad manum sunt rerum testimonia. Non enim dianoëtica duntaxat habetur Primi Entis cognitio, ex contemplatione & macrocosmi & microcosmi Acquisita ; sed & unicuique Insita existit supremi Dei conscientia, & noëtica certitudo : quæ animis hominum tam penitus infixa hæret, inque iis tam altùm est radicata ut in congressu cum homine sanæ mentis, cui hanc veritatem persuasam cupimus, non tam opus fit multâ ratiocinatione, quam solâ potius obtestatione ; quâ si id impetres, ut propriás mentis suæ tabulas seriò tantum inspicere dignetur, salva res est : adeò inveniet id, quod quidam cupiunt controversum, naturâ suâ esse per se notissimum. Quod, ne quis erret, non sic accipi velim, quasi vocum, quibus profertur hoc effatum, Deus existit, ac significationis earundem, notitia nobis citra ullam institutionem ab ipsa natura ingenita sit : neque etiam, quasi Entis perfectissimi necessariò existentis actualis idea quæpiam aut repræsentamen menti hominis jam inde à primo nativitatis momento obversetur, & de facto percipiatur. Minime ! Istud ipsi signorum vocalium quibus res & conceptus nobis exprimuntur naturæ adversatur ; quatenus vocabula ex solo instituto significant res, quibus denotandis sunt imposita, ut eorundem nulla possit esse naturalis notitia, verum ea omnis necessariò sit acquisita ; postquam videlicet adultiori constat de arbitrio & usu hominum, qui in eadem societate viventes, hac significatione, non alia, voces inter sese valere voluerunt. Hoc verò nimium adversatur statui isti, in quo anima embryonis existit, tum in ipso utero materno, tum etiam mox à nativitate, quippe qui minimè actualis cogitationis, quapropter nec cognitionis istiusmodi aut repræsentaminis, existit capax : quod alibi, in Animadversionibus nostris in Narrationem de controversiis in Academia Ultrajectina motis, fusè demonstravimus. Non etiam dixisse sufficit, innatam Dei notitiam esse facultatem quandam in nobis, quâ demonstrationis pro existentia Dei veritatem, & conclusionis istius certitudinem, levi negotio percipere, facilemque ei assensum præbere, apti nati sumus : quàmvis enim hoc minimè sit negandum, non tamen, ut dixi, sufficit ; quoniam, quantumvis facilis, re verâ tamen acquisita est talis notitia & discursiva, non ingenita & per se nota. Quid ergo ? Id volumus, ut verbo dicam, hujus propositionis Deus existit, in ordine ad cognitionem nostram, eandem esse conditionem, quæ est V. C. istius, Totum est majus suâ parte; aut similium veritatum, quæ principiorum per se notorum, ac propositionum immediatarum nomine vulgò nobis venire solent. Videlicet, nemo sanæ mentis, cui facta est occasio intelligendi res vocibus Totum, Partis, Majoris, significatas, ambigit amplius, utrum Totum sit suâ parte majus, sed è vestigio hoc ipsum per sese verrissimum esse ita certò percipit, ut mox sponte, nullâ exspectatâ demonstratione, ruat in assensum. Pari modo contendimus, animum cujusvis hominis mentis compotis, oblatâ hac propositione, ac ritè intellectâ prævià verborum explicatione, Deus existit, adeo per se in ejus assensum esse pronum, ut nullam, ad ejus certitudinem menti ingenerandam, necesse habeat quærere demonstrationem; dum majorem in hac ipsa veritate reperit convictionis vim, quam ab ullis argumentationibus queat exspectare: ut non minus facilis & inclinata mens sit ad assentiendum huic effato sine ulla probatione, quam ad ampleētendam cujusvis firmissimæ demonstrationis conclusionem.
units.tr: the man himself as the perpetual minister of the liturgy. He does not stop at the outward appearance of the Temple itself, but by penetrating into its inner parts he searches out, marvels at, acknowledges, worships and adores the immortal Deity: best in so great a usefulness of things, greatest in so great a vastness, most beautiful in so great a comeliness, richest in so great a variety, most constant in so great a perpetuity of these same things. So it is the most wonderful of all wonders that there should be men who cast themselves so far beneath all sense and reason that they dare to attribute this most august work of God, the best and greatest, which cannot be traced by any grasp of the craftsman, to I know not what spontaneous concourse of corpuscles and to the chance cohesion of the smallest particles. Epicurus seems largely to have bequeathed this inheritance of his ridiculous folly to certain philosophers of our age, who introduce a whirling world formed by mechanical motion of matter alone, so that in its whole arrangement there is almost no mention, or at least a very rare one, of the Creator. But indeed, if it is a crime to deal with creatures and omit the craftsman, as Socrates long ago judged, and rightly, no door wider than this way of philosophizing can be opened to atheism; by which, above all, the mind is so drawn away from meditating on the craftsman that it vanishes in contemplating the work. That pious admiration, raising the mind higher, of the royal psalmist pleases me more: O Jehovah, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! When I behold your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you have set in place: what is man, that you are mindful of him; or the son of man, that you visit him? You have made him ruler over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet, etc. O Jehovah, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! But if anyone, however made of iron, should still claim to be moved neither by the force of demonstration nor by the stupor of admiration, nevertheless this most splendid light of truth so strikes even eyes closed by blind fury that by its shining it fills the whole soul and makes him feel, against his will, how unjustly he labours to suppress the knowledge of the Deity. So readily at hand, in this respect, are the testimonies of things, more effective than any kind of proof. For the knowledge of the First Being is not held to be merely discursive, acquired from contemplating both the macrocosm and the microcosm; but the conscience of the supreme God also exists in everyone, innate, and a noetic certainty, which clings so deeply to men's minds and is so firmly rooted in them that in dealing with a man of sound mind, whom we wish to be persuaded of this truth, there is less need of long reasoning than of simply appealing to him; if you can obtain this, that he deigns to look seriously at the tablets of his own mind, all is well: he will find that what some wish to be disputed is in its own nature most evident through itself. I would not have this taken, lest anyone err, as if the knowledge of the words by which this statement is expressed, God exists, and of their meaning, were innate in us from nature itself without any teaching; nor again as if some idea or representation of an actually existing most perfect and necessary Being were present to the human mind from the first moment of birth and were actually perceived. By no means! That would run counter to the very nature of vocal signs by which things and concepts are expressed to us; since words signify things, to which they have been assigned, only by convention, so that there can be no natural knowledge of them, but all such knowledge is necessarily acquired; once, namely, it is established for an adult that by the decision and usage of men, living in the same society, they chose words to have value among themselves in this meaning and not another. But this is strongly opposed to the state in which the soul of the embryo exists, both in the mother's womb and also soon after birth, since it is by no means capable of actual thought, and therefore not capable of knowledge or representation of this kind; which we have demonstrated at length elsewhere, in our Animadversions on the Narrative concerning the controversies raised in the Academy of Utrecht. Nor is it enough to say that the innate knowledge of God is a certain faculty in us, by which we are fitted by nature to perceive with little effort the truth of the demonstration for God's existence and the certainty of that conclusion, and to give it ready assent; for although this must by no means be denied, it is not enough, as I have said; since, however easy, such knowledge is in fact acquired and discursive, not innate and self-evident. What then? To put it in a word, we maintain that this proposition, God exists, in relation to our knowledge, stands in the same condition as that of the proposition, The whole is greater than its part, or of similar truths which are commonly called self-evident principles and immediate propositions. Clearly, no one of sound mind, who has been given the opportunity of understanding the things signified by the words whole, part and greater, doubts any longer whether the whole is greater than its part, but at once perceives with such certainty that this very thing is wholly true, that he rushes spontaneously into assent without awaiting any demonstration. In the same way we contend that the mind of any man in his right senses, once this proposition, God exists, has been put before him and rightly understood after a prior explanation of the words, is so inclined by itself to assent to it that he has no need to seek a demonstration in order to produce certainty in his mind; since he finds in this very truth a greater force of conviction than he could expect from any arguments. So the mind is no less ready and inclined to assent to this statement without any proof than to accept the conclusion of any most firm demonstration.

units.la: Talem aliquam πεόληψιν sive anticipationem de Deo homini à natura esse insitam, firmissimè demonstrat innata conscientia turpis & honesti. Nimirum, attendamus practica principia, qualia sunt, Unicuique suum tribuendum; Alium non est laedendus; &c. concessa quibusvis, qui rationalitatem, id est, humanitatem ipsam non plane exuerunt. Has veritates per se notas existere, carundemque sensum ab ipsa natura animis omnium esse insculptum, docet illarum maxima universalitas, & unanimis quarumvis gentium in hæc placita consensus. Etenim in tanta ingeniorum varietate fieri nequaquam potest, ut omnes idem prorsus sentiant de iis rebus, quarum cognitionem ipsi nobis investigamus & aliunde acquirimus: earum imprimis quarum in vita nostra observatio ardua adeò est & molesta. Adde, quæ has veritates comitatur, vim obligatoriam, suâ sponte efficacissimè se exerentem in animis mortalium; ita ut homines etiam indomiti, nullumque quem metuant in terris agnoscentes, scelerum, quamvis occultissimorum, furiisagitati, in mortis quoque articulo ista patiantur animi tormina, quæ clarè monstrant, harum veritatum transgressores hominum iràmajus aliquid meruisse. Ex quibus conficitur ingenitam esse horum principiorum notitiam: nec simpliciter tantum ingenitam, sed & naturâ notas esse has veritates sub forma legis, munitæ revera sanctione poenali; cui subjecta sit omnis creatura rationalis cum obligatione ad poenam, si sese ejus constituerit violatorem. Jam verò si sit à natura innata notitia Legis, utique etiam Legislatoris, à qua lex illa lata sit tanta cum obligandi potestate. Antecedentis membri veritas ex dictis manifesta est. De sequelæ necessitate nulli potest esse dubium, quandoquidem Lex & Legislator relata sunt, quorum natura est talis, ut cognitione existant simul, quatenus in notione unius per se includitur respectus ad aliud, atque adeo etiam ipsa notio illius alterius, ad quod hoc prius relationem dicit. Hunc autem Legislatorem cujus insitam notitiam arguit innatus Legis Naturalis sensus, esse Numen de quo nobis hic disquiritur, nullo negotio patescit. Etenim qui innotescit tanquam potestatem legislatoriam habens in conscientiam hominis, creaturæ omnium nobilissimæ, is simul cognoscitur tanquam supremus rerum Dominus, cui jus convenit suâ naturâ αὐτοχεφάλοιχον & indepen-dens; imprimis cum simul is menti occurrat tanquam occultæ quoque impietatis testis καρδιογνώστης & omniscius, ejusdemque etiam post hanc vitam vindex justissimus & quàvis creaturâ potentior: quæ ipsa prædicata Deitatem digito quasi monstrant clarissimè. Atque hæc ipsa illa ratiocinatio est, quâ alibi utitur tanta cum emphasi infallibilis Gentium Doctor Paulus, urgens vehementer τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου γεγραμμένον ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν, Opus Legis scriptum in cordibus suis; quod & ostendant Gentes, quoque impelluntur sic, ut φύσει, Natura, ea faciant quæ legis sunt; cuique, pro bene vel male factis, per excusatrices aut accusatrices cogitationes attestatur conscientia.
units.tr: Such a preconception or anticipation of God is implanted in man by nature, as the innate conscience of right and wrong most firmly demonstrates. Let us consider the practical principles, such as "To each his own should be given" and "One must not harm another," and so on, which are granted by all who have not wholly stripped off rationality, that is, humanity itself. That these truths are known through themselves, and that the sense of them has been engraved on the minds of all by nature itself, is taught by their very great universality and by the unanimous agreement of all nations in these tenets. For amid such great variety of minds it is in no way possible that all should think exactly the same about those things whose knowledge we ourselves investigate and acquire from elsewhere, especially those whose observation in our life is so difficult and troublesome. Add to this the binding force that accompanies these truths, which of its own accord most effectively asserts itself in the minds of mortals; so that men even untamed, raging with the furies of crimes, however hidden, and acknowledging no one on earth whom they fear, suffer in the very moment of death those torments of the soul which plainly show that the transgressors of these truths have deserved something greater than the wrath of men. From these things it follows that the knowledge of these principles is innate: and not merely innate, but that these truths are known by nature in the form of a law, indeed backed by a penal sanction, to which every rational creature is subject, with the obligation to punishment should it make itself their violator. Now, if there is a knowledge of the Law innate by nature, then surely there is also knowledge of the Lawgiver, by whom that law was enacted with such binding power. The truth of the antecedent is manifest from what has been said. Of the necessity of the consequence there can be no doubt, since Law and Lawgiver are correlatives, whose nature is such that they exist together in knowledge, inasmuch as in the notion of the one there is included by itself a relation to the other, and thus also the notion of that other, to which the first refers. That this Lawgiver, whose innate knowledge the innate sense of the Natural Law argues for, is the Deity of whom we are inquiring here, is made plain without any difficulty. For he who makes himself known to the conscience of man, the most noble of all creatures, as having legislative power, is at the same time known as the supreme Lord of things, to whom there belongs by his nature a right that is autocephalous and independent; especially since at the same time he presents himself to the mind as the heart-knower and omniscient witness of even hidden impiety, and the most just avenger of it also after this life, and more powerful than any creature: and these very attributes show the Deity as clearly as if pointing with a finger. And this is that very reasoning which the infallible Teacher of the Gentiles, Paul, uses elsewhere with such emphasis, urgently declaring that the work of the law is written in their hearts [τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου γεγραμμένον ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις αὐτῶν], the work of the Law written in their hearts; which the Gentiles also show, since they are driven so that, by nature [φύσει], they do the things of the law; and their conscience bears witness to each, according to good or evil deeds, through thoughts accusing or else excusing them.

units.la: Atque ita supremi Numinis Existentiam, simul & Naturalem ejusdem Notitiam, veritatem omnium quæ in universa Philosophia occurrunt primam facilè ac longè præcipuam, suis adstruximus quantùm satis est argumentis: quibus docuimus cognosci Deum, & argumentando, tum etiam admirando, tanquam Ens entium, & quo, ceu alterius cujusvis entitatis fonte & scaturigine, fluit & pendet quicquid ab eo diversum existit in tota hac rerum natura; & immediato quoque conscientiæ testimonio, quo idem universi primum principium etiam invitis sese manifestat Regem & Dominum supremum, suo arbitrio jura ferentem, eisque suas creaturas auctoritate cui nemo refragari potest adstringentem, tum etiam secundum illa plenissimum in eadem imperium exercentem. Quibus duobus capitibus, quatenus ea arguunt creaturarum, speciatim rationalium, ab opifice suo absolutissimam dependentiam, non realem duntaxat, sed & moralem, comprehenduntur fundamenta omnis religionis ac cultus naturalis Deo debiti. Plurima eaque pulcherrima subjici possent hujus Demonstrationis Consectaria; atqui suis quaeque locis rectius deinceps ea tradentur, quando istuc invitabit occasio, quam abunde ipsa rerum tradendarum series suppeditabit.
units.tr: And so we have established, as far as is sufficient, by our arguments the existence of the supreme Deity, together with the natural knowledge of him, the first and by far the chief of all truths that occur in the whole of Philosophy: by which we have shown that God is known both by reasoning and also by wonder, as Being of beings, and as the one from whom, as from the source and spring of every other entity, flows and depends whatever exists apart from him in the whole of this natural order of things; and also by the immediate testimony of conscience, by which the first principle of the universe reveals himself, even against our will, as King and supreme Lord, giving laws by his own will, binding his creatures to them by an authority that no one can resist, and exercising in addition full dominion over them by means of those laws. By these two heads, insofar as they show the absolute dependence of creatures, especially rational ones, upon their Maker, not merely real but also moral, are comprehended the foundations of all religion and natural worship owed to God. Very many and very beautiful consequences of this demonstration could be added; but these will be set out more fittingly in their own places hereafter, when occasion invites, as the very series of the things to be treated will abundantly supply.
THE THIRD EXERCISE, ON SPECULATIVE ATHEISM.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Atheismi summa & perniciosa absurditas. II. Controversiæ de Atheis Speculativis sensus aperitur. III. Ejus negativa compluribus adstruitur. IV. Pro affirmativa adductæ rationes diluuntur. V. Dubitatio de Dei Existentia, ut à Cartesio tradita & palliata, proponitur. VI. Ejus cum summo periculo conjuncta absurditas detegitur.
units.tr: I. The sum and the pernicious absurdity of atheism. II. The sense of the controversy about speculative atheists is set out. III. The negative view is supported by several arguments. IV. The arguments brought for the affirmative are refuted. V. The doubt about the existence of God, as Descartes delivered and disguised it, is proposed. VI. The absurdity joined with its great danger is exposed.

units.la: Ppofita juxta fe posita usque eò elucescere, ut eadem fit illorum scientia, non frustrà docent Logicorum filii. Quam ob rem, quum proximè diffcruerimus de prima veritate, nimirum de Existentiæ Divinæ naturali notitia, & certitudinis illius fundamentis, ex ordinis lege tranfeundem nunc foret ad excutiendam contrariam ei falfitatem, Atheismum. Ejus num fit absurditas major, num impietas, merito dubites. Nullum profecto commentum æquè ac hoc existit fui everfivum: quando qui agnoscere nolunt, absque quo tamen esse nequeunt, Deum, eò tandem abire coguntur, ut quam summo Numini detrahunt indcpendentiam ac divinitatem, reclamante omni rationis & experientiæ sensu, ridiculâ non minus quam monstrificâ apotheosi, in hoc ipsum Universum transcribant. Quumque prima veritas eadem fit summa bonitas, quid mirum, fi tanta, quâ tam protervè ab illa recedītur, stultitia existat unica cujusvis in humano genere impietatis causa & origo. Quod adeo verum, ut etiam optimus quisque quotics in via virtutis deficit ac labitur, fi fe fatis attendat, alium nullum inveniat erroris fontem, quam animi ab intima supremi Numinis conscientia recessum. Scitè in hanc rem ille:
units.tr: That propositions set side by side become so clear that their knowledge is the same for all is taught by the sons of the logicians, and not in vain. Since we have lately discussed the first truth, namely the natural knowledge of the existence of God and the grounds of that certainty, it is now fitting, by the law of order, to examine the falsehood opposed to it, atheism. One may rightly doubt whether its absurdity or its impiety is the greater. Certainly no invention is so self-destructive as this one. Those who refuse to acknowledge God, without whom they cannot exist, are at last driven to such a place that, while they take from the supreme Deity its independence and divinity, they transfer that very Universe, in a ridiculous and monstrous apotheosis, to itself, against the whole sense of reason and experience. And since the first truth is the same as the highest goodness, it is no wonder that so great a folly, by which people so shamelessly withdraw from that truth, is the sole cause and origin of every impiety in the human race. This is so true that even the best of men, whenever he falls and slips from the path of virtue, if he attends to himself carefully, will find no other source of error than a departure from the inner consciousness of the supreme Deity. The poet aptly says on this matter:
Whoever sins, (otherwise he would fear to sin)

units.la: Esse sibi nullum fingit in orbe Deum.
units.tr: Imagines there is no God in the world for himself.

units.la: Determinam hanc pestem diligentius aliquanto retegere hujus loci foret: verum in ea quâ nostras has Exercitationes circumscripsimus brevitate nefarii dogmatis profunda anxiè scrutari non licet. Atquì neque lubet; nec multum quoque attinet: dum fatis huic monstro incifi sunt nervi, quamdiu stant adduƈtæ à nobis pro Primi Entis existentia rationcs. Neque opus est Iliada scribere post Homerum: adeo, pro more suo, plenè ac solidè quicquid hùc pertinet pertraƈtavit, venerandæ nobis memoriæ Præceptor & Collega, Celeberrimus Gifbertus Voctius, Part. 1. Select. Difp. de Atheismo. Paucis unum duntaxat atque que alterum attingemus, quod hodie magis controversum praecipuam prae aliis cum Theologia Naturali habet affinitatem.
units.tr: It would be worthwhile to uncover this deadly plague a little more carefully here, but in the brevity to which we have confined these Exercises we may not anxiously search out the depths of this wicked dogma. Nor do we wish to, nor is it of much importance: while the sinews of this monster are cut by the arguments we have brought forward for the existence of the First Being, they remain cut. Nor is there need to write a second Iliad after Homer. Our venerable teacher and colleague, the most celebrated Gisbertus Voetius, has treated everything that pertains to this, fully and soundly, as was his way, in Part. 1. Select. Disp. de Atheismo. We shall touch briefly on only one or two points, which are now more disputed and have a special affinity with Natural Theology.

units.la: Eō praeprimis spectat agitatissima quaestio, de Atheis Speculativis, utrum dentur? Sunt qui affirmant; etiam, quod merito mireris, ex eorum numero, qui quibusvis innatam Dei ideam, eamque omnium quae in mente nostra exsistunt clarissimam ac distinctissimam, simul tradunt: quae qui cohaerent dogmata, non satis me intelligere, lubens fateor. Sentiunt nostro judicio sanius, atque apti sunt Atheismum redarguere efficacius, qui negant. Loquimur autem, ne quis ex perperam intellecto quaestionis statu hallucinetur, de subjecto actualis de Deo cognitionis capaci, id est, de homine sanae mentis, quique in aliis veritatibus cognoscendis ratione sua recte utitur: nè quis nobis infantes objiciat, aut mente captos, aut similes, quos ignorare posse veritatem, quam nondum actu queunt percipere, vel etiam forte negare, quam non intelligunt, minimè est inficiandum. Neque quaeritur, an sint, qui sic procul ab omni Numinis reverentia vivunt, quasi nullus exsistat Deus, qui sit scelerum testis simul & judex? Non etiam, utrum reperiantur, qui, negando Dei Unitatem, Omniscientiam, Immutabilitatem, Providentiam, similesque perfectiones, re ipsa per legitimam sequelam e medio tollant Divinitatem? Neque tandem, num quis ore tenus negare queat primae causae exsistentiam, atque affirmantibus quoad verba contradicere? Clamat, proh dolor: tristis experientia, omne hoc Atheorum genus exsistere abundè, ac nimium indies accrescere numerum eorum, qui variis modis veritatem injustè detinent, ac malitia suâ tantum non opprimunt. Id ergò τὸ κεχινόμενον est, An quis detur mortalium, uti ratione potens, qui ipsam Dei exsistentiam directè sic neget, ut ex interiori animi sententia securus acquiescat in salsissima hac falsitate, Non existit Deus, tanquam in theoremate, de cujus veritate certò se persuasum putet? Atque hunc talem Atheum non dari, neque etiam dari posse, nos credimus.
units.tr: The most hotly debated question concerns the speculative atheists: do they exist? Some affirm that they do, and, what is surprising, some of them belong to the number of those who at the same time hold that the idea of God is innate in everyone and is the clearest and most distinct of all the things that exist in our mind. I freely confess that I do not understand well how these doctrines cohere. In our judgment, those who deny the existence of such atheists think more soundly, and they are better able to refute atheism more effectively. But, so that no one may be misled by a wrong understanding of the state of the question, we speak of a subject capable of actual knowledge of God, that is, a man of sound mind who uses his reason rightly in knowing other truths. Let no one object to us infants, or the mentally impaired, or those who, as is certainly not to be denied, cannot yet actually perceive a truth, or perhaps even deny what they do not understand. Nor is the question whether there are people who live so far from all reverence for the Deity as if there were no God who is both witness and judge of crimes. Nor is the question whether there are those who, by denying the unity, omniscience, immutability, providence and similar perfections of God, by a legitimate consequence in fact remove the Divinity. Nor finally is the question whether anyone can deny in words the existence of the First Cause and contradict those who affirm it. Sad experience, alas, cries out that every kind of atheist of this sort exists in abundance, and that the number of those who unjustly hold back the truth in various ways, and all but crush it by their wickedness, grows day by day to excess. So the point at issue is this: is there any mortal, endowed with reason, who so directly denies the very existence of God that, from the inner conviction of his mind, he rests securely in this most false falsehood, God does not exist, as in a theorem of whose truth he thinks himself firmly persuaded? We believe that such an atheist neither exists, nor can exist.

units.la: Fidem huic sententiae facit totum quod de naturali Dei notitia, tum acquisita, tum innata, hactenus docuimus. Non tantum facili adeò diligentiâ supremi Entis exsistentiam in unaquaque creatura nobis obvia elucere, ut vix aliquo discursu indigeamus, evicimus; verum etiam, *si quoque ratiocinari hic lubeat, ostendimus, nullâ longâ ac operosâ demonstrationis serie hic opus esse, sed totum hoc confici proximâ consequentiâ ex immotis principiis, tantâ certitudinis evidentiâ, ut nulla alia dianoëtica notitia sit facilior. Quapropter quicunque aliarum veritatum vim percipere aptus est, hujus etiam efficaciam non sentire non potest. Verùm magis attendi velim, de qua antè diximus, noëticam atque omnibus ingenitam Dei notitiam. Certè, quæ secundum se simpliciter naturalia sunt, ea exui nequeunt, nisi exutâ pariter naturâ ipsâ; adeo quod congenitum est recurrit usque. Quid? quod ipsum rationis lumen (quo nemine ratione utentem destitui clarum est) non in alio consistat, quam in primarum & per se notarum veritatum cognitione; junčta cum facultate, eliciendi indè legitimâ sequelâ quæ in eis latent conclusiones. Jam verò anticipationibus istis insitis annumerandam quoque esse hanc propositionem, Deus existit, antè planum fecimus. Quumque primarum veritatum ratione necessitatis & certitudinis æqualis inter se sit conditio, utique, si nihil obstat quo minus unam quis ex animo ejicere queat, etiam omnes extirpare poterit: quod qui concedendum arbitratur, hominem re verâ ponit non-hominem; à quo scilicet id maximè alienum erit, quod ipsum hominem facit rationalem, id est, hominem. Adde, quod demonstravimus quoque, innatum hoc rationis dictamen, in quantum actiones nostras spectat, vim legis habere. Atqui omnem naturalis legis notitiam (cum quâ pari passu ambulat notitia Legislatoris) ita radicitùs exscindi posse, ut nullus omnino ejus maneat sensus, nemo, nisi ipse ab omni rationis lege remotus, dixerit. Saltem haud parum Gentium ἀναπολόγηta diminuitur, si tam debilis ac parum efficax in iis statuatur opus Legis, ut quis suâ resistentiâ obligationis ejus sensum suffocare penitus queat. Quin charakterem hujus legis vivum & indelebilem poscit inprimis gloriosa Legislatoris Majestas, quæ in hoc potissimum omni finitâ potestate apparet major, quod jura dicat ista cum imperii plenitudine atque efficacia, ut subditi conscientiam moralis, atque adeo omnigenæ, dependentiæ à suo Rege exuere, etiamsi quam maximè velint, non tamen possint, sed quam suâ malitiâ nolunt. lunt, cogantur nihilominus tremente animo agnoscere Judicis auctoritatem. Hunc demum in modum plenè victrix est Dei potestas: cui & ipsi in malo confirmati Dæmones testimonium dicunt, quando quod exhorrescunt, exístere tamen non credere non possunt, Numen. Atque indè factum arbitror (quod silentio prætermittere nequeo, cum maximi sit hoc loco momenti) egregium atque infallibilem Naturalis Theologiæ doctorem & assertorem Paulum, quando alienatum à vero Dei cultu Gentilium statum, ac deploratam eorum malitiam fusè describit, vanos quidem factos narrare in ratiocinationibus ac stultos per obtenebratum intelligentiâ carens cor, eo usque ut debitâ gratiarum actione non tantum Deum non glorificaverint, sed & crasså idololatriâ incorruptibilis Dei gloriam adeo obscuraverint, ut veritatem Dei in mendacium transformaverint; nusquam tamen in isto scelerum catalogo quem subtexit quicquam hujus Atheismi, qui procul dubio inexcusabilis ἀναπολόγητος existit argumentum, meminisse. Osores Dei inter alios numerat Apostolus; non existentiæ Divinæ abnegatores: minimè præteriturus crimen, quod, si detur, omnium cæterorum flagitium est ac quasi compendium. Quin ex adverso passim inculcat, in tanta malitia homines & noviße Deum, & agnoviße δικαίωμα ℨ Θεῦ, & conscientiæ ac cogitationum testimonio ostendiße opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis. Tam nullus tradi potest ἐις ἀδίκημον, ut desinat in eo manifestum esse quod de Deo cognoscitur, quatenus id unicuique mortalium Deus manifestavit.
units.tr: What we have taught so far about the natural knowledge of God, both acquired and innate, makes this view credible. We have shown not only that, with such easy diligence, the existence of the supreme Being shines forth in every creature that meets us, so that we hardly need any reasoning; but also, if it pleases us to reason here, we show that no long and laborious chain of demonstration is needed here, but that the whole matter is established by a immediate consequence from fixed principles, with such evident certainty that no other intellectual knowledge is easier. Therefore whoever is able to grasp the force of other truths cannot fail to feel the efficacy of this one too. But I would have you attend more closely to that noetic knowledge of God which, as we said before, is innate in all. Certainly those things which are by their own nature simply natural cannot be stripped away unless nature itself is stripped away at the same time; so what is innate keeps returning. What is more, the very light of reason (and it is clear that no one who uses reason is deprived of it) consists in nothing other than the knowledge of the first and self-evident truths, joined with the faculty of drawing from them, by a legitimate sequence, the conclusions that lie hidden in them. Now we have already made clear that this proposition, God exists, must be counted among those innate anticipations. And since the first truths are equal in their necessity and certainty, then surely, if nothing prevents someone from casting one of them out of his mind, he will also be able to root out all of them. Whoever thinks this must be conceded makes a man in reality a non-man, one from whom, clearly, what makes man rational, that is, man, would be most remote. Add that we have also demonstrated that this innate dictate of reason, so far as it concerns our actions, has the force of law. But that the whole knowledge of natural law (with which the knowledge of the Lawgiver walks side by side) could be so radically cut out that no sense of it at all remains, no one, unless he were himself quite removed from every law of reason, would say. At least a good deal of the excuselessness of the Gentiles [ἀναπολόγητα] is diminished, if the work of the law is held to be so weak and so ineffective in them that someone could completely suffocate the sense of its obligation by his resistance. Indeed, the glorious Majesty of the Lawgiver above all demands a living and indelible character of this law, a Majesty which appears greater than any finite power in this, that it lays down these laws with such fullness and efficacy of command that subjects, even if they most strongly wish it, cannot strip away the consciousness of moral dependence on their King, and of every kind of dependence, but are compelled, though they unwillingly will it, to acknowledge with trembling spirit the authority of the Judge. In this way the power of God is fully victorious, and to it even the demons, confirmed in evil, bear witness, when, though they shudder at it, they cannot fail to believe that the Deity exists. From this, I think (which I cannot pass over in silence, since it is of the greatest importance here), it came about that Paul, the outstanding and infallible teacher and defender of Natural Theology, when he describes at length the state of the Gentiles, alienated from the true worship of God, and their desperate wickedness, says that they became vain in their reasonings and foolish, with a heart darkened and lacking understanding, so far that they not only did not glorify God with due thanksgiving, but also, by gross idolatry, obscured the glory of the incorruptible God to such a degree that they changed the truth of God into a lie. Yet nowhere in the catalogue of crimes that he appends does he mention anything of this atheism, which undoubtedly exists as a reason for being [ἀναπολόγητος], without excuse. The Apostle counts haters of God among others, not deniers of the existence of God, since he would by no means pass over a crime which, if it exists, is the disgrace of all the others and as it were their summary. Indeed, on the contrary, he everywhere insists that, in so great a wickedness, men both know God, and acknowledge the righteous decree of God, and by the testimony of conscience and thoughts show the work of the law written in their hearts. So no one can be given over [εἰς ἀδίκημα] to wrongdoing in such a way as to cease to find in himself what is known of God to be manifest, inasmuch as God has manifested it to every mortal.

units.la: Et hæc quidem præcipua sunt nostræ sententiæ firmamenta; quibuscum conferendum minimè censemus quicquid à quibusdam pro Atheismo Speculativo movetur. Adducunt ex Psalmo Stultum, qui in corde dicat, non esse Deum. Verum de Practico potius Atheo isthic sermonem esse, ex textûs totius compagine, ejusque cum parallelis collatione, jam dudùm monstrârunt Theologi; quibus eum curatius expendendum relinquimus. Levius est, quod, testimonio Plutarchi ac Ciceronis, referunt de Diagora, Theodoro Cyrenensi, Evemero Tegeate, Euripide Tragico, pluribusque; qui Deos esse negaverint. Etenim quis est qui ignorat, apud Gentiles Atheos passim vocatos fuisse, non qui nullum credebant Deum, sed qui non eadem quæ ipsi admittebant Numina. Socratem ipsum, virum certè sapientissimum, & omni vitæ instituto etiam à suspicione tanti criminis remotissimum, istius quoque impietatis narrant accusatum à quadruplatoribus Atheniensibus; tantùm quod non eosdem, quos concives, colerët Deos. Quicquid sit, istos enumeratos fuisse Speculativos Atheos, quales antè descripsimus, nondum ullâ rationis specie demonstratum vidi. Gravius urget, quem adferunt in medium, Atheismi Apostolus & pro eo Martyr Julius Cæsar Vaninus, qui præfractè Deum negans, postquam per pestilentissimos libros, Æternæ providentiæ Divinæ theatrum, item Dialogos, virus nefarii dogmatis tectè in animos hominum insinuare conatus fuerat, tandem convictus debitum pertinaci impietati supplicium Tholosæ igne exsolvit, etiam ad extremum usque nequicquam à blasphemia remittens. Non vacat disquirere, quibus modis & artibus in casses suos tam profundè trahere potuerit hominem diabolus? Theologici id fori est. Hæc aliaque prætermittens, id unum ajo, tot & tantis rationibus scelestam unius hominis vocem nihil detrahere: qui enim primam veritatem negare audet, quid non ausit? Quare, sic animo re verâ sensisse, uti verbis præ se tulit, prudentis non est credere ex solo impii ac mendacis oris testimonio. Tandem gentes integras in aciem educunt, quæ ex innata feritate nullum Numen agnoscant. Verum testimonium hoc negativum est; quatenus, si qui sunt qui sic narrant, potissimum narrant nihil cultûs religiosi per illud tempus quo inter eas commorati fuerunt, se observare potuisse. Quod si tamen qui ista de gentibus quibusdam testantur scriptores, longiori ac familiariori convictu populorum de quibus loquuntur & linguam & mores perspectos satis & cognitos habuissent, longè aliud, quam quod de iis tradiderunt, fuissent experti: uti & experti fuerunt alii, qui propriori indagine edocti contrarium de iisdem illis testati sunt; & communi consensu confirmarunt illud Ciceronis, quæ eadem nostra conclusio erit, Nulla gens tam feræ, nemo omnium tam immanis, quem non imbuerit Deorum (Dei) opinio.
units.tr: And these are indeed the chief supports of our position, and we do not think anything that some people put forward in favour of speculative atheism should be compared with them. They cite from the Psalm, The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. But theologians have long since shown, from the structure of the whole text and its comparison with parallel passages, that the reference there is rather to practical atheism. We leave it to them to weigh this more carefully. What they report about Diagoras, Theodorus of Cyrene, Euhemerus of Tegea, the tragic poet Euripides and many others, who are said to have denied that there are gods, on the testimony of Plutarch and Cicero, is weaker. For who does not know that among the Gentiles, atheists were often so called, not those who believed in no god, but those who did not admit the same divinities as themselves? They also relate that Socrates himself, a man most certainly wise and by the whole course of his life far removed even from suspicion of such a crime, was accused of this same impiety by the four informers at Athens, merely because he did not worship the same gods as his fellow citizens. Whatever the case, I have not yet seen it shown by any rational argument that these men listed were speculative atheists of the kind we described above. A more serious argument is that brought forward by the apostle of atheism, and its martyr, Julius Caesar Vanini, who, obstinately denying God, after he had tried through most pestilential books, the Theatre of the Eternal Divine Providence, and likewise his Dialogues, to insinuate the poison of his impious doctrine secretly into men's minds, was at last convicted and paid the due penalty of his stubborn impiety by fire at Toulouse, retracting his blasphemy to the very end to no avail. It is not the time to inquire by what methods and arts the devil was able to draw the man so deeply into his snares. That belongs to the court of theology. Setting these and other things aside, I say this only: the wicked voice of one man, however many and great the reasons, detracts nothing; for he who dares to deny the first truth, what will he not dare? Therefore, that he truly felt in his heart as he professed in words is not a matter for a prudent man to believe on the sole testimony of an impious and lying mouth. Lastly, they bring forward whole nations which, from innate savagery, acknowledge no divinity. But this testimony is negative; for even if there are those who so report, they chiefly report that during the time they lived among these peoples they could observe no religious worship at all. Yet if those writers who bear witness to such things about certain nations had known both the language and the customs of the peoples they speak of, from a longer and more familiar acquaintance, they would have experienced something quite different from what they handed down about them. Others did experience it, who, taught by a closer investigation, bore witness to the contrary about these same peoples, and by common consent confirmed that saying of Cicero, which will be our own conclusion as well: No nation is so savage, no man so monstrous, that the opinion of the gods (of God) has not imbued him.

units.la: Verum ab aperta Atheismi professione (propter ipsam horridi dogmatis cruditatem, cui digerendæ ferreus paucorum tantum spirituum
units.tr: But the open profession of atheism is not so much to be feared by truth and piety, on account of the very crudity of that horrid doctrine, the digestion of which requires an iron stomach, such as only a few strong spirits possess,
V. Doubt

units.la: spirituum fortium ventriculus par est) non tam est metuendum veritati & pietati, quam potius ab istis artibus, quibus nonnulli, sive scientes, sive ignorantes, sub specioso veritatis inquirendæ prætextu, latam blasphemiæ portam aperiunt. Hasinter (aliis nunc missis) primo loco collocandam censeo methodum illam, quâ Philosophaturo præcipitur, in acquirenda cognitione, uti aliarum rerum, ita quoque ipsius Dei, initium faciendum esse a dubitatione. Ergò pauca etiam de hac controversia, Utrum de Dei Existentia naturaliter dubitare liceat? Ita quæstionem proponit Cartefius, Epist. x. Part. ii. ubi & de ea disserit pluribus; quorum summa hùc redit. Contendit, eos omnes, qui existentiam Dei evidenter demonstrare nequeunt, posse (separata fide) naturali ratione examinare, an sit Deus aliquis? atque ita intellectu suo de Deo dubitare. Quotquot autem sic de Deo dubitant, si sibi pro scopo non habeant in re tanti momenti velle pendere in dubio, sed hanc sibi dubitationem proponant tanquam medium ad clariorem veritatis cognitionem acquirendam, rem facere omninò piam & honestam; ut non peccet, qui propter hunc finem totam quam de Deo habere potest cognitionem ad tempus ex animo summovet. Quod nisi lubitum fuerit in re seria nugari, abutendo nimium voce dubitationis, sique quod res est dicere licet, nihil ista volunt aliud, quam omnes illos rem piam facere & honestam, qui ad tempus Athei fieri intendunt, ut deinceps Athei esse desinant. Nec enim video, quid re verà differitatis intercedat inter Atheum, atque illum qui totam quam de Deo habere potest cognitionem ex animo summovet. Quod enim subjicit Auctor, etiam nos, quotiescunque dormimus, aut aliud quicquam agimus, seponere in id tempus totam cognitionem quam de Divinitate habere possumus, id uti falsum, ita oppidò ridiculum est, & merum ἀρησφὼγετον, ad horridam sententiam, si quo colore fieri possit, palliandam. Certè, quicunque pius, aliud agens, de Deo non cogitat, is quidem actualem de Divina existentia cogitationem negative non elicit, quatenus plures diversarum rerum notiones in eadem mentis actione simul non subsistunt; attamen servat constantem animi propensionem ac habitualem aliquem assensum in hanc propositionem, Deus existit, tanquam verifsi-
units.tr: a stomach such as only a few strong spirits possess) as much as by those arts with which some, whether knowingly or unknowingly, under the specious pretext of inquiring after truth, open a wide gate to blasphemy. Here (other matters now set aside) I think the first place should be given to that method which is prescribed to the one who philosophizes, that in acquiring knowledge, both of other things and of God himself, one must begin from doubt. Therefore, a few words also on this controversy: Whether one may naturally doubt the existence of God? Descartes proposes the question in this way, Epistle 10, Part 2, where he also discusses it at length, and the substance of it comes to this. He contends that all those who cannot clearly demonstrate the existence of God may (with faith set aside) examine by natural reason whether there is some God, and so in their understanding doubt concerning God. But however many doubt about God in this way, if they do not make it their aim to remain in doubt about a matter of such importance, but propose this doubt as a means of gaining a clearer knowledge of the truth, they do a thing wholly pious and honourable; so that he does not sin who, for this end, removes from his mind for a time all the knowledge of God that he can have. Unless it pleases us to trifle in a serious matter, abusing the word doubt too much, and, to say what is the case, these men want nothing else than that all those who intend to become atheists for a time, so that afterwards they may cease to be atheists, do a pious and honourable thing. For I do not see what real difference there is between an atheist and one who removes from his mind all the knowledge of God that he can have. As for what the author adds, that we too, whenever we sleep or do anything else, set aside for that time all the knowledge of the Godhead that we can have, this is as false as it is utterly ridiculous, and a mere ἀρησφὼγετον [absurd conclusion], intended to cloak a horrid opinion with some colour, if that were possible. Certainly, whoever is pious, while occupied with something else, does not think of God; he indeed does not elicit an actual thought of the divine existence, inasmuch as several notions of different things do not subsist together in one act of the mind; yet he preserves a constant inclination of the soul and a habitual assent to this proposition, God exists, as most true and most certain.

units.la: de Dei Existentia, ut à Cartefio tradita & palliata, proponitur. verissimam ac certissimam ; ut talis nequaquam omnem quàm de Deo habere potest cognitionem ex animo summoveat, nec positivo actu mentis circa ejus existentiam assensum suspendat, quod ad dubitationem Cartesianam omninò pertinet. Nisi dicendum sit, Cartesium, quando in mundo suo vorticoso digerendo laborabat, de Meditationibus suis earumque veritate dubitasse, quòd tum temporis de illis forte non cogitaverit? Pinguis ista profectò subtilitas est, & mysterium sapientiæ non vulgaris! Verum tanti est ea cudere dogmata, quorum, dum candidum patrocinium aperte suscipere pudet, turpem nuditatem fictis tegere nugamentis tutius habetur. Et quis vel sando audivit, unquam fuisse controversum, an teneamur indesinenter cogitare, quod existat Deus? Aliud ergò planè est, dubitare de re quapiam, id est, pendere in dubio (ut ipse hoc loco Auctor) aliud, de ea non cogitare: nisi velit nova methodus, quando jubet dubitare de omnibus, de iis tantum non esse cogitandum. Plura sunt in paucis illis lineis paris acuminis, aliàs forte ex professo excutienda. Nunc quæ præ manibus est quæstio tribus verbis absolvenda.
units.tr: concerning the existence of God, as set forth by Descartes and disguised, is put forward. Such a person by no means removes from his mind all the knowledge of God that he can have, nor suspends by a positive act of the mind his assent to God's existence, which pertains entirely to the Cartesian doubt. Unless it must be said that Descartes, when he was labouring to arrange his vortical world, doubted his own Meditations and their truth, because perhaps at that time he did not think about them? That is a fat subtlety indeed, and a mystery of no common wisdom! But such doctrines are worth coining only as long as one is ashamed openly to take up their open defence, and it is considered safer to cover their shameful nakedness with fictitious trifles. And who has ever heard, even in jest, that it was a controversy whether we are bound to think unceasingly that God exists? It is one thing, therefore, to doubt some matter, that is, to remain in suspense about it (as the author himself here does), and another not to think about it at all; unless this new method, when it bids us doubt everything, bids us think about none of it. There are many matters in those few lines of equal shrewdness, which perhaps will be examined at length on another occasion. But the question now before us can be settled in three words.

units.la: Licitum est procul dubio argumenta quærere ad thesin hanc, Existit Deus, variis modis magis magisque stabiliendam: itâ tamen ut conclusionis inferendæ veritas, tanquam dubia, ab argumentis adhuc investigandis minimè suspendatur, sed inquirenti argumenta supponatur tanquam certa, tantùm aliis rationibus confirmanda. Itaque, sicuti in vita nostra quotidiè res millenæ nobis occurrunt, quas ipsi certissimas atque indubias esse sumus persuasissimi, quaque nihilominus, si quis forte negaverit, sine ulla certitudinis in mente nostra diminutione, alteri persuadere nitimur rationibus hunc in finem inquirendis; ita quoque inquirantur argumenta ad confutandum Atheum, nobis tamen ipsis indubia interim semper sit & maneat, veritas hæc, Existit Deus. Etenim quicunque ab ejus certa persuasione quicquam remittit (uti remittit omnis qui dubitat; quatenus certum & dubium in mente nostra opposita sunt, quorum alterum alterius contagione imminui necesse est) tanto propius ad Atheismum accedit, quanto à certitudine hujus thesèos recedit longius. Horret certè animus ac meminisse refugit, tanto co
units.tr: Doubtless it is lawful to seek arguments for this thesis, God exists, so as to establish it more and more firmly in various ways; yet in such a way that the truth of the conclusion to be drawn is not suspended, as if doubtful, pending the arguments still to be searched out, but that the arguments are assumed by the inquirer as certain, to be confirmed only by other reasons. Thus, just as in our life countless things daily present themselves to us, which we ourselves are most firmly persuaded are certain and beyond doubt, and which nevertheless, if someone happens to deny them, we attempt to persuade him of by reasons sought for this purpose, without any diminution of certainty in our own minds; so arguments may be sought for refuting the atheist, while this truth, God exists, remains and always stays unshaken for us in the meantime. For whoever gives up anything of this firm persuasion (as everyone who doubts does give it up; since the certain and the doubtful are opposed in our mind, and one of them must be diminished by the contagion of the other) draws so much nearer to atheism as he withdraws further from the certainty of this thesis. Certainly the mind shudders and shrinks from remembering how far...
VI.

units.la: natu commendari hodiè methodum, quâ inter Existentiæ Divinæ certam notitiam & ipsum Atheismum homo in isto ponitur bivio, in quo dubiam trahit sententia mentem, an sit aliquis Deus? Quid? quod qui de Deo dubitat, necesse habeat unà dubitare de sua ab ipso dependentia, suaque ad legis naturalis dictamen obligatione; cujus diminutà reverentiâ nulla rectior ad Atheismum datur via. Ad hæc, si de Dei existentia dubitare li-cuerit, etiam dubitationi subducenda non erunt quævis alia principia per se nota, quæ in eodem cum illa stant ordine. Quod si sic, invenit, de quo sibi gratuletur, Atheismus & Scepticis-mus propugnaculum inexpugnabile; quatenus hi non nisi beneficio quarundam immediatarum veritatum certò supponendarum everti queunt. Et quid ipsi Cartefianæ Philosophiæ evenient, quæ hoc pacto omni nudatur certitudinis spe? Cum enim per ejus placita nihil cuiquam possit esse certum, nisi præcognitâ Dei minimè fallacis existentia, hac dubiâ datâ, nihil unquam in ea erit indubium: si enim omnia, cum Deo, dubia, quâ obscero ratione, & ex quo principio, primùm de Deo, mox etiam de rebus aliis, evademus certi? Adde & innatam esse hanc veritatem, quod antè docui: ut nec fatis possibilis sit, nec utilis, de ea dubitatio; quatenus suæ certitudinis vi omnem eam sic excludit, ut antè se sentiri faciat, quam de dubitatione con-silium capescere alicui licet. Quod si qui nihilominus ejus ful-gentem certitudinem affectatâ dubitatione obscurare, & sic re verâ injustè detinere erumpentem veritatem nitantur, viderint tales, ne incidant in judicium gentium, quàs, quia visum non fuit eis Deum in notitia retinere, tradidit Ipse in mentem omnis judicii expertem. Utinam nulli isti dubitatores id sint experti, nec existant inter eos, qui istis Spirits suffocati, non possint non parùm reverenter habere deiitceps Numen, de quo præfracte primùm dubitare voluerunt!
units.tr: Is it commended today as a method by which a man is placed at this crossroads between the certain knowledge of God's existence and atheism itself, a crossroads where doubt draws the mind to ask whether there is any God at all? What is more, whoever doubts God must also necessarily doubt his own dependence on Him and his obligation to the dictate of natural law; and once reverence for these is diminished, no more direct road to atheism is open. Moreover, if it is allowed to doubt the existence of God, then no other self-evident principles that stand in the same order as that one will be exempt from doubt either. If so, atheism and skepticism have found, and may congratulate themselves on, an impregnable bulwark, since they can be overthrown only with the aid of certain immediate truths that must be taken for granted. And what will become of the Cartesian philosophy itself, which in this way is stripped of every hope of certainty? For by its tenets nothing can be certain to anyone unless the existence of a God who is not a deceiver is known beforehand; if that is granted to be doubtful, nothing in it will ever be beyond doubt. For if everything, God included, is in doubt, by what reasoning and from what principle shall we emerge certain, first about God and then also about other things? Add too that this truth is innate, as I taught earlier, so that doubt about it is neither sufficiently possible nor useful; since by the force of its own certainty it excludes every doubt in such a way that it makes itself felt before anyone can even take up a plan of doubting. But if some nevertheless try, by feigned doubt, to obscure its shining certainty, and so in fact unjustly to hold down the truth as it breaks forth, let such men see to it that they do not fall under the judgment upon the Gentiles, because they did not see fit to retain God in knowledge, God gave them up to a reprobate mind. Would that none of these doubters experience this, and that there be none among them who, choked by such spirits, cannot help holding in rather little reverence from then on the Deity about which they first stubbornly wished to doubt!
EXER-

units.la: EXERCITATIO QUARTA DE DEO INDEPENDENTE. SUMMARIUM.
units.tr: FOURTH EXERCISE ON THE INDEPENDENT GOD. SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Primi alicujus & fundamentalis quasi conceptús de Deo formandi necessitas. II. Perperam ratione Independentiæ Deum Cartesio dici esse à se positivè. III. Quid tamen positivi Independentia Divina includat ? IV. Independentiam Deo competere ,, & hujus conceptum aliis omnibus in Deo esse præmittendum , ostenditur: V. Illi junčta Spiritualitas descriptionem quasi Dei conficit. VI. An; & quo sensu , ex natura Verus Deus cognosci dicendus sit ? VII. Omnimodæ Dei Independentiæ agnitio præcipua veræ Religionis basis. VIII. Ex notione Independentiæ perperam concludi, unam tantum dari substantiam. IX. Sententiæ hujus Atheismus paucis detegitur.
units.tr: I. The necessity of forming some first and fundamental concept of God. II. It is wrongly said, on account of Independence, that God is positively from himself, according to Descartes. III. What positive content, however, does divine Independence include? IV. It is shown that Independence belongs to God, and that its concept must be placed before all other things in God. V. Spirituality, joined to it, makes up as it were the description of God. VI. Whether, and in what sense, the true God is said to be known from his nature. VII. The acknowledgement of God's Independence in every respect is the chief basis of true religion. VIII. It is wrongly concluded from the notion of Independence that only one substance exists. IX. The atheism of this opinion is briefly exposed.

units.la: D formandum distinctiorem rei cujusfibet conceptum, tum etiam ad notitiam ejus acquirendam & certiorem & pleniorem, recte præcipiunt Philosophi, inter omnia quæ menti occurrunt prædicata, unum aliquod esse investigandum ante alia, quod rei præ cæteris sit intrinsecum, ac rationem ejus formalem sive essentiam quasi constituat; in quo, ceu immoto fundamento, pedem figere liceat, atque unde, tanquam ex fonte aliquo, continuatâ demonstrationis serie quævis alia ejusdem attributa deriventur. Quapropter, postquam summi Numinis Existentiam naturali rationis lumine non uno modo innotescere proximè evicimus, non rectius, quantum capiunt ingenioli nostri angustiæ, & Quid sive
units.tr: Philosophers rightly teach that, in order to form a more distinct concept of any thing, and to acquire a more certain and fuller knowledge of it, one must investigate, among all the predicates that occur to the mind, one that is more intrinsic to the thing than the rest, and that as it were constitutes its formal reason or essence. On this, as on an immovable foundation, one may set one's foot, and from it, as from a certain source, every other attribute of the thing may be derived by a continuous series of demonstration. For this reason, since we have just shown in more than one way that the existence of the highest Divinity is known by the natural light of reason, we shall understand what and who God is, so far as the narrowness of our little wits allows, in no more correct way than by laying down, as the foundation of all our thoughts about God, some first and, as I may say, essential concept.

units.la: I. Primi alicujus & fundamentalis quasi conceptús de Deo formandi necessitas. sive Quis, & Qualis Deus sit, intelligemus, quam si omnibus nostris de Deo cogitationibus primum aliquem & , ut ita dicam , essentialem conceptum substernamus. Id quotquot negligunt præsenti gravissimorum errorum periculo sese exponunt, ista sæpiusculè Deo tribuentes, quæ à summæ perfectionis statu non tantum sunt alienissima, sed & quæ altius introspecta ipsam naturam Divinam penitus evertunt. Neque hîc satis juvat notio Dei confusè tantùm concepti tanquam Entis infinitè perfecti (in quam facile, quotquot Deum exiʃtere credunt, consentiunt) nisi ad manum sit manifestum indicium, quo id quod re verâ perfectionem notat discriminetur ab eo quod imperfectum est; quodque adeo conceptibus quibusvis de Deo formandis normam ponat ac mensuram primam & prorsus infallibilem. Talé prædicatum, nostro judicio, Independentia est: quæ cum ipsa natura Divina, in quantum ea sub captum nostrum cadit, unum idemque notare videtur; & quam qui unicè sequitur tanquam cynosuram in formandis quibuslibet de Deo cogitatis, certus is esse poterit, se non salli, hanc quamdiu servat sartam tectamque.
units.tr: I. The necessity of forming some first and fundamental, as it were, concept of God. Or, who and what God is. Those who neglect this expose themselves to the present danger of very serious errors, attributing to God many things that are not only most alien to the state of supreme perfection but which, looked into more deeply, utterly overturn the divine nature itself. Here, the notion of God conceived only confusedly, as a Being infinitely perfect, is not enough (all who believe that God exists readily agree on this), unless there is at hand a clear sign by which what truly denotes perfection is distinguished from what is imperfect, and which therefore sets down for forming any concepts of God a first and wholly infallible norm and measure. Such a predicate, in my judgement, is Independence. This, so far as it falls under our grasp, seems to denote the same thing as the divine nature itself; and whoever follows it alone, as a guiding star in forming any thoughts about God, may be certain that he is not deceived, as long as he keeps it whole and unimpaired.

units.la: Independentiam cum appello, aliquid significatum volo tum negativi, tum etiam positivi. In mera negatione subsistendum, in quantum excluditur qualiscunque dependentia, sive passiva emanatio ab influxu cujuscunque causæ. Removetur ergo omnis omninò ratio causalitatis, sive intrinsecam eam quis cogitet, ratione Dei ipsius; sive extrinsecam, ratione alicujus principii extra Deum. Et hanc quidem manifestè excludit primitas in causarum subordinatarum seriè, respuens omne superius, atque inferens principium sine principio. Illam verò ipsa notio causalitatis arguit contradictionis atque absurditatis; quatenus si quid sui ipsius causa foret, sibi id dedisset quod jam habuisset, nec tamen habuisset quod dedisset. Quæ cum sint evidentia, mirum, quid in mentem venerit Cartesio, quando iterùm iterùmque inculcat, Deum à se esse, non negativè, sed quam maximè positivè; sic ut, quia ille ipse est, qui se re verâ conservat, videatur non nimis impropriè dici posse sui causa: quatenus ejus potentiam tam exsuperantem agnoscit, ut planè fit causa, cur ille esse perseveret; quippe qui, dum in eo tantum est potentia
units.tr: When I call it Independence, I mean something both negative and positive. We must rest in the mere negation, insofar as every kind of dependence is excluded, that is, every passive emanation from the influence of any cause whatever. Therefore all rationale of causality is removed, whether one thinks of it as intrinsic, with respect to God himself, or as extrinsic, with respect to some principle outside God. Primacy in the series of subordinate causes clearly excludes this, rejecting everything superior and implying a principle without a principle. The very notion of causality, moreover, shows that the other is contradictory and absurd: for if anything were the cause of itself, it would have given to itself what it already had, and yet it would not have had what it gave. Since these things are evident, it is strange what came into Descartes' mind when he again and again insists that God is from himself, not negatively, but most of all positively; so that, because he is himself the one who really conserves himself, he may seem not too improperly to be called the cause of himself: insofar as he recognises his power to be so exceeding that he plainly becomes the cause why he persists in being; since, while in him there is only power

units.la: II. Perperam ratione Independentiæ Deum Cartesio dici esse à se positive. tentia, ut rem extra se positam conservet, omnino tanto magis seipsum suâ propriâ potentiâ conservas. Ut nobis omnino liceat cogitare, illum quodammodo idem praestare respectu sui ipsius, quod causa efficiens respectu sui effectus: nec videat, cur nomen causae tantopere sit fugiendum, cum potius illo uti perutile ac propemodum necessarium esse videatur. Quod si Viro placuisset paulò clarius ac distinctius philosophari, saltem, quid aliquid assereret diligentius attendere, videre facile potuisset, nihil istis inconcinnius dici posse. Quandoquidem enim notiones causae ac causati indivisam ac reciprocam involvunt relationem eorum, quorum alterum naturâ prius est altero, utique nullus eis in hac materia relinquitur locus. Nisi concipere liceat quodammodo, ac dicere non nimis improprie, sed perutiliter ac propemodum necessario, essentiam Divinam naturâ priorem esse se ipsâ; id est, eam id sibi dedisse, quod jam possidebat. Ut jam sileam istud longè crudius, quo ita Deum vult sui ipsius causam, ut cum se conservare dicat per eandem potentiam, per quam res extra se positas conservat.
