Quæ, si non nimis improprie accipiantur, quodammodo, quin plane necessario, inferunt, conceptum potentiae Divinae, uti aliarum rerum creatarum essentiis, ita quoque existentiae Dei, esse praemittendum: quod, qui potest, capiat! Quin, cum conservatio sit quaedam continuata creatio, per ista jam allegata cogitandum erit ac pronunciandum, nec nimis improprie, sed perutiliter ac propemodum necessario, Deum statuendum esse creatorem sui ipsius, uti est suarum creaturarum; quarum esse, ut primum, sic quoque continuatum, ad potentiae divinae exsuperantem causalitatem est referendum. Quae omnia cùm sint quam maximè absurda & in Divinam perfectionem contumeliosa, certè ferendi sunt conceptus istiusmodi ac phraseologiae nullo modo, nec proprie nec improprie, nedum perutiliter aut necessario, sed plane ac plenè ab hoc negotio removendi. Eoque sensu optimè hactenus dictum (quatenus respectus habetur alicujus, qualiscunque ea fuerit, causalitatis) Deum nullo modo esse à se positivè, sed tantum merè negativè, omne sui principium excludendo.
units.tr: II. It is wrongly said, on account of Independence, that God is positively from himself, according to Descartes. power, to conserve a thing placed outside himself, he conserves himself all the more by his own power. So that we may altogether be permitted to think that he does in some way the same for himself that an efficient cause does for its effect: and he sees no reason why the name of cause should be so much shunned, since rather its use seems to be most useful and almost necessary. If the man had been pleased to philosophise a little more clearly and distinctly, at least by attending more carefully to what he asserts, he could easily have seen that nothing more incongruous could be said than these things. For since the notions of cause and effect involve an indivisible and reciprocal relation of those things of which one is prior to the other by nature, no room is left for them in this matter. Unless one may conceive in some way, and say not too improperly, but most usefully and almost necessarily, that the divine essence is by nature prior to itself; that is, that it gave to itself what it already possessed. Let me pass over, for now, that far cruder claim by which he wishes God to be the cause of himself in such a way that he says he conserves himself through the same power by which he conserves things placed outside himself. If these things are taken not too improperly, they imply, in some way, indeed plainly necessarily, that the concept of divine power, like the essences of other created things, so also the existence of God, must be placed first: let whoever can grasp that! Indeed, since conservation is a certain continued creation, it must be thought and pronounced, by what has been alleged above, not too improperly, but most usefully and almost necessarily, that God must be held to be the creator of himself, just as he is of his creatures; and the continued being of these, like their first being, must be referred to the exceeding causality of divine power. Since all these things are most absurd and insulting to divine perfection, such notions and phraseology must certainly be borne in no way, neither properly nor improperly, much less usefully or necessarily, but must be plainly and fully removed from this discussion. And in that sense it has been rightly said hitherto (insofar as a relation to some kind of causality, whatever it may be, is in view) that God is in no way positively from himself, but only merely negatively, by excluding every principle of his own.

units.la: Interim, semoto omni omninò causalitatis conceptu, haud gravatim admittimus, Independentiam à parte rei esse aliquid quam
units.tr: Meanwhile, with every concept of causality entirely set aside, we readily admit that Independence, on the side of the thing itself, is something

units.la: III. Quid tamen quam maximè positivum : quam ob rem quidam eam Asseitatis nomine exprimere maluerunt. Etenim, cum ne vilissimæ at-que imperfectissimæ quidem rei essentia in præ-dicato negativo consistat, imprimis cogitandum est, meram negationem debiliorem esse quam ut sufficiat ad ponendum primum & radicale prædicatum illius Entis, quod præ omni alio summè positivum est. Quid ? quod etiam ipsum purum putum nihil dici possit suo sensu negativè independens; quatenus nullius causæ influxui debet suum esse, quod nullum habet. Itaque, cum Deum Independentem asserimus, id volumus, illi ex se & per se con-venire perfectissimam Sufficientiam ad existendum; adeo ut se ipso, modo eminentissimo & ab omni causalitate longè diverso, existentiam possideat, quam suam alia quævis entia suis debent causis. Attamen cum ista ratio existendi consummatissima, & à parte rei procul dubio maximè realis & positiva, à nobis tanquam positiva concipi non posset, nisi mox in alicujus causalitatis ideam incidamus (quæ tamen, uti docuimus, præprimis hic arenda est) jure merito ac longè tutissimè mens nostra, suæ imperfectionis sibi conscia, ne quid cogitet Deo indignum, acquiescit in negativa Independentiæ notione, quatenus ea offert Dei essentiam nullius ad existendum indigam.
units.tr: III. What positive content does divine Independence include? Therefore some have preferred to express it by the name Aseity. For, since not even the essence of the meanest and most imperfect thing consists in a negative predicate, it must first be considered that mere negation is too weak to suffice for positing the first and radical predicate of that Being which is supremely positive above every other. Moreover, even pure and simple, nothing can be said to be independent in a negative sense, since it owes its being to the influence of no cause, because it has nothing. Therefore, when we assert God to be Independent, we mean that to him belongs, from himself and through himself, the most perfect sufficiency for existing; so that he possesses existence in himself, in a most eminent way and far removed from all causality, whereas all other beings owe their existence to their causes. Yet since this most consummate manner of existing, which is certainly most real and positive in the reality of the thing, could not be conceived by us as positive unless we soon fall upon the idea of some causality (which, however, as we have taught, must here above all be avoided), our mind, conscious of its own imperfection, rightly and by far most safely rests, lest it think anything unworthy of God, in the negative notion of Independence, insofar as that notion presents the essence of God as needing nothing for existing.

units.la: IV. Independentiam Deo competere, & hujus conceptum aliis omnibus in Deo esse præmittendum, ostenditur.
units.tr: IV. It is shown that Independence belongs to God, and that its concept must be placed before all the other things in God.

units.la: Non jam laborabo in demonstranda Dei Independentia, quum de ea ex ante dictis abunde constet. Quod enim in omni cau-sarum ordine primum est (quale Deum esse evicimus ante, cum à finita causarum subordinatarum serie pro ejus existentia argumentabamur) id ab alterius influxu nihil plane accepisse potuit: quumque tamen existat, utique per se atque ex se id existere, est necesse. Cæterum, uti ab omni causa, ita quoque alio quovis modo Independentem esse Deum, eâdem demonstratione conficitur. Quandoquidem enim omne aliud dependentiæ genus eam quæ à causa est supponere & involvere constat, utique in quod Ens hanc cadere non posse ostendimus, ab eodem omnem alterius ordinis dependentiam esse removen-dam, per se manifestum est. Id ergò potius inquirendum, de quo lis moveri posset, utrùm conceptus Independentiæ, pro modo cogitandi nostro, cæteris omnibus in Deo occurrentibus prædicatis præmittendus sit, tanquam maximè essentialis & intrinse-
units.tr: I will not now labour to demonstrate God's Independence, since it is already sufficiently established from what has been said. For whatever is first in the whole order of causes (as we proved earlier, when we argued for God's existence from the finite series of subordinate causes) could have received nothing at all from another's influence; and since it nonetheless exists, it must necessarily exist through itself and from itself. Moreover, the same demonstration shows that God is independent of every cause and of every other kind of dependence. For since every other kind of dependence is known to presuppose and involve dependence on a cause, and we have shown that this cannot fall upon the Being in question, it is plain that every dependence of another order must likewise be removed from him. The question that could be raised is therefore a different one: whether the concept of Independence, in our way of thinking, should be placed before all the other predicates that occur in God, as the most essential and intrinsic of them.

units.la: positivi Divina Independentia includat? trinsecus? Nobis quidem sic omnino videtur: &, quia Independentia ex nullo priori deduci, sed duntaxat à posteriori de Deo probari, potest; &, quia quævis aliæ in Deo obviæ perfectiones ex ipsa Independentia, tanquam ex fonte, à priori quasi queunt demonstrari: uti de singulis docebit sequens nostet tractatus. Cui verò prædicato duo ista requisita conveniunt, id rectè habetur pro ratione rei formali, distinguenda ab attributis, tanquam prædicatisillius, uti vulgò loquuntur, consecutivis. Nec obscurè Deus ipse nobis in hoc conceptu præiisse videtur, quando sese manifestavit nomine יהוה tanquam Memoriali suo. Videlicet, id uti derivatur ab הוה fuit, ita in nativa significatione notat aliquid quod est absolutissimè ex se ipso: quapropter & illud Deo essentiale esse ac proprium, nec ulli alteri communicabile, docent Theologi & Philologi; ex quibus consuli potest facillimus harum rerum explanator, Præceptor ac Collega honorandus, Cl. Johannes Leusden, Philolog. Hebr. Quamvis autem omnia quæ Deo conveniunt, ipsa etiam ejus Spiritualitas, sive Vita rationalis, essentiam notans ab omni materia remotam, & intelligendo ac volendo actuosam, facilè ex Independentia deduci queant, atque ideo solius hujus conceptus, ad Dei essentiam pro modulo repræsentandam, sufficere videatur; attamen, quoniam Rationalitas ista Dei sive Spiritualitas fermè pari passu cum Independentia ex creaturarum contemplatione, ut suprà vidimus, nobis innotescit, quumque etiam nos assueti simus in concipienda aliarum rerum natura duo prædicata essentialia distinctè notare, quorum prius magis est commune, posterius rei magis proprium ac specificum; facilè admittimus, ne nimium à communi concipiendi modo recedamus, analogico quodam modo (excludendum enim omne imperfectionis fundamentum) conceptum nostrum de natura Divina comprehendi posse duabus notionibus, quarum altera ejus Spiritualitatem (cujus etiam suo modo participes exstant rationales creaturæ) altera conjunctam, quin identificatam cum illa, Independentiam offerat. Ut supremi Numinis brevis, & ad captum nostrum accommodata, talis esse queat descriptio: Deus est Spiritus Independens. Aliæ, quæcunque circumferuntur definitiofinitiones, vel verbis tantum ab hac differunt, re ipsa conveniunt, ut cum Deus dicitur, v. c. Essentia spiritualis se ipsa viveus; aut, Ens entium; &c. vel minus existunt accuratæ, quòd non primum prædicatum, sed attributum aliquod, essentia divina pro modo concipiendi posterius, assumant; quales sunt quæ Deum describunt, v. c. Ens necessario existens;. aut, Ens infinitè perfectum; &c. Sed harum examen, servamus illis locis, quibus de Necessitate existendi, Infinitate perfectionum, &c. sumus aduri. Imprimis verò silenter hic praetermittere non deberem praeposteram philosophationem Neotericorum, omnem Divinam essentiam frigida solius Cogitationis idea circumscribentium; nisi ejus absurditatem pluribus detexissem, peculiari Exercitatione de Cogitatione, quae sit mens humana. Quapropter & istud nunc missum facio.
units.tr: Does Divine Independence include something positive, intrinsically? To us it certainly seems so, for two reasons: because Independence cannot be deduced from anything prior but can only be proved of God a posteriori, and because every other perfection found in God can, as it were, be demonstrated a priori from Independence itself as from a source; as the following treatise will teach concerning each of them. Whatever predicate has these two requirements is rightly regarded as the formal reason of a thing, to be distinguished from its attributes, which are, as they commonly say, consequent predicates of it. Nor does God himself seem to have obscurely gone before us in this concept, when he made himself known by the name [יהוה] as his memorial. Namely, this name, derived from [הוה] was, in its native meaning signifies something that is most absolutely from itself; hence both theologians and philologists teach that this name is essential and proper to God and not communicable to any other. On these matters the most easy expounder of them may be consulted, our honoured teacher and colleague, Cl. Johannes Leusden, in his Philolog. Hebr. Although all the things that belong to God, including his Spirituality, that is, his rational life, which denotes an essence removed from all matter and active in understanding and willing, can easily be deduced from Independence, and although the concept of this alone seems sufficient to represent the divine essence in due measure, nevertheless, since this rationality or spirituality of God becomes known to us almost step by step with Independence from the contemplation of creatures, as we saw above, and since we are accustomed in conceiving the nature of other things to note distinctly two essential predicates, of which the first is more common and the second more proper and specific to the thing, we readily admit, so as not to depart too far from the common manner of conceiving, that our concept of the divine nature can be comprehended, in an analogical way (for every ground of imperfection must be excluded), by two notions: one of which presents his Spirituality (in which rational creatures also share in their own way), and the other, joined with it and yet not distinct from it, presents Independence. So a brief description of the supreme Deity, adapted to our understanding, may be: God is an Independent Spirit. The other definitions that are in circulation differ from this only in words, agreeing with it in substance, as when God is called, for example, a spiritual essence living of itself, or the Being of beings, etc.; or they are less accurate, in that they take as the first predicate not the essence of God but some attribute that comes later in our way of conceiving it, as are those that describe God as a Being existing necessarily, or a Being infinitely perfect, etc. But we reserve the examination of these for the places where we are dealing with the necessity of existence, the infinity of perfections, and so on. Above all, I ought not to pass over in silence here the preposterous philosophising of the modern writers who circumscribe the whole divine essence with the cold idea of mere Thought; unless I had exposed its absurdity at length in a separate Exercitation on what thought is, namely the human mind. Therefore I now set that aside as well.

units.la: Caeterum, ex dictis de Independentia, quae eadem sit cum Essentia Divina, liquet, ni fallor, quid respondendum sit ad quaestionem, An ex natura cognoscatur verus Deus? Rationem dubitandi fecit quibusdam, cum S. Trinitatis per naturalis rationis lumen nescientia, tum profunda Gentilium idololatria; quarum illa veri Dei ignorantiam, haec ejusdem quoque abnegationem inferre videtur. Nemo tamen, qui ἀχειρώς ratiocinari ac loqui hic cupit, id simpliciter negaverit, nisi qui pariter neget, Ens Independens, aut verum Deum esse, aut ex rationis lumine innotescere: quorum utrumlibet esse certissimum, jam demonstravimus. An verò quod de Deo cognosci potest, quodque Deus ipse Gentibus manifestum fecit, aeterna videlicet Divinitas & potentia, non solius veri Dei characteres sunt, sed ficti quoque idoli elogia? Quasi Jus Dei, ac opus Legis Gentium cordibus insculptum, Deum aliquem non-verum, per cujus notitiam reddita sint inexcusabiles, conscientiis earundem manifestaverit! Verbo, cum non-verus Deus re verâ sit nullus Deus, utique vel verus Deus ex natura cognosci potest, vel nullus planè cognoscitur. Id qui admittere non vult, hoc concedere cogitur: quo ipso omnis naturalis Dei notitia unâ litura expungitur. Fateor, Gentiles ex obsenebrati cordis caecitate turpissimè errasse, dum illum veri Dei conceptum, quem opus conscientiae aequè ac creationis abundè suppeditabat, mirâ fatuitate tate applicuerunt istis rebus quæ naturâ Deus non erant, sicque inciderunt in crassissimam idololatriam; at indè non rectius conficitur, eos verum Deum non cognovisse, quam inserre licet, aurifabrum v. c. quempiam non cognoscere naturam veri auri, quia fortè in dubia luce per aliquam visus fallaciam oblatum aurichalcum verum aurum putat. Imò verò in hoc præcipuè sunt gentes inexcusabiles, quòd, cum verum Deum cognoverint, non tamen ut talem glorificaverint, sed ejus gloriam in fœdum idolum transformaverint. Etiam SS. Trinitatem ignorasse, largior; at non ideo ignorarunt verum illum Deum, qui re ipsâ Triunus est, etsi hos in ipso subsistendi modos, atque indè pendentem totam salutis œconomiam, per ignorantiam puræ negationis nescīverint. Aliud enim est, notitiam, quam quis de Deo habet, imperfectam esse, nec salutarem; aliud, objectum imperfectæ talis cognitionis non esse verum Deum. Quapropter, si accurato loquendi modo sit inhærendum, nequaquam potest categoricè negari, verum Deum ex natura cognosci posse, nisi quis periculosa phrasi in extremum discrimen adducere velit universam Theologiam Naturalem; quippe quæ, nisi pro objecto habeat verum Deum, in merum phantasma chimærici alicujus idoli re verâ convertitur. Hoc cum nolint quotquot contra Socinianos istam tuentur rectè sentientes, crediderim facilè, hanc, quatenus inter illos agitatur, de nomine præcipuè esse controversiam: quamobrem nec latius eam prosequor.
units.tr: Moreover, from what has been said about Independence, which is the same as the divine essence, it is clear, unless I am mistaken, what must be answered to the question: Can the true God be known from nature? Some have been led to doubt this both by the ignorance of the Holy Trinity through the light of natural reason and by the deep idolatry of the Gentiles; the former seems to imply ignorance of the true God, the latter his very denial. Yet no one who wishes to reason and speak here [accurately, ἀκριβῶς] would simply deny it, unless he also denied that the Independent Being is the true God or is made known by the light of reason; and we have already demonstrated that each of these is most certain. But is that which can be known of God, and which God himself has made manifest to the Gentiles, namely his eternal divinity and power, only the marks of the true God, or also the praises of a false idol? As if the righteous requirement of God and the work of the law written in the hearts of the Gentiles had revealed to their consciences some not-true god, through whose knowledge they were made without excuse! In short, since a not-true god is in truth no god, either the true God can be known from nature, or no god at all is known. Whoever is unwilling to admit this is forced to concede it, and by that very concession all natural knowledge of God is wiped out with a single stroke. I grant that the Gentiles, through the blindness of their darkened heart, erred most shamefully, when with wondrous folly they applied that concept of the true God, which the work of conscience as well as of creation abundantly supplied, to things that were by nature not God, and so fell into the grossest idolatry. But it does not follow from this more correctly that they did not know the true God, than one could infer that a goldsmith, for example, does not know the nature of true gold because in a dim light, through some fault of sight, he takes brass offered to him for true gold. Indeed, the Gentiles are inexcusable chiefly in this, that although they knew the true God, they did not glorify him as God, but changed his glory into a vile idol. I grant too that they were ignorant of the Holy Trinity; but they were not thereby ignorant of the true God, who in truth is Triune, even though through ignorance of pure negation they did not know the modes of subsistence in him, on which the whole economy of salvation depends. For it is one thing that the knowledge a person has of God is imperfect and not saving; it is another that the object of such imperfect knowledge is not the true God. Therefore, if we must keep to a strict manner of speaking, it cannot be categorically denied that the true God can be known from nature, unless someone, by a dangerous phrase, wishes to bring the whole of Natural Theology into the greatest peril; for unless it has the true God as its object, it is turned into the mere phantom of some chimerical idol. Since all who rightly think and defend this against the Socinians are unwilling to do this, I should readily believe that this controversy, as it is carried on among them, is chiefly about a name; therefore I do not pursue it further.

units.la: Porrò, hæc Dei, cujus essentia sit ipsa Independentia, notio, plurimas suppeditat ac pulcherrimas observationes, quarum amplissimus in Theologia universa, tam Naturali quam Revelata, usus conceptûs hujus elegantiam mirè commendat. Per omnes ac singulas ire curta pagina non permittit. Conabor hoc uno, quo absolvam, totum comprehendere: Nihil quicquam tribuendum Deo, quod non sit omni ratione Independens; quodque absolutè Independens est, Illi soli id adscribendum. Novâ demonstratione non indiget hæc veritas. Quandoquidem enim attributa quævis & operationes sequuntur conditionem rei à qua fluunt, utique etiam res ista, cujus solius tota natura est ipsa Independentia, sibi soli vindicat prædicata quæcunque Independentiam involventia, & alia quævis aliquid dependentiæ connotantia, tantia, tanquam è diametro sibi adversa, prorsus respuit. Ex hoc uno canone neglecto, uti nati sunt omnes de Dei natura & perfectionibus errores, omnisque adeo idololatria ac haeresis; ita contrà hic idem unus accuratè observatus securam reddit omnem nostram de Deo ac Creatura cogitationem. Tribue Deo intrepidè quicquid visum est, dummodo salvas independentiam, ex vero tribuis: De creatura in ordine ad Deum ut lubet philosophare, tantum si per omnia agnoscas dependentem, rectè philosophaberis. Ex adverso: Detrahe Deo quicquam quod spirat Independentiam; aut tribue creaturae vel minimam Independentiae speciem, mox blasphemus es simul ac sacrilegus. Atque haec prima ac praecipua illa Reformatae nostrae Religionis laus est & gloria, quòd una prae caeteris tota sit in eo, ut per omnia Deo sua constet Independentia, sua creaturis dependentia. Ut, si quid erret, in hoc solo erret, quod Deum nimium Deum, Creaturam nimium Creaturam agnoscat. Hic verò cum errari neutiquam possit, nequit etiam ullo pacto fieri, ut haec de Deo doctrina exstat falsa. Ita Reformatae nostrae fidei, atque uni nostrae, plaudit ac testimonium efficacissimum dicit ipsa recta ratio; dum circa Deum ac res divinas modis indignissimis sine ratione, ac contra rationem, delirat universa secus sentientium cohors; quorum omnis error fundamentalis, ac perpetuum πεσιτον ... exstitit, Deum solum non agnoscere omnimodè Independentem. Cujus contrarium quoniam religiosè observant orthodoxi, illis per solam supremi Numinis Independentiam stat victrix Dei Gratia, cadit inimicus illi corruptae naturae typhus.
units.tr: Furthermore, this notion of God, whose essence is Independence itself, supplies very many and beautiful observations, and the wide use of this concept, in all Theology both natural and revealed, greatly commends its elegance. A short page does not allow me to go through each and every one. I will try to comprehend the whole in this one principle, with which I will conclude: Nothing is to be attributed to God that is not Independent in every respect; and what is absolutely Independent is to be ascribed to him alone. This truth needs no new demonstration. For since every attribute and every operation follows the condition of the thing from which it flows, that thing alone, whose whole nature is Independence itself, claims for itself whatever predicates involve Independence, and utterly rejects, as diametrically opposed to itself, any others that connote some dependence. When this one canon is neglected, from it all errors about the nature and perfections of God arise, and so all idolatry and heresy; conversely, when this same one canon is carefully observed, it makes all our thinking about God and the creature secure. Attribute to God boldly whatever seems fit, provided you preserve his independence, and you attribute it rightly. Concerning the creature in relation to God, you may philosophise as you please, provided you acknowledge it in every respect as dependent; then you will philosophise rightly. On the other side: take from God anything that breathes Independence, or grant the creature the least species of Independence, and at once you are blasphemous and sacrilegious. And this is that first and principal praise and glory of our Reformed Religion, that above all others it is wholly directed to this: that in every respect God's Independence stands firm and the creature's dependence stands firm. So, if it errs at all, it errs only in this, that it acknowledges God as too much God and the creature as too much creature. But since here it can by no means err, it also cannot in any way come about that this doctrine of God is false. Thus the very right reason applauds our Reformed faith and, as it were, gives it the most effective testimony; while the whole band of those who think otherwise rages about God and divine things in the most unworthy ways, without reason and against reason. Their every fundamental error, and their perpetual [πρῶτον ψεῦδος], has been this: not to acknowledge God as absolutely Independent. Since the orthodox observe the contrary religiously, for them the grace of God stands victorious through the Independence of the supreme Deity alone, and the enemy's pride of corrupt nature falls.
VIII.

units.la: Etsi verò soli Deo Independentiae omnimodae gloriam sic adscrucrimus, nihil tamen commune nostram philosophationem habere volumus cum conceptibus eorum, qui, longè alio modo instituentes, in rerum natura neque dari neque dari posse contendunt plures substantias quam unam, quae necessario exstat, & essentiam habeat infinitè perfectam atque inexhaustam, quaeque constet infinitis attributis, quorum quodlibet infinitam essentiam infinitè exprimat. Ut per Mundum intellectum velint modum qui Dei attributum aliquod certo ac determinato modo exprimit: per partes autem mundi, quas ipsi vocant res particulares, res, nihil aliud nisi Dei attributorum affectiones sive modos, quibus Dei attributa certo atque determinatò exprimuntur: adeo ut quælibet res particularis sit modificatio Dei, utque, quatenus una res particularis ab alia re particulari differt, ita Deus aliter atque aliter modificetur. Quæ profecto verba, in quamcunque flectantur formam, si quem habent sensum, alium nullum dare possunt, quam, unam duntaxat esse substantiam, quæ sit solus Deus; multiplices interim esse unius illius substantiæ modos, qui sint res quælibet particulares in hoc universo nobis obviæ, v.c. cogitantes, extensæ, &c. quæ omnes in una illa substantia subsistentes cum ea faciant complexum quoddam, puta substantiam unam modis variis modificatam. Ut ex hac hypothesi ea- dem res, si consideretur ratione substantiæ, omnes modos sustinentis, Deus dicatur, quæ eadem, spectata ratione modorum particularium, omnium simul ad absolvendum hoc Universum concurrentium , Natura vulgò appellari consuevit. Id est, ut verbo dicam, Mundi nullam esse substantiam præterquam quæ Dei ipsius est: ut Mundus & Deus non nisi considerandi modo differre videantur. Hùc planè aurigantur, quæ de partis unius universi ab alia dependentia tradunt, nullà factà mentione Dei. Nempe statuunt „quamlibet rem particularem quæ finita est & „determinatam habet existentiam, non posse existere nec ad o„perandum determinari, nisi ad existendum & operandum de-„terminetur ab alia re quæ etiam finita est & determinatam ha„bet existentiam, & hæc rursus ab alia, quæ etiam finita est& „determinatam habet existentiam ; & sic in infinitum. Num quid clarius pro Naturæ apotheosi dici potest?
units.tr: Although I have ascribed the glory of absolute independence to God alone, I nevertheless want our philosophising to have nothing in common with the notions of those who, proceeding in quite a different way, maintain that in the nature of things there are not, and cannot be, more substances than one. That one substance necessarily exists, has an infinitely perfect and inexhaustible essence, and consists of infinite attributes, each of which expresses the infinite essence infinitely. They wish the world to be understood as "the mode which expresses some attribute of God in a certain and determinate way," and the parts of the world, which they call "particular things," as "nothing but affections or modes of God's attributes, by which God's attributes are expressed in a certain and determinate way." So every particular thing is a "modification of God," and insofar as one particular thing differs from another, God is modified differently. However these words are bent into whatever form, if they have any meaning, they can give no other sense than this: there is one substance only, which is God alone, and there are manifold modes of that one substance, which are whatever particular things we meet in this universe, for example thinking things, extended things, and so on. All of these, subsisting in that one substance, make with it a certain complex, namely one substance modified in various ways. So on this hypothesis, the same thing, considered under the aspect of the substance sustaining all the modes, is called God, and the same thing, considered under the aspect of the particular modes all concurring together to complete this universe, is commonly called Nature. In a word, the world has no substance except that which belongs to God himself, so that the world and God seem to differ only in the mode of consideration. These men clearly drive at this in what they teach about the dependence of one part of the universe on another, with no mention of God. Namely, they lay down that "any particular thing which is finite and has a determinate existence cannot exist, nor be determined to operate, unless it is determined to exist and operate by another thing which is also finite and has a determinate existence, and this again by another, which is also finite and has a determinate existence; and so on to infinity." What clearer thing can be said for the deification of Nature?

units.la: Re ipsâ itaque universa hæc philofophatio aliud nihil est, quam recoctus quidam Atheismus Plinii aliorumque, præter hunc noftrum mundum nullum Numen agnoscentium, hoc est, re vera planè nullum. Tam enim nemo rationis compos sibi persuadedere potest Deum esse quodcunque videmus, ut nulla in hoc universo res oculis obvia existat, quæ non, undecunque eam intueamur, omnibus atque singulis prædicatis suis reclamet, testaturque suâ dependentiâ, finitudine, mutabilitate, contingentiâ, insufficientiâ, &c. nihil sibi divinum inesse. Vide Exercitat. III.§.I. Quumque jam centies confutata fit ista impietas, miror, Philosophiam, totam his fundamentis superstructam, cà subtilitatis specie se hodiè posse commendare tanquam unicè masculam: miror, desiderari toties viris etiam minimè indoctis & malis, ut prodeat tandem aliquis, qui accuratam det stupidi commenti refutationem; cum detexisse tantum rem hic verè sit refutasse. Quod ipsum neque ignoravit sectæ princeps, quando tam ambiguis, obscuris, tortis phrasibus mentem involvit, ut religiosissimi quoque horum arcanorum interpretes fateantur, obscurè & durè se virum illum explicuisse, per verba durissima, & primo aspectu incomprehensibilia. Nimirum aliam evasionis rimam non inveniunt, ad declinandam hanc Atheismi notam; quâ notâ omnem ei perituraм gratiam norunt. Interim ipsi cavent quoque sedulò, ne, missis verbis durissimis & incomprehensibilibus, ideoque merito hactenus rejectis, per phrases claras ac distinctas mentem suam hic faciant planam; quod facere decebat omninò tantorum mysteriorum Sacerdotes, ut desinant tandem (quod conqueruntur passim) à paucissimis intelligi tam profundæ sapientiæ cogitationes. Has interim cui debeamus primo auctori vel inventori, forsan percipietur inspicienti Cartesii Princ. Part. I. Art. LI. ubi sic ille: „Per substantiam nihil aliud intelligere possumus, quam rem quæ ita „existit, ut nullâ aliâ re indigeat ad existendum. Et quidem „substantia quæ nullâ planè re indigeat, unica tantum potest „intelligi, nempe Deus. Alias verò omnes non nisi ope concursus Dei existere posse percipimus. Atque ideo nomen substantiæ non convenit Deo & illis univocè, ut dici solet in „scholis; hoc est, nulla ejus nominis significatio potest distinguè intelligi, quæ Deo & creaturis sit communis. Conferre hæc cum istis prioribus possunt queis vacat. Nos ad ea revertimur quæ ad institutam nostræ Meditationis seriem pertinent.
units.tr: In fact, therefore, this whole philosophy is nothing other than a rehashed atheism of Pliny and others, acknowledging no deity beyond this our world, that is, really no deity at all. For no one in possession of reason can persuade himself that God is whatever we see; no thing existing before our eyes in this universe fails, from whatever side we look at it, to cry out against all and each of its predicates, and to attest by its dependence, finitude, mutability, contingency, insufficiency, and so on, that nothing divine is in it. See Exercitation III, §1. Since this impiety has now been refuted a hundred times, I wonder that a philosophy built entirely on these foundations can still commend itself, under the appearance of subtlety, as uniquely manly. I wonder that, although it has so often been asked for by men who are not at all learned and are even ill-disposed, no one has yet come forward to give an accurate refutation of this foolish invention; for to have uncovered it here is truly to have refuted it. The leader of the sect himself did not fail to know this, since he wrapped his thought in such ambiguous, obscure, twisted phrases that even the most devout interpreters of these mysteries confess that "that man explained himself obscurely and harshly, through very harsh words, incomprehensible at first sight." Surely they find no other crack of escape to avoid this mark of atheism, the mark from which they know all grace is lost to him. Meanwhile they also take care not to make their thought plain through clear and distinct phrases, dropping the harsh and incomprehensible words which have therefore rightly been rejected so far. Yet the priests of such great mysteries ought entirely to do this, so that at last they might cease (as they complain everywhere) to have such thoughts of profound wisdom understood by very few. Meanwhile, to whom we owe these thoughts, that is, to their first author or inventor, will perhaps be perceived by one who looks at Descartes, Principles, Part I, Art. LI, where he says thus: "By substance we can understand nothing other than a thing which so exists that it needs no other thing in order to exist. And indeed, substance which needs no thing at all can be understood as one only, namely God. But all others we perceive can exist only with the aid of God's concurrence. And therefore the name substance does not apply to God and to those others univocally, as is commonly said in the schools; that is, no signification of that name can be distinctly understood which is common to God and to creatures." Those who have leisure may compare these words with the earlier ones. We return to what pertains to the course of our Meditation as set out.

units.la: EXERCITATIO QUINTA DE DEI ATTRIBUTIS, in communi.
units.tr: FIFTH EXERCITATION ON THE ATTRIBUTES OF GOD, in general.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Pluribus & inadæquatis conceptibus Divinæ perfectiones nobis apprehendendæ. II. Absurdè statuuntur duo tantum Attributa Dei Interna, Intellectus & Voluntas. III. Attributorum Divinorum cum Accidentibus creaturarum collatio. IV. Objectionibus eorum, qui Accidentia esse contendunt, occurritur. V. Qualis inter essentiam & Attributa Dei intercedat distinctio, pressius exponitur. VI. Attributa Dei alia Independentiam, alia Spiritualitatem ejusdem, sequuntur.
units.tr: I. Divine perfections must be grasped by us through many concepts, and each of them is inadequate. II. The view that God has only two internal attributes, Intellect and Will, is absurdly maintained. III. The divine attributes are compared with the accidents of creatures. IV. Objections from those who contend that the attributes are accidents are met. V. The distinction between the essence of God and his attributes is set out more precisely. VI. Some attributes follow from God's Independence, others from his Spirituality.

units.la: Rudentis Philosophi est, quoties cognoscenda occurrit res perfectionibus suis captum nimium excedens, eam, ne planè non intelligat, intelligere ut potest; atque adeo notiones de ea formare, si non re ipsâ dignas, menti saltem suæ approportionatas. Sicubi, certè hîc, ubi de Deo sermo est, id locum habet: is enim tanto perfectionum splendore mentis finitæ aciem perstringit, ut pulchrè dixerit ille, habere se intellectum nostrum ad contemplationem primi Entis, ut se habet oculus noctuæ ad intuitum Solis. Quapropter, quicunque non cupit, quanto diutius considerat, tanto sibi Deum videri obscuriorem (quæ desperantis in
units.tr: It is the mark of a sound philosopher, whenever a thing to be known presents itself that far exceeds the measure of his capacity, to understand it as far as he can, so that he does not fail to understand it altogether, and to form notions of it that, if not worthy of the thing itself, are at least proportioned to his own mind. If this holds anywhere, it certainly holds here, where the subject is God. For he so dazzles the edge of the finite mind with the splendour of his perfections that someone aptly said our intellect is to the contemplation of the first Being as the eye of an owl is to the sight of the sun. Therefore, whoever does not wish God to appear more obscure to him the longer he considers him (a cry, as Cicero reports, of Simonides in despair)

units.la: F in hoc negotio Simonidis vox est, apud Ciceronem) suæ imperfectioni ante omnia hic est consulendum; ut, quod uno mentis actu adæquatè comprehendere nequit, uti in se est, id pluribus conceptibus inadæquatè apprehendat saltem, uti ipse potest. Indè factum, ut, quamvis nihil existat in Deo quod non sit ipsissimum ejus Esse, nos tamen pro modulo Eum cogitaturi necesse habeamus, & plura in eo concipere prædicata, & illorum alia supponere quasi essentialia constitutiva, ut loquuntur, alia ex illis deducere, quasi sint essentialia consecutiva. Atque ista quidem esse diximus Spiritualitatem Independentem, vel si mavis, Independentiam Spiritualem. Verùm, quantæ sit sufficientiæ & amplitudinis iste conceptus, tum demum intelligemus rectius, quando suo ordine ex fonte illo scaturientes Perfectiones lustraverimus; quippe quæ instar radiorum totidem manifestius nobis manifestabunt, Quale sit hoc Ens exsuperantissimum. Solent istæc omnia vulgò venire generali nomine Attributorum Divinorum: per quæ intelligimus, quaslibet perfectiones, quæ conceptum Essentiæ Divinæ, ceu Spiritûs Independentis, necessariò sequuntur, quatenus de essentia illa, per ipsam essentiam, quasi à priori possunt demonstrari.
units.tr: in this matter must above all take thought for his own imperfection. What he cannot grasp adequately in a single act of the mind, as it is in itself, he should at least grasp inadequately, through many concepts, as best he can. Hence it happens that, although nothing exists in God that is not his very Being, we, thinking of him according to our measure, must necessarily conceive in him many predicates. Some of these we suppose to be essential constituents, as they say, and others we deduce from these as essential consequences. These we have said are Independent Spirituality, or, if you prefer, Spiritual Independence. But we shall understand more rightly how great the sufficiency and range of this concept is only when we have surveyed, in their order, the perfections springing from that source. For like rays they will show us more clearly what this most supreme Being is like. All these are commonly called by the general name of Divine Attributes, by which we mean whatever perfections necessarily follow from the concept of the Divine essence as Independent Spirit, insofar as they can be demonstrated from that essence, as it were a priori, through the essence itself.

units.la: II. Dicebam, Attributa esse Perfectiones; quatenus non tantum imperfectionem aliquam à Deo removent, sed & in ipso notant prædicata positiva ac realia; etsi sæpè, ex conceptuum nostrorum & vocabulorum penuria, negativâ notione repræsententur, negativâ voce exprimantur. Ut minimè rei hic satisfaciat tenuis illa philosophatio quorundam, qui contendunt duo duntaxat, proprie loquendo, esse Attributa Dei interna, Intellectum & Voluntatem; reliqua tantum denominationes externas esse, aut relationes, aut negationes, ad essentiam Dei internam proprie non spectantes, sed illi tantum tributas in ordine ad homines, aut alias quasdam res externas. Id quidem minimè negandum est, fateor, in concipiendis pro modulo Attributis Divinis mentem nostram frequenter de Deo cogitare cum relatione ad res quæ sunt extra ejus essentiam, uti id experimur, quoties nobis repræsentamus Æternitatem, Immensitatem, &c.: verum, quamvis hinc conficiatur, istiusmodi respectus ad res extra Deum juvare intellectum tellectum nostrum in formandis notionibus Divinarum perse-ctionum, nullâ tamen legitimæ sequelæ specie hinc inferre licet, Attributa ista secundum suum formale in ipsa natura Divina purâ relatione aut negatione absolvi. Quasi quæ Deo simpliciter tanquam Spiritui conveniunt prædicata, magis illi sint interna, & plus dicant realitatis, quam quæ eidem quà Independenti competunt! Cum tamen natura Spiritualis Deo & creaturis rationalibus analogico modo sit communis; Independentia verò imprimis propria illi existat atque essentialis, uti demonstravimus. Ex quibus sicuti conficitur, Deum maximè ratione suæ Independentiæ à creaturis distare, ita ex mente eo-rum qui sic philosophantur pariter sequi necesse est, Eundem à creaturis potissimùm differre quibusdam relationibus, aut negationibus, aut denominationibus; id est, aliquibus non-entibus. An verò credendum, non existentibus creaturis, atque adeò cessantibus ejuscemodi relationibus, denominationibus, negationibus, plerisque suis attributis exui naturam Divinam? Quin, cum Independentia prædicatum sit à parte sui non minus positivum, quam ipsa Spiritualitas, idque ipsum ante alios im-primis velint hi auctores, nescio quam ob causam illa Deo ma-gis interna sint Attributa ac positiva, quæ Spiritualitatem comi-tantur, quam quæ fluunt ex Independentia. Scio, illos contendere, omnia quæ sunt in Deo esse meram cogitationem; cui per se nihil volunt esse intrinsecum, præter intellectum & vo-luntatem: verum de hypothecseòs hujus falsitate alibi nobis actum est. Cæterùm instantias hic adderem desumptas ab existendi Necessitate, Simplicitate, Immutabilitate, Æternitate, Immensitate, similibusque Perfectionibus, quas nec merum Intellectum esse aut Voluntatem, nec tamen meras negationes, aut denominationes, aut relationes, docerem, nisi id intelligendum foret rectius ex singularum explicatione, quæ infrà tradenda erit suis locis. Conferatur interim Exercitatio nostra de Cogitatione quæ sit ipsa mens humana; ubi & alia in hanc rem adduximus, assertionem istam confodientia.
units.tr: II. I said that the attributes are perfections, insofar as they not only remove some imperfection from God but also signify in him positive and real predicates, although often, because of the poverty of our concepts and words, they are represented by a negative notion and expressed in a negative word. So that thin philosophy of certain people will not satisfy the matter, those who contend that, strictly speaking, there are only two internal attributes of God, Intellect and Will. The rest, they say, are merely external denominations, or relations, or negations, not properly concerning the internal essence of God, but attributed to him only in relation to men or certain other external things. This, I grant, must certainly not be denied: in conceiving the Divine attributes according to our measure, our mind often thinks of God in relation to things outside his essence, as we experience whenever we represent to ourselves Eternity, Immensity, and so on. But although it follows that such respects to things outside God help our intellect in forming notions of the Divine perfections, no legitimate inference allows us to conclude from this that these attributes, according to their formal character, are wholly resolved into a pure relation or negation within the Divine nature itself. As if predicates that belong to God simply as Spirit were more internal to him and said more of reality than those that belong to him as Independent! Yet the spiritual nature is common to God and rational creatures in an analogical way, whereas Independence is especially and essentially proper to him, as we have demonstrated. From this it follows that God differs from creatures most of all in respect of his Independence. And from the mind of those who philosophise in this way it must equally follow that he differs from creatures chiefly by certain relations, negations or denominations, that is, by some non-entities. But is it to be believed that, if creatures did not exist, and such relations, denominations and negations ceased, the Divine nature would be stripped of most of its attributes? Indeed, since Independence is a predicate on its own side no less positive than Spirituality itself, and these authors especially insist on this very point, I do not know for what reason those attributes that accompany Spirituality should be more internal and positive to God than those that flow from Independence. I know they contend that everything in God is mere thought, and that nothing is intrinsic to him in itself except intellect and will. But we have already dealt elsewhere with the falsity of this hypothesis. Otherwise I would add here instances drawn from necessity of existence, simplicity, immutability, eternity, immensity and similar perfections, which I would show are neither merely intellect nor will, nor yet mere negations, denominations or relations. But this will be better understood from the explanation of each, which will be given below in its place. Meanwhile let our Exercitation on the thought that is the human mind itself be consulted, where we have also brought forward other arguments striking at this assertion.

units.la: Quandò dicimus, Perfectiones hasce sequi conceptum essentiæ Divinæ, cave sis, ne idcirco vera Accidentia esse cogites, aut dispositiones quasdam ab essentia verè distinctas, eandemque accessu sui modificantes ; uti id obtinet in creaturis, quæ reci- piendo adjuncta quædam in se, eo ipso majorem quasi perfectionis gradum consequuntur, dum acquirunt quod naturâ suâ in se ipsis non poterant. Omnem istiusmodi pluralitatem, atque indè fluentem compositionem, respuit tum Independentia Dei, jam demonstrata, tum perfectionum in ipso Infinitas proximè demonstranda: de quibus quoniam agendum erit pluribus, ubi erit dicendum de Simplicitate Dei, nihil attinet ista hic loci antevertere. Interim hanc ipsam ob causam cautelæ ergò dicebam, Perfectiones hasce sequi, non ipsam Dei essentiam, sed potius essentiæ Divinæ conceptum: ut omnis tum pluralitas, tum prioritas ac posterioritas hic intelligenda duntaxat sit, uti loquuntur, in signo rationis, ac pro modo concipiendi nostro; quatenus mens nostra ex pluribus prædicatis, quæ sese in Deo pro nostro captu offerunt, notionem unius alicujus præmittit, ex qua cætera à priori quasi demonstret: ad instar scilicet accidentium, quæ de creaturis, à quibus realiter distinguuntur, ex suis veris causis demonstrantur. Scitè hunc in sensum alibi priscæ Ecclesiæ Doctor: „Sapienter dicitur, nihil accidere substantiæ Dei, quoniam in se ipsa persecta est: sed tamen cogimur nonnunquam quasi accidentia, „etiamsi non omninò accidant Deo, hæc dicere, & mente „accidentium modo concipere.
units.tr: When we say that these perfections follow from the concept of the Divine essence, take care not to think that they are therefore true accidents, or certain dispositions really distinct from the essence and modifying it by their addition. This is the case with creatures, which, by receiving certain adjuncts into themselves, thereby attain, as it were, a greater degree of perfection, since they acquire what they could not have by their own nature. All such plurality, and the composition flowing from it, is rejected both by the Independence of God, already demonstrated, and by the Infinity of the perfections in him, which is to be demonstrated shortly. Since these matters will need to be treated at length when we speak of the Simplicity of God, it is pointless to anticipate them here. Meanwhile I said, for this very reason and by way of caution, that these perfections follow not the Divine essence itself but rather the concept of the Divine essence. Thus all plurality, and all priority and posteriority, is to be understood here only, as they say, in the sign of reason and according to our manner of conceiving. Insofar as our mind, from the many predicates that present themselves in God according to our capacity, puts first the notion of one of them, from which it demonstrates the rest as it were a priori, it does so in the manner of accidents, which are demonstrated of creatures, from which they are really distinct, from their true causes. In this sense a teacher of the early Church rightly said elsewhere: "It is wisely said that nothing accidents the substance of God, since it is perfect in itself; yet we are sometimes compelled to say these things as if they were accidents, even though they do not strictly accrue to God, and to conceive them in the manner of accidents."

units.la: Neque objici potest, omnia rei alicujus Attributa esse debere ejusdem accidentia ab essentia distincta; in quantum nihil de se ipso potest demonstrari. Quamvis enim idem, cogitatum quatenus prorsus idem, de se ipso demonstrctur; nihil tamen obstat, cur non idem de eodem queat demonstrari, si tantum sufficienti fundamento idem bis diversimodè concipiatur. Multæ profectò Disciplinæ institiuunt demonstrationes affectionum à subjecto re ipsa non distinctarum. Pneumatica de Anima hominis demonstrat Intellectum ac Voluntatem; cum tamen nec hæc facultas ab illa, nec alterutra à suo subjecto, realiter differre videatur. Quis afferat, Impenetrabilitatem, Divisibilitatem, Figurabilitatem, Mensurabilitatem, &c. à materia distincta accidentia esse; demonstrat tamen hæc de eadem Physica. Ipsa Mathesis, speciatim Geometria, quæ methodum thodum demonstrativam peculiari quodam quasi jure suam fecit, demonstrat v. c. de triangulo rectangulo, potentiam rectum angulum subtendentis caeterorum duorum laterum potentiae esse aequalem; item, cujusvis trianguli rectilinei duo latera tertio esse majora; tres angulos internos aequivalere duobus rectis; &c. At quis, nisi ineptus nimium, ista trianguli praedicata totidem ejus accidentia, re vera ab essentia distincta, dixerit? Urgent quidam regulam Philosophi: Quod in uno est accidens, id non est substantia in alio. Quasi inde sequatur, ex. gr. Sapientiam, Justitiam, Misericordiam, aut in Deo non esse ipsam ejus substantiam; aut eadem illa in nobis non esse accidentia: quorum posterius esse salsissimum, est manifestum. Verum nulla haec difficultas est, si cogitaverimus, effatum hoc verissimum esse de illis praedicatis, quae in pluribus rebus sese habent eodem prorsus modo. Ergo, si Sapientia Dei & nostra in idem genus univocum, ut vocant, convenirent, stringeret, fateor, argumentatio: at nunc, cum non nisi ad similitudinem qualemcunque & modum valde analogicum eadem Sapientia Deo tribuatur atque creaturis (ut deinceps videbimus) nihil utique obstat, cur non quae Deo inest Sapientia sit ipsa ejus essentia, quippe quae sine illa non esset talis; nostra vero sit accidens, utpote quae nobis inest plane contingenter.
units.tr: Nor can it be objected that all the attributes of a thing must be accidents of it distinct from its essence, on the ground that nothing can be demonstrated of itself. For although the same thing, insofar as it is wholly the same, is not demonstrated of itself, nothing prevents the same thing from being demonstrated of the same, provided it is conceived in two different ways on a sufficient foundation. Indeed, many disciplines rest on demonstrations of affections from a subject not really distinct from them. Pneumatology demonstrates of the human soul intellect and will, though neither this faculty seems really to differ from the soul, nor either of them from its subject. Who would assert that impenetrability, divisibility, figurability, measurability and so on are accidents distinct from matter? Yet physics demonstrates these of the same matter. Mathematics itself, and especially geometry, which has made the demonstrative method its own by a kind of peculiar right, demonstrates, for example, of a right-angled triangle that the square on the side subtending the right angle equals the squares on the other two sides; likewise that in any rectilinear triangle two sides together are greater than the third; that the three internal angles equal two right angles; and so on. But who, unless utterly inept, would say that these predicates of the triangle are so many accidents of it, really distinct from its essence? Some press the rule of the Philosopher: "What is an accident in one thing is not a substance in another." As if it followed, for example, that wisdom, justice and mercy either are not in God his very substance, or are not accidents in us. The latter is manifestly most absurd. But there is no difficulty here if we consider that this saying is most true of those predicates which stand in the same way in many things. Therefore, if the wisdom of God and ours agreed in one univocal genus, as they say, the argument would, I grant, be binding. But now, since the same wisdom is attributed to God and to creatures only by some likeness and a very analogical mode (as we shall see later), there is certainly nothing to prevent the wisdom that is in God from being his very essence, since without it he would not be such, while ours is an accident, as it inheres in us quite contingently.

units.la: Ut autem ista percipiantur melius, videamus paucis, qua ratione, quo modo & fundamento, Attributa Dei ab ejus essentia distinguantur? Realem inter illa intercedere diversitatem, qua sint vere plura, jam negavimus. Nec tamen a sola mente nostra unice pendet discrimen, quasi ea pro mero lubitu de eadem re conceptus variet & multiplicet: sic enim Attributa haec non tam aliquid quod fluit ex ipsa Divina natura, sed meri potius conceptus (quidni ingenii nostri lusus?) essent. Ergo ab intellectu nostro quidem est quod inter essentiam Dei & Attributa ejusdem intercedit discrimen; ita tamen, ut notiones illae, quibus idem ens simplicissimum ac quam maxime indivisum pluribus dissimilibus atque inaequalis concipiendi modis pro captu nostro a nobis apprehenditur, fundamentum suum habeant in re; quod distinctionis genus vulgo in scholis vocant rationis ratiocinatae. Fundamentum vero, cujus memini, aliud nullum esse videtur, quam ipsa infinita Divinæ naturæ excellentia; quâ dum intellectûs omnis creati angustias longissimè excedit, apta tamen est, pro vario ad res varias respectu, in eodem termine varios ac multiplices concipiendi modos. Ut re verâ sit ipsa Divina in ordine ad nostras cogitationes Incomprehensibilitas (de qua latius suo loco); quâ fit, ut quod unicâ notione simul ac semel menti nostræ præsens sistere non possumus, accommodatè ad captum nostrum id nobis repræsentemus iteratis mentis actibus, ac notionibus plurimùm differentibus. Qui concipiendi modus in nobis, uti nullam ponit in Deo imperfectionem, verùm potius supremam quandam ac verè Deo dignam perfectionis eminentiam; ita quoque idem, licet arguat mentis nostræ ad tantam rem cogitandam disproportionem, nullam infert in istiusmodi conceptibus falsitatem: & quia omnis abest notionum unio, quæ sola falsitati subest; & quia talium conceptuum, uti dixi, sufficiens datur in re fundamentum & necessitas, quibus prorsus destituitur falsitas qua talis. Tantùm id hic attendendum est, ut imperfecti istius atque analogici concipiendi modi probè nos semper nobis simus conscii, nec unquam qualescunque illas nostras de Deo cogitationes normam constituamus earum, quæ de Deo ipso sint judicanda. Ex quo uno neglecto fermè profluxit, quicquid plurimi circa Dei Attributa errant graviter; à quo periculo aberimus longissimè, si accurato semper judicio imbecilli nostræ perceptioni subveniamus.
units.tr: But so that these things may be better understood, let us see briefly by what reason, in what manner, and on what foundation the attributes of God are distinguished from his essence. We have already denied that a real diversity lies between them, by which they are truly many. Yet the distinction does not depend solely on our mind, as though the mind varied and multiplied one and the same thing by mere whim, conceiving it in different ways. For in that case these attributes would be not something flowing from the divine nature itself, but mere concepts (perhaps the play of our wit?). So the distinction between the essence of God and his attributes does arise from our understanding; but in such a way that those notions, by which the same most simple and most undivided being is apprehended by us, according to our capacity, under several dissimilar and unequal modes of conception, have their foundation in the thing itself. The schools commonly call this kind of distinction a distinction of reasoned reason (rationis ratiocinatae). The foundation I have mentioned seems to be nothing other than the infinite excellence of the divine nature itself. Although this excellence far exceeds the narrow limits of every created understanding, it is nonetheless suited, according to the various respects in which it bears on various things, to be conceived under the same term in various and manifold ways. So the divine incomprehensibility itself is, in relation to our thoughts, the reason (of which more in its proper place) why we cannot present to our mind at once, in a single notion, what we represent to ourselves, to suit our capacity, by repeated acts of the mind and by notions very different from one another. This mode of conceiving, while it posits no imperfection in God, rather points to a certain supreme eminence of perfection truly worthy of God. Likewise, although it argues a disproportion between our mind and so great a subject, it introduces no falsity into such concepts: both because the union of notions, which alone underlies falsity, is absent, and because, as I said, there is a sufficient foundation and necessity in the thing for such concepts, and falsity as such is wholly lacking from them. Only this must be attended to here: that we should always be well aware of this imperfect and analogical mode of conceiving, and never make whatever thoughts we have of God the standard for those things which are to be judged concerning God himself. From neglect of this one point almost all the grave errors of the many people who go wrong about the attributes of God have flowed; we shall keep far from this danger if we always assist our feeble perception with accurate judgment.
VI.

units.la: Denique de Attributorum Divinorum ordine ac divisione multi multùm solliciti sunt. Nobis ea tractâsse sufficiet eâ serie, quâ quælibet eorum tum ex ipsa Dei natura, tum alia ex aliis, optimè deduci queunt. Non tamen displicet, si quis universa revocaverit ad duas classes; quarum altera sub se comprehendat perfectiones illas, quæ ex Independentia Dei qua tali fluunt; altera illas, quæ ex Spiritualitate ejusdem qua tali demonstrantur. Etenim quùm jam antè ad ista duo capita ipsum Essentiæ Divinæ conceptum reduxerimus, ut Attributa (quæ essentiæ suæ conditionem sequi solent) pariter ad illa duo referantur, rectæ methodo consentaneum videtur. Quamvis autem istic conceptui Independentiæ eum qui est Spiritualitatis quasi communiorem substraverimus, hic tamen visum est præmittere tractationem Attributorum quæ sequuntur Indepen-dentiam qua talem, eis quæ comitantur Spiritualitatem. Etiamsi enim & hoc verum sit, in Attributis Independentiæ concipiendis, etiam Spiritualitatis, in iis omnibus dominantis, accuratam semper habendam esse rationem, placet nihilominus inversus ordo: tum quia Spiritualitas sub ipsius Independentiæ conceptu quodammodo comprehenditur, non vero conceptus Independentiæ sub eo qui Spiritualitatis est; tum etiam, quia, quemadmodum solius Spiritualitatis notio, non Deum qua talem, sed abstractam potius rei cujusvis spiritualis naturam offert, ita quoque attributa Spiritualitatis per se nimium in communi subsistunt, nec satis tanquam Divina agnoscuntur, nisi per Attributa quæ fluunt ex Independentia pro modo concipiendi nostro exaltentur quasi, donec Deo digne cogitentur. Et hæc eadem ratio est, ob quam hactenus Theologi & Philosophi duas statuerunt Attributorum Divinorum series, quarum altera Incommunicabilium sit, Communicabilium altera. Rectè quidem: quatenus ut ipsius Spiritualitatis, ita perfectionum inde resultantium, expressio quædam analogica relucet in rationalibus creaturis; quo nomine etiam Dei imaginem gerere in Sacris dicuntur: at vero Independentiæ cum annexis nullum in eis vestigium; in quantum sufficientiæ talis ad exis-tendum ex se citra cujuscunque causæ influxum, eorumque quæ ex illa fluunt prædicatorum, nulla creata natura quocunque modo exstitit capax. Non nescio, obstrigillare hisce quosdam, claris suis ac distinctis ideis in omni scirpo nodum quærentes, ne quid scilicet exstat in Theologia aut Philosophia, quod non sit Novæ sapientiæ lumine collucтratum; verum tales sunt quas adscrunt objectiunculæ, ut ex dictis eis satisfiat facillimè, neque necesse videatur in præsentiarum pluribus super hac re cum illis congredi.
units.tr: Finally, many people have been much concerned about the order and division of the divine attributes. It will suffice for us to treat them in that sequence in which each of them can best be deduced, both from the very nature of God and from others out of others. Nevertheless, it does not displease me if anyone reduces them all to two classes: one of which comprehends those perfections that flow from the Independence of God as such, the other those that are demonstrated from his Spirituality as such. For since we have already earlier reduced the very concept of the divine essence to these two heads, so that the attributes (which usually follow the condition of their essence) are likewise referred to those two, this seems consistent with the right method. Although here we have placed the concept of Independence, which is the more general, under the concept of Spirituality, yet it has seemed good here to put first the treatment of those attributes which follow Independence as such, before those which accompany Spirituality. For even if it is true that, in conceiving the attributes of Independence, an accurate account must always be taken also of Spirituality, which dominates all of them, nonetheless the inverted order pleases me: partly because Spirituality is in a sense comprehended under the concept of Independence, but not the concept of Independence under that of Spirituality; and partly because, just as the notion of Spirituality alone presents not God as such but rather the abstract nature of any spiritual thing whatever, so too the attributes of Spirituality subsist in themselves too much in general, and are not sufficiently acknowledged as divine unless they are raised up, as it were, through the attributes that flow from Independence, according to our mode of conceiving, until they are thought worthily of God. This is also the reason why theologians and philosophers have hitherto established two series of divine attributes: one of the Incommunicable, the other of the Communicable. And rightly so: inasmuch as an analogical expression of Spirituality, and of the perfections resulting from it, shines forth in rational creatures (for which reason they are also said in the Sacred Writings to bear the image of God); but of Independence with its adjuncts there is no trace in them, inasmuch as no created nature, in any way whatever, has been capable of such sufficiency to exist from itself without the influx of any cause, nor of the predicates that flow from it. I am not unaware that some men, seeking a knot in every rush with their clear and distinct ideas, object to these things, as though nothing exists in theology or philosophy that has not been illuminated by the light of the New Wisdom; but the little objections they bring forward are such that they are very easily satisfied by what has been said, and it does not seem necessary at present to engage with them at length on this matter.

units.la: EXERCITATIO SEXTA. DE DEO INFINITE PERFECTO.
units.tr: SIXTH EXERCISE. CONCERNING GOD AS INFINITELY PERFECT.

units.la: I. Infinitatis Perfectionis explicatio ceteris Dei Attributis cur praemittenda? II. Eam esse Attributum, Essentiam Dei consequens, ostenditur. III. Persectio generatim spectata quid, & quotuplex. IV. Triplex modus Perfectiones continendi Deo applicatus. V. Perfectiones Divinas cognosci, non ex Idea innata intuitu, sed ex creaturarum contemplatione, probatur. VI. Quo pacto huic negotio subserviat triplex via, Causalitatis, Negationis, & Eminentiae. VII. Perfectionis Infinitatem Deo, & quidem soli, convenire, demonstratur. VIII. Perfectionis Divinae rite cogitatae in studio pietatis utilitas.
units.tr: I. Why should the explanation of infinite perfection be placed before the other attributes of God? II. That it is an attribute following from the essence of God is shown. III. Perfection considered generally: what it is, and how many kinds there are. IV. The threefold mode of attributing perfections to God. V. That the divine perfections are known not from an innate idea by intuition but from the contemplation of creatures, is proved. VI. In what way the threefold way of causality, negation and eminence serves this business. VII. That infinity of perfection belongs to God, and to him alone, is demonstrated. VIII. The usefulness, in the pursuit of piety, of a rightly considered divine perfection.

units.la: Nter omnia praedicata, quae ex natura Dei deducenda intellectui nostro sese offerunt, primum locum merito sibi vindicat Infinita ejus Perfectio. Ea enim non tam est Attributum, quam potius quaedam Attributorum omnium complexio; quâ mens nostra brevi quasi compendio, conceptu interim minus distincto ac satis obscuro, apprehendere nititur quicquid de Deo cogitandum venit. Cui accedit, quòd, quamvis ingens sit sententiarum divortium in concipiendis & Deo tribuendis his aut illis Attributis, in hoc unum tamen conveniant omnes, quotquot planè Athei non existunt, Dei nomine intelligi ens infinitè perfectum; quo scilicet majus atque excellentius existit nihil : unde trita ac recepta quibusvis elogia, quibus Deus agnoscitur ac praedicatur, Optimus, Maximus. Id quidem hominum errore contingit, ut ista quandoque à quibusdam Enti summo adscribantur, quae re ipsa imperfectionem arguunt; nemo tamen Illi tribuit quicquam, quod non ipse perfectionem notare saltem putet. Adeo ut, quandò deinceps erit disputandum, num hoc vel illud praedicatum Deo conveniat, nec ne? tantum fermè sit inquirendum, utrum id dicat perfectionem? Si notare evicteris, quin in Deo locum habet, nemo ambiget.
units.tr: Among all the predicates that present themselves to our intellect as deducible from the nature of God, his infinite perfection rightly claims the first place. For it is not so much an attribute as a certain complex of all the attributes, by which our mind tries to grasp, as if in a brief summary, whatever has to be thought about God, though with a concept that is less distinct and rather obscure. To this must be added that, although there is great disagreement in conceiving of and ascribing this or that attribute to God, all who are not altogether atheists agree on this one point: that by the name of God is understood a being infinitely perfect, than which nothing greater or more excellent exists. Hence the trite and accepted epithets by which God is acknowledged and proclaimed, Best, Greatest. It is true that, through human error, some of these things are sometimes ascribed by some to the highest being, which in fact indicate imperfection; yet no one attributes to him anything that he himself does not at least think denotes perfection. So that when later it will be disputed whether this or that predicate belongs to God or not, it is almost only necessary to inquire whether it denotes perfection. If you prove that it does not, no one will doubt that it has no place in God.

units.la: Ajebam, omnimodam hanc Perfectionem esse quasi compagem omnium Attributorum, quippe quae universa uno hoc titulo comprehenduntur. Quare minus placet conceptus; quo Perfectionum Infinitas statuitur primum ac radicale ipsius essentiae Divinae praedicatum; quia scilicet ipsa quoque Independentia, seu Perfectio quaedam, sub Infinita Perfectione continetur, & sic haec illa pro modo concipiendi sit prior. Verum tamen eam Divinis Attributis rectius accenseri, facilè intelligemus, si attendamus, Perfectionis nomine, ex accurato loquendi modo, non rei illius, cujus esse dicitur perfectio, indicari essentiam ipsam, sed illa ejusdem praedicata, quae addita essentiae nihil illi deesse faciunt eorum, quorum ipsa est capax; ut omnis Perfectio supponat naturam cujus perfectio dicitur. Imprimis hic observandum venit, intellectum nostrum, quando existentiam summi Numinis demonstrat ex finita causarum subordinatarum serie, per eam primò ac directè duci ad Deum agnoscendum simpliciter tanquam causam primam, seu Ens Independens. Simul quidem innotescit, fateor, tanquam rerum quarumvis àse pendentium perfectiones continens; at non ilicò nobis hoc ipso offertur tanquam ens absolutè atque omni modo perfectum: quae notio ex Independentia demùm quasi a priori eruitur, ut ex iis quae mox sequentur manifestum fiet. At verò quodcunque ex alio priori demonstratur, id ipsam rei essentiam non constituere, evidens est. Si quis nihilominus malit voce Perfectionis intelligere omne praedicatum quod rei quomodocunque inest, sive essentiam constituat, sive sequatur (quo sensu liquet homine Infinitae Perfectionis etiam Independentiam comprehendi) cum tali, etsi minus accuratè philosophari videatur, multum litigandum non erit, quoniam nominalem controversiam hactenus facere videtur.
units.tr: I was saying that this all-embracing perfection is as it were the framework of all the attributes, since they are all comprehended under this one title. Hence the concept by which the infinity of perfections is set down as the first and radical predicate of the divine essence itself is less pleasing. For independence, or a certain perfection, is itself contained under infinite perfection, and so the latter is prior only in the mode of conceiving. Yet we will easily understand that it is more rightly reckoned among the divine attributes if we attend to the following: in the strict manner of speaking, the name of perfection indicates not the essence itself of the thing of which it is said to be the perfection, but those predicates of it which, added to the essence, make nothing lacking to it of those things of which it is capable; so that every perfection presupposes the nature whose perfection it is said to be. Here it must first be noted that our intellect, when it demonstrates the existence of the supreme Deity from the finite series of subordinate causes, is led through this primarily and directly to acknowledge God simply as first cause, or independent being. At the same time it becomes known, I grant, as containing the perfections of all things that depend on it; but it is not immediately offered to us in this way as a being absolutely and in every respect perfect. That notion is drawn out, as it were a priori, from independence, as will become clear from what follows. But it is evident that whatever is demonstrated from something prior does not constitute the essence of the thing itself. If anyone nevertheless prefers to understand by the word perfection every predicate that belongs to a thing in any way, whether it constitutes the essence or follows it (in which sense it is clear that independence too is included in infinite perfection), there will not be much quarrel with such a person, although he seems to philosophise less accurately, since so far he seems to be raising a merely verbal controversy.

units.la: Per ipsam autem Perfectionis Infinitatem tale Dei prædicatum intelligimus, cujus ratione Essentia Divina omnes omninò Perfectiones possidet, modo sibi convenientes, id est, infinito ac consummatissimo. Perfectionem in genere vocant id omne quo secluditur aliquis defectus: unde Perfectum vulgò describunt, id cui nihil deest. Aliquid verò alicui deesse dicitur vel negativè, vel privativè. Negativè deest, quod quidem secundum se perfectionem notat, cujus tamen hoc aut illud subjectum non est capax: quo sensu lapidi v. c. deest perfectio intelligendi, loquendi, &c. Privativè alicui aliquid deest, quando abest aliquod prædicatum, cujus subjectum omninò erat capax: hoc facto homini idiotæ deest perfectio eruditionis, aut muto loquela, &c. Saltem Perfectio propriè sic dicta semper notat aliquod positivum; ut hactenus non malè definiatur: Perfectio est quæ in unoquoque est melior ipsa, quam non ipsa. Videlicet, ex duobus terminis contradictoriis ille perfectionem notat, qui exprimit aliquid quod à parte rei est reale ac positivum; ille autem imperfectionem, qui reale ac positivum prædicatum removet ac tollit. Adeo ut, quantum unaquæque res habet Entitatis, tantundem quoque habeat Perfectionis; cum Perfectio parum aut nihil differat ab ipsissima rei Bonitate, quam cum ente reciprocari, rectè docent Metaphysici. Cavendum interim, ne nostris conceptibus ac vocibus examinemus, utrùm aliquid positiva perfectio sit, nec ne? Frequenter enim mentis imbecillitas ac vocabulorum penuria, istic negativis notionibus ac signis uti cogit, ubi res ipsa est quam maximè positiva. Conferri possunt quæ hanc in rem antè diximus, occasione Independentiæ, Exercit. iv. §. iii. Præterea, neque hic negligenda est non inutilis distinctio Perfectionum, quâ aliæ earum dicuntur esse simpliciter simplices, sive absolutæ; aliæ tales tantùm secundum quid, sive limitatæ. Illæ sunt, quæ, qua tales, in essentiali suo conceptu nullam supponunt, includunt, aut inferunt imperfectionem, sed ubicunque reperiuntur notant puram putam perfectionem, quales v. c. sunt, Scientia, Voluntas, Simplicitas, &c.
units.tr: By the infinity of perfection itself, however, we understand such a predicate of God that, by reason of it, the divine essence possesses absolutely all perfections that are fitting to it, that is, in an infinite and most consummate way. They call perfection, in general, whatever excludes some defect; whence they commonly describe the perfect as that to which nothing is lacking. But something is said to be lacking to something either negatively or privatively. It is lacking negatively when it indeed denotes perfection in itself, but this or that subject is not capable of it: in this sense, for example, the perfection of understanding or speaking, etc., is lacking to a stone. It is lacking privatively to something when a predicate is absent of which the subject was altogether capable: in this way the perfection of learning is lacking to an unlearned man, or speech to a mute, etc. At any rate, perfection properly so called always denotes something positive; so that it has been well defined thus far: Perfection is that which is better in each thing than the thing would be without it. That is, of two contradictory terms, the one denotes perfection which expresses something real and positive in the thing; the other denotes imperfection, which removes and takes away a real and positive predicate. So that, as much as each thing has of entity, so much also it has of perfection; since perfection differs little or not at all from the very goodness of the thing, which the metaphysicians rightly teach is convertible with being. Meanwhile we must take care not to judge by our concepts and words whether something is a positive perfection or not. For often the weakness of the mind and the poverty of words compel us to use negative notions and signs where the thing itself is most positive. What we said earlier on this matter, on the occasion of independence, Exercit. iv, §iii, may be compared. Moreover, here too the not unuseful distinction of perfections must not be neglected, by which some of them are said to be simply simple, or absolute, and others such only in a certain respect, or limited. Those are the ones which, as such, in their essential concept suppose, include or imply no imperfection, but wherever they are found they denote pure perfection, such as Knowledge, Will, Simplicity, etc.

units.la: Hæ sunt, quæ quidem prout in certo subjecto existunt, perfectionem notant ̓, in quantum illi subjecto tali prædicato gaudere conducibilius est, quam non gaudere; attamen vel adjunctum habent, vel supponunt saltem aliquid imperfectionis, in cujus remedium & levamen sint concessæ. Sic facultas discurrendi ex. gr. est Perfectio; sed in homine, quatenus is plurima ejus beneficio cognoscit, quæ absque ejus usu prorsus ignoraret. Nutritio pari modo perfectio est; sed in vivente corpore, in quantum absque ejus ope, ob continuam partium dissipationem, diu in suo esse perseverare non posset.
units.tr: Those are the others which, indeed, as they exist in a certain subject, denote perfection, in so far as it is more advantageous for that subject to possess such a predicate than not to possess it; yet they either have some imperfection attached to them, or at least presuppose it, and they are granted as a remedy and alleviation of it. Thus the faculty of reasoning, for example, is a perfection; but it is so in a man insofar as through it he knows many things that he would be wholly ignorant of without its use. Nutrition likewise is a perfection; but it is so in a living body, insofar as without its aid it could not long persevere in its being, on account of the continual dissipation of its parts.

units.la: Et ista quidem si generatim bene percepta fuerint, rei quæ præ manibus est lumen affundent haud exiguum. Nimirum, quando diximus, Essentiam Divinam omnes omninò Perfectiones possidere, universas intelligimus conceptibiles & possibiles; quascunque exfuerint, seu absolutæ, seu limitatæ. Quod tamen recte intelligendum; neque enim eodem modo has possidet, quo illas. Id innuebamus, cum addebamus, Deum illas continere modo sibi conveniente; qui qualis sit ? videndum jam est aliquanto propius.
