Tribus modis res quæpiam Perfectiones aliquas continere vulgò dicitur; quos suo more exprimunt Scholastici, cùm ajunt rem aliquid in se habere Formaliter, Eminenter, Virtualiter. Scilicet, cui aliqua Perfectio inest simpli citer secundum propriam suam definitionem, illi ea inesse dicitur Formaliter; quasi dicas inesse secundum intrinsecam suam formam sive essentiam: quo modo intellectui humano inest v. c. facultas judicandi, aut discurrendi. Quod si Perfectio quaedam, prout existit in hoc vel isto subjecto, adjunctam habeat aliquam imperfectionem, quae tamen eadem, remotâ omnis imperfectionis notâ, gradu ac modo longè eminentiori, in alia re continetur, dicitur ea ab hac re contineri Eminenter (quamvis non eodem modo omnes hæc explicent): quo sensu v. c. Intellectus Divinus intellectum humanum in se continet. Denique, quæcunque Perfectio ab alio quo produci potest, etsi fortè nec formaliter nec eminenter in eo continetur, dicitur in illo esse Virtualiter; quia scilicet virtute istius causæ actuari potest: atque ita v. c. Pictor perfectiones picturæ suæ, Architectus perfectiones domûs à se fabricatæ, in se continet. Quæ si transtransferantur ad Deum, atque ejus omnimodam Perfectionem, sic paucis statuendum est. Quæ Perfectiones simpliciter & absolutè tales sunt, neque quicquam imperfectionis habent admixtum, ea quoque quicquam simpliciter secundum definitionem suam, sive formaliter, Deo tribuendæ sunt. Sic Deus formaliter est Æternus, Simplex, Intelligens, Volens, &c. Quæcunque prædicata notant Perfectionem aliquam limitatam & secundum quid, ea, in quantum separatis imperfectionibus manent aliquid perfectionis, eminenter in Deo locum habent, quatenus, præcisâ omni imperfectione, gradu ac modo excellentissimo, ei tantum tribuuntur. Ita Deo competit v. c. Ubi, Quando, Intellectus, Voluntas, &c. rerum creatarum; quatenus ab eis removetur omnis dependentia, finitudo, successio, divisio, mutabilitas, &c. Denique, quæcunque Persectiones secundum quid ab omni adhærente imperfectione ita ut concipi possint χωρίς separari nequeunt, ex duntaxat in Deo continari dicuntur virtualiter, tanquam in causa prima, quæ eas uti sunt in creaturis extra se poterit producere. Atque hoc modo in Deo sunt v. c. Visus, Loquela, Motus, Figura, & quælibet alia rerum corporearum attributa.
units.tr: If these things are grasped generally, they will shed no small light on the matter at hand. Namely, when we said that the divine essence possesses all perfections absolutely, we mean all those that can be conceived and are possible, whether absolute or limited. This, however, must be rightly understood, for God does not possess these in the same way as those. This we were hinting at when we added that God contains them in a manner suited to himself; what this manner is must now be considered somewhat more closely. A thing is commonly said to contain some perfections in three ways, which the Scholastics express in their own fashion when they say that a thing has something in itself formally, eminently, virtually. That is, that to which some perfection inheres simply according to its own definition is said to have it formally, as if you were to say that it inheres according to its intrinsic form or essence: in this way the faculty of judging or reasoning inheres, for example, in the human intellect. But if a certain perfection, as it exists in this or that subject, has some attached imperfection, which nevertheless, with every mark of imperfection removed, is contained in another thing to a far more eminent degree and in a far more eminent manner, it is said that the perfection is contained by this thing eminently (although not all explain this in the same way): in this sense, for example, the divine intellect contains the human intellect within itself. Finally, whatever perfection can be produced by something else, even if perhaps it is contained in that thing neither formally nor eminently, is said to be in it virtually, because it can be brought into act by the power of that cause: thus, for example, the painter contains in himself the perfections of his picture, and the architect the perfections of the house he has built. If these are transferred to God and his all-embracing perfection, the matter may be settled briefly as follows. Those perfections which are simply and absolutely such, and have no imperfection mixed in, are to be attributed to God simply according to their definition, that is, formally: thus God is formally eternal, simple, intelligent, willing, etc. Whatever predicates denote some limited perfection and perfection only in a certain respect, insofar as, with the separated imperfections, they retain something of perfection, have a place in God eminently, inasmuch as, with all imperfection set aside, they are attributed to him alone in the most excellent degree and manner. Thus there belong to God, for example, Where, When, Understanding, Will, etc., as predicated of created things, insofar as all dependence, finitude, succession, division, mutability, etc., is removed from them. Finally, whatever perfections in a certain respect cannot be separated from every adhering imperfection, so that they cannot be conceived apart from it, are said to be contained in God only virtually, as in the first cause, which can produce them in creatures outside itself as they are. And in this way there are in God, for example, Sight, Speech, Motion, Figure, and any other attributes of corporeal things.

units.la: Ex quibus liquet, hos modos, quibus Deus Perfectiones quasvis possidere concipitur, relationem involvere ad perfectiones rerum creatarum, ex quarum contemplatione Dei perfectiones cogitare discimus. Ridcontent, sat scio, albis dentibus hanc omnem philosophationem hodierni quidam magistri, qui, explosis istis, scilicet! nugis, jam dudum se reperisse sibi imaginantur viam longè magis compendiosam, ad Infinitas Dei Perfectiones secundum se cognoscendas, absque creaturarum ope, ex solo intuitu Entis infinitè perfecti ideæ, quam se mente sua circumgestare innatam jactitant claram & distinctam. Verum μεγαλοφυΐα ista vel id abundè refellit, quod nihil illi attributorum Divinorum ex ista idea hactenus deprompserint, quod non jam olim de Deo demonstrarunt alii, qui ex creaturarum contemplatione occasiones sumpserunt philosophandi de primi entis Perfectionibus. Quin utinam illi, qui à trita via hic recesserunt, ideæ istius figmento non ita corrupissent plerarumque Divinarum perfectionum conceptus, ut, nisi tandem licentiæ tiæ fiat finis, brevi Deus aliquis orbi hactenus ignotus sit introducendus! Absit, quod ominantur prudentiores! Neque ominari immeritò, docebunt errores quos isti committunt circa plurimas perfectiones divinas, suis locis inferius notandi: uti quoque plenius de hac entis infiniti clara idea agendum erit, cum Incomprehensibilitatem sumus tractaturi. Nobis religio est, etiam hoc loco quicquam recedere ab ista methodo, quâ hactenus ad Divinarum perfectionum conceptum ex creaturarum perpensione ascenderunt viri maximi. Atque illas ih hisce, tanquam in speculo, relucere, nemo, nisi Atheismo nimium velificans, negaverit. Ut nescium, quid sibi velint, qui Attributorum Divinorum notitiam ex creaturarum consideratione hauriri neque posse, neque debere, hodiè contendunt. Alia profectò mens Regio Vati, cui hæ enarrabant gloriam Dei fortis, ac magnificum per universam terram nomen. Alia item Apostolo, qui ex τῆς ποιήματων aeternam Divinitatem & potentiam intelligi, inculcat; Deumque beneficiis suis se οὐκ ἀμαρτύρων reliquisse, testatur. Cui veritati ratio quoque suffragatur & experientia; quippe quæ docet, nullas Dei perfectiones à nobis cognosci, quarum scientiarum occasio aliqua non sit facta ex contemplatione creaturarum: quod petenti per inductionem demonstrari posset facili negotio. Quin, ex illis Dei attributis quæ lumine naturæ cognoscimus, ea concipimus facilius & magis positivè, quorum præ aliis vestigium in creaturis exstat expressum. Nihil est, quod obiiciunt, inter Perfectiones Infinitas Creatoris & finitas creaturæ nullam dari proportionem, atque ideò notitiam harum non posse suppeditare conceptum illarum. Hoc, inquam, nihil est, quandoquidem conceptum hunc analogicum duntaxat esse fatemur, non directè repræsentantem Perfectiones Dei prout in Deo sunt, sed tantum pro modulo, quo earum capax est mens creata: at verò ad talem conceptum fundandum, intercedente rationis usu, sufficiunt ipsæ etiam creaturarum rerum imperfectiones; cum nuspiam magis verum sit quam hic illud Logicorum, oppositorum eandem esse scientiam.
units.tr: From these points it is clear that the modes by which God is conceived to possess any perfections involve a relation to the perfections of created things, from whose contemplation we learn to think of God's perfections. Some of today's masters, I know well, will laugh with white teeth at all this philosophising. They imagine that, having cast aside these "trifles", they have already found a far shorter road to knowing the infinite perfections of God in themselves, without the help of creatures, from the mere inspection of the idea of an infinitely perfect Being, which they boast is innate in their minds, clear and distinct. But that great genius is sufficiently refuted by the fact that, so far, they have drawn from this idea no attribute of God that other men had not already demonstrated long ago, men who took their occasions for reasoning about the perfections of the First Being from the contemplation of creatures. Indeed, I wish that those who have left the beaten path here had not so corrupted the concepts of most of the divine perfections with their fiction of this idea. Unless an end is put to their licence, some God unknown to the world up to now will soon have to be introduced! May it not happen, as the wiser men fear. And I do not fear this without reason: the errors which these men commit concerning very many divine perfections will show themselves in their proper places further on. Likewise, this clear idea of an infinite Being will have to be treated more fully when we come to discuss incomprehensibility. For our part, we hold it a matter of conscience to depart in any way, even in this place, from that method by which the greatest men have so far ascended to the concept of the divine perfections through the consideration of creatures. That these perfections shine forth in creatures as in a mirror, no one will deny unless he sails too far on the wind of atheism. They do not know what they mean, those who today contend that the knowledge of the divine attributes can be drawn neither from the consideration of creatures nor ought to be. The mind of the royal prophet was quite different: "The heavens declared the glory of the strong God, and his magnificent name throughout the whole earth." Alia item Apostolo, quite different too was that of the Apostle, who teaches that the eternal divinity and power are understood from the things that are made [τῶν ποιημάτων], and testifies that God did not leave himself without witness [οὐκ ἀμάρτυρον] by his benefits. Reason also supports this truth, and experience, which teaches that no perfections of God are known to us for which some occasion has not been provided by the contemplation of creatures. This could be shown easily by induction to anyone who asks. Indeed, of those divine attributes which we know by the light of nature, we conceive more easily and more positively those whose trace stands out in creatures more clearly than others. As for the objection that there is no proportion between the infinite perfections of the Creator and the finite perfections of the creature, and that therefore knowledge of the latter cannot supply a concept of the former, this is nothing. For we confess that this concept is only analogical, not directly representing the perfections of God as they are in God, but only according to the measure in which a created mind is capable of them. Yet to found such a concept, the very imperfections of created things are sufficient, with the use of reason intervening, since nowhere is that saying of the logicians more true than here: that the knowledge of opposites is the same.

units.la: Ut hæc capiantur melius, non est hoc loco prætereunda via, quâ ex perceptis entium finitorum attributis, ad cognitionem perfectionum in infinito Deo assurgimus. Triplex illa est, Diony-
units.tr: So that these things may be better understood, we must not pass over here the way by which, from the perceived attributes of finite beings, we rise to the knowledge of the perfections in the infinite God. That way is threefold, Diony-

units.la: Dionysio Areopagitæ vulgò adscripta: puta, Causalitatis, Negationis, & Eminentiæ. Nimirum, quoties rem creatam tanquam dependentem cogito, nihil in ea invenio perfectionis, quin statim per viam Causalitatis mens ducatur ad cogitationem, easdem saltem perfectiones contineri in causa ejusdem prima; cum perspicuum sit, nihil esse in effectu, quod idem non fuerit in causa. Inquirens porrò, quo modo id sit in Creatore, quod suo modo video inesse creaturæ, mox percipio, in creatura id multâs annexas habere imperfectiones, quæ cum Creatoris independentia prorsus pugnant: succurrit ergò via Negationis, id omne removens, ob quod tale prædicatum enti Independenti tribui proprie non poterat. Verum cum ex imperfectionis remotione sequatur oppositæ perfectionis positio, mox conatur mens nostra viâ Eminentiæ eo usque amplificare istius perfectionis conceptum, donec aliquid cogitare videatur Deo dignum, quodque ei absque independentiæ præjudicio tribui queat. Observo (ut totum exemplo illustrem) durare creaturam: indè colligo per viam Causalitatis, etiam ergò durare Creatorem. Sed duratio creaturæ dependens est, finita, contingens: non ita, cogito per viam Negationis, durat independens Creator. Quâ ergò ratione durat hic? Modo infinities perfectiore, quam qui à me concipi potest, addit via Eminentiæ. Unde tandem perfectionis Divinæ, quæ Æternitas appellatur, resultat, qualis in mentem nostram cadit, conceptus. Ita mutuas sibi operas præstant hæ viæ; quas quò quis accuratius in suis de Dei perfectione cogitationibus formandis observat, eò puriores de ipsa habebit notiones.
units.tr: commonly ascribed to Dionysius the Areopagite: namely, of Causality, of Negation, and of Eminence. Indeed, whenever I think of a created thing as dependent, and find in it some perfection, the mind is at once led by the way of Causality to the thought that the same perfections are contained in its first cause, since it is plain that there is nothing in an effect which was not also in its cause. Then, inquiring how that which I see to be in the creature in its own way can be in the Creator, I soon perceive that in the creature this is bound up with many imperfections which are utterly incompatible with the independence of the Creator. Then the way of Negation comes to mind, removing everything on account of which such a predicate could not properly be attributed to the Independent Being. But since the positing of the opposite perfection follows from the removal of the imperfection, our mind next strives, by the way of Eminence, to enlarge the concept of that perfection until it seems to think of something worthy of God, which can be attributed to him without prejudice to his independence. To illustrate the whole by an example: I observe that a creature endures; from this I infer by the way of Causality that the Creator too endures. But the duration of a creature is dependent, finite, and contingent; by the way of Negation I think that the independent Creator does not endure in this way. In what way, then, does he endure? By the way of Eminence, in a manner infinitely more perfect than any I can conceive. Thence at last there results the concept, such as falls into our mind, of that divine perfection which is called Eternity. Thus these ways render mutual service to one another, and the more carefully anyone observes them in forming his thoughts about the perfection of God, the purer notions of it he will have.

units.la: VII. Perfectionis Infinitatem Deo, & quidem soli, convenire, demonstratur.
units.tr: VII. That infinite perfection belongs to God, and to God alone, is demonstrated.

units.la: Cæterum, explicatâ sic omnimodâ Dei Perfectione, id fuerit, ut accedamus ad ejus demonstrationem, quæ facili negotio ex ipsius Independentia adstruitur hoc modo. Quod est independens, tam perfectum est quam esse potest. Quod tam perfectum est quam esse potest, infinitè perfectum est. Ergò, quod independens est, infinitè perfectum est. Propositio certa est: nam quodcunque non tam perfectum est quam esse potest, id à perfectione possibili, quæ sibi addi potest, dependet; atque hactenus non absolutè independens est. Assumtio indubia existit; quoniam ideo aliquid finitè perfectum est, quia aliquid majus ei addi potest: at quod tam perfectum est quam esse potest, ei quicquam addi nequit; necessariò itaque, quod tam perfectum est quam esse potest, id infinitè perfectum est. Manet ergò Deum, quia Independens est, esse infinitè perfectum: quod demonstrandum erat. Iterùm: Omnis omninò perfectio possibilis vel dependens est, vel independens. Quæcunque independens est perfectio, ea, hoc ipso quia esse potest, etiam est: mera enim possibilitas, existentiam actualem excludens, est pura denominatio facta à potentia rei, in cujus sinu latet, & à qua produci potest; quod ipsum independentiæ è diametro adversatur. Jam verò si omnis independens perfectio ipso actu existat, non alibi quærenda erit quam in independenti essentia: ea enim quæ dependens est independentis perfectionis non est capax; cum nullum attributum excedat conditionem fui subjecti. Possidet ergo ens independens ipso facto in sese omnes omninò perfectiones independentes. Quod ad dependentes attinet, ea vel ab aliquo dependenti dependent, vel ab independenti. Si hoc, ergò à Deo ipso, qui solus est independens, dependent; consequenter is eàdem, tanquam causa, virtualiter in se continet. Sed & omnes illæ perfectiones quæ à dependenti principio pendent, per subordinationem rerum dependentium finitam (de qua antè) tandem reducendæ sunt ad omnis rei dependentis principium primum independens, quod ipse Deus est. Continet ergo Deus, quia Independens est, ipso facto omnes omninò perfectiones possibiles; atque hoc ipso existit infinitè perfectus: quod demonstrandum erat. Plura addere nihil attinet. Uti nec opus est, multis probare, hanc perfectionis infinitatem soli Deo convenire; nec ullam dari posse creaturam perfectissimam, de quo latè Scholastici. Constat de utroque abundè ex eo, quod demonstratum jam sit, Perfectionis Infinitatem indissolubilem nexum habere cum Independentia Divina; cujus nullam speciem alteri esse communicabilem, retrò docuimus.
units.tr: Having thus explained God's perfection in every respect, let us proceed to its demonstration, which follows with little difficulty from his independence, in this way. What is independent is as perfect as it can be. What is as perfect as it can be is infinitely perfect. Therefore what is independent is infinitely perfect. The major premise is certain: for whatever is not as perfect as it can be depends on a possible perfection that could be added to it, and so is not absolutely independent so far as that goes. The minor premise is beyond doubt, since a thing is called finitely perfect because something greater can be added to it, but nothing can be added to what is as perfect as it can be. It necessarily follows, then, that what is as perfect as it can be is infinitely perfect. Thus God, because he is independent, is infinitely perfect, which was to be demonstrated. Again: every possible perfection whatsoever is either dependent or independent. Any independent perfection, simply because it can exist, also does exist. For a mere possibility, which excludes actual existence, is nothing but a label drawn from the potency of a thing, in whose bosom it lies hidden and from which it can be produced; and that is directly opposed to independence itself. Now if every independent perfection actually exists, it must be sought nowhere else than in the independent essence; for what is dependent is not capable of an independent perfection, since no attribute exceeds the condition of its subject. Therefore the independent being possesses in itself, by the very fact, all independent perfections without exception. As for dependent perfections, they depend either on some dependent being or on an independent one. If the latter, then they depend on God himself, who alone is independent, and consequently he contains them virtually in himself as their cause. But also all those perfections which depend on a dependent principle must, through the finite subordination of dependent things (of which we spoke above), ultimately be traced back to the first independent principle of every dependent thing, which is God himself. Therefore God, because he is independent, contains by that very fact all possible perfections without exception, and by this very fact he exists infinitely perfect, which was to be demonstrated. There is no need to add more. Nor is it necessary to prove at length, by many arguments, that this infinity of perfection belongs to God alone, or that no most perfect creature can be given, a matter on which the Scholastics write at length. Both points are abundantly clear from what has now been demonstrated: the infinity of perfection has an indissoluble bond with the divine independence, of which we taught earlier that no species can be communicated to another.

units.la: Ex iis quæ de Perfectione Dei infinita hactenus disputavimus, hanc nobis figamus regulam, Nihil unquam præcipitanter de Deo esse effutiendum, sed diligenter prius & seriò attendendum, num quod de Deo affirmamus aut negamus, infinitâ tā perfectione sit satis dignum, ne unquam deprehendamur in eam injurii. At non id sufficit. Etiam in illam injurii erimus, nisi quasvis rerum creatarum perfectiones finitas semper cogitemus ac dependentes; rivulos scilicet, uti deductos ex immenso divinarum perfectionum oceano, sic in eundem reducendos. Ita qui sublimare assuevit suas de perfectionibus rerum finitarum cogitationes, semper & ubique is Creatorem inveniet manifestatum in creaturis; quarum quot notat perfectiones, tot observat reflexos ab iis Divinæ bonitatis ac perfectionis radios. Hac dulci meditatione verè nobis
units.tr: From what we have so far disputed about the infinite perfection of God, let us fix this rule for ourselves: nothing is ever to be rashly uttered about God, but we must first diligently and seriously consider whether what we affirm or deny of God is worthy of his infinite perfection, lest we ever be caught doing him wrong. Yet this is not enough. We will also do him wrong unless we always think of every finite perfection of created things as dependent, as streams which, drawn from the immense ocean of the divine perfections, are likewise to be led back into it. Thus the one who has accustomed himself to raise his thoughts about the perfections of finite things will always and everywhere find the Creator made manifest in creatures; and as many perfections as he notes in them, so many reflected rays of divine goodness and perfection he observes shining from them. In this sweet meditation, truly,

units.la: Præsentem referet qualibet herba Deum; &, secundum illud Senecæ, Deus erit id quod videmus, & id quod non videmus. Hac vilescet vel totius Universi Imperfecta quævis perfectio; quæ sine Deo nulla, absque qua etiam Deus Perfectissimus. O hominum Rector! quam late nominis exit Fama Tui; & terras Virtus Tua sparsa per omnes In mutis etiam loquitur de Numine rebus!
units.tr: every herb will bring God before us as present; and, in the words of Seneca, God will be that which we see, and that which we do not see. Every imperfect perfection of the whole Universe, which is nothing without God, and without which God would not be most perfect, grows worthless by comparison. O Ruler of men! How far the fame of your name goes forth, and your virtue, spread over all the lands, speaks of the Deity even through dumb things!

units.la: EXERCITATIO SEPTIMA, DE DEO NECESSARIO EXISTENTE.
units.tr: EXERCITATION SEVEN, CONCERNING GOD AS A NECESSARILY EXISTING BEING.
SUMMARY

units.la: I. Inter Dei Attributa primum est Necessitas existendi. II. Eam perfectionem, Contingentiam imperfectionem esse, ostenditur. III. Deum esse Necessa-
units.tr: I. Among the attributes of God, the first is necessity of existence. II. It is shown that contingency, the opposite of this, is an imperfection. III. It is demonstrated that God is a Being necessary in existing.

units.la: rium in existendo, demonstratur. IV. An pariter sit Necessarius in operando, & quo sensu, explicatur. V. Præter Deum nil esse in existendo absolutè Necessarium, probatur.
units.tr: IV. It is explained whether he is likewise necessary in acting, and in what sense. V. It is proved that, apart from God, nothing exists with absolute necessity.

units.la: TA quoque in compendio quasi, Qualis sit Deus, pro ingenioli nostri captu & modulo vidimus, Ens videlicet Infinitæ perfectum. Verum cum hic conceptus tantum sit confusa notio alicujus aggregati, puta collectionis cujuspiam quarumcunque quæ dari aut concipi possunt perfectionum, ad distinctiorem hujus rei notitiam acquirendam omninò pertinet, lustrare sigillatim saltem aliquas earum Perfectionum, quæ pro modo concipiendi nostro istum immensæ perfectionis cumulum conficiunt. Dico, saltem aliquas earum nobis esse considerandas: omnes enim atque singulas enumerare, nedum explicare, sphæram finiti & creati intellectûs excedit longissimè, ac solius infinitæ mentis, sc incomprehensibilem comprehendentis, prærogativa est, sicuti suo loco videbimus. Inter eas quarum notitiam naturali rationis lumine manifestare nobis voluit Creator, numerandam primo loco censemus jure merito Existendi Necessitatem. Ut enim primum cujuslibet rei prædicatum, quod in omnia alia ejusdem perfectione supponitur atque includitur, est ipsa Existentia, absque qua unumquodque nihil eorum est quæ est; ita ex cæteris Dei Attributis illa præmittenda videntur, quæ præ aliis Existentiam ejus proximè comitantur & sequuntur: qualis sine dubio est Existentiæ Necessitas. Atque hac ratione moti quidam hanc existendi Necessitatem numerarunt, non inter Attributa, sed inter illa prædicata, quæ sunt Essentiæ Divinæ constitutiva: ast perperàm, quandoquidem ea ex Independentia Divina quasi à priori potest demonstrari; uti ex dicendis intelligetur.
units.tr: We have also seen, as in a summary, what God is, so far as the measure and capacity of our small intellect allow: namely, a Being perfect to infinity. But since this concept is only a confused notion of some aggregate, that is, of a collection of whatever perfections can be given or conceived, it belongs entirely to acquiring a more distinct knowledge of the matter to examine, one by one at least, some of those perfections which, according to our manner of conceiving, make up this mass of immeasurable perfection. I say "at least some," for we must consider only some of them. To list all of them, let alone explain them, far exceeds the scope of a finite and created understanding; it is the prerogative of an infinite mind alone, which comprehends the incomprehensible, as we shall see in its place. Among those attributes whose knowledge the Creator has willed to make manifest to us by the natural light of reason, we rightly judge that necessity of existence should be counted first. For just as the first predicate of anything, which is presupposed and included in all its other perfections, is existence itself, without which a thing is nothing of what it is, so among God's other attributes those should be placed first which most closely accompany and follow his existence. Such is undoubtedly the necessity of existence. Moved by this reasoning, some have counted this necessity of existence not among the attributes but among those predicates which constitute the divine essence. But they are wrong, since it can be demonstrated a priori, as it were, from the independence of God, as will be understood from what follows.

units.la: Est verò Necessitas existendi in Deo, tale Ejus Attributum cujus ratione naturæ Divinæ absolutè repugnat non-existere. Nimirum Necessitati opposita est Contingentia; quæ notat, rem existen-
units.tr: Now the necessity of existence in God is that attribute of his by reason of which it is absolutely repugnant to the divine nature not to exist. Contingency is, of course, the opposite of necessity; it signifies that a thing which exists can, without contradiction, not be

units.la: H existentem citra contradictionem posse non-esse. Ut quidem Contingens omne existat, atque hactenus sit aliquid reale (si enim existentiam non haberet, non jam Contingens proprie foret, sed merum duntaxat possibile, & non-ens) interim tamen eo usque sit affine nihilo, ut saltem repugnantiam non dicat ad id, ut nihil fieri possit. Hinc, quemadmodum citra controversiam perfectius est esse, quam non-esse (quum recte notent Metaphysici, unumquamque rem tantum habere bonitatis & perfectionis, quantum habet entitatis) ita etiam procul dubio perfectius est non posse non-esse, quam posse non-esse: quo quid enim ab imperfecto longius distat, quoque illi magis adversatur, eo etiam perfectius id est habendum. Quum itaque τὸ Aliquid perfectius sit τοῦ Nihilo, perfectior quoque erit ille existendi modus quo res quaepiam sic est Aliquid, ut Nihil esse plane non possit, quam si sic sit Aliquid; ut fieri interim possit purum Nihil; cujus uti nullae sunt affectiones, ita nec ullae perfectiones.
units.tr: existing. Although every contingent thing does exist, and so far is something real (for if it had no existence it would no longer properly be contingent, but merely possible and a non-being), nevertheless it is so close to nothing that it does not imply any repugnance to its coming to nothing. Hence, just as it is beyond dispute that being is more perfect than non-being (since the Metaphysicians rightly note that each thing has as much goodness and perfection as it has entity), so too it is without doubt more perfect not to be able not to exist than to be able not to exist. For the further a thing is from the imperfect, and the more it opposes it, the more perfect it must be held to be. Since, then, the Something [τὸ Aliquid] is more perfect than the Nothing [τοῦ Nihilo], that mode of existence will also be more perfect by which a thing is such a Something that it cannot at all be Nothing, than one by which it is such a Something that a pure Nothing may nevertheless come to be. Such a Nothing has no affections, and therefore no perfections either.
III.

units.la: Quibus perceptis, dubium esse nequit, quin Deus, propter Infinitatem suae Perfectionis, sit Ens necessariò existens. Quum enim existendi Necessitatem esse simplicem & absolutam perfectionem, jam demonstraverimus, utique ex ipsis terminis & per se nota est haec propositio, Quod existit infinitè perfectum, existit necessariò: quoniam praedicatum hujus enunciationis in subjecto ejusdem includitur & continetur. Quod enim infinitas perfectiones possidet, ei unam earum, puta existendi Necessitatem, negari non posse, res ipsa clamat. Non istis tamen probamus methodum Recentiorum, concludentium necessariam Dei existentiam (non, uti nos, ex suppositu vel demonstrata jam ante simplici ejusdem existentia) sed ex idea quapiam entis infinitè perfecti, quam se in sua mente reperire ajunt: de qua re vide Exercit. II. §. VI. Caeterum, etiam cum Dei Independentia immediatè cohaeret ejusdem in existendo Necessitas. Etenim omne Contingens secundum se indifferens est ad hoc, ut vel sit, vel non-sit. Si namque in se ipso aliquid contineret, quod faceret potius id esse, quam non-esse, utique, eo ipso quod aliquam talem existendi rationem in sua essentia contineret, Necessarium, non Contingens, foret. Itaque quando Contingens existit, semper extra illud aliquid quæri potest, quod causa sit, cujus influxu res, ex sese indifferens ad utrumlibet, determinata sit ad existendum potius, quam non-existendum. Quam dependentiam à cujuscunque causæ influxu quum Inde-pendentia Divina prorsus respuat, respuit quoque eadem omnem pariter Contingentiam, dependentiam istiusmodi involventem s consequenter, oppositam illi Necessitatem existendi eam includere, manifestum est. Nec tantùm omnimoda Dei Independentia & Perfectio Necessitatem ejusdem in existendo inserunt; sed & eam arguit efficaciter ipsa rerum creatarum Contingentia. Utì enim plurimæ res contingentes nobis passim obviæ sunt, ita in earum causam, per quam existant, inquirere licet; cum, uti demonstratum, eæ ex se & per se existere non possint. Illam si contingentem assignaveris, & ipsa, per jam dicta, suam ite-rum habebit causam. Hæc si rursus detur contingens, eadem denuo redibit quæstio: quæ cum in infinitum (propter causarum subordinatarum seriem necessariò finitam, de qua antè) repeti non possit; utique oportet illud, in quo tanquam in pri-ma rerum contingentium causa subsistimus, esse ens Necessarium in existendo. Ast hoc ipsum demonstrandum fuit.
units.tr: Having grasped these points, there can be no doubt that God, on account of the infinity of his perfection, is a Being existing necessarily. For since we have already demonstrated that necessity of existence is a simple and absolute perfection, this proposition is surely evident from the very terms and known in itself: what exists infinitely perfect, exists necessarily, since the predicate of this statement is included and contained in its subject. That which possesses infinite perfections cannot be denied one of them, namely necessity of existence; the thing itself cries out for this. Yet we do not prove this by the method of the more recent writers, who conclude the necessary existence of God not, as we do, from a previously assumed or already demonstrated simple existence of him, but from a certain idea of a Being infinitely perfect, which they say they find in their own mind. On this matter see Exercitation II, §. VI. Moreover, necessity of existence in God is also immediately bound up with his independence. For every contingent thing, considered in itself, is indifferent to whether it is or is not. If it contained within itself something that made it rather be than not be, then, by the very fact that it contained such a mode of existence in its essence, it would be necessary and not contingent. Therefore, whenever a contingent thing exists, something can always be sought outside it that is its cause, by whose influence the thing, which of itself is indifferent to either, has been determined to exist rather than not exist. Since the independence of God utterly rejects this dependence on the influence of some cause, it is equally manifest that it rejects all contingency, which involves such dependence; and consequently it includes the opposite necessity of existence. Not only does the complete independence and perfection of God imply his necessity of existence, but the very contingency of created things proves it effectively. For just as many contingent things are everywhere met with by us, so we may inquire into the cause through which they exist, since, as has been shown, they cannot exist of themselves and through themselves. If you assign a contingent cause, that cause will again, by what has already been said, have its own cause. If this in turn is some contingent thing, the same question will return again. Since this cannot be repeated to infinity (because of the necessarily finite series of subordinate causes, mentioned above), it must be that the thing on which we rest, as on the first cause of contingent things, is a Being necessary in existing. But this very point was what had to be demonstrated.

units.la: Juvat hoc loco tribus verbis expedire huic materiæ affinem controversiam à variis variè definitam, An Deus, uti est ens absolutè Necessarium in existendo, ita pariter absolutè necessarius sit in operando? Facilis erit dubii solutio, si observemus, duo-bus modis à nobis spectari posse Dei actionem; vel absolutè, prout se habet à parte Dei & secundum sese, nulla habita ratione ob-jectorum, effectorum, aut modi operandi; vel relativè, quatenus includit respectum ad has vel istas res hac vel ista ratione existentes, in quibus actionem Dei terminari concipimus. Isto mo-do si consideretur, jubet Dei Simplicitas (infrà demonstranda) credere, actionem Dei ab essentia ejus actuosa nullâ parte distin-gui. Quapropter etiam tantùm abest ut essentia sine actione hic esse queat, ut quæ essentiæ, eadem quoque actioni cum essentia identificatæ conveniat absolutissima Necessitas. At verò, si spectemus Dei actionem cum relatione ad has aut istas creaturas, hoc vel istoc modo ab actuosa Dei essentia fluentes, certum est, eam omnem esse non-necessariam, sed indifferenter liberam, sive objectum
units.tr: It is worth settling in a few words here a controversy related to this subject, which has been defined in various ways by various people: whether God, as he is a Being absolutely necessary in existing, is likewise absolutely necessary in acting. The solution to this doubt will be easy if we observe that we can consider God's action in two ways: either absolutely, as it stands on God's side and in itself, with no regard to objects, effects, or manner of acting; or relatively, insofar as it includes a reference to these or those things, existing in this or that way, in which we conceive God's action as terminating. If it is considered in this way, God's simplicity (to be demonstrated below) requires us to believe that his action is not distinguished in any part from his essence, which is active. Therefore, far from its being possible for his essence to exist without action, the most absolute necessity belongs to the essence, and likewise to the action, which is identified with the essence. But if we consider God's action in relation to these or those creatures, flowing from his active essence in this or that way, it is certain that all of it is not necessary but indifferently free, that is, as to the object

units.la: IV. An pariter Deus Necessarius sit in operando, & quo sen-su ? explicatur. objectum actionis species, sive modum operandi. Talis enim agendi modus cum sit perfectissimus, ut maximè etiam congruus tum Independentiæ Creatoris, tum dependentiæ omnimodæ creaturarum, enti perfectissimo & independenti planè tribuendus est. Atque ita verissimum illud tritum Theologorum: Actiones Dei ad extra sunt indifferenter liberæ. Sed de hisce alibi plura.
units.tr: IV. Whether God is likewise necessary in acting, and in what sense, is explained. as to the object of the action, or the species, or the mode of acting. For such a manner of acting, since it is most perfect, and most fitting both to the independence of the Creator and to the complete dependence of creatures, must be wholly ascribed to the most perfect and wholly independent Being. And so that well-worn saying of the theologians is most true: God's actions outwardly are indifferently free. But more on these matters elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc ex dictis abundè intelligitur, absolutam talem existendi Necessitatem solius Dei attributum esse, nec ulli communicabile. Nam ut Ipsi uni convenit Independentia, absque qua Necessitas ejusmodi non consistit, ita omne quod existit præter Deum ab influxu ipsius procreante & conservante pendet; qui cum sit, ut dixi, in egressu suo indifferenter liber, etiam res quæcunque ab eo procedentes suâ naturâ indifferentes erunt ad existendum vel non existendum; id est, erunt prorsus contingentes. Convenit quidem suo modo quibusdam creaturis aliqua Necessitas, vel potius Immutabilitas quædam, ratione quorundam prædicatorum; sed non ideò illa prædicata absolutè & secundum se necessariò existunt, cum quod sint, id vel fluat indè, quod aliquod aliud prædicatum Deus in rebus posuerit, quod illa sibi habet connexa tanquam non realiter à se distincta; quo sensu substantia aliqua necessariò est divisibilis, figurabilis, &c. posito Deum eam creasse extensam: vel fluit à lege quapiam naturæ, quam Deus rebus tulit, ut secundum eam innato impetu agant; quo pacto Sol necessariò movetur: vel denique indè procedit, quod Deus certitudinem connexionis fecerit inter duas res, ut si earum una sit, altera sequatur; quâ ratione, posità corporis humani totali indispositione, necesse est animam à corpore separari. Itaque cum omnis ejusmodi Necessitatis ratio derivanda veniat ab aliquo extrinseco, puta à Deo, qui tales naturas creare, tales leges ferre, talem antecedentis cum suo consequente concatenationem facere, liberrimè voluit, cum, si placuisset, eorum omnium nihil planè ponere potuisset, facilè liquet, ab omnibus istis qualiscunque Necessitatis speciebus toto coelo distare illam, quam Deo asseruimus, absolutam existendi Necessitatem. Verum de istis quoque uberius dicendi alibi locus est.
units.tr: From what has been said, it is now abundantly clear that this absolute necessity of existence is an attribute of God alone and cannot be communicated to anything else. For just as independence belongs to him alone, without which such necessity does not exist, so everything that exists apart from God depends on his creating and conserving influence. Since, as I have said, God in his going forth is indifferently free, all things proceeding from him will by their nature be indifferent to existing or not existing; that is, they will be wholly contingent. Some necessity, or rather a certain immutability, does indeed belong in its own way to some creatures, by reason of certain predicates. But those predicates do not therefore exist absolutely and of themselves necessarily. Either they flow from this, that God has placed in things some other predicate, which they have joined to themselves as not really distinct from themselves; in this sense some substance is necessarily divisible, capable of figure, and so on, given that God created it extended. Or they flow from some law of nature which God gave to things, so that they act by an innate impulse; in this way the sun is necessarily moved. Or finally they proceed from this, that God made a certainty of connection between two things, so that if one of them is, the other follows; for this reason, given the total indisposition of the human body, the soul must be separated from the body. Thus, since every reason for such necessity is derived from something extrinsic, namely from God, who most freely willed to create such natures, to give such laws, and to make such a chain of antecedent and consequent, and who, had it pleased him, could have posited none of these things at all, it is easily clear that that absolute necessity of existence which we have ascribed to God is removed by the whole heaven from all these kinds of necessity, of whatever sort. But there is also room elsewhere to speak more fully about these matters.
EIGHTH EXERCITATION, CONCERNING THE ETERNAL GOD.
SUMMARY

units.la: I. Inter Necessitatem existendi & Æternitatem quæ sit respectu durationis distinctio. II. Æternitatis à Tempore, ratione carentiæ terminorum, discrimen. III. Altera Æternitatis, ratione carentiæ successionis, à Tempore differentia. IV. Dei Æternitatem esse interminabilem, docetur. V. Eandem esse successionis expertem, demonstratur. VI. Neque obstat ejus cum nostris temporibus successivis coexistentia. VII. Relatio ad temporalia spatia, seu vera, seu possibilia, qui juvet nostrum Æternitatis conceptum? VIII. Æternitatem esse Dei solius prærogativam, ex demonstratis conficitur.
units.tr: I. There is a distinction, with respect to duration, between the necessity of existing and eternity. II. There is a difference between eternity and time, according to the lack of limits. III. There is another difference between eternity and time, according to the lack of succession. IV. God's eternity is taught to be without limit. V. It is shown that it is free of succession. VI. Its coexistence with our successive times is no obstacle. VII. Would a relation to temporal spaces, whether real or possible, help our concept of eternity? VIII. From what has been shown it follows that eternity is the prerogative of God alone.

units.la: Ic, Deum existere necessariò, ostensum satis. Porrò videndum, an, & quâ ratione existat Alicubi & Aliquando? Nam etiam hæc duo Attributa cum ipsa rei cujusvis Existentia immediatè cohærere videntur. Istud nobis explicabit conceptus Immensitatis; hoc, ÆTERNITATIS. Quibusdam quidem Æternitas confunditur cum ipsa Necessitate existendi, quasi hæc idem sonent; rectius tamen ista duo distinguuntur. Non quidem nego, quemadmodum contingens, hoc ipso quod tale est, est temporarium, ita quoque omne absolutè Necessarium in existendo. do, ideo quod tale est, esse Æternum: attamen conceptus Necessariæ existentiæ competit Deo simpliciter tanquam existenti ; Æternitas vero eidem potius tribuitur tanquam duranti, seu permanenti in ista sua existentia. Indè & hæc à quibusdam definitur, Infinita Dei duratio. Non est autem quod quem in hoc negotio offendat vox durationis, quasi hic minus accurata sit. Id enim uti lubens concedo, si peream præcisè indigitetur continuatio alicujus existentiæ successivæ, qualis est nostra duratio, per lapsum annorum, mensium, &c. ita ex adverso nil video, ob quod vocem hanc fugere hic debeamus, si abstractè sumatur, eâque simpliciter intelligatur qualiscunque rei in existendo perseverantia. Hoc sensu, quatenus ϑ durare opponitur τῷ cessare in existendo, non capio, quomodo quis durationem de Deo negare possit, qui non oppositum ejus, defectum puta in existendo, de eodem absurdissimè affirmet.
units.tr: Now that it has been sufficiently shown that God exists necessarily, we must consider whether, and in what manner, he exists somewhere and at some time. For these two attributes also seem to cohere immediately with the existence of any thing whatever. The concept of immensity will explain the first; the concept of ETERNITY the second. For some indeed confuse eternity with the necessity of existing, as if the two meant the same thing; yet it is more correct to distinguish them. I do not deny that, just as the contingent is temporary by the very fact that it is such, so too everything absolutely necessary in its existence is eternal by the very fact that it is such. Still, the concept of necessary existence belongs to God simply as existing, whereas eternity is attributed to him rather as enduring, or persisting, in that existence of his. Hence some also define it as the infinite duration of God. Nor should anyone be troubled by the word duration in this matter, as if it were less accurate here. I gladly concede that if it is taken to mean precisely the continuation of some successive existence, such as our duration through the passing of years, months, and so on, then the word should be avoided. But on the contrary, I see no reason why we should avoid it here, if it is taken abstractly and understood simply as the perseverance of any thing in existing. In this sense, insofar as to endure [ϑ durare] is opposed to to cease in existing [τῷ cessare in existendo], I do not see how anyone could deny duration of God, unless he were to assert most absurdly of him the opposite, namely a failure in existing.

units.la: Describunt alii Æternitatem negativè, Durationem principio, fine, & successione carentem; alii positivè, durationem quæ tota & perfecta sit simul. Nobis non displicet nota omnibus ac celebris definitio Boëtii, utramque explicationem miscentis, quando ait: Æternitas est interminabilis vita tota simul & perfecta possessio. Minutatim eam non jam excutiam. Nostro instituto faciet satis duo in ea observasse, per quæ Æternitas à spatiis nostris temporalibus longissimè distat. Primo, Interminabilis dicitur Æternitas; non tantùm quia re ipsâ terminos quoscunque, sive principium & finem, excludit ac removet, sed & quia illos omnes conceptibiles sic excedit, ut ne quidem terminos istiusmodi pati possit, quatenus ens Æternum sic Sempiternum est, ut nunquam cogitari queat posse aliquando vel non-fuisse, vel non-fore. Aliter res temporariæ, quæ, quia suos ortus habent & interitus, durratione gaudent certis terminis circumscriptâ. Dantur quidem earum quædam (v. c. animæ rationales) quarum existentia nunquam deficiet; quo sensu Ævum, temporì strictè dicto oppositum, à quibusdam cis adscribitur: attamen eæ, quamvis durationem de facto terminatam non habeant, habent saltem citra contradictionem terminabilem, in quantum ex natura rei præsens durationis momentum cum futura adeo nullam connexionem habet, ut quovis temporis articulo finem ei imponere, si velit, possit Deus. Quin, si paulò diligentius hæc introspicere lubet, deprehendemus, etiam has ipsas res in suo esse permanere duratione quovis existentiæ momento ipso facto terminatâ; quatenus per fluxum instabilis suæ existentiæ, ac labentem quandam sui innovationem, perpetuò amittunt illum durationis articulum, quem modò possidebant; acquirunt alium, quo modò carebant: atque ita, tametsi duratio earundem in infinitum sit producenda, ea tamen quam actu habent, vel habuerunt unquam, præsenti momento in quo jam versantur ipso facto finitur, dum quas adhuc in futuro habituræ sunt durationis partes, necdum eis in præsenti gaudent.
units.tr: Others describe eternity negatively, as a duration without beginning, end, or succession; others positively, as a duration that is whole and perfect all at once. I am not displeased with the well-known and celebrated definition of Boethius, which combines both explanations when he says: Eternity is an interminable life, wholly and perfectly possessed all at once. I shall not examine it piece by piece. It will be enough for my purpose to note two features in it by which eternity is very far removed from our temporal spans. First, eternity is called interminable, not only because in reality it excludes and removes all limits whatever, whether beginning or end, but also because it so surpasses all such limits that it cannot even admit them. Being an eternal being, it is so everlasting that it can never be conceived as having at some time either not been or not going to be. Temporal things are otherwise: since they have their origins and their deaths, they enjoy a duration bounded by certain limits. There are indeed some of them (for example, rational souls) whose existence will never fail; in this sense some ascribe Aevum, which they set against strict time, to such things. Yet although these have in fact no limited duration, they have at least a duration that can be limited without contradiction, insofar as, by the nature of the thing, the present moment of its duration has so little connection with the future that God could, if he wished, put an end to it at any point of time. Indeed, if we care to examine these things a little more carefully, we will find that even these things remain in their being through a duration that is terminated by the very fact of each moment of their existence. For through the flow of their unstable existence, and a certain sliding renewal of themselves, they constantly lose the portion of duration they now possess and acquire another that they lacked before. And so, although their duration is to be produced to infinity, the duration they actually have, or have ever had, is ended by the very fact of the present moment in which they now stand, while the parts of duration they are yet to have in the future they do not yet enjoy in the present.

units.la: Sed & secundò, durationem suam omnem simul totam ac perfectam possidet quod est Æternum: id est, durat invariabili quâdam existentiæ perseveratione, absque ulla minutorum sibi succedentium lapsu. Aliter res temporariæ, quæ singulis momentis novum quasi incipiunt esse; quippe quæ tempori subjectæ, quemadmodum ipsa tempora, cum temporibus mutantur, nec unquam omnem illam habent durationem, quam habere possunt. Sequitur hic quod elapsum est præteritum præsens, sed non nisi istud fuerit elapsum; hoc excipiet mox futurum, at non nisi eo ipso evanescat præsens. Neque, quia res olim fuit, ideo jam est; aut non, quia jam est, aliquanto post erit; dum hic fuisse esse potest sine esse, esse stare potest sine fore. Quod verò absolutâ Æternitate gaudet, dum perfectissimâ existit durationè, gaudet necessariò eâ tantâ, quantâ gaudere potest: quæ durationis perfectio cum in nullum succesivum cadat, utique ab Æternitate secundum se penitus removendum omne fuisse, omne fore, quod non sit ipsum esse. Ut per Æternitatem res durans ponatur in momento eodem & perpetuo, quod quasi semper stat, partibus caret, in fluxum nunquam progreditur, in se ipso manet: unde quidam non inelegantèr eam dixerunt, Nunc semper stans. Scitè hanc temporis striète dictiab Æternitate propriè sumpta differentiam (cujus accurata observatio unica ad Æternitatem ritè concipiendam via est) paucis expressit magnus Augustinus, cujus hæc verba ex Enarrat. in Psalm. cx. huc transscribere non pigebit. Ita commentatur Doctor in verba hæc Vatis : In generatione generationum anni tui. „Sed qui anni tui ? Qui , nisi qui non ve-„nient ut transeant ? Qui, nisi qui non ideo veniunt ut non „sint ? Omnis enim dies in hoc tempore ideo venit , ut non „,fit , omnis hora , omnis mensis , omnis annus : nihil ho„rum stat , antequam veniat erit , cum venerit non erit. Illi „ergò anni tui æterni , anni tui qui non mutantur , in gene-„ratione generationum erunt .... Non enim aliud anni Dei, „& aliud ipse Deus ; sed anni Dei, Æternitas Dei est. Æter-„nitas ipsa Dei substantia est , quæ nihil habet mutabile. Ibi „nihil est præteritum , quasi jam non sit ; nihil est futurum, „quasi nondum sit. Sed non est ibi nisi est ; non est ibi fuit „& erit : quia & quod fuit , jam non est; & quod erit, non-„dum est : sed quicquid ibi est , non nisi est.
units.tr: But second, what is eternal possesses all its duration whole and perfect all at once: that is, it endures with a certain unchanging perseverance of existence, without any passing of successive moments. Temporal things are otherwise: they almost begin to be anew at each moment; for, being subject to time, like time itself they change with time, and never have the whole duration that they could have. From this it follows that what has passed is past, and what is present is present only so long as it has passed; the future will follow this, but only when the present has vanished. Nor, because a thing once was, is it therefore now; nor, because it now is, will it be some time later; for what has been can be without being, and what is standing can be without going to be. But that which enjoys absolute eternity, since it exists in the most perfect duration, necessarily enjoys as much of duration as it can enjoy. Since this perfection of duration falls into no succession, it follows that everything that is not being itself must be utterly removed from eternity in itself: everything that was, everything that will be. Thus a thing that endures through eternity is placed in one and the same perpetual moment, which, as it were, always stands still; it has no parts, does not proceed into flux, but remains in itself. Hence some have not inelegantly called it Now always standing. The great Augustine has neatly expressed this difference between eternity properly so called and time strictly so called (the accurate observation of which is the only way to conceive eternity rightly) in a few words; I shall not hesitate to transcribe here his words from the Enarrations on Psalm 101 (cx). The Doctor thus comments on the words of the prophet: In generatione generationum anni tui. "But which are your years? Those which do not come to pass? Those which do not come so that they may pass away? For every day in this time comes so that it may not be; every hour, every month, every year: none of these stands; before it comes it will be, when it has come it will not be. Those, then, are your eternal years, your years which do not change; they will be in the generation of generations ... For the years of God are not one thing and God himself another; the years of God are the eternity of God. Eternity itself is the substance of God, which has nothing changeable in it. There is nothing past there, as if it were no longer; nothing future, as if it were not yet. But there is nothing there except is; there is not was and will be there; for what was is no longer is, and what will be is not yet is; but whatever is there, is only is."

units.la: IV. Æternitatem Dei esse intermina-bilem, docetur.
units.tr: IV. That the eternity of God is without end is taught.

units.la: Verùm ad horum demonstrationem accedamus propius. Prius quidem nostræ descriptionis membrum, quo Æternitatem asseruimus Interminabilem, admiserunt haud gravatim quotquot unquam veram Deitatem agnoverunt sapientiores. Certè ipsis fanioribus Ethnicis ridicula visa fuit, quam quidam eorum vates tradiderunt, Θεογονία. Dei semper fuerunt , nati nunquam sunt, æterni sunt futuri, alibi Cicero. Nec difficile est adstruere , quod clamant quævis Dei prædicata ; adeo se undique rationes offerunt , sive Independentiam ejus spectes , sive Perfectionis infinitatem , sive existendi Necessitatem. Hanc si consideres , prohibet ea à Deo omnes existentiæ limites ; dum ab ipso removet omne non-existere. Etenim ubi est aliqua durationis extremitas, ibidem ipsum τὸ non-existere habet locum. Itaque ubi non-existere locum habere nequit, ibi nec ullum existentiæ principium; quod quicquid agnoscit, aliquando non fuit: neque ejusdem finis; quem quicquid exspectat, aliquando non erit. Præterea , cum omnis duratio æstimanda sit ex natura entium quæ durare dicuntur , ea nulla Enti perfectissimo nisi perfectissima est adscribenda. Jam verò unamquamque durationem eo magis perfectam esse quo minus angustis terminis est circumscri-pta , per se claret. Ea ergò demùm Deo summè perfecto erit digna , quæ nullo modo limitata. Denique , aut jam semper Deus extitit , aut ne nunc quidem exstitit. Si enim aliquando nonnon-fuerit, unde obscuro esse coepit? Num ex sese? At quod non est, non magis se actuare potest, quam idem esse simul potest & non-esse. An ab alio vis productum? Verum sic totam tollis Independentiam; hoc est, omnem re ipsâ Deitatem. Pari ratione, si nunc Deus est, semper quoque erit: cum nec intrinseca aliquâ indigentiâ deficiat Perfectissimum; nec extrinseca vi aboleatur Independens. Ne addam, causas subordinatas finitæ durationis reduci debere vel ad seriem aliquam earundem in qua primam invenire non detur (quam implicare, antè ostendimus); vel ad aliquod earum principium primum, quod extitit semper sine principio, &c, quia sine principio, etiam sine fine.
units.tr: But let us come nearer to the proof of these points. As for the first part of our definition, in which we asserted that eternity is interminable, nearly everyone who has ever acknowledged the true Deity, and the wiser among them, has accepted it without reluctance. Even the most frenzied heathens found ridiculous the Theogonia [Θεογονία] that some of their poets handed down. Elsewhere Cicero says: the gods have always existed, were never born, and will be eternal. Nor is it difficult to establish what every predicate of God proclaims, for reasons present themselves on every side, whether you consider his independence, the infinity of his perfection, or the necessity of his existence. If you consider this last, it excludes from God every limit of existence, since it removes from him all non-existence. For wherever there is some end to duration, there non-existence has its place. Therefore, where non-existence cannot have a place, there is no beginning of existence either. Whatever acknowledges such a beginning once did not exist, and whatever has no end is one that will never cease to exist. Moreover, since all duration must be judged by the nature of the beings said to endure, no duration can be ascribed to the most perfect Being except the most perfect duration. And it is clear in itself that each duration is the more perfect the less it is confined within narrow limits. Therefore that duration alone will be worthy of the most perfectly perfect God which is in no way limited. Finally, either God has always existed, or he has not existed even now. For if he had at some time not existed, from what did he begin to be? From himself? But what does not exist cannot bring itself into act any more than the same thing can at once both be and not be. Or was he produced by force from another? But then you remove all independence altogether, that is, all true Deity. By the same reasoning, if God now exists, he will also always exist, since the Most Perfect cannot fail through any intrinsic need, nor can the Independent be abolished by any external force. I need not add that the subordinate causes of finite duration must be traced back either to some series of them in which a first cannot be found (which we have already shown to be self-contradictory), or to some first principle of them, which has always existed without beginning, etc.; and because it is without beginning, it is also without end.

units.la: Sed definio probare quod minùs controversum. Potiùs ad alteram nostræ descriptionis partem progredior, quâ Simultaneam esse Æternitatis durationem, diximus. Eam impugnare laborant Socini & Vorstii sectatores; qui, dum nimiè sibi plaudunt in quibusdam quas hic urgent argutiis, re ipsâ parùm se subtiles probant in hoc negotio, quando non attendunt, quam malè cohæreat, eandem durationem affirmare infinitam, & tamen per temporum intervalla successivè fluentem: quo nihil dici potest crassius atque ineptius. Id enim manifestissimum est, omnem successivam durationem partibus constare; ob ipsum enim partium sibi succedentium lapsum successiva est & dicitur. Ergò rogare lubet, quas illi infinitæ assignare velis partes, quos annos, quæ sæcula; aut saltem (ne de vocibus laboremus) quas spatii temporalis partes illis æquipollentes? Vis eas finitas? At sic clarè negas totius durationis infinitatem. An verò infinitas? Sume ergò v. c. sæcula infinita. At jam quos annos statues? Etiam, opinor, infinitos. Fuerit itaque infinitorum annorum numerus numero infinitorum sæculorum vel major, vel æqualis, vel minor. Majorem non dixeris, nisi infinitum negaveris numerum sæculorum: quandoquidem infinitum omne majus suâ naturâ respuit. Æqualem si volueris, vel etiam minorem, omnibus, quantum à ratione recedas, palam facies nimiùm. Nullius ergò successionis capax est quæ infinita existit duratio. His adde, permanentiam rei successivam, quemadmodum includit fuisse & fore, ita quoque involvere non-esse. Quod enim fuit, quà tale haud amplius est; quod erit, nondum est; quod jam
units.tr: But I will undertake to prove what is less disputed. I now proceed to the second part of our definition, in which we said that the duration of eternity is simultaneous. The followers of Socinus and Vorstius labour to attack this. While they applaud themselves too much for certain subtleties they press here, they in fact show themselves not very subtle in this matter, since they do not notice how poorly it fits together to affirm that the same duration is infinite and yet flows successively through intervals of time. Nothing can be said that is cruder or more absurd. For it is most evident that every successive duration consists of parts, since it is successive and is called so precisely because its parts succeed one another and pass away. Therefore I should like to ask what infinite parts you wish to assign to it, what years, what ages; or at least (not to quarrel over words) what parts of temporal space equivalent to them? Do you want them to be finite? Then you clearly deny the infinity of the whole duration. Or do you want them infinite? Then take, for example, infinite ages. But what years will you then assign to them? Infinite ones too, I suppose. So the number of infinite years would be either greater than, equal to, or less than the number of infinite ages. You could not say greater, unless you denied that the number of ages is infinite, since by its nature every infinite thing rejects being greater. If you want it equal, or even less, you will make it plain to everyone how far you have departed from reason. Therefore an infinite duration is capable of no succession whatever. Add to this that what is permanent in its successive form, just as it includes having been and being about to be, so too it involves not-being. For what has been is, as such, no longer; what will be is not yet; what now is will soon not be. Therefore contingency accompanies such succession, and this absolutely no necessity of existing, already demonstrated in God, can suffer at all.

units.la: V. Eandem esse successionis expertem, demonstratur. jam est, mox non erit. Successionem ergò talem comitatur contingentia*: hanc verò planè nullam patitur omnimoda Necessitas exstiendi, de Deo jam demonstrata. Quid? quod duratio per temporum articulos fluens nunquam fit infinitè perfecta, adeoque nec perfectionis Divinæ infinitati congrua. Quæ enim duratio est in continuo fluxu, dum singulis momentis sumit incrementa, nunquam dici potest esse tanta, quanta esse potest: quæ tamen infinitatis proprietas est. Confer quæ hanc in rem jam attulimus, §. iii. Denique, quodcunque continuò est actuandum id Independens esse nequit, neque cadit in rem cujus ipsa intrinseca natura est pura puta Independentia. Hæc in extrema semper est actualitate, cum quantum in unoquoque ente est potentiæ, tantundem in eo sit dependentiæ. Actuandum autem esse de novo omne successivum, patet, quia quod succedet, nondum est, sed, quatenus aliquando erit, nunc in præsenti tantum esse potest. Liquet ergò ex dictis, cui durationi nec origo dedit initium, nec casus dabit finem, eidem neque tempora dare incrementum. Liquet, quæ momentaneum & quotidie orientem nobis fingit Deum alium & eundem, Æternitatem, quam verbis ponit, re ipsâ tollere opinionem. Quod demonstrandum erat.
units.tr: V. That it is free from succession is demonstrated. What is more, a duration that flows through the moments of time is never infinitely perfect, and so is not congruent with the infinity of divine perfection. For a duration that is in continual flux, since it gains increments at each moment, can never be said to be as great as it can be; yet this is the property of infinity. Compare what we have already brought forward on this point in section iii. Finally, whatever must be continually actuated cannot be Independent, nor does it belong to a thing whose intrinsic nature is pure Independence. This is always in extreme actuality, since in every being there is as much dependence as there is potency. Now it is clear that all successive duration must be actuated anew, because what is to succeed does not yet exist, and insofar as it will at some time be, it can now be only in the present. It is therefore clear from what has been said that to a duration to which no origin gave a beginning, and to which no accident will give an end, time cannot give any increase either. It is clear that the opinion which, in words, posits an eternity, but which imagines a God who is momentary, newly arising for us each day, and other and yet the same, in fact removes eternity. This was what had to be demonstrated.
VI.

units.la: Ita facilè hujus veritatis certitudo ostenditur: at non ideo perinde claram eam habemus per omnia idem. Sic enim fermè nobiscum comparatum est, ut quæ à finitis creaturarum perfectionibus recedunt nimiùm, vix ea nisi negativè & conceptu satis confuso concipiamus. Quapropter ne quicquam curabimus prævaricationem inferentium, simultaneam Dei durationem haud esse, eo quod sic neutiquam nostræ successivæ durationi coëxistere posset, nisi hoc ipso admittatur, nostrum præsens, præteritum, & futurum existere simul, quippe quæ eidem indivisæ Æternitati pariter coëxistant. Verum reddere isti debebant necessitatis rationem, ob quam nequeant coëxistere sibi duæ res disparis naturæ, & quarum altera se alio habeat modo ac altera. Speciem haberet objectio, si assereremus, Deo convenire verum aliquod præteritum & futurum, quod cum præsenti ejusdem sit idem. Sequeretur enim tunc, uti Dei præteritum coincidit cum præsenti, ita quoque nostrum præteritum, quod
units.tr: In this way the certainty of this truth is easily shown, yet we do not have it equally clear in every respect. For we are so constituted that we can scarcely conceive, except negatively and in a rather confused concept, those things which depart too far from the finite perfections of creatures. So we shall not trouble ourselves over the sophistry of those who infer that God's duration is not simultaneous, on the ground that it could in no way coexist with our successive duration unless it were granted that our present, past and future exist all at once, since these would coexist alike with the same undivided Eternity. But they ought to give the reason of necessity why two things of unlike nature, one of which is related in a different way from the other, cannot coexist. The objection would have some appearance if we asserted that some true past and future belongs to God, which is the same as his present. For it would then follow that, just as God's past coincides with the present, so too our past, which coexisted with the divine past, ought to coincide with our present. But since we have long since entirely removed from the Eternity of God all those differences of time which rule in our duration, there is no consequence in this inference.

units.la: * quod coëxtitit præterito divino, coincidere debere cum nostro præsenti. Atqui cum jam dudum omnes istas temporum diffe- rentias, quæ in nostra duratione dominantur, penitus ab Æternitate Dei secluserimus, nulla est in hac illatione sequela. Habent interim hic recentiores Doctores nodum, quem claris suis & distinctis ideis solvent nunquam: imprimis quando ipsi pari argumentandi modo tam vehementer in Immensitatis divinæ negotio urgent, non posse Deum per essentiam suam rebus extensis præsentem esse, nisi hæc ipsa pariter sit extensa. An verò statuent quoque, non posse coëxistere Deum nostræ durationi successivæ, nisi pariter ipse successivè duret? Sumant Viri acu- tum, & istis se expediant, si possint! Si nequeant, videant tandem famosæ suæ illationis imbecillitatem.
units.tr: Meanwhile, the more recent Doctors here have a knot which they will never untie with their clear and distinct ideas, especially when they themselves, using the same kind of argument, press so vehemently in the matter of the divine Immensity that God cannot be present to extended things through his essence unless he is himself likewise extended. But will they also hold that God cannot coexist with our successive duration unless he too endures successively? Let the sharp men take up the question and extricate themselves, if they can! If they cannot, let them at last see the weakness of their famous inference.

units.la: Etsi verò Divina duratio adeo nostræ sit dispar, atque coe- xistentia illius cum hac nihil planè faciat ad ipsam Æternita- tis secundum se consideratæ naturam (nihilo enim illa extitit imperfectior ante conditum hoc universum, cum nulla ei co- extitit, vel adextitit potius, creatura) non tamen nego, quin, ad juvandum nostrum qualemcunque de Æternitate conceptum, utile sit eam cogitare per relationem aliquam ad spatia re- rum temporalium: ita ut mens nostra sibi facilius illam repræsentet, nec incommodè, tanquam durationem excedon- tem omnia spatia, non tantum quibus creaturæ aliquæ durâ- runt, sed & quibus durare quandocunque vel potuerunt, vel poterunt. In quo repræsentamine includitur successio (absque qua durationem aliquam concipere difficile nobis est, si non impossibile) at non à parte Æternitatis, sed à parte rerum quæ Æternitati adexistere saltem potuisse concipiuntur. Ita, si vellim mihi repræsentare Deum secundum Æternitatem suam ante mundi primordia existentem, non potero distinctius, quam si concepero, tam perfectam esse Divinam durationem, ut si qualiscunque conceptibilis duratio successiva ante initium hujus Universi extitisset, illi simultaneâ suâ Æternitate coëxtitisset Deus. Et hæc sunt spatia illa imaginaria temporalia, tanto hodiè conatu impugnata à multis; qui procul dubio metuunt, ne sint satis subtiles, nisi ipsum quoque nihil sibi sumant impugnandum.
units.tr: Although the divine duration is so unlike ours, and its coexistence with ours makes no difference at all to the nature of Eternity considered in itself (for it was no less perfect before this universe was created, since no creature coexisted with it, or rather, adexisted to it), I nevertheless do not deny that, to help our conception of Eternity, however imperfect it may be, it is useful to think of it through some relation to the spans of temporal things. In this way our mind represents it more easily, and not inappropriately, as a duration exceeding all spans: not only those through which some creatures endure, but also those through which they have been able, or will be able, to endure at any time. This representation includes succession (without which it is difficult, if not impossible, for us to conceive any duration), but not on the side of Eternity; it is on the side of things which are conceived as being able at least to adexist to Eternity. Thus, if I wished to represent to myself God existing before the beginnings of the world according to his Eternity, I could do no more distinctly than by conceiving the divine duration to be so perfect that, if any conceivable successive duration had existed before the beginning of this Universe, God would have coexisted with it by his simultaneous Eternity. These are the imaginary temporal spans so vigorously attacked today by many, who doubtless fear that they are not subtle enough, unless they also take on the refutation of nothing itself.

units.la: An verò mallent illis realia spatia temporalia substituere? Sic videtur:
units.tr: But would they rather substitute real temporal spans for these? It seems so:

units.la: VII. Relatio ad temporalia spatia, seu vera, seu possibilia, qui juvet nostrum Æternitatis conceptum. VIII. Æternita-
units.tr: VII. Relation to temporal spans, whether real or possible, which helps our conception of Eternity. VIII. Eterni-

units.la: videtur : ne scilicet mundum, qui iis nullos extensionis suæ fines habet, durationė non satis amplum nobis imaginemur. Saltem hinc non multum abesse mihi videntur, qui possibilem mundi Æternitatem asserunt difficulter refelli posse ; tantum si statuatur Æternitas mundi alterius generis, quam illa Dei. Verùm, cujuscunque generis statuatur mundi duratio, semper saltem successiva est ; sic prorsus exigente ejusdem in exsistendo contingentiâ. Talem autem Æternam esse non posse, §. v. firmissimè jam demonstravimus. Alia, quæ ipsa Creaturæ notio suppeditat, argumenta hic transeo, infrà forsan urgenda suo loco. Exemtus nostri sic solus ab ordine secli, Temporibus leges qui das / Tibi tempora leges Nulla dabunt, nullam ponunt cui tempora metam. Nostra quidem assiduo labuntur tempora motu, Dum nova sunt semper, tacitisque senescimus annis : Tu verò Tibi semper eras, Tibi semper es idem; Cui mors exactos veniens non supputat annos. Ut semel ergo Tibi sapiamus, lubrica vitæ Tu nos fata doce, & quo se mora porrigat ævi; Ut mens juncta Deo studiis det tempora sacris!
units.tr: Namely, lest we imagine the world, which has no limits of extension in these spans, as not ample enough in duration. At least from this, those who assert that the possible eternity of the world can hardly be refuted do not seem to me far off, provided only that an eternity of a different kind is ascribed to the world than that of God. But whatever kind of duration is given to the world, it is always at least successive, since its contingency in existing absolutely demands this. That such a duration cannot be eternal we have already most firmly demonstrated in §. v. Other arguments which the very notion of creature supplies I pass over here, to be pressed perhaps later in their proper place. You who alone are set apart from the order of the age, who give laws to times: no times will give laws to you, and they set no limit upon you. Our times slip away with constant motion, always new while we grow old through silent years; but you were always for yourself, you are always the same, and death, coming, does not count your exhausted years. So that we may once for all become wise toward you, teach us the slippery fates of life and how far the delay of our age extends, so that the mind joined to God may give its times to sacred studies!
EXERCITATION NINE, ON THE IMMENSE GOD.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Immensitas Divina quæ; & quâ ratione ab Omni-præsentia distincta? II. Spatia Imaginaria quid; & quis eorum in Immensitate Dei concipienda usus? III. Car-
units.tr: I. What is divine immensity, and how is it distinguished from omnipresence? II. What are imaginary spaces, and what use do they have in conceiving the immensity of God? III. Car-

units.la: III. Cartesianorum de Omnipræsentia Dei philosophatio; & quædam in eam animadversiones. IV. Immensitatis Divinæ contra Vorstium & Socinianos demonstratio. V. Omnipræsentiæ Divinæ essentialis contra Cartesianos assertio. VI. Difficultatibus quibusdam horum obviam itur. VII. Immensitatem, non Ubiquitatem strictè dictam, solius Dei esse, probatur.
units.tr: III. The Cartesians' philosophizing on the omnipresence of God, with some remarks on it. IV. A demonstration of divine immensity against Vorstius and the Socinians. V. An assertion of the essential omnipresence of God against the Cartesians. VI. Some difficulties of these men are met. VII. It is proved that immensity, and not ubiquity strictly so called, belongs to God alone.

units.la: Idimus, quo modo se habeat Deus in ordine ad nostrum tempus per Æternitatem; videndum qui sese habeat Numen in ordine ad spatia localia per Immensitatem. Quæ duo cum valdè sint analoga, quanto rectius perspecta fuerit natura illius, tanto facilior erit meditatio hujus. Eâ notamus supereminentiam illam divinæ perfectionis, quâ per essentiam suam, modo tamen perfectissimo ac sibi convenienti, exsistit Deus ubicunque corpus est, vel esse potest. Observandum imprimis, cum dixi existere Deum, ubi exsistit, modo perfectissimo ac sibi convenienti, ante omnia me velle hic remotissimum habere conceptum cujuscunque propriè dictæ diffusionis aut extensionis; quæ, uti partes involvit, ita naturæ spirituali atque independenti planè repugnat. Magnus Deus noster est, sed sine quantitate, atque ideo Immensus: uti scitè alibi Augustinus. Absit ergò, ut hoc loco Deum nobis imaginemur per modum subtilissimi corporis cuncta pervadentis; quod quidam non sine calumnia objiciunt. Dico, non sine calumnia: nam jam olim vetus schola asseruit, Deum itâ totum esse in toto mundo, ut totus pariter sit in singulis ejus partibus; i. e. ut mundo divisibili ac partes habenti ipse coexistat quidem, verum absque partibus sui, ac modo prorsus indivisibili. Sed & illud attendendum est in antecessum, non tantùm hic notari Omnipræsentiam vel Ubiquitatem strictè dictam, quatenus dicit relationem veræ præsentiæ ad corpora de facto existentia. Latius patet Immensitatis conceptus; quippe qui, & Ubiquitatem includit, & insuper ponit, etiam istic existere.
units.tr: We have seen how God stands in relation to our time through eternity; now we must consider how the Deity stands in relation to local spaces through immensity. Since these two are very closely analogous, the more accurately the nature of the one is understood, the easier will be the consideration of the other. By this we mark that supreme excellence of the divine perfection by which God exists, through his essence, wherever a body is or can be, in a most perfect manner and one fitting to himself.
