It must be observed above all that, when I said God exists wherever he exists, in a most perfect manner fitting to himself, I wish first of all to have here the most remote concept of any properly so called diffusion or extension. Such extension, since it involves parts, is entirely repugnant to a spiritual and independent nature. Great is our God, but without quantity, and therefore Immense, as Augustine says elsewhere, wisely. Far be it, then, that in this place we should imagine God to us after the manner of a most subtle body pervading all things; which some object, not without calumny. I say not without calumny, for long ago the old school asserted that God is so wholly in the whole world that he is equally whole in each of its parts; that is, that he coexists with the divisible world, which has parts, yet without parts of himself, and in a wholly indivisible manner. But it must also be noted beforehand that what is marked here is not only omnipresence or ubiquity strictly so called, insofar as it denotes the relation of true presence to bodies actually existing. The concept of immensity is wider, since it includes ubiquity and moreover posits that God exists even where there is no body at present.

units.la: { } Ubiquitatem strictè dictam: see Vorstius. exi-stere Deum, ubi quidem jam corpus non est, attamen per potentiam Divinam esse saltem potest. In quantum ergo vera præsentia, per actualem creaturæ cujuspiam coëxistentiam, ad Immensitatem per se nihil pertinet, facilè intelligimus, quomodo Immensus extiterit Deus, nullo etiam existente corpore; & quâ ratione ipse sibi dicatur esse locus. Hoc sensu rectè ille:
units.tr: { } Ubiquity strictly so called: see Vorstius. God exists where indeed no body is now, yet is at least able to be there through divine power. Insofar, then, as true presence, through the actual coexistence of some creature, pertains in itself nothing to immensity, we easily understand how God was immense even when no body existed, and in what sense he is said to be a place to himself. In this sense that poet rightly says:

units.la: Dic ubi tunc esset, cum praeter eum nihil esset?
units.tr: Tell me where he then was, when nothing existed besides him?

units.la: Tunc, ubi nunc; in se: sibimet nam sufficit ipse.
units.tr: Then, where he is now: in himself; for he suffices to himself.

units.la: Interim, uti ante dixi Æternitatem, etsi nihil nostri temporis involvit, rectè tamen, ad conceptum nostrum juvandum, cogitari cum respectu ad nostra tempora; ita quoque Immensitas per modum alicujus præsentiæ, etsi eam actualem non necessariò includat, non incommodè nobis repræsentatur. Ita enim Deus absolutissimè existit in se ipso, etiam illic ubi nunc nullum existit corpus, ut tamen, si ibi, ubi nunc nihil est, per potentiam divinam poneretur aliquod corpus, illi etiam essentiâ suâ Deus intimè coëxisteret præsens: quemadmodum scilicet ante hujus Universi productionem in se ipso sic extitit ubi nunc est mundus, ut, simulac hic existere cœpit, mox ei verè coëxiterit præsentissimus Deus. Et hic est conceptus ille, nimium à quibusdam hodiè vexatus, qui vulgò venit nomine Spatiorum Imaginariorum: quem quomodo citra contradictionem rejicere possint, quotquot mundi nostri extensionem non agnoscunt infinitam, haud equidem video. Certè, admissis aliquibus Universi hujus limitibus, evidentissimum est, extra illos, ubicunque demum fuerint, per inexhaustam Dei vim corpus aliquod poni posse. Etiam per mox demonstranda patebit, non posse tale corpus poni, nisi Deus vi infinitæ suæ perfectionis eidem coëxistat præsens. At dum ista cogito, eo ipso & spatia imaginaria, id est, corpora quædam possibilia, & pariter Immensitatem divinam per relationem aliquam ad ista spatia, concipio. Quapropter, cum hujus conceptûs fundamenta sint, & mundi finitudo ab una parte, & exsuperantia tum perfectissimæ Infinitatis tum etiam incomprehensæ Potentiæ divinæ ab altera parte, mirum mihi semper visum fuit, res adeo claras & distinctas capere non posse, vel potius non velle, illos qui tanto conatu hæc spatia exagitant, tanquam nescio quæ absurditatum portenta & chimæras. Sed hinc illæ lacrymæ! Vorticosum suum mundum re verâ infinitum ponere necessum habent; atque indè nullum corpori possibilirelinquunt extra eum locum: imò ( si quod res est dicere liceat ) dum duo immensa repugnant, quam mundo affingunt infinitatem Immensitatis, Deo re ipsâ derogant.
units.tr: Meanwhile, as I said before of eternity, although it involves nothing of our time, it is nevertheless fitting, to help our concept, to think of it with reference to our times; so too immensity, though it does not necessarily include actual presence, is not inappropriately represented to us by way of some presence. For God exists most absolutely in himself even there where at present no body exists, yet so that, if some body were placed there by divine power where now there is nothing, God would coexist there with it, present in his essence, intimately. Just as before the production of this universe he existed in himself where the world now is, so that, as soon as the world began to exist here, God, most present, truly coexisted with it. And this is that concept, too much harassed by some today, which commonly goes by the name of imaginary spaces. How those who do not acknowledge the infinite extension of our world can reject it without contradiction, I indeed do not see. Certainly, once some limits of this universe are admitted, it is most evident that beyond those limits, wherever they may be, some body can be placed through the inexhaustible power of God. It will also become clear from what is about to be demonstrated that such a body cannot be placed unless God, by the power of his infinite perfection, is present and coexistent with it. But while I think these things, I conceive at the same time of imaginary spaces, that is, of certain possible bodies, and likewise of the divine immensity through some relation to those spaces. Therefore, since the foundations of this concept are, on the one side, the finitude of the world, and on the other the transcendence both of most perfect infinity and of the incomprehensible power of God, it has always seemed to me strange that those who with such effort worry over these spaces, as if they were some monstrous absurdities and chimeras, cannot, or rather will not, grasp things so clear and distinct. But hence those tears! They must posit their vortical world as truly infinite, and so leave no place for a possible body outside it. Indeed (if it is permitted to say what is the case), while they assert two immense things at once, the infinity of immensity they ascribe to the world actually detracts from God.

units.la: Leve enim fuisset de Imaginariis Spatiis controversiam movere, nisi quoque in discrimen adduceretur vera Dei Παντοχωρία, & essentialis Omnipræsentia. Socino ac Vorstio jam olim placuit, Deum essentiâ suâ omni mundo præsentem esse, negare. Riserunt quoque alii præsentiam Dei atomicam & atopicam, ut ipsi ajunt. Impia verò hæc semper visa fuerunt, & in Dei Immensitatem injuria quam maximè, rectum sentientibus; qui omnibus illis semper oppositum illud vulgare,
units.tr: For the controversy about imaginary spaces would be a light matter, were not the true Pantochoria of God and his essential omnipresence also brought into danger. Long ago it pleased Socinus and Vorstius to deny that God is present to the whole world by his essence. Others also mocked the presence of God as "atomic" and "atopic," as they call it. But these views have always seemed impious to those who think rightly, and especially an injury to the immensity of God; and against all of them they have always set that common saying:
Essentially, presently: God is here and everywhere, powerfully.

units.la: Istorum tamen insignia qui sibi aptent hodiè deesse minimè videntur. Non meis hæc dicam verbis, sed Cl. Vogelsangii, qui itâ hac de re alibi disserit. „Cartesius è tripode veluti pronunciat, Deum ubique non existere: sed ubique tamen esse ratione suæ potentiæ. Quia scilicet in Deo nulla sit extensio substantiæ, sed potentia duntaxat, &c. Ita visum Cartesio fuit sive vaticinari, sive incassum furere. Quem tota armenta sequuntur. Itaque nuperi quidam Theologi, etiam Reformatæ communionis, abnegatâ Numinis Immensitate, prorsus ad gustum pravitatis hæreticæ Vorstianorum, Socinianorum, & Remonstrantium, definiunt, Omnipræsentiam Dei nihil aliud esse, quam extrinseçam denominationem, natam ex operatione Dei, qua in omnibus rebus corporeis operatur, & propter illam operationem iis præsens esse dicitur. Vel, Omnipræsentiam Dei nihil aliud esse, quam efficacissimam Dei voluntatem, qua omnia sustentat & gubernat, explicandam ab operatione, qua extra se aliud producit. Immensitatem essentiæ, quâ Deus excedat mundi terminos, quaque citra dimensionum interstitia limitesve Deus ante mundum conditum incola fui fuerit, uti neque potuerit ullam creaturam producere, cui non adforet intimè per essentiam suam sine ulla mutatione fui, planè tollunt: atque fundamentum
units.tr: Those who would now claim these marks for themselves seem by no means lacking. I shall not put this in my own words but in those of the distinguished Vogelsang, who discusses the matter this way elsewhere. "Descartes pronounces, as if from the tripod, that God does not exist everywhere, yet he is everywhere by reason of his power. Namely because in God there is no extension of substance, but only power, etc. Whether Descartes was prophesying or raving to no purpose, that is how it seemed to him. Whole herds follow him. And so certain recent theologians, even of the Reformed communion, having denied the immensity of God, define quite in the taste of the heretical perversity of the Vorstians, the Socinians and the Remonstrants: the omnipresence of God is nothing other than an extrinsic denomination, arising from the operation by which God works in all corporeal things, and on account of which he is said to be present to them. Or: the omnipresence of God is nothing other than the most efficacious will of God, by which he sustains and governs all things, to be explained from the operation by which he produces something outside himself. They plainly remove the immensity of essence, by which God exceeds the limits of the world, and by which, without any interval of dimensions or limits, God was present before the world was made, just as he could not have produced any creature to which he was not intimately present through his essence without any change in himself. And they make the foundation

units.la: „ Omnipræsentiæ Divinæ nullum aliud faciunt, quàm Dei potentiam, sive potentissimam illius operationem. Neve tamen „Deum toto mundo veluti proscribere videantur, commenti „ sunt, essentiam Dei, prout nempe creaturis illa præsens intelligi „debet, nihil aliud esse, quam cogitationem Dei fœcundam, cœli „terræque creatricem, conservatricem, atque gubernatricem. Hæc ille Theologus eruditissimus. Egregiam verò laudem referre merentur, qui in gratiam unius Cartefii sic hoc loco philosophari amant, ut nihil tandem reliquum faciant, quo rectum sentientium sententia à Socini ac Vorstii errore distinguatur. Neque enim putandum est, quod quidam velint, omnem hanc litem meram tandem logomachiam fore, quum iidem auctores passim etiam largiri videantur, Deum quoque per essentiam creaturis suis esse præsentem. Nam ignota non sunt artificia, quibus quod mentem aperit apertius mox interpretatione in speciem meliori palliatur. Si nihil sibi cum istorum sententia commune velint Cartefii asseclæ, candidè repudium mittant crudis istiusmodi phrasibus. Id quamdiu non palam faciunt, nunquam credendum, viros sapientes in re ardua lusus velle facere in mera voce, recedendo citra ullam necessitatem à communi loquendi modo, mox tamen ad eum revertendo. Laudandus mihi hic est candor saltem Poireti; cujus viri vix unquam sine præfatione honoris mentionem faciunt Novatores. Is clarius ista mysteria nobis revelat, cum dicit rotundo ore, Cartefium, Wittichium, Forgæum, aliosque Cartefianos, quando dixerunt, Deum omnibus rebus præsentem esse essentiâ, essentialiter, ratione essentiæ, difficultatum quarundam causâ, usos fuisse vocibus deceptricibus, ex usu ordinario non significantibus verum, sed ipsi verborum significationi reluctantibus. Et quidem dum hoc pronunciat, Cartefium recté philosophantem se sequi profitetur. Cogit. Rat. Pag. 31. Ecquis istas logomachias habeat? Ecquis fidem adhibeat amplius viris utentibus, difficultatum quarundam causa, vocibus deceptricibus, nec significantibus verum? Cavendum profectò iis, qui vocibus deceptricibus decipi hic nolunt; nec credendum facilè Viris qui quandò difficultatibus urgentur, confugere non metuunt ad voces non significantes verum!
units.tr: of divine omnipresence nothing other than the power of God, or rather his most powerful operation. Yet lest they seem to banish God wholly from the world, they have devised that the essence of God, namely as it ought to be understood to be present to creatures, is nothing other than the fruitful thought of God, creator, conserver and governor of heaven and earth. So says that most learned theologian. But they deserve distinguished praise, those who love to philosophise on this point so much for the sake of Descartes alone that in the end they leave nothing by which the opinion of those who think rightly is distinguished from the error of Socinus and Vorstius. For it is not to be thought, as some want, that this whole dispute will finally be mere logomachy, since the same authors everywhere seem to concede that God is also present to his creatures in essence. For the tricks are not unknown by which what reveals the mind more openly is soon cloaked in a more pleasing interpretation. If the followers of Descartes want nothing in common with that opinion, let them frankly send away such crude phrases. As long as they do not do this openly, one must never believe that wise men want to play with mere words in a difficult matter, departing without any necessity from the common way of speaking, yet soon returning to it. Here the candour of Poiret alone deserves praise; the novelists scarcely ever mention that man without a preface of honour. He reveals these mysteries to us more clearly when he says plainly that Descartes, Wittich, Forgé and the other Cartesians, when they said that God is present to all things in essence, essentially, by reason of essence, for the sake of certain difficulties, had used deceptive words, which in ordinary usage do not signify the truth but resist the very meaning of the words. And indeed, while he pronounces this, he professes that he follows Descartes in philosophising correctly. Cogit. Rat. Pag. 31. Who would put up with these logomachies? Who would give further faith to men who use, for the sake of certain difficulties, deceptive words, not signifying the truth? Surely one must beware of those who here refuse to be deceived by deceptive words; nor should one readily believe men who, whenever they are pressed by difficulties, are not afraid to take refuge in words that do not signify the truth!

units.la: Nos candor delectat: atque ideò simpliciter probamus communem munem orthodoxorum sententiam, quæ semper contra quosvis definivit, summum Numen ratione Immensitatis existere & in omni mundo, & extra eundem in infinitum; nec tantum <bl>ἐνεργητικῶς</bl>, sive quoad operationes & potentiam, sed & <bl>ἀντωδῶς</bl>, per ipsam essentiam suam & naturam. Id nullo negotio demonstratur adversus eos, qui Deo ratione essentiæ aliquod saltem Ubi tribuunt; quales qui cum Socino faciunt Vorstius aliique. Definiunt hi, cœlum cœlorum locum esse in quo sic habitet Divina natura, ut indè per providam tantum operationem suis adsit creaturis: haud aliter ac Sol essentia suâ in medio cœli positus vim suam indè per omnem mundum diffundit; vel, uti Rex in palatio habitans curam suam per omnes regni partes extendit. Sed quam nihil Deo dignum istiusmodi comprehendant cogitata, facilè illi intelligunt, qui, quis Deus sit, satis tantùm attendunt. Certè quodcunque ab aliquo limitatur quomodocunque, etiam ratione sui Ubi, id pendet ab eo quod in causa exististit, cur ipsum sit limitatum, & tanto Ubi, non majori, quasi circumscriptum. Si quod ergò Ubi Independenti Dei essentiæ tribuendum est, id ei assignandum, quod sit omninò independens; nullisque adeò artatum limitibus, nullis definitum terminis. Tale verò neque cœli ambitu, neque ipsius mundi finitis spatiis comprehenditur, sed omnia illa excedit infinities. Porrò, cum in Ens perfectissimum nil cadat nisi quod perfectio sit, etiam <bl>ᾱ</bl> Ubi, quod essentiæ Divinæ tribuitur, erit perfectio. Quæcunque autem Deo tribuitur perfectio, ea prorsus infinita est. Ubi ergò essentiæ Divinæ congruum tantum id est, quod est infinitum & <bl>ἄπειρον</bl>. Quid? quod in locis hisce inferioribus Deum saltem actuali operatione & providentiâ præsentem largiantur adversarii. Ubi autem operatur Deus, ibidem essentiâ suâ existit præsens. Nam, ut agere supponit esse, ita hic agere supponit hic esse; cum nihil agere in distans sit certissimum. Stringit efficaciter imprimis hæc ratio, si Deum non nisi immediatè per essentiam operari posse cogitemus. Nec enim ejusdem patitur Independentia, ut causarum intermediarum, seu instrumentorum, adhibitus sit in effectu quopiam producendo ministerio. Talem tamen alienæ opis indigum Deum necesse habent statuere, qui essentiam
units.tr: We like candour, so we simply approve the common opinion of the orthodox, which has always been defined against all comers: the supreme Deity exists by reason of immensity in every world and beyond it to infinity; and not only energetically [ἐνεργητικῶς], that is, as to his operations and power, but also essentially [ἀντωδῶς], through his very essence and nature. This is demonstrated without any trouble against those who ascribe to God some kind of Where, at least with respect to his essence. Such are Vorstius and others who side with Socinus. They define the heaven of heavens as the place in which the divine nature dwells in such a way that from there it is present to its creatures only by its providential operation: just as the sun, placed in the middle of the heavens, spreads its power through the whole world by its essence, or as a king who lives in a palace extends his care through all parts of his kingdom. But those who pay sufficient attention to what God is will readily understand how little such notions are worthy of God. Certainly whatever is limited in any way, even by its own Where, depends on something in the cause that determines why it is limited, and is circumscribed by just so much place and no more. If, therefore, any Where is to be attributed to the independent essence of God, it must be assigned to him in the sense that he is wholly independent, and so is bound by no limits and defined by no boundaries. Such a being is not contained within the circuit of heaven, nor within the finite spaces of the world itself, but exceeds all those infinitely. Furthermore, since nothing falls into the most perfect Being except what is perfection, the Where that is attributed to the divine essence will also be a perfection. But whatever perfection is attributed to God is altogether infinite. Therefore the only Where fitting the divine essence is that which is infinite and [ἄπειρον] boundless. What of the fact that our opponents grant God to be present in these lower places at least by his actual operation and providence? But where God operates, there he exists present by his essence. For as operating presupposes being, so operating here presupposes being here, since it is most certain that nothing acts at a distance. This argument presses especially hard if we think of God as able to operate only immediately, through his essence. For his independence does not allow the use of intermediate causes or instruments in producing some effect. Yet they must hold that God, who in essence is confined to heaven, nonetheless needs the help of another and grants that he operates on earth, in places far removed from heaven.

units.la: K tiam cœlo includunt, operari tamen in terris, locis tantùm à cœlo remotis, largiuntur. Postremùm, dicant isti, obsecrò, quid respondendum censeant, si rogavero, num totum cœlum essentia Divina occupet, num aliquam tantum ejus inhabitet partem? Si modicam cœli regionem Deo habitaculum assignent, nisi ei affixum velint Numen, cogitare licebit exspatiari ipsum subindè, ac mutare domicilium. Si toti cœlo præsentem malint Dei essentiam, scire lubet, cur istis tantum mundi spatiis sese includerit ille, cui omnis hæc ingens machina quasi nihilum est? Quæve tandem istæ sint causæ, quibus tantum Numen à cæteris mundi regionibus secludatur? Nimis crassum est ac insipidum, quod hic metuunt, ne Deo malè fit a vicinia rerum sordidarum. Sordida profectò cogitatio, nec responsione digna! Cum enim ne creatus quidem spiritus sordibus leprosi corporis inquinetur, quanto minus essentiæ supereminentissimæ quicquam labis affricabit corporum terrestrium immundities? Quidque ineptius cogitari queat nescio, quam longâ locorum intercapedine sibi consulere necesse habere Numen, ne puritati immineat periculum à rebus, quas ipsum liberrimè condidit atque conservat. Hàc firmiores cum non sint quæ pro oppositâ sententia aliæ militant rationes, frustrà iis refellendis immorarer. Demonstrasse sufficit, essentiæ Divinæ aut nullum esse tribuendum Ubi; aut, si quod tribuendum sit, aliud tribui non posse, quam quod nullis limitibus exstitit terminatum; adeoque nec cœlo, nec mundo, nec ulli finito spatio affixum. Quod demonstrandum erat.
units.tr: Finally, I beg these men to say what they think should be answered if I ask whether the divine essence fills the whole heaven or inhabits only some part of it. If they assign God a small region of heaven as his dwelling, then unless they want the Deity to be fixed there, one may suppose that he wanders about from time to time and changes his abode. If they prefer the divine essence to be present throughout the whole heaven, I should like to know why he who to whom this vast machine is almost nothing should shut himself up in just these regions of the world. And what, finally, are the reasons by which the Deity should be cut off from the other regions of the world? What they fear, lest God be harmed by the nearness of filthy things, is too crude and silly. That is a filthy thought, and not worth an answer! For if even a created spirit is not polluted by the filth of a leprous body, how much less will the impurity of earthly bodies stain the most supremely exalted essence? I do not know what could be thought more absurd than that God must take care to keep himself at a great distance from places, lest his purity be endangered by things which he himself freely created and preserves. Since the arguments on the opposite side are no firmer, it would be pointless to linger in refuting them. It is enough to have shown that either no Where is to be attributed to the divine essence, or, if some is to be attributed, nothing else can be attributed than that it is bounded by no limits, and so is fixed neither to heaven, nor to the world, nor to any finite space. This was to be demonstrated.

units.la: V. Omnipræsentiæ Divinæ essentialis contra Cartesianos assertio.
units.tr: V. Assertion of the essential omnipresence of God against the Cartesians.

units.la: Id cum satis capiant Cartesiani, Socinianis longè hic subtilius se philosophaturos autumant, si Deum ratione essentiæ plane nullibi esse pronunciaverint. Ita quod cœlum hi volunt esse Dei habitaculum, ne quidem isti ei faciunt reliquum. Quid sibi ista velint, quis satis intelligat? Quid monstri alant, quove tandem sint abitura? forsan dies dabit. Profectò, nisi planam viam struere cupiant ad Atheismum, haud gravatim, si vel leviter attendere velint, intelligere possunt qui sic instituunt, quam re ipsâ vel nihil dicant, vel sibi aperte contradicant. Etenim quando Deum ratione operationis ubique, ratione essentiæ nullibi esse afferunt, dicant mihi, quo sensu contendant Deum ratiratione operationum esse alicubi? Voluntne operationem illam, cujus intuitu Deus alicubi esse dicitur, considerandam esse ratione Dei ipsius operantis; an potius ratione rei creatae, in quam operatio illa terminatur? Posteriori modo sumta Dei operatio non Deus est, aut aliquod Dei attributum, sed re verâ existit ipsissima creaturae essentia, à Deo operante producta & fluens. Hoc itaque sensu non Deus erit alicubi, sed Dei duntaxat effectum; quod cum essentiam habeat & attributa ab essentia & attributis Dei prorsus distincta, nequit id Ubi quod creaturae competit Creatori tribui, nisi improprissimè, per aliquam tantum denominationem, quae Rhetoribus dicitur metonymia; in qua latebras quaerere haud decet virum sapientem. Quod si operationem Dei spectandam velint à parte Dei ipsius operantis, eam ab essentia Dei distinctam non esse, largiri coguntur quotquot tuentur simplicitatem divinam. Ex quo conficitur, eadem quae operationi, essentiae quoque, tribuenda esse praedicata. Ut, quoties essentiae denegatur, quod operationibus Divinis conceditur, Ubi, mirifica sint aenigmata, quorum mysteria forte clarius evolvent isti Auctores temporibus magis opportunis, quibus necesse non habebunt, difficultatum quarundam causa, mundo imponere vocibus deceptricibus, & non significantibus verum; ut audivimus loquentem Poiretum. Verbo, cum Deus operetur modo simplicissimo & maximè independenti, id est, per essentiam, absque evidenti contradictione dici nequit, Deum alicubi operari, nec tamen ibi, ubi operatur, per essentiam exister. Imprimis nequeunt non nobiscum sentire, quos aliqua tangit Mysteriorum Fidei cura. Credimus, quotquot confitemur Dominum Jesum, secundam S. S. Trinitatis personam naturam humanam assumsisse in plenitudine temporis. Hanc assumtionem factam esse per unionem substantialem, uno ore docent orthodoxi: nam per solam operationem Divinae naturae in humanam unionem hanc esse factam, Nestorianum est, & à tota veteri Ecclesia condemnatum. Sic alicubi Doctissimus Walaeus. Id verò certum est, rem aliquam cum altera uniri non posse alio modo, quam quo illi coëxistit praesens: quandoquidem omnis unio praesentiam supponit. Eligendum ergò alterutrum: vel unionem duarum naturarum in Christo Mediatore factam esse, non ratione essentiæ, sed per denominationem duntaxat externam ab operationibus desumtam; vel naturam divinam cum humana unitam esse verè secundum essentiam. Prius hæreticum pronunciat Fidei analogia. Posterius infert, etiam ergò Divinam naturam verè secundum essentiam saltem Alicubi esse. Hoc si detur, facilè probatur eo quo diximus modo Immensa; idque iisdem prorsus rationibus, quibus articulo præcedenti contra Vorstium ac Socinum fuimus usi.
units.tr: The Cartesians, though they understand this well enough, think they will philosophize far more subtly than the Socinians if they declare that God is in no place at all in respect of his essence. So these men, who want heaven to be God's dwelling, do not even leave him that. What they mean by this, who can sufficiently understand? What monsters they are nurturing, or where they will eventually go, perhaps time will tell. Certainly, unless they wish to pave a plain road to atheism, those who reason in this way can, if they are willing to pay even slight attention, see that they either say nothing at all in fact, or openly contradict themselves. For when they assert that God is everywhere in respect of operation and nowhere in respect of essence, let them tell me in what sense they maintain that God is anywhere in respect of operations at all. Do they want that operation, on account of which God is said to be somewhere, to be considered in relation to God himself as the one operating, or rather in relation to the created thing into which that operation terminates? Taken in the latter way, God's operation is not God, nor any attribute of God, but in truth is the very essence of the creature, produced and flowing from God operating. In this sense, therefore, God will not be somewhere; rather, the effect of God will be. Since this has an essence and attributes wholly distinct from the essence and attributes of God, the Where that belongs to a creature cannot be attributed to the Creator except most improperly, by some mere denomination, which the rhetoricians call metonymy; and a wise man ought not to seek hiding places there. But if they want the operation of God to be considered from the side of God himself as operating, then all who defend the divine simplicity are forced to concede that it is not distinct from the essence of God. From this it follows that the predicates which belong to the operation must belong also to the essence. Thus, whenever the Where which is granted to the divine operations is denied to the essence, these are wonderful riddles, whose mysteries perhaps these authors will unfold more clearly at more opportune times, when they will not need, on account of some difficulties, to impose on the world deceptive words and words not signifying the truth, as we heard Poiret saying. In short, since God operates in the most simple and most independent way, that is through his essence, it cannot be said without a plain contradiction that God operates somewhere and yet does not exist through his essence in the place where he operates. Above all, they cannot fail to agree with us, those whom any concern for the mysteries of the faith touches. We believe, all of us who confess the Lord Jesus, that the second person of the Holy and Blessed Trinity assumed human nature in the fullness of time. The orthodox teach with one voice that this assumption was made through a substantial union; for that this union was made through the operation of the divine nature alone in the human nature is Nestorian, and has been condemned by the whole ancient Church. So the most learned Walaeus, somewhere. But it is certain that one thing cannot be united with another except in the way in which it coexists present with it, since every union presupposes presence. Therefore one of two things must be chosen: either the union of the two natures in Christ the Mediator was made not in respect of essence but only by an external denomination taken from the operations; or the divine nature was united with the human truly according to essence. The first is pronounced heretical by the analogy of faith. The second infers that the divine nature, too, truly according to essence, exists at least somewhere. If this is granted, it is easily proved in the way we have stated that God is immense; and that by exactly the same arguments with which, in the preceding article, we proceeded against Vorstius and Socinus.

units.la: Manifestat quidem Deus suam nobis præsentiam per opera creationis & providentiæ; at non ideo Immensitas ipsa ejus Providentia est: quæ duo, hactenus distincta habita, inaudità absurditate confundunt Novatores. Etenim, sepositò omni providentiæ conceptu, ex ipsa perfectissima Dei natura per se fluit, eam existere ubicunque corpus esse potest. Quapropter merito Theologi & Philosophi saniores ab omni ævo Immensitatem ad attributa Dei retulerunt, Providentiam ad operationes ejusdem: quæ duæ notiones quantum distent, nemo nisi ignorantissimus ignorare potest. Deus Immensus, fateor, omnia sustentat & gubernat: verùm, neque ipsâ Immensitate suâ, formaliter & proprie loquendo, omnia sustentat; neque ideò Immensus existit, quia res sustentat. Omnem enim operationis transeuntis conceptum notio Immensitatis antecedit, quatenus, ut jam dixi, operari supponit esse; non contrà: ergò & ubique operari supponit ubique esse; non contrà. Nec metuendum, ne, quando essentiam Dei rebus extensis coëxistere asserimus, aliquid ideo extensionis eidem tribuamus: quæ cogitatio, etsi mirè placeat Recentioribus, re verâ non minus ridicula est, quam istud nugamentum, quod essentiam Dei sordidis locis adesse non vult, ne ipsa sordescat. Verum de hisce, aliisque quæ similia huc quandoque adferuntur, toti pluribus egimus Exercitat. de Nullibitate Spirituum: quapropter istic dicta hic repetere nil necesse est. Conferantur quoque quæ adduximus, Exercitat. de Cogitatione, quæ sit ipsa Mens humana. Concludo ex hactenus disputatis, non posse phrasi magis convenienti exprimi excellentiam Divinæ Immensitatis, quam quâ usi sunt antiquiores, quando Deum celebrarunt 'Ἐνκέϛμιον, Πει-χέϛμιον. κύκλιον, Ὑπερκόσμιον, Ὑπερέφανιον : quasi dicas, In-mundanum, Circa-mundanum, Supra-mundanum, Supra-cœlestem.
units.tr: God does indeed make his presence known to us through the works of creation and providence; but his immensity is not for that reason his providence itself. The Novatores confuse these two things, which have hitherto been regarded as distinct, with an unheard-of absurdity. For, setting aside every notion of providence, it follows of itself from the most perfect nature of God that he exists wherever a body can exist. Therefore, rightly, theologians and sounder philosophers have from all ages referred immensity to the attributes of God and providence to his operations. How far apart these two notions are, no one can fail to know except the most ignorant. I grant that the immense God sustains and governs all things; but he does not formally and properly sustain all things by his immensity itself, nor does he exist as immense because he sustains things. For the notion of immensity precedes every concept of transient operation, inasmuch as, as I have already said, operating presupposes existing, not the reverse; therefore he also presupposes that he is everywhere when he operates everywhere, not the reverse. Nor need we fear that, when we assert that the essence of God coexists with extended things, we thereby ascribe some extension to him. That notion, although it greatly pleases the more recent writers, is in fact no less ridiculous than that silly trifle which holds that the essence of God is not present in filthy places, lest it itself be defiled. But concerning these and other similar objections which are sometimes brought forward here, we have treated at length in our Exercitation on the Nullibity of Spirits; therefore there is no need to repeat there what was said here. Let what we have adduced in our Exercitation on Thought, what the human mind itself is, also be compared. I conclude from what has been disputed so far that the excellence of divine immensity cannot be expressed in a more suitable phrase than that which the earlier writers used when they celebrated God as Enkosmion [ἔγκοσμον], Perikosmion [περίκοσμον], Kyklion [κύκλιον], Hyperkosmion [ὑπερκόσμιον], Hyperouranion [ὑπερουράνιον]: as if you were to say, In-worldly, Around-worldly, Supra-worldly, Supra-heavenly.

units.la: Cæterùm, Immensitatem unius Dei prærogativam esse, liquet eo quod actualem ratione § Alicubi includat infinitatem. At nulla cujuscunque infinitatis species locum habere potest in essentia finita; qualem esse illam omnem, quæ à Deo distincta & dependens est, jam antè ostendimus. Specialius, nùm corpus quodpiam, v. c. hic noster Mundus, sit aut esse possit mole infinitum, adeoque suo quoque modo Immensum? excussimus; ac negativam compluribus rationibus evidenter demonstravimus, Exercitatione de Infinito: quapropter nunc ista transimus. Longè tamen alia quæstio est, an res creata possit esse Ubique, vel Omnipræsens? Explicui jam supra, §. 1. quâ ratione, & vi vocum, & significationis usu, plurimum distent à se vocabula Immensitatis & Ubiquitatis. Id quicunque attendit, nemo, nisi quæstionem de nomine facere malit, negare poterit, Universum nostrum ipso facto exístere Ubique; id est, occupare omne spatium de facto corpore repletum, etsi non occupet omne omninò spatium possibile: quod postremum uti propriè est Immensitatis, non strictè dictæ Ubiquitatis, ita ad præsentem quæstionem nihil pertinet. Verùm jam dudum Immensitas præfixam brevitatis nostræ mensuram excurrit. At sic jussit rei momentum satis grave. Nunc de aliis; & brevius!
units.tr: Moreover, that immensity is a prerogative of the one God alone is clear from the fact that it includes, by the reasoning of the § Alicubi, actual infinity. But no kind of infinity can have a place in a finite essence, which is what all that is distinct from God and dependent upon him is, as we showed earlier. More particularly, whether some body, for example this our world, is or could be infinite in mass, and so in its own way immense, we have examined, and by several arguments we have clearly demonstrated the negative in our Exercitation on the Infinite; therefore we pass over these matters now. But the question whether a created thing can be everywhere, or omnipresent, is a quite different one. I explained above, §. 1., how far apart the terms immensity and ubiquity are from one another, by the force of the words and the usage of their meaning. Whoever attends to this, no one, unless he prefers to make a question about a name, will be able to deny that our universe in fact exists everywhere; that is, it occupies all the space filled by the actual body, although it does not occupy every space whatever that is possible. This last, which properly belongs to immensity and not to ubiquity strictly so called, has nothing to do with the present question. But now immensity has long exceeded the measure of brevity we set ourselves. Yet the importance of the matter demanded this. Now on to other things, and more briefly!

units.la: VII. Immensitatem, non Ubiquitatem strictè dictam, solius Dei esse, probatur.
units.tr: VII. That immensity, not ubiquity strictly so called, belongs to God alone, is proved.

units.la: Note: marginal side-notes, right margin: "Immensita-tem, non Ubiquitatem strictè di-ctam, solius Dei esse, probatur."
units.tr: Immensity, not ubiquity strictly so called, is proved to belong to God alone.
THE TENTH EXERCISE, CONCERNING THE ONE GOD.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Unitas Dei demonstratur, & illi soli vindicatur. II. SS. Trinitatis mysterium ex rationis naturalis lumine non innotescere, ostenditur.
units.tr: I. The unity of God is demonstrated, and it is claimed for him alone. II. It is shown that the mystery of the Holy Trinity cannot be known from the light of natural reason.

units.la: UM Alicubi & Aliquando pari passu ambulat Unitas; quum & hæc & ista sint communissimæ quædam affectiones, quæ enti simpliciter quà enti spectato conveniunt. Multa quæ re ipsâ plura sunt, Unum quid esse quandoque dicuntur, quatenus ea in ejusdem generis vel speciei conceptu convenire apta sunt. Verum uti hæc Unitas est fidta tantum per mentis cogitationem, sic re ipsâ id demum modo quodam excellenti ac perfectissimo est Unum, quod ita suâ naturâ existit Singulare, ut absolutè nihil planè admittat sibi simile, quodque sit ejusdem communis essentiæ secum. Et hanc talem, quando eam Deo tribuimus, innuimus Unitatem. Verbo, nec esse, nec esse posse, plures Deos, contendimus. Cujus veritatis tanta existit evidentia, ut nec ipsi gentiles in suis sibi Deastris satisfacere potuerint, nisi reductâ tandem omni illâ pluralitate ad Unum aliquem, qui pariter sit Θεὸν πάντῃ ἑνὶ ἑσῇ ἀνδρῶν. Sed more nostro philosophemur potius! Vel solam cogitemus divinæ perfectionis, antè demonstratam, infinitatem. Hanc absolutam istiusmodi Unitatem secum trahere dico. Demonstro. Sunto, si ita vis, duo pluresve Dii, Jupiter v. c. & Mars. Neutrum horum Deum agnoveris, nisi pariter agnoveris utrumque infinitè perfectum, id est, re
units.tr: Unity walks side by side with "somewhere" and "sometimes," since both are very common affections that belong to being considered simply as being. Many things that are in fact several are sometimes called one thing, insofar as they are fit to agree in the concept of the same genus or species. But just as this unity is merely feigned by the thought of the mind, so in reality that alone is one in a certain excellent and most perfect way which exists by its own nature as singular, so that it absolutely admits nothing at all similar to itself, and which shares the same common essence with itself. When we attribute this kind of unity to God, we mean this unity. In a word, we maintain that there are not, and cannot be, several gods. The evidence of this truth is so great that even the Gentiles themselves could not satisfy themselves with their own godlings unless, all that plurality having at last been reduced to a single one, there was one who is likewise God in every way one and equal to men [Θεὸν πάντῃ ἑνὶ ἑσῇ ἀνδρῶν]. But let us rather philosophize in our own manner! Or let us consider only the infinity of divine perfection, demonstrated above. I say that this absolute kind of unity follows from it. I demonstrate it. Let there be, if you like, two or more gods, Jupiter for instance, and Mars. You will not recognise either of them as God unless you likewise recognise each as infinitely perfect, that is, really possessing whatever can come under any name of perfection in any way at all.

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] re verâ possidentem id ipsum quodcunque modo qualicunque perfectionis nomine venire potest. Nunc scire lubet, an easdem numero perfectioncs Jupiter contineat, quas ipsas continet Mars; nec ne? Si neges, utique Jovem infinitè perfectum non agnoscis; cum extra eum dentur aliæ adhuc infinitæ perfectiones in Marte, quibus ipsis non gaudet Jupiter: at verò extra infinitum nihil dari potest aut concipi. Necessum ergò erit, ut Jupiter, si Deus sit, in se omnes omninò contineat perfectiones, adeoque & eas quæ Martis sunt. At quì poterit? nisi, vel cum Marte fuerit idem numero Numen; adeoque non duo: vel, nisi Martis perfectiones Jupiter, tanquam causa, in se complectatur, easque Marti communicaverit. Ast hoc ipso Martis destruitur plane, uti Indcpendentia, ita Deitas. Ex quibus apparet, non minus contradictoria esse duo entia infinitè perfecta, quam sunt duæ extensiones undiquaque infinitæ. Ut enim nemo has sibi imaginatus fuerit, nisi eas se mutuo penetrare, id est, vel utramque re ipsa unam, vel neutram earum veram esse extensionem, cogitaverit; sic nemo mente apprehenderit duo entia infinitè perfecta, nisi alterius perfectiones sub altero contineri, atque ita illa revera vel duo non esse, vel infinitè perfecta non esse, conceperit. Quamobrem duo pluresve Dii nec sunt, nec esse possunt: adeo πλανῆτης est re ipsa quædam veræ Deitatis abnegatio, & crassa ἀθεότης. Atque hoc argumentum unum nobis instar omnium erit: nam, quæ alii urgent defumta ab unitate mundi, ab harmonia universi, à plurium Deorum pugna, ab omnipotentia eorundem, aliaque istis similia, nostro judicio, vel tantum probant, uti loquuntur, ad hominem; vel illustrationes potius quædam sunt & allegoriæ, quam solidæ probationes; vel talia denique, quorum vis omnis à nostra hac demonstratione pendet. Porrò, Deo soli attributum hoc esse proprium, docet dependens & finita rerum quarumvis ab infinito principio pendentium natura; quæ uti augmentum sui in infinitum pati potest, ita nihil continet, quod adversetur productioni alterius similis sibi naturæ individui. Quumque mundo æquè hæc possint applicari, ac cuivis alteri rei creatæ, patet, errare eos, qui plurium mundorum possibilitatem negantes, eo ipso absolutam Unitatem non solius Dei privilegium vilcgium vilegium esse, profitentur. Etiam liquet ex traditis, quid respondendum ad quæstionem a quibusdam motam: Num Deus sit thema universale, num singulare? Hoc nimirum eligendum est. Cui non obstat Personarum in eadem essentia pluralitas: non enim ea notat, naturam Divinam pluribus essentiis numero distinctis esse communem; quod ad universalem naturam requiritur.
units.tr: [illegible, about three letters] really possessing. Now I should like to know whether Jupiter contains the same perfections in number that Mars contains, or not? If you deny it, you certainly do not recognise Jupiter as infinitely perfect, since outside him there would be other infinite perfections in Mars, which Jupiter does not enjoy; but nothing can be given or conceived outside the infinite. It will therefore necessarily follow that Jupiter, if he is God, contains in himself all perfections without exception, and so also those that belong to Mars. But how can he? Unless either the divine power is numerically the same as Mars's, and so not two; or Jupiter, as cause, embraces the perfections of Mars in himself and has communicated them to Mars. But by this very thing the independence of Mars is plainly destroyed, and his deity along with it. From these points it appears that two infinitely perfect beings are no less contradictory than two extensions that are infinite on every side. For just as no one can imagine these as existing unless he thinks that they penetrate each other, that is, either that both are really one, or that neither is a true extension; so no one can grasp in the mind two infinitely perfect beings unless the perfections of the one are contained under the other, and so he has conceived them either not to be two, or not to be infinitely perfect. Therefore two or more gods neither are, nor can be. So much so that to wander [πλανῆτης] in this way is really a certain denial of the true Deity, and gross atheism. This one argument will serve us in place of all. For the arguments that others press, drawn from the unity of the world, from the harmony of the universe, from the strife of several gods, from their omnipotence, and other things like these, in our judgment either prove only what they say, as they put it, ad hominem; or are rather illustrations and allegories than solid proofs; or finally are such that all their force depends on this demonstration of ours. Moreover, that this attribute belongs properly to God alone is taught by the nature of all things, which are dependent and finite and depend on an infinite principle; for such a nature, while it can undergo an increase of itself to infinity, contains nothing that opposes the production of another individual of a like nature. And since these considerations can be applied to the world just as well as to any other created thing, it is plain that those err who, while denying the possibility of several worlds, thereby profess that absolute unity is not the privilege of God alone. It is also clear from what has been said what must be answered to the question raised by some: Is God a universal or a singular theme? Clearly the latter must be chosen. The plurality of Persons in the same essence does not stand in the way of this: for it does not signify that the Divine nature is common to several essences numerically distinct from one another, which is what a universal nature requires.

units.la: Dum plurium in Deo Personarum mentionem facio, huc pertinere videtur, ut verbo tangam controversiam, An, uti essentiæ Divinæ Unitas, ita Personarum in ea Trinitas ex naturali rationis lumine sciri queat? Affirmantes frustra mihi hic esse videntur. In ipsa saltem Dei Optimi Maximi essentia, quatenus natura innotescit, nihil occurrit, quod talem Personarum pluralitatem inferat. Contemplatio quoque creaturarum ea tantum de Deo nobis cognoscenda præbet, quæ essentiæ qua tali, omnibusque adeo Personis in communi, conveniunt. Qui dissentiunt, hac palmaria utuntur ratione. Constat, ajunt, Deum se intelligere; at hoc ipso generat imaginem sibi simillimam; quæ Filius est. Pergunt: Deus Pater amat Filium; at per hunc actum amandi ab utroque procedit Spiritus Sanctus. Non desunt, scio, viri etiam Doctissimi, quibus haud displicent hæ Scholasticorum subtilitates. Sed qui stare queant, non video. Certè intelligere se & amare actus Dei sunt, non personales, sed essentiales; atque ideo à parte Dei nec ab essentia Divina simplicissima, nec inter se distinguuntur, uti suo modo distinguuntur personæ. Quin, quia essentiales sunt, si quid ab intelligente & amante distinctum producerent, non personam producerent, sed essentiam. Et si vel maximè personam, cum unaquæque persona tum se tum alias intelligat ac velit, personarum processus hoc pacto multiplicari posset in infinitum. Alii saltem inæstimabile arcanum per similia de creatis quibusdam rebus adducta conantur illustrare. Ast neque horum institutum probandum videtur: tanta enim per omnia elucet disparitas, ut extraneis non sine ludibrii periculo istiusmodi pictu-ræ proponantur. Adferunt alii, ut ostendant hoc dogma lumine naturæ gentilibus fuisse familiare, priscos eorum Philosophos ac Poëtas. Verùm de multorum testimoniorum fide vix constat satis : plerorumque etiam verba trahuntur in sensum à mente auctorum manifestò diversum : ad summum nil produnt, nisi reliquias quasdam valdè corruptas doctrinæ Hebræorum, ut ipsis illis scriptoribus non satis intellectas, ita tam rudi modo expressas, ut hæreticis deinceps occasionem præbuerint blasphemandi. Constat equidem non aliundè natas esse hæreses tum Tritheitarum tum Antitrinitariorum, quam quòd naturæ lumine rimari voluerint venerabile mysterium, quod humili tantum pietate mirari debuissent. Hujus temeritatis infelicissimo successu admonerinos decet, ut de hisce aliundè non scisciteamur quam ex verbo Dei; utque fidei docilitate, non rationis acumine, in hanc meditationem incumbere curæ sit.
units.tr: Since I am mentioning the several Persons in God, it seems relevant here to touch briefly on the controversy: whether, just as the unity of the Divine essence can be known from the natural light of reason, so too the Trinity of Persons in it can be known? Those who affirm it seem to me to labour in vain. In the very essence of God, Best and Greatest, so far as it is known by nature, nothing occurs that would imply such a plurality of Persons. The contemplation of creatures also presents to us only those things about God to be known that belong to the essence as such, and so to all the Persons in common. Those who disagree use this outstanding argument. It is established, they say, that God understands himself; but by this very act he begets an image most like himself, who is the Son. They go on: God the Father loves the Son; but through this act of loving, the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. I know there are not lacking men, even most learned, who are not displeased by these subtleties of the Scholastics. But I do not see how they can stand. Certainly to understand oneself and to love are acts of God that are not personal but essential; and so on God's side they are distinguished neither from the most simple Divine essence nor from each other, as persons are distinguished in their own way. Indeed, because they are essential, if they produced something distinct from the one who understands and loves, they would produce not a Person but an essence. And even if they produced a Person, since each Person both understands and wills both himself and the others, the procession of Persons could in this way be multiplied to infinity. Others at least try to illuminate this inestimable mystery by similar examples drawn from certain created things. But the purpose of these men does not seem to be approved either: for such a disparity shines out in every respect that such pictures are offered to outsiders not without danger of mockery. Others adduce the ancient philosophers and poets of the Gentiles, to show that this doctrine was familiar to them by the light of nature. But there is hardly enough certainty about the trustworthiness of many testimonies: and the words of most of them are also twisted into a meaning clearly different from the intention of their authors. At most they reveal nothing but certain very corrupted remnants of the doctrine of the Hebrews, understood by those writers themselves only imperfectly, and expressed in so crude a manner that they afterwards gave heretics occasion to blaspheme. It is indeed certain that the heresies both of the Tritheists and of the Antitrinitarians arose from no other source than that they wished to search out by the light of nature a venerable mystery, which they ought only to admire with humble piety. The most unhappy outcome of this rashness ought to warn us not to seek information about these matters from anywhere but the Word of God, and that our care should be to apply ourselves to this meditation with the docility of faith, not with the sharpness of reason.
EXERCITATION ELEVEN, ON THE SIMPLE GOD.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Simplicitatis Divinæ notio quid inferat? II. Divinæ Simplicitatis per varias rationes adstructio. III. Difficultatum quarundam hic occurrentium amotio. IV. Divinæ Simplicitatis persuasio quam multis modis utilis? V. Simplicitatem inter Dei, & quidem solius, Attributa esse numerandam.
units.tr: I. What does the notion of the divine simplicity imply? II. The divine simplicity established by various arguments. III. Removal of certain difficulties that arise here. IV. How many useful ways is the persuasion of the divine simplicity? V. Simplicity is to be counted among the attributes of God, and indeed of God alone.

units.la: Nitatem cujusvis entis ejusdem sequitur Identitas ; quatenus quod indivisum est in se, quia est indivisum in se, divisum est ab alio quovis. Undè conficitur, omne absolutè unum & idem etiam esse summè simplex. Quod enim compositum est, non tantum hoc unum, verum etiam aliud est, quod cum illo priori idem non est, sed ex cujus cum illo unione hoc qua compositum resul-tet. Merito itaque, postquam contemplati sumus Deum ceu Unum, meditationem nostram proximè convertimus ad cogitandum Eum tanquam Simplicem. Hac notione notatam volumus quorumcunque quæ Divinæ essentiæ tribuuntur prædicatorum cum ea ipsa perfectissimam quandam identitatem. Ut in Deo Essentia & Attributum, vel Attributum & Attribu-tum, non sint (quemadmodum sæpè sunt in creatis) ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο; sed quæcunque hic intercedit diversitas solius duntaxat sit rationis, orta ex intellectus finiti imperfectione, quà quod idem est tanquam tale non valet concipere, sed potius dissimilibus id sibi conceptibus repræsentat. Verbo, id contendimus, nil adeò realis discriminis inter ea quæ Deo essentialia sunt intercedere, ut quicquid hoc modo in Deo est sit ipsa ejus essentia; per quàm est quicquid est, citra ullam plurium verè distinctorum aggregationem. Quod acutè expressit alibi Augustinus, cum Deum simplicem esse asserit, quoniam quod habet, hoc est. Longè diversum sentiunt, qui volunt, per Attributa, quibus nobis concipitur Deus, intelligenda esse accidentia quædam seu qualitates realiter ab essentia cui tribuuntur distinctas. Contrà, rectè docent sanjores, removendum esse penitùs à Deo omnem omninò compositionis modum: ut non tantum Deus ex pluribus verè diversis coädunatus non sit; verum nec cum alio à se distincto ad compositum cum eo constituendum concurrere possit.
units.tr: From the unity of any being its identity follows, inasmuch as what is undivided in itself, because it is undivided in itself, is divided from every other thing. From this it is concluded that whatever is absolutely one and the same is also supremely simple. For what is compound is not only this one thing but also something else, which is not the same as that first thing, and by whose union with it the compound results. Rightly, therefore, after we have contemplated God as One, we turn our meditation next to thinking of Him as Simple. By this notion we mean that whatever predicates are attributed to the divine essence have with it a most perfect identity. So in God the essence and the attribute, or attribute and attribute, are not (as they often are in created things) [ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο] something different and something else; rather, whatever diversity lies here is merely of reason, arising from the imperfection of our finite understanding, by which it cannot conceive what is the same as such, but represents it to itself by dissimilar concepts. In a word, we contend that there is no real distinction between those things that are essential to God, such that whatever is in God in this way is his very essence, by which he is whatever he is, without any aggregation of several things truly distinct. Augustine expressed this acutely elsewhere when he asserts that God is simple, because what he has, that he is. Those who hold that the attributes by which God is conceived by us must be understood as accidents or qualities really distinct from the essence to which they are attributed think quite otherwise. On the contrary, the sounder teachers rightly teach that every mode of composition must be entirely removed from God: so that God is not only not made up of several truly different things, but cannot even concur with another thing distinct from himself to constitute a composite with it.

units.la: Prius hoc indubitabile facit summi Numinis & Independentia & Perfectionis infinitas. Profectò, quicquid compositum est ex pluribus, id quà tale posterius est iis rebus ex quibus tanquam partibus componitur, atque ab iisdem tanquam naturâ prioribus dependet. Quin & pars altera compositi pendet ab altera, in quantum illa perfectionem hujus ex se non habet, sed eam acceptam ferre debet unioni cum hac, additâ sibi & à se distinctâ. Verum omne quod modo qualicunque aliquam vel minimam dicit dependentiam, è diametro id Deitati adver-sari, jam dudum demonstravimus. Quapropter, vel Deus per omnia Deus, id est, ens Independens, non est: vel Ipse habet id quod habet, aut potius est id omne quod est, planè inindependenter ; hoc est, citra ullam fui ex pluribus composi-tionem. ἀνάγκη τὸ πρῶτον καὶ ἀσυλλόγιστον εἶναι : ut recté alibi in Epictetum ipse Simplicius. Et quis neget, perfectiorem esse essentiam, quæ sic per se ipsam existit perfectissima, ut nullis ad perfectionem suam consummandam indigeat acciden-tium appendicibus, quam est illa, quæ non sui, sed additarum qualitatum beneficio, perfectiones possidet quas possidet. Si autem prius illud perfectius quid sonet quam hoc, utique non hic, sed ille, perfectiones possidendi modus Deo enti perfectissimo tribuendus erit. Et quæ aǝ quales, obsecro, illæ erunt perfectiones essentiæ Divinæ superadditæ ? Nunquid eas in se continebit essentia Dei ? Si non : non etiam hæc erit infi-nitè perfecta; quare nec Divina. Si contineat : quid ergo at-tinet eas essentiæ per sese illas possidenti superaddere ? Demùm, quæ illa esse poterit ab essentia Divina realiter distincta persectio ? An finita erit; an infinita? dependens; an independens ? creata; an increata ? Si finita, dependens, creata, nil continet Deo dignum. Si infinita, independens, increata, & tamen entitatem habens ab essentia Dei reapse distinctam, qui non secundum rem plures statuantur Dii ? non video. Quibus om-nibus quandoquidem per adversariorum hypotheses exitus dari planè nequit, liquet, omninò esse concludendum, quod con-cludendum erat, Deum actum purißimum ac simplicißimum esse, nec ullo modo capacem attributorum ab essentia sua, aut ab invicem, realiter diversorum. Ast neque eadem Dei essentia ad instar partis cum alio in idem compositum coalescere potest: jam enim ostensum, in taliplurium rerum ad compositum proprié dictum constituendum concursu conspicuam esse mu-tuam quandam partium dependentiam, ac, ut ita loquar, perfectibilitatem ; quatenus ipsa notio partis per se & suâ naturâ notione totius inferior est, dum defectum involvit per istam sui ad unum totum compositum constituendum ordinationem & habitudinem. Neque ergò ex partibus componi, neque pars ipsa esse, potest Deus.
units.tr: The first point is made indubitable by the independence and infinite perfection of the supreme Godhead. Indeed, whatever is composed of several things, as such is posterior to those things out of which it is composed as parts, and depends on them as prior by nature. Moreover, one part of a composite depends on another insofar as the one does not have its perfection from itself, but must owe it to its union with the other, which is added to it and distinct from it. But that everything which in any way implies even the slightest dependence is diametrically opposed to Deity, we have long since demonstrated. Therefore either God is not God in every respect, that is, is not an independent being, or he has what he has, or rather is all that he is, wholly independently; that is, without any composition of several things. [ἀνάγκη τὸ πρῶτον καὶ ἀσυλλόγιστον εἶναι] The first must be necessary and uncompounded, as Simplicius himself rightly says elsewhere on Epictetus. And who would deny that that essence is more perfect which exists through itself so perfectly that it needs no appendages of accidents to complete its perfection, than that which possesses the perfections it possesses not by its own power but by the benefit of added qualities? If the former is the more perfect, then surely it is not the latter but the former mode of possessing perfections that must be attributed to God, the most perfect being. And what, I ask, will those perfections be that are added to the divine essence? Will the essence of God contain them within itself? If not, then this essence will not be infinitely perfect either, and so not divine. If it does contain them, why then is there any point in adding them to an essence that already possesses them through itself? Finally, what perfection could be really distinct from the divine essence? Will it be finite or infinite? dependent or independent? created or uncreated? If finite, dependent, and created, it contains nothing worthy of God. If infinite, independent, and uncreated, yet having a being really distinct from the essence of God, why should not several gods be posited in fact? I do not see. Since by none of these hypotheses of the adversaries can a way out be found, it is clear that we must conclude what had to be concluded: that God is a most pure and most simple act, and in no way capable of attributes really different from his essence or from one another. But neither can the same essence of God coalesce with another thing into one composite as a part; for it has already been shown that in such a concurrence of several things to constitute a composite properly so called, there is a conspicuous mutual dependence of the parts, and, so to speak, a capacity for perfection; inasmuch as the very notion of a part is by its own nature inferior to the notion of a whole, since it involves a defect in its ordering and relation to constitute one whole composite. Therefore God can be neither composed of parts nor be a part.

units.la: Fatendum omninò, magnam esse in Divinorum Attributorum conceptu varietatem. Sed tantum in conceptu, sive, ut ajunt, in sensu formali, & à parte modi concipiendi in nostra mente , per distinctionem rationis ratiocinatæ ; non à parte rei per diversitatem realem. Confer , quæ jam suprà hanc in rem diximus , Exercit. v. §. iii. iv. v. Nec putandum Decretorum divinorum obstare tum pluralitatem , tum indifferentem libertatem ; quasi clarum sit , talia cum una essentia , eaque maxime necessaria , non posse esse eadem. Non enim qui sic arguunt satis Θεωρητικῶς concipere rationem Divinæ Voluntatis, evincent clarissimè quæ dicenda erunt infrà , ubi de Decretis Dei erit agendum. Solutu difficilius est , quod adferunt de Trium Personarum in eadem Essentia Divina subsistentia. Has ante mentis operam ab essentia & inter se distinctos esse τέρτιας ὑπὸστάσεως ; verè tamen unitas in eadem essentia , sic ut sint τὸ ὁμοούσιον , docet nos Christiana fides. Haud difficiteor , me non clarè & distinctè capere , quo modo cum absoluta Simplicitate triplex talis subsistendi modus consistat : at neutiquam indè sequitur , hunc cum ista revera consistere planè non posset. Nullus dubito , quin facilè ista concilianda nobis forent , si , & quid formaliter sint istæ Personalitates , & quâ ratione ab invicem & ab Essentia propriè distinguantur , & quo modo in eadem singulari Natura subsistant , intimè & satis evidenter habueremus perspectum. Nunc ea, quæ tantùm captum nostrum excedunt , adducere Fidei arcana , ad apertam veritatem naturâ notam impugnandam , nimium est præposterum & intempestivum. Mihi sufficit , quâ Philosopho scire , Deum esse Simplicem, quia sic exigit divina perfectio; quâ Christiano credere , Deum esse personis Trinum , quia sic testatur exertim Dei verbum : si quæ in istis conciliandis occurrit difficultas , ingenii tenuitas , non alterutrius dogmatis falsitas, indè evincitur. Et sic in tantarum rerum meditatione merito acquiescit modestia sapientis in certitudine veritatis utriusque agnitæ , non in evidentia alterius cum altera connexæ. Paria dicenda sunt de altero illo magno pietatis Mysterio , quo Deus Filius manifestatus est in carne , per sui cum hac unionem hypostaticam. Sed nos hæc Theologis relinquimus explicanda , quæ tantum naturæ sphæram excedunt, ut forte beati cœlites, quorum privilegium est Dominum Jesum videre sicuti est, istis ritè concipiendis soli exi-stant pares.
units.tr: It must be altogether admitted that there is great variety in the concept of the divine attributes. But this is only in the concept, or, as they say, in the formal sense, and on the side of the mode of conceiving in our mind, by a distinction of reasoned reason; not on the side of the thing, by a real diversity. Compare what we have already said on this matter above, Exercit. v. §§ iii, iv, v. Nor should it be thought that the plurality of the divine decrees, or their indifferent freedom, stands in the way; as if it were clear that such things cannot be the same with one essence, and that a most necessary one. For those who argue thus do not sufficiently conceive the reason of the divine will [Θεωρητικῶς] theoretically, and will not prove what must be said below, where we shall treat of the decrees of God. The point that they adduce about the subsistence of the three Persons in the same divine essence is more difficult to solve. We are taught by the Christian faith that these, as far as our mental effort goes, are distinct from the essence and from one another as three hypostases [τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις]; yet that they are truly one in the same essence, so that they are one substance [τὸ ὁμοούσιον]. I readily admit that I do not grasp clearly and distinctly how such a threefold mode of subsisting can exist together with absolute simplicity; but it by no means follows from this that it cannot in fact exist together with it at all. I have no doubt that these matters could be reconciled for us, if we had an intimate and sufficiently evident grasp of what these personalities formally are, in what way they are distinguished from one another and from the essence properly, and how they subsist in the same single nature. As things stand, to bring forward the mysteries of faith, which exceed our capacity, in order to assail a truth plainly known by nature, is far too rash and ill-timed. It is enough for me, as a philosopher, to know that God is simple, because the divine perfection requires it; and, as a Christian, to believe that God is three in persons, because the word of God so clearly attests it. If some difficulty arises in reconciling these, that is proof of the slenderness of our wit, not of the falsity of either doctrine. And so, in meditating on such great matters, the modesty of the wise rightly rests in the certainty of the truth of both, known, and not in the evidence of their connection with each other. The same must be said of that other great mystery of piety, by which God the Son was manifested in the flesh, through the hypostatic union of the divine nature with it. But we leave these things to the theologians to explain: they so far exceed the sphere of nature that perhaps only the blessed inhabitants of heaven, whose privilege it is to see the Lord Jesus as he is, are fit to conceive them rightly.
... / removal.

units.la: Quum autem quæ ante de Dei Simplicitate demonstrata sunt, deducantur & fluant ex ipsa Divina natura, valdè perperam pulcherrima hæc doctrina quibusdam habetur subtilitas quæpiam Scholastica, absque necessitate induĉta. Frigidum imprimis est, quod Apologistæ alibi, adulaturi Socinianis, eam arenâ steriliorem pronuncient. An verò arenâ sterilius dogma, citra quod Deo sua nequit esse salva Independentia, Perfectio, Unitas? Quid? quod Simplicitas hæc fundamentum sit immotum Divinæ Immutabilitatis: quæ, uti purioris Religionis est palladium, ita caput exstitit præcipuum, à quo pendet bona pars Theologiæ inter nos & illos controversæ: ut minus mirum, eos niti tantopere rei hujus momentum extenuare. Et quæ cogitatio dulci consolatione & piâ reverentiâ fœcundior esse queat, quam quæ Deum, quicum nobis res est, menti repræsentat esse, hinc quidem ipsam infinitam Sanctitatem, Justitiam, &c. indè verò ipsam infinitam Misericordiam, Bonitatem, Sapientiam, Potentiam, &c. Certè cui hæc, similesque quas notio Simplicitatis suppeditat, cogitationes arenâ steriliores sunt, ejus pectus esse oportet sterilis valdè affectûs erga supremum Numen. Denique, quis nisi hospes planè in hisce, ignoret, quanti usus sit in re Theologica novisse, An, & quo sensu, quicquid est in Deo sit ipse Deus? An de essentia & de se invicem prædicari possint Attributa, non in concreto tantum, sed & in abstracto? An nulla Attributa intendantur aut remittantur? Deo magis & minus sint essentialia? Alia aliis priora & posteriora? quæque iis affinia ex hoc dogmate de Simplicitate tum confirmanda sunt, tum illustranda.
units.tr: Since the things demonstrated above about the simplicity of God are derived from and flow out of the divine nature itself, it is very wrongly held by some that this most beautiful doctrine is a certain scholastic subtlety, introduced without need. It is especially cold of the Apologists, who elsewhere, fawning on the Socinians, call it more barren than sand. But is there a doctrine more barren than sand, apart from which God's independence, perfection and unity cannot remain intact? Moreover, this simplicity is the immovable foundation of the divine immutability, which is the guardian of the purer religion, and it has been the chief point on which a large part of the theological controversy between us and them depends. So it is hardly surprising that they labour so hard to belittle the importance of this matter. And what thought can be more fruitful of sweet consolation and holy reverence than that which presents to the mind the God with whom we have to do as, on the one hand, infinite holiness and justice, and so on, and on the other, infinite mercy, goodness, wisdom, power, and so on? Certainly, anyone for whom these and similar thoughts, which the notion of simplicity supplies, are more barren than sand must have a heart very barren of affection towards the supreme Deity. Finally, who, unless a complete stranger to these matters, does not know how much it matters in theology to know whether, and in what sense, whatever is in God is God himself? Whether attributes can be predicated of the essence and of one another, not only in the concrete but also in the abstract? Whether no attributes are intensified or relaxed? Whether some are more essential to God than others? Whether some are prior and some posterior to others? And whatever is related to these must be both confirmed and illustrated from this doctrine of simplicity.

units.la: Dubium quibusdam visum fuit, num inter Dei Attributa rectè numeretur Simplicitas? Frustrà autem quidam negant. Quamvis enim largiamur lubentes, eam respicere omnes omnino Divinas perfectiones, quatenus earumdem notat intimam identitatem: non tamen pro modo concipiendi nostro Simplicitas est prima perfectionum Divinarum scaturigo; quippe quæ ipsa ex Independentia, & Infinitate perfectionis firmissimè, quasi à priori, poterit demonstrari, ut jam docuimus. Cæterùm, solum Deum absolutè simplicem, seu, ut loquuntur, actum purum esse, tum hoc quod dixi evincit; tum illud quo-que, que, quod omnis quæ præter Deum existit effentia, ut limitata, ita dependens fit. Quapropter nil obstat, cur non ei semper arbitrio primi entis à quo pendet nova addi qucat perfectio: quæ fi addatur (quandoquidem à præexiftente subjecto realiter distinguitur, idque fui accessu perficit) necessariò cum illa faciet compositum. Et sic dictat experientia, etiam creaturas omnium fimplicifimas, quales procul dubio sunt Angeli & Animæ rationales, multa possidere attributa, quibus absolutè carere possent: adeoque & illas ex subjecto & accidentibus modisque esse compositas. Quamòbrem & nulla earum dici potest Actus purus modificabilis: quod mirificum quorundam hodiè de mente humana vaticinium est.
units.tr: It has seemed doubtful to some whether simplicity is rightly counted among the attributes of God. Yet some deny it in vain. For although we gladly grant that all the divine perfections, insofar as they signify their intimate identity, bear on simplicity, nevertheless, according to our manner of conceiving, simplicity is not the first source of the divine perfections. Indeed it can be demonstrated most firmly from independence and the infinity of perfection, as it were a priori, as we have already taught. Moreover, that God alone is absolutely simple, or, as they say, pure act, is proved both by what I have said and by this too: every essence that exists apart from God is, as limited, also dependent. Therefore nothing prevents a new perfection from always being added to the primary being on which all things depend. If it is added (since it is really distinct from the pre-existing subject and perfects it by its coming), it will necessarily make a composite with it. And so experience shows that even the simplest of creatures, such as undoubtedly angels and rational souls are, possess many attributes which they could lack altogether, and so they too are composed of subject, accidents and modes. Wherefore none of them can be called pure modifiable act, which is the wonderful prophecy of some today concerning the human mind.
Exercitation Twelve: On the Immutable God.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Immutabilitas Deo adscripta ratione Essentiæ, Attributorum, & Operationum. II. Immutabilitatis Divinæ respectu Attributorum demonstratio. III. Deus solus, in rerum omnium mutationibus, Immutabilis.
units.tr: I. Immutability is ascribed to God with respect to his essence, his attributes and his operations. II. A demonstration of divine immutability with respect to the attributes. III. God alone is immutable amid the changes of all things.

units.la: Implicitati cohæret Immutabilitas; quâ innuimus, naturæ Divinæ repugnare, ut, ejus aliquo remanente, illi aliquid quo antè caruit de novo accedat, vel etiam quicquam quod antè habuit decedat: sic quidem, ut qui semel est, is idem semper maneat nullâ sui parte alius quam olim aut fuit aut erit. Tribus considerandi modis quibusdam spectatur hæc Immutabilitas : tum ratione Essentiæ Divinæ, tum ratione Proprietatum, tum etiam ratione Operationum. At censent alii, non nisi Attributorum & Operationum respectu Deo Immutabilitatem tribui debere. Non quod Essentiam Dei hi velint mutabilem ; sed quod perfectionem, quam illi Immutabilitatem Essentiæ vocant, malint hi vocare Necessitatem existendi: nam, ajunt, ipsa essentia, ut aliarum rerum, ita Dei, quemadmodum in indivisibili consistit, sic nullam variationem ratione sui potest subire. Per annihilationem quædam essentiæ interire possunt, verùm cum nullum tali casu relinquatur mutationis subjectum, etiam totalis rei interitus non; nisi satis impropriè, mutatio dicenda est. Unde concludunt, sicuti id, cujus essentia ipsa destrui potest ut non amplius sit, rectius dicitur contingens quam mutabile; ita ex adverso id, cujus essentia ipsa destrui non potest, rectius dici Necessarium quam Immutabile. Quæ ut accuratius dici largior, sic de nomine tamen contendere nolim. Cæterum de essentiæ Divinæ Immutabilitate, vel potius existendi Necessitate, dictum est, quantùm sufficit, suprà. Tantum de Immutabilitate Dei ratione Attributorum hic agemus. Quâ ritè perceptâ, quæ Immutabilitas operationum Deo tribuenda sit, facilè intelligitur. Sed de hac aptius agemus infrà, quando dicendum erit de Dei Intellectu & Voluntate.
units.tr: Immutability goes together with simplicity. By it we mean that it is repugnant to the divine nature that anything should be added to God, which he previously lacked, while he himself remains, or that anything he previously had should be taken away. In such a way, indeed, that what has once been remains always the same, with no part of it other than it was or will be. This immutability is regarded in three ways: with respect to the divine essence, with respect to the properties, and also with respect to the operations. Others, however, judge that immutability should be ascribed to God only with respect to his attributes and operations. They do not wish the divine essence to be mutable; rather, they prefer to call the perfection that the others call immutability of essence the necessity of existing. For, they say, the essence itself, as with the essences of other things, so also that of God, since it consists in indivisibility, can undergo no variation in itself. Some essences can perish by annihilation, but since no subject of change remains in such a case, even the total destruction of a thing should be called change only in a rather improper sense. Hence they conclude that just as that whose essence can itself be destroyed, so that it no longer is, is more correctly called contingent than mutable, so, conversely, that whose essence cannot itself be destroyed is more correctly called necessary than immutable. I would allow these things to be stated more precisely, but I would not wish to contend over the name. Otherwise, what suffices has been said above concerning the immutability of the divine essence, or rather the necessity of existence. Here we shall treat only of the immutability of God with respect to his attributes. Once this is rightly understood, it is easily grasped what immutability is to be ascribed to God's operations. But we shall treat of this more fitly below, when we come to speak of the intellect and will of God.

units.la: II. Immutabilitatis Divinæ respectu Attributorum demonstratio.
units.tr: II. A demonstration of divine immutability with respect to the attributes.

units.la: Nullam verò essentiam Divinam subire, aut subire posse, mutationem ratione hujus vel illius attributi, evincunt pariter ista omnia quæ continuatâ serie de Deo hactenus demonstrata fuerunt. Quamvis certè mutabilitatem supponere plurium prædicatorum veram distinctionem, earundemque possibilem inter se unionem, aut ab invicem disunionem, per se evidens adeò est & certum, ut mutabile nemo, nisi compositum, aut saltem, ut itâ dicam, componibile simul, fingat Numen. Verum Simplicem jam demonstravimus Deum; qui quemadmodum essentiam habet, nil admittentem quod ipsa essentia non sit, ita nihil in eo concipi potest quod manet altero recedente, nihil cui existenti alterum queat accedere. Et quis perfectissimo modo id Unum esse dixerit, quod usque eo in se divisum est, ut aliquid ejus absque altero existere queat? Nec saltem ratione loci mutabile est quod Immensitate suâ existit ipso facto, ubicunque aliquid unquam existere potest. Nec temporibus ille variatur, qui secundum perfectissimam Æternitatem sic simultaneè durat, ut
units.tr: Indeed, all those things that have so far been demonstrated of God in a continuous series prove equally that the divine essence neither undergoes, nor can undergo, any change with respect to this or that attribute. For it is so evident and certain in itself that mutability presupposes a true distinction of several predicates and their possible union with one another or separation from one another, that no one would imagine a Deity that is mutable unless it were composite, or at least, as I may say, capable of being composed at the same time. But we have already demonstrated that God is simple.
