Just as he has an essence admitting nothing that the essence itself is not, so nothing can be conceived in him which remains when another thing departs, nothing to which another can be added while he exists. And who would say that that is one in the most perfect way which is so divided within itself that something of it could exist without something else? Nor is that mutable with respect to place which exists by its immensity wherever anything at all can exist. Nor does he vary in time, who according to most perfect eternity so endures at once that
Time from eternity

units.la: Ire jubens, stabilisque manens, dat cuncta moveri.
units.tr: Commanding motion while he himself remains steady, he gives all things to move.

units.la: Non etiam patitur talem, qualis in omni mutatione includitur, hujus aut illius entis & non-entis successionem ipsa existendi Necessitas. Procul dubio qualis est rei cujuspiam essentia, talia existunt ejusdem attributa; quippe quæ ejus ex quo fluunt induunt naturam: quapropter qui in essentia, is in singulis quoque prædicatis essentialibus conspicuus erit idem necessitatis gradus. Ēt quâ quæso ratione mutabitur Numen infinitæ persectionis? cui nihil addas, nihil detrahas, quin pariter agnoscas, tantas non esse in eo perfectionum divitias, quantæ sunt rei verâ gaudentis infinitate; cujus natura omnem diminutionem & augmentum respuit. An verò quod accedet ad Deum, aut recedet ab eo, nil ad infinitas ejus perfectiones pertinere dices? At sic nihil quoque ad Deum ipsum pertinet. Erit nimirum quod Deo de novo adveniet vel creatum, vel increatum; vel dependens, vel independens; vel finitum, vel infinitum. Priora illa enti increato, independenti, infinito addi non posse, res ipsa clamat. Posteriora non magis Deo addi possunt, quam Deus addi potest sibi; dum præter Deum nil increatum, independens, infinitum existere, suis locis docuimus. Verbo, si subeat mutationem Deus, vel in parem transfibit statum, vel in melius mutabitur, vel in deterius. Istud ridiculum est. Horum quicquid dixeris, imperfectionem id notat vel præteritam, vel præsentem, vel futuram. Denique, quid esse mutabile est aliud, quam esse in potentia ad perfectionem aliquam vel recipiendam vel amittendam? Quod qui cadere queat in ens Independens, quis concipiat? Et quid tandem istud erit, quod Numen mutari faciat? Num quid extrinsecum? Non id finit primi entis Æcitas. Nec ipse se mutat propter aliquid in se, cum nihil in se quod secum pugnet continet. Neque etiam mutat se propter aliquid extra se; cum extra se nihil habeat, quod non sit à se, ut dependens, ita nullo negotio, si velit, mutandum. Luce meridiana hæc omnia sunt lucidiora. Quapropter hinc facessant, qui obfirmatâ mentis cæcitate Deum inducunt, qui in horas fit alius & idem. Sanctius de istis philosophatur Apostolus, quando tam magnificè de Deo testatur, apud eum ne quidem esse τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα. Scilicet ipse Sol in eclypsi sui luminis, si non mutationem, obumbrationem saltem patitur: at ne sic quidem Pater luminum, in quo ne minimum mutationis simulacrum.
units.tr: Nor does the necessity of existence itself admit that succession of this or that being and non-being which is included in every change. Surely, whatever is the essence of a thing, such are its attributes, since they flow from it and take on its nature. Therefore whatever is necessary in the essence will be seen in each of the essential predicates to the same degree of necessity. And by what reasoning, I ask, would the Deity of infinite perfection be changed? To him you can add nothing and take nothing away without at the same time acknowledging that the riches of perfections in him are not as great as those of a being that truly possesses infinity, whose nature rejects every diminution and augmentation. But will you say that what comes to God or departs from him pertains nothing to his infinite perfections? Then nothing pertains to God himself either. Surely there will be something that newly comes to God, whether created or uncreated, dependent or independent, finite or infinite. The reality itself cries out that the first of these cannot be added to the uncreated, independent, infinite being. The latter cannot be added to God any more than God can be added to himself, since we have shown in their places that nothing uncreated, independent or infinite exists besides God. In a word, if God underwent change, he would pass into an equal state, or be changed for the better, or for the worse. That is absurd. Whatever of these you say, it signifies imperfection, either past, present or future. Finally, what is it to be mutable but to be in potency toward some perfection, either to receive or to lose it? How anyone could conceive that this could befall an independent being, who could conceive? And what, finally, would that be which would make the Deity change? Something extrinsic? The eternity of the first being does not allow this. Nor does he change himself on account of something in himself, since he contains nothing in himself that conflicts with himself. Nor does he change himself on account of something outside himself, since he has nothing outside himself which is not from himself, and so, being dependent, could be changed with no trouble, if he were willing. All these things are clearer than the noonday light. Therefore let those depart from here who, with a hardened blindness of mind, introduce a God who becomes now one thing, now another, hour by hour. The Apostle philosophizes more holily about these matters when he testifies so magnificently of God that with him there is not even a shadow of turning [τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα]. Surely the sun itself, in the eclipse of its light, suffers at least obscuration, if not change; but not even so does the Father of lights, in whom there is not the least semblance of change.

units.la: III. Deus solus, in rerum omnium mutationibus, Immutabilis.
units.tr: III. God alone is immutable amid all the changes of things.

units.la: Semotâ sic omni Mutabilitate à Deo, nil opus erit ire per singulas mutationum species, & docere, Deum esse Incorruptibilem, &c. ex dictis enim ista facilè eruuntur. Etiam solius Dei hanc esse prærogativam, multâ jam demonstratione non indiget. Id evincit, tum hujus cum aliis Divinis perfectionibus concatenatio, jam ostensa; tum quoque dependens & finita rerum creatarum natura, quæ, quemadmodum probat illam omnem esse compositionis capacem, ita pariter evincit, eandem esse mutationi obnoxiam, casu quo quicquam perfectionis ei addere vel demere voluerit Deus. Nec si id fecerit, Immutabilitati ejus hoc quodammodo præjudicare credendum est: quum operis vicissitudo Opificis constantiæ nil detrahat. Mira hinc mihi visa fuit semper ista Cartefii philosophatio, & tanto ingenio parùm digna, quando alibi ex Immutabilitate Dei, eandem semper motûs quantitatem in universo hoc conservari concludit, ne quæ, si secus fiat, inconstantia indè in Numine arguatur. Ineptè profecto! Etiam judicio divini Vatis; cui alia planè mens, quando in maximis quas facit Divina providentia vicissitudinibus imprimis Immutabilem agnoscit & celebrat Deum, cum canit: Tu, Deus! usque manes, nullo mutabilis ævo, Victurumque omni tempore nomen habes. Principio solidæ fundasti pondera terræ, Altaque sunt digitis sidera facta tuis;
units.tr: With all mutability thus removed from God, there will be no need to go through each kind of change and to teach that God is incorruptible, and so on, for these things are easily drawn out from what has been said. That this is a prerogative of God alone does not need much demonstration. The interconnection of this attribute with the other divine perfections, already shown, proves it. So too does the dependent and finite nature of created things, which, just as it proves that such a nature is capable of composition, likewise proves that it is subject to change, in case God should wish to add or take away some perfection from it. Nor, if he did so, should it be thought that this in any way prejudices his immutability, since the variation of the work takes nothing from the constancy of the Maker. That philosophizing of Descartes has always seemed strange to me, and little worthy of so great a mind, when elsewhere he infers from the immutability of God that the same quantity of motion is always conserved in this universe, lest, if it were otherwise, inconstancy be charged against the Deity thereby. Foolishly indeed! So too by the judgment of the divine poet, whose mind is quite different, when among the greatest changes made by divine providence he above all acknowledges and celebrates God as immutable, singing: O God, you remain for ever, mutable in no age, and you have a name that will endure in every time. In the beginning you founded the weights of the solid earth, and the lofty stars were made by your fingers;

units.la: Cælorum series mutâ compage peribit,Ut per longa perit tempora vestis honor;Hosque laborarum tanquam mutabis amittum,Nec speciem poterunt usque tenere suam:Semper at es, nullo casu mutabilis, idem, Invadetque annos nulla senecta tuos.
units.tr: The series of the heavens will perish with a changed structure, as the honour of a garment perishes through long periods of time; and you will change them like a worn garment, and they will not be able to keep their appearance for ever; but you are always the same, changeable by no chance, and no old age will overtake your years.
EXERCITATIO DECIMA-TERTIA, DE DEO OMNISUFFICIENTE.
SUMMARIUM.

units.la: I. Sufficientiæ Divinæ varia consideratio. II. Omnisufficientiæ Dei, quæ hujus est loci, explicatio. III. Ejusdem plenior demonstratio. IV. Summum bonum nullum, nisi unicus Deus Omnisufficiens.
units.tr: I. A varied consideration of the sufficiency of God. II. An explanation of the omnisufficiency of God, which is the subject of this place. III. A fuller demonstration of the same. IV. There is no supreme good except the one God, who is omnisufficient.

units.la: Tà quædam consideravimus prædicata, quorum ratione Deus in se ipso sibi perfectissimus est, & tanquam talis nobis innotescit. Nunc ea proximè expendenda veniunt, quæ propiorem dicunt habitudinem ad creaturas, tum omnes, tum rationales imprimis. In isto genere princeps Dei Attributum est Sufficientia, tam undiquaque absoluta, ut merito dicatur Omni-sufficientia. Spectari ea potest, vel quatenus ad Deum ipsum refertur, vel quatenus respicit res existentes extra Deum. Si Sufficientem Deum cogitaveris ratione suæ existentiæ, in quantum nullâ re extra se ad hoc ut existat indiget, sic occurrit ipsa primi Entis Independentia, seu Aseitas; de qua antè. Si Sufficientiam eandem attendas, tendas, quatenus eâ notatur, Ens independens sic plenissimè abundare omni perfectionum genere, ut nulla earum species aut gradus ei desit, sic ipsa Perfectionis Infinitas est; de qua etiam dictum suo loco. Quod si Sufficientiam conceperis, quatenus perfectissimum Numen sibi suæ istius immensæ perfectionis intimè est conscium, ejusque amplitudinem ita perfectè intelligit, ut in ea summa cum tranquillitate acquiescat, sic erit Beatitudo Dei, quâ ipse perfectissimus perfectionibus suis fruitur perfectissimè: quod prædicatum rectius infrà tractabitur, ubi præmissa fuerit consideratio Divini Intellectûs & Voluntatis.
units.tr: We have considered certain predicates by which God is most perfect in himself and is made known to us as such. Now we must weigh those attributes which denote a closer relation to creatures, to all of them, but especially to rational ones. In this class the chief attribute of God is sufficiency, so absolute in every respect that it may rightly be called all-sufficiency. It can be viewed either as it relates to God himself or as it regards things existing outside God. If you think of the sufficient God with respect to his existence, in that he needs nothing outside himself in order to exist, there presents itself the independence of the first Being, or aseity, of which we spoke earlier. If you attend to the same sufficiency as it is denoted by this, that the independent Being so abundantly overflows with every kind of perfection that no species or degree of them is lacking to him, this is the infinity of perfection, which was also discussed in its place. But if you conceive sufficiency as the most perfect Deity's inmost awareness of his own immense perfection, and his understanding of its greatness is so complete that he rests in it with perfect tranquillity, then it will be the blessedness of God, by which he, most perfect, enjoys his perfections most perfectly. This predicate will be treated more fully below, once the consideration of the divine intellect and will has been set out.

units.la: Ergò hujus duntaxat loci erit ista plenitudo perfectionis, quâ Deus ex se & per se omni alteri à se esse potest omnia in omnibus. Tantam nimirum bonitatis in Deo abundantiam notat, ut nihil excogitari queat in omni bonorum genere, seu honestum id fuerit, seu utile, seu jucundum, quo non quolibet in casu satiare queat quamlibet creaturam. Sua etiam rebus quibusdam creatis convenit Sufficientia, sed tantùm ratione hujus aut illius defectûs, quem excludere possunt aut compensare suâ præsentiâ; nulla eis competit talis, quâ in omni indigentia esse queant omnia in omnibus. Sufficit v. c. Cibus ad satiandum famelicum; verum idoneus non est reficere sitientem. Respondet Honor appetitui ambitiosi: at idem non explet desideria avari. Satisfacit sensibus Voluptas corporis; sed valetudinem conservare nequit eadem. Hæc similiaque aliquid sunt alicui; nihil corum est omnibus omnia. Quin ne quidem in isto perfectionis genere, in quo quædam Sufficientiæ species creaturæ competit, tantum præstat alicui, ut non plerumque majora desiderare & capere possit. Longè aliter se habet Sufficientia entis perfectissimi; quæ si se exerat ut potest, id rebus dabit, ultra quod ne quicquam cogitare queant, cujus appetant fruitionem. Et talis Deus ex sese est. Non alterius gratiâ, uti creaturæ; quarum qualiscunque Sufficientia rivulus est duntaxat profluens ex oceani istius abundantia, qui si suum inhibuerit influxum, exaresceet is penitus, nullamque per se, dum per se nihil est, compensare valebit indigentiam.
units.tr: Therefore the fullness of perfection by which God, from himself and through himself, can be all in all to every other being belongs to this place alone. It denotes such an abundance of goodness in God that nothing can be thought of in any kind of good, whether it be honourable, useful or pleasant, which he cannot in any case satisfy for any creature whatever. Sufficiency also belongs to certain created things, but only by reason of this or that defect, which they can remove or make up for by their presence. No created thing possesses that sufficiency by which all things can be all in every need. Food, for example, is sufficient to satisfy the hungry, but it is not fit to refresh the thirsty. Honour answers the appetite of the ambitious, but the same does not satisfy the desires of the greedy. Bodily pleasure satisfies the senses, but it cannot preserve health. These and similar things are something to someone; none of them is all things to all. Indeed, even in that kind of perfection in which a certain sufficiency belongs to a creature, it does not supply anyone so fully that he is not for the most part able to desire and grasp greater things. The sufficiency of the most perfect Being is quite otherwise: if it exerts itself as far as it can, it will give to things more than they could think of, so that they would seek to enjoy it. And God is such from himself. He is not sufficient for the sake of another, as creatures are. Their sufficiency, whatever it may be, is only a stream flowing from the abundance of that ocean; if the ocean were to halt its influx, the stream would wholly dry up, and since in itself it is nothing, it would be unable to make up for any need by its own power.

units.la: Atque istæc omnia talia sunt, ut operosâ demonstratione minimè indigeant. Conferatur duntaxat rerum quarumcunque natura finita & dependens, cum Independentia & Infinitate Divinæ perfectionis; ac mox intelligetur, & Omnisufficientem esse Deum, & solum illum esse talem. Id certum est, finiti ad infinitum nullam esse proportionem; contrà, infiniti supra finitum immensum esse excessum. Excedit ergò infinities infinita Dei perfectio finitam cujusvis rei finitæ indigentiam. Quod si tantum excedat, utique si se infinitum finito communicaverit Deus, saltem omnem in eo defectum plenè ac planè supplere poterit: sive id fecerit mediatè, unius creaturæ defectum alterius substitutione compensando; sive etiam immediato suavissimæ fruitionis sui ipsius sensu, qui tanto est jucundior, quanto sunt dulciores quæ ex ipso fonte bibuntur aquæ. Verbo, vel nihil quicquam Sufficientiæ habet in rerum natura, vel quicquid Sufficientiæ universis inest creaturis, in Deo tanquam in causa earundem suprema continetur, modo Deo convenienté, id est, infinitè perfecto: consequenter, quod universæ creaturæ esse possunt earundem alicui uni, id solus Deus multò magis esse potest iis universis. Fatear, non quidem illa efficit semper, quibus sufficit, Deus. At abundantiæ bonitatis in causa mensura idonea non est effectus. Ut non hoc arguat aliqualem Sufficientiæ defectum, sed indépendentis tantum arbitrii libertatem dispensationem; quà non ad instar causæ brutæ seipsum communicat quo usque potest, sed unicuique suarum creaturarum sapientissimo voluntatis consilio tantum sui largitur quantum visum est. Neque eidem Sufficientiæ quid detrahit quæ conspicua est in obviis causis secundis qualiscumque, uti efficientia, ita Sufficientia: quanto enim hæc est major, tanto illustrius manifestat plenitudinem fontis, ex quo scaturit. Deus itaque, quemadmodum per se sibi satis est, ita per se sufficit ad id, ut sit omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: All these things are such that they need no laborious demonstration. Let the finite and dependent nature of any things whatever be compared with the independence and infinity of the divine perfection, and it will at once be understood both that God is all-sufficient and that he alone is so. It is certain that there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite; on the contrary, the excess of the infinite above the finite is immense. Therefore the infinite perfection of God exceeds any finite need of any finite thing an infinite number of times. And if God, being infinite, has communicated himself to the finite, then at least he can fully and completely supply every defect in it, whether he does so mediately, by compensating the defect of one creature through the substitution of another, or immediately, through the sense of his own most sweet enjoyment, which is all the more pleasant as the waters drunk from the very spring are sweeter. In short, either nothing of sufficiency exists in the nature of things, or whatever sufficiency is in all created things is contained in God as in their highest cause, provided it is God in a manner befitting him, that is, infinitely perfect. Consequently, what all created things can be to any one of them, God alone can be to all of them, and far more so. I grant that God does not always bestow those things with which he suffices. But the measure of an effect is not a fit measure of the abundance of goodness in the cause. This does not prove any defect of sufficiency, but only the freedom of his independent will in dispensing his gifts: he does not communicate himself as far as he can, like a blind cause, but to each of his creatures he gives of himself only as much as seemed good in his most wise counsel of will. Nor does the sufficiency of secondary causes, whatever it may be, which is visible in them as their efficiency is, detract from that sufficiency. For the greater it is, the more clearly it shows the fullness of the spring from which it flows. Thus God, as he is sufficient for himself through himself, is also sufficient through himself to be all in all.

units.la: Verum quid ista cogitâsse juvat, si tantum cogitentur, nec altius in pectus descendant? Quid Sufficientem Deum scimus, factis tamen abnegamus? Quid tam anxiè Voluptates, Opes, Honores venamur, tantamque in iis locamus Sufficientiam; quæ sicuti omnia in omnibus non sunt, ita satis esse minimè quCunt appetitui, cujus desideria infinitum spirant & æternum. Saltem, si quærimus, quid ita quærimus, ut quæ subordinata sunt turpi sacrilegio divellamus? Facimus id, quoties stulti creaturis secundum se aliquam tribuimus Sufficientiam; quasi ex sejunctae à principio suo, cujus influxui suam qualemcunque debent Sufficientiam, non omni re ipsâ exuantur Sufficientiâ. Imò quid adeo infinitis dolorum, metuum, curarum, affectibus torquemur, quoties deficit insufficientissima Sufficientia creata? Scilicet, ut inania captamus, ita quoties eis destituimur, nimium dolemus, quia non animo satis obversatur יהוה אל שדי, Jehova, Deus sufficiens: quo qui fruitur, beatus ille nactus est statum omni bonorum genere affluentem, cui nihil detrahit creaturae cujuscunque recessus, nihil addit vel totius Universi additamentum; quippe quod absque Omnisufficiente sufficit nihil, absque quo Omnisufficiens solus ipse est omnia in omnibus. Facessant ergo, cum trecentis illis de Summo Bono gentilium ineptiis, nostra pariter perversa hac parte vitae studia! Sat jam sæpe tulit vaga per divortia mentem Hinc Thetis, hinc Tellus, arduus inde Polus. Vel totum injectis mundum si metiar ulnis, Non tamen hæc ulnis par erit ulna meis. Quod neque sideri claudunt amplexibus orbes, Id voto spes est resque petita meo. Hactenus, heu fateor! vacuas dum prendimus auras, Semper ab amplexu mens male lusa suo est. Sis mihi Terra, Deus; mihi Tu Mare; Tu mihi Cœlum! Sis Tu cuncta mihi; Te sine, cuncta nihil!
units.tr: But what does it help to have thought these things, if they are only thought and do not sink more deeply into the heart? Why do we know that God is sufficient, yet by our deeds deny it? Why do we hunt so anxiously after pleasures, riches and honours, and place in them such sufficiency, which, since they are not all in all, cannot satisfy the appetite whose desires breathe infinity and eternity? At least, if we seek, why do we seek in such a way that we tear apart in shameful sacrilege the things that are subordinate to God? We do so whenever, in our folly, we attribute to creatures some sufficiency of their own, as if, separated from their origin, on whose influence they depend for whatever sufficiency they have, they were not stripped of every real sufficiency. Nay, why are we tormented by such infinite affections of pain, fear and care, whenever the most insufficient created sufficiency fails us? Clearly, as we grasp at empty things, so when we are deprived of them we grieve too much, because the name Jehovah, God All-sufficient, [יהוה אל שדי] does not sufficiently present itself to the mind. Whoever enjoys him has attained a state of blessedness overflowing with every kind of good, from which the departure of any creature takes nothing, and to which the addition of the whole universe adds nothing; for without the All-sufficient, the creature suffices for nothing, and without whom the All-sufficient alone is all in all. Away, then, with the three hundred foolish notions of the Chief Good held by the Gentiles, and likewise with our own perverse pursuits in this part of life! Often enough has the mind, wandering through diverse paths, been carried hither by the sea, hither by the earth, and thither by the lofty pole. Even if I should measure the whole world with outstretched arms, this span will not be equal to my arms. What the orbs of the stars do not embrace is the hope and the thing I seek with my desire. Hitherto, alas, I confess, while we grasp at empty air, the mind is always deceived in its embrace. Be thou my earth, O God; be thou my sea; be thou my heaven! Be thou all things to me; without thee, all things are nothing!
Exercise Fourteen, On the Incomprehensible God.
Summary.

units.la: I. Nullius Sensitivæ perceptionis unquam Deus esse potest objectum. II. Humanæ menti Deum, & solum quidem, esse Incomprehensibilem, docetur. III. Etiam beatis Cœlitibus Deus incomprehensibilis exístit. IV. Perperam in intellectu finito claram ac distinctam Dei ideam statui, offenditur. V. Non nisi modestissimè de Incomprehensibili Numine philosophandam. VI. Deus, quia Incomprehensibilis, etiam Ineffabilis.
units.tr: I. God can never be the object of any sensory perception. II. It is taught that God, and God alone, is incomprehensible to the human mind. III. God is incomprehensible even to the blessed inhabitants of heaven. IV. It is shown to be wrong to hold that a clear and distinct idea of God is possible in a finite intellect. V. Concerning the incomprehensible Deity, we must philosophise only most modestly. VI. God, because he is incomprehensible, is also ineffable.

units.la: SIc quidem Deus Omnisufficiens est. At talem tantum esse haud sufficit, nisi quoque tantum quam talem cognoscendum sese & agnoscendum exhibuerit istis, qui ejus pro modulo sunt capaces. Nunc itaque videndum, quo pacto se habeat tanta perfectionis plenitudo in ordine ad duplicem istam facultatem, quâ præ omni alia pollet rationalis, creatura, Intellectum puta & Voluntatem. Vim nostram percipientem quod attinet, notandum hic in antecessum diligenter, puram huc adferendam esse mentem atque elevatam longissimè supra id omne quod Sensus afficit: Insensibilis namque Deus est. Neque tantum isto communiori modo, quo, ob extensionis & corporeárum qualitatum, quæ organa afficere aptæ natæ sunt, carentiam, quivis Spiritus sensum fugit; verum ratione quâdam peculiari ac Deo propriâ, quatenus sentiri posse consistere nequit cum perfectionis Infinitate, neque cum Immensitate, neque cum Simplicitate. Non ergò Imaginabilis est interiori sensui, cujus nullum fingi potest phantasma, quod tanquam ectypon aliquam Dei, ceu archetypi sui, referat similitudinem. Neque eandem ob causam Effigiabile esse potest Numen; quandoquidem nemo vel statuâ quapiam vel pictura exprimere valet, cujus vel in cerebello suo delineatam nequit habere imaginem. Ut nimiùm contra ipsum luminis naturalis dictamen anthropomorphiticis idolis sacra sua polluant, qui incorruptibilis Dei gloriam foedissimum in modum mutant in similitudinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis, puta v. c. Senis, aut Juvenis: nec tantum hominis, sed & quadrupedis ac volucris, Agni videlicet, Columbæ, &c. Cæterùm, qui sensûs interni objectum esse nequit, idem nec externo Visu aut Tactu percipi potest. Tangitur id duntaxat, quod molis suæ resistentiâ obvium nostrum corpus potest afficere: quapropter absque palpabili errore nemo Deum neget Impalpabilem. Neque minus idem Invisibilis: quippe qui neque lumine suo neque colore oculo materiali se manifestare potest, dum essentiam possidet simplicissimam, nullos luminis radios aut emittentem aut remittentem. Quumque ista per se atque immediatè fluant ex ipsa Entis perfectissimi natura, tum etiam ex propria atque nativa sensuum nostrorum constitutione, absurdissimè opinantur nonnulli, beatos saltem cœlites corporeo oculo essentiam Dei intueri posse; elevato scilicet (ajunt) Sensu per potentiam Divinam ad actum istiusmodi eliciendum, quem viribus ipse suis naturalibus elicere non valet. Verum hoc qui contendere volunt, dicant illi pari cum subtilitatis acumine, visum elevari posse, ut percipiat sapores; aut auditum, ut sentiat colores: quæ certè minus sunt absurda, quam videri quod est absolutè & per naturam invisibile; quippe quod evidentem notat contradictionem.
units.tr: So God is indeed all-sufficient. But it is not enough that he be such, unless he has also shown himself to be known and acknowledged, as far as he is such, by those who are capable of him according to their measure. We must now consider how this great fullness of perfection stands in relation to the twofold faculty by which the rational creature excels all others, namely the intellect and the will. As for our power of perception, it must be noted here at the outset, with care, that the mind must be brought forward pure and raised far above everything that affects the senses, for God is insensible. Nor does he escape the senses merely in that more common way in which any spirit escapes them, through lacking extension and those corporeal qualities that are fitted to affect the organs. He escapes them for a certain peculiar reason proper to God: being perceptible cannot be reconciled with the infinity of his perfection, nor with his immensity, nor with his simplicity. Therefore he is not imaginable to the inner sense, since no phantasm can be formed of him that would represent some likeness of God as a copy of its archetype. For the same reason the Deity cannot be depicted, since no one can express in a statue or a picture what he cannot even have as a delineated image in his own little brain. So far do people go against the very dictate of the natural light that they defile their sacred things with anthropomorphic idols, who change the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, for example of an old man or a young man; and not only of man, but also of a four-footed beast and a bird, namely a lamb, a dove, and so on. Moreover, what cannot be the object of the inner sense cannot be perceived by outer sight or touch either. Only that is touched which can affect our body by the resistance of its mass; therefore, without a palpable error, no one can deny that God is Impalpable. He is no less Invisible: indeed he cannot make himself manifest to the material eye by his light or his colour, since he possesses a most simple essence, emitting or reflecting no rays of light. And although these things follow directly and immediately from the very nature of the most perfect Being, and also from the proper and native constitution of our senses, some absurdly maintain that at least the blessed inhabitants of heaven can behold the essence of God with the bodily eye, the sense, they say, being elevated by divine power to produce such an act, which it cannot produce by its own natural powers. But let those who wish to maintain this say, with equal subtlety, that sight can be elevated so as to perceive tastes, or hearing so as to perceive colours. Those things are certainly less absurd than to see what is absolutely and by nature invisible, for that involves an evident contradiction.

units.la: Non ergò corporeis organis quoquo modo sentiendum sese dare potest Deus. Et nos tamen, dum animâ constamus pariter & corpore, usque adeo sensationibus adsuncti sumus in hac vita, ut absque earum adminiculo vix quicquam cogitemus, difficillimè saltem attendamus ad ea, quæ imaginationi præsentia
units.tr: Therefore God cannot give himself to be sensed by bodily organs in any way at all. Yet we, since we consist of soul and body alike, are so bound to our sensations in this life that we can hardly think anything without their help, and at least find it very difficult to attend to those things which are not present to the imagination.

units.la: tia non sint. An verò idcirco quoque Dominus alibi, Non me videbit homo, & vivet? Imò, non videbit Numen propius, qui non attulerit intellectum à sensuum inquinamentis puriorem, quam qui nobis in hoc unionis statu obtingit. Quin, vel si sola mens, eaque purissima, huc accedat, ne ea quidem huic contemplationi par est: tanta Numinis est Incomprehensi- BILITAS. Tot scilicet & tantarum cuilibet intellectûs aciem huc intendenti sese offert perfectionum cumulus, ut ei sicuti in se est plenè intelligendo nullum unquam ingenium creatum sufficiat. Elegans istæc est metaphora, quâ cognitionem nostram vel Comprehensivam, vel Apprehensivam, dixerunt Philosophi. Nimirum, quemadmodum manus corpora se minora sic tangit, ut omni parte ambiens & excedens illa tota circumplectatur; se autem majora aliquâ quidem parte tenet, itâ tamen ut alia portione ab eis excedatur: sic Intellectus noster rem dicitur comprehendere, quàm plenè & perfectè cognoscit per idèam ipsi objecto adæquatam, atque omnia ac singula ejus prædicata intimè penetrantem; à qua cognitionis plenitudine quoties intellectus deficit, non omnia ut in se sunt, sed quædam duntaxat attributa rei, & qualicunque modo, sibi repræsentans, toties aliquid tantùm apprehendere dicitur. Atque ex hoc posteriori cognitionis genere est omnis creaturarum, quam de Deo habent, notitia. Quod facilè demonstratur. Videlicet, de natura finiti est, ut nulla plane inter ipsum & infinitum existat proportio; neque istud, quantumvis amplum, huic æquari unquam queat. Itaque cum indè perfectiones in Deo cognoscibiles sint omni modo infinitæ, hinc verò vis cognoscens in omni creatura sit finita, utique illæ quascunque cogitationes hujus longissimo intervallo post se relinquent, neque vel omnium simul creaturarum captu plenè ac perfectè intelligentur: eritque adeo Deus verè secundum excessum suarum perfectionum cuivis finito intellectui Incomprehensibilis. Quod idem de nulla creaturarum affirmari potest: quarum etsi forte pleræque à nulla mente creata secundum omnia sui prædicata comprehendantur, absolutè tamen, etiam à finito captu, comprehendi saltem possunt; sine dubio quoque ipso facto à Divino intellectu comprehenduntur. Cæterum, hoc Attributum ad creatam mentem totum retuli. Quandoquidem enim perfecta sui cognitio non minima perfectio est, ambiguum esse nequit, quin Ens infinitè perfectum se ipsum intelligat plenissimè, perfectissimè. An verò hæc plena sui notitia Comprehensio dici debeat (de quo quidam contendunt) mera lis de voce esse videtur.
units.tr: tia non sint. Does the Lord therefore also say elsewhere, "No man shall see me and live"? Indeed, no one will see the Deity more nearly than one who brings an intellect purer from the defilements of the senses than the one that falls to us in this state of union. Indeed, even if the mind alone, and that most pure, approaches, it is still not equal to this contemplation: so great is the Incomprehensi-BILITY of the Deity. For a heap of so many and so great perfections presents itself to the gaze of any intellect that directs itself to it, that no created intelligence is ever sufficient to understand it fully as it is in itself. This is an elegant metaphor, by which the philosophers called our knowledge either comprehensive or apprehensive. Just as the hand touches smaller bodies in such a way that it embraces and surrounds them on every side, but holds larger ones only in part, so that another portion of them extends beyond it, so our intellect is said to comprehend a thing when it knows it fully and perfectly through an idea adequate to the object itself, penetrating intimately all its predicates, one by one. Whenever the intellect falls short of this fullness of knowledge, and represents to itself not all things as they are in themselves but only certain attributes of the thing, and in some sort, then it is said to apprehend only something. And all the knowledge that creatures have of God belongs to this latter kind. This is easily demonstrated. Namely, it is of the nature of the finite that no proportion at all exists between it and the infinite, and that the finite, however large, can never be made equal to the infinite. Therefore, since the perfections knowable in God are infinite in every way, while the knowing power in every creature is finite, those perfections will leave behind any thoughts about them by a very long interval, and they will not be fully and perfectly understood even by the grasp of all creatures taken together. And so God is truly incomprehensible to any finite intellect, in respect of the excess of his perfections. This cannot be said of any creature, for although perhaps most creatures are not comprehended in all their predicates by any created mind, yet they can at least be comprehended absolutely, even by a finite grasp, and without doubt they are also comprehended, by the very fact, by the divine intellect. Moreover, I have referred this attribute wholly to the created mind. For since perfect self-knowledge is no small perfection, there can be no doubt that the infinitely perfect Being understands himself most fully and most perfectly. Whether this full self-knowledge ought to be called comprehension (as some contend) seems to be a mere dispute about a word.

units.la: Quamvis autem ista ignorari nequeant vel leviter rem attendentibus, dissentiunt tamen multi Doctores Scholastici, distinguentes inter illam Dei cognitionem quam hic in via habemus, atque eam quam olim habituri sumus in patria. Viatoribus quidem haud aliam quam imperfectam & apprehensivam Dei notitiam reliquam faciunt; ast qui vivunt in cœlis beatos Comprehensores ipsi appellant. Absurdè! Non nego, inconceptibilibus modis Theologiam Visionis, quæ per lumen Gloriæ cœlitibus obtingit, superare illam nostram quam habemus in hujus vitæ stadio per lumen Naturæ, vel etiam Gratiæ. Etenim quas nos in speculo quasi relucentes contemplamur primi entis perfectiones, eadem illi, absque istis imbecillis naturæ nostræ adminiculis, familiariori revelatione propius, ceu de facie ad faciem, teste S. Paginâ, intuentur. Verumtamen quæcunque etiam fuerit immediata magis illa Divinarum perfectionum manifestatio, nunquam ea creatæ mentis captum sic elevabit, ut approportionatum reddat perfectè concipiendæ immensæ illi infinitorum prædicatorum latitudini: neque enim aut finitam mentem infinitate donabit, aut infinitum Deum intra finitudinis limites coarctabit; absque quorum altero creatum intellectum nullam comprehensivam Dei notionem habere posse, ostendimus. Neque cœlitum consummatæ felicitati quicquam obstat inadæquata Dei notitia, quandoquidem perfecta satis est, quæ omnem subjecti capacitatem replet, etsi non omnem objecti amplitudinem exhaurit. Summus potius ille videtur beatitatis gradus, si quis ne mente quidem suâ satis capere valeat excellentiam boni, quo frui se sentit. Quin ipsa hac ratione optimè cœlestis gaudii æterna esse poterit sine fastidio satietas.
units.tr: Although these matters cannot be ignored by anyone who attends to the thing even slightly, nevertheless many Scholastic teachers disagree, distinguishing between that knowledge of God which we have here on the way and that which we shall one day have in our homeland. They leave to wayfarers only an imperfect and apprehensive knowledge of God, but they themselves call the blessed in heaven comprehenders. This is absurd! I do not deny that the vision of God, which comes to the inhabitants of heaven through the light of glory, surpasses in inconceivable ways that knowledge of ours which we have in this stage of life through the light of nature, or even of grace. For the perfections of the first Being, which we contemplate as shining back to us as in a mirror, they see more nearly, by a more intimate revelation, as face to face, as Holy Scripture attests, and without those feeble aids of our nature. Yet however immediate that manifestation of the divine perfections may be, it will never so raise the grasp of the created mind as to make it proportionate to that immense breadth of infinite predicates, which is to be conceived perfectly. For it will neither endow the finite mind with infinity, nor confine the infinite God within the limits of finitude; and we have shown that without one of these the created intellect cannot have any comprehensive notion of God. Nor does an inadequate knowledge of God stand in the way of the consummate happiness of the inhabitants of heaven, since that knowledge is perfect enough which fills the whole capacity of the subject, even though it does not exhaust the whole breadth of the object. Indeed, that seems rather to be the highest degree of blessedness, if someone cannot grasp even with his mind the excellence of the good in which he feels himself to rejoice. Indeed, in this very way the satiety of heavenly joy may well be eternal without weariness.

units.la: Istoc Scholasticorum errore minus tolerabilis est hac parte opinio Cartesii, in hac ipsa vita omnium mortalium, tantùm citra præjudicium propriæ mentis tabulas intuentium, animis ob-
units.tr: This opinion of Descartes is less tolerable in this respect than the error of the Scholastics, since it asserts that in this very life there presents itself to the minds of all mortals, provided they look only at the tablets of their own mind without prejudice,

units.la: obversari afferentis insculptam quandam ideam Dei talem, quâ quamvis summas ejus perfectiones non comprehendamus, nihilominus tamen ipsas clarius & distinctius, quam ullas res corporeas, intelligere possimus. Quid ista sibi velint mysteria, jam dudum me haud satis intelligere, lubens fateor. Constat equidem rerum corporearum attributa omnia, sic ut in se sunt, à finito intellectu comprehendi saltem posse. Constat pariter ex antè dictis, rei infinitè perfectæ omnia ac singula prædicata, uti in se sunt, à finito intellectu comprehendi omninò non posse. Etiam denique per se manifestum est, eo clariorem ac distinctiorem esse cognitionem, quo magis est perfecta, quòque altius rem cognoscendam penetrat. Quæ si sint vera, uti sunt, quâ, obsecro, ratione dici potest, omni aliâ re clarius à nobis cognosci Deum, quem omnium minimè secundum omnia ac singula prædicata, prout in se sunt, mens sibi sistere potest præsentem? Non ista sententia stetit Apostolo, quando universam nostram de Deo in his terris notitiam, etiam illam quam revelationis supernaturalis gratia cordibus fidelium infundit, similem pronunciat ænigmati; cujus totam rationem in ipsa obscuritate consistere, notum est. Cogitationem nostram, fateor, magis implent Divinæ perfectiones, quam ullæ aliæ. Sed vel ideo intelliguntur obscurius, quia usque adeò mentem implent, ut totam obruant. Scilicet, non ea tantum confusa nobis sunt & inevidentia, quæ infra vim percipiendi subsistunt, eamque non satis afficiunt; verum & illa quæ longius eam excedunt, ac plus justo in eandem agunt. Æquè hic peccat nimium, atque parum; dum utroque modo recedítur ab ista proportione, quæ inter subjectum percipiens & objectum percipiendum necessariò requiritur, ad id ut perceptio clara sit ac distincta. Scitè hoc innuit Philosophus, quando mentem nostram ad contemplationem rerum nimis excellentium se habere dixit, uti se habet oculus noctuæ ad intuitum luminis meridiani. Et quis est, qui non sit expertus ardentis facis flammam longè clarius videri quam Solis splendorem; etsi hic oculum lumine multo magis impleat, quam illa? Plura qui cupit, conferat nostram Exercitat. de Infinito, ubi de hisce, quæque iis affinia sunt, actum est fusius. Plus modestiæ est in illa cautela, quâ Cartesius philosophaturum alibi monet utendum, ut tutò & sine errandi periculo rem aggrediatur, quæque, cum mirè huc pertineat, silentio prætereunda hoc loco non videtur. Vult, ut semper „quam maximè recordemur, & Deum auctorem rerum esse „infinitum, & nos omninò finitos. Itâ si fortè nobis Deus de „se ipso vel aliis aliquid revelet, quod naturales ingenii nostri „vires excedat, qualia jam sunt mysteria Incarnationis & „Trinitatis, non recusabimus illa credere, quamvis non clarè „intelligamus: nec ullo modo mirabimur, multa esse, tum in „immensa ejus natura, tum etiam in rebus ab eo creatis, quæ „captum nostrum excedant. Aurea regula! Cujus si aliquanto diligentius recordatus fuisset ipse ejus Auctor & sequaces, in tractandis Sacris plus reverentiæ, in Philosophicis plus modestiæ, conspicuum foret. Non illorum majestatem profanasset impius ex hac cavea Philosophus, Scriptura Interpres infallibilis; non horum latitudinem arctasset Cartesius intra angustos propriæ suæ perceptionis terminos. Quid addam de Scholasticorum audacia, atque Hæreticorum petulantia? qui quasi non sit Incomprehensibilis Deus, divina quæque ad captûs sui pedem metiri passim nihil metuunt. O! quanto rectius, dum isti suâ sibi temeritate cruces figunt, acquiescit hic sæpè mens sobriè sapientis, non in evidentia rei introspectæ, sed in altitudine veritatis occultæ! Ita qui capi cupit ab eo, quem capere se non posse capit, reverenter is habebit Incomprehensibilem majestatem, à gloria nunquam opprimendus, nisi gloriosè.
units.tr: a certain engraved idea of God, such that although we do not comprehend his supreme perfections, we can nevertheless understand them more clearly and distinctly than any corporeal thing. I readily confess that I have not for a long time understood well what these mysteries mean. It is certainly agreed that all the attributes of corporeal things, as they are in themselves, can at least be comprehended by a finite intellect. It is likewise agreed from what has been said above that the individual predicates of an infinitely perfect thing, as they are in themselves, cannot be comprehended at all by a finite intellect. Finally, it is also self-evident that knowledge is the clearer and more distinct the more perfect the object is and the more deeply it penetrates the thing to be known. If these things are true, as they are, by what reasoning, I ask, can it be said that God is known by us more clearly than any other thing, when the mind can least of all place before itself God's presence in all his individual predicates, as they are in themselves? That view did not stand with the Apostle, when he declares that our whole knowledge of God in this earthly life, even that which the grace of supernatural revelation pours into the hearts of believers, is like a riddle; and it is well known that its whole character consists in that very obscurity. I grant that the divine perfections fill our thought more than any others. But for that very reason they are understood more obscurely, because they fill the mind so completely that they overwhelm it. Certainly, it is not only those things that remain below the power of perceiving, and so do not sufficiently move it, that are confused and not evident to us, but also those that go beyond it and act upon it more than is right. Here one errs as much by excess as by deficiency, since both ways depart from that proportion which is necessarily required between the perceiving subject and the object perceived, if the perception is to be clear and distinct. The Philosopher hints at this aptly, when he said that our mind is related to the contemplation of things that are too excellent as the eye of an owl is related to the sight of the midday light. And who has not experienced that the flame of a burning torch is seen far more clearly than the splendour of the sun, although the sun fills the eye with light much more than the torch does? Whoever wishes for more should consult our Exercitatio de Infinito, where these matters and those akin to them are treated at greater length. There is more modesty in that caution which Descartes advises to be observed by one who philosophises elsewhere, so that he may approach the matter safely and without danger of error; and since it bears most directly on this point, it does not seem to be passed over in silence here. He wishes that we always remember most carefully that God, the author of things, is infinite, and that we ourselves are wholly finite. Thus, if God perhaps reveals to us something about himself or about other things that exceeds the natural powers of our intellect, such as now the mysteries of the Incarnation and the Trinity, we will not refuse to believe them, although we do not understand them clearly; nor will we at all wonder that there are many things, both in his immeasurable nature and also in the things created by him, that exceed our grasp. A golden rule! If its author himself and his followers had remembered it somewhat more diligently, there would have been more reverence in treating sacred matters and more modesty in philosophical ones. The impious "Philosopher, infallible interpreter of Scripture" would not have profaned their majesty from that cage; Descartes would not have narrowed their breadth within the narrow limits of his own perception. What shall I add about the audacity of the Scholastics and the wantonness of the heretics, who, as if God were not incomprehensible, fear nothing in measuring all divine things by the measure of their own grasp? O, how much more rightly does the mind of the soberly wise rest, while these men set up crosses of their own rashness, not in the evidence of a thing examined within, but in the depth of a hidden truth! Thus whoever desires to be grasped by him whom he grasps he cannot grasp will reverently regard the incomprehensible majesty, never to be overwhelmed by glory, except gloriously.

units.la: Cæterum, præter Sensum, tum etiam Intellectum, aliud adhuc in homine occurrit, referendum ad ejus perceptionem, tanquam ejusdem interpres atque nuncius, Sermo puta externus; ad quem quomodo se habeat Deus, idcirco obiter quoque hic erit attingendum. Verbo: quandoquidem voces sunt signa conceptuum, neque signo plus exprimi potest, quam in signato continetur, tanta exstitit inter λόγον ἐνδιάθετον & λόγον πρoφορικòν convenientia, ut quod intellectus capere nequit, idem lingua efferre non valeat; utque quod verbo mentis est Incomprehensibile, idem verbo oris sit Ineffabile. Quumque prius jam de Deo sit demonstratum, de posteriori quoque dubium esse haud potest. INEFFABILE dico Numen; non quod plane nihil de eo dicere liceat, nam sic ne Ineffabile quidem a nobis jam praedicari posset: verum quatenus nullum tantum sermonis apparatum excogitare datur, qui quid exprimat, quod infinitis Dei perfectionibus plene exprimendis dignum sit ac sufficiens, & cujus etiam amplissima significatione non infinities amplior sit res significata. Nomen יהוה non absque multis fabulis ἀνεκφώνητον perperam contendunt Judaei: quam litem Philologicam praeclare excussam vide a Venerando Collega Cl. Leusdeno, Phil. Hebr. Dissert. XXVIII. & seqq. Quamvis vero erret, qui non de ipsa potius quam de Nomine sic sentit, multo tamen tolerabilior est illa superstitio, quam multorum hodie profani & inanes garritus de Deo Ineffabili; de quo sine timore ac tremore nemo unquam balbutire incipit, qui debita tangitur Numinis reverentia: usque adeo etiam vera de Ineffabili effari res est sollicitudinis atque periculi plena.
units.tr: Moreover, besides sense and also intellect, there is yet another thing in man that is to be referred to his perception, as its interpreter and messenger: namely, outward speech; and how God stands in relation to this must here be touched on in passing. In short, since words are signs of concepts, and a sign can express no more than what is contained in the thing signified, there is such a correspondence between the inner word [λόγος ἐνδιάθετος] and the spoken word [λόγος προφορικός] that what the intellect cannot grasp, the tongue also cannot utter; and what is incomprehensible to the word of the mind is likewise unspeakable to the word of the mouth. And since the former has already been demonstrated concerning God, there can be no doubt about the latter. I call the Deity UNSPEAKABLE; not because nothing at all may be said about him, for in that case even "unspeakable" could not now be predicated of him by us; but insofar as no such array of language can be devised as would express, in a way fitting and sufficient to express the infinite perfections of God, what is signified, and even in its most ample signification the thing signified is not infinitely greater. The Jews wrongly contend, not without many fables, that the name [יהוה] is [ἀνεκφώνητον] unpronounceable; for this philological dispute, admirably thrashed out, see our venerable colleague, the learned Leusden, Philologus Hebraeus, Dissertation XXVIII and following. Although he errs who thinks thus about the name rather than about the thing itself, that superstition is nevertheless much more tolerable than the empty and profane chatter of many today about the Ineffable God; no one who is touched by the due reverence for the Deity ever begins to stammer about him without fear and trembling. So much is it a matter full of anxiety and danger even to speak truly about the Ineffable.

units.la: EXERCITATIO DECIMA-QUINTA, DE DEO ADMIRABILI, ET AMABILI. SUMMARIUM.
units.tr: EXERCISE FIFTEEN, ON THE ADMIRABLE AND LOVABLE GOD. SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Animo finito Numen infinitum existit summè Admirabile. II. Uberior ejus rei confirmatio & illustratio. III. Amabilitatis Divinæ consideratio. IV. Ea tanta, ut nihil amandum non propter Deum.
units.tr: I. The infinite Deity exists, supremely admirable, in the finite mind. II. A fuller confirmation and illustration of this. III. Consideration of the divine lovableness. IV. This lovableness is so great that nothing is to be loved except on account of God.

units.la: ATque itâ quidem se habet Deus ad creatæ Mentis perceptionem. Nunc, quâ ratione se habeat ad finitæ Voluntatis appetitum, paucis quoque videamus! Missis, quæ in hanc rem adferri possent, aliis plurimis, unam duntaxat atque alteram attendemus voluntatis nostræ motionem facilè principem, Admirationem puta, atque Amorem; quæ duæ junctæ præcipuum existunt genuinæ, quam Numini debemus, Reverentiæ ac Cultûs fundamentum. ADMIRABILIS Deus est, quatenus animum cujusvis creaturæ, se diligentius contemplantis, repentinâ quâdam occupatione sic afficit, ut totus in Ipso hæreat, tanquam in re rarissima, & præ aliis maximâ consideratione digna. Multa quidem mirabilia occurrunt in natura rerum; ea scilicet, quæ intrinsecâ suâ essentiâ aliquid continent, quod latens & reconditum non omninò assequimur, inque cujus intuitu animus hæhæret suspensus, ulteriori sciendi desiderio flagrans: verùm nihil eorum omnium est, quod cuivis necessariò & semper admirandum videatur; quatenus absolutè saltem unumquodque finitum à finito intellectu sic penetrari potest, ut nulla superfit stuporis causa. Oritur enim omnis Admiratio ex quadam rei novæ ignorantia, conjuncta cum desiderio eam plenius cognoscendi: ut, quamvis ignorantiæ filia sit Admiratio, excitet ea tamen sciendi cupiditatem. Undè maximè Philosophi esse hunc affectum, nec aliud esse Philosophiæ principium, quam ipsam Admirationem, merito censuit Plato: uti non minus rectè Pythagoras, se ex Philosophia id parasse ajebat, ne quid admiraretur. Scilicet, qui rerum omnium adeo omnibus numeris perfectam notitiam sibi habet, ut nihil quod in ea continetur ipsum fugiat, nil is miratur: quæ res, judice Poeta, prope una est,
units.tr: Thus God stands in relation to the perception of the created mind. Now let us briefly see how he stands in relation to the appetite of the finite will. Setting aside the many other things that could be brought to bear on this, we will attend to one or two motions of our will that are easily the chief, namely admiration and love. These two joined together form the principal foundation of the genuine reverence and worship we owe to the Deity. God is admirable insofar as he so affects the mind of any creature who contemplates him more carefully, by a sudden seizure, that the mind clings wholly to him as to a thing most rare and most worthy of consideration above all others. Many marvels indeed occur in the nature of things, namely those which contain within their intrinsic essence something hidden and recondite that we do not wholly grasp, and upon whose sight the mind hangs suspended, burning with a further desire to know. But none of them is such that it necessarily and always seems admirable to everyone, inasmuch as each finite thing, at least absolutely, can be penetrated by a finite intellect so that no cause of astonishment remains. For all admiration arises from a certain ignorance of a new thing, joined with a desire to know it more fully; so that, although admiration is the daughter of ignorance, it nevertheless arouses the desire to know. Hence Plato rightly judged that this feeling is especially proper to philosophers, and that admiration itself is the only beginning of philosophy. Pythagoras, no less rightly, said that he had prepared himself through philosophy so as to admire nothing. Clearly, one who has such a perfect knowledge of all things in every respect that nothing contained in them escapes him admires nothing. This, in the judgment of the poet, is nearly the only thing,
And the only thing that can make and keep one blessed.

units.la: Atque hæc ratio est, cur hoc Dei attributum restrinxerim ad animum creatum. Ens enim infinitum, quemadmodum sese plenissimè intelligit, & modo quodam perfectissimo se ipso fruitur, ita in intelligentia, ut aliarum rerum, sic quoque sui, nihil habet obvium, quod rarum videatur nec satis plenè cognitum, quodque ideò repentinâ commotione ad ulteriorem sui considerationem incitet.
units.tr: And this is the reason why I have restricted this attribute of God to the created mind. For an infinite being, just as it understands itself most fully and enjoys itself in a most perfect way, so in its understanding, both of other things and of itself, has nothing before it that seems rare and not sufficiently fully known, and which would therefore stir it by a sudden movement to further consideration of itself.

units.la: II. Uberior ejus rei confirmatio & illustratio.
units.tr: II. A fuller confirmation and illustration of this.

units.la: Sola creatura rationalis est, eaque omnis, cui attendenti non potest non continuò aliquid rari in Numine occurrere & admirandi. Quod non in hoc tantum rerum statu obtinet, sed & in maxima ejusdem, quantam obtinere potest, perfectione. Quandoquidem enim jam antè satis docuimus, usque adeò Divinas perfectiones omnem finitæ mentis captum excedere, ut nunquam non ei sint & maneant Incomprehensibiles, etiam non potest non tanta altitudo veritatis occultæ plurima semper in recessu habere, quæ sedulo inquirenti nova occurrant, animumque creatum in admirationem rapiant & stupore percellant. Quin, quum in aliarum rerum notitia quo magis proficimus, eo minus miremur, hic ex adverso tanto stupemus magis, quanto plus cognoscimus: in quo vel uno maximè mirandum exstitit Numen. Et quid demonstratione opus est? Sive essentiam dividivinam spectes, sive perfectiones, sive actiones, offerunt sese ubique rerum admirandarum thesauri inexplicabiles. Quis, nisi sordidus nimium Numinis contemplator, absque animi haesitatione cogitet Deum existentem sine causa; sine successione praeteriti ac futuri durantem; sine situ, sine loco, sine extensione, universa implentem; sine compositione omnia in uno possidentem; sine mutatione omnia mutantem; uno mentis ictu infallibiliter contingentia praevidentem; immutabili voluntatis actu quaevis libera decernentem; irresistibili potentiae determinatione voluntates indifferentes flectentem; creantem omnia sine indigentia; conservantem omnia sine labore; gubernantem omnia sine molestia; poenitentem sine dolore; irascentem sine motu? Ut jam de mirabili Mundi structura nil addam, in qua quisquis mirabilia Opificis non stupet, stupet ille profecto nimium. Suae aetatis sapientissimus habitus Socrates orientem Solem immotis membris eisdemque vestigiis stans attonitus mirabatur saepius. At quae nos abriperet sanctae admirationis ἔκστασις, si ut fas est ad tantum Numen meditandum animum adjicere mus satis! Unica certe votorum nostrorum summa foret, ut ab eo, quem capere non possumus, caperemur; quam quidam narrant fuisse ultimam vocem Philosophi, cum dispendio vitae, alternos rapidi maris cursus nimium admirantis.
units.tr: Only the rational creature exists, and every such creature, attending to God, cannot fail to continually find something rare and admirable in the Deity. This holds not only in the present state of things but also in the greatest perfection that the creature can attain. For since we have already shown sufficiently that the divine perfections so far exceed the grasp of the finite mind that they always remain incomprehensible to it, so too that great depth of hidden truth cannot but always keep much in reserve that presents itself as new to the one who inquires diligently, seizing the created mind in wonder and striking it with amazement. Indeed, whereas in the knowledge of other things the more we advance the less we wonder, here on the contrary we are amazed the more, the more we know. In this one respect especially the Deity shows itself to be admirable. And why is demonstration needed? Whether you look at the essence, the perfections or the actions of the divine nature, inexplicable treasures of admirable things present themselves everywhere. Who, unless he were an excessively sordid contemplator of the Deity, could think without hesitation of God as existing without cause; enduring without succession of past and future; without situation, without place, without extension, filling all things; possessing all things in one without composition; changing all things without change; foreseeing with a single stroke of the mind things that happen infallibly; decreeing by an immutable act of will whatever is free; bending indifferent wills by an irresistible determination of power; creating all things without need; preserving all things without labour; governing all things without trouble; repenting without grief; being angry without passion? Not to add anything now about the wonderful structure of the world, in which whoever is not amazed at the marvels of the Maker is surely too amazed himself. Socrates, considered the wisest man of his age, often stood wondering at the rising sun, standing with unmoving limbs and the same posture. But what ecstasy [ἔκστασις] of holy admiration would carry us away, if we applied our minds enough, as is right, to meditate on so great a Deity! Surely the sole sum of our prayers would be that we be grasped by him whom we cannot grasp. This, some relate, was the last word of the Philosopher who, at the cost of his life, admired too much the alternating rush of the swift sea.

units.la: Sic Deus, quatenus tanquam Maximus ab intellectu nostro non comprehenditur, animo Admirabilis est; qui idem interim, quatenus tanquam Optimus a mente apprehenditur, voluntati occurrit ceu summe Amabilis. Amabilis, inquam; & quidem modo quodam peculiari ac sibi proprio, in quantum dignus existit, quem unum prae aliis quibuscunque, tantum propter se, quanta potest virium intentione summo votorum studio prosequatur creatura rationalis. Bonum id esse, jam olim dixit Philosophus, quod omnia appetunt. Et jure merito. Quod enim sibi congruum est, non potest non appetere voluntas, tendens semper in maximam, quantam obtinere valet, sui perfectionem; atque ideo annitens, bono, quo semetipsam in se ipsa sentit desitui, ex alterius secum unione frui. Inde quicx rationis praescripto agit, mensuram sui amoris ponit ipsam objecti bonitatem; quam ultra citrave quoties fertur affectus, totics ties errantis judicii ductum inordinato motu sequitur voluntas. Ut in omni amore peccare semper queat, tum nimium, tum parum. Tantum hic amor nimium non patitur. Quin parum est, quicquid hoc loco minus est maximo. Perfectissimum namque Optimum pariter existit; quod, quæ in re quapiam secundum se spectata est Perfectio, eadem relata ad appetitum sit Bonitas. Numen itaque infinitè perfectum, hoc ipso infinitè bonum est. Ast, ut jam ostendi, quo quid bonum magis, eo magis amabile. Quod ergò infinito bonitatis excessu finito quovis bono melius est, quanto est illo melius, tanto dignius existit omni sincerae charitatis affectu. Dignus idcirco Optimus Deus tanto amore, quanti ne quidem res finita capax est.
units.tr: Thus God, insofar as he is apprehended by our intellect as the Greatest, is admirable to the soul; and the same God, insofar as he is apprehended by the mind as the Best, presents himself to the will as supremely lovable. Lovable, I say, and indeed in a certain peculiar way proper to himself, inasmuch as he is worthy to be pursued by the rational creature alone above all others, for his own sake, with the full intensity of its powers and the highest zeal of its desires. That is good, the Philosopher said long ago, which all things desire, and rightly so. For the will cannot but desire what is suited to it, always tending toward the greatest perfection of itself that it can obtain; and therefore, striving, it seeks to enjoy by union with another the good of which it feels itself deprived within itself. Hence whoever acts according to the prescription of reason sets the measure of his love by the very goodness of the object. Whenever the affection is carried beyond or short of this, the will, by disordered motion, follows the lead of an erring judgment. So in every love one can always sin, both by too much and by too little, yet this love does not suffer too much; indeed, whatever is less than the greatest is little. For the most perfect is likewise the Best. What is perfection in a thing considered in itself is the same, when related to the appetite, as goodness. Therefore God, infinitely perfect, is thereby infinitely good. But, as I have now shown, the more a thing is good, the more it is lovable. What therefore is better than any finite good by an infinite excess of goodness is worthy of every sincere affection of charity, in proportion as it is better than that good. Therefore the Best God is worthy of a love such as no finite thing is even capable of.

units.la: Ut revera, quotquot animum adjiciunt ad aliquid amandum non in ordine ad Deum, amori enti perfectissimo debito tantum detrahant, quantum ejus in creaturam transfundunt. Stulti profectò, qui umbratica veris, inania solidis, modica infinitis præferunt. Adeò præter Deum rationali appetitui non potest quicquam ambire esse non propter Deum: in quo uno quemadmodum est omne bonum, omne pulcrum, omne delectabile, ita solus amandus est propter se. Nec aliud ad ipsam nostram beatitudinem pertinet; quum unus Deus plus possideat, quam nos finiti in æternum, ut nobis bene sit, concupiscere possumus. Quamobrem in hoc solo amore desiderium est cum satietate, & satietas cum desiderio; in quo nec desiderium dolorem generat, nec satietas fastidium. Cæterum, referebam iterum hoc Attributum ad voluntatem creatam: etsi negandum minimè sit, ut suo loco videbimus, etiam Deum infinitum amare se ipsum infinitè. Atquì alterius prorsus ordinis hic amor est ab eo, quo fertur creatura in Deum; quippe qui, remotus ab omni concupiscentia & desiderio, solà absolvitur complacentiâ; ideoque non est, quemadmodum iste, motus quidam in bonum à se diversum, sed potius mera tranquillitas, quâ mens perfectissima in suis perfectionibus sibi placet & acquiescit.
units.tr: Truly, all who apply their minds to love anything not in relation to God detract from the most perfect love due to him just as much as they transfer to the creature. Surely foolish are those who prefer shadows to truths, empty things to solid, small things to infinite. Thus apart from God the rational appetite can desire nothing that is not for God's sake. In him alone, as in all good, all beauty and all delight, so he alone is to be loved for his own sake. Nor does anything else pertain to our very blessedness, since God alone possesses more than we finite beings could desire for ourselves through eternity, that we might be well. Wherefore in this love alone there is desire with satiety, and satiety with desire; in it desire does not produce pain, nor satiety loathing. Moreover, I was referring this attribute again to the created will, although it must by no means be denied, as we shall see in its place, that the infinite God also loves himself infinitely. But this love is of an entirely different order from that by which the creature is carried toward God. For that love, remote from all concupiscence and desire, is completed by complacency alone. So it is not, as the creature's love is, a certain motion toward a good different from itself, but rather pure tranquillity, by which the most perfect mind is pleased with its own perfections and rests in them.
EXERCITATION SIXTEEN, ON GOD AS THE OBJECT OF WORSHIP.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Cultûs cujusvis, ejusque fundamenti, generalis consideratio. II. Deus Adorabilis tantum ob infinitam Sufficientiæ excellentiam. III. Actus & Signa divini cultus paucis notati. IV. Deus & solus & semper Adorabilis existit. V. Religiosus cultus neque gradus patitur, neque vi Dei irrefiftibili nititur.
units.tr: I. A general consideration of worship of any kind, and of its foundation. II. God is adorable only because of the infinite excellence of his self-sufficiency. III. The acts and signs of divine worship, briefly noted. IV. God alone and always exists as adorable. V. Religious worship admits of no degrees and does not rest on the irresistible power of God.

units.la: {a}X utroque affectu, tum Admirationis, tum Amoris, nasci solet alius, qui Existimatio dicitur; notatque inclinationem animi in rem quam miratur aut amat, ortam ex opinione quam habemus de excellentia magnitudinis & bonitatis in re mira aut amata. Quod fi Exiftimatio rei cujufpiam tanta fuerit, ut judicemus dignam cui nos vel nostra subjiciamus, abit ea in Venerationem five Cultum: qui, fi fummus fit, omnimodamque fubmiffionem involvat, religiosus dicitur, seu Divinus; atque à primario quodam ejus exercitio, tanquam à principali parte, Adoratio nuncupatur, indeque Deus ipse ADORABILIS; idest, dignus ob summam excellentiam à creatura rationali honorari cultu religioso. Hic autem quo pacto conveniat Deo, cum fatis intelligi nequeat, nisi perspecta natura Cultûs five Honoris, pauca de illo præernotanda veniunt in antecessum. Omnis Cultus aliquam dicit honorantis subjectionem; approportionatam scilicet rei honoratæ dignitati atque excellentiæ. Etenim O quifquisquis major est & præstantior nunquam quâ talis minorem proprië dicto cultu prosequitur: minor verò qua talis, quoties rem se majorem cognoscit, non potest non, si ex ratione agat, tanto se facere inferiorem, quanto illam agnoscit superiorem. Ex quibus intelligitur, genuinum omnis cultûs fundamentum esse sufficientiam ac præstantiam rei quam colimus: ut accuratissimè dixerit alibi Cicero, Habet venerationem justam quicquid excellit. Quod adeò verum est, ut inter homines quisquis perfectione aliquâ eminet, quantum eâ eminere creditur, tantæ quoque existimationis & venerationis sit apud alios. Undè & quæcunque hominem exornant dotes fundamentum existunt civilis alicujus honoris: uti manifestum est, & in bonis animi, qualia sunt, mentis perspicacitas, judicii dexteritas, sapientia, fortitudo, mansuetudo, &c. & corporis, uti sunt, robur, pulchritudo, &c. & denique, ut vocant, fortunæ, quo pertinent, nobilitas, divitiæ, ætas provectior, &c. Quæ omnia, quanto præstantiora sunt in aliquo, tanto magis existimationem intendunt. Etiam quidem, fateor, rerum gestarum magnitudo honorem meretur; sed non per se, verùm duntaxat quatenus opus virum indicat, atque argumentum existit sufficientiæ quæ in agente latet: qua de causa quæcunque fortuito, etiamsi feliciter, accidunt, quatenus nullam arguunt agentis sapientiam & industriam, nullam etiam erga illum excitare solent venerationem. Neque eis quæ de honore dixi obstat, quod etiam homines nequissimi, ob scelera ipsa, v.c. strenuam compotationem, scortationem, &c. nonnunquam honorentur à quibusdam; non enim id fit, nisi ab eis, qui depravato judicio aliquid excellentiæ in ejusmodi quoque flagitiis se reperire autumant: ut quidem in speciem honorentur tales, attamen re verâ honorandi minimè sint. Cæterùm, cùm ipso cultu minimè confundendum est ejus signum externum; quippe quod ad essentiam illius per se non pertinet: etsi necessarium existat inter eos, quibus de interna animi venerationE non aliter, quam per adhibita istiusmodi testimonia externa, constare potest. Mitto plura, quæ pro dignitate hujus rei dicenda præsens pagina non capit. Nunc pro nostro instituto satis erit hæc de Honore prænotasse: quippe quæ ad Religiosum Cultum translata, illi explicando sufficient.
units.tr: From each of the two feelings, admiration and love, there usually arises another, which is called esteem. It denotes an inclination of the mind towards a thing that we admire or love, arising from our opinion of the excellence of its greatness and goodness. If our esteem for some thing is so great that we judge it worthy of us to submit ourselves or our possessions to it, this becomes veneration or worship. If this worship is of the highest degree and involves complete submission, it is called religious, or divine. From one chief part of it, as from its principal element, it is called adoration, and so God himself is called ADORABLE, that is, worthy, because of his supreme excellence, to be honoured by a rational creature with religious worship. But since this cannot be sufficiently understood unless the nature of worship or honour is first thoroughly grasped, a few points about the latter must be noted in advance. All worship implies some subjection of the one who honours, proportioned to the dignity and excellence of the one honoured. For whoever is greater and more eminent, as such, never receives proper worship from someone lesser; and the lesser, as such, whenever he recognises the other as greater, cannot, if he acts rationally, fail to make himself inferior in proportion as he acknowledges the other as superior. From this it is understood that the true foundation of all worship is the sufficiency and eminence of the thing we worship, as Cicero said very accurately elsewhere: Whatever excels has a just claim to reverence. This is so true that among men, whoever stands out by some perfection is held in as much esteem and reverence by others as he is believed to excel in that perfection. Hence whatever gifts adorn a man are the grounds of some civil honour. This is plain both in goods of the mind, such as keenness of intellect, skill in judgement, wisdom, courage, gentleness and so on, and in goods of the body, such as strength and beauty, and finally in what are called goods of fortune, to which belong noble birth, riches, advanced age and so on. All of these, the more eminent they are in someone, the more they increase esteem. I admit that the greatness of deeds also deserves honour, but not in itself; only so far as the deed reveals the man and is evidence of the sufficiency that lies hidden in the doer. For this reason, things that happen by chance, even if fortunately, since they show no wisdom or diligence in the agent, usually do not arouse reverence for him. Nor does it count against what I have said that even most wicked men are sometimes honoured by some people for their very crimes, for example for hard drinking, whoring and the like. This happens only among those who, with a corrupt judgement, suppose that some excellence is to be found even in such shameful acts. Such men may be honoured in appearance, but in truth they are in no way worthy of honour. Moreover, the external sign of worship must not be confused with the worship itself, since it does not belong by itself to its essence, although it is necessary among those who can know of someone's inward reverence only through such outward testimonies. I pass over many other points, which the present page does not have room for, given the importance of this matter. For our purpose it will be enough to have noted these things about honour, since, when applied to religious worship, they will suffice to explain it.

units.la: Est itaque Cultus Religiosus, Veneratio Entis sufficientissimi, per omnimodam sui submissionem. Quandò objectum religiosi cultûs assigno Ens sufficientissimum, pariter ejusdem indico fundamentum; quod est absoluta sufficientia, omnes omninò perfectiones involvens. Quandoquidem enim jam ostendimus, venerationis cujuscunque fundamentum esse rei honoratæ præstantiam, etiam supremi honoris, qualis religiosus est, fundamentum aliud nullum esse potest, quam summa perfectionis excellentia. Quo sensu præclarè Epicurus, apud Ciceronem, tam eximiam esse, ait, & præstantem naturam Deorum (Dei), ut ea debeat ipsa per se ad se colendam allicere sapientem. Atque hinc rectè observarunt quidam Theologi, non satis accuratè dici, Deum quà Creatorem, Christum quà Mediatorem, esse adorandum. Quamvis enim verissimum sit, Deum, qui Creator est, Christum, qui Mediator est, adorandum esse; imò etiam, Deum, quia Creator est, Christum, quia Mediator est, esse adorandum (quatenus Creationis ac Redemptionis consideratio efficacissimè nos impellit ad cultum Deo debitum, tanquam gratitudinis officium, præstandum) minus tamen istæ phrases probandæ videntur, quatenus in speciem præ se ferunt, ac si Dei Adorabilitas fundetur in beneficio Creationis aut Redemptionis, & non potius in sola atque unica intrinseca Dei præstantia. Hæc (ut pergam) cum jam antè demonstrata sit infinita, omnisque honor, quemadmodum ostendi, suo fundamento debeat esse approportionatus, per se liquet, nullum cultum Deo infinitè perfecto dignum à creatura finita præstari posse, qui non sit quousque esse potest quasi infinitus, id est, conjunctus cum totali atque omnimoda sui submissione.
units.tr: Religious worship, therefore, is the veneration of the most sufficient Being through complete submission of oneself. When I assign the most sufficient Being as the object of religious worship, I at the same time indicate its foundation, which is absolute sufficiency, involving all perfections without exception. For since we have already shown that the foundation of any veneration is the eminence of the thing honoured, and since religious honour is the highest kind, its foundation can be nothing other than the supreme excellence of perfection. In this sense Epicurus, in Cicero, rightly says that the nature of the gods (God) is so exceptional and excellent that it ought by itself to attract the wise man to worship it. Hence some theologians have rightly observed that it is not sufficiently precise to say that God as Creator, or Christ as Mediator, is to be worshipped. For although it is most true that God, who is Creator, and Christ, who is Mediator, are to be worshipped, and even that God is to be worshipped because he is Creator, and Christ because he is Mediator (inasmuch as the consideration of creation and redemption powerfully moves us to render the worship due to God as a duty of gratitude), yet these phrases seem less acceptable, in that they give the impression that God's adorability is grounded in the benefit of creation or redemption, and not rather in God's own intrinsic excellence alone and unique. Since this excellence has already been shown to be infinite, and since all honour, as I have shown, must be proportioned to its foundation, it is clear of itself that no worship worthy of the infinitely perfect God can be rendered by a finite creature unless it is, as far as possible, as it were infinite, that is, joined with a total and complete submission of oneself.

units.la: Et in hoc uno essentia ac anima Religiosi Honoris consistit; absque quo quicquid præstatur venerationis, nihil habet divini cultûs. Ex adverso quicquid à nobis fit ex istius subjectionis conscientia, etsi pro objecto immediato habeat res hujus vitæ, totum tamen revera divinus cultus est. Neque enim ullo pacto Deo nosmet magis submittere possumus, quam si ipsum agnoscamus actionum nostrarum quarumcunque (etiam quarum ipsi quodammodo, per arbitrii libertatem, videri poteramus domini) arbitrum unicum ac supremum. Estque hic conceptus primarium genuinæ ac masculæ Ethicæ fundamentum; quatenus ex Regno Dei morali, quod in creaturas suas rationales Is exercet, fluit quicquid æqui & boni in actionibus humanis reperire datur. Quod fusiùs aliquando demonstrare, si Deus vitam dederit & vires, conabimur, deducturi Moralem Philosophiam ex primis Juris Naturalis elementis: cujus rei neglectus nobilissimam disciplinam mirè reddidit sterilem. Nunc istum oceanum ingredi non sinunt praefixi huic tractatui brevitatis termini.
