Illis iisdem prohibemur excutere singulos actus, quibus religiosa haec submissio absolvitur, quales sunt, Numinis Invocatio, Gratiarum actio, Fiducia, &c. quæ ut Pietatis partes sunt, & veræ Probitatis bases, ita ex professo in Ethica tractanda veniunt. Quo eodem pertinet disquisitio de Signis, per quæ interiorem animi venerationem coram Deo & hominibus testatam facimus. Verbo, ipsa rei natura docet, ea debere esse humillima, quatenus talia sola satis congrua sunt, ad exhibendam debitam animi Deo devoti submissionem.
units.tr: In this one thing lies the essence and soul of religious honour; without it, whatever veneration is offered has nothing of divine worship in it. On the other hand, whatever we do with an awareness of this subjection, even if its immediate object is a thing of this life, is in truth entirely divine worship. For in no way can we submit ourselves more to God than by acknowledging him as the sole and supreme judge of all our actions, including those of which we might seem, through the freedom of our will, to be in some sense the masters. This concept is the primary foundation of genuine and manly ethics, since whatever is just and good to be found in human actions flows from the moral kingdom of God, which he exercises over his rational creatures. If God grants us life and strength, we shall try some time to demonstrate this more fully, deducing moral philosophy from the first elements of natural law. The neglect of this has made the noblest discipline wonderfully barren. For now, the limits of brevity set for this treatise do not allow us to enter that ocean. For the same reason we are prevented from examining individually the acts by which this religious submission is carried out, such as invocation of the divinity, thanksgiving, trust and so on. Since these are parts of piety and the true foundations of uprightness, they are dealt with at length in ethics. To the same subject belongs the inquiry into the signs by which we display our inward veneration before God and men. In short, the very nature of the thing teaches that these signs ought to be most humble, since only such signs are sufficiently fitting to express the proper submission of a mind devoted to God.

units.la: Cæterum eo, quem jam explicuimus, modo Adorabilis est Deus & solus, & semper. Semper Adorabilis Deus est. Etsi enim ipso facto ab æterno, nullo existente præter se, adoratus non fuerit; erat nihilominus etiam tunc dignus, quem, casu quo existeret, reipsa religioso cultu veneraretur rationalis creatura. Quod tamen nullam arguit mutabilitatem in Numine, dum se honorari vult, tantùm quia dignus est; non quod sibi à nostro quicquam perfectionis accedat æstimio. Solus quoque imprimis Adorabilis existit Deus, quoniam nusquam extra eum reperire datur Omni-sufficientiam, unicum Religiosi cultûs fundamentum. Ut quivis alius alterius rei cultus religiosæ venerationi subordinandus sit: nullâ parte ei æquandus; multo minus præferendus. Imò verò sic pari passu ambulant Adorabilitas & Deitas, ut omne Adorabile merito concludatur esse verum Deum; quodque naturâ Deus non est, id neque Adorabile sit aut haberi debeat. Nulli enim, ut dixi, præterquam Deo religiosi cultûs fundamentum competere potest. Quapropter mirè contumeliosi sunt in Deum, atque abominabili læsæ Majestatis Divinæ crimine sese polluunt, qui Angelos, aliasve creaturas, quantumvis Sanctas & excellentes, religiosè adorandas esse contendunt dunt: cum tamen nihil habeant, ut Divinitatis, ita Adorabilitatis. Quo eodem fundamento ipsa ratio Idololatriæ reos arguit quoque illos, qui Christum Dominum nudum hominem credentes, religiosè tamen Adorandum contendunt. Quæ omnia uti reipsa <bl>ꝏ</bl> inducunt, ita mirum est patronos invenire posse inter eos, qui pro uno Numine agnoscendo præ aliis stare videri cupiunt.
units.tr: Moreover, in the manner I have now explained, God alone is adorable, and always. God is always adorable. For although from eternity, when nothing existed besides himself, he was not actually worshipped, he was nonetheless then worthy of being worshipped with religious worship by a rational creature, had one existed. This does not, however, indicate any change in the Deity, in that he wishes to be honoured only because he is worthy, and not because any increase of perfection comes to him from our estimation. God alone is also above all adorable, since nowhere outside him can omni-sufficiency be found, which is the sole foundation of religious worship. Therefore any other object of religious worship must be subordinated to the veneration of God; it must not be equal to him in any respect, much less preferred to him. Indeed, adorability and deity walk so closely together that every adorable thing is rightly concluded to be the true God, and whatever is not God by nature is neither adorable nor ought to be regarded as such. For, as I said, the foundation of religious worship can belong to no one but God. Therefore those who contend that angels, or other creatures however holy and excellent, are to be worshipped with religious worship are extremely insulting to God, and defile themselves with the abominable crime of injured divine majesty, since such creatures have nothing of adorability, just as they have nothing of deity. On the same foundation, the very reasoning of idolatry convicts of guilt also those who, while believing Christ the Lord to be a mere man, nevertheless contend that he is to be worshipped with religious worship. All these things, as they truly lead into idolatry, it is strange that defenders can be found among those who wish to seem to stand out above others in acknowledging the one Deity.

units.la: Adhæc, concidit ex traditis inepta & frivola distinctio inter Latriam & Duliam, tanquam diversas cultûs religiosi species; excogitata quibusdam ad turpem suam idololatriam palliandam. Cum enim ostensum sit, nullam venerationem esse religiosam, nisi quæ sit tanta, quanta esse potest, conjuncta scilicet cum omnimoda animi submissione, facilè intelligimus, Duliam, si sit cultus verè religiosus, Latriæ debere esse æqualem; aut, si æqualis non sit, sed aliquâ parte minor, ne quidem cultum religiosum esse. Porrò liquet ex demonstratis, errare Hobbesium vehementer; quando Religiosæ venerationis fundamentum revocat ad solam irresistibilem Dei potentiam. Quo ipso omnis genuinæ pietatis basin penitus subvertit. Etenim si in solius potentiæ existimatione consistat honor, utique servilis metus fuerit unica & vera religio; qui tamen pœnæ tantum formidinem, non virtutis amorem, generare aptus est. Nisi forte pessimi quique, ipsique adeo Diaboli, Deum quoque ritè honorare credendi sint; quippe qui non possunt non agnoscere & æstimare vim irresistibilem Numinis, cujus potentem manum sentiunt atque experiuntur. Excusandi saltem in tantum, juxta hanc hypothesin, Indi, quando se cultum Diabolo deferre profitentur eo fine, ne noceat. Absit à nobis, ut probemus, quod per hanc sententiam probatur, illud Poetæ, Primus in orbe Deos fecit timor. Denique apparet, Naturalem Theologiam esse quam maxime Practicam, dum non tantum cognoscendum Deum explicat, sed & religiosè colendum monstrat: etsi in his naturæ nostræ tenebris ignoret prorsus salutarem istius cultûs modum. Quem dum frustrà quæsiverunt gentiles, coeperunt ϑελοπεχνῶν, mixtis imperfectis Theologiæ Naturalis reliquiis depravatis Revelatæ Theologiæ traditionibus: unde malè compositæ Religionis insipida ϰεχοςς, longissimè recedens ab isto cultu, quo qui clariori lumine ducuntur, per Dominum Jesum Unitatem in Trinitate, ac Trinitatem in Unitate supplices adorant.
units.tr: Furthermore, the inept and frivolous distinction, handed down from earlier writers, between latria and dulia falls to the ground. It is treated as two different kinds of religious worship, and it was devised by certain people to cloak their shameful idolatry. For since it has been shown that no veneration is religious unless it is as great as it can be, namely joined with complete submission of the mind, we easily understand that dulia, if it is truly religious worship, must be equal to latria; or, if it is not equal but is somewhat less, then it is not religious worship at all. Moreover, it is clear from what has been demonstrated that Hobbes is greatly mistaken, when he traces the foundation of religious veneration back to God's irresistible power alone. By this very thing he utterly overturns the basis of all genuine piety. For if honour consists only in the estimation of power, then servile fear will be the only and true religion, and yet fear of this kind is apt to produce only dread of punishment, not love of virtue. Unless perhaps the worst of men, and the Devil himself, are to be believed to honour God rightly, since they cannot but acknowledge and esteem the irresistible force of the Deity, whose mighty hand they feel and experience. According to this hypothesis, at least the Indians would be excused, insofar as they profess that they pay worship to the Devil for this purpose, that he may not harm them. Far be it from us to approve what this opinion proves, that saying of the poet, Fear was the first to make gods in the world. Finally, it appears that natural theology is above all practical, since it not only explains that God is to be known, but also shows that He is to be worshipped religiously, although in the darkness of our nature it entirely lacks the saving manner of this worship. Since the Gentiles sought this in vain, they began to devise [ϑελοπεχνῶν], mixing the imperfect remnants of natural theology, corrupted, with the traditions of revealed theology; whence came the insipid [ϰεχοςς] of a poorly composed religion, very far removed from that worship by which those who are led by a clearer light, through the Lord Jesus, worship as suppliants Unity in Trinity and Trinity in Unity.

units.la: V. Religiosus cultus neque gradus patitur, neque vi Dei irresistibili nititur.
units.tr: V. Religious worship neither admits of degrees, nor rests upon the irresistible power of God.
DISPUTATION SEVENTEEN, ON THE LIVING GOD.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Vita Dei ipsa ejus essentia rationaliter actuosa. II. Esse hoc modo Deum Viventem demonstratur. III. Vita Dei Independens & Immortalis. IV. Vita Dei quot modis actuosa ?
units.tr: I. The life of God, which is his very essence, is rationally active. II. That God is living in this way is demonstrated. III. The life of God is independent and immortal. IV. In how many ways is the life of God active?

units.la: V Idimus praecipuas quasdam, quae cum Independentia Dei immediatè connexae sunt, Perfectiones; quarumque ideò, qua talium, nullum in rebus finitis deprehendere datur vestigium. Nunc ad illas contemplandas nos convertimus, quae communiorem Spiritualitatis conceptum sequuntur, quibusque hactenus simile quid & analogum reperitur in quibusdam creaturis: etsi modus eas possidendi sit dissimilLimus; dùm quod in Deo existit ratione quâdam simplicissimâ, infinitâ, essentiali, idem datur in rebus creatis mixtum, imperfectum, adventitium. Suntque haec potissimum, Intellectus, Voluntas, Potentia; & si quae alia ista comitentur. Supponunt illa Vitam Dei Spiritualem: quapropter de ea pauca dicemus in antecessum. Notamus illâ ipsam Divinam essentiam, ex se ipsa modo rationali absolutissimè actuosam. Num quid ab essentia verè distinctum dicat creaturarum vita? quibusdam disquiritur. Rectius, nostro judicio, sentiunt, qui negant. Verum hoc loco de eo disputare, parùm attinet; quandoquidem, quicquid etiam istius statuatur, in Deo saltem Vitam inter & essentiam nullum reapse discrimen esse admittendum, dum, evincit abundè demonstrata antè Simplicitas: quâ Deus Vivens ipsa sua Vita est, & vitalis operatio; ipse nimirum sua intellectio, suus amor, suum gaudium, sua beatitas. Caeterum, etsi unaquaeque vita in suo genere tam sit nobilis, ut non dubitet Paroemiastes canem vivum leoni mortuo praeferre, cum tamen non ejusdem ordinis sit quorumvis viventium Vita, quae illa Deo digna hujus loci sit, examinandum. Scilicet, quae essentia perfectissima ipsa Vita est, ejusdem, ut essentia, ita Vita, non potest non esse perfectissima. Semota ergò plurimum existit à Vita ista materiali & corporea, quam vivunt suo quodam modo, vegetativo Plantae, sensitivo Animantia. Nihil cum istis imperfectionibus commune habet ens perfectissimum, cujus sublimioris ordinis Vita est, totaque actuosâ quâdam rationalitate absolvitur: cujusque quatenus ectypon quoddam pro suo modulo exprimunt mentes creatae, etiam, inter alia, hoc sensu ipsae solae Imaginem Dei referre dicuntur.
units.tr: We have considered certain chief perfections that are immediately connected with the independence of God, and for that reason, as such, no trace of them can be found in finite things. Now we turn to those perfections that follow the more common concept of spirituality, and of which something similar and analogous is found in some creatures, although the manner of possessing them is most dissimilar. For what exists in God in a certain most simple, infinite and essential way is found in created things mixed, imperfect and adventitious. These are chiefly the intellect, the will and the power, together with whatever others accompany them. They presuppose the spiritual life of God, so we shall say a few things about that life beforehand. We note that the divine essence itself is, of itself, in a rational way, most absolutely active. Whether the life of creatures signifies something truly distinct from their essence is disputed by some. In our judgement, those who deny it judge more rightly. But it is of little concern to argue about this here, since, whatever is decided on that point, no real distinction between life and essence in God is to be admitted, as the Simplicity demonstrated at length above proves. By it God, being alive, is his own life and vital activity: that is, his own understanding, his own love, his own joy and his own blessedness. Moreover, although the life of each kind of being is so noble in its own kind that the proverb-maker does not hesitate to prefer a living dog to a dead lion, still, since the life of all living things is not of the same order, we must examine which life is worthy of God in this place. Clearly, that essence which is most perfect is itself life; and it, as its essence is most perfect, so its life cannot but be most perfect. Therefore it is far removed from that material and bodily life which living things have in their own fashion: the vegetative life of plants and the sensitive life of animals. The most perfect being has nothing in common with these imperfections; its life is of a higher order and is wholly completed by a certain active rationality. Created minds express this life, each according to its measure, as a kind of ectype [ἔκτυπον], and for this reason, among other things, they alone are said to bear the image of God in this sense.

units.la: Et vel ob hoc unum dubium esse nequit, quin rationaliter vivat Spirituum, rationaliter viventium, Pater & causa unica. Nisi vitâ careat origo & scatebra illa, ex qua quaecunque vivunt vitam hauriunt, & vitales facultates motusque arcescunt. Neque profectò perfectionis divinae infinitas patitur, ut iners & torpidum sit ens optimum, coque careat praedicato, quod omnium caeterorum quasi anima est, & absque quo foret, ut ne suis quidem beatitatibus frui valeret Deus. Quin ipse res inanimes testimonium dicunt huic veritati, quando mirissimo fui artificio, ipsoque bruto quo in suos quaeque fines tendunt impetu, sui Creatorem ac Gubernatorem arguunt sapientissimè viventem, isto eas moventem vitali influxu, ut & quae non vivunt vivere tamen videantur. Quapropter gentilium etiam sapientissimi adeò non Viventis Moderatoris imperio ea omnia quae nobis obvia sunt subducere potuerunt, ut Divinam mentem mundi animam fingere maluerint, cujus aurae particulam possideat unaquaeque pars universi; dum Spiritus intus alit, totamque infusa per artus Mens agitat molem, magno se corpore miscens.
units.tr: And for this reason alone it cannot be doubted that the Father and sole cause of spirits, which live rationally, lives rationally too. For otherwise that origin and fountain, from which all living things draw their life and from which they derive their vital powers and motions, would lack life. Indeed, the infinity of divine perfection does not allow that the best being should be inert and torpid and lack that predicate which is, as it were, the soul of all others, and without which God could not even enjoy his own blessednesses. Nay, even inanimate things bear witness to this truth: by their wonderful workmanship, and by the very blind impulse with which each tends to its ends, they proclaim a Creator and Governor who lives most wisely, moving them by that vital influence, so that even things that do not live seem to live. Therefore the wisest of the Gentiles could not so withdraw all those things that lie before us from the rule of a non-living Governor that they preferred to imagine a divine mind as the soul of the world, of which every part of the universe possesses a portion of the breath: "the Spirit feeds within, and the Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass, mingling itself with the great body."

units.la: Viventem ergò cogitet Deum oportet, quicunque rerum omnium causam primam ritè intelligere cupit, quae citra vitalem influxum nihil eorum facit, quæ facit. Atque hinc gravissima subest ratio, cur in Sacris passim promissionibus suis atque comminationibus Dominus adjiciat emphaticum illud, הַאֲנִי Vivo ego. Vivit videlicet qui ista annunciat, manu suâ certò perfecturus, quod jam mente suâ ab æterno formaverat consilium semper actuosus Deus. De quibus infrà plura.
units.tr: Therefore whoever wishes to understand rightly the first cause of all things must think of God as living, since without a vital influence he does none of the things that he does. And hence there lies a most weighty reason why the Lord, in his promises and threats throughout the Sacred Writings, adds that emphatic formula, As I live [חַי אֲנִי]. Surely he who announces these things lives, certain to bring about by his own hand what from eternity he had already formed in his mind as a purpose, since God is always active. More on these matters below.

units.la: Nunc adhuc prætercundum hoc loco haudquaquam est, etiam prorsus Independenter vivere Numen; quod quam diligentissimè observasse, usus erit in sequentibus longè maximi. Nimirum actio unaquæque conditionem sui principii refert, & unumquodque eo modo est actuosum, quo existit: quare non potest non independenter vivere id, cujus prima & essentialis perfectio ipsa Independentia est. Adeo ut, quemadmodum peculiari quodam suo jure ὁ ὤν, ita etiam ὁ ζῶν; nec minus אֶהְיֶה, quam אֶהְיֶה, dici queat Deus: qui ut primum Ens, ita primum pariter Vivens est; dum, nort uti cætera, vitam possidet mutuatitiam ac precariam, sed vitam suam habet in se ipso ex se ipso. Atque hoc demùm eminentissimam facit in Deo vivendi rationem, eam largiens absolutissimam perennis vitæ possessionem, quam neque intrinsecus defectus, neque extrinseca vis, ullâ unquam morâ interrumpere, ullo unquam fine terminare, potest: quo nomine, cum Vita, Immortalitatem in se ipso habet solus. Sed de hisce jam satis.
units.tr: Nor is it at all to be passed over here that the Deity lives also in a wholly independent way. To have observed this most carefully will be of very great use in what follows. Indeed, each action reflects the condition of its principle, and each thing is active in the manner in which it exists. Hence he whose first and essential perfection is independence itself cannot but live independently. So, just as God may rightly be called, in a peculiar sense, ho ōn [ὁ ὤν], so also ho zōn [ὁ ζῶν]; and as well as ehyeh [אֶהְיֶה], he may be called ehyeh [אֶהְיֶה] again. As he is the first Being, so he is equally the first Living: since, unlike other things, he does not possess a borrowed and precarious life, but has his life in himself and from himself. And this finally makes the manner of living in God most eminent, granting him an absolutely perfect possession of eternal life, which neither internal defect nor external force can ever interrupt with any delay or terminate with any end. On this account he alone has immortality in himself, together with life. But enough has been said of these matters now.

units.la: Porrò, quâ ratione actuosa sit vivens illa Dei natura, expendamus! Et quâ aliâ, quam quæ maximè est rationalis? Secum videlicet Intelligendo & Volendo quæcunque; tum etiam Potentiæ suæ efficaci exercitio extra se ponendo, quicquid sapientissimo consilio præter se exists vult. Ut non malè jam pridem hic notaverint eruditi, quemadmodum duplex Actionum genus, Immanentium videlicet & Transeuntium, ita quoque tres quasi Facultates, tanquam totidem operum divinorum principia; Dirigens primum, quod Intellectus est; Imperans alterum, quod Voluntas; Exequens tertium, quod Potentia. Quorum quomodo nullum cum altero in signo rationis sit confundendum, sequens hujus rei docebit pertractatio. Dixi, ne quis errret, in signo rationis: neque enim re verâ alterum hic ab altero diversum est, sed omnia à parte Dei actus idem purissimus. Quæ eadem causa erat, ob quam quasi Facultates eas appellavi, ne quis hic actum primum cogitet, qui ipsâ re alius sit quam actus secundus. De quibus plura suis locis.
units.tr: Next, let us consider in what way that living nature of God is active, and in what way other than the most rational. Clearly, by understanding and willing all things within himself; and also by placing outside himself, through the effective exercise of his power, whatever by his most wise counsel he wills to exist beyond himself. As learned men have not badly noted here before now, just as there are two kinds of actions, namely immanent and transient, so there are also three faculties, as it were, as so many principles of the divine works: the first, which directs, is the intellect; the second, which commands, is the will; the third, which executes, is the power. How none of these is to be confused with another in the reason of things, the following treatment will show. I said "in the reason of things," lest anyone err: for in reality they are not different from one another on God's side, but all are one most pure act. This was the same reason why I called them "as it were" faculties, lest anyone should think of a first act which in reality is other than a second act. More on these matters in their proper places.

units.la: EXERCITATIO DECIMA-OCTAVA, D E DEO INTELLIGENTE.
units.tr: EXERCITATION EIGHTEEN, CONCERNING GOD'S UNDERSTANDING.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Intellectus Dei explicatus & demonstratus. II. Modus intelligendi in Deo perfectissimus. III. Et nominatim quidem, Independens: IV Imò etiam Simplicissimus, & Immutabilis. V. Denique, Æternus quoque, Infallibilis, & Adæquatus. VI. Modi nostri cognoscendi imperfecti à Numinis Intellectu removendi. VII. Deus sese intelligit; & quo modo? VIII. Res quasvis à se alias Deum perfectè cognitas habere, demonstratur. IX. Possibilium Scientia in Deo datur per eorundem Ideas. X. Idque citra Divinæ Voluntatis decretum. XI. Futurorum, etiam contingentium, certa est in mente Divina Præscientia. XII. Existentia quælibet Deus plenissimè cognoscit. XIII. Etiam minima quaeque ac vilissima. XIV. Scientiæ Divinæ in Necessariam & Liberam divisio. XV. Media Scientia quid, & quo fine à suis inventoribus excogitata? XVI. Absur-
units.tr: I. The understanding of God is explained and demonstrated. II. The manner of understanding in God is most perfect. III. And in particular, it is independent. IV. Indeed, it is also most simple and immutable. V. Finally, it is also eternal, infallible, and adequate. VI. Our imperfect modes of knowing must be removed from the understanding of the Deity. VII. How does God know himself? VIII. It is demonstrated that God has a perfect knowledge of all things other than himself. IX. The knowledge of possibles exists in God through their ideas. X. And this apart from the decree of the divine will. XI. Certain foreknowledge of future things, even contingent ones, is in the divine mind. XII. God knows every existence most fully. XIII. Even the very smallest and most worthless things. XIV. The division of divine knowledge into necessary and free. XV. What is middle knowledge, and for what purpose was it devised by its inventors? XVI. Its absurdity, detected by several instances. XVII. The solution of the chief difficulties in this matter. XVIII. The mysteries of divine wisdom are to be acknowledged with reverence.

units.tr: Its absurdity, detected by several instances. XVII. The solution of the chief difficulties in this matter. XVIII. The mysteries of divine wisdom are to be acknowledged with reverence.

units.la: Primo orsurus, non immoror vocibus Intellectus & Cognitionis; quarum illa ex usu vulgari intelligendi vim, haec ipsum ejus exercitium magis exprimit, quemadmodum vocabulis Scientiae, Intelligentiae, Sapientiae, similibusque hic utimur, fermè ad variam cognitionis divinae excellentiam preßius exhibendam. Nobis promiscuus erit fere harum omnium vocum usus, per eas intelligentibus, Actum Dei Viventis perfectissimum, quo omnis omninò scibilis intimè sibi exstat conscius. Conscium sibi dico Deum, quatenus mente suâ comprehendit sibi praesentissima, quaecunque intelligit. Quae ut clarius perciperentur nobis, qui vix satis distinctè alios intelligendi actus quam qui sunt nostri concipimus, conferendae hic erunt nostrae perceptiones cum divina scientia: verum post pauca rectius id fiet. Intelligere Deum, prius demonstrandum est: si multum fit necesse. Recte enim Philosophus: Si mens divina nihil intelligat, sed ita se habeat ut dormiens, quodnam praecellens erit? Scilicet quis causam primam eâ exuat perfectione, quae inter alias una etiam princeps est. Neque agere potest ullo modo nisi rationaliter, quod neque casu agit aut bruto impetu, neque ad certos fines ab alio dirigitur: quorum utrumlibet respuit planè tum independens Divinae vitae perfectio, tum omnis haec Universi constitutio, istis librata, exaesciata, perfecta, ponderibus, mensuris, numeris, ut nox noti quoque indicet scientiam Opificis tantam, quantae nullus exstat numerus. Et quid conscientiae testimonio efficacius? Numen quis agnoscat, quod non adoret? Quis verò, nisi idololatra nimium ἀσέβεια, adoret, quod intelligentiâ non praeditum arbitretur? Sed mitto rem nimium manifestam. Potius, quo modo Deus cognoscat quae cognoscit? quantum cognoscere poterimus, examinemus. Ex antè dictis jam satis intelligitur, eum non posse non esse perfectissimum. Neque enim minus quam perfectissimum esse potest, quicquid ad consummatam entis perfectissimi perfectionem pertinet; præter quod ad Deum nihil pertinet. Ut haud ritè Dei Intelligentiam æstimet, qui tantam non agnoscit, quantus est ipse Deus. Atque evidentior generalis hæc veritas est, quam ut cujuspiam patiatur contradictionem: ut si tam facilis esset omnium consensus in ea, quæ perfectissimus ille sciendi modus re verâ involvit, nulla ulterior disquisitione hic opus foret. At nunc febriculosa quorundam philosophemata de Scientia media, quâ Numen speculetur suarum creaturarum actiones liberas; vel etiam de conjectura, quâ divinet futura contingentia, necessitatem imponunt cogitationibus nostris in rebus cæterum satis certis nonnihil hærendi, atque universæ hujus impietatis fundamenta hic suffodiendi. Non autem rectius tantarum rerum pro modulo nostro formabimus conceptum, quam si probè in mentem revocaverimus ea, quæ antehac de singulis perfectionibus Dei essentialibus notavimus; quibus conformis agnosci debet Divina scientia: nisi ens primum naturæ suæ non convenienter agere statuendum sit absurdissimè. Tùm etiam diligenter advertendum crit, quid imperfectionis adhæreat nostris cognoscendi modis, à Divinis procul dubio removendum: nisi anthropomorphiticas cogitationes de Deo nimium fovere velimus; quas fovent re verâ, quotquot unquam hac parte erraverunt.
units.tr: Before beginning, I will not dwell on the words "understanding" and "knowledge." The former expresses more the power of understanding in common usage, the latter its actual exercise. So too we use here the terms science, intelligence, wisdom and the like, mostly to express more strongly the varied excellence of divine knowledge. For us, these words will be used almost interchangeably, to mean the most perfect act of the living God, by which he is intimately and wholly aware of everything that can be known. I say God is conscious to himself insofar as he comprehends by his mind whatever he understands, all of which is most present to him. So that these things may be perceived more clearly by us, who scarcely conceive other acts of understanding distinctly enough except those that are our own, our perceptions will here be compared with divine knowledge; but this will be done more correctly a little later. That God understands must first be demonstrated, if it is necessary to say much. For the Philosopher rightly says: If the divine mind understood nothing, but were disposed as one asleep, what would be pre-eminent? Clearly, whoever would strip the first cause of that perfection, which is also one of the chief among the others. Nor can it act in any way except rationally: it does not act by chance or blind impulse, nor is it directed to certain ends by another. The independent perfection of the divine life plainly rejects either of these, and so does the whole constitution of the universe, balanced, weighed, perfect, by weights, measures and numbers, so that the very night indicates to the knowing the Maker's wisdom, which is beyond any number. And what is more effective than the testimony of conscience? Who would acknowledge a deity and not worship it? Who, unless he were an extreme idolater in his impiety, would worship what he thinks lacks understanding? But I pass over a matter that is too manifest. Rather, let us examine how God knows what he knows, as far as we are able to know it. From what has been said before, it is already sufficiently clear that he cannot but be most perfect. For whatever pertains to the complete perfection of the most perfect being cannot be less than most perfect, and nothing pertains to God in a way that is not. He does not properly estimate the understanding of God who does not acknowledge it to be as great as God himself is. And this general truth is more evident than that it could admit of any contradiction; if agreement were as easy about what that most perfect mode of knowing really involves, no further inquiry would be needed here. But as it is, the feverish philosophies of some people about middle knowledge, by which the Deity is supposed to contemplate the free actions of his creatures, or even about the conjecture by which they divine future contingent things, impose necessity upon our thoughts, causing them to stumble somewhat over matters otherwise quite certain, and lay here the foundations of this whole impiety. Yet we will not form a concept of such great things in proportion to our capacity more correctly than if we carefully recall to mind those things that we noted before about the individual essential perfections of God, to which the divine knowledge must be acknowledged as conformed; unless we are to hold that the first being does not act in accordance with its own nature, which is absurdly supposed. Then too, we must attentively observe what imperfection clings to our modes of knowing, which must undoubtedly be removed from the divine ones; unless we wish to foster too much anthropomorphic thoughts about God, which in truth are fostered by all who have ever erred in this respect.

units.la: Istis accuratè observatis, intelligemus primùm, scire Deum quicquid scit Independenter. Certè, quod ens per Independentiam est id ipsum quod est, non potest id quicquam scire modo sibi congruo, nisi eo quo existit, id est, independenti: quemadmodum & jam dudùm demonstravimus, nihil esse Divinum, quod non sit independens. An verò quod sibi sufficit ad existendum, non pariter sibi sufficiet ad intelligendum? Et quis non intelligit, qui intellectu non caret, longè perfectius esse independenter scire, quam dependenter? Si sic, utique, si dependens esset, perfectissima non esset, Divina scientia. Et quid, obsecrò, tandem istud crit, à quo pendeat prima Intelligentia? Non saltem, ut in nobis, vim percipien-tem tem movent oblata objecta ; cum ista omnia processerint à causa prima tanquam ab agente , non bruto , sed maximè rationali ; atque adeò universa ista sui ideis jam mente divinâ comprehensa fuerunt , antequam extiterunt. Ut non ex operefuo formato notionem ejus haurire necesse habeat supremus Τεχνίτης ; sed contrà res quævis mensuram sui habeat Divinum Intellectum , tanquam causam exemplarem ad cujus amussim producta est. Easdemque ob causas ex nullis cognoscendi principiis genita esse potest vis Dei intelligendi præstantissima ; nullius ideò indiga sensationis , experientiæ , ratiocinationis , similiumque imbecillium humanæ cognitionis adminiculorum. Nihil ergò vel dari vel concipi potest extra Deum , à quo ejusdem Intellectus ortum haberet quomodocunque. Cui minimè repugnat Dei Decretum, quod infrà Præscientiæ futurorum basin sumus posituri : non enim sic inducitur aliquid à Deo diversum, scientiam ejus precedens, sed ordo tantùm aliquis concipitur inter ea , quæ diversimodè à nobis cogitata , re ipsâ idem sunt. Ordo verò noster concipiendi nullam infert dependentiam; cum nihil à se ipso dependere dici possit.
units.tr: Having observed these things carefully, we will understand first that God knows whatever he knows independently. Certainly, a being that is what it is through independence cannot know anything in a manner suited to itself except in the way in which it exists, that is, independently; just as we have already demonstrated that nothing is divine that is not independent. But will that which is sufficient to itself for existing not likewise be sufficient to itself for understanding? And who that lacks no understanding does not grasp that to know independently is far more perfect than to know dependently? If so, surely, if the divine knowledge were dependent, it would not be most perfect. And what, I beg you, would that be, on which the first understanding depends? Not, as in us, is the power of perceiving moved by presented objects; since all those things have proceeded from the first cause as from an agent that is not blind but most rational; and therefore all those things were comprehended in the divine mind by their ideas before they existed. So the supreme Artificer does not need to draw the notion of a thing from his work once formed; rather, on the contrary, each thing has its measure in the divine understanding, as in an exemplary cause by whose rule it was produced. And for the same reasons, the most excellent power of divine understanding cannot have arisen from any principles of knowing; therefore it needs none of the aids of human knowledge, such as sensation, experience, reasoning, and similar weak helps. Nothing, therefore, either exists or can be conceived outside God from which his understanding could in any way have its origin. The decree of God, which we shall lay down below as the basis of the foreknowledge of future things, does not contradict this: for something different from God, preceding his knowledge, is not thereby introduced; rather only some order is conceived among those things which, though thought of by us in different ways, are in reality the same. Our order of conceiving, however, implies no dependence, since nothing can be said to depend on itself.

units.la: Cæterum , quemadmodum ex Independentia divinæ naturæ omnes ejusdem perfectiones fluunt, sic quoque ex independentia divini Intellectûs alia ejusdem attributa facilè innotescunt. Videlicet, quia independens , etiam Simplicissimus est in Deo cognoscendi modus ; ut nec pluribus actibus veŕ distinctis intelligat , nec ipse intelligendi actus ab intelligentis essentia' quid diversum existat. Si enim alterius eorum ab altero aliqualis hic foret divisio , etiam , ut ista divisa in unum conveniant , parilis eorundem inter se requireretur compositio. Verum omnem compositionis speciem absolutæ independentiæ prorsus repugnare, ubi de primi entis simplicitate egimus, probavimus sat multis: ut illa hic repetere nil sit necesse. Sufficit, rerum omnium causam supremam semet ipsum scire per semet ipsum, eodemque mentis in ictu cernere quæ sint, quæ fuerint, veniantque ; quatenus in ipso continentur quæcunque unquam sunt vel esse possunt , ut nulla ei opus sit, ad alia à se cognoscenda, notionum à se distinctarum formatione vel multiplicatione. Atque hoc est , quod vulgò dicunt , Deum intelligere per essentiam :
units.tr: Moreover, just as all the perfections of the divine nature flow from its independence, so from the independence of the divine understanding other attributes of the same are easily known. Namely, because it is independent, the mode of knowing in God is also most simple: so that he does not understand by several truly distinct acts, nor does the act of understanding itself exist as anything different from the essence of the one understanding. For if any division of these into one another were here, then, for these divided things to agree in one, a like composition of them among themselves would be required. But we have proved sufficiently often, when we treated of the simplicity of the first being, that every species of composition absolutely repugns absolute independence; so it is unnecessary to repeat those arguments here. It is enough that the supreme cause of all things knows itself through itself, and by one instant of the mind perceives what things are, what have been, and what are to come; inasmuch as whatever ever is or can be is contained in it, so that it has no need, in order to know other things apart from itself, of forming or multiplying notions distinct from itself. And this is what they commonly say, that God understands through his essence:

units.la: {•} ˆ ~ tiam : cujus eminentissimæ perfectionis nimiùm in mentes creatas hodiè transfundunt, qui actionem cogitandi ab essentia earundem neutiquam distinctam arbitrantur : de quo alibi plura. Sed & Immutabilis est Dei scientia, ab objectis independens, ideoque nec eorum mutationibus subjecta, quæ ipsa potius constans est rerum mutabilium mensura. Planè ut oculus citra ullam sui vertiginem rotulæ circumactæ varios gyros intuetur; ita mens divina, ullius mutationis ignara, nullam patitur à rebus mutationibus infestis mutationem.
units.tr: ...whose most eminent perfection they pour too freely into created minds today, those who think that the act of thinking is in no way distinct from the essence of those minds. I have said more about this elsewhere. But the knowledge of God is also immutable, independent of its objects, and therefore not subject to their changes. It is rather itself the steady measure of changeable things. Just as the eye, without any dizziness of its own, watches the various turns of a wheel as it spins, so the divine mind, ignorant of all change, suffers no change from the things that are subject to change.

units.la: Ex quibus Æternam, omnisque etiam successionis expertem, eandem esse, nullo negotio conficitur; quatenus quod Ens sapientiæ suæ thesauros independenter possidet in se ipso ex se ipso, nulliusque rei ignotæ novam adipisci potest notitiam, ob immutabilitatem, id ante tempora seculorum, absque principio ullo, scivisse quod scit, manifestum est. Eàdem sequelà summa & infallibilis Certitudo Divino Intellectui convenit. Quæ enim cognitio neutiquam pendet à rebus ipsis incertis, nec ullâ novâ certioris medii luce confirmari potest, nequit in eadem aliquem locum habere dubitatio, aut ulla oppositi formido. Tandem Adæquatâ concipiendi perfectione novit Deus quicquid novit; intimè penetrans omnem rerum essentiam, ac funditùs exhauriens qualiacunque earundem attributa. Ut absolutissimè Deus sciat quidlibet quod scibile est, & quousque scibile est; adeo ut quod ipse non scit (si fit fas itâ loqui) quemadmodum prorsus nihil est, ita sciri nullâ ratione unquam possit. Etenim quòd quædam quandoque non plenè & clarè percipiantur, tantum oritur ex dependentia cognitionis ab objecto; quod quoties secundum se totum vim perceptivam non satis vividè afficit, conceptum sui parit imperfectum & obscurum. Quod itaque per independentiam suam objectis neutiquam subjicitur, etiam nullas istiusmodi patitur imperfectæ cognitionis causas. Alia quæ huc pertinent infrà. Nunc liquet, quam jure merito Deus cognoscere dicatur Comprehensivè, dum quâdam mentis suæ quasi comprehensione rem omnem complectitur; item Intuitivè, claro scilicet & distincto quasi intuitu totum quod in re cognosci potest pervidendo. Non aliæ desunt rationes, quibus amplius confirmari queat multiplex illa, quam jam demonstravimus, mentis Divinæ in modo cognoscendi eminentia. Verum & ista sufficiunt quæ attulimus, & mox quoque occasio dabitur alia quædam attingendi.
units.tr: From these points it follows without any difficulty that this knowledge is eternal and free of all succession. Since it possesses the treasures of its wisdom independently, in itself and from itself, and since, by reason of its immutability, it can acquire no new knowledge of anything unknown, it is plain that it knew before the ages of time, without any beginning, what it knows. By the same reasoning, supreme and infallible certainty belongs to the divine intellect. For knowledge that in no way depends on uncertain things themselves, and cannot be confirmed by any new light from a surer means, cannot admit any doubt or any fear of the opposite. Finally, by a perfect and adequate way of conceiving, God knows whatever he knows, penetrating every essence of things and exhausting to the bottom whatever attributes they have. So God knows, in the most absolute way, whatever can be known, and to the full extent that it can be known; so that what he does not know (if it is lawful to speak so) is, just as it is nothing at all, never able to be known in any way. For the fact that some things are sometimes not perceived fully and clearly arises only from the dependence of knowledge on its object. Whenever the object, taken in itself, does not strike the power of perception vividly enough, the concept it produces is imperfect and obscure. Therefore that which by its independence is in no way subject to objects also suffers none of the causes of such imperfect knowledge. Other matters that pertain here will be treated below. Now it is clear with what good reason God is said to know comprehensively, since he embraces every thing in a kind of comprehension of his own mind; and likewise intuitively, that is, by a clear and distinct kind of intuition, seeing through everything that can be known in a thing. There are no lack of other reasons by which that manifold eminence of the divine mind in its manner of knowing, which we have already demonstrated, could be further confirmed. But the ones we have brought forward are enough, and soon there will also be an occasion to touch on some others.

units.la: Nunc operæ pretium erit attendisse diligentius (quod supra obiter tangebamus) immensam differitatem, quâ ratio cognoscendi Divina distat à nostra. Tribus verbis præcipua quædam hujus rei capita recensebo; ex quibus lumen longè clarissimum tractatui nostro sequenti affulgebit. Nimirum, Nulla est in Deo scientia habitualis, quiescens quandoque, quandoque in actum transiens. Nullis indiget mens Divina cognoscendi instrumentis aut occasionibus. Nullas proprie loquendo format rerum notiones, nullas fingit imagines, quibus suæ intelligentiæ res sistat præsentes. Nulla hic rei ignotæ comparatur scientia; nulla rei notæ inducitur oblivio, nulla obliteratæ notitiæ excitatur reminiscentia. Nulla in præscientia futurorum locum habet sagax conjectura; nulla præsentium vel præteritorum per experientiam acquisita certitudo. Nulla extra Deum datur conditio, à qua scientia divina suspendatur. Nunquam componit aut dividit mens Divina; neque ullos abstractos habet rerum conceptus. Nullas ex rerum convenientia ac discrepantia rationes conserit; nullas ex causis conclusiones nectit. Hi omnes, & si qui plures his similes, nostri cognoscendi modi, quemadmodum facillime demonstrantur Scientiæ Independenti, Simplicissimæ, Immutabili, Æternæ, Certissimæ, ac Comprehensivæ in plurimis adversari, tanquam perfectissimâ intelligentiâ prorsus indigni, diligentissimâ curâ ab ea sunt removendi. Si quis conqueratur, istis omnibus abjectis, tenue superesse quod de Divina mente cogitet; regero ego illi, superesse infinita; sed, quia infinita, conceptibus finitis altiora: cujus enim cogitationes non sunt sicuti nostræ cogitationes, ejusdem modus cognoscendi nostro sublimior est, quantum cœlum altius est terrâ. Quam sublimitatem qui conscendere non potest (ut nulla potest creatura) potius quam temerario scrutinio vertiginem patiatur, humili eam modestiâ miretur: quæ via in tam nobis inviis longè tutissima.
units.tr: Now it will be worthwhile to consider more carefully (as we touched on in passing above) the immense difference by which the divine way of knowing differs from ours. In a few words I shall list the chief heads of this matter, from which a much clearer light will shine on our following treatise. Namely: in God there is no habitual knowledge, resting at one time and passing into act at another. The divine mind needs no instruments or occasions for knowing. Properly speaking, it forms no notions of things, and feigns no images by which it sets the things of its understanding before itself as present. Here no knowledge of an unknown thing is acquired; no forgetting of a known thing is brought on; no reminiscence of an obliterated knowledge is stirred up. In foreknowledge of future things no shrewd conjecture has a place; nor any certainty of present or past things acquired through experience. No condition exists outside God on which the divine knowledge depends. The divine mind never composes or divides; nor does it have any abstract concepts of things. It does not weave arguments from the agreement or disagreement of things; nor does it tie conclusions to causes. All these ways, and whatever others are like them, of our knowing, as is very easily shown, are in many respects opposed to a knowledge that is independent, most simple, immutable, eternal, most certain and comprehensive. As wholly unworthy of the most perfect understanding, they must be removed from it with the greatest care. If someone should complain that, with all these things cast aside, only a slight notion of the divine mind remains for him to think about, I answer him: infinite things remain; but because they are infinite they are higher than finite concepts. For whose thoughts are not as our thoughts, his manner of knowing is as much higher than ours as heaven is higher than earth. Whoever cannot climb to that height (as no creature can), rather than suffer dizziness from rash scrutiny, let him admire it with humble modesty; this is by far the safest way in matters so closed to us.

units.la: Enitendum tamen quousque finit nostra imbecillitas. Conducet huc plurimùm, considerare sigillatim res circa quas Divina vina Scientia modis jam recensitis actuosa est; tum etiam varias hujus, pro illarum vario statu, divisiones. Jam ante monuimus, extendi eam ad omne omnino scibile, ut vere sit & dici debeat Omni-scientia. De eo constabit clarissimè, si per partes agamus. Primarium primæ Intelligentiæ objectum absque dubio Numen ipsum est. Quandoquidem enim sui ipsius cognitio secundum se spectata perfectio est, nullaque congnitionis perfectio à perfectissimo cognoscente potest abesse, etiam ea Deo denegari nequit. Neque finit, Deum sufficientissimum se ignorare, ejusdem (de qua suo loco plenius) Beatitudo. Etenim qui virtutum suarum plenitudinem haud intelligit, is neque in eisdem rationaliter potest acquisere; quatenus, sicuti ignoti boni nulla est cupido, ita quoque felicitatis non intellectæ, quantumvis magnæ, nulla esse potest cum complacentia fruitio. Et quod, obsecrò, perfectissimâ scientiâ dignius objectum esse aut cogitari potest, quam ipsum ens perfectissimum? Pulchrè Philosophus: Manifestum est, mentem divinam intelligere quod divinissimum & honorabilissimum est; quo fit ut se ipsam intelligat. Et profectò, se nisi cognoscat Deus, cognoscit nihil planè: quippe qui, propter independentem ac simplicissimum cognoscendi modum, supra Deo vindicatum, extra se nihil cognoscere potest, nisi ex se & per se. Adde, res omnes à Deo diversas esse ab eodem prorsus dependentes; ut tanquam tales cognosci nequeant, nisi cognito ipso principio à quo pendent. Sed jam dudum nimius sum in re manifesta. Non interim, ut nos Deum, sic ipse se intelligit: qui enim quæcunque novit novit adæquatè, etiam non potest is non consummatâ concipiendi perfectione penitus intimèque sibi esse notissimus. Quin ne actu quidem reflexo ad se penetrandum indiget, qui ipse simplicissimus idem est & cognoscens, & cognitio, & cognoscibile. Estque hæc sublimis illa Dei ipsius Theologia: cujus quidam in mente creata relucentes radii existunt Ectypon, referens pro subjecti capacitate qualicunque modo Archetypi sui perfectiones.
units.tr: Yet we must strive as far as our weakness allows. It will greatly help to consider one by one the things about which the divine knowledge is active in the ways already listed; and also the various divisions of that knowledge according to the varying state of those things. We have already noted before that it extends to absolutely everything knowable, so that it truly is, and ought to be called, omniscience. This will be made very clear if we proceed part by part. Without doubt the primary object of the first understanding is the Deity himself. For since the knowledge of himself, considered in itself, is a perfection, and no perfection of knowing can be absent from the most perfect knower, it cannot be denied to God either. Nor does it suit that God should be ignorant of his own fullness, which is his blessedness (of which more fully in its place). For whoever does not understand the fullness of his own powers cannot rationally acquire them; and just as there is no desire for an unknown good, so too there can be no enjoyment with delight of a happiness that is not understood, however great it is. And what object, I beg you, can be more worthy of the most perfect knowledge than the most perfect being himself? The Philosopher said well: It is manifest that the divine mind understands what is most divine and most honourable; whence it comes that it understands itself. And indeed, if God does not know himself, he knows nothing at all; for since he knows by his independent and most simple manner of knowing, which we have claimed for him above, he can know nothing outside himself except from himself and through himself. Add that all things other than God are wholly dependent on him, so that they cannot be known as such unless the principle on which they depend is known first. But I have already been too long on a matter that is plain. Meanwhile, just as we know God, so he understands himself: for he who knows whatever he knows adequately cannot fail, with a perfect and complete way of conceiving, to be most thoroughly and intimately known to himself. Nor does he even need a reflexive act to penetrate himself, since he is himself most simple, both knower, knowledge and knowable. And this is that sublime theology of God himself, of which certain rays shining in the created mind are an ectype [ἔκτυπον], representing in whatever way the capacity of the subject allows the perfections of its archetype.

units.la: Præter se novit Deus alia quævis à se, q ualiacunqncea fuerint, & in quocunque statu. Si enim vel minimum quicquam fugeret Divinam Scientiam, non jam hoc ipso foret præstantissima ; quatenùs negari nequit, perfectiorem esse notitiam quæ nihil prorsus ignorat, quam cui quædam subducuntur. Quin tantæ necessitatis hæc veritas est, ut si quid rerum aliquando Deum lateat, id nunquam Ipsum scire posse, dicendum sit. Tam omnem sciendi novitatem excludit scientiæ independentis simplicitas, immutabilitas, & æternitas. Et quid est, cujuscunque fuerit conditionis, quod non totum Deo tanquam causæ primæ subordinetur? Quæcunque verò Deo subordinantur, principium sui eum agnoscunt, non brutum, sed maximè rationale : quod arguit tum agentis primi vita perfectissima, tum varii in rebus productis perfectionum gradus ; qui nulli forent, si ad extremum virium (quod est causæ rationE destitutæ) ac non certo potius selectu atque ex rationis præscripto, operaretur Numen. Nihil itaque est eorum quæ quocunque modo à causa prima dependent, quod non per omnia quo usque à se pendet, Deus habeat exploratissimum. Quæ rationes omnes quum non minus spectent possibilia, quam præsentia ; futura, quam præterita ; contingentia, quam necessaria ; voluntaria, quam naturalia ; cogitata, quam patrata ; conditionata, quam absoluta ; singularia, quam universalia ; minima, quam maxima ; etiam nihil eorum omnium agnoscimus, quod non æquali necessitate à mente divina plenissimè cognosci, fit statuendum. Neque profectò metuendum est, ne (quod nobis frequenter accidit) tot tantarumque rerum vel varietate distrahatur, vel multitudine confundatur, vel magnitudine obruatur, vel exilitate fatigetur Intellectus Dei. Ita qui cogitat, non se satis attendere offendit modum intelligendi divinum, tum independentem esse, ut nullâ opus sit sciendorum investigatione; tum etiam simplicissimum, quo fit ut eodem actu parilique facilitate omnia ac unum intelligat. Quarum perfectionum à nostra cognitione absentia, tantum in ea parit defectum & molestiam, ut præstantissimarum quoque rerum scientiam sapientum .scientissimus Salomon pronunciare non dubitaverit occupationem malam, quam qui multiplicat multiplicet dolorem.
units.tr: Besides himself God knows all other things than himself, whatever they may be and in whatever state. For if he were to escape the divine knowledge even in the smallest thing, it would not on that account be the most excellent knowledge; since it cannot be denied that a knowledge which is ignorant of nothing at all is more perfect than one from which some things are withheld. Indeed this truth is of such necessity that, if anything at some time were hidden from God, it would have to be said that he could never know it himself. So completely does the simplicity, immutability and eternity of independent knowledge exclude any novelty of knowing. And what thing, of whatever kind, is not wholly subordinated to God as first cause? Moreover, all things subordinated to God acknowledge him as their principle, not as something blind, but as supremely rational. This shows both the most perfect life of the first agent and the various grades of perfection in the things produced; and these would not exist if the Deity acted by the last extremity of power (which is the mark of a cause lacking reason) rather than by sure selection and according to the prescription of reason. Therefore, of all the things that in any way depend on the first cause, there is nothing which God does not know most thoroughly, in every respect, insofar as it depends on him. Since all these relations regard possible things no less than present ones, future things no less than past ones, contingent things no less than necessary ones, voluntary things no less than natural ones, things thought of no less than things done, conditional things no less than absolute ones, singular things no less than universal ones, the least things no less than the greatest, we must hold that none of all these is not known most fully by the divine mind with equal necessity. Nor indeed is there any fear that the intellect of God might be distracted by the variety, or confused by the multitude, or overwhelmed by the magnitude, or worn out by the minuteness of so many and so great things, as often happens to us. The one who thinks this fails to pay enough attention to the divine manner of understanding: it is independent, so that there is no need of searching out things to be known; and it is also most simple, so that it understands all things and one thing in the same act and with equal ease. The absence of these perfections from our knowledge produces in it so much defect and trouble that even the most learned of the wise, Solomon, did not hesitate to pronounce a grievous occupation: he who multiplies knowledge multiplies sorrow.
IX. The Knowledge of Possibles

units.la: Atquì, ne ullum superfit in hoc negotio dubium, earum rerum quas recensuimus præcipuas quasdam species breviter viter percurremus, eas imprimis in quibus aliqua sese offert difficultas; ostensuri, & illas Deo cognosci, & simul, quo fundamento : utriusque enim hujus consideratio ad alterutrius intelligentiam, ut claram, ita certam, plurimum confert. Possibilia, qua talia, puram denominationem dicere à potentia aliqua activa, quæ eis in actum deducendis sufficit, cujusque ideo tanquam objecta considerantur, notum est. Indè quicunque perfectè intelligit causæ cujuspiam potentiam, nihil is eorum possibilium ignorare potest, quæ in perfectione istius causæ virtualiter continentur. Ex quo conficitur, nihil saltem illorum Deum latere posse,. quæ in ipso, tanquam in causa, exstiunt; qualia sunt quævis Possibilia. Neque putandum est, præter ista quæ ratione Divinæ virtutis Possibilia dicuntur, quædam etiam esse quæ sint potentiæ alicujus alterius objecta; atque ideo Deo per cognitam suam potentiam non ilicò perspecta. Quum enim cujusvis rei creatæ virtus absolutissimè à Deo dependens sit, nihil certè à causa secunda produci verè potest, quod non priori quodam jure possibile sit causæ primæ; atque ideò illi tanquam tale exploratissimum. Et quid possit Deus, quod non intelligat? Nisi absurdissimè dicendus sit aliquid posse ad instar causæ brutæ. Quoties enim agenti rationali aliquid possibile esse cogitamus, tantumque attendimus vim exsequentem, nil cogitantes de Intellectu tanquam de principio dirigente, mox id tanquam agens rationale cogitare definimus. Quæ veritas tantæ evidentiæ est, ut non minus rerum omnium producibilium Ideas, quam virtutem eas extra se ponendi, in Deo admiserint Gentium sapientiores. Verum de sublimi illa materia, in qua Philosophiæ Platonicæ cardo vertitur, brevitatis causâ satis hoc loco dicere non possumus; quare nec parùm dicere volumus. Verbo tantum moneo, per has rerum possibilium in mente divina Ideas nos nihil aliud intelligere, quam ipsam essentiam Divinam, à se ipsa perfectissimè cognitam, tanquam sufficientem ad suas quasdam perfectiones modo analogico & infinitè vario extra se exprimendas.
units.tr: But, so that no doubt remains in this matter, we shall briefly run through certain principal kinds of those things we have listed, especially those in which some difficulty presents itself, intending to show both that they are known to God and on what ground. For the consideration of each of these contributes greatly to a clear and certain understanding of the other. It is well known that possibles, as such, take their name purely from some active power that is sufficient to bring them into act, and are therefore considered as its objects. Hence, whoever understands perfectly the power of any cause can be ignorant of none of those possibles that are contained virtually in the perfection of that cause. From this it follows that God cannot fail to know at least those things that exist in him as in their cause, such as all possibles. Nor should we think that, apart from those things which are called possible by reason of the divine power, there are also some things that are the objects of some other power, and so are not at once perceived by God through his own known power. For since the power of any created thing depends most absolutely on God, nothing can truly be produced by a secondary cause that is not possible to the first cause by some prior right; and so it is most fully known to him as such. And what could God do that he does not understand? Unless it is said, most absurdly, that he can do something in the manner of a blind cause. For whenever we think of something as possible to a rational agent, and attend only to the executing force, without thinking of the intellect as the directing principle, we soon define that thing as being done by a rational agent. This truth is of such evidence that the wiser of the Gentiles admitted in God no less the ideas of all producible things than the power of setting them outside himself. But we cannot say enough about that lofty matter, on which the hinge of Platonic philosophy turns, in this place, for the sake of brevity; therefore we do not wish to say too little. I merely advise in a word that by these ideas of possible things in the divine mind we understand nothing other than the Divine Essence itself, most perfectly known by itself, as sufficient to express outside itself certain perfections of its own in an analogical and infinitely varied manner.
X.

units.la: Nullam in toto hoc negotio mentionem feci divinæ Voluntatis: quam uti recentiores Philosophi genuinum statuunt possibilitatis fundamentum, ita, Deum possibilia non cognoscere nisi vi decreti sui, contendunt. Perperam certè. Uti enim Deus suæ sibi perfectionis intimè conscius existit, absque ullo actu voluntatis intercedente, ita quoque & se intelligit sufficientissimum, & simul illa omnia quæ cum sufficientia ista immediato nexu cohærent, qualia sunt possibilia, absque ulla voluntatis liberæ determinatione: à qua non magis suspendi potest possibilitas rerum, quam ipsa Dei Potentia, quæ re vera est ipsa ejusdem Sufficientia. De quibus plenius constabit infrà, ubi de Potentia Dei dixerimus: quo loco etiam hujus opinionis fundamenta erunt refellenda, nimirum, Potentiam Dei à Voluntate ejusdem nulla ratione differre; item, Deum posse etiam efficere, ut contradictoria existant. Caeterùm, quid de Impossibilibus hic sit sentiendum, quæ de Possibilibus tradita sunt satis docent. Scilicet, nihil est absolutè Impossibile, quod idem non sit contradictorium; id est, tale cujus alterum prædicatum sic alterum evertit, ut nec cogitatione quidem, ob mutuam destructionem, simul uniri queant. Cognoscit ergo Deus Impossibile, quousque id cognosci potest. Extrema scilicet quæ in Impossibili occurrunt, seorsim spectata, cognoscit plenissimè. Etiam unionem inter illa fieri non posse, id est, eandem cum suis perfectionibus non consistere, intelligit; qui quicquid suæ sufficientiæ adversatur non minus intelligit, quam quod ex eadem fluit. Extrema ergo tanquam inter se unita non concipit, qui nihil concipit quod non suis perfectionibus continetur; ob quod ipsum neque ea unita producere potest. Nec ullus hinc sequitur scientiæ defectus, sed maxima potius ejusdem perfectio: cum enim quod absolutè est impossibile sit purum putum nihil, utique qui impossibile non scit, nihil non scit. Et quid est nihil non scire, aliud quam omnia scire?
units.tr: I have made no mention of the divine Will in this whole matter. Recent philosophers hold it to be the genuine ground of possibility, and they contend that God knows possibles only by virtue of his decree. They are certainly wrong. For just as God exists intimately conscious of his own perfection, without any act of the will intervening, so too he understands himself to be most sufficient, and at the same time all those things which cohere with that sufficiency in an immediate connection, such as possibles, without any determination of the free will. The possibility of things can no more be suspended from that will than the very power of God, which in reality is his own sufficiency. These matters will be made clearer below, where we speak of the power of God; in that place also the foundations of this opinion will have to be refuted, namely, that the power of God in no way differs from his will, and that God can also bring it about that contradictories exist. Moreover, what must be thought here about impossibles is sufficiently taught by what has been handed down about possibles. Namely, nothing is absolutely impossible unless it is a contradiction; that is, something whose one predicate so overthrows the other that they cannot be united together even in thought, because of their mutual destruction. God therefore knows the impossible as far as it can be known. He knows most fully the extremes that occur in the impossible, considered separately. He also understands that a union between them cannot take place, that is, that they cannot coexist with his perfections; and he understands what opposes his sufficiency no less than what flows from it. He therefore does not conceive the extremes as united with one another, since he conceives nothing that is not contained in his perfections; for which reason he cannot produce them united either. Nor does any defect of knowledge follow from this, but rather the greatest perfection of it. For since what is absolutely impossible is pure nothing, surely one who does not know the impossible does not know nothing. And what is not knowing nothing, other than knowing all things?

units.la: XI. Futurorum etiam contingentium, certa est in mente Divina Præscientia.
units.tr: XI. The certain foreknowledge of future contingents is also in the divine mind.

units.la: Possibilitatem rerum excipit earundem Futuritio & Non-suturitio. Atque hanc non minus quam illam penetrat divina mens, distinctissimè & perfectissimè cognoscendo tum ipsas creaturas futuras, tum etiam quænam re ipsâ fierent à singulis secundum omnem statum, quem toto temporis successu habebunt, quâvis hypothesi factâ, quâvis occasione oblata. Quæ occasiones cum sint infinities infinitæ, omnium maximè immensam vastitatem, amplitudinem, ac profunditatem Divinæ Sapientiæ declarant ; nobis quidem incomprehensibilem, non tamen minus veram. Sileo, quæ tot futurorum contingentium eventus præcesserunt, illustria Vaticinia, totidem hujus Præscientiæ testes locupletissimos. Nobis ratione agendum est. Quando Futurum dicimus, rem denotamus, quæ, cum nondum sit, ad hoc tamen est definita, ut existat aliquandò : si enim ad hoc definita non sit, non magis futura dici potest, quam non-futura. Jam verò manifestum est, non posse quicquam suæ futuritionis esse causam : etenim quod ex se hactenus merum nihil est, nullam etiam sibi determinationem tribuere potest ad hoc, ut aliquandò, potius quam nunquam, existat. Causam ergò aliquam suæ futuritionis requirit quodvis futurum extra se. Nec eam qualemcunque; sed istam, quæ fecerit, ut de futuro nunquam verè dici potuerit, fuisse aliquandò non-futurum. Quæ enim res aliquando futura est, jam ab æterno fuit talis; cùm, si nunc verum sit rem hanc aliquandò fore, idem ab æterno etiam verum fuerit. Æterna itaque futuritio æternum sui fundamentum exigit; quale nullum excogitare datur, nullumque aliud patitur divina independentia, præter æternam Æterni entis voluntatem, cujus æternâ definitione quod unquam futurum dici potest, jam ab æterno futurum fuit. Quumque Voluntatis suæ perfectissimo actu non possit non conscium sibi esse ens perfectissimum; utique futura quæcunque ignorare non potest, qui id per & propter quod singula futura sunt, quæ futura sunt, habet exploratissimum. Quid? quod rerum existentium nulla esse posset certa ac sapienter ordinata connexio (qualem esse, tum res ipsæ clamant, tum Primæ causæ sapientia postulat) nisi earundem seriem jam antè digesserit mens divina. At qui potuit, ni ea sic futura, non aliter, uti ordinaverit, ita præsenserit. Ut nulla re verâ agnosci possit Numinis Providentia, nisi quanta ejusdem agnoscitur Prævidentia. Estque rerum Non-futurarum, ex oppositο, similis ratio. Neque futurorum contingentium contingentiæ quicquam obstat hæc Præscientiæ divinæ, in Dei decreto fundata, certitudo. Ipsum enim præfinitione suâ rei cuique suas quidem aptavit causas; sed non omnes secundum naturam suam necessarias & immutabiles: quare, si eæ secundum se variabiles sint, nulloque certo nexu per se cum effectu cohærentes, merito hic illarum intuitu dicitur contingens. Aliam enim contingentiam fingere quam quæ tota ad causas secundas veniat referenda, non permittit necessaria causæ primæ & in intelligendo perfectio, & in causando independentia.
units.tr: The possibility of things is followed by their futurity and non-futurity. The divine mind penetrates this no less than that, knowing most distinctly and perfectly both the creatures that will be in the future, and also what would in fact come about from each one, in every state it will have through the whole succession of time, under any supposition whatever, on any occasion offered. Since these occasions are infinitely infinite, they declare the immense vastness, breadth, and depth of divine wisdom, incomprehensible to us, but no less true. I pass over the many events of future contingents that have gone before, the famous prophecies, so many most abundant witnesses of this foreknowledge. We must argue by reason. When we say "future," we denote a thing which, although it does not yet exist, is nevertheless determined to exist at some time; for if it were not determined to this, it could be called no more future than non-future. Now it is plain that nothing can be the cause of its own futurity: for what is of itself until now pure nothing cannot give itself any determination to exist at some time rather than never. Therefore any future thing requires some cause of its futurity outside itself. Nor any cause whatever, but one that has made it so that of the future it could never truly be said that it had at some time been non-future. For a thing that is at some time future was already such from eternity; since, if it is now true that this thing will be at some time, the same would also have been true from eternity. Eternal futurity therefore demands an eternal ground for itself; no other can be devised, and divine independence admits no other except the eternal will of the Eternal Being, by whose eternal determination whatever can ever be called future has already been future from eternity. And since the most perfect being cannot but be conscious to itself of its most perfect act of will, it certainly cannot be ignorant of any future things, since it has most fully known that through which and on account of which each single future thing is what it is. What more? Since no certain and wisely ordered connection of existing things could exist (such as both the things themselves cry out that there is, and the wisdom of the First Cause demands), unless the divine mind had already arranged their series beforehand. But it could not have foreseen them as it did, unless it had ordained them to be future in that way and not otherwise. So the providence of the Deity can in truth be recognised in nothing except insofar as its foreseeing is recognised. And the same reasoning holds, conversely, for non-future things. Nor does this certainty of divine foreknowledge, founded on God's decree, stand in the way of the contingency of future contingents. For by his predestination he has indeed assigned to each thing its causes; but not all of them necessary and unchangeable according to their nature. Therefore, if those causes are variable in themselves, and not connected with the effect by any fixed bond in themselves, the effect is rightly called contingent with respect to them. For the necessary character of the First Cause, both in understanding and in causing its independence, does not allow us to feign any contingency other than that which is referred wholly to secondary causes.

units.la: Tandem, quemadmodum quæ futura olim erant juxta Decretum Dei, suo tempore per actualem ejusdem Providentiam existunt Præsentia; sic etiam quemadmodum Deus illa futura prævidet vi decreti, donec tempus advenerit quo producantur, ita actu eodem immutabili eadem pervidet Præsentia vi actualis providentiæ,. simulatque hoc tempus affulserit. Hac de re dubitare non finit totalis cujusvis creaturæ secundum omnia sui prædicata à Creatoris sui influxu dependentia; quæ non patitur quicquam in ea existere, quod non, quantum habet entitatis, tantundem habeat dependentiæ. At jam antè probavimus, quicquid à Deo pendet pendere ab eo rationali modo: quapropter nihil quoque ab eo productum est, nisi cum influxus sui, tum procreantis, tum conservantis, tum gubernantis, intimâ conscientiâ. Ex quo rursùm infero, vel nullam esse Numinis Providentiam; vel, si sit Providentia circa res creatas, non minorem esse earundem penes Deum, ita loquar, Pervidentiam. Scitè de hoc negotio Augustinus: „Non multæ, sed una sa-„pientia est, in qua sunt immensi quidem atque infiniti thesauri „rerum intelligibilium; in quibus sunt omnes invisibiles atque „incommutabiles rationes rerum, etiam visibilium & mutabi„lium, quæ per istam factæ sunt: quoniam Deus non aliquid „nesciens fecit, quod nec de quolibet homine artifice recte dici „potest. Porro, si sciens fecit omnia, ea utique fecit quæ „noverat. Ex quo occurrit animo quiddam mirum, sed ta„men verum, quod iste mundus nobis notus esse non posset, „nisi esset: Deo autem nisi notus esset, esse non posset.
units.tr: Finally, just as those things which were future under God's decree in time past now exist as present through his actual providence, so also God foresees those future things by virtue of his decree until the time comes when they are brought into being, and by that same unchanging act he sees the same things as present, by virtue of his actual providence, as soon as that time dawns. Nor does the total dependence of any creature, in all its attributes, on the influence of its Creator allow us to doubt this. That dependence does not permit anything to exist in the creature which does not depend on God to the same extent as it has being. But we have already proved that whatever depends on God depends on him in a rational way. Therefore nothing has been produced by him without his influence being known to him intimately, both as creating, preserving and governing. From this I infer again that either there is no providence of the Deity, or, if there is a providence over created things, then there is no less a perfect foresight of them in God, if I may so speak. Augustine has written wisely on this matter: "There is not many wisdom but one, in which are the immense and infinite treasures of intelligible things; in it are all the invisible and unchangeable reasons of things, even of visible and changeable things, which were made through it. For God did not make anything in ignorance, which cannot rightly be said of any human craftsman. Moreover, if he made all things knowingly, then he surely made those things which he knew. From this there comes to mind something wonderful but yet true: that this world could not be known to us unless it existed, while it could not exist unless it were known to God."

units.la: Turpissimus itaque error est plurimorum Scholasticorum, quando ad Singularia scientiam Dei extendi debere negant; æstimantes nimirum divinum intellectum ex inopia propriæ mentis, in difficilibus suis de Universalibus nugis miserè sese torquentis. Quin, validissimis istis rationibus moti, nil nos metuimus affirmare, Divinam mentem in numerato habere omnes ac singulos ververmiculos, omnes muscas, animalia omnia & partes singulorum, omnes pilos animantium, omnes arenas littoris, omnes guttas maris, omnes pluviarum stillas; omnes omnium figuras, qualitates, conditiones, situs, motiunculas, momenta, modos, habitudines, tempora, loca; omnes omnium hominum cogitationes, affectus, & intentiones. Hæc omnia & singula ut à Deo absolutissimè pendent, ita eadem adeo clarè & perfectè ipse intuetur, penetrat, & comprehendit, ac si tota vis mentis illius in unum duntaxat illorum intenta foret. Neque ullam ista sciendo sibi conciliat ignominiam Deus magis quam faciendo; cum vel minima quoque creando suam propalaverit Omnipotentiam. Et quis ignoret minima, qui non pariter ignorare dicendus sit maxima; quorum momenta à minimis haud rarò pendent? Neque eadem causæ laborare nos hic sinunt de malis, falsis, imperfectis; quæ, uti eveniunt permittente Numine, & permittente ista non minus rationaliter, quam bona, vera, perfecta producente, etiam non magis quam hæc illi possunt ignorari. Adde, & ista frequenter rerum optimarum ac perfectissimarum esse occasiones; neutiquam ergo ignoranda illi, qui hasce habet sine dubio perspectas. Ut absolvam, quod Numen demonstravimus cognoscere se ipsum infinitum infinitè per se ipsum; & in perfectissima sua Potentia, Possibilia omnia; in liberrimo Voluntatis suæ decreto, Futura omnia; in efficaci sua Providentia, Actualia omnia; id ipsum merito dicitur perfectissimo sciendi modo cognoscere omninò omnia. Atqui hoc ipsum est quod de Deo demonstrandum ab initio sumebamus.
units.tr: Therefore it is a most shameful error of many Scholastics when they deny that the knowledge of God ought to extend to singulars. They evidently judge the divine intellect by the poverty of their own minds, which wretchedly torment themselves over their trifles about universals. Indeed, moved by these most weighty reasons, we do not hesitate to affirm that the divine mind has in its reckoning every single worm, every fly, all animals and the parts of each, every hair of living things, every grain of sand on the shore, every drop of the sea, every drop of rain; all the shapes, qualities, conditions, positions, little movements, moments, modes, relations, times and places of all things; all the thoughts, affections and intentions of all men. God depends on all these things and each of them in the most absolute way, and so he sees, penetrates and comprehends them as clearly and perfectly as if the whole force of his mind were directed to any one of them alone. Nor does God gain any dishonour by knowing these things, any more than by making them, since in creating even the smallest things he has displayed his omnipotence. And who would not know that the smallest things are not to be called unknown to one who does not likewise fail to know the greatest, since the importance of the greatest often depends on the smallest? Nor do the same difficulties trouble us here about evils, falsehoods and imperfections. As these come about through the permission of the Deity, and as he permits them no less rationally than he produces good, true and perfect things, so they can no more be unknown to him than those others. Add to this that these often give occasion for the best and most perfect things, and therefore they should by no means be unknown to him, who doubtless has a clear view of them. To conclude: we have shown that the Deity knows himself as infinite, infinitely through himself; in his most perfect power he knows all possible things; in the most free decree of his will, all future things; in his effective providence, all actual things. For this reason he may rightly be said to know absolutely all things in the most perfect manner of knowing. And this is precisely what we took from the beginning as the thing to be demonstrated about God.

units.la: Cæterum ex hoc vario objectorum genere varia resultat Scientiæ Divinæ consideratio, & non una ejusdem, etsi in se ipsa simplicissimæ, divisio. Missis nunc præ brevitate aliis, celeberrima ac receptissima ejus est distinctio in Scientiam Necessariam & Liberam. Illa est, quâ Deus ea cognoscit, quæ in alio statu, quam quo cognoscuntur, cognosci ab ipso absolutè non possunt; qualia sunt, tum Deus ipse; tum, quæ ex Divina Sufficientia per se immediatè fluunt, Possibilia.
