Hæc est, quâ Deus intelligit ea, quæ, si aliud decreto suo definire voluisset, etiam sub alio statu menti Divinæ objici potuissent. sent, quam quo de facto nunc objiciuntur: qualia sunt omnia omninò tum Futura, tum Non-futura. Prior illa nullam decreti Divini determinationem supponit, sed fundatur in ipsa perfectissima Dei natura; unde & Naturalis dici solet: etiam simplicis Intelligentiæ; etsi quidam hanc sumant strictius, pro Scientia Naturali restricta ad objectum suum secundarium, videlicet Possibilia: etiam Theoretica, vel Abstractiva, quibusdam nuncupatur, quatenus cogitatur abstractè ipsas possibiles rerum essentias considerare, nulla habita ratione futuritionis. Posterior hæc, sive Libera Dei Scientia, in signo rationis, sequitur actum divinæ voluntatis decernentem de rerum futuritione aut non-futuritione; unde etiam Visionis appellatur, quatenus eâ Deus ab æterno prævidet res in quacunque temporis differentia vi decreti extituras, vel absolutè non-extituras: Practicam quoque alii vocant, quandoquidem objectum ejus sunt res, quatenus aliquando sunt in actum deducendæ, vel in perpetuum ab omni actuali existentia excludendæ. Ex quibus distributionis hujus non sensus tantum intelligitur, verum etiam sufficientia. Nihil enim tanquam scibile potest cogitari, quod non sit vel ipse Deus, vel quid à Deo dependens; atque hoc iterum vel fluens ex ipsa Dei natura, vel ex indifferenti voluntatis placito. Quorum illud & istud Scientiæ Necessariæ, hoc Visionis, objectum est.
units.tr: Moreover, from this varied kind of objects there results a varied consideration of the divine knowledge, and not a single division of it, although in itself it is most simple. Setting aside the others for the sake of brevity, the most famous and generally accepted distinction of it is into Necessary and Free knowledge. The former is that by which God knows those things which cannot be known by him absolutely in any state other than that in which they are known; such are God himself, and the possibles which flow immediately from the divine sufficiency through themselves. The latter is that by which God understands those things which, if he had wished to define otherwise by his decree, could have been presented to the divine mind even under another state than that in which they are in fact now presented; such are all things absolutely, both future and non-future. The former presupposes no determination of the divine decree but is grounded in the most perfect nature of God itself; for this reason it is also commonly called Natural, or the knowledge of simple intelligence. Some, however, take this more narrowly, as Natural knowledge restricted to its secondary object, namely possibles; and some call it Theoretical or Abstractive, inasmuch as it is conceived as considering abstractly the possible essences of things, with no regard to their future existence. The latter, that is the Free knowledge of God, follows, in the order of reason, the act of the divine will decreeing the future or non-future existence of things; for this reason it is also called Vision, inasmuch as by it God from eternity foresees things that will exist, by virtue of his decree, at whatever point of time, or that will absolutely not exist. Others call it Practical as well, since its objects are things as they are to be brought into act at some time, or to be excluded for ever from all actual existence. From this distinction not only the meaning but also the adequacy is understood. For nothing can be conceived as knowable which is not either God himself or something dependent on God; and this again either flows from the nature of God or from the indifferent pleasure of the will. The former of these, both that and this, is the object of Necessary knowledge; the latter is the object of Vision.

units.la: Non tamen ista veritatis simplicitas satisfacit, quibus indifferens voluntatis suæ libertas, quam elegerunt propugnandam, unica philosophandi regula est, quique potius quascunque veritates divinas turbare volunt, quam ut huic idolo quicquam decedere patiantur. Ἐvρηµα invenerunt superiori seculo Jesuitæ; foverunt dein quivis liberi arbitrii patroni diligenter. Nimirum, hinc quidem pudebat certam futurorum liberorum præscientiam Deo detrahere, cum Socinianis: indè tamen cum ea conciliare desperabant supremam illam, quam ipsi fingunt, creaturarum rationalium ἀνπξεσίαν. Quid ergo? Quo tutius tantis de rebus nugarentur, tertiam quandam placuit fingere Dei Scientiam, camque inter istas duas interponere MEDIAM; sic dictam, quod sit mixtæ quasi conditionis, conveniens scilicet partim cum scientia Naturali, quòd omnem divinæ voluntatis luntatis actum antecedat; partim cum Libera, quia (ut Auctores illi loquuntur) sicut Deus per scientiam Liberam potuisset res futuras non-cognoscere, si statuisset eas non-producere, ita etiam per scientiam Mediam potuisset non-praescire, quae creaturae re vera facturae sunt, si pro sua libertate non ea suissent facturae, sed aliquid aliud. Itaque eam versari volunt circa actiones liberas creaturarum rationalium, quatenus quid ipsae, si quando in his vel illis circumstantiis ponerentur, facturae sint secundum liberam voluntatis suae inclinationem, praevidet Deus; idque (in quo rei cardo vertitur) ante ullum suae voluntatis hac de re decretum. Qui rerum eventus quoniam a certa conditione sunt suspensi, atque sub conditione a Deo cognosci statuuntur, etiam scientiam hanc inde vocant Conditionatam. Ubi & hoc observandum est, ejusmodi contingentium conditionatorum tam antecedens quam consequens actu in certa temporis differentia hactenus non poni; sed de hoc definiendum esse per decretum, post istam per scientiam Mediam praevisionem. Atque hoc pacto unice salvari posse jactant & agentis creaturae libertatem, & scientis Creatoris certitudinem. Postquam enim praevidit Deus, quo creaturae liberum arbitrium, in his vel istis circumstantiis collocatum, sese sit inclinaturum, jam demum pro re nata decernit; atque ita praevisae causae alicujus creatae volentiae suam dein quoque adjicit voluntatem.
units.tr: Yet this simplicity of truth does not satisfy those who have chosen to defend the indifferent liberty of their will as the only rule of reasoning, and who would rather disturb all divine truths than suffer anything to yield to this idol. The Jesuits devised this invention [εὕρημα] in the last century, and afterwards all the advocates of free will diligently fostered it. Certainly, on the one hand, they were ashamed to take from God the sure foreknowledge of future free acts, along with the Socinians; but on the other hand they despaired of reconciling that foreknowledge with the supreme self-determination [αὐτεξουσίαν] of rational creatures, which they themselves imagine. What then? In order that they might trifle more safely on such great matters, they chose to devise a third kind of knowledge in God, and to place it between those two as a MIDDLE knowledge. It is called so because it has a mixed kind of condition, agreeing partly with Natural knowledge, in that it precedes every act of the divine will, and partly with Free knowledge, because (as those authors put it) just as God, by Free knowledge, could have failed to know future things if he had decided not to produce them, so by Middle knowledge he could have failed to foreknow what creatures would in fact do, if in their freedom they were not going to do those things but something else. They therefore want it to be concerned with the free actions of rational creatures, inasmuch as God foresees what they themselves will do, in accordance with the free inclination of their will, if at some time they were placed in these or those circumstances; and this (on which the whole point turns) before any decree of his will concerning the matter. Since these events are suspended on a certain condition, and are held to be known by God under a condition, they also call this knowledge Conditional. Here it must also be observed that such conditional contingents, both antecedent and consequent, are not yet posited in any actual point of time, but that this must be defined by decree after that foreknowledge through Middle knowledge. And by this method they boast that they alone can preserve both the liberty of the acting creature and the certainty of the knowing Creator. For after God has foreseen in what direction the free will of the creature, placed in these or those circumstances, will incline itself, then at last he decrees according to the situation, and so he adds his own will afterwards to the foreseen volition of some created cause.

units.la: At nostro judicio nullum unquam fingi potuit commentum stultius atque absurdius. Primum quidem ipsam rerum sciendarum naturam hanc scientiam prorsus repuere, satis evincunt, quae §. xiv. in hanc rem allata sunt. Gravius est, quod in Divinas perfectiones non uno modo arietet hoc dogma. Enimvero quis ferendam putet in causa prima scientiam, quae primitatem ejusdem ac independentiam prorsus evertit? Nimirum praeit, ex se ipsa determinando suo quodam jure semet ipsam, causa creata. Mox illam creaturae praedefinitionem, sua tum scientia, tum voluntate, sequitur Creator. Imo sequitur vix passibus aequis. Nullus enim excogitari potest circumstantiarum ordo, qui sufficiat fundandae vel probabili conjecturae, nedum certae scientiae, de electione liberi arbitrii; siquidem (quod contendunt adversarii) natura ejus in hoc sita est, quod fit facultas quæ, positis etiam omnibus ad agendum requisitis, agere possit vel non-agere. De Fato verò quid dicemus; cujus omnium fortissimos se destructores gloriantur isti? Certè id fatuissimum inducitur, & plus quam Stoicum; quatenus citra Divinæ voluntatis præfinitionem aliquid statuitur futurum, idque tanquam tale à Deo cognosci, proptereaque ab ipso decerni. Etiam de Divinæ voluntatis libertate quid fiet? Hanc nullam citra indifferentiam consistere volunt. Ne quid ergò ea in homine patiatur detrimenti, fingunt prævideri determinationem voluntatis creatæ, antequam definiat voluntas Creatoris. At nullam hoc pacto huic relinqui libertatem, quatenus ipsa nil determinare potest, nisi id præcisè quod jam ante electuram præscit creaturam, quis non videt? Et quâ obsecro ratione futurum id sciri potest, in quo nullum planè fundamentum reperire datur, ob quod futurum potius credatur, quam nonfuturum? quandoquidem præter ipsum Dei decretum (quod totum quam anxiè possunt hinc remotum volunt isti) nihil unquam cogitare datur, cujus vi ab æterno aliquid scientiæ divinæ objiciatur tanquam futurum: cui difficultati nemo dederit exitum. Adde, quem hæc scientia infert, discursum, ac successivum cognoscendi modum, Deo jam dudum negatum. Videlicet, nihil determinandum est Numini, quod non se, facere oportere collegerit ex prævisa actione suæ creaturæ. Pudeat profectò tueri tantum sacrilegium, Dei pariter ac creaturæ naturam penitus subvertens, tamquè mille modis in illam contumeliosum!
units.tr: But in our judgment no more foolish or absurd invention could ever have been devised. First, that this science utterly rejects the very nature of knowable things is sufficiently shown by what was adduced on this point in §. xiv. More serious is that this dogma strikes at the divine perfections in more than one way. For who could think it tolerable to posit in the First Cause a knowledge that utterly overthrows its primacy and independence? The created cause goes first, determining of itself by some right of its own, and the Creator follows with his knowledge and will upon that predefinition of the creature. Indeed, he hardly follows with equal steps. For no order of circumstances can be devised that would suffice to found even a probable conjecture, let alone certain knowledge, about the choice of free will; since (as the adversaries contend) its nature lies in this, that it is a faculty which, even with all the requisites for acting posited, can act or not act. But what shall we say of Fate, whose most determined destroyers these men boast themselves to be? Surely this is made most foolish, and more than Stoic, inasmuch as, apart from any predefinition of the divine will, something is established as future, is known by God as such, and is therefore decreed by him. What will become of the freedom of the divine will too? They hold that it cannot exist without indifference. Lest it suffer any loss in man, they feign that the determination of the created will is foreseen before the will of the Creator determines. But who does not see that in this way no freedom is left to God, since he can determine nothing except precisely what the creature, whom he foreknows, will first choose? And by what reason, I ask, can that be known as future for which no foundation at all can be found that would make it more likely to be future than not future? For apart from God's own decree (which these men most anxiously try to keep far removed from this matter), nothing can ever be conceived by which anything is set before the divine knowledge from eternity as future. No one will ever resolve this difficulty. Add the discursive and successive mode of knowing which this science introduces, long since denied to God. Clearly, nothing is to be determined by the Deity which he has not gathered, from the foreseen action of his creature, that he ought to do. It is shameful to defend such sacrilege, which wholly subverts the nature of God and of the creature alike, and insults both in a thousand ways!

units.la: Non tamen hujus patronis suæ desunt subtilitates, quibus ceu rationibus eam commendent. Multùm adferunt Logicorum effatum, quo duorum contradictoriorum alterum semper verum, alterum falsum, pronunciatur. Unde sequi putant, cum futurum & non-futurum contradictoria sint, etiam ab æterno, antecedenter quoque ad Dei decretum, alterutrum eorum suam habuisse veritatem; consequenter Intellectui Divino (quem nulla latet veritas) ante voluntatis determinationem, per scientiam hanc Mediam, cognitam. Verùm, si quod res est attenderent satis, intelligerent nullo negotio, ante Dei decretum rebus competere posse affectionem nullam, præter meram possibilitatem : ut hactenus omnia sint & à Deo cognoscantur non alio modo, quam tanquam (si ita vis) non-futura : sed merè negativè; idest, tanquam talia, de quorum positivo ac definito statu, sive futuritionis, sive non-futuritionis, hactenus nil certi sit, aut sciri possit. Etiam in ore habent frequenter enunciationes hypotheticas, quibus rerum, earum quoque quæ nunquam evenerunt, conditionata passim in Sacris prædicitur futuritio : undè & Scientiam Dei, cujus per enunciationem aliquam talem conditionatam fit manifestatio, conditionatam esse concludunt. Sed errant longissimè. Potest enim absolutæ scientiæ signum esse enunciatio conditionalis. Quod facilè intelligitur, si attendamus, duarum rerum possibilium per voluntatem Dei factam esse potuisse ab æterno connexionem, ut tamen neutram earum unquam futuram decreverit & præviderit. Atque hæc talis duarum rerum connexio ad fundandam conditionatæ enunciationis veritatem sufficit, etsi nulla sit ipsius consequentis tanquam futuri per scientiam Mediam prævisio. Exemplis parcere jubet brevitas. Etiam cognitio hujus rei facilior erit, ubi actum fuerit suo loco de Decretis Divinis. Imprimis verò, per absolutam Dei prævisionem, citra Mediam scientiam, libertati nostræ vim inferri, vociferantur. Et fatemur lubentes eam inferri illi, non quam nos habemus, sed quam ipsi nos habere fingunt; junctam scilicet cum absoluta quadam αὐτεξουσία atque omnimoda istiusmodi indifferentia, quâ quis, positis etiam omnibus ad agendum requisitis, agere potest vel non-agere. Hanc libertatem uti non patitur dependens creaturarum natura, ita eandem destrui per indépendentem Creatoris præscientiam, ipsa veritas est. Quid? quòd facilè fit demonstrare, ne quidem stante hac Scientiâ Mediâ, salvam esse posse talem voluntatis nostræ ἀδιαφορίαν. Id sufficit, si rationali complacentiæ (quæ vera libertatis anima est) nihil obstet futurarum nostrarum actionum certa ac definita per Scientiam Visionis cognitio; quæ aliquam quidem arguit rei prævisæ necessitatem, nullam interim ei infert vim coactivam, quam libertati adversari uti damus, ita longissimè distare dicimus ab ea quam tuemur scientia. Sed & hæc ex infrà dicendis clariora evadent.
units.tr: Nor do the advocates of this view lack subtleties with which to commend it, as if they were reasons. They bring forward at length the logicians' maxim, by which it is declared that of two contradictories one is always true and the other false. From this they think it follows that, since future and not-future are contradictories, even from eternity, and even prior to the decree of God, one of them had its own truth, and consequently was known to the Divine Intellect (which no truth escapes) before the determination of the will, through this Middle Knowledge. But if they had attended well enough to what the matter is, they would understand without any difficulty that before the decree of God things can have no affection at all beyond bare possibility. So all things, until then, are known by God in no other way than as (if you like) not-future, but merely negatively; that is, as things of which, in respect of their positive and definite state, whether of being future or not being future, nothing is certain or can be known. They also frequently have on their lips hypothetical statements, by which conditional futurition is everywhere foretold in the Sacred Writings of things that never came to pass; hence they conclude that the knowledge of God, which is manifested through some such conditional statement, is itself conditional. But they are gravely mistaken. For a conditional statement can be the sign of an absolute knowledge. This is easily understood if we consider that a connection between two possible things could have been made from eternity by the will of God, while he neither decreed nor foresaw that either of them would ever be future. And such a connection of two things is sufficient to ground the truth of a conditional statement, even if there is no foreseeing, through Middle Knowledge, of the consequent itself as future. Brevity forbids me to give examples. The knowledge of this matter will also be easier once the Divine Decrees have been treated in their proper place. Above all, they cry out that our liberty is violated by absolute foreknowledge of God apart from Middle Knowledge. And we gladly admit that it is violated, not the liberty we have, but the liberty they pretend we have: namely, one joined with an absolute autexousia [αὐτεξουσία] and with that complete indifference [adiaphoria ἀδιαφορία] by which one can, even with all the requisites for acting posited, act or not act. That this liberty is not allowed by the dependent nature of creatures, and is in turn destroyed by the independent foreknowledge of the Creator, is itself the truth. Indeed, it is easy to demonstrate that even if this Middle Knowledge is set aside, such indifference of our will cannot be preserved. It is enough that nothing hinders rational delight (which is the true soul of liberty) from being joined with a certain and definite knowledge of our future actions through the Knowledge of Vision. This knowledge indeed implies some necessity of the foreseen thing, yet it introduces no coercive force, which we grant is opposed to liberty; so we say that this knowledge is as far from that as the science we defend. But these points will become clearer from what is to be said below.

units.la: At verò, detur etiam in hisce aliquid menti nostræ occurrere, quod non sit ei satis perspicuum. Non unum hoc est in infinita Dei
units.tr: But indeed, let it be granted that in these matters something presents itself to our mind which is not sufficiently clear to it. This is not the only thing in the infinite God
XVIII. The Wisdom of God, a my-

units.la: Dei Sapientia mysterium. Singula quæ de ea hactenus tradidimus maximam merentur Admirationem, pari cum Veneratione conjunctam. Hæc piam mentem docet, satiusque esse suam agnoscere in hisce ritè cogitandis curtam supellectilem, quam temerario ausu immensæ profunditatis tentare fundum: quippe quæ novit, non alibi magis quam in hac ipsa sublimitate sese commendare tantarum rerum majestatem. Eadem illa silere jubet, quoties scientiarum Deus, vel naturali rationis lumine docet, vel sublimiori revelatione dictat veritates, cogitatione nostrâ altiores, ingeniolo nostro impervestigabiles. Qui mutit hic quicquam, tantum sapientiæ infinitati detrahit, quantum eâ rationis decempeda minor est. Beatus ille unus, qui in istum oceanum mentem suam totam transfundit atque immergit! Sed & quam hinc discimus Modestiam in pervestigandis tam sapientis Dei operibus! quorum summam exploratam habere, atque ipsorum perfectissimas in mente divina ideas ad plenitudinem usque cognoscere, idem profectò est. Jactent ergò alii suam hic quandam quasi omniscientiam; putent nihil sibi occultum ex tot naturæ mirabilibus; definiant audacter de singularum rerum ortu atque constitutione, haud aliter ac si supremo Artifici fuissent à consiliis! Nobis tutius erit, curiosos nimium animi motus inhibere: quippe quibus persuadet tanta Creatoris sapientia, plurima esse, quæ nos nescire voluit maximus Magister, quæque etiam scire non velle, erudita inscitia sit. Denique, quid animi nobis esset omnibus, si continuò obversaretur Numen Omniscium, quod quæ nos cernimus auditque videtque, ipsisque animis nostris interest, mediisque cogitationibus intervenit testis αὐτόπτης? Quem non ista vel cogitâsse dispudet, dum adeò nullam sentit esse suam sub oculis tanti Domini humilem reverentiam!
units.tr: The Wisdom of God is a mystery. Each of the things we have so far delivered about it deserves the greatest admiration, joined with equal reverence. This teaches a pious mind that it is better to acknowledge how meagre is its own equipment for rightly thinking about these things, than with rash daring to try to sound the bottom of an immeasurable depth; for it knows that the majesty of such great things commends itself nowhere more than in this very sublimity. The same wisdom bids us be silent whenever God teaches the truths of knowledge, either by the natural light of reason or dictates them by a higher revelation, truths higher than our thought and unsearchable by our wit. Whoever murmurs anything here detracts from the infinity of wisdom just as much as his measuring-rod of reason is smaller than it. Blessed is he alone who pours and plunges his whole mind into that ocean! But how much modesty do we learn from this in searching out the works of so wise a God! To have their sum fully explored, and to know their most perfect ideas in the divine mind to the full, is surely the same thing. Let others therefore boast here of a kind of omniscience of their own; let them think nothing hidden from them among so many wonders of nature; let them boldly define the origin and constitution of each thing, as if they had been counsellors to the supreme Artificer! It will be safer for us to restrain the overly curious motions of the mind, since the great Creator's wisdom persuades us that there are very many things which the greatest Teacher wished us not to know, and which not to wish to know is learned ignorance. Finally, what would be the state of our minds, all of us, if the All-knowing Deity were constantly before us, who hears and sees what we perceive, who is present to our very souls and intervenes among our thoughts as an autoptes [αὐτόπτης] witness? Who is not ashamed to have thought such things, while he feels so little humble reverence under the eyes of so great a Lord!
While I think these things silently in my mind, stupor
and torpor bind my senses;
my spirit wavers, when Your wonder
weighs this knowledge:
sooner shall I count the number of the sand on the shore,
how many bodies the tides roll,
though my eyes, ever wakeful,
shall never grant themselves sweet sleep.
Exercise Nineteen, Concerning the Willing God.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Voluntas Dei paucis explicata & asserta. Voluntas Divina non nisi perfectissimo modo actuosa.
units.tr: I. The will of God is explained and asserted in a few words. The divine will is active only in the most perfect manner.
III. The will of God is to be acknowledged as wholly independent.

units.la: IV. Eadem Liberrima est; & quo sensu Indifferens quoque? V. Dei Voluntas Simplicissima, Immutabilis, Æterna. VI. Affectus omnes à perfectissima Voluntate removendi. VII. Deus semet ipsum vult perfectâ quadam complacentiâ. VIII. Alia quævis à se vult Deus; Possibilia nominatim, & futura. IX. Præsentia quaeque Deus vult; etiam Mala, & quo modo? X. Distributio Voluntatis Divinæ in Beneplaciti & Signi. XI. Alia ejusdem in Occultam & Revelatam distinctio. XII. Pro concilianda altera illarum cum altera, monita duo observanda. XIII. Voluntas Dei Decernens vel Approbans; & hæc quæ? XIV. Decretum Divinum quid; & circa quæ versetur? XV. Decreti Divini existentia rationibus adstructa. XVI. Decretum Dei nullum multiplex, mutabile, suspensum. XVII. Difficultates hic occurrentes breviter discussæ. XVIII. Quâ modestiâ cautelâ arcana hæc Dei cogitanda. XIX. Problematis, de Decreto Dei positivo etiam circa Non-futura, brevis consideratio.
units.tr: IV. The same will is most free; and in what sense is it also indifferent? V. The will of God is most simple, unchanging and eternal. VI. All emotions are to be removed from the most perfect will. VII. God wills himself with a certain perfect complacency. VIII. God wills all other things apart from himself, possible things and future things by name. IX. God wills all present things, even evil ones; and in what way? X. The division of the divine will into that of good pleasure and that of sign. XI. Another distinction of the same will into hidden and revealed. XII. Two points are to be observed in order to reconcile one of these with the other. XIII. The will of God as decreeing or approving; and what is this? XIV. What is the divine decree, and what does it concern? XV. The existence of the divine decree is supported by arguments. XVI. The decree of God is not manifold, changeable or suspended. XVII. The difficulties arising here are briefly discussed. XVIII. With what modesty and caution these mysteries of God are to be considered. XIX. A brief consideration of the problem of God's positive decree even concerning things that are not future.

units.la: AD alterum Actionum Divinarum Principium progredimur, vita Voluntatem; Actum illum Dei Viventis perfectissimum quo sibi placet in se ipso, atque etiam, propter se, in omnibus aliis à se. Non moneo, actum volendi primum cum actu secundo in Deo prorsus coincidere, neque adeò hoc loco de eisdem ab invicem distinguendis quicquam esse laborandum; cum id ex iis quæ de Simplicitate Dei jam antè dicta sunt intelligatur abundè. Nil interimid obstat, quò minus Voluntas hic à nobis concipiatur ad instar Facultatis, indefinenti exercitio volendi perpetim operosæ: talis enim notio distinctius pro modulo concipiendi ac pressius permanentem Dei perfectionem, non tanquam Actionem, sed Attributum, actionis principium, nobis repræsentat. Pleniorem rei hujus intelligentiam dabunt sequentia. Dari verò in Deo Voluntatem, multis in antecessum demonstrare operæ pretium vix videtur; tantæ ea veritas necessitatis atque evidentiæ existit. Certè præcipuum rationalitatis prædicatum Voluntas est, atque indivisio nexu cum Intellectu cohærens: ut neutiquam eâ carere queat, cui jam antè Intellectum asseruimus, summa Ratio. Quid? quod sit perfectio inter alias quàsvis facilè prima, dominum esse suarum actionum per supremam quandam ἀνπξυσίαν; quam qui in Deo non concipit, non jam is Numen concipit, sed brutum prorsus idolum. Et quæ possit esse rei Adorabilitas, penes quam nulla secundum Voluntatem boni malive est dispensatio. Adde pulcherrimum hunc Universi ordinem, ac miram illam totius naturæ in tanta partium vicissitudine constantiam: quæ refundere velle vel in Epicuri oberrantem vago casu fortunam, vel in Porticus ferream fatorum seriem (ut ea hodiè vulgò explicatur) insanientis stultitiæ est, non sanæ mentis Philosophi; qui quocunque oculos circumfert, ista cumulatim obvia habet ubiquè, quæ ne cogitari quidem queunt, absque dominio sapientissimi Numinis, definito quodam perfectissimæ Voluntatis consilio istæc omnia producentis, conservantis, gubernantis. Et quæ esse queat Voluntas in creatura, cujus non exsuperans plenitudo, modo Ipsi convenienti, existat in Creatore? Desino alia adferre, ne nimius sim in re obvia.
units.tr: We now come to the second principle of the divine actions, the will: that most perfect act of the living God by which he pleases himself in himself, and also, for his own sake, pleases himself in all other things apart from himself. I do not warn that the act of willing and the act of the will coincide entirely in God, nor is there any need here to labour over distinguishing them, since this is sufficiently understood from what has already been said about the simplicity of God. Nothing stands in the way of our conceiving the will here as a faculty, constantly busy with the unending exercise of willing, for such a notion, as far as our capacity allows and more closely, presents to us the permanent perfection of God not as an action but as an attribute, the principle of action. What follows will give a fuller understanding of the matter. That there is a will in God hardly seems worth demonstrating at length beforehand, so great is the necessity and evidence of this truth. Certainly the chief mark of rationality is the will, joined by an indivisible bond to the intellect, so that that supreme Reason, whom we have already asserted to possess intellect, cannot be without it. Moreover, to be lord of one's actions through a supreme self-determination [αὐτεξουσίαν] is easily the first of all perfections; whoever does not conceive this in God does not conceive a deity at all, but a utterly brutish idol. And what could be the worthiness of worship in a being in which there is no disposition of good and evil according to will? Add to this the most beautiful order of the universe, and that wonderful constancy of all nature amid such great changes of its parts. To refer these things either to the wandering chance of Epicurus or to the iron chain of fates (as that is commonly explained today) is the folly of a madman, not of a sound-minded philosopher. Whichever way he turns his eyes, he sees these things heaped up everywhere, which cannot even be thought of without the lordship of the most wise Deity, producing, preserving and governing all these things by a definite counsel of most perfect will. And what could will be in a creature, if its fullness, surpassing in a manner suited to it, does not exist in the Creator? I cease to bring forward other points, lest I be tedious about a matter so obvious.

units.la: Altioris indaginis est, & quænam Deus velit; & quo modo? Posterius hoc totum complector verbo unico, si dixero, actum volendi Divinum esse Perfectissimum. Neque, opinor, erit, quisquis Numen ens perfectissimum agnoscit, qui expressè assertioni nimiùm manifestæ ausit contradicere. Contradicunt tamen revera plurimi, haud aliam fere formantes notionem de entis primi Voluntate, quam qualem suppeditat suæ propriæ voluntatis imperfectissimæ conscientia: nil attendentes immensum discrimen, quod est inter Voluntatem quæ ipsa subjecta est rebus, qualis est hæc nostra, atque eam cui subjiciuntur res ipsæ, qualis est illa Dei. Hic spiritus ille est, atque, ut ita dicam, quintessentia istius veneni, quo universam penè Divinorum Mysteriorum doctrinam virulenta Pelagianismi hydra fœdissimum in modum conspurcavit; hæc una radix tot sacrilegorum dogmatum, ac contumeliosissimorum in supremum Numen errorum, quibus, quæ verbis asseritur, re ipsa subvertitur, Divinæ Voluntatis perfectio. Distinctius ergò notare juvabit quædam capita, in quibus cardo hujus rei potissimum vertitur; sed pro instituta brevitate paucis tangenda potius, quam pertractanda.
units.tr: It is a more difficult inquiry both what God wills and in what manner he wills. I comprehend the latter entirely in one word if I say that the divine act of willing is most perfect. Nor, I think, will there be anyone who, acknowledging the Deity as the most perfect being, would dare expressly to contradict an assertion so manifestly true. Yet very many do contradict it in fact, forming almost no other notion of the will of the first being than that which is supplied by the consciousness of their own most imperfect will. They take no account of the immense difference between a will that is itself subject to things, such as ours, and a will to which things themselves are subject, such as God's. This is the spirit, and, so to speak, the quintessence of that poison, with which the virulent hydra of Pelagianism has foully defiled almost the whole doctrine of the divine mysteries; this is the single root of so many sacrilegious dogmas and most insulting errors against the supreme Deity, by which the perfection of the divine will, asserted in words, is in fact overthrown. It will therefore be helpful to note more distinctly certain heads on which the hinge of this matter chiefly turns; yet, given the brevity I have set myself, they are to be touched on briefly rather than treated at length.

units.la: Ac primò quidem loco firmiter tenendum est, omni omninò modo Independentem esse Divinam Voluntatem. Etenim, si communi quodam omnium sensu (eorum imprimis quibuscum hic agimus) rerum creatarum unaquæque eo cæteris creditur præstantior, quo pleniori quodam suo jure fruitur, minusque alterius arbitrio obnoxia utitur voluntate; utique manifestum est, tantum cuique voluntati deesse perfectionis, quantum illi detrahitur Independentiæ: ut quæ perfectissima agnoscenda est Voluntas, hoc ipso ab omni dependentiæ specie prorsùs sit absolvenda. Etiam unumquodque naturæ suæ convenienter operatur quicquid operatur. Itaque cujus entis esse est ipsum Independens esse, illius quoque activitas in volendo non potest non per omnia parilem cum essentia involvere Independentiam. Et à quo, obsecro, pendeat arbitrium entisindependentis, nisi ab aliquo à se independenti? Tale verò præter Deum cogitare, meram esse contradictionem, jam antè demonstravimus. Ergò, si præter Deum nihil independens, utique nec quicquam existit, quod non pendeat ab eo qui solus est independens. Verùm, non quovis modo à Deo pendet, quod ab ipso pendet, sed maximè rationali; ut nihil sit quod non sit ab Ipso productum, utì scienter, ita volenter, ut ita dicam. Ex quibus luce meridianâ clarius est, unumquemque qui non cupit fingere ens extra Deum à Deo independens (id est, aliquid præter Deum Deo æquale, aut majus) fateri debere, nihil omninò cogitari posse à quo pendeat Voluntas illius, qui nihil extra se agnoscit, quod ipsum à sua non pendeat Voluntate. Quæ cum ita sint, frustrà sunt quicunque aliquid concipiunt, à quo, vel tanquam ab objecto, vel tanquam à causa procatarctica, vel ratione quâvis aliâ, suspendatur qualicunque modo actus volendi in ente primo; quod tanquam prima ratio neutiquam agnoscitur, nisi sic suo singula disposuerit arbitrio, ut non independentis consilii mensura sit res volita, sic loquar, sed rei volitæ norma unica sit consilium Numinis independens.
units.tr: And first of all it must be firmly held that the divine will is independent in every way whatever. For if, by a common sense of all (especially of those with whom we are dealing here), each of the created things is believed to be the more excellent the more it enjoys a fuller right of its own and uses a will less subject to another's control, then it is clearly manifest that each will lacks as much perfection as it lacks independence; so that the will which must be acknowledged as most perfect must, for that very reason, be wholly freed from every kind of dependence. Also, everything operates whatever it operates in accordance with its nature. Therefore the activity in willing of that being whose very being is to be independent cannot fail to involve independence in every respect equal to its essence. And on what, I beg you, should the will of an independent being depend, except on something independent of itself? That to conceive any such thing apart from God is sheer contradiction, we have already demonstrated before. Therefore, if nothing is independent apart from God, then assuredly nothing exists that does not depend on him who alone is independent. Yet what depends on God does not depend on him in just any way, but chiefly in a rational way, so that there is nothing which has not been produced by him, knowingly and willingly, if I may so put it. From these things it is clearer than noonday light that anyone who does not wish to imagine a being outside God that is independent of God (that is, something beside God equal or greater to God) must admit that nothing at all can be thought of on which the will of him depends, who acknowledges nothing outside himself that does not depend on his own will. Since these things are so, they are wrong who conceive anything on which the act of willing in the first being is suspended in any way whatever, either as its object, or as a procatarctic cause, or on any other ground; for that thing is by no means acknowledged as the first reason, unless he has so disposed each single thing by his own will that the thing willed is not, so to speak, the measure of an independent counsel, but the sole rule of the thing willed is the independent counsel of the Deity.

units.la: Atque hanc Voluntatis Divinæ independentiam comitatur omnimoda ejusdem Libertas. Coactio saltem nulla cadit in ens quod non alterius lege, sed à se agit, independenti quâdam sui arbitrii complacentiâ. Scilicet, Spontaneitatem in agendo poscit Independentia; Rationalitatem, Intellectus Dei: hæc illi junƈta ipsa Libertas est. Non tamen eâ solâ absolvitur quicquid in voluntate Divina existit libertatis: Indifferentiam quoque ad utrumlibet oppositorum eidem tribuimus. Tantùm ne ad quævis eam extendamus, cavendum est. Etiam (quod docebimus infrà) semet ipsum vult Deus, & quicquid perseƈtissimam suam naturam indiviso nexu comitatur, qualia esse possibilia suo loco ostendemus: verum minimè indifferenter; quandoquidem summa complacentia in summo bono summa quædam perfeƈtio est, atque ideò ab ente perfeƈtissimo omninò indivisa. Ex quo eodem principio fluit, ad ipsum actus volendi exercitium minimè quoque indifferenter sese habere naturam Divinam. Neque enim plane non-velle potest, quod se saltem non-velle non potest. Quin & actus volendi secundum sese perfectio si sit (uti est; citra hoc enim ne unquam quidem in ens perfectissimum cadere posset) inseparabilis existit ab illa natura, quæ in se comprehendit consummata plenitudine quodvis perfectionum genus. Imò, non potest non indesinenter velle, quod à nullo externo, propter independentiam, vel in volendo impediri, vel ad volendum excitari potest. Quid ergò? Eadem illa voluntatis independentia, quæ non sinit Deum nonvelle, arguit cum hoc vel illud præter se velle summâ cum αὐταρκείᾳ; quum nihil eorum quæ extrà Deum sunt, quicquam necessariæ connexionis habeat cum natura Divina persectissima. Vult ergò Deus rerum quarumcunque extra se contingentes status, affectiones, nexus, indifferenti prorsus voluntatis suæ determinatione ad hoc ut sint vel non-sint, tales vel aliæ sint, sic vel aliter cohæreant, &c. Atque hinc natum axioma, Actiones Dei ad extra esse indifferenter liberas; de quo suo loco plura.
units.tr: Together with this independence of the divine will goes its complete liberty. Coercion certainly cannot fall upon a being which acts not under another's law but of itself, by an independent complacency in its own choice. Clearly, independence demands spontaneity in acting; the intellect of God demands rationality; liberty is precisely these things joined together. Yet not everything in the divine will that is free is accounted for by that alone: we also ascribe to it indifference toward either of two opposites. We must only take care not to extend this to everything. Also (as we shall teach below) God wills himself, and whatever accompanies his most perfect nature by an indivisible bond, as we shall show in its place are possible; yet not indifferently at all, since supreme complacency in the supreme good is a certain supreme perfection, and therefore wholly undivided in the most perfect being. From this same principle it follows that the divine nature does not stand in an indifferent relation even to the very exercise of the act of willing. For it cannot not-will plainly what it cannot at least not-will. Indeed, if the act of willing is perfection in itself (as it is; for without this the most perfect being could never exist at all), it is inseparable from that nature which comprehends in itself, in consummate fullness, every kind of perfection. Indeed, it cannot but will without ceasing, since, by reason of its independence, it cannot be hindered in willing, or roused to willing, by anything external. What then? That same independence of will, which does not allow God not to will, implies that he wills this or that apart from himself with the utmost self-sufficiency [αὐταρκείᾳ]; since none of the things that are outside God has any necessary connection with the most perfect divine nature. God therefore wills the contingent states, affections and connections of all things outside himself, by a wholly indifferent determination of his will, that they be or not be, that they be such or otherwise, that they cohere thus or otherwise, and so on. Hence arises the axiom that the actions of God toward the outside are indifferently free; of which more in its place.

units.la: Insuper Simplicissima Divina Voluntas est: actus scilicet unus idemque, quantacunque etiam fuerit multiplicis objecti varietas; imò nec ab essentia Volentis Dei diversus. Neque enim sinit retrò demonstrata Dei Simplicitas, quicquam, quod ipse non sit, in Deo dari. Ut omnis quæ hic concipitur distinctio meræ rationis sit. Quod objiciunt de volitione Dei, ab essentia ejusdem necessariò reapse diversa, quòd hæc libera non sit, ut illa, sed necessaria, nullius id momenti esse, evincunt modo dicta de necessaria ipsius actûs volendi in Deo existentia; etsi libera sit & indifferens actûs istius necessarii in hoc aut illo objecto, secundum se contingente, terminatio. Ex quibus Volitionis hujus in Deo Immutabilitas sponte suâ sequitur. Quod enim perfectè simplex est, ac cum essentia immutabili unum idemque, id, manente eâdem essentiâ, non posse non manere idem & immotum, necessum est. Et quæ causa excogitabitur, quæ Numen perfectissimum & independens nolle faciat, quod voluit; aut velle, quod noluit? Omnis profectò secto consilii mutatio aut ex mera animi levitate oritur; aut ex quadam vel imprudentia vel impotentia, quando videlicet improvisi casus intercedentes. quos vel avertere vel mutare in manu non est, ea capere cogunt nova consilia, quae apta sunt novis atque inopinatis mutatorum rerum circumstantiis. Eum vero fingere in Numine aut sapientiae aut potentiae defectum, ut rebus a se pendentibus suum subjicere arbitrium habeat necesse, stoliditatis profecto est ac stultitiae omnem modum superantis. Absit itaque a Numine mutanda voluisse! quod, ut scite ille, Majestatis diminutio est, & erroris confessio. Denique, si entis independentis atque infinite perfecti perfectio sit immutabilis & simplex voluntas (uti esse ostendimus) dubium esse nequit, quin eadem quoque sit ac esse debeat Æterna, expers principii, carens fine, nullique obnoxia successioni: de quibus quandoquidem ex dictis constat, quicquam addere non est necesse.
units.tr: Moreover, the divine will is most simple: it is one and the same act, however great the variety of its multiple objects, and indeed it is not even different from the essence of God who wills. For the simplicity of God, demonstrated above, does not allow that anything exists in God which he himself is not. So every distinction conceived here is a distinction of reason alone. As for the objection that God's volition, which is really distinct from his essence, is not free as that essence is but necessary, the points just made about the necessary existence of the act of willing in God show that this objection is of no weight. Yet the will is free, and its determination of this necessary act toward this or that object, which is contingent in itself, is indifferent. From these points the immutability of this volition in God follows of its own accord. For what is perfectly simple, and one and the same with an immutable essence, must necessarily remain the same and unmoved while that essence remains the same. And what cause could be devised that would make the most perfect and independent Deity not wish what he has willed, or will what he has not wished? Every change of plan surely arises either from mere fickleness of mind, or from some lack of foresight or of power, when unforeseen events that intervene, and which cannot be averted or altered, compel one to adopt new plans suited to the new and unexpected circumstances of changed affairs. To imagine a deficiency of wisdom or power in the Deity, such that he must submit his will to things dependent on himself, is truly the height of stupidity and folly beyond all measure. Far from the Deity be the thought that he has willed things that must be changed! This, as a certain writer rightly says, is a diminution of majesty and a confession of error. Finally, if the perfection of the independent and infinitely perfect Being is an immutable and simple will (as we have shown), there can be no doubt that it is also eternal, without beginning, without end, and subject to no succession. Since these points are plain from what has been said, there is no need to add anything.

units.la: Quæ omnia cum ita sint, neque per independentis naturæ absolutam perfectionem aliter sese habere possint, liquet, quam jure merito supra audacissimæ temeritatis reos egerimus hominiones, quos non pudet, ad suæ qualiscunque voluntatis modulum revocare tam stupenda supereminentis illius quæ in Numine exstitit mysteria. Eo usque tamen quidam eorum processerunt anthropomorphiticæ insaniæ, ut Deum suis etiam laborare Affectibus contendant, affectu profecto nimium stolido ac perverso. Quasi scilicet in tranquillissima mente leves isti ac parum stabiles dominentur animi motus! quibus jactatur humana voluntas, ex hoc uno, quod sibi ex se ipsa stabilitatem promittere non valeat, sed indigentiæ ac votorum suorum complementum ab extrinseco arcessere debeat, sæque illis plerumque rebus affigat, quas in potestate sua nequaquam habet, & quæ, si vel maximè haberet, tamen, dum ipsæ instabiles sunt ac aurâ leviores, se ipsis firmiora quietis fundamenta animo præstare neutiquam possunt. Cæcutit profecto plane, qui non ex dictis videt clarissimè, longè aliam esse debere volendi rationem, & ab istis mutationibus atque imperfectionibus remotissimam, in eo, qui nullas suæ voluntatis causas extra se à quibus impellatur, agnoscere potest, sed qui ipso suæ voluntatis
units.tr: Since these things are so, and since, by the absolute perfection of an independent nature, they cannot be otherwise, it is clear that we were right to charge with the guilt of the most audacious rashness those men who are not ashamed to bring those stupendous mysteries of that supereminent Being down to the measure of their own will, whatever it may be. Yet some of them have gone so far in their anthropomorphic madness as to contend that God too labours under passions of his own, a passion surely too foolish and perverse. As if in the most tranquil mind those light and unstable movements of the soul rule, by which the human will is tossed about, for the single reason that it cannot promise itself stability from itself, but must seek from outside the fulfilment of its needs and desires, and attaches itself mostly to those things which it does not in any way have in its power, and which, even if it had them completely, could not, being themselves unstable and lighter than air, provide the mind with firmer foundations of rest than themselves. He is surely quite blind who does not see clearly from what has been said that the manner of willing must be quite different, and most remote from such changes and imperfections, in the one who can recognise no causes of his will outside himself by which he might be driven, but who subjects all things to the command of his own will.

units.la: tatis imperio sibi subjicit universa. Sunto animi Passiones perfectiones in illis, in quibus perfectio est appetere quod deest, fugere quod obest! non tamen sunt in Illo, cujus voluntas sui solius sufficientiâ satiatur usque adeo, ut ne cogitare quidem detur, quod ullam Ei adferre possit vel intentionem vel remissionem: dum nihil aliunde boni potest accipere, quod desideret; nihil Ei imminere mali, quod metuat; nihil idcirco objici, cujus impulsu immoto suo statu moveatur. Et certè quicunque Numen sibi fingunt adeò variabile, æstuans odio, percitum ira, amans, dolens, gaudens, poenitens, sperans, desiderans, optans, ineptissimè ne istas quidem persectiones in Deo agnoscunt, quas in suo Sapiente requirebant Stoici. Hunc sibi constare, in se divitem esse, non poenitere, &c. affirmabant. Et affirmabant verè de perfecto sapiente; qualis cum sit nemo mortalium, illa quidem grandiloquentia statum delineat qui supra hominum esse videtur imbecillitatem, at qui dignissimus tamen est solo sapiente Deo. Tribuunt passim Numini Affectus Auctores sacri pariter ac profani, fateor; at cavendum, ne quid istis verbis innui putemus, quod sit praeter voluntatis infinitè perfectæ decentiam. Quid ergò? Humano loquendi modo ea Deo tribuuntur ob similitudinem tantùm effectûs, quæ in nobis existunt secundum proprietatem Affectûs. Nos v. c. Poenitentiâ ducti, cum ipso consilio mutamus opus; quodque antè & fecimus, & facere voluimus, dein quantum in nobis est destruimus, dum jam id esse nolumus. Deum poenitere alicujus rei dicimus, quoties destruit quod fecerat; etiamsi nulla accidat ei voluntatis mutatio. Sufficit interim illa in opere externo convenientia ad fundandum de imparibus rebus parem loquendi modum. Cæterùm re ipsâ is, quem nec mœsta perturbant, nec læta demulcent (ut alibi scitè Augustinus) amat, nec æstuat; zelat, & secuntur est; poenitet eum, & non dolet; irascitur, & tranquillus est: nimirum, opera mutat, sed non consilium.
units.tr: Let there be passions of the mind in those beings in whom it is a perfection to seek what is lacking and to flee what hinders. Yet they are not in him whose will is so satisfied by its own sufficiency that one cannot even think of anything that could bring to him either an increase or a diminution of intention: since he can receive no good from elsewhere that he might desire, no evil hanging over him that he might fear, and so nothing can be set before him by whose impulse his unmoved state would be stirred. And certainly those who imagine a God so changeable, boiling with hatred, stirred by anger, loving, grieving, rejoicing, repenting, hoping, desiring, wishing, most foolishly do not even recognise in God those perfections which the Stoics sought in their wise man. They affirmed that he is consistent with himself, rich in himself, that he does not repent, and so on. And they affirmed this truly of the perfect wise man; and although no mortal is such, that lofty language sketches a state which seems to rise above human weakness, yet it is most fitting for the wise God alone. The sacred and profane authors alike, I admit, everywhere ascribe affections to the Deity; but we must take care that we do not suppose anything to be implied by those words beyond the fitness of an infinitely perfect will. What then? In human manner of speaking these things are attributed to God only because of a similarity of effect with what exists in us according to the nature of the affection. For example, when we are moved by repentance, we change our plan along with our work, and we destroy, as far as in us lies, what we had done before and had wished to do, now that we no longer want it. We say that God repents of something whenever he destroys what he had made, even though no change of will befalls him. Meanwhile, that agreement in the external work is enough to found a common manner of speaking about unlike things. But in fact he whom neither sorrow disturbs nor joy soothes (as Augustine wisely says elsewhere) loves, yet does not rage; is jealous, yet is secure; repents, yet does not grieve; is angry, yet is calm: that is, he changes his works, but not his purpose.

units.la: Transeo ad illa expendendâ circa quæ Divina Voluntas suâ actuositate versatur. Ea sunt omnia omninò, quousque secundum rationis dictamen volibilia esse possunt. Non enim ca perfectissima Voluntas esset, quæ non velit quæcunque velle potest.
units.tr: I pass on to consider those things with which the Divine Will is concerned by its activity. These are all things without exception, so far as they can be willed according to the dictate of reason. For that would not be the most perfect will which does not will whatever it is able to will.
VII.

units.la: teft. Si namque ei subducas aliquid, quod non velit actu, velle tamen posset Deus, detrahis revera ejusdem infinitæ amplitudini, independentiæ, immutabilitati, atque æternitati: quæ omnia à Divina voluntate non magis separari posse, quam ipsa voluntas separari potest à Deo, jam firmiter demonstravimus. Sed de singulis verbo! Inter ea quæ vult Deus, primarium objectum Ipse sibi est. Quum enim & summè persectus existat, & adæquatâ concipiendi ratione istius suæ perfectionis intimè sibi sit conscius, non potest non complacentia summè rationalis planè in eo acquiescere, in quo intellectus nihil reperit, quod displicere queat. Ut objectum perfectissimâ voluntate dignissimum sit ens perfectissimum, in quo prorsus acquiescat: quæ ipsa in se ipso sine motu quies Beatitudo illa Dei est; de qua deinceps. Imo revera nihil vellet Deus, aut velle posset, nisi vellet id, propter quod vult quicquid velle potest; quatenus ob aliud, quam quod ipse est, nihil velle potest, qui dependenter ab alio velle non potest. At non ideo cogitandum, ac si Dei voluntas, quæ alia à Deo esse facit, etiam ipsum existere faci t, aut in esse perseverare, per modum causæ efficientis; ut hac ratione Numen dici deberet esse à se ipsum maximè positivè: id enim quam sit absonum, dudum ostendimus, ubi de Dei Independentia ac Sufficientia fuit agendi locus. Quapropter nudâ duntaxat complacentiâ quicquid Dei circa se Voluntatis est absolvitur.
units.tr: teft. For if you take away from him something which he does not will in act, though God could will it, you really detract from that same infinite greatness, independence, immutability and eternity. We have already firmly demonstrated that all these cannot be separated from the divine will any more than the will itself can be separated from God. But let us take each point in turn! Among the things God wills, the primary object is himself. Since he exists most perfectly and is inwardly aware of this perfection by an adequate mode of conception, he cannot fail to rest in himself with the most rational complacency, since the intellect finds in him nothing that could displease it. Thus the most perfect being is the object most worthy of the most perfect will, the being in which it rests entirely. This resting in himself without motion is that blessedness of God, of which more later. Indeed, God would will nothing, nor could he will anything, unless he willed that for which he wills whatever he can will. For one who cannot will dependently on another can will nothing for any reason other than what he himself is. Yet we should not think that God's will, which makes other things exist, also makes himself exist or persist in being, by way of an efficient cause. In that case the Deity would have to be called self-existent in the most positive sense. How absurd this is we showed long ago, when there was occasion to treat of God's independence and sufficiency. Therefore whatever the will of God concerns itself with is accomplished by bare complacency alone.

units.la: Etiam quævis alia à se Deus vult; ut quanta in eis est entitas, tanta sit Dei circa illa complacentia. Quicquid enim præter Deum est, quemcunque id habuerit statum, cum omnem dependenter habet ab illo qui solus est independens. At quicquid pendet à Deo, pendet ab ipso summâ cum ejusdem complacentiâ; quatenus non minus hæc, quam ipsa conscientia, in modo operandi qui rationalis est involvitur: cum nihil rationaliter aliquid producat, in quo sibi displicet, dum id producit. Si quid ergò esset nolente Deo, id à Deo non foret; sine quo tamen eorum quæ sunt nihil esse potest. Sed per partes! Possibilia Deus non potest non velle, qui suam Sufficientiam, quæ possibilium radix, non velle non potest. Nolim tamen Possibilia ad Voluntatem Dei sic referre, quasi hæc, determinando illa ad statum possibilitatis, eorundem esset causa. Nullo tali voluntatis actu hic opus esse, ad hoc ut res sit merè possibilis, palàm fiet ex iis quæ de Potentia Dei suo loco venient di-cenda. Conferantur & ea quæ jam in hanc rem dicta sunt, Exercitat. xviii. §. x. Suffecerit, simpliciter sibi placere Deum in sua Sufficientia, concepta ab intellectu suo ut est expressibilis extra se modis infinitè multis ac variis. Alia verò Futu-rorum ratio est. Futuritio enim, cum sit determinatio rei pos-sibilis ad hoc ut aliquando transeat à non-esse ad esse, aliquam sui causam necessariò requirit. Eam in futuro ipso non-existente reperire non datur, quoniam antequam est merum nihil est, nec magis suâ naturâ definitum ad hoc ut aliquando, quam ut nunquam, sit. At neque, ut possibilia, ita Futura indivifim fluunt ex essentiali aliqua ac necessaria Dei perfectione. Non alibi ergò Futuritionis causam reperire datur quam in solo Entis Primi arbitrio, cui, hæc vel ista olim esse futura, ab omni æternitate secum definire placuit. Quæ determinatio cum sit actio Voluntatis, etiam Deum Futura velle, dicendum est: de quibus post pauca plura.
units.tr: God also wills other things apart from himself, so that God's complacency in them is as great as their entity. For whatever exists apart from God, in whatever state it may be, has all its dependence on him who alone is independent. And whatever depends on God depends on him with his supreme complacency, inasmuch as this complacency is involved no less than his consciousness in the rational mode of his operation, since nothing that is produced rationally is produced in a way that displeases the producer. If, then, anything were to exist against God's will, it would not be from God, yet without him nothing of what exists could be. But let us go through the parts in order! God cannot fail to will possibilities, since he cannot fail to will his own sufficiency, which is the root of possibilities. Yet I would not wish to refer possibilities to the will of God as if they were the cause of their own possibility by his willing them into that state. That no such act of will is needed for a thing to be merely possible will become plain from what will be said about the power of God in its proper place. Let what has already been said on this matter in Exercitat. xviii, §. x, also be compared. It is enough that God is pleased with himself in his sufficiency, conceived by his intellect as expressible outside himself in infinitely many and various ways. The case of future things is different. Futurition, being the determination of a possible thing to pass at some time from non-being to being, necessarily requires some cause of itself. This cannot be found in the future thing itself, since before it exists it is pure nothing, and by its nature it is no more determined to be at some time than never to be. Nor do future things flow necessarily from any essential and necessary perfection of God, any more than possibles do. Therefore the cause of futurition is found nowhere but in the sole decision of the First Being, to whom it has pleased to determine from all eternity that this or that is to be future. Since this determination is an act of the will, we must say that God also wills future things, of which we shall say a few more things after a little.

units.la: De Præsentibus nihil laborandum; cum tota eorum existen-tia ab actuali Dei influxu pendeat: quem quum non nisi liberrimè exerat Deus, patet nihil existere, quod non existere velit. Major de actionibus moraliter malis, sive de Peccatis, difficultas esse videtur. Non tamen de malitiæ istius subjecto, sive physica actione; quippe quæ secundum se positiva, adeoque bona est, & in tantum voluntate Dei comprobata. Verum de ipsa ἀνομία, sive actionis malitia morali quid dicemus? Ea procul dubio boni privatio est; atque hactenus rationalis com-placentiæ, quæ tantum in bono est, objectum esse nequit. Et tamen eam accidere nolente prorsus Deo, etiam dici non po-test; cum multiplex Numinis circa mala istiusmodi Providentia (infrà probanda) efficaciter evincat, ea Voluntati Divinæ haud planè subduci: utì neque ullus esset defectus, si boni absentis præsentiam efficaci voluntate ponere, utì potest, ita vellet, Deus. Nunc ergò, cum non ponat eam, vult pro-cul dubio non producere bonum, ad quod producendum non tenetur. Quorum illud voluntatem Dei permittentem circa mala
units.tr: There is no difficulty about present things, since their whole existence depends on God's actual influx, which he exercises only most freely. It is plain that nothing exists which he does not will to exist. A greater difficulty seems to lie with morally evil actions, that is, with sins. Yet this is not about the subject of that evil or its physical action, which in itself is positive and therefore good, and is so far approved by the will of God. But what shall we say of the lawlessness [ἀνομία] itself, that is, of the moral wickedness of the action? Without doubt this is a privation of good, and so far it cannot be the object of rational complacency, which is only in good. Yet it cannot be said that it happens with God utterly unwilling, since the manifold providence of the Deity concerning such evils (to be proved below) effectively shows that they are not wholly withdrawn from the divine will. Nor would there be any defect if God, by an effective will, could posit the presence of the absent good, as he can, and yet did not wish to. Now, since he does not posit it, he without doubt wills not to produce the good, which he is not bound to produce. Of these two, the first concerns the permissive will of God regarding evils.

units.la: IX. Præsentia quæque Deus vult, etiam Ma-la, & quo modo ? mala versari evincit ; hoc tamen istâ voluntatis permissione nihil labis Deo affricari, docet. Quæ difficilia videri possent in hoc negotio, ea intelligentur rectius, ubi suo loco dixerimus de Dei circa peccata creaturarum rationalium Providentia actuali; quæ æterni hujus consilii est quasi executio.
units.tr: IX. Whatever God wills in the present, even evils, and in what way; he proves that evils are present, but teaches that by this permissive will no stain is brought upon God. What might seem difficult in this matter will be understood more correctly when, in its proper place, we speak of God's actual providence concerning the sins of rational creatures, which is, as it were, the execution of this eternal counsel.

units.la: Expendenda sequitur varia Divinæ Voluntatis, pro varia objectorum diversitate, ac vario nostro considerandi modo, distributio; nihil ejusdem secundum se spectatæ detrahens tum simplicitati, tum immutabilitati, tum independentiæ. Vulgaris illa est, quâ alia Signi dicitur, Beneplaciti alia. Hæc significat ipsum volendi actum prout is in Deo est: Illa notat eundem illum volendi actum, quatenus eum nobis manifestavit Deus signo qualicunque. Non lubet disquirere, Num, quæ dicitur Voluntas Signi, appellari potius debeat Signum Voluntatis? Ubi enim de re constat, de voce litigare nihil attinet. Imprimis quandoquidem appellatio illa hoc loco nequaquam incongrua videtur, propterea quod nullum signum inane hic occurrit, sed id omne suum signatum certò connotat atque includit. Signa verò præcipua quibus Numen suam voluntatem rationalibus creaturis plerumquè patefacere consuevit, haud malè ad quinque referuntur, comprehensa versiculo: Prædicit, Prohibet, Permittit, Præcipit, Implet. Ex quo liquet, non omnem manifestationis modum pertinere præcisè ad Mandata; etsi synecdochicâ locutione voluntas Signi etiam Mandati dici solet. Excellens nimirum voluntatis Signi species est voluntas Mandati, quâ Deus creaturis rationalibus præscribit legem, cui ceu normæ adstrictas vult carundem actiones: quam ob rem quidam hanc voluntatem etiam dixerunt Moralem; cujus usus longè maximus est in Philosophia Practica, ubi de Regno morali quod Deus exercet in homines agitur.
units.tr: Next there follows a discussion of the various distribution of the divine will, according to the diversity of objects and our varying manner of considering it. This distribution takes nothing away from the simplicity, immutability or independence of the will, considered in itself. The common one is that by which one is called the will of Signi (of sign), another the will of Beneplaciti (of good pleasure). The first signifies the act of willing itself as it is in God; the second denotes that same act of willing, insofar as God has made it known to us by some sign or other. I do not wish to inquire whether the will called the will of sign ought rather to be called the sign of the will. For where the thing is agreed, it is pointless to dispute about the word. This term seems in no way unsuitable here, especially because no empty sign occurs here, but every sign certainly connotes and includes its signified. The chief signs by which the Deity is accustomed to make his will known to rational creatures are, rightly enough, referred to five, comprehended in the verse: Foretells, Forbids, Permits, Commands, Fulfils. From this it is clear that not every mode of manifestation pertains precisely to the commands, although by a synecdochic way of speaking the will of sign is also commonly called the will of Mandati (of command). The excellent species of the will of sign is indeed the will of command, by which God prescribes a law to rational creatures and wills their actions to be bound to it as to a norm. For this reason some have also called this will moral. Its use is by far the greatest in practical philosophy, where we treat of the moral kingdom which God exercises over men.

units.la: Cæterùm, quandoquidem existunt plurima, de quibus definivit quidem Deus secum, nihil tamen nobis aut per prophetias, aut per præcepta, aut per eventum, aut alio quocunque modo manifestavit, haud de nihilo in ordine ad nos Voluntas Dei dispescitur in Occultam & Revelatam, distinctione illi priori affini, si non ferè eādem. Ridicula quidem visa ea fuit quibusdam; sed sine ratione. Etenim, non omnia saltem nos latere quæ Deus vult, palam est, ipsæque docent res præteritæ, quas ut extitisse, ita non sine voluntate Dei extitisse, omnes novimus. Ab altera parte, plurima eorum nobis occulta esse, quæ jam voluntate Dei definita sunt, arguunt, tum immensa Divinæ Voluntatis cum intellectus nostri angustiis comparatæ amplitudo, tum etiam qui quotidie accidunt, non sine æterna supremi Numinis providentia, ηδ ἰδιοπινάτι nobis rerum casus. Quid hic carpat inscitia? Duntaxat cavendum est sedulò (quod neglectum ansam dedit cavillandi) ne unquam voluntatem Revelatam, sive Signi, illi quæ est Occulta, sive Beneplaciti, opponamus: quasi nimirum Deus voluntate Revelatâ aliquid velit, cujus oppositum placeat ac decreverit voluntate Occulta; vel contrà. Non ferre istusmodi pugnam inter voluntatis suæ signum & beneplacitum, veracissimum Dei candorem, infrà videbimus.
units.tr: Furthermore, since there are very many things which God has indeed decided within himself but has not made known to us, whether by prophecies, by precepts, by the event, or in any other way, the will of God is divided with respect to us, not without reason, into Occultam & Revelatam (hidden and revealed), a distinction akin to the former, if not nearly the same. Some have found this ridiculous, but without reason. For it is plain that not all things that God wills are hidden from us, and past events teach this, since we all know that they have occurred and that they did not occur without the will of God. On the other hand, that many things are hidden from us which have already been decided by the will of God is shown both by the immense range of the divine will compared with the narrowness of our intellect, and also by the chances of things that happen daily, not without the eternal providence of the supreme Deity, by unexpected chances. What can ignorance carp at here? Only this must be carefully guarded against (and neglect of it has given occasion for cavilling): we must never set the revealed will, or the will of sign, against that which is hidden, or the will of good pleasure, as if God by his revealed will wished something whose opposite he pleased and decreed by his hidden will, or the reverse. That such a conflict between the sign of his will and his good pleasure does not bear with God's most truthful sincerity, we shall see below.

units.la: Quid ergò? dicat quis. Nonne præcipere potest Deus creaturæ, ut faciat, quod tamen facere re verà non vult? Nonne prædicere peccata, quæ vult non-fieri? Potest ista Deus: sed non ideo signum suo signato vel minimùm erit difforme. Etenim Præceptum signum est, non istius quod Deus re verà aliquandò evenire vult, verum obligationis tantùm ad officium, cui creaturam suam adstrictam se velle, præcepto manifestat. Iterùm, Prædictio signum est, manifestans Dei voluntatem, non de obligatione creaturæ imposita ad hoc faciendum quod prædicitur; sed de eo, quod simpliciter, etiam sæpissimè præter debitum creaturæ rationalis officium, aliquandò est futurum. Conferatur ergò Præceptum cum voluntate Dei obligante, cujus est signum; Prophetia cum voluntate Dei decernente, cujus est signum; &c. nec quicquam in hoc toto negotio esse poterit difficultatis. Maximè, si id quoque observemus, non alio sensu signa à nobis debere accipi, quam quo ex intentione Dei offeruntur. Potest tacitâ conditione ex mente Dei restringi signum, quod parum attendenti videri potest absolutum; potest quandoque (quod potest quisque, sine veritatis dispendio, imò cum laude prudentiæ, vir bonus) ex parte suam voluntatem manifestare Deus, quam totam manifestasse putabit imperitus. His similibusque casibus diligenter cavendum, ne extendamus signum latius, quam quousque id extendi voluit Deus, ipse signorum à se datorum interpres omnium optimus. Exemplis hæc non illustramus, brevitatis causâ. Interim si hæc ipsa, lumine naturæ de Divina voluntate notissima, satis accuratè attendisset eximius cæterum Theologus pariter ac Philosophus, nunquam ei excidisset, quod excidisse merito nollent viri doctissimi, Fidei Divinæ posse subesse falsum. De quo agendum alibi ex professo.
units.tr: Well then, someone may say: can God not command a creature to do what he in fact does not wish it to do? Can he not foretell sins which he wishes not to happen? God can do both, but for that reason his sign will not be in the least at odds with what is signified. For a precept is a sign not of what God truly wishes to come to pass at some time, but only of the obligation to duty, to which by the precept he makes clear that he wishes his creature to be bound. Again, a prediction is a sign making known the will of God, not concerning an obligation laid on the creature to do what is predicted, but concerning what simply will at some time be, often even beyond the duty owed by a rational creature. Let the precept therefore be compared with the obligating will of God, of which it is a sign, and the prophecy with the decreeing will of God, of which it is a sign, and so on; and there will be no difficulty at all in this whole matter. This is especially so if we also observe that signs ought to be understood by us only in the sense in which God offers them according to his intention. By a tacit condition a sign may be restricted by the mind of God, so that to one who does not attend closely it may seem absolute. Sometimes (as any good man may do, without loss of truth and indeed with credit to his prudence) God may reveal part of his will, while the unskilled man will think he has revealed the whole. In such cases we must take care that we do not extend a sign more widely than God wished it extended, he being the best interpreter of the signs he has given. We do not illustrate these points with examples, for the sake of brevity. Meanwhile, if he had attended with sufficient care to this very matter, which is most well known from the light of nature concerning the divine will, that otherwise distinguished theologian and philosopher would never have let slip what learned men rightly would not wish to have slipped: that falsehood could underlie divine faith. This must be treated elsewhere expressly.

units.la: Non desunt, quibus voluntas Beneplaciti eadem statuitur cum voluntate Decernente. Sed minus accuratè. Etsi enim verissimum est, Decretum Dei esse ipsum beneplacitum ejusdem circa rerum futuritionem, non tamen hæc duo æquè latè patent. Etiam circa se ipsum ac merè possibilia versatur Deus suo Beneplacito; non tamen id, uti docebunt sequentia, Decretum dici debet. Ut sileam res præteritas & præsentes; quæ, quæ tales, & in quantum futuræ esse desierunt, rigidè loquendo, Decreti non quidem, Beneplaciti nihilominus, objecta sunt. Accuratius itaque dicemus voluntatem Beneplaciti, vel Decernentem esse, vel Approbantem: quarum quemadmodum illa infert rei nondum existentis futuritionem, ita hæc entis cujuscunque existentis comitatur prædicata realia qualiacunque. Ut revera quæ ante rei existentiam dicebatur voluntas decernens, eadem illa, re jam existente, vocetur approbans. Unde componere licebit controversiam, an & quo sensu dicere liceat, Decreta Dei habere finem? Sed de Decreto plura, ubi aliquid de Approbante voluntate præmiserimus. Notat ea summam illam complacentiam, quâ Numen & in se ipso, & in omnibus aliis à se diversis, in quantum à se sunt, tanquam voluntati perfectissimæ conformibus, acquiescit. Quæ quomodo intelligenda sint, satis jam est explicatum §. vii. viii. ix. ut ea hoc loco repetere non sit necesse. Id interim hic præterundum minimè est, unamquamque rem, quemadmodum ea existit vera, quia refert perfectiones quas complectitur exemplar ejus in mente divina, ita quoque pariter esse metaphysicè bonam, hoc ipso quòd approbante Divina voluntate existat. Non interim putandum est, hanc voluntatem approbantem re productâ verè esse posteriorem. Neutiquam: sed simul sunt, rem produci à Deo, & comprobari; cum causæ rationalis sit, nihil agere, in quo non sibi, dum id agit, placeat; imo &, in cujus idea in sua mente, etiam ante rem productam, non perfectissimâ complacentiâ acquieverit. Sed de voluntate Dei Decernente, sive Decreto, philosophandum est aliquanto diligentius.
units.tr: There are those who identify the will of good pleasure with the decreeing will. But this is less accurate. For although it is most true that the decree of God is his very good pleasure concerning the futurition of things, these two do not extend equally widely. God also exercises his good pleasure concerning himself and merely possible things; yet, as the following will show, that cannot rightly be called a decree. To pass over things past and present, which, strictly speaking, are objects not of a decree but nevertheless of good pleasure, insofar as they are such and insofar as they have ceased to be future. More accurately, therefore, we shall say that the will of good pleasure is either decreeing or approving. Just as the former brings about the futurition of a thing not yet existing, so the latter accompanies whatever existing thing with whatever real attributes it has. Indeed, the will that was called decreeing before the thing existed is the same will, now that the thing exists, called approving. Hence it will be possible to settle the controversy whether, and in what sense, it may be said that the decrees of God have an end. But we shall say more about the decree once we have first premised something about the approving will. This will denotes that supreme complacency by which the Deity rests both in himself and in all other things distinct from himself, insofar as they are in conformity with his most perfect will. How these things are to be understood has already been sufficiently explained in §§ vii, viii, and ix, so that there is no need to repeat them here. Meanwhile this must by no means be passed over: each thing, as it truly exists, because its exemplar in the divine mind contains the perfections it embraces, is likewise metaphysically good, for the very reason that it exists by the approving divine will. Yet we must not think that this approving will is truly posterior to the thing produced. Not at all: the production of the thing by God and its approval are simultaneous. For it belongs to a rational cause to do nothing in which it is not pleased with itself while it does it; indeed, in whose idea in its own mind it has rested in most perfect complacency even before the thing was produced. But the decreeing will of God, or the decree, must be philosophised about somewhat more carefully.

units.la: DECRETUM quandò dicimus, intelligimus actum Divinae voluntatis perfectissimum, quo possibilia quaevis determinata sunt ad hoc, ut futura sint, vel non-futura. Huic actui quatenus summa veluti praelucet sapientia, Consilii nomine frequenter is venire solet: remoto tamen à voce metaphorica omni isto, qui in nostris consiliis habet locum, deliberandi modo, juncto scilicet cum multiplici ignorantia ac longa inquirendi mora, nec non addubitatione molesta, quâ animus saepe hùc illùc dividitur; quae omnia Intellectum Dei perfectissimum prorsus repuere, docent quae hac de re suo loco dicta fuerunt. Praecognitio etiam nonnunquam dicitur: verùm metonymicè; quatenus ipsum decernendi actum practica futurorum scientia individuum comitatur. Sed rem prosequamur! Ea omnis absolvitur determinatione possibilium ad statum (liceat & nunc & deinceps ita loqui) futuritionis vel non-futuritionis. Quandoquidem autem futuritio non nisi rebus non-existentibus convenit, atque non-entis nullae sunt affectiones, liquet hunc actum Dei immanentem esse, qui qua talis nihil ponit extra Deum, sed denominationem futuritionis duntaxat infert in ipso fundatam. Decretum notabam versari circa possibilia; id est, circa ipsas perfectiones Divinas, mente Divinâ conceptas tanquam expressibiles extra Deum per potentiam. Harum quasdam futuras esse, facit Decretum. Id verò sciendum, nomine Futurorum etiam tum Praesentia tum Praeterita comprehendi hoc loco: ut enim ista omnia aliquando non-extiterunt, ita quoque antequam extiterunt aeterno Decreto objecta fuerunt, tanquam futura, etsi postquam extiterunt futura esse desierint; quod idem in omni futuro, quando actu exstet, obtinebit. Dixi, Decreto finita esse possibilia, ad hoc ut sint futura; potius quae Deo sint producenda: futuritio enim suo sensu ad eis, quae ad efficientiam Divinam referri pro qualia sunt mala turpia, sive peccata. Decreti Divini in Effectivum, & Permissivum : quorum illud notat voluntatem Dei de rebus bonis in tempore efficaciter producendis; hoc voluntatem ejusdem de malis turpibus in creaturis rationalibus permittendis, sive non-impediendis.
units.tr: When we say DECREE, we mean the most perfect act of the divine will, by which any possible things whatever are determined to be future or not future.
