To this act, insofar as the highest wisdom shines through it as it were, the name of Counsel is often given; but removed from this metaphorical word is all that mode of deliberation which has a place in our counsels, namely, the combination of manifold ignorance, long delay in inquiry, and also troublesome hesitation by which the mind is often pulled this way and that. All these things, the things said on this matter in their proper place show, utterly reject the most perfect intellect of God. It is sometimes called foreknowledge too, but metonymically, insofar as the practical knowledge of future things accompanies the very act of decreeing. But let us proceed! The whole matter is completed by the determination of possibles to the state (let us speak thus both now and henceforth) of futurition or non-futurition. Since futurition belongs only to things not existing, and non-beings have no affections, it is clear that this act of God is immanent, which, as such, posits nothing outside God, but merely introduces a denomination of futurition grounded in himself. I have noted that the decree is concerned with possibles, that is, with the divine perfections themselves, conceived in the divine mind as capable of being expressed outside God through power. The decree makes some of these future. Yet it must be known that by the name of future things, here, both present and past things are included: for just as all these at some time did not exist, so before they existed they were objects of the eternal decree as future, although after they existed they ceased to be future; which will hold good of every future thing when it actually exists. I have said that possibles are determined by the decree to be future, or rather to be produced by God; for futurition, in its sense, relates to those things which are referred to divine efficiency, or to those evils, base things, or sins which are of such a kind. The divine decree is divided into the Effective and the Permissive: the former denotes God's will to bring about efficaciously in time good things; the latter his will to permit, or not to hinder, base evils in rational creatures.

units.la: Dari in Deo Decretum circa res futuras, admittunt facile quotquot Providentiam dari admittunt: unde & sine dubio æternæ Providentiæ nomine idem passim venire solet. Et prosecto, quum manifestum sit, non esse sapientis quicquam agere, cujus secum non ante iniverit certas rationes, deque quo intentionis scopum ac ordinem non formaverit, utique de Numine sapientissimo minime dubitare fas est, quin id universa operetur secundum consilium illud voluntatis, quod jam ante rerum productionem secum constituit. Imo, nisi vi Decreti, nequiquam ut futurum praescire potest Deus. Unde enim sciet obsecro, nisi ex se, qui scire nihil potest dependenter ab alio à se? Ex se ergo si scit quod futurum est, in se utique fundamentum futuritionis ipsum continere oportet. Verum nullum tale excogitare datur, præter hoc divinæ voluntatis beneplacitum, cujus vi, hæc vel ista, quæ futura scit, ideo futura sciat, quia se illa ad futuritionem ordinasse novit. Pari ergo passu ambulant in Deo futurorum præscientia, atque eorundem per Decretum ad istum statum præordinatio: quapropter etiam hanc Præcognitionis vocabulo insigniri, jam ab initio notavimus. Et certè ipsa futuritionis vox involvit connotationem alicujus causalitatis quà aliquando erit, quod hactenus non est. Si sic, utique in causam causarum tandem illa resolvi debet; à qua uti res futurae pendent rationaliter, ita omninò scienter volenter. Etiam, nisi sit aliquod dominans primæ voluntatis in futura imperium, ac certus eorundem selectus, quid causæ est cur non quot possibilia, totidem sint futura? Et, cur non jam quondam fuerint, quæ olim erunt, aut unquam esse possunt? Datur ergo Decretum, si detur Deus à quo pendeant ...
units.tr: That there is a decree in God concerning future things, all who admit that there is a providence readily admit; hence also, undoubtedly, the same thing is commonly called by the name of eternal providence. And indeed, since it is manifest that it is not the mark of a wise agent to do anything for which he has not first laid down certain reasons with himself, and has not formed the aim and order of the intention, surely it is right not to doubt that the most wise Deity works all things according to that counsel of will which he had already constituted with himself before the production of things. Indeed, apart from the force of the decree, God could not foreknow a thing as future. For, I ask you, whence would he know it, unless from himself, since he can know nothing dependently on anything other than himself? If, then, he knows from himself what is future, it must surely be that he contains in himself the ground of futurition. But no such ground can be devised except this good pleasure of the divine will, by whose force he knows this or that as future because he knows that he has ordained it to futurition. Thus the foreknowledge of future things in God and their predetermination to this state through the decree walk side by side; wherefore we noted from the outset that this is also signified by the word Foreknowledge. And certainly the very word futurition involves a connotation of some causality by which a thing will be at some time what hitherto it has not been. If so, it must surely be resolved at last into the cause of causes, from which future things depend rationally, and indeed wholly knowingly and willingly. Also, unless there is some dominating command of the first will over future things and a certain selection of them, what is the cause why not as many things are future as are possible? And why have not those things which will one day be, or ever can be, already once been? A decree therefore exists, if there is a God on whom they depend...

units.la: Imo tantà hujus veritatis vis est, ut negare non tam conentur ... tum, quam tale potius fingere quale poscunt præ... uris opiniones, exigentes iniquissimâ temeritate ... supereminentiam ad volitiunculæ nostræ finitæ simulacrum. Isti bene multa ei subducere mallent, si auderent: dum ejus suppudet, inducunt saltem nobis Decretum, quod causas morales habeat extra Deum & temporariam originem; quod multiplex sit & diversum; quod ambulatorium sit & mutabile; & quid non? Tale nimirum, quod verbis ne quidem ponit, re ipsâ penitus tollit, dignum voluntate optimâ maximâ Consilium. Nos omnibus istis simul & semel viam jam præclusimus unâ istâ voce perfectissimi. Perfectissimam enim voluntatem esse non posse, nisi sit absolutè independens, liberrima, simplicissima, immutabilis, æterna, invictis rationibus planum fecimus §. II. III. IV. quæ istic dicta, cum huc imprimis pertinent, non jam denuò inculcabimus. Concidunt iisdem argumentis, quas tantopere depereunt hodierni liberi arbitrii patroni, plenæ absurditatis distinctiones, quibus ipsum decernendi actum adversarii (non enim eos nostros notamus, qui commodum, objectorum ratione, vocabulis quibusdam istis tribuunt significatum) alium Efficacem faciunt, Inefficacem alium; alium Absolutum, Conditionatum alium; alium Antecedentem, Consequentem alium; alium Generalem, Specialem alium. Nos verò, secundum antè demonstrata, non minimam partem pii istius sensûs ac religionis, quam creatura rationalis Deo suo debet, in eo consistere credimus, ut nullum Decretum agnoscatur Divinum, quod non à parte sui & Efficax sit, & Absolutum, & Antecedens, & Speciale.
units.tr: Indeed, the force of this truth is so great that they do not even try to deny it outright, but rather try to feign a God such as their own opinions demand, insisting with the most unjust rashness on a supereminence reduced to the image of our finite little will. Those men would prefer to take much away from him, if they dared; but since they are ashamed of him, they at least attribute to us a Decree that has moral causes outside God and a temporary origin, that is manifold and diverse, that is wandering and changeable, and whatever else. Such a decree, which in words they scarcely even assert, they in fact wholly destroy, a counsel unworthy of the best and greatest will. We have already closed off all of these at once with that single word most perfect. For we have shown by unanswerable arguments (§§ II, III, IV) that a will cannot be most perfect unless it is absolutely independent, most free, most simple, immutable and eternal. Since those points were made there, and concern this matter above all, we will not now repeat them. The same arguments overthrow those absurd distinctions, on which the modern champions of free will so eagerly depend, by which they make the decreeing act itself of their opponents (I do not mean our own writers, who for convenience attach a certain meaning to these terms according to the nature of the objects) one act efficacious and another inefficacious; one absolute and another conditional; one antecedent and another consequent; one general and another special. But we, following what has been demonstrated above, believe that no small part of that devout feeling and religion which a rational creature owes to its God consists in this: that no decree is acknowledged as divine unless it is, in itself, efficacious, absolute, antecedent and special.

units.la: Neque ad admittenda in Deo ista multiplicium, ac suspensorum, ac mutabilium Decretorum commenta nos cogunt illa, quæ obmurmurat corruptæ rationis immodestia ac malesana subtilitas. Fatum Stoicum hac sententiâ induci, importunè vociferantur. Sed re verâ satis fatuè. Quid enim commune habet series causarum per se ex invicem fluentium, ipsumque Deum involventium (ita enim Stoicos sensisse volunt. An benè? vel unus Seneca meritò dubitare facit) cum catena rerum, quæ nullam per se connexionem habere, sed omnem illam unicè debere asseritur liberrimo solius Dei concatenantis placito? Quin potius, quantum à Stoicismo pariter ac Epicureismo (uniuntur enim in hac chimæra duo hæc contradictoria) isti absint, qui aliquam rebus ex sese tribuunt futuritionem, citra disponentis Dei arbitrium? equidem non video. Urgent, nostram thesin abolere omnem contingentiam. Sed frustrà. Ut enim res unaquæque in hoc contingens est, quod intrinsecam nullam habeat necessitatem, vel etiam nullam ex natura rei cum causis secundis & proximis connexionem, ita nihil ei detrahit absoluta Dei voluntas. Interim ratione decernentis Dei nihil dici aut cogitari debere contingens, tam aserimus intrepidè, quam sumus certi, nullam posse ponitalem contingentiam, quæ non tantundem secum trahat indépendentiæ; cujus vel speciem creatura nulla admittit. Neque etiam mediorum usum hoc pa-cto è medio tollimus. Non enim minus de mediis, eorumque cum fine connexione, ordinatum dicimus per Decretum, ac de fine ipso. An verò medii tollitur necessitas, quando docetur, tantum per illud, juxta decretum, obtineri posse finem? Gravius est, quod objiciunt, absoluto Decreto inferri necessitatem peccandi; eâque posità, peccati culpam transferri ex creatura in Deum. Verùm omnis necessitas hæc extrinseca duntaxat est, quæ non tollit spontaneitatem illam intrinsecam, quâ creatura facere non vult, quæ sui officii esse novit, idque consilio deliberato, ex propria malitia, nihil intuens divinum decretum. Nec denique naufragium patitur nostra libertas. Non enim illa consistit in indifferenti contingentia respectu Dei, quæ revera supremæ cujusdam independentiæ est, sed in rationali complacentia: at hæc magis stabiliri non potest, quam si immutabili decreto statuatur definitum esse, non nisi cum tali complacentia hoc vel istud acturam fore creaturam rationalem.
units.tr: Nor do those objections, which the immodesty of corrupt reason and a diseased subtlety mutter against us, compel us to admit these fictions of many, suspended and changeable decrees in God. They loudly and tiresomely cry out that this view introduces the Stoic fate. But in truth they do so quite foolishly. For what does the chain of causes that flow from one another of themselves, and that involve God himself (for so the Stoics are said to have thought; whether rightly, Seneca alone is enough to make us doubt), have in common with a chain of things which, it is asserted, has no connection of its own but owes its whole connection solely to the most free pleasure of God who links them? Indeed, how far those people who ascribe to things a futurition from themselves, apart from the will of the disposing God, are removed from Stoicism and Epicureanism alike (for these two contradictory doctrines are joined in this chimera), I do not see. They press that our thesis abolishes all contingency. But in vain. For just as each thing is contingent in this respect, that it has no intrinsic necessity, or indeed no connection with secondary and proximate causes arising from the nature of the thing, so the absolute will of God takes away nothing from it. Meanwhile, with respect to the decree of God, we assert fearlessly that nothing ought to be said or thought contingent, just as we are certain that no contingency can be posited which does not carry with it an equal degree of independence; no creature admits even the appearance of this. Nor do we, by this means, remove the use of means. For we say no less that the means, and their connection with the end, are ordained by the Decree than that the end itself is. Nor is the necessity of means removed when it is taught that the end can be obtained only through them, according to the decree. Their more serious objection is that from an absolute Decree a necessity of sinning follows, and that, this being posited, the guilt of sin is transferred from the creature to God. But all this necessity is merely external, and it does not take away that intrinsic spontaneity by which the creature does not wish to do what it knows belongs to its duty, and does so by deliberate counsel, from its own malice, paying no heed to the divine decree. Nor finally does our liberty suffer shipwreck. For it does not consist in an indifferent contingency with respect to God, which is in truth a kind of supreme independence, but in rational complacency; and this cannot be more firmly established than when it is settled by an immutable decree that a rational creature will act in this or that way only with such complacency.

units.la: XVIII. Quâ modestiæ cautelâ hæc arcana Dei cogitanda.
units.tr: XVIII. With what caution of modesty these secrets of God are to be considered.

units.la: Acquiescet istis facilè devota Deo mens, cui arridet maximè sobria sapientia in illis quæ sine timore atque tremore etiam cogitasse summum existit nefas. Suam voluntatem divinæ pedisse quam mavult humiliter agnoscere, quam absurdo ludibrio Numini affingere voluntatem, quæ aliunde præstoletur determinationem. Polluant non uno modo tantarum rerum mysteria sophistæ; irrumpant in hæc adyta importunâ curiositate temerarii; metiantur ad sui sensûs hebetudinem infinitam volendi vim stolidi: ipsâ humi repere habet tutius, quam altius assurgendo. gendo pennas amittere in sublimi, gravissimoque lapsu Icarii conatus debitas luere poenas. Nondum, quantum quæ sunt Dei excedant humana, intelligunt satis, qui non id unicè satagunt, ut quâ parte acies oculi caligat ad tantum splendorem, istic imprimis attendant, ne quam decernendi vilitatem transscribant Numini perfectissimo. Cæterùm utilior cura est, vias suas humili reverentiâ, &, quæ indè nascitur, piâ quâdam, ut ita dicam, securitate, commendare arbitrio Illius, à cujus nutu pendet quicquid rerum existit. Et satisfacit sibi hic facilè, qui revelatæ voluntatis legem religiosâ observantiâ unicam agnoscit & habet agendorum normam; quippe qui certus est, talibus non nisi saventissima esse occultæ voluntatis consilia. Plura scire, ut sua nihil refert, ita ea tutò mirari, quam cum periculo rimari, mavult. Confer Exercit. xvii. §. xviii.
units.tr: A mind devoted to God, which delights most in sober wisdom, will readily acquiesce in these things, a wisdom that regards it as the greatest impiety even to have thought, without fear and trembling, about those things. It prefers humbly to acknowledge that its own will falls short of the divine will, rather than, in an absurd mockery of the Divinity, to ascribe to him a will that waits for determination from elsewhere. Sophists defile the mysteries of such great matters in more ways than one; rash men with unseemly curiosity break into these sanctuaries; fools measure the infinite power of willing by the dullness of their own sense. It is safer to creep upon the ground than to rise higher, and to lose one's wings in the heights, and to pay the due penalty of Icarus's attempt in a grievous fall. Those who do not chiefly take care to see where the eye's sight is dimmed by so great a brightness, and who are not most of all on their guard lest they transfer some baseness of decreeing to the most perfect Deity, do not yet understand well enough how far the things of God exceed human things. A more useful care is to commit one's ways to the judgment of him, on whose nod everything that exists depends, with humble reverence, and with that devout, so to speak, security which arises from it. And he who recognizes the law of revealed will as the one rule of his actions, and keeps it with religious observance, easily satisfies himself here; for he is certain that the counsels of the hidden will can be nothing but most favourable to such people. As it is no concern of his to know more, so he prefers to wonder at these things safely rather than to search into them with danger. Compare Exercit. xvii. §. xviii.

units.la: Coronidis loco verbo tangendum nobilissimum Problema: Num Deus possibilia Non-futura tantum negativè non voluerit esse talia; an verò ea non-futura decreverit actu voluntatis non minus positivo, quam quo versatur circa ea quæ sunt futura? Nobis posterior sententia habetur verior, quippe quæ Decreti Divini perfectioni magis videtur congrua. Quandoquidem enim constat, possibilia quævis suâ naturâ esse (venia sit voci) decernibilia, quumque sit de conceptu Decreti perfectissimi ad omnia quæ objectum ejus esse queunt sese extendere, res ipsa loqui videtur, partem possibilium longè maximam, Non-futura puta, ab infiniti Decreti amplitudine minimè esse removendam. Et profectò, uti non-futurum plus dicit quam merum possibile, ita quoque aliquod non-futuritionis fundamentum, ultra id quod meræ possibilitatis est, venit agnoscendum. Id verò non sufficit sola decernendi non-actio; ea enim rem merè possibilem à non-futura qua tali non discernit, cum & antecedenter ad decretum in signo rationis circa purè possibilia considerari queat actionis decernendi negatio. Et quid si nil unquam extra se producere voluisset Deus; num ideò ab eo removendum foret omne decretum? Utique foret, nisi de non-futuris quoque id esse statuendum sit. Quumque indubium existat, Deum scire non-futura, quid aptius dicemus, quam cum illa scire vi decreti, quo ea talia voluit? Certè nisi sic, id tandem cogitandum erit, necessum habere Deum lustrare quasi rerum vi decreti futurarum seriem, ut inde demum, quid non futurum sit, ex opposito concludat. Atqui à perfectissima scientia nimium alienus est talis cognoscendi modus. Adde, nullam dari viam compendiosiorem ad exitum dandum plerisque, iisque gravissimis, difficultatibus pro adstruenda Scientia Media adferri solitis, quam si cogitemus rerum non-futurarum, uti ipsam non-futuritionem, ita quoque nexus quosvis possibiles Deo vi sui Decreti existere exploratos. Quo dato, ridiculum prorsus est quicquid ex enunciationibus conditionatis res nonfuturas spectantibus in hanc rem operosè adferunt Molinistæ, eorumque sequaces. Confer. Exercitat. precedent. §.xvii.
units.tr: By way of a crown, let us touch briefly on a most noble problem: whether God has not willed possible things that are non-future merely negatively, that they should not be such; or whether he has decreed those non-future things by an act of will no less positive than that by which he is concerned with those things that are future. The latter opinion seems to us the truer, since it seems more consistent with the perfection of the Divine Decree. For since it is agreed that every possible thing is by its nature (let the word be pardoned) decreeable, and since it belongs to the concept of the most perfect Decree to extend itself to all things that can be its object, the matter itself seems to say that by far the greater part of possibles, namely non-future things, must by no means be removed from the scope of an infinite Decree. And indeed, just as the non-future says more than the merely possible, so some ground of non-futurition, beyond what belongs to mere possibility, must also be acknowledged. But the mere non-action of decreeing is not enough for this; for it does not distinguish the merely possible thing from the non-future as such, since the negation of the act of decreeing can be considered, in the order of reason and prior to the decree, with respect to purely possible things. And what if God had wished never to produce anything outside himself? Would every decree then have to be removed from him? Certainly it would, unless it is to be established that the same holds for non-future things. And since it is beyond doubt that God knows non-future things, what more fitting account can we give than that he knows them by virtue of the decree by which he willed them to be such? Certainly, unless it is so, it will finally have to be thought that God must, as it were, survey the series of things that will be by virtue of his decree, so that from that he may at last conclude, by the opposite, what will not be. But such a mode of knowing is far too alien from most perfect knowledge. Add that there is no more compendious way of answering the many, and very serious, difficulties usually brought forward in support of Middle Knowledge, than to think that non-future things, like non-futurition itself, and any possible connections, are known to God by virtue of his own Decree. Given this, whatever the Molinists and their followers laboriously bring forward on this point from conditional propositions concerning non-future things is utterly ridiculous. Compare Exercitat. precedent. §. xvii.

units.la: EXERCITATIO VIGESIMA, DE DEO SANCTO. SUMMARIUM.
units.tr: EXERCITATIO VIGESIMA, DE DEO SANCTO. SUMMARIUM.

units.la: I. Virtutes quo sensu Deo tribuendæ; & earum à nostris discrimen. II. Sanctitatis Divinæ notio quid involvat? III. Dei Benignitas, Gratia, Misericordia, Amor. IV. Veracitas Divina explicata & asserta. V. Deum fallere posse, si velit; vel verbale mendacium proferre, absurdè dici, oftenditur. VI. Justitiæ Divinæ, nominatim Vindicativæ, brevis consideratio. VII. Deum, vi Justitiæ, non posse non punire peccata, monstratur. VIII. Palmariæ difficultati paucis obviam itur.
units.tr: I. The senses in which virtues are to be ascribed to God, and how they differ from ours. II. What the notion of the divine holiness involves. III. The goodness, grace, mercy and love of God. IV. The divine veracity explained and affirmed. V. It is shown that God could deceive if he willed, or utter a verbal lie, and that this is absurdly said. VI. A brief consideration of the divine justice, especially its vindictive form. VII. It is shown that God, by virtue of his justice, cannot but punish sins. VIII. The chief difficulty is briefly met.

units.la: Ut enim ad creatæ Voluntatis debitam perfectionem pertinent Virtutes Morales, ad promptam observantiam illius quod ex rectæ rationis dictamine bonum est atque honestum animum disponentes, ita nequaquam superna hæc rationalis entis ornamenta Divinæ Vo-
units.tr: For just as the moral virtues belong to the due perfection of a created will, disposing the soul to the ready observance of what is good and honourable according to the dictate of right reason, so these lofty adornments of a rational being are by no means to be denied to the divine Will

units.la: I. Virtutes quo sensu Deo tribuendæ; & earum à nostris discrimen. Voluntati sunt deneganda. Nimirum, dictaminis rationis sive æternæ legis, auctor atque conditor ipse Deus est; quippe qui unus ipse summa ratio est. Quod itaque Numen necessariò sibi placet in se ipso, id in nullo sibi placere potest, quod non sibi ipsi, tanquam summæ rationi, sit congruum. Scilicet, sibi placere in eis quæ sibi adversantur nequit, qui ipsi sibi simplicissimo adversari nequit. Interim quales sunt nostræ, tales etiam primi entis Virtutes esse, nequaquam cogitandum est. In creatura rationali ex accessoriæ quædam qualitates sunt; quæ uti abesse quandoque prorsus possunt, sic quoque suam patiuntur per gradus intensionem ac remissionem. In Deo Virtus occurrit, quæ sit, non adventitium accidens, sed ipsa perfectissima Numinis voluntas, quatenus constantissimè ea vult quæ sibi existunt conformia. Vexata non minus atque celebris illa est Jurisconsultorum definitio, quâ ipsis describitur Justitia, Constans voluntas jus suum cuique tribuendi. Haud perperàm qui accuratius philosophantur eruditi complures jam olim in ea notarunt, Virtutem nullam nostram, si exactè loqui velimus, dici posse ipsam nostram voluntatem, quandoquidem ea omnis quoddam illius existit adjunctum; ac tale, cujus haud illa est constantia, ut non sæpissimè in suo exercitio, etiam in optimo quoque, deficiat. De Deo secundum exactam verborum proprietatem solummodo dixeris, Virtutem ejus esse ipsam constantem ejusdem voluntatem. Tollit enim simplicitas Divina virtutem inter & essentiam discrimen; respuit immutabilitas ejusdem vel minimam inconstantiam. Quamobrem, qui non tam virtute præditum, quam potius nil nisi Virtutem Deum esse dixerit, Deo digne loquetur. Ad hanc collata nostra virtus ejus vix umbram assequitur; dum quæ maxima nostra perfectio est, ut in nobis est, in Deum ne quidem cadere potest. Etiam quam dissimile Numen suis existit creaturis, in illis ipsis quoque, quorum ratione hæ imaginem illius gerere dicuntur! Ut virtutes intelligant neque suas, neque Dei, quos nostrarum, ita loquar, semi-virtutum imperfectiones Deo adscribere non pudet.
units.tr: I. The senses in which virtues are to be ascribed to God, and how they differ from ours. Are to be denied to the divine Will. Certainly, God himself is the author and founder of the dictate of reason, or of the eternal law, since he alone is supreme Reason. Therefore whatever pleases the Deity necessarily in himself, it can please in nothing that is not congruous with himself as supreme Reason. Certainly, he who is most simple cannot be opposed to himself, and so he cannot take pleasure in things that are opposed to him. Meanwhile, we must by no means think that the virtues of the first Being are of the same kind as ours. In a rational creature there are certain accidental qualities, which, as they can sometimes be wholly absent, so also undergo increase and decrease by degrees. In God there is a virtue which is not an adventitious accident, but the most perfect will of the Deity itself, insofar as he most constantly wills those things which are conformable to himself. That famous and much-disputed definition of the jurists, by which justice is described as the constant will to render to each his due, is also well known. Several learned men who have philosophized more carefully have long since observed, not without reason, that if we wish to speak exactly, no virtue of ours can be called our will itself, since every will has a certain accident joined to it, and of such a kind that its constancy is never so firm that it does not very often fail in its exercise, even in the best of people. Of God, one may speak with exact propriety only by saying that his virtue is his very constant will. For the divine simplicity removes any distinction between virtue and essence, and his immutability rejects even the smallest inconstancy. Wherefore, one who says that God is not so much endowed with virtue as that he is nothing but Virtue, will speak worthily of God. Compared with this, our virtue scarcely reaches a shadow of his, since what is our greatest perfection, as it is in us, cannot even apply to God. How unlike the Deity is to his creatures, even to those very beings by whose reason they are said to bear his image! Since they do not understand virtues, neither their own nor God's, they are not ashamed to ascribe to God the imperfections of what I may call our half-virtues.

units.la: Cæterum, universum Bonitatis istius Moralis in Numine complexum rectè unico Sanctitatis nomine comprehenditur quo aliud nihil intelligimus, quam ipsissimam illam constantem Divinæ voluntatis cum sua natura conformitatem, de qua jam diximus. Tantum notandum, non duntaxat ipsum in se Sanctum esse Deum, sed & hanc Entis primi Sanctitatem alterius cujusvis Sanctitatis in rebus creatis normam primam existere, atque exemplar perfectissimum, in exacta affectuum conformatione cum illa divinæ rationis rectitudine imitandum. Qua una in re quemadmodum consistit creaturarum rationalium puritas omnis ac moralis integritas, ita imprimis hoc pacto quanta possunt assimilatione infinitæ bonitatis referunt imaginem, suamque summam obtinent perfectionem atque pulchritudinem. Sed de hisce alibi plura: nunc ad ipsius Dei Sanctitatem redeo. Ea varie sese exerens circa varia objecta variam plurium Virtutum subit denominationem. De earum in nobis diversitate disputant Ethici: sed ista contentio parum utilis visa fuit quibusdam, qui non absque ratione arbitrati fuerunt veram virtutem non nisi unam in homine reperiri. Ejus quicquid fuerit, hoc altem loco de virtutum numero nil erit laborandum, ubi omnem veram pluralitatem secludit indivisa simplicissimi entis per omnia sui identitas. Atque inde distinctarum virtutum tantum Deo tribuendam dixi denominationem. Omnem illam pertransfire nec mentis nostræ est, nec hujus chartæ.
units.tr: Moreover, the whole range of this moral goodness in the Deity is rightly comprehended under the single name of Holiness, by which we understand nothing other than that very constant conformity of the divine will with his nature, of which we have already spoken. It is only to be noted that God is not only holy in himself, but that this holiness of the first Being is also the first standard of every other holiness in created things, and the most perfect exemplar to be imitated in the exact conformity of our affections with that rectitude of divine reason. In this one thing consists all the purity and moral integrity of rational creatures, and so especially in this way, by the greatest possible likeness to infinite goodness, they bear its image and attain their highest perfection and beauty. But more on these matters elsewhere; now I return to the holiness of God himself. Displaying itself variously in relation to various objects, it takes on the varied names of many virtues. Ethicists dispute about their diversity in us, but that controversy seemed of little use to some, who not without reason thought that true virtue is found in man only as one. Whatever the truth of that may be, here at least we need not labour over the number of virtues, since in the simplest Being the undivided identity in all its aspects excludes every real plurality. And so I said that only the name of distinct virtues is to be ascribed to God. To run through all of them belongs neither to our mind nor to this paper.

units.la: III. Dei Benignitas, Gratia, Misericordia, Amor.
units.tr: III. The Kindness, Grace, Mercy and Love of God.

units.la: Paucis itaque tantum attingemus nobilissimum illud par, Veracitatem scilicet, & Justitiam; duo illa omnis genuinæ pietatis ac cultus Deo debiti columina firmissima & longè præcipua: nisi tertium adjungere velis, BENIGNITATEM. Est hæc, constans illa voluntas, quâ creaturis suis, in quantum à se sunt ac sibi conformes, benevult Deus. Quæ Benevolentia etiam GRATIA quandoque dicitur, etiam MISERICORDIA, etiam AMOR; ad indigitandam scilicet ejusdem vehementiam, simul & objectorum circa quæ se exerit varium statum. Sensus ejus fugere nequit aliquem, quem non plane fugit sua omnimoda à supremi Numinis liberrima dispensatione dependentia. Testis ejus locupletissimus ista Dei beneficentia, quâ, etsi suis contentus existeret opibus nostrisque nihil indigus, suas tamen perfectiones, nullâ adactus naturæ necessitate, nullo obligatus meriti debito, ex pura bonitatis abundantia, modis tam infinitè tè variis, voluit liberalissimâ munificentiâ communicare rebus extra sese, homini præ omnibus illis. Sed cum magis ardua tractanda præ manu sint, non prosequimur rem facilioris studii, cujusque nimis quam manifesta in quovis Dei opere obvia sunt vestigia.
units.tr: We shall therefore touch briefly only on that most noble pair, namely Truthfulness and Justice, the two firmest pillars of all genuine piety and of the worship owed to God, and by far the chief ones, unless you wish to add a third, KINDNESS. This is that constant will by which God wishes well to his creatures, insofar as they are from him and conformed to him. This benevolence is sometimes called GRACE, sometimes MERCY, and sometimes LOVE, to indicate both its intensity and the varied condition of the objects on which it is exercised. No one can escape its sense who does not wholly escape his own complete dependence on the most free disposal of the supreme Deity. Its most abundant witness is that beneficence of God by which, although he would be content with his own riches and in need of nothing of ours, nonetheless, compelled by no necessity of nature, bound by no debt of merit, out of the pure abundance of his goodness, he willed in ways infinitely varied to communicate his perfections with the most generous munificence to things outside himself, and to man above all of them. But since more difficult matters lie before us, we do not pursue a subject of easier study, whose traces are all too manifest and present in every work of God.

units.la: Ad Veracitatem itaque Dei! Notat hæc constantem illam Dei voluntatem, quâ homini nihil unquam manifestat aut manifestare potest, quod non suæ menti simul ac rebus ipsis ad amussim sit conforme. Perindè vero est, num immediatè Deus aliquid manifestet, num in ista manifestatione certis quibusdam utatur signis. Quòd enim Veracitas nostra in signis potissimum eorumque cum mente nostra conformitate locum habeat, indè est, quod aliis nihil nos persuadere queamus absque signorum adminiculo. Eisdem frequenter utitur Deus; & quando utitur, signa semper exactè sunt conformia tum animi sensui, tum rebus ipsis: ut utramque veritatem & Ethicam & Logicam hac Veracitate comprehendi velimus. Et si de priori constiterit, nullum de posteriori poterit esse dubium reputanti animo suo ea, quæ de exacta rerum omnium cum intellectu divino congruentia diximus, quando de Intellectu divino diximus? Nunc ergò, numquid quod sit contra animi sensum Deus revelare queat? videndum est. An verò dubitari poterit, utrum simplicissimus Deus loquens sibi eidem sententi queat adversari? Manifesta certè ista foret Dei secum ipso pugna. Et qui posset summa ratio rationalem creaturam ad id credendum obligare, quod alienum est à rei veritate (quæ cum mente Dei pari passu ambulat) id est, quod alienum est à recta ratione, sive quod contrariatur lumini intelligendi quod Deus ipse rationali creaturæ indidit? Juberet ergò rationem à se conditam abnegare, si quod revera falsum est credere juberet. At tale quid juberet, si falsa revelaret: cum omnis revelatio Divina, simulac nobis patefit, vim obligandi ad credendum quod revelatur secum ferat. Imò, quæcunque excogitari queunt mendacitatis causæ, omnes ex absunt longissimè ab ente perfectissimo. Nos Insipientiâ nostrâ atque Imprudentiâ ipsi falsum pro vero amplectentes uti haud raro erramus, sic sæpè incauti alios nobiscum in errores trahimus: tale nihil pati Omniscientiam Dei, claclarum est.Etiam Malitia sua atque veritatis odium ad falsum dicendum homines nonnunquam impellunt; nec non invidia, jactantia, similesque pravi affectus: quos omnes procul habere primam Veritatem, Bonitatem, Sanctitatem, manifestum est. Denique Impotentia nostra, quâ fit ut scopum sæpè obtinere nequeamus, nisi dolo circumveniatur quicum nobis res est, mendacii saltem officiosi usum nobis commendare videtur, si non ut licitum, tamen ut quasi necessarium: sed neque illiusmodi necessitas urget Omnipotentem rerum gubernatorem, qui nutu suo flectit quarumcunque creaturarum voluntatem ad sibi præstitutos fines & scopos. Respuit itaque prorsus perfectissima natura divina, uti omnes falsiloquii causas, itâ ipsam quoque, quamcunque fingas, mendacitatem.
units.tr: Let us come, then, to the Truthfulness of God! This denotes that constant will of God by which he never reveals, or can reveal, anything to man that is not exactly conformed both to his own mind and to the things themselves. It makes no difference whether God reveals something immediately or uses certain signs in that revelation. For that our truthfulness chiefly takes place in signs, and in their conformity with our mind, arises from the fact that we can persuade others of nothing without the help of signs. God frequently uses them, and when he uses them the signs are always exactly conformed both to the sense of the mind and to the things themselves, so that we would have both truths, the ethical and the logical, comprehended under this Truthfulness. And if the former is established, can there be any doubt about the latter for anyone who reflects on what we said about the exact agreement of all things with the divine intellect, when we spoke of the divine Intellect? Now, then, let us see whether God can reveal anything contrary to the sense of the mind. Or can it be doubted whether the most simple God, speaking, could contradict his own judgment? That would be a manifest contradiction in God with himself. And how could the highest reason oblige a rational creature to believe what is alien to the truth of the thing (which walks step by step with the mind of God), that is, what is alien to right reason, or what runs counter to the light of understanding that God himself has implanted in the rational creature? He would then be ordering reason, which he himself established, to deny itself, if he ordered it to believe what is in fact false. But he would be ordering just such a thing if he revealed falsehoods, since every divine revelation, as soon as it is made known to us, carries with it the force of obliging us to believe what is revealed. Indeed, whatever causes of lying can be imagined, all are far removed from the most perfect being. We, through our ignorance and imprudence, embracing the false as true, often err ourselves, and so, being careless, we often draw others with us into error; that the omniscience of God should suffer anything of the kind is clearly absurd. Also, malice and hatred of the truth sometimes impel men to speak falsely, as do envy, boastfulness and similar depraved affections; and it is manifest that the first Truth, Goodness and Holiness keeps all of these far away. Finally, our impotence, by which it happens that we often cannot attain our goal unless we deceive the one with whom we are dealing, seems to recommend to us at least the use of a helpful lie, if not as lawful, yet as in some way necessary. But no such necessity presses on the Omnipotent governor of things, who by his mere nod bends the will of whatever creatures you please to the ends and goals he has set for them. Thus the most perfect divine nature rejects utterly all the causes of falsehood, and likewise falsehood itself, however you may imagine it.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, mirandum profectò est, inveniri posse hodiè, qui tanquam sapientiæ haud vulgaris arcanum persuasissimum esse cupiunt, id pertinere ad suam Numini asserendam tum sapientiæ tum potentiæ infinitatem, ut credamus, nihil illi deesse ad struendam fallaciam, satisque eum habere sagacitatis ad consuendas artificiosè fraudes, ut Deus fallere, si velit, possit. Assertio certè cruda, neque assensum impretratura ullius, cujus non in dictata Cartesii sit obsequiosus magis affectus, quam pia ad Sanctissimi Dei Veracitatem attentio. Is (ut alia præteream ipsius hac parte placita) quando benè negarat, Deum mentiri, vel esse deceptorem, mox, quasi nimium dixisset, sese correcturus, inepta limitatione thesin universim verissimam absurdè restringit. Se enim, ait, ibi de mendacio quod verbis exprimitur non fuisse locutum, &c. Ut „ nolit reprehendere illos, qui „concedunt Deum per Prophetas verbale aliquod mendacium „(qualia sunt illa Medicorum, quibus ægrotos decipiunt ut ip„sos curent, hoc est, in quo desit omnis malitia deceptionis) „proferre posse. Hoc si sit verum, nullum unquam Divinum lumen sive naturæ, sive gratiæ, sive gloriæ, certam animis persuasionem ingenerare poterit, de infallibili rei patefactæ veritate. Si enim verbale mendacium, ad instar Medici, proferre possit Deus, quis, non id passim eum fecisse in plurimis, de quibus Rationis & Scripturarum lumine constare putamus, evicerit? Ad mendacium præcisè verbale hic recurrere nil juvat; quandoquidem qui verbis manifestare potest falsum, etiam quovis alio modo id potest. An vero ille hic forte latteret (quod absit!) Atheismus, posse quidem Deum mentiri in Sacra Pagina, in qua signis verbalibus utitur; non autem in naturali ratione, in qua nobis res manifestat, ut illi volunt, per innatas ideas, sine verbali sermone? Horret animus tantæ blasphemiæ rimari mysteria. Interim, quid aliud quam hoc ipsum revera contendant ex illa cavea doctores, qui rotundè profitentur, S. Scripturam in rebus naturalibus sapius loqui secundum erroneam vulgi opinionem? vix video. Verbis enim erroneis id proferre quod neque menti dicentis est conforme, neque rei consonum, quodque eo fine profertur ne quis in suo errore turbetur, est formaliter mentiri, sive verbale mendacium proferre; quum præter ista tria ad mendacium qualificatum, ut ita loquar, nihil amplius requiri videatur. Quantum enim ad damnum attinet, quod quis in mendacio alicui adferre intendit (in quo omnem mendacii malitiam ponere videtur Cartesius, uti docet exemplum Medici ab eo allatum) id ad mendacium qua tale nil pertinet: cum hoc idem etiam per veritatem quis intendere quandoque possit. Quam pulchrè interim de fide nostra mercantur, qui Divinis oraculis verbalium mendaciorum nubem istam offendunt, clarioribus scilicet Cartesii ideis dissipandam, viderint Theologi, qucis istarum rerum custodia imprimis commissa est. Nos intrepidè asserimus, de nulla re naturali (alia alterius loci sunt) in tota Sacra Pagina extare enunciationem vel unicam, quæ non exactissimè cum accurata & Philosophica rei veritate queat conciliari. Verum tanti est, reclamante Deo naturæ auctore, ista cudere pseudo-philosophemata, quæ sua constare nequit veritas, nisi divina cadat auctoritas. Ajunt quidem isti (ut ad primam assertionem redeam) se duntaxat dicere, Deum fallere posse, si velit; at nunquam velle, nunquam velle posse. Verum, etiam plus dicere, jam audivimus. Et, si vel hoc tantum dicerent, num ergò concipiendam in Deo potentiam arbitrantur, quæ voluntatis fræno coerceatur, ne in mendaciorum fagitia prorumpar? Apage impietatem! Plane non potest quod velle non potest, qui quod potest, non nisi rationaliter potest; id est, non nisi præeunte, ut intellestu, sic voluntate. Et quid dicis, posse, si velit, quem velle non posse constat, quod dicis posse? Pari jure dixeris, v.c. arborem posse loqui, si velit; quam id per naturam suam velle non posse, intelligis. Pudeat nugacissimæ vanitatis in re gravissima! cujus momentum aliquanto diutius hic nos detinuit: quapropter alia quæ hujus loci sunt præterimus in præsens.
units.tr: Since these things are so, it is truly astonishing that there should be found today people who, wishing to be most firmly persuaded that they hold a secret of no ordinary wisdom, maintain that it pertains to asserting the infinity of the Deity both in wisdom and in power that we should believe nothing is lacking to him for devising deceit, and that he has enough shrewdness to stitch together frauds skilfully, so that God could deceive, if he willed to. This assertion is certainly crude, and it will win the assent of no one whose affection is not more obsequious to the dictates of Descartes than is his pious attention to the most holy Veracity of God. Descartes (to pass over other of his opinions on this point) when he has well denied that God lies or is a deceiver, soon, as if he had said too much and intended to correct himself, absurdly restricts this most true thesis by an inept limitation. For he says that he had not spoken there of a lie that is expressed in words, etc., so that he does not wish to reprove those who concede that God can utter, through the Prophets, some verbal falsehood (such as those lies of physicians by which they deceive the sick in order to cure them, that is, in which all malice of deception is absent). If this is true, no divine light, whether of nature, of grace or of glory, will ever be able to produce in our minds a certain persuasion about the infallible truth of a revealed matter. For if God can utter a verbal lie, like a physician, who could prove, from the light of Reason and of the Scriptures, that he has not done so in very many matters, of which we think we are certain? To recur here to a lie that is precisely verbal helps nothing, since whoever can make a falsehood manifest by words can also do so by any other means. Or is there perhaps hidden here (God forbid!) some atheism, which holds that God can indeed lie in Sacred Scripture, where he uses verbal signs, but not in natural reason, where, as they would have it, he makes things manifest to us through innate ideas, without verbal speech? My mind shudders at searching out the mysteries of so great a blasphemy. Meanwhile, what else do those teachers from that school, who openly profess that Sacred Scripture speaks in natural matters quite often according to the mistaken opinion of the common people, actually contend? I hardly see. For to utter in erroneous words what conforms neither to the mind of the speaker nor to the thing, and what is uttered for this end, that no one may be troubled in his error, is formally to lie, that is, to utter a verbal lie; since beyond these three things nothing further seems to be required for a qualified lie, so to speak. As for the harm that someone intends to inflict on another by a lie (in which Descartes seems to place the whole malice of a lie, as his example of the physician shows), this pertains nothing to a lie as such, since the same harm can sometimes be intended even through the truth. How nicely, meanwhile, do they bargain away our faith, who bring that cloud of verbal lies against the divine oracles, to be dispelled, of course, by the clearer ideas of Descartes! Let the theologians see to it, to whom the custody of these matters is chiefly committed. We confidently assert that in the whole of Sacred Scripture there is no single statement about any natural matter (other matters belong to other places) that cannot be reconciled most exactly with the accurate and philosophical truth of the thing. But it is not worth the cost, with God, the author of nature, protesting, to coin these pseudo-philosophical notions, whose truth cannot stand unless divine authority falls. Those people say indeed (to return to the first assertion) that they only say God can deceive if he wills; but that he never wills it, and never can will it. But we have already heard them say more than this. And if they said only this much, do they then think there is to be conceived in God a power which is restrained by the bridle of the will, lest it break out into the shameful acts of lying? Away with such impiety! He who can do a thing only rationally, that is, only with the intellect going before and likewise the will, plainly cannot do what he cannot will. And what do you mean by saying that he can deceive if he wills, when it is established that he cannot will it? By the same right you might say, for example, that a tree can speak if it wills; since you understand that by its nature it cannot will this. Let us be ashamed of such most trifling vanity in a matter of the greatest weight! Its importance has detained us here somewhat longer than we intended, so for the present we pass over the other matters belonging to this place.

units.la: Ad Justitiam Dei progredior, Constantem illam voluntatem id retribuendi creaturæ rationali, quod ipsius est secundum legem: nimirum, vel, post consummatam omnem ejus obedientiam, remunerando bonum, ex liberali pacto secundum gratuitam promissionem, quâ, supereminenti suæ bonitati convenienter, unicuique se tanquam summum bonum quærenti pollicitus est beatam sui fruitionem ac communionem; vel etiam, propter sanctissimæ legis violationem, poenas irrogando, ex merito, secundum sanctionis poenalis, legi adversus immorigeros ejus transgressores adjectæ; formulam. Ad debitam tantæ rei discussionem plura spectant, ardua non minus ac utilia, quàm quæ capit angustia hujus nostri tractatus. Quapropter de posteriori hac Justitia, quæ Vindicativa appellari consuevit, pauca dixisse erimus contenti. Objectum ejus duntaxat est creatura rationalis; quippe quæ una & legis argumentum, & legislatoris potestatem, & suam ad illum subjectionem, & denique qui ex transgressione resultat reatum, intelligere potest atque agnoscere. Neutiquam ergò, uti quibusdam visum fuit, huc pertinent bruta, quæ per ipsam suam naturam mentis expertem, uti non legis, sic nec poenæ proprie dictæ, existunt capacia. Quin & jus infligendi poenas ad solam creaturam peccatricem restringendum esse, clamat notio poenæ, demeritum peccati evidenter supponens. Ut ad oppositam sententiam nimium forsan accedere videantur, qui, jure quodam dominii, innocentem etiam creaturam malis tristibus affligere posse Deum, contendunt. Quasi id ferat conformitas cum beatissimo Numine! quasi infinitæ bonitati congruum sit, odisse opera manuum suarum! quasi deceat justissimum judicem adeo non dispari modo habere hactenus fidelem suæ Majestatis cultorem atque improbum perduellem! Cæterum jus poenas sumendi à legis suæ transgressoribus Deo competere, nemo negare potest, qui non voluerit. luerit plane tollere e medio dominium Dei in creaturam rationa-lem, atque hujus ab illo moralem dependentiam. Etenim quae cogitari potest suprema potestas legislatoria, quae non armata sit pari potestate legis executoria? Sine hac nullam veram vim obligandi illa haberet: absque ea enim liberum foret unicuique ei sese subducere impune, atque ita re vera a legis observantia sese suo arbitrio, ut ita dicam, dispensare. Quam itaque evidens est creaturarum rationalium dependentia in genere moris, tam per se clarum est jus hoc Dei, tanquam dependentiae istius vinculum necessarium atque insolubile.
units.tr: I come now to the justice of God: that constant will to render to a rational creature what is due to it under the law. This takes one of two forms. Either, after the creature has completed all its obedience, God rewards the good by a free covenant, according to his gratuitous promise, in which, consistent with his surpassing goodness, he has pledged to everyone who seeks him as the highest good the blessed enjoyment and fellowship of himself. Or, on account of the violation of his most holy law, God inflicts punishment as merited, according to the penal sanction attached to the law against those who disobey and transgress it. A proper discussion of so great a matter involves much that is as difficult as it is useful, more than the scope of this treatise can hold. I shall therefore be content to say only a little about this latter justice, which is commonly called vindictive. Its object is the rational creature alone. Only the rational creature can understand and acknowledge the law, the lawgiver's authority, its own subjection to him, and finally the guilt that results from transgression. Therefore, as some have thought, brute animals have no place here. Lacking mind by their very nature, they are capable neither of law nor of punishment properly so called. Indeed, the very notion of punishment cries out that the right to inflict penalties must be restricted to the sinful creature, since it plainly presupposes the demerit of sin. Those who maintain that God, by a certain right of dominion, may afflict even an innocent creature with grievous evils seem perhaps to come too close to the opposite view. As if such a thing agreed with the most blessed Deity! As if it befitted infinite goodness to hate the works of its own hands! As if it became the most just judge to treat in no different way the faithful worshipper of his Majesty and the wicked traitor! Moreover, no one who is unwilling to do so can deny that God has the right to exact punishment from those who transgress his law. Anyone who wished to abolish altogether God's dominion over the rational creature and its moral dependence upon him would have to do so plainly. For what supreme legislative power can be conceived that is not also armed with equal power to execute the law? Without this power the law would have no real binding force. For without it, each person would be free to withdraw from it with impunity, and so would in fact exempt himself from observing the law by his own will, so to speak. Just as clear as the dependence of rational creatures in the sphere of morals is, so plainly is this right of God, as the necessary and indissoluble bond of that dependence.

units.la: Ita quidem facile intelligitur ex natura τὸ δικαίωμα § Θεῦ, quo qui aeternam legem transgrediuntur approportionata tanto delicto poena existunt digni. An vero tales aliquando ipso facto, sic exigente natura divina, sint necessario puniendi? quaestio gravis est ac tremenda. Istuc redit res omnis: An ex libera voluntatis indifferentia, per absolutam potentiam, Deus remittere queat peccata citra satisfactionem; an vero, posito peccato, Justitiae Vindicativae exercitium per naturam Dei sit prorsus necessarium? De absoluta potentia sermo est: non de ordinata, juxta decretum; de qua lis nulla esse potest inter orthodoxos. Iterum, de ipsa poena quaestio est: non de ejusdem vel modo, vel gradu, vel tempore; in quibus omnibus ex aequo atque sapienter dispensandis plurimam valere Dei tum Clementiam, tum Dominium, omnes etiam lubenter agnoscunt. Istis suppositis restrictionibus, propositae quaestionis partem posteriorem tenendam arbitramur, utpote maxime congruam et sanctissimae naturae divinae, et omnimodae creaturarum dependentiae, et denique nostrae fidei mysteriis. Rejectis bene multis quae huc pertinent in aliam occasionem, unam breviter adferam rationem, quae quidem nobis invicta esse videtur atque instar omnium. Non posse esse creaturam rationalem absque obligatione ad colendum Deum tanquam talem, per se claret. Obligationem hanc derivandam esse haud aliunde quam a lege, non minus manifestum est. Legem absque sanctione poenali legem non esse, sed potius consilium, liquet, quia ea non addita impune licet vivere arbitrio, non legis, sed suo. Jam ergo commisso peccato, eoque sine satisfactione remisso, missio, quærere lubet, quo demùm pacto tali in casu peccatrix creatura maneat sublex ? Non certè ratione obedientiæ activæ; ab ea enim peccator peccando defecit, & factum infectum fieri nequit. Non etiam ratione obedientiæ passivæ; reatum enim cum pœna remissum supponimus. Ecce ! renunciat creatura obligationi legis quod ad observantiam activam, peccando; renunciat Deus obligationi legis quoad pœnam, remittendo: soluto itaque utroque hoc obligationis vinculo, præter quod tertium non datur, solvitur re verâ actus aliquis moralis alicujus creaturæ ab omni obligatione legis divinæ. Hoc cum fieri nequeat citra abnegationem divinæ excellentiæ, manifestum est, etiam peccata impunita remittere, Deo haud esse possibile.
units.tr: From the nature of God's righteous requirement [τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ], it is easily understood that those who transgress the eternal law are worthy of a punishment proportioned to so great a crime. But are such persons ever necessarily to be punished by the very fact, since the divine nature demands it? This is a weighty and fearful question. The whole matter comes to this: whether God, by the free indifference of his will and by his absolute power, can remit sins without satisfaction, or whether, sin having been posited, the exercise of vindictive justice is wholly necessary by the nature of God. The question concerns absolute power, not ordained power, which depends on the decree; and no dispute about that can exist among the orthodox. Again, the question concerns punishment itself, not its manner, degree or timing. In all these matters, which are to be dispensed equitably and wisely, everyone also gladly acknowledges that both the clemency and the dominion of God have great weight. With these restrictions laid down, we think the latter part of the question should be upheld, as most consonant with the most holy nature of God, with the total dependence of creatures, and finally with the mysteries of our faith. Setting aside the many points that belong here but would require another occasion, I shall briefly adduce one argument, which seems to us unanswerable and worth all the rest. That a rational creature cannot exist without an obligation to worship God as such is clear in itself. That this obligation can be derived from nothing other than the law is no less manifest. That a law without penal sanction is not a law but rather a counsel is clear, because without such a sanction one may live at will with impunity, by one's own will and not by the law. Now, therefore, let us ask this: once sin has been committed and then remitted without satisfaction, in what way does the sinful creature remain under obligation? Certainly not in respect of active obedience, for by sinning the sinner has fallen away from it, and what has been done cannot be undone. Nor in respect of passive obedience either, for we have supposed the guilt and the punishment to be remitted. See! The creature renounces its obligation to the law as regards active observance, by sinning. God renounces the law's obligation as regards punishment, by remitting it. Thus, with both of these bonds of obligation loosed (and there is no third), some moral act of a creature is in truth released from every obligation to the divine law. Since this cannot happen without denying the divine excellence, it is plain that for God to remit unpunished sins is not possible.

units.la: Ad quæ quod regeri posset, ego quidem nihil planè video. Objectiones omnes sigillatim excutere, non finit brevitas. Interim hoc ipso nostro argumento jam suppeditavimus, quo facilè prosternitur fortissimus ille pro adversa sententia Hercules. Actiones Dei, ajunt, ad extra, quas inter est punitio, sunt indifferenter liberæ. Verum abusus canonis verbo detegitur. Etiam legislatio procul dubio actio Dei ad extra est. An ergò indifferenter quoque libera ? Imò libera : sed quo pacto? Ab æterno indifferenter liberum erat Deo hominem condere, aut non-condere; consequenter etiam, legem ferre, aut non-ferre. Verum, posito jam conditum esse, neutiquam moralis ejus dependentia Deo relinquit indifferenter liberam legislationem. Pari ratione, peccatum permittere, cut nonpermittere, Deo ab æterno fuit indifferens; atque hactenus etiam punire, aut non-punire. Sed, posito peccato, non jam quod per se liberum erat Deo, scilicet punire, indifferens ei relinquit moralis creaturæ rationalis à Deo dependentia: uti demonstravimus. Alia & plura qui cupit, consulendus illi Gisbertus Voetius, Præceptor quondam noster & Collega memoriæ perquam venerandæ, qui egregium hac parte accurationis experimentum dedit in sua Diatriba de Jure & Justitia Dei, quæ extat Select. Disp. Part. Primâ. Absolvo isto Virgiliano :
units.tr: To this argument I can see absolutely nothing that could be answered. The brevity of this work does not permit me to examine every objection one by one. Meanwhile, by this very argument of ours we have already provided the means by which that most mighty Hercules on the opposing side is easily overthrown. They say that the actions of God toward the outside, among which punishment is one, are indifferently free. But the misuse of the rule is exposed by its own wording. Legislation is undoubtedly also an action of God toward the outside. Is it then indifferently free as well? Indeed it is free, but in what way? From eternity it was indifferently free for God to create man or not to create him, and consequently to enact a law or not to enact one. But once man has been created, his moral dependence upon God by no means leaves legislation indifferently free. In the same way, it was a matter of indifference for God from eternity to permit sin or not to permit it, and so far also to punish or not to punish. But once sin has been posited, the moral dependence of the rational creature upon God no longer leaves to him the indifference that he had, namely to punish, which was in itself free. This we have demonstrated. Whoever desires more and further instruction should consult Gisbertus Voetius, once our teacher and colleague of most venerable memory, who gave an outstanding example of accuracy in this part in his Diatriba de Jure et Justitia Dei, which is found in the Select Disputations, first part. I conclude with that line of Virgil:

units.la: Discite Justitiam moniti, & non temnere Numen !
units.tr: Learn justice, you who have been warned, and do not despise the Godhead!
EXERCITATIO VIGESIMA-PRIMA, DE DEO POTENTE.
SUMMARIUM.

units.la: I. Potentiæ cum Intellectu & Voluntate Dei connexæ demonstratio. II. Ejus interim à Voluntate Divina distinctio rationibus adstructa. III. Atque à difficultatibus quibusdam vindicata. IV. Potentia Deo asserta Simplex, Independens, Infinita, Irresistibilis. V. Divinam Potentiam nulli posse fieri communem. VI. Objectum Divinæ virtutis neque Deus ipse, neque contradictoria. VII. Possibilitas rei quâ talis nihil reale est, sed denominatio tantum externa. VIII. Radix proxima Possibilium est Dei Potentia; prima, Intellectus ejusdem. IX. Potentiæ Divinæ in Absolutam & Ordinatam divisio explicata & asserta.
units.tr: I. A demonstration that the power of God is joined with his intellect and will. II. Its distinction from the will of God, supported by reasons. III. And its defence against certain difficulties. IV. The power of God is asserted to be simple, independent, infinite and irresistible. V. The divine power cannot be made common to anyone else. VI. The object of divine power is neither God himself nor contradictories. VII. The possibility of a thing, as such, is nothing real, but only an external label. VIII. The proximate root of possibilities is the power of God; the first root is his intellect. IX. The division of the divine power into absolute and ordained, explained and asserted.

units.la: D considerandam supremi Numinis POTENTIAM progredimur: Sufficientiam istam vi-ventis Dei, quâ extra sese ponere quæcunque perfectiffimæ rationi haud repugnant ei est promptissimum. Tantam videlicet possidet Ens perfectissimum Sufficientiæ abundantiam, ut non duntaxat ipsi sibi infinito sufficiat, sed &, quia sibi infinito, producendæ cuivis alteri finitæ entitati, quæ præter ipsum vel concipi potest. Quæ tamen, nequis erret, ratione plurimùm dispari intelligenda veniunt. Etenim quæcunque possibilis est præter Deum bonitas, per omnia dependentiam notat ab ista prima Sufficientia, tanquam à fonte suo ac causa suprema: quà verò sibi Numen sufficit Sufficientia, propter ipsam suam independentiam, omnem cujuscunque causalitatis notionem atque vel umbram à se quam longissimè. Commodum autem hujus Attributi tractationem ei quæ fuit Divinæ Voluntatis subjicimus, quando nihil unquam ipso facto extra Deum ponit Potentia, de quo non jam ante æterno Voluntatis decreto penes Deum exactè fuerit prædefinitum. Quid? quod efficax atque independens suique juris intelligi nequeat voluntas, quæ non comitem habere cogitatur tantam in exequendo virtutis facilitatem, quantam habet in formando consilio tum sapientiam tum constantiam. Adeò cum Intellectu & Voluntate perfectissima connexa est Potentia, ut priora rectè in Deo non agnoscat, qui de posteriori quoquo modo dubitat. Quin, quisquis non Deum negat, Potentem Deum neget nemo: tam exstitit manifestum, independentiam id nequaquam possidere atque perfectionis infinitatem, quod non sibi suâ virtute quidvis subjicere valet, potentiqúe efficientiâ quicquid extra se perfectionis esse potest ex sui ipsius perfectione derivare sufficiens est. Et quæ ulla dependentium causarum dari queat Potentia, quæ non ultimâ analysi in causam causarum primam & independentem debeat tandem resolvi? Non id nescivernunt Gentiles; quando quem supremum hominumque Deūmque Patrem finxerunt, eundem passim Omnipotentem celebrarunt.
units.tr: We proceed to consider the power of the supreme Divinity. That sufficiency of the living God, by which he can most readily posit outside himself whatever does not conflict with most perfect reason, is the first thing to note. The most perfect Being possesses such an abundance of sufficiency that he suffices not only for himself, who is infinite, but also, because he is infinite, for producing any other finite entity that can be conceived apart from himself. Yet, lest anyone err, these things must be understood in a very different way. For whatever goodness is possible apart from God signifies in every respect a dependence on that first sufficiency, as on its source and supreme cause. But insofar as the Divinity suffices for himself, by reason of his own independence, he is remote, as far as possible, from any notion of causality, not even its shadow. We now turn to the treatment of this attribute, which is suitable to the consideration of the divine will, since power never posits anything outside God without its having been precisely predefined in God by an eternal decree of the will. What then? A will cannot be understood as effective, independent and its own master unless it is thought to have with it such ease of power in executing, as it has in forming a plan, both wisdom and constancy. So closely is the most perfect power joined with intellect and will, that one who doubts the latter in any way does not rightly acknowledge the former in God. Indeed, whoever does not deny God will deny no one that God is powerful. It is so plain that independence and infinity of perfection do not possess that which cannot by its own virtue subject anything to itself, and that it is enough that, by its efficient power, it derives from its own perfection whatever perfection can exist outside itself. And what power of dependent causes could there be that does not, in the final analysis, have to be resolved into the first and independent cause of causes? The Gentiles did not fail to know this; when they imagined the supreme Father of men and gods, they everywhere celebrated him as Almighty.

units.la: Etsi verò cohæreat indivisim cum perfectissimo Intellectu & Voluntate Potentia perfectissima, attendendum tamen est quam diligentissimè, ne pro modo concipiendi nostro conceptus hujus cum notione alterutrius illorum confundatur. Perèam id agunt, cum Scholasticis qnibusdam, novellæ sapientiæ antistites. Quandò scilicet ex præconcepta opinione istam Dei formarunt ideam, quæ nihil menti exhibeat præter meram cogitationem perfectissimam, quæque omnis intelligendo ac volendo absolvatur, non nisi alterutro modo Deum extra se actuosum esse posse, sequitur: quamobrem & quævis actio Dei transiens eisdem nihil esse dicitur, præter efficacem ejusdem voluntatem. Verùm non unam hæc sententia involvit absurditatem. Dictum jam est Divinæ Potentiæ conceptum ad eum qui Omnisufficientiæ est prorsus pertinere. Hanc autem à Voluntate Dei distinctum attributum esse, nemo inficias ire poterit, cui non lubitum fuerit mirâ confusione universam Divinæ perfectionis infinitatem, quæ Omnisufficientiæ existit basis, solius voluntatis notione absolvere. Adde, quòd jam ab æterno volucrit quæcunque sunt aut erunt, etiam cum non fuerunt, omnisque adeò volentia actio immanens sit, per se nihil actu constituens extra Deum; cum contrà actuale Potentiæ exercitium rem ponat ipso facto existentem: qui modus operandi ratione effectorum diversissimus nisi sufficiat fundandæ distinctioni rationis ratiocinatæ, ut vocant, Potentiam inter & Voluntatem, haud scio, quid tandem remansurum sit cujus intuitu attributa Divina ab invicem distinguere licucerit. Neque hoc tantum: etiam actuosa Dei voluntas circa non-entia versatur; illa quoque quæ nullam unquam habitura sunt actualem existentiam, qualia sunt non-futura, quippe quæ idcò talia, quia ad hunc statum positivo decreto sunt determinata. Jam verò quærere lubet, num asserendum etiam videatur, Deum ab æterno actuosâ suâ Omnipotentiâ id fecisse, ut eorum multa, quæ esse possunt, sint non-futura? Ita scilicet actuale Omnipotentiæ exercitium in nihilum tandem terminari poterit, nisi à Voluntate distinguatur. Porrò, in Sacris scripturis ea Deus posse dicitur expresse, quæ tamen haud cum voluisse experientiâ constat. Quis huic rei, sine Voluntatis à Potentia distinctione, dabitur exitus? Imò, & sese velle Deum modo perfectissimo, jam demonstravimus. Quumque potuisset Deus, si ita visum fuisset, pro liberrimo placito, se tantum velle, nec quicquam præter se, potuisset utique actuosa esse Voluntas citra exercitium Potentiæ. Nisi quoque hæc philosophatio contendere velit, Numen haud minus sese posse ac velle. Sileo monstrificorum conceptuum syrma, quod ista Potentiæ divinæ cum Voluntate confusio secum trahit insolubili nexu; qualia sunt, v. c. Omne possibile esse futurum; quodque futurum non est neque idem possibile esse. Adeoque &, possibile potuisse fieri impossibile, atque impossibile possibile. Hinc, potuisse etiam Deum efficere ut duo contradictoria sint vera. Cum, ante decretum nihil debeat dici possibile. bile. Sic ut, omnis Dei scientia visionis dici debeat, quatenus ad res extra Deum refertur. Ista similiaque multa, quibus universa rei Theologicæ facies immutatur, tueri necesse habent, atque reipsa etiam hodiè tuentur, qui ¦Potentiam Dei à Voluntate nullâ parte distinctam esse contendunt. Denique, nisi quæ sit inter illaduo differitas, haud equidem capio, quo demùm pacto isti Doctores asserant, Deum posse facere ut contradictoria sint vera, si velit; fallere posse, si velit; &c. An verò multeâ subtilitate dicendum erit, Deum velle ista, si velit; aut, posse, si possit? Num potius inaudita absurditate contendent, Deum etiam velle facere contradictoria, etiam velle fallere? Utique; si dicendus sit ea posse, atque inter posse ac velle Dei distinguendum non veniat.
units.tr: Although the most perfect power cleaves inseparably to the most perfect intellect and will, we must nonetheless attend very carefully that, owing to our manner of conceiving, the concept of this power is not confused with the notion of either of them. Certain Scholastics, leaders of the new wisdom, do precisely this. For, having formed from a preconceived opinion that idea of God which presents to the mind nothing but a bare and most perfect thought, and which is completed entirely by understanding and willing, they conclude that God can be active outside himself only in one of these ways. Hence they say that every transient action of God is nothing but his effective will. But this opinion involves not one absurdity. It has already been said that the concept of divine power belongs entirely to that of omnisufficiency. Now, no one who has not been pleased, through a strange confusion, to reduce the whole infinity of divine perfection, which is the basis of omnisufficiency, to the notion of will alone, will be able to deny that this attribute is distinct from the will of God. Add that from eternity he has willed whatever is or will be, even before they existed; and so all willing is an immanent act, which in itself constitutes nothing outside God. On the other hand, the actual exercise of power posits a thing that exists by the very fact. If this difference in the mode of acting, so very great in its effects, does not suffice to ground the distinction of reasoned reason, as they call it, between power and will, I do not know what will finally remain by which the divine attributes could be distinguished from one another. And this is not all. The active will of God is also concerned with non-beings, including those things which will never have actual existence, such as non-future things, which are called such precisely because they have been determined by a positive decree to this state. Now, I should like to ask whether it does not also seem necessary to assert that God, by his active omnipotence, has brought it about that many of the things that could be should be non-future? In this way, indeed, the actual exercise of omnipotence could finally come to nothing, unless it is distinguished from the will. Furthermore, in the Holy Scriptures God is said expressly to be able to do things which, nevertheless, it is clear from experience he has not willed. What outcome can there be for this matter without a distinction of will from power? Indeed, we have already demonstrated that God wills himself in the most perfect manner. And since God, if it had so seemed good to him by his most free pleasure, could have willed only himself and nothing besides himself, his will could certainly have been active without the exercise of power. Unless, indeed, this philosophizing wishes to maintain that the Divinity can no less than he wills. I pass over the train of monstrous concepts which this confusion of divine power with will drags along in an inseparable bond: for example, that everything possible will be future; and that what is not future is not also possible. And so also that what was possible could have become impossible, and what is impossible possible. Hence, that God could also bring it about that two contradictories are true, since nothing ought to be called possible before the decree. Thus all the knowledge of God ought to be called knowledge of vision, insofar as it is referred to things outside God. Those who contend that the power of God is in no part distinct from his will must maintain these and many similar things, by which the whole face of theology is altered; and indeed they still maintain them today. Finally, unless there is a difference between those two things, I truly do not see how these teachers can assert that God can make contradictories true if he wills, can deceive if he wills, and so on. Or must we say, with great subtlety, that God wills these things if he wills, or can them if he can? Or will they rather contend, with unheard-of absurdity, that God even wills to make contradictories, even wills to deceive? Certainly they will, if it must be said that he can do these things, and if the distinction between God's power and his will is not to come into play.

units.la: III. Atque à difficultatibus quibusdam vindicata.
units.tr: III. Defended against certain difficulties.

units.la: Neque metuendum est, nec, si admittatur inter divinam Voluntatem & Potentiam quam urgemus differentia, sequatur, voluntatem Dei inefficacem esse; quippe quæ per se nihil ponat, sed à Potentia ad agendum debeat applicari. Uti enim Intellectus non ideò inefficax dici debet, quòd Deus tantum intelligendo nullum opus externum efficit, ita nullo majori jure id de Voluntate cogitare licet. Est sua, ut Intellectûs divini, ita quoque Voluntatis, si sic loqui lubet, efficacia in hoc, quod nullâ unquam parte aut iste in præcognita rerum certitudine fallatur, aut hæc in prædeterminata earundem futuritione fruftretur: idque eo ipso, quòd omnia per insuperabilem infinitæ Potentiæ actuositatem talia reipsâ suo tempore constituantur extra Deum, qualia ab æterno ea, quemadmodum decrevit, ita præscivit. Quod si inefficacem quis idcirco Voluntatem divinam appellare voluerit, quòd non ipsa immediatè ponat rerum existentiam simpliciter volendo, viderit is, ne pari sequela eandem insipientem arguat, propterea quòd non Voluntas res præsciat, formaliter loquendo, sed Intellectus. Fortior non est objectiuncula, quâ inferunt, omnia Dei opera passim referri ad ejusdem Voluntatem, tanquam ad causam suam & fontem. Hoc enim ut concedimus, ita nullam videmus rationem, ob quam opponi debeant hoc loco, quæ re verâ subordinata quasi sunt. Utique per Voluntatem suam res producit, qui citra ejus decretum nil producit; quique cum volentiæ suæ nutu conjungit effiefficientiam suæ manûs. Scilicet, etiam Sapientiâ suâ Numen agere quicquid agit haud absurdè dixeris, quatenus cunEta su-perno ducit ab exemplo. Sit ergò imperans rerum omnium principium Voluntas divina ! Sed non id obstat, quo minùs exse-quens principium statuatur Potentia: uti dirigens principium Intellectus est. Neque multùm moramur difficultatem, quam occurrere ajunt in concipienda aliqua actuositate causæ primæ, quæ non sit ipsa volitio. Ut enim nos minimè ii sumus, qui rerum omnium, etiam divinarum, claras ac distinctas jactamus ideas, ita facilè damus, modum operandi infinitè perfectum à finito ingeniolo exhauriri non posse. Quo tamen minimè compellimur, ad ea confundenda, quæ suo modo distinguenda esse, non una ratio efficaciter evincit. Imprimis, cum nec ipsi adversarii satis explicare queant, quo pacto tantùm volendo Deus res extra se constituat. Verùm desino addere plura, cum jam dudum in his sim prolixior. Sed aliquanto diligentius confutandus erat error, cui multi alii haud levis momenti suam debent orginem.
units.tr: Nor need we fear, nor does it follow, if we admit the difference between the divine Will and the Power that we press, that the will of God is inefficacious. For the will by itself posits nothing, but must be applied to acting by the power. Just as the intellect cannot rightly be called inefficacious because God, by understanding alone, produces no external work, so we may think of the will in no lesser way. The divine will has its efficacy, as the divine intellect does, if it is lawful to speak so: in this, that neither the one is deceived in its foreknowledge of things with a certainty beyond doubt, nor the other is frustrated in the predetermined future of those same things. This is so because, by the unconquerable activity of infinite power, all things are actually brought into being outside God at their appointed time, just as he decreed them from eternity and foreknew them. But if anyone should want to call the divine will inefficacious because it does not directly produce the existence of things by simply willing them, let him see that he does not thereby charge it with folly by the same inference, since it is not the will, strictly speaking, but the intellect that foreknows things. The little objection they bring is no stronger: that all the works of God are everywhere referred to his will as to their cause and source. We grant this, but we see no reason why it should be set against us here, since these things are in truth in some sense subordinate. Certainly he produces things through his will who produces nothing apart from its decree, and who joins the efficiency of his hand to the nod of his will. Indeed one may not unreasonably say that the Deity also acts by his wisdom in whatever it does, inasmuch as all things are led from the heavenly pattern. Let the divine will be the principle that commands all things! But this does not prevent the executing principle from being named power, just as the directing principle is the intellect. Nor do we dwell long on the difficulty they say arises in conceiving any activity of the first cause that is not itself volition. For we are by no means those who boast of clear and distinct ideas of all things, even divine ones; so we readily grant that a mode of operating infinitely perfect cannot be exhausted by a finite intellect.
