Yet we are not thereby compelled to confuse things which, in their own way, must be distinguished, as a single argument effectively proves. Above all, since the adversaries themselves cannot sufficiently explain how God, merely by willing, constitutes things outside himself. But I stop adding more, since I have already been rather lengthy on these points. Yet the error on which many other no small matters depend had to be refuted with some care.

units.la: Itaquè posse Deum, constat; & sic quidem, ut posse ejusdem non sit ipsum velle. Quod tamen accipiendum tantùm est pro eo concipiendi modo, quo sese ista duo menti nostræ offerunt. A parte rei enim adeo respuit divina simplicitas omnium plurium verè distinctorum diversitatem, ut fatendum sit, Potentiam Dei esse ipsam actuosam ejus essentiam, quatenus ea sufficit coëxistentem sibi ponere creaturam quamcunque. Abest ergò ut perfici concipiatur ab ullo superaccedente actu; quales sunt vel habitus in operando facilitantes, vel actus secundi quibus ab otio ad exercitium transit agendi facultas, vel qualescunque modificationes aut determinationes undecunquè oriundæ. Estque ea haud minima Numinis perfectio, quòd etiam in operando actus purus sit, atque agens per essentiam; quam qui quocunque modo ad creaturas transferre conaretur, in entis simplicissimi eminentiam injurius is nimium soret. Etsi enim cum quibusdam sentiam, nullâ sufficienti ratione demonstrari posse, potentias rerum creatarum ab essentiis earundem reapse differre; ipsæ tamen haud exeunt in actum absque multiplici mutatione, dum in operatione ab habitibus juvantur, ab obje-
units.tr: So it is established that God can, and in such a way that his power is not the same as his willing. This, however, must be taken only as the manner in which these two present themselves to our minds. For in reality the divine simplicity so rejects any diversity of many things truly distinct that we must confess the Power of God to be his very active essence, insofar as that essence suffices to posit any creature whatever co-existing with itself. It is therefore far from being conceived as perfected by any added act, such as habits that facilitate operation, or second acts by which the faculty of acting passes from rest to exercise, or any modifications or determinations arising from whatever source. And it is no small perfection of the Deity that in acting it is pure act and acts through its essence. Whoever tried in any way to transfer this to creatures would do grave wrong to the eminence of the most simple Being. For although I agree with some that it cannot be shown by any sufficient reason that the powers of created things really differ from their essences, still these powers do not pass into act without manifold change: they are aided in operating by habits, moved by objects,

units.la: ctis âtis moventur, ac deniquè quiescunt modo, pro re nata, modo operantur. Quod discrimen inter illam Dei Potentiam ac nostram accuratè notandum, ut quod subindè humano modo de Deo cogitamus, non nisi Deo dignè huic tribuendum esse, probè discamus. Interim non simplicissima tantum sed imprimis quoque independens agnoscenda est divina virtus; ut nullum sibi hic locum vendicet vel ratio motiva quâ ad agendum extrinsecùs excitetur, vel causarum instrumentalium in efficiendo necessitas. Supervacaneum foret id hoc loco adstruere, quando jam antè pluribus evicimus, nihil divinum dici debere, quod non omni modo sit independens. Cumque pariter demonstratum sit, indivisim connexa esse independentiam & infinitatem, non minus infinita quam independens Dei virtus æstimanda est. Infinita scilicet omni modo, sive ipsam ejus perfectionem inexhaustam spectes secundum se, sive modum operandi impervestigabilem, sive immensam rerum producibilium amplitudinem. Testis existit hæc ipsa visibilis creatura, jam inde à mundo condito manifestans æternam sui Creatoris ut Divinitatem sic Potentiam: quemadmodum alibi instituit Gentium Doctor. Quæ cum itâ sint, nullam excogitare datur resistentiam, quæ Deo, exercere volenti eam quâ pollet independentis virtutis infinitatem, obicem ponere, vel moram ullam injicere queat aut difficultatem. Estque hæc victricis Potentiæ divinæ irresistibilitas, juncta cum æterno immutabilis Voluntatis consilio, atque absoluta infallibilis Præscientiæ certitudine, unicum omnis sanioris Theologiæ palladium: quo salvo, salva demum sua existit primæ causæ independens activitas, atque intemerata sua primo motori potestas atque gloria.
units.tr: and at last they rest or operate according to circumstance. This difference between that power of God and ours must be carefully noted, so that we may rightly learn that whatever we sometimes think of God in a human way is to be attributed to him only in a manner worthy of God. Meanwhile the divine virtue must be acknowledged not only as most simple but above all as independent, so that no motive reason by which it might be externally stirred to act, nor any necessity of instrumental causes in producing effects, can claim any place here. It would be superfluous to establish this here, since we have already shown at length before that nothing should be called divine which is not independent in every way. And since it has likewise been demonstrated that independence and infinity are inseparably connected, the divine virtue must be esteemed no less infinite than independent. Infinite in every respect, certainly, whether you regard its perfection in itself as inexhaustible, or its unsearchable manner of operating, or the immense range of things that can be produced. This very visible creation bears witness to it, manifesting from the founding of the world the eternal Divinity as well as the Power of its Creator, as the Teacher of the Gentiles has shown elsewhere. Since these things are so, no resistance can be devised that could place an obstacle, cause any delay, or present any difficulty to God when he wishes to exercise the infinity of independent virtue in which he excels. And this irresistibility of the divine victorious power, joined with the eternal counsel of an unchangeable will and the absolute certainty of infallible foreknowledge, is the one bulwark of all sounder theology. With it safe, the independent activity of the first cause stands safe, and so too its unimpaired power and glory as first mover.

units.la: Quandoquidem verò talis est Divina Potentia, qualem jam delineavimus, per se liquidissimum est, haud alteri cuicunque eam esse communicabilem. Non enim illa quæ Dei est communicata dici potest, nisi communicata fit & simplicissima, & independens, & infinita, & denique ea cujus unica radix est inexhausta Omnisufficientiæ plenitudo. Talia creaturæ transscribere quis potest, qui non prorsus confundere velit, illius cum ea quæ Dei est, notionem? Imò, neque finitum subjectum infinitæ virtutis capax est, nec infinita virtus ab infinita natura separabilis esse potest. Ut mirum profecto sit, chimaericum istiusmodi conceptum etiam Doctoribus quibusdam Christianis in mentem venire potuisse. Quae isti objiciunt de mystica duarum naturarum in Domino Jesu unione, deque ea, quam inde fluere opinantur, idiomatum communicatione reali à natura ad naturam, cum fori Theologici sint, praeterea. Verbo expedienda difficultas alia, oriunda ex operibus sphaeram finitae activitatis longissime excedentibus, quae tamen etiam creaturas quasdam produxisse credimus, historiae Sacrae divinâ fide persuasi. Sed notandum, illam miraculorum stricte dictorum patrationem ad virtutem propriam causarum secundarum, earundemque efficientiam realem referendam minime esse; sed omnem, quae in effecti miraculosi productione exeritur physica activitas, esse unius Dei: quippe qui solus, tanquam naturae universae auctor & dominus supremus, hujus legibus non adstringitur; atque ideo de eisdem ex plenitudine potestatis pro arbitrio dispensare potest. Id illius nequaquam esse, quod tanquam creatum naturae legibus subest, res ipsa loquitur. Et tamen, fateor, hominibus quibusdam miracula istiusmodi passim tribuuntur. Neque sine causa. Cooperati scilicet sunt ii circa miraculi patrationem moralem saltem quandam causalitatem exercendo, subjectum ad ejus fidem disponendo, divinas promissiones applicando, complementum earum Deum flagitando, symbolo quopiam prodigia obsignando, similibusque aliis operandi modis, quibus, si proprie loqui volerimus, miraculi patratio vestitur potius, quam ipso facto causatur. Ut nihil hic comparet, quod, quatenus ad creaturam pertinet, non sit finitae potentiae, quodve quicquam detrahat eis, quae pro vindicanda soli Deo Omnipotentiae gloria adduximus.
units.tr: Since, however, the divine power is such as we have now outlined, it is perfectly clear in itself that it cannot be communicated to any other being whatever. For that cannot be said to be communicated which is of God, unless what is communicated is both most simple, and independent, and infinite, and finally that whose sole root is the inexhaustible fullness of all-sufficiency. Who can transfer such attributes to a creature without wanting utterly to confuse the notion of what is of God with that of the creature? Indeed, a finite subject is not capable of infinite virtue, nor can infinite virtue be separated from an infinite nature. So it is indeed strange that such a monstrous conception could have come into the minds of certain Christian teachers. What they object concerning the mystical union of the two natures in the Lord Jesus, and the real communication of properties from nature to nature which they think flows from it, belongs in any case to the theological forum. Another difficulty must be briefly dealt with, arising from works that far exceed the sphere of finite activity, though we believe that God did produce some such works, persuaded by the divine faith of sacred history. But it should be noted that the performance of miracles, strictly so called, is by no means to be referred to the proper virtue of secondary causes or to their real efficiency; rather, all the physical activity that is exerted in producing a miraculous effect belongs to God alone. For he alone, as author and supreme lord of all nature, is not bound by its laws, and so can dispense with them at will from the fullness of his power. That this belongs to no creature, which is subject to the laws of nature as created, the thing itself makes plain. Yet, I admit, such miracles are often ascribed to certain men. And not without cause. Those men, of course, co-operated in the moral performance of the miracle, exercising at least some kind of causality: by disposing the subject to faith in it, by applying divine promises, by asking God to fulfil them, by sealing the prodigies with some sign, and by similar modes of acting, by which the performance of a miracle is, strictly speaking, clothed rather than actually caused. So nothing appears here that, insofar as it pertains to a creature, is not within finite power, nor anything that takes away from what we have adduced to vindicate the glory of Omnipotence for God alone.
VI.

units.la: Nunc, quaenam ista sint quae infinitâ suâ Virtute possit Deus? ordine nobis expendendum venit. Innuebam id jam ab initio, quando ajebam, per Potentiam Deo promptissimum esse extra se ponere, quaecunque perfectissimae rationi haud repugnant. Scilicet, ea duntaxat divinae Potentiae objiciuntur, quae extra Deum existere apta sunt: ut circa semetipsum aut proprias suas perfectiones potentiae suae exercitio actuosum Numen concipi nequaquam debeat. Etenim, quandoquidem omnis vis activa cogitanda necessariò est tanquam causalitas quæpiam, omnisque causa causato suo naturâ existit prior, quis non videt, rationi planè adversum esse, siquis statuat entis alicujus attributum, qualis est Potentia, ipsius sui subjecti essentiam vel procreare posse vel conservare ? Ut liqueat, quam hac parte clarè & distinctè philosophetur Cartesius, quando nihil dubitat, Dei Potentiam tam exsuperantem agnoscere, ut planè sit causa cur ille esse perseveret; quia videlicet, in quo tantum est potentia, ut rem extra se positam conservet, omnino tanto magis se ipsum sua propria potentia conservat. Profectò, vel absona ista nimium vox est, vel absurdissima assertio ! Verùm de hisce etiam actum nobis retrò, Exercit. iv. §. ii. Tantum ergò objecta extra Deum respicit de qua agimus Potentia. Sed quæ illa ? Dixi, quæcunque rationi perfectissimæ haud repugnant; sive, quorum ideam Deus in sua mente gerit; qualia sunt absolutè omnia omninò quæ concipi queunt citra contradictionem, seu mutuam prædicatorum essentialium repugnantiam. Quæ enim usquè adeò incompatibilia sunt prædicata, ut intellectui ne quidem repræsentari possint, istæc omnia à Potentia divina secludimus, ob ipsam ejus perfectionem. Ob ipsam, inquam, divinæ virtutis perfectionem: quippe quæ non finit eam cogitare ad instar bruti impetûs; quo pacto tamen concipienda foret, si quod intelligere nequit producere posset Deus. Ut nefas sit primæ rationi tribuere Virtutem, quæ citra prævium intellectûs actum, quicquam quod non mente conceperit, formare queat. Atque hic iterum ad partes vocandus foret Cartefius; ex cujus mente, liquet, Deum non potuisse determinari ad faciendum, ut verum foret, quod contradictoria nequeant esse simul; ac proinde, potuisse illum statuere contrarium. Verùm, quam sit absurdum hoc Weigelianæ sapientiæ mysterium, nunc non ostendam, qui jam dudum plurimis instantiis urgentissimis id præstiti Exercitat. peculiari, quâ expendebam, An Deus possit contradictoria? In illo labore brevitatis causa in præsens acquiesco.
units.tr: Now we must consider in order what things God can do by his infinite power. I hinted at this from the beginning, when I said that God is most readily able, by his power, to set outside himself whatever does not contradict the most perfect reason. That is, only those things are subject to the divine power which are fit to exist outside God, so that the active Deity should by no means be conceived as acting upon himself or upon his own perfections by the exercise of his power. For since every active power must necessarily be thought of as some kind of causality, and every cause is by nature prior to its effect, who does not see that it is plainly contrary to reason to hold that an attribute of a being, such as power, could produce or preserve the essence of its own subject? It is clear how clearly and distinctly Descartes philosophizes on this point when he does not hesitate to acknowledge God's power to be so surpassing that it is plainly the cause of God's persisting in being; for, he says, in whom there is so much power that he preserves a thing placed outside himself, he much more completely preserves himself by his own power. Truly, this is either too absurd an expression or an utterly absurd assertion! But I have dealt with these matters before, in Exercit. iv, §. ii. So the power we are discussing regards only objects outside God. But what are these? I said: whatever does not contradict the most perfect reason, or whose idea God holds in his own mind. Such are absolutely all things that can be conceived without contradiction, that is, without the mutual repugnance of essential predicates. For those predicates which are so incompatible that they cannot even be represented to the intellect, all these we exclude from divine power, on account of its very perfection. On account of the perfection of the divine virtue, I say: for it does not allow us to think of it as a brute impulse; yet it would have to be conceived in that way if God could produce what he cannot understand. So it is impious to attribute to the first reason a power that could form, without a prior act of the intellect, anything it has not conceived in mind. And here Descartes must again be called to account, for from his mind, it is clear that God could not have been determined to make it so that what contradictories cannot both be true would be true; and therefore he could have decreed the contrary. But how absurd this mystery of Weigelian wisdom is I shall not now show, since I have already done so long ago, with very urgent instances, in a separate exercise in which I examined Whether God can do contradictories? In that work, for the sake of brevity, I rest content for the present.

units.la: Ex dictis concludere licet, quid statuendum sit de rerum possibilitate, ejusque Radice seu fundamento; de quibus tot difficiles nugas tradunt Scholastici Doctores. Ipsa videlicet rei possibilitas per se spectata aliud nihil notat, quam puram putam dedenominationem, desumptam à potentia causæ, cujus efficien- tiâ id quod possibile dicitur aptum est transfire à non-esse ad esse. Quæ denominatio cum à parte rei possibilis nihil reale sit, sed meram tantum dicat relationem, rectè ratiocinari hoc loco vi-dentur, qui possibilia quamdiu non exi&tunt non-entibus annu-merant; planè ad instar rerum futurarum, quæ quamdiu & in quantum merè futuræ sunt, nihil reale continent, sed de-nominationem duntaxat à divinæ voluntatis decreto derivandam. Quapropter frustrà entitas quæpiam fingitur nominalis, quæ rebus possibilibus æquè ac exi&tentibus sit communis; frustrà ab essentia existentia distinguitur, ut illa etiam possibilibus, hæc eis solummodò quæ extra causas posita sunt, convenire dicatur; frustrà, ut verbo absolvam, tam immensâ inutililium notionum hùc pertinentium multitudine nimiùm oneratur, ac bonam partem sterilis atque fœda redditur pars Philosophiæ nobilissima, omniumque facilè princeps, Metaphysica.
units.tr: From what has been said we may conclude what must be held about possibility and its root or foundation, concerning which the Scholastic doctors deliver so many difficult trifles. Possibility itself, considered in itself, signifies nothing other than a pure extrinsic denomination, derived from the power of a cause by whose efficiency that which is called possible is apt to pass from non-being to being. Since this denomination is nothing real on the side of the possible thing, but signifies merely a relation, those seem to reason rightly here who count possibles among non-beings as long as they do not exist; just as with future things, which, as long as and insofar as they are merely future, contain nothing real but have a denomination to be derived solely from the decree of the divine will. Therefore it is in vain that some nominal entity is invented, common to possible things as well as to existing ones; in vain is it distinguished from essence, so that existence is said to belong to possibles as well, while essence belongs only to those things placed outside their causes; in vain, to put it briefly, is that most noble part of philosophy, and easily the prince of all, Metaphysics, burdened with such an immense multitude of useless notions pertaining to this matter, and made in good part barren and foul.

units.la: Clarum est ex allatis, ut ad rem redeam, proximum omnis possibilitatis fundamentum esse causæ primæ atque universalis Potentiam activam: ut ideò quid sit habendum possibile, quia id Deus suâ potentiâ producere potest. Verùm, an hìc prorsus subsistendum sit, num verò aliqua ratio prior reddi queat, cur hoc Deus possit, illud non possit? nova quæstio est. Nos sanè ex iis quæ jam de Dei potentia disseruimus clarè omninò arbitra-mur, reddi posse ac debere. Est nimirum Idea in mente divina rerum producibilium principium dirigens, Potentia exequens: consequenter, quemadmodum, saltem pro modo concipiendi, in causa rationali ordine naturæ prius est rem concipere, quam producere, itâ quoque prius erit rem concipi posse, quam pro-duci posse. Si itaque quæras, quid pro primo, sive ultimo, ut appellare lubet, possibilitatis fundamento sit habendum, respondemus, id esse Intellectum divinum, quatenus is horum aut illorum prædicatorum est repræsentativus. Ut si accuratè philosophari cupiamus, dicendum sit, rem quampiam esse possibilem, quia Deus eam potest producere; posse autem Deum eam producere, quia in ejusdem idea in divina mente nulla involvitur con-tradictio. Atque hoc sensu possibilitatem hanc, quam vocant intrinsecam, illà, quæ extrinseca dicitur, priorem esse, apertum est. Solet fermè hoc loco de his atque istis singularibus rebus disquiri, num eas posse dicendus sit Deus, nec ne? Verum quum major harum quæstionum pars parùm utilis sit, saltem plus justo curiosa, nos secundum ea quæ jam demonstrata sunt, tutissimum habemus, unam duntaxat regulam hanc generalem probè observasse: Quæcunque contradictionem non involvere certò constat, ea Deum posse, docet ejus Sufficientia; quæ eam involvere omninò certum est, ea non posse Deum, docet ejusdem Sapientia; de quibus non clarè liquet, temerarium est atque profanum in alterutram partem definire. Nominatim, de ultimo possibili, num id à Deo produci ipso facto possit? disputant. In controverso sensu negandum videtur. Certè, quotcunque & quantascunque res creatas Deus unquam produxerit, eas omnes suâ naturâ finitas semper esse, necessum est. Ab altera parte, tanta Dei est Potentia, quanta ejus existit perfectio, id est, infinita. Quumque finiti ad infinitum nulla sit proportio, concludendum restat, nunquam perfectionum creatarum amplitudinem existere posse tantam, quæ re ipsâ adæquata sit immensæ virtuti Divinæ, sicque hujus plenitudinem exhauriat.
units.tr: It is clear from what has been said, to return to the matter, that the nearest foundation of all possibility is the active power of the first and universal cause, so that whatever is to be held possible is possible because God can produce it by his power. But whether we must stop here entirely, or whether some prior reason can be given why God can do this and cannot do that, is a new question. We for our part, from what we have already argued about the power of God, think it can and must be clearly given. There is indeed in the divine mind the idea of producible things, as the directing principle, and the power as the executing principle. Consequently, just as in a rational cause, at least in our mode of conceiving, it is prior in the order of nature to conceive a thing than to produce it, so also it will be prior for a thing to be conceivable than to be producible. If therefore you ask what must be held as the first, or last, as one may prefer to call it, foundation of possibility, we answer that it is the divine intellect, insofar as it is representative of this or that predicate. So, if we wish to philosophize accurately, it must be said that a thing is possible because God can produce it, and God can produce it because no contradiction is involved in his idea of it in the divine mind. And in this sense it is evident that the so-called intrinsic possibility is prior to that which is called extrinsic. Usually at this point one inquires about these and those particular things, whether God can be said to be able to do them or not. But since the greater part of these questions is of little use, and at least more curious than is right, we have, according to what has now been demonstrated, the safest course of carefully observing this one general rule: whatever it is certain does not involve a contradiction, that God can do, as his sufficiency teaches; whatever it is entirely certain does involve one, that God cannot do, as his wisdom teaches; but concerning those things which are not clearly settled, it is rash and profane to define in either direction. Specifically, they dispute about the last possible, whether God can actually produce it. In the controverted sense it seems to be denied. Certainly, however many and however great created things God has ever produced, it is necessary that they should all be finite by their nature. On the other hand, the power of God is as great as his perfection, that is, infinite. And since there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite, it remains to conclude that the magnitude of created perfections can never be so great as to be really equal to the immense divine virtue, and so exhaust its fullness.

units.la: Cæterùm, quo rectius percipiatur, quem ad modum eadem res Deo quandoque possibilis pariter atque impossibilis dici queat, notanda venit Potentiæ divinæ distinctio vulgaris, quâ in Absolutam & Ordinatam dispescitur. Illa meram Dei Sufficientiam significat, quatenus ejus vi existere potest id omne quodcunque in primæ causæ intellectu non involvit contradictionem; nullamque ea relationem ad decretum connotat, quandoquidem pro modo concipiendi actum voluntatis decernentis antecedit, dum ei suum objectum, puta merè possibilia, subsisternit. Hæc notat Sufficientiam Divinam, quatenus per eam re ipsâ aliquando sunt ponenda quæ æterno decreto ad existentiæ statum determinata sunt; sive notat virtutis divinæ determinationem, ad illa certa possibilium genera actuanda, quæ liberrimo voluntatis placito à se facienda fore Deus ordinavit. Ex quo apparet, plurima nunc ipso facto Deo esse impossibilia, ex hypothesi scilicet immutabilis decreti & infallibilis præscientiæ, imò etiam prædictionis nonnunquam, quæ eadem, si meram NumiNuminis Potentiam spectes, secundum se possibilia dici debent. Parco exemplis, etiam in Sacris obviis. Non nescio, hanc Potentiae divisionem improbari hodie quibusdam, qui mallent omne possibilitatis negotium ita in solidum ad Dei Voluntatem referre, ut illius solius determinationi tribuendum foret, quod haec vel ista res possibilis sit, alia non item. Verum nos, uti voluntatem complacentiae minime hinc secludimus, sic opinamur, in concipiendis possibilibus tanquam talibus nullas Decreto partes esse, sed solius Intellectus ac Potentiae divinae considerationem sufficere. Cum ipsa namque perfectione causae primae, a se intellecta tanquam quomodocunque expressibili extra se, possibilia immediate cohaerent. Quumque istam perfectionem suam Ens primum non possideat aut intelligat vi decreti, etiam possibilia vi decreti non sunt facta talia. Sed jam §. 11. inter alia allata sunt plurima, quae huc transferre, ad distinctionis hujus tum utilitatem tum necessitatem confirmandam, vel leviter attendenti fuerit facillimum.
units.tr: Furthermore, so that it may be understood more correctly how the same thing can at one time be called both possible and impossible to God, the common distinction of the divine power is to be noted, by which it is divided into absolute and ordained. The former signifies the mere sufficiency of God, insofar as by its force whatever does not involve a contradiction in the intellect of the first cause can exist; and it connotes no relation to a decree, since in our manner of conceiving it precedes the act of the decreeing will, while its object, namely merely possible things, subsists. The latter signifies the divine sufficiency insofar as through it those things are really to be posited at some time which have been determined by an eternal decree to the state of existence; or it signifies the determination of the divine virtue to actualize those certain kinds of possibles which God has ordained to be brought about by the most free pleasure of his will. From this it appears that many things are now, by the very fact, impossible to God, on the hypothesis, namely, of his immutable decree and infallible foreknowledge, and sometimes even of prediction, which same things, if you regard only the mere power of the Deity, ought to be called possible in themselves. I spare examples, even though they are common in the Sacred Writings. I am not unaware that this division of power is disapproved today by some, who would prefer to refer the whole business of possibility so entirely to the will of God that it would be attributed to his determination alone that this or that thing is possible and another is not. But we, while not excluding from this the will of complacency, think that in conceiving possibles as such there is no part for the decree, but that the consideration of the divine intellect and power alone is sufficient. For possible things cohere immediately with the very perfection of the first cause, as understood by itself as expressible in some way outside itself. And since the First Being does not possess this perfection, or understand it, by virtue of a decree, possible things also are not made such by virtue of a decree. But many other things have already been adduced in §. 11, which it would be very easy for one who attends even slightly to transfer here, to confirm both the usefulness and the necessity of this distinction.

units.la: EXERCITATIO VIGESIMA-SECUNDA, DE DEI MAJESTATE ET BEATITUDINE.
units.tr: EXERCITATION TWENTY-SECOND, ON THE MAJESTY AND BLESSEDNESS OF GOD.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Majestas Dei conspicua in absoluto & independenti Ejus in quaevis Dominio. II. Dominium Dei concipiendum non nisi sanctissimum; & in sola Ejus per-
units.tr: I. The majesty of God is seen in His absolute and independent dominion over all things. II. The dominion of God is to be conceived only as most holy, and founded solely in His per-

units.la: perfectione fundatum. III. Dominium Dei Morale per Legislationem, ejusdemque Executionem. IV. Non omnem Legem nobis Moralem fluere ex ipsa Dei natura. V. Majestatem Dei non rite æstimari nisi humillimo venerationis affectu. VI. Beatitudo Dei tanta quanta in Eo perfectionis plenitudo.
units.tr: fection alone. III. God's moral dominion rests on legislation and on the execution of that legislation. IV. Not every law that is moral for us flows from the very nature of God. V. The majesty of God is not rightly esteemed except with the most humble affection of reverence. VI. The blessedness of God is as great as the fullness of perfection in Him.

units.la: Uum ergò non quantæ sunt vires Divinæ Omnipotentiæ tanta sit ejusdem efficientia, verùm infinita possibilium multitudo in abyssô perfectionis primæ causæ sit relicta, atque illa ipsa quæ ex ea educuntur ratione attributorum & circumstantiarum existere possent modis longè diversis ab eis quibus nunc actu existunt, de tanti selectûs origine merito cogitatur. Et quam illam dabimus aliam, præter absolutissimam Numinis Potestatem? ad quam idcirco nonnihil nobis hic subsistendum est. Per eam intelligimus, supremum jus disponendi de rebus quibuscunque tanquam suis pro liberrimo voluntatis divinæ placito. Cujus Dominii independentia quandoquidem legis omnis ab alio præscriptæ prorsus est impatiens, ipsumque corusçat stupendâ incomprehensibilis Gloriæ effulgentiâ, Potestas hæc Dei, sumtâ voce in sensu plenissimo ac maximè emphatico, Majestas rectissimè nuncupatur. Eam Deo convenire, tam evidens est, ut vix sit operæ pretium de eo disquirere. Deum solum independentem esse, jam olim demonstravimus. Tantum ergò cætera omnia habent dependentiæ à Numine, quantum habent perfectionis; atque ideo totum quod sunt Dei sui sunt. Notissimum verò, unicuique in rem suam competere jus ac potestatem de ea faciendi quod lubet. Unde nec enti perfectissimo hæc prærogativa est deneganda. Ex quo simul facilè colligitur, infinitum esse hoc Dei Dominium. Sic postulat infinita Dei perfectio, sic dependens creaturarum natura, quæ non finit quicquam earum subduci arbitrio illius, cujus merâ munificentiâ sunt id omne quod sunt.
units.tr: Since, therefore, the extent of divine omnipotence is not matched by its exercise, but the infinite multitude of possibles has been left within the abyss of the first cause's perfection, and since those same things that could be drawn out of it, given its attributes and circumstances, could exist in ways far different from those in which they now actually exist, we rightly consider the origin of so great a selection. And what shall we call this other than the Power of the Deity in its most absolute sense? On this we must dwell here for a while. By it we mean the supreme right to dispose of all things as one's own, according to the most free pleasure of the divine will. Since the independence of this dominion cannot bear any law prescribed by another, and since it shines with the stupendous brightness of an incomprehensible glory, this power of God, taking the word in its fullest and most emphatic sense, is most rightly called Majesty. That this belongs to God is so evident that it is hardly worth inquiring into. We have already shown that God alone is independent. Therefore all other things depend on the Deity exactly as far as they have perfection, and so whatever they are, they are God's. It is well known that each person has the right and power to do as he likes with his own property, so this prerogative must not be denied to the most perfect Being. From this it is easily gathered that this dominion of God is infinite. The infinite perfection of God demands it, and so does the dependent nature of creatures, which does not allow any of them to be withdrawn from the will of Him by whose sheer bounty they are all that they are.

units.la: Fateor, non ad istos actus extendenda Numinis Potestas, quibus ipsum suæ Sanctitati, aliisve perfectionibus, adversaretur. Non tamen ideò infinitè perfecta esse definit. Utì enim perfectioni alicui adversari maxima imperfectio est, itâ id demum habendum omni modo perfectum, quod suâ naturâ nulli perfectioni repugnare potest. Ex quo sequitur, quum primi entis Sanctitas & Potestas pari passu ambulent, etiam Potentiam ejus & Potestatem æquè latè patere; ut quantæ sunt in Deo vires tantum sit jus, & quantum vicissim jus ejus tantæ pariter vires. Atque hoc Divinæ Potestatis fastigium est, quòd illi & quod lubet liceat, & quod licet possit. Subsidet longè infra eam quicquid est sic dictæ in hominibus Majestatis, quæ viribus quandoque utitur ultra jus, & sic in tyrannidem abit; vel jus suum paribus viribus nequit exsequi, atque ita contempta vilescit. In Deo uno conspirant παντοκρατορία καὶ πᾶσα ἐξουσία, Omni-potentia & Omni-potestas. Nec jam longè quærendum erit Potestatis hujus fundamentum. Certè, ea infinita & indepéndens jam demonstrata est, atque ideo nihil adscititium pro basi sua agnoscit. Sola est infinita & independens Dei perfectio, quæ infinitum & independens Dominium fundare apta est. Quid? quod sua Deo competat Potestas in ipsa possibilia; in quibus uti nihil reale est, ita nihil invenire datur, unde Deo in ea nascastur jus. Res ipsa loquitur, quando experientia dictat, non omnia fieri, quæ fieri possunt. Unde? Nisi quod sic suo jure de eis disponat causa prima, in cujus virtute ea continentur. Non ergò satis attendunt sublimem illum titulum, quo Deus rerum omnium Dominus est, qui hic confugiunt ad Dei beneficium, vel creaturæ maleficium, vel aliud quodcunque quod Deus ipse non est. Quasi modis quibusdam acquirendi, utì nos, indigeret Numen, ad vindicandum sibi in rem quampiam Dominium!
units.tr: I grant that the power of the Deity does not extend to those acts by which it would be opposed to His holiness or to His other perfections. Yet this does not make Him infinitely perfect by definition. Just as to be opposed to some perfection is the greatest imperfection, so that alone is to be held perfect in every way which by its nature cannot be contrary to any perfection. It follows that, since the holiness and the power of the first Being go hand in hand, His potency and His authority also extend equally far: as great as the powers in God are, so great is His right, and conversely, as great as His right is, so equally great are His powers. And this is the summit of divine power: that what He wishes is permitted to Him, and what is permitted He is able to do. Far below it lies whatever is called majesty among men, which sometimes uses its power beyond its right and so passes into tyranny, or cannot carry out its right with equal power and so becomes contemptible. In God alone there come together παντοκρατορία καὶ πᾶσα ἐξουσία, omnipotence and omni-authority. Nor do we need to look far for the foundation of this power. Certainly it has already been shown to be infinite and independent, and so it acknowledges nothing adventitious as its basis. The infinite and independent perfection of God alone is fit to found an infinite and independent dominion. What then of the fact that God has power over the possibles themselves? In these there is nothing real, so nothing can be found from which a right over them could arise for God. The matter itself speaks: experience tells us that not everything that can be done is done. Why so? Only because the first cause, in whose power they are contained, disposes of them by its own right. Those, therefore, who take refuge here in God's beneficence, or in the creature's wrongdoing, or in anything else that God Himself is not, do not sufficiently attend to that sublime title by which God is Lord of all things. As if God, like us, needed some means of acquiring in order to claim dominion over some thing!

units.la: Præter generale hoc Proprietatis Dominium, quo Deus de quibusvis rebus statuit pro arbitratu, eas conservando, vastando, donando, &c. speciaḷioris considerationis est Dominium Jurisdictionis strictè dictæ, cujus territorium quasi est universa creaturarum rationalium multitudo. Nimirum, quantum quid habet à primo ente dependentiæ, tantum in id juris habet
units.tr: Besides this general dominion of property, by which God decides about all things at His pleasure, preserving, destroying, giving and so on, there is a more particular dominion, strictly called jurisdiction, whose territory is, as it were, the whole multitude of rational creatures. Namely, whatever has dependence on the first Being, to that extent God has right over it.

units.la: Y habet Deus. Quamobrem necesse est, Deo esse peculiare quoddam Dominium in creaturarum rationalium rationalitatem ipsam, ejusque exercitium; quod ipsum tanquam tale ad res alias ratione carentes extendi nequit. Involvit hoc Potestatem significandi rebus rationalibus tanquam subditis moralem suam dependentiam à Numine, atque ad eam agnoscendam obligationem omnimodam. Quod cum sine Lege fieri non possit, utique jus habet Deus ferendi leges, quas regulas esse velit obedientiæ sibi præstandæ à subjecto, uti moralis dependentiæ, itâ præcepti, capace. Ex quo Jus aliud sequitur, sanciendi nempe legem pœnali comminatione; quatenus absque ea potestas legislatoria vim obligatoriam vix satis efficaciter exerit; cum citra ipsam penes rebellem subditum stet sese impune istâ suâ erga superiorem obligatione eximere. Undè porro fluit jus infligendi pœnas propter demeritum violatæ legis, secundùm sanctionem pœnalem. Per quæ omnia apparet, concipi non posse rationalem creaturam, in quam Deo non competat plenissima Potestas tum legislatoria, tum legis executoria. Quam quomodo Deus, tanquam Rex pariter & Judex, ipso facto circa hominem exerceat, non hujus loci est disputare, sed ad actualis Providentiæ considerationem pertinet. Quæ speciatim Dei Potestas sit circa peccati permissionem, imputationem, punitionem, dispensationem, & quæ sexcenta istius commatis huc spectant plura, cum paucis expediri nequeant, nihil in præsentiarum de iis dicere malumus quam parum.
units.tr: And God has it. Therefore God must have a peculiar dominion over the rationality of rational creatures themselves, and over its exercise; and this dominion, as such, cannot be extended to other things that lack reason. It involves the power of signifying to rational beings, as subjects, their moral dependence on the Deity, and their complete obligation to acknowledge it. Since this cannot be done without a law, God surely has the right to enact laws, which He wishes to be the rules of obedience to be rendered to Him by the subject, as capable of command as moral dependence is. From this another right follows, namely that of sanctioning the law with a penal threat, since without such a threat the legislative power would hardly exert its binding force effectively enough, for without it the rebellious subject could free himself from his obligation to his superior with impunity. Thence further flows the right to inflict punishment for the guilt of a violated law, according to the penal sanction. From all this it appears that no rational creature can be conceived over whom God does not have the fullest power, both legislative and executive. How God, as King and Judge alike, actually exercises this over man is not the place to discuss; that belongs to the consideration of actual Providence. What exactly God's power is concerning the permission, imputation, punishment and dispensation of sin, and the countless other matters of this kind that bear on the question, cannot be settled in a few words, so for the present we prefer to say nothing about them rather than too little.

units.la: Tantum plane præterire non possumus nobilissimam controversiam, Num Deo etiam jus sit præscribendi suis creaturis rationalibus præceptum aliquod, tanquam morale, quod tamen ex natura sua aut essentialibus perfectionibus minimè fluat? Prænoto (nequis in voce lusus fiat) id morale dici, quod homini universim naturâ notum est tanquam regula morum. Nescio, quomodo affirmativa videri possit quibusdam dubia, quin falsa. Saltem Deum legem ferre posse homini, quæ non fluat ex sua natura, indubium est. Quid si tulerit circa res de quibus hodiè lege nihil est definitum? Quid si omnes eâ obligatos velit? Quid si tanquam naturæ auctor conscientiis hominum eam inscripserit? Non posse, undè demonstrabitur? Imò verò vero imprimis ad declarandam Divinæ Majestatis excellentiam, & plenissimi in hominem juris demonstrationem pertinere videtur, quòd præceptis etiam positivis, sive officiis, quæ non aliter bona sunt nisi propter arbitrariam Dei jussionem, creaturam rationalem adstringere possit. Specimen luculentum exhibet in ipso integritatis statu (si ex fide Christiana id huc adferre licuerit nobis Philosophis) mandatum circa arborem scientiæ boni & mali. Quin & hodiè præcepta de Incestu, Polygamia, Furto, ut plura sileam, quæ nobis juris naturalis & moralis sunt, esse re verâ juris divini positivi atque liberrimi, luce meridianâ clarius videtur. Saltem rationes audire lubet, quibus conficiatur, ista omnia mandata necessariò fluere ex perfectissima Dei natura. De quibusdam tamen aliis posterius verè dici, largimur. Displicet idcirco vehementer illa in oppositum plane abiens quorundam sententia, quæ tam amplam concipit Dei potestatem, ut omnium quæ præcepit contrarium præscribere, si voluisset, potuisse contendat. Medium tenere suadet ratio.
units.tr: We cannot pass over altogether the most noble controversy: whether God also has the right to prescribe to His rational creatures some precept as moral, which nevertheless does not flow from His nature or from His essential perfections. Let it first be stated (lest any play be made on the word) that what is called moral is what is known to man in general by nature as a rule of conduct. I do not see how the affirmative can seem doubtful to some rather than false. At least it is certain that God can give man a law that does not flow from his nature. What if He has enacted something about matters on which no law has yet been laid down? What if He wishes all men to be bound by it? What if, as author of nature, He has written it on the consciences of men? Who will prove that He cannot? Indeed, it seems to pertain above all to declaring the excellence of the divine majesty and to demonstrating the full right He has over man, that He can bind a rational creature even by positive precepts, or duties, which are good only on account of God's arbitrary command. A striking example is shown in the very state of integrity (if we philosophers may bring this in from the Christian faith), in the command concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Indeed, even today the precepts against incest, polygamy and theft, to say nothing of many others that are for us matters of natural and moral law, clearly appear, more plainly than noonday light, to be in truth of divine, positive and most free law. At least we are willing to hear the reasons by which it is proved that all these commands necessarily flow from the most perfect nature of God. Yet we grant that some other precepts may truly be said to be of this later kind. Therefore that opinion of some, which goes completely the other way and conceives God's power so broadly as to maintain that, had He wished, He could have prescribed the contrary of everything He has commanded, greatly displeases us. Reason advises us to take the middle course.

units.la: Sed desino scrutari Majestatem; cujus arcana perve-stigare nefas eis, queis devoti obsequii gloria relicta tantum est, cum submissa humillimæ venerationis æstimatione. O! si tantæ effulgentiæ radii mentis oculos ut decet perstringerent, quam non adeò securè philosopharemur de Potestate Domini, cujus amplius est hoc ipso universo territorium! Quid, si de ea persuasi satis essemus ut oportet, superbiremus usque eò sæpè vermiculi, & non potius istius lucis fulgore contabesceremus ad instar ceræ, viribusque plane concideremus? Quid, si hæc cordi sint nobis, tanti Numinis leges sanctissimas totiès transgredimur petulanter, neque vindicem manum metuimus Judicis, cujus non minor est in exequendo suo jure Potentia, quam in ferendis legibus Potestas? Sed & quæ ista Regum hujus seculi fascinatio est, simulac aliquam in universi puncto quod inhabitamus particulam suo subjecerunt imperio, supremam nescio quam somniantium legibusque solutam potestatem? Altior profecto est istis altis; cujus gratiâ precariò tantùm imperant potentissimi terrarum domini, hujus Regis mancipia duntaxat & servi. Quid itaque illorum indignationem totiès plus justo metuimus, & non multo magis horremus violatæ Divinæ Majestatis crimen? Venerabiles etiam sunt summo jure Magistratus, in quibus aliquam suæ Majestatis relucere voluit Deus imaginem: sed imaginem tantum; ut discamus primo loco eum revereri cujus delegatâ auctoritate ipsi imperant, cujusque sceptrum cœlestes etiam venerantur potestates. Denique, quid passim de Providentia primæ causæ fumus queruli; cujus gloriæ servire bonum majus est, quam totius mundi tenere imperium. Intendat tantum mens debitis tanto Domino obsequiis: critque hæc via brevissima ad obtinendam veram ac imperturbabilem animi tranquillitatem; dum tutelam in omni fortuna certissimam promittit fideli subdito amica cum immensæ Potentiæ pariter ac Potestatis Monarcha, societas. Cavcamus ante omnia religiosè, ne fœdissimo sacrilegio quid nostrum unquam fingamus, perquod quicquam limitetur summa Majestas; cujus sese ubique tanta prodit effulgentia, ut ipsa ratio dictet abundè, probandam esse ceu optimam præ aliis Religionem, cujus prima ac præcipua cura est, suam Divino Numini per omnia semper & ubique afferere supremam Legibusque solutam potestatem.
units.tr: But I will stop searching into the Majesty, whose hidden things it is wrong for anyone to investigate, since to them is left only the glory of devoted obedience, together with a humble and submissive esteem of reverence. O! If the rays of so great a brightness struck the eyes of the mind as they ought, we would not philosophize so carelessly about the power of the Lord, whose territory is more than this whole universe! What if we were persuaded of Him as we ought to be? Would we so often, as mere worms, swell with pride, instead of melting like wax in the brightness of that light and utterly losing our strength? What if this truly mattered to us? Would we so wantonly break again and again the most holy laws of so great a Divinity, and not fear the avenging hand of the Judge, whose power to execute His right is no less than His authority to enact laws? And what is this bewitchment of the kings of this age, as soon as they bring under their rule some small part of the point of the universe that we inhabit, dreaming of I know not what supreme power loosed from all laws? Surely He is higher than the highest, and for His sake the most powerful lords of the earth rule only on loan; they are merely the bondsmen and slaves of this King. Why then do we so often fear their anger more than is right, and not much more dread the crime of violating the Divine Majesty? Magistrates too, in whom God willed some image of His Majesty to shine forth, are rightly to be honoured with the highest right; but it is only an image, so that we may learn first of all to revere Him by whose delegated authority they govern, and whose sceptre even the heavenly powers worship. Finally, why do we everywhere complain so fretfully about the providence of the First Cause? It is a greater good to serve His glory than to hold dominion over the whole world. Let the mind only apply to so great a Lord the obedience He is due: this will be the shortest way to obtain a true and unshakeable tranquillity of soul, since the Monarch of immense power and authority, joined in friendship with the faithful subject, promises the most certain protection in every fortune. Above all let us take care, with religious caution, that we never devise, in the most foul sacrilege, anything by which the supreme Majesty might be limited; its brightness shows itself everywhere so greatly that reason itself declares plainly that that religion is to be approved above others as the best, whose first and chief concern is to assert that the power of the Divine Majesty is always and everywhere supreme and loosed from all laws.

units.la: Tandem de Dei Beatitudine addam verbum; ut quę Divinorum Attributorum meditatio ab Infinitate perfectionis fecit initium, in eadem contemplatione finiatur. Est enim nihil aliud Dei Beatitas, quam ipsissima perfectionum infinitas, quatenus in ejus fruitione perfecta cum complacentia acquiescit. Ut sit in Deo quædam quasi sui ipsius tanquam boni sese satiantis, constantissima, maxima cum voluptate, absque ægritudinis ullius mixtura, fruitio. De ea demonstranda nihil laborandum. Felicitatem jam olim quis dixit statum bonorum omnium congregatione perfectum. Infinita ergò quum sit Numinis perfectio, etiam minor esse nequit ejusdem Beatitudo. Imò sese fruitur ex se ipso per se ipsum, qui per independentiam suam & simplicitatem solus ipse sibi & Beatitudo est, & beatus, & beatitudinis fruitio. Sed nimium tantæ detraherem excellentiæ, si balbutire pergerem de re, quam mens nulla assequi, lingua nulla effari, potest; cujusque idcirco anhelanda potius fruitio, quam scrutanda plenitudo: quippe quæ non nisi sensu ipso percipitur ab eis, quos ritè ad se accedentes in tanti boni communionem admittere, atque hoc ipso terque quaterque beare, dignatum aliquando fuerit benignum Numen.
units.tr: Finally, I will add a word on the Blessedness of God, so that the meditation on the Divine Attributes, which began from the Infinity of perfection, may end in the same contemplation. For the Blessedness of God is nothing other than the very infinity of perfections, insofar as in their perfect enjoyment it rests with complacency. It is thus a kind of constant and most delightful enjoyment in God of Himself, as of a good that satisfies itself, without any admixture of distress. Nothing need be laboured in proving this. Someone long ago defined happiness as the state of all good things brought together into one. Since, then, the perfection of the Deity is infinite, its blessedness cannot be less. Indeed, He enjoys Himself from Himself through Himself, who by His independence and simplicity is alone both His own blessedness and blessed, and the enjoyment of blessedness. But I would detract too much from so great an excellence if I went on stammering about a thing that no mind can grasp and no tongue express; it is therefore to be longed for in enjoyment rather than searched out in its fullness, for it is perceived only by feeling itself, by those whom the benign Deity has at some time deigned to admit, as they approach Him rightly, to communion in so great a good, and thereby to bless them thrice and four times over.

units.la: Ergò sub alarum velut umbra tecta Tuarum Mortales stauent corda quieta fide. Hic velut irrigua saturos pinguedine pascet Fortunata Tua diuitis aula penus. Plena voluptatum potos ad flumina duces, Deliciis saturent omnibus unde sitim. Tu fons ille sacer, Tu vena beata salutis, In vitam latices dans salientis aquæ. Ite igitur nigro torpentia flumina cæno! Non bibit e vili gurgite nostra sitis. Ite! Sitit superi dias mens fluminis undas, Cervus ut irrigui fontis anhelat aquas. I. Productio rerum à Deo facta non indigentiæ sed sufficientiæ argumentum. II. Creatio quid; & ad quæ sese extendat? III. Admittendæ Creationis necessitas demonstrata. IV. Difficultatibus præcipuis in hoc negotio occurrentibus obviam itur. V. Creandi vis ita solius Dei est, ut in ejus societatem nulla veniat creatura. VI. Creandi actio numquid notet à Deo diversum? VII. Productio creaturarum Deo, uti liberrima, ita facillima. VIII. Mundum ab æterno creatum fuisse, repugnat. IX. Quando tamen præcisè fuerit productus, natura non docet. X. Creationis universæ tum ordo tum modus per naturæ lumen incertus planè. XI. Cartesii in eo omni definiendo notata temeritas. XII. Cartesiana mundi Genesis Mosaicæ quam multis modis adversa. XIII. Frustrà palliata ab Auctore fictionis audacia. XIV. Mundus hic creatus, nobis quidem indefinitæ, re ipsa tamen finitæ amplitudinis. XV. Indeque majorem, imò & plures alios, creare potest Deus. XVI. Difficultatum hic moveri solitarum amotio. XVII. Finis creati mundi, ultimus Dei gloria, subordinatus homo, rectè statuitur. XVIII. Objectæ à Cartesio in oppositum rationes paucis excusse. XIX. Ex visibilibus creaturis majestatem Creatoris invisibilem venerari discit pia mens.
units.tr: Therefore under the shadow, as it were, of Your wings, mortals keep their hearts quiet in faith. Here, as if from well-watered pasture, Your fortunate and rich court shall feed them full of fatness. You will lead them, drinking, to the river full of delights, where they may satisfy their thirst with every pleasure. You are that holy fountain, You the blessed vein of salvation, giving to life the streams of leaping water. Go then, sluggish rivers, to your black mire! Our thirst does not drink from the vile whirlpool. Go! The mind thirsts for the divine waters of the river, as the hart pants for the waters of the watered spring. I. The production of things by God is a proof not of need but of sufficiency. II. What is creation, and to what does it extend? III. The necessity of admitting creation is demonstrated. IV. The chief difficulties that arise in this matter are met. V. The power to create belongs to God alone, so that no creature comes into fellowship with it. VI. Does the act of creating signify something different from God? VII. The production of creatures is by God as free as it is easy. VIII. That the world was created from eternity is contrary to reason. IX. Yet nature does not teach precisely when it was produced. X. Both the order and the manner of the whole creation are quite uncertain by the light of nature. XI. The rashness of Descartes in defining all of this is noted. XII. The Cartesian genesis of the world is opposed to the Mosaic in many ways. XIII. The audacity of the author of the fiction, though covered over, is in vain. XIV. This created world has, for us indeed, an indefinite extent, but in fact a finite one. XV. Hence God can create a greater world, indeed also many others. XVI. The removal of the difficulties usually raised here. XVII. The end of the created world, the ultimate glory of God, with man subordinate, is rightly laid down. XVIII. The reasons Descartes brings against this are briefly examined. XIX. From visible creatures a pious mind learns to venerate the invisible majesty of the Creator.

units.la: Tiamsi, ob eam quam hactenus per partes prosecuti fuimus pro modulo perfectionis infinitatem, ex se ipso per se ipsum Beatissimum existat Numen, haud tamen illi repugnat opulentiæ suæ manifestare immensitatem, extra se aliquid producendo; quo ostendat, non duntaxat sibi, sed & rebus aliis extra se, sufficere tantam plenitudinis abundantiam. Ut nimium ineptiat argutatio Epicureorum, inferentium, non posse Deum agnosci Universi auctorem, quòd sic vel frustrà, vel ex inopia consortii suæ creaturæ, id produxisse dicendus foret; quorum illud Numinis sapientia, hoc ejusdem sufficientia non patitur. Verùm, neque Deum intelligunt, neque rem à Deo diversam, qui sic philosophantur. Saltem jam dudùm, ubi de Independentia Dei egimus, probavimus, nec hujus nec illius naturam id sinere, ut quicquam existat, quod non vel ipse Deus sit, vel res à Deo dependens. Quid ergò? Rei cujuslibet productio per se arguit tantummodò, indè quidem causæ producentis sufficientiam, hinc verò rei productæ omnimodam ab ipso suo principio dependentiam. Quamobrem nihil existit efficacius ad illustrandam causæ primæ perfectionem, quam ipsa rei præ aliis excellentissimæ Creatio : planè quemadmodum non melius quanta fit Solis perfectio intelligitur, quam ex copiosissimis quos quaquaverfum ex corpore suo emittit radiis. Verbo, quodcunque operatur Deus, non id vel frustranei laboris, vel indigentis naturæ existit argumentum, sed luculentum potius exundantis bonitatis testimonium. Quæ ut percipiantur rectius, quem hactenus in fe Maximum cogitavimus Deum, nunc eundem in operibus Optimum contemplari fuerit pretium operæ. Sic autem videbimus amictum Majestate & Gloria ex adyto quasi fui prodeuntem in hoc Universum rerum omnium Creatorem, Conservatorem, Gubernatorem, potentissimum, benignissimum, sapientissimum. Atque ultimus iste erit Meditationis nostræ de Deo tractatus, ut utilissimus, itå minimè hic prætercundus ; quippe qui conferet plurimum ad amplius persuadendam certitudinem omnium, quæ huc usquè docuimus. Neque enim fieri potest, ut non vehementer in suo quem de Deo habet sensu mens nostra confirmetur, quando videt non alium Eum apparere in operibus, quam qualem debere in semet ipso existere ex Independentia jam, à priori quasi, demonstravimus.
units.tr: Although, from the infinity of perfection which we have so far pursued part by part according to our measure, the Deity exists most blessed of itself and through itself, it nonetheless does not thereby lack the power to show forth the immensity of its wealth by producing something outside itself, so that it may show that such an abundance of fullness suffices not only for itself but also for other things outside itself. The subtle argument of the Epicureans is too silly, which infers that God cannot be acknowledged as the author of the universe, because in that case He would be said to have produced it either in vain or from lack of company with His creature; the wisdom of the Deity does not allow the former, nor its sufficiency the latter. But those who philosophize in this way understand neither God nor the thing that is distinct from God. At least we have already, when we treated of the Independence of God, proved that neither His nature nor that of anything else permits anything to exist that is not either God Himself or a thing dependent on God. What then? The production of anything by itself argues only this: on one side, the sufficiency of the producing cause, and on the other, the complete dependence of the produced thing on its own principle. Therefore nothing exists more effective for illustrating the perfection of the First Cause than the creation of a thing most excellent beyond others; just as the perfection of the Sun is not better understood than from the most abundant rays it sends out from its body on every side. In a word, whatever God works is the proof not of a useless labour or of a needy nature, but rather a clear testimony of overflowing goodness. That we may perceive this more rightly, it will be worth our while to contemplate now as the Best in His works the God whom we have hitherto thought of in Himself as the Greatest. Thus we shall see the Creator, Preserver, Governor of all things, most powerful, most kind, most wise, coming forth into this universe as it were from the sanctuary of Himself, clothed in Majesty and Glory. And this will be the last treatise of our meditation on God, as the most useful, and it must not be passed over here; for it will contribute greatly to more firmly persuading us of all that we have taught so far. For it cannot be that our mind is not strongly confirmed in its sense of God, when it sees that He appears in His works as none other than He must be in Himself, which we have already demonstrated from Independence, as it were a priori.

units.la: Primum quod in qualibet re spectandum occurrit, est prima ejus positio, seu primum existentiæ momentum ; ac cui causæ & causalitati illud debeat. Idcirco etiam primo loco illa Dei actio spectanda venit, cujus vi existere ceperunt quæcunque existunt. CREATIONIS nomine ea vulgò occurrit ; sumtà voce quatenus notat, Actionem Dei transeuntem, quâ quicquid existit à fe diversum ex nihilo produxit. Transeuntem Dei actionem dico ; per fe scilicet aliquid constituentem extra Deum: quo nomine à Decreto distinguitur. Hoc rei creandæ futuritionem duntaxat ponit; illa actualem rei creatæ existentiam. Ut minus accuratè Creatio quibusdam definiatur efficax Dei voluntas : ea enim per fe extra fe nihil efficit, sed tota tantum immanens est. Verùm hac de re etiam suprà egimus, ubi de Divina Potentia differebamus. Facit autem hæc actio creaturam transire ipso facto à nihil ad aliquid ; ut quod antè non-erat jam fit, quodque prius dici poterat solum possibile, aut futurum ad summum, nunc actu verè existat. Parùm autem refert, num id de Nihilo absolutè & simpliciter sic dicto acc ipias, num etiam de nihilo illius rei quæ producitur; qualis actio est, quâ quid efficitur ex materia per se secundum ordinem & leges naturæ inhabili ad id, ut indè fiat, quod per virtutem divinam ex illa producitur. Neque enim posterior hæc, Mediata vulgò dicta, minus propriè Creatio est ac illa prior, sive Immediata; quandoquidem cjusdem virtutis est aliquid producere ex puro nihilo, ac est id conficere ex subjecto nullo modo apto, adeoque non plus quam merum nihil ad rei noviter ex se producta existentiam conferente. Cæterùm, ad illa quæ existunt à Deo diversa Creationem restringimus. Ut enim ens primum citra contradictionem concipi non potest unquam transitum fecisse à non-esse ad esse, ita nullam actionem cogitare datur, quâ vel ipsum circa se, vel aliud circa ipsum creando versetur. Restat itaque, illa solùm Creationis objecta esse, quæ tam debilis sunt entitatis, ut, nisi potentioris causæ influxus accedat, ex se nihil sint; qualia sunt contingentia quævis, quæ ob hoc ipsum possunt non-esse quod sunt, quia quod sunt aliquando non-fuerunt. Atque hùc pertinent omnia quæ existunt præter Deum, totumque adeò qua latè patet hoc Universum: solius enim Independentis Dei privilegium esse existendi necessitatem, jam dudùm ostendimus.
units.tr: The first thing to consider in any thing is its initial position, or the first moment of its existence, and to what cause and causality it owes that. So the first place to consider is that action of God by whose power all things that exist began to exist. This is commonly called CREATION, taking the word as it denotes the transient action of God by which he produced out of nothing whatever exists apart from himself. I say transient action, meaning that it establishes something outside God in its own right; by this name it is distinguished from the Decree. The Decree posits only the future existence of the thing to be created, whereas creation posits its actual existence. Some define Creation less accurately as God's effective will, for that will effects nothing outside itself and is wholly immanent. But I have already dealt with this matter above, where I discussed the Divine Power. This action makes the creature pass, by the very fact, from nothing to something, so that what did not exist before now actually exists, and what could previously be called merely possible, or at most future, now truly is. It matters little whether we take this to be out of nothing absolutely and simply so called, or out of the nothing of the thing that is produced. Such is the action by which something is effected from matter which of itself, according to the order and laws of nature, is unfit for that result, but which by divine power is produced from it. This latter, commonly called Mediate, is no less properly Creation than the former, which is called Immediate. For it belongs to the same power to produce something out of pure nothing as to make it from a subject in no way apt for it, and so the matter contributes no more than pure nothing to the existence of the thing newly produced from it. Moreover, we restrict Creation to those things that exist apart from God. For just as the first being cannot, without contradiction, be conceived ever to have passed from non-being to being, so we cannot conceive of any action by which he would be occupied either with himself or with anything else around himself through creating. It remains, then, that the objects of Creation are only those things of such feeble entity that, unless the influence of a more powerful cause is added, they are nothing of themselves. Such are all contingent things, which for that very reason can fail to be what they are, because what they now are, they once were not. To this belong all things that exist besides God, and indeed this whole universe, as far as it extends. For we have shown long ago that necessity of existence is the privilege of God alone, who is Independent.

units.la: Suppeditat autem hæc ipsa, de qua loquor, rerum nobis obviarum contingentia fundamentum pulcherrimi argumenti, pro demonstranda Creationis non tantum possibilitate, sed & (data hypothesi, existere Mundum) necessitate: in quo negotio laborarunt plurimi, sæpè minus accuratè; cum tamen certum sit, vix aliud dogma occurrere in universa Philosophia, quod plus afferat momenti, quam hoc ipsum solidè adstructum, ad Religionem Christianam confirmandam, contra Atheorum atque Epicureorum insultus. Ut verbo dicam: Nisi ex nihilo producta sint res quæ sunt, unde illud est, quod earum quælibet ad non existendum per se æquè sint indifferentes quam ad existendum? Sed juvat paulò explicatius urgere vim ratiocinii, quod imprimis efficax arbitror ad totum hoc conficiendum. Neminem ejus vires latere poterunt, quicunque revocaverit in mentem duas veritates jam ante firmissimè adstructas. Prior est, Independentiam sic unius Dei praedicatum esse, ut per naturam suam nulli alteri attribui possit. Evidens hoc postulatum est, sive ipsam in se attendas Independentiam, prout ea suo loco à nobis explicata fuit; sive infinitatem perfectionis, quam & Deo soli propriam, & cum Independentia insolubili vinculo connexam esse, jam ante ostendimus. Si itaque mundus hic noster Deus ipse non sit (quem non esse, docet absentia perfectionum hactenus de Deo demonstratarum) utique neque Independens est: quod si non independens, neque etiam Necessariò existens; per ea quae retrò Exercitat. VII. §. v. demonstravimus. Est ergò mundus ens contingens, quod ex sese haud magis existit, quam non-existit; atque ideò, hoc ipso quod existit, causam aliquam sui arguit extra se, quae faciat cum existere potius quam non-existere. Si enim aliquam extantiae suae rationem in sese contineret, ipso facto neque dependens foret, neque contingens. Existit ergò hoc universum virtute alicujus causae. Sed quomodo? Sic ut in existentia sua perseveret: atque ita quidem, ut ejus hodiè non sit heri, neque heri hodiè, neque cras alterutrum illorum. Ecce itaque durationis lapsum ex praeterito per praesens in futurum; consequenter & partes, partiumque successionem! Ea verò ubi dominantur, istic aeternitatem locum habere non posse, invictè jam Exercitat. VIII. §. v. probavimus. Atque istud alterum eorum erat, quae hoc loco praenotari cupiebam. Ex quibus pro eo quod nunc intendebam brevi collectione sic infero. Per ea quae jam allata sunt, Mundus neque fuisse ab aeterno, neque sine causa sui existere potest. Quumque quod aeternum non est, necessariò aliquando non-fuerit, manifestissimum evadit, mundum quidem aliquando non-fuisse, attamen virtute suae causae deinceps extitisse; sive, quod eodem redit, eum per potentiam efficientis transfiisse à non-esse ad esse. Atquì hoc ipsum est, productum esse per Creationem; cujus rei veritatem demonstrandam sumseramus.
units.tr: This very contingency of the things we encounter, of which I speak, supplies us with the foundation of a most excellent argument for demonstrating not only the possibility of Creation but also its necessity (granting the hypothesis that the world exists). Many have laboured at this matter, often less accurately; yet it is certain that scarcely any other doctrine in all of philosophy is of greater moment than this one, when it is soundly established, for confirming the Christian religion against the assaults of Atheists and Epicureans. To put it in a word: unless the things that exist have been produced out of nothing, how is it that each of them is by its own nature as indifferent to not existing as to existing? But it is worth pressing the force of the reasoning a little more fully, which I judge especially effective for establishing this whole matter. No one who recalls to mind two truths already firmly established earlier will fail to see its strength. The first is that Independence is a predicate of God alone, such that by its nature it cannot be attributed to any other. This postulate is evident, whether we consider Independence in itself, as we explained it in its proper place, or the infinity of perfection, which we showed earlier belongs to God alone and is joined with Independence by an indissoluble bond. If therefore this world of ours is not God himself (and the absence of the perfections hitherto demonstrated of God shows that it is not), then it is certainly not Independent either. And if it is not independent, neither is it Necessarily existing, by what we demonstrated above in Exercitation VII, §. v. Therefore the world is a contingent being, which of itself no more exists than does not exist. Hence, by the very fact that it exists, it proves some cause outside itself that makes it exist rather than not exist. For if it contained within itself some reason for its existence, it would by that very fact be neither dependent nor contingent. Therefore this universe exists by the power of some cause. But how? So that it persists in its existence; and indeed in such a way that today it is not yesterday, nor yesterday today, nor tomorrow either of those. Here, then, is the flowing of duration from past through present into future, and consequently parts and the succession of parts! Where these prevail, eternity cannot have a place, as we have already proved unassailably in Exercitation VIII, §. v. This second point was one of the things I wished to set forth in advance here. From these, with a brief summary, I now draw my conclusion for what I now intend. From what has been adduced, the world can neither have existed from eternity nor exist without a cause of itself. And since what is not eternal must at some time have not existed, it becomes most manifest that the world indeed did not exist at some time, but thereafter has existed by the power of its cause; or, which comes to the same thing, that by the power of an efficient cause it has passed from non-being to being. But this very thing is to have been produced by Creation, and it was the truth of this matter that we had undertaken to demonstrate.

units.la: Neque virbus hujus argumenti quicquam detrahet, qui ad id declinandum studuerit excipere, dici posse, genitum fortè esse hoc universum ex materia quapiam praejacente; uti inter an-
units.tr: Nor will anything be taken away from the force of this argument by someone who, in order to evade it, has tried to object that this universe may perhaps have been generated out of some pre-existing matter, as

units.la: antiquiores in Ethnicismo Philosophos plurimi opinati fuerunt: adeoque ex ante dictis non sequi ejusdem ex nihilo Creationem. Etiamsi enim lubens largiar, non mihi videri solum rationis naturalis lumen suppeditare demonstrationes, quibus plenè conficiatur, mundum hunc ex nulla praevia materia formatum esse, stat nihilominus suo talo nostra ratiocinatio. Ex quocunque enim praeexistente corpore hanc universi molem originem suam traxisse finxeris, de illo eadem facilitate eadem demonstrantur, quae jam de mundo ipso demonstravimus; scilicet, nec independens, nec aeternum id esse posse. Atque adeo, uti mundi ipsius, ita rei cujusvis alterius contingentis, ultima tandem analysis fiet (an mediatè, an immediatè, parum facit ad rem praesentem) in causam quampiam, quae eam fecerit esse, cum ante non-fuerit; id est, quae eam creaverit. Sufficiet autem ad sobrietatem sapere cupienti adstructa jam tam evidentis veritatis necessitas, tametsi intellectûs captum excedat modus ille operandi quo ex nihilo fiat aliquid. Profectò, non, si sapimus, mirum videbitur, aliquid hîc occurrere nobis inaccessum. Nempè vix claram & distinctam notionem habemus istius activitatis, quae à finita causa procedit, exeriturque secundum naturae leges jam constitutas & obvias: quanto minus comprehendemus illam, quae ipsam naturam spectat ut primum constituendam, eam sicuti antecedens ita longissimè excedens; quaeque fluit non ab ente quopiam finito legibus naturae adstricto, sed ab eo qui incomprehensibilem aeternae suae divinitatis & potentiae amplitudinem hac ipsâ actione manifestare intendit. Quare, nisi conceptus ejusdem nobis hominionibus foret inconceptibilis, neque ipsa operi tam admirabili excitando sufficiens foret, neque Deo digna, quam exindè enarrat coelorum expansum, gloria. Sit itaque impervestigabilis tanti Numinis via, dummodo nihil includat contradictionis; quam involvere hanc alicujus ex nihilo productionem, haudquaquam putandum est. Per se quidem notum videtur illud tritum, Ex nihilo nihil fit; quatenus scilicet ex nihilo, per ipsum nihilum, sive virtute ipsius nihili, nihil produci potest; nihilque adeo alicujus principium esse nequit. Verum haudquaquam illi repugnat, cum qui sufficientissimus est non sibi tantum sed & aliis à se, facere, ut ex nihilo, tanquam à termino à quo, uti loquuntur, ab ipsa potentiæ suæ infinitate, tanquam à principio, id existere incipiat, cujus antè dabatur nihil. Prorsus ut rei contingenti nunc existenti minimè adversatur, si, destituta influxu causæ cujus vi existit, existere desinat, sicque quod est aliquid fiat nihil.
units.tr: many of the more ancient philosophers among the Gentiles supposed. For even if I willingly grant that the light of natural reason does not seem to me to supply demonstrations that fully establish that this world was formed from no prior matter, our reasoning nonetheless stands firm on its own footing. For whatever pre-existing body you might feign as the origin of this vast universe, the same things are demonstrated of it with the same ease as we have already demonstrated of the world itself: namely, that it can be neither independent nor eternal. And so, just as with the world itself, so with any other contingent thing whatever, the final analysis will arrive (whether mediately or immediately makes little difference to the present point) at some cause which has made it to be, when it was not before; that is, which has created it. But for one who wishes to be sober in wisdom, the necessity of a truth so evident, once established, will suffice, even though that mode of operating by which something is made out of nothing exceeds the grasp of the intellect. Indeed, if we are wise, it will not seem strange that something here is inaccessible to us. For we scarcely have a clear and distinct notion of that activity which proceeds from a finite cause and issues forth according to the laws of nature already established and familiar. How much less shall we comprehend that which regards nature itself as something to be first constituted, and which, as it precedes nature, so far exceeds it; and which flows not from some finite being bound by the laws of nature, but from him who by this very action intends to manifest the incomprehensible vastness of his eternal divinity and power. Hence, if the conception of it were not inconceivable to us men, it would be neither sufficient for stirring up so admirable a work nor worthy of God, the glory that the expanse of the heavens recounts from it. Let the way of so great a Deity be unsearchable, provided it involves no contradiction; and it is by no means to be thought that the production of something out of nothing involves a contradiction. The well-worn saying, Out of nothing nothing comes, seems self-evident, in so far as nothing can be produced out of nothing, through the nothing itself, or by the power of nothing itself; and so nothing can be the principle of anything. But it by no means conflicts with this that he who is most sufficient, not only for himself but also for others, should bring it about that something begins to exist out of nothing, as from the terminus a quo, as they say, by the infinity of his own power as from a principle, a thing of which there had previously been nothing. Just as it is by no means contrary to a contingent thing that now exists, if it ceases to exist, deprived of the influence of the cause by whose power it exists, and so what was something becomes nothing.

units.la: Interim, quamvis infinito Numini Creationem minimè faciat impossibilem hæc difficultas, haud tamen adeò nullam eam esse arbitror, quin conficiat omninò, quavis finità virtute majorem requiri ad id ut quicquam crescetur. Certè nihilum rei creatæ principium esse non potest, jam diximus. Ipsum itaque creans rei creatæ in solidum omnem quam per creationem habet essentiam dare debebit. At qui poterit creatura? Num suam suæ creaturæ dabit essentiam? Non utique, nisi unum à se ipso hoc pacto divisum, & sic re verà plura, fiat; vel sese saltem in aliud transmutet. Num potius quam ipsa non habet alteri dabit essentiam? Atqui in effectu nihil esse posse quod non in causa præextiterit, certa veritas est. Restat ergò, creare illius solius esse, qui modo incomprehensibili ob perfectionum suarum infinitatem aliis de suo potest dare, neque ipse tamen ideò habere minus. Imò, quam nulla sit in nihilo aptitudo ad aliquid, ritè cogitemus; consequenter quam nulla inter ista duo proportio. Agere verò absque ulla proportione inter terminum à quo & terminum ad quem, ut cum Schola loquar, neutiquam ejus est, cujus, quemadmodum essentia, sic potentia, omnem proportionem excedere, hoc est, infinita esse nequit. Adhuc, Creatio actio est, naturam in suo esse constituens. Quid autem clarius, quam quod naturam constituit referendum id duntaxat esse ad virtutem ejus, qui naturæ rerum, tanquam auctor ejusdem, præest; non ad debilem efficientiam illius, cujus omnis vis naturæ legibus adstricta subest. Et qui sufficiat aliis à se creandis, quod ipsi sibi conservando sufficiens non existit; qualis non existit quævis per se contingens creatura? Quam ridiculum, statuere, id facere posse ut nihil fiat aliquid, quod facere nequit, ut aliquid non fiat nihil. Atque evertunt hæ rationes Creationem creaturæ posse sibilem, non immediatam tantum, sed & mediatam: utramque
units.tr: Meanwhile, although this difficulty does not make creation impossible for the infinite Deity, I do not think it is so slight that it does not show that, for anything to be created, a power greater than any finite power is required. Certainly, as we have already said, nothing cannot be the principle of a created thing. The Creator must therefore give the created thing its whole essence, all that it has through creation. But how could a creature do this? Will it give its own essence to its creature? Certainly not, unless one and the same thing were divided in this way from itself and so there were really more than one, or unless it were changed into something else. Will it rather give to another what it does not itself have? But it is a certain truth that nothing can exist in an effect that did not previously exist in its cause.
