It remains, therefore, that creating belongs to him alone who, by the incomprehensible infinity of his perfections, can give to others from his own store, and yet does not thereby have any less himself. Indeed, if we think rightly, nothing has no aptitude at all for anything, and consequently there is no proportion between the two. But to act without any proportion between the term from which and the term to which, to use the language of the Schoolmen, does not belong to him whose power, just like his essence, exceeds every proportion, that is, cannot be infinite. Moreover, creation is an action that establishes a nature in its being. Now what is clearer than that the establishing of a nature must be referred only to the power of him who presides over the nature of things as their author, and not to the feeble efficacy of one whose every power is bound by the laws of nature? And how could he suffice to create others, who does not even exist self-sufficiently to preserve himself, as no contingent creature existing through itself does? How ridiculous it is to say that he who cannot make something from nothing can make nothing into something! These arguments overturn the view that creature can create, not only immediately but also mediately. Both are overturned.

units.la: Creandi vis tã solius Dei est, ut in ejus societatem nulla veniat creatura. que enim ejusdem virtutis esse, ob non majorem subjecti inha-bilis, quam ipsius puri nihili, ad opus creandum ineptitudinem, §. 11. notavimus. Quin, ne instrumentalem quidem causalitatem hac parte creaturæ relinquimus, quandoquidem tota instrumenti natura in aptitudine ad usum constitit; qualis re verò in eo nulla est, nisi in ordine ad subjectum in quod agit, vel circa quod versatur. Atqui subjectum hic vel plane nullum est, vel, quod eodem redit, nullo modo aptum ad productionem rei, quæ per Creationem ex eo efficitur. Detestandum itaque sacrilegium est eorum, qui non dubitant Angelos aliasve creaturas cum Deo in Creationis societatem admittere, saltem ut comministros; nimium profectò obscurantes effulgentem in opere creationis divinæ Majestatis gloriam. Quæ à miraculis per creaturas patratis petita hic objici pollent, jam supra Exercitat. xxi. §. v. diluta sunt.
units.tr: The power of creating belongs to God alone, so that no creature may share in his fellowship. For it is not of the same power, because of the unfitness of the subject, which is no greater than the unfitness of pure nothing for the work of creating, as we noted in §. 11. Nor do we leave to creatures even an instrumental causality in this respect, since the whole nature of an instrument consists in its aptitude for use; but there is no such aptitude in a thing except in relation to the subject on which it acts or with which it is concerned. Now here the subject is either altogether nonexistent or, which comes to the same thing, in no way apt for the production of the thing that is brought about out of it by creation. It is therefore a detestable sacrilege of those who do not hesitate to admit angels or other creatures into fellowship with God in creation, at least as fellow-workers; they greatly obscure the glory of the divine Majesty shining forth in the work of creation. What might be objected here from miracles wrought through creatures has already been answered above in Exercitat. xxi. §. v.

units.la: Quandò autem solum Deum rerum omnium Cratorem statui-mus, attendendum est diligenter, ne quid cogitationibus no-stris admisceamus quod perfectissimo perfectionum quarumvis creatarum Auctori quicquam detrahat. Removenda hinc est quam longissimè primo loco omnis sive compositio sive mutatio, qualem inferunt operationes creaturarum; quæ, quemadmodum agunt per actionem ab essentia distinctam, ab otio transeunt ad actum, ab actu redeunt ad quietem. Errat, qui concipit Creationem tanquam aliquid quod Deus ipse non sit, sed ei in tempore superaccesserit. Certè in Deo nihil est, quod, ob Simplicitatem jam antè demonstratam, Deus non sit; nihil in creatura, quod non, ob dependentiam ejus & contingentiam, sit creatum: atque ideò nulla fingenda creatio, quæ non à parte Creatoris activè spectata ipse Deus creans sit, à parte Creaturæ passivè considerata ipsa res creata. Tertium quid, quod nec Deus sit, nec creatura, monstrificum prorsus est, omnique rationi nimiùm adversum. Quamobrem si, prout se à parte rei habet, Creationem menti distinctiùs repræsentare voluerimus, ipsa æterna Dei sufficientia cogitanda venit, quatenus ejus vi in tempore Deo coëxistere incipit res alia à Deo, idque cum omnimoda ab ea tanquam à principio suo dependentia. Talis res ex nihilo producta cum nulla Deo ipso facto coëxtiterit ab-æterno no, neque etiam extitit ab æterno illius denominationis, quà Deus Creator dicitur, fundamentum: atque ideò minus accuratè Deus ab æterno dicetur fuisse Creator; etiamsi possederit quicquid in actu creandi absolutæ perfectionis involvitur.
units.tr: When we affirm that God alone is the Creator of all things, we must take care not to mix into our thoughts anything that would detract in any way from the most perfect Author of all perfections. First and foremost, therefore, every composition or change of the kind that the operations of creatures involve must be removed as far as possible. Creatures, when they act through an action distinct from their essence, pass from rest into activity and return from activity into rest. He is in error who conceives creation as something that God himself is not, but that came to him in time. Certainly in God there is nothing that is not God, on account of his simplicity, already demonstrated earlier; and in a creature there is nothing that has not been created, on account of its dependence and contingency. Therefore no creation should be imagined which, viewed actively on the side of the Creator, is not God himself creating, and, viewed passively on the side of the creature, is not the created thing itself. A third something, which is neither God nor creature, is utterly monstrous and altogether too contrary to reason. Wherefore, if we wish to represent creation to the mind more distinctly, as it stands in reality, we must consider God's own eternal sufficiency, insofar as by his power something other than God begins to coexist with God in time, and that with complete dependence on him as its principle. A thing produced out of nothing in this way never coexisted with God from eternity, nor did it ever exist from eternity as the foundation of that designation by which God is called Creator. Hence God will be said less accurately to have been Creator from eternity, even though he possessed from eternity whatever is included in the absolute perfection of the act of creating.

units.la: Porrò, nequaquam sentire fas est, ex aliqua naturæ necessitate Deum creasse quod creavit, ad instar causæ, quam vocant, emanativæ. Sicuti enim res quævis extra Deum Divinæ perfectionis infinitati, si sint, nihil addunt, si non sint, nihil detrahunt; ita nulla inter perfectissimi Numinis essentiam, & productarum ab ipso creaturarum existentiam, ex natura rei est connexio. Atque ideò, liberrimè creasse Deum quod creavit, certum est; ut vel nihil plane creare, vel aliud creare, vel alio modo atque ordine creare, si voluisset, potuisset. Qua de re dubitare non finit quod antè observavimus, tum de modo operandi enti perfectissimo tribuendo non nisi perfectissimo, qualis procul dubio est liberrimus; tum speciatim de Dei absoluto atque supremo in possibilia quævis Dominio ac Potestate. Tenendum deniquè, absque labore, mora, ac defatigatione operatum fuisse Deum, quandò creavit. Sic exigit independens infinitæ activitatis efficacia, cui nihil resistere aptum est, cujusque eminentiam maximè commendat prompta ad nutum Creatoris rei creatæ extantia. Adde, quæ idem postulat, immediatam nihili atque entis oppositionem: ea, ut mixturam extremorum non patitur, ita respuit successivum à nihilo ad aliquid transitum, & cum eo languidam ac moram trahentem creandi actionem. Unde liquet, quam parum magnificè de re tanta, sentiant, qui serie bene longa eam nobis delineant novam mundi genesin, quæ regulis mechanicis adstricta, tantùm successiva particularum configuratione & concursatione absolvitur. Quasi verò vectibus atque machinis eguerit Numen in Universi fabricatione! quæ Velleji apud Ciceronem stoliditas est. Sed plura hanc in rem dicenda erunt: de eis enim quæ nostri hujus mundi Creationem speciatim concernunt nonnihil adhuc differendum.
units.tr: Further, it is by no means right to think that God created what he created from some necessity of nature, in the manner of what they call an emanative cause. For just as things outside God add nothing to the infinity of the divine perfection if they exist, and take nothing away if they do not exist, so there is no connection by the nature of the thing between the essence of the most perfect Deity and the existence of the creatures produced by him. Hence it is certain that God created what he created most freely; so that, if he had willed, he could have created nothing at all, or something else, or in another way and order. This is confirmed by what we observed earlier, both that the most perfect being must be ascribed a mode of acting that is nothing but most perfect, such as is undoubtedly the freest, and especially that God has absolute and supreme dominion and power over all possible things. Finally, we must hold that God acted without labour, delay, or fatigue when he created. The independent efficacy of infinite activity demands this, to which nothing can be opposed, and whose eminence is most commended by the created thing standing forth ready at the nod of the Creator. Add that the same efficacy requires the immediate opposition of nothing and being. As this does not admit a mixture of the extremes, so it rejects a successive transition from nothing to something, and with it an action of creating that is sluggish and drawn out. From this it is clear how poorly those think of so great a matter who, at considerable length, describe for us a new genesis of the world, which, bound by mechanical rules, is accomplished only by the gradual arrangement and collision of particles! As if the Deity needed levers and machines in fashioning the universe! This is the stupidity of Velleius in Cicero. But more must be said on this point, for we must still defer somewhat the discussion of those matters that specifically concern the creation of this our world.

units.la: Et quidem de productionis hujus Universi tum tempore, tum etiam ordine atque modo, disquiritur. Primum quantum attinet, in genere dictat ratio, sic saltem necessariò aliquod primum extitisse Creationis momentum, ut ab æterno Mundus hic creatus neque fuerit, neque fuisse potuerit. Contrarium enim quisquis tueri vellet, statuere cogeretur, mundum creatum ab aeterno potuisse vere coexistere suo Creatori; cum, ut jam notavimus, citra ejusmodi rei creatae & causae creantis coexistentiam, Creatio, si proprie loqui cupiamus, non consistat. Atqui aeternitatem perfectionem esse in imperfectam illam durationem, quae successiva est, minime cadentem, semel iterumque jam evicimus. Conferatur, §. iii. Imo etiam aeterna Creatio aeternam, atque ideo re vera infinitam, causarum subordinatarum seriem secum trahit: cujus consequentis absurditatem demonstravimus clare; Exercitat. ii. §. iii.
units.tr: Indeed, the question is raised both concerning the time of this universe's production and concerning its order and manner. As to the first, reason in general dictates that some first moment of creation must necessarily have existed, so that this world, created, neither was from eternity nor could have been. For whoever wished to maintain the contrary would be forced to hold that a created world could truly have coexisted from eternity with its Creator; whereas, as we have already noted, without such coexistence of a created thing and a creating cause, creation, to speak properly, does not exist. But we have already shown, more than once, that eternity is not a perfection in that imperfect duration which is successive and which does not fall to God. Compare §. iii. Indeed, even an eternal creation would bring with it an eternal, and therefore really infinite, series of subordinate causes; the absurdity of this consequence we have demonstrated clearly in Exercitat. ii. §. iii.

units.la: Quin ipsam tantum Creationis notionem secundum se si attendamus, nectit ea hic nodum insolubilem. Quis enim cogitet actionem, quae faciat creaturam transire a non-esse ad esse, qui non hoc ipso concipiat hujus non-esse antecedere ejusdem esse? Verum de quo dici potest, quod antequam esset non-fuerit, de eo interminata existentia affirmari nequit. Aeternus ergo non est mundus creatus, ideo quia creatus. Neque obstat, quam huc adferunt quidam, Potentia Dei; quae, ajunt, ut ipsa aeterna est, ita arguit quolibet momento possibili, id est, ab aeterno, mundum creari potuisse. Etsi enim certum sit, aeternam esse divinam potentiam, nihil tamen inde conficitur aliud, quam ab aeterno possibile fuisse ut mundus existat; existat nimirum naturae suae convenienter, id est, duratione, uti successiva, ita principium habente. Potuit ergo aeterna potentia ab aeterno quolibet possibili momento initium existentiae dare huic universo. Sed quemadmodum citra contradictionem non potest creaturae dare essentiam cujus duratio successiva ipso facto omne possibile momentum temporis collective includat, sic neque aeternam creaturam creare potest. De aeterno Dei decreto minus laborandum est, cum id sit actio immanens, nihil aeternum a Deo diversum per se constituens; quale quid reapse constitueret aeterna Creatio: quapropter ab illo ad hanc nulla legitima atque efficax est hac parte sequela.
units.tr: Indeed, if we attend to the bare notion of creation in itself, it ties us to an insoluble knot. For who can think of an act that makes a creature pass from non-being to being without at once conceiving that this non-being precedes its being? Whatever can truly be said to have not existed before it existed cannot be affirmed to have unending existence. The world, then, is not eternal, because it was created. Nor is there force in the argument some bring forward from the power of God, which, they say, being eternal, could have created the world at any moment possible, that is, from eternity. For although it is certain that the divine power is eternal, nothing further follows from this than that it was possible from eternity for the world to exist, existing, of course, in a manner consistent with its nature, that is, with a duration that is successive and so has a beginning. Therefore the eternal power could from eternity have given this universe a beginning of existence at any possible moment. But just as, without contradiction, it cannot give a creature an essence whose successive duration by its very nature takes in every possible moment of time collectively, so it cannot create an eternal creature either. We need not trouble ourselves much over the eternal decree of God, since it is an immanent act, establishing nothing eternal distinct from God; whereas eternal creation would actually establish something of that kind. Hence there is no legitimate or valid inference from the former to the latter on this point.

units.la: IX. Quando tamen praecise fuerit pro-
units.tr: IX. When, however, precisely it was produced

units.la: Interim, accurate loquendo, mundus non tam in, quam potius cum tempore, est productus: id est, una cum productione mundi initium cepit duratio ejus successiva, quae est ipsum
units.tr: Meanwhile, speaking accurately, the world was produced not so much in time as together with time: that is, together with the production of the world its successive duration began, and that is time itself.
To have existed before it is contradictory.

units.la: ipsum tempus. Ut mustea fit eorum subtilitas, qui rem crea- tam ante tempus esse potuisse afferunt; quia tempus contendunt non esse fine motu, ac potuisse Deum materiam creare quiescentem. Sed attendere debuissent, motum esse aliquid tempore accidentarium, non essentiale (nam & ipsi motui sua fucceffiva duratio, five tempus, competit) quatenus in dime-tiendis temporum partibus nos pro mensura motum sumimus. Quâ autem anni tempestate initium sumserit tempus mundanum, five, ut rectius dicam, in quo Zodiaci signo in prima rerum productione sol extiterit, ne quidem in subsidium vocatâ sacrâ Auctoritate, expediri satis potest. Pro solstitio hyemali vix ulli, pro æstivo pauci; pro æquinoctio alterutro plærique definiunt: sed debili nimis fundamento, quam ut huic rei immorari debeamus. Quod idem ferè dicendum de primi creationis momenti à nostro hoc præsenti tempore distantia. Etsi enim Chronologia Sacra collata cum profanis annalibus sextum millenarium præter propter exindè elapsum esse doceat, solum tamen naturæ lumen ne quidem probabili conjecturæ locum facit. Quandoquidem enim nullos ætatis suæ characteres sibi impressos habet mundus, & non nisi ex effectis de causæ liberrimæ actionibus concludere datur, nemo nisi temerarius quicquam de hac re definiverit. Non desunt tamen nobis, qui citius aut serius mundum creari potuisse, strenuè negant. Atquì, cum solius æterni sit non posse existere vel citius vel serius, quid isti sibi velint, nescio. Nisi forsan hoc pacto viam struere contendant opinioni, quæ nullos agnoscit in Universi hujus ut extensione, sic quoque duratione, limites. Alias enim, si non nimium nugari lubitum fuerit, otiosam excitando logomachiam (quandoquidem nullus de Deo rectè sentiens ignorat, in ordine ad Divinam æternitatem nihil citum aut serum dici debere, aut posse) quo modo ex naturæ lumine negari potest, citius aut serius creari id potuisse, de quo quando creatum sit, ne quidem per naturam constat? Et quid ni, situ corporum cœlestium (à quibus quemadmodum mensuram temporis sumimus, ita etiam durationis longioris aut brevioris determinationem) existente hodiè qualis est, sol hic ab initio sui, si Deo visum fuisset, absolvere potuisset per Zodiacum non sexies mille, sed vel centies mille circuitus? Verùm desino esse copiosior in re manifesta.
units.tr: How empty is the subtlety of those who maintain that a created thing could have existed before time, on the ground that they contend time cannot exist without motion, and that God could have created matter at rest. But they ought to have considered that motion is something accidental to time, not essential to it (for motion too has its own successive duration, or time), inasmuch as we take motion as the measure when we divide off the parts of time. But in what season of the year the world's time began, or, to put it more correctly, in which sign of the Zodiac the sun stood at the first production of things, cannot be settled sufficiently even by calling in sacred authority. Scarcely anyone defines it as the winter solstice, few as the summer solstice, and most as one of the equinoxes; but these rest on too weak a foundation for us to linger over the question. Much the same must be said of the distance of the first moment of creation from our present time. For although Sacred Chronology, compared with profane annals, shows that roughly six thousand years have since elapsed, the light of nature alone does not afford even a probable conjecture. For since the world bears no marks of its age impressed upon it, and it can be inferred only from the effects of a most free cause, no one but a rash person would define anything about this matter. Yet there are not wanting those among us who stoutly deny that the world could have been created sooner or later. But since it belongs only to the eternal not to be able to exist either sooner or later, I do not know what these men mean, unless perhaps they are trying by this route to pave the way for the opinion that recognises no limits to this Universe, either in extension or in duration. For otherwise, if it is not too trifling to stir up an idle logomachy (since no one who thinks rightly of God is ignorant that, in relation to the divine eternity, nothing can or should be called sooner or later), how can it be denied, by the light of nature, that that which was created at a time not established even by nature could have been created sooner or later? And why not? With the present position of the heavenly bodies (by which we measure time, and so also determine longer or shorter duration), could this sun, if it had pleased God, from the beginning of its course have completed the circuits of the Zodiac not six thousand times, but even a hundred thousand? But I stop being more copious on a plain matter.

units.la: De modo & ordine, quem servaverit causa prima in excitanda hac mundi mole, ex solo naturali lumine non magis liquet, quam de præcisô creationis tempore. Quicquid enim ratio manifestat de Divina operandi ratione, id totum vel à priori quasi, deducendum est ex perfectissima Opificis natura, vel, quasi à posteriori, colligendum ex inspecta ipsius operis constitutione. Neutra contemplatio quicquam ad negotium hoc satis expediendum conferre potest. Deum si spectes, independens ejus libertas atque supremum in res quasvis dominium, cum infinita tum sapientia tum potentia conjunctum, non finit nos ullam ejusmodi Creationis methodum excogitare, ut non mille aliis viis ea æquè facilis atque expedita esse potuerit Creatori. Neque juvat obvia universi dispositio. Qualemcunque enim assignaveris originis modum (dummodo talis sit, qui neque perfectioni divinæ, neque hodiernæ mundi syntaxi atque phænomenis in eo obviis, manifestè adversetur) is omnis, ob jam memoratam sapientissimi ac potentissimi agentis plenissimam in operibus extra se producendis libertatem, fermè æquè probabilis videri potest: nulla saltem istius exigitit necessitatis, ut certa atque indubitata haberi debeat. Solus ipse Deus, quid hic volucrit, cum modo alio atque alio agere potuerit, de suo opere testari aptus est. Atque ita Christiani coelesti oraculo didicimus, sextiduanâ Creationis morâ surrexisse hanc Mundi machinam: eâ operationis serie, ut cum ipso primi diei exordio exordium sumserit universa mundi materia, ab ipsa jam prima sui origine Cœlo constantem, Terrâque à cœlo divisâ, ac Mari ubique diffluo circumfusâ; mox altero hæmisphærio illustrata luce primigenià, quæ triduanâ, Solis nondum conditi vicaria, suâ circumvolutione noctúrna diurnaque tempora discriminabat. Jactis hisce nascentis mundi quasi fundamentis, orbem terrarum primùm habitabilem fœturus Creator, atque exundante liquore evoluturus, altero die bonam aquarum partem in altum subvectam jussit constituere Nubes: daturas in sublimi admiranda mundi spectacula Meteora. Tertiâ luce fecit ascendere montes, descendere valles, Mari sic suis ostiis concluso
units.tr: Concerning the manner and order that the First Cause followed in bringing forth this mass of the world, nothing is clearer from natural light alone than the precise time of creation. Whatever reason makes plain about the divine way of working must be drawn either a priori from the most perfect nature of the Maker, or, as it were a posteriori, gathered from an examination of the structure of his work itself. Neither line of inquiry can contribute enough to settle this matter. If you consider God, his independent freedom and supreme dominion over all things, joined with both infinite wisdom and infinite power, does not allow us to devise any method of creation by which the Creator could not have achieved the same result as easily and conveniently by a thousand other ways. Nor does the obvious arrangement of the universe help. For whatever mode of origin you assign (provided it is one that does not manifestly conflict with the divine perfection, nor with the present construction of the world and the phenomena that appear in it), that mode can seem almost equally probable, because of the fullest freedom, already mentioned, of the most wise and most powerful Agent in producing works outside himself. At least no necessity of that kind exists that would require it to be held as certain and beyond doubt. God alone, who knows what he willed here, and who could have acted in another way, is fit to bear witness about his own work. And so we Christians have learned from the heavenly oracle that this machinery of the world arose over a period of six days of creation, in such a sequence of operations that the whole matter of the world began with the very beginning of the first day, being at once from its first origin consisting of heaven, with earth separated from heaven, and surrounded everywhere by the flowing sea. Then, with the primal light shining on one hemisphere, which over three days, standing in for the sun not yet made, marked off night and day by its revolution. With these foundations, as it were, of the emerging world laid, the Creator, about to bring forth first the inhabitable globe and to lay it bare as the overflowing liquid withdrew, on the second day commanded that a good part of the waters be raised on high and set up as clouds, which were to provide the wondrous spectacles of the meteors in the upper air. On the third day of light he made mountains rise and valleys sink, and the sea, thus shut up with its doors and bolted as if by a bar at the divine command, so that the waters withdrew and the land was laid bare everywhere; then, the soil being adorned with plants, he made the most pleasant garden of the world. On the following day of the origins, the Maker vaulted the sky, the arched roof of our world, with perpetual lights of the world, set forth on the ethereal stage: the Sun, the Moon, and the dancing bands of countless other stars. With the dwelling thus prepared, the inhabitants were given their seats: on the fifth day, from the common womb of the waters, the whole brood of birds and fishes was brought forth, the former released into the air, the latter kept in the maternal bosom. To complete this living world, the generation of land animals was added on the sixth day; soon after it came the holier animal, the epitome of beauty scattered everywhere, man himself, formed indeed from the clay of the earth but after the image of the Maker of the cosmos, destined to be lord of created things and to dedicate them to their Creator.

units.la: concluso cluso, ac divino imperio veluti vecte oppeffulato, quo refi- dua aquarum diffusione detecta passim terra; mox, picturato Plantis solo, extituraamænissimum mundi viridarium. Sequenti originum die concameratam orbis nostri testudinem Cœlum cælavit opifex perpetuis mundi luminibus, in scenam ætheream productis Sole, Luna, reliquisque innumerorum syderum choragiis. Parato hunc in modum domicilio, quæque suis sedibus datæ fuerunt incolæ: progenitâ quinto die ex communi aquarum gremio omni avium atque piscium sobole; illis in aëra dimissis, his in materno sinu retentis. Quibus, ad consummandum mundi vivarium, addita fuit sexto die terrestrium animantium genesis; quam mox excepit sanctius his animal, pulchritudinis passim sparsæ compendium, ipsus homo, de terræ quidem limo, ad Cosmopæi tamen imaginem, formatus, rerum creatarum futurus dominus, qui easdem suo Creatori devoveret.
units.tr: Shut up with its doors, and bolted as if by a divine command, like a bar, the waters having flowed back and spread out, the dry land was everywhere uncovered. Soon the ground, painted over with plants, became the most pleasant garden of the world. On the following day of the origins, the Creator and craftsman vaulted the arched roof of our world, the heavens, with the perpetual lights of the universe, the Sun and Moon and the dances of countless other stars, brought onto the ethereal stage. With the dwelling thus prepared, the inhabitants were given their places: on the fifth day, from the common bosom of the waters, a whole brood of birds and fishes was brought forth, the former released into the air, the latter kept in their mother's bosom. To these, to complete the living world, the creation of land animals was added on the sixth day. Soon after them came the more sacred creature, a summary of the beauty scattered everywhere, man himself, formed indeed from the clay of the earth but in the image of the Cosmopoeus, destined to be lord of created things and to dedicate them to their Creator.

units.la: Hanc universi operis ideam, ex natura non sciendam, delineant sacræ Ephemerides: quæ indubitatæ fidei esse oportet inter quosvis, qui infallibilem divinorum oraculorum auctoritatem ritè se agnoscere profitentur. Non tamen hodiè eorum numerus deest, quos juvat, contemptâ, sepositâ saltem, narratione Mosaicâ, totos sese tradere confictis pro lubitu hypothesibus toto cœlo ab ea recedentibus. Quod Ethnici pro suo quisque captu alia atque alia finxerint atque pinxerint rerum primordia, à genuinis istis originibus longè diversa, condonari utcunque poterat hominibus in meris tenebris hac parte palpantibus. Sed quòd isti quoque, quibus cœlitus patefactum est tanti operis mysterium, usque eo suis hic ausint indulgere ideis, ut à tam clara luce recedere nihil metuant, id verò facinus indignissimum existit, neque ulli cui Creatoris gloria cordi est ferendum. Iliada commentorum canit Cartesius, Principiorum suæ Philosophiæ parte Tertiâ & Quartâ: ubi tantâ confidentiâ de mechanica hujus mundi, ut structura, sic quoque origine, disserit, ut majori haud potuisset, etiamsi vel Deo conditori extitisset à consiliis. Quod si aliquanto major fuisset Viri erga Sacras Scripturas reverentia, abstterrere debuisset à temerariis conatibus vel una illa gravissima Dei concio, quæ ex-tat
units.tr: The sacred Ephemerides outline this idea of the whole work, which cannot be known from nature. It ought to be of indubitable faith among all who properly profess to acknowledge the infallible authority of the divine oracles. Yet today there is no lack of those who, having despised or at least set aside the Mosaic narrative, delight in surrendering themselves entirely to hypotheses invented at will, which depart from it by the whole breadth of heaven. That the heathen, each according to his capacity, imagined and painted various other beginnings of things, far removed from those genuine origins, might somehow be pardoned in men groping in pure darkness on this point. But that these men also, to whom the mystery of so great a work has been revealed from heaven, dare to indulge their own ideas here to such an extent that they fear no departure from so clear a light, this is truly a most unworthy crime, and one that cannot be tolerated by anyone to whom the glory of the Creator is dear. Descartes sings an Iliad of inventions in the third and fourth parts of his Principles of Philosophy, where he discourses on the mechanics of this world, its structure and likewise its origin, with such confidence that he could not have shown more had he been a counsellor of God the Creator himself. But if the author had shown somewhat greater reverence for the Sacred Scriptures, that one most weighty speech of God should have deterred him from rash attempts, the speech which stands in the final chapters of the sacred book of Job.

units.la: XI. Cartesii in eo omni definiendo notata temeritas. tat ultimis in sacro Jobi codice capitibus. Provocat ibi Creator industriam humanam, ad expedienda, si possit, stupenda vasti operis miracula: quorum interim minutissimas rationes exploratissimas se habere sibi persuadent nuperi homines; percunctanti Deo ad singula respondere parati ex solis Cartesii sui, si sint vera hujus vaticinia, principiis. Cogitatio profecto parum est modesta, ne dicam in Deum contumeliosa, ea velle mente comprehendere, quibus excogitandis nulla par est, nisi infinita supremi Numinis, intelligentia: cujus solius existit definire modum, quo omnia facta sint, aut fieri etiam potuerint. Sed qualem nobis narret idealis mundi vorticosus conditor genituraм, audire, nisi res longa foret, esset operae pretium. Totum negotium, ut verbo dicam, merá arte mechanicá absolvitur, materiâque secundùm regulas ejus motá. Mentio Dei, quae apud Mosen in tanto opificii molimine utramque facit paginam, vix rara alicubi aspersa est, neque multo saepius, quam tantum ut ne credas Lucretium te legere aut Epicurum. Neque id mirum. Nullam enim planè in Coeli Terraeque formatione Deo reliquam facit operationem nova Mundi Genesis, praeterquam materiae (forsitan aeternae, vel undecunque suppeditatae; neque enim de ejus origine quicquam Auctor laborat) per inditum motum in particulas divisionem, earumque per servatam eandem motûs quantitatem diversimodam motionem. Quae pauca sufficere ei videntur, ut ex iis, tanquam causis, omnes qui in hoc mundo apparent effectus secundum leges naturae oriantur. Usque eo, ut non putet alia simpliciora, vel intellectu faciliora, vel etiam probabiliora rerum principia posse excogitari.
units.tr: XI. The rashness of Cartesius in defining all of this. tat ultimis in sacro Jobi codice capitibus. There, in the final chapters of the sacred book of Job, the Creator challenges human ingenuity to explain, if it can, the stupendous marvels of his vast work. Yet modern men persuade themselves that they have the smallest details thoroughly worked out, and are ready to answer God on every point from the principles of Cartesius alone, if his prophecies are true. Surely it is rather immodest, not to say insulting to God, to wish to grasp with the mind those things for whose devising no one is equal to God's supreme intelligence, the only intelligence able to define the manner in which all things were made, or could have been made. But it would be worth hearing what sort of genesis of the material world this whirling architect of his ideal universe would tell us, if the matter were not too long. The whole business, to put it in a word, is accomplished by mere mechanical art, with matter moved according to its rules. The mention of God, which in Moses fills both pages in so great an enterprise of construction, is scarcely found here and there, and not much more often than to keep you from thinking you are reading Lucretius or Epicurus. Nor is this surprising. For the new Genesis makes God perform no operation at all in the formation of heaven and earth, except the division of matter (perhaps eternal, or supplied from somewhere; for the author does not trouble himself about its origin) into particles by an impressed motion, and the various motion of those particles by the same quantity of motion kept constant. These few things seem to him sufficient, so that from them, as causes, all the effects that appear in this world arise according to the laws of nature. To such a degree that he does not think that other, simpler principles of things, or ones easier to understand, or even more probable, could be devised.

units.la: Quam haec prorsus indigna sit Divinâ Majestate philosophatio, quamque nihil contineat quod assurgat ad illam grandiloquentiam, quâ ipse suum opus in Sacris commendat Creator, utcunquè jam notavimus. Quam malè inter se cohaerat ista vorticosarum fabellarum textura, nisi id physici potius fori foret, non uno modo unicuique vigilantius ad cernenda vera oculos deducenti, ostenderem facillimè. Tantùm, quam existant historiae Sacrae inimica, atque Viro Dei Mosi in barbam contradicentia, illa nudiusquartus in Cartesii cerebello nata commenta, non possum non planum facere hoc loco instantiâ solum-
units.tr: How utterly unworthy of the Divine Majesty this philosophising is, and how little it contains that rises to that lofty style by which the Creator himself commends his work in the Scriptures, we have already noted in some measure. How badly the texture of these whirling fables hangs together I could easily show, were this a matter for the natural philosopher's forum, where eyes are led in many ways to see the truth more carefully. I cannot fail, at least, to make plain here, by this single instance, how these fancies, hatched in the little brain of Cartesius, are hostile to sacred history and flatly contradict Moses, the man of God.

units.la: XII. Cartesiana mundi genesis Mosaicae quam multis modis adversa. lummodò unâ atque alterâ, ab unius Telluris productione petità. Cæterùm, ex ungue leonem! In ipso primi dici rerumque omnium exordio æquè Terram creatam fuisse ac Cœlum, exertim narrat Genesis Mosaïca: Cœlos tamen fluidos præextitisse jam dudum, ac non nisi post plurium indè æstatum lapsum, efformatam fuisse Terram, fingit Genesis Cartesiana. Triduum antè productas Stellas extitisse globum nostrum terraaquecum, docet Genesis Mosaïca; Ipsam stellam eum primitùs fuisse, quæ, multo tempore post Solis & Fixarum existentiam, maculis tandem involuta, ac varià crustâ crassiori tecta, indèque in motu suo languescens à valentiore vicini Solis vortice absorpta, atque in istam orbitam in qua hodiè oberrat circa solem compacta, in corpus solidum & opacum abierit, tellusque qualis nunc est esse cœperit, prolixè fabulatur Genesis Cartesiana. Unius tantum telluris, tanquam partis universi principalioris, ac cœlis contradistinctæ, meminit Genesis Mosaica: Planetis eam annumerat in Solis cœlo cum cæteris fluitantem; camque non unam tantum, sed, si mechanicis suis regulis convenienter philosophari cupiat, in infinitis vorticibus sine fine multiplicatam, fingere necesse habet Genesis Cartesiana. Aquis ab origine sui tectam, ac tertio primùm die emergentem, telluris faciem exhibet Genesis Mosaica: aridæ verò ubique superficiei, paulatim factæ rimosæ, collabente crustâ, ac quibusdam ejus fragmentis substratarum aquarum fundum petentibus, sicque superfluitante liquore, erupisse mare, pingit Genesis Cartesiana. Sed quid διχοτομίαν tantam paucis comprehendere laboro? cui, si singula, uti rei momentum postulat, prosequi vellem, volumen Cartesii Principiis grandius conscribendum foret. Etsi verò de re tanta in præsentiarum non liceat adferre in medium quicquid istùc pertinet, non tamen planè hoc loco silenter transmittere poteram Helenam, cujus amoribus ad furorem usque infatuatur hodiè orbis eruditus, etiam Christianus.
units.tr: XII. The Cartesian genesis of the world is in many ways opposed to the Mosaic. One instance alone, drawn from the production of the earth alone. But: judge the lion by its claw! At the very beginning of time and of all things, the Mosaic Genesis expressly narrates that the earth was created just as the heaven was; the Cartesian Genesis, however, imagines that the heavens existed long before as a fluid, and that the earth was formed only after many ages had passed. The Mosaic Genesis teaches that our globe of earth and water came into being before the stars three days earlier; the Cartesian Genesis fabulously tells at length how the star itself was first, which, long after the existence of the Sun and the fixed stars, at length became enveloped in spots and covered with a varied thicker crust, and then, its motion slackening, was absorbed by the vortex of the nearer and stronger Sun, and compacted into that orbit in which it now wanders about the sun, and turned into a solid and opaque body, and the earth began to be what it now is. The Mosaic Genesis mentions only one earth, as a principal part of the universe distinct from the heavens; it counts it among the planets floating in the heaven of the Sun along with the others. The Cartesian Genesis is obliged to imagine not one earth only, but, if it wishes to philosophise in accordance with its mechanical rules, infinitely many earths multiplied without end in infinite vortices. The Mosaic Genesis presents the face of the earth at its origin covered by waters, and emerging only on the third day; the Cartesian Genesis paints the dry surface, gradually made full of cracks, with its crust collapsing and some fragments of it sinking to the bottom of the underlying waters, so that the liquid overflowed and the sea burst forth. But why do I labour to comprehend such a dichotomy [διχοτομίαν] in a few words? If I wished to pursue each point, as the weight of the matter demands, a volume larger than Cartesius's Principles would have to be written. And although, for the present, it is not permitted to bring forward in the midst all that pertains to so great a matter, I could not altogether pass over in silence here Helen, for whose love the learned world today, even the Christian part of it, is infatuated to the point of madness.
XIII.

units.la: Alibi quidem novæ Genesis Auctor testatur, se, quando in Mosaicam historiam incidérat, miratum fuisse ejus cum suis hac parte cogitatis consensum. Mirum autem, pro eo demonstrando nihil unquam eum tentasse. Quod tamen fecisse imprimis mis cordi esse debuisset homini, cui nihil magis in votis erat, quam suam ubique locorum in Academias Christianorum inducere Philosophiam. Quin, quam parum suas hypotheses Mosaizare ipse crediderit, vel istud evincit, quod, quo loco illud docere imprimis oportuisset, praefari istic maluerit, se ad res naturales melius explicandas, causas earum repetere altius, quam ipsas unquam extitisse existimet. Modesta quidem illa videri possent, nisi pelluceret artificium prudentioribus rerum aestimatoribus. Quid enim ad illustrandam veram mundi syntaxin pertinet ejusdem adeo operosa per confictas sine fine hypotheses constructio? Nisi ex mendacio suum veritati accedere splendorem, credendum sit. Aliud itaque auctor intendebat, si, quod hic sese manibus palpandum offert, dicere liceat. Animus erat suo arbitrio res naturales tales fingere, quales ipse somniabat. Fidem facturus inauditis commentis, via paranda erat, accommodando eis nativitatem praeconcepto somnio saventem. Eam ut veram neminem facile sanae mentis admissurum, sat praevidebat. Ergo homo callidus in ipso exordio profitetur, se duntaxat hypotheses narraturum, de quibus credere liceat, non omnes esse veras. Itaque, postquam lectoris sui mentem longiori progressu vorticosis ideis assuefecit, primum ei minus ridicula videri poterant quae jam facta familiaria; mox saltem possibilia; dein non prorsus improbabilia; denique verissima; quin etiam talia, ut, nisi Deum non summe bonum ac veracem habere volucrimus, in mathematicarum demonstrationum numerum ea sint recipienda; quando quae de Mundo scripsit, vix aliter quam a se explicata sunt, intelligi posse putet. Princip. iv. Art. ccvi. Mirum foret, nisi quantum crescit fingendi licentia, crescerct pariter asseverationis confidentia. Verum jam dudum in his excelsi quem huic tractatui praestitui modum. Vorticosi mundi subversio alterius laboris erit, neque valde difficilis; si vitae vires addere voluerit Deus.
units.tr: Elsewhere, indeed, the author of the new Genesis testifies that when he had come upon the Mosaic history he was amazed at the agreement of his thoughts with it in this part. But it is strange that he never attempted to demonstrate this. Yet this was especially what ought to have been dear to a man who desired nothing more than to introduce his philosophy into the Christian academies everywhere. Indeed, how little he himself believed his hypotheses to be Mosaic, this very fact proves: in the place where he especially ought to have taught this, he preferred to say in a preface that he wishes to explain natural things better, and to trace their causes further back than he thinks they ever existed. Those words might seem modest, were it not that the trick is transparent to the more prudent judges of things. For what does the so laboured construction of the same world, built up through invented hypotheses without end, contribute to illustrating the true arrangement of the world? Unless one is to believe that he adds his own splendour to truth by falsehood. He was therefore aiming at something else, if one may say what here offers itself to be felt with the hands. His purpose was to imagine natural things, by his own judgement, such as he himself dreamed them. Intending to win belief for unheard-of fancies, he had to prepare a way, by accommodating to them a birth favourable to the dream he had conceived beforehand. He foresaw well enough that no one of sound mind would easily admit this as true. So the crafty man at the very outset professes that he will only narrate hypotheses, which it is permissible to believe, not all of which are true. Accordingly, after he had accustomed his reader's mind, through a longer course, to whirling ideas, at first those things which had become familiar could seem to him less ridiculous; soon, at least, possible; then not altogether improbable; at last most true; indeed of such a kind that, unless we are willing to hold God not to be supremely good and truthful, they must be received in the number of mathematical demonstrations, since he thinks that what he wrote about the world can hardly be understood otherwise than as he has explained it. Principles, part 4, art. 206. It would be strange if, as the licence of feigning grows, the confidence of assertion did not grow equally. But I have long since set in these lofty matters the measure that I proposed for this treatise. The overthrow of the whirling world will be another labour, and not very difficult, if God is willing to add strength to life.
XIV.

units.la: Quam amplum hoc Universum condiderit Creator? amplius quaeri potest. Equidem tam vaste diffusionis menti nostrae occurrit hoc naturae domicilium, ut finium quibus clauditur distincta imaginatio cadere non videatur in humanam cogitationem, omnem quantitatis mensuram fere fumentem a modica magnitudine tudine rerum in terræ nostræ superficie visui sese offerentium. Multa quidem de exacta cœlorum à tellure distantia tam præcisè definiunt quidam Astronomi, ac si nudius-tertius cœlo delapsi forent; sed id totum mera atque omni idoneo fundamento destituta nugatio est. Quin, si vel maximè res haberet ut isti vaticinantur, nec sic quidem negotium hoc expediri posset. Dato enim stellarum errantium & fixarum altitudinem ad perfectum calculum à nobis revocari posse, non tamen idcirco intelligimus, quæ & quanta ultra fixarum ambitum forte sese diffundant vastissima cœlorum spatia; ut sensui inaccessa, sic menti nostræ non nisi temerè definienda. Quamobrem hæc Geometria illi relinquenda, qui cœlos extendit solus, eosque definita à se mensurâ formavit. Etsi verò isti suaviter delirent, qui tantum sibi tribuunt, ut exactam mundi mensuram se animo comprehendere arbitrentur, gravius tamen errant hodiè qui, in alterum extremum abeuntes, tantam huic Universo adscribunt magnitudinem, ut re ipsâ immensam nullosque extensionis fines habentem agnoscant. Quantum enim Divinæ eminentiæ decedat, si quicquam præter ipsum Numen quocunque modo aut sensu admittatur infinitum, docent quæ de divinæ perfectionis Infinitate suo loco diximus. Quibus solvendis minimè satisfacit inanis distinctiuncula inter infinitatem perfectionis, atque extensionis; quarum scilicet hæc mundo tribui queat, citra præjudicium illius. Quando enim, ut illi contendunt, corporis essentiam constituit ipsa extensio, manifestum evadit, extensionis & essentiæ infinitatem passu pari hoc loco ambulare. Quumque quod essentiâ infinitum est etiam idem necessariò tale sit omnibus suis attributis (quæ suâ naturâ subjecti sui conditionem sequuntur) apparet, vel nullam, vel omnimodam, mundo tribuendam esse infinitatem. Verum de hac hallucinatione longè gravissima prolixè disputavimus Exercitat. de Infinito: quâ, & quæ mens sit novi Philosophi hac parte genuina, & quibus sese tueatur rationibus, & quam multis modis absurdum dogma incurrat in proprietates tum Creatoris tum creaturæ, tam plenè exposuimus, ut si quid vellemus addere, actum ageremus.
units.tr: How large has the Creator made this Universe? One may ask further. Indeed, this dwelling-place of nature presents itself to our minds as so vast in its extent that the bounds by which it is enclosed cannot be grasped by a distinct imagination, and the measure of its quantity almost escapes human thought, starting from the modest size of the things that present themselves to sight on the surface of our earth. Some astronomers define the exact distance of the heavens from the earth so precisely that one would think they had come down from heaven only the day before. But all of this is mere trifling, lacking any sound foundation. Indeed, even if the matter were as those prophets claim, the question still could not be settled in this way. Grant that the heights of the wandering and fixed stars can be brought by us to a perfect calculation. Still we do not thereby understand what and how great are the most vast spaces of the heavens that may extend beyond the sphere of the fixed stars. Inaccessible to the senses, they are likewise to be defined by the mind only rashly. Therefore this geometry must be left to him alone who extended the heavens and shaped them with a measure defined by himself. Yet although those men are pleasantly deluded who attribute so much to themselves as to think they can grasp the exact measure of the world in their minds, those today err more gravely who, going to the opposite extreme, ascribe to this Universe such great magnitude that they acknowledge it in fact to be immense and without any limits of extension. For how much is taken from the divine eminence if anything whatever, by any mode or sense, is admitted to be infinite besides the Deity itself, the things we said in their proper place concerning the Infinity of the divine perfection teach us. A hollow little distinction between the infinity of perfection and the infinity of extension does not at all suffice to resolve these matters. Namely, the former could be ascribed to the world without prejudice to the latter. For when, as they contend, extension itself constitutes the essence of body, it becomes plain that the infinity of extension and of essence walk here with equal step. And since what is infinite in essence must necessarily also be such in all its attributes (which by their nature follow the condition of their subject), it appears that either no infinity or every kind of infinity must be ascribed to the world. But we have disputed at length about this by far the most grievous delusion in our Exercitatio de Infinito. There we set out fully, both what the mind of the new philosopher genuinely is on this point, and with what arguments he defends himself, and in how many ways the absurd dogma runs into the properties both of the Creator and of the creature, so that if we wished to add anything, we would be doing work already done.
XV.

units.la: Intra suos limites (ubicunque etiam locorum illi fuerint) coërcoërcita hujus Universi diffusione, cumque ea collatâ Divinæ potentiæ immensitate, quamvis rei finitæ perfectionem longissimè excedente, facilè apparet, potuisse Creatorem, si ita lubitum fuisset, majus fecisse hoc universum; cum quod majus minusve, quam reipsa est, non existat, res sit solo indifferenti Dei arbitratu definita. Atque eodem hoc fundamento ex mero naturalis rationis lumine solvi nequit dubitatio, num unius hujus mundi productione omne Creationis opus absolverit Deus; num verò alios etiam huic similes extra ejus fines constituerit? Quandoquidem enim saltem id potuit, ac noluisse ipsum, hoc universum per se non docet, neque ex ipsa Creationis natura, neque ex mundi creati contemplatione colligere datur, quam in partem liberrimam voluntatem hîc determinaverit Deus. Temerarius, fateor, est, quisquis plures rerum universitates asserit, quia quod asserit nullâ rationis specie firmare potest: maximè, cum præter Creationem hujus Cœli atque Terræ, omnisque qui in utroque existit exercitus, aliam nullam agnoscat Sacra Dei Pagina. Verum, câ sepositâ, neque is qui pluralitatem mundorum negat, ejus quod negat ullam, nisi negativam, rationem reddere valet. Qui autem, nec creari quidem alium mundum posse, præter eum qui existit, affirmat, haud leviter is in primæ causæ valentiam existit injurius, quando omnem ejus infinitatem operis unius finiti Creatione exhaustam esse, necesse habet profiteri.
units.tr: Within its own limits (wherever those limits may be placed), with the diffusion of this Universe thus confined, and that compared with the immensity of the divine power, which far exceeds the perfection of any finite thing, it is easily seen that the Creator could, had it so pleased him, have made this universe greater. For a greater or smaller world than the one that actually exists does not exist, so the thing is determined by the indifferent decision of God alone. On this same ground, the doubt cannot be resolved by the mere light of natural reason, whether God, by the production of this one world alone, completed the whole work of creation, or whether he also set up other worlds like this one beyond its bounds. For since he was at least able to do so, and the fact that he did not do so is not shown by this universe itself, nor can it be gathered either from the nature of creation or from the contemplation of the created world, in which direction God determined his most free will here. I admit that whoever asserts a plurality of universes of things is rash, because he cannot support what he asserts by any kind of reason, especially since the Sacred Page of God acknowledges no other creation besides the creation of this heaven and earth and the whole host that exists in both. But setting that aside, neither can he who denies a plurality of worlds give any reason for what he denies except a negative one. Yet he who affirms that another world cannot even be created beside the one that exists does not lightly do injury to the power of the first cause, since he is bound to profess that all its infinity of work has been exhausted in the creation of one finite thing.

units.la: Quam enim hic venantur contradictionem, ex eo quod se perspicuè intelligere affirmant, mundi hujus materiam jam occupare omnia omninò spatia, in quibus alii isti mundi esse deberent, ea nulla re verâ est; cum totum hoc sit purum præjudicium, natum ex crasso errore de infinita mundi extensione; quem jam notavimus. Levius est, quod de impossibili plurium mundorum sive contactu, sive distantia, adferunt. Etsi enim sese tangerent, haud ideò opinandum, eos hoc ipso fore ordinatos ad constituendum unum corpus harmonicum, cujus partes sint mutuo adjumento; quod tamen imprimis, ad constituendam naturam rei quæ ex aggregatione una est, requiritur. Et si distarent, nil vetat, ob eandem rationem, interjici corpus quodcunque tertium intermedium, ad neutrius extremi essen
units.tr: The contradiction which they hunt here, from the fact that they affirm they clearly understand that the matter of this world already occupies all the spaces in which other worlds ought to be, is in truth no contradiction at all. For this whole objection is pure prejudice, born of the gross error about the infinite extension of the world which we have already noted. Lighter still is what they bring forward about the impossibility of several worlds, whether touching or distant. For even if they were to touch one another, it is not therefore to be supposed that they would by that very fact be ordered to constitute one harmonious body, whose parts are mutually helpful, which nevertheless is required above all to constitute the nature of a thing that is one by aggregation. And if they were distant, there is nothing to prevent, for the same reason, some third intermediate body from being placed between them, so that neither extreme loses its essence

units.la: XVI. Difficultatum hic moveri solitarum amotio. tiam & integritatem ex ordinatione Creatoris pertinens. Quid si etiam nullo interposito corpore distarent? Nullum in eo contradictionis periculum; nisi quod isti sibi fingunt ex infantili praejudicio, dum à pueritia observarunt, corpora quaeque nobis obvia intergerino tertio ab alio separari. Ast hoc de natura distantiae ipsius esse, & non potius quid accidentarium, demonstrandum foret: qua de re alibi agendum ex professo. Omnium maximè clumbis est cavillatio ex voce Universi; quasi id, quippe complectens omnia, extra se quicquam existere non sinat. Certè Universum hic mundus est, quatenus compages est universorum corporum sibi ad sui integritatem debitorum. Jam verò tale quid ni maneat, etiamsi alia corporum qualiumcunque, sed ad mundi nostri constitutionem atque integritatem (cujus unica mensura existit Dei opificis idea & ordinatio) nil pertinentium, detur compages? Caeterum, cum absolutè loquendo ne mundorum quidem plurium Creatio contradictionem implicet, quanto minus negandum venit, Deum infinitum, si velit, creare posse alias adhuc rerum species, praeter illas finitas quae creatae hodiè existunt? Quo pacto id dubium, quin falsum, videri possit iis qui infinitam Numinis sufficientiam agnoscunt, nescio. Neque dicere juvat, eas non-productas rerum species clarâ ideâ nobis non intelligi: quis enim homuncio, sine sacrilegii nota, ausit suas ideas virtutis divinae facere normam, ultra quas nihil causa prima actuare queat? Sufficit, Opificem intelligere suarum facturarum rationes; creaturis suis eas imprimere cur debuerit, nulla causa est. Sed in Narratore nostro Confutato, sive Animadversionibus in Cel. Collegae D. Burmanni Narrationem de Controversiis nuper in Academia Ultrajectina motis §. 11. etiam de hoc nobis est actum.
units.tr: XVI. The removal of the difficulties usually raised here. ... and integrity pertaining to the ordering of the Creator. What if they were even distant with no body interposed? There is no danger of contradiction in that, except what they imagine to themselves from childish prejudice, since from boyhood they have observed that all bodies that meet us are separated from one another by some third thing in between. But it would have to be demonstrated that this belongs to the nature of distance itself and is not rather something accidental. That matter must be treated expressly elsewhere. Most absurd of all is the quibble drawn from the word Universe, as if the term, since it embraces all things, does not allow anything to exist outside itself. Certainly this world is the Universe, insofar as it is the compound of all bodies bound together as their integrity requires. But why should such a whole not remain, even if there were a compound of other bodies, of whatever kind, that pertain in no way to the constitution and integrity of our world (whose sole measure is the idea and ordinance of God the Maker)? Moreover, since, speaking absolutely, not even the creation of several worlds involves a contradiction, how much less must it be denied that God, being infinite, can, if he wishes, create still other species of things besides those finite ones which now exist as created? How this could seem doubtful, if not false, to those who acknowledge the infinite sufficiency of the Deity, I do not know. Nor is it helpful to say that those unproduced species of things are not understood by us through a clear idea. For what little man, without the stain of sacrilege, would dare to make his own ideas the rule of divine power, beyond which the First Cause could bring nothing into act? It is enough that the Maker understands the reasons of his works; why he ought to impress them on his creatures, there is no cause. But in our Narrator Refuted, or Animadversions on the Reverend colleague D. Burman's Narration concerning the Controversies recently stirred up in the University of Utrecht, §. 11, this too has been treated by us.

units.la: Priusquam finiam has de Creatione cogitationes, de Fine tanti operis paucula dicenda supersunt. Principalem illum atque supremum esse Divinae Majestatis per tam illustria infinitae sapientiae, potentiae, ac bonitatis documenta, manifestationem, arguit Dei in omni causarum genere primitas; quae non finit ob alium esse haec omnia, nisi ob ipsum à quo sunt omnia; ut ita, qui in causarum efficientium ordine prima exsistit cujusvis veritatis origo, idem sit in finium subordinatione ultimus mus bonitatis terminus, ipsumque summum bonum. Parùm huic veritati consonum est, quod alibi Cartesius: Puerile esset & absurdum, afferre in Metaphysicis, Deum, ad similitudinem hominis superbi, non habuisse alium finem in constituendo mundo, quam hunc ut laudaretur ab hominibus. Dura certè, imò nec[?] satis quidem pia, hæc est supremi Domini cum superbo homine comparatio absurdissima. Atqui, parum erat Atheismo tradidisse argumentum pro existentia Dei à causarum efficientium subordinatione petitum; pariter alterum ex simili finium serie deductum è medio tollendum fuit. Vicinus existit huic alter ejusdem error, quo negat conditi mundi finem subordinatum esse Hominem: etsi id tenuerint communi consensu sapientiores quivis, ipsi quoque Gentiles; quorum illustria hanc in rem testimonia adferre, prohibet brevitas. Et profectò, quid tum Creatoris sapientiæ, tum ipsarum rerum creatarum naturæ convenientius existit, quam cætera imperfectiora ordinata esse ad usum istius rei, quæ in omni creaturarum genere eminet tanquam perfectissima, qualis est homo? infrà cujus dignitatem longè subsidet quicquid in hoc Universo contemplationi nostræ est obvium. Maximè, cum unus homo sit, qui ex omni creaturarum coetu suam Deo Creatori laudem poterit accinere. Quid itaque pronius cogitare, quam ejus usibus omnia destinata esse, cujus solius animo atque ore ad Deum redire poterat suus ex opere creationis honor & gloria. Sed & exertim sic definit ipsius Conditoris vox, in Sacris ita de sui operis fine testantis, ut totum id hominem spectet & ad ipsum referatur; ne astris quidem, vastissimis illis & à terra nostra remotissimis corporibus, exceptis. Indè quoque omnia homini, angelis solis paululum inferiori, dicuntur subjecta scilicet homini, ad Dei imaginem, tale Dominium inferentem, condito; quo quando excidit, etiam universa creatura vanitati subjecta fuit; usque adeò, ut tota seculi hujus consummatio tantùm præstoletur beandorum hominum plenitudinem, obfirmatorum in peccatis poenas. Quid? quod ipse ordo, quem in formando homine servavit Creator, cæterorum omnium in hominis commodum ordinationem inferat; quatenus quæ in executione præcedunt, respectu eorum quæ ultimò sequuntur, medii ferè rationem hahabent. Vidit quodammodo harum consequentiarum vim, quam fusius prosequitur S. Codex, ex ipsa crepera naturae luce Metamorphoseon scriptor, cum canit: Sanctius his animal, mentisque capacius altae Deerat adhuc, & quod dominari in caetera posset. Natus homo est; &c. Quem Finxit in effigiem moderantum cunctia Deorum.
units.tr: Before I finish these thoughts on Creation, a few words remain to be said about the End of so great a work. That the principal and supreme end is the manifestation of the divine Majesty through such illustrious proofs of infinite wisdom, power, and goodness is shown by God's primacy in every kind of cause. He is not the end of all these things except as the one from whom all things are; so that he who stands as the origin of every truth in the order of efficient causes is also the last term of goodness in the subordination of ends, and the supreme good itself. What Descartes says elsewhere agrees little with this truth: It would be puerile and absurd to affirm in Metaphysics that God, in the likeness of a proud man, had no other end in constituting the world than that he might be praised by men. Certainly this comparison of the supreme Lord with a proud man is harsh, nay not even pious enough, and most absurd. Yet it was not enough to have handed over to atheism the argument for the existence of God drawn from the subordination of efficient causes; the other argument, deduced from a similar series of ends, had likewise to be removed from the midst. Close to this stands another error of the same kind, by which it is denied that Man is the subordinate end of the world created: although the wiser men of every sort, the Gentiles themselves included, have held this by common consent. Brevity forbids me to bring forward their illustrious testimonies on this point. And indeed, what is more fitting both to the wisdom of the Creator and to the nature of the created things themselves than that the other, more imperfect things were ordered to the use of that one which stands out in every kind of creature as most perfect, such as man is? Beneath his dignity lies far below whatever in this Universe is open to our contemplation. Especially since he is the one man who, out of the whole company of creatures, can sing his own praise and glory to God the Creator. What, then, could be thought more natural than that all things were destined for the uses of him alone, through whose mind and mouth alone the honour and glory of the work of creation could return to God? And indeed the voice of the Creator himself so defines this end, bearing witness in the Sacred Writings concerning the end of his work, that the whole of it looks to man and is referred to him; the stars alone are excepted, those vast bodies very remote from our earth. From this too it follows that all things are said to be subject to man, who is only a little lower than the angels, namely subject to man, made in the image of God, bearing such dominion; and when he fell from it, the whole creation also was subjected to vanity; so that the entire consummation of this age awaits only the fullness of the blessed men and the punishment of those hardened in sins. What more? The very order which the Creator observed in forming man implies the ordering of all other things for the benefit of man, insofar as what precedes in execution stands, with respect to what finally follows, almost in the relation of means. The writer of the Metamorphoses, from the very light of nature, saw in some measure the force of these consequences, which the Sacred Codex pursues more fully, when he sings: A more holy animal, more capable of lofty mind, was still lacking, one that could rule the rest. Man was born; etc. Whom he fashioned in the likeness of the gods who govern all things.

units.la: Tam nulla tamen haec omnia sunt Cartesio, ut qui quod adstruximus tuentur, eos de se superbe nimis sentire, pronuncict; cum haec sententia ei nequaquam sit vero simili, imo in physica consideratione ridicula & inepta. Et cur obsecro talis? Quia, inquit, non dubitamus, quae multa exstiterunt, vel olim extiterint, jamque esse desierint, quae nunquam ab ullo homine visa sunt aut intellecta, nunquamque ullum usum ulli praebuerunt. Subtilis equidem collectio! Quasi quae incognita existunt ideo sua careant utilitate, quin & necessitate quandoque, quia incognita! Millena nobis inscitis usum quotidie praestare longe maximum, nemo ignorat, nisi rei Medicae atque Physicae prorsus ignarus. Imo, si multa visa non sint aut intellecta, qua fide narratur, ea nullum omnino cuiquam mortalium, sive directum sive indirectum, sive proximum sive remotum, praestitisse usum? Assignet talia, si possit: si nequeat, quid praesumit judicare de rebus, earumque usu, quarum nullas habet ideas? Sed aliud pectore volvebat consilium, ad quod haec hypothesi praestruendus erat gradus. Animus erat mundum fabricare ex infinito vorticum numero coagmentatum, in quo plures forsan oberrent terrarum orbes, quam in nostra hac tellure vivunt homines. Et haec procul dubio ista sunt nunquam ab homine visa vel intellecta, quae nunquam ullum usum ulli praebuerunt; sed quae hoc loco proseri intempestivum videbatur. Id autem minime capio, quo sensu velit, esse in Ethicis pium, dicere, omnia a Deo propter nos facta esse, ut nempe tanto magis ad agendas ei gratias impellamur; ejusque amore incendamur. Frigida profecto pietas, imo vero mera superstitio, quae ad Deo gratias agendas impellit animum suppositionibus quibusdam superbis, nonverosimilibus, ridiculis, ineptis! Quid, quod alibi expresse sic instituat: Si concipiamus nihil esse extra coelos praeter spatia imagimaria, cœlosque omnes non nisi terrâ causâ factos esse, terram verò hominis; hinc fiet ut propendeamus ad cogitandum, terram hanc esse præcipuam nostram sedem, hacque vitâ melius nihil ad nos pertinere. Vol. I. Epist. VII. Ergò in Ethicis id dicere pium erit, quod idem per se comparatum est ad reddendos homines Epicureos! Imò, neque intelligo, quid Cartesiano homini multo plus solatii post hanc vitam futurum sit in istis extra cœlum nostrum circumactis vorticibus, quam in aliorum spatiis imaginariis. Nisi forte animulæ eorum vagulæ, postquam terram hanc tanquam sedem minus-præcipuam derelinquerunt, in hoc delicias sint habituræ, quod, ad instar comectarum, ex uno vortice in alium absque fine modo ac mensura sint trajiciendæ, ac sine quiete per peregrinos cœlos vagaturæ. O pulchras sedes, quas manibus defunctorum paravit Cartesianæ sapientiæ pietas!
units.tr: Yet these things are not so much to Descartes that he pronounces those who defend what we have asserted to be too proud of themselves, since this opinion is by no means likely to be true, and indeed in physical consideration ridiculous and foolish. And why, I beg you, is it so? Because, he says, we do not doubt that many things have existed, or once existed and have now ceased to be, which were never seen or understood by any man, and never offered any use to anyone. A subtle inference indeed! As if things that exist unknown therefore lack their usefulness, or even their necessity at times, simply because they are unknown! That thousands of unknown things furnish us daily with very great use, no one is ignorant except one utterly ignorant of medicine and physics. Indeed, if many things have not been seen or understood, on what grounds is it reported that they have offered no use at all to anyone, whether direct or indirect, near or remote? Let him name such things, if he can. If he cannot, on what basis does he presume to judge things and their use, of which he has no ideas at all? But he was turning over another plan in his mind, for which this hypothesis had to be laid as a step. His purpose was to fabricate a world put together from an infinite number of vortices, in which perhaps more earth-orbs wander than men live on this our earth. And these are without doubt the things never seen or understood by man, which never offered any use to anyone; but it seemed out of place to bring them forward at this point. I do not at all grasp, however, in what sense he wishes it to be pious in ethics to say that all things were made by God for our sake, namely so that we might be the more driven to give thanks to him and be kindled with his love. A cold piety indeed, or rather mere superstition, which drives the mind to give thanks to God by means of certain proud, unlikely, ridiculous, foolish suppositions! What of the fact that elsewhere he expressly lays it down thus: If we conceive that there is nothing outside the heavens except imaginary spaces, and that all the heavens were made for the earth's sake alone, and the earth for man's; hence it will come about that we incline to think this earth is our chief abode, and that nothing pertains to us better than this life. Vol. I, Letter VII. Therefore it will be pious in ethics to say what in itself tends to make men Epicureans! Indeed I do not understand what much greater comfort there will be for a Cartesian man after this life in those vortices whirled about outside our heaven, than in the imaginary spaces of others. Unless perhaps their little wandering souls, having left this earth as a less-chief abode, are going to find their delight in this: that, like comets, they must be carried from one vortex into another without end or measure, and wander without rest through foreign heavens. O fine abodes, which the piety of Cartesian wisdom has prepared for the departed!

units.la: XIX. Ex visibilibus creaturis majestatem Creatoris invisibilis venerari discit pia mens.
units.tr: XIX. From visible creatures a pious mind learns to venerate the majesty of the invisible Creator.

units.la: Verùm desino plura addere. Sic hîc altercandum, ne pietas amittatur. Quamobrem satius est parcius de hisce disputare, interim diligentius id agere, ut ad suos unaquæque, ad quos à Creatore Deo condita est, creatura fines diligenter ipso facto referatur. Sed quantum hac parte deficit etiam optimi cujusque cura! Scelus esse jam olim dixit Socrates, de creaturis agere, & Opificem omittere. Quis, ehcu! hoc crimine insons planè? Omnia propter hominem formata esse, allubescit facilè plerisque. Ast ipsum hominem ad hoc esse conditum, ut universa illa Deo Creatori suo reddat, se persuasum habere, quis est qui ipso opere testetur, ut oportet? Inexcusabiles pronunciat alibi Gentium Doctor, qui, quam ex creati mundi factura mente perspicere debuissent æternam Divinitatem & potentiam, cum debita gratiarum actione non fuerunt ritè venerati; quando, quem ignorare non potuerunt Creatorem, non glorificarunt. Utinam duntaxat in gentiles idololatras id quadret! & non peculiari quadam ratione in nostros quoque homines, qui quodcunque pulchrum ac delectabile occurrit in creaturis, à Creatore id descendisse parùm cogitant, deque eo ad Illius gloriam ordinando nil sunt solliciti. Etiam hi Idololatræ pessimi: bonitatem non-dependentem, quæ solius Dei est, adscribentes creaturis; atque ita incorruptibilis Numinis gloriam re ipsâ mutantes tantes in corruptibilis creaturæ similitudinem, atque huic servientes hunc in modum [?] Imò, præter Creatorem colunt creaturas, qui toti harum utilitati inhærentes, eis non ex Creatoris lege utuntur, sed suo quodam suuntur arbitrio, ingrati tantarum opum usufructuarii. Recurvæ nimiùm in terram animæ indignæ erecto vultu, quo sublimiora quam quæ præ pedibus sunt meditari monentur, cœlumque potius sublatis in altum oculis tueri, cumque qui creavit hæc omnia Deum. Ita fas erat publicam hanc Naturæ domum cogitare Dei Optimi Maximi Templum, divina omnipræsentia consecratum: cui pro ara, humanus animus; pro dedicandis muneribus, obviæ quæque naturæ opes; pro liturgo perpetuo, ipse homo, qui obsequioso sacrificio creaturas universas suo devoveat Creatori. Hoc intuitu quicunque contemplantur tantæ summæ opificium, non illi in externa templi specie atque apparatu hærent, sed piâ mente ad intimum ejusdem penetrant [?]; iisque solis occurrit hoc Universum, tanquam visibile invisibilis Majestatis monumentum. Beati ter & amplius, quels accessibile tantum sacrarium in quo fruuntur ineffabili voluptatis dulcitudine, quando mirantes [?] Deum, discunt indè, ut oportet, in tanta rerum utilitate Optimum, in tanta amplitudine Maximum, in tanto decore Pulcherrimum, in tanta varietate Ditissimum, in tanta vicissi tudine Constantissimum, in tanta earundem constantia Immortalem, investigare, agnoscere, colere, adorare, Cosmopœum. Juvat cum Regio Vate, de universis Creationis operibus, deque tota natura longè latèque homini tributaria, omnium Conditori lætanter sic paucis applaudere:
units.tr: But I will stop adding more. Thus we must not dispute here, lest piety be lost. Therefore it is better to discuss these matters more sparingly, and meanwhile to take greater care that each creature is diligently referred, by its very action, to the ends for which it was made by God the Creator. But how far even the care of the best men falls short in this respect! Socrates long ago said that it was a crime to treat of creatures and to omit the Maker. Who, alas, is entirely free of this charge? It readily pleases most people that all things were formed for the sake of man. But who bears witness by his very works, as he ought, that man himself was made for this purpose, to render all those things back to God his Creator? The Teacher of the Gentiles declares elsewhere that they are without excuse, who, though they ought to have perceived from the making of the created world the eternal Divinity and power, did not duly honour him with due thanksgiving, since they did not glorify the Creator whom they could not fail to know. Would that this applied only to the Gentile idolaters, and not in a peculiar way to our own people as well, who, whatever beautiful and delightful thing they meet with among creatures, think little that it has descended from the Creator, and are not concerned to direct it to his glory! These too are the worst idolaters: ascribing to creatures a goodness not dependent on another, which belongs to God alone; and so by their deeds changing the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible creatures, and serving these in this way [?]. Indeed they worship creatures besides the Creator, clinging wholly to their usefulness, and they use them not according to the law of the Creator but are carried along by some arbitrary will of their own, ungrateful users of such great riches. Souls too much bent down to the earth, unworthy of the upright face by which they are admonished to think of things higher than what lies at their feet, and to gaze rather upon heaven with eyes lifted on high, and upon God who made all these things. Thus it was fitting to regard this public house of Nature as the Temple of God, the Best and Greatest, consecrated by the divine omnipresence: with the human mind for its altar; with the riches of nature at hand for the offerings to be dedicated; with man himself as the perpetual minister, who by a dutiful sacrifice devotes all creatures to their Creator. Those who contemplate the workmanship of so great a Sum with this in view do not cling to the outward form and furnishings of the temple, but with a pious mind penetrate to its inmost part [?]; and to them alone this Universe presents itself as a visible monument of the invisible Majesty. Thrice blessed, and more, are they, who have access to this sanctuary, in which they enjoy the ineffable sweetness of delight, when, marvelling at God [?], they learn thence, as they ought, to search out, acknowledge, worship, adore, the Best in so great a usefulness, the Greatest in so great an extent, the Most Beautiful in so great an adornment, the Richest in so great a variety, the Most Constant in so great a succession of changes, the Immortal in so great a constancy of the same things, the Maker of the world. It pleases us, with the royal prophet, to applaud gladly, in few words, the Creator of all, concerning all the works of creation, and the whole of nature stretching far and wide, tributary to man:

units.la: O Domine! O magni Fabricator maxime Mundi,
units.tr: O Lord! O greatest Maker of the great world,

units.la: Quam celebre est toto nomen in orbe Tuum!
units.tr: How renowned is Your name throughout the whole earth!
When the mind gazes on the heavens, their order and beauty,
Which Your skilful fingers have fashioned;
When I behold the varied moon, and the fiery globes,
And the beautiful stars scattered over the bright sky:

units.la: Tunc ego: Quid sumus! Et pietas quæ tanta subegit,
units.tr: Then I say: What are we! And what piety has moved You so greatly,
That, mindful of man, You gave these things for human uses?

units.la: Quo Tibi tam potuit soboles humana placere, Ut res dilectas inter & ante loces! Das etenim facili dominetur in omnia nutu, Archetypi recipit dum simulacra Tui: Mille greges pecudum, genus omne volatile coeli, Squammigerum quicquid per mare sulcat aquas. O Domine! O magni Fabricator maxime Mundi, Quam celebre est totonomen in orbe Tuum!
units.tr: For You, how could the human offspring please You so much, that You place them among Your beloved things and before them! For You grant that he should rule over all things at a easy nod, while he receives the likenesses of Your archetype: a thousand flocks of cattle, every kind of bird of the air, whatever scaly creature furrows the waters of the sea. O Lord! O greatest Maker of the great world, how renowned is Your name throughout the whole earth!

units.la: EXERCITATIO VIGESIMA-QUARTA, DE DEO PROVIDENTE PER CONSERVATIONEM.
units.tr: EXERCITATION TWENTY-FOURTH, CONCERNING GOD PROVIDING BY CONSERVATION.
SUMMARY

units.la: I. Providentiae Divinae circa hoc Universum consideratio generalis. II. Prioris Providentiae actus, Conservationis, specialior explicatio. III.
