Eam positivum in creaturam durantem influxum notare, demonstratur. IV. Imo re ipsa esse quandam continuatam Creationem. V. Difficultatum quarundam hic obviarum solutio. VI. Qualescunque creaturas conservat Deus, influxu immediato, ac sibi proprio. VII. Quaecunque conservat Numen eadem annihilare, si velit, potest. VIII. Annihilatio latio nil positivi dicit, sed meram non-conservationem.
units.tr: I. A general consideration of the Divine providence concerning this universe. II. A more detailed explanation of the first act of providence, conservation. III. It is shown that conservation signifies a positive influx into the creature that endures. IV. Indeed, in fact, that conservation is a certain continued creation. V. The solution of certain difficulties met with here. VI. God conserves creatures of whatever kind by an immediate influx, and one that is his own. VII. God can, if he wishes, annihilate the things he conserves. VIII. Annihilation signifies nothing positive, but merely the non-conservation.

units.la: Ic fuit Creatio. Verùm non illâ solâ quicquid ex-tra se sese operatur causa prima absolvitur. Ergò cir-ca creaturas jam productas mox alter Dei actus contemplationi nostræ sese offert; ille nimirum, qui Providentiæ nomine vulgò venit. Actualis scilicet: vox enim ista frequenter etiam notat, tum Dei voluntatem quâ jam ante tempora seculorum rerum omnium futurarum rationes penes ipsum exactissimè definitæ extiterunt; tum etiam æternam earundem juxta decretum præscientiam. Nostræ hic consideracionis est utriusque illius in creatura, per creationem jam existente, executio: quæ quoniam in eventu æterni consilii intentioni ad amussim respondet, nil mirum si diversis cæterùm rebus idem commune nomen sit impositum. Generatim sumtum Providentiæ vocabulum hoc loco significat, Curam Dei Creatoris circa suas jam productas creaturas. Hanc qualemcunque admittere minimè quidem sufficit (quod fusius & per partes infrà ostendetur); interim universam qui negarunt vix extiterunt, nisi qui Deum mundi auctorem & opificem esse pariter negarunt. Tanta videlicet nexus necessitate ista duo cohærent, ut jam dudum communi consensu in axioma quasi abierit: Si Deus est, ergò mundus regitur Providentiâ. Epicuri gregem quod attinet, etiamsi viderint volucrint agnoscere Numinis existentiam, rectè tamen existimasse videntur eruditi, parùm revera eum ab Atheismo absuisse, ob negatam ejusdem Providentiam. Multò saniora hac parte extiterunt, & præ aliis pulcherrima, Stoicorum philosophemata; quæ procul dubio jam dudum applausum meruissent plerorumque, nisi obstitissent eorundem de Fato (sed malè intellecta; ut ego quidem arbitror) sententia: de qua forsan ex professo aliàs differemus. Nunc, si Deus Universi hujus Auctor sit, quam esse Exercitatione proximâ evicimus, quam pariter providens ejusdem Curator agnosci debeat, est ostendendum. Neque difficile est demonstrare, ex collata Divinæ naturæ excellentiâ cum multiplici creatæ rei imperfectione, non fine sine custode stare tantum opus , ut alibi Seneca. Verùm multo evidentior erit veritatis hujus evictio, si singulos potius Providentiæ Divinæ actus circa res ab ipsa pendentes consideraverimus.
units.tr: That was Creation. But the first cause does not complete all that it works outside itself by Creation alone. Therefore, concerning creatures already produced, another act of God presents itself to our contemplation, namely the one commonly called by the name of Providence. Actual, that is: for this word often denotes also both God's will, by which the reasons of all future things were most exactly determined in him before the ages of time, and his eternal foreknowledge of them according to his decree. It is the execution of both of these in a creature, now existing through creation, that concerns our consideration here. Since this execution corresponds exactly to the intention of the eternal counsel in its outcome, it is no wonder that the same common name has been given to two different things. Taken generally, the word Providence in this place means the care of God the Creator for the creatures he has already produced. It is not enough to admit this care in any form whatever (as will be shown more fully and in parts below); meanwhile, hardly any have existed who denied universal providence, except those who likewise denied that God is the author and maker of the world. These two things are joined by such a necessary bond that by common consent it has long since passed into something like an axiom: If God exists, then the world is governed by Providence. As for Epicurus' herd, although they were willing to acknowledge the existence of a Deity, learned men rightly judge that they were in truth hardly removed from atheism, because they denied his providence. The Stoic teachings were much sounder in this respect, and among the others the most beautiful; without doubt they would long since have won the applause of most people, had not their doctrine of Fate (though, as I think, misunderstood) stood in the way. Perhaps we shall treat that doctrine expressly at another time. Now it must be shown that, if God is the Author of this universe, as we proved in the preceding exercitation, he must likewise be acknowledged as its provident Curator. It is not difficult to demonstrate, from comparing the excellence of the divine nature with the manifold imperfection of created things, that so great a work cannot stand without a guardian, as Seneca says elsewhere. But the proof of this truth will be far clearer if we consider the individual acts of divine providence concerning things that depend on him.

units.la: In unaquaque re per Creationem jam producta duo observare licet, quorum alterum ab altero est diversissimum, Permanentiam ejus in existendo, & Activitatem ejusdem in operando. Secundum illa duplex occurrit distinctè notandus Providentiæ Divinæ actus, Conservatio & Gubernatio. Illa est efficax Providentiæ Divinæ actio, quâ Deus creaturas suas omnes atque singulas, quamdiu esse non desinunt, facit manere eas quæ sunt factæ per creationem. Quibusdam quidem Conservationis vocabulum hoc loco minus appositum videtur; quasi notet plurium causarum sociarum in eadem re servanda coöperationem : cum tamen solius Dei sit actio illa, de qua hîc sermo est. Sed pepercisse potuissent isti supervacuâ crisi, si attendere voluissent, rectè dici Conservationem, quasi servat.onem rei cum illa essentia, quàm jam ab initio sui per Creationem acceperat. Verum ad rem potius accedo. In qua concipienda nequid erremus, diligenter cavendum est, ut non hic intelligi putemus qualemcunque illam conservationem, vulgò sic dictam, quâ quid simpliciter non-destruit, quod destruere si voluisset, potuisset omninò. Ludunt hac vocis ambiguitate, qui, admittentes quasi Divinam conservationem, interim ad continuandam rem creatam in sua existentia nullum realem actum aut positivum influxum Dei requiri, arbitrantur, contendentes, sufficere puram destructionis negationem; sic ut creatura, postquam existere cœperit per creationem, ad porrò existendum usque adeò sibi sufficiat, ut nullo ad id indigeat u'lteriori Dei auxilio, sed mero duntaxat indultu, qui otiosè sinat eam manere quod est. Istis ut occurreremus, describebamus nos Conservationem, efficacem Dei actum, quo creaturam permanere re ipsâ facit. Planè ad instar Solis diem, dum durat, conservantis. Nequaquam is meridianum lumen tantùm nondestruit, sed virtute quam maximè positivâ, nec minus efficaci quam quâ primam auroram produxit, ad ejus conservationem operatur.
units.tr: In every thing already produced by Creation two things may be observed, of which one is quite different from the other: its permanence in existing, and its activity in operating. Corresponding to this twofold aspect, there appears a distinct act of divine providence to be noted: Conservation and Government. The former is the effective action of divine providence by which God causes all and each of his creatures, for as long as they do not cease to be, to remain what they were made by creation. For some, the word Conservation seems less appropriate in this place, as if it signified a cooperation of several co-operating causes in the thing to be preserved; yet the act we are discussing here belongs to God alone. But those men could have spared themselves this superfluous quibble had they been willing to notice that Conservation is rightly so called as if it were a keeping (servatio) of the thing together with (cum) that essence which it had received from the beginning through creation. But I come rather to the matter itself. In conceiving it, we must take care not to suppose that the kind of conservation here meant is that common so-called conservation by which something merely does not destroy what, if it had wished to destroy it, it could have destroyed altogether. Those who, while admitting a kind of divine conservation, nevertheless think that no real act or positive influx of God is required to continue a created thing in its existence, play with this ambiguity of the word, contending that the mere negation of destruction is sufficient. Thus a creature, once it has begun to exist through creation, is so far sufficient to exist further that it needs no further help from God, but only a bare permission which idly allows it to remain what it is. To meet these men, we have described Conservation as an effective act of God by which he really makes the creature to remain. It is just like the sun conserving the day while it lasts: it does not merely fail to destroy the midday light, but by a power that is most positive, and no less effective than that by which it produced the first dawn, it works for its conservation.

units.la: Suppeditat huic nostræ assertioni fundamenta firmissima ipsa creaturarum rerum in suo esse permanentia, si jus tantum imperfectiones ritè cogitemus. Eam & dependentem esse, & contingentem, & successivam, res ipsa clamat, nec quisquam negaverit, qui creatam non negaverit. Sed & certum est, rei cujuscunque in suo esse permanentiam haud esse omninò nihil: sic enim res nihil fieri inciperet, simulac durare inciperet; quo nihil fingi potest absurdius. Est itaque duratio verum aliquid ac reale. Neque hoc tantum, sed & continuata duratio à primo ejusdem momento realiter est distincta; quandoquidem certum est, rem aliquam durationis suæ initium accipere potuisse, ut tamen ea, quousque prolongari posset, non prolongetur. Quandoquidem autem jam sæpius demonstravimus, nequicquam quod spirat indepéndentiam creaturæ tribui posse, clarum est, permanentiam in existendo, quæ sit aliquid verum & reale, in ea locum habere non posse, nisi ab independenti Deo, tanquam à vera & reali causa, per veram & realem influxum, procedat. Hic verò influxus est ipsa, quam explicuimus, Conservatio. Contingentiam creaturarum ratione durationis si attendas, idem suadet eadem. Nimirum, quod contingenter durat, per sese non magis est determinatum ad permanendum in suo esse, quam ad non-permanendum. Si enim ex se ad permanendum sit determinatum, non jam contingenter durat, sed necessariò. Quod si non ex intrinseca necessitate res duret, utique causæ alicujus influxui tribuendum erit quod duret. At cujus? nisi illius, quæ ut rem possibilem & ex se non-existentem per creationem fecit existere, ita & eandem contingentem & ex se non-durantem faciat durare. Cum durationis contingentia si junxerimus ejusdem successivum per partes lapsum, pulchra imprimis indè resultat argumentatio. Nempè, momenta durationis quæ in re contingente & successiva occurrunt, ex se nullam inter se connexionem habere, multo minus alterum eorum in alterum influere posse, facilè ostenditur. Certè, non ideo nunc sum, quia ante horam fui; neque ero post horam, quia jam sum × aliàs in durando contingens non forem. Iterùm, ob successivum durationis meæ lapsum, non ero post horam quod ero, nisi quod nunc sum esse desiero; neque sum quod nunc sum, nisi quod ante horam fui esse desierim. At verò, quod fuit, & jam non est, non erit, cum non erit id quod jam est : quodque jam est, mox non erit, cum non erit id quod jam est, vi ejus quod jam est, esse non potest causa illius quod mox erit. Ecce ! per se insufficiens est ad durandum vel per momentum, quicquid durat permanentiâ contingenti ac successiva. Necessaria ergò est vis externæ causæ, quæ ut suam durationem perfectissimo modo ex se esse possidet, ita durationis cujusvis alterius extra se existat fons & origo, per verum & realem, de quo loquimur, Conservationis influxum.
units.tr: The very permanence of created things in their being supplies the firmest foundations for this assertion of ours, if we rightly consider their imperfections alone. The thing itself proclaims that this permanence is dependent, contingent and successive, and no one who denies that a creature is created will deny this. But it is also certain that the permanence of any thing in its being is not altogether nothing: for in that case a thing would begin to become nothing as soon as it began to endure, and nothing can be imagined more absurd. Duration is therefore something true and real. And not only that, but continued duration is really distinct from its first moment; for it is certain that a thing could have received a beginning of its duration, yet it is not prolonged as far as it could be prolonged. Since, moreover, we have often shown already that independence cannot be ascribed to a creature, it is clear that permanence in existing, which is something true and real, cannot have a place in it unless it proceeds from the independent God, as from a true and real cause, through a true and real influx. And this influx is precisely the Conservation we have explained. If you consider the contingency of creatures with respect to their duration, the same conclusion follows. For what endures contingently is not, of itself, any more determined to remain in its being than to not remain. For if it were determined of itself to remain, it would not endure contingently but necessarily. And if a thing does not endure by an intrinsic necessity, it must necessarily be attributed to the influx of some cause that it endures. But of what cause? Surely of that one which, as it made a thing that was possible and not existing of itself to exist through creation, so also makes that same contingent and not self-enduring thing to endure. If we join to the contingency of duration its successive passing by parts, a fine argument results from this. Namely, it is easily shown that the moments of duration which occur in a contingent and successive thing have no connection among themselves of their own nature, much less can one of them flow into another. Certainly, I am not now because I was an hour ago; nor shall I be after an hour because I am now, otherwise I should not be contingent in enduring. Again, because of the successive passing of my duration, I shall not after an hour be what I shall be, unless I cease to be what I now am; nor am I what I now am, unless I have ceased to be what I was an hour ago. But what has been and now is no more, will not be, since it will not be what now is; and what now is will soon not be, since it will not be what now is. By the power of what now is, it cannot be the cause of what will soon be. Behold: whatever endures with a contingent and successive permanence is insufficient of itself to endure even for a moment. A force of an external cause is therefore necessary, which, as it possesses its own duration from itself in the most perfect manner, so it exists outside itself as the source and origin of every other duration, through the true and real influx of Conservation of which we speak.

units.la: Ex demonstratis abundè liquet, minimè superfluam esse hanc, de qua locuti fuimus, conservandi actionem : quod opinantur, qui contendunt, unamquamque rem per seipsam id omne quod illi semel datum fuit per Creationem retinere facilè posse, etiamsi nihil amplius in eam conferatur, modò tantum non auferatur quod datum jam antè fuit. In cujus sententiæ confirmationem ajunt, frustrà ac nullâ ratione urgente, quin absurdè, poni actionem novam ac realem, cujus nullum effectum proprium ac positivum potest assignari. Verùm ex dictis totum hoc prorsùs corruit. Etiamsi enim cuique creaturæ per Creationem simul & semel sua detur existentia ; duratio tamen ejusdem, quam successivam esse jam diximus, quemadmodum, ob ipsum illum successivum sui lapsum, simul & semel existere non potest, ita ea unicâ momentaneâ actione simul & semel secundum se totam in creaturam quampiam conferri non potest. Quapropter, ad ponendam continuatam creaturæ existentiam, opus omninò est continuatâ productione ; id est, Conservatione. Consequenter, proprium ac specificum Conservationis effectum est rei conservatæ existentia ; non quatenus primum ex nihilo prodiit (sic ad Creationem pertinet) sed in quantum ultra primum illud emersionis suæ ex nihilo initium longius longiusque extenditur. Atque hanc ob causam rectè dictum fuit, Conservationem re ipsâ nihil aliud esse quam Creationem continuatam. Quæ enim Dei actio Creatio dicitur, in quantum existere facit, quod antè non erat, eadem illa Conservationis nomine venit, quatenus ejusdem generis influxu atque efficaciâ id permanere facit in suo esse, quod quidem antè extitit, sed quod absque continuato hoc influxu jam non amplius extitiffet, verum in pristinum suum nihilum, ex quo per Creationem emerserat, fuisset relapsurum.
units.tr: From what has been demonstrated it is abundantly clear that this action of conserving, of which we have spoken, is by no means superfluous. Those who contend that each thing can easily retain by itself all that was once given to it through Creation, even if nothing more is conferred on it, provided only that what was already given is not taken away, think otherwise. In confirmation of this opinion they say that a new and real action is posited to no purpose and for no pressing reason, indeed absurdly, when no proper and positive effect of it can be assigned. But from what has been said, all this utterly collapses. For even if existence is given to each creature through Creation, at once and in a single act, its duration, which we have already said is successive, cannot be conferred on it all at once by that single momentary action, just as it cannot exist all at once because of its own successive lapse. Therefore, to posit the continued existence of a creature, there is absolutely need of continued production, that is, of Conservation. Consequently, the proper and specific effect of Conservation is the existence of the conserved thing: not insofar as it first came forth from nothing (this pertains to Creation), but insofar as its existence is extended longer and longer beyond that first beginning of its emergence from nothing. And for this reason it has been rightly said that Conservation is really nothing other than Creation continued. For the action of God which is called Creation, insofar as it makes to exist what previously was not, is called by the name of Conservation insofar as, by an influx and efficacy of the same kind, it makes that persist in its being which indeed previously existed, but which, without this continued influx, would no longer have existed, and would have relapsed into its former nothingness, from which it had emerged through Creation.

units.la: Continuatam Creationem dicebam Conservationem; non repetitam : ne quis hic alternationem quandam rei existentis atque nihili sibi imaginetur, quasi hoc momento res creata esse ex sese desinat, mox vero sequenti momento nova creatione à Deo reproducatur ? idque toties quoties. Ut abfurdiffimus hic conceptus est, ita nihil is habet commune cum nostra jam explicata de Conservatione sententia. Multò minus difficilis est difficultas alia, petita ab artificibus, quorum imprimis laudatur industria, fi struant machinas, quibus manum admovere ad earundem conservationem nihil est necesse. Undè arguunt, minorem longè agnosci Dei quam hominum sapientiam ac potentiam, nisi fateamur, cum saltem producere posse creaturas, quæ ipsæ per sese subsistere queant, solo Numinis indultu, citra ullum istiusmodi continuatum Conservationis influxum. Sed non attendunt isti, quam, quæ duo tanquam paria hic componunt, toto cœlo revera sint disparia. Dedero quod ipsi contendunt; fi machinæ cujufpiam à suo opifice tantam esse dependentiam demonstraverint, quanta creaturæ cujuscunque est à suo Creatore. Profecto, uti fuperemineutis perfectionis atque excellentiæ nota est, res etiam perfectiffimas à fui tanquam causæ efficientis influxu habere pendentes omni modo (tantum fi id contingat absque labore & defatigatione illius à quo pendent) ita non absque ingenti tantæ perfectionis abnegatione hac fe prærogativâ exueret causa perfectiffima. Exueret autem re verâ, fi quid tale produceret, quod perpetuâ suâ manutenentiâ quamdiu existit non indigeret. Dixi, fi fine labore id fiat & defatigatione: absque qua quatenus artifex in rem artefactam nec influit nec influere potest, industriæ alicujus atque peritiæ argumentum exiftit, opera fabricare, quæ quam diutissimè per sese subsistant & durent citra architecti fui manum atque curam. Sed quid hæc omnia ad illum mundi custodem attinent, qui nullâ unquam operis magnitudine distrahitur aut fatigatur, cujusque activitas idcirco non absque contumeliæ nota cum laborioso nostrorum fabrorum conamine confertur.
units.tr: I was calling Conservation continued Creation, not repeated Creation; lest anyone here imagine a certain alternation of existing and nothing, as if at one moment the created thing ceased of itself to exist, and then in the following moment it were reproduced by God through a new creation, and that as often as you like. As this notion is most absurd, so it has nothing in common with our doctrine of Conservation as now explained. Far less difficult is another objection, drawn from craftsmen, whose industry is especially praised when they build machines to which there is no need to put a hand for their conservation. Hence they argue that the wisdom and power of God are acknowledged to be far less than those of men, unless we grant that God can produce creatures which can subsist through themselves, by the sole grant of the Deity, without any such continued influx of conservation. But these people do not notice how far apart the two things they put together as if they were equals really are, by the whole breadth of heaven. Let me grant what they contend, namely, that they have shown a machine to depend on its maker to the same degree that any creature depends on its Creator. Indeed, just as dependence on an efficient cause is a mark of supereminent perfection, and things most perfect also depend in every way on their cause (provided this happens without labour and fatigue on the part of him on whom they depend), so the most perfect cause would not, without a great denial of such perfection, strip itself of this prerogative. It would indeed strip itself, if it produced something that did not need its perpetual upholding as long as it exists. I said, provided this happens without labour and fatigue: for without this, insofar as the artisan neither influences nor can influence the artefact, it is a proof of some industry and skill to make works which subsist and endure as long as possible through themselves, without the hand and care of their architect. But what do all these things have to do with that guardian of the world, who is never distracted or wearied by any magnitude of work, and whose activity is therefore not compared, without a mark of insult, with the laborious effort of our craftsmen?

units.la: Ostensa sic est Conservationis à nobis descriptæ veritas non tantum, sed & necessitas. Quæ quia se extendit ad omnia quæ in esse successivo perseverant, non erit opus ambulare per singulas rerum conservatarum classes. Quæcunque durant alia à Deo, eidem dependenti contingenti ac successivæ durationi subjiciuntur ex æquo omnia, atque ideò pari virtute Dei, ut Creatoris, sic Conservatoris, ad existentiam sui indigent. Magna illa fuerint num parva, visia num pretiosa, nil attinet; cum nulla excellentia tam magna existat quæ hanc dependentiam transcendat, nulla vilitas tam parva quæ infra eandem subsidat. Quin tantum abest, ut res nobis minimi momenti visæ ab hac Conservatione excipi debeant, ob abjectam sui conditionem, ut, si quod majus aut minus hic locum habere posset (utì non potest in cis, quæ quantum habent entitatis tantundem habent dependentiæ) quo quid existit imperfectius, eo minus id sibi sufficere primæque causæ sustentatione carere posse, cogitandum foret. Porrò, cum cum in modum nulla creatura abalia pendeat aut pendere queat, quo ipsæ omnes pendent à Deo, facilè patet hunc actum conservandi solius Dei esse privilegium. Neque de eodem dubitare sinunt quæ de Conservationis cum Creatione identitate jam disputavimus: ex qua fluit, vel Conservare non posse creaturam; vel, si conservare possit, etiam creare posse. Atquì creare non posse, suo loco satis efficaciter evicimus. Etiam quidem nonnunquam creatura alteram conservare dicitur, vel quatenus eam non-destruit, vel in quantum particulæ quæpiam unius in locum particularum dissipatarum alterius substituuntur (quod fieri quotidiè, observamus in corporum illorum continuatione quæ alimento indigent) sed quam hæc nulla fit ejusdem ordinis cum illa de qua hic agimus Dei Conservatione, nemo vel leviter ad antè tradita attendens ignorare potest. Undè intelligitur, omnem Conservationem, si spectes modum operationis divinæ, immediatam semper esse: etiamsi ratione causarum secundarum, quarum usum qualemcunque, eo quo jam dictum est modo, admittit aliquando, aliquando omninò præterit Deus, in Mediatam & Immediatam dispesci soleat.
units.tr: Thus the truth, and indeed the necessity, of the Conservation described by us has been shown. Since it extends to all things which persist in successive being, there is no need to go through each class of conserved things one by one. Whatever things endure other than God are all equally subject to a dependent, contingent and successive duration, and therefore, by the same power of God, as Creator and likewise as Conserver, they all need him for their existence. Whether those things are great or small, precious or cheap, does not matter; for no excellence is so great that it transcends this dependence, and no baseness so small that it sinks below it. Indeed, so far is it from being the case that things which seem to us of least moment should be excepted from this Conservation because of their abject condition, that, if any greater or lesser distinction could have a place here (as it cannot in things which have as much dependence as they have being), one would have to think that the less perfect a thing is, the less it can suffice for itself and be without the support of the First Cause. Moreover, since no creature depends on another in the way that all of them depend on God, or can so depend, it is easily clear that this act of conserving is the sole privilege of God. Nor do the things we have already discussed about the identity of Conservation with Creation allow us to doubt this: from which it follows that either a creature cannot conserve, or, if it could conserve, it could also create. But that it cannot create we have sufficiently and effectively proved in its place. It is true that sometimes one creature is said to conserve another, either insofar as it does not destroy it, or insofar as some particles of one are substituted in place of particles dissipated from another (which we observe happening daily in the continuation of those bodies which need food). But that this is not of the same kind as that Conservation of God of which we are speaking, no one can fail to know, even if he attends only slightly to what was handed down above. Hence it is understood that all Conservation, if you look at the mode of divine operation, is always immediate; although, by reason of secondary causes, whose use of whatever sort God sometimes admits in the way already stated and sometimes altogether passes over, it is customarily divided into Mediate and Immediate.

units.la: Istud denique probè tenendum est, Conservationem, non minus
units.tr: Finally, this must be held firmly: that Conservation, no less

units.la: VI. Qualescunque creaturas conservat Deus, influxu immediato, ac sibi proprio.
units.tr: VI. God conserves creatures of whatever kind by an immediate influence, which is his own.

units.la: VII. Quæcunque minus quam Creationem, omnemque aliam actionem Dei ad extra, liberrimam esse ac purè arbitrariam; quandò perfectissima independentis causæ natura postulat, ut non diutius conservare teneatur, quam quo usque lubuerit. Neque mirum; cùm ad Entis primi perfectionem nequaquam pertineat continuata suarum creaturarum existentia. Quamobrem quâ facilitate omnia creavit olim Deus, quàque etiamnum ea conservat, eádem, si velit, quicquid præter se existit abolere potest. Neque, si conservare aliquid desineret Numen, quicquam idcirco decederet illius vel constantiæ vel immutabilitati; quandoquidem illis non magis adversatur rei existentis abolitio, quam nova rei nondum existentis productio: quæ quo pacto cum immutabilitate consistat, quando egimus de Creatione, vidimus. Mira hinc semper mihi visa fuit illa Cartesii collectio, quâ ex Divina immutabilitate eandem motûs quantitatem in hoc universo conservari debere concludit. Gravius tamen est, quod contendunt hodiè multi ex ista cavea Philosophi, Deum nec universum hoc totum, nec partem aliquam illius, annihilare posse. Et cur nequeat? Ne spatiis imaginariis fortè fiat locus; ac pulcherrima ista mundi, tanquam nullos extensionis fines habentis, idea periclitetur. Sed jubet brevitas mittere dogma, quod penitus abnegat liberrimum Dei Conservatoris in rem à se conservatam dominium.
units.tr: VII. Whatever is less than Creation, and every other outward action of God, is wholly free and purely arbitrary; since the most perfect nature of an independent cause requires that it is not bound to conserve anything for longer than it pleases. Nor is this surprising, since the continued existence of his creatures by no means pertains to the perfection of the First Being. Therefore, by the same ease with which God once created all things, and by which he still conserves them, he can, if he wishes, abolish whatever exists besides himself. Nor, if God were to cease conserving anything, would anything of his constancy or immutability thereby be lost; since the abolition of an existing thing is no more opposed to these than the new production of a thing not yet existing. How this agrees with immutability, we have seen when we treated of Creation. Hence that famous inference of Descartes has always seemed to me remarkable, by which from the divine immutability he concludes that the same quantity of motion ought to be conserved in this universe. More serious, however, is what many philosophers today, coming out of that same cage, contend: that God can annihilate neither this whole universe nor any part of it. And why should he be unable? Perhaps lest room be made for imaginary spaces, and that beautiful idea of the world, as having no limits of extension, be endangered. But brevity bids us pass over a dogma which utterly denies the most free dominion of God the Conserver over what he conserves.

units.la: Cæterùm cum Annihilationis mentionem feci, minimè per eam actum aliquem positivum intellectum volui; qualem quidam eam habent: sed perperam. Revera enim in ejusmodi conceptu tacitè supponitur, ac si in creatura aliquid sit, quod à mero Conservationis influxu non pendeat. Si enim pendeat, utique tantùm cessante influxu isto, cessabit existere ejus effectum, id est, creatura hactenus conservata. Quare superfluus planè est positivus annihilandi actus. Imò & absurdus. Quo pacto enim quo nihil planè ponitur, actus positivus dici potest? Et quis nisi conceptu monstrifico cogitet, perfectissimum agens omnipotenti suo influxu producere plane nihil? Rectius itaque sentiunt, qui opinantur, ad Annihilationem nil prorsus pertinere præter purum causæ primæ non-influxum. Scilicet, ut ante mundum conditum præter Deum nihil erat, tantùm quia Deus extra
units.tr: Moreover, when I mentioned annihilation, I did not mean by it any positive act, as some understand it, but wrongly so. For in such a concept it is tacitly assumed that there is something in a creature that does not depend on the mere influx of conservation. If it did depend on it, then, once that influx ceased, its effect, that is, the creature hitherto conserved, would certainly cease to exist. So a positive act of annihilating is plainly superfluous. Indeed it is absurd as well. For how can an act be called positive when it posits absolutely nothing? And who would think that the most perfect agent, by his almighty influx, produces absolutely nothing, unless he has a monstrous concept in mind? Those who hold that annihilation involves nothing at all beyond the mere non-influx of the first cause judge more rightly. Just as, before the world was made, nothing existed besides God, only because God worked nothing outside himself,

units.la: VIII. Annihilatio nil positivi dicit, sed meram non-conservationem.
units.tr: VIII. Annihilation signifies nothing positive, but merely non-conservation.

units.la: tra se nihil operabatur; ita quoque nunc, si duntaxat Deus extra se operari desineret, nihil eorum quae ante exịstebant existeret, redirentque in nihilum, quae fuerant quondam nihil. Ut Annihilatio sit re vera non-actio, & quaedam quasi nonConservatio. Prorsus se res habet quemadmodum in aeris nostri, quae nocte accidit, obtenebratione. Nullam ea arguit luminis diurni, quod ante extitit, per positivam actionem solis abolitionem; sed sufficit hujus in nostrum hemisphaerium merus noninfluxus, non-illuminantio.
units.tr: ...outside himself. So too now, if God merely ceased to work outside himself, nothing of those things that existed before would exist, and those things that once were nothing would return to nothing. Annihilation is thus in truth a non-action, a kind of non-conservation. The matter stands just as with the darkening of our air that comes on at night. That darkening does not indicate any positive action of the sun abolishing the daylight that existed before; the mere non-influx of the sun's light, its failure to illuminate our hemisphere, is enough.

units.la: EXERCITATIO VIGESIMA-QUINTA ET ULTIMA, DE DEO PROVIDENTE PER GUBERNATIONEM. SUMMARIUM.
units.tr: EXERCITATION TWENTY-FIFTH AND LAST, CONCERNING GOD'S PROVIDENCE THROUGH GOVERNANCE. SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Alter Providentiae actus, Gubernatio, meditationis difficillimae ac periculosae. II. Error afferentium, solum Deum omnia, creaturas nihil operari. III. Alter error illi oppositus, nullum Dei in operantes creaturas influxum agnoscens. IV. Vera Dei efficientia in causarum secundarum actiones asserta: V. Atque a difficultatibus quibusdam praecipuis vindicata. VI. Utriusque causae, primae & secundae, eadem esse docetur in effectu quopiam producendo actio. VII. Dubiorum in hac sententia occurrentium brevis solutio. VIII. Tres hujus Providentiæ quasi actus, Præcursus, Concursus, & Gubernatio strictè dicta. IX. Virium ad operandum largitio ad hos Providentiæ actus neque sufficit, neque pertinet. X. Præcursus quid, & quo usque actione creaturæ prior? XI. Præcursus Divini actionem creatam prædeterminantis necessitas demonstrata. XII. Influxus Dei generalis & determinabilis aliorum quam sit non uno modo in Deum contumeliosus? XIII. Præmotionis Dei efficacis cum libertate creaturæ conciliandæ difficultas unde potissimum oriunda? XIV. Duplex in hanc rem prænotanda magni momenti observatio. XV. Creatæ causæ libertas, uti non indépendens, ita nec prorsus indifferens, statui potest. XVI. Alterius causæ veram libertatem cum determinatione alterius consistere, & ex natura rei, & ex adversa hypothesi ipsa, docetur. XVII. Prædeterminans Providentia neque Deum peccati auctorem statuit, neque peccantem creaturam excusat. XVIII. Eadem neque Deum injustitiæ arguit, neque causarum secundarum potentiæ activæ præjudicat. XIX. Concursus Dei agnoscendus tanquam causæ totalis, immediatæ, & principalis. XX. Concursu Dei continuato indiget creatura quamdiu in operando perseverat. XXI. Gubernantis Providentiæ Divinæ necessitas paucis demonstrata. XXII. Ea ad quasvis creaturarum actiones extendenda; etiam minimas, contingentes, liberas, malas. XXIII. Gubernatio Dei tota sanctissima, independens, irresistibilis, sapientissima, constantissima. XXIV. Providentiæ Divinæ in Ordinariam & Extraordinariam; item, in
units.tr: I. The second act of Providence, governance, is a most difficult and hazardous subject of meditation. II. The error of those who hold that God alone does all things and creatures do nothing. III. The opposite error, which acknowledges no influx of God into creatures that act. IV. The true efficiency of God is asserted in the actions of secondary causes. V. And is defended against certain chief difficulties. VI. The same action of the first and second causes is taught in producing any given effect. VII. A brief solution of the doubts arising in this opinion. VIII. The three quasi-acts of this Providence: Precursus, Concursus, and governance strictly so called. IX. The bestowal of powers for acting belongs neither sufficiently nor properly to these acts of Providence. X. What is Precursus, and how far is it prior to the action of the creature? XI. The necessity of a divine Precursus that predetermines the created action is demonstrated. XII. In how many ways is a general and determinable influx of God, as others conceive it, insulting to God? XIII. From what source does the difficulty of reconciling the efficacious premotion of God with the freedom of the creature chiefly arise? XIV. A twofold observation of great importance to be noted beforehand on this matter. XV. The freedom of the created cause may be established as neither wholly independent nor altogether indifferent. XVI. That the true freedom of one cause consists together with the determination of another is taught both from the nature of the thing and from the adverse hypothesis itself. XVII. Predetermining Providence neither makes God the author of sin nor excuses the sinning creature. XVIII. The same does not charge God with injustice, nor prejudice the active powers of secondary causes. XIX. The concursus of God must be acknowledged as that of a total, immediate, and principal cause. XX. The creature needs the continued concursus of God for as long as it persists in acting. XXI. The necessity of governing divine Providence is demonstrated briefly. XXII. It is to be extended to all actions of creatures, even the smallest, contingent, free, and evil. XXIII. The governance of God is wholly most holy, independent, irresistible, most wise, and most constant. XXIV. The division of Providence into ordinary and extraordinary; likewise into

units.la: Realem & Moralem, divisio. XXV. Moralis Providentiæ consideratio unicum genuinæ Philo- sophiæ Moralis Fundamentum. XXVI. Trac- tatus de Deo, ejusque Providentia, Epilo- gus.
units.tr: Real and Moral Division. XXV. The consideration of moral Providence is the sole genuine foundation of moral philosophy. XXVI. Epilogue of the treatise on God and his Providence.

units.la: ALTERUM Divinæ Providentiæ actum transeo, sive ad curam Dei circa rerum creatarum activitatem, Gubernationem puta; sumtâ voce generaliori significatu: nam & aliàs specialius aliquam quasi hujus Providentiæ partem notare solet. Quæ eadem ambiguitas in vocabulo Concursus observanda: uti ex infrà dicendis intelligetur. Attentione verò attentissimâ ac multo majori hic opus erit, quam in ullo capite de Deo hactenus tractato; tam ardua & periculi plena est hæc meditatio. Nimirum, vix imò vix concipiendæ alicui activitati par est nostra cogitatio, quam non exigat ad actionum quas in nobismet ipsis deprehendimus mensuram. Atquì illæ se-se hic nobis offerunt viæ, quæ quantum cœlum tellure nostrâ est altius, tantùm exi-stunt viis nostris sublimiores. Quamobrem quisquis curâ minus circumspectâ ac pede parum stabili incomprehensibilis mysterii altitudinem conscendere nititur, etiam ex levissimo lapsu præceps devolvitur in errores profundissimos; quorum quidem initia primâ specie apparent tenuia, incrementa verò exi-stunt tanta, ut nullo unquam dogmate purioris rei Theologicæ facies conspurcata fuerit fœdius, quam perperam intellectâ hac Providentiæ divinæ parte. Est hæc re verâ hæresium quarumcumque corculum: quandoquidem una fermè omnium summa exi-stit, ex impiis corruptæ rationis elementis hanc saniorem impugnare doctrinam; quâ vitiatâ facilis via est, ad profanandum universum divinarum perfectionum sacrarium, eumque obtrudendum Deum, qui reipsâ iners atque impotens prorsùs sit idolum. Ex adverso, nulla æquè pia est de Numine persuasio, quam quod ejusdem provido consilio & efficaci manu regatur omnis qua latè patet universi machina. Hic nu-di deus & medulla est puriorum de Deo cogitationum; absque quo nunquam erit, ut quis ritè agnoscat & veneretur adorandam supremi Regis majestatem. Ejus gratiâ freti tantarum rerum meditationem aggredimur: sed modestam; quando hic tutius est humi serpere, quam in sublimi pati vertiginem.
units.tr: I pass over the second act of divine Providence, namely God's care for the activity of created things, which is to say governance, taking the word in its more general sense, since elsewhere it is customary to denote by it some more specific part of this Providence. The same ambiguity must be observed in the word concursus, as will be clear from what is said below. Here, however, much more attentive and careful thought will be required than in any chapter on God treated so far, so arduous and full of danger is this meditation. Indeed, our thought is scarcely, or rather hardly, equal to conceiving any activity that does not demand the measure of the actions we find in ourselves. Yet the paths that present themselves here are as much higher than our paths as heaven is higher than our earth. Therefore, whoever with careless attention and an unsteady foot tries to climb the height of an incomprehensible mystery is hurled headlong, even by the slightest slip, into the deepest errors. Their beginnings at first sight seem slight, but their growth is so great that no purer theological matter has ever been defiled more foully than by this part of divine Providence when misunderstood. This is in truth the little heart of all heresies, for nearly the whole sum of them amounts to this: to attack this saner doctrine with the impious elements of corrupted reason. Once this is corrupted, there is an easy way to profane the whole sanctuary of the divine perfections and to thrust upon us a God who is in reality an idol, utterly inert and powerless. On the contrary, no conviction about the Deity is as pious as that the whole machine of the universe, however widely it extends, is ruled by his provident counsel and efficacious hand. Here is the very core and marrow of purer thoughts about God; without it no one will ever rightly acknowledge and worship the majesty of the supreme King. Relying on his grace, we undertake the meditation of such great matters, but a modest one, since here it is safer to creep along the ground than to suffer vertigo on high.

units.la: Intelligimus per hunc Providentiæ actum, omnem illum causæ primæ influxum, quem præbet ad quascunque quarumcunque suarum creaturarum, sive causarum secundarum, actiones. Duplex in hoc negotio sese offert causa, utraque verè operativa: interim altera alteri sic subordinata, ut quicquid agit inferior, id agat acta à superiore; indeque idem effectus duplici causæ sese debeat, Deo scilicet & creaturæ. Notandum itaque hic occurrit duplex principium ἐνεργητικὸν, sive operativum; una tamen ἐνέργεια, sive operatio, à gemino illo principio fluens; atque unum denique ἐνέργημα, sive opus productum. De hoc quidem dubitari nequit. De isto constabit facilè, quandò illud planum fecimus. Ut ergò à primò faciamus initium, asserimus, effecta quævis, quæ à causis suis naturali ratione procedunt, & Deo tribuenda esse, & creaturæ; utrique tanquam causæ proximæ & totali in suo genere. Adversatur nostræ huic thesi duplex error, in extremâ è diametro oppositæ secedens. Alter creaturas nihil agere, sed solum Deum; alter Deum nihil agere, sed solas creaturas, contendit: quorum ille etsi sit stultissimus, hic profanus quoque, neuter tamen suis destituitur propugnatoribus. Priorem opinionem rejectam suscitarunt quidam Scholastici, docentes, nihil activitatis creaturis competere, sed duntaxat Deum agere ad earum præsentiam. Admodum vicina huic sententiæ exstitit illa hodierna Cartesiana Philosophatio, quæ (exceptâ mente humanâ) præter materiam ac varios cjus modos in creaturis admittit nihil. Quum enim illa duo sint merè passiva, sequitur exinde, res omnes creatas omni prorsus activitatis principio destitui, nec quicquam extra se producere posse. Imò, ne mens humana quidem hic excipi potest, quandoquidem eam contendunt meram esse cogitationem; quæ quam nullum effectum extra se ponere apta sit, clarum est. Sileo deliria fanaticorum, non se, sed solum Deum in se, agere, quod agere dicuntur, contendentium. Et hos quidem efficacissimè redarguere poterat vel propria suorum facinorum conscientia; quorum culpam sanctissimo Deo, ceu causæ, transscribere, abhorrentius est ab omni pietatis sensu, quam ut à nobis confutari debeat. Istos verò refellit evidenter constans Universi harmonia, conservata per adjumentum mutuum quod sibi præstant ejusdem partes; quippe quæ sibi invicem id præstare nequeunt absque alterius in alteram influxum & causalitatem. Adde Dei variam in creaturis ad naturarum varietatem accommodatam operationem: frustrà profectò huic accommodatam, nisi sic postulante varia rerum creatarum activitate; quandoquidem divina virtus, si per se solam cogitetur, in quovis subjecto quidvis operatur eâdem operandi facilitate. Verùm, quoniam de Dei potius quam creaturarum activitate agendum nobis est in præsens, desino pluribus confirmare, quod (ne nimium ab eo quod præmanibus est argumento) hypothesis instar hoc loco rectius à nobis assumitur.
units.tr: By this act of Providence we understand that whole influx of the first cause which it gives to all the actions of its creatures, that is, of the secondary causes. In this matter two causes present themselves, both truly operative; yet one is so subordinated to the other that whatever the inferior agent does, it does as acted upon by the superior. Hence the same effect is owed to a twofold cause, namely God and the creature. It must be noted here that there is a twofold operative principle (energetikon), yet one energy or operation (energeia) flowing from that twofold principle, and finally one product of the work (energema). Of this there can be no doubt, and about the rest it will easily be settled once we have made this plain. So, to begin at the beginning, we assert that whatever effects proceed from their causes by natural reason are to be attributed both to God and to the creature, each as proximate and total cause in its own kind. Our thesis is opposed by a twofold error, each departing to an extreme opposite the other. One contends that creatures do nothing, but God alone; the other that God does nothing, but the creatures alone. Of these, the former is most foolish, the latter profane, yet neither lacks defenders. The first opinion, though rejected, was revived by certain Scholastics, who taught that creatures have no activity at all, but that God alone acts in their presence. Very close to this view is the modern Cartesian philosophy, which admits nothing in creatures except matter and its various modes, with the exception of the human mind. For since those two are purely passive, it follows that all created things are wholly destitute of any principle of activity and cannot produce anything outside themselves. Indeed, the human mind cannot even be excepted here, since they contend that it is mere thought, and it is clear that thought is not apt to produce any effect outside itself. I pass over the ravings of the fanatics, who contend that they themselves do not act, but that God alone acts in them whatever they are said to do. The very consciousness of their own crimes could refute these most effectively; to transfer their guilt to the most holy God as cause is too abhorrent to every sense of piety to need refutation by us. But the constant harmony of the universe, preserved by the mutual aid which its parts give one another, plainly refutes the others; for these parts could not give that aid to one another without the influx and causality of one upon another. Add God's varied operation in creatures, accommodated to the variety of natures: this would surely be accommodated in vain, unless the varied activity of created things demanded it, since divine power, if thought of by itself alone, would work in any subject whatever with the same ease. But since at present we must treat of God's activity rather than that of creatures, I cease to confirm at greater length what, lest I stray too far from the argument at hand, is more rightly assumed here by us as a hypothesis.

units.la: De altero itaque errore videndum erit diligentius; illo scilicet, qui citra ullum verum Dei influxum causas secundas operari contendit. Agmen hic ducunt, post Atheos, Epicurei, qui nihil hujus Providentiæ Diis suis faciunt reliquum, verentes eosdem ex suis intermundiis ab otio voluptuoso vocare ad negotium. Exertim, ex eorum mente, Lucretius: Natura videtur, Libera continuo dominis privata superbis, Ipsa sua per se sponte omnia Dis agere expers.
units.tr: Concerning the other error, then, we must look more carefully: namely, the error that contends that secondary causes operate without any true influx of God. Leading this band, after the atheists, are the Epicureans, who leave nothing of this Providence to their gods, fearing that they would be called from their voluptuous idleness to business out of their intermundane spaces. Especially Lucretius, in their view: Nature seems free, continually stripped of her proud masters, of her own accord doing all things by herself, without any need of the gods.

units.la: Quibuscum in partem societatis veniunt Peripatetici, illi qui mundum sublunarem divinæ curæ subducunt. Ruunt quidem hæc omnia per ea quæ jam antè de Creatione & Conservatione nobis disputata sunt, ut solo comtemptu vindicanda videri posset sacrilega impietas; nisi inter ipsos Christianos jam olim Durando, nuperius quoque Taurello, cum suis, libuisset eandem recoquere, negando cum actionibus causarum secundarum concurrere Deum. Atque utinam negent isti soli! Etiam hodiè Jesuitæ & Sociniani, cum socienis suis, etiamsi, ad declinandam negatæ divinæ Providentiæ invidiam, vafro consilio verbis ferè utantur modestioribus, quando tamen ad rem ipsam ventum est, cumprimis autem ad concursum Dei in liberas rationalium creaturarum actiones, sic consulunt libero suo arbitrio bitrio per efficacis divini influxûs divortium, ut supremo cœlorum terrarumque Regi tribunt re verà pro sceptro arundinem. Istud ergò nobis hoc loco ponendum est fundamentum, cui firmum superstruatur ædificium, ac tale quod sustinere queat Sophistarum quorumcunque insultus. Summa rei est, nullam à creatura qualicunque fluere actionem, qua talem, quæ non pariter proficiscatur ab efficientia Dei, tanquam causæ ejusdem veræ ac realis. Hanc assertionem si demonstratam dederimus, faciliori negotio superabimus quicquid circa Providentiæ hujus modum ab adversariis movetur difficultatis. Ergò hoc agamus! & paucis quidem: quandoquidem res omnis conficitur, attendendo duntaxat notionem tum Creaturæ tum Creatoris. Faciam (dicam cum Seneca) rem non difficilem, causam Deorum (Dei) agam.
units.tr: With them in partnership come the Peripatetics, those who withdraw the sublunary world from divine care. All of these indeed collapse under what has already been argued about Creation and Conservation, so that their sacrilegious impiety might seem to be dismissed by contempt alone. But among Christians themselves, Durandus long ago, and more recently Taurellus with his followers, were pleased to reheat the same view, denying that God concurs with the actions of secondary causes. Would that these alone had denied it! Even today the Jesuits and the Socinians, with their allies, though to avoid the odium of denying divine Providence they use rather more modest words with a crafty design, yet when it comes to the thing itself, and especially to God's concurrence in the free actions of rational creatures, they so provide for free will by divorcing it from efficacious divine influx that they in fact give the supreme King of heaven and earth a reed in place of a sceptre. Therefore this must be laid here by us as the foundation, on which a firm building is raised, one able to withstand the assaults of whatever sophists. The sum of the matter is this: no action whatever flows from any creature, as such, which does not likewise proceed from the efficiency of God as from his true and real cause. If we give this assertion as demonstrated, we shall more easily overcome whatever difficulty the adversaries raise concerning the manner of this Providence. Let us therefore do this, and briefly indeed, since the whole matter is settled by attending merely to the notions of both creature and Creator. I shall make the matter not difficult, I shall say with Seneca, I shall plead the cause of the gods (God).

units.la: Multà demonstratione jam sæpius evicimus, indubitatum esse axioma, tantum esse in creaturis relatis ad suum Deum dependentiæ, quantum est in eis entitatis. Nunc itaquè scire lubet, num quid entitatis quæcunque creaturæ actio includat? Si includat (ut includit; nisi forsan actio creaturæ nihil sit) tantundem ergò includit dependentiæ. Dependentiæ scilicet talis, qualis est cujusvis entitatis; id est, istius, quà Dei tanquam suæ causæ influxui vero ac positivo se totam debet. Quamobrem, vel nihil planè est creaturarum actio, vel si quid positivi sit, id totum à Deo habet tanquam à principio sui. Item: planum jam antè fecimus, à Deo tanquam à causa sui pendere creaturam quamvis, quousque ab eo pendere potest. At si solius essentiæ non item operationis suæ respectu, à positivo Dei influxu penderet creatura, minus certè à Deo penderet, quam ab ipso pendere posset. Nisi quis contendere cupiat, actiones creaturarum ipsâ suâ naturâ ab alio pendere non posse; id est, divinas esse & infinitè perfectas. Quin, cum modus operandi eum qui essendi est sequatur, creatura autem quolibet existentiæ momento vi efficacis Dei influxûs, sive Conservationis, subsistat, negari nequit, eandem in operationibus suis pari Dei influxu, sive Concursu, indigere. Et quis concipiat rem, cujus tota substantia Dei est; cujusque tamen accidentia, actiones puta, eodem cum sua substantia modo ad Deum nil pertinent? Subjectum ergò dependens erit, ad-
units.tr: By a long demonstration we have already proved many times the indubitable axiom that creatures depend on their God to the same extent that they have entity. Now we wish to know whether the action of any creature includes some entity. If it includes it (as it does, unless perhaps a creature's action is nothing), then it includes just as much dependence: namely that dependence which belongs to any entity, that is, the dependence by which it owes itself wholly to the true and positive influx of God as its cause. Therefore either the action of a creature is nothing at all, or, if it is something positive, it has the whole of it from God as from its principle. Likewise: we have already made plain that a creature depends on God as its cause as far as it can depend on him. But if a creature depended on God's positive influx only with respect to its essence and not likewise with respect to its operation, it would certainly depend on him less than it could. Unless someone wishes to contend that the actions of creatures cannot by their very nature depend on another, that is, that they are divine and infinitely perfect. Moreover, since the mode of operating follows the mode of being, and a creature subsists at every moment of its existence by the power of God's efficacious influx, or Conservation, it cannot be denied that in its operations it needs the same divine influx, or Concurrence. And who could conceive of a thing whose whole substance is God's, yet whose accidents, namely its actions, in the same way pertain nothing to God? The subject, then, will be dependent, the ad-

units.la: IV. Vera Dei efficientia in causarum secundarum actiones asserta. adjunctum independens? Creaturæ secundaria & subordinata erunt entia, prima interim nec ulli causæ obnoxia agentia? Videmus clarè, quam nemo affirmare possit, Deum minus influere in actiones causarum secundarum per Concursum, quam influit in essentiam earundem per positivam Creationis & Conservationis efficientiam, quicunque non monstrosò contradictione, eandem rem simul agnoscere velit dependentem, id est creaturam, in essendo, & independentem, id est Deum, in operando. Sufficient ista: quapropter alia addere desino. Tantum notari velim, hisce rationibus non solùm nos ostendisse ejus Providentiæ de qua agimus veritatem, sed & universalem ejusdem necessitatem; atque adeò simul confecisse, extendere se eam ad quasvis quarumcunque creaturarum actiones. Quandoquidem enim eas cruimus ex ipsa natura creaturæ qua talis considerate, nequeunt, citra hujus abnegationem, illi magis subduci sublunares actiones, quam cœlestes; liberæ, quam necessariæ; malæ, quam bonæ; minimæ, quam maximæ. Quatenus enim omnes in eadem creatæ entitatis categoria includuntur, etiam pariter eidem subsunt dependentiæ. Quæque interim suo modo atque ordine: de quo constabit ex sequentibus plenius.
units.tr: IV. The true efficacy of God, asserted in the actions of secondary causes. Is the adjunct independent? Will creatures be secondary and subordinate beings, while the first cause is an agent subject to no other cause? It is plain that no one can affirm that God influences the actions of secondary causes by concurrence less than he influences their essence by the positive efficacy of creation and conservation. Anyone who is not willing to hold a monstrous contradiction must acknowledge that one and the same thing is at once dependent in its being, that is, a creature, and independent in its acting, that is, God. These points are sufficient, so I stop adding others. I would only have it noted that by these arguments we have shown not only the truth of the providence we are discussing but also its universal necessity; and so we have at the same time established that it extends to all the actions of any creatures whatever. For since we judge that creatures have such actions from the very nature of the creature considered as such, then, unless we deny this, sublunary actions cannot be withdrawn from this dependence any more than heavenly ones, free actions any more than necessary ones, evil actions any more than good ones, the smallest any more than the greatest. For insofar as all of them are included in the same category of created being, they are equally subject to the same dependence, each in its own way and order, as will be made clearer from what follows.

units.la: V. Atque à difficultatibus quibusdam præcipuis vindicata.
units.tr: V. And defended against certain chief difficulties.

units.la: Difficultates quæ nostræ sententiæ obstare videntur, nunc prius amovendæ sunt. Nil moror Epicureorum fatuitatem, metuentem, ne nimiis rerum molestiis implicetur Numen, s cunctis nostris actionibus præsit. Toto cœlo ea aberrat ab omni conceptu saniori de Deo; quem qui cum molesto conatu ac fatigatione concipit actuosum, ne Deum quidem concipit. Æquè frivolum est, quod urgent de bonis quæ malis, de malis quæ bonis in hac vita frequenter eveniunt; quodque minimè futurum autumant, si cura justi ac benigni Dei circa singulas rerum actiones versaretur. Sed solvit jam dudum egregiè hunc nodum Seneca, in suis de Providentia dissertationibus. Itaque, quid alii hùc adferant, videamus potius. Urgent imprimis, superfluum esse talem Dei in nostras actiones influxum: si enim certum sit, creaturas tanquam causas principales naturali sibique indita ac sufficiente virtute præditas esse ad operandum, sequi omninò putant, eas causas superioris auxilio non indigere. Sed consequentia inconsequens est. Etenim, sit causa secunda sufficiens ad operandum, etiam tanquam causa principalis; non hoc ipso sufficiens est ad operandum tanquam causa prima. Aliud enim est, sufficiens esse ad operandum in suo genere; aliud, prorsus independens esse, nulloque primi entis auxilio indigere. Sufficientia causæ creatæ secludit omnem causalitatem quæ sit ejusdem secum generis ac naturæ; non subordinationem ad efficientiam illam, à qua quemadmodum pendet ipsa causæ creatæ virtus, ita non minus actio ab ea procedens, cum dependentia à causa prima utrique illi æquè sit essentialis. Itaque, si subordinata non pugnare cogitaverimus, facilè intelligemus, dependentiam à causa prima nil præjudicare sufficientiæ ad operandum quæ competit creaturæ in genere causæ secundæ. Si instes, causæ creatæ suarum actionum perfectiones in se ipsis continent, facilè ergo ex se & per se eas producere poterunt, citra alterius auxilium: regero, speciem habituram fore hanc objectionem, si creaturæ actionum suarum perfectiones in se continerent à se & ex se. Atqui id est salsissimum. Quamobrem, quemadmodum creaturæ actionum suarum perfectiones in se non continent ex se, sed dependenter a causa prima, quæ eas in illis posuit; ita quoque eadem ex se elicere non poterunt, nisi dependenter ab influxu ejusdem causæ, qui eas faciat ipso facto illas exferre. Ut verbo dicam, tribue creaturæ virtutem operandi quantumvis sufficientem, nil repugno; duntaxat si, quantam in ea ponis sufficientiam ad agendum, tantam agnoscas in agendo dependentiam.
units.tr: The difficulties that seem to stand in the way of our view must now be removed first. I need not dwell on the folly of the Epicureans, who fear that the Deity would be entangled in too many troubles if he presided over all our actions. This is wholly far from any saner conception of God; whoever conceives of him as active only with a troublesome effort and fatigue does not conceive of God at all. Equally trivial is their objection about the good things that often happen to the bad, and the bad to the good, in this life; they claim this would not happen if the care of a just and kind God were concerned with each single action of things. But Seneca long ago solved this knot well, in his discourses on providence. So let us rather see what others bring forward here. They press chiefly that such an influence of God on our actions is superfluous: for if it is certain that creatures, as true causes, are endowed with a natural and implanted power sufficient for acting, they think it follows altogether that such causes do not need the help of a superior. But the inference does not follow. For though a secondary cause is sufficient to act even as a principal cause, it is not thereby sufficient to act as a first cause. For it is one thing to be sufficient to act in one's own kind, and another to be wholly independent and in need of no help from the first being. The sufficiency of a created cause excludes every causality of the same kind and nature as itself, not subordination to that efficacy on which the power of the created cause depends, and the action proceeding from it no less, since dependence on the first cause is essential to both alike. Therefore, if we consider that subordinate things do not conflict, we shall readily understand that dependence on the first cause does nothing to prejudice the sufficiency for acting that belongs to a creature as a secondary cause. If you insist that created causes contain the perfections of their actions in themselves, and so can easily produce them from themselves and through themselves without the help of another, I answer that this objection would have force only if creatures contained the perfections of their actions from themselves and out of themselves. But that is most false. Wherefore, just as creatures do not contain the perfections of their actions out of themselves, but depend on the first cause, which placed them in them, so neither can they draw them forth from themselves except in dependence on the influence of that same cause, which makes them bring them forth in the very act. To put it in a word: I have no objection to your attributing to a creature a power of acting however sufficient; only acknowledge in its acting as much dependence as you place in it as sufficiency for acting.

units.la: Manet itaque firmum, nullam actionem itá in solidum causæ creatæ tribui posse, ut non ea pariter agnoscat causam sui Deum. Verùm, num utrumque hoc principium influat in eundem effectum eádem numero actione; an potius distincta in hoc negotio statuenda sit actio Dei, & alia ab ea quæ creaturæ est? quæritur. Mercturque hoc dubium eo diligentius hoc loco expendi, quia eodem utitur Durandus, ad evertendum quem jam adstruximus Dei influxum. Si Deus, inquit, ageret immediatè ad productionem effectuum causæ secundæ, aut ageret eádem actione, quà creatura; aut aliâ. Non eádem; quia impossibile est, eandem numero actionem esse à duobus vel pluribus agentibus ita, ut à quolibet sit immediatè & perse stè. Non aliâ ; quia , &c. Nos hìc respondendum censemus cum eis qui sentiunt , Deum agere cum creatura actione numero eâdem cum ea quâ agit creatura. Atque arbitror , si sic sentiamus , multo facilius expediri haud paucas difficultates , quæ sese in hoc Providentiæ negotio offerunt. Id certum est, præter Deum & res à Deo productas nihil dari in rerum natura. Quod si actionem Dei cogitaverimus , prout sese habet activè à parte principii sui , Dei, non minus certum est , eam nihil creaturæ esse , sed ipsissimum simplicissimo modo actuosum Deum. Passivè ergò spectanda venit , prout extra Deum terminatur in creaturam. Atque sic consideratam nihil aliud esse posse asserimus, quam ipsam actionem causæ secundæ , quatenus eà à prima quoque causa procedit. Prorsus quemadmodum Creatio : quæ non concipienda venit ut actio , indè à creatoris , hinc à creaturæ natura distincta ; sed tanquam ipse creator , si activè spectetur, vel tanquam ipsa res creata , si consideretur passivè. Sicuti verò præter ista duo tertium quodcunque in creatione nec dari nec concipi potest, ita pari ratione dicendum hoc loco , illum divinæ virtutis influxum, de quo agimus , à parte Dei quidem ipsum Deum esse , verum à parte operantis causæ secundæ , ipsissimam actionem creaturæ. Imò, nisi eâdem numero actione Deus agat & creatura , non potest actio creaturæ Deum habere causam sui proximam , sed remotam duntaxat : quod immediatæ creaturarum à Deo dependentiæ planè adversatur. Tandem , si Dei actio non eadem sit cum illa creaturæ , quid ni pari necessitate illa actio Dei , quâ actio creaturæ absea distincta producitur , aliâ indigeat iterùm efficientiâ à se distinctâ , quâ producatur ipsa hæc ? Si sic , influxus influxibus cumulandi erunt absque fine. Id ergò ne fiat, in prima actione Dei , quæ cum actione creaturæ una eademque sit , erit subsistendum.
units.tr: It remains therefore firmly established that no action can be attributed to a created cause so entirely that it does not also acknowledge God as its cause. But whether both these principles flow into one and the same effect by one and the same numerical action, or whether we should rather posit in this matter a divine action distinct from that of the creature, is the question. This doubt is the more carefully weighed here because Durandus uses it to overthrow the influence of God that we have just established. "If God," he says, "acted immediately to produce the effects of a secondary cause, he would act either by the same action as the creature, or by another. Not by the same, because it is impossible that one and the same numerical action should be from two or more agents such that it is immediate and per se from each. Not by another, because, etc." We think that here we should answer with those who hold that God acts with the creature by an action numerically the same as that by which the creature acts. And I think that if we think this way, many of the difficulties that present themselves in this matter of providence are resolved much more easily. It is certain that apart from God and the things produced by God there is nothing in the nature of things. But if we consider the action of God as it stands actively on the side of its principle, which is God, it is no less certain that it is not anything of the creature, but God himself, acting in the simplest manner. It must therefore be regarded passively, insofar as it terminates outside God in the creature. And so considered, we assert that it can be nothing other than the very action of the secondary cause, insofar as it also proceeds from the first cause. Just as with creation, which is not to be conceived as an action distinct from the nature of the creator on one side and of the creature on the other, but as the creator himself, if considered actively, or as the created thing itself, if considered passively. And just as in creation no third thing can either be given or conceived beyond these two, so by the same reasoning we must say here that the influence of divine power of which we speak is, on God's side, God himself, but on the side of the operating secondary cause, the very action of the creature. Indeed, unless God and the creature act by one and the same numerical action, the action of the creature cannot have God as its proximate cause, but only as a remote one; and this flatly contradicts the immediate dependence of creatures on God. Finally, if the action of God is not the same as that of the creature, why should not that action of God, by which the action of the creature distinct from it is produced, need by the same necessity yet another efficacy distinct from itself, by which it in turn is produced? If so, influences will have to be piled upon influences without end. To prevent this, we must stop at the first action of God, which is one and the same with the action of the creature.

units.la: Quod asserunt, sieri non posse, ut actio numero eadem à duobus agentibus procedat, itâ ut à quolibet sit immediatè & perfectè, id totum verissimum esse damus in causis coordinatis; quarum mutua indepéndentia cundem ab utroque procedentem influxum non admittit. Verùm longè dispar ratio est illarum causarum, quarum una per omnia sui omnimodam & totalem dependentiam dicit
units.tr: As to their claim that it cannot happen that one and the same numerical action proceeds from two agents, so that it is immediate and perfect from each, we grant that this is entirely true of coordinate causes, whose mutual independence does not admit the same influence proceeding from each. But the case is far different for those causes of which one has complete and total dependence on it in all respects.

units.la: VII. Dubiorum in hac sententia occurrentium brevis solutio.
units.tr: VII. A brief solution of the difficulties arising in this view.

units.la: ab altera; uti hic obtinet. Cui rei simile exemplum in rerum natura nullum exstare, cum jam ante monuerimus, frustrà laboratur in adserendis hùc instantiis ab obviis causis desumtis; quippe quæ nimiùm existunt dissimiles, ad fundandam argumentationem contra allatæ à nobis demonstrationis evidentiam. Sed, inquiunt alii, eidem actioni eadem necessariò conveniunt prædicata. Si itaque Dei & creaturæ actio numero una hìc sit, quod peccatum huic adhæret, etiam illi adhærere dicendum erit: quod tamen omni modo à divina sanctitate abhorret. At, tametsi sit verum, ejusdem actionis secundum se spectatæ easdem esse affectiones reales ex natura illius actionis fluentes, non tamen id quadrat in peccatum, quod proprie loquendo privatio est alicujus boni, atque idcò potissimum æstimandum venit ex modo quo se agens habet ad suam illam actionem, quæ peccaminosa existit. Jam verò parili modo & Deum & creaturam ad eandem illam suam actionem habere se, id est quod nego. Producit Deus actionem; non comproducit bonitatem moralem: atquì non tenebatur. Producit creatura eandem illam actionem; nec comproducit bonitatem moralem: atquì hæc omninò tenebatur. Negativè ergò se habet Deus, privativè creatura: consequenter, eadem in eàdem actione absentia respectu hujus rationem peccati habet, illius respectu nequaquam. Verum de hisce deinceps quoque dicendum erit. Nunc, ut absolvam, contentus ero demonstrasse, quod ab initio demonstrandum propositum; videlicet, quodcunque opus à creatura productum, etsi in se sit unum, duplex tamen agnoscere sui principium subordinatum, Deum & creaturam; à quo utroque fluat per unam & eandem utriusque actionem. Quæ qui rectè perceperit, viam ad sequentem tractatum is stratam sibi experietur planam atque expeditam.
units.tr: from the other, as obtains here. No similar example exists in nature, since we have already pointed out that it is futile to bring forward here instances taken from ordinary causes, which are too dissimilar to found an argument against the evidence of the demonstration we have given. But others say that the same predicates necessarily belong to the same action. So if the action of God and of the creature is numerically one here, whatever sin clings to it must be said to cling to the other as well, which is wholly abhorrent to divine holiness. But although it is true that the real affections flowing from the nature of that action, considered in itself, are the same, this does not fit with sin, which properly speaking is the privation of some good. Sin must therefore be judged chiefly by the way the agent stands toward that action which is sinful. Now that God and the creature stand in the same way toward that same action, I deny. God produces the action but does not co-produce its moral goodness, and he was not bound to. The creature produces that same action and does not co-produce its moral goodness, and this it was wholly bound to do. God therefore stands in a negative relation to the action, the creature in a privative one. Consequently the same absence in the same action has the character of sin with respect to the creature, and not with respect to God. These matters will be discussed further later. For now, to conclude, I am content to have shown what was proposed to be shown from the beginning: namely, that whatever work is produced by a creature, though it is one in itself, nevertheless acknowledges a twofold subordinate principle, God and the creature, from both of which it flows through one and the same action of each. Whoever has rightly grasped this will find the road to the following treatise laid out plain and unobstructed for him.

units.la: Nequaquam verò sufficit, generatim agnovisse Divinam Providentiam, quæ in omnibus creaturis operetur omnia; nisi quoque istius efficientiæ modus statuatur ille, qui tanti Numinis independentia atque primitate sit omninò dignus. Quod arduum negotium quo distinctius à nobis concipiatur, plurimùm juvabit tria sigillatim attendisse, quæ in quavis causæ secundæ operatione intellectui nostro se offerunt. Occurrit primò agentis cujusvis prima applicatio ad agendum; hanc mox sequitur ipsa ejusdem activitas; quam denique excipit actionis universæ ad suos fines specialis determinatio. Quumque in istis omnibus dominetur Dei influxus, non male etiam hic tripliciter considerari: vel quatenus primo instanti quiescentem anuè creaturam potenter excitat ad agendum; vel quatenus agentem jam creaturam, quamdiu agit, indesinenter promovet in agendo; vel tandem, quatenus in præstitutos abs se fines actionem totam sapienter regit atque gubernat. Illo modo spectata Providentia, Præcursus; isto, Concursus; hoc, Gubernatio dici commodè potest: sumtis vocabulis aliquanto strictius ac sæpè accipiuntur, quando absque discrimine singula pro universa Dei Providentia usurpantur. Cavendum verò, ne quis hic trinam Dei actionem verè distinctam concipiat: idem enim unusquisque re vera influxus est, qui variè conceptus cum relatione ad actionis creatæ, vel initium, vel progressum, vel finem, pro vario hoc considerandi modo, variam subit denominationem.
units.tr: It is by no means enough to have acknowledged in general the divine providence which works all things in all creatures, unless the mode of this efficacy is also established as one truly worthy of the independence and primacy of so great a Deity. To conceive this difficult matter more distinctly, it will greatly help to consider separately three things which present themselves to our understanding in any operation of a secondary cause. First there is the initial application of any agent to acting; this is soon followed by its own activity; and finally comes the special determination of the whole action to its ends. Since God's influence governs all of these, it may here be considered in three ways: either insofar as at the first instant he powerfully stirs the creature, previously at rest, to act; or insofar as, while the creature is already acting, he continually promotes it in its acting; or finally, insofar as he wisely directs and governs the whole action to the ends he has appointed. Viewed in the first way, providence may conveniently be called Precursus; in the second, Concursus; in the third, Gubernatio. These terms are taken somewhat more strictly than they are often used, when each is employed without distinction for the whole of divine providence. Care must be taken, however, that no one conceives here a threefold divine action truly distinct. For it is one and the same influence in reality, which, conceived variously in relation to the beginning, progress or end of the created action, takes on a different name according to this different mode of consideration.

units.la: Quæ percipientur multo facilius, ubi de singulis dixerimus. Suppono semper & ubique in hac dissertatione, Deum creaturas instruxisse viribus ad agendum idoneis, sive facultates naturales eæ fuerint, sive etiam habitus: quin & eundem vires istas in eisdem continuare suo influxu. Id tam manifestè arguit creaturarum à Deo dependentia, ut de eo vix dubitet quisquam eorum omnium, qui aliquem saltem Dei Concursum admittunt. Tantum falluntur vehementer, quotquot hoc uno omnem Providentiam divinam absolvi putant, neque progrediuntur longius. Si sic, non jam Deus ipsius actionis creatæ auctor foret; quem esse necessariò, jam demonstravimus. Quandoquidem enim potentiæ atque habitus frequenter existunt otiosi omnique actu secundo destituti, certè non is qui facultatem agendi concessit, vel habitum infudit, ideò actionis indè fluentis haberi potest vera causa. Quumque actio ipsa aliquid sit ab istis agendi principiis verè distinctum, etiam in actionem qua talem, non tantum in agendi facultatem, Deum influere, tenendum est. Imò, illa Dei actio quâ creaturis vires ad operandum dedit, si accuratè loqui cupiamus, non tam Providentiæ est, quam potius Creationis: sicuti illa, quâ vires semel concessas permanere facit, proprie non Concursus est, sed Conservationis. Praerequisita ergo illa tantum sunt specialis istius Providentiae, de qua hic agimus.
units.tr: These points will be grasped much more easily once we have spoken of each. I assume always and everywhere in this dissertation that God has equipped creatures with powers suited to acting, whether these be natural faculties or habits, and that he continues these powers in them by his influence. This so clearly shows the dependence of creatures on God that hardly anyone who admits at least some concurrence of God would doubt it.
