Those are greatly mistaken, however, who think that the whole of divine providence is discharged by this alone and go no further. If that were so, God would not be the author of the created action itself, which we have already shown he necessarily is. For since powers and habits often exist idle and destitute of every second act, certainly he who granted the faculty of acting or infused the habit cannot for that reason be held the true cause of the action that flows from them. And since the action itself is something truly distinct from these principles of acting, we must hold that God influences the action as such, and not merely the faculty of acting. Indeed, that divine action by which he gave powers to creatures for working belongs, if we wish to speak accurately, not so much to Providence as to Creation; just as that by which he causes powers once granted to remain is properly not Concurrence but Conservation. These are therefore only the prerequisites of that special providence with which we are dealing here.

units.la: In ea sese primum offert Praecursus: qui quatenus naturae ordine creaturae activitatem antecedit, etiam Praedeterminatio, seu Praemotio, aliis quoque Concursus praevius vel praedeterminans, dici consuevit. Designatur eo nomine, ipsa Providentia Divina, quatenus creaturarum vires, quotiescunque sunt operaturae, efficaciter ad agendum excitat & applicat. Dicebam, hunc actum Praecursum dici, eo quod ordine naturae activitatem creaturarum antecedat: quandoquidem enim jam ostendimus, non alia atque alia, sed eadem numero actione & Deum agere & creaturam, per se manifestum est, nullam temporis prioritatem hic locum habere posse; nisi quid se ipso prius extitisse dicatur. Probe id observandum est adversus adversariorum nostrorum hac parte calumnias, quibus affingere nobis solent, ac si sentiamus, primo temporis momento Deum reali efficientia creaturam ad agendum excitare, deinceps sequenti temporis articulo creaturam sic motam, istaque vi externa impulsam, cum aliter nequeat, operari quoque. Absona ista sunt, uti a natura rei, ita a nostra opinione. Imo vero, Concursum concomitantem & simultaneum, ut ipsi vocant, ab hoc concursu praevio, ac si gemina actio sit, ne quidem re ipsa distinguimus: sed inchoatum Concursum, quatenus is ordine naturae creaturam agentem praecedit, Praecursum vocamus; qui idem Praecursus continuatus, quatenus ratione temporis cum actuosis creaturis prorsus simul est, Concursus dicitur. Tantum ergo volumus, Deum non duntaxat simultaneitate temporis agere cum causis secundis, sed & prioritate naturae agere in causas secundas. Etiamsi autem haec communis etiam opinio fit plurimorum ex Doctoribus Scholasticis, qui inde Praedeterminantes appellati sunt, quales exstiterunt prae aliis Thomistae & Dominicani, adversantur tamen ei imprimis quotquot Scientiae mediae commentum sunt amplexi, quos inter excellunt Jesuitae. Videndum itaque, quae ratio suadeat, Deo tribuendam esse hanc in operando prioritatem, quoties per ejus influxum agunt creaturae.
units.tr: In this, Precursus first presents itself. Insofar as it precedes the activity of the creature in the order of nature, it is also customarily called predetermination or premotion, and by others prior or predetermining concurrence. By this name is designated divine providence itself, insofar as it efficaciously stirs up and applies the powers of creatures whenever they are about to act. I said that this act is called Precursus because it precedes the activity of creatures in the order of nature. For since we have already shown that God and the creature act not by different actions but by one and the same action numerically, it is self-evident that no priority of time can have a place here, unless something is said to have existed before itself. This must be carefully observed against the calumnies of our adversaries on this point, with which they are accustomed to charge us: as if we held that at the first moment of time God stirs up the creature to act by real efficacy, and then at the following moment the creature, so moved and impelled by an external force, also acts, since it cannot do otherwise. These notions are absurd both by the nature of the thing and by our opinion. Indeed, we do not even distinguish in reality the concomitant and simultaneous concurrence, as they call it, from this prior concurrence, as though there were a twofold action. We call the inchoate concurrence, insofar as it precedes the creature acting in the order of nature, Precursus; and this same continued Precursus, insofar as in respect of time it is altogether simultaneous with the active creatures, is called Concursus. We mean only that God acts not merely simultaneously in time with secondary causes, but also acts prior in nature to them. Although this is also the common opinion of many Scholastic doctors, from whom those called Predeterminants took their name, such as above all the Thomists and Dominicans, yet those who have embraced the fiction of middle knowledge oppose it, chief among them the Jesuits. We must therefore consider what reason suggests: that this priority in acting is to be attributed to God whenever creatures act through his influence.

units.la: Demonstratum jam dedimus, nihil agere creaturam, nisi influente Deo. Influente nimirum efficacia sese digna, atque conveniente cum Independentiae suae excellentia. Non finit haec, pares facere Deum & creaturam, ita ut nulla sit causae primae praesecunda eminentia. Atqui quae haec erit, si tantum cum creaturis concurrat Deus? Nam & itidem cum Deo concurrunt creaturae. Nihil ergo sic Deo fiet relictum, praeter causae mere sociae gloriam, pari passu cum creatura progredientis, habentisque non nisi divisum cum ea imperium. Imo vero, prima atque secunda causa nomina duntaxat erunt absque re; quando primae nulla re vera erit prioritas prae secunda, secundae nulla ad primam subordinatio. Adde (quod suis locis a nobis est ostensum) jam ab aeterno suam stare efficaci Dei consilio absolutam immutabilitatem, suam divinae praescientiae infallibilem certitudinem. Qui autem stet, nisi intentionis ordini respondeat ad amussim eventus complementum? Et quo pacto hoc illi respondeat, nisi provida cura Numinis intercedat, praevio suo imperio ad id agendum creaturas excitans, quod ipsas in tempore acturas ab aeterno & praeordinavit & praevidit? Neque hujus illationis vim ignorant adversarii: quamobrem ad aeternae providentiae seriem cum actuali ejusdem executione conciliandam, quam ut agnoscant supremi Numinis super suis creaturis in agendo primitatem, cerea & ambulatoria illi decreta, ac speculantem quasi ex conjectura scientiam, tribuere malunt. Atque hac de causa universum hoc negotium plane ac plene confici posset vel illis rationibus solis, quibus jam dudum Divini Intellectus & Voluntatis asseruimus independentiam. Unum, quo absolvam, adjiciam. Nisi alteram causam ab altera hic praedeterminari statuamus, scire lubet rationem & modum istius connexionis inter actionem utriusque, qua fit ut utraque in eodem opere producendo concurrat? Non id forte fortuna fieri, clarissimum est. Neque tamen extra Deum & creaturam quicquam existit, cui id adscribi queat: nisi fatuissimum fatum quis inducere cupiat, cujus legibus utrumque agens, aeque primum ac secundum, sic sit adstrictum, ut altero operante mox coöperetur alterum. Quando ergo nullum tertium impellat Deum & creaturam ad simultaneam actionem, restat, nexus istius rationem quaerendam esse vel in Deo, qui faciat creaturam concurrere secum; vel in creatura, quæ faciat Deum concurrere secum. Posterius quis est qui palam ausit ampledi? Nemo enim nôn manibus palpat, si causæ secundæ id tribuatur imperii in actiones causæ primæ, ut illa quoties lubitum fuerit hanc vocet in operis sui societatem, idem prorsus hoc esse, ac Numen habere non Universi gubernatorem, sed apparitorem potius; qui scilicet attentissimè creaturarum suarum nutus observare teneatur, atque ilicò præsto esse, simulac hilce ad opus quodpiam se accingere placuerit.
units.tr: We have already demonstrated that a creature does nothing unless God influences it, and influences it with an efficacy worthy of himself and agreeing with the excellence of his independence. This does not allow God and the creature to be made equal, so that there is no eminence of the first cause over the second. But what would that eminence be if God merely concurred with creatures? For creatures likewise concur with God. Nothing would thus be left to God except the glory of a merely associated cause, proceeding side by side with the creature and having only a divided dominion with it. Indeed, the names first and second cause would be empty of reality, since there would be no real priority of the first over the second, and no subordination of the second to the first. Add to this (as we have shown in their place) that from eternity there stands in God's effective counsel an absolute immutability, and in his divine foreknowledge an infallible certainty. But how could this stand unless the completion of the event corresponded exactly to the order of intention? And how could it so correspond unless the providential care of the Deity intervened, previously stirring creatures by his command to do that which he had from eternity both predestined and foreseen they would do in time? Nor do our adversaries ignore the force of this inference. Therefore, in order to reconcile the series of eternal providence with its actual execution, they prefer to attribute to the supreme Deity, not that primacy in acting over his creatures which they would have to acknowledge, but wavering and changeable decrees, and a knowledge that speculates as it were by conjecture. For this reason the whole matter could be completely settled by those arguments alone by which we have long since asserted the independence of the divine intellect and will. I will add one thing to finish. Unless we hold that one cause is here predetermined by the other, may we know the reason and mode of the connection between the action of each, by which it comes about that each concurs in producing the same work? It is most clear that this does not happen by chance. Yet there is nothing outside God and the creature to which it could be ascribed, unless someone wishes to introduce the most foolish fate, by whose laws each agent, first and second alike, is so bound that once the one is operating the other immediately cooperates. Since, then, no third thing impels God and the creature to simultaneous action, it remains that the reason for this connection must be sought either in God, who makes the creature concur with him, or in the creature, which makes God concur with it. Who would dare openly to embrace the latter? For no one fails to see, as plainly as with his hands, that if such a power of command over the actions of the first cause were attributed to the secondary cause, so that whenever it pleased it could summon the first into partnership in its work, this would be exactly the same as the Deity having not the governor of the universe but rather a servant: one who would be bound to watch most attentively the nods of his creatures, and to be at hand at once whenever they chose to set about some work.

units.la: Et profectò tantum harum demonstrationum est pondus, ut eo precisi Adversarii apertè quod res est profiteri vix ausint, sed tutius habeant latebras quærere in ambagibus verborum; at quorum sensum si detexeris, detexeris pariter eandem, verum palliatam tantum, quam nunc impugnavimus, impietatem absurdissimam. Nimirùm, influxum Dei admittere videri planè volunt: at verò ita se mox explicant, ut non agnoscant alium, quam generalem, indifferentem, determinabilem; specificandum scilicet & determinandum ad alterutrum oppositorum à libero rationalis creaturæ arbitrio. Ut fermè Deum in hoc negotio se habere cogitandum sit ad instar hominis, qui organi alicujus pneumatici tubos aëre quidem inflat, totam tamen hujus ad hunc vel istum sonum producendum determinationem arbitrio & actioni musici relinquit. Indè fingunt, loco Præcursûs jam à nobis explicati & demonstrati, concursum nescio quem, oblatum, uti vocant, quo voluntatem nostram prædeterminari negant; quippe qui existat talis, ut eum creatura libera sic habeat in sua potestate, ut eo uti vel non uti, ad hoc vel ad oppositum efficiendum uti, queat. Qua in re eo usque progredi non verentur, ut doceant, hominem uti posse pro suo arbitratu Dei concursu, non aliter ac si esset habitus inhærens. Atque hisce principiis suam debent originem omnia illa sententiarum portenta, quibus ab omni ævo hæreticorum furor victricem Dei efficaciam in salutis nostræ negotio impugnavit. Qualis est imprimis gratia illa conversionis resistibilis, quæ quidem sufficiens sit, si forsan incidat in piæ dispositionis animum, cà ritè uti paratum; per se tamen nequaquam efficiens, quippe quæ nullo negotio à contumaci peccatore possit repui. Nos, relictis Theologis posteriori rioribus hisce, ista priora à detestando sacrilegio absolvere non possumus, propter rationes quibus præcedente articulo firmiter evicimus, Deum non tanquam Deum agnosci, nisi agnoscatur primus motor, quascunque causarum secundarum operationes efficaciter sibi subordinans. Atqui per ista creaturæ subordinatur creator; pars magna divini influxus irrita redditur & frustranea; independens determinatio actionis quæ Dei est dependenti creaturæ asseritur; omnipotentiæ divinæ per creaturam ponitur obex; divinæ præscientiæ certitudo evertitur; consiliorum divinorum constantia infringitur; omnis divinæ gubernationis ordo confunditur; utque uno dicam verbo, sic in supremo dominationis throno collocatur humana voluntas, divinæ Providentiæ nexibus emancipata, ut Deo inane duntaxat relinquatur simulacrum imperii, quippe quod sit mancum, pendulum, consusum, precarium, enervatum, ac mixtum cum plurima ad creatum arbitrium submissione. Quorum omnium cum ex antè dictis facilis sit demonstratio, brevitatis causâ eis inhærere desino. Certè rem quâ oportet attentione examinanti dubium jure merito videri posset, an non tolerabilior re verâ sit Epicureismus, omnem Dei gubernationem penitus expungens, quam tam mera providentiæ creato arbitrio sic subditæ, ac ne speciem quidem summæ Majestatis præ se ferentis, umbra.
units.tr: Indeed these demonstrations carry such weight that our opponents hardly dare to state plainly what the matter is, and they prefer to seek safer hiding places in verbal ambiguities. But if you uncover their meaning, you will find the same most absurd impiety, though disguised, which we have now attacked. They clearly want to appear to admit the influence of God, but they then explain it so that they recognise only a general, indifferent influence, one that is determined and specified to either of two opposites by the free choice of the rational creature. It is as if God, in this matter, were to be pictured like a man who blows air into the pipes of some pneumatic organ, but leaves the determination of this or that note entirely to the choice and skill of the musician. From this they invent, in place of the Premotion we have already explained and demonstrated, some concurrence or other, which they call "offered" concurrence, by which they deny that our will is predetermined. Such a concurrence, they say, exists in such a way that the free creature has it so in its power that it may use it or not use it, and use it to bring about this or the opposite. In this they do not hesitate to go so far as to teach that man may use God's concurrence at his own pleasure, not otherwise than if it were an inherent habit. And from these principles arise all those monstrous opinions by which the fury of heretics, in every age, has assailed the victorious efficacy of God in the business of our salvation. Chief among them is that grace of conversion which is resistible: it is indeed sufficient, should it perhaps fall upon a mind of pious disposition ready to use it rightly, but in itself it is not at all efficacious, since it can be rejected without any trouble by a stubborn sinner. We cannot, leaving aside these later theologians, absolve these earlier ones from the detestable sacrilege, for the reasons by which in the preceding article we firmly proved that God is not acknowledged as God unless the first mover is acknowledged, one who efficaciously subordinates to himself the operations of all secondary causes. But by these views the Creator is made subordinate to the creature; a great part of the divine influence is rendered vain and fruitless; a determination of action independent of God is asserted for a dependent creature; a barrier is placed to the divine omnipotence through the creature; the certainty of divine foreknowledge is overthrown; the constancy of the divine counsels is broken; the whole order of divine government is confounded. And, to say it in one word, the human will is thus placed on the supreme throne of dominion, emancipated from the bonds of divine Providence, so that to God there is left only the empty image of rule, which is maimed, dangling, confused, precarious, enfeebled, and mixed with a great deal of submission to the created will. Since the demonstration of all these points from what has been said before is easy, I cease, for the sake of brevity, to dwell on them. Surely, to one examining the matter with the attention it deserves, it could rightly seem doubtful whether Epicureanism, which removes all government of God altogether, is not in truth more tolerable than such a mere shadow of providence, subjected to the created will and not even bearing the appearance of supreme Majesty.

units.la: Duas autem præ aliis admovent machinas, ad quasdam Divinæ Prædeterminationis certitudinem, ejusdem hostes. Altum ante omnia clamorem tollunt de libertate nostra, quam primi omninò vociferantur, si divinæ præmotioni humani arbitrii actus eo quo dictum est modo subjiciantur. Nimirùm, necessitatem quandam agendi induci per hunc Præcursum efficaciter excitantem, manifestum evadit. Atqui quod in operando necessitati cuipiam subest, id liberè agere non posse, contendunt; quatenus per necessitatem destruitur ad utrumlubet oppositorum indifferentia; quam ipsi pro anima libertatis habent. Atque hæc illa Helena est, quæ dedit, non decennale bellum, sed omnium fermè seculorum Theomachiam. Nobis nunc paulo præsius cum isto Achille est congrediendum, & nùm tantus sit, ad conficiendum quod isti volunt, ac vulgò habetur, cominùs experiundum est. Dederjn ab initio, in con-
units.tr: There are, however, two engines which the enemies of the divine Predetermination bring forward before others, to shake its certainty. First of all, they raise a loud outcry about our liberty, which they cry out above all others as lost if the acts of the human will are made subject to divine premotion in the way described. Clearly, it is evident that a certain necessity of acting is induced by this Premotion, which efficaciously excites the will. But they contend that whatever is subject to some necessity in acting cannot act freely, inasmuch as indifference to either of two opposites is destroyed by necessity; and this indifference they regard as the very soul of liberty. This is that Helen who caused not a ten-year war but a almost universal battle against God, extending over nearly all the ages. We must now engage with this Achilles a little more closely, and see, by close combat, whether he is strong enough to accomplish what they want, and what is commonly held.

units.la: XIII. Præmotionem Dei efficacem cum libertate creaturæ conciliandæ difficultas unde potissimum oriunda?
units.tr: XIII. From what source does the chief difficulty of reconciling the efficacious premotion of God with the liberty of the creature arise?

units.la: conciliando hoc Dei cum creata voluntate Præcursu aliquid latere, quod obstat, quo minus omnem hic difficultatem superare queam. Dederim, inquam, hoc: neque mirum id videri poterit; neque tale, quod quicquam faveat adversariis. Mirum accidere nequit; præcipuum enim fundamentum ex quo ratio conciliandæ nostræ libertatis cum divino Præcursu est eruenda, pendet à clarè & distinctè percepto modo illo quo causa prima in creatam voluntatem operatur: illo enim non planè perspecto, necessariò etiam hærebimus in comprehendenda habitudine, quam ex ipso hoc operandi modo causa prima dicit ad creaturæ voluntatem. Atqui quid dignius existit incomprehensibili Deo, quam incomprehensibiles fateri quas servat nobiscum agendi vias. Decentior itaque Deo ac veritati magis congrua videri debet nostra sententia, vel ob hoc ipsum, quia aliquid mirabile in ea latet, quam illa adversariorum, quæ nihil difficultatis, ut illi opinantur, hic reliquum facit. Interim in ea quam asseruimus veritate ipsi quoque minus invenirent scrupuli, si didicissent satis à sublimitate tantarum rerum humiles istos & abjectos influendi modos removere, qui nobis in creaturis sunt obvii. Id quia negligunt, nodos ipsi sibi nectunt in hoc negotio insolubiles: quos magnam partem potuissent declinare, si attendere voluissent, indè quidem nullam causam creatam tam intrinsecam esse posse alteri, quam Deus existit creatæ voluntati; hinc verò, nullam causam creatam tam ab alia pendere posse, quam à Deo pendet sua creatura. Quo observato, sponte suâ evanescit præcipua hujus loci difficultas, ex iniquâ istiusmodi comparatione maximè oriunda. Sed & ab initio aliquid hujus præmonuimus.
units.tr: I grant, I say, that in reconciling this Premotion of God with the created will something lies hidden which stands in the way of our being able to overcome every difficulty here. I grant this, and it will not seem strange, nor is it something that favours our adversaries in any way. It could not be otherwise; for the chief foundation from which the account of reconciling our liberty with divine Premotion must be drawn depends on that mode, clearly and distinctly perceived, by which the first cause works in the created will. If we have not thoroughly grasped that mode, we shall necessarily also stick fast in understanding the relation which the first cause, from this very mode of operating, bears to the will of the creature. But what is more worthy than to confess that there are ways of acting with us which we cannot comprehend, in the case of God who is himself incomprehensible? Therefore our opinion ought to seem more becoming to God and more agreeable to truth, if only for this reason, that something wonderful lies hidden in it, than that of our adversaries, which, as they suppose, leaves no difficulty here. Yet, in the truth we have asserted, they would have found fewer scruples, had they learned well to remove from the sublimity of such great things those lowly and base modes of influence which meet us among creatures. Because they neglect this, they tie for themselves knots in this matter that cannot be untied; most of which they could have avoided, had they been willing to attend to this: that no created cause can be as intrinsic to another as God is to the created will, and, on the other hand, that no created cause can depend on another as the creature depends on God. Once this is observed, the chief difficulty of this place, which arises chiefly from an unfair comparison of this kind, vanishes of its own accord. But I have already given some warning of this from the beginning as well.

units.la: Quicquid sit, quod nos ignorare mirum non est, nequaquam id creare debet præjudicium veritati, de qua sumus aliundè certò persuasi. Deum non posse non omnibus creaturarum actionibus præesse, ex perfectissima ejus natura jam demonstravimus: creaturæ rationalis voluntatem non posse non liberam esse, ipsi in nobis ipsis experimur abundè. Nunc pone, in connectendis istis duabus veritatibus me hæsitare: num ideò non-cognita connexionis ratio abnegare faciet alterutrum extremorum certissimè exploratorum An verò etiam id scire non velle debebo quod
units.tr: Whatever the case may be, and it is no wonder that we do not know it, it must by no means create prejudice against the truth, of which we are certainly persuaded from elsewhere. That God cannot but preside over all the actions of creatures, we have already demonstrated from his most perfect nature; that the will of the rational creature cannot but be free, we experience abundantly in ourselves. Now suppose that I hesitate in joining these two truths: will the unknown manner of their connection therefore make me deny one of the two extremes most certainly established? Or shall I also be obliged not to wish to know what

units.la: XIV. quod scio, quia quo pacto eorum quæ scio alterum cum altero cohæreat, nescio? Quin imò, ut nulli non constet, quam absurdus sit adversariorum in hoc negotio processus, grandius quid dabo, nunquam tamen concedendum. Fingamus, demonstratle eos, concipi non posse causæ primæ prædeterminationem qualem descripsissimus, nisi hoc ipso aliquam patiatur libertas nostra diminutionem. Quid si jam ego rationibus saltem non minus firmis demonstratum dedero (uti dedi) neque concipi posse causæ secundæ libertatem qualem illi describunt, nisi hoc ipso aliquam patiatur indepen-dens Dei dominium diminutionem? Cujusnam hîc sententia alteri præferri debeat? res ipsa clamat. Nos à Deo initium facientes, quid ejus perfectio postulet, unicè primùm attendimus; atque modum operandi illi convenientem postquam collocavimus in tuto, de salvanda demùm omni meliori modo nostra libertate cogitamus. Adversarii à semet ipsis initium facientes, id anxiè primo loco agunt, ut quam amplissimam atque absolutissimam creatæ voluntati asserant libertatem; quâ in arce collocatâ, de Deo deinceps cogitare incipiunt, totiesque ejus decreta, præscientiam, potentiam, influxum, fingunt refinguntque, donec eam illis omnibus induerint formam, quâ nihil detrahatur præconceptæ voluntatis humanæ libertati. Quis rectius hic philosophetur, judicet æquus quilibet rerum arbiter! Profectò, quanto existit tutius in hominem injurium, quam in Deum sacrilegum esse, tanto securius quis, potius quam ut Deo quicquam detrahat, aliquid suæ abneget libertatis.
units.tr: XIV. what I know, because I do not know how one of the things I know coheres with the other? Indeed, as is plain to everyone, how absurd is the procedure of our adversaries in this matter. I will grant something greater, though it must never be conceded. Let us suppose that they have demonstrated that the predetermination of the first cause, such as we have described, cannot be conceived unless our liberty thereby suffers some diminution. What if I now have shown (as I have shown) by reasons no less firm that the liberty of the secondary cause, as they describe it, cannot be conceived unless the independent dominion of God thereby suffers some diminution? Whose opinion ought to be preferred to the other here? The matter itself cries out. We, beginning from God, attend first of all only to what his perfection requires; and once we have set the mode of operating fitting to him in safety, only then do we think how our liberty may be saved in the best possible way. Our adversaries, beginning from themselves, are anxious above all to assert for the created will the fullest and most absolute liberty; once this is established as their citadel, they begin to think about God, and they feign and refashion his decrees, foreknowledge, power and influence, again and again, until they have clothed them in a form from which nothing is taken away from the preconceived liberty of the human will. Let any impartial judge of things decide who philosophises more rightly here! Surely, as it is safer to do wrong to a man than to be sacrilegious towards God, so one should rather deny something of one's own liberty than take anything away from God.

units.la: Verùm enim verò neque hujus quicquam fieri necessum est. Stante quoque divinâ prædeterminatione, nobis salva manet libertas; vera scilicet; non illa quam suo sibi arbitrio fingunt isti. Confundunt perperam duas distinctissimas notiones, ac si idem planè sint voluntatis libertas, atque ἀδιαφορία sive indifferentia; putantque nihil huic detrahi posse, quin tantundem & illi decedat: undè nata famosa illa, quam vulgò circumferunt, libertatis definitio, tanquam facultatis, quâ quis, positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, agere possit, vel non-agere. Sed confictam eam totam esse, nos dicimus ac prorsus erroneam. Nulla enim ex hac hypothesi esse potest vera libertas quæ non fit.
units.tr: But neither does any of this need to happen. Even with the divine predetermination in place, our freedom remains intact: true freedom, that is, not the kind these men invent by their own arbitrary whim. They wrongly confuse two very distinct notions, as if freedom of the will and ἀδιαφορία (indifference) were exactly the same thing, and they think nothing can be taken from the one without the same being lost from the other. Hence arose that notorious definition of freedom which they commonly circulate, namely as a faculty by which someone, with all things required for acting present, can either act or not act. But we say that this whole notion is fabricated and utterly mistaken. For on this hypothesis there can be no true freedom that is not
XV.

units.la: fit independens : quatenus dependens esse, & tamen tam absolutum in suas actiones habere dominium, ut, positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis (etiam ratione illius à quo dependet) agere quid possit vel non-agere, aperte contradictoria sunt. Quisquis ergò dicere noluerit, Deum creando creaturam liberam, eandem pariter creasse independentem, is neque admittere poterit quem illi nobus cudunt libertatis conceptum. Nescio, quid hic Cartesio in mentem venerit, quando concedit quidem, contradictionem implicare, ut voluntatis nostræ actiones à Dei voluntate non pendeant; interim simul fatetur, nos liberum arbitrium si ad nos tantum attendamus non posse non pu are independens: eo usque, ut liberum nostrum arbitrium nos Deo aliquo modo pares efficiat, ejusque imperio eximere videatur. Voces profectò nimium (ut dicam mollissimè) rudes in re delicata, quam ut ferri debeant! Sed ad rem redeo, quæ præ manibus est. Consistere absque indifferentia libertatem, vel id quoque evincit efficacissimè, quod quo perfectior est voluntatis libertas, co minor sit ejusdem indifferentia. Res claret in Deo ipso, nec non in beatis cœlitibus, quorum libertas perfectissima procul dubio est, sejuncta tamen prorsus ab indifferentia; quippe immobili constantia determinata ad hoc unum, ut non nisi quod bonum existit amant aut amare possint. Est itaquè indifferentia-per se adjunctum duntaxat libertatis, & quidem separabile. Ex quo conficitur, rectius hic sentire, qui ad libertatem, ut sic spectatam, sufficeic statuunt rationalem complacentiam, sive facultatem agendi ex prævio judicio intellectûs & concomitante lubentia voluntatis.
units.tr: it becomes independent. To be dependent and yet to have such absolute dominion over its own actions that, with everything required for acting in place (including the causality of that on which it depends), it can either act or not act, are plainly contradictory. Whoever does not wish to say that God, in creating a free creature, created it equally independent, cannot accept the concept of liberty that they hammer out for us. I do not know what came into Descartes's mind here, when he grants that it implies a contradiction that the actions of our will should not depend on the will of God, and yet at the same time admits that our free choice, if we attend to ourselves alone, cannot but think itself independent, to the point that our free choice seems in some way to make us equal to God and to exempt us from his command. These are words far too crude (to put it most gently) for so delicate a matter, and not fit to be put forward! But I return to the matter in hand. That liberty can exist without indifference is proved most effectively by the fact that the more perfect the liberty of the will, the less its indifference. This is clear in God himself, and likewise in the blessed inhabitants of heaven, whose liberty is undoubtedly most perfect and yet wholly separate from indifference; for they are fixed by an unchanging constancy to this one thing, that they love, or are able to love, only what is good. Indifference, therefore, is merely an accompaniment of liberty, and indeed a separable one. From this it follows that those think more rightly who hold that, for liberty considered as such, a rational pleasure suffices, that is, the faculty of acting from a prior judgment of the intellect and an accompanying delight of the will.

units.la: Quibus positis, ne hilum nostræ libertatis per prævium Dei concursum evertitur. Sic enim suaviter infinitæ virtutis suæ efficaciam intra creatum animum Deum insinuare docemus, ut quam creaturam rationalem agere facit, faciat agere non nisi ex rationali ductu proprii judicii & plenissimo suæ voluntatis lubitu. Quo ipso divina præmotio firmat nostram libertatem ac verum ei addit vigorem; quatenus nil magis liberè agit, quam quod efficaciter ad liberè agendum sic est determinatum, ut non-liberè agere planè non possit. Abest itaquè hinc longissimè omnis necessitas, quà vel ex bruto ac ratione destituto
units.tr: With these things laid down, not a whit of our liberty is overturned by God's prior concurrence. For we teach that God, in a gentle manner, insinuates the efficacy of his infinite power into the created mind, so that he who makes a rational creature act causes it to act only from the rational guidance of its own judgment and the fullest pleasure of its own will. By this very fact the divine premotion confirms our liberty and adds to it true vigour; inasmuch as nothing acts more freely than that which has been so effectively determined to act freely that it cannot possibly act unfreely. Thus all necessity is far removed from this, by which a rational creature would be impelled either by the instinct of something brute and devoid of reason,
Ec 3

units.la: instinctu, vel ex coactione per illatam vim externam contra propensionem impellatur rationalis creatura: quam utramlibet sicuti libertati adversari lubenter concedimus, ita omnem aliam necessitatem, praeter eam quam jam removimus, cum illa consistere posse, asserimus. Caeterum, ad detegendum amplius, quam nullarum virium sit haec sophisticatio, cui, ad destruendam Divinam Praedeterminationem, nihil non tribuunt isti imaginariae suae libertatis patroni, juvaret imprimis ostendere, quam pulchrè quicquid hùc adducunt retorqueri posset in ipsam eorum sententiam, quâ divinum concursum submittunt arbitrariae creaturarum determinationi. Si namque idcirco creatae voluntatis libertatem laedi credendum sit, quòd actiones ejus divini influxùs determinationi subordinentur; quid ni pari jure inferre licuerit, laedi ex opposito divinae voluntatis libertatem, quando actiones ejusdem arbitrii creati determinationi subjiciuntur. Non dabunt huic difficultati exitum in aeternum quot-quot indifferentiam cum libertate statuunt eandem. Sed verbum unum non addam, cum jam dudum in hoc argumento fuerim justo prolixior.
units.tr: instinct, or from compulsion by external force applied against inclination, the rational creature is driven: both of which we gladly concede are opposed to freedom, just as we assert that every other necessity, apart from that which we have already removed, can coexist with it. Moreover, to show further how baseless this sophistry is, the one to which these patrons of their imaginary freedom ascribe everything in order to destroy the divine predetermination, it would chiefly help to show how neatly whatever they bring forward could be turned back upon their own view, by which they subject the divine concurrence to the arbitrary determination of creatures. For if the freedom of the created will is to be believed impaired because its actions are subordinated to the determination of divine influence, why should it not equally follow that the freedom of the divine will is impaired when the actions of that created will are subjected to determination? All who hold indifference to be the same as freedom will never give this difficulty a way out. But I will not add a word more, since I have already been rather too long on this argument.

units.la: De Deo tamen solliciti quoque videri volunt, qui quam asseruimus non admittunt divinae Providentiae Praedeterminationem. Si enim, ajunt, ad quascunque actiones per Praecursum incitetur creatura; de malis ejusdem actionibus id intelligendum erit aequè ac de bonis: quumque ratione istius Praemotionis auctor & causa prima harum statuatur Deus, etiam perinde istarum auctor dici debebit. Ut in summi Numinis sanctitatem & justitiam haud leviter existat injuria haec sententia; quippe quae necesse habet nostrorum scelerum labem optimo Deo affricare. Sic arguunt isti; sed perperam. Quoties quid bonum operatur creatura, duo occurrunt, ipsa videlicet actio, tum etiam talis ejusdem modificatio, cujus ratione ea legi conformis, atque ideò moraliter bona, est. Ad utramque hanc Deus suo influxu rationalem creaturam excitat; consequenter utriusque, non actionis tantum quâ actionis, sed & qua bonae, totiusque adeò complexi, vera causa exsistit. Secus sese res habet in peccante creatura; in qua quidem itidem sese offert tum actio ipsa, tum conformitatis cum lege abscntia, quae est malitia ejusdem : atquì Dei ad utramque illam minimè eadem , sed dispar planè , est habitudo. Incitat is creaturam ad agendum vero influxu ; atque hactenus actionis qua talis vera existit causa. Non-influit interim in bonitatem moralem ; ad quam Præmotionis fufpenfionem sequitur quidem in actione creata legalis rectitudinis carentia, attamen non ideò hujus causa dici debet Deus ; propterea , quia non-influendo suspendit duntaxat efficaciam suæ gratiæ , ejusque indebitæ. Indebitæ, inquam : ut intelligamus , nihil in hoc negotio à Numine committi , quod sanctissimæ suæ naturæ adversetur ; quin potius hoc omne , quatenus à Deo est, bonum esse ; neque tantum metaphysicè bonum , sed & moraliter. Interim quam actionem, se quod attinet, bonam producit Creator, in eadem producenda volens suo vitio deficit creatura , illamque privativo suo non-influxu sic inquinat , ut vitiositatis qua talis vera ac solitaria existat, si sic loqui liceat, deficiens causa. Dices: Criminis culpam nihilominus in Deum conjicere poterit creatura, quippe quæ idcirco peccat, quia Deus non-influit. Verùm nihil eo efficitur, quamdiu probatum non est, illum Dei non-influxum talem creatæ voluntati imponere necessitatem; quæ cum libertate ejusdem consistere nequeat. Quam id salsum sit, ex præcedentibus proximè articulis abundè licet colligere. Equidem extra omnem controversiam esse nos inter & adversarios opinor, alteri cuicunque culpam peccati imputare posse neminem, qui id committit non nisi liberrimè, plenissimoque sui judicii ac voluntatis consensu & arbitrio. Quum itaque, non obstante Providentiâ Prædeterminante, salvam & integram esse creaturæ rationali in omni sua actione libertatem, jam demonstraverimus, utiquè manet, non posse hanc sui sceleris iniquitatem Deo aspergere, prætextu alicujus necessitatis, quæ nihil prorsus plenissimæ peccatoris libertati detrahit; cujusque utì sensum nullum, ita neque ullam habuit, dum peccavit, rationem.
units.tr: Yet those who do not admit the predetermination of divine Providence which we have asserted also wish to appear concerned for God. For, they say, if a creature is stirred by prior concurrence to whatever actions, this must be understood of its evil actions just as of its good ones; and since by reason of that premotion God is established as the author and first cause of these, he must likewise be called the author of them too. This opinion does a not slight injury to the holiness and justice of the highest Deity, since it must smear the stain of our sins upon the best of Gods. This is how they argue, but wrongly. Whenever a creature does something good, two things present themselves: the action itself, and also its particular modification by which it is in conformity with the law and therefore morally good. To both of these God, by his influence, stirs the rational creature; consequently he is the true cause of both, not of the action only as action, but also as good, and so of the whole complex. It is otherwise with a sinning creature, in which there likewise present themselves both the action itself and the absence of conformity with the law, which is its wickedness. But God's relation to these two is by no means the same; it is entirely different. He stirs the creature to act by a true influence, and so far the true cause of the action as such exists. Yet he does not influence its moral goodness. From the suspension of the premotion there does indeed follow, in the created action, a lack of legal rectitude; nevertheless God ought not on that account to be called its cause, because by not influencing he merely suspends the efficacy of his grace, and that grace is not owed. Not owed, I say: so that we understand that nothing in this business is committed by the Deity which is opposed to his most holy nature; rather, all of this, insofar as it is from God, is good, and good not merely metaphysically but also morally. Yet in respect of the action, which the Creator produces as good, the creature, wishing to produce that same action, fails through its own fault, and by its privative non-influence it so taints the action that the vice, as vice as such, exists truly and alone, if one may so speak, with a deficient cause. You will say: nevertheless the creature can lay the blame of its crime upon God, since it sins precisely because God does not influence. But nothing is gained by this, so long as it has not been proved that God's non-influence imposes on the created will a necessity which cannot coexist with its freedom. How false this is may be gathered amply from the articles immediately preceding. Indeed, I think it is beyond all controversy between us and our opponents that no one can impute the guilt of sin to another who commits it only most freely, with the fullest consent and choice of his own judgement and will. Since, therefore, we have already demonstrated that, notwithstanding the predetermining providence, the freedom of the rational creature in every one of its actions remains safe and whole, it certainly follows that this iniquity of its own wickedness cannot be cast upon God under the pretext of some necessity, which takes absolutely nothing away from the full freedom of the sinner; and which, while he sinned, had no sense in him and no reason either.

units.la: Instabis: Saltem bonitati ac justitiæ divinæ nequaquam congruum existit, suâ lege officium ab homine postulare, quod hic præstare non potest: utì nihil legis præstare potest, quandò Deus gratiæ suæ influxum suspendit. Ad quod probè notandum tandum venit, proprie loquendo, actualem praedeterminationem nullam tribuere subjecto in quod influit agendi potentiam; sed tantum ad operandum excitare creaturam, quae jam ante potentiam talem possidebat. Quamobrem, sicuti Providentiae divinae influxus potentiam agendi in creatura supponit1, non in eam confert; ita plane ex opposito Providentiae divinae non-influxus potentiam agendi in creatura integram relinquit, non aufert. Habet ergo creatura rationalis, in integritate sua spectata, potentiam praestandi omne opus legis; eamque illam habet, sive in actum ipsum influat causa prima, sive noninfluat. Sinimus itaque facile tantam creaturae rationali tribui potentiam ad obediendum Deo per omnia (loquor, ne quis erret, de ea prout venit ex manu Dei) quantam quis concipere voluerit aut potuerit: tantum si non fingas independentem, quam neque Creatoris neque creaturae conditio ferre potest. Nisi vero ad sceleris condemnandum hominem, & ab omni injustitiae specie absolvendum Numen, sufficiat creatam potentiam tam amplam, tam perfectam, tam sufficientem statuere, quam in suo genere statui potest; quid sufficiat? equidem non video. Nobis saltem id sufficit, qui indubitabilibus rationibus sumus persuasi, citra divinae perfectionis abnegationem aliter statui non posse; relinquentes de cetero suam curiositatem eis, queis nefas non videtur scrutari minutatim supremum independentis Dei in suam creaturam dominium: quorum istud quemadmodum nostri est officii, ita hoc temeritatis profecto nimiae exitiit atque inexcusabilis. Ne tamen nesciant Sophistae, nec nobis deesse quo eis os batuatur, unum addam. Ipsi in vetitorum actuum effectione hactenus saltem admittunt concursum Dei, ut influxui creaturae liberae in peccaminosam actionem vergentis, influxum suum ad eam producendam extemplo Numen jungere, fateantur. Nunc ego illos obtestor, si per concursum nostrum praevium, eorum judicio, statuatur malí auctor, dicant mihi, cur non eadem sequela per concursum eorum simultaneum Deus evitat mali fautor? Expediant hic sese! Experienturque, si quam inveneint viam, illam nobis non minus ac ipsis eundem monstrare exitum. Si expedire non se possint, sileat tandem calumnia!
units.tr: You will press further: at least it is in no way consistent with the goodness and justice of God to demand by his law an obligation from man which man cannot perform, just as he can perform nothing of the law when God suspends the influence of his grace. To this it must be carefully noted that, properly speaking, actual predetermination confers no power of acting on the subject into which it influences; it merely stirs the creature to act, the creature already possessing such a power beforehand. Therefore, just as the influence of divine Providence presupposes the power of acting in the creature, and does not confer it, so, on the contrary, the non-influence of divine Providence leaves the power of acting in the creature whole and does not take it away. The rational creature, then, considered in its integrity, has the power to perform every work of the law, and it has this power whether the first cause flows into the act itself or does not flow in. We therefore readily allow that so great a power to obey God in all things is ascribed to the rational creature (I speak, lest anyone err, of it as it came from the hand of God) as anyone may wish or be able to conceive, provided you do not imagine it independent, which the condition neither of the Creator nor of the creature can bear. Unless, indeed, it is enough, in order to condemn man for sin and to absolve the Deity from every kind of injustice, to establish a created power as ample, as perfect, and as sufficient as can be established in its own kind; what, then, would be enough? I for my part do not see. It is enough for us, at least, who are persuaded by indubitable reasons that it cannot be established otherwise without denying the divine perfection, leaving to others their curiosity, to whom it seems no sin to scrutinise minutely the supreme dominion of the independent God over his creature. Of these two things, the first is indeed our duty; the second is certainly a matter of excessive and inexcusable rashness. Yet, lest the sophists not know, nor we lack a means of stopping their mouths, I will add one thing. They themselves, at least up to now, admit that God concurs in the effecting of forbidden acts; let them confess that, when the free creature inclines to a sinful action, God immediately joins his own influence to the production of it. Now I beseech them: if, by our prior concurrence, the author of evil is held to be God in their judgement, let them tell me why, by the same consequence, through their simultaneous concurrence, God does not avoid being the patron of evil? Let them extricate themselves here! And if they find some way out, they will discover that it shows us the same exit as it shows them. If they cannot extricate themselves, let calumny at last be silent!

units.la: Agit ergò Deus in creaturas per Præcursum ; sed & cum iisdem agit per Concursum : actum illum Providentiæ, quo causa prima una cum causis secundis potenter coöperatur in producione effectuum naturalium ab hisce procedentium. Dico, effectuum naturalium : quæcunque enim in hoc Universo producuntur opera præter & extra naturæ ordinem, ea quemadmodum causarum creatarum activitatem secludunt & removent, sic non per aliquem Dei cum creatura Concursum, sed per unius Dei tanquam solitarii principii vim producuntur. De hoc Concursu demonstrando nil laborabimus. Sufficiunt abundè huic rei quæ jam antè probata dedimus, tum de efficaci Providentia Dei in genere, tum speciatim de Præcursu ; à quo ratione tantùm Concursum distingui, dudum notavimus. Addendum solummodò, in Præcursu præcipuè attendi ad activitatem creaturæ, quatenus ea à causæ primæ influxu excitatur ; in Concursu etiam imprimis rationem haberi ipsius effectûs, ab utriusque causæ causalitate procedentis. Interim nihil hic novum occurrit aut difficile, cujus intelligentiam ex antè dictis non liceat haurire. Verbo igitur de quibusdam hic monendi potius sumus, quam docendi. Cavendum, ne nomen Concursûs decipiat, mentemque inducat ad cogitandum hoc loco duas causas concurrentes partiales ; quarum exempla in creatis ubique obvia. Absit longissimè istce conceptus ! Partialis causalitas, uti non sufficit ad effectum totum producendum, nisi ab alia concausa juvetur, independente & sufficientissimo Numine prorsus indigna existit. Verè totalis causa est tum Deus, tum creatura ; quatenus in effectu nihil est, quod non sese totum debeat & Illi & huic, unicuique in suo genere atque ordine. Ut ridicula hoc loco sint Scholasticæ sapientiæ mysteria, quibus universali causæ Deo in omni opere à creatura producto respondere fingitur universale effectum, puta existentiam. Quasi effecti cujuslibet à creatura procedentis tantùm existentia (si vel maximè hæc ab essentia distingueretur ; quod illi perperàm contendunt) Deo debeatur, & non potius omnia omninò & essentialia & accidentalia prædicata ! Nec peccatum obstat, nam & illius, in quantum aliquid positivi est, Deus verè causa totalis est ; etsi non sit causa adhærentis privationis sive vitiositatis : de quo actum proximè. Neque est absonum, cjusdem effecti duo agnoscere principia totalia; dummodo existunt, subordinata: quæ ut non pugnant, sic alterum eorum alteri nihil præjudicare potest, quo minus utrumque in suo genere vere sit totalis causa. Eandem ob rationem immediata quoque effectorum, ad quæ concurrit, causa existit Deus; qui quemadmodum vi Immensitatis suæ per essentiam omnibus rebus intimè est præsens, ita quoque pari ratione immediatè in eisdem operatur. Quæ omnia pulcherrimè cogitare possumus, si eandem concipiamus esse & Dei & creaturæ actionem: quâ de re Art. vi. vii. egimus. Denique, Principalis quoque causa Deus est eorum, quorum per Concursum causa est: nequit enim ens independens agere, nisi suâ virtute, quâ principatum obtineat in agendo. Quod attendere negligunt isti, &, qui efficientiam Dei circa liberas creaturarum rationalium actiones moralem solummodò agnoscunt; qualis tantum est causæ minus-principalis, sive procatarcticæ: &, qui Concursum Dei statuunt determinabilem à causa secunda; haud aliter ac si causa prima suis creaturis ad instar instrumentalis causæ subserviat.
units.tr: God therefore acts upon creatures through Preconcurrence, but he also acts together with them through Concurrence: that act of Providence by which the first cause powerfully co-operates with secondary causes in producing the natural effects that proceed from them. I say natural effects, for whatever works are produced in this Universe beyond and outside the order of nature are not produced by any Concurrence of God with a creature. Just as they exclude and remove the activity of created causes, so they are produced by the power of God alone as a solitary principle. We will not labour to demonstrate this Concurrence. What we have already proved, both concerning God's efficacious Providence in general and concerning Preconcurrence in particular, is more than enough for the matter, and we have long since noted that Concurrence is distinguished from Preconcurrence only by reason. It need only be added that in Preconcurrence attention is directed chiefly to the activity of the creature, insofar as it is stirred up by the influx of the first cause, while in Concurrence account is taken above all of the effect itself, proceeding from the causality of both causes. Nothing new or difficult arises here whose understanding cannot be drawn from what has been said before, so here we are to be reminded of certain points rather than taught. Care must be taken that the name of Concurrence does not deceive us and lead the mind to think of two partial concurrent causes, of which examples are everywhere obvious among created things. Far be such a notion! Partial causality, which is not sufficient to produce the whole effect unless it is helped by another concause, is utterly unworthy of an independent and wholly sufficient Deity. Truly, both God and the creature are total causes, insofar as there is nothing in the effect which does not wholly owe itself both to him and to it, each in its own kind and order. So the mysteries of Scholastic wisdom are ridiculous here, by which it is pretended that a universal effect, namely existence, corresponds to God as universal cause in every work produced by a creature. As if the existence alone of any effect proceeding from a creature were owed to God (even if this were distinguished from essence, as they wrongly contend), and not rather all predicates whatsoever, both essential and accidental! Nor does sin stand in the way: God is truly the total cause of it too, insofar as it is something positive, although he is not the cause of the adhering privation or vitiosity, which we will treat shortly. Nor is it absurd to acknowledge two total principles of one and the same effect, provided they exist in subordination. As they do not conflict, so neither can one of them prejudice the other, so that each truly is total cause in its own kind. For the same reason God is also the immediate cause of the effects to which he concurs. Just as by the power of his immensity he is intimately present to all things through his essence, so in like manner he operates immediately in them. All these things we can conceive most beautifully if we conceive the action to be one and the same of God and of the creature, a matter on which we treated in Articles 6 and 7. Finally, God is also the principal cause of those things of which he is the cause through Concurrence, for an independent being cannot act except by its own power, by which it holds primacy in acting. Those men fail to attend to this who acknowledge God's efficiency concerning the free actions of rational creatures only as moral, which is the mark of a less-principal or procatarctic cause alone; and also those who hold that God's Concurrence is determined by the secondary cause, quite as if the first cause served its creatures as an instrumental cause.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus per se sequitur, quod unum in hoc negotio observandum superesset, Concursum hunc Dei non duntaxat esse restringendum ad aliquod primum creatæ actionis momentum; ac & Numen dē cætero, citra sui influxûs continuationem, sinat solummodo creaturam continuare inchoatam actionem, uti observamus v. c. pilam à manu semel impulsam, ad hoc ut aliquamdiu moveri pergat. renovato manûs influxu non indigere. Minimè sic cogitandum. Imò verò, si creaturam, quamdiu in operis productione occupatur, in agendo Concursu suo continuato non ipso facto promoveat causa prima, utique effectum ex parte tantùm & remotè ad Deum referri posset; quandoquidem id suam perfectionem consummatæ demum actioni debet. Consequenter Deus causa illius totalis, immediata, ac principalis nequaquam existeret: quod jam demonstratis è diametro adversatur. Adde, non minus à Deo pendere causæ secundæ operationem continuatam, quam eadem ab ipso pendet inchoata, quia illa majoris quam hæc, perfectionis esse non potest ; esset vero , nisi illa eodem modo ac hæc à Deo foret dependens. Et quis dubitet , cujuscunque creatæ actionis eam esse contingentiam, ut quolibet sui momento ex se deficere queat , adeoque non hoc ipso quod est inchoata continuari debeat ? Nempè , quodcunque creatæ actionis momentum nullam certam ex natura sua cum a'io ejusdem insequenti momento continuandæ habet connexionem. Si sic , manifestum evadit , causas secundas in quovis activitatis suæ articulo æquali Dei influxu indigere. Quemadmodum itaquè suo loco ostendimus, non posse ens creatum in existendo perseverare , nisi singulis continuatæ existentiæ momentis eådem vi , quâ primùm id ex nihilo fecit existere , influat Deus ; itâ pariter concludendum erit ( si creaturæ modum operandi tribuere velimus, qui modo ejusdem existendi sit approportionatus) non posse ens creatum in operando perseverare, nisi singulis continuatæ operationis momentis eâdem vi in eam influat Deus , quâ primum id ex nonoperante operans fieri fecit.
units.tr: From all these things it follows of itself that one point remains to be observed in this matter: this Concurrence of God is not to be restricted merely to some first moment of the created action, so that God, for the rest, without continuing his influence, allows the creature merely to continue the action begun, as we observe, for example, a ball once struck by a hand keeps moving for a while without needing the hand's influence to be renewed. By no means is it to be thought so. Indeed, if the first cause did not, by its continued Concurrence, actually promote the creature while it is occupied in producing the work, the effect could be referred to God only in part and remotely, since it owes its perfection to the completed action. Consequently God would not be the total, immediate, and principal cause of it at all, which is diametrically opposed to what has now been demonstrated. Add that the continued operation of a secondary cause depends no less on God than its begun operation does, for the former cannot be of greater perfection than the latter; yet it would be so if it did not depend on God in the same way as the latter. And who would doubt that the contingency of any created action is such that it can of itself fail at any moment, and so it must not be continued merely because it has been begun? Indeed, any moment of a created action has, by its nature, no certain connection with its continuation in the following moment. If so, it becomes manifest that secondary causes, at every point of their activity, need an equal influx from God. Just as we showed in its proper place that a created being cannot persist in existing unless God influences it at each moment of its continued existence with the same power by which he first made it exist out of nothing, so in like manner it must be concluded (if we wish to ascribe to the creature a mode of operating proportionate to its mode of existing) that a created being cannot persist in operating unless God influences it at each moment of its continued operation with the same power by which he first made it, from non-operating, become operating.

units.la: Interim, dum hoc pacto causa prima creaturas per Præcursum ad agendum præmovet & per Concursum in agendo pro-movet, simul eâdem illâ efficientiâ & actiones & effecta causarum secundarum ,· pro liberrimo suæ voluntatis placito , ad præstitutos à se fines ducit & gubernat. Atque hic est tertius actus istius influxûs , quem Deus circa creaturarum actiones ex-ferit : tertius nimirum pro modo concipiendi nostro; qui qua-lis hîc sese offerat , jam monui ab initio. Estque hæc propriè illa Gubernatio , quæ strictissimâ significatione Providentia vocatur. Per eam dicimus Numen omnem creaturarum activitatem dirigere ad fines , quos ipse ei prædefinivit. Videlicet, primùm quidem ad proximos , aliisque ulterioribus subordina-tos ; sic tamen ut omnia tandem redeant ad manifestandam glo-riam multiplicis perfectionis istius principii , cujus abundanti bonitati & se & omnes suas actiones agentia creata debent. Itâ demum omni modo patefit Deus tanquam Alpha & Omega ; quando qui in genere causarum efficientium existit prima , à qua derivanda rerum quarumcunque genesis ,· idem is in ordine causarum finalium occurrit ultima , in quam terminetur omnis rei creatæ analysis. Tanti est hanc Providentiæ partem, ut decet, agnoscere! absque quo nemo Deum ceu Universi Regem rite veneratur. Risit quidem eam præ aliis Epicureorum fatuitas, nescio quid insaniens de cæca fortuna & mero casu, quo volvantur rerum omnium in hoc Universo vicissitudines: verùm ad confutandum cæcum furorem multo apparatu non est opus. Tantùm eis quæ antè demonstravimus inhæreamus. Æternum decretorum divinorum ordinem, atque infallibilis præscientiæ certitudinem jam dudùm adstruximus. Atqui res secum ordinare ab omni ævo, easque ordinatas prævidere, sapienter & certò nemo potest, qui non in tempore ipso facto potenti dispensatione sic eas moderetur, ut æterno consilio respondeat ad amussim eventùs complementum. Et quorsum omnis, quem probavimus hactenùs, tum Præcursus, tum Concursus, nisi ei hæc accedat Gubernatio? Nulla profectò constat illi sapientia, nisi certo fine impellat causas secundas, quas impellit, Numen. Quare, vel frustrà tanta molitur Deus, quod ne hominis quidem est non planè insipidi; vel quod agit in & cum creaturis, sic agit, ut ad certos id dirigat fines. Infinitas rationes suppeditat Universi hujus contemplatio; cujus harmonia, vicissitudo, constantia, & quid non, uno ore vociferantur, nil eorum quæ fiunt fieri citra potentissimum pariter ac sapientissimum primæ causæ mentis præsidium & moderamen. Verùm tam millies hæc cocta sunt ac recocta à multis, & ab hominum impiorum cavillatiunculis vindicata, ut non sine tædio fusus essem in re trita. Imprimis, quoniam ex eis quæ sæpius inculcavimus facile est hùc transferre, quod rem omnem nullo negotio conficiat.
units.tr: Meanwhile, in this way the first cause pre-moves creatures to act through Preconcurrence and promotes them in acting through Concurrence, and at the same time, by that same efficiency, it leads and governs both the actions and the effects of the secondary causes, according to the most free pleasure of his will, to the ends he has set. This is the third act of that influx which God exerts upon the actions of creatures, third that is in our manner of conceiving it, the character of which I have already said from the beginning. This is properly that Government which, in the strictest sense, is called Providence. Through it we say the Deity directs every activity of creatures to the ends he has predetermined for it: first indeed to the proximate ends and to others subordinated to them, yet in such a way that all things finally return to the manifestation of the glory of that manifold perfection, by whose abundant goodness both creatures themselves and all their actions owe their being. Thus God is at last revealed in every way as Alpha and Omega, since he who is first in the genus of efficient causes, from whom the genesis of all things is to be derived, is the same who appears last in the order of final causes, in which every analysis of a created thing terminates. This part of Providence is to be acknowledged as great as it deserves, for without it no one duly venerates God as King of the Universe. The folly of the Epicureans has mocked this more than other things, raving about I know not what blind fortune and mere chance, by which the vicissitudes of all things in this Universe are turned. But no great apparatus is needed to refute this blind frenzy; we need only adhere to what we have demonstrated before. We have long since established the eternal order of the divine decrees and the certainty of infallible foreknowledge. But no one can arrange things in order from all eternity and foresee them wisely and certainly unless, in time itself, by actual and powerful disposition, he so governs them that they correspond exactly, to the completion of the outcome, with the eternal counsel. And to what end would all the Preconcurrence and Concurrence we have so far proved be, unless this Government were added to them? That wisdom surely does not belong to God unless the Deity impels the secondary causes it impels toward certain ends. Therefore either God labours in vain at so much, which is not even true of a man who is not altogether foolish, or what he does in and with creatures he does in such a way that he directs it to certain ends. The contemplation of this Universe supplies infinite reasons: its harmony, its vicissitude, its constancy, and whatever else, all cry out with one voice that nothing that happens comes about without the most powerful and equally wise protection and governance of the mind of the first cause. But these things have been cooked and recooked a thousand times by many, and vindicated against the petty cavils of impious men, so that I would be tediously prolix in a worn-out subject. Especially since, from what we have often impressed, it is easy to carry over here what settles the whole matter without any trouble.
XXII.

units.la: Cæterùm, si, ut jam ostendimus, cum decreto, præscientia, præcursu & concursu pari passu ambulet Dei Gubernatio, illisque omnes omninò actiones creatæ subjiciantur, de hac quin idem sit asserendum, dubium esse nequit. Absurdi sunt, qui nimis minutas censent quasdam creaturarum operationes, quam ut earum curam gerat Deus. Quasi scilicet quo quid exstit minus, eo magis haberi id debeat independens! Quin, quæ nos minima habemus, in eodem ordine cum maximis hic esse collocanda, vel ipse Deus nos experientiâ docet, quoties minimis utitur ad consciendas res maximas. Et, nisi minimarum, cur non nullarum actionum potius dicatur Gubernatio ; quandoquidem totum quoque hoc universum coram infinito Numine quid minimum existit ? Contingentium eadem plane ratio est. Præterquam enim quod tantùm causarum secundarum respectu, nequaquam in ordine ad primum motorem, actionum quarundam contingentiam admittimus ; etiam contingentia ipsa tantæ imperfectionis prædicatum est, ut, si ulla alia, saltem ea quæ contingens est actio, ideò quia contingens est, moderamine causæ cujusdam necessariæ indigeat. Imò verò, præprimis in contingentibus ludit frequenter stupendum in modum divina Providentia : ut non aliundè clarius elucescat sapientissima Dei œconomia ac in ipsa contingente, tam opportuna sæpè quam improvisa, contingentium causarum connexione. Idem easdem ob causas de liberis rationalium creaturarum actionibus tenendum. * Fateor, causam quamcunque liberam existere actionum suarum dominam ; at non supremam & independentem : nisi quantum homini in suas actiones imperii concessit Deus, tantum dominii in eum ipse sibi dextraxisse credendus sit. Sed de eo satis liquet ex Act. xiii. xiv. xv. xvi. Tandem malas quoque actiones divinæ Gubernationi subesse, nemo neget, qui non magnâ imperii parte Numen exuere velit; quandoquidem pleræque rerum humanarum mutationes, omniumque fermè regnorum ac rerumpublicarum revolutiones, peccaminosis mortalium machinationibus suas debent origines, incrementa, exitus. Certè, ad peccati cujusvis actum substratum Deum & præcurrere & concurrere, jam dudùm demonstravimus. Frustrà profectò, imò nec sanctè, nisi totum complexum & limitare, & in bonum finem ordinare ac dirigere, ipso facto & velit & possit. Atque hoc sensu, non alio, Nostri physicam peccati permissionem, eamque Efficacem, Deo adscribere solent. Ut mirum sit, etiam eo nomine nobis impingi impium dogma de Deo auctore peccati. Stultè! Quo pacto enim peccati causa evadat cà actione, quæ peccatum quasi supponit ; quin potius, quæ flagitio hominum ad optimos fines, ut ita loquar, abutitur ? Scilicet, aliquid Numine dignius sentiunt, qui sic philosophantur hoc loco de nuda permissione, ac si decussatis manibus sedeat Deus in hoc negotio spe-
units.tr: But if, as we have already shown, God's government moves step by step with his decree, foreknowledge, going before and concurrence, and if all created actions are subject to it, there can be no doubt that the same must be asserted of this part too. Those are foolish who think certain operations of creatures too minute for God to care for. As if, forsooth, the less a thing exists, the more it ought to be held independent! Indeed, God himself teaches us by experience that the things we count least must be placed in the same order as the greatest, whenever he uses the smallest things to bring about the greatest. And if we speak of government over the smallest things, why not of some actions rather? For what is this whole universe, before the infinite Deity, but something least? The same plain reasoning applies to contingent things. For apart from the fact that we admit the contingency of certain actions only with respect to secondary causes, and never in relation to the first mover, contingency itself is such a mark of imperfection that a contingent action, if any action is, needs the governance of some necessary cause, precisely because it is contingent. Indeed, divine Providence especially plays in contingent things, often in a wonderful manner, so that the most wise economy of God shines out nowhere more clearly than in the connection of contingent causes, which is as often timely as unforeseen. The same must be held for the same reasons concerning the free actions of rational creatures. I grant that any free cause is master of its own actions, but not a supreme and independent master. Unless God has granted to man dominion over his actions, we must believe that God has drawn to himself the whole dominion over them. On this the Act. xiii. xiv. xv. xvi. make the matter sufficiently clear. Finally, no one will deny that even evil actions are subject to the divine government, unless he wishes to strip the Deity of a great part of his rule; for most changes in human affairs, and nearly all the revolutions of kingdoms and commonwealths, owe their origins, growth and outcomes to the sinful schemes of mortals. Certainly we have long since demonstrated that God both goes before and concurs with the substratum of every act of sin. It would be in vain, and indeed not holy, unless God, by the very fact, both wills and is able to limit the whole complex and to order and direct it to a good end. It is in this sense, and in no other, that our writers are accustomed to ascribe to God the physical and, as they call it, efficacious permission of sin. So it is strange that they charge us with the impious dogma that God is the author of sin on this account too. Foolishly! For how can a cause of sin come from that action which in a manner presupposes sin, rather than from that which, so to speak, turns human wickedness to the best ends? Clearly those who philosophize here about bare permission think more meanly of the Deity than is fitting, as if God sat with folded hands in this business.

units.la: * Fateor ... ator. Quæ permissio re ipsa est otiosa non-providentia: quippe quæ infert, necessariò, vel inscio Deo committi peccata; vel invito; vel nec volente nec nolente, id est, nil curante omninò.
units.tr: * I grant ... otherwise. This permission is in fact an idle non-providence: for it implies necessarily that sins are committed either with God not knowing, or against his will, or with him neither willing nor unwilling, that is, not caring at all.

units.la: Etiamsi autem circa peccaminosas æquè ac circa quascunque alias creaturarum operationes versari statuamus hunc Divinæ Providentiæ actum, universam tamen ejus rationem agnoscimus Sanctissimam; quandò non aliam admittimus, quam quæ divinæ puritati & justitiæ sit planè congrua, quâque nihil sibi contrahat labis ex actionum, quas suâ dispensatione moderatur, vitio. Interim non minus cogitandum est, absolutissimam exist-ere hujus Gubernationis Independentiam; convenientem scilicet enti ex natura sua per omnia independenti. Ut nullam admittamus præambulam hominis voluntatem, quam præstolet-ur Deus, cujusque determinationibus se attemperet; quod subservientis potius est ministri, quam suo jure gubernantis domini. Aut neque independens esset hoc Dei regimen, si quæ vis creata ejus manum posset avertere. Quamobrem potentissimum pariter exist-it hoc summi Numinis imperium, insuperabili efficientiâ omnem omninò creaturarum activitatem flectens in eos quos Ipse illi prædefinivit fines. Absque quo neque sapientissima agnoscitur hæc Providentia ; à qua nihil est abhorrentius , quam excidere suis scopis , aut quicquam frustrà mo-liri. Moderatur verò prudentissimè omnia ordinatissimà catisfarum serie Deus , per varios casus aptis mediis universa diri-gens in præstitutos eventus , idque naturis causarum secundarum convenienter. Non semper , fateor , tanti operis elegan-tissimum ordinem comprehendit nostra stupiditas : ubi amen rerum exitus attendimus, aperit sese in hac supremæ rationis Gubernatione sapientia impervestigabilis, in iis maximè rebus quæ nobis homuncionibus omnium perplexissimæ videntur. Ex quibus sponte suâ sequitur imperii divini immutabilitas , clarè relucens in tanta tam mutabilis Universi constantia. Et , si sapientem sibi constare fas est , necessariò Numen sapientissimum procul habet mutatas quavis sui regiminis formas.
units.tr: Although we hold that this act of divine Providence is concerned with sinful actions equally as with any other operations of creatures, we nevertheless acknowledge its whole plan to be most holy, since we admit no plan but one that is wholly consistent with divine purity and justice, and by which God incurs no stain from the faults of the actions which he governs by his disposition. Meanwhile we must not think less of this that the government is most absolutely independent, befitting a being that is by its nature independent in all things. Thus we do not admit any human will that goes before, which God waits for and to whose decisions he accommodates himself; that would belong to a serving minister rather than to a lord governing by his own right. Otherwise this rule of God would not be independent, if any created power could turn his hand aside. Wherefore this dominion of the supreme Deity is equally most powerful, bending every activity of creatures, by an invincible efficacy, to those ends which he himself has predetermined for it. Without this, his providence would not be recognized as most wise; and nothing is more foreign to it than to fall short of its aims or to attempt anything in vain. God governs all things most prudently, in the most orderly series of causes, directing the universe through various events, by apt means, to the appointed outcomes, and this in a manner agreeing with the natures of secondary causes. I grant that our dullness does not always grasp the most elegant order of so great a work; but when we attend to the outcomes of things, the wisdom of this supreme government of reason opens itself, unsearchable, especially in those matters which seem to us poor mortals most perplexing. From these things it follows of its own accord that the divine rule is unchangeable, shining clearly in such constancy of so changeable a universe. And if it is lawful for a wise being to be consistent with itself, the most wise Deity is necessarily far from any change of forms of his government.

units.la: Neque obstant prodigia , quorum meminit divina pagina: ea enim uti consuetam naturalium causarum efficientiam quod ad cætera non perturbant, ita exceptiones quædam sunt naturæ regulas confirmantes quam efficacissimè; quandoquidem non casu ea accidunt, sed Dei consilio & nutu singulari, ad declarandum supremum ejusdem & independens in res suas dominium. Sed de miraculis minus nobis laborandum, qui qua Philosophi ea fermè ignoramus; id tantum scientes, liberrimum Deum creaturarum legibus esse superiorem, atque ideò ab eisdem quoties volucrit recedere posse. Hoc loco igitur de Providentiæ in Ordinariam & Extraordinariam distributione fusius non agam. Alia occurrit, eaque momenti longè maximi, ejusdem in Realem & Moralem divisio. Nimirùm, duum generum dantur creaturæ, brutæ ac rationales: unde duplex obvia earundem actívitas; alia ex mero naturali impetu fluens, alia non nisi liberè & prævio rationis consilio suscepta. Utrique præest summi Numinis Gubernatio, quæ rem unamquamque regit aptè congruenterque istis perfectionibus ac viribus agendi, quas illi in prima creatione concessit, inque ea continuatò suo influxu conservat. Præter illam ergò Providentiam, quæ potentissimo quodam regimine sese extendit ad omnes omninò creaturas, consideratas simpliciter tanquam actuosa principia causæ primæ subordinata (de qua hactenus potissimum diximus) specialioris consideration est creaturarum intellectualium, tanquam talium, per juris moderamen Gubernatio; quæ ab appropriato objecto Moralis scitè appellatur. Ejus admittendæ necessitas neminem fugere potest, attendentem duntaxat intimam creaturarum per omnia sui à suo Deo dependentiam: ea enim, cum tanta sit quanta esse potest, non finit causarum rationalium rationem à prima ratione esse independentem. Et cum agentia cætera quæcunque ordini naturæ à summo Deo præscripto, secundum nativam indolem quam in eis posuit Creator, obediant accuratissimè, negari plane nequit, rationales creaturas etiam suo modo, id est rationali, juxta rationis lumen sibi ingenitum, suum quoddam proprium, id est, rationale obsequium debere rationali Deo.
units.tr: Nor do the miracles, of which the divine page speaks, stand in the way. For these, as they do not disturb the usual efficiency of natural causes in other respects, are certain exceptions which most effectively confirm the rules of nature; since they do not happen by chance, but by the counsel and singular command of God, to declare his supreme and independent dominion over his own affairs. But we need not labour much over miracles, we who as philosophers know little about them, knowing only this: that the most free God is superior to the laws of creatures, and so can depart from them whenever he wills. Therefore I shall not here treat at length of the division of Providence into ordinary and extraordinary. Another division presents itself, and one of very great importance: the division of Providence into real and moral. Namely, there are two kinds of creatures, brute and rational, whence there is a twofold activity of each that lies open to view: one flowing from mere natural impulse, the other undertaken only freely and after prior deliberation of reason. Over both presides the government of the supreme Deity, which rules each thing fittingly and congruently with those perfections and powers of acting which he granted to it in the first creation, and preserves them in it by his continuous influence. Therefore, besides that Providence which extends by a most powerful rule to all creatures without exception, considered simply as active principles subordinate to the first cause (of which we have so far spoken chiefly), there is a more particular consideration: the government through the rule of right of intellectual creatures as such, which is aptly called moral from its proper object. The necessity of admitting it can escape no one who attends merely to the intimate dependence of creatures in all things upon their God. For that dependence, being as great as it can be, does not allow the reason of rational causes to be independent of the first reason. And since all other agents obey most exactly the order of nature prescribed by the supreme God, according to the native disposition which the Creator placed in them, it cannot be denied that rational creatures too, in their own way, that is rationally, according to the light of reason innate to them, owe to the rational God a certain obedience of their own, that is, a rational obedience.
