units.la: Atque itâ nostræ meditationi Deus hic sese offert tanquam supremum Dominum, in creaturas quasvis mentis capaces ceu subditos suos exercentem imperium pro suo arbitrio, rationali tamen
units.tr: And so, in our meditation, God presents himself here as the supreme Lord, exercising his dominion at his own discretion over all creatures capable of mind, as his subjects; yet a dominion suited to both natures, that is, rational.

units.la: XXV. Moralis Providentiæ consideratio. tamen utriusque naturæ congruum. Hujus verò duplicem observare licet œconomiam ; alteram immediatam, mediatam alteram. Videlicet ipse Deus per se in hoc Regno regit, quatenus conscientiis hominum se manifestat, & tanquam Legislatorem supremum, potestate architectonicâ jura dantem, eisque illas adstringentem; dictando officia quæ à quolibet præstanda sint Deo tanquam Regi, sibi tanquam Subdito, aliis hominibus tanquam Concivibus in hoc regno morali : & tanquam Judicem, indè quidem justissimâ severitate rebelles subditos punientem secundum sanctionem legis poenalem; hinc cives morigeros præmiantem ex gratuita promissione. Interim & aliis administrationis partem quadantenùs commisit; Magistratibus nimirum, tanquam suis in hoc regno vice-Regibus, qui potestate coactivâ armati invigilent debitæ societatis humanæ sub suo Rege Deo conservationi. Et his paucis continentur fundamenta omnis sanioris doctrinæ tum Ethicæ, tum Politicæ : quas nobilissimas Philosophiæ partes fœdissimum in modum polluunt plurimi, qui, nihil attendentes moralem hominis à Deo dependentiam, unicam, vel sui, vel etiam societatis, conservationem sibi sumunt morum regulam; abnegantes sic re verâ summi Numinis in creaturas suas imperium, ac genuinum inducentes Atheismum : quorum monstrorum ferax, eheu ! nimium existit hoc nostrum seculum. Verùm, tam est illustre hoc argumentum, ut nihil de eo dicere præstet, quando quod sufficit dicere in præsentiarum non licet. Juslam ergò ejus explicationem servabimus Tractatui peculiari de Regno Dei Morali: cujus Sciagraphiam nobiscum affectam jam habemus; quemque dabimus forlàn aliquandò, si Deus vitam dederit atque vires. Nunc ostendisse verbo sat est, ibi principium sumere Philosophiam Moralem, ubi existit Theologiæ Naturalis finis.
units.tr: XXV. Consideration of Moral Providence. Suited to both natures. Of this dominion one may observe a twofold economy: one immediate, the other mediate. God himself rules in this kingdom directly, insofar as he makes himself known to the consciences of men, and as supreme Legislator, giving laws by architectonic power and binding them to them, dictating the duties which are to be performed by each toward God as King, toward himself as subject, and toward other men as fellow citizens in this moral kingdom; and as Judge, punishing rebellious subjects with most just severity according to the penal sanction of the law, and rewarding obedient citizens from free promise. Meanwhile he has also committed a part of the administration, in some measure, to others, namely to magistrates, as his vice-kings in this kingdom, who, armed with coercive power, watch over the preservation of due human society under their King, God. And in these few words are contained the foundations of all sounder doctrine, both ethical and political; which very many men foully pollute in regard to these most noble parts of philosophy, who, attending to nothing but man's moral dependence on God, take for their sole rule of morals the preservation either of themselves or of society; thus in truth denying the dominion of the supreme Deity over his creatures, and introducing genuine Atheism. Alas, this our age is all too fertile of such monsters! But this subject is so illustrious that it is better to say nothing of it, since what is sufficient to say cannot be said at present. We shall therefore reserve its proper explanation for a separate treatise of the Moral Kingdom of God: whose outline we already have in mind, and which we shall perhaps publish sometime, if God grants us life and strength. For now it is enough to have indicated in a word that Moral Philosophy takes its beginning where the end of Natural Theology is.

units.la: Itâ benigna Numinis Providentiâ nostram hanc qualemcunque de Divinis Perfectionibus Meditationem absolvimus. Unum Deum per omnia independentem atque supremum docere, scopus fuit : in quo si quid fuit erratum, ipsâ pietate erratum fuit; quâ quanto erratur difficilius, tanto in his cogitationibus acquiescimus tutius. Interim quem cognoscimus, utinam agnoscamus talem ! Neque agnoscemus, nisi altùm præprimis animo semper inhæreat firmissima de Divina Providentia, submissa cum veneratione iuncta, persuasio. Hæc una potens existit liberare nos idololatriâ, quâ optimus etiam quisque tantopere adhæret creaturis; quarum tamen nulla in sua extantia est permanentia, nulla in opere producendo efficacitas, nisi motore primo conservante, excitante, adjuvante, moderante. Ea si sat infixa sedeat menti opinio, nunquam id eveniet, ut diffidentes abjiciamus spem, simulac carundem destituimur auxilio; superbiamus fatui, quoties inferiorum causarum suppetit abundantia. Quin potius in solum Numen fiduciam collocabimus, mente quidem sedulitate debitâ rebus agendis ex Ejus voluntate intentâ, cæterum vero securâ, atque obsequioso silentio acquiescente in cura illa, quâ prudentissimus Pater suam unicuique nostrum distribuit sortem, eamque suo arbitratu adversâ modo, modo prosperâ varietate, dispensat. Hæc una meditatio in periculis pariet securitatem, in terroribus fortitudinem, in turbulentis tranquillitatem, in adversis tolerantiam, in futurorum exspectatione æquanimitatem. Abśunt longissimè ab hac felicitate quotquot suâ, quam Dei, vivere malunt providentiâ: quippe qui sese subducentes petulanter Providentiæ dirigenti ad vitam, incidunt justissimè in Providentiam ducentem ad mortem. Absit à nobis tanta calamitas! Et aberit, si datum fuerit, devoto animo Numinis vias non-pervestigabiles sic mirari, leges sanctissimas sic revereri, ut studium nobis sit indefessum, rerum omnium Statorem ac Moderatorem mente contemplari, factis venerari, dictis celebrare, per omnia Optimum Maximum.
units.tr: By the kind providence of the Deity we have completed this meditation of ours on the divine perfections, such as it is. My aim was to teach that God is one, independent in all things and supreme. If there was any error in this, it was an error of piety itself. The more difficult such an error is to fall into, the more safely we rest in these reflections. Meanwhile, may we acknowledge in practice the God we have come to know! We will not acknowledge him unless a firm persuasion of divine providence, joined with humble reverence, always clings deeply to our minds. This alone is able to free us from idolatry, to which even the best of people cling so strongly, although no creature has any permanence in its existence, or any efficacy in producing its effects, except through the first mover, who conserves, stirs up, assists and governs it. If this opinion sits firmly enough in our minds, we will never, when we are deprived of the help of creatures, abandon hope in despair, nor, when the abundance of lesser causes is at hand, grow proud in our foolishness. Rather, we will place our trust in the Deity alone. We will apply ourselves to our tasks with due diligence, directed by his will, but otherwise we will be untroubled and will rest in quiet obedience in that care by which the most wise Father assigns each of us our lot, and dispenses it at his own judgment, now with adverse and now with prosperous variety. This one meditation will produce security in dangers, courage in terrors, calm in disturbances, endurance in adversity and equanimity in expectation of the future. Far from this happiness are all those who prefer to live by their own providence rather than God's. Withdrawing themselves wantonly from the providence that leads to life, they most justly fall into the providence that leads to death. May such a calamity be far from us! And it will be far from us, if it is granted us with devoted hearts to wonder at the Deity's untraceable ways and to revere his most holy laws, so that it becomes our unwearied endeavour to contemplate in mind the Establisher and Governor of all things, to venerate him in deeds, to celebrate him in words, and to honour him in all things as the Best and Greatest.
To the Reader, Greetings

units.la: Ut in plerisque nostris hisce de Deo cogitationibus fuimus contrariores, ita & in eis quae spectant Providentiam ejus Moralem. Hujus vis omnis cum ferme consistat in obligatione hominis quâ tenetur universa sua actiones practico rectae rationis dictamini praestare conformes, placuit hanc, quae ad manum erat, quadamque paucis completi conati fuimus praecipuam hujus rei summam, de Lege Naturae Exercitationem, Coronidis instar, addere. Neque loco alieno; quando tota aurigatur eo, ut demonstret, quod diximus, nullam veram stare Moralem Philosophiam, nisi Naturalis Theologiae fundamentis innixam.
units.tr: Just as in most of these our reflections on God we have been rather contrary, so also in those that concern his moral providence. Since almost all its force consists in the obligation by which a human being is bound to render all his actions conformable to the practical dictate of right reason, it has pleased us to add, as a kind of crown, this exercise on the law of nature, which was at hand, and which we have completed in a few words as a chief summary of the matter. Nor is it out of place, since the whole of it is directed to showing what we have said, that no true moral philosophy stands except one that rests on the foundations of natural theology.

units.la: EXERCITATIO PHILOSOPHICA, DE LEGE NATURÆ. SUMMARIUM
units.tr: PHILOSOPHICAL EXERCITATION ON THE LAW OF NATURE: A SUMMARY

units.la: I. Providentiae Divinae subest quicquid existit rerum. II. Ex quo fluit Numinis in universas creaturas Imperium. III. Quod quatenus circa hominem versatur peculiarem meretur considerationem. IV. Regui Dei Moralis instrumentum est Lex Naturae. V. Ea est practicum rectae rationis dictamen: VI. Innatum, quoad habitualem animi in id proclivitatem: VII. Praecipue quidem quod ad generalia honesti principia. VIII. Lex haec est, & quidem propriè dicta. IX. Ejus existentia tam manifesta, quam omnimoda hominis à Deo dependentia. X. Citra eam nulla existere potest rationalis creatura. XI. Legislatoriae potestatis basis Divinae naturae eminentia.
units.tr: I. Whatever exists is subject to the providence of God. II. From this flows the dominion of the Deity over all creatures. III. That which concerns man, insofar as it bears on him, deserves a particular consideration. IV. The Law of Nature is the instrument of God's moral kingdom. V. It is the practical dictate of right reason: VI. innate, as to a habitual inclination of the mind towards it: VII. chiefly with respect to the general principles of what is honourable. VIII. This is a law, and properly so called. IX. Its existence is as manifest as man's complete dependence on God. X. Apart from it no rational creature can exist. XI. The basis of legislative power is the eminence of the divine nature.

units.la: XII. Obligationis ad eam agnoscendam sensum infert dependentiæ suæ in creatura conscientia. XIII. Jus Dei Legislatorium malè ad Ejus beneficia, vel solam potentiam, refertur. XIV. Innatæ Legis præcepta quædam sunt Juris Divini Naturalis; XV. Ut alia præscribere per ipsam suam naturam Numen nequiverit: XVI. Quædam tamen Juris Divini merè Positivi. XVII. Quæ sententia & Divinæ Majestati planè congrua est; XVIII. Et naturali hujus Legis sensui nihil detrahit. XIX. Arbitraria præcepta cadere possunt sub Dei dispensationem. XX. Lex Naturæ lata & omni, & soli creaturæ rationali. XXI. Ut nulla cæterorum animantium hic haberi debeat ratio. XXII. Triplicem, ad promovendum Regnum Dei, imponit hæc Lex obligationem: XXIII. Cui minimè satisfacit sola Societatis Civilis confervandæ consideratio; XXIV. Cum multorum officiorum antiquior longè sit obligatio: XXV. Quam qui non admittit Atheismum Politicum revera inducit. XXVI. Lex Naturæ necessariò munita Sanctione Pœnali; XXVII. Quâ æquissimo jure immorigeros exstirpatio ex hoc Regno manet: XXVIII. Uti obsequiosos ejus cultores beata Dei, Regis sui, fruitio. XXIX. Unde ipso naturæ lumine Lex hæc ut formula Fœderis operum innotescit. XXX. His paucis continueri universæ Moralis Philosophiæ fundamenta.
units.tr: XII. The consciousness of its dependence on God in the creature produces the sense of obligation to acknowledge it. XIII. God's legislative right is wrongly referred only to His benefits, or to His power alone. XIV. Some precepts of the innate Law are of the Divine Natural Right; XV. since God could not prescribe others by His own nature: XVI. yet some are of purely Positive Divine Right. XVII. This opinion is wholly consistent with the Divine Majesty, XVIII. and takes nothing away from the natural sense of this Law. XIX. Arbitrary precepts may fall under God's dispensation. XX. The Law of Nature is given to all, and to the rational creature alone. XXI. So no regard is to be had here to the other living beings. XXII. This Law imposes a threefold obligation to promote the Kingdom of God: XXIII. which the consideration of preserving civil society alone by no means satisfies; XXIV. since the obligation of many duties is far older. XXV. Whoever does not admit this in fact introduces political atheism. XXVI. The Law of Nature is necessarily fortified with a penal sanction; XXVII. by which, by the most just right, the disobedient remain to be cut off from this Kingdom: XXVIII. while its obedient worshippers enjoy the blessed fruition of God, their King. XXIX. Whence this Law, by the light of nature itself, is known as the formula of the covenant of works. XXX. In these few points the foundations of all Moral Philosophy are contained.

units.la: Etus verbum est: Si datur Deus, ergò mundus regitur Providentiâ. Et verissimum! Quisquis enim Creatoris excellentiam cum creaturarum imperfectionibus ritè conferre instituit, necesse habet fateri, quam Deus totâ suâ naturâ independens est, tam esse ab influxu Dei dependentes per omnia sui quasvis creaturas. Si sic, sponte suâ sequitur, tantam existere Creatoris circa suas creaturas Providentiam, quanta est creaturarum à suo Creatore dependentia. Huic cum nil creaturæ queat subduci, neque etiam illi quicquam ejusdem potest subtrahi.
units.tr: Its saying is: If God exists, therefore the world is governed by providence. And most true! For whoever undertakes to compare rightly the excellence of the Creator with the imperfections of creatures must necessarily confess that, just as God is wholly independent by His whole nature, so all His creatures, in every respect, are dependent on the influence of God. If so, it follows of its own accord that the providence of the Creator over His creatures is as great as the dependence of the creatures on their Creator. Since nothing can be taken away from this, nothing can also be subtracted from that.

units.la: Quæ veritas quemadmodum immota basis est omnis Imperii, quod suo jure atque suprema legibusque soluta potestate diffundit Numen per omnes omnino res universi hujus Macrocosmi ambitu comprehensas, ita eadem præcipuum existit fundamentum specialioris illius Providentiæ, quâ semet ipsum Regem Microcosmi, sive Hominis, manifestat Divina Majestas: quæ quo proximior est Homini atque magis propria, eo diligentiorem ejusdem meretur attentionem.
units.tr: This truth is as firm a basis for every dominion which, by its own right, by supreme power and loosed from laws, the Deity extends over all things comprehended within the compass of this Macrocosm of the universe; so the same truth is also the chief foundation of that more particular providence by which the Divine Majesty reveals itself as King of the Microcosm, that is, of Man. The nearer and more proper this providence is to man, the more careful attention it deserves.

units.la: Etiamsi enim nihil quicquam in universo Providentiæ opere tam est minutum, quod non animi nostri & admiratione summâ & veneratione profundissimâ sit dignissimum, tanto tamen quâ Deus moderatur hominum genus, eâ quæ cæteri mundi est, excellentior existit gubernatio, quanto præ omni alia re corporea eminentioris naturæ, atque ideò imperii cujusdam sublimioris capacior, est homo. Creatus nimirum mentis particeps, & ipse in suas actiones habet dominium; atquì, quia creatus talis, etiam hoc ipso Creatoris sui dominio subjectus.
units.tr: For although nothing in the work of providence in the universe is so small that it is not most worthy of our minds' highest admiration and deepest veneration, yet the government by which God rules the human race is more excellent than that of the rest of the world, in proportion as man, being of a nature more eminent than any other corporeal thing, is therefore more capable of a certain higher dominion. Created, no doubt, as a sharer in mind, he himself also has dominion over his own actions; but being created as such, he is by this very fact also subject to the dominion of his Creator.

units.la: Subjectus, inquam, dominio Dei, ceu Regis sui, gubernantis rationalem creaturam peculiari modo, & illi prorsus congruo, & sese maximè digno; quandò rationali imperio actionibus quibusvis rationalibus suam, tanquam primæ rationis, voluntatem proponit homini normam, ut imitandam semper religiosè, sic violandam nunquam impunè. Atque hùc spectat Regnum Dei Morale in genus humanum; cujus omnis tum vis tum exercitium consistit in præceptis illis, quæ vulgò Juris, sive Legis, Naturalis nomine veniunt. Circa quæ generaliora quædam in præsens paucis notare, animus est.
units.tr: Subject, I say, to the dominion of God as his King, who governs the rational creature in a peculiar manner, one wholly fitting to Him and most worthy of Himself; since by rational authority He sets before man, in all rational actions, His own will as the norm of the first reason, to be always imitated with reverence, and never violated with impunity. To this pertains the Moral Kingdom of God over the human race, whose whole force and exercise consists in those precepts which commonly go by the name of Natural Right or Natural Law. I intend here to note briefly some of their more general features.

units.la: Est autem Naturæ Lex, Innatum creaturæ rationali rectæ rationis dictamen, quatenus illam obligat ad actiones suas ei præstandas conformes. Innatum dico esse rationis dictamen, quatenus id à naturæ humanæ auctore Deo à prima ejus origine ei est insculptum, sic ut in hac vita perpetuò eam comitetur.
units.tr: Now the Law of Nature is the innate dictate of right reason in the rational creature, insofar as it binds him to perform actions conformable to it. I say the dictate of reason is innate, insofar as it has been engraved on him from his first origin by God, the author of human nature, so that it accompanies him perpetually in this life.

units.la: Quem in sensum Naturæ Legem Philosophus scitè appellavit, Δικαιον ἐμψυχον; atque gentium Doctor emphaticè alibi, ἔγγιστα τῷ νόμῳ χαρτὸν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις.
units.tr: In this sense the Philosopher aptly called the Law of Nature "a living right" [Δικαιον ἔμψυχον]; and the Teacher of the Gentiles, elsewhere with emphasis, "close to the law, written in their hearts" [ἔγγιστα τῷ νόμῳ γραπτὸν ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις].

units.la: Quæ tamen non itâ accipienda veniunt, ac si Legis Naturæ notitia actualis menti à primo nativitatis momento obversetur; cujus ea in omni suo statu, nominatim infantili, non semper est capax: sed intellectam volumus constantem quandam & habitualem quasi animi dispositionem, quâ ipse suapte naturâ proclivis est, simulac ei fit idonea Legis hujus argumentum percipiendi occasio, & ad ruendum absque ulla hæsitatione ac citra demonstrationem in ejusdem assensum, & ad agnoscendam suam erga eam obligationem.
units.tr: These words, however, are not to be taken as if an actual knowledge of the Law of Nature were present to the mind from the first moment of birth; the mind is not always capable of this in every state, especially in infancy. Rather we mean a certain constant and habitual disposition of the mind, by which it is by its own nature inclined, as soon as an opportunity of perceiving the subject-matter of this Law is given to it, to assent to it at once without any hesitation and without demonstration, and to acknowledge its own obligation towards it.

units.la: Ad hæc, Innatum dicimus Legis Naturalis sensum: non quasi omnium præceptorum ad eam pertinentium immediata persuasio in omnium ac singulorum hominum animis reperiatur; sed quatenus in unaquaque rationis compote creatura suâ luce radiant generalia saltem honesti atque turpis principia, unde menti, si rectâ ratione hac parte uti voluerit, pronum existit, plurimas elicere per ratiocinationem legitimam conclusiones firmissimas; relictâ quoque eidem, pro re nata & varia circumstantiarum exigentia, prudenti omnium applicatione. Quod observasse operæ pretium fuerit, ne quid vel perfectionis vel certitudinis decedere huic Legi opinemur, per diversissima sæpè hominum de Officiis quibusdam eâ præscriptis judicia.
units.tr: Moreover, we call the sense of the Natural Law innate, not as though the immediate persuasion of all the precepts belonging to it were found in the minds of all and each of men; but insofar as the general principles of the honourable and the base, at least, shine with their own light in every creature endowed with reason. From these the mind, if it is willing to use reason rightly in this part, is readily able to draw, by legitimate reasoning, very many firm conclusions; while to each man is left, according to the occasion and the varying demands of circumstances, the prudent application of all these. It will be worth observing that we should not think this Law loses anything of its perfection or certainty because of the very diverse judgments of men about certain duties prescribed by it.

units.la: Nugantur autem hic nimiùm, qui contendunt, Jus hoc Naturæ proprie loquendo Legem non esse; eò quod scriptum non sit, neque oratio ejus qui jure imperat, sed tantum conclusiones quædam ratione intellectæ. Posterius hoc quam sit salsum, jam vidimus: & res ipsa clamat; quas enim conclusiones ratio intelligat absque suis præmissis principiis? Prius quod attinet, non id urgeretur, si attendere placeret, scripturam nequaquam de Legis essentia esse, sed tantum ad id pertinere, ut alteri per eam de voluntate Legislatoris constet. Atquì non tenuibus istis adminiculis eget supremus Legislator, qui suæ mentis placita immediatè conscientiis suarum creaturarum efficacius intimare valet, quam ullus mortalis Legislator suam voluntatem alteri declarare potest per scripturam, vel signa alia qualiacunque.
units.tr: Those trifle too much here who contend that this Right of Nature is not properly speaking a Law, because it is not written, nor is it the utterance of one who commands by right, but only certain conclusions understood by reason. How false the latter is we have already seen, and the matter itself cries out: for what conclusions could reason understand apart from their principles? As for the former, the point would not be pressed if one cared to consider that writing is by no means of the essence of a law, but pertains only to making the will of the Legislator known to another by it. But the supreme Legislator does not need such slender supports, since He is able to make the decrees of His mind known immediately to the consciences of His creatures more effectively than any mortal legislator can declare his will to another by writing or by any other signs whatsoever.

units.la: Agnoscendam autem esse istiusmodi Legem animis ingenitam, evincunt abunde quae initio hujus Dissertationis praemisimus; quae & idcirco praemisimus. Nimirum, simulac homo nascitur, propter omnimodam ab Opifice sui dependentiam, nascitur ejusdem subjectus; id est, talis, qui quemadmodum se totum suo Creatori debet, ita obligatus est se suaque omnia debita cum observantia illius arbitrio submittere, ejusdemque summam prae se venerari excellentiam. Atqui cum nulla obligatio aliunde quam a legis imperio derivari queat, manifestum evadit, tam naturalem esse creaturae rationali innatam Legem, quam illi naturale est simulac producitur rationaliter a Deo dependere, tique sese totam debere.
units.tr: That a law of this kind is to be acknowledged as implanted in minds is amply shown by what we set out at the beginning of this Dissertation, and therefore we set it out. Namely, as soon as man is born, on account of his complete dependence on his Maker, he is born His subject; that is, such a one who, just as he owes himself wholly to his Creator, so he is bound to submit himself and all his debts to His will with reverence, and to venerate above all His supreme excellence. But since no obligation can be derived from any source other than the command of a law, it becomes manifest that the Law is as natural and innate to the rational creature as it is natural for him, as soon as he is produced, to depend rationally on God and to owe himself wholly to Him.

units.la: Errant itaque, qui autumant, creare Deum posse creaturam sanctam, interim ex-legem, soliusque amoris vinculo sibi religatam. Errant; cum ne quidem ad hunc amoris actum eliciendum obligatio citra legis mandatum concipi queat. Et quocunque in statu hominem fingere volueris, semper saltem est subjectum Legis à Deo ferendae, si ità placuerit, capax; consequenter de facto semper obligatur animum saltem habere paratum, ad Legem divinam, casu quo praescribitur, humili cum pietatis affectu excipiendam atque observandam. Atqui, dico iterum, unde haec ipsa obligatio, si creatura cogitetur prorsus ex-lex?
units.tr: They are therefore wrong who maintain that God can create a holy creature that is nevertheless free from law and bound to him by the bond of love alone. They are wrong, since not even the obligation to elicit this act of love can be conceived apart from a command of the law. And whatever state you wish to imagine man in, he is always at least capable of being made subject to a law given by God, if God so pleases; consequently he is always obliged, in fact, to have a mind at least ready to receive and observe the divine law, with humble affection of piety, whenever it is prescribed. But again I ask: from what source would this obligation come, if the creature were thought of as wholly without law?

units.la: Ut vero ex dictis satis intelligimus, ut naturae nostrae sic Legis ei insculptae auctorem esse eundem D. O. M. ita non obscure ex iis percipimus, quodnam sit in Deo potestatis hujus legislatoriae fundamentum? Infinita nempe perfectissimae naturae eminentia: qua ipsa digna existit tanta existimatione atque veneratione, quanta in animum finitum cadere potest. Ex quo conficitur, Deum jus habere plenissimum creaturis suis praescribendi mandata, in quorum exacta observantia agnoscatur re ipsa infinitae perfectionis Numen, ac Dominus earundem supremus.
units.tr: As we understand well enough from what has been said, the same God, the Most Good and Greatest, is the author both of our nature and of the law engraved on it. From these things we also perceive clearly what is the foundation of this legislative power in God. It is, namely, the infinite pre-eminence of his most perfect nature, by which he is worthy of as much esteem and reverence as a finite mind can conceive. From this it follows that God has the fullest right to prescribe commands to his creatures, in whose exact observance the Deity of infinite perfection and their supreme Lord is recognised in fact.

units.la: Cujus supereminentis in ente summè perfecto potestatis, suaeque infra eam, ut ita loquar, subsidentiae conscientia quoniam neminem creaturam rationalem fugere potest; liquet, hanc sese illius imperio subducere nunquam posse, citra evidentem tem rationalis suæ naturæ quandam quasi abnegationem. Ex quo fluit, rationalem creaturam qua talem, eo ipso quod tallis est, obligari ad officiorum à Deo Rege suo sibi præscriptorum præstationem: eâque necessitate quâ se ipsam intelligit rationalem, etiam non posse non agnoscere omnimodam suam, hac quoque parte, à primæ rationis imperio dependentiam.
units.tr: Since no rational creature can escape the consciousness of this supereminent power in the Most Perfect Being, and of its own subordination beneath it, so to speak, it is plain that it can never withdraw itself from his command without a manifest denial, as it were, of its own rational nature. From this it follows that a rational creature, simply as such and because it is such, is obliged to perform the duties prescribed to it by God its King; and by that same necessity by which it understands itself to be rational, it cannot fail to acknowledge its total dependence, in this respect too, upon the authority of the First Reason.

units.la: Errant idcirco toto coelo, qui jus Dei legislatorium fundatum arbitrantur in creatione, conservatione, similibusve beneficiis: hæc enim, tametsi ad actuale hujus potestatis exercitium prærequirantur, non tamen ponunt, sed supponunt, Divinæ perfectionis infinitatem; genuinum, ut jam ostendimus, hujus potestatis principium. Nec minùs errant, qui jus imperii Deo competere asserunt duntaxat ob irresistibilem potentiam, quâ inferior exi-stat humana infirmitas: cum sola potentia irresistibilis, præcisa Dei bonitate, æquitate, sanctitate, justitiâ, vim quandam quasi tyrannicam potius sapiat, quam dignam tanto Numine potestatem.
units.tr: Therefore they are utterly wrong who think that God's legislative right is grounded in creation, preservation or similar benefits. For these, although they are required beforehand for the actual exercise of this power, do not establish it but presuppose it: the infinity of divine perfection is, as we have already shown, the genuine principle of this power. Nor are they less mistaken who assert that the right of rule belongs to God merely on account of an irresistible power by which human weakness is far inferior. For irresistible power alone, apart from the goodness, equity, holiness and justice of God, savours rather of a certain tyrannical force than of a power worthy of so great a Deity.

units.la: Sed quo usque in condenda Naturæ Lege hac suâ potestate usus fuerit, vel uti saltem potuerit, Numen? non omnes idem sentiunt. Id certum est, non potuisse non Deum vi suæ perfectionis, ea saltem suis creaturis rationalibus præscribere officia, quæ ex natura tum sua tum harum indivisio nexu sequuntur; quale saltem est præceptum de agnoscendo Deo, tanquam supremo Domino, ut in sese beatissimo, ita sufficientissimo rebus quibusvis aliis extra se, atque ideò perfecto amore & honore prosequendo.
units.tr: But how far the Deity made use of this power in framing the law of nature, or at least could have used it, not all think alike. This is certain: by the force of his perfection God could not but prescribe to his rational creatures at least those duties which follow from their nature and from the indissoluble bond between them; such as the precept to acknowledge God as supreme Lord, who is as most blessed in himself as he is most sufficient for all other things outside himself, and who is therefore to be pursued with perfect love and honour.

units.la: Ut minimè ferenda sit assertio universum Legis naturalis argumentum ad merum jus Dei positivum sic referentium, ut, quicquid eâ continetur à pura liberrimæ voluntatis Divinæ determinatione in solidum id pendere contendant. Quod crudum profectò dogma est, atque à sanctissima Dei natura nimium abhorrens; quando per se indifferens inducit Numen ad id, ut vel coli velit à suis creaturis, vel abnegari: sive, cui perindè sit, vel obligare, si velit, suos subditos ad sui abnegationem, id est Atheismum, vel ad agnitionem sui tanquam talis, qualis revera existit.
units.tr: The assertion is quite unacceptable that refers the whole argument of natural law to mere positive divine right in such a way that they contend that whatever it contains depends entirely on the bare determination of the most free divine will. This is indeed a crude dogma, and too far removed from the most holy nature of God; for it makes the Deity, who is in himself indifferent, such that he may will either to be worshipped by his creatures or to be denied; or, what comes to the same thing, that he may oblige his subjects, if he wishes, to deny him, that is to atheism, or to acknowledge him as he truly is.

units.la: Ast neque eorum hic probamus sententiam, qui in aliud extremum tremum abeuntes, nulla officia per Naturæ Legem Deum hoc mini præscripsisse, vel etiam præscribere potuisse, asserunt, quam quæ vel sua, vel à se pendentium creaturarum natura, necessariò postulet: cæterum nullas hoc in negotio partes esse juris divini merè positivi. Equidem, nisi hos abripuisset totos contentionis Sabbathicæ fervor, contrarium docere potuisset, ut alia multa sileam, vel sola prohibitio incestús: qui quo pacto per sese naturæ vel divinæ vel humanæ necessariò adversetur, ex alterutra illa firmiter demonstratum à nemine vidi, neque etiam solidè demonstrari posse confido.
units.tr: But neither do we here approve the opinion of those who, passing to the other extreme, assert that God has prescribed through the law of nature to man no duties except those which the nature of the creatures, either their own or of those dependent on them, necessarily requires; and that in this matter there is no part of mere positive divine right. Indeed, had the fervour of the Sabbatarian controversy not carried them away entirely, they could have taught the contrary, to say nothing of many other things, from the prohibition of incest alone. How this is necessarily opposed, through itself, to the nature of God or of man, in either sense, I have never seen firmly demonstrated by anyone, nor do I trust that it can be solidly demonstrated.

units.la: Deo dignius, nostro judicio, sentiunt, qui quidem Legis Naturæ magnam partem esse Juris divini naturalis concedunt; sed & bene multa in eadem occurrere opinantur, quæ sint juris divini prorsus arbitrarii ac purè positivi, quorumque non tam facilis est ex natura vel Dei vel nostri demonstratio, quam quidem eorundem existit efficax per immediatum quendam sensum in nobis persuasio. Hæc sententia, ut ab una parte sanctissimum legislatorem ponit Deum, qui in Lege sua nihil eorum exprimere prætermisit, quæ ad perfectissimæ suæ naturæ agnitionem pertinent, ita ab altera illimitatam simul agnoscit divinæ potestatis in suas creaturas amplitudinem, quando hic imperasse sufficit, etiam ea in quibus stat pro ratione solius imperantis arbitrium.
units.tr: In our judgement those think more worthily of God who concede that a large part of the law of nature is of divine natural right; but they also think that many things occur in it which belong purely to arbitrary and positive divine right, the demonstration of which from the nature of God or of ourselves is not so easy, but whose persuasion is effectively present in us through a certain immediate sense. This view, on the one hand, holds God to be the most holy lawgiver, who in his law has omitted nothing that pertains to the knowledge of his most perfect nature; and on the other hand, it acknowledges the unlimited extent of divine power over his creatures, since it is enough that he has commanded, even in those matters in which the will of the commander alone is the rule.

units.la: Neque idcirco definit naturale esse nobis ejusmodi aliquod præceptum. Non enim hoc loco id naturale dicimus, quod ex natura nostra necessariò fluit, sed potius id omne quod naturam nostram humanam in hoc naturæ statu in quo versamur indivisim comitatur. Non posse autem Deum cum natura nostra connectere notitiam quarundam rerum, quarum demonstrativa certitudo ex contemplatione nostri vel sui erui nequeat, hactenus à quoquam probatum non audivi: oppositumque vel solæ evincunt imbelles rationes quæ pro prohibito incestu indè petitæ vulgò adferuntur; quem tamen jure naturali turpem & illicitum habendum esse utrimque constat.
units.tr: Nor does this view therefore hold that any such precept is natural to us. For here we do not call natural that which flows necessarily from our nature, but rather all that which accompanies our human nature inseparably in this state of nature in which we live. But I have not heard anyone prove hitherto that God cannot connect with our nature the knowledge of certain things whose demonstrative certainty cannot be drawn from the contemplation of ourselves or of our own nature; and the opposite is shown by the feeble arguments which are commonly brought forward on this matter against incest, arguments which in any case both sides agree that incest, by natural law, is to be held shameful and unlawful.

units.la: Quæ si ritè percepta fuerint, viam planam faciunt ad expediendam agitatissimam controversiam, quanta sit Divini Numinis potestas circa Legis Naturæ vel mutationem, vel dispensationem ? Tanta scilicet ea statuenda, quanta est ejusdem in condenda hac Lege libertatis indifferentia. Quatenus enim non nisi suo arbitrio præcepta quædam dedit, quæ, si placuisset, etiam planè non dare potuisset, liquet, eâdem libertate posse cum, si velit, vel ejusmodi præceptis quasdam personas eximere, vel eadem quoque prœtus abrogare. Quod tamen ad officia quæ sunt juris Deo naturalis extendendum non est; ob rationes antè datas. An verò facta sit aliquandò re ipsâ talis aliqua vel mutatio vel dispensatio, quæstio tantùm facti est; adeòque nec hujus loci.
units.tr: If these points are rightly understood, they open a plain path for settling the much-disputed question of how great is the power of the divine Deity over the law of nature, both as to its change and its dispensation. It must be determined to be as great as is the indifference of his freedom in framing this law. For insofar as he gave certain precepts only by his own will, which, had he pleased, he could entirely not have given, it is plain that with the same freedom he can, if he wills, either exempt certain persons from such precepts or abrogate them altogether. This, however, is not to be extended to the duties which belong to natural divine right, for the reasons given above. Whether any such change or dispensation has ever actually been made is a question of fact only, and therefore does not belong to this place.

units.la: Porrò, quandò jam sæpius dictum fuit, Legem Naturæ constitere in rectæ rationis dictamine, à Deo menti impresso, ad id ut sit actionum rationalium norma, clarum est, quinam isti sint, quibus hæc lex lata est ? Creaturæ scilicet rationales: eæque tum solæ, tum omnes. Solæ; quia solæ Legis præcepta intelligere, auctoritatem Legislatoris agnoscere, suasque actiones ad ejus modulum componere possunt. Omnes; quia omnium æqualis est à Deo tanquam Rege suo moralis hac parte dependentia.
units.tr: Further, since it has been said often enough that the law of nature consists in the dictate of right reason, impressed by God on the mind, so that it may be the rule of rational actions, it is clear who are those to whom this law has been given? Namely, rational creatures; and these both alone and all of them. Alone, because only they can understand the precepts of the law, acknowledge the authority of the Lawgiver, and fashion their actions according to its measure. All of them, because the moral dependence of all upon God as their King is equal in this respect.

units.la: Absona quapropter, etiamsi trita, est ea Juris Naturalis definitio, quâ describitur esse, quod natura omnia animantia docuit. Præterquam enim quod jam millies notatum sit, & ex dictis clareat, Jus sive Legem in res ratione carentes nullum cadere, vel cadere posse; etiam id minimè prætereundum, ingenti errore Legis hujus præcepta restringi ad istos tantum actus, quorum vestigia in brutis obvia sunt: quâ exceptione descriptionis hujus absurditatem vulgò palliare solent. Sed nihil agunt.
units.tr: Therefore that definition of natural right, though commonplace, is out of tune, by which it is described as what nature has taught all living creatures. For apart from the fact that it has been noted a thousand times already, and is clear from what has been said, that right or law falls upon, or can fall upon, creatures without reason not at all; we must also not pass over the fact that by a huge error the precepts of this law are restricted to those acts alone whose traces are found in brute beasts; and by this exception people commonly try to cover up the absurdity of this description. But they achieve nothing.

units.la: Etenim pleraque officia Lege Naturali mandata, eaque longè præcipua, talia exi-stunt, ut ne quidem quoad actum materialem, ut loqui solent, in bruta cadant: quod liquet intuenti omnia quæ ea jubet circa Deum, plurima quæ injungit homini circa se ipsum ac proximum observanda.
units.tr: For most of the duties the Law of Nature prescribes, and by far the most important ones, the material act itself does not fall on brute beasts, as people usually put it. This is plain to anyone who looks at everything the Law orders concerning God, and at most of what it requires man to observe concerning himself and his neighbour.

units.la: Qua de re dubitari amplius nequit, si porrò proprium hujus Legis finem attendamus; quem alium nullum esse, res ipsa clamat, quam ut sit instrumentum Moralis istius Imperii quod Deus in hominum tanquam Subditorum suorum animos exercet: dum hoc vinculo adstringuntur rationales creaturæ ad promovendam vendam pro viribus Divini hujus Regni amplitudinem, ea fideliter præstando officia, quæ ex Legis requisito earum unaquæque Deo debet tanquam Regi suo, sibimet ipsi tanquam Dei Subdito, aliis omnibus hominibus tanquam suis in eodem Regno, sub eodem Principe Deo, Concivibus.
units.tr: There can be no further doubt on this point if we also consider the proper end of this Law. The thing itself cries out that its only end is to serve as the instrument of that moral rule which God exercises over the minds of men as his subjects. By this bond rational creatures are bound to advance, as far as their strength allows, the greatness of this divine kingdom, faithfully performing those duties which the requirement of the Law says each of them owes: to God as her King, to herself as a subject of God, and to all other men as her fellow citizens in the same kingdom under the same Prince, God.

units.la: A qua saniori Legis Naturalis consideratione longissimè recedit philosophatio omnium ferè qui de Jure Naturali scribunt hodiè Auctorum, autumantium, unicum Philosophiæ moralis Fundamentum, atque adeò præcipuam Legis Naturæ summam absolvi unicâ societatis civilis culturâ. Ex qua una hypothesi fluxerunt tot monstrifici in hoc negotio conceptus Hobbesii, aliorumque; non, ut oportet, Politicæ fundamenta ex Ethica petentium, sed ordine prorsus inverso universam Ethicam Politicæ hominum societati subordinantium.
units.tr: Far removed from this saner view of the Law of Nature is the philosophy of nearly all the writers on natural law today, who maintain that the sole foundation of moral philosophy, and the chief sum of the Law of Nature, is fulfilled by the single cultivation of civil society. From this one hypothesis have flowed so many monstrous notions in this matter, those of Hobbes and others. They do not seek the foundations of politics from ethics, as they ought to, but in a completely inverted order they subordinate the whole of ethics to the political life of human society.

units.la: Hominem quidem suâ naturâ esse animal sociale, certum est: verùm uti hæc ad societatem civilem colendam inclinatio hominis naturam sequitur, non constituit, itâ longè altius petenda sunt officiorum homini qua tali præstandorum fundamenta, quam ex civilis convictûs regulis. Imò verò, homini secundum se consideratò, ut antè vidimus, ipsâ suâ naturâ vi hujus Legis incumbit obligatio, ad Deum colendum, proximum amandum, temperanter vivendum, etiamsi nulla ei ad corpus civile, cujus sit membrum, accesserit relatio.
units.tr: That man by nature is a social animal is certain. But just as this inclination to cultivate civil society follows human nature without constituting it, so the foundations of the duties that man as such must perform are to be sought much deeper than in the rules of civil intercourse. Indeed, man considered in himself, as we saw above, lies under an obligation by the very nature of this Law to worship God, love his neighbour, and live temperately, even if no relation to the civil body of which he is a member had arisen for him.

units.la: Jejunum est regerere, etiam pietatem, temperantiam, similesque virtutes, quarum citra convictum civilem cum aliis dari potest exercitium, nihilominus ad societatem politicam referri posse, tanquam ejusdem firmiora vincula, quæque ad eam colendam hominem reddant aptiorem. Etenim quis non videt, profanum nimium esse, pietatem, temperantiam, &c. sic subordinare politicæ societati, ut si fine iis salva hæc esse posset, minor exisseret ad earum cultum nostra obligatio? Ista tamen Atheismi Politici, nimium hodiè, proh dolor! succrescentis, infelicia existunt semina.
units.tr: It is groundless to say that piety, temperance and similar virtues, whose exercise can exist without civil intercourse with others, can nevertheless be referred to political society as firmer bonds of it, which make man more fit to cultivate it. For who does not see that it is too profane to subordinate piety, temperance and so on to political society in such a way that, if the safety of society could be preserved without them, our obligation to cultivate them would be smaller? Yet these are the unhappy seeds of political atheism, which, alas, is growing far too much today.

units.la: Cæterum, quandoquidem morali suæ dependentiæ à Deo rationalem creaturam pro suo arbitrio sese eximere posse, omnimoda ejus dependentia nort finit; interim tamen omninò posset, quandò vellet, si ei impunè liceret à Legis Naturæ præceptis recedere, manifestum est, perfectam undiquaque obligationem hac Lege homini non imponi, nisi munita ea fuerit Sanctione Pœnali, in quam incurrentes Legis transgressores, experiantur nolentes per passivam obedientiam suam à Deo tanquam Judice dependentiam, quam volentes per obedientiam activam à Deo tanquam æquissimo Legislatore agnoscere noluerunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, since a rational creature cannot at its own pleasure free itself from its moral dependence on God, its total dependence does not cease. Yet it is plain that, if it were allowed with impunity to depart from the precepts of the Law of Nature whenever it wished, it could do so altogether. So this Law does not impose a perfect obligation on man unless it is backed by a penal sanction. Transgressors of the Law will, against their will, experience through their passive obedience the dependence on God as Judge, which, willing, through active obedience, they refused to acknowledge in God as the most just Lawgiver. ## XXVII.

units.la: Quanta verò præcisè pœna ejusmodi perduellibus à Deo sit definita, non tam exacto Lumen Naturæ docere videtur. Id manifestum est, jus Dei esse, ut morte digni habeantur quotquot existunt Legis, quà Regnum suum moderatur, violatores. Qui enim eo fine à Numine sunt conditi, ut tanquam morigeri cives vivant in honorem sui Regis Dei, quandò tales vivere nolunt, justissimo supplicio, tanquam inofficiosi cives, ejiciuntur ea civitate, cujus membra esse se nolle factis declararunt: id est, jure merito tales ex hominum numero per mortem tolluntur. Imò, nullâ parte propitium sibi Numen promittere posse, qui ipsi communioni inter Deum tanquam Regem suum & se tanquam ejus subditos renunciarunt, rescisso ejusdem vinculo, quod in integra Legis hujus observantia consistit, res ipla clamat.
units.tr: How exactly great a punishment God has fixed for such traitors, the light of nature does not seem to teach with precision. This much is clear: it is God's right that all who violate the Law by which he governs his kingdom be held worthy of death. For those who were formed by the Deity for this purpose, to live as obedient citizens to the honour of their King God, when they are unwilling to live thus, are cast out by most just punishment, as unfaithful citizens, from the state of which by their deeds they have declared they are unwilling to be members. That is, by right such people are removed from the number of men by death. Indeed, the thing itself cries out that no one can promise himself a favourable Deity in any way who has renounced the communion between God as their King and themselves as his subjects, the bond being broken which consists in the full observance of this Law.

units.la: Sicuti verò Justitiæ Dei conveniens est, debitâ pœnâ animadvertere in eos, qui sese per hujus Legis violationem reos constituerunt criminis Læsæ Majestatis Divinæ, itâ quoque naturæ lumen prorsus suadere videtur, Bonitati Numinis esse congruum, ut religiosis Legis suæ cultoribus semetipsum præstet talem, qualem cum ipsi in pia observantia hujus Legis agnoscunt. Nempe, quem Deum instituit amare creatura rationalis ac toto corde venerari tanquam Regem suum unicum, in cujus perfectissimo obsequio ac humillima sub eo submissione omnis sua consistat beatitudo, quo modo ea non benignum sibi ac favente m experietur Regem Optimum Deum?
units.tr: But just as it befits God's justice to punish with due penalty those who have made themselves guilty of the crime of injured divine majesty by violating this Law, so too the light of nature seems wholly to suggest that it is congruous with the goodness of the Deity to show himself to the pious observers of his Law as they recognise him to be when they piously observe it. Indeed, whom a rational creature is bound to love and venerate with its whole heart as its only King, in whose most perfect obedience and most humble submission to him all its blessedness consists, how could it fail to experience God, the best King, as kind and favourable to it?

units.la: Atque itâ per ipsum rationis lumen sponte quasi ducimur, ad considerandum Naturæ Jus, non simpliciter tantùm ut Legem, sed & tanquam Formulam alicujus Societatis sive Fœderis, intercedentis inter Deum, tanquam Regem, fœderis conditiones pro sua quidem eminentia, interim perfectissimæ suæ naturæ, nominatim tum justitiæ tum bonitati convenienter, præscribentem ; & creaturam rationalem , tanquam subditum , in easdem conditiones , tanquam quæ rectæ rationis judicio non possunt non æstimari æquisIimæ , animo lubenti consentientem atque acquiescentem.
units.tr: And thus, by the very light of reason, we are led, as it were spontaneously, to consider the Law of Nature not merely as a law but also as the formula of a certain society or covenant between God as King and the rational creature. God, in his eminence yet most perfect nature, prescribes the conditions of the covenant, suitably to justice and goodness in particular, and the rational creature, as a subject, consents to and acquiesces in those conditions with a willing mind, since by the judgment of right reason they cannot but be judged most equitable.

units.la: Progrediendum foret , ad expendendas Actiones humanas à Lege Naturæ regendas; Conscientiam , hâc Lege informandam; Virtutem denique moralem , quatenus est constans animi propositum ad actiones omnes huic Legi præstandas conformes : verùm jam dudum Exercitationis Academicæ angustiæ limites ponunt nostræ meditationi : cui, nisi hoc obstitisset impedimentum , volupe sæpius fuisset , latius se nonnihil diffundere in multis , in quibus ad ampliores cogitationes passim invitabat rerum sublimium Majestas. Nunc itaquè sufficerit ', & paucis exhibuisse prima illa fundamenta , quibus Moralem Philosophiam inædificandam censemus , & simul qualecunque specimen dedisse , cùm nostrarum hac parte cogitationum , tùm methodi, quâ res has tractandas putamus. In quo acquiescere cogemur, donec , quæ ad conatus tales perficiendos requiruntur, & otia & vires largiri voluerit benignus Deus.
units.tr: We should proceed to examine human actions to be governed by the Law of Nature, conscience to be informed by this Law, and finally moral virtue, insofar as it is a constant purpose of the mind to perform all actions conformable to this Law. But the limits of an academic exercise have long since set bounds to our meditation. Had this hindrance not stood in the way, it would often have been pleasant to spread out somewhat more widely on many matters, in which the majesty of sublime things everywhere invited fuller thought. For now let it suffice to have briefly set out those first foundations on which we think moral philosophy should be built, and at the same time to have given some sort of specimen both of our thinking in this part and of the method by which we think these matters should be treated. In this we shall have to rest content, until the kindly God is pleased to grant both leisure and strength for carrying such efforts to completion.

units.la: DISSERTATIONIS DE INFINITO SECTIO PRIOR; Quæ est de CONCEPTU INFINITI.
units.tr: ON THE NATURE OF THE INFINITE, FIRST SECTION: CONCERNING THE CONCEPT OF THE INFINITE.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Quæcunque existunt humanæ menti pervestigabilia, præterquam Infinitum. II. De Infinito tamen mens nostra, etsi finita, rectè disputat. III. Neque ideò quicquam quod finitatem suam excedat conari, credendum est. IV. De Infinito disputari, cur noluerit re verâ Cartesius ? V. Triplex circa Infiniti in nostra mente conceptum controversia. VI. Ad cujus intelligentiam præstructæ tres hypotheses. VII. Infiniti conceptum esse negativum, evincit ejus ad mentem creatam disproportio : VIII. Nec non Infiniti secundum rem & conceptum indivisibilitas. IX. Iniqua inter ideam negativam tenebrarum, & eam quæ Infiniti est, comparatio. X. Negativum Infiniti conceptum mens nostra quo modo formet ? XI. Positivam Infiniti ideam non arguit, quod plus in Infinito esse intelligitur realitatis, quam in finito. XII. Conceptum Infiniti eo qui finiti est in mente nostra priorem non esse, demonstratur. XIII. Neque obstat, defectum finiti intelligi ex comparatione majoris, puta Infiniti. XIV. Si naturæ ordine idea Infiniti in mente nostra sit prior, non sibi constare novam methodum, docetur. XV. Infinitum clarâ & distinctâ ideâ à finita mente concipi, repugnat. XVI. Neque satisfacit distinctio inter conceptum totius Infiniti, & singularum in eo perfectionum. XVII. Non etiam juvat plus realitatis, quod in idea Infiniti, præ omni alia, contineri dicitur. XVIII. Res in quibus minus perfectionis est clarius plerumque nobis intelligi, ostenditur. XIX. Errores circa ideam Infiniti perpetuum Meditationum Cartesianarum
units.tr: I. Whatever exists can be investigated by the human mind, except the Infinite. II. Yet our mind, though finite, reasons rightly about the Infinite. III. Nor is it therefore to be believed that we should attempt anything that goes beyond its finitude. IV. Why did Descartes, in truth, not want to dispute about the Infinite? V. There is a threefold controversy about the concept of the Infinite in our mind. VI. Three hypotheses laid down in advance for understanding it. VII. The concept of the Infinite is shown to be negative, by its disproportion to the created mind. VIII. Nor is the Infinite indivisible only in reality and not in concept. IX. An unfair comparison between the negative idea of darkness and the idea of the Infinite. X. How does our mind form the negative concept of the Infinite? XI. That the Infinite is understood to contain more reality than the finite does not prove a positive idea of it. XII. The concept of the Infinite in our mind is prior to that of the finite: it is demonstrated that it is not. XIII. Nor does it stand in the way that the defect of the finite is understood from comparison with the greater, namely the Infinite. XIV. It is taught that if, in the order of nature, the idea of the Infinite is prior in our mind, the new method does not agree with itself. XV. That the Infinite can be conceived by a finite mind through a clear and distinct idea is contradictory. XVI. Nor does the distinction between the concept of the whole Infinite and of the individual perfections in it give satisfaction. XVII. Nor does it help that more reality is said to be contained in the idea of the Infinite than in any other idea. XVIII. It is shown that things in which there is less perfection are usually understood more clearly by us. XIX. The errors concerning the idea of the Infinite throughout the Cartesian Meditations.
I.

units.la: Quæcunque existunt humanæ menti perceptibilia, præterquam Infinitum.
units.tr: Whatever things exist are perceptible to the human mind, except the Infinite.

units.la: Leganter ille & sapientissimè, Quantum est quod ignoramus! Experiuntur id quotidiè, quotquot unquam haud plane hebetes, exteriori cortice non contenti, sese dederunt severioribus meditationibus, eisdemque, interiorem rerum substantiam & medullam exhaurire conati sunt. Itâ nimirùm voluit providus naturæ Auctor Deus inde quidem abstergere sciendi nauseam, quo semper infixum hærcat illud, Plus ultra; hinc verò lusu elegantissimo fatigare industriam & laborem mortalium, tanto magis suam unicuique detegens ignorantiam, quanto altius in rerum scientia profecit: ut credas merito, unumquemque quo scit plura, eo scire magis, se scire pauca. Causam si quæramus, cur adeò sint multa, in quorum contemplatione sic hæremus, ut initium facilius inveniamus quam exitum, reperiemus plerumque eam esse, non tam ipsam rei difficultatem, quam potius inopiam administriculorum, quibus occlusa ad rerum notitiam via reseratur; quod unum hic & opus & labor est. Fallitur quicunque eas sibi imaginatur mentis humanæ angustias, ut non apta existat quævis cacapere, modo ad manum sint media idonea; quorum defectu sæpè contingit, ut subsistere cogatur atque acquiescere in qualicunque sapientiæ modulo. Unum duntaxat est quod omnem mentis nostræ vim longissimè excedit, ipsaque suâ naturâ, ut in se est, ab ea cognosci nequit; Infinitum puta. Id, quia nullam planè ad finitum nostrum ingeniolum habet proportionem, tanto fermè magis nostram fugit meditationem, quanto diligentius in id inquirimus; & in hoc potissimum à nobis tanquam Infinitum cognoscitur, quòd mens humana ejus plenitudinem & perfectionem concipere nequeat." Ut mirum sit, non deesse hodiè Philosophos, qui, quidvis sibi de se promittentes, secundum methodum suam philosophantibus polliceri audent Infiniti idem, non claram tantum & distinctam (id parùm) sed omnium quoque quas quis habere potest clarissimam & distinctissimam. Quam verè? constabit ex hac Dissertatione nostra; quâ, aspirante Ente Infinito, de Infinito promodulo disputare constitui.
units.tr: That wise man spoke elegantly and most wisely: How much there is that we do not know! Every thinking person who was not utterly dull, and who was not content with the outer bark but gave himself to more serious meditation and tried to drain the inner substance and marrow of things, has found this out every day. God, the provident Author of nature, willed in this way, on the one hand, to wipe away the nausea of knowing, so that the saying Plus ultra should always remain fixed in us; and on the other hand, in a most elegant sport, to wear out the effort and labour of mortals, revealing to each person his own ignorance the further he has advanced in knowledge, so that one may rightly believe that the more a man knows, the more he knows that he knows little. If we ask why there are so many things in whose contemplation we get stuck, so that we find it easier to make a beginning than to reach an end, we shall find that the cause is usually not so much the difficulty of the thing itself as the lack of aids by which the closed way to knowledge of things is opened; this alone is both the work and the labour here. He is mistaken who imagines such narrowness of the human mind that no thing is fit to be grasped, provided suitable means are at hand; for when these are lacking it often happens that he is forced to remain content with whatever small measure of wisdom he has. There is only one thing which far exceeds the whole power of our mind and, in its own nature as it is in itself, cannot be known by it: the Infinite, that is. Because it has no proportion at all to our finite little wit, it escapes our meditation almost in proportion as we inquire into it more diligently; and it is known by us chiefly as the Infinite in this, that the human mind cannot conceive its fullness and perfection." So it is no wonder that there are philosophers today who, promising themselves anything about themselves, dare to promise to those who philosophize by their method a clear and distinct idea of the Infinite, not merely clear and distinct (which is too little), but the clearest and most distinct of all that anyone can have. How truly? This will be established by this Dissertation of ours, in which, with the Infinite Being aiding us, I have determined to dispute a little about the Infinite.

units.la: Verùm in ipso hic limine necessitas imponitur vindicandi hoc institutum à censura quorundam, quibus ipso Dissertationis titulo graviter impingere videbor, dum disputare aggredior de re, de qua nunquam disputandum esse, dictant. Cartef. Princip. 1. §. 26. Quod si verum sit, unâ litura quicquid hîc meditamur inducitur. Mihi quidem mira semper hæc visa fuit philosophatio, ac parùm congrua eorum hypothesibus, qui conceptum Infiniti positivum, & quidem clarum ac distinctum, quin omnium qui in mente existunt evidentissimum se habere gloriantur. Si sic, quid ni disputare liceat de Infinito? Equidem quod clarè & distinctè cognoscimus, etiam priusquam concipimus finitum, quid ni de eo judicare liceat ista, quæ sic concipimus? Ast de quo judicare licet, de eo quoquè disputare non tantum licet, verum etiam sæpè necessum est. Quum enim variorum de eadem re judicia esse soleant varia, & non raro opposita, facilè eveniet (quod passim evenire docet experientia; docebit hæc ipsa pagina, quâ de Infinito quandoque disputandum esse, contra negantem id Cartesium evincimus) ut quis in suo de Infinito judicio erret; quem errorem refutare, ac veram de Infinito sententiam vindicare, unusquisque tenetur, cui
units.tr: But at the very threshold a necessity is laid upon me to defend this undertaking against the censure of certain people, by whom I seem to be gravely struck by the very title of the Dissertation, since I begin to dispute about a matter about which they pronounce that one must never dispute. Cartes. Princip. 1. §. 26. If that were true, everything we meditate here would be wiped out with one stroke. To me this kind of philosophizing has always seemed strange, and hardly consistent with the hypotheses of those who boast that they have a positive concept of the Infinite, and indeed a clear and distinct one, and even the most evident of all those that exist in the mind. If so, why should it not be permitted to dispute about the Infinite? For if we know clearly and distinctly what the finite is, even before we conceive it, why should it not be permitted to judge those things about it which we conceive in this way? But about whatever it is permitted to judge, it is not only permitted to dispute, but often necessary. For since the judgments of various people about the same matter are usually various and not rarely opposed, it will easily happen (as experience shows everywhere, and as this very page will show, in which we prove against Descartes, who denies it, that we must sometimes dispute about the Infinite) that someone errs in his judgment about the Infinite; and everyone to whom truth is dear, lest it be overwhelmed by errors, is bound to refute that error and to vindicate the true opinion about the Infinite. ## II.

units.la: II. De Infinito tamen mens nostra, etsi finita, recte disputat. cui veritas, ne erroribus opprimatur, cordi est. Ecquid autem id est aliud, quam de Infinito disputare? Atque hoc fundamento Metaphysici, Entis affectiones tractantes, de Infinito non minus agunt quam de Finito; Pneumatici Spiritum in Finitum & Infinitum dividunt, atque utriusque differentias explicant; Ethici de Bono summo seu Infinito, an & quale detur, disquirunt; Mathematici & Physici de Quantitate Infinita disputant; Theologi de Deo Infinito toti differunt. Absurdi omnes & inepti, si Cartesio credimus, qui sese fatigarunt disputationibus de re, de qua disputandum sit nunquam. Tandem de ipso Cartesio quid judicabimus, qui determinare passim audet de Infinito plurima, eaque vindicare ab objectionibus, puta, Infiniti Ideam positivam esse, & ideam finiti priorem, esse omnium maximè claram & distinctam, &c. Ut taceam quae de mundo, ejusque materia Infinita, docet alibi; de quibus infrà suo loco.
units.tr: Yet our mind, though finite, disputes rightly about the Infinite. And what else is this but to dispute about the Infinite? On this foundation Metaphysicians, treating the affections of Being, deal with the Infinite no less than with the finite; Pneumatologists divide Spirit into finite and infinite and explain the differences of each; Ethicists inquire whether and of what kind there is a Supreme or Infinite Good; Mathematicians and Physicists dispute about infinite quantity; Theologians discourse about the Infinite God as a whole. All of them would be absurd and foolish, if we believe Descartes, who have "wearied themselves with disputations" about a matter about which one must never dispute. Finally, what shall we judge of Descartes himself, who everywhere dares to determine many things about the Infinite, and to defend them against objections, namely that the idea of the Infinite is positive, that it is prior to the idea of the finite, that it is the clearest and most distinct of all, and so on? Not to mention what he teaches elsewhere about the world and its infinite matter, which will be discussed in its proper place below.
III.

units.la: Sed cur, obsecrò, nullis unquam de Infinito disputationibus locum relinquit Cartesius? Cum simus, inquit, finiti, absurdum esset nos aliquid de Infinito determinare, atque sic illud quasi finire ac comprehendere conari. Itane? De nulla ergo re aliquid determinare licet, nisi quam intellectu nostro finimus ac comprehendimus? Profectò de re omninò nulla, ne minima quidem, sic quicquam determinare forsan licuerit; cum certè non simus, nos vel unicam comprehensivè intelligere. Instantias, quibus vanitatem illationis ostendam, non longè petam. Attributorum Divinorum ne unum quidem nos comprehendere notum est; at quoties non imponitur necessitas disputandi de Æternitate, Simplicitate, Immensitate, Immutabilitate, Præscientia infallibili, Decreto immutabili, Providentia efficaci, &c. si vindicare voluerimus independentem Divinæ Majestatis gloriam à plurimorum eam temerè vellicantium cavillationibus? Ut addam aliud: exemplo sit Chiliogonum, quo ipso alibi utitur Cartesius, quodque hùc imprimis facit, quippe cujus ne claram quidem & distinctam imaginationem nos habere largitur, nisi tantum, quatenus ad unum aut alterum ejus latus se extendit nostra attentio. Numquid autem idcircò dubitabis de eo contra negantem disputare, atque afferere, id esse æquiangulum, si sit æquilaterum; in æquiangulo duo latera quovis tertio esse majora; esse minus circulo cui inscribitur; esse majus circulo circa quem describitur; & quae alia similia ex Matheseos principiis de Chiliogono non minus certò demonstrari possunt, quam de Trigono aut Pentagono, quae quod ad omnia & singula sui latera atque angulos comprehendis? Vides (ut plura hūc adferre desinam) non ideò nos aliquid comprehendere, quia de eo disputamus? Nec mirum. Sufficit de re quapiam disputaturo, si satis habeat, ob quod suam tuetur opinionem, fundamenti, ex quo dubia circa rem controversam mota possit decidere: habet autem satis fundamenti, si praedicatum, de quo disputare aggreditur, percipiat cognitione certâ; qualis apprehensiva esse potest non minus quam comprehensiva. Itaque sufficiens nequaquam est haec ratiocinatio ad prohibendas quaslibet de Infinito disputationes. Non saltem tales, quibus omnes nostri intellectus vires sic in eo contemplando occupare conamur, ut non tam Infinitum capere laboremus, quam ab ipso potius capi: uti ipse loquitur Cartesius, de Infiniti Dei in mente nostra idea differens. Modestis ejusmodi de Infinito dissertationibus nihil praejudicant mentis nostrae, quibus id comprehendere prohibemur, angustiae. Modestis, inquam; nequis autumet, nos hic quicquam ullo pacto patrocinari velle curiosis, temerariis, ac non raro profanis hac parte Scholasticorum quaestionibus ac decisionibus, quibus infinitis eximium hunc de Infinito tractatum turpem in modum polluerunt homines inaniter atque otiosè subtiles, nihilque de se humile in tractandis rebus etiam maximè sublimibus sentientes.
units.tr: But why, I beg you, does Descartes leave no room at all for disputations about the Infinite? Since we are finite, he says, it would be absurd for us to determine anything about the Infinite, and so to try to finish it off and comprehend it. Really? So we may determine nothing about any thing except what we bound and comprehend by our understanding? Indeed, we might perhaps not determine anything at all about any thing, not even the smallest, since certainly we do not comprehensively understand even one thing. I shall not seek far for instances by which to show the emptiness of this inference. We know that we do not comprehend even one of the divine attributes. Yet whenever there is no necessity to dispute about Eternity, Simplicity, Immensity, Immutability, infallible Foreknowledge, immutable Decree, effectual Providence, and so on, how shall we defend the glory of the divine Majesty, independent of the cavils of the many who rashly pluck at it? To add another example: take the chiliagon, which Descartes himself uses elsewhere, and which is especially pertinent here, since he grants that we do not even have a clear and distinct image of it, except insofar as our attention extends to one or another of its sides. Will you therefore doubt that one may dispute about it against someone who denies it, and assert that it is equiangular if it is equilateral; that in an equiangular figure any two sides are greater than a third; that it is smaller than the circle in which it is inscribed; that it is greater than the circle about which it is described; and other similar things that can be demonstrated from the principles of mathematics about the chiliagon no less certainly than about the triangle or pentagon, which you comprehend in all its sides and angles? You see (to stop bringing up more) that we do not comprehend something merely because we dispute about it? No wonder. It is enough for one who is about to dispute about some thing that he has sufficient ground for defending his opinion, from which he can settle the doubts raised about the matter in question. And he has sufficient ground if he perceives the predicate about which he undertakes to dispute with certain knowledge; such knowledge can be apprehensive no less than comprehensive. Therefore this reasoning is by no means sufficient to forbid every disputation about the Infinite. Not, at least, those by which we try to employ all the powers of our intellect in contemplating it, not so much labouring to grasp the Infinite as rather to be grasped by it, as Descartes himself puts it, distinguishing this from the idea of the infinite God in our mind. The narrowness of our mind, by which we are forbidden to comprehend it, is no obstacle to such modest dissertations on the Infinite. Modest, I say; lest anyone suppose that we here wish in any way to defend the curious, rash, and not seldom profane questions and decisions of the Scholastics on this point, with which men, vainly and idly subtle, and thinking nothing humble of themselves even in treating the most sublime things, have shamefully polluted this excellent subject.

units.la: An verò humilitatis conscientia genuina causa fuerit, ob quam de Infinito disputare noluerit Cartesius; an potius aliud eum movarit ad hanc utendum praecautione, conjectare licet ex iis quae mox ipse addit. Nimirum, pro ea quâ excellebat mentis subtilitate, praevidebat facilè, quot difficultatibus, & quam prorsus insolubilibus, premenda essent quae de mundi nostri infinitate, seu nullis ejusdem terminis nisi imaginariis, traditurus erat deinceps. Neque tamen mittendum erat repudium opinioni, quam alibi agnoscit unum ex praecipuis, suoque judicio certissimis, Physicae suae fundamentis. Epist. Vol. I, p. 187. Itaque via praescindenda erat omnibus istiusmodi rationibus & instantiis, quibus extensio hujus universi intra limites coërceri atque compelli validè posset. Hinc istâ sibi suisque hypothesibus cavet prolepfi, monendo in antecessum lectorem, istis fe disputationibus fatigandum minimè esse. Sic enimmoxpergit: Non igitur respondere curabimus iis, qui quærunt, an, fi daretur linea infinita, ejus media pars esse: etiam infinita; vel, an numerus infinitus fit par an imp ir, & talia; quia de iis nulli viderentur debere cogitare, nisi qui mentem suam infinitam esse arbitrantur. En callidum consilium! quo uno quasi ictu secare nititur infinitos nodos, quibus mundum suum nullos extensionis terminos habentem constringendum fore præsagiebat, quibusque rite solvendis neque ipse par erat, neque ullus unquam sufficiet mortalium. Pulcrè profecto! Dicta bit de Infinito quod placet Dominus Cartefius. In contrarium fi objicias rationes, non iis respondere curabit; causatus mentis finitudinem. Benè habet, quòd hodiè didicerimus viam ratiocinandi brevem & compendiariam; quâ eâdem, & vacui poffibilitatem, & plurium mundorum non-repugnantiam, & spirituum cum corporibus essentialem coëxiftentiam, & alia quævis dogmata, novam sapientiam subvertentia, absque multa circuitione tueri datur facillimè.
units.tr: Whether genuine consciousness of humility was the real cause for which Descartes was unwilling to dispute about the Infinite, or whether something else moved him to use this caution, we may conjecture from what he adds presently. Doubtless, with the keenness of mind in which he excelled, he easily foresaw by how many difficulties, and how utterly insoluble, the matters would be pressed which he was going to set forth concerning the infinity of our world, or its lack of any limits except imaginary ones. Yet the rejection of an opinion which he elsewhere acknowledges as one of the chief foundations of his Physics, and most certain by his own judgment. Epist. Vol. I, p. 187. had not to be sent away. Therefore he had to cut off the way to all reasons and instances of this kind by which the extension of this universe could strongly be confined and compelled within limits. Hence he guards his hypotheses with this preemptive remark, warning the reader in advance that he need not be wearied with such disputations. For he continues thus: Therefore we shall not take care to answer those who ask whether, if an infinite line were given, its middle part would also be infinite; or whether an infinite number is even or odd, and suchlike; because no one should seem to think about these things except those who believe their own mind to be infinite. Behold the crafty counsel! With one stroke, as it were, he tries to cut through the infinite knots by which he foresaw his world, which has no limits of extension, would be bound; and neither he himself was equal to untying them properly, nor will any mortal ever be sufficient for that. Admirably indeed! Let him say about the Infinite whatever pleases Mr. Descartes. If you object reasons against him to the contrary, he will not take care to answer them, alleging the finitude of his mind. It is well that we have today learned a short and compendious way of reasoning, by which, with no long detour, one can very easily defend both the possibility of a vacuum and the non-repugnance of several worlds, and the essential coexistence of spirits with bodies, and any other doctrines that overturn the new wisdom.

units.la: Quum itaquè nihil nobis re verâ obstet mentis finitas, quo minus disputare de Infinito liceat, age! paulo propius cum Nobili Auctore congrediamur, acturi & de Infiniti in nostra mente notione, & de re ipsa quoque: utrobiquè enim haud leviter errare videtur. Utque indè faciamus initium, triplex circa Infiniti conceptum occurrit expendenda controversia. Primùm, An positivus is fit, an potius negativus? Indè fluit fecundò, Utrum conceptus altero prior fit, Finiti, an Infiniti? Denique, An idea Infiniti in mente nostra existens fit clara & distincta, quin omnium quas habemus clarissima ac diftinctiffima? Conceptum Infiniti & positivum esse; & conceptu Finiti priorem esse; & omnium maximè clarum & distinctum esse, tuetur Cartefius, Medit. iii. Nobis opposita sententia verissima videtur & certiffima. Quo autem diftinctius de his omnibus philosophemur, quædam in antecessum notari velim, quorum non levis crit in his quæstionibus decidendis usus.
units.tr: Since therefore nothing in fact stands in the way of our disputing about the Infinite on account of the finitude of our mind, come, let us engage a little more closely with this noble author, treating both the notion of the Infinite in our mind and the thing itself; for in both he seems to err not lightly. And to make a beginning from this, a threefold controversy about the concept of the Infinite presents itself for examination. First, whether it is positive or rather negative. From this follows, secondly, whether the concept of the Finite or that of the Infinite is prior to the other. Lastly, whether the idea of the Infinite existing in our mind is clear and distinct, indeed the clearest and most distinct of all that we have. That the concept of the Infinite is positive, and prior to the concept of the Finite, and most clear and distinct of all, Descartes maintains in the Third Meditation. The opposite opinion seems to us most true and most certain. But that we may philosophize more distinctly about all these things, I would like some points to be noted in advance, whose use will not be slight in deciding these questions.

units.la: I. Distinguendus est accuratè conceptus formalis, uti loquuntur, ab objectivo, five notio rei in nostra mente, à re ipsa quæ notione. tione repræsentatur. Quod si attendamus, deprehendemus ili- cò, distinguendum planè esse conceptum rei positivum à conceptu rei positivæ. Illic τὸ positivum est affectio conceptûs seu notionis, exprimens modum, quo mens rem sibi repræsentat: hic verò τὸ positivum est affectio objecti repræsentati, indicans id esse verum quid & reale. Ex quo conficitur, quemadmodum rei perfectæ dari potest conceptus imperfectus, & vice versa, itâ quoque non repugnare, rei positivæ dari conceptum negativum: quod ipsum plurimis instantiis cuique obviis confirmare facillimum existit. Hic nobis quæstio est, non de conceptu Infiniti positivi, sed de conceptu positivo Infiniti: i. e. non disquiritur, an Infinitas à parte rei sit positiva perfectio, quod nemo negaverit, qui expendet ea quæ de Infinito ipso deinceps trademus; sed quæstio est an Infinitas, etsi verè sit à parte sui quid positivum, etiam modo positivo à nobis concipiatur? Neque inanem hanc esse subtilitatem, sed controversiam magni momenti, vel hoc unum evincit, quod hinc pendeat omnis vis & robur argumenti Cartesiani, petiti ab infiniti Dei idea, ad probandam ejusdem existentiam; uti ex infrà dicendis percipietur. II. Distinguendum quoque est inter nudam ideam, rem immediatè & directè per solam apprehensionem simplicem menti offerentem, atquè inter perceptionem istiusmodi, quæ, ex pluribus mentis actibus composita, superaccedente judicio & discursu quasi perficitur.
