Secundum ista evenire potest, nos firmiter tenere, prædicatum quodpiam esse positivum, non quia id tanquam positivum simpliciter concipimus, sed quia sufficientes sunt rationes, quæ nos compellunt ad credendum, quod negativo duntaxat modo ob mentis imbecillitatem concipimus, re verâ tamen esse positivum, quamvis tanquam tale nobis sit inconceptibile. Aliud itaquè est, Infinitum simplici ideâ, eâque positivâ & positivo modo concipere; aliud, ope judicii & discursûs intelligere, Infinitum, quamvis negativè conceptum, esse tamen re ipsâ positivum. Non de isto quæritur, sed de illo. III. Distinguenda denique est res quæ Infinita est, ab ipsa Infinitate; consequenter, distinguendus quoque conceptus rei Infinitæ à conceptu ipsius Infinitatis tanquam talis. Ille compositus quasi est ex duabus notionibus, & rei ipsius, & adjunctæ Infinitatis; hic est simplex idea, Infinitatem.
units.tr: I. The formal concept, as they say, must be carefully distinguished from the objective concept, that is, the notion of a thing in our mind from the thing itself which is represented by the notion. If we attend to this, we shall immediately perceive that the positive character of the concept of a thing must be plainly distinguished from the positive character of the thing conceived. In the former, the positive is an affection of the concept or notion, expressing the mode in which the mind represents the thing to itself; in the latter, the positive is an affection of the represented object, indicating that it is something true and real. From this it follows that, just as an imperfect concept may be given of a perfect thing, and vice versa, so also it is not repugnant that a negative concept be given of a positive thing; which is very easy to confirm by very many instances obvious to everyone. Here our question is not about the concept of the positive Infinite but about the positive concept of the Infinite; that is, the inquiry is not whether infinity, on the side of the thing, is a positive perfection, which no one will deny who weighs what we shall afterwards set forth about the Infinite itself; but the question is whether infinity, although it is truly something positive on the side of the thing, is also conceived by us in a positive mode. That this is no empty subtlety, but a controversy of great moment, is shown by this alone: that on it depends all the force and strength of the Cartesian argument, drawn from the idea of the infinite God, for proving his existence, as will be perceived from what is said below. II. It must also be distinguished between the bare idea, which presents the thing immediately and directly to the mind through simple apprehension alone, and the perception of this kind, which is composed of several acts of the mind and is, as it were, completed by the addition of judgment and discourse. According to these, it can happen that we firmly hold a predicate to be positive, not because we conceive it simply as positive, but because there are sufficient reasons which compel us to believe that what we conceive only in a negative way, owing to the weakness of the mind, is nevertheless in fact positive, although it is inconceivable to us as such. It is therefore one thing to conceive the Infinite by a simple idea, and that a positive idea, in a positive mode; it is another to understand, by means of judgment and discourse, that the Infinite, although conceived negatively, is nevertheless in fact positive. It is not of the latter that we are inquiring, but of the former. III. Finally, the thing which is infinite must be distinguished from infinity itself; consequently, the concept of the infinite thing must also be distinguished from the concept of infinity as such. The former is composed, as it were, of two notions, that of the thing itself and that of the added infinity; the latter is a simple idea, representing infinity in the abstract.

units.la: II. Ii 3 tatem in abstracto repræsentans. Illum, quod ad rem attinet cui Infinitas tribuitur, posse esse positivum, non negamus; hunc (de quo nobis quæstio est) dicimus in finita mente positivum neque esse, neque esse posse.
units.tr: II. ...tatem in abstracto repræsentans. We do not deny that the thing to which infinity is ascribed can be positive. But we say that infinity itself, which is the matter in question, is neither positive in a finite mind nor can be.

units.la: Ista præmittere visum fuit ad statum controversiæ rectius intelligendum. Nunc Cartesium audiamus! Nec, ait, pw'are debeo, me non percipere infinitum per veram ideam, sed tantum per negationem finiti, ut principio quietem & tenebras per negationem motus & lucis; nam contrà manifeste intelligo, plus realitatis esse in substantia infinita, quam finita. Ego verò prorsus autumo, conceptum Infiniti, qua talis, in nostra mente esse negativum, non positivum. Demonstro. Quicquid positivè concipimus id intellectui nostro tanquam illi approportionatum occurrit. Fieri namque non potest, ut aliquid positivè à mente nostra attingatur, quod captum ejus excedit, in quantum nimirum eum excedit; quoniam implicat, intellectum nostrum positivo modo versari circa illud, quod suâ naturâ est extra ejus sphæram activitatis. Jam verò Infinitum tanquam tale, sive ipsam Infinitatem, finitæ menti, ejusve vi perceptivæ, neutiquam esse approportionatum, imò nec approportionari posse, adeò clarum est, quam quod clarissimum; quandoquidem finitum quoticscunque sumptum nunquam potest Infinitum excedere: qui tamen possibilis uniusfupra alium excessus in eis requiritur, quæ aliquam habent ad se mutuo proportionem. Si itaque majus quid & amplius concipiendum sit in Infinitate, quam quod à mente nostra attingi potest, ptopter nullam illius ad hanc proportionem; sequitur utique, Infinitatem nos alio modo concipere non posse, quam cogitando, nullis unquam finitis conceptibus Infiniti perfectionem absolvi posse. Quod profectò clarè notat, Infinitatem qua talem tantum nobis cogitari negativè; removendo limites quoscunque vel conceptos, vel etiam conceptibiles.
units.tr: It seemed right to set this out first, so that the state of the controversy may be understood more correctly. Now let us hear Descartes! Nor, he says, ought I to think that I do not perceive the infinite through a true idea, but only through the negation of the finite, as I perceive rest and darkness through the negation of motion and light; for on the contrary I clearly understand that there is more reality in an infinite substance than in a finite one. But I for my part maintain flatly that the concept of the Infinite, as such, in our mind is negative, not positive. I prove it. Whatever we conceive positively presents itself to our intellect as proportioned to it. For it cannot happen that something is positively grasped by our mind which exceeds its capacity, insofar as it exceeds it; since it implies that our intellect is occupied in a positive way with that which by its nature lies outside its sphere of activity. Now that the Infinite as such, or infinity itself, is in no way proportioned to a finite mind or to its power of perception, nor can even be proportioned, is as clear as anything most clear; for however a finite thing is taken, it can never exceed the Infinite, whereas a possible excess of one thing over another is required only among things that have some proportion to one another. If, therefore, there is something greater and fuller to be conceived in infinity than what our mind can attain, and this because there is no proportion of it to our mind, it follows surely that we cannot conceive infinity in any other way than by thinking that the perfection of the Infinite can never be completed by any finite concepts. This clearly shows that infinity, as such, can be thought by us only negatively, by removing whatever limits, either conceived or conceivable.

units.la: VIII. His addo, Infinitatem ejusmodi prædicatum esse, quod (quemadmodum infrà docebimus) in indivisibili consistit, quare uti ipsi, ita & conceptui, ei respondenti, nihil addi potest aut detrahi. At verò omnes conceptus nostri, in quantum sunt positivi, finiti sunt, cum conditionem ipsius mentis finitæ non excedant; adeoque semper iis addi potest & detrahi. Restat ergò conceptum ceptum Infiniti in nostra mente non esse positivum. Si malis, clarius forsan sic arguam: Infiniti qua talis vel totum concipit mens nostra, vel aliquam partem, vel nihil. Totum infinitum concipere est nihil aliud, quam suo conceptu id exhaurire & comprehendere, quod mentis finitatem omnino excedit. Partem Infiniti concipere, mera contradictio est; cum infinitas suâ naturâ omnis partitionis sit expers. Restat ergo, dum positivo conceptu nec totum infinitum, nec partem ejus concipere possumus, si quo modo id concipimus, alio quam negativo id nos concipere non posse; per remotionem puta termini cujusvis conceptibilis. Talis autem conceptus negativus, sicuti magis & minus non admittit, sed in indivisibili consistit, itâ unicè idoneus videtur ad rem indivisibilem, Infinitatem nempè, intelligendam. Neque attinet pluribus confirmare certam veritatem, quam & Cartefius ipse, quod mireris, Opponenti suo largiri cogitur, dum inquit: Quantum ad rationem formalem Infiniti, sive Infinitatem, etiamsi illam intelligamus esse quam maximè positivam, non tamen nisi negativo quodam modo intelligimus; ex hoc scilicet, quod in re nullam limitationem advertamus. Respons. Prim. p. 59. Quod si non, nisi negativo modo, intelligamus Infinitum, quare negat, ut audivimus, nos Infinitum tantum per negationem finiti percipere, uti quietem percipimus per negationem motûs? Neque hic juvat distinctio inter Infinitatem & rem quæ infinita est, quasi non Infinitatem, sed ipsam rem quæ est infinita, positive intelligamus. Nam de Infinito concepto qua tali est quæstio, ut antè monuimus, non de eo quatenus aut spiritus, aut ens, aut substantia est; quo sensu quis unquam mortalium asseruit, Infiniti conceptum negativum esse?
units.tr: VIII. To this I add that infinity is a predicate of such a kind that (as we shall teach below) it consists in indivisibility; hence, just as nothing can be added to or taken from infinity itself, so nothing can be added to or taken from the concept corresponding to it. But all our concepts, insofar as they are positive, are finite, since they do not exceed the condition of the finite mind itself; and so something can always be added to them or taken from them. It remains, therefore, that the concept of the Infinite is not positive in our mind. If you prefer, I shall argue more clearly perhaps as follows: our mind conceives the Infinite as such either as a whole, or in some part, or not at all. To conceive the infinite whole is nothing other than to exhaust and comprehend by its concept that which altogether exceeds the finitude of the mind. To conceive a part of the Infinite is a plain contradiction, since infinity by its nature admits no partition. It remains, then, that since we can conceive neither the infinite whole nor a part of it by a positive concept, if we conceive it in any way, we cannot conceive it otherwise than negatively, namely by removing the boundary of whatever is conceivable. Moreover such a negative concept, just as it does not admit more and less, but consists in indivisibility, seems to be the only one fitted to understand a thing that is indivisible, namely infinity. Nor is it worth while to confirm at length a certain truth, which Descartes himself, to your surprise, is forced to concede to his opponent when he says: As regards the formal reason of the Infinite, or infinity, even if we understand it to be as positive as possible, we nevertheless understand it only in a certain negative way; namely because we notice no limitation in the thing. Reply to the First Objections, p. 59. But if we understand the Infinite only in a negative way, why does he deny, as we have heard, that we perceive the Infinite only through the negation of the finite, as we perceive rest through the negation of motion? Nor does the distinction between infinity and the thing that is infinite help here, as though we understood positively not infinity but the thing that is infinite itself. For the question concerns the Infinite as conceived as such, as we said before, not insofar as it is a spirit, or a being, or a substance; in what sense has any mortal ever asserted that the concept of the Infinite is negative?

units.la: Verùm, neque prætermittendum est, esse valdè ambiguè dictum à Cartefio, Nec putare debeo, me non percipere infinitum per veram ideam, sed tantum per negationem finiti, ut percipio quietem & tenebras per negationem motus & lucis.
units.tr: But it must not be passed over that Descartes has spoken very ambiguously: Nor ought I to think that I do not perceive the infinite through a true idea, but only through the negation of the finite, as I perceive rest and darkness through the negation of motion and light.

units.la: Ambigua, inquam, sunt ista. Vel enim respiciunt duntaxat simplicem concipiendi modum, vel notant simul judicium quod de re concepta formamus, quodque notionem illam ferè comitatur. Si solam ideam attendas, quatenus in mente nostra simplici apprehensione absolvitur, liquet ex antè demonstratis, verissimum hactenus esse, nos Infini-
units.tr: These statements, I say, are ambiguous. For they either refer merely to the simple mode of conceiving, or they signify at the same time the judgement we form about the thing conceived, which usually accompanies that notion. If you attend only to the idea, insofar as it is completed in our mind by simple apprehension, it is clear from what has been demonstrated above that it is most true up to this point that we Infini-

units.la: IX. Iniqua inter ideam negativam tenebrarum, & eam quæ Infiniti est, comparatio. Infinitum non percipere per positivam ideam, sed tantum per finium remotionem, uti percipimus quietem & tenebras per negationem motus & lucis. Verùm si notionem Infiniti spectes, quatenus eam comitatur judicium de re quam negativâ notione percipimus, longè hoc loco disparratio est inter conceptum Infiniti, atque eum qui est quietis aut tenebrarum. Videlicet, quando conceptu negativo cogito quietem aut tenebras, simul intelligo, non tantùm conceptum formalem, quem vocant, sive ipsum concipiendi modum negativum esse; verùm etiam judico, conceptum objectivum, sive tenebras ipsas à parte sui, esse duntaxat privationem luminis, quietem tantùm privationem motûs, taque itâ reale nihil in se includere, quemadmodum in idea eorum nihil reale offertur menti. At verò, quamvis Infiniti quâ talis conceptus formalis, sive modus concipiendi, sit negativus, certò tamen judicamus, conceptum objectivum, seu Infinitum ipsum prout à parte rei existit, esse quam maximè positivum. Atque hactenus conceptus negativus tenebrarum aut quietis à conceptu negativo Infiniti distat quam plurimùm. Illam notionem & negativam esse, & rei negativæ scimus; hanc negativam esse, sed rei positivæ, novimus. Ut reverà minus accuratè hactenus institutatur inter conceptum tenebrarum & Infiniti comparatio.
units.tr: IX. The comparison between the negative idea of darkness and the idea of the Infinite is unfair. To perceive the Infinite not through a positive idea, but only through the removal of limits, just as we perceive rest and darkness through the negation of motion and light. But if you look at the notion of the Infinite insofar as it is accompanied by the judgement about the thing that we perceive by a negative notion, then at this point the disparity between the concept of the Infinite and that of rest or darkness is very great. For when I think of rest or darkness by a negative concept, at the same time I understand not only that the formal concept, as they call it, or the mode of conceiving itself, is negative, but I also judge that the objective concept, or darkness itself on its own side, is merely a privation of light, and rest merely a privation of motion, and so includes nothing real in itself, just as nothing real is presented to the mind in the idea of them. But although the formal concept of the Infinite as such, or its mode of conceiving, is negative, we nevertheless certainly judge that the objective concept, or the Infinite itself as it exists on the side of the thing, is as positive as possible. And so far the negative concept of darkness or rest differs very much from the negative concept of the Infinite. We know that the former notion is negative, and that it is of a negative thing; we know that the latter is negative, but of a positive thing. Indeed, the comparison between the concept of darkness and that of the Infinite has so far been set up in a rather inaccurate way.

units.la: Ut verò nihil amplius dubitemus, quin Infinitum, prout sub conceptum nostrum finitum cadit, non nisi negativè à nobis apprehendatur, per terminorum seu limitum remotionem, operæ pretium fuerit attendere paulo diligentius modum, quo, teste experientiâ, Infiniti notio à mente nostra formatur. Exemplo sit Æternitas, spectata simpliciter in quantum est duratio infinita: nam & successionis carentiam in ea includi novimus; atquiquam hic non jam attendemus. Eam conceptur tanquam talem, obviam quamcunque durationem apprehendo; finitam quidem, sed quam, factâ sæpius multiplicatione, amplifico quantum possum, & quam latissimè patentem concipere annitor. Indè quidem experior, ex finita duratione multoties aucta & multiplicata resultare tandem aliquam, cujus definitam magnitudinem non intelligo, utpote distinctum meum captum fugientem; non tamen ideò me Infinitam eam concipere probè novi, quippe qui mihi conscius sum, finiti ad infinitum nullam esse proportionem, neque adeò multiplicationis finitæ, quantumvis magnæ, productum unquam esse, aut esse posse, Infinitum. Nunc itaquè, nisi de-sperabundus omnem prorsùs de Infinita duratione cogitationem abjicere velim, nihil restat aliud, quam ut cogitem rem infinitè durantem, tanquam aliquid quod omnem mihi conceptibilem durationem excedit. Quæ verò duratio conceptibilem omnem dura-tionem excedere cogitatur, eo ipso concipitur negativè: quan-doquidem manifestam notat contradictionem, aliquid omne conceptibile excedere, & tamen simul à me positivè intelligi. Quodcunque enim, ut antè docui, concipitur positivè, in quantum concipitur positivè, mentem non excedit; & contrà, quod mentem excedit, hoc ipso quod excedit, mentem non afficit, & sic non nisi negativè cogitatur. Et profectò modum concipien-di, ad quem nos ducit Spiritus Sanctus in Sacris, si attendamus, deprehendemus à finito fieri initium, & per finium seu limitum remotionem conceptum hunc terminari. Quid enim vult aliud, quando de Æternitate (ut tantùm assumam hoc de quo jam di-ximus) sermo est, illud antropopathicum, Anni tui non deficiunt? Ecce, durationem Deo tribuendam, sive æternitatem, conceptam finitam primùm per modum annorum! Ecce, factam infinitam, pro modo concipiendi nostro, per remotionem ter-minorum! Mirum, balbutire voluisse itâ Spiritum S. nobiscum, si Infinitatis positivum habere conceptum adeò sit facile, quam contendunt isti.
units.tr: But so that we may have no further doubt that the Infinite, insofar as it falls under our finite concept, is apprehended by us only negatively, through the removal of terms or limits, it will be worth our while to consider a little more carefully the manner in which, as experience attests, the notion of the Infinite is formed by our mind. Let eternity serve as an example, considered simply insofar as it is infinite duration; for we know that the absence of succession is included in it, but we shall not now attend to this. I conceive it as such: whatever duration presents itself to me, I apprehend as finite, but I amplify it as much as I can by repeated multiplication, and I strive to conceive it as extended as widely as possible. From this I indeed experience that from a finite duration increased and multiplied many times there at last results something whose definite magnitude I do not understand, as it escapes my limited grasp; yet I do not on that account well know that I conceive it as infinite, since I am aware that there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite, and that no product of finite multiplication, however great, has ever been or can be infinite. Now, therefore, unless I wish, in despair, to cast off altogether all thought of infinite duration, nothing remains but to think of a thing enduring infinitely, as something that exceeds every duration conceivable to me. But a duration that is thought to exceed every conceivable duration is by that very fact conceived negatively, since it marks a manifest contradiction, that something should exceed everything conceivable and yet at the same time be understood by me positively. For whatever is conceived positively, as I taught above, insofar as it is conceived positively, does not exceed the mind; and conversely, what exceeds the mind, by the very fact that it exceeds it, does not affect the mind, and so is thought only negatively. And indeed, if we attend to the mode of conceiving to which the Holy Spirit leads us in the Sacred Scriptures, we shall find that the beginning is made from the finite, and that this concept is terminated by the removal of finite limits. For what else does it mean, when there is talk of eternity (to take only this instance of which we have just spoken), than that anthropopathic saying, Thy years shall not fail? Behold, duration to be ascribed to God, or eternity, conceived first as finite, after the manner of years! Behold, made infinite, according to our manner of conceiving, by the removal of terms! It would be strange if the Holy Spirit had wished to stammer thus with us, if it were as easy to have a positive concept of infinity as these men contend.

units.la: Neque pro positiva Infiniti idea facit, quod tanquam funda-mentum assertioni suæ subjicit Cartesius, quandò ait: Manifestè intelligo, plus realitatis esse in substantia infinita, quam in finita. Nam, quamvis sit certissimum, nos meritò ob validas rationes judicare, id quod in re infinita plus est quam in finita, & per quod res infinita constituitur in esse Infiniti, esse à parte rei quam maximè positivum, negatur tamen, ob antè demonstrata, te illud plus realitatis, quod in re Infinita est, eamque Infinitam facit, ideâ quadam positivâ concipere; quod docere omninò necesse fuerit, ad concedendum, nos Infinitum per veram ideam, & non tantum per negationem finiti percipere. Neque multò aliter solvendum aliorum argumentum huic non valdè absimile. Idea, inquiunt, substantiæ infinitæ est positiva; quia infinita substantia illa est , quæ omnes omninò perfectiones cogitabiles perfectissimè possidet : ast istud aliquid positivum est. Quamvis enim negandum non fit , τὸ[?] possidere omnes perfectiones perfectissimè notare à parte ipsius possidentis quid quam maximè positivum & reale, non tamen indè conficitur, reale illud positivâ idcâ, pro modo concipiendi nostro , à nobis intelligi. Quis certè est, qui positivè concipiat, & omnes omninò perfectiones cogitabiles, & perfectissimam earundem possessionem ? Quin, quis non potius experitur secum , se hæc concipere , removendo istiusmodi impersectiones & modos possidendi imperfectos, quos in creaturis observamus ? Quamobrem , Deum omnes omninò perfectiones perfectissimo modo possidere, quoties dicimus, non id exprimi-mus quod simplici ideâ eâque positivâ, de Numine nobis repræsentamus , sed , quod, quamvis nobis positivè inconceptibile esse sentiamus, ratiocinando tamen Divinæ naturæ convenire novimus. Quo sensu ille, piè non minus quam eleganter, Nobis de Deo affirmanda esse & qua concipimus, & qua non concipimus.
units.tr: Nor does what Descartes sets down as the foundation of his assertion support a positive idea of the Infinite, when he says: I clearly understand that there is more reality in an infinite substance than in a finite one. For although it is most certain that we rightly judge, for weighty reasons, that what is more in an infinite thing, and through which the thing is constituted in the being of the Infinite, is in its reality most positive, it is nevertheless denied, for the reasons demonstrated above, that we can conceive by some positive idea that surplus of reality which is in the infinite thing and makes it infinite. This would have to be taught before we could grant that we perceive the Infinite through a true idea, and not merely through the negation of the finite. The argument of others, not very different from this, is to be answered in much the same way. They say: the idea of an infinite substance is positive, because that infinite substance is the one that possesses perfectly all conceivable perfections in the most perfect way; but this is something positive. For although it must not be denied that to possess all perfections in the most perfect way is, on the part of the possessor himself, something most positive and real, it does not follow from this that we understand that reality by a positive idea, according to our manner of conceiving. Who, indeed, conceives positively both all conceivable perfections and their most perfect possession? Rather, who does not find in himself that he conceives these things by removing such imperfections and imperfect modes of possession as we observe in creatures? Therefore, when we say that God possesses all perfections in the most perfect manner, we do not express what we represent to ourselves of the Deity by a simple and positive idea, but what, although we feel that it is positively inconceivable to us, we know by reasoning to belong to the divine nature. In this sense that writer, no less piously than elegantly, said: Of God we must affirm both what we conceive and what we do not conceive.

units.la: Progredior ad alteram de conceptu Infiniti controversiam , cujus decisio ex priori facillima est. Dico nimirum, Conceptum finiti in mente nostra priorem esse eo qui est Infiniti. De hoc dubitare non sinunt jam allata. Scilicet, quod à mente nostra positivè percipitur, eidemque sic satis est approportionatum (quale esse finitum ostendimus) id procul omni dubio prius percipitur eo quod neque positivè menti offertur, neque ullá ratione illi approportionari potest; quale est Infinitum. Ad ea enim concipienda mentem imprimis pronam esse & facilem, quæ maximè ei sunt approproportionata; item, conceptum positivum negativo priorem esse, per se clarum est. Quin, si, ut opinantur qui sentiunt oppositum, finitum tantùm concipi queat per remotionem majoris alicujus puta Infiniti jam antè nobis concepti, sequitur, ea concipi plane non posse finita, quæ ipsa Infinita quoque concipi nequeunt. Sumamus V. G. Extensionem vel Numerum. Ea quando concipio finita, dici nequit præcessisse in mente meâ ideam extensionis aut numeri Infiniti, per cujus remotionem extensionem vel numerum hunc aut istum finitum concipio; nam (quod deinceps docebimus) itâ contradictoria & sui everfiva est extensio vel numerus infinitus, ut ejus positivam ideam habere ne quidem quisquam possit. Atque haec ratio efficacissima est, & vel una sufficit, ad evincendum, conceptum Infiniti notionem finiti suâ naturâ non antecedere. Et quid quaeso de istis dicemus hominibus, qui per omnem vitam vix unquam serió de Infinito cogitarunt, multò minus positivo conceptu id unquam conceperunt; quos tamen res quaevis obvias tanquam finitas clarè & distinctè concipere, notum est? Evidenti profectò argumento, non praecedere in nostra mente conceptum Infiniti notionem finiti; sed finitum concipi omninò posse ab aliquo qui nequidem de Infinito cogitat. Adde deniquè, ipsum Spiritum Sanctum non uno loco nos manu ducere ad concipiendum Infinitum ex finito; non contrà, finitum ex Infinito: cujus exemplum, ne alia adducam, dedimus in Æternitate Divina concipienda per durationem à qua removentur fines. Non addam plura; sufficiunt haec ad demonstrandum, falsum esse, quod asserit Cartesius, priorem quodammodo in nobis esse perceptionem Infiniti, quam finiti.
units.tr: I proceed to the second controversy about the concept of the Infinite, whose decision follows very easily from the former. I say, namely, that the concept of the finite is prior in our mind to that of the Infinite. The things already adduced leave no room for doubt on this. Clearly, what is positively perceived by our mind, and is sufficiently proportioned to it (as we have shown the finite to be), is without doubt perceived before that which is neither positively presented to the mind nor can be proportioned to it in any way, such as the Infinite. For the mind is especially prone and apt to conceive those things which are most proportioned to it; and it is clear in itself that a positive concept is prior to a negative one. Indeed, if, as those who hold the opposite opinion think, the finite can be conceived only by the removal of some greater thing, namely the Infinite, already conceived by us beforehand, it follows that those finite things cannot be conceived at all which themselves cannot be conceived as infinite. Let us take, for example, extension or number. When I conceive these as finite, it cannot be said that the idea of infinite extension or infinite number had come first into my mind, by whose removal I conceive this or that finite extension or number; for (as we shall show later) infinite extension or number is so self-contradictory and self-subverting that no one can even have a positive idea of it. This argument is most effective, and by itself suffices to prove that the concept of the Infinite does not precede the notion of the finite by its nature. And what, I ask, shall we say of those men who, throughout their whole life, have hardly ever seriously thought about the Infinite, much less conceived it by a positive concept, yet who are known to conceive clearly and distinctly all the things that lie before them as finite? This is surely strong evidence that the notion of the Infinite does not precede the notion of the finite in our mind, but that the finite can be conceived perfectly well by someone who does not even think of the Infinite. Finally, add that the Holy Spirit himself, in more than one place, leads us by the hand to conceive the Infinite from the finite, and not, conversely, the finite from the Infinite. Of this we have given an example, to pass over others, in conceiving the divine eternity through duration from which ends are removed. I will add no more; these things suffice to demonstrate that what Descartes asserts is false, namely that in us the perception of the Infinite is in some way prior to that of the finite.

units.la: Neque stringunt, quae pro sententia sua subjicit: Qua enim ratione intelligerem me dubitare, me cupere, hoc est aliquid mihi deesse, & me non esse omnino perfectum, si nulla idea entis perfectioris in me esset, ex cujus comparatione defectus meos agnoscerem? Nam non prorsùs idem sunt, se ipsum concipere finitum; &, concipere aliquid sibi deesse ex comparatione alicujus perfectioris. Prior conceptus absolutus est; posterior comparativus: &, si benè attendamus, hic ex illo sequitur. Videlicet, primum positivè intelligo, me hoc vel illud praedicatum possidere hactenus; mox negativè cogito, non ergò me possidere majus, v. c non duplum, aut triplum, &c. multo minus id me possidere sine ullis limitibus & modo perfectiore quam unquam positivè intelligere possum, id est, infinito. Quamvis itaque verum sit, me non posse concipere in me ipso comparativè minus, quin connotetur conceptus majoris (minus enim & majus, tanquam relata, sunt simul, uti natura, ita quoque cognitione) nihil tamen hinc conficitur aliud, quam, quoties finitum cogitare incipimus comparativè, tanquam minus Infinito, conceptum Infiniti in hoc mentis actu involvi. At non indè sequitur, hunc ideò priorem esse illo: non magis, quam si inferrem ego, conceptum finiti priorem esse notione Infiniti, quia nimirum nunquam concipere possum Infinitum tanquam majus finito, quin in me existat idea entis finiti, ex cujus comparatione excessum Infiniti supra finitum intelligam. Comparativè itaquè si spectentur Finitum & Infinitum, quatenus alterum altero majus est aut minus, intelliguntur, uti dixi, simul; ut ne quidem in comparativo hoc sensu ex vero dicatur, priorem quodammodo esse perceptionem infiniti quam finiti. Concidit itaque omnis haec Cartesii philosophatio. Quod enim ad conceptum Infiniti absolutum (non comparativum tanquam alicujus finito majoris) cum conceptu finiti in nobis esse posteriorem, commate proximè precedente, invitè docuimus.
units.tr: Nor do the things he adduces in support of his view press the point: For by what reasoning would I understand that I doubt, that I desire, that is, that something is lacking to me and that I am not wholly perfect, if there were no idea in me of a more perfect being, by comparison with which I might recognise my defects? For to conceive oneself as finite and to conceive that something is lacking to oneself by comparison with something more perfect are not altogether the same. The former concept is absolute; the latter is comparative; and, if we attend carefully, the latter follows from the former. Namely, first I understand positively that I possess this or that predicate so far; then I think negatively that I therefore do not possess something greater, for example not double or triple, and so on; much less do I possess it without any limits and in a more perfect mode than I can ever understand positively, that is, infinitely. Although it is therefore true that I cannot conceive in myself something comparatively less without the concept of something greater being implied (for less and greater, as correlatives, are simultaneous in nature and so also in our knowledge), nothing else follows from this than that, whenever we begin to think of the finite comparatively, as less than the Infinite, the concept of the Infinite is involved in that act of the mind. But it does not follow from this that the latter is therefore prior to the former: no more than if I were to infer that the concept of the finite is prior to the notion of the Infinite, because I can never conceive the Infinite as greater than the finite without the idea of a finite being existing in me, by comparison with which I understand the excess of the Infinite over the finite. So if the Finite and the Infinite are regarded comparatively, insofar as one is greater or less than the other, they are understood, as I have said, simultaneously; so that not even in this comparative sense is it rightly said that the perception of the infinite is in some way prior to that of the finite. Thus this whole philosophy of Descartes collapses. For as to the absolute concept of the Infinite (not the comparative, as of something greater than some finite thing), that it is posterior to the concept of the finite in us, we have reluctantly taught in the immediately preceding paragraph.

units.la: Id verò mirum est, si, quod contendit Cartesius, perceptio Infiniti, hoc est Dei, prior quodammodo in homine fit, quam finiti, hoc est sui ipsius, cur non Nobilis Auctor Meditationum suarum initium fecerit ab idea Dei potius tanquam Infiniti, quam sui tanquam dubitantis; quoniam, si ei credimus, nulla ratione intelligere possumus nos dubitare, sine comparatione entis perfectioris. Certè, si sint haec vera, non est nova methodus satis congrua ideis, prout ex nativo quasi ordine menti nostrae sese offerunt. Quin, quandò ipse Cartesius adhuc omnia pro falsis habebat, sic ut supponeret, nullum esse Deum, totumque hoc de Deo daret esse fictitium, omnemque adeò de Deo, hoc est Infinito, cogitationem planè seponeret, intelligebat nihilominus etiam tum, se existere tanquam dubitantem, hoc est, tanquam finitum, cui aliquid defit; nec tamen adhuc intelligebat, aliquid existere se majus, ex cujus comparatione se tanquam finitum & dubitantem intelligere poterat. Parum congrua ergò fuerit, nullâ habitâ ratione Infiniti, ejusque conscientiâ in alium locum rejectâ, tam operosa & profunda de mente dubitante, atque ex dubitatione ipsa suæ sibi finitudinis conscia, philosophatio. Videmus, ad concipiendum finitum supponendum non esse conceptum priorem Infiniti, ea ipsa si attendamus, quæ tradunt novi methodistæ.
units.tr: It is indeed remarkable that, if Descartes contends that the perception of the Infinite, that is of God, is in some way prior in man to that of the finite, that is of himself, the noble author of his Meditations did not begin with the idea of God as infinite rather than with the idea of himself as doubting; since, if we believe him, we can in no way understand that we doubt without a comparison with a more perfect being. Certainly, if these things are true, it is not a new method sufficiently agreeing with ideas as they present themselves to our mind in a kind of native order. Indeed, when Descartes himself still held everything to be false, so that he supposed that there is no God, and that all this about God was a fiction, and so wholly set aside all thought of God, that is of the Infinite, he nevertheless understood even then that he existed as doubting, that is, as a finite being to whom something is lacking; yet he did not yet understand that there exists something greater than himself, by comparison with which he could understand himself as finite and doubting. It would therefore be little consonant, with no regard had to the Infinite and with consciousness of it thrust into another place, to construct so laborious and profound a philosophy about a doubting mind, and about its consciousness of its own finitude arising from the doubt itself. We see, if we attend to those very things which the new methodists teach, that to conceive the finite one need not presuppose a prior concept of the Infinite.

units.la: Propero ad tertiam, de conceptu Infiniti in nobis, quæstionem: An nimirum idea Infiniti in nostra mente sit clara & distincta; quin, uti loquitur Auctor, maximè clara & distincta? Ad ejus solutionem multa hùc congerere necesse non erit. Si enim, quod demonstravimus, idea Infiniti, & negativa sit, & finiti idea posterior, quis dubitet, clarius & distinctius à nobis finitum percipi quam Infinitum? An verò maximè clara & distincta erit idea ejus, quod, ipso teste Cartesio, non nisi negativo quodam modo intelligimus; ex hoc scilicet, quod in re nullam limitationem advertamus? Respons. Prim p. m. 59. Ea ergò idea maximè clara & distincta erit, quæ est rei, quam totam simul animo complecti non possumus, quamque non nisi finitâ, & ad modulum ingenii nostri accommodata cognitione intelligere nos, fatetur? Ibidem. Ecquis extitit unquam, qui non, vel leviter ipsas duntaxat voces attendens, intellexerit, id quod menti approportionatum est, atque, absolutè loquendo, totum ab ipsa comprehendi potest, quale est finitum, longè clarius & distinctius intelligi à nobis, quam quod nullam planè per se & ex suâ naturâ ad mentem dicit proportionem, quale est Infinitum? Hoc enim, ut jam antè notavimus, neque secundum se totum prout in se est intelligere possumus, ob mentis percipientis finitatem; neque intelligere id possumus per partes, quas ipsa Infiniti natura respuit: undè nihil aliud de Infinito qua tali concipere licet, quam quod inæstimabili magnitudine & modo prorsus inconceptibili, omnem omninò vis nostræ intellectivæ finitudinem excedat. Hæccine idea maximè clara est & distincta? Concipiant ista qui possint, dicant qui ausint! Ego, me quod attinet, sic omninò habeo, præclarè hac de re disseruisse Auctorem Objection. Prim. p. 49. hunc in modum: Interrogabit nonnemo; clarene distincteque cognoscis ens infinitum? Quid ergo sibi vult tritum istud & vulgo notum: Infinitum qua infinitum est ignotum. Si enim ego cum de chiliogono cogito figuram aliquam confusè mihi repræsentans, non chiliogonum ipsum distincte imaginor aut cognosco, quia mille ejus latera non distincte intueor; sane rogabit ille, quomodo infinitum ut infinitum distincte & non confusè tantum cogitet, si infinitas ejus perfectiones, quibus constat, clare & velut ad oculum videre non possit.
units.tr: I hasten to the third question, concerning our concept of the Infinite: namely, whether the idea of the Infinite in our mind is clear and distinct, or, as the Author puts it, most clear and distinct. It will not be necessary to pile up many arguments for its solution. For if, as we have demonstrated, the idea of the Infinite is negative, and the idea of the finite is prior to it, who would doubt that we perceive the finite more clearly and distinctly than the Infinite? But will the idea of that thing be most clear and distinct which, on Descartes' own testimony, we understand only in a certain negative way, namely from our not noticing any limitation in the thing? (Reply to the First Objections, p. 59.) Will that idea then be most clear and distinct which, as he himself admits, is the idea of a thing we cannot grasp as a whole all at once, and which we understand only by a finite cognition accommodated to the measure of our intellect? (Ibid.) Has anyone ever existed who, paying even slight attention to the words themselves, did not understand that what is proportionate to the mind, and which can, strictly speaking, be wholly comprehended by it, such as the finite, is understood by us far more clearly and distinctly than what has no proportion whatever to the mind by its own nature, such as the Infinite? For, as we have already noted, we cannot understand the Infinite as it is in itself, as a whole, because of the finitude of the perceiving mind; nor can we understand it by parts, which the very nature of the Infinite rejects. Hence we can conceive of the Infinite, as such, only as something of immeasurable magnitude and of a wholly inconceivable mode, exceeding all the finitude of our power of understanding. Is this the most clear and distinct idea? Let those who can conceive such things conceive them; let those who dare say so say it! As for me, I am entirely of the opinion that the Author of the First Objections, p. 49, argued excellently to this effect: Someone will ask: do you know the infinite Being clearly and distinctly? What then does that hackneyed and commonly known saying mean: the Infinite, qua infinite, is unknown? For if, when I think of a chiliagon, I represent some figure to myself confusedly, I do not distinctly imagine or know the chiliagon itself, because I do not distinctly see its thousand sides; surely that man will ask how one can think of the Infinite, as infinite, distinctly and not merely confusedly, if one cannot see clearly, as it were before the eyes, the infinite perfections of which it consists.

units.la: Neque ullâ parte iis satisfecit Cartesius, respondendo, Resp. Prim. p. 59. Confusè imaginamur chiliogonum, cum omnia simul ejus latera complectimur, sed potest valde clara & distincta esse imaginatio chiliogoni, si tantum ad unum aut alterum ejus latus se extendat. Simili ratione, &c. Perindè enim id est, ac si dicam, posse esse valdè claram & distinctam imaginationem leonis, cujus non omnia nit & sinmembra video, sed aliquem tantùm unguem. Certè chiliogonum tanquam tale clarè & distinctè neutiquam concipitur, nisi id ad minimum concipiatur quod chiliogono est essentiale, videlicet non unum, non alterum, non tertium latus, quod & in decagono observare licet, sed mille præcisè latera totidem angulis inter se unita: quæ nisi concipias, re verà chiliogonum non concipis tanquam tale; nedum ut id conciperes clarè & distinctè. Quæ si Infinito applicemus, res est evidentissima. Nam neque Infinitum tanquam tale clarè & distinctè concipitur, nisi omnes perfectiones quæ Infinitum absolvunt, & sine quibus omnibus Infinitum tale non est, & positivè tanquam tale menti non occurrit, clarè & distinctè concipiantur. Quapropter, quemadmodum mens nostra in formando repræsentamine chilogoni, laterum multitudine, imaginationi non approportionatâ, sic obruitur, ut chiliogoni tanquam talis clarum & distinctum conceptum nunquam acquirat; itâ quoque mens nostra in formatione notionis Infiniti, multitudine perfectionum ad Infinitum requisitarum, & inconceptibile quantùm captum nostrum excedentium, sic obruitur, ut Infiniti qua talis conceptum clarum & distinctum nec habeat, nec per finitam suam naturam ad infinitum collatam habere possit.
units.tr: Descartes did not satisfy these objections in any part, when he replied: We imagine a chiliagon confusedly when we take in all its sides at once; but the imagination of a chiliagon can be very clear and distinct if it extends only to one or another of its sides. (Reply to the First Objections, p. 59.) In a similar way, and so on. For this is just the same as if I were to say that one can have a very clear and distinct imagination of a lion of which one sees not all the limbs and members, but only some single claw. Certainly a chiliagon is not conceived clearly and distinctly as such unless at least what is essential to a chiliagon is conceived, namely not one side, not another, not a third side (which can be observed also in a decagon), but precisely a thousand sides united with as many angles. Unless you conceive these, you do not in fact conceive the chiliagon as such, much less conceive it clearly and distinctly. If we apply this to the Infinite, the matter is most evident. For the Infinite is not conceived as such clearly and distinctly unless all the perfections which make up the Infinite, and without all of which the Infinite is not such, are conceived clearly and distinctly, and unless it presents itself to the mind positively as such. Therefore, just as our mind, in forming the representation of a chiliagon, is so overwhelmed by the multitude of sides, which is not proportionate to the imagination, that it never acquires a clear and distinct concept of the chiliagon as such, so also our mind, in forming the notion of the Infinite, is so overwhelmed by the multitude of perfections required for the Infinite, which exceed our capacity beyond all conception, that it has no clear and distinct concept of the Infinite as such, nor can it have one through its finite nature compared with the infinite.

units.la: Nititur quidem Cartesius, ideam Infiniti in mente nostra præ cæteris quam maximè esse claram & distinctam, hinc imprimis probare, quod illa plus realitatis quam ulla alia contineat. Sed frustrà est. Neque enim eo clarior semper est & distinctior idea, quo plus realitatis objectivæ continet. Sive, ut loquar clarius, non eò evidentius & distinctius rem concipimus, quo plures in re concepta perfectiones existere judicamus, nisi simul illud plus realitatis, vel plures illas perfectiones ipsas, quarum ratione res concepta alias excedit, clarè & distinctè intelligamus. Etenim aliud prorsùs est, intelligere rem quampiam esse perfectiorem, aliud, ipsas illas perfectiones, per quas res hæc existit illâ perfectior, clarè & distinctè concipere: quorum hoc imprimis ad claram & distinctam rei perfectioris ideam pertinet. Jam verò, ut illud plus realitatis, quo Finitum ab Infinito excedittur, clarè & distinctè intelligas, tantùm abest, ut ipse necesse habeas post pauca fateri, alia innumera in Deo (Infinito) esse, quæ forte ignoras, nec forte forte etiam attingere cogitatione ullo modo potes: adeò ut, quantum ad ipsam Infinitatem, illam non nisi negativo quodam modo intelligamus. Tu ergò, qui in Infinito innumera (quorum respectu Infinitum exstitit tale) ignoras, sic ut ea cogitatione ullo modo attingere nequeas, & non nisi negativo quodam modo intelligas, dices nihilominus, Infiniti claram & distinctam, & quidem quam maximè claram & distinctam, te habere ideam? Capiat ænigmata istiusmodi qui potest!
units.tr: Descartes indeed strives to prove that the idea of the Infinite in our mind is above all others most clear and distinct, and he proves this chiefly by saying that it contains more reality than any other. But this is in vain. For an idea is not always clearer and more distinct the more objective reality it contains. Or, to speak more clearly, we do not conceive a thing more evidently and distinctly the more perfections we judge to exist in the conceived thing, unless at the same time we understand clearly and distinctly that additional reality, or those very perfections, by reason of which the conceived thing surpasses others. For it is one thing to understand that some thing is more perfect, and quite another to conceive clearly and distinctly those very perfections through which this thing is more perfect; and the latter pertains above all to the clear and distinct idea of the more perfect thing. Now, far from your being able to understand clearly and distinctly that additional reality by which the Finite falls short of the Infinite, you must yourself soon admit that in God (the Infinite) there are countless other things which you perhaps do not know, nor perhaps can you in any way attain them in thought: so much so that, as far as the Infinity itself is concerned, we understand it only in a certain negative way. So you, who do not know the countless things in the Infinite (with respect to which the Infinite exists as such), so that you cannot in any way attain them in thought, and understand only in a negative way, will nevertheless say that you have a clear and distinct idea of the Infinite, and indeed a most clear and distinct one? Let whoever can accept such riddles accept them!

units.la: Juvat rem hanc paucis illustrare, quo veritas eorum quæ diximus ab imperitissimo quoque manibus palpetur. Similis omninò est universa hæc Cartesii philosophatio assertioni alicujus Geometræ, jactantis, longè clarius & distinctius se concipere figuram indefinitorum angulorum, quam trium; eo scil. fundamento, quod, cum in idea Trianguli tres tantum sese offerant anguli, ex adverso Indefinitanguli conceptus plus angulorum contineat, quam ulla alterius figuræ idea: licet ipse interim experiatur, in Indefinitangulo innumeros esse angulos, quos ignorat, nec etiam attingere cogitatione ullo modo potest. Aut tantundem est, ac si quis glorietur imaginem Solis se habere multò clariorem & distinctiorem quam ardentis alicujus candelæ; quoniam intelligit in sole esse plus luminis quam in flamma candelæ, innumeros nimirum radios, sed quos omnes nec videt, nec visu suo ullo modo attingere potest. Si quis hæc ritè perpenderit, nihil dubito, quin omnis, qui non volens hìc exercutire cupit, intelligat clarissimè & distinctissimè, longè salsissimum esse & absurdissimum, tanto clarius & distinctius rem aliquam nos intelligere, quanto plura ei inesse judicamus prædicata, etiamsi ea nobis sint inconceptibilia. Quid? quod experientia quotidiana nos doceat, verissimum esse, non raro rem imperfectissimam, cui pauca duntaxat insunt prædicata, longè clarius & distinctius nobis concipi (dum mens omnes & singulas ejus perfectiones magis quasi penetrat & plenius exhaurit) quam aliam multò quidem perfectiorem, sed ipsâ prædicatorum suorum multitudine & magnitudine intellectui inaccessam nec ullo modo approportionatam. Obtinet hoc imprimis in rebus quæ infinitis suis perfectionibus, sic mentis aciem perstringit, ut confundat, neque quid tandem percipiat, ipsa satis sciat, nisi forte hoc unum, rem in hoc à se Infinitam agnosci, quod perperceptione finitâ percipere nequeat ea quæ in re Infinita percipienda sunt. Hæccine est idea maximè clara & distincta? Rectæ rationis hac parte dictamini conformia magis existunt dictata Spiritus Sancti, asserentis, Deum ratione infinitarum suarum perfectionum lucem inhabitare, sed finitis nobis homuncionibus sic inaccessam, ut & in tenebris habitare dicatur; adeò quidem, ut singulari etiam gratiâ illuminatorum in hac vita cognitio de Infinito Deo similis sit ænigmati, cujus ipsam rationem formalem in obscuritate & confusione consistere, notissimum est.
units.tr: It is worth illustrating this matter briefly, so that the truth of what we have said may be felt by even the most unskilled. This whole philosophizing of Descartes is quite like the assertion of some geometer who boasts that he conceives the figure of an indefinite angle far more clearly and distinctly than that of a triangle; on the ground, namely, that while in the idea of a triangle only three angles present themselves, the concept of an indefinite angle, on the contrary, contains more angles than the idea of any other figure; although he himself meanwhile experiences that in an indefinite angle there are innumerable angles which he does not know and cannot in any way attain in thought. Or it is just as if someone should boast that he has an image of the sun far clearer and more distinct than that of some burning candle, since he understands that there is more light in the sun than in a candle flame, namely countless rays, which however he neither sees all nor can in any way attain with his sight. If anyone weighs these things properly, I have no doubt that everyone who does not wish to exercise himself here in vain will understand most clearly and distinctly that it is most absurd and utterly foolish to say that we understand a thing the more clearly and distinctly the more predicates we judge to belong to it, even if those predicates are inconceivable to us. Moreover, does not daily experience teach us that it is most true that a very imperfect thing, to which only a few predicates belong, is often conceived by us far more clearly and distinctly (since the mind, as it were, penetrates each and every one of its perfections more and exhausts them more fully) than another, far more perfect, but inaccessible to the intellect and in no way proportionate to it because of the multitude and magnitude of its predicates? This holds above all for things which, by their infinite perfections, so dazzle the edge of the mind that it is confused, and itself knows scarcely what it finally perceives, except perhaps this one thing: that the thing is recognized as infinite in that it cannot, by a finite perception, perceive the things that are to be perceived in an infinite thing. Is this the most clear and distinct idea? The utterances of the Holy Spirit agree more with the dictate of right reason in this respect, affirming that God dwells in light by reason of his infinite perfections, but is so inaccessible to us finite little men, that he is also said to dwell in darkness; so much so that even by the singular grace of those enlightened in this life, the knowledge of the Infinite God is like a riddle, whose formal nature is well known to consist in obscurity and confusion.

units.la: Ex hactenus demonstratis liquet abundè, conceptum Infiniti, tanquam talis, in mente nostra & negativum esse; & notione finiti posteriorem; & denique non nisi obscurum & confusum: quæ ipsa de Infiniti idea probanda sumseramus. Quibus ritè intellectis, ad oculum apparet, quam parùm concinna sit methodus Cartesii, quam servat in famosis illis suis de prima Philosophia Meditationibus. Nititur enim hæc omnis eâ, quam jam profligavimus, sententiâ, de idea Infiniti in mente nostra & positiva, & ideâ finiti priore, & clara maximè ac distincta. Nominatim liquet, nullam omninò esse decantatam illam demonstrationem, quam adfert pro demonstranda summi Numinis existentia ex innata quadam nobis Dei, tanquam entis infinitè perfecti, idea, omnium quas habemus clarissima ac distinctissima, atque ideò maximè vera. Concidunt istæc omnia, quæque iis connexa sunt sexcenta, subruto hoc de idea Infiniti fundamento; quod conceptibus suis ac demonstrationibus ubique Cartesius substernit. Verùm novæ Methodi ἀμεθόδευτοι, & gravissima illarum Meditationum λανθασμέναι, alias fortè detegemus pluribus & ex professo. Nunc circa Infiniti ideam hæc observasse sufficerit.
units.tr: From what has been demonstrated so far it is abundantly clear that the concept of the Infinite, as such, is in our mind both negative, and posterior to the notion of the finite, and finally only obscure and confused. These are the very things we had undertaken to prove about the idea of the Infinite. Once these points are rightly understood, it is plain how little consistent the method of Descartes is, which he follows in his famous Meditations on First Philosophy. For all of it rests on that opinion which we have now overthrown, namely that the idea of the Infinite in our mind is positive, and that the idea of the finite is prior, and clear and distinct above all. In particular it is evident that there is no such celebrated demonstration at all, which he offers for proving the existence of the supreme Deity from a certain innate idea of God in us, as of an infinitely perfect being, the clearest and most distinct of all the ideas we have, and therefore most true. All these things fall, together with the countless others connected with them, once this foundation concerning the idea of the Infinite is overthrown, which Descartes everywhere lays beneath his concepts and demonstrations. But the ἀμεθόδευτοι ["without method"] of his new Method, and the very grave λανθασμέναι ["errors"] of those Meditations, we shall perhaps uncover at another time, more fully and on purpose. For now it will be enough to have made these observations about the idea of the Infinite.

units.la: DISSERTATIONIS DE INFINITO SECTIO POSTERIOR; Quæ est de EXTENSIONE INFINITA.
units.tr: THE LATER SECTION OF THE DISSERTATION ON THE INFINITE, CONCERNING INFINITE EXTENSION.
SUMMARY.

units.la: XX. De Infinita materiæ extensione quæstio est longissimæ consequentiæ. XXI. Infinitam Universi dissusionem agnoscit præ aliis rotundè Epicurus. XXII. Cartesianorum in indefinita mundi extensione vorticum cum innumeris Epicuri in infinito universo mundis consensus. XXIII. Universi extensionem verè infinitam statuere, æquè ac Epicurus, necesse habet Cartesius. XXIV. Cui difficultati frustrà sese hic subducere laborat. XXV. Cartesii dissertatio, quâ suam aperit de Infinito universo sententiam. XXVI. Alia ejusdem in eandem rem adducta loca præcipua. XXVII. Philosophationis Cartesianæ summa omnis capitibus quibusdam comprehensa. XXVIII. Veram extensionis Infinitatem eis asseri, observatione unâ atque alterâ ostenditur. XXIX. Distinctio Cartesii inter Infinitum & Indefinitum nil hic aufert difficultatis. XXX. Mundi extensio quo sen-su su affirmanda Infinita , Indefinita , Finita. XXXI. Finitas partes nulli Infinitæ extensioni constituendæ sufficere, ostenditur. XXXII. Etiam partes numero infinitas in Infinita extensione admitti non posse, docetur. XXXIII. Neque ex partibus extensione infinitis Infinitam extensionem componi , evincitur. XXXIV. Imò ne altera quidem parte infinitas partes extensionem totam Infinitam conficere posse, demonstratur. XXXV. Ex quibus omnibus , extensum nullum , ob ipsam fui extensionem , Infinitum dari , aut dari posse , concluditur. XXXVI. Quod idem ex rei corporeæ natura & attributis quibuslibet pluribus inftantiis conficitur. XXXVII. Effentia solius Dei Infinita extensionis cujusvis Infinitatem evertit. XXXVIII. Immenfitas Divina extensionem mundi Infinitam non patitur. XXXIX. Divinæ Potentiæ infinitas, & liberrimum in rem creatam dominium, cum Infinita hujus extensione non consistit. XL. Denique , extensionis Infinitas inimica existit Divinæ Sapientiæ, Unitati , Incomprehenfibilitati, atque æternitati. XLI. Difficultas de spatiis imaginariis, quæ veram in suo conceptu involvant extenfionem, aufertur : XLII. Quamque ea fit inefficax, ad impugnandam finitam mundi extensionem, duplici instantiâ ostenditur. XLIII. Non qui mundi extensionem finitam cogitat , quicquam sentit de fe superbum , de Deo minus magnificum. XLIV. Non ad extensionem quamlibet finiendam aliud corpus ambiens cum Epicuro admittere neceffum est : XLV. Cum id corpori accidat , non qua simpliciter finito , sed qua parti Universi. XLVI. Omnipotentiæ Divinæ Immenfitas pro possibili extensione Infinita finita finita nil concludit. XLVII. Detegitur indè petita sophisticatio, non unà in hanc rem allatà infantiâ. XLVIII. Demonstrationis de extensione necessariò finita Porismata, Cartesianam Physicam subvertentia.
units.tr: XX. The question of the infinite extension of matter has consequences of the greatest reach. XXI. Epicurus openly acknowledges the infinite diffusion of the universe beyond all others. XXII. The agreement of the Cartesians, who posit whirlpools in an indefinite extension of the world, with the countless worlds of Epicurus in an infinite universe. XXIII. Descartes, like Epicurus, is bound to hold that the extension of the universe is truly infinite. XXIV. He labours in vain here to withdraw himself from this difficulty. XXV. Descartes' dissertation, in which he sets out his view on the infinite universe. XXVI. Other principal passages of his cited on the same matter. XXVII. The whole sum of the Cartesian philosophy, gathered under certain heads. XXVIII. That true infinity of extension is asserted by them is shown by one or two observations. XXIX. Descartes' distinction between the Infinite and the Indefinite removes none of the difficulty here. XXX. In what sense the extension of the world is to be affirmed as infinite, indefinite or finite. XXXI. It is shown that finite parts are not sufficient to constitute any infinite extension. XXXII. It is taught that parts infinite in number cannot be admitted in an infinite extension either. XXXIII. It is proved that an infinite extension cannot be composed of parts that are infinite in extension. XXXIV. Indeed it is demonstrated that not even parts infinite in the other respect can make up the whole extension as infinite. XXXV. From all of these it is concluded that no extended thing is, or can be, infinite on account of its own extension. XXXVI. The same is established from the nature of a corporeal thing and from several of its attributes, by many instances. XXXVII. The essence of God alone overturns the infinity of any infinite extension whatever. XXXVIII. The immensity of God does not allow the infinite extension of the world. XXXIX. The infinity of divine power and its most free dominion over created things do not agree with the infinity of this extension. XL. Finally, the infinity of extension is hostile to divine wisdom, unity, incomprehensibility and eternity. XLI. The difficulty about imaginary spaces, which in their concept involve a true extension, is removed. XLII. And it is shown by a double instance how ineffective that difficulty is for attacking the finite extension of the world. XLIII. He who thinks of the world's extension as finite feels nothing proud about himself and nothing less magnificent about God. XLIV. It is not necessary, with Epicurus, to admit some other body surrounding a given extension in order to bound it. XLV. Since this happens to a body not as simply finite, but as a part of the Universe. XLVI. The immensity of divine omnipotence concludes nothing about a finite extension, as against a possible infinite one. XLVII. The sophistry drawn from this is exposed, not the only childishness brought forward for this purpose. XLVIII. Corollaries of the demonstration that the extension is necessarily finite, overturning the Cartesian physics.

units.la: Ad rem ipsam progredior; in qua non minus, quam in ejusdem idea, graviter hallucinatum fuisse Cartesium, paucis ostendere constitui. Missis autem aliis, quæ plurima de Infinito disputari possunt, unam duntaxat, eamque longè præcipuam, excutere fert animus controversiam, de materia, sive extensione, infinita. Neque inutilis erit disquisitio, quum indè pendeant controversiæ vexatissimæ, quales sunt v. c. de Spatiis Imaginariis, de possibilitate plurium Mundorum, quæque iis sunt affines; imò & gravissimæ, disputationes de primæ causæ potentia & providentia circa hoc universum totum, atquè etiam plurimas ejus partes: de quibus omnibus aliter atque aliter statuendum est, prout mundi nostri extensionem vel finitæ quantitatis agnoscimus, vel infinitæ. Ut forsan vix alia exstat materia, quæ tantum consequentiarum syrma in re Theologica æquè ac Philosophica post sese trahit, quam hæc ipsa. Quæstionem quibus eam verbis vates Physicus Lib. 1. de Nat. Rer. proponit, & ipse proponam ego: Nunc age summam ecquenam sit finis eorum, Nec nesit, evolvamus: item, quod inane repertu 'st, Seu locus, ac spatium, res in quo quaeque genantur, Pervideamus, utrum finitum funditus omne Consistet; an immensum pateat vel adusque profundum.
units.tr: I now come to the matter itself, in which I intend to show briefly that Descartes went no less grievously astray than in his idea of the infinite. Setting aside the many other things that may be argued about the infinite, I am minded to examine only one question, and that by far the chief one: the question of infinite matter, or extension. Nor will this inquiry be useless, since on it hang the most troublesome controversies, such as those about imaginary spaces and the possibility of many worlds, and those akin to them; indeed also the most weighty disputes about the power and providence of the First Cause over this whole universe and very many of its parts. On all these matters we must judge one way or another, according as we acknowledge the extent of our world to be of finite quantity or of infinite. Perhaps there is scarcely any other subject that draws in its train so great a chain of consequences in theology as well as in philosophy as this one. The question the poet and natural philosopher puts in the first book of On the Nature of Things, I too will put in the same words: Now come, let us unroll the sum of the ends of things, and of what is not; and let us see whether the void, or place and space in which all things are carried on, is found to be wholly finite, or whether it lies open immeasurably and down to the depths.

units.la: Inter Antiquiores varii à variis recensentur, qui voluerint Mundum, aut saltem materiam ejus, infinitè extensam esse. Ità sensisse fertur Anaximander, Diogenes, aliique; qui tamen non eodem modo ac sensu mundi infinitatem explicuisse atque asseruisse videntur: sed hæc latè prosequi vix operæ pretium. Ex recentioribus Franciscus Patricius & Guiljelmus Gilbertus, capita portentosarum novitatum feracissima, mundum mole infinitum propugnarunt. In hæretico Hermogene, faciente materiam infinitam, jam olim opinionem hanc tanquam Orthodoxæ Fidei inimicam notavit gravissimus auctor Tertullianus. Quamvis autem Christianis doctoribus passim commentum hoc de materiae infinitate vehementer displicuerit, ipsumque cordatioribus etiam Gentilibus fuerit explosum, placuit tamen Cartesio illis omnibus, uti in Physicis saepius, ita quoque hac in parte praeferre Epicurum, quippe cujus opinio hypothesibus novae sapientiae mirum in modum exstitit congrua. Ipse Epicurus rotunde: Ἀλλὰ μὲν οὖν καὶ τὸ πᾶν ἄπειρόν ἐστι, apud Laert. Lib. x. Unde Cicero de Divinat. Lib. ii. Videsne Epicurum, quem hebetem & rudem dicere solent Stoici, quemadmodum quod in natura rerum Omne esse dicimus, id infinitum esse concluserit. Atqui idem, Lib. i. de Natura Deorum: Cujus operam profecto non desideraretis, ait Vellejus, si immensam & interminatam in omnes partes magnitudinem regionum videritis, in quam se injiciens animus & intendens, ita longe lateque peregrinatur, ut nullam tamen oram ultimi videat, in qua possit insistere. In hac igitur immensitate latitudinum, longitudinum, altitudinum, infinita vis innumerabilium volitat atomorum, &c. Contendit nimirum Epicurus, per infinitum Universi spatium ferri atomos infinitas, quae alibi atque alibi concurrentes, innumerabilia mundorum systemata constituerunt; isticenim mundum nasci voluit, ubicunque congrua atomorum congeries per proprias quasdam earundem convolutiones coaluit. Quae atomorum coagmentatio cum in infinito universo non potuerit non plurimis locis fieri, etiam non potuit non evenire, quin inde quoque innumerabilis mundorum multitudo in hoc universo extiterit. Quo pertinet illud notum Metrodori, Ἄλοπον εἶναι ἐν μεγάλῳ πεδίῳ ἕνα σπόρον γεννᾶσθαι, καὶ ἕνα κόσμον ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ: Absurdum esse in magno agro nasci unam spicam; & sic pariter absurdum esse in infinito unum nasci mundum. Sed Lucretium audiamus, rem omnem dilucide sub finem Lib. ii. De Nat. Rer. ita exsequentem: Principio nobis in cunctas undique partes, Et latere ex utroque, infra, supraque, per omne Nulla'st finis; uti docui, res ipsaque per se Vociferatur, & elucet natura profundi. Nullo jam pacto verisimile esse putandum est, (Cum quoquo versus spatium vacet infinitum, Seminaque innumero numero summaque profunda Multi modis volitent aeterno percita motu) Hunc unum terrarum orbem, coelumque creatum, Nil agere illa foris tot corpora materiai: Cum praesertim hic sit natura factus, & ipsaSponte sua forte offensando semina rerumMulti modis temere, incassum, frustraque coalta,Tandem coaluerint ea, quae conjecta repenteMagnarum rerum fierent exordia semper, Terrai, maris, & coeli, generisque animantum. Quare etiam atque etiam taleis fateare necesse estEsse alios alibi congressus materiai, Qualis hic est, avido complexu quem tenet aether. Praeterea, cum materies est multa parata, Cum locus est praesto, nec res nec causa moraturUlla, geni debent nimirum & confieri res. Etc.
units.tr: Among the ancients, various writers are recorded by various authorities as having held that the world, or at least its matter, is infinitely extended. Anaximander, Diogenes and others are said to have thought so; yet they seem not to have explained or asserted the infinity of the world in the same way or with the same meaning, but it is hardly worth the trouble to pursue these matters at length. Among more recent writers, Francesco Patrizi and William Gilbert, most fertile producers of monstrous novelties, have championed a world infinite in mass. Long ago the most weighty author Tertullian noted this opinion, in the heretic Hermogenes, who made matter infinite, as hostile to the Orthodox Faith. Although this fiction about the infinity of matter has commonly displeased Christian teachers strongly, and was rejected even by the more sensible among the Gentiles, Descartes nonetheless chose, as he often does in physics, to prefer Epicurus to all of them in this respect as well, since Epicurus' opinion fits wonderfully with the hypotheses of the new wisdom. Epicurus himself stated it plainly: "But indeed the whole is infinite" [Ἀλλὰ μὲν οὖν καὶ τὸ πᾶν ἄπειρόν ἐστι], as reported in Laertius, Book x. Hence Cicero, On Divination, Book ii: "Do you see that Epicurus, whom the Stoics are accustomed to call dull and crude, concluded that what we say is in the nature of things is infinite?" And yet the same man, in Book i of On the Nature of the Gods, says through Velleius: "You would surely not need his labour, if you saw the immense and boundless magnitude of regions in every direction, into which the mind, throwing itself and straining forward, wanders so far and wide that it nonetheless sees no edge at which it might stand. In this immensity of breadths, lengths and heights, an infinite host of innumerable atoms flits about," etc. Epicurus, of course, maintained that infinitely many atoms are carried through the infinite extent of the Universe, and, meeting here and there, they constitute innumerable systems of worlds; for he held that a world is born wherever a suitable collection of atoms has come together by certain proper convolutions of its own. Since such a coming-together of atoms could not fail to happen in many places in an infinite universe, it also could not fail to come about that an innumerable multitude of worlds should exist in this universe. To this belongs the well-known saying of Metrodorus: "It is absurd that in a great field one ear of corn should be born, and so likewise absurd that in the infinite one world should be born" [Ἄλοπον εἶναι ἐν μεγάλῳ πεδίῳ ἕνα σπόρον γεννᾶσθαι, καὶ ἕνα κόσμον ἐν τῷ ἀπείρῳ: Absurdum esse in magno agro nasci unam spicam; & sic pariter absurdum esse in infinito unum nasci mundum.]. But let us hear Lucretius, who sets out the whole matter clearly near the end of Book ii of On the Nature of Things: "First, on every side, in all directions, both on the sides and below and above, through the whole, there is no end, as I have taught; and the thing itself by its own nature cries out, and the nature of the deep shows itself. Now in no way is it to be thought probable that, since space lies empty without limit in every direction, and seeds in countless number and in unfathomable sum are flying about, driven by eternal motion in many ways, this one orb of earth and heaven was created, and that those so many bodies of matter do nothing outside it; especially since it was made by nature, and the seeds of things, colliding of their own accord by chance in many ways, to no purpose and in vain, at last came together, so that such things as, being suddenly thrown together, would always become the beginnings of great things, of land, sea and sky, and of the race of living creatures. Therefore, again and again, you must admit that there are elsewhere other gatherings of matter like this one, which the air holds in its eager embrace. Moreover, since matter is abundantly ready, since there is room, and since nothing and no cause stands in the way, things must necessarily be made and come to be." Etc.

units.la: Non piguit Poëtæ textum pleniorem exhibere, quo & mentem Epicuri assequamur rectius, & intelligamus simul, cui sapientiæ nova Physica suas debeat hypotheses. Mirum enim, quam concinnè hunc infinitorum mundorum in universo infinito exortum Epicurcum referat vorticum innumerabilium in indefinita Universi extensione naturæ genesis Cartesiana. Ut istic audis ex alio & alio atomorum in diversa infiniti hujus universi loca concursu genitos esse complures Mundos; ita hic supponitur materiam hujus Universi, in qua nullos extensionis limites agnoscunt, divisam fuisse in particulas fermè æquales, & magnitudine mediocres, quæ circa centra sua circumactæ constituerunt vortices ut vastissimos, ita innumeros: in quibus corpora stellarum, tum fixarum, tum planetarum, quos inter numeranda nostra Tellus, quæque in iis dantur res naturales, originem traxerint ex solo confluxu & cohæsione particularum tantùm ratione magnitudinis, figuræ, situs atquè motus diversarum. Vide Cartesii Princip. Lib. III. §. XLVI. & seqq. Item, Lib. IV. ab initio. Et re verà ipsissimos infinitos in infinito universo Epicuri mundos in Cartesiana hypothesi, si propius attendamus, renatos videbimus: cum vortices Cartesianos inter & mundos Epicureos quantum hactenus interfit discriminis? non videam. Ecquid enim aliud mundorum nomine intellexisse Epicurum credamus, quam plura systemata planetaria, nostro huic in quo nos degimus in plerisque similia ? At verò ex hypothesibus Cartesianis vix evenire potuit aliter, quam ut quilibet vortex hujus universi, uti suum meditullium habet proprium Solem, itâ suis quoque gaudeat Planetis, ipsisque etiam Terris; ad instar vorticis hujus, in quo nos terricolæ circa solem nostrum oberramus. Neque multum aberit hæc sententia ab opinione quam alibi Plutarchus tribuit Heraclidi & Pythagoreis, qui senserint innumeras stellas per universi immensitatem dispersas totidem exister mundos.
units.tr: It is no trouble to give the poet's text in fuller form, so that we may grasp Epicurus' mind more correctly, and at the same time understand what wisdom the new Physics owes its hypotheses to. For it is remarkable how neatly the Cartesian genesis of nature in the indefinite extension of the universe reproduces this Epicurean rise of infinite worlds in the infinite universe, namely of countless vortices. As you hear there that many worlds were born from the concourse of atoms in various places of this infinite universe, so here it is supposed that the matter of this universe, in which they recognise no limits of extension, was divided into particles nearly equal and of moderate size, which, turned about their own centres, constituted vortices, as vast as they are innumerable. In these the bodies of the stars, both fixed and planetary (among which our Earth must be counted), and whatever natural things are found in them, have drawn their origin from the mere confluence and cohesion of particles differing only in size, shape, position and motion. See Descartes, Principles, Book III, §46 and following. Likewise Book IV, from the beginning. And indeed, if we attend more closely, we shall see the very infinite worlds of Epicurus in infinite universe reborn in the Cartesian hypothesis. What difference, so far as I can see, is there between the Cartesian vortices and the Epicurean worlds? For what else can we believe Epicurus meant by worlds, than many planetary systems, in most respects like this one in which we live? Indeed, from the Cartesian hypotheses it could hardly come about otherwise than that each vortex of this universe, just as it has its own Sun at its centre, so also enjoys its own planets and even its own Earths, like this vortex in which we earth-dwellers wander about our sun. Nor will this opinion differ much from the view which Plutarch elsewhere attributes to Heraclides and the Pythagoreans, who held that the countless stars scattered through the immensity of the universe are as many worlds.

units.la: {}Egregiam verò laudem merentur, qui deliramenta istiusmodi, sapientibus quibusvis, Gentilibus pariter ac Christianis, dudùm explosa, & jam silentio ac contemptu sepulta, in lucem revocant, & orbi literato novo habitu aucta & ornata proponunt. Etenim quamvis multa sua habeat Cartesius, in quibus conspicua est ejus ab Epicuro dividia, in hoc tamen tertium (ut alia, quæ hujus loci non sunt, taceam plurima) prorsùs consentit utraque hypothesis, quod absque Universi extensione infinita nec ista nec hæc consistat. Uti enim jam olim ex mente Epicuri cecinit Lucretius, Lib. I.
units.tr: Truly they deserve great praise who recall to light such follies, long since exploded by all wise men, Gentile and Christian alike, and buried in silence and contempt, and set them before the literary world, renewed in a new dress and adorned. For although Descartes has many doctrines of his own, in which his departure from Epicurus is evident, yet in this third point (to pass over many others which do not belong to this place) both hypotheses wholly agree: that neither of them can stand without the infinite extension of the universe. For as Lucretius long ago sang, in the mind of Epicurus, in Book I:

units.la: Ante etiam alterutrum nisi terminet alterum eorum, Simplice & natura patet Totum immoderatum, Nec mare, nec tellus, nec cœli lucida templa, Nec mortale genus, nec Divum corpora sanctaExiguum possent horai sistere tempus. Nam dispulsa suo de coetu materiaiCopia ferretur magnum per inane soluta: Sive adeo potius nunquam concreta creassetUllam rem, quoniam cogi disperso nequisset.
units.tr: Unless the one of them bounds the other, the whole is plainly immeasurable in its nature: neither sea, nor earth, nor the bright temples of heaven, nor the mortal race, nor the holy bodies of the gods could endure even for a brief hour. For the scattered store of matter would be carried off and dissolved through the great void; or rather it would never have created any thing joined together, since it could not have been gathered from a dispersed state.

units.la: Uti, inquam, hisce arguit Lucretius, nisi Universum sit infinitum, fore, ut dissipatæ atomi æternùm ferantur, neque compositionem ullam faciant; itaque rectè Cartesium monuit H. Morus, Lib. I. Epist. LXVI. debere ex ejus hypothesibus Universi expansionem statui infinitam, quia, hoc nisi supponatur, materia, ait, tuorum vorticum à centris suis recedet, totaque mundi machina in dissipatas atomos vagosque abibit pulviSculos.
units.tr: As Lucretius argues from these things, I say, unless the universe is infinite, the dissipated atoms will be carried on forever and will make no composition at all. So H.
