More rightly warned Descartes, Book I, Letter LXVI, that from his hypotheses the expansion of the universe must be held to be infinite, because, unless this is supposed, "the matter of your vortices," he says, "will recede from their centres, and the whole machine of the world will go off into dissipated atoms and wandering dust."

units.la: {}Cum itaquè sit manifestum, absque infinita materiæ extensione, non magis consistere posse Cartesii mundum vorticosum, quam Epicuri universum atomicum, frustrà sunt, nimiumque fibiipfis adversi Recentiores, quandò difficiles adeò existunt in exponenda sua sententia de vera universi infinitate; quæ negari nequit, nisi simul convellatur unicum & præ cæteris necessarium novæ Physicæ fundamentum. Neutiquam verò hic sese exsolvit Cartesius, quando respondet Moro: Cum dico, extensionem materiæ esse indefinitam, sufficere hoc puto, ad impediendum nequis extra illam locus fingi queat, in quem meorum vorticum particulæ abire possint. Ubicunque enim locus ille concipiatur, ibijam, juxta meam hypothesin, aliqua materia est; quia dicendo eam esse indefinite extensam, dico ipsam latius extendi quam omne id quod ab homine concipi potest. Non, inquam, sic sese exsolvit satis Cartesius. Si enim aliquis re ipsâ sit inter vortices ultimus (eum tanquam talem an concipias, nec ne, parum refert) utique partes hujus dissilient, & à centro, secundum regulas motus, necessariò recedent; quod ne admittere cogaris, necesse omninò est ut vorticem quemcunque alio vortice re ipsa existente cingi statuas, nullusque adeò admittatur in hoc Universo verè extremus. Quod aliud nihil est quam ipso facto Universum asserere infinitum. Nequaquam hæc ignorasse opinor Cartesium. Verùm, cum facilè videret, quot & quantis se difficultatibus involveret, si aperte sibi sumeret defendendam extensionem mundi infinitam, eam non palam profiteri, sed crudum dogma palliare, prudenter maluit, quæsito effugio in voce Indefiniti, in qua mirè ludit. Saltem declinandum sibi hoc argumentum duxit, quo usque potuit: quod ipsum quoque profitentem mox audiemus. Quicquid fuerit, quidnam hypothesibus suis de vorticibus convenienter Cartesius sentire debuerit de vera universi ratione extensionis infinitate, satis quæ jam diximus docent.
units.tr: Since therefore it is clear that, without the infinite extension of matter, the Cartesian vortical world can no more stand than the Epicurean atomic universe, the more recent writers are vainly and too much at odds with themselves, when they are so difficult in setting out their opinion on the true infinity of the universe; which cannot be denied unless at the same time the one and most necessary foundation of the new Physics is overthrown. But by no means does Descartes extricate himself here, when he answers More: "When I say that the extension of matter is indefinite, I think this is enough to prevent any place from being imagined outside it into which the particles of my vortices could pass. For wherever that place is conceived, there, according to my hypothesis, some matter already is; because in saying that it is indefinitely extended, I say that it extends more widely than anything that man can conceive." No, I say, Descartes does not extricate himself sufficiently in this way. For if there really is some last vortex among the vortices (whether you conceive it as such or not matters little), then surely its parts will fly apart and, by the rules of motion, will necessarily recede from the centre; and lest you be forced to admit this, you must necessarily suppose that any vortex whatever is surrounded by another vortex actually existing, and so no vortex at all is admitted in this universe to be truly outermost. This is nothing other than to assert, by the very fact, that the universe is infinite. I do not suppose Descartes was ignorant of these things. But since he easily saw how many and how great difficulties he would involve himself in, if he openly undertook to defend the infinite extension of the world, he preferred not to profess it openly but to dress up his bare dogma, and wisely sought an escape in the word "indefinite," in which he plays cleverly. At least he judged that this argument should be avoided as far as he could manage; which we shall soon hear him admitting himself. Whatever the case, what Descartes ought consistently to have thought, given his hypotheses about vortices, concerning the true nature of the universe's infinite extension, what we have already said sufficiently shows.

units.la: XXV. Cartesii dissertatio, quâ suam aperit de infinita universi materia sententiam.
units.tr: XXV. Descartes's dissertation, in which he sets out his opinion on the infinite matter of the universe.

units.la: Verumtamen, cum, ut Cartesius ipse, itâ quoque Cartesiani adeò hac parte sint varii & inconstantes, ut nullibi magis (itâ ajunt, negant, dubitant, nesciunt) ipsique passim conquerantur de calumnia quâ Cartesio affingantur opiniones à mente ejus alienæ, age! de Infinita mundi extensione quid ipse docuerit, videamus! Fusè imprimis hac de re agit, Lib. 1. Epist. xxxvi. Totus istic loci est in hac dissertatione, diluituros objectiones, quas Regina Suecia Christina proposuerat in eam, quam ipse mundo tribuit, diffusionem. Dabo integrum textum: nam dedisse operæ pretium erit. Quicquid, ait, in hoc argumento noverim conabor hic exponere. Primo memini Cardinalem Cusanum, Doctoresque alios plurimos supposuisse mundum infinitum, neque tamen propterea ab ecclesia unquam fuisse correptos: contra videtur ad Dei cultum pertinere ut ejus opera amplissima censeantur; meaque, quam illorum sententia, commodius admitti posset, quia non dico mundum esse infinitum, sed tantum indefinitum. Quae quidem duo inter se haud parum differunt: ad hoc enim ut quis dicat infinitum quid esse, ratione aliqua niti debet, qua probet rem ita se habere, quod de Deo tantum probari potest; sed ad hoc ut dicam esse quid indefinitum, satis est si nulla sit ratio, qua probari possit id esse finitum. Mihi autem videtur probari non posse, imo neque concipi, ullos esse fines materiae ex qua constat universus orbis. Cum enim materiae hujus naturam perscrutor, invenio, positam esse totam in eo, quod extensa sit secundum longitudinem, latitudinem, & profunditatem; ita ut quicquid praeditum est tribus hisce dimensionibus, sit materiae hujus pars. Neque vero potest spatium ullum dari omnino vacuum, hoc est, quod nullam contineat materiam, quia tale spatium concipere nequimus, quin tres hasce in illo dimensiones, & proinde materiam concipiamus. Mundum autem finitum supponendo, concipiuntur ultra ejus fines spatia quaedam tribus hisce dimensionibus prædita, & proinde non pure imaginaria, quæ Philosophi vocant, sed continentia in se materiam; quæ cum alibi esse nequeat, quam in mundo, liquet mundum extra fines ipsi præscriptos extendi. Cum ergo rationem nullam noverim, quà probem, imo neque concipere queam, mundi fines ullos esse, illum indefinitum voco; sed negare tamen nequeo, illius forsan fines aliquos esse Deo notos, licet illis comprehendendis impar sim: quare non dico absolute esse infinitum. Quæ de Cusano Cardinale, deque Ecclesia Romana sententiam de infinito mundo non corripiente, hic narrat Cartesius, unde habuerit, facile erit colligere inspicienti Lib. 11. Epist. cv. ubi sic suo Mersenno: Quæso rescribe mihi, an de extensione mundi quicquam fuerit in fide definitum, utrum nempe sit finitus, an vero potius infinitus; atque, utrum spatia illa, quæ vocant imaginaria, sint corpora creata & vera: nam, licet non erat animus hanc quæstionem movere, tamen puto invito mihi tractandam fore.
units.tr: However, since the Cartesians themselves are as varied and inconsistent on this point as Descartes was, so that nowhere do they more often affirm, deny, doubt and profess ignorance (as they say), and since they often complain that opinions alien to his mind are fastened upon Descartes by slander, come, let us see what he himself taught about the infinite extension of the universe! He treats this matter at length, Book 1, Letter xxxvi. The whole of that passage is devoted to answering the objections which Queen Christina of Sweden had raised against the extension which he attributes to the world. I shall give the full text, for it will be worth the effort: Whatever I have learned on this subject I will try to set out here. First, I recall that Cardinal Cusanus and many other teachers have supposed the world to be infinite, and yet they were never on that account rebuked by the Church. On the contrary, it seems to belong to the worship of God that his works be judged very ample; and my opinion can be admitted more conveniently than theirs, because I do not say the world is infinite, but only indefinite. These two things differ not a little from each other: for in order that someone may call something infinite, he must rest on some reason by which he proves that the thing is so, which can be proved only of God; but in order that I may say something is indefinite, it is enough if there is no reason by which it can be proved to be finite. Now it seems to me that it cannot be proved, nor even conceived, that there are any limits to the matter of which the universe is made. For when I examine the nature of this matter, I find that it consists wholly in this, that it is extended in length, breadth and depth; so that whatever has these three dimensions is a part of this matter. Nor can any space be given that is entirely empty, that is, that contains no matter, because we cannot conceive such a space without conceiving in it these three dimensions, and therefore matter. But when we suppose the world to be finite, there are conceived beyond its limits certain spaces endowed with these three dimensions and therefore not purely imaginary, as the philosophers call them, but containing matter in themselves; and since this matter can be nowhere else than in the world, it is clear that the world extends beyond the limits prescribed for it. Since therefore I know no reason by which I can prove, nor even conceive, that the world has any limits, I call it indefinite; yet I cannot deny that perhaps some limits of it are known to God, although I am unequal to comprehending them: therefore I do not say that it is absolutely infinite. How Descartes came by what he relates here, concerning Cardinal Cusanus and the Roman Church not censuring the opinion of an infinite world, will be easy to gather for anyone who looks at Book 2, Letter cv., where he writes thus to his Mersenne: Please write back to me whether anything has been defined in the faith about the extension of the world, whether it is finite or rather infinite; and whether those spaces which they call imaginary are created and true bodies: for although I had no intention of raising this question, I think I shall be forced to deal with it against my will.
XXVI.

units.la: Cæterum, etiam cum H. Moro prolixa fuit Cartesio de Infinita Mundi extensione concertatio. Summa hùc redit. Objecerat Mo-
units.tr: Moreover, Descartes also had a lengthy dispute with H. More about the infinite extension of the world. The gist of it comes to this. More had objected:

units.la: Morus : Indefinitam tuam mundi extensionem non intelligo. Extensio enim illa indefinita , vel simpliciter infinita est , vel tantum quoad nos. Si intelligis extensionem infinitam simpliciter, cur mentem tuam obscuras vocabulis nimium suppressis ac modestis ? Si tantum quoad nos infinitam, re vera erit finita extensio; neque enim mens nostra aut rerum aut veritatis mensura est. Ac proinde materia tuorum vorticum à centris suis recedet, &c. Respondet Cartefius, Epift. lxvii. Lib. i. Neque vero affectata modestia est , sed cautela , meo judicio, necessaria , quod quaedam dicam esse indefinita potius quam infinita ; solus enim Deus est quem positive intelligo esse infinitum : de reliquis , ut de mundi extensione , de numero partium in quas materia est divisibilis , & similibus an sint simpliciter infinita, nec ne, me profiteor nescire, scio tantum me in illis nullum finem agnoscere . atque idcirco respectu mei dico esse indefinita. Quumquè instaret Morus : Haud tamen latere te potest, quin sint vel simpliciter infinita , vel re vera finita; quamvis utrum horum sint, tam facile statuere non possis. Quod autem vortices tui non diffrumpantur & fatisfcant, non obscurum videtur indicium , Mundum re vera esse infinitum. Etc. Ista, inquam, quum iterato urgeret Morus, clarius fe explicat Cartefius, & confidentius loquitur, Epift. lxix. his verbis: Repugnat conceptui meo , five , quod idem est, puto implicare contradictionem, ut mundus fit finitus vel terminatus , quia non possum non concipere spatium ultra quoslibet praefuppofitos mundi fines; tale autem spatium apud me est verum corpus : nec moror quod ab aliis imaginarium vocetur , & ideo mundus finitus existimetur; novi enim ex quibus praejudiciis error iste profectus fit. Quibus convenienter itâ , Princip. Part. iii. §. i. 2. De mundi aspectabilis constructione ut rectè philosophemur , duo sunt imprimis observanda. Unum, ut attendentes ad infinitam Dei potentiam & bonitatem, ne vereamur nimis ampla , & pulchra, & absoluta ejus opera imaginari : sed e contrario caveamus, nisi quos forte limites , nobis non certo cognitos, in ipsis supponamus , non satis magnifice de Creatoris potentia sentire videamur. Alterum , ut etiam caveamus, ne nimis superbe de nobis ipsis sentiamus. Quod fieret non modo, si quos limites, nobis nulla cognitos ratione , nec divina revelatione , mundo vellemus affingere , tanquam si vis nostra cogitationis, ultra id quod à Deo re vera factum est, ferri posset ; sed, &c. Adde quae extant Ibid. Part. ii. §. 21. 22. Cognoscimus praeterea hunc mundum , sive substantiae corporeae universitatem, nullos extensionis suae fines habere. Ubicunque enim fines illos esse fingamus, semper ultra ipsos aliqua spatia indefinite extensa, non modo imaginamur, sed etiam vere imaginabilia, hoc est, realia, esse percipimus; ac proinde etiam substantiam corpoream indefinite extensam in iis contineri. Hincque etiam colligi facile potest ..... non plures mundos, sed unum tantum, esse posse: quia perspicue intelligimus, illam materiam, cujus natura in eo solo consistit quod sit substantia extensa, omnia omnino spatia imaginabilia, in quibus alii isti mundi esse deberent, jam occupare. Nec denique praeteriri debet insignitè huc pertinens locus, ex Lib. 1. Epist. xxxv. Si insuper attendamus ad infinitudinem potentiae ejus (Dei) per quam tam multa crevit, quorum pars summus minima ....... denique hinc tenuitatem nostram, inde rerum omnium creatarum magnitudinem perpendendo, & qua ratione ille a Deo pendeant, illaque modo potentiae ejus congruo aestimando, non vero pyxide veluti quadam concludendo (quod ii faciunt qui volunt mundum esse finitum) harum omnium rerum meditatio, &c.
units.tr: More: I do not understand your indefinite extension of the world. For that extension is either simply infinite, or infinite only in relation to us. If you mean an extension simply infinite, why do you obscure your meaning with such suppressed and modest words? If it is infinite only in relation to us, the extension will in fact be finite; for our mind is the measure neither of things nor of truth. And accordingly the matter of your vortices will recede from their centres, etc. Descartes replies, Letter lxvii, Book 1: Nor is this affected modesty, but, in my judgement, a necessary caution, because I say that some things are indefinite rather than infinite; for God alone is the one I positively understand to be infinite. As for the rest, such as the extension of the world, the number of parts into which matter is divisible, and similar things, whether they are simply infinite or not, I confess I do not know; I know only that in them I recognise no end; and for that reason I say, with respect to myself, that they are indefinite. When More pressed the point, You cannot fail to see that they are either simply infinite or really finite, although you cannot easily determine which of these they are. But that your vortices do not burst apart and fall to pieces seems to be an obscure indication that the world is really infinite, etc. When More urged these things again, Descartes explained himself more clearly and spoke more confidently, Letter lxix, in these words: It is repugnant to my conception, or, which is the same, I think it implies a contradiction, that the world should be finite or bounded, because I cannot help conceiving a space beyond any limits of the world that may be supposed; and such a space, in my mind, is a true body. Nor do I mind that others call it imaginary and so think the world finite; for I know from what prejudices that error has arisen. In agreement with these things he says, Principles, Part 3, §§ 1–2: In order to philosophise rightly about the construction of the visible world, two things must above all be observed. The first is that, attending to the infinite power and goodness of God, we should not be afraid to imagine his works very ample, beautiful and perfect; but on the contrary we should take care not to seem to think too meanly of the power of the Creator, unless we suppose some limits in them which we do not know for certain. The second is that we should also take care not to think too proudly of ourselves. This would happen not only if we wished to attribute to the world some limits, known to us by no reason, nor by divine revelation, as if the power of our thought could be carried beyond what God has in fact made; but, etc. Add what is found in the same Part 2, §§ 21–22: Moreover we recognise that this world, or the whole of corporeal substance, has no limits to its extension. For wherever we pretend that those limits are, we perceive that beyond them there always are spaces indefinitely extended, which we not only imagine but also perceive to be truly imaginable, that is, real; and accordingly we perceive that corporeal substance indefinitely extended is contained in them as well. And from this it can also easily be gathered ..... that there can be not many worlds, but only one; because we clearly understand that that matter, whose nature consists solely in this, that it is extended substance, already occupies all the imaginable spaces in which other such worlds would have to be. Finally, the passage bearing notably on this point must not be passed over, from Book 1, Letter xxxv: If we further consider the infinitude of his power (God's), by which so many things have grown, of which the smallest part is the greatest ....... finally, weighing on the one hand our own littleness, and on the other the greatness of all created things, and how they depend on God, and estimating them by the mode of his power that is fitting, not concluding them as if in some little box (which is what those do who want the world to be finite), the meditation on all these things, etc.

units.la: Atque ista, si non omnia, pleraque saltem sunt & praecipua, quae de mundo, ejusve materia sive extensione, Finita, & Infinita, extant in scriptis Cartesii. Juvat quae istic sparsa jacent in ordinem cogere, & ad quaedam capita revocare universam rei summam: neque erit opinor, cui amplius de mente Viri superesse queat dubium. I. Animum non fuisse, ait, hanc quaestionem movere; sed invito sibi tractandam fore. Gravem profecto causam fuisse oportet, ob quam invitus trahatur ad tractandam rem, ad quam expediendam sponte potius advolare debuisset; cum citra infinitam extensionem vorticosam mundi structuram non consistere, jam observaverimus. II. Anxie percunctatur, numquid de mundi extensione, finita an infinita, in fide fuerit definitum? Innuens sic satis, in quam sententiam animus inclinaret; de finito enim mundo opinionem, ut pervulgatam & ubique receptam, ita fide nunquam fuisse damnatam, qui nesciat nemo est. III. De indefinito interim mundo, an quid ab Ecclesia sit definitum, nihil istic inquirit. Deinceps ergo demum incidit de indefinito cogitatio; ut sua scilicet, quam illorum qui mundum esse infinitum dicunt, sententia commodius admitti posset. IV. Caeterum asserit, sibi videri, probari non posse, imo neque concipi, ullos esse fines mamaterie, ex qua constat universus orbis ; nec rationem ullam novisse, quâ probet, imò vel concipere quεat, mundi fines nullos esse. v. Excusat opinionem supponentem mundum infinitum, quod non meminerit, propterea Cardinalem Cusanum, Doctoresque alios, ab Ecclesia unquam fuisse correptos. vi. Quin contrà commendat hanc sententiam : quod videatur ad Dei cultum pertinere, ut ejus opera amplissima censeantur. vii. Tam ampla videlicet, ut rerum creatarum magnitudinem potentia divinæ infinitudini congruè æstimemus. viii. Quod non faciant, qui volunt mundum esse finitum ; quippe qui pyxide veluti quâdam eum concludunt. ix. Quinque adeò non magnificè satis de Creatoris potentia sentire videntur; quando limites quos, non certo cognitos, in Dei operibus supponunt. x. Quales superbè nimis de se ipsis sentiant ; dum limites, nullà cognitos ratione vel revelatione, mundo volunt affingere. xi. Cum vis nostræ cogitationis ultra id quod à Deo re verâ factum est, ferri nequeat. xii. Ut morandum hic non sit spatium imaginarium ; quia quod spatium ultra quoslibet præsuppositos mundi fines concipimus, verum corpus est ; quoniam in eo substantia corporea indefinitè extensa continetur. xiii. Utque error sit, ex præjudiciis profectus, id imaginarium vocare, & ideò mundum finitum existimare. xiv. Quoniam dari non potest aut concipi spatium ullum omninò vacuum, hoc est, quod nullam contineat materiam. xv. Ut hinc facilè colligi possit, non plures mundos, sed unum tantùm, esse posse. xvi. Quia nempè perspicuè intelligimus, materiam hujus universi omnia omninò spatia imaginabilia, in quibus alii mundi esse deberent, jam occupare. xvii. Ut tandem cognoscamus, hunc mundum, sive substantiæ corporeæ universitatem, nullos extensionis suæ fines habere. xviii. Repugnetque conceptui, sive, quod idem est, implicet contradictionem, ut mundus sit finitus vel terminatus.
units.tr: Although these are not all, they are at least most and the chief points that Descartes has written about the world, or its matter or extension, finite and infinite. It helps to gather what lies scattered here into order and reduce the whole matter to certain heads. I think no one could have any further doubt about the man's mind. I. He says that he did not intend to raise this question, but it will have to be handled against his will. There must surely have been a grave reason why he is unwillingly drawn into treating a matter which he ought rather to have hastened to explain of his own accord, since we have already observed that the vortical structure of the world does not stand without an infinite extension. II. He anxiously asks whether it has been defined in the faith that the extension of the world is finite or infinite. In this he sufficiently hints in which direction his mind inclines. For no one is ignorant that the opinion of a finite world, as commonly held and received everywhere, has never been condemned by the faith. III. Meanwhile, he inquires nothing here about the indefinite world, whether the Church has defined anything about it. Only then does the thought of the indefinite come in, namely that his own opinion, that of those who say the world is infinite, could more conveniently be admitted. IV. Moreover, he asserts that it seems to him that it cannot be proved, indeed not even conceived, that there are any limits of the matter from which the whole universe consists; nor does he know any reason by which he could prove, or even conceive, that the world has no limits. V. He excuses the opinion that supposes the world infinite, because he does not recall that on this account Cardinal Cusanus and other teachers were ever rebuked by the Church. VI. Indeed, on the contrary, he commends this opinion, because it seems to pertain to the worship of God that his works be judged most ample. VII. Ample indeed, so that we may fitly estimate the greatness of created things by the infinitude of divine power. VIII. Those who want the world to be finite do not do this, since they enclose it as if with a certain box. IX. Indeed, they seem not to think magnificently enough of the power of the Creator, when they suppose limits in God's works not known for certain. X. Such men think too proudly of themselves, while they wish to attach to the world limits known by no reason or revelation. XI. Since the power of our thought cannot be carried beyond what has truly been made by God. XII. So we need not linger here over imaginary space, because the space that we conceive beyond any supposed limits of the world is a true body, since corporeal substance indefinitely extended is contained in it. XIII. And it is an error, arising from prejudices, to call it imaginary and therefore to judge the world finite. XIV. Since no space at all can be given or conceived entirely empty, that is, one containing no matter. XV. From this it can easily be gathered that not several worlds, but only one, can exist. XVI. For we clearly understand that the matter of this universe already occupies all the imaginable spaces in which other worlds would have to be. XVII. So at last we recognise that this world, or the totality of corporeal substance, has no limits to its extension. XVIII. And it is repugnant to the concept, or, what is the same, implies a contradiction, that the world be finite or bounded.

units.la: Talia cui exciderunt, non semel, non aliud agenti, is quo pacto mundum non re verâ habuerit extensione infinitum ? ego quidem non video. Cæteris quidem admiscet, fateor, molliora quædam, v. c. cum se nescire profitetur, an mundi extensio sit simpliciter finita, nec ne ; scire tantum, se in illa nullum finem agnoscere; negare se non posse, illinc forsan fines aliquos esse Deo notos ; &c. Verum ista similiaque merito referenda esse ad vocabula nimium suppressa & modesta, quibus mentem suam obscurare nititur, facilè credat cum Moro, quisquis eorum quæ hic exhibuimus continuum filum atque universæ cogitationis Cartesianæ non interruptam seriem, quam dedimus, vel leviter attenderit. Saltem, quicunque etiam cæteris quæratur color, in quemcunque verba deflectantur sensum, tres postremi à nobis notati articuli tantæ sunt in hoc negotio evidentiæ, ut quàvis exceptione exístant majores. Certè qui asserit, alios mundos esse non posse, eo quod intelligat perspicuè, materiam hujus nostri omnia spatia, in quibus alii esse deberent, jam occupare, qua obscuro ratione illi dubium esse potest, num ipso facto infinitum sit nostrum universum? Hoc enim qui se nescire profitetur, quo fundamento ponit se perspicuè intelligere, omnia spatia in quibus alii mundi esse deberent jam occupari ab hoc nostro. Si enim sint forsan fines quidam Deo noti, nec id negare queas; qui potes negare Deum forsan extra illos aliquid creare posse? En, ut pelluceat artificium! Sed & quid clarius isto: Cognoscimus, hunc mundum nullos extensionis sua fines habere? Non ait negativè, Non cognoscimus, ullos fines mundum habere, quod potuisset videri magis pertinere ad cognitionis imperfectionem, quam ad rei cognitæ actualem infinitatem: verum exertim & positivè inquit, cognoscimus, nullos habere mundum fines. Imprimis verò quid dici poterat hic plenius & planius, quam: Puto implicare contradictionem, ut mundus sit finitus vel terminatus? An verò credemus, aliquem sanæ mentis id à se impetrare posse, ut dubium id habeat, num sit nec ne, quod ipsum putat implicare contradictionem. Adde expressimis hisce Cartesii effatis consentire, ut jam antè notavimus, hypothesin ejusdem de mundo vorticoso, cui omnis recentior physica inædificata existit; quaque salvari nullâ ratione potest, nisi Universi extensio supponatur actu infinita. Quæ cum ità sint, judicium penes lectorem esto, num tantas habeant Cartesiani causas conquerendi, suam Philosophiam opinione de mundi extensione actu infinita iniquè gravari?
units.tr: To one who has let such things slip, not once and not while doing something else, how could it be that the world is not in fact infinite in extension? I for one do not see how. He does mix in, I admit, some softer statements, for example when he professes that he does not know whether the extension of the world is simply finite or not; he only knows that he recognises no end in it; he cannot deny that perhaps some limits are known to God; and so on. But these and similar things should rightly be referred to words too much suppressed and modest, by which he strives to obscure his mind. Whoever has glanced even lightly at the continuous thread of what we have set out here, and at the uninterrupted sequence of the whole Cartesian line of thought that we have given, will easily believe with More. In any case, whatever colour is sought for him, and whatever sense his words are bent to, the last three articles that we have noted are of such clarity in this business that they outweigh any exception. Certainly, one who asserts that other worlds cannot exist, because he clearly understands that the matter of our world already occupies all the spaces in which others would have to be, by what obscure reasoning can he doubt whether our universe is infinite by the very fact? For he who professes that he does not know on what ground he clearly understands that all the spaces in which other worlds would have to be are already occupied by this one of ours? For if there are perhaps certain limits known to God, and you cannot deny it, how can you deny that God can perhaps create something beyond them? See how the artifice shines through! But what is clearer than this: We recognise that this world has no limits to its extension? He does not say negatively, We do not recognise that the world has any limits, which might have seemed to pertain more to imperfection of knowledge than to the actual infinity of the thing known. Rather, he says plainly and positively, we recognise that the world has no limits. Above all, what could be said more fully and plainly here than: I think it implies a contradiction that the world be finite or bounded? Or shall we believe that anyone of sound mind could bring himself to be in doubt whether it is or is not so, when he himself thinks it implies a contradiction? Add that, as we noted earlier, Descartes' hypothesis of the vortical world agrees with these most explicit sayings of his, and on it all the more recent physics is built; and it cannot be saved in any way unless the extension of the universe is supposed to be actually infinite. Since these things stand so, let the reader judge whether the Cartesians have such cause to complain that their philosophy is unjustly burdened by the opinion of an actually infinite extension of the world.

units.la: Nos quod attinet, ne hisce quidem litigiis inhærere necesse habemus, quandoquidem Dissertationi huic nostræ sat amplum campum aperit materia hujus Universi, si non Infinita, Indefinita saltem: in qua distinctione cum mirum in modum sibi placeat Cartesius, quid illi inter duo ista discriminis intercedat, videndum est paulò accuratius. Textum Auctoris, quo hac de re disserit, dedimus §. xxv. ex Epist xxxvi. Lib. i. Addam illi verba clara & perspicua, quæ occurrunt Reponf. prim. p. 59. Et quidem, ait, hic distinguo inter indefinitum & infinitum, illudque tantum proprie infinitum appello, in quo nulla ex parte limites inveniuntur; quo sensu solus Deus est infinitus: illa autem in quibus sub aliqua tantum ratione finem non agnosco, ut extensio spatii imaginarii, multitudo numerorum, divisibilitas partium quantitatis, & similia, indefinita quidem appello, non autem infinita, quia non omni ex parte fine carent. Ex quibus liquet, duas ob causas Cartesium maluisse mundum hunc appellare indefinitum, quam infinitum: Primùm, quia id tantum vult proprie dici Infinitum, quod ratione aliquâ probetur esse tale; id Indefinitum, quod nullâ ratione probari potest esse finitum, qualis est materia ex qua constat universus orbis. Deinde, quia in mundo sub aliqua tantum ratione, videlicet respectu extensionis duntaxat, finem nullum agnoscit; cum Infinitum hoc tantum censeat appellandum, in quo nulla ex parte, respectu nullius prædicati aut perfectionis, limites inveniuntur. Atqui nequicquam Cartesium juvare potest hæc distinctio, ad declinandam vim efficacissimarum rationum, quæ pro finita mundi extensione urgeri queunt. Quandoquidem enim de Infinitate mundi, non omni ex parte, sed tantum sub aliqua ratione, scil. extensionis, hic disputatur; & quidem itâ, ut quæratur, an hoc respectu mundum Infinitum non esse, firma ratione probari possit, utique in hac controversia planè coïncidunt hactenus, atque unum idemque sonant, Indefinitum Cartesii, & Antagonistarum ejus Infinitum. Quibus rite intellectis, nemo hic sibi patietur imponi per τὸ Indefinitum, sub cujus umbone in hac controversia Recentiores fere delitescere, quodque instar caput Gorgonis identidem objicere, consueverunt; perturbantes itâ quantum possunt quæstionis statum, atque in litigiosis vocibus, quandò se rationibus impares experiuntur, præsidium quærentes: quod profectò disputatoris est flexiloqui & parùm generosi.
units.tr: As for us, we do not need to cling to these quarrels either, since the matter of this universe, if not infinite, at least indefinite, opens a fairly broad field for this dissertation of ours. Since Descartes is so pleased with this distinction, it must be looked at a little more carefully: what difference lies between these two. We have given the Author's text in which he discusses this matter, at §25, from Letter 36 of Book 1. I will add his clear and plain words, which occur in the First Reply, p. 59. He says: And indeed, here I distinguish between the indefinite and the infinite, and I call only that properly infinite in which no limits are found in any respect; in which sense God alone is infinite. But those in which I do not recognise an end only in some respect, such as the extension of imaginary space, the multitude of numbers, the divisibility of the parts of quantity, and the like, these I indeed call indefinite, not infinite, because they are not without end in every respect. From these words it is clear that Descartes preferred to call this world indefinite rather than infinite, for two reasons. First, because he wants to call properly infinite only that which is proved in some way to be such; and indefinite that which cannot be proved in any way to be finite, such as the matter from which the whole universe consists. Second, because in the world he recognises no end only in some respect, namely in respect of extension alone; whereas he thinks that only that should be called infinite in which no limits are found in any respect, with regard to no predicate or perfection. But this distinction cannot help Descartes at all, for turning aside the force of the most effective arguments that can be urged for the finite extension of the world. For since the question here concerns the infinity of the world not in every respect but only in some respect, namely extension, and since it is asked whether the world can be firmly proved not to be infinite in this respect, then in this controversy, up to now, Descartes' indefinite and his opponents' infinite agree exactly and sound the same. Once this is rightly understood, no one here will allow himself to be deceived by the indefinite, under whose shield the more recent writers mostly hide in this controversy, and which they habitually hold up like the head of the Gorgon. In this way they throw the state of the question into confusion as much as they can, and when they find themselves unequal to the arguments, they seek refuge in disputed terms. This is certainly the mark of a debater who is smooth of speech and not very high-minded.

units.la: Nos candidè agere instituimus: atque ideò, ut nullus maneat ambiguitati, in qua ludatur, locus, tribus articulis, quæ nostra sit de extensione universi Infinita, Indefinita, Finita, sententia, clarè & distinctè sic paucis definiemus. i. Infinitam mundi hujus
units.tr: We intend to argue openly. So that no room remains for ambiguity to be exploited, we will state our view clearly and distinctly, in a few words, on three points concerning the extension of the universe: whether it is Infinite, Indefinite, or Finite. First, the extension of this world is Infinite

units.la: XXX. Mundi extensio quo sensu affirmanda Infinita. jus extensionem esse & dici posse potentiâ, ut loquuntur, quatenus sese nunquam eo usquè diffundit, ut non in infinitum ulterius & u'terius extendi atque ampliari queat, tantùm abesse ut negemus, ut contrà hoc ipsum quam maximè contendamus: nequit enim admitti hæc infinitas potentialis in mundi diffusione, nisi actualis ejusdem terminatio omninò supponatur. II. Indefinitam hujus universi extensionem etiam faciles admittimus: si ejus nomine veniat magnitudo tam vasta, ut ejus termini, ubi definitè sint, & quantum ab invicem distent, præcisè à nobis definiri nequeant. Atque itâ mundum agnoscimus Indefinitum, quo sensu indefinitum dicimus V. C. numerum arenarum in littore maris, aut amplitudinem Terræ Australis incognitæ, aut profunditatem maris, aut altitudinem Solis, &c. quæ omnia certo certius cognoscimus aliquos re verâ habere suæ magnitudinis terminos ac limites, licet eorundem definitum ubi nequeamus assignare. At si sumatur acceptione Cartesianâ vox Indefiniti, aut pro re in qua sit vera infinitas, etsi certâ tantum ratione, puta respectu extensionis; aut pro re, quæ nullâ ratione probari queat finita, prosùs negamus, mundum posse aut debere dici Indefinitum. Quin ex adverso asserimus, III. Finitum esse re ipsa hoc Universum, ut omni modo, itâ nominatim respectu extensionis; idque solidâ ratione non tantum probari posse, verùm etiam argumentis compluribus eisque efficacissimis, Universi hujus, sive materiæ ejusdem, diffusionem nec à parte rei esse, nec à parte mentis concipi posse Infinitam, citra multiplicem contradictionem, demonstratu esse facillimum, contendimus. Hoc si ostendamus, procul dubio verum faciemus elenchum; quum Cartesium contrarium ejus expressissimè asserere audiverimus.
units.tr: XXX. In what sense the extension of the world is to be affirmed as infinite. I say that its extension can be called infinite in potentiality, as they put it, insofar as it never extends so far that it cannot be spread further and further, and enlarged without end. Far from denying this, we strongly insist on it. For this potential infinity in the diffusion of the world cannot be admitted unless its actual termination is wholly presupposed. II. We also readily admit that the extension of this universe is Indefinite, if by that word is meant a magnitude so vast that its limits, where they lie, and how far apart they are, cannot be precisely determined by us. In this sense we acknowledge the world as indefinite, just as we call indefinite, for example, the number of grains of sand on a seashore, or the extent of the unknown Southern Land, or the depth of the sea, or the height of the sun, etc. Of all these we know, with greater than certain knowledge, that in fact they have some terms and limits of their magnitude, although we cannot assign where those limits lie. But if the word "indefinite" is taken in the Cartesian sense, either for a thing in which there is true infinity, even if only in a certain respect, such as extension, or for a thing that cannot be shown by any reasoning to be finite, we flatly deny that the world can or ought to be called indefinite. On the contrary, we assert, III. that this Universe is Finite in fact, in every way, and especially with respect to extension. We contend that this can be proved not only by solid reasoning but also by several most effective arguments; and that it is very easy to demonstrate that the diffusion of this Universe, or of its matter, can be conceived as infinite neither in reality nor in the mind, without manifold contradiction. If we show this, we will undoubtedly make a sound refutation, since we have heard Descartes asserting the opposite most explicitly.
XXXI.

units.la: Non explicabo aciem, neque omnes adducam argumentorum classes, adversus mundi extensionem, quæ sit, aut esse possit, militantes infinitas. Tantùm quas hic rationes suppeditat tum mundi creati conditio, tum Dei Creatoris perfectio, notabo. Neque has quidem omnes urgebo; contentus, unam aut alteram fortius adstrinxisse, alias istùc pertinentes paucis attigisse. Ut verò quæ res ipsa clamat audiamus primum, attendi velim diligenter ad corporum, ex quibus constat hoc Universum, naturam. Intima eorum essentia (urgentibus id præ aliis quibuscum cum nobis hic res est) extensionem necessariò involvit. Ea quum sine partibus neque fit, neque concipi possit, nullâ ratione mundo partes integrantes denegari possunt. Et hæc quidem, ut opinor, extra controversiam collocata sunt. Jam verò, quodcunque partibus constat, id Infinitum nec esse, nec esse posse, invitè conficitur ratiocinio hoc, quovis Hercule fortiore. Partes nimirum, quibus constabit totum extensione Infinitum, à parte rei vel finitæ erunt, vel infinitæ. Tertium hic ne cogitari quidem potest; propter membrorum oppositionem contradictoriam, medium quovis respuentem. Neutras autem infinitum corpus admittere, sic ostendo. Non finitas; est enim manifestissimum, extremæ partis terminationem eandem omninò esse cum terminatione totius: ut toti, ex finitis partibus conflato, non magis deesse possit terminus & extremitas, quam ipsi cjusdem ultimæ parti finitæ. Quæ quamvis luce meridianâ sint clariora, neque ullâ ulteriore confirmatione egere videantur, ne quid tamen in argumento nostro desiderent importuni disputatores, qui quidvis sæpè negare malunt, quam suis valedicere hypothesibus, age! etiam assertionem hanc nostram demonstremus clarè & distinctè! Indubitatum est, partes omnes simul sumtas & unitas ipsum totum esse, adeoque illas huic existere prorsùs adæquatas. Pariter itaquè indubitatum existit, inter partes & totum, hoc ipso quia illæ huic adæquatæ existunt, rationem vel proportionem dari. At finiti ad Infinitum ullam dari, aut dari posse, proportionem, nemo dixerit, cujus non insania sit sine ulla proportione infinita. Rationem habere inter se dicuntur quantitates, quæ possunt multiplicata sese mutuo superare. Def. 5. v. Eucl. Multiplicetur autem finitum quotiescunquè, nunquam superabit Infinitum: nunquam enim finitum finito additum finiti naturam exuit; nec partes unquàm toti dabunt, quam ipsæ non possident, perfectionem. Quin, si finitis partibus constare queat totum Infinitum, quid evenict, si nova cis pars finita addatur? (Finitis verò finitum addi, quid vetat?) Numquid hoc casu totum Infinitum adauctum dices? Quis neget; cum addita de novo pars suam toti, quâ antè caruit, adjecerit quantitatem? Quis tamen affirmet, qui non simul necesse habeat largiri, unum Infinitum altero Infinito finitâ quâdam sui parte posse esse majus? Quæ quam sit insulsa cogitatio, nemo non videt; atquè ex infrà dicendis constabit abundè. Est itaquè plus quam certum, contradictionem non unam ponere, si quis asserat, Infinitum totum ex finitis partibus constare posse. Quod demonstrandum erat.
units.tr: I will not set out the whole line of battle, nor bring forward all the classes of arguments that stand against an infinite extension of the world, whether it actually is or could be. I will only note the reasons that the condition of the created world, and the perfection of God the Creator, supply here. Nor will I press all of these; I am content to have pressed one or another more strongly, and to have touched on the others that belong here in a few words. But that we may first hear what the matter itself cries out, I would have you attend carefully to the nature of the bodies of which this Universe consists. Their inner essence (and this presses especially against those with whom we have to do here) necessarily involves extension. Since this can neither exist nor be conceived without parts, the world cannot in any way be denied integral parts. And these points, I think, have been placed beyond controversy. Now it follows, with an argument stronger than any Hercules, that whatever consists of parts is not, and cannot be, infinite. For the parts out of which a whole that is infinite in extension would consist must be either finite or infinite in reality. A third possibility cannot even be thought, because of the contradictory opposition of the members, which rejects any middle ground. But that an infinite body admits neither of these, I show as follows. Not finite parts: for it is most obvious that the termination of the extreme part is wholly the same as the termination of the whole. So a whole made up of finite parts can no more lack a terminus and an extremity than its own last finite part can. These points are clearer than noonday light and seem to need no further confirmation. Yet, lest the troublesome disputants, who would rather deny anything at all than give up their hypotheses, find something in our argument to complain of, come! let us also demonstrate this assertion of ours clearly and distinctly! It is beyond doubt that all the parts taken together are the whole itself, and so the parts exist as wholly adequate to it. Likewise it is beyond doubt that, because the parts exist as adequate to the whole, there is a ratio or proportion between the parts and the whole. But no one would say that there is, or could be, any proportion of the finite to the Infinite, unless he were mad enough to posit a proportion without any infinite term. Quantities are said to have a ratio to one another when they can, multiplied, exceed one another. Def. 5, Euclid. However often a finite quantity is multiplied, it will never exceed the Infinite. For a finite quantity added to a finite quantity never loses the nature of the finite, nor will parts ever give to the whole a perfection that they do not themselves possess. Indeed, if a whole that is infinite could consist of finite parts, what would happen if a new finite part were added to it on this side? (For what forbids finite things being added to finite things?) Will you say that in this case the infinite whole has been increased? Who would deny it, since the part newly added has contributed to the whole a quantity it lacked before? Yet who would affirm this without at the same time being obliged to grant that one Infinite can be greater than another Infinite by some finite part of itself? How foolish this thought is, everyone sees, and it will be made abundantly clear from what is said below. It is therefore more than certain that whoever asserts that the whole Infinite can consist of finite parts sets down not one contradiction. This was to be demonstrated.

units.la: Verùm neque partes infinitas Infinita hujus Universi moles, vel quantitas quævis alia, admittit; seu numero eas infinitas dixeris, seu extensione. Aliam autem, præter hanc alterutram, infinitatem partibus tribui nullam posse, clarum est. Certè partium numerus infinitatem omnem prorsùs respuit: nisi numerus admittendus sit verè innumerus, talis nempè, cujus unitates absolutè colligi nequeunt; id est, qui revera sit non-numerus. Quid enim aliud est numerare, quam singulas unitates percurrere, & à paucioribus ad multiplicatiores gradatim ascendere? Quis numerus, qui non decades, centurias, chiliades, &c. complectatur; quinque adeò non constet partibus finitis? ex quibus Infinitum totum resultare non posse, planum modò fecimus abundè. Quis numerus, qui non subductâ unitate fiat minor; additâ unitate, major? Quumque Infinitum, qua tale, suâ naturâ se majus non admittat, neque etiam minus, non tantum ea admittet infinitus numerus, sed & absolutam suam infinitatem unitati debebit; adeò ut unius unitatis adjectione vel detractione, infinitus numerus finito succedat immediatè, & finitus infinito. Itâ insanire fas est eos, qui in extensione Infinita infinitas numero partes admittunt. Sed & aliud hic occurrit planè insolubile. Pone, si lubet, partes illas numero infinitas, ex quibus hoc universum Infinitum conflari contendis, pone, inquam, eas palmaris magnitudinis, vel etiam majores, minoresve, pro arbitrio; eodem enim vis demonstrationis redibit: tantùm si divisibiles posueris; de quo nulla nobis contentio. Singulis palmis quaterni continentur digiti; totidemque grana singulos iterum componunt digitos; atque itâ porrò quævis pars major plures minores in se complectitur in infinitum. Continebunt ergò semel infiniti palmi quater infinitos digitos; & decies sexies infinita grana; sicque in infinitum; quoniam hic in corpore progressus à partibus majoribus ad minores continuari potest sine fine. Elige nunc, obsecro! num in Infinito corpore palmorum numerum numero digitorum, granorum, &c. statuere velis æqualem, an minorem. Æqualem si ponas (uti exigit natura Infiniti; quod, cum sit quid maximum atque absolutissimum in suo genere, inæqualitatem omnem respuit) tot unitates admittes in corpore, quot quaterniones, &c. utque uno verbo absolvam, directè incurres in 9. Axiom. 1. Eucl. statuendo, partem toti æqualem. Fac ergò palmorum numerum eo qui est digitorum minorem; (quod natura partium exigit) sed dic simul, unum numerum Infinitum altero numero Infinito infinities esse minorem. Quasi quod Infinito minus est, possit nihilominus verè esse Infinitum! Quasi de ulla re creata dici debeat, quod de sola Divinarum persectionum plenitudine cogitare fas est, eam esse infinities infinitam in infinitum, & ab infinitis sine fine participabilem. Hisce omnibus cum exitus dari queat planè nullus, constat certo certius, Infinitam quantitatem ex partibus numero infinitis nullâ ratione componi posse. Quod demonstrandum erat.
units.tr: But neither the Infinite mass of this Universe, nor any other quantity, admits parts that are infinite, whether you call them infinite in number or in extension. It is clear that no other infinity, besides one or other of these, can be attributed to parts. Certainly the number of parts rejects every kind of infinity, unless the number to be admitted is truly innumerable, namely one whose units cannot be gathered together absolutely; that is, which is in fact a non-number. For what else is counting than running through the single units, and ascending gradually from fewer to more? What number is there that does not comprise tens, hundreds, thousands, and so on? Indeed, what number does not consist of finite parts? From which the whole Infinite cannot result, as we have just made abundantly plain. What number is not made smaller by subtracting a unit, and larger by adding one? And since the Infinite, as such, by its nature admits neither greater nor smaller, an infinite number will not only admit this, but must also owe its absolute infinity to the unit; so that by adding or taking away a single unit, an infinite number would immediately give way to a finite one, and a finite one to an infinite one. It is thus mad of those who, in Infinite extension, admit parts infinite in number. But there is also another point here that is quite insoluble. Suppose, if you like, that those parts, infinite in number, out of which you contend this Infinite universe is compounded, are of a palm's size, or even larger or smaller, as you please; for the force of the demonstration will come to the same thing, provided you posit them divisible, which is not in dispute between us. Each palm contains four fingers, and as many grains again make up each finger; and so on, so that every larger part contains several smaller parts within itself, without end. Therefore an infinite number of palms will contain four times an infinite number of fingers, and ten times six infinite grains; and so on without end, since in a body the progression from larger to smaller parts can continue without end. Now choose, I beg you! Do you wish to set the number of palms in an Infinite body equal to the number of fingers, grains, and so on, or smaller? If you posit it equal (as the nature of the Infinite requires, since it is the greatest and most absolute thing in its kind and rejects all inequality), you will admit as many units in the body as there are quaternions, etc., and to put it in one word, you will fall straight into Axiom 9 of Euclid's first book, by positing a part equal to the whole. So let the number of palms be smaller than the number of fingers (as the nature of parts requires), but say at the same time that one infinite number is infinitely smaller than another infinite number. As if what is less than the Infinite could nevertheless truly be Infinite! As if one should say of any created thing what it is right to think only of the fullness of the Divine perfections: that it is infinitely infinite, and participable without end by infinite things. Since no exit from these difficulties can be found at all, it is more than certain that an infinite quantity cannot in any way be composed of parts infinite in number. This was to be demonstrated.

units.la: Superest, ut tandem cogitetur, quod unum restat, an non partes mundi Infiniti integrantes esse queant magnitudinis infinitæ. Verùm nec hoc monstrum absque multiplici contradictione sibi quis imaginatus fuerit. Etenim partem aliquam talem mundi Infinitam statuesque toti mundo æqualem, nec ne? Inæqualem non dixeris, nisi pariter unius Infiniti præ altero Infinito admiseris excessum, ob quem alterum alteri inæquale dicatur. At Infinitum quodvis nullum excessum ultra se admittit, quoniam de natura Infiniti qua talis est, ut contineat totam plenitudinem prædicati, cujus ratione Infinitum dicitur: adeò ut extensio Infinita tanta sit, quanta absolutè dari potest; consequenter ea, quâ major cogitari nequit. Quin, ne quidem excessum unius Infiniti ultra aliud Infinitum cogitaveris absque evidenti repugnantia. Quis enim excessum concipiat, nisi limites supponantur in re, quæ ab altera se majorce excedditur; limites, inquam, ultra quos excedens excessum excedat? Infinitum itaquè si excedi ab alio cogites, terminatum id concipis istic, ubi excessum patitur. Quæ autem contradictio sit, nisi hæc sit? nescio. Id ergò solum reliquum est, ut partem Infiniti mundi Infinitam toti mundo Infinito æqualem statuas: quod rursùs è diametro adversatur, &9. Axiom. 1. Eucl. Totum parte majus est; & 1. Def. v. Pars est magnitudo magnitudinis, minor majoris, cum metitur majorem. Quid? quod ex partibus infinitum extensis (sint, v. c. A. & B.) propter ipsam earundem infinitatem, ne quidem totum componi possit. Vel enim pars altera A alterius B extensionem in se continebit; vel non. Si A in se contineat extensionem B, utique frustrà ad totius complementum parti A addetur pars B; quoniam pars B comparti A nihil adjungere poterit, quod non pars A jam antè in se continuit. Non ergo hoc casu B concurret cum A ad constituendum totum; adeòque ne quidem B pars erit; quod manifestè est contra hypothesin. Dic itaquè (quod superest) partem A infinitam in se non continere extensionem suæ compartis B. Verùm hac ratione pars A Infinita revera non erit; quoniam (ut res ipsa monstrat) de natura Infiniti est tantum esse quantum esse potest. Quapropter si parti A addi possit extensio partis B, prioris partis extensio tanta non fuit, quanta esse potuit; consequenter neque Infinita. Denique, ipsa totius integralis notio partium componentium Infinitatem penitus excludit. Totum nullum continuum datur aut dari potest, sine partium extensarum unione; nullum contiguum, sine mutuo earundem contactu. At quæ partium extensarum unio, quis contactus, conceptibilis est, qui non supponat partium unitarum in puncto unionis, vel contactus, terminationem? Unde & recepta est continui definitio, tanquam Magnitudinis cujus partes communi termino copulantur. Quoniam ergò possibilis non est partium infinitarum in unum continuum unio, vel etiam in contiguo contactus, etiam possibilis non crit quantitas continua, vel contigua, ex partibus in infinitum extensis constata.
units.tr: It remains that we consider the one question still open: whether the parts that make up an infinite world can be of infinite magnitude. But no one could imagine even this monster without many contradictions. For suppose you posit some infinite part of the world equal to the whole world. Or not equal? You cannot call it unequal unless you admit that one infinite exceeds another infinite, so that one is said to be unequal to the other. But no infinite admits any excess beyond itself, since it is of the nature of the infinite, as such, to contain the whole fullness of the attribute by which it is called infinite. So an infinite extension is as great as it can absolutely be, and consequently is such that no greater can be conceived. Indeed, you cannot even conceive of one infinite exceeding another infinite without an obvious contradiction. For who could conceive an excess unless limits are supposed in the thing that is exceeded by the other, larger thing, limits, I say, beyond which the excess would go? So if you think of an infinite being exceeded by another, you conceive it there as bounded, where it suffers the excess. But what contradiction there would be, if this were not so, I do not know. The only remaining option, then, is to posit an infinite part of the infinite world equal to the whole infinite world. This again is directly opposed to Axiom 1 of Euclid's Elements, "The whole is greater than the part," and to Definition 1 of Book 5, "A part is a magnitude of a magnitude, the smaller of the greater, when it measures the greater." What is more, a whole cannot be composed even of parts extended to infinity (say A and B), because of their very infinity. For either the one part A will contain within itself the extension of the other part B, or it will not. If A contains within itself the extension of B, then clearly part B is added to part A in vain for completing the whole, since B can add nothing to A that A did not already contain in itself. So in this case B will not combine with A to constitute the whole, and therefore B will not even be a part, which is clearly against the hypothesis. Therefore say, as is left, that the infinite part A does not contain within itself the extension of its companion part B. But on this view the part A will not really be infinite, since (as the thing itself shows) it is of the nature of the infinite to be only as great as it can be. Hence, if the extension of part B can be added to part A, the extension of the former part was not as great as it could be, and consequently it was not infinite. Finally, the very notion of a whole composed of parts wholly excludes infinity. No continuous whole exists, or can exist, without the union of extended parts; no contiguous whole without their mutual contact. But what union of extended parts, what contact, can be conceived that does not presuppose a termination of the united parts at the point of union or contact? Hence the accepted definition of a continuum is also that of a magnitude whose parts are joined by a common term. Since, therefore, a union of infinite parts into one continuum is impossible, or even a contact of them in a contiguous whole, a continuous or contiguous quantity made up of parts extended to infinity will likewise be impossible.

units.la: Nec quicquam quod hisce opponi possit video, nisi forte hoc unum, nostrâ demonstratione tantum confici, partes, quæ ad totum Infinitum constituendum concurrunt, debere quidem finitas agnosci cà parte quâ inter se uniuntur, sed nihilominus. versus alteras partes, quibus ab invicem recedunt, posse esse sine fine extensas; ut scil. partium altera sit infinita hinc, altera indè, totum verò ex iis conflatum Infinitum existat undecunquè. Quasi nempe linea B C B D A E C
units.tr: I see nothing that can be set against these points, except perhaps this one objection: that our demonstration proves only that the parts which combine to constitute an infinite whole must indeed be recognised as finite by the side on which they are joined to one another, yet nevertheless, towards their other sides, from which they recede from each other, they may be extended without end, so that one part is infinite on this side and the other on that, and the whole made of them exists as infinite on every side. As if, namely, the line B C were thought of as composed of two lines, A B and A C, finite indeed on the side A, where they are joined together, but on the other side, both towards B and towards C, extended to infinity; so that from the two infinite lines A B and A C, one whole line B C, infinite in both directions, is made.

units.la: composita cogitetur ex duabus lineis A B, & A C, finitis quidem dem à parte A, quâ inter sese uniuntur, sed ab altera parte utrimque, & versus B, & versus C, protensis in infinitum: sic ut ex duabus A B, A C, infinitis altera parte, una fiat tota linea B C, Infinita utrinque. Verum ista altius introspecta nequicquam hic auferunt difficultatis. Ut mittam alia, tantum cogitemus, lineas A B & A C, infinitum, uti vis, extensas versus B & C, partes sui agnoscere, & tanquam tales includere, lineas A D, & A E. Hæ cum undiquaque existant finitæ, utique tota linea infinita B C, ex hac sententia, componetur ex partibus quibusdam finitis, puta A D, A E; & aliis quibusdam infinitis, scil. D B, E C. At verò, quod antè demonstravi, finiti ad infinitum nulla proportio est; qualis semper esse debet inter partes & totum: quapropter lineæ finitæ A D, A E, nequidem considerari possunt tanquam partes totius lineæ infinitæ B C; nedum ut ex infinito & finito chimærica istiusmodi & quovis monstro monstrosior fiat mixtio. Præterea, ex junctis in puncto A lineis A B, & A C, altera parte infinitis, ita ut tota B C utrimque existat infinita, pars quæpiam circa A auferatur, puta D E, unitis rursum inter se punctis D & E. Quid jam? Num adhuc linea tota composita erit Infinita? At verò minor facta est per ablatam partem D E. Sic ergò iterùm statuetur Infinitum infinito parte aliquâ finitâ minus; quod jam antè ostendimus implicare. Nec evades, si dixeris, lineam B C factam esse finitam, sublatâ parte D E: est enim contra omnem rationem, ut particula finita D E, quæ nullam omninò ad Infinitum dicit proportionem, si adjecta fuerit vel abjecta, ex Infinito faciat finitum, ex finito Infinitum. Contradictionem itaquè multiplicem involvit magnitudo Infinita ex partibus infinitis quomodocunquè composita. Quod demonstrandum erat.
units.tr: But this view, looked into more deeply, in no way removes the difficulty. Setting other things aside, let us suppose that the lines A B and A C, extended towards B and C, however infinite you like, acknowledge parts of themselves and include, as such, the lines A D and A E. Since these are finite on every side, the whole infinite line B C, on this view, will be composed of certain finite parts, namely A D and A E, and certain other infinite parts, namely D B and E C. But, as I showed earlier, there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite, and there must always be such a proportion between a part and its whole. Therefore the finite lines A D and A E cannot even be regarded as parts of the infinite line B C, much less does a mixture of the infinite and the finite arise, a chimaera of this kind and a monster more monstrous than any other. Further, take the lines A B and A C, joined at the point A and infinite on one side, so that the whole B C is infinite on both sides, and let some part near A be removed, say D E, the points D and E being again joined together. What now? Will the whole composite line still be infinite? But it has become smaller by the removal of the part D E. So again we shall have posited an infinite that is less than an infinite by some finite part, which we have already shown to be self-contradictory. Nor will you escape by saying that the line B C has become finite once the part D E is removed. For it is against every reason that a small finite particle D E, which bears no proportion at all to the infinite, should, when added or taken away, make the infinite finite or the finite infinite. Therefore an infinite magnitude, however composed of infinite parts, involves manifold contradiction. This was to be demonstrated.

units.la: Nequit igitur mundi extensio, Infinita si sit, constare ex partibus & numero & magnitudine finitis. Neque etiam ex partibus, vel numero, vel magnitudine, infinitis. Neque aliæ partes præter illas vel dantur, vel dari possunt. Interim partibus carere nequit. Restat itaquè, ut universi extensio nec sit, nec esse possit, infinita. Quod demonstrandum erat. Estque hujus nostri ratiocinii per omnes sui partes vis & efficacia tanta, ut evidentissimâ certitudine & certissimâ evidentiâ certet cum demonstratione quavis
units.tr: Therefore the extension of the world, if it is infinite, cannot consist of parts finite in number and magnitude. Nor can it consist of parts infinite in number or magnitude. Nor are there, or can there be, any parts other than these. Yet it cannot be without parts. It remains, therefore, that the extension of the universe neither is, nor can be, infinite. This was to be demonstrated. And the force and efficacy of this our reasoning, throughout all its parts, is so great that it vies, with the most evident certainty and the most certain evidence, with any mathematical demonstration.

units.la: N n 2 vis mathematica ; cujus rei judicium lubens quibuscunque, qui ad singula & omnia ejus membra sine præjudicio attendere dignati fuerint, committo. Me quod attinet, sic habeo, omnes omnium Novatorum in unum congestas claras & distinctas ideas minimè sufficere infringendo robori tam immotis rectæ rationis fundamentis inædificati argumenti. Ausim universam illorum familiam hic obtestari per omnia quæ sacra eis sunt in Patriarchæ sui hæreditate, per cjus libros Principiorum quatuor, per Meditationes de Prima Philosophia sex, per Responsiones ejusdem Primas, Secundas, Tertias, Quartas, Sextas, Quintas & Septimas, dent exitum huic rei aliquem, si possint ! Atqui quid possint isti, quod ipse non potuit Cartesius ? Is, cum nihil quod hisce opponeret inveniret, quod unum supererat, necesse habuit negare, de infinito disputandum esse; nimirum, ut respondere non curaret iis, qui quærunt, an si daretur linea infinita, ejus mediapars esset etiam infinita; vel, an numerus infinitus sit par, anve impar; &c. Principia I. §. 26. Benè habet ! Veritati sat triumphi in eo est, si adversarios ipsa suos redegerit ad terminos non respondendi. Nulli interim extra partes constituto satisfaciet, opinor, turpis ejusce modi tergiversatio; quippe quæ minimè arguit animum candidum, & veritati cedere paratum, sed manifestissimum potius existit invincibilis pertinaciæ argumentum. Confer Dissertat. hujus §. IV.
units.tr: I leave the judgement on this matter to all those who have been willing to attend, without prejudice, to each and every member of this argument. As far as I am concerned, I hold that all the clear and distinct ideas of all the innovators gathered into one body are by no means sufficient to shake the strength of an argument built on such immovable foundations of right reason. I would venture to call upon that whole family of theirs here, by all that is holy to them in the inheritance of their patriarch, by his four books of the Principles, by his six Meditations on First Philosophy, and by his Replies, the First, Second, Third, Fourth, Sixth, Fifth and Seventh, let them, if they can, provide some answer to this matter! But what can they do that Descartes himself could not? He, when he found nothing with which to oppose these arguments, was obliged to deny that the one remaining point was to be disputed, namely that the question concerns the infinite; so that he would not take the trouble to answer those who ask whether, if an infinite line were given, its middle part would also be infinite; or whether an infinite number is even or odd; etc. Principles I, §26. Very well! It is triumph enough for truth if it has driven its adversaries to the point of not answering. Yet, I think, such shifty evasion will satisfy no one outside the party; for it does not show a candid mind ready to yield to truth, but is rather a most manifest sign of unconquerable obstinacy. Compare this Dissertation, §IV.
XXXVI.

units.la: Itâ cum ostenderimus invictè, extensioni, quæ Recentioribus ipsam corporis naturam constituit, adeò adversari Infinitatem ut eam penitus evertat, non necesse erit plura congerere, quibus mundi diffusio intra terminos coërceatur. Tantum, ne in unica ratione omnis veritati præsidium esse videatur, alias nonnullas, quas ad modum prioris efficacissimè urgere facile fuerit, digito monstrabo. Nimirum, Mundus si sit extensione Infinitus, essentiâ pariter Infinitus erit. Si enim extensio sit ipsa corporis essentia, res per se manifesta est. Si sit, ut placet aliis, aliquis corporis modus, eodem res redit; cum essentia finita attributi nullius Infiniti sit capax. Creaturæ verò cujuscunque essentiam Infinitam quis admiserit, qui non rectam sternat ad Atheismum viam? Avertat Deus, quæ prudentiores meritissimo jure suspicari facit hæc de mundo Infinito opinio! Porrò, Si Mundus sit extenextensione Infinitus, omnium quoque attributorum suorum ratio-ne infinitus erit. Extensio enim infinita, uti docui, necessariò arguit essentiam Infinitam. At quod effentiâ Infinitum est , infinitum pariter est omnibus suis prædicatis ; quoniam attributa quævis conditionem fui subjecti sequuntur. Erit ergò mundus non minus Infinitus ratione durationis , & cujusvis alterius perfectionis , quam ratione extensionis. Quid ad atheifticam naturæ ἀπροθώσιν desideretur amplius ? non video. Verum de hisce mox plura. Nunc & hoc notetur, Si mundus fit extensione Infinitus, omnia ei ex adverso detrahenda erunt attributa, quæ corpori sunt propria. Divisibilis non erit ejus magnitudo : neque enim in partes finitas resolvi poterit , neque infinitas ; uti probavimus. Nec diminui ea poterit : Infinito enim nihil detrahi posse, ex antè dictis manifestum est. Neque ullâ fui parte augeri poterit : quia non minus incrementum respuit Infinitudo, quam decrementum. Nec figurâ aliquâ prædītus erit : magnitudinis enim terminationem Infinito tribuere mera contradictio est. Nec mobilis erit : nam nullum Infinito relinquitur spatium quo feratur. Nec menfurabiliserit : non enim ei applicari poterit mensura finita, quippe quæ Infinitum nunquam exæquare potest; neque Infinita, cum ipsa infinitas mensuram destruat. Nec situm partium habebit : nullus namque is dari potest fine ordine, quem omnem Infinitas excludit ? Nec distantia quibusvis ejus partibus in ordine ad alias conveniet : nisi alicubi Infinita; quæ re verâ nulla est. Verbo uno ut absolvam, neque, quo me ducit argumenti fertilitas, excurram in infinitum, extensionis Infinitas corpus omnibus exuit suis proprietatibus : adeò ut, mundum corpus non esse, fi Infinius fit; aut Infinitum non esse, fi corpus fit, existat absolutè necessarium. Nec tantùm ipsam corporis naturam prorsùs evertit , omnesque ejus proprietates planè tollit Infinita hujus Universi extensio , sed & in plurimas Dei Creatoris perfectiones eadem existit injuria haud leviter, neque uno modo. Certè, solius supremi Numinis prærogativam esse essentiæ Infinitatem , unanimi consensu tradiderunt haftenus Doctores Christiani , ipsique inter Gentes sapientiores. Et merito. Nam eam cum Indepen dentia, quæ omnium Divinarum perfectionum fons est & origo , nexum habere essentialem & insolubilem, facile est demonftratu: quemadmodum & ex hac
units.tr: Thus, since we have shown invincibly that infinity is so opposed to extension, which the Moderns make the very nature of body, that it utterly overturns it, it will not be necessary to heap up more arguments by which the spread of the world is confined within limits. Only, lest it seem that the whole defence of truth rests on a single reason, I will point out with a finger some others, which could easily be pressed as effectively as the former. Namely: if the world is infinite in extension, it will be infinite in essence as well. For if extension is the very essence of body, the thing is plain in itself. If it is, as others prefer, some mode of body, the result is the same, since a finite essence cannot be capable of any infinite attribute. But who would admit an infinite essence in any creature without laying a straight road to Atheism? God forbid! What this opinion of an infinite world makes the wiser sort rightly suspect! Furthermore, if the world is infinite in extension, it will be infinite in all its attributes too. For infinite extension, as I have shown, necessarily implies an infinite essence. But what is infinite in essence is infinite likewise in all its predicates, since every attribute follows the condition of its subject. Therefore the world will be infinite no less in duration and in every other perfection than in extension. What more is wanted for the atheistic ἀπροθώσιν of nature? I do not see. But more on these things shortly. Now let this also be noted: if the world is infinite in extension, all the attributes proper to body must be stripped from it. Its magnitude will not be divisible: for it cannot be resolved into finite parts, nor into infinite ones, as we have proved. Nor can it be diminished: for that nothing can be taken from the infinite is clear from what was said above. Nor can it be increased in any part: since infinity rejects increase no less than decrease. Nor will it have any shape: for to ascribe a termination of magnitude to the infinite is sheer contradiction. Nor will it be mobile: for no space is left to the infinite in which it could move. Nor will it be measurable: for no finite measure can be applied to it, since a finite measure can never equal the infinite; nor an infinite one, since infinity destroys measure. Nor will it have a position of parts: for what order can there be where infinity excludes every order? Nor will any distance of its parts from others be consistent: unless somewhere infinite, which in truth there is not. To sum up in one word, and not to run on into infinity as the fertility of the argument leads me, the infinity of extension strips the body of all its properties: so that the world is not a body if it is infinite, nor infinite if it is a body; this is absolutely necessary. Nor does the infinite extension of this universe merely overturn the very nature of body and wholly remove all its properties; the same wrong is done, not lightly and not in one way only, to very many perfections of God the Creator. Certainly the Christian teachers up to now, and the wiser among the Gentiles themselves, have unanimously taught that infinity of essence is the sole prerogative of the supreme Deity. And rightly so. For it is easily demonstrated that this has an essential and indissoluble bond with independence, which is the source and origin of all the divine perfections; just as also from this

units.la: XXXVII. Effentia solius Dei Infinita extensionis cuiusvis Infinitatem everfit.
units.tr: XXXVII. The essence of God alone, being infinite, overturns the infinity of any extension whatever.

units.la: Infinitate Dei deducitur firmissimâ sequelâ, ejusdem Æternitas, Immensitas, Immutabilitas, Primitas, Unitas, aliaque ejus generis attributa, Incommunicabilia vulgò dicta. Hinc omnium voce celebratus semper Deus, tanquam qui unus existit, uti Optimus, itâ Maximus. At non jam solius excellentissimæ Majestatis hæc erit eminentia, sed in societatem admittetur Mundus, extensione suâ eodem gaudens cum suo Opifice privilegio. Impia profectò, nec sine sacrilegio profana, cogitatio ! quam magno mercentur Athei, qui naturam Σωτηρίαν. Non nescio, quisabsurditati obducatur color. Aliam planè esse, ajunt, atque alterius ordinis Infinitatem, quæ mundo competat, quam quæ Deo. Hanc dicere Infinitatem omnibus numeris absolutam, cùm ratione ipsius essentiæ, tùm ratione omnium omninò, quæ dari aut cogitari queunt, perfectionum: illam verò, quæ mundo convenit, Infinitatem ad solam restringi extensionem; quam in ente perfectissimo locum habere non posse, certò intelligimus. Speciosè, fateor, hæc dicuntur, at minus verè; neque ea altiùs introspecta quicquam hic tollunt abFurditatis. Quamvis enim differitatem agnoscant hi auctores inter essentiam Dei & Mundi, quodillla, ut ipsi loquuntur, sit cogitatio, hæc extensio; manet nihilominus firmissimum, admissâ magnitudine hujus Universi infinitâ, extensioni creatæ non minus, quam cogitationi increatæ, essentialem Infinitatem esse tribuendam. Contendunt enim hi auctores (quod & antè observavimus) ipsam corporis essentiam in extensione consistere: quapropter, cum mundus sit in genere rerum corporearum, imò verò corporum omnium compages, nequit ejus essentiæ negari, quæ ejusdem extensioni tribuitur, Infinitas. Ex quibus clarissimè conficitur, admissâ infinitâ mundi extensione, Infinitatem essentiæ tale prædicatum esse, quod secundum se, non tantùm Deo proprium non est, verum quod cadat etiam in rem longè imperfectissimam, quale est corpus, sive extensio. Quæ quidem evidentia adeò sunt, ut vel manibus sese offerant palpanda. Neque tandem dici poterit, non saltem omnimodam ratione cujusvis perfectionis Infinitatem, uti Deo, itâ mundo infinitè extenso, tribui. Dato enim, quod jam evicimus, mundum, si sit extensione infinitus, ipsâ essentiâ infinitum esse, non potest non Infinitus pariter hic agnosci ratione cujusvis jusvis attributi; quùm, ut jam antic. prox. docui, proprietates subjecti sui conditionem necessariò sequantur. Unde & ex essentiae Divinae Infinitate quarumvis in ipso perfectionum Infinitatem rectè adstruunt Theologi ac Philosophi. Manet itaquè, aut solum Deum essentiâ Infinitum non esse, quod à blasphemia non multùm distat; aut Mundum nostrum extensione esse finitum: quod demonstrandum erat.
units.tr: From the infinity of God there is deduced, by a most firm sequence, his eternity, immensity, immutability, primacy, unity, and other attributes of that kind, commonly called incommunicable. Hence God is celebrated by the voice of all as ever one who alone exists, as the Best, so also the Greatest. But this eminence will no longer belong to his excellent majesty alone, for the world will be admitted into fellowship, enjoying by its extension a privilege equal to that of its Maker. A truly impious thought, and profane not without sacrilege! How dearly do the Atheists pay for it, who make nature Σωτηρίαν [Saviour]. I know what colour is put over the absurdity. They say that the infinity which belongs to the world is of another kind, and of a different order, from that which belongs to God. That infinity is called absolute in every respect, both with regard to the essence itself and with regard to all the perfections that can exist or be conceived; but the infinity which belongs to the world is restricted to extension alone, which we clearly understand cannot have a place in the most perfect being. These things are said plausibly, I grant, but less truly; nor, looked into more deeply, do they remove any of the absurdity. For although these authors acknowledge a difference between the essence of God and that of the world, in that the former is, as they themselves say, thought, the latter extension, it nevertheless remains most firm that, once the magnitude of this universe is granted to be infinite, essential infinity must be ascribed no less to created extension than to uncreated thought. For these authors contend (as we noted before) that the very essence of body consists in extension; therefore, since the world is the framework of corporeal things in general, indeed of all bodies, the infinity that is attributed to its essence, namely to its extension, cannot be denied.
