From which it is most clearly concluded that, granting an infinite extension of the world, infinity of essence is a predicate which, in itself, is not only not proper to God alone, but falls also upon a thing far more imperfect, such as body or extension. These things are so evident that they offer themselves to be touched with the hands. Nor can it finally be said that infinity is not ascribed to the world, if it is infinitely extended, in every way, in respect of any perfection, as it is to God. For granting what we have already proved, that the world, if it is infinite in extension, is infinite in essence itself, it cannot but be acknowledged infinite likewise in respect of any attribute; since, as I have already shown in the immediately preceding section, properties necessarily follow the condition of their subject. Whence theologians and philosophers rightly also infer the infinity of all perfections in God from the infinity of the divine essence. It remains, therefore, either that God alone is not infinite in essence, which is not far from blasphemy, or that our world is finite in extension: which was to be demonstrated.

units.la: In Immensitatem Divinam non minus incurrit crudum dogma. Ejus nomine hactenùs intellexère Philosophi & Theologi, illam primi entis supereminentem perfectionem, quâ ipsum existit suâ essentiâ, non tantùm ubi corpus est, verùm etiam ubicunquè id esse potest. Sed neque hac parte mundus, si fit extensione Infinitus, quicquam Deo cedit; quippe qui, non minus quam Ille, existit suâ essentiâ ubicunquè corpus dari potest. Facilis admitto, in hac mundi Immensitate diffusionem partium involvi, quae eadem ab Immensitate simplicissimi Dei planè est removenda; ut in aliquo quidem rei modo videam discrimen: attamen in re ipsâ nullum id mihi hîc esse videtur, dum nusquam in infinitum admittitur Deus non-extensus, ubi pariter non sit mundus extensus. Non profectò talis fuit idea, quam de Divina Immensitate habuit, à Deo ipso edoctus optimè, sapiens non minus per omnia Philosophus, quam Regius Propheta Salomon, quandò Deum Immensum cogitans, negavit Ipsum capi cælo, imo vel cælo cælorum. Quem eundem in sensum scitè alibi Dionysius Deum celebrat ὑπερκόσμιον, ὑπερουράνιον, ὑπερουσιον, quasi dicas, Immundanum, Circummundanum, Supermundanum, Supercœleftem. Scio, non admitti hos conceptus Novellis Doctoribus, qui, cum clarè videant per mundum suum Infinitum & Immensum nullum relinqui locum Immensitati illi divinae, quam hactenùs credidit orbis Christianus, hanc totam, quasi aliquid sapiat corporeum, expungere ipsa malunt, eique substituere creationis & providentiae ideas; quasi videlicet Immensitas Dei nihil sit aliud quam efficacissima Dei voluntas, quâ omnia producit, sustentat ac regit. Verùm uti ante nostra tempora inter Orthodoxos inauditum fuit hoc dogma, itâ etiam id longè esse absurdissimum ac periculosissimum, ostendimus alibi; nominatim in Dissertat. de Nullibitate Spiritum. Sufficit in præsens monstrasse, aut mundum, si sit extensione Infinitus, non minus Immensum esse, quam ipsum Deum; aut, si solus Deus existat Immensus, mundum non esse ubicunque corpus esse poterit, atque ideo neque extensione Infinitum. Quod demonstrandum erat.
units.tr: The crude dogma conflicts no less with the divine Immensity. Under this name philosophers and theologians have hitherto understood that supereminent perfection of the first being by which it exists by its essence not only where body is, but wherever it can be. But neither in this respect, if the world is infinite in extension, does it yield anything to God; for it, no less than He, exists by its essence wherever a body can be. I readily admit that in this immensity of the world the diffusion of parts is involved, which must be entirely removed from the immensity of the most simple God; so that in a certain mode of the thing I do see a difference. Yet in the thing itself no such difference seems to me to exist here, since nowhere is an unextended God admitted to infinity where the extended world is not likewise. Certainly that was not the idea which the Divine Immensity had, as taught most excellently by God Himself, a philosopher no less in all things than the royal prophet Solomon, when, thinking of God as immense, he denied that He could be contained by heaven, nay even by the heaven of heavens. In the same sense Dionysius elsewhere wisely celebrates God as hyperkosmion, hyperouranion, hyperousion [ὑπερκόσμιον, ὑπερουράνιον, ὑπερουσιον], as if you should say Immundane, Circummundane, Supermundane, Supercelestial. I know these concepts are not admitted by the newer teachers, who, since they clearly see that through their infinite and immense world no place is left for that divine Immensity which the Christian world has hitherto believed in, prefer to expunge this whole thing entirely, as if it smacked of something corporeal, and to substitute for it the ideas of creation and providence; as if, to be sure, the Immensity of God were nothing other than the most efficacious will of God by which He produces, sustains and governs all things. But just as this dogma was unheard of among the Orthodox before our time, so we have shown elsewhere that it is far more absurd and dangerous, namely in the Dissertation on the Non-Locality of Spirits. It is enough for the present to have shown that either the world, if it is infinite in extension, is no less immense than God Himself; or, if God alone exists as immense, the world is not wherever body can be, and so is not infinite in extension. Which was to be demonstrated.

units.la: Non etiam cum interminabili Potentiæ Divinæ amplitudine, liberrimaque, quam habet summum Numen in opera creationis & providentiæ, potestate, consistere potest Infinita Universi quantitas. Theologorum & Philosophorum axioma est receptissimum, Opera Dei ad extra esse indifferenter libera. Verum per hanc sententiam id stare nequit; dum quæ adferunt argumenta inferunt, non tantum mundum actu esse in infinitum extensum, verum etiam alium quam Infinitum esse non posse. Ex quo sequitur, Deum ex necessitate quadam mundum produxisse tantum, quantus existit, neque ex indifferenti voluntatis placito minorem producere potuisse. Sed de hisce infra latius. Nunc observari velim, infinitam liberrimi Creatoris vim creaturæ cujusvis perfectiones longissimè semper & in immensum excedere; quandoquidem res adeo dispares nullam ad se mutuo dicere posse proportionem, luce meridiana existit clarius. Ex quo concluditur firmissimè, eam esse creatæ cujusvis naturæ essentiam, ut nunquam sit, aut quoquè esse possit, in extrema, uti loquuntur, actualitate, id est, in perfectionis gradu ac complemento absolutè ultimo: quod vulgò ajunt, creaturam perfectissimam non posse dari. Quamobrem neque ullum rei creatæ prædicatum unquam esse potest tantum, ut non amplius subsit activæ Creatoris potentiæ; utque adeo non existat in potentia passiva ad recipiendos plures perfectionis gradus, quos necdum habet, liberrimo tamen Omnisufficientis Dei nutu & arbitrio habere poterit. Jam vero corpus Infinitum ad ampliorem sui diffusionem potentiam nullam passivam admittere, liquet, quòd antè demonstravimus, Infinito majus nihil dari posse, neque id vel tantilli incrementi, per ipsam naturam Infinitatis, existere capax. Unde sequitur, admisso mundo Infinito, immensam omnipotentis Dei vim de novo in hoc universo nec muscam quidem aut pulicem ex nihilo creare posse. Quemadmodum & ex adverso ex eadem fluit hypothesi, per absolutam Dei potentiam, ne pulviisculum quidem, aut quamcunque vel minimam hujus universi particulam, annihilari posse; quoniam implicat, per
units.tr: Nor can the infinite quantity of the universe stand together with the boundless greatness and most free power that the supreme Deity has in the work of creation and providence. It is the most widely accepted axiom of theologians and philosophers that God's works outside himself are free in a way that allows either option. Yet this view cannot hold if their arguments are right, for they infer not only that the world is actually extended to infinity, but that it cannot be anything other than infinite. From this it follows that God produced the world, as it exists, out of a certain necessity, and could not have produced a smaller one by an indifferent choice of his will. But more on this below. For now I would have it noted that the infinite power of the free Creator always far exceeds the perfections of any creature, and to an immeasurable degree. Since things so unequal can have no proportion to one another, this is clearer than noonday light. From this we firmly conclude that it is the essence of any created nature that it never is, nor ever can be, in what they call extreme actuality, that is, in a degree and completion of perfection that is absolutely ultimate. This is why people commonly say that a most perfect creature cannot be given. Therefore no predicate of a created thing can ever be so great that it no longer lies under the active power of the Creator, and so it is not in a passive potency to receive further degrees of perfection, which it does not yet have, but which the most free will of the all-sufficient God can give it. Now, that an infinite body admits no passive potency for wider diffusion is plain, since we showed earlier that nothing greater than the infinite can exist, and by the very nature of infinity it is not capable of even the smallest increase. Hence it follows that, if an infinite world is granted, the immense power of the almighty God could not create anew in this universe even a gnat or a flea out of nothing. And conversely, from the same hypothesis it follows that, by God's absolute power, not even a speck of dust, or any smallest particle of this universe, could be annihilated, since it implies, through

units.la: XXXIX. Divinæ Potentiæ infinitas, & liberrimum in rem creatam dominium, cum Infinita hujus extensione non consistit. per antè demonstrata, Infinitum finitâ sui parte posse diminui. Vel itaquè (ut sileam quæ istius generis plura hùc adducere possem) si mundi extensio finibus caret, ad extremum deducta fuerit Dei potentia, ejusdemque sublatum indifferens & liberrimum in suam creaturam dominium; vel, si hæc cogitare nefas sit ac summo Numine indignum, mundus extensione Infinitus nequaquam esse potest: quod demonstrandum erat.
units.tr: XXXIX. The infinity of divine power and its most free dominion over created things do not agree with the infinite extension of this world, since, as shown before, the infinite can be diminished by a finite part of itself. Or, to pass over the many other arguments of this kind that I could adduce here: if the extension of the world has no limits, then the power of God is reduced to an extreme, and his indifferent and most free dominion over his creature is taken away. Or, if it is wrong even to think this and unworthy of the supreme Deity, then the world can by no means be infinite in extension, which was to be demonstrated.

units.la: Et quid de Divina Sapientia dicemus? Ea quo modo salvari queat in productione hujus Universi, si extensionem ejus nullos limites habere statuamus, non video. Certè, extensum aliquod sine partibus concipere, pura puta contradictio est. At partes (sive finitas eas volueris, sive infinitas) in Infinito citra repugnantiam cogitari absolutè non posse, fusè jam demonstravimus rationibus firmissimis atque omni exceptione majoribus. Quid ergò? An extensionis Infinitæ à se producendæ ideam habuisse Creatorem, credendum erit? At illa sui eversiva est; nedum ut cadat in mentem perfectissimam. An verò sic habebimus, Artificem summum ad instar causæ brutæ, absque prævio tanti operis in suo intellectu exemplari, id produxisse, cujus conceptum ne quidem habere per ipsam rei naturam quiverit? Absit! Quin potius concludo, talem hujus Universi materiam creasse Deum, qualis sine contradictione concipi potest, id est, necessariò finitam. Addi hisce possent & alia, quibus ostendatur, admissâ mundi Infinitate, communicanda esse eidem absolutam Unitatem, Incomprehensibilitatem, similiaque Deo propria prædicata: quò ut deveniat, non facilè à se impetrabit devotus Deo animus. Etiam minimâ operâ demonstrari posset, Æternitatem hujus Universi cum ejusdem extensione infinita pari passu ambulare; ut illam negare nequeat, quicunque hanc tuetur: per quæ nec solus Deus æternus erit. Verùm per singula hæc non jam me diffundam, qui finire laboro hunc de Infinito laborem, ne & ipse excurrat in infinitum. Autumo, quæ hactenùs adversus hunc nullos extensionis fines habentem mundum adduximus, tùm ex natura ipsius creatæ materiæ, tùm ex perfectionibus Dei Creatoris, esse omninò talia, in quibus non possit non acquiescere, quicunque adfert animum veritatis studiosiorem, quam vorticosis Cartesii ideis ex præjudicio addictiorem. Me quod attinet, sic habeo, ipso sole meridiano clarius ex demonstratis intelligi, vix ullam in universa Philosophia opinionem è diametro magis rectæ rationis lumini adversari, vix ullam includere sequelas tot portentosas & tam in Deum Creatorem atrociter injurias, quam quæ sententia creaturæ corporeæ vel umbram tribuit Infinitatis cujuscunque.
units.tr: And what shall we say of divine wisdom? I do not see how it can be preserved in the production of this universe, if we hold that its extension has no limits. Certainly, to conceive of something extended without parts is simply a contradiction. But we have already demonstrated at length, by most firm reasons, which admit of no exception, that parts (whether you call them finite or infinite) cannot be thought of in the infinite without contradiction. What then? Must we believe that the Creator had an idea of an infinite extension to be produced by himself? But that idea destroys itself, not to mention that it could not enter the most perfect mind. Or shall we hold that the supreme Artificer, like a blind cause, without a prior exemplar of so great a work in his intellect, produced something of which by the very nature of the thing he could not even have a concept? Far from it! Rather, I conclude that God created the matter of this universe such as can be conceived without contradiction, that is, necessarily finite. Other points could be added, by which it might be shown that, if the world is granted to be infinite, absolute unity, incomprehensibility, and similar attributes proper to God would have to be communicated to it. A devout mind will not easily bring itself to that. It could also be demonstrated with very little labour that the eternity of this universe walks step by step with its infinite extension, so that whoever defends the one cannot deny the other; by which God would not be the only eternal being. But I will not go into each of these points at length, since I am trying to bring this labour on the infinite to an end, lest it too run on to infinity. I maintain that the arguments we have so far brought against this world with no limits of extension, both from the nature of created matter itself and from the perfections of God the Creator, are wholly of such a kind that anyone who approaches the matter with a mind more devoted to the search for truth, and less inclined by prejudice to the whirling ideas of Descartes, cannot but acquiesce in them. As for me, I hold that from what has been demonstrated it is clearer than the noonday sun that hardly any opinion in all of philosophy is more directly opposed to the light of right reason, and hardly any includes so many monstrous consequences and such atrocious wrongs against God the Creator, as the view that gives even a shadow of infinity of any kind to a corporeal creature.

units.la: Solvendæ supersunt difficultates, quæ contra Finitam mundi extensionem objiciuntur. Earum summa præcipuè redit ad duo capita quæ apud Cartesium occurrunt, locis ex Libris Principiorum jam suprà allegatis. Priori sic infert: Cognoscimus hunc mundum, sive substantiæ corporeæ universitatem, nullos extensionis suæ fines habere. Ubicunque enim fines illos esse fingamus, semper ultra ipsos aliqua spatia indefinitè extensa, non modo imaginamur, sed etiam vere imaginabilia, hoc est, realia, esse percipimus; ac proinde etiam substantiam corpoream indefinitè extensam in iis contineri. At ego salsissimum esse dico, ex vero ultra quoscunque mundi fines spatia extensa & VERE REALIA ESSE, percipi. Etenim quoties intellectus noster ultra fines, quibus mundum alicubi saltem terminari certò certius novit, suas diffundit cogitationes, tantùm abest, ut ibi esse veram extensionem percipiat, ut ex adverso nihil prorsùs istic esse percipiat, præter puram omnis omninò veri corporis atque extensionis carentiam. Fateor, quandò animum simul subit de Divina tum Immensitate tum Omnipotentia cogitatio, occurrit menti nostræ fundamentum concipiendi extra suppositos quoscunque mundi fines corpora: atqui non, quæ verè existant ac realia sint; sed planè contrà, quæ, cum non sint, per inexhaustam Dei vim, si sic visum fuerit, poni possunt ubi reapse nunc est nihil, ac mera duntaxat possibilis corporis negatio. Et hæc sunt illa tam nullo suo merito miserrimum in modum vexata hodiè spatia imaginaria: quorum sensus unicè est, extra nostrum hunc mundum de facto existere planè nihil, producitamen extra eundem posse corpora; quæ, si quandò producantur, realia erunt; nunc in sola nostra imaginatione, non tanquam realia, sed tanquam pure possibilia, subsistunt. Neque alicujus momenti existit, quod de extensione vera, adeoque reali corpore, in his spatiis contento, ingeminat centies ad ravim usque Cartesius. Non enim hic occurrit conceptus extensionis verè exiexistentis, sed, ut dixi, tantum merè possibilis. Quæ verò scimus merè possibilia esse, quæque nos non nisi tanquam talia cogitare probè novimus, ea cum veris ac realibus corporibus confundere, tam est ineptum & ridiculum, ac si dicam, quandò concipio, Principiorum Cartesii Libris Quatuor addi potuisse de viventibus Quintum, de homine Sextum, hoc ipso duos hosce libros me non modo mihi imaginari, sed & verè imaginabiles, hoc est, reales esse, percipere. Non invenio, quibus mentem clarius exprimam in hoc negotio, quam quibus suam, Lib. 1. Epist. xxxvi. de indefinita mundi duratione effert ipse Cartesius. Sic ille: Quod objicitur de indefinita mundi duratione, mihi videtur tantum occasionem præbere putandi, nullum posse ante mundi creationem concipi tempus, quo Deus, si voluisset, non potuisset illum creare. Neque est cur exinde quispiam concludat, fuisse re vera mundum ante tempus indefinitum creatum; quia existentia mundi actualis, sive vera, quam retro abhinc quinque aut sex millibus annorum habuit, cum ejus existentia possibili, sive imaginaria, quam antea habere potuit, necessariam connexionem non habet. Dicam ego, mutatis tantum mutandis: Quæcunque de spatiis imaginariis objiciuntur, mihi videntur tantum occasionem præbere putandi, nullum posse extra mundi fines concipi corpus, sive spatium, si mavis, quod Deus, si voluisset non potuisset extra illos creare. Neque est cur exinde quispiam concludat, fuisse re vera corpus tale, sive spatium, creatum extra fines mundi; quia existentia corporis, seu spatii actualis, sive vera, quam abhinc usque ad sui terminos mundus habet, cum spatio seu corpore possibili, sive imaginario, quod extra fines suos sibi adjiciendum habere potest, necessariam connexionem non habet. Scio, postremam periodum negare hoc ipso loco Cartesium: verùm si demonstrationem exigas, redibit vetus de extensione actuali in omni spatio conceptibili cantilena; quæ eadem facilè illi occinitur de duratione mundi, quæ potuerit antevertere id quo nunc cepit durare principium, nec ipsa absque actuali mundi existentia concipienda.
units.tr: There remain difficulties to be solved, which are raised against the finite extension of the world. Their sum comes down chiefly to two heads that occur in Descartes, in passages from the Principles already cited above. He infers the first as follows: We know that this world, or the totality of corporeal substance, has no limits to its extension. For wherever we imagine those limits to be, we perceive that beyond them there are always some spaces indefinitely extended, which we not only imagine but also perceive to be truly imaginable, that is, real; and therefore the corporeal substance indefinitely extended is contained in them. But I say that it is most absurd to perceive that extended spaces that are TRULY REAL exist beyond any limits of the world. For whenever our intellect spreads its thoughts beyond the limits by which we know with certainty that the world is bounded somewhere, it is so far from perceiving there any true extension that, on the contrary, it perceives nothing at all there except the pure absence of every true body and of extension. I grant that when the thought of the divine immensity and omnipotence comes to mind, there occurs to our minds the basis for conceiving bodies beyond whatever limits of the world we assume; but these are not things that really exist and are real, but quite the contrary: things that, since they do not exist, can by the inexhaustible power of God, if he so willed, be placed where in fact there is now nothing, and only the mere negation of a possible body. And these are those imaginary spaces, so miserably harassed today, though they deserve it in no way: their sense is only that outside our world there in fact exists nothing at all, yet God can produce bodies outside it; and these, if ever they are produced, will be real; for now they subsist only in our imagination, not as real, but as purely possible. Nor is there any weight in what Descartes repeats a hundred times, and to the point of tedium, about true extension, and therefore real body, contained in these spaces. For the concept here is not of an extension that truly exists, but, as I said, only of one that is merely possible. And to confuse what we know to be merely possible, and what we know we can only think of as such, with true and real bodies, is as silly and ridiculous as if I were to say, when I think of it, that a fifth book on living things and a sixth on man could have been added to Descartes's four books of the Principles, and by this very fact I perceive that these two books are not only imagined by me but are truly imaginable, that is, real. I do not find words by which I can express my mind on this matter more clearly than those by which Descartes himself puts forward his own, Book 1, Letter 36, on the indefinite duration of the world. He speaks thus: What is objected concerning the indefinite duration of the world seems to me only to give occasion for thinking that no time can be conceived before the creation of the world in which God, if he had willed, could not have created it. Nor is there any reason why anyone should conclude from this that the world was really created after an indefinite time; because the actual or true existence which the world has had for five or six thousand years back from now does not have a necessary connection with its possible or imaginary existence, which it could have had before. I will say, changing only what needs changing: whatever is objected concerning imaginary spaces seems to me only to give occasion for thinking that no body, or space if you prefer, can be conceived outside the limits of the world which God, if he had willed, could not have created outside them. Nor is there any reason why anyone should conclude from this that such a body or space was really created outside the limits of the world; because the actual or true existence of the body or space, which the world has from now up to its own bounds, does not have a necessary connection with the possible or imaginary space or body, which it can have to be added beyond its own limits. I know that Descartes denies the last clause at this very point; but if you demand a proof, there will return the old song about actual extension in every conceivable space; and the same song is easily sung to him about the duration of the world, which could have preceded the beginning from which it now began to endure, and which itself cannot be conceived without the actual existence of the world.

units.la: Ut verò neminem lateat, quanta sit Cartesiani ratiocinii absurditas, addam duo, quibus ut clarè & distinctè satisfaciant ejus patroni, cupio. Primum suppeditat ipsa Epistola citata, eoque se frustrà istic expedire laborat. Nimirum, eadem sequela, quà hîc impugnatur finis extensionis hujus Universi, impugnari quoque potest initium durationis. Quidni enim inferre liceat eodem arguendi modo, iisdem penè verbis: Cognoscimus hunc mundum, sive substantiae corporeae universitatem, nullum durationis suae initium habere. Quandocunque enim initium illud esse fingamus, semper ultra ipsum aliqua spatia temporalia indefinitè exte nfa, non modo imaginamur, sed etiam vere imaginabilia, hoc est, realia, esse percipimus; ac proinde etiam substantiam corpoream indefinite durantem in iis contineri. Respondeatur solidè ad hanc nostram illationem, atque erit quo ipso satisfiat argumentationi Cartefianæ. Alterum quod hoc loco notari cupiebam est, hac ratiocinatione Cartefii, fi fit vera, confici necessario, non tantum hunc mundum posse esse Infinitum, sed & Deum alium quam Infinitum producere nequivisse. Quin sequitur, ne quidem ullum finitum corpus à Deo creari posse. Si enim possit, produxerit ergò Deus hoc solum, in quo ista scribo, musæum. Atqui de hoc ipso eâdem viâ concludere dabitur, nullos id quoque extensionis fines habere. Ubicunque enim, dicam, fines illius esse video, semper ultra ipsos aliqua spatia indefinite extensa, non modo imaginor, sed etiam vere imaginabilia, hoc est, realia, esse percipio; ac proinde etiam substantiam ejus esse indefinitè extensam. Ex quibus instantiis, ad oculum patet, vel nullam omninò esse, quam tanti faciunt & invictam arbitrantur Recentiores, argumentationem hanc Cartefii; vel, fi quid valeat, câ evinci re verâ, quodlibet corpus non posse non infinitum esse simul & æternum. A quo quicunque non abhorret, viderit is, ne hac ratione rectam struat ad Atheismum viam.
units.tr: So that no one may be unaware of how great the absurdity of the Cartesian reasoning is, I will add two points, which I wish its defenders would answer clearly and distinctly. The first is supplied by the Epistle cited, where Descartes labours in vain to extricate himself. Indeed, by the same inference by which the end of this Universe's extension is here attacked, the beginning of its duration can also be attacked. For why should it not be allowed to infer, by the same mode of argument and almost in the same words: We know that this world, or the totality of corporeal substance, has no beginning of its duration. For whatever beginning we may suppose it to have, we perceive that beyond it there are always temporal spaces extended indefinitely, which we not only imagine but which are truly imaginable, that is, real; and therefore the corporeal substance, enduring indefinitely, is also contained in them. Let someone answer this inference of ours solidly, and by that very act the Cartesian argument will be satisfied. The second point I wished to note here is that, if Descartes' reasoning were true, it would necessarily follow not only that this world can be infinite, but also that God could not have produced anything other than something infinite. Indeed, it follows that not even any finite body can be created by God. For if he could, then God would surely have produced this very thing in which I am writing, a fly. Yet by the same road it will be possible to conclude of this very thing that it too has no limits of extension. For wherever I say I see its limits, I not only imagine but also perceive that beyond them there are always some spaces extended indefinitely, which are truly imaginable, that is, real; and therefore its substance is also extended indefinitely. From these instances it is plain that either the argument of Descartes, which the moderns so highly value and consider unanswerable, is wholly without any force, or, if it has any force, it proves in fact that any body whatever cannot fail to be at once infinite and eternal. Whoever does not shrink from this, let him see whether he is not by this reasoning building a straight road to atheism.
XLIII.

units.la: Altera, quam tollendis Mundi limitibus Cartefius admovet, machina hæc est. Attendentes, ait, ad infinitam Dei potentiam & bonitatem, ne vereamur nimis amplas, & pulchras, & absoluta ejus opera imaginari: sed e contrario caveamus, ne, fi quos forte limites, nobis non certo cognitos, in ipsis supponamus, non fatis magnifice de Creatoris potentia sentire videamur. Etiam caveamus, ne nimis superbè de nobis ipsis sentiamus. Quod fieret, fi quos limites, nobis nulla cognitos ratione, nec divina revelatione, mundo vellemus affingere, tanquam fi vis cogitationis ultra id quod a Deo revera factum est ferri possit. Itâ scilicet Viri modestiam simulant, cujus velo absurdam de Infinito mundo ideam pallient, qui ipsi in enarrandis Universi versi hujus orginibus ex materia & motu ad stuporem usque exi‑stunt temerarii & audaces, tantâque de omnium ac singularum in eo partium fabrica & structura definiunt confidentiâ, ut majori non possint, si vel Deo à consiliis fuissent. Rem quod attinet, magna procul dubio temeritas est quorundam Mathematicorum, istó supercilio præcisam mundi magnitudinem definientium, ac si spithama vastissima ejus spatia fuissent dimensi; de quibus rectè Plinius, Lib. II. Cap. I. Furor est, mensuram ejus animo quosdam agitasse, atque prodere ausus. Verùm cum istiusmodi deliriis nihil habet commune nostra assertio, ad nullam determinatam quantitatem descendens, subsistensque duntaxat in generali thesi, de agnoscendis saltem aliquibus in hoc Universo limitibus, ubicunque demùm isti fuerint, & quantumcunque ab invicem distent, Quam veritatem, juxta rectæ rationis non uno modo firmissimè eam persuadentis dictamen, agnoscere non velle, metu nescio cujus superbiæ, aut defectûs erga magnificentiam Divinam reverentiæ, præposteræ est modestiæ. An verò etiam de se superbè, de Creatoris potentia non satis magnificè, sentit, qui negat muscam esse concipiendam ad instar elephantis? Profectò conceptus rebus ipsis conformes formare, atque opera Dei concipere qualia se produ‑xisse ipse Creator lumine rationis manifestum facit, ea demùm vera sapientia est. Quumque operum divinorum norma & mensura sit, non absoluta Dei potentia, verùm liberrima ejusdem voluntas, possumus utique, si eis plus tribuamus perfectionis, quam largiri illis voluit Creator, possumus, inquam, etiam hac parte à vero aberrare, illa nobis imaginando ampla nimis, & pulchra, & absoluta: quique hic cogitationum suarum excessum ad id quod rei naturæ congruum est restringit, nullâ parte injurius existit in Deum, quippe qui non ideò definit Illum habere Optimum atque Maximum. Quid? Quod ipsi non sentiant sat magnificè de Creatoris potentia & bonitate, qui eam creaturæ productione exhaustam esse fateri coguntur: uti coguntur, qui mundi extensionem finitam negant; quemadmodum ostendimus. Adde, de Opificis bonitate & potentia, nec non de operis ipsius amplitudine, pulchritudine & perfectione, nec potissimùm, nec semper, judican‑dum esse ex magnitudine molis. In minimo non raro ars maxi‑ ma: magisque relucent sapientiæ, potentiæ & bonitatis Divinæ radii ( si nobis homuncionibus fas sit tantarum rerum instituere comparationes ) in unius hominis ad imaginem Dei conditi minuta machina, quam in totius macrocosmi amplissima structura. Deniquè, constat sua Deo bonitas infinita & potentia, sua huic Universo amplitudo, pulchritudo, & perfectio, etsi id ab æterno extitisse non concipiamus; cur minus, si extensione infinitum negemus? An verò neque hîc sat magnificè cogitabimus de Creatoris potentia & bonitate, nisi, ut extensionis, ita quoque durationis principium omne Universo detrahamus? An quoque hîc de nobis ipsis sentiemus superbè, tanquam si vis nostræ cogitationis, ultra id quod à Deo re verâ factum est, ferri possit? Mirum, nili probent hi modestiæ patroni, & tam sollicitæ de Creatoris magnificentia animæ, quæ de hoc Universo Plinius, Loc. cit. Mundum numen esse credi par est, aeternum, immensum, neque genitum, neque interiturum unquam. Hujus extera indagare, nec interest hominum, nec capit humana conjectura mentis. Sacer est, aeternus, immensus, totus in toto, imo vero ipse totum, &c. Quæ quò tendant, nemo ignorat, qui Atheismum Plinii non ignorat.
units.tr: The second contrivance, which Descartes brings to bear in removing the limits of the world, is this. Let us attend, he says, to the infinite power and goodness of God, and not be afraid to imagine his works as very large, and beautiful, and perfect. On the contrary, let us take care that, if we suppose in them some limits which we do not know for certain, we do not seem to think unworthily of the power of the Creator. Let us also take care not to think too proudly of ourselves. This would happen if we chose to attribute to the world limits which we know by no reason, nor by divine revelation, as though the power of our thought could be carried beyond what has really been made by God. Thus, of course, they put on the appearance of modesty, by which they try to cover up their absurd idea of an infinite world, while they themselves, in describing the origins of this turning universe from matter and motion, are bold and daring to the point of astonishment, and they define the construction and structure of all and each of its parts with such confidence that they could not be more certain if they had been counsellors of God. As to the matter, there is surely great rashness in certain mathematicians who, with this haughty air, define the precise magnitude of the world, as if they had measured its vast spaces with a span. Of them Pliny rightly says: Lib. II. Cap. I. It is madness for some to have agitated in their minds its measure, and to have dared to publish it. But our assertion has nothing in common with such follies. It descends to no determinate quantity, and rests merely on the general thesis that at least some limits must be acknowledged in this Universe, wherever they may be and however far apart they may be. To be unwilling to acknowledge this truth, which right reason, in more than one way, most firmly persuades us of, out of fear of I know not what pride, or from a reverence that is deficient towards the divine magnificence, is a misplaced modesty. Indeed, does he think proudly of himself, or unworthily of the power of the Creator, who denies that a fly is to be conceived on the scale of an elephant? Certainly, to form concepts conformable to the things themselves, and to conceive the works of God as the Creator himself has made manifest to the light of reason that he produced them, that is true wisdom. And since the rule and measure of the divine works is not the absolute power of God but his most free will, we can indeed, if we attribute to them more perfection than the Creator was willing to bestow upon them, go astray in this respect too, by imagining them too large, and beautiful, and perfect. And he who here restricts the excess of his thoughts to what agrees with the nature of the thing does no wrong to God in any part, since he does not for that reason define that God has the Best and the Greatest. What then? Do not those who are forced to confess that the power of the Creator is exhausted by the production of the creature think unworthily of his power and goodness? So too are those forced who deny the finite extension of the world, as we have shown. Add that the goodness and power of the Maker, and likewise the greatness, beauty and perfection of the work itself, are to be judged neither chiefly nor always by the size of the mass. Often the greatest art is in the smallest thing, and the rays of divine wisdom, power and goodness (if it is permitted us, little men that we are, to make comparisons of such great things) shine more brightly in the minute mechanism of one man made in the image of God than in the vast structure of the whole macrocosm. Finally, it is established that God's goodness and power are infinite, and this Universe's greatness, beauty and perfection are its own, even though we do not conceive that these existed from eternity; why then should we deny them less, if we deny that it is infinite in extension? Or shall we not think magnificently enough here of the Creator's power and goodness, unless we also strip the Universe of every beginning of duration, as well as of extension? Or shall we here also think proudly of ourselves, as though the power of our thought could be carried beyond what has really been made by God? It would be strange if these patrons of modesty, and souls so anxious for the magnificence of the Creator, did not approve what Pliny says of this Universe: Loc. cit. It is fitting to believe the world to be a god, eternal, immense, neither begotten nor destined ever to perish. To investigate its outside is neither the business of men nor within the grasp of human conjecture. It is holy, eternal, immense, wholly in the whole, nay indeed itself the whole, etc. Where these words tend, no one is unaware who is not unaware of the atheism of Pliny.

units.la: Aliæ quædam solvendæ superstunt argutiæ, quæ quandoquè pro Infinita hujus Universi mole à quibusdam adferuntur. Ajunt: Quicquid finitum est, ab aliquo ambiente finitur & terminatur. Itaque, si sit finitus mundus, ultra ejus extremitates corpus aliquod, cujus complexu & circuitu terminctur, admittere erit necesse. Id verò contradictorium est. Quandoquidem enim omne corpus est pars Universi, nunquam cogitari potest corpus finiens mundum, quin hoc ipso cogitetur mundus longius adhuc extensus, idest, re verâ nondum finitus. Ex quibus concludunt, sine repugnantia mundum finitum concipi non posse. Si quid autem video, eadem hæc prorsùs ratio est cum ea, quâ jam olim Epicurus probare nitebatur, Universum hoc esse Infinitum. Ciceronem audiamus, Lib. II. de Divinat. Videsne Epicurum, quem hebetem & rudem dicere solent Stoici, quemadmodum, quod in natura rerum Omne esse dicimus, id infinitum esse concluserit? Quod finitum est, inquit, habet extremum. Quis hoc non dederit? Quod habet extremum, id cernitur ex alio extrinsecus. Ne hoc quidem negari potest. Omne igitur, cum nihil habeat extremum, infinitum
units.tr: There remain some other subtleties to be answered, which are sometimes brought forward by certain people in support of the infinite mass of this Universe. They say: Whatever is finite is bounded and terminated by some surrounding thing. Therefore, if the world is finite, it will be necessary to admit some body beyond its extremities, by whose embrace and circuit it is terminated. But this is self-contradictory. For since every body is a part of the Universe, a body terminating the world can never be conceived without thereby conceiving the world extended still further, that is, in truth not yet finite. From these things they conclude that a finite world cannot be conceived without contradiction. But if I see anything, this reasoning is exactly the same as that by which Epicurus long ago tried to prove that this Universe is infinite. Let us hear Cicero, Lib. II. de Divinat.: Do you see how Epicurus, whom the Stoics are accustomed to call dull and crude, concluded, as to what we say in the nature of things is all, that it is infinite? What is finite, he says, has an extremity. Who would not grant this? What has an extremity is seen from something else outside it. This too cannot be denied. Therefore the All, since it has no extremity, is infinite.

units.la: XLIV. Non ad extensionem quamlibet finiendam aliud corpus ambiens cum Epicuro admittere necessum est: nitum sit necesse est. Videsne, ut ad rem dubiam concessis rebus pervenerit? Accinit vates Epicureus; cujus quaedam hic referam; ut intelligat unusquisque, quibuscum antiquatis, atque orbi erudito explosis dudum, à Novatoribus nuper instauratis, conceptibus, pugnandum hodie sit. Sic ille, Lib. 1. de Rer. Nat. Omne quod est igitur, nulla regione viarum Finitum'st: namque extremum debebat habere. Extremum porro nullius posse videtur Esse, nisi ultra sit quod finiat, ut videatur, Quo non longius haec sensus natura sequatur. Nunc extra summum quoniam nil esse fatendum est, Non habet extremum: caret ergo fine modoque. Nec refert quibus adsistas regionibus ejus, Usque adeo quem quisque locum possedit, in omneis Tantundem partes infinitum omne relinquit.
units.tr: XLIV. It is not necessary, with Epicurus, to admit some other body surrounding it in order to limit any extension whatever: it must be finite. Do you see how, from matters conceded, he arrived at a doubtful point? The Epicurean bard sings. I shall quote some of his lines here, so that everyone may understand against which concepts we must contend today. These were long since worn out and driven from the learned world, and have lately been revived by the Innovators. Thus he writes, Lib. 1. de Rer. Nat.: Whatever exists, therefore, is not finite in any region of space, for it would have to have an end. But nothing can have an end unless there is something beyond it that bounds it, and so it seems that sense cannot follow the thing further. Now since we must confess that there is nothing outside the whole, it has no end, and therefore lacks limit and measure. Nor does it matter in which regions you stand; each place that anyone occupies leaves the whole infinite to the same extent in every direction.

units.la: Quo eodem pertinent, quae post pauca sequuntur: Postremo ante oculos rem res finire videtur: Aër disjepit colleis, atque aëra montes, Terra mare, & contra mare terra terminat omneis. Omne quidem vero nihil est quod finiat extra.
units.tr: To the same point belong the lines that follow a little later: Lastly, before our eyes one thing seems to bound another: air separates the hills, and the mountains the air, earth bounds the sea, and in turn the sea the earth. Yet the All, which is nothing, has nothing outside it to bound it.

units.la: Usque adeo passim patet ingens copia rebus
units.tr: Everywhere, so widely, the vast abundance of things spreads out

units.la: Finibus exemtis in cunctas undique partes. Facilis autem est universæ difficultatis solutio attendenti, salsissimum esse, quod ceu fundamentum huic ratiocinio substernitur, videlicet, id postulare rei finitæ finitudinem ut extrinseco quo ambiente terminetur. Equidem, in conceptu finitatis, qua tali, includitur nihil, quam rem non extendi quousque extendi potest. Cujus causa non est quid ambiens, sed arbitrium efficientis, rei extensionem tantam, non majorem, tribuentis. Itaque unaquæque res suis ipsa definitur perfectionis extremitatibus, non termino ambeuntis. Quod idem in mundo obtinet; qui terminatur ibi, ubi nullum amplius corpus producere Deo Creatori placuit. Etenim pone, hanc solam terram, quanta nunc existit, creasse Deum præterea nihil, finita illa erit certò certius, nec tamen ambiente corpore circumscripta. Nisi quis tueri malit, corpus nullum à Deo potuisse produci, nisi simul hoc ambiens infinita extensio producta fuerit. De quo absurdo jam antè dictum. Sed
units.tr: with its boundaries removed, on every side into all parts. The solution of the whole difficulty is easy for one who attends to it: the premise that is laid down as the foundation of this reasoning is utterly false, namely that the finitude of a finite thing requires that it be terminated by some external surrounding body. Indeed, the concept of finitude, as such, includes nothing except that a thing is not extended as far as it could be extended. The cause of this is not a surrounding thing but the will of the efficient cause, which grants to the thing an extension so great and no greater. Thus each thing is defined by the extremities of its own perfection, not by the boundary of what surrounds it. The same holds for the world, which is bounded where God the Creator was pleased to produce no further body. For suppose that God created only this earth, as large as it now is, and nothing besides; it would certainly be finite, and yet not circumscribed by any surrounding body. Unless someone prefers to maintain that no body could have been produced by God unless at the same time an infinite extension surrounding it had been produced. This absurdity has been dealt with already above. But

units.la: XLV. Sed aperiendus nonnihil clarius fons argumentationis, non nisi ex infantili præjudicio ortum trahentis. Nimirùm ab ineunte ætate hi observarunt, cum Lucretio, montes cingi æræ, terras mari, nullamque Universi partem nobis esse conspicuam, cujus terminatam superficiem non tangat proximè aliud corpus vicinum. Indè de extremis mundi partibus idem cogitare instituerunt. Atqui perperam; dum ipsam Finitatem ab eo quod per accidens in hoc universo cum comitatur non distinxerunt satis. Per accidens, dico: quamvis enim quodcunque ab alio ambitur finitum sit, non tamen idcirco finitum est, quia ab alio ambitur. Nam non ideò esse mutuo tangunt Universi partes, ut altera alterius diffusioni ponat limites (ad quos sufficit mera ulterioris extensionis carentia) verum quia mediantibus causis secundis rerum naturalium operationes peragi voluit Deus. Quum enim solo motu intervenient corpus in corpus agat, nec ullus possit esse corporis moti in aliud quiescens influxus, nisi per contactum ei fuerit approximatum, planè necesse fuit, partes hujus universi contiguas esse, si, ex intentione Dei Creatoris, coöperaturæ sint omnes, tanquam causæ secundæ, in mutuum auxilium ad totius universi conservationem. Atque hæc vera causa est, cur quævis corpora in hoc universo vicinis aliis corporibus cingantur: non verò eorundem finitas, quæ, sublato etiam quovis ambiente, eadem planè manet. Sufficit enim ad corporis finitatem, ut id tantum non sit quantum esse potest. Cæterùm, an quod ei addi potuisset existat re verà, & corpus finitum tangat, an saltem existere idque tangere possit, nihil omninò refert. Atque hoc posteriùs in mundo obtinet: qui quamvis à nullo corpore ambiatur, finitus nihilominus est, quia, uti suprà docuimus, magnitudini ejus potest fieri accessio, adeòque ea tanta non est, quanta esse potest: quod unum prædicatum hic sufficit, tanquam Finitati proprium & essentiale; quale non est ab extrinseco tangi.
units.tr: XLV. But the source of the argument, which arises from nothing but childish prejudice, must be opened somewhat more clearly. Indeed, from early age people have observed, together with Lucretius, that mountains are surrounded by air, lands by sea, and that no part of the Universe is visible to us whose bounded surface is not touched immediately by another neighbouring body. From this they came to think the same about the extreme parts of the world. But they reason wrongly, since they have not sufficiently distinguished finitude itself from what accompanies it in this universe only by accident. By accident, I say: for although whatever is surrounded by another is finite, it is not therefore finite because it is surrounded by another. For the parts of the Universe do not touch one another so that one sets limits to the diffusion of the other (for a mere lack of further extension suffices for those limits), but because God willed that the operations of natural things be carried out by means of secondary causes. For since a body can act upon a body only by motion, and no influence of a moved body upon a resting one is possible unless it has been brought near by contact, it was plainly necessary that the parts of this universe be contiguous, if, by the intention of God the Creator, all of them were to co-operate, as secondary causes, in mutual aid for the preservation of the whole universe. And this is the true cause why any bodies in this universe are surrounded by other neighbouring bodies; not, however, their finitude, which remains exactly the same even if every surrounding thing is removed. For it is enough for a body's finitude that it is not as large as it can be. Moreover, whether that which could have been added to it actually exists and touches the finite body, or only could exist and touch it, makes no difference at all. And this holds for the world as well: although it is surrounded by no body, it is nonetheless finite, because, as we have taught above, its magnitude can be increased, and so it is not as great as it can be. This one predicate suffices here as proper and essential to finitude; being touched from outside is not such a predicate.

units.la: XLVI. Nec denique præsidium hîc est in Divina Omnipotentia junçta cum ejusdem Immensitate; unde quidam hunc in modum argumentantur. Deus, ajunt, ubicunque existit, inibi potest operari, & corpus extra se producere: At verò ipse existit ubicunque corpus est vel esse potest; Ergò etiam potest corpus producere, ubicunque corpus esse potest. Quodcunque autem corpus est ubicunquè corpus esse potest, id necessariò infinitum est: si enim finitum supponatur, nondum est ubicunquè corpus esse poteft. Atque hoc ratiocinio arbitrantur confici corpus Infinitæ extensionis, si non detur, saltem dari posse. At, si sat diligenter totum hoc expendamus, mera est sophisticatio, orta ex conjunctione tu ubicunque corpus esse potest, modò cum potentia divina, modò cum producti corporis existentia. Quamvis enim recte dicas, Deus ubicunque potest creare corpus; non tamen recte dixeris, Deus potest creare corpus ubicunque existens: illud enim ex perfectione Divina fluere, facilè demonstratur; hoc verò cum corporis natura non consistere, jam antè ostendimus. Ut ista duo toto cœlo sint diversa. Itaquè potest Deus distributivè in quolibet spatio conceptibili creare corpus finitum; at non ideò collectivè in omni simul spatio conceptibili potest creare corpus Infinitum. Planè, quemadmodum Deus potuit producere mundum quandocunquè Ipse extitit ab æterno: ab æterno nimirùm potuit; sed non potuit condere mundum ab æterno existentem. Quapropter, uti æternus Deus ab æterno potuit condere cum quovis temporis initio mundum non-æternum; itâ Immensus Deus in immensum potest condere in quolibet spatio vel ubi mundum Finitum.
units.tr: XLVI. Nor finally is there any support here in the divine omnipotence joined with the immensity of God; from which some argue in this way. God, they say, wherever he exists, can operate there and produce a body outside himself. But he exists wherever a body is or can be. Therefore he can also produce a body wherever a body can be. Now whatever body is, wherever a body can be, is necessarily infinite: for if it is supposed to be finite, then it is not yet wherever a body can be. By this reasoning they think that a body of infinite extension is established, if it is not given, at least that it can be given. But if we weigh the whole of this carefully enough, it is mere sophistry, arising from the conjoining of that a body can be anywhere, now with divine power, now with the existence of the produced body. For although you may rightly say that God can create a body anywhere, you may not rightly say that God can create a body existing anywhere: the former is easily shown to flow from divine perfection, while the latter is not consistent with the nature of body, as we have already shown above. So these two things are wholly different. Thus God can create a finite body distributively in any conceivable space; but he cannot therefore create collectively an infinite body in all conceivable space at once. Just as God could produce the world at whatever time he existed from eternity: he could, of course, have done so from eternity; but he could not have founded a world existing from eternity. Therefore, just as the eternal God could from eternity found a non-eternal world with any beginning of time, so the immense God can found a finite world in immensity, or in any place whatever.

units.la: Instabis forte: Potest Deus tamen creare tantum corpus quantum creare potest. Supponamus ergò, tantum creare ipso facto, quantum creare potest; illud vel finitum erit, vel infinitum. Non finitum; quia quolibet finito potest à Deo fieri majus. Ergò Infinitum. Potest itaquè Deus producere corpus infinitum. Ut verbo expediam: negò unquam ex vero dici posse, Deum tantum corpus creasse, quantum creare potest; quandoquidem id non minus perfectibilitati creaturæ quam inexhaustæ perfectioni Divinæ repugnat; de quibus suprà actum est abundè. Ut autem clarè deprehendatur, quam nihil solidi sit in hoc argumento, tantùm attendamus has illi similes illationes. Puta: Deus creare potest tantum corpus finitum, quantum potest creare. Supponamus ergò tantum creare ipso facto, quantum creare potest: illud vel finitum erit, vel infinitum. Non finitum, alias Deus non posset facere majus finito; quod absurdum. Ergò corpus illud finitum erit Infinitum. En contradictionem explicitam! Iterùm dicam: Deus potest tantum quadrangulum creare quantum potest. Crect ergò : illud vel finitum erit, vel infinitum. Non finitum* sic enim nondum maximum esset, cum quovis finito possit fieri majus. Ergò quadrangulum fieri poterit infinitum. Quis concedat ? Rursùm arguam : Deus potest creare spiritum tam perfectum, quam creare potest. Crect ergò : ille vel finitus crit, vel infinitus. Non finitus; is enim tam perfectus non est quam esse potest. Ergò Deus creare potest spiritum infinitè perfectum; id est, alium Deum. Absurdissimè ! Sufficiunt hæ instantiæ, ad demonstrandum, quam sit nullarum virium hæc argutatio, pro extensione mundi quæ saltem Infinita esse possit.
units.tr: You will perhaps object: God can nevertheless create just as much body as he is able to create. Let us then suppose that he in fact creates as much as he can create; that will be either finite or infinite. Not finite, because to any finite amount God could make something greater. Therefore infinite. Thus God can produce an infinite body. To put it briefly: I deny that it can ever truly be said that God has created as much body as he can create, since this contradicts the perfectibility of the creature no less than the inexhaustible perfection of God, about which we have spoken at length above. But so that it may clearly be seen how little solid there is in this argument, let us consider inferences similar to it. Suppose: God can create as much finite body as he can create. Let us then suppose that he in fact creates as much as he can create: that will be either finite or infinite. Not finite, otherwise God could not make anything greater than the finite; which is absurd. Therefore that finite body will be infinite. Behold an explicit contradiction! Again I say: God can create as large a square as he can create. He creates it; that will be either finite or infinite. Not finite, for thus it would not yet be the largest, since to any finite size something larger can be made. Therefore a square will be able to become infinite. Who would grant this? Again I shall argue: God can create a spirit as perfect as he can create. He creates it; that will be either finite or infinite. Not finite, for it is not as perfect as it can be. Therefore God can create a spirit infinitely perfect, that is, another God. Most absurd! These examples are enough to show how devoid of any real strength is this subtle argument for an extension of the world that could at least be infinite.

units.la: Desino alia addere. Satis est, per hactenùs disputata lascivienti hujus Universi extensioni præfixos esse fines, ubicunquè locorum illi fuerint; solique Deo Optimo Maximo vindicatam stare Infinitatis gloriam. Tantùm coronidis loco recolligam quædam nostræ demonstrationis Porismata, quorum & in ipso tractatu subindè facta est mentio. Quamobrem & tribus verbis ea notasse habebo satis. Ex mundi nostri extensione finita, eâque concipiendâ tanquam tali, sequitur : I. Recte concipi spatia imaginaria : i. e. extra Universi fines, ubi nunc nihil est, corpora quædam per omnipotentiam divinam produci posse. II. Dari Posse plures mundos: si enim aliquod corpus extra hoc universum esse queat, quid ni corporum Systema, nostro, in quo vivimus, per omnia simile; quod ipsum Mundus dicitur. III. Imò, ex natura non constare, hunc mundum tantùm esse unum : cum ejus unitas fluat non ex natura rei, sed ex libera Divinæ voluntatis determinatione. IV. Mundo huic tribui posse Ubiquitatem, non Immensitatem; quatenus hæc Infinitatem involvit, non ista. V. Per absolutam potentiam posse dari vacuum: cum enim extra mundum actu sit corporis carentia negativa, cur non in ipso, absolutè loquendo, esse queat absentia ejusdem privativa ? VI. Mundum mechanicum ex vorticibus compositum adversari legibus motûs : quatenus partes extremorum vorticum, mox etiam proximorum, à centro sui motus, juxta naturæ legem, recedentes, necessariò per inane dissilirent. Quæ omnia cum sint clara & distincta, viderint quotquot Universi extensionem Infinitam admittere nolunt, num Cartesiani hic esse possint, & amplecti Physicam, cujus, nullos agnoscere in mundi extensione fines, præcipua basis est & fundamentum.
units.tr: I cease to add other matters. It is enough, from what has been argued so far, that limits have been set to the wanton extension of this Universe, wherever they may lie, and that the glory of Infinity stands claimed for God alone, Best and Greatest. Merely by way of a crown, I will gather up some of the corollaries of our demonstration, which were also mentioned from time to time in the treatise itself. Therefore I shall consider it enough to note them in three words. From the finite extension of our world, and from conceiving it as such, it follows: I. That imaginary spaces are rightly conceived: that is, that certain bodies could be produced by divine omnipotence beyond the bounds of the Universe, where at present there is nothing. II. That several worlds can exist: for if some body can exist outside this universe, why not a system of bodies, wholly like our own, in which we live, which itself is called a world? III. Indeed, it does not follow from nature that this world is only one: since its unity flows not from the nature of the thing but from the free determination of the divine will. IV. That Ubiquity, not Immensity, can be attributed to this world; inasmuch as the latter involves infinity, the former does not. V. That by absolute power a vacuum can exist: for since outside the world there is actually a negative lack of body, why, speaking absolutely, could not a privative absence of body exist within it? VI. That the mechanical world, composed of vortices, is contrary to the laws of motion: inasmuch as the parts of the outermost vortices, and soon also of the nearer ones, withdrawing from the centre of their motion according to the law of nature, would necessarily leap apart into the void. Since all these points are clear and distinct, let those who are unwilling to admit the infinite extension of the Universe consider whether Cartesians can exist here at all, and embrace a physics whose chief basis and foundation is that it recognises no limits in the extension of the world.

units.la: * Non finitum sic enim nondum maximum esset
units.tr: * For what is not finite would thus not yet be greatest.
A Disquisition on the Nowhereness of Spirits.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Nullibitatis nomen merito in hac Disquisitione usurpatum, neque sine exemplo. II. Nullibismi spiritwithuum assertor primarius Cartesius: III. Contendens, non nisi operationum respectu spiritus dici posse Alicubi esse. IV. Præivit olim hac sententia Cartesio Valentinus Weigelius. V. Opinionis Weigelianæ atque Cartesianæ consensus. VI. Ex operationibus spirituum in aliquo Ubi essentialis eorundem in illo præsentia infertur. VII. Frustra ad actionem spiritus transeuntem ejus Alicubi restringi. VIII. Iis imprimis, qui motus corporis cum actione spiritus nihil habere per se commercii opinantur. IX. Arctissima mentis humanæ cum corpore conjunctio præsentiam spiritus essentialem valide adstruit. X. Nec non mystica, quam dictat fides, duarum naturarum in eandem Christi personam unio. XI. Essentialem Dei Omnipræsentiam Nullibistica sententia palam evertit. XII. Cœlumque beatorum inducit reperiendum nusquam locorum. XIII. Nequaquam ex vulgi errore natum axioma, Omne quod est, Alicubi est.
units.tr: I. The name "Nullibity" is rightly used in this Disquisition, and not without precedent. II. The chief advocate of the nullibism of spirits is Descartes: III. contending that spirit can be said to be somewhere only with respect to its operations. IV. Valentinus Weigel held this opinion before Descartes. V. The agreement of the Weigelian and Cartesian opinions. VI. From the operations of spirits in some place, their essential presence in that place is inferred. VII. It is in vain to restrict the place of a spirit to its transient action. VIII. Especially to those who think that bodily motion has no intrinsic connection with the action of spirit. IX. The closest conjunction of the human mind with the body powerfully establishes the essential presence of spirit. X. And also the mystical union of the two natures in the one person of Christ, as faith dictates. XI. The Nullibist view openly overturns God's essential omnipresence. XII. It also introduces a heaven of the blessed to be found nowhere in place. XIII. The axiom "Whatever is, is somewhere" is by no means born of popular error.

units.la: XIV. Neque spirituum Ubi obstat spatium, quod cum corpore sit idem. XV. Quale sit spiritum Alicubi, & quâ ratione nobis concipiendum? XVI. Spirituum Alicubi non tollit non-extensa illorum natura. XVII. Forgæi in hanc rem dictum, & quædam in id observatiunculæ. XVIII. Corporis, cui spiritus coëxistit, aucta vel diminuta quantitas hujus Alicubi nil præjudicat. XIX. Solo spiritu, nullo corpore, existente, etiam illi suum competit Ubi; & quo modo? XX. Actio spiritus transiens, cum hic aut illic esse non facit, sed tantùm indicat. XXI. Nullibiftis nulla de affectis sibi opinionibus querelarum causa. XXII. H. Mori in Nullibiftas dicto Disquisitio clauditur.
units.tr: XIV. Nor does space, which is the same as body, stand in the way of the where of spirits. XV. What kind of thing is it for a spirit to be somewhere, and in what way are we to conceive it? XVI. The non-extended nature of spirits does not remove their being somewhere. XVII. Forgaeus's saying on this matter, and some small observations on it. XVIII. An increase or decrease in the quantity of the body with which the spirit coexists does nothing to prejudice this somewhere. XIX. With only the spirit existing and no body, it too has its own where; and in what way? XX. The transient action of a spirit, when it does not make it here or there, but only indicates it. XXI. The Nullibists have no cause for complaint about the opinions attributed to them. XXII. The Disquisition closes with H. More's saying against the Nullibists.

units.la: Omnia rebus & conceptibus, quibus significandis inserviunt, convenientia esse oportet. Quapropter, quùm hâc Dissertatione examinare constituissem illam quorundam assertionem, quâ, Spiritus esse Nullibi, contendunt, conceptui novo subtilissimo exprimendo conveniens omninò & dignus videbatur novus titulus. Neque res est absque exemplo. Simili planè aliorum errori, nec minus prodigioso, sed abeunti prorsùs in oppositum, de Omnipræsentia corporis Christi, notum est deberi voces Ubiquitatis, Ubiquitismi, ac Ubiquitistarum, in scholis Thelogorum tritissimas. Pari in casu pari jure hic uti quis vetet? Maximè cùm hac ipsa quoquè in re præeuntes nobis habeamus alios. Audiamus, si lubet, Henricum Morum, Enchirid. Metaph. Part. I. Cap. xxvii. Is uti quosdam Philosophos ait Spiritus naturam sic describere, quasi sit totus in toto, & totus in qualibet sui spatii parte, itâ aliam quoque esse sententiam, atque huic è diametro oppositam, eorum „qui, „tametsi Res incorporeas in rerum natura existere non gravatè agnoscunt, eas tamen in tota rerum Universitate Nusquam esse, „perquam acriter contendunt. Quæ quidem opinio, quanquam „vel prima fronte satis ridicula videtur, ab ejus tamen Assertori‐„bus, non sine aliquo fastu ac supercilio, aut occulto saltem con‐„temptu aliorum philosophorum, qui aliter sentiunt, tanquam „minus Intellectualium, & Imaginationi nimium quantum indul‐„gentium, mordicus tenetur. Hi igitur, propterea quod Spi‐„ritus Nullibi esse tam audacter affirmant, Nullibiftarum titulum„ sibi merito conciliaverunt.
units.tr: Everything ought to agree with the things and the concepts they serve to signify. Therefore, when I had decided to examine in this dissertation that assertion of certain people, by which they contend that spirits are nowhere, a new title seemed wholly fitting and worthy for expressing this most subtle new concept. Nor is the matter without precedent. For a quite similar error of others, no less monstrous but veering entirely to the opposite extreme, concerning the omnipresence of Christ's body, it is well known that the words Ubiquity, Ubiquitism and Ubiquitarians, most common in theological schools, were coined. In a similar case, why should anyone forbid using the same right here? Especially since we have others going before us in this very matter. Let us listen, if you please, to Henry More, Enchiridion Metaphysicum, Part I, chapter xxvii. He says that just as some philosophers describe the nature of spirit as if it were wholly in the whole and wholly in every part of its space, so there is another opinion, diametrically opposed to this, held by "those who, although they do not hesitate to acknowledge that incorporeal things exist in the nature of things, nevertheless contend most vigorously that they are nowhere in the whole universe of things. This opinion, although even at first sight it seems quite ridiculous, is nevertheless held stubbornly by its advocates, not without some haughtiness and arrogance, or at least hidden contempt for other philosophers who think otherwise, as being 'less intellectual and too much indulgent to imagination.' Therefore these men, because they so boldly affirm that spirit is nowhere, have rightly earned for themselves the title of Nullibists."

units.la: Novi dogmatis Auctorem primum & fautores idem ibidem hunc in modum describere pergit: „Nullibiftarum quidem, ait, pri‐ „mus Author exstitisse videtur festivum illud caput Renatus Carte‐„sius, qui, jocularibus suis Meditationibus Metaphysicis, In‐„geniis satis sobriis alias atque acutis, sed in hac parte ob nimiam Cartesii admirationem minus cautis, facultates rationales ita lu‐„xavit ac distorsit, ut partim commentitia ac praestigiosa subtilitate,„partim authoritate deceptí, ea sibi persuaserint verissima clarissi‐„maque esse, quae, nisi hisce praejudiciis occæcati essent, nun‐„ quam existimaturi fuissent possibilia. Itaque tam sedulò ab ipso„edocti & diligenter instructi, ut à nullo, ne potentissimo qui‐„dem & malignissimo deceptore Deo, falli possent, non satis sibi„caverunt, nec à mero homine, sed perfacto quidem, quan‐„quam astuto satis & abstruso, decipcrentur illuderenturque.„ Quemadmodum clarè patebit, postquam rationes hujus Opinio‐„ nis Nullibiftarum ab ipsa stirpe exquisivimus. Hoc idem praesta‐re nobis propositum est: verum itâ, ut hujus Auctoris rationes, nec non hypotheses ejusdem de Spiritu extenso, similesque, minimè adoptemus. Eas intactas suo linquimus loco ac pretio: contenti eundem errorem confutasse argumentis magis firmis ac solidis, quam multis fortasse videbuntur illa Mori.
units.tr: "The first author of this new dogma and its supporters, he goes on to describe in this way: 'The first author of the Nullibists seems to have been that witty fellow René Descartes, who, in his playful Metaphysical Meditations, dislocated and distorted the rational faculties of men who are otherwise fairly sober and sharp, but in this matter less cautious through excessive admiration for Descartes. So, partly deceived by a fictitious and deceptive subtlety, partly by his authority, they persuaded themselves that those things were most true and most clear which, unless they had been blinded by these prejudices, they would never have thought possible. And so, being so diligently taught and carefully instructed by him that they could not be deceived by anyone, not even by the most powerful and most malicious deceiver, God, they did not take sufficient care for themselves, and they were deceived and mocked not by a mere man, but by a thoroughly made-up one, though fairly clever and abstruse.' As will be clearly shown, after we have sought out the reasons for this opinion of the Nullibists from its very root. It is our purpose to do the same; but in such a way that we do not at all adopt this author's reasons, nor his hypotheses about extended spirit and similar ones. We leave them untouched in their place and value, content to have refuted the same error with arguments more firm and solid than those of More will perhaps seem to many."

units.la: Sed necessarium fuerit ante omnia rectè percepisse Nullibiftarum mentem; quae abunde & clarè innotescit ex iis, quae occurrunt apud Claubergium, de Cognit. Dei & nostri, Exercitat. LXV t. ubi ad eam, quam sibi pertractandam istic sumit, Quaestionem, An omne quod est, Alicubi sit; adeo ut hoc axioma à Deo & Creatura (convenientius iis, quae apud ipsum sequuntur, dixisset, à Spiritu & Corpore) sit abstractum? inter alia respondet, §. 2. Subjectum de quo dicitur quod sit Alicubi, non est res intellectualis seu incorporea, sed corporea tantum, sive materialis, quae in longum, latum & proprofundum est extensa. Et §. 16. Res intellectuales non possunt aliter dici esse Alicubi, quam efficaciter agendo. In eandem sententiam alii asserunt, Spiritum in se consideratum non posse dici Hic esse, aut Illic, aut Ubique; quippe qui conceptus ei non magis quadrent, quam coloris aut saporis. Atque ideò secundum verborum & conceptuum proprietatem non verè dici, ajunt, Spiritum per suam essentiam Hic, Illic, aut Ubique esse; sed tantùm per operationem, quam circa corpus exerit, acquirere denominationem, quòd Hic sit aut Illic: corpore verò non dato, non posse de eo rectè dici, quod Hic aut Illic existant. Atque hoc ipsum est, quod rejicimus, cujusque antithesin asserimus esse verissimam: Spiritus scil. citra ullam operationem in corpore sic Hic aut Illic existere, ut etiam ratione essentiae accuratè & propriè dici & concipi debeant esse Alicubi.
units.tr: But first of all it will be necessary to have rightly grasped the mind of the Nullibists, which becomes abundantly and clearly known from what occurs in Clauberg, De Cognitione Dei et nostri, Exercitatio LXV, where he takes up the question he undertakes to treat there, whether everything that is is somewhere; so that this axiom is abstracted from God and creature (he would more fittingly have said, from what follows in his own work, from spirit and body)? Among other things he answers, §2: The subject of which it is said that it is somewhere is not an intellectual or incorporeal thing, but only a corporeal or material thing, which is extended in length, breadth and depth. And §16: Intellectual things cannot be said to be somewhere in any other way than by acting effectively. To the same effect others assert that spirit, considered in itself, cannot be said to be Here, or There, or Everywhere, since these concepts fit it no more than colour or taste. And therefore, according to the proper meaning of words and concepts, they say it is not truly said that spirit exists by its essence Here, There or Everywhere; but only that it acquires the designation of being here or there through the operation it exerts on a body; and when no body is given, it cannot rightly be said of it that it exists here or there. This is precisely what we reject, and we assert that its opposite is most true: namely, that spirit, without any operation on a body, so exists here or there that it ought to be accurately and properly said and conceived to be somewhere, even by reason of its essence.

units.la: Id priusquam planum facio, minimè praetereundum videtur, non itá in solidum subtilissimi hujus de Spirituum Nullibitate conceptûs laudem Cartesio tribuendam, ut non in ejus partem admittendi sint & alii. Famosissimum est fanatici hominis Valentini Weigelii nomen. Is, praeter alia, ex Paracelsi veterumque haereticorum lacunis potissimùm hausta deliria, etiam asserit, Spiritus Nullibi esse. Verùm illi hac quoque in parte, fui inter Orthodoxos antagonistae non defuerunt. Celebris in his est Johannes Crocius, qui Antiweigelii sui Part. 1. Cap. iv. Quaest. 1. versatur totus in examinanda controversia, An Angelus sine neque Hic, neque Illic? Sed lubet ipsa Weigelii verba referre, ut à Crocio exhibentur. Ea ex Germanico in Latinum versa sic sonant: Summus intellectus omnem crassam imperfectionem removet, ac reperit, neque Deum, neque Angelos ulla sede corporea aut quopiam externo indigere, verum eos neque Hic esse; neque Illic; sed esse in se ipsis actuosos, uti Deus est. Corpus certo in loco esse debet, sed Spiritus eget nullo loco. Huic assertioni Weigelianae communi Orthodoxorum nomine hanc aliam opponit Crocius Anti-Weigelianam, camque, loco citato, variis tùm Testimoniis S. Scripturae, tùm Rationibus naturalibus, tum Patrum Auctoritatibus confirmat. Angelos, inquit, non indigere loco circumscribente, modo corporum, quae propter quantitatem suam loco commensurantur, agnoscunt Catholici. An-
units.tr: Before I make this plain, it seems not to be passed over that the praise for this most subtle concept of the Nullibity of spirits is not to be attributed so wholly to Descartes that others are not also to be admitted to his party. The name of the fanatical man Valentinus Weigel is most notorious. He, among other things, drawing chiefly from the swamps of Paracelsus and the older heretics, also asserts that spirits are nowhere. But Orthodox antagonists were not lacking to him in this part either. Prominent among them is Johannes Crocius, who in Antiweigelius his, Part I, chapter iv, question 1, is wholly occupied in examining the controversy, whether an angel is neither here nor there? But it pleases me to report Weigel's own words as Crocius presents them. Translated from German into Latin, they sound thus: "The highest intellect removes every gross imperfection, and finds that neither God nor angels need any corporeal seat or any external thing, but that they are neither here nor there; but are active in themselves, as God is. A body must be in a certain place, but spirit needs no place." Against this common Weigelian assertion, in the name of the Orthodox, Crocius sets another, anti-Weigelian one, and confirms it, in the place cited, with various testimonies of Holy Scripture, natural reasons, and the authority of the Fathers. "Angels," he says, "do not need a circumscribing place, the mode of bodies, which because of their quantity are measured by place; this is what the Catholics acknowledge. An-

units.la: IV. Praivit olim hac sententia Cartesio Valentinus Weigelius. Angelos non indigere aliquo ræu, seu Ubi, in quo existant, non agnoscunt. Quin imò Angelos Hic & Illic esse affirmant; sua natura spirituali convenienter.
units.tr: Long before this, Valentin Weigel held this opinion, which Descartes later adopted. They do not acknowledge that angels need any place, or Where, in which they exist. Indeed they affirm that angels are Here and There, in keeping with their spiritual nature.

units.la: Parallelismum utriusque & Weigelianæ & Cartefianæ sententiæ, atque hanc in illa à Crocio Catholicorum nomine rejectam & confutatam, quis hic non videt ? Quisve etiam miretur, consentire conclusiones, ubi principia amicè adeò inter sese conspirant. Expendantur quæ Crocius, Ibid. Quest. 11. citat. ex Mystica Philosophia Weigelii. Qui dicunt, Angelus in Persia non est simul in Græcia, ii saltem perpendunt, Angelum visibilem corporeum, juxta corpus assumptum, & non juxta veram substantiam Angelicam, quæ potest esse Ubique. Quid verò Neoterici ? Contendunt hi, Angelos in duobus spatiis esse posse; quin, ne id parùm videatur, Mentem nostram, quamvis divina non sit, toti Universo posse esse præsentem. Essent forte quos impelleret tantus Virorum inter se in dogma non ubiquè obvium consensus, ad suspicandum, vitulo Weigelii arafse Cartefium. Ego verò benignius sentio, ac forte fortuna potius in eandem cum Weigelio sententiam hunc incidisse; ipsumque ideò (deficiente jam fermè familiâ Weigeliana) lubens, cum Moro, agnosco hodiernorum nostrorum Nullibistarum caput atque principem. Operæ pretium interim erat, hanc utriusque auctoris in eodem placito notare harmoniam: ut exemplo hoc nunc obvio appareat, quam hodiè eveniat sæpè, ut illa quoque paradoxa non raro applausum inveniant apud multos, tanquam reconditioris sapientiæ arcana, quibus assurgere deceat orbem erudituм, quæ ipsa jam olim, tanquam fanatica, & veritati atque orthodoxiæ prorsus inimica, damnarunt & confutarunt viri magni. Si menti infixum hæreret illud: Viatrita, viatuta, non tam frequenter qui per diverticula incedunt cum erronibus inciderent in foveam eandem. Sed ad rem!
units.tr: Who here does not see the parallel between Weigel's view and Descartes's, and the way Crocius, speaking for the Catholics, rejects and refutes it? Who would be surprised that the conclusions agree when the principles so readily coincide? Let us weigh what Crocius quotes from Weigel's Mystical Philosophy, in the same place, question 11: Those who say that an angel is not in Persia and in Greece at the same time, at least consider only a visible angel, a bodily one, according to the body he has assumed, and not according to his true angelic substance, which can be everywhere. What then do the modern writers say? They contend that angels can be in two places at once; and, lest this seem too little, that our mind, though it is not divine, can be present to the whole universe. Some might be moved by such a striking agreement of men who otherwise differ on doctrine to suspect that Descartes ploughed with Weigel's calf. I judge more kindly, and think he perhaps happened by chance on the same opinion as Weigel. So, since the Weigelian school is now almost extinct, I gladly acknowledge him, with More, as the head and chief of our present-day Nullibists. Meanwhile it was worth noting this harmony between the two authors on the same point, so that this example, lying ready to hand, shows how often it happens today that such paradoxes win applause from many, as hidden marks of a more recondite wisdom to which the learned world ought to rise, though great men long ago condemned and refuted them as fanatical and wholly hostile to truth and orthodoxy. If the saying Viatrita, viatuta had stuck in their minds, those who wander off the beaten road with the erring would not so often fall into the same pit. But to the matter!

units.la: Pro confirmatione nostræ assertionis, assumam primum, quod ultrò largiuntur adversarii, Spiritus alicubi esse, saltem ratione operationum, quas circa corpora exercent. Possunt autem hæ spectari duobus modis, vel à parte Spiritûs operantis; vel à parte corporis actionem istam recipientis. Priori modo, si credimus Recentioribus, quibus Spiritus non existunt actuosi nisi simpliciter volendo, sunt nihil aliud quam ipsissimæ Spiritum Cogitationes. nes. Posteriori verò sunt ipsi corporis motus, illas cogitationes comitantes. Neutro sensu stare potest Nullibistica opinio. Si enim verum est illud tritum, uti est verissimum, Agere præsupponit esse, & Modus operandi sequitur modum essendi, utique certissimum est & hoc, Hic aut Istic agere præsupponit Hic aut Istic esse. Quod si jam operationes Spiritum, prout se habent à parte ipsorum, nihilque aliud sunt quam meræ Cogitationes, verè sint alicubi, quis etiam essentiam Spiritum verè alicubi esse neget? Imprimis, quis id neget eorum, qui omnem rei intellectualis rationem formalem in sola Cogitatione consistere affirmant?
