Et profectò non video, qui, hoc sensu, cum iis, quas suprà ex Claubergio aliisque exhibuimus, assertionibus consistat hæc illius thesis, quæ occurrit §. 17. cuique planè similia alii etiam Nullibistæ subindè tradunt. Nec proinde, inquit, opponenda sunt in rebus intellectualibus, quod essentia, virtute, actione sint præsentia; cum hæc omnia in ipsis realiter idem sint, licet ratione nostra distinguantur. Quid enim? An non opponitur essentia Spiritus actioni ejusdem, cum hæc alicubi esse conceditur, illa esse negatur? Certè opponitur; nisi idem prædicatum de eodem subjecto affirmari simul & negari posse citra oppositionem, deinceps statuendum sit. Sed age! non sint hoc loco opponenda, uti contendit Claubergius, spirituum essentia eorundem actioni, verùm sint ea unum idemque. Quid indè sequitur aliud, quam invictam hanc esse & firmissimam nostram illationem: Quodcunque præsens est alicubi virtute & actione, etiam præsens est essentia. At Spiritus verè & proprie loquendo præsens alicubi est virtute & actione. Sequitur ergò, etiam Spiritum verè & proprie loquendo præsentem alicubi esse suâ essentiâ. Quod ipsum volebamus.
units.tr: To confirm our assertion, I shall first assume what our opponents themselves freely grant: spirits are somewhere, at least by reason of the operations they carry out upon bodies. These operations may be viewed in two ways: either on the side of the spirit that acts, or on the side of the body that receives the action. In the first way, if we believe the more recent writers, for whom spirits are active only by simply willing, the operations are nothing other than the very thoughts of the spirit. In the second way, they are the motions of the body that accompany those thoughts. The Nullibist opinion cannot stand in either sense. For if that well-worn saying is true, as it is most true, to act presupposes to be, and the mode of acting follows the mode of being, then it is most certain also that to act here or there presupposes being here or there. But if the operations of spirits, considered on their own side, are nothing but mere thoughts, who would deny that they really are somewhere? Above all, who would deny it among those who affirm that the whole formal nature of an intellectual thing consists in thought alone? And indeed I do not see how this thesis of Clauberg's, which occurs in §17 and which other Nullibists also sometimes put forward in nearly the same words, agrees in this sense with the assertions I have already cited from Clauberg and others. Therefore, he says, in intellectual things, essence, power and action should not be set against one another as present, since all these are really the same in them, although we distinguish them by our reasoning. For is the essence of a spirit not set against its action, when the one is granted to be somewhere and the other denied? It certainly is set against it, unless we are to hold that the same predicate can be affirmed and denied of the same subject at once without opposition. But come! Let us grant that, as Clauberg contends, the essence of spirits is not to be set against their action, but that they are one and the same. What follows from this except that our inference is unshakeable and most firm: whatever is present somewhere by power and action is also present by essence. But a spirit, speaking truly and properly, is present somewhere by power and action. It follows, therefore, that a spirit, speaking truly and properly, is present somewhere by its essence. This is what we wished to show.

units.la: VII. Frustrà ad actionem Spiritus transeuntem ejus Alicui restringi.
units.tr: VII. It is in vain to restrict the action of a spirit to its transient action.

units.la: Sed jam præsentisco, respondendum fore à Nullibisticæ sententiæ fautoribus, nullius esse hanc nostram argumentationem, quòd Spiritus tantum sibi dicantur esse alicubi ratione actionis, non immanentis, sed transeuntis ad extra. Verùm, quicquid sit de soliditate hujus exceptionis (de qua mox) non saltem eâ se tueri potest Claubergius, qüiqüe hac in parte ejus premunt vestigia. Exiis enim quæ ipse, loco citato, ad confirmationem suæ sententiæ affert, evidentissimum est, ei intelligi operationes, quatenus se habent à parte Spirituum ipsorum, tanquam immanentes. Nempè, pè, ut doceat Spiritus duntaxat per operationes alicubi esse, ad imitationem illius axiomatis Metaphylici, Ut unumquodque est, ita & verum est, format hoc aliud §. 15. Ut unumquodque est, ita & Alicubi est; sive, Qualis est existentia rei, talis etiam ejus est praesentia. Ratio similis est, inquit (sui, ut videtur, prorsùs oblitus) quoniam N. B. per Entitatem suam Alicubi est, sive praesens est per suam existentiam. In eo autem, pergit §. 16. confisus, ταῦτα esse rerum intellectualium, quod sint actus: existentia enim actuosa est ipsarum vita, vis, efficacia. Itaque si unumquodque uti est, ficetiam Alicubi est, res intellectuales non possunt aliter dici Alicubi esse, quam efficaciter agendo. Clarissimum est, in toto hoc discursu sermonem esse de Spirituum actionibus immanentibus, seu ipsis cogitationibus, quatenus sunt in mente; non de iisdem quatenus sese circa corpus exerunt. Nisi dicendum sit, res spirituales amplius actus non esse, adeòque omni existentia actuosa, vita, vi & efficacia destitui, quando ab omni corpore separatae existunt, nec quicquam in eo ad extra operantur. Quod minimè velint Nullibismi spiritualispatroni.
units.tr: But I already foresee that the defenders of the Nullibist opinion will reply that this argument of ours is worthless, because spirits are said to be somewhere only by reason of an action that is not immanent but transient, directed outward. Whatever the soundness of this exception (which I shall examine presently), Clauberg cannot be defended even on this ground, though his followers tread in his footsteps here. For from the passages he cites in support of his view in the place mentioned, it is quite evident that he understands the operations, so far as they are on the side of the spirits themselves, as immanent. Indeed, to teach that spirits are somewhere only through their operations, following that metaphysical axiom as a thing is, so is it true, he formulates this other axiom in §15: as a thing is, so it is also somewhere; or, as is the existence of a thing, so is its presence. The reasoning is similar, he says (quite forgetting himself, as it seems): since N.B. is somewhere through its entity, that is, is present through its existence. Relying on this, he goes on in §16: that these are properties of intellectual things, that they are acts; for active existence is their life, power and efficacy. So if each thing is as it is, and is somewhere as it is, intellectual things cannot be said to be somewhere in any other way than by acting efficaciously. It is quite clear that the whole of this discussion concerns the immanent actions of spirits, that is, their thoughts, so far as they are in the mind, and not those same actions so far as they exert themselves upon a body. Unless we are to say that spiritual things are no longer acts, and so are deprived of all active existence, life, power and efficacy when they exist apart from every body and do nothing outwardly in it. This the patrons of a spiritual Nullibism would by no means wish to say.

units.la: Verùm neque satis convenienter suis hypothesibus ratiocinantur quoties ajunt, Spiritus alicubi esse ratione operationum, quas producunt in corporibus. Nullae enim tales existunt quarum mentem causam agnoscant proprie dictam: statuunt enim ipsi, rem intellectualem non esse actuosam nisi cogitando, itâ ut in sese operetur, quicquid operatur. Motus corporeos quod attinet, qui in nobis conspicui sunt, eos à mente tanquam à vera & reali causa pendere negant, quippe qui, mente etiam non data, in corpore humano, tanquam in automato, peragi nihilominus possint. Quin tantùm abest, ut mentem habeant motuum corporeorum principium, ut nullum illi in hos imperium concedant, nisi quatenus, ex sola Dei voluntate, ejus actiones volendi corporeis actionibus conjunguntur. Quod si ergò motus in corpore non sint operationum mentis effecta, sed solummodò quaedam ejus concomitantia, eaque ne reciproca quidem, sed talia quae quoque existere in corpore possint, mente non operante, quin non data; sequitur, ineptissimum esse afferere, Spiritus esse alicubi duntaxat ratione operationum ad extra, quas producunt in corporibus, cum ne ullas tales mentem in corpore verè producere credant ipsi & contendant.
units.tr: But they do not reason consistently with their own hypotheses whenever they say that spirits are somewhere by reason of the operations they produce in bodies. For no such operations exist whose cause, properly so called, is the mind. They themselves maintain that an intellectual thing is not active except by thinking, so that whatever it does, it does within itself. As for the bodily motions that are visible in us, they deny that these depend on the mind as on a true and real cause, since such motions could nevertheless be carried out in the human body, as in an automaton, even when the mind is not present. Indeed they are so far from holding the mind to be the principle of bodily motions that they grant it no rule over them, except insofar as, by the will of God alone, its acts of willing are joined to bodily actions. If, then, the motions in the body are not effects of the operations of the mind, but only certain accompaniments of it, and not even reciprocal ones, but such as can exist in the body even when the mind does not operate, indeed when it is not present at all; it follows that it is most absurd to assert that spirits are somewhere only by reason of the outward operations they produce in bodies, since they themselves neither believe nor contend that the mind truly produces any such operations in the body.

units.la: Qq tendant. Quid itaque attinebit spiritui tribuere alicubi ratione motus ejusmodi corporei, qui tam nullis perticis cum essentia spiritus ejusque activitate quicquam commune habet, ut ne quidem haec illius vera causa cogitari possit aut debeat? Verum missa haec facio Claubergiano discursu, quo res omnis absolvitur & conficitur plenissime: Ut unumquodque est, ita alicubi est: At per essentiam suam, quae illis in nuda cogitatione consistit, non per operationes extra se in corpore productas, Spiritus est: Ergò per essentiam suam, non per operationes extra se in corpore productas, Spiritus alicubi est. Quod erat demonstrandum.
units.tr: ...contend. What then will it avail to ascribe to a spirit a location by reason of such bodily motion, which has so little in common with the essence of a spirit and its activity that not even this motion can rightly be thought to be its true cause? But I set aside this Claubergian argument, by which the whole matter is settled and fully concluded: Whatever a thing is, so it is somewhere; but a spirit is by its essence, which for them consists in bare thought, and not by operations produced outside itself in a body; therefore a spirit is somewhere by its essence, not by operations produced outside itself in a body. Which was to be demonstrated.

units.la: IX. Arctissima mentis humanae cum corpore conjunctio praesentiam spiritus essentialem validè adstruit.
units.tr: IX. The closest conjunction of the human mind with the body strongly proves the essential presence of the spirit.

units.la: Si deinceps animo cogitemus arctissimam illam Spiritus cum corpore in idem suppositum unionem, qualis observatur naturalis in quolibet nostrum, mystica creditur in Christo Domino, validissimum ea contra opinionem Nullibisticam suppeditat argumentum; quin efficax adeò, ut, qui ejus ictum declinare possint Novatores, non videam. Nam id quidem extra controversiam est, omnem plurium rerum inter se conjunctionem praesentiam earundem mutuam, unioni isti convenientem, supponere. Jam verò anima rationalis humano corpori unita existit, non per assistentiam duntaxat, & ratione operationum transeuntium quas inibi exercet, sed re verà per essentiam & personaliter. Si enim nulla sit unio inter mentem & corpus, citra influxum operationum illius in hoc, utique ea cessante, sublata quoque erit inter partes hominis essentiales unio personalis. Si sic; ergò moritur homo, omnisque animae cum corpore unio tollitur, quoties in lypothymiam, syncopen, apoplexiam, similesve graviores cerebri assectiones, omne mentis imperium in corpus suspendentes incidit: contrà revivisset, quoties, recedente paroxismo, ad se redit, mensque iterum in corpore operari incipit, Non jam miremur amplius bis-mortuos opus est, quandò cum vel centies mortuis res nobis est quotidiè. Adeò est per novam sapientiam à morte ad vitam facilis regressus! Addere possem, ex hac sententia admittendum esse, Angelum cum corpore in quo operatur, non minus unam constituere hypostasin, quam anima nostra constituit cum corpore nostro. Sed ulteriorem hujus rei pertractationem servo peculiari Diatribae, quà examinare constitui Neotericorum conceptum de Unione humanae mentis cum corpore. Nunc indicasse ista sufficit, ut appareat, citra manifestam absurditatem negari non posse, Mentem, adeòque & Spiritum, per essentiam verè alicubi esse, etiam ubi extra se nihil operatur.
units.tr: If next we consider in our minds that closest union of spirit and body in one suppositum, such as is observed naturally in each of us, and is believed to be mystical in Christ the Lord, it supplies a most powerful argument against the Nullibistic opinion; indeed I do not see how the Innovators can avoid its blow, so effective is it. For it is beyond dispute that every conjunction of several things among themselves presupposes their mutual presence, suited to that union. Now the rational soul exists united to the human body not merely by assistance and by way of the transient operations it carries on therein, but truly and personally by its essence. For if there is no union between mind and body apart from the influx of the mind's operations into the body, then, that influx ceasing, the personal union between the essential parts of man will also be removed. If so, man dies, and all union of soul with body is dissolved whenever he falls into lipothymia, syncope, apoplexy, or similar more serious affections of the brain which suspend all the mind's command over the body; conversely he would revive whenever, the paroxysm receding, he comes to himself and the mind begins again to operate in the body. Let us no longer wonder at men twice dead, since we have to do with them daily, even a hundred times dead! So easy, by the new wisdom, is the return from death to life! I might add that on this view one must admit that an angel, together with the body in which it operates, constitutes no less one hypostasis than our soul constitutes with our body. But I reserve the fuller treatment of this matter for a separate Diatribe, in which I have resolved to examine the modern concept of the union of the human mind with the body. For now it is enough to have indicated these points, so that it appears that, without manifest absurdity, it cannot be denied that the mind, and therefore the spirit, is truly somewhere by its essence, even where it operates nothing outside itself. Which was to be demonstrated.

units.la: Suppositâ porrò ex fide duarum Naturarum in Christo Mediatore unione hypostaticâ, simile incommodum sententiam Nullibisticam premit; sed tanto gravius, quanto periculosus magis hic error est. Si enim Spiritus non aliter possint dici esse alicubi, quam efficaciter agendo, nec dicantur verè secundum verborum & conceptuum proprietatem per essentiam suam Hic aut Illic esse, sed tantum per denominationem ab operationibus in corpore; (quod Nullibistas disertè asserere, audivimus) non poterit etiam verè ac proprie dici, essentiam naturæ Divinæ unitam fuisse in Christo cum natura humana, sed tantum per denominationem ab operationibus ad extra in corpore desumptam. Ubiergò vera Unio personalis? quam Theologus doctissimus Junius ait proprie definiri, quòd sit duarum naturarum perfectissima & Substantialis in unam personam conjunctio. Viderint itaque Theologi, an hactenus sententia Nullibistica absolvi possit à consequentia Nestorianismi, non aliam hic admittentis unionem personalem, quam κ̓ παράςασιν vel ταυτοζωλίαν, per assistentiam, vel voluntatis consensum. Per Solam operationem, inquit Walæus, Divinæ Naturæ in humanam unionem hanc esse factam, Nestorianum est, & à tota Veteri Ecclesia condemnatum. Sed nos manum de hac tabula. Sat nobis est evicisse, sive rationem attendamus, sive revelationem, ex personali spiritu um cum corpore unione admitti debere, non tantùm per operationes, sed & per essentiam illos esse alicubi. Quod erat demonstrandum.
units.tr: Furthermore, given the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ the Mediator, which we hold on the basis of faith, a similar inconvenience presses upon the Nullibistic opinion; and it is the more grave as this error is the more dangerous. For if spirits cannot be said to be somewhere otherwise than by acting efficaciously, and are not said truly, according to the proper meaning of words and concepts, to be here or there by their essence, but only by denomination from operations in the body (which we have heard the Nullibists plainly assert), then it will also not be possible to say truly and properly that the essence of the divine nature was united in Christ with the human nature, but only by denomination drawn from operations outside itself in the body. Where then is the true personal union, which the most learned theologian Junius says is properly defined as the most perfect and substantial conjunction of two natures into one person? Let the theologians themselves see whether the Nullibistic opinion can so far be freed from the consequence of Nestorianism, which admits no personal union here other than [παράστασιν] presence or [ταυτοζωλίαν] agreement, by assistance or consent of will. That this union of the human nature was made by the sole operation of the divine nature, says Walaeus, is Nestorian, and has been condemned by the whole ancient Church. But I leave this subject. It is enough for us to have shown, whether we consider reason or revelation, that a personal union of spirits with the body must be admitted, and that they are somewhere not only by operations but also by essence. Which was to be demonstrated.

units.la: Ulterius, Si Spiritus non aliter dici possint alicubi esse, quam per denominationem ab operationibus in corpore derivatam, non autem verè & propriè per essentiam, quid de Divina Immensitate & vera ταυταχωσία dicendum erit? Eam contra Vorstium, ejusdemque asseclas, ità asseruerunt hactenus saniores Theologi & Philosophi, ut (verba sunt Walæi) Omnes orthodoxi, Deum Ubique per essentiam, tam in cœlo quam in terra, præsentem esse, rectè contendant; & contrariam sententiam blasphemiæ condemnent. Ubi interim invaluit apud quosdam opinio Nullibistica, nullis non modis orthodoxa hæc doctrina sugillata fuit passim atque luxata. Præivit vit Cartesius ipse hunc in modum, Epist. Part. 1. p. 205. Videris (Moro respondet) Infinitatem Dei in eo ponere, quod ubique existat; cui opinioni non assentior. Sed puto, Deum ratione suae potentiae ubique esse; Ratione autem suae essentiae nullam plane habere relationem ad locum. Antesignanum suum gnaviter secuti alii, hypothesi Nullibisticae convenienter, affirmarunt, Omnipraesentiam Dei nihil aliud esse, quam efficacissimam ejusdem voluntatem, qua omnia extra se sustentat ac gubernat. Quae thesis, etsi plurimos jam dudum gravissimè offendit, itàtamen Nullibistis in deliciis est, ut post alios nuperrimè quidam eorum publicè contenderit, illam neque pietati neque rectae rationi adversam, sed quaestionem purè Philosophicam esse. Uti quondam Vorstius cum Sociis, quò tutius controversiam subterfugerent, atque Orthodoxorum censuram declinarent, controversiam de essentiali Omnipraesentia Divina subtilitatem Scholasticam esse, praetenderunt, ejusque modum nusquam in Verbo Dei esse patefactum. Quin rideri coepit apertè versiculus Orthodoxis hac in re explicanda tritus: Enter, Praesenter, Deus hic & Ubique Potenter. Nam, qui statuunt Dei Immensitatem esse triplicem, nempe Essentiae, Potentiae, ac denique Praesentiae, illi nugas agunt, diserte Auctor Append. Demonstr. Princip. Cartef. p. 114. Verùm missa haec facio, alibi quoque nobis notata pluribus.
units.tr: Further, if spirits cannot be said to be somewhere otherwise than by denomination derived from operations in the body, and not truly and properly by essence, what must be said of the divine immensity and true omnipresence? The more sober theologians and philosophers have hitherto so vigorously asserted this against Vorstius and his followers that (in Walaeus's words) all orthodox men rightly maintain that God is present everywhere, by essence, both in heaven and on earth, and condemn the contrary opinion as blasphemy. Yet meanwhile the Nullibistic opinion has gained ground among some, and this orthodox doctrine has been everywhere disparaged and distorted. Descartes himself led the way in this manner, Epist. Part. 1, p. 205. You seem (he answers Morus) to place the infinity of God in his existing everywhere; with which opinion I do not agree. But I think God is everywhere by reason of his power; yet by reason of his essence he has plainly no relation to place. Others vigorously following their champion, in agreement with the Nullibistic hypothesis, have affirmed that the omnipresence of God is nothing other than his most efficacious will, by which he sustains and governs all things outside himself. This thesis, although it has long since gravely offended very many, is nevertheless a delight to the Nullibists, so that, after others, one of them has recently maintained publicly that it is neither contrary to piety nor to right reason, but a purely philosophical question. Just as Vorstius once did with his associates, in order to escape the controversy more safely and avoid the censure of the orthodox, they pretended that the controversy about the essential omnipresence of God is a Scholastic subtlety, and that its manner is nowhere revealed in the Word of God. Indeed the little verse, worn threadbare by the orthodox in explaining this matter, Enter, Praesenter, Deus hic & Ubique Potenter, has begun to be openly laughed at. For those who hold that the immensity of God is threefold, namely of essence, of power, and finally of presence, are trifling, says the author plainly in the Append. Demonstr. Princip. Cartef. p. 114. But I set these things aside, since they have been noted by us elsewhere at greater length.

units.la: Aliud contra Nullibitatem Spirituum argumentum subjicerem, ostendendo, parem hic esse rationem rē Ubi & Quando: ideòque cùm posterius Spiritibus, operationum non tantùm, verùm essentiae quoque ratione tribuendum esse, non inviti largiantur Neoterici, etiam prius iisdem denegandum minimè esse. Universalem porrò eruditorum consensum adducerem, rem omnem singularem hactenus determinantium per Hoc, Hic, Nunc; & pro generali ac firmissimo axiomate habentium illud. Quod Nullibi est, non est. Verùm quae jam in medium adduximus sufficiunt restituendo Spiritibus suum Ubi, unde nullo suo merito à Recentioribus fuerunt exturbati. Neque per haec singula ire sinunt, praefixi brevitatis termini. Quapropter nec urgebo argumenta Scripturaria, quibus Deus asseritur coelorum coelos non capi, ubi tamen nil extra se operatur; Animae damnatorum abiisse dicuntur in infernum, tanquam in Locum suum; Beatorum Spiritibus promittuntur parata
units.tr: I would put forward another argument against the non-location of spirits, showing that the reason is the same for where and when. Therefore, since the modern thinkers willingly grant that the latter must be attributed to spirits not only by reason of their operations but also of their essence, the former also must by no means be denied them. Moreover I would bring forward the universal consent of the learned, who have hitherto determined every singular thing by this, here, now, and hold as a general and most firm axiom that what is nowhere, is not. But what we have already brought forward is enough to restore to spirits their where, of which by no merit of their own they were driven out by the more recent writers. Nor does the limit of brevity I have set allow me to go through each of these points. Therefore I shall not press the scriptural arguments either, by which God is asserted not to be contained by the heaven of heavens, though he operates nothing outside himself; by which the souls of the damned are said to have gone into hell, as into their own place; by which the spirits of the blessed are promised prepared places

units.la: Loca in cœlis, tanquam in Domo patris, ubi Mansiones multæ; quæque sexcenta occurrunt in Sacris hisce similia. Ad quorum vim elidendam, quæ mira Scripturarum interpretamenta, Cartesianæ Philosophiæ radiis illustrata, ab iis quibus Novæ sapientiæ lux affulsit, excogitata sint? non est hic ostendendi locus. Novum certè, & de quo nulla unquam audiverunt tempora, à quo invaluit opinio Nullibiftica fabricari cœpit cœlum; quod nimirùm nusquam re verâ datur, statumque tantum significet non locum, inque quod migratio mutationem statûs duntaxat dicat non loci. Aberrarunt itaque tota viâ à vero cœlo, & nusquam inveniendum quæsiverunt, quotquot id hactenus quæsiverunt absque præambula hac face Cartesiana de Nullibitate spirituum; ductura scilicet ad cœlum quod inveniri possit nusquam gentium. Notus est gravissimi Theologi Petri Martyris serius il'e jocus, quo Bullingero se jamjam excessurum è vivis consolanti dicto Pauli, de fidelium Politia quæ sit in cœlo, respondit, Sed non in cœlo Brentii, quod est nusquam. Itâ tunc temporis Doctores Reformati; qui ignorabant cœlum quod sit sine loco status solummodò, & nil nisi quiddam novus cogitandi modus, in quo pacem habitura sit mens cum glandula pineali, cujus motibus hodiè adsistit mancipata. Solentur suas animulas spe cœli ejusmodi Cartesiani, qui velint ? nobis Paulinum placet, quærendum supra, in quod olim Dominus Jesus corpore suo ascendit, quo & hodiè capitur, & ex quo visibiliter modo rediturum novissimo consummati hujus seculi die exspectamus. A qua fidei simplicitate quisquis abduci semet ipsum patitur ἀλλ' ἀ φιλοσοφίας, viderit is ne sic tandem hic aberret, ut inveniat nunquam, quod quærit nusquam.
units.tr: in heaven, as in the house of the Father, where there are many mansions; and the countless similar passages in these sacred books. What wonderful interpretations, illuminated by the rays of Cartesian philosophy, have been devised by those on whom the light of the new wisdom has shone, to overturn their force? This is not the place to show. Certainly a new heaven, of which no age ever heard, has begun to be fabricated by those from whom the Nullibistic opinion gained ground; a heaven which in truth is nowhere given, and which signifies only a state and not a place, and into which migration means only a change of state and not of place. Therefore all who have sought heaven hitherto without the preliminary torch of the Cartesian doctrine of the non-location of spirits have gone wholly astray from the true heaven, and have sought it where it is nowhere to be found; for that doctrine would lead them to a heaven which can be found nowhere in the world. The grave theologian Peter Martyr's witty remark is well known: when Bullinger consoled him as he was about to depart this life with Paul's saying about the citizenship of the faithful, which is in heaven, he replied, But not in the heaven of Brentius, which is nowhere. So in those days the Reformed teachers, who did not know a heaven that is only a state without place, and nothing but some new mode of thinking, in which the mind would have peace with the pineal gland to whose motions it is now bound as a slave, were ignorant. Let the Cartesians, who wish, console their little souls with hope of such a heaven; we prefer the Pauline one, which is to be sought above, where the Lord Jesus once ascended in his body, where he is also today contained, and from which we await his return in a visible manner on the last day of the consummation of this age. Whoever allows himself to be drawn away from this simplicity of faith but of philosophy [ἀλλ' ἀ φιλοσοφίας], let him see that he does not at last go so far astray here that he finds never what he seeks, because it is nowhere.

units.la: Sed properandum est ad expendendas rationes, ob quas Spiritum omnem ad Atopiam, dicam, an Utopiam, relegandum censent Nullibiftæ: ut appareat, quam ἀτόπως Atopica sententia confirmetur. Subjectum (inquit Claubergius, loc. cit. §. 2. 3.) de quo dicitur, quod sit Alicubi, non est res Intellectualis, sed Corporea tantum: id quod probatur, primò ab eorum sensu, qui hoc Axioma (Omne quod est, Alicubi est) invenerunt & usurparunt. Qui id primi introduxerunt sunt vulgus hominum, qui nihil solent nisi corporeum cogitare, deque eo solo sermones miscere. Mirum equidem argumentum! de quo unde constet Claubergio, nescio. Eruditos primes controversum canonem introduxisse, eumque consequenter non corporibus tantum, quæ sola vulgus fere concipere solet, sed & Spiritibus applicandum esse, æquali certitudine affirmet alius. Quin hoc hic probet ex universali regula Platonis (Viri procul dubio haud vulgaris, ac immateriali-um rerum ideis contemplandis satis assueti) quam ex Parmenide ipse citat Claubergius, Quod Nusquam est, nihil penitus est. Verum esto! Introduxerit vulgus! Nihilne adeo à vulgo bene dictum aut conceptum, ut quicquid id fuerit, ilicò totum sit reiiciendum, quia tale? Si hoc axioma à vulgo introductum est, etiam aliud ei simile, Quod nunquam est, non est, pari ratione ab eodem descendit. At hoc etiam ad Spiritus extendi debere, ipsi largiuntur dissentientes. Quæ igitur consequentia, Effatum hoc à vulgo fuit usurpatum primitus, ergo rebus Intellectualibus applicari nequit? Et quicunque demùm fuerit, qui axioma hoc introduxit, demonstratum à nobis, non absque gravi causa Auctores gravissimos, Sacros pariter & profanos, de rebus etiam intellectualibus pronunciasse, quod fortè ex vulgo quidam nil nisi corporeum cogitantes, rebus tantum extensis applicuerunt. Perquam jejunum est, Claubergium, ostensurum idem hic secum sentire (de axiomate videlicet vulgi Spiritibus non applicando) eruditos, Theologos scil & Philosophos, duos §. 4. & 7. adducere textus, alterum Platonis, Augustini alterum, in quo neutro vel quod hùc spectet, occurrit. Asserit duntaxat uterque, corpora sine Ubi esse non posse: at verbum apud eos nullum, quo Spiritus ab eo excludant; quod probandum sumserat Claubergius. Rectius allegasset illa, quæ nos ex Weigelio suprà exhibuimus, quippe quæ verbotenùs mentem Nullibisticam exprimunt.
units.tr: But we must hasten on to weigh the reasons why the Nullibists think every spirit should be relegated to Atopia (or, shall I say, Utopia), so that it may appear how atopically [ἀτόπως] the Atopian opinion is supported. The subject of which it is said that it is somewhere (says Clauberg, loc. cit. §§ 2, 3) is not an intellectual thing but only a corporeal one. This is proved, first, from the view of those who devised and used this axiom (Whatever is, is somewhere). The ones who first introduced it were the common people, who are accustomed to think of nothing but corporeal things and to talk of that alone. A marvellous argument indeed! How Clauberg knows this, I do not know. Another writer affirms with equal certainty that the learned first introduced this disputed rule, and that it should consequently be applied not only to bodies, which the common people almost alone are wont to conceive, but also to spirits. Indeed, he would prove this here from Plato's universal rule (a man surely not of the common sort, and well accustomed to contemplating the ideas of immaterial things), which Clauberg himself cites from Parmenides: What is nowhere is nothing at all. But granted! Let the common people have introduced it! Is nothing said or conceived well by the common people, so that whatever it may be must be wholly rejected simply because it comes from them? If this axiom was introduced by the common people, then another similar to it, What never is, is not, descends from the same source by the same reasoning. Yet the dissenters themselves concede that this too must be extended to spirits. What, then, is the consequence: this saying was originally used by the common people, therefore it cannot be applied to intellectual things? And whoever it was who introduced this axiom, we have shown that, not without serious cause, the most weighty authors, sacred and profane alike, have pronounced also about intellectual things, whereas some of the common people, thinking only of corporeal things, may have applied it only to extended things. It is very feeble of Clauberg, who wants to show that he himself thinks the same here (namely, that the axiom of the common people is not to be applied to spirits), to adduce learned men, theologians and philosophers, in §§ 4 and 7, two texts, one of Plato and the other of Augustine, in neither of which is anything that bears on the point. Each merely asserts that bodies cannot be without a Where; but there is no word in either by which they exclude spirits, which is what Clauberg had undertaken to prove. He would have done better to allege those passages which we have set out above from Weigel, since they express the Nullibist view word for word.
XIV.

units.la: Pergit Claubergius §. 8. Necratio permittit, ut latius extendatur axioma: nam causa hujusce veritatis, quod omne quod est Alicubi sive in aliquo spatio sit, alia non est, quam quod corpus omne sit extensum, & spatium etiam sit extensum: adeo ut idem re vera sit, extensum esse, & spatium esse, & in spatio esse, &c. Ad quæ autem causa axiomatis applicari nequit, ad illa nec ipsum debet applicari. In quibus omnibus supponitur, spatium esse corpus ipsum quod in spatio est, nec quicquam inter ista duo intercedere discriminis; quod plurimi, nec sine ratione, negant: ut qui autumant, errorem hunc, spatium cum corpore locato confundentem, non aliunde ortum duxisse, quam ex infantili praejudicio, quo mens nostra jam inde à primis annis occupata esse solet, dum ab incunte aetate observavimus, omnia spatia, nobis designabilia, corpore esse repleta. At distinctius rem cogitantes, ac omnipotentiam Divinam ritè expendentes, facilè percipere asserunt, etiam dari posse spatium sine corpore, seu distantiam inter duo corpora nullo tertio interposito, quam vacuum appellant. Et quamvis hi ex vero sic philosophari nobis videantur, hoc loco tamen de spatio corporis, num sit idem cum ipso, nùm quid ab eo diversum, disputare nil attinet. Nam, utrumlibet supposueris, id certum, neminem eorum, qui asserunt Spiritus esse Alicubi, eo absurditatis descendisse, ut Spiritus in spatio esse volucrit per modum corporum, quibus proprium est, per partes sui spatio suo ejusque partibus coexistere, idque sic occupare, ut omne aliud corpus ex eodem spatio excludant. Quis enim est qui ignoret vulgarem Alicubi distinctionem in Circumscriptivum, Definitivum & Repletivum? Et cui non audita recepta antiquitùs formula, de Spiritu, qui sit in spatio toto totus, & totus in qualibet ejus parte? Ista Alicubi distinctio, hic coexistentiae modus, expugnanda fuissent, non verò de spatio corporum differendum, cum id totum sit à re praesenti alienissimum; nisi in antecessum demonstratum fuerit, aliud Ubi, praeter id quod Corporum est, admittendum non esse: quod hoc saltem Claubergiano argumento non evincitur, nisi per principii petitionem. An autem, & quae sint causae, ob quas hoc Axioma non corporibus duntaxat, verùm etiam Spiritibus sit applicandum, jam vidimus abundè.
units.tr: Clauberg goes on in §8: Nor does reason permit the axiom to be extended more widely. For the cause of this truth, that everything that is is somewhere, that is, in some space, is no other than that every body is extended and space too is extended, so that to be extended and to be space and to be in space, etc., are really the same thing. But to whatever the cause of the axiom cannot be applied, neither should the axiom itself be applied to them. In all these things it is assumed that space is the very body which is in space, and that there is no difference between the two; many deny this, and not without reason. Those who maintain that this error, which confuses space with the located body, did not arise from any other source than an infantile prejudice, with which our mind is usually occupied from our earliest years, since from early age we have observed that all the spaces we can mark out are filled with body. But those who think about the matter more distinctly, and weigh the divine omnipotence rightly, readily perceive, they assert, that space without body can also exist, or a distance between two bodies with no third body interposed, which they call a vacuum. And although these men seem to us to philosophize truly in this, it is not relevant here to dispute whether the space of a body is the same as the body, or something different from it. For whichever you suppose, this is certain: none of those who assert that spirits are somewhere has fallen into such an absurdity as to want spirits to be in space in the manner of bodies, which by their nature coexist with their space and its parts part by part, and occupy it so as to exclude every other body from the same space. For who does not know the common distinction of Where into circumscriptive, definitive and repletive? And who has not heard the formula received from antiquity, of a spirit which is wholly in the whole of space and wholly in every part of it? That distinction of Where and this mode of coexistence ought to have been attacked; rather than disputing about the space of bodies, which is wholly foreign to the present matter, unless it were first demonstrated that some Where other than what belongs to bodies must not be admitted. This, at least, is not proved by Clauberg's argument, except by begging the question. But as to whether, and what the causes are for which this axiom must be applied not only to bodies but also to spirits, we have already seen this amply.

units.la: Instabis forte, quale ergo erit τὸ Alicubi Spiritūum, sinon aliquam involvit extensionem? Nihil aliud quam tale corundem attributum, quo per essentiam suam in rerum corporearum spatiis, seu veris seu possibilibus, exsistunt modo indivisibili. Notatque adeò, ut verbo dicam, absque sui extensione spiritum esse, ubi corpus est, vel esse saltem potest. Ita V. C. Anima nostra in corpore humano est, tanquam in suo Ubi, quatenus essentiā suā corpori ejusve spatio intimè ac verè coexistit; sed naturae suae spirituali convenienter, i.e. absque sui partibus. Sic quoque Deus, etiam
units.tr: You will perhaps object: what, then, will the being-somewhere of spirits be, if it does not involve some extension? Nothing other than a certain attribute of theirs, by which, through their essence, they exist in the spaces of corporeal things, whether real or possible, in an indivisible mode. And so, to put it in a word, a spirit is without extension of its own where a body is, or at least can be. Thus, for example, our soul is in the human body as in its Where, insofar as it coexists intimately and truly with the body, or with its space, by its essence; but in a manner agreeable to its spiritual nature, that is, without parts of itself. So too God, also

units.la: {y} Quale sit Spiritum Alicubi, & qui ratione nobis concipiendum? etiam ante mundum conditum, Alicubi fuit, quatenus ipse infinitus omnisque extensionis expers verè tunc extitit, ubi nunc mundus est, tunc esse poterat. Quæ, cum clarissima sint & distinctissima, qui non capit, cum vel indocilem esse oportet, qui hæc intelligere non possit, vel malignum, qui non velit. Quapropter neque plura addo; imprimis quandoquidem quædam adhuc infrà dicenda venient, quæ ad plenissimam horum explicationem conducent plurimùm, quæque cum eis quæ jam diximus collata, facillimam facient solutionem omnium, quæ vel eadem, vel ex istis principiis deducta, in citata sæpius Claubergii Exercitatione de Spirituum Nullibi occurrunt. Nominatim concidunt, quæ adfert §. 12. Unde & ipsum Axiomatis nostri, Omne quod est, Alicubi est, praedicatum satis innotuefcit; nihil enim aliud significat tò Alicubi esse, quam in aliquo loco esse, per spatium aliquod extensum esse, &c. adeoque corporeo modo quantum esse. Id enim quamvis daretur verum esse de Ubi corporum, nulla tamen inde, uti ostensum, ad Ubi Spirituum formari potest consequentia. Disquiri porrò posset, qui cohæreat, quod Auctor §. 1. asserit, idem re vera esse, extensum esse, & spatium esse & in spatio esse, cum eo quod immediatè sequitur, §. 9. Alicubi esse solum est intelligendum de his & illis rebus particularibus, quæ portiones quædam sunt Universi; non de ipso Universo, seu toto mundo, vel corpore in genere. Quasi totum Universum, vel corpus in genere extensum non sit! Verùm cum de Ubi corporum nunc agere non constituerim, hæc, aliaque quæ hùc spectant in Dissertatione Claubergiana plura, transeo, pergoque potius tollere alias nonnullas, quas contra Spirituum Ubi passim urgent difficultates Nullibiftæ.
units.tr: {y} What it is for a spirit to be somewhere, and how we are to conceive it: even before the world was created, God was somewhere, insofar as he, being infinite and free of all extension, truly existed then where the world now is, and then could be there. Since these things are very clear and distinct, whoever does not grasp them must be either unteachable, being unable to understand them, or malicious, being unwilling to. Therefore I add no more, especially since some things yet to be said below will contribute greatly to the fullest explanation of these matters, and which, compared with what we have already said, will make the solution of all the difficulties easy, difficulties which, whether the same or deduced from these principles, occur in Clauberg's Exercitatio on the Nowhere of Spirits, cited so often. Those things in particular are overturned which he adduces in §12: Hence also the predicate of our axiom, Whatever is, is somewhere, is sufficiently known; for to be somewhere signifies nothing other than to be in some place, to be extended through some space, etc., and so to be as large as a body in a corporeal manner. For even if this were granted as true of the Where of bodies, no consequence can be drawn from it, as has been shown, for the Where of spirits. One might further inquire how it coheres that the author asserts in §1 that to be extended, to be space, and to be in space are really the same thing, with what immediately follows in §9: To be somewhere is to be understood only of those and those particular things which are certain portions of the Universe, not of the Universe itself, or the whole world, or body in general. As if the whole extended universe, or body in general, were not extended! But since I have not determined now to treat of the Where of bodies, I pass over these and the many other points in Clauberg's Dissertation that bear on this, and proceed rather to remove some other difficulties which the Nullibists everywhere press against the Where of spirits.

units.la: Trita est & ad nauseam usque plus millies reposita Novatorum contra Spirituum Alicubi objectio, desumpta ab eorundem non-extensione. Inconceptibile est, inquiunt, neque ullà ratione fieri potest, ut res non-extensa atque indivisibilis per essentiam suam coëxistat rei extensæ & divisibili. Quapropter (pergunt) quicunque rebus Spiritualibus tò Alicubi tribuunt ratione essentiæ, pariter in iisdem extensionem concipere necesse habent; si non crassam, saltem subtilem. At hoc absurdissimum. Verum universi hujus discursûs fundamentum unicum est, non posse res plures sibi mutuo coëxistere, nisi inter se ejusdem prorsùs sint nanaturæ & conditionis : quod totum salsissimum est. Quid enim? An non æterna Dei duratio, omnis mutationis ac successionis expers, totaque adeò, uti loquitur Philosophus Christianus, simul & perfecta, coëxistit spatiis hisce nostris temporalibus, annis, horis, &c. quæ fluunt continuò & mutantur? Quis neget, nisi qui simul, vel Deum nunc durare, vel durationem ejusdem successivam non esse, neget? At quod obtinet in rerum diversissimarum Quando, idem in earundem Ubi obtinere quid ni queat? Quæquè, obsecrò, ratio erit, cur, si res eadem & immutabilis coëxistere queat rebus successivis earumque mutationi, absque tamen ulla suæ durationis mutatione aut successione, cur, inquam, non pari ratione res non-extensa & indivisibilis, qualis est Spiritus, coëxistere possit rei extensæ & divisibili, puta corpori, absque extensione aut divisibilitate sui? Vidit jam olim consequentiæ hujus vim & robur Vorstius cum Sociis: unde etiam factum, ut, postquam ridere coeperunt essentialem Dei Omnipræsentiam, ut vocabant, Atomicam & Atopicam, simul etiam negaverint, ejusdem Æternitatem successionis ac mutationis expertem esse. Similibus hypothesibus qui utuntur, caveant ne in consequentiam incidant eandem: & qui queant non incidere? ostendant, velim. Nos terrent vestigia. Concedo itaque, quantum ad rem ipsam, quoties Spiritus Alicubi concipitur, concipi pariter extensionem; at non in Spiritu qui est Alicubi, sed in eo cui Spiritus coëxistere concipitur, nempe in corpore, vel, si ità vis, in spatio quod extensum & corporeum est, aut tanquam tale concipitur. Rectè ergò instituis: Si spiritus essentia extensione caret, ergò neque per essentiæ suæ extensionem corpori potest coëxistere præsens. Quod totum uti verissimum est, sic minimè concludit, etiam spiritum corpori præsentem esse non posse modo sibi convenìente, id est, indivisibili; quod unum contendunt Nullibistarum antagonistæ.
units.tr: The objection of the Innovators against the Alicubi of spirits is worn out and has been repeated more than a thousand times, to the point of nausea. It is taken from the non-extension of spirits. They say that it is inconceivable, and that by no means can it happen, that a thing which is non-extended and indivisible should coexist by its own essence with a thing that is extended and divisible. Therefore (they continue), whoever attributes to spiritual things an Alicubi by reason of their essence must also conceive extension in them, if not a gross extension then at least a subtle one. But this is most absurd. The sole foundation of this whole argument is that several things cannot coexist with one another unless they are altogether of the same nature and condition; and this is utterly false. For does not the eternal duration of God, free from all change and succession, and whole at once, as the Christian philosopher puts it, simultaneously and perfectly, coexist with our temporal spans, years, hours, and so on, which flow continually and change? Who would deny this, unless he denied either that God now endures or that his duration is successive? But why should what holds for the When of very diverse things not also hold for their Where? And what reason, I beg you, is there why, if a thing that is the same and unchangeable can coexist with successive things and their change, without any change or succession in its own duration, a thing that is non-extended and indivisible, such as a spirit, cannot in the same way coexist with an extended and divisible thing, say a body, without extension or divisibility of its own? Vorstius and his associates long ago saw the force and strength of this consequence. Hence it also came about that, after they began to mock the essential omnipresence of God, as they called it, atomic and atopic, they at the same time denied that his eternity is free from succession and change. Those who use similar hypotheses should take care not to fall into the same consequence; but who can avoid falling into it? Let them show me, I would like to see it. Their footsteps frighten us. I concede, then, so far as the matter itself goes, that whenever a spirit is conceived as being somewhere, extension is likewise conceived; but not in the spirit which is somewhere, rather in that with which the spirit is conceived to coexist, namely in a body, or, if you prefer, in a space which is extended and corporeal, or is conceived as such. You therefore rightly argue: If the essence of a spirit lacks extension, then by the extension of its essence it cannot be present with a body. Although all of this is most true, it by no means follows that a spirit cannot be present to a body in a mode suited to itself, that is, indivisibly; and this alone is what the opponents of the Nullibitarians contend.

units.la: Quibus dum solvimus objectum argumentum, simul satisfecimus difficultati, quam movet De la Forge, Tractat. de Mente Hum. Cap. XIII. cum inquit: „Philosophia Scholastica, cum „ex una parte doceat, essentiam mentis in eo consistere quod non „sit extensa, & ex altera statuat, naturam unionis duarum sub„stantiarum consistere in locali præsentia unius cum altera, simul „aufert hoc modo omnia media concipiendi mentis ac corporis uni-„onem. Quomodo enim quis comprehendat mentem, id est, „secundum eos substantiam cujus natura consistit in eo quod non „est extensa, posse fieri extensam? Nam nullo alio pacto concipe„re possumus, quomodo præsens esse possit substantiæ alicui ex-„tensæ, nisi ipsam etiam extensam concipiamus, &c. Ad quæ notetur: 1. Nullo modo necessum esse, ut extensum sit id omne, aut tanquam tale concipiatur, quod alicui extenso coëxistit; uti demonstratum satis. Quapropter etiam, ad difficultatem hanc evitandam, nullatenus indigemus distinctione inter extensionem realem & virtualem, adeò ut per hanc res spiritualis corpori esset quasi coëxtensa; quam Auctor impugnat deinceps. Non magis quam in explicanda Æternitate Dei, successivæ rerum creatarum durationi coëxistente, opus est concipere virtualem successionem à reali distinctam. II. Si nullo alio pacto concipere possumus, quomodo Spiritus præsens esse possit substantiæ extensæ, nisi ipsum etiam extensum concipiamus, viderit Auctor, quâ aut fide, aut prudentiâ, sub finem Cap. xii. professus sit, se nolle negare, Deum non etiam per suam essentiam suamque substantiam rebus omnibus esse præsentem. Profectò, nisi lectori suo hic verba dare voluerit, omninò secundum ista necesse habet fateri, vel Dei substantiam extensam se concipere, cum eam rebus corporeis præsentem esse fatetur; vel falsò dici, non alio pacto concipi posse, quomodo spiritus rei extensæ sit præsens, nisi concipiatur extensus. III. Quod ad unionem Spiritùs cum corpore attinet, non quidem ea, nostro judicio, in locali præsentia consistit; attamen hanc ad illam omninò prærequiri, firmiter in superioribus probavimus. IV. Observetur, Auctorem diserte fateri, Philosophiam Peripateticam docere, essentiam mentis in eo consistere, quod non sit extensa; & (uti addit paulò inferius) non esse mentem, nisi propterea quod non habeat extensionem. Audiant ista nostri Novatores! qui quamvis ignorare nequeant, hanc esse adversariorum suorum mentem perpetuam & assertionem constantem, nihilominus, plane contra officium viri boni, objicere illis non desinunt iterum iterumque, eos Spiritum sibi imaginari per modum subtilis corporis ac tenuis extensionis. Cætera, quæ habet hac de re Auctor, transeo; quippe quæ, uti magnam partem ex Claubergio petita, itâ quoque cum hunc refutavimus refutata sunt. Alii, ut probent Spiritibus Alicubi tribui non posse citra absurditatem, vehementer urgent, quid sit futurum, si pars istius corporis, cui Spiritus coexistit, auferatur, V. C. si manus homini amputetur; vel si extensio ea augeatur, ut cum puer accrescit, &c. Rogantque, an eo in casu adhuc Spiritus maneat in eodem Ubi, nec ne? Quibus respondeo, in eodem Ubi manere, quamdiu eidem spatio, coexistit. Membrum resectum quod attinet, ci mens simpliciter non amplius exsistit praesens, absque ullo tamen sui motu, divisione, aut diminutione. Habet res se per omnia, uti in aeterna Dei duratione nostris temporibus coexistente. De ea si quis quaerat quid futurum sit, si mundus existere desinat? dicendum, extiturum Deum, uti semper extitit, citra ullam suae durationis contractionem. Quapropter quae a quibusdam hoc loco quaeruntur, An Spiritus essentia dividatur, minuatur, prorepat in partes de novo additas, vel retrocedat seseque contrahat in caeterum membrum, atque ibi intumescat? quaeque sexcenta moventur his similia, ridicula prorsus sunt, & inepta adeo, ut responsum nullum mereantur. Oriuntur quippe difficultates illae & quaestiones absurdissimae ex absurdo conceptu, quem de Spirituum praesentia sibi formant, aliosque secum formare autumant. Videlicet supponunt, & sic sentire dissentientes fingunt, quasi ita dicatur & concipiatur Spiritus corpori coexistere, quemadmodum ex. gr. vapor, vel aliud quod tenue corpus, corporis alterius porosi, v. c. spongiae, interstitia replet, in ea se insinuat, perque ea diffunditur; unde necessarium fit, ut, si corporis ejusmodi pars abscindatur, etiam simul auferatur aliqua pars corporis subtilioris, per id diffusi eique inhaerentis, nisi hoc se contrahat ac in caeteram illius partem se recipiat. Verum nisi quis ex hactenus explicatis didicerit alios formare conceptus de Spirituum Ubi, ac intelligere longissimum discrimen quod intercedit inter spiritus cum corpore coexistentiam, & hanc tenuis corporis in poros alterius insinuationem, frustra laborabo discutere crassas illas corporearum idearum nebulas: quae sua sponte evanescunt, superioribus duntaxat rite perceptis.
units.tr: While we answer the objection put forward, we have at the same time satisfied the difficulty raised by De la Forge, in his Tractatus de Mente Humana, chapter XIII, when he says: "Scholastic philosophy, while on the one hand it teaches that the essence of the mind consists in its not being extended, and on the other hand holds that the nature of the union of two substances consists in the local presence of one with the other, at the same time removes in this way all the means of conceiving the union of mind and body. For how can anyone grasp the mind, that is, according to them a substance whose nature consists in not being extended, as able to become extended? For we can conceive in no other way how something can be present to an extended substance, unless we also conceive it as extended, etc." On these words, note the following. 1. It is by no means necessary that everything which coexists with an extended thing be extended, or be conceived as such; as has been sufficiently demonstrated. Therefore, to avoid this difficulty, we have no need at all of the distinction between real and virtual extension, so that by it a spiritual thing would be, as it were, co-extended with a body; which the author attacks afterwards. No more is it necessary, in explaining the eternity of God coexisting with the successive duration of created things, to conceive a virtual succession distinct from a real one. II. As for "If we can conceive in no other way how a spirit can be present to an extended substance unless we also conceive it as extended," let the author see with what faith or prudence, near the end of chapter XII, he professed that he is unwilling to deny that God is also present to all things through his essence and his substance. Certainly, unless he wishes to deceive his reader here, he must by these very words either admit that he conceives the extended substance of God, since he confesses that it is present to corporeal things; or else it is falsely said that there is no other way to conceive how a spirit is present to an extended thing, unless it is conceived as extended. III. As for the union of spirit with body, it indeed does not, in our judgment, consist in local presence; yet we have firmly proved in what precedes that this presence is entirely prerequisite for that union. IV. Let it be noted that the author plainly admits that Peripatetic philosophy teaches that the essence of the mind consists in its not being extended, and (as he adds a little lower) that the mind is not a mind except because it has no extension. Let our Innovators hear these things! Although they cannot be ignorant that this is the constant and perpetual assertion of their opponents, nevertheless, quite contrary to the duty of a good man, they do not cease to object to them again and again that they imagine a spirit after the manner of a subtle body and a thin extension. As for the rest of what the author has on this matter, I pass it over; since, being for the most part taken from Clauberg, it has been refuted together with him when we refuted him. Others, to prove that an Alicubi cannot be ascribed to spirits without absurdity, urge vehemently what would happen if a part of that body with which the spirit coexists were removed, for example if a hand were amputated from a man; or if that extension were enlarged, as when a child grows, etc. And they ask whether, in that case, the spirit still remains in the same Where or not. To these I answer that it remains in the same Where as long as it coexists with the same space. As for a severed limb, the mind simply no longer exists there as present, yet without any motion, division, or diminution on its part. The matter is in every way like the eternal duration of God coexisting with our times. If someone asks about this what will happen if the world ceases to exist, the answer is that God will still exist, as he always has, without any contraction of his duration. Therefore the questions raised here by some, whether the essence of a spirit is divided, diminished, creeps into newly added parts, or retreats and contracts itself into the remaining member and there swells up; and the countless similar questions that are stirred up, are altogether ridiculous and so inept that they deserve no answer. Those difficulties and most absurd questions arise from the absurd concept which they form for themselves of the presence of spirits, and which they claim others form too. Namely, they suppose, and feign that dissenters think so, that a spirit is said and conceived to coexist with a body in the way that, for example, vapour, or some other thin body, fills the interstices of another porous body, such as a sponge, insinuates itself into it, and is diffused through it; whence it becomes necessary that, if a part of such a body is cut off, some part of the more subtle body, diffused through it and adhering to it, is also removed at the same time, unless this contracts and withdraws into the remaining part of it. But unless someone has learned from what has been explained so far to form other concepts of the Where of spirits, and to understand the very great difference that lies between the coexistence of a spirit with a body and this insinuation of a thin body into the pores of another, I shall labour in vain to dispel those gross mists of corporeal ideas; which vanish of their own accord, provided only the foregoing has been rightly grasped.

units.la: Majoris momenti est argumentum quod pro Nullibitate Spirituum desumunt quidam ab eo, quod Spiritus solos producere potuerit Deus, nullis creatis corporibus. Nempe inquiunt, hoc
units.tr: The argument that some draw for the nonlocation of spirits is of greater weight. It rests on the fact that God could have produced spirits alone, with no created bodies. Granted this, they say, would spirits still be somewhere?

units.la: R r 2 posito, etiamnùm Spiritus Alicubì forent ? Si non; utiquè inseparabile Spirittuum attributum non erit τὸ Alicubi esse, sed id eis conveniet, non sui ratione, sed ex accidente tantùm, ratione corporum in quibus operantur, quæque verè sunt Alicubi. Si verò non existente corpore, Spiritus nihilominus forent alicubì, admittendum etiam erit, Spiritum à Spiritu distare, alterumque alteri propiorem esse, &c. At quis ista concipiat sine existentia extensionis intermediæ ? Ad quæ observandum, fore omninò, spiritus alicubi, etiamsi soli existerent, quatenus essentia eorum esset, ubi corpora esse possent, itâ ut, si hæc producerentur, Spiritus iisdem verè coëxisterent, quod ad Ubi Spituum concipiendum sufficere, antè fuit dictum. Atque hoc sensu Immensus Deus etiam ante creatum mundum extitit Alicubi, quoniam fuit, ubi tunc fuit nihil, extensio tamen esse potuit. Quod additur de intermedia extensione, cujus respectu Spiritus distare deberent, id supponit, extensionem & spatium & distantiam coincidere prorsùs, nec hæc posse esse sine illa; quod falsum autumamus. Sed latioris id indaginis est, quam quod in præsens, hæc absolvere festinans, pertractare possim. Conferantur quæ in hanc rem notavimus. §. xiv.
units.tr: If not, then being somewhere [τὸ Alicubi esse] will not be an inseparable attribute of spirits. It will belong to them not by their own nature but only by accident, by reason of the bodies in which they act and which truly are somewhere. But if, with no body existing, spirits would nonetheless be somewhere, it must also be admitted that spirit is at a distance from spirit, and one nearer to another, and so on. But who can conceive this without an intervening extension existing? To this it must be observed that spirits would certainly be somewhere even if they alone existed, insofar as their essence is such that bodies could be where they are. So if these were produced, the spirits would truly coexist with them. As was said before, this is enough for conceiving the "where" of spirits. In this sense the immense God also existed somewhere before the world was created, since there was extension where then there was nothing, yet it could have been. What is added about an intervening extension, with respect to which spirits would have to be distant, supposes that extension, space and distance coincide entirely, and that none of these can exist without the others. We hold this to be false. But this is a matter of wider scope than I can treat now, since I am hastening to finish. Let the things we have noted on this subject be compared: §. xiv.

units.la: Urgent alii : Si mens per se & ratione suæ essentiæ alicubi esset, procul omni dubio hujus sui attributi sibi foret conscia, noviset- que adeò ubinam præcisè exisseret. At nullo modo ejus sibi conscia est. Imò, addunt, ignoraremus penitus, utrùm Spiritus hic aut illic sint, nisi id concluderemus ex operationibus eorundem externis & transeuntibus; quas ubi nullas observamus, illicò incerti sumus, utrùm quis adsit Spiritus, nec ne. Ex quibus manifestum esse putant, non per essentiam, sed tantùm per operationes in corporibus, Spiritus esse alicubi. Verùm salva res omnis est, si distinxerimus inter causam, uti vocant, essendi & cognoscendi. Fateor, non nisi ex operationibus transeuntibus nobis innotescere, Spiritum in hoc aut illo determinato Ubi existere: cum enim sit res quæ sensus non afficit, quæque in intellectum nostrum rarò immediatè agit, nos verò, ceu cognitionis nostræ administris, utamur sensibus, quid mirum, si ignoremus, in hoc aut illo determinato Ubi Spiritum existere, quamdiu se suis operationibus inibi non manifestat ? Sed & sæpissimè corporis alicujus tenuioris,
units.tr: Others press the point: "If the mind were somewhere by its own essence and by the nature of its being, it would beyond doubt be conscious of this attribute of its own, and so would know exactly where it is. But it is in no way conscious of this. Indeed," they add, "we would be utterly ignorant whether spirits are here or there, unless we concluded it from their external and transient operations; and where we observe no such operations, we are at once uncertain whether any spirit is present or not. From these things they think it evident that spirits are somewhere not through their essence, but only through their operations on bodies." But the whole matter is settled if we distinguish between the cause, as they call it, of being and that of knowing. I grant that we come to know that a spirit exists in this or that determinate place only from its transient operations. For since it is a thing that does not affect the senses, and rarely acts immediately upon our intellect, while we use the senses as the servants of our knowledge, what wonder is it if we do not know that a spirit exists in this or that determinate place, so long as it does not make itself manifest there by its operations? But very often also a body of a rather thin nature,

units.la: XX. Actio spiritus transiens, cum hic aut illic esse non facit, sed tantùm indicat.
units.tr: XX. A spirit's transient action does not make it be here or there, but only indicates it.

units.la: nobisque ob subtilitatem suam insensibilis, præsentia à nobis non percipitur, nisi quædam ejus operationes externæ sensus nostros afficiant. At, quemadmodum nequaquam indè colligere licet, corpus tale verè iltic præsens non fuisse, quamdiu conspicuas nobis operationes non produxit, itâ neque de Spiritu concludere id licet. Cæterùm, parvi momenti est, quòd dicatur mens sibi non esse conscia sui alicubi: plura enim sunt prædicata, quorum sæpè mens sibi conscia non est, quæ nihilominus verè ei conveniunt. Ne longè abeamus, dic, quæsò! estne sibi satis conscia mens, in qua parte corporis humani immediatè operetur? Si est; unde ergò tam diversa de sensorio communi inter ipsos eruditos sententia? Si non; num & ideò negandum, mentem in aliqua corporis nostri parte immediatè agere? Inquies forsan, bene attendenti id satis notum esse potest. At (ne jam inquiram, quam hoc sit vel verum vel falsum) idem à me tibi responsum puta; mecumque idcirco agnosce, haud licere menti denegare attributum quodpiam, ex hoc quod ejus sibi non sit immediatè conscia. Nempè, non immediatè, sed argumentando ferè devenimus in cognitionem plerarumque proprietatum nostræ mentis: quam argumentationem quisquis secum instituit diligenter & accuratè, actutum is certus erit nobiscum, Mentem etiam verè alicubi esse, atque esse debere.
units.tr: and because of its subtlety insensible to us, its presence is not perceived by us unless certain of its external operations affect our senses. But just as one cannot at all infer from this that such a body was not truly present there so long as it produced no visible operations, so neither may one conclude this about a spirit. Moreover, it is of little weight that the mind is said not to be conscious of itself as being somewhere: for there are many predicates which the mind is often not conscious of, yet which truly belong to it. Not to go far afield, tell me, I pray: is the mind sufficiently conscious of the part of the human body in which it acts immediately? If it is, whence then comes such a diversity of opinion among the learned themselves about the common sensorium? If it is not, must we therefore also deny that the mind acts immediately in some part of our body? You will perhaps say that to one who attends carefully this can be known well enough. But (not to inquire now how true or false this is) take the same answer from me, and so agree with me that it is not permitted to deny the mind any attribute merely because it is not immediately conscious of it. Indeed, we arrive at the knowledge of most properties of our mind not immediately but by reasoning; and whoever carefully and accurately works this reasoning out for himself will soon be certain with us that the mind also truly is somewhere, and must be somewhere.

units.la: Ex omnibus hactenus allatis concludimus, Spiritus jure merito esse revocandos ex exilio, ad quod eos nullo suo merito damnarunt, & non ultra Garamantas tantùm & glacialem oceanum relegarunt, sed terrâ marique, infemi coelique sedibus, totiusque Universi finibus expulsos, proscripserunt Nullibistæ: aut deliberantes, aut ludentes, vafreque ac obliquè insinuantes, mentem, quatenus est substantia incorporea, tanquam chimeram inutileque figmentum, ex tota rerum Universitate esse exterminandam, inquit H. Morus. Quousquè hæc verè? judicent alii! Ipsi quid ad hæc? Jam mihi eos more suo videor audire conquerentes de injuriis & calumniis, quibus iniquè graventur. Non enim se eos esse, qui negent Spiritus, etiam ratione essentiæ, esse alicubi; sed, qui accuratius solùm explicent, Quomodo alicubi sint; idque ordine meliori quam hactenùs factum sit à Scholasticis. Videlicet, tantùm se velle, ut concipiamus gradatim Spiritum esse Alicubi; primùm quidem per operationes externas; hinc per potentiam; inde denique per essentiam. Ast hoccine est, quod rotundè affirmare audivimus, Spiritus alicubi esse non aliter quam efficaciter agendo ; tantum per operationem ; non vere ; non proprie per essentiam, &c. Quis, hæc cum illis conferens, non miretur vel prodigiosam contradicendi libidinem, vel vaferrimam in palliativa hac cura astutiam? Non itâ solent qui pacem & veritatem amant candidi. Si dissentiant ab iis qui statuunt Spiritus alicubi esse ratione essentiæ, etiamsi extra se nil operentur, quid Viros pudet suæ sententiæ? Curam per verum elenchum oppugnatam non fatentur? Quidve adeò conquerantur de injuriis amplius & calumniis? Quod si cum affirmantibus idem re vera sentiant, quid attinet his obloqui non tantùm, sed & eos tam immeritò & acerbè passim traducere? Cur non missas faciunt phrases oppositum sonantes, inusitatas, periculosas, ac turbantes docentium & discentium scholas? Atquì cum stupidis istis, scilicet! Peripateticis idem sentire, affirmabunt, sat scio, nunquam: tam animulis istis voluptè est esse Nullibi, ne videlicet corporum contagio ipsæ quoque extensæ fiant, atque itâ omni suâ excidant cogitatione.
units.tr: From all that has been adduced so far we conclude that spirits are rightly to be recalled from the exile to which they were condemned through no merit of their own. The Nullibists have not merely banished them beyond the Garamantes and the icy ocean; they have also expelled them from land and sea, from the abodes of hell and heaven, and from the bounds of the whole universe, and proscribed them: whether deliberately or in jest, and craftily and obliquely insinuating that the mind, insofar as it is an incorporeal substance, must be banished from the whole universe of things as a chimera and a useless fiction, says H. More. How true this is, let others judge! What do they themselves say to this? Already I seem to hear them, in their usual manner, complaining of the injuries and calumnies with which they are unjustly burdened. For they say they are not the ones who deny that spirits are somewhere, even by reason of essence. Rather, they only explain more accurately how spirits are somewhere, and in a better order than the Scholastics have hitherto followed. Namely, they wish only that we conceive gradually that spirit is somewhere: first through external operations, then through power, and finally through essence. But is this what we have heard them assert outright, that spirits are somewhere in no other way than by acting effectively, only through operation, not truly and not properly through essence, and so on? Who, comparing these statements with those people, would not marvel either at their prodigious itch for contradiction or at the very crafty cunning of this palliative cure? Those who love peace and truth do not usually act so sincerely. If they dissent from those who hold that spirits are somewhere by reason of essence, even when they operate nothing outside themselves, why are they ashamed of their opinion? Do they not confess that their cure has been assailed by a true refutation? Or why do they complain further of injuries and calumnies? But if they really think the same as those who affirm it, what is the point of not only contradicting them but also slandering them everywhere so unjustly and bitterly? Why do they not drop their phrases that sound the opposite, unusual, dangerous, and disturbing to the schools of teachers and learners? But with those dull Peripatetics! They will certainly never affirm that they think the same, I am sure of it. Such is the delight these little souls take in being nowhere, lest, by contagion with bodies, they too should become extended and so lose all their thought.
XXII.

units.la: Uti orsus sum, itâ pertexam hanc Dissertatiunculam verbis H. Mori, qui, loco citato, ad verba illa Ludovici de la Forge, Quando dico Deum esse omnibus rebus præsentem per suam Omnipotentiam, nolo negare eum etiam per suam Essentiam suamque Substantiam ibi esse præsentem, sic disserit : „Audin' tu, mi Nullibista! quid aperte „profitetur unus è præcipuis Condiscipulis tuis, & religiosissimis „stupendi vestri Arcani, Nullibismum intelligo, Symmystis, „Deum etiam per essentiam vel substantiam suam omnibus materiæ „partibus adesse? Et tamen vos non pudet interim asseverare, nec „Deum nec Spiritus ullos creatos Alicubi esse posse? Quo nihil „repugnantius dici potest vel excogitari, & ab omni ratione alienius. Quamobrem cum tam prope ad veritatem accedant Nullibista, impossibile videtur, ut adeo ex inopinato eam rursus refugerent, nisi superstitiosa Metaphysicæ Cartesianæ admiratione „occæcati essent, & jocularibus illius subtilitatibus præstigiosisque „abstractionibus illusi, effascinati, & dementati. Concludituque demum : „Quod quicquam exstat, nec tamen sit usquam in „tota rerum Universitate, tam malesana vox est & ab omni ratione aliena atque absona, ut à nemine mentis compote, nisi „per
units.tr: As I began, so I will continue this little dissertation with the words of H. More, who, in the passage already cited, responding to those words of Louis de la Forge, When I say that God is present to all things by his Omnipotence, I do not wish to deny that he is also present there by his Essence and his Substance, argues as follows: "Do you hear this, my Nullibist! See what one of the chief fellow-disciples of yours, and one of the most devout adherents of your wonderful mystery, openly professes. I mean Nullibism, you fellow-initiates: that God is present to all parts of matter even by his essence or substance. And yet you are not ashamed meanwhile to assert that neither God nor any created spirit can be anywhere? Nothing more contradictory can be said or imagined, and nothing more alien to all reason. Therefore, since the Nullibists come so near to the truth, it seems impossible that they should so suddenly flee from it again, unless they had been blinded by a superstitious admiration for the Cartesian metaphysics, and had been deceived, bewitched, and driven mad by its playful subtleties and deceptive abstractions. And at last he concludes: That something exists and yet is nowhere in the whole universe of things is such a mad expression, and so alien and discordant with all reason, that no one in his right mind could utter it except as a joke, as we have already noted. Therefore those are the more to be pitied who, captivated and blinded by admiration for the first author of so absurd an opinion, embrace it so seriously and so solemnly, and elaborate it so diligently."

units.la: H. Mori in Nullibistas dicto Disquisitio clauditur. „per deridiculum possit proferri ; prout suprà monuimus. „ Unde magis dolendæ sunt eorum vices, qui, admiratione „primi Authoris tam absurdæ sententiæ capti & occæcati, eam „tam serió sanctoque amplectuntur, tamque diligenter ex„poliunt.
units.tr: Here the Disquisition against the Nullibists by H. More ends. "...could be uttered only as a joke, as we have already noted. Hence the more pitiable is the lot of those who, captivated and blinded by admiration for the first author of so absurd an opinion, embrace it so earnestly and so solemnly, and work it out so diligently."
DISSERTATION ON THE AUTOMATON MAN.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Assumptarum hypothesium falsitas fertilis plerorumque errorum causa. II. Admissi in brutis motus automatici iisdem in hominibus admittendis viam parant. III. Hominem Automaticum quem, & quo sensu, admittat Cartesius ? IV. Per eum inane reipsa redditur & superfluum animæ rationalis in corporis motus imperium. V. Deleturque prorsus efficax mentis, tanquam verè causæ, in motus corporeos influxus. VI. Obstat eidem impeditus corporis motus ad mentis ægritudinem, abstractam meditationem, & separationem ejus à corpore in morte. VII. Opinio de Homine Automatico patronos suos incertos reddit, num bona hominum pars anima rationali gaudeat? VIII. Operationes brutorum pro automaticis hominis motibus nihil concludunt. IX. Operationes hominis multæ rationem habent causam, etsi inconsultâ eâ fieri videantur. X. Etiam purè animales actiones à rationali anima proficisci possunt. XI. Motus corporis qui passiones animi comitantur mentem habent principium sui, & voluntarii sunt. XII. Convulsionum motus ipse ab anima est; inordinatio ejus à perturbata corporis dispositione. XIII. Automata artefacta pro rerum naturalium motibus automaticis concludendis nihil prosunt.
units.tr: I. The falsity of assumed hypotheses is a fertile cause of most errors. II. What is admitted about automatic motion in brutes prepares the way for admitting it in men. III. What Descartes admits concerning the Automaton Man, and in what sense. IV. Through him the rule of the rational soul over the motions of the body is in fact made empty and superfluous. V. And the efficacy of the mind, as a true cause, in bodily motions is utterly destroyed. VI. Against this stands the hindered motion of the body in the mind's sickness, in abstract meditation, and in its separation from the body at death. VII. The opinion about the Automaton Man makes its defenders uncertain whether a good part of mankind enjoys a rational soul. VIII. The operations of brutes prove nothing about the automatic motions of man. IX. Many human operations have a reasoned cause, even if they seem to be done without deliberation. X. Even purely animal actions can proceed from the rational soul. XI. Bodily motions that accompany the passions of the mind have the mind as their principle, and are voluntary. XII. The motion of convulsions is itself from the soul; its disorder is from the disturbed disposition of the body. XIII. Artificial automata are of no help in proving the automatic motions of natural things.

units.la: A ubi pedem figam, & totam Terræ molem dimovebo loco, quondam Geometræ Syracusani vox erat. Adeò facile est, datis postulatis etiam valdè exiguis, grandia quævis moliri. Atque id in veritatis inquisitione non tantùm obtinet, ubi ex principiis valdè paucis & tenuibus infinita deducitur conclusionum continuâ demonstrationis concatenatione connexarum multitudo, cujus rei specimen exhibet elegantissimum Geometria; sed & falsitatis atque erroris par, si non major, existit fertilitas. Nimirùm non solum in ratiocinando consequentiæ inconsequentes nectuntur sæpius, verùm legitimâ etiam firmæ sequelæ necessitate dogmata deducuntur sat nitidè ex hypothesi falsa, quæ tamen ob vitium præmissorum principiorum, iisdem nihilo sunt aut firmiora aut veriora. Quæ cogitantes haud mirabimur, eum, qui vel semel hypothesin falsam pro vera assumsit, ex una falsitate incidere in aliam, nec sæpè ante quiescere in præcipiti hoc lapsu, quàm continuo descensu venerit ad imum; istud nimirum absurditatis barathrum, in quod descendere potuisse rationis compotem negares, ni viam noscas quâ istuc pervenerit. Scilicet, uti nemo de repente fit pessimus, quoniam quisque sceleratus sentit reluctantis conscientiæ morsus, quos simul & semel superare difficillimum est & vix possibile; itâ nemo facilè per saltum in extrema incidit absurda, cohibente hominem aliquatenus & aliquamdiu lumine rationis menti ingenito. Idcirco sensim plerumque sine sensu à minori ad majus hic fit progressus; donec error, initio parvus & contemnendus, dum errorem trahit, accrescat eundo, atque in fine magnus evadat & monstrosissimus. Itā ut quisque paulo ingeniosior promittere jure posset: Da ubi pedem figam (in falsa hypothesi), & totum scicutiarum orbem movebo loco.
