units.tr: "Give me a place where I may stand, and I will move the whole earth," was once the saying of the Syracusan geometer. So easy is it, given postulates however very slight, to construct any great thing whatever. And this holds not only in the inquiry after truth, where from very few and slender principles an infinite multitude of conclusions is deduced, linked together in an unbroken chain of demonstration (of which the most elegant geometry offers an example); there is also an equal, if not greater, fertility of falsehood and error. For not only in reasoning are inconsequent consequences often joined together, but also by the necessity of a sound inference, doctrines are deduced quite neatly from a false hypothesis, which nonetheless, because of the fault of their premises and principles, are in no way firmer or truer for that. Thinking on these things, we will not be surprised that whoever has once assumed a false hypothesis as true falls from one falsity into another, and often does not rest in this headlong slide until, by continuous descent, he reaches the bottom: that abyss of absurdity into which you would deny that a man in his right mind could have fallen, unless you know the path by which he arrived there. Indeed, just as no one becomes wicked all at once, since every criminal feels the bites of a resisting conscience, which it is most difficult and scarcely possible to overcome at once and in a single moment, so no one easily falls by a leap into the extreme absurdities, since the light of reason, innate in the mind, restrains a man to some extent and for some time. Hence the progress is usually made gradually, from the lesser to the greater, almost without notice; until the error, small and contemptible at the beginning, grows as it goes on drawing other errors after it, and at last becomes great and most monstrous. So that any man a little more clever could rightly promise: Give me a place where I may stand (in a false hypothesis), and I will move the whole orb of the sciences.

units.la: Rei hujus fidem facit, neque uno specimine, hodierna Philosophorum secta, cui placita Cartesii placent. Insolens ei non est, quaedam praemittere dogmata, quae primo intuitu minoris momenti videri possunt, & toleranda saltem tanquam ingeniosae subtilitatis inventa; quibus tamen si quis inhaeserit, iisque convenienter philosophari perrexerit, absurditatibus involvetur longè maximis: quibus tamen (ut pessimo more fieri solet) repudium mittere deinceps recusabit, ne in praeconceptis hypothesibus errasse deprehendatur. Sit unum instar omnium! Coepit antehac Recentioribus defendi, Bruta quicquid agunt agere ad instar machinae cujusdam pneumaticae aut hydraulicae; per solam nimirum partium dispositionem, & sanguinis ac spirituum motum tantùm ab extrinseco impressum, citra ullius animae, quae sit intrinsecum ac substantiale sensus & cognitionis principium, praesidium aut moderamen. Quamvis autem hujus sententiae patroni primùm non proderent, se opinari, idem quoque in corpore humano evenire posse, haud tamen jam tum deerant inter eruditos prudentes viri, qui, attendentes quanta sit & organorum & operationum externarum in bruto & homine similitudo, facilem ab illo ad hunc transitum & consequentiam aliquandò faciendam, praevidebant. Indè non pauci vel ob hoc solum concedendum neutiquam arbitrabantur dogma de brutis, quae sine principio substantiali intrinseco agant ad instar horologiorum, quòd crederent, viam per illud sterni, ad humana quoque corpora in ejusdem generis machinas automaticas convertenda; sicque tandem mentem substantialem penitus ab iisdem excludendam.
units.tr: The present-day school of philosophers, whose tenets please Descartes, furnishes proof of this, and not by one example alone. It is not unusual for them to put forward certain doctrines which at first glance may seem of little importance, and which may be tolerated at least as inventions of clever subtlety. Yet if anyone clings to these and goes on philosophizing accordingly, he will be entangled in the greatest absurdities; and yet (as is commonly done in the worst fashion) he will then refuse to cast these off, lest he be found to have erred in his preconceived hypotheses. Let one example stand for all! Recent writers have begun to defend the view that brutes, whatever they do, act in the manner of some pneumatic or hydraulic machine: namely, by the mere arrangement of parts and by the motion of blood and spirits impressed only from without, without the help or direction of any soul, which is the intrinsic and substantial principle of sensation and cognition. Although the defenders of this opinion did not at first profess that the same could happen in the human body, nevertheless there were not lacking, even then, prudent men among the learned who, considering how great is the similarity between brute and man both in their organs and in their external operations, foresaw that at some time an easy transition and consequence would be made from the one to the other. Hence not a few thought that the doctrine about brutes, that they act without an intrinsic substantial principle like clocks, should by no means be granted even for this reason alone: they believed that a way was being paved through it for turning human bodies also into automatic machines of the same kind; and so at last the substantial mind would be utterly excluded from them.

units.la: Neque hic metus fuit omninò vanus: re verà enim Cartesius corpus humanum considerare coepit tanquam ergasterium quinque accidentium, Motus, Quietis, Situs, Figurae, & Magnitudinis; quodque adeò vivere posset & moveri absque animae rationalis lis praesidio, æquè ac brutum. Ipsum audire operæ pretium fuerit. Epist. LIV. Part. I. Externarum nostrarum actionum nulla est, praeter loquelam, quà possit cuipiam illas examinanti constare, corpus nostrum non esse automatum, sed insuper inesse illi animam, quæ cogitandi facultate polleat. Ecce! Actiones nostras omnes corporeas, loquelâ exceptâ, ad corpus, tanquam ad automatum referri posse, opinatur. Atque iterum clarè, Epist. LXVII. Nullam agnoscimus rationem, propter quam, ubi est talis membrorum conformatio, qualem in animalibus videmus, cogitatio etiam debeat adesse; atque ideo majori admiratione dignum est, quod mens aliqua reperiatur in unoquoque humano corpore, quam quod nulla sit in ullis brutis. Transeo quæ hùc spectantia occurrunt plurima in Tractatu ejusdem gemino, tùm de Homine, tùm de Passionibus animi: quem utrumque quisquis unquam evolvit diligentius, super hanc unam hypothesin, tanquam primum ac præcipuum fundamentum, ædificatum stare, nullo negotio deprehendet. Quin imò, si ad ipsas Viri Philosophationes attendere velimus potius quam ad phraseologias quasdam modestiores, quibus illas evitandæ offensionis gratiâ de industria nonnunquam involvisse videtur, intelligemus facilè, genuinam illi mentem fuisse, hominis corpus vivere non tantum posse sine animæ rationalis influxu, sed & re ipsâ absque ejusdem præsidio vivere & moveri. Quibus convenienter passim hodiè docent istius opinionis fautores: Vitam nostram in solo corporeo motu consistere; eam cum belluis nos communem habere; non dependere à mente, cum, hac non data, in automato, omnia suâ operâ potuisset defungi. Item, Hominem moveri ab anima, & mortem ejus à carne divortium esse, non simpliciter esse asserendum: Ut Molitor molam non movet, sed motam regit, sic animam non tam motum, quam ejus modos facere, suâ directione, &c. Et hic Homo, cujus corpus, licet forte animâ rationali non careat, haud tamen ab ea moveatur (quem meritò idcirco Automaticum dicimus) num admittendus sit? hac Exercitatione disquiremus.
units.tr: Nor was this fear altogether vain. For in fact Descartes began to consider the human body as a workshop of five accidents: motion, rest, position, figure, and magnitude; and so it could live and move without the help of the rational soul, just as a brute does. It will be worth our while to hear him himself. Letter 54, Part I: Of our external actions there is none, except speech, by which anyone examining them could be assured that our body is not an automaton, but that a soul endowed with the faculty of thought is also present in it. See! He thinks that all our bodily actions, except speech, can be referred to the body as to an automaton. And again, quite clearly, Letter 67: We recognize no reason why, where there is such a conformation of limbs as we see in animals, thought should also be present; and therefore it is more worthy of admiration that some mind is found in every human body than that none is found in any brute. I pass over the many things pertinent to this which occur in his twofold treatise, both On Man and On the Passions of the Soul. Whoever has ever read either of these more carefully will easily see that it rests upon this one hypothesis as its first and chief foundation. Indeed, if we attend to the Philosopher's own reasonings rather than to certain more modest phrases, by which he seems to have deliberately wrapped them up now and then to avoid offence, we will easily understand that his genuine mind was that the human body can not only live without the influence of the rational soul, but in fact does live and move without its help. The defenders of this opinion teach today, accordingly, in many places: that our life consists in bodily motion alone; that we share it with the beasts; that it does not depend on the mind, since, the mind being absent, the automaton could have performed all its functions by its own work. Likewise: It must not be simply asserted that man is moved by the soul, and that his death is the separation of the soul from the flesh. As the miller does not move the millstone but governs it when it is moved, so the soul does not so much cause motion as direct its modes, by its guidance, etc. And here we shall inquire, in this Dissertation, whether this Man, whose body, though perhaps not lacking a rational soul, is nevertheless not moved by it (and for that reason we rightly call him the Automaton), is to be admitted.

units.la: Videtur autem nobis sententia affirmativa, uti salsissima, ita periculosissima. Id demonstraturi supponemus, certum esse, nos ipsos in nobis experiri Animam rationis participem, essentiæ à corpore nostro distinctæ, ad cujus nutum & arbitrium motus nostri
units.tr: It seems to us that the affirmative view is as absurd as it is dangerous. To prove this we shall assume that it is certain that we experience in ourselves a soul, a partaker of reason, distinct in essence from our body, at whose nod and will our motions...

units.la: IV. Per cum inane re ipsa reddiint & superfluum
units.tr: IV. Per cum inane re ipsa reddiint & superfluum

units.la: nostri corporis passim excitantur & peraguntur. Jam verò si motus isti corporis etiam citra animæ moderamen oriantur, aut oriri possint, cui, obsecro, fini mens corpori unita sic fuerit, ut illius imperio hujus actiones subsint, talesque quales sunt existant ? Certè, dicis causà hæc duo connectere noluit sapientissimus rerum opifex; qui, uti pondere, mensurâ, numero fecit omnia, itafrustrà produxit nihil. Quasi necesse fit, motorem addere navi, quæ ipsa ex sese, ventis solis & fluctibus agitata, apta satis est moveri, & viam sic conficere ut nullo motoris auxilio indigeat. Quasi sapiens sit, qui famulum assistere perpetuo jubet horologio, citra admotæ manûs opem horas indicare parato. Quin nihil jam aliud restare videtur, quam ut credamus, animam nostram corpus, cujus motibus non tam præest ex hac opinione quam potius subjecta existit, pro vero carcere duntaxat habere : quæ quondam Platonicorum erant deliria, sapientioribus dudùm rejecta & explosa. Quantò fuerit concinnius, & sapientiæ ac bonitati Divinæ, nec non animæ rationalis dignitati, congruum magis, sic omninò habere, movendæ nobili & structuræ præ omni alio in hoc Universo corpore admirandæ machinæ nobilem destinatam esse Divinâ providentiâ motricem Mentem, quæ ipsa suo sic imperio ei præsit, ut absque ea nihil possit moles per se iners atque omni actuositate destituta.
units.tr: of our body are everywhere aroused and carried on. Now, if those motions of the body arise, or can arise, even without the governance of the soul, then, I beg you, to what end would the mind be so united with the body that the body's actions are subject to its command and exist as they do? Surely, you will say, the most wise Maker of things did not wish to connect these two for no purpose; he who made all things by weight, measure and number has not produced anything in vain. As if a ship needed a pilot added to it, when it is of itself, driven by winds and waves alone, fit enough to move and to make its course without any help from a pilot. As if he were wise who ordered a servant to stand beside a clock forever, ready to show the hours without the touch of a hand being applied. Indeed, nothing else seems left than that we should believe our soul holds the body, whose motions it does not so much rule under this opinion as exist subject to them, merely as a true prison. This was once the delirium of the Platonists, long since rejected and exploded by wiser men. How much more fitting it would be, and more congruous with the wisdom and goodness of God and with the dignity of the rational soul, to hold that by divine providence a noble mind, moving the body, has been appointed to move this noble machine, the most admirable structure in this universe, and that it presides over it by its own command, so that without it the mass, inert in itself and destitute of all activity, could do nothing.

units.la: Quin, propius expensa Mentis nostræ cùm Corpore Unio prorsus infert necessariam motuum corporeorum à mente dependentiam. Consistere illam volunt Recentiores in hoc, quod ad varios corporis motus anima nostra variè cogitet, & vicissim ad varias animæ volitiones varii sequantur motus in corpore. Scire autem lubet, an volitiones illæ mentis, quibuscum connexi sunt motus nostri corporis, se habeant ut veræ horum causæ. an verò ut aliquod duntaxat concomitans, quod quidem cum eis existat simul, itâ tamen ut hi ab efficientia & influxu causali alterius non pendeant ? Si prius, habemus utique quod intendimus, quatenus evidens existit, effectum nullum dari sine causa; consequenter neque motus in corpore sine influxu animæ rationalis. Neque excipere juvabit, sic tantùm evinci, motus corporeos ipso quidem facto à mente dependere tanquam à causa, at non hinc sequi, eos in corpore sine mente dari planè non posse. Nam, præterquam
units.tr: Moreover, if we examine more closely the union of our mind with the body, it plainly implies a necessary dependence of bodily motions on the mind. The more recent writers want this union to consist in this: that our soul thinks variously in response to the various motions of the body, and conversely that various motions follow in the body upon various volitions of the soul. But we may ask whether those volitions of the mind, with which our bodily motions are connected, stand as the true causes of those motions, or only as some accompanying thing which exists together with them, but in such a way that these motions do not depend on the efficiency and causal influence of the other. If the former, we certainly have what we intend, since it is evident that no effect exists without a cause; consequently there is no motion in the body without the influence of the rational soul. Nor will it help to object that this only proves that bodily motions in fact depend on the mind as on a cause, but that it does not follow from this that they cannot occur in the body without the mind. For, apart from

units.la: V. Deleturque prorsus efficax mentis, tanquam veræ causæ, in motus corporeos influxus. quam quod ista adferre nequeant, qui vitam nostram à mente dependere corpusque hominis ab ea moveri negant, etiam superflua fuerit mentis illa causalitas, quâ de facto corpus movet, quod etiam sine ea hoc modo moveri potuisset: quod & Deo, & homine, & mente indignum est. Itaque eligendum posterius, Mentem videlicet nullam veram exercere causalitatem in producendis corporis motibus: quod ipsum hodiè velle videntur plerorumque Recentiorum phrases, atque hùc etiam aurigantur omnes eorundem hac parte assertiones. Atqui non uno absurdo premitur hæc sententia. Nimirùm, sequetur hinc, Mentem à corpore quopiam absentem, cum eo nihilominus re verà posse esse unitam; quin & eam unam eandemque unitam posse esse eodem tempore pluribus corporibus loco & spatio longè dissitis. Sume (itâ dispensante Divinâ Providentiâ) ad animæ meæ voluntatem moveri corpus quodpiam existens Romæ, aliud etiam Parisiis, idque eodem tempore. An ergò eadem mea mens, hîc unita existens meo corpori, simul unita fuerit corpori alteri Romæ existenti, & simul alteri, quod est Parisiis? Si non; reddatur, obsecro, ratio! Sufficit etenim ad unionem, ex hac opinione, cogitationum & motuum corporeorum simultanea existentia, citra realem influxum & causalitatem: at illam hîc habemus. Si sic; videsis, nemeritò stupidior habearis stipite, quicum mentem tuam uniri posse in idem suppositum credis. Et tamen ista profiteri non metuunt Neoterici; idque hypothesibus suis convenienter. Sic enim ajunt: Quoniam mentis cum corpore unio decreto Divino d int axat hæret, non est absolutè necessarium, ut hæc unio localis sit, sive ut mens præsentialiter parti alicui corporis præsideat: cum, tamen sive gr. esset in cœlis, non eo minus hæc cogitatio &c. hæc glandulæ, spirituum, aut actionum determinatio, se invicem immediatè excipirent, unirenturque in unico durationis nunc. Stupeat oportet mecum, qui hæc audit: simul autem notet, quò abducat de motibus nostri corporis à mentis influxu & causalitate non dependentibus, conceptus. Istis adde, si motus nostri corporis à mente, tanquam à vero principio & proprie dicta causa, non pendeant, etiam animam rationalem nullius actionis externæ, consequenter neque ullius operis corporei peccaminosi, causam proprie dictam haberi posse. Neque enim unquam, ex hac sententia, rea esse poterit Anima nostra, quod quicquam per corpus suo influxu & causalitate effecerit, sed duntaxat, quod tale quid fieri voluerit; quæ voluntas. ex hac hypothesi, non tanquam facti istius peccaminosi causa spectanda erit, sed tantum tanquam conditio sine qua non, ut loquuntur, sive prærequisitum. Per quæ concidit trita peccati in cogitatum, dictum, factum, divisio: ne plura accumulem, quæ in re Sacra hinc fluunt, absurda.
units.tr: V. And the efficacious influence of the mind, as a true cause, on bodily motions is utterly abolished. This: that those who deny that our life depends on the mind and that the human body is moved by it cannot advance this point; even that causality of the mind by which it in fact moves the body would be superfluous, since the body could have been moved in this way even without it, which is unworthy of God, of man, and of the mind. Therefore the latter must be chosen: namely, that the mind exercises no true causality in producing motions of the body. This is indeed what the phrases of most of the more recent writers seem to wish today, and all their assertions on this point are driven toward it. Yet this opinion is burdened with more than one absurdity. For it will follow from this that the mind can be really united with a body while absent from it, and that the same single mind can be united at the same time to several bodies widely distant in place and space. Suppose (by divine providence so dispensing) that some body existing at Rome is moved at the will of my soul, and another also at Paris, and that at the same time. Then is this same mind of mine, existing here united to my body, at the same time united to the other body existing at Rome, and at the same time to the other, which is at Paris? If not, let a reason be given, I beg you! For, on this opinion, the simultaneous existence of thoughts and bodily motions suffices for union, without real influence and causality; but here we have that. If so, you would be rightly considered more stupid than a log, if you believe your mind can be united to the same supposit as well. And yet the moderns do not fear to profess this, and in keeping with their hypotheses. For they say: Since the union of mind with body hangs only on the Divine decree, it is not absolutely necessary that this union be local, or that the mind preside over some part of the body in a present way: since, even if it were in heaven, nevertheless this thought, and this determination of the gland, of the spirits, or of the actions, would follow one another immediately and be united in a single instant of duration. Whoever hears this must be astonished along with me; and let him also note to what concept of bodily motions not dependent on the influence and causality of the mind this leads. Add to these: if the motions of our body do not depend on the mind as on the true principle and properly so-called cause, then the rational soul also cannot be considered the proper cause of any external action, and consequently of no sinful bodily work either. For on this view our soul can never be guilty of having effected anything through the body by its influence and causality, but only of having willed that such a thing be done; and that volition, on this hypothesis, is to be regarded not as the cause of the sinful deed but only as a condition without which it cannot occur, as they say, or as a prerequisite. By this the familiar division of sin into thought, word and deed collapses; I will not pile up the further absurdities that flow from this in sacred matters.

units.la: Experientiam porrò si consulamus, dictat ea non uno modo, motus corporeos ab impulsu & præsidio animæ rationalis prorsùs esse dependentes. Impediri eosdem & turbari videmus, quoties mens ægritudine confecta est, vel aliis modis affligitur; quatenus scilicet iis nimium detenta minus in regendo corpore occupatur: quùm contrà, mente existente vegeta, prompti atque agiles in corpore nostro exerceantur motus. Quin, absque debita Animæ nostræ attentione nullus existit in nobis usus organorum sensationi, consequenter & motui animali, inservientium. Quis nostrum non expertus est sæpius, quandò mens altius immersa fuit conceptibus profundioribus circa res à sensibus remotas, etiam tunc corpus obriguisse, neque motum aut affectum fuisse ab objectis externis, oblatis etiam satis clarè organis coporeis undiquaquè bene habentibus? Certo argumento, non instar machinæ alicujus automaticæ corpus nostrum moveri & impelli unitè à rebus extra nos positis; quod volunt, & sentire debent, qui motus corporis à mente pendere negant. Et quid in morte hominis eveniat, attendamus! Nempe, simulac Anima corpus socium deserit, quiescunt quoque operationes corporis & motus ejusdem animales. Cur quæsò? nisi motus illi, omnisque corporis activitas, ab Animæ præsentia, ejusque impulsu, sic pendeant, ut citra eam produci plane non possint. Nec moror objectiunculam, quam quidam movent, desumptam à qualicunque membrorum contractione, aut partium vibratione, quæ ad tempus etiam in cadavere superesse observatur: neque enim ordinatus iste motus est, neque diutinus adeò, quin referri facilè possit ad spiritus animales, ante mortis articulum ab anima impulsos, & in isto suo motu aliquamdiu perseverantes. Non parùm confirmabitur nostra ratiocinatio, si, quid ipsa hominis mors sit, cogitemus. Consistit ea in separatione seu disunione Animæ rationalis à corpore, quicum unita ante fuerat in eandem personam. Id docet Scriptura, confirmat ratio, clamat quorumvis eruditorum cujusvis seculi & sectæ consensus. Jam verò morti vitam opponi privativè, notum est. Itaque ut in disunione mentis à corpore mors, ita ex opposito in eorundem inter se unione vita hominis constistit. Illâ igitur sublatâ, etiam hæc tollitur. At ipsâ vita sublatâ, quis actiones vitales superstites manere posse, affirmet? Non ignoro distinctionem adversariorum inter vitam hominis animalem & rationalem: verum, quamvis negandum neutiquam sit, toto cœlo distinctas esse actiones mentis cogitativas à motibus corporis, hoc tamen loco inane esse hoc effugium, patet, quia hos ab illis dependere ex ipsa unionis natura, prout ea à Recentioribus explicatur, jam demonstravimus.
units.tr: Further, if we consult experience, it shows in more than one way that bodily motions depend entirely on the impulse and governance of the rational soul. We see them impeded and disturbed whenever the mind is worn out by sickness or is afflicted in other ways, since, being too much absorbed in these, it is less occupied in governing the body; whereas, when the mind is vigorous, prompt and agile motions are carried on in our body. Indeed, without due attention of our soul there is no use in us of the organs that serve sensation and, consequently, animal motion. Which of us has not often experienced that, when the mind was deeply immersed in more profound concepts about things remote from the senses, the body then also grew stiff, and was not moved or affected by external objects presented even to organs that were quite clearly well disposed in every way? This is a sure argument that our body is not moved and driven, like some automatic machine, solely by things placed outside us; those who deny that the motion of the body depends on the mind must want this and must feel it. And let us consider what happens at a man's death! Namely, as soon as the soul deserts its companion the body, the body's operations and its animal motions also cease. Why, I ask? Unless those motions, and all the activity of the body, depend on the presence and impulse of the soul in such a way that they cannot be produced at all without it. Nor do I dwell on the small objection some raise, drawn from any contraction of limbs or vibration of parts that is observed for a time even in a corpse: for that motion is neither ordered nor lasting enough not to be easily referred to the animal spirits, which the soul set moving before the moment of death and which persist for some time in that motion. Our reasoning will be considerably confirmed if we think about what death itself is. It consists in the separation or disunion of the rational soul from the body with which it was previously united in one person. Scripture teaches this, reason confirms it, and the agreement of learned men of every age and sect cries it out. Now it is well known that death is opposed to life as privation is. So just as death consists in the disunion of mind from body, so, conversely, the life of a man consists in the union of the two with each other. When that union is removed, so is this life. But once life itself is removed, who would affirm that vital actions can remain behind? I am not unaware of the opponents' distinction between the animal and the rational life of man: yet, although it must by no means be denied that the thinking actions of the mind are utterly distinct from the motions of the body, this escape is empty in the present place, since we have already shown that these depend on those, from the very nature of the union as the more recent writers explain it.

units.la: Præter ista, militat contra motum hominis automaticum generale argumentum, quo evincitur, nullas operationes à sola partium dispositione & motu, aliisve accidentibus aut modis, citra principii substantialis influxum, oriri posse, ex eo quod accidentia operativa non sint, nisi virtute alicujus substantiæ, cujus beneficio ut exsistunt ità operentur; quandoquidem modus operandi sequitur eum qui est essendi: nedum, ut actiones tam variæ & elegantes, quales plurimas, etiam præter loquelam, in humano corpore observare datur, ab iisdem proficisci queant. Verùm non lubet actum agere: videatur nostra Dissertatiuncula de Operationibus Brutorum. Unum præterire hic nequeo, eoque absolvam. Obtestor universos qui hic dissentiunt à nobis, dicant mihi, si operationes in corpore humano obviæ mentis influxu absolutè non indigeant, sed absque eo excitari queant, dicant mihi, inquam, bonâ fide, qui sciant, aut unde certi sint, fœtui humano in lucem hanc prodeunti inexistere mentem? Nunquam, sat scio, se hic expedient: nullam enim adferre poterunt obviam in eo operationem, præter motus quos ipsi automaticos esse contendunt. Si dicant, ineptum esse, qui indè concludat, Animam rationalem in illis non dari; nihil dicunt quod ad rem faciat. Nec enim ego infero, mentem in iis non exstitere; sed ab iis peto, ut ipsi inferant ullo firmo ratiocinio, eam omninò in iis dari: quod quamdiu non præstitum, temeritatis videtur, Philosopho imprimis, credere sine ratione, mentem iis inesse. Si hominem adferas
units.tr: Besides these, a general argument tells against the automatic motion of man: no operations can arise from the arrangement and motion of parts alone, or from other accidents or modes, without the influence of a substantial principle. Operative accidents do not act except by virtue of some substance, through whose benefit they exist and so act, since the mode of operating follows the mode of being. Still less could actions so varied and elegant, of which many are observed in the human body even apart from speech, proceed from such sources. But I do not wish to go into the matter at length here; see our little dissertation On the Operations of Brutes. There is one point I cannot pass over, and with it I will finish. I beg all who dissent from us to tell me, in good faith, if the operations found in the human body do not absolutely need the influence of the mind but can be excited without it: how do they know, or on what grounds are they certain, that a mind exists in the human foetus that is coming into this light? They will never, I am quite sure, extricate themselves here, for they can point to no operation in it apart from the motions which they themselves claim are automatic. If they say it would be foolish to conclude from this that no rational soul is present in them, they say nothing to the point. For I do not infer that a mind does not exist in them; I ask them to infer, by some firm reasoning, that a mind is indeed present in them. Until this is done, it seems rash, especially for a philosopher, to believe without reason that a mind is in them. If you bring forward

units.la: VII. Opinio de Homine Automatico suos patronos iucertos reddit, num bona homi-num pars animâ rationali gau-deat. adferas dormientem, in quo mens sit, quamvis nihil ejus deprehendi possit; respondeo, me facilè credere, mentem ei inesse, quippe qui sic habeo, ne quidem actiones istas animales in dormiente superstites citra activitatem principii substantialis dari posse: at tu illam ei inesse in æternum non probabis, nisi infirmâ conjecturâ, quòd & ante & post somnum corpori illi adsit. Neque evades, urgendo, mentem parvulorum actuosam esse, nihil repugnare, licet nihil tale nobis appareat. Etenim, dato, nihil repugnare. An quicquid nihil repugnat, Philosopho credendum est actu esse? Etiam certè nihil repugnat, ex tua hypothesi, parvulorum corpora vivere sine mente. Primo itaque biennio aut triennio à nativitate, priusquam sese rationis usus gestu & loquelâ prodere incipit, infantulo mentem inesse, demonstrare Cartesiano homini fuerit impossibile: quod ipsum volebam. Ne addam, per omnem vitam quosdam rationis usu ab ipsa infantia destitui, nec ullo cum signo unquam prodere; de quibus ergò per omnem vitam liceat dubitare, num mente gaudeant? Per quæ stant inconcussa, quæ quondam alibi de hoc ipso argumento hunc in modum differebam: Non mirabimur amplius (si absque Animæ rationalis præsentia vivere possumus) homines Arimaspos, Sciapodas, Strutiocæphalos, Fanesios, Satyros, Cynocephalos, Pygmæos, aliaque hominum portenta, quæ nobis delineat Plinius; cum non jam quibusdam corporis partibus, sed & Anima carere possit corpus humanum, & nihilominus, imò fortè commodius, vivere. Impii Paracelsi homunculum artificiolem, qui istud admittit, non pariter admittat? Quin si hoc itâ sit, quis novit, an non frequenter (etiam dum hæc scribimus) res nobis sit cum larvatis hominibus, speciatim talibus, cæterùm omni Mente prorsus destitutis? Et si forte in plerisque, quibuscum quotidiè agimus, aliquid occurrat, quod nos suspicari facit, inesse iis quoddam ratiocinandi principium, nihil tamen ejusmodi (ex hypothesi adversâ) deprehendere poterimus in puero paucos menses nato, phrenetico, similibusque aliis, idoneis signis, se aliquid rationaliter agere, indicare non valentibus. Quare cum in iis nullæ nobis observandæ occurrant operationes, præterquam tales, quales hi Philosophi, citra ullius Animæ substantialis adjumentum, à sola partium dispositione ac ,, motu proficisci posse afferunt, merito dubitabimus, an quidem ,,ii, quos enumeravimus, Mente gaudeant. Quæ si semel obti-,,neat insania, actum est de charitatis officiis, omnisque dissoluta ,,sunt societatis ac humanitatis vincula. Ista quidem tunc. Nunc, si cum Theologo, cui nova placet opinio, res foret, monerem serió, caveat ipse sedulò, ne ad ægrotos mentis & linguæ usu alienatos vocatus, incautus preces sæpius fundat pro defunctis; si-quidem ex novellis hypothesibus, nihil fieri poterit & facilius & frequentius, quam ut anima rationalis jam dudùm absit à corpo-re, in quo conspicui adhuc sunt motus, quos in agonizantibus passim observamus. Itâ non uno modo sine mente philosophari necesse habent, qui corpus suum sine mente regi posse conten-dunt.
units.tr: VII. The opinion of the Automatic Man leaves its supporters uncertain whether a good part of mankind enjoys a rational soul. a sleeping man, in whom there is a mind though nothing of it can be detected, I answer that I readily believe a mind is in him, since I hold that even those animal actions which survive in a sleeper cannot occur without the activity of a substantial principle. But you will not prove that it is in him forever, except by a weak conjecture, namely that it is present in that body both before and after sleep. Nor will you escape by urging that the mind of infants is active, and that there is nothing repugnant in it, even though nothing of the kind appears to us. For granting that nothing is repugnant, is whatever is not repugnant to be believed by a philosopher to be actual? Certainly, on your hypothesis, it is also not repugnant that the bodies of infants live without a mind. So it would be impossible to demonstrate to a Cartesian man that an infant, in the first two or three years from birth, before he begins to show the use of reason by gesture and speech, has a mind; and that is exactly my point. Not to add that some men are deprived of the use of reason from infancy and never show any sign of it throughout life: about such men, then, may we not doubt throughout life whether they enjoy a mind? By these arguments, which I once set out elsewhere on this same question in this way, stand unshaken: We shall no longer wonder (if we can live without the presence of a rational soul) at the Arimaspians, Sciapodes, Strutiocephali, Fanesii, Satyrs, Cynocephali, Pygmies, and other monstrous men that Pliny depicts for us; since a human body can now lack not only certain parts but also a soul, and nevertheless, perhaps even more conveniently, live. Does not the impious Paracelsus, who admits this, equally admit the artificial homunculus? Indeed, if this is so, who knows whether we do not often (even as we write these things) have to do with masked men, especially such as are wholly destitute of mind? And if perhaps in many of those with whom we daily deal something occurs that makes us suspect a certain principle of reasoning in them, yet on your adverse hypothesis we could detect nothing of the kind in a boy a few months old, in a frenzied man, or in others like them, who cannot show by suitable signs that they act rationally. Therefore, since no operations present themselves to us for observation in them, except such as these philosophers claim can arise from the arrangement and motion of parts alone without the aid of any substantial soul, we shall rightly doubt whether those I have listed enjoy a mind. If this madness once prevails, the duties of charity are at an end, and all the bonds of society and humanity are dissolved. Such are the consequences then. Now, if the matter concerned a theologian who likes the new opinion, I would seriously warn him to take great care, lest, when called to the sick who have lost the use of mind and speech, he rashly pour out prayers for the dead too often; for from these novel hypotheses nothing could happen more easily or more frequently than that a rational soul has long since left a body in which the motions we commonly observe in the dying are still visible. Thus those who maintain that a body can be governed without a mind are bound to philosophise in a mindless way in more than one respect.

units.la: Quæ tamen pro sua quoque sententia adducant ipsi, examinemus? Primarium novæ assertionis fundamentum est similitudo simillima, quæ datur inter plerasque, si non omnes (loquelam imprimis si exceperis) hominum & brutorum operationes externas. Quumque has supponant oriri à sola partium dispositione, & sanguinis spiritvery umque motu, absque ullius animæ substantialis moderamine, facili indè inferunt sequelâ, absurdum haberi non debere, si eodem quo corpus bruti movetur modo hominis quoque corpus moveri existimemus. Fateor, satis consequentem videri hanc consequentiam. Neutiquam enim repugnat, quin potius summè probabile est, duas machinas, adeò quod ad ossa, nervos, musculos, sanguinem, spiritus, omnemque organorum apparatum & structuram similes, simili quoque modo impelli & moveri. Ast verò antecedens illud, de Brutis operantibus ad instar horologii, vel ob hanc ipsam consequentiam, falsum esse ac neutiquam admittendum, censeo: de quo & ab initio dixi. Neque in præsens id agam, ut ostendam multis, operationes brutorum motus ejusmodi automaticos non esse. Satis fuè hæc de re disserui, allegatâ jam de Operationibus Brutorum Exercitatione: quæ si hic conferatur, suffecerit ad superandum quicquid hâc parte hærere potest difficultatis.
units.tr: But shall we examine what they themselves bring forward in support of their opinion? The chief foundation of the new assertion is the very great similarity that exists between most, if not all, of the external operations of men and brutes (speech above all excepted). Since they assume that these arise from the arrangement of parts and the motion of blood and spirits alone, without any moderation by a substantial soul, they easily infer the consequence that it should not be thought absurd if we suppose that a man's body is moved in the same way as a brute's body. I grant that this inference seems quite consistent. For it is by no means repugnant, indeed it is highly probable, that two machines, so similar as regards bones, nerves, muscles, blood, spirits, and the whole apparatus and structure of their organs, are driven and moved in a similar way. But I judge that the premise, that brutes act like clocks, is false and by no means to be admitted, precisely because of this very consequence; and I have said as much from the beginning. Nor do I intend here to show to many that the operations of brutes are not automatic motions of this kind. I have argued enough on this matter, the Exercitation on the Operations of Brutes already cited; if that is consulted here, it will suffice to overcome whatever difficulty may cling to this part.

units.la: Verùm neque Brutis forte indigent, qui in homine ipso sat multa inveniunt, ad stabiliendam suam thesin. Ipsum audiamus Cartesium! ,, Fit plerumque, ait, ut ambulemus aut comeda-,,mus, „mus , neutiquam cogitantes de eo quod agimus ; quin imo ea „quae nobis noxia sunt repellimus , aut etiam ictus quibus peti„mur declinamus tam inconsulta ratione , ut quamvis dedita „opera vellemus manus nostras capiti non praetendere cum cadi„mus , tamen non esset penes nos id non facere. Credo etiam
units.tr: But perhaps those who find enough in man himself to establish their thesis do not need brutes. Let us hear Descartes himself: "It happens for the most part," he says, "that we walk or eat without at all thinking about what we are doing; indeed we repel those things that are harmful to us, or even dodge the blows with which we are attacked, with such thoughtless haste that, even if we deliberately wished not to put our hands before our head when we fall, it would not be in our power not to do so. I believe too

units.la: „nos brutorum instar manducaturos , sine praevia institutione, „si cogitatione nulla essemus praediti : & certe, dicunt eos, qui „per somnum obambulant , ejusmodi fluvios nonnunquam tra„nare, ex quibus experecti nunquam emersuri essent. Epist. Part. 1. p. 107. Quibus ut satisfiat, cum plurimis Philosophis eruditissimis , distinguendum venit , inter actiones hominis animales & rationales; seu, ut alii loquuntur, inter actiones hominis & humanas; quarum illae ab homine fluunt, quatenus est animal, hae ab ipso proficiscuntur, quatenus praecise homo est. Posterioris generis actiones ab homine nunquam quidem eliciuntur, fateor, citra praeviam mentis cogitationem & imperium, attamen & hoc certum est, frequenti usu & exercitio tantam saepe promptitudinem & facilitatem earum acquiri , ut peragantur animae attentione tam exigua , ut singula minus expendenti ea videri possit nulla. Quis nostrum sibi conscius est distinctae cogitationis & imperii mentis circa singula verba quae proferimus , quoties ex tempore dissertationem saepe satis prolixam de re quapiam instituimus? Indubium tamen existit , multiplicem hic requiri Animae attentionem, & ad res singulas, & ad rerum notiones, & ad unumquodque verbum quo notionem efferimus, & ad totam orationis texturam ac verborum connexionem logicam simul & grammaticam. Atque vel hoc unum evincit satis, non absque mentis cogitatione & praesentia fieri, quaecunque nonnunquam primo intuitu absque ea fieri videntur. Sit v. c. ( ut aliud addam frequens & obvium ) Studiosus, qui meditabundus Academiam adit lectionem auditurus. Non raro evenit, eum, dum altius meditationibus immersus est, videri sibi venisse ad auditorium, absque ulla cogitatione de via , qua eundem fuit. Interim certum, non absque aliqua mentis attentione & imperio motum progressivum pedum & totius corporis, per varias platearum ambages & longos viarum circuitus, directum fuisse praecise ad Academiam ; uti vel inde evincitur, quod a via & praestituto loco aberret , si nimia fuerit animi per alias cogitationes distractio. Quæ omnia docent abundè, plurimas nostras actiones, quæ citra fixam, statam, & morosam, ut itâ dicam, cogitationem à nobis peraguntur, non tamen carere imperio incidentis alicujus & fugacis cogitationis; quæ semper adeò omnes nostras actiones comitatur, ut verum nequaquam sit, quod hîc dicitur, nos neutiquam cogitantes de eo quod agimus, plerumque ambulare, comedere, ictus repellere, &c. Noctambulones quod attinet, tantum abest, ut credendum sit, eos idem acturos quod agunt, etiamsi nulla cogitatione essent praediti, ut experientia contrà doceat, eos vigilantes sæpissimè sibi probè conscios esse ejus, quod fecerunt somniantes; certo indicio, non sine voluntatis imperio eos fecisse, quod fecerunt. Negandum tamen non est, minus distinctè eos affici ab objectis per organa minus rectè disposita confusè & inordinatè oblatis; undè &, dum singulas rerum circumstantias minus percipiunt, sine timore agunt, atque itâ in tranandis fluminibus, &c. pericula quæ ignorant, felicius evadunt.
units.tr: that we would eat like brutes without prior instruction, if we were endowed with no thought at all; and certainly they say that those who walk in their sleep sometimes swim across rivers, from which, when they awoke, they would never have emerged. Epist. Part. 1. p. 107. To satisfy these points, we must, with most learned philosophers, distinguish between the animal and the rational actions of man; or, as others put it, between the actions of man and human actions. The former flow from man as he is an animal, the latter proceed from him as he is precisely man. I grant that actions of the latter kind are never elicited from man without a prior thought and command of the mind. Yet it is also certain that by frequent use and practice there is often acquired such readiness and facility in them that they are performed with so little attention of the soul that to one who does not weigh each detail carefully they may seem to have none at all. Which of us is conscious of distinct thought and command of mind about each word we utter, whenever we deliver a fairly lengthy speech on some subject on the spur of the moment? Yet it is beyond doubt that here a manifold attention of the soul is required: to the things themselves, to the notions of things, to every word by which we express a notion, and to the whole texture of the sentence and the logical and grammatical connection of the words together. This alone is enough to prove that whatever sometimes seems at first sight to be done without it is not done without thought and the presence of mind. Take, for example (to add another frequent and common case), a student who goes to the Academy, lost in thought, to hear a lecture. It often happens that, while he is deeply immersed in his meditations, he seems to himself to have come to the lecture hall without any thought of the way he took. Yet it is certain that the progressive motion of his feet and of his whole body, through the winding streets and long circuits of the roads, was not without some attention and command of mind, and was directed precisely to the Academy; as is shown even by this, that he strays from the road and the appointed place if his mind is too much distracted by other thoughts. All these things abundantly teach that many of our actions, which we perform without a fixed, settled, and, as it were, burdensome thought, nevertheless are not free from the command of some passing and fleeting thought; and this thought so accompanies all our actions that it is by no means true, as is said here, that we walk, eat, repel blows, etc., "for the most part without thinking at all about what we are doing." As for sleepwalkers, it is so far from being credible that they would do what they do even if they had no thought at all, that experience teaches the contrary: that when awake they are very often well aware of what they did while dreaming; a sure sign that what they did was not done without the command of the will. It must not be denied, however, that they are affected less distinctly by objects, which are presented confusedly and disorderly through organs not rightly disposed; hence, since they perceive the individual circumstances of things less, they act without fear, and so in swimming rivers, etc., they escape more fortunately the dangers they do not know of.
X.

units.la: Utautem omnis, qui hærere adhuc posset scrupulus, eximitur penitus, cogitemus in nobis aliud quod genus actionum occurrere, scilicet merè animalium. Eas plurimas etiam citra ullam vel minimam cogitationem fieri, quid si dederim? Ab anima hominis idcirco non proficisci, neque hâc indigere, demonstratum hactenus non vidi. Quin contrarium ejus probant Infantes, Lethargici, Apoplectici, aliique qui neque per cogitationem agunt quæ agunt, neque tamen absque animæ præsentia & influxu operantur; utì jam pluribus evicimus. Nec obstat, quòd anima, quippe spiritus, tantùm cogitando dicatur esse actuosa: undè inferunt, eas quæ sine cogitatione fiunt operationes animam cogitantem non habere principium. Non, inquam, id obstat; antecedens enim verum est de anima secundum se consideratâ, & quatenus merus existit spiritus, idque in ordine ad actiones immanentes: minimè tamen id admittendum quod ad actiones transeuntes, quæ abeadem proficiscuntur quatenùs cum corpore unita hujus existit forma; quales plurimas, præter cogitativas, ex mero naturæ instinctu à Deo primùm indito profluere posse ab eadem, quis negaverit? Atque itâ animam humanam per gradus in corpore quicum unitur esse actuosam, ab omni ævo, experientiæ convenienter, admisere eruditi cum Philosopho, eleganter id innuente, quandò ait, hominem primùm vivere vitam plantæ, tantùm per nutritionem crescendo; mox bestiæ, sentiendo etiam, appetendo, & se loco movendo; demùm hominis, intelligendo, volendo, &c. Neque multum hic alicui difficultatis hærere potest, cui non infixa sedet opinio de mente-humana quæ nil sit nisi cogitatio. Qua de re alibi.
units.tr: Moreover, so that every scruple that could still cling to us may be wholly removed, let us consider that there is another kind of action in us, namely actions that are merely animal. What if I grant that very many of these take place without any thought at all? I have not yet seen it demonstrated that they do not proceed from the soul of man, nor that they need it. Indeed, infants, the lethargic and the apoplectic, and others who do not act by thought, yet do not act without the presence and influx of the soul, prove the contrary, as we have already shown at length. Nor does it stand in the way that the soul, being a spirit, is said to be active only by thinking; from which they infer that operations performed without thought do not have a thinking soul as their principle. No, I say, this does not stand in the way: the premise is true of the soul considered in itself, and insofar as it exists as a mere spirit, and that with respect to immanent actions; but it is by no means to be admitted of transitive actions, which proceed from the soul insofar as it exists as the form united with the body. Who would deny that many such actions, besides thinking ones, can proceed from it by the mere instinct of nature first implanted by God? And so, in keeping with experience, learned men from all ages have admitted, together with the Philosopher, who hints at this elegantly when he says that man first lives the life of a plant, by nutrition and growth alone; then that of a beast, by also sensing, desiring and moving from place to place; and finally that of a man, by understanding, willing, and so on. Nor can anyone who has not fixed in his mind the opinion that the human mind is nothing but thought find much difficulty here. On this matter, elsewhere.

units.la: Minimè verò passionum nostrarum motus evincunt, operationes nostri corporis ab anima non procedere; quasi clarissimum sit, illos à cogitandi facultate non pendere, quandoquidem invitis nobis sæpenumero exoriuntur. Cartes. Ibid. p. 108. Non hæc faciunt pro Homine Automatico. Ut enim nunc taceam quæ modò dicta sunt de actionibus ab anima orientibus ex mero naturæ instinctu (quales esse nostros affectus contendunt, qui eosdem in facultate animæ sensitiva, seu inferiori, uti vocant collocant; quibusque facile exstit hic respondere, Affectus ab anima oriri, licet non præcisè ab ea proficiscantur, quatenus cogitandi facultate prædita est) ista, inquam, taceo: nobis enim videtur, motus corporeos, qui passiones animi comitantur, non magis nobis invitis exoriri, quam nobis invitis exoriuntur ipsæ illæ passiones. Videlicet, & hæ sæpenumero invitæ sunt, quod ad actus nostræ voluntatis qui eosdem vel antecedunt vel sequuntur. Mens enim nostra objecti, cujus bonitas vel malitia animi perturbationem in nobis excitavit, prædicata omnia & singula, postquam desæviit nonnihil affectus, expendens accuratius, errorem judicii deprehendit, indeque ordinatum inordinatum animi motum, sicque pœnitentiâ ducitur affectûs, quo non itâ pridem laborabat. Atque hactenus uti affectus ipse, itâ motus corporis cum eo conjunctus, invitus censeri potest. At verò, uti nemo aliquâ animi passione laborat, nisi, quo tempore eâ laborat, sic affectus esse velit (est enim passio animi in homine reverà nihil aliud, quam intensior ejusdem volitio aut nolitio; at nemo invitus unquam vult, aut velle potest) itâ quoque nemo afficitur motu corporis inordinato, quatenus is passionem animi voluntariam comitatur, nisi sic affectus esse hactenùs velit. Dico, eum hactenùs velle, in quantum nimirùm simpliciter is est motus corporeus; non quatenus hæc aut illa effecta aut consequentia secum trahit. Itâ nemo volucrit febrim, quam ex vehementiori ira, eaque voluntaria, sibi forte contraxit. Qui igitur nostras Passiones animi comitantur corporis motus non minus in suo exortu ab anima nostra pendent, quam ipsæ passiones: quamobrem & nequicquam nobis hic adversantur.
units.tr: Yet the motions of our passions by no means prove that the operations of our body do not proceed from the soul, as if it were "most clear that they do not depend on the faculty of thinking, since they often arise in us against our will." Descartes, ibid., p. 108. These words do not favour the Automaton Man. For, to pass over for now what has just been said about actions arising from the mere instinct of nature (which they contend our affections are, placing them in the sensitive or, as they call it, inferior faculty of the soul; and to which it is easy to reply here that affections arise from the soul, even if they do not proceed from it precisely insofar as it is endowed with the faculty of thinking), I say, let these pass. For it seems to us that the bodily motions which accompany the passions of the mind do not arise against our will any more than the passions themselves do. Indeed, these passions too are often against our will, as regards the acts of our will which either precede or follow them. For our mind, weighing more carefully all the features of the object whose goodness or badness has stirred up a disturbance in us, once the emotion has raged for a while, detects an error of judgment, and from this the disordered motion of the soul is brought back to order, and so repentance of the affection overtakes us, which previously we had been suffering from. And so far the affection itself, and the bodily motion joined with it, may be regarded as involuntary. But just as no one suffers from some passion of the mind unless, at the time he suffers from it, he wishes to be so affected (for a passion of the mind in man is really nothing other than a more intense volition or nolition of the same; and no one ever wills, or can will, against his will), so too no one is affected by a disordered motion of the body, insofar as it accompanies a voluntary passion of the mind, unless he wishes to be so affected up to that point. I say he wishes this up to that point, namely insofar as it is simply a bodily motion, not insofar as it draws after it this or that effect or consequence. Thus no one would wish for a fever which he has perhaps contracted from a more violent and voluntary anger. Therefore the bodily motions which accompany our passions of the mind depend no less on our soul in their arising than the passions themselves do; and so they are of no use to our opponents here.

units.la: Neque convulsiones demonstrant, corpus humanum posse vivere & moveri sine mente, qua de re ità Cartesius: „Certum est „in corporibus animalium, ut etiam in nostris, esse ossa, nervos, „musculos, sanguinem, spiritus animales, & reliqua organa ita „disposita, ut se solis, absque ulla cogitatione, omnes motus „quos in brutis observamus ciere possint. Quod patet in convul„sionibus, cum mente invita machinamentum corporis vehemen„tius sæpè & magis diversis modis solum se movet, quam ope vo„luntatis soleat moveri. Rag. 89. De organis brutorum quæ se solis motus ciëant nunc nihil dicere attinet; quùm de iis & ante, & alibi. Quod ad Convulsiones, eas nihil facere pro Homine Automatico facilè intelligimus, si in iis distinguamus inter motum simpliciter animalem qua talem, & motùs istius inordinationem. Illum ab anima nostra excitari dicimus, vel ex cogitatione & voluntate prævia, vel ex instinctu merè naturali; de quibus suprà. Quantum ad ἀταξίαν & inordinationem motùs, quam in convulsionibus observamus, agnoscimus eam omnem oriri à sola partium dispositione perturbata & non-naturali; atque hactenus mente invitâ accidere, non est negandum. Sed ista nihil nobis obest; quatenus in motibus ejusmodi ciendis anima, tanquam actus corporis organici, uti bene eam vocat Philosophus, prorsùs est organica, atque omni modo à bona machinæ corporeæ dispositione dependens. Tam ergò elegans atque efficax est hoc argumentum à convulsionibus desumtum, ad demonstrandum motus animales absque ulla anima cieri posse, ac si quis inferat, organum pneumaticum se solo, absque ulla cogitatione organistæ, edere posse sonum musicum; quia scilicet, quandò tubi obstructi sunt, aut rimosi, aut aliquo alio modo non rectè dispositi, invito artifice, machinamentum organi vehementius sæpè & magis diversis modis movetur, edendo bombum vel alium quem confusum sonum, quam voluntate musici moveri solet.
units.tr: Nor do convulsions show that the human body can live and move without the mind. Descartes says of this: "It is certain that in the bodies of animals, as in ours, there are bones, nerves, muscles, blood, animal spirits, and the other organs so arranged that, by themselves and without any thought, they can produce all the motions which we observe in brutes. This is evident in convulsions, when, against the will of the mind, the machinery of the body often moves by itself more violently and in more varied ways than it is usually moved by the power of the will." Rag. 89. It is not necessary now to say anything about the organs of brutes which produce motions by themselves, since we have spoken of them before and elsewhere. As for convulsions, we readily understand that they do nothing in favour of the Automaton Man, if in them we distinguish between motion that is simply animal as such and the disorder of that motion. We say that the former is excited in us either by prior thought and will, or by mere natural instinct, as discussed above. As regards the disorder and irregularity of motion which we observe in convulsions, we acknowledge that all of it arises from the disturbed and unnatural disposition of the parts alone; and that it happens against the will of the mind so far, we do not deny. But this does nothing against us: in producing motions of this kind the soul, as the "act of an organic body", as the Philosopher rightly calls it, is wholly organic and entirely dependent on the good disposition of the bodily machine. So this argument drawn from convulsions is just as elegant and effective for proving that animal motions can be produced without any soul, as if someone were to infer that a pneumatic organ can of itself, without any thought of the organist, produce a musical sound; because, namely, when its pipes are blocked, or cracked, or otherwise not properly arranged, the mechanism of the organ, against the craftsman's will, often moves more violently and in more varied ways, producing a booming or some other confused sound, than it is usually moved by the will of the musician.

units.la: Pergit Cartesius: „Rationi consentanCum videtur, cum ars „sit naturæ imitatrix, possintque homines varia fabricare auto„mata, in quibus sine ulla cogitatione est motus, ut natura etiam „sua automata, sed artefactis longe praestantiora, nempe bruta „omnia, producat, praesertim cum nullam cognoscamus rationem propter quam, ubi est talis membrorum conformatio, qualem in animalibus videmus, cogitatio etiam debeat adesse; atque „ideo majori admiratione dignum sit, quod mens aliqua reperiatur in unoquoque humano corpore, quam quod nulla sit in ulis brutis. Vis omnis hujus argumenti, in quantum huc pertinet, sita est in collatione automati alicujus artefacti cum re naturali. Facile foret ejus inefficaciam monstrare, & ostendendo, hac ratione nullum tandem admittendum fore specificum & essentiale discrimen inter res naturales atque artefactas, cum magis & minus non varient speciem; & docendo artem, quamvis naturam imitetur, nunquam tamen eo usque perfectionem hujus assequi, ut non immensum ab ea deficiat, tum ratione ipsarum operationum, tum ratione earundem principii. Brevitatis causa ista similiaque nunc mittam; daboque, admittendam esse sequelam ab artefactis ad naturalia: tantum nunc aequa sit, quae hic instituitur comparatio, nunc videamus! Profecto automata artefacta nequaquam moventur a sola partium dispositione, sed ab adjuncto ab artifice, applicante naturale activum passivae machinae, principio motus qualicunque; quale in horologio v. c. est pondus appensum, vel quid huic analogum. Ex quo concludo: Quemadmodum horologium etiam optime dispositum se solo nullis motibus movetur, verum hi omnes proficiscuntur ab addito motus principio, tanquam a causa sui; ita quoque corpus animalis, quantumvis bene habens, se solo nullos motus exercet, verum eos omnes debet addito alicui motus principio; quod hic nobis est anima. Neque evades, excipiendo, corpus animalis, etiam sine anima vivens, non carere suo motore, etsi non interno, externo tamen, quatenus ab objectis per radios luminis, aliisque modis, huc illuc impellitur, uti v. c. mola circumagitur a vento: talem namque explicationem refutat abunde, tum experientia in nobis ipsis, qui deprehendimus corpus nostrum moveri, non ab extrinseco aliquo motore, sed ab animae nostrae, tanquam principii interni, impulsu & directione; tum, quod, licet daretur sufficere motionem factam ab extrinseco ad operationem qualemcunque, nequaquam tamen ad illud referri queant operationes tam variæ & admirandæ, quales in animalium corporibus obviæ sunt; tùm denique quod sic re ipsa omnia animalia verâ causalitate atque activitate priventur, quoniam arte facta, ab extrinseco mota, non tam agunt, quam potius aguntur: cujus theseos periculum, ut & alia huc pertinentia, plenius excutere, alterius loci est, nimiumque ab Homine nostro Automatico recederet. Sufficiunt hactenus allata: quæ talia putamus, ut Homo Automaticus merito habendus videatur, quicunque, ista non capiens, pugnare amplius pro Homine Automatico ausit.
units.tr: Descartes goes on: "It seems reasonable, since art imitates nature, and men can make various automata, in which there is motion without any thought, that nature too should produce her own automata, far more excellent than artificial ones, namely all brutes; especially since we know of no reason why, where there is such a conformation of limbs as we see in animals, thought should also be present; and so it is more worthy of wonder that some mind should be found in every human body than that none should be in the other brutes." The whole force of this argument, insofar as it bears on our question, lies in comparing some artificial automaton with a natural thing. It would be easy to show its ineffectiveness, and by showing that, on this reasoning, no specific and essential difference would finally be admitted between natural and artificial things, since more and less do not vary the species; and by teaching that art, although it imitates nature, never attains such perfection in it that it does not fall immeasurably short of it, both in the operations themselves and in their principle. For the sake of brevity I will set these and similar points aside; and I will grant that the inference from artefacts to natural things must be admitted; only let us now see whether the comparison instituted here is fair. Surely artificial automata are by no means moved by the mere arrangement of their parts, but by a principle of motion of some kind, a natural active force applied by the craftsman to the passive machine from outside; such as, in a clock, for example, is a hanging weight or something analogous to it. From which I conclude: just as a clock, however well arranged, does not move by itself with any motion, but all its motions proceed from an added principle of motion, as from a cause of itself; so too the body of an animal, however well it is, does not by itself exercise any motion, but must have all its motions from some added principle of motion, which for us is the soul. Nor can you escape by saying that the body of an animal, even when living without a soul, does not lack its mover, though it is not an internal one but an external one, insofar as it is pushed hither and thither by objects through rays of light and in other ways, just as a mill is turned by the wind. For this explanation is thoroughly refuted: first by experience in ourselves, who perceive that our body is moved not by some external mover but by the impulse and direction of our soul as an internal principle; second, because even if an external motion were granted to suffice for some sort of operation, yet the operations so varied and admirable as those found in the bodies of animals could by no means be referred to it; and finally because in this way all animals would be deprived of true causality and activity, since, being moved from outside as artefacts are, they do not so much act as are acted upon. The danger of this thesis, like the other points pertaining to it, belongs to be examined more fully in another place, and it would take us too far from our Automaton Man. What has been said so far is enough: we think these points are such that the Automaton Man rightly seems to be held, whoever, not grasping them, dares to fight any longer for the Automaton Man.
A DISSERTATION CONCERNING CONTRADICTORIES POSSIBLE TO GOD.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Contradictoria Deum posse, præter Weigelium, vix quisquam ante Cartesium contendit. II. Hujus in hanc rem allegati textus, qui mentem ejusdem plenius explicant. III. Contradictoriorum possibilitas cum primæ causæ sapientia nequaquam consistit. IV. Non nostræ mentis finitudo, sed ipsa rei contradictoriæ repugnantia causa exstiit, cur ejus idea formari nequeat. V. Omnipotentia Divina in veram rem terminatur, non in nihilum; adeoque nec in in contradictoria. VI. Si contradictoria Deo possibilia sint, nihil fingi tam absonum potest, quod non efficere possit Deus. VII. Si facere queat Deus ut contradictoria sint simul, etiam res contradictorias credendas proponere potest. VIII. Admissa contradictoriorum possibilitate, nullius momenti exi-stunt quaecunque ab absurdo consequenti petita argumenta. IX. Quin, subvertuntur omnia omnium disciplinarum atque universae quam unquam habere potest homo certitudinis fundamenta. X. Potentiae Dei cum Voluntate ejusdem confusio praecipua novae assertionis basis. XI. Objectorum diversitas evidens distinguendae Divinae Potentiae a Voluntate fundamentum. XII. Eandem distinctionem evincit habens se aliter Potentiae aliter Voluntatis. Divinae exercitium. XIII. Neque, quando Potentia Dei a Voluntate distinguitur, ideo minus efficax aut perfecta haec agnoscitur. XIV. Productio rerum cur ad Voluntatem Dei saepe referatur, nulla facta mentione Potentiae? XV. Rerum possibilitat fundandae sola sufficit Dei Sufficientia, citra ullam de Voluntate ejus cogitationem. XVI. Nihil perseEționis divinæ libertati detrahitur, si contradictoria Deum efficere posse, negetur. XVII. Possibilia, tametsi ad indifferentem primæ causæ voluntatem non reducantur, à Deo nihilominus dependent. XVIII. Quæ aliæ esse potuissent naturæ rerum contradictoriorum possibilitatem minimè probant. XIX. Nullâ parte immodestiæ reus exististit, qui contradictoria infinitæ potentiæ subducit. XX. Propositæ quæstionis decisionem Philosopho minimè subterfugiendam esse, osten-ditur.
units.tr: I. Apart from Weigel, hardly anyone before Descartes has maintained that God can bring about contradictories. II. The texts he cites for this matter, which explain his meaning more fully. III. The possibility of contradictories is by no means consistent with the wisdom of the first cause. IV. It was not the finitude of our mind but the very repugnance of the contradictory thing that caused its idea to be impossible to form. V. Divine omnipotence terminates in a true thing, not in nothing, and so not in contradictories. VI. If contradictories are possible to God, nothing so absurd can be imagined that God cannot bring about. VII. If God can make contradictories be simultaneously true, he can also propose contradictory things to be believed. VIII. Once the possibility of contradictories is admitted, all arguments drawn from absurd consequences are of no weight. IX. Indeed, the foundations of all the disciplines, and of whatever certainty man can ever have, are overturned. X. The confusion of God's power with his will is the chief basis of the new assertion. XI. The evident diversity of objects is the foundation for distinguishing divine power from will. XII. The exercise of divine power differs from that of will, which shows the same distinction. XIII. Nor, when God's power is distinguished from his will, is it thereby recognised as less efficacious or perfect. XIV. Why is the production of things so often referred to the will of God, with no mention made of his power? XV. For grounding the possibility of things, God's sufficiency alone is enough, without any thought of his will. XVI. Nothing is taken away from the divine perfection of freedom if it is denied that God can effect contradictories. XVII. Possibilities, although they are not traced back to the indifferent will of the first cause, nonetheless depend on God. XVIII. Whatever other natures of things might have been, they in no way prove the possibility of contradictories. XIX. He who withdraws contradictories from infinite power is guilty of no immodesty. XX. It is shown that the decision of the question proposed must by no means be evaded by the philosopher.

units.la: ditur. XXI. Absurdè dicitur Deus per Potentiam posse, quod idem efficere nequeat per Bo- nitatem.
units.tr: ...ditur. XXI. It is absurd to say that God can do by his power what he cannot bring about by his goodness.

units.la: ERemendum quid omnique nostrâ cogitatione majus existit Divina Potentia, cujus tam immensa est summa cum perfectione conjuncta amplitudo, ut nulla de re circumspectâ magis cautelâ atque attentiore attentione quam hic philosophari oporteat. Nusquam æquè facilè ac hoc loco impingitur, ubi inter duo præcipitia tenere medium prudentiæ est planè non-vulgaris: adeò Dei virtutem hinc quidem absque causa restringunt arctius quam decet; indè alii temerè eandem extendunt latius quam fas est. Displs-cuerunt eo nomine modestioribus ingeniis jam dudum illæ maximâ sui parte inutiles, periculosæ plerumquè, etiam non raro prosanæ, de eo quod possit Deus, quæstiones ac determinationes, decisæ non minus temerè quam motæ à Scholasticis Doctoribus, hominibus otiosè laboriosis & inaniter subtilibus, nimiumque hac parte negligentibus metum istum ac venerationem, quâ sacra hæc tractare jubet & Divini Numinis supereminentia, & humanæ mentis imbecillitas. Atquì horum parùm memores adeò audaci scrutinio universa hæc mysteria contaminarunt, ut nihil à vanis suis speculationibus intactum reliquerint, neque quicquam tam absurdum hîc unquam à quoquam fuerit excogitatum, quod non in hoc hominum genere suum invenerit patronum. Vix tamen, quod sciam, omnium unus eo processit ineptiarum, qui contradictoria Deo possibilia esse contenderit. Ut omninò licuerit sperare, reperiundum fore deinceps neminem, qui suum faceret dogma, cui illorum nullus suum commodare ausus fuit patrocinium. Imprimis tale nihil exspectandum videri poterat, postquam risu & contemptu omnium explosus fuit fanaticus & plus quam transcendentaliter ineptus homo Valentinus Weigelius, interalia ridicula suæ stultitiæ mysteria, nulli sanæ mentis homini intelligibilia, nescio quid garriens de possibili Contradictoriorum combinatione. Atquì eo vivimus seculo, quo illa quoque fieri videmus passim, quæ fieri potuisse negassent avi. Hi quidem prudenter sic habebant (& nos cum illis) multa Deum posse, quæ nos non intelligimus: ideòque nullâ demonstratâ repugnantiâ, pro evitanda temeritate, ad quæstionem, An istud vel illud Deus possit, ajebant ferè lubentius quam negabant; sæpè judicium suspendebant potius quam ut definirent temerè; dum semper subibat cogitatio, hoc vel istud, de quo quærebatur, forsitan esse ex illorum numero, quæ quidem existunt in classe possibilium, superant tamen nostrum captum, quo minus ea possibilia esse putemus. Ità piè atque modestè in tuto collocabant Divinæ Omnipotentiæ ad sui ingenioli captum comparatæ incomprehensibilitatem. Non hoc interim erat impedimento, quo minus nihil addubitantes rotundè simul pronunciarent, à perfectissima causa nequaquam ista fieri posse, quæ verâ involvere contradictionem, evidenter & certò demonstrari potest. Et profectò nè fidem quidem adhibere potuissent vaticinanti, extituros brevi inter nepotes benè multos, qui affirmarent, nos determinare non posse, an Deus ea possit quæ contradictionem implicant: quin Deum facere potuisse, ut bis duo non quatuor sint, sed quinque forsan vel septem, ut trianguli tres anguli non æquipolleant duobus rectis, &c. Et tamen, etiam in medio orbe Reformato, nunc ista defendi audimus. Tam nihil amplius absurdum videtur quicquid assertionis enixum est cerebellum Cartesii, postquam eo usque invaluit apud plurimos, quo usque nostro tempore invaluit, ejus auctoritas. Hic scilicet opinionis absurdissimæ, quatenus hodiè inter suos viget, est architectus. Etsi verò ad Johannis Crocii Anti-Weigelium, ubi Quæst. II. Liminari hoc commentum confutatur abundè, amandandus Vir cum sequacibus videri queat; quâ tamen ejus sectæ Philosophi illum venerantur existimatio operæ pretium faciet, ut in hanc assertionem paulò diligentius inquiramus, ostendamusque, posse nos, quin debere affirmare, Deum contradictoria producere non posse.
units.tr: It must be remembered that the divine power is greater than anything we can think, and its vastness is so immense and joined with such perfection that one must philosophize about it with more caution and closer attention than about any other subject. Nowhere is one more easily driven onto the rocks than here, where to keep the middle course between two precipices is a rare kind of prudence. Some narrow God's power too much, without cause, and others extend it too widely, which is not permitted. Modest minds have long disliked those questions and decisions about what God can do, questions for the most part useless, often dangerous, and not seldom even profane. Scholastic doctors, men idly laborious and vainly subtle, decided them no less rashly than they raised them, and in this matter they neglected that fear and reverence which both the supereminence of the divine majesty and the weakness of the human mind require when such holy matters are handled. Yet those who forgot these things so boldly pried into all these mysteries that they left nothing untouched by their empty speculations, and nothing so absurd was ever devised by anyone that it did not find its advocate in this class of men. Yet, so far as I know, hardly any one of them has gone so far in folly as to contend that contradictories are possible for God. One might have hoped that no one would afterwards adopt a doctrine which none of them had dared to defend. Such a thing could especially have been expected to be absent after Valentin Weigel, a fanatic and a man more than transcendentally foolish, had been hooted down and despised by everyone. Among his other ridiculous mysteries, unintelligible to any sane person, he babbled about I know not what possible combination of contradictories. Yet we live in an age in which we see everywhere those things done which our grandfathers would have denied could be done. Those men, to be sure, reasoned prudently (and we with them) that God can do many things which we do not understand. So, when no contradiction had been demonstrated, and to avoid rashness, they were more inclined to say yes than no when asked whether God could do this or that. Often they suspended judgment rather than define rashly, since the thought always came to them that the thing in question might perhaps be among those which indeed belong to the class of possibles but which exceed our grasp, so that we should not think them possible. In this way they devoutly and modestly placed in safety the incomprehensibility of divine omnipotence, which is fitted to the measure of our small intellect. Nevertheless, this did not stop them from pronouncing outright, without any doubt, that those things which involve a true contradiction cannot be produced by the most perfect cause, a thing that can be clearly and certainly demonstrated. Indeed, they could not have given credence to a prophet who foretold that, before long, among their grandsons there would be many who would assert that we cannot determine whether God can do those things which imply a contradiction; nor that God could have made it so that twice two are not four but perhaps five or seven, or that the three angles of a triangle do not equal two right angles, and so on. Yet, even in the midst of the Reformed world, we now hear these things defended. Nothing seems more absurd than whatever the brain of Descartes has brought forth, now that his authority has prevailed among so many, to the extent that it prevails in our time. He is, to be sure, the architect of this most absurd opinion, as far as it flourishes today among his followers. Although that man may seem to be one whom his followers should be pardoned, since in John Croce's Anti-Weigelius, in question II, Liminaris, this fiction is thoroughly refuted, it will be worth the trouble for the philosophers of his sect, whom he is venerated by, if we inquire into this assertion a little more carefully, and show that we can, and indeed must, affirm that God cannot produce contradictories.

units.la: Verùm audiendus est antè Cartesius. Sic is, Respons. Sext. §. 6. Repugnat Dei voluntatem non fuisse ab æterno indifferentem ad omnia quæ facta sunt, aut unquam fient, quia nullum bonum, vel verum, vel faciendum, vel omittendum fingi potest, cujus idea in intellectu Divino prius fuerit, quam ejus voluntas se determinavit ad efficiendum ut
units.tr: But first Descartes must be heard. He says, in the Responsio Sexta, §6: It is repugnant that the will of God was not from eternity indifferent to all the things that have been done or ever will be done, because no good, or truth, or thing to be done or omitted can be imagined whose idea was in the divine intellect before his will determined itself to bring it about.

units.la: II. Huius in hanc rem allegati textus, qui mentem ut id tale esset. Neque hic loquor de prioritate temporis, sed ne quidem prius fuit ordine, vel natura, vel ratione ratiocinatâ, ut vocant, ita scilicet ut ista boni idea impulerit Deum ad unum potius quam aliud eligendum. Nempe, exempli causa, non ideo voluit mundum creare in tempore, quia vidit melius sic fore, quam si creasset ab aeterno: nec voluit tres angulos trianguli aequales esse duobus rectis, quia cognovit aliter fieri non posse, &c. Sed contra, quia voluit mundum creare in tempore, ideo sic melius est, quam si creatus fuisset ab aeterno: & quia voluit tres angulos trianguli necessariò aequales esse duobus rectis, idcirco jam hoc verum est, & fieri aliter non potest, atque ita de reliquis. Ibid §. 8. Nec opus etiam est quaerere, quâ ratione Deus potuisset ab aeterno facere, ut non fuisset verum bis 4 esse 8, &c. Fateor enim id a nobis intelligi non posse; atque, &c. Quibus principiis convenienter itâ alibi instituit. Part. II. Epist. VI. Alibi non videtur de nullâ re, sed nam re esse dicendum, ipsam a Deo fieri non posse; cum enim omnis ratio veri & boni ab ejus omnipotentia depen-deat, nequidem dicere ausim, Deum facere non posse, ut mons sit sine valle, vel ut unum & duo non sint tria; sed tantum dico, illum talem mentem mihi indidisse, ut à me concipi non possit mons sine valle, vel aggregatum ex uno & duobus quod non sit tria, &c. atque talia implicare contradictionem in meo concepru, &c. Clarius vero, Part. I. Epist. CXV.
