Quantum ad difficultatem concipiendi, qui Liberum & indifferentem fuerit Deum efficere, ut non sit verum, quod tres anguli trianguli sint duobus rectis aequales, aut universum quod contradictoria nequeant esse simul vera; id facile solvi potest, considerando, potentia divina limites nullos esse posse, deinde etiam, advertendo, mentem nostram esse finitam, atque ita creatam, ut possit concipere tanquam possibilia ea quae Deus re vera voluit esse possibilia; sed non ita, ut possit etiam concipere tanquam possibilia, ea quae Deus potuisset quidem possibilia reddere, sed quae tamen ipse voluit reddere impossibilia. Ex priore enim consideratione liquet, Deum non potuisse determinari seu cogi ad faciendum ut verum foret, quod contradictoria nequeunt esse simul; ac proinde potuisse illum statuere contrarium. Deinde vero altera nos monet, quod licet id verum sit, non tamen debemus laborare, ut id comprehendamus, quia natura nostra huic comprehendendo impar est. Quanquam autem Deus voluerit nonnullas veritates esse necessarias, minim, tamen sequitur id illum necessario voluisse, aliud enim prorsus est velle illas esse necessarium, aliud velle necessario, seu ad id volendum cogi. Unde exertim & rotundè, Ibid. Epist. cx. Dico fuisse Deo aeque liberum facere, ne verum foret, omnes lineas ductas a centro circuli ad peripheriam esse aequales, atque creare mundum. Ne quis de Cartesii mente ambigat, istæc verbotim exhibuisse visum fuit. Nunc recta propero ad examen thesèos principalis, puta, potuisse Deum statuere, ut contradictoria sint simul.
units.tr: II. The texts cited on this matter, which show what his mind was on this point. I am not speaking here of priority in time; but there was not even a priority in order, or in nature, or in what they call reasoned reason, so that the idea of the good would have moved God to choose one thing rather than another. For example, he did not will to create the world in time because he saw that it would be better so than if he had created it from eternity; nor did he will that the three angles of a triangle be equal to two right angles because he knew that it could not be otherwise, and so on. Rather, on the contrary, because he willed to create the world in time, therefore it is better so than if it had been created from eternity; and because he willed that the three angles of a triangle necessarily be equal to two right angles, therefore this is now true and cannot be otherwise, and so on for the rest. Ibid., §8: Nor is there any need to ask by what reason God could from eternity have brought it about that twice four would not be eight, and so on. For I confess that this cannot be understood by us. And so on. In agreement with these principles he set out the matter elsewhere, Part II, Letter VI: Elsewhere it seems that one must say not that a thing cannot be made by God, but that the thing itself cannot be made by God. For since every reason of truth and good depends on his omnipotence, I would not dare to say that God cannot make it so that a mountain be without a valley, or that one and two are not three; but I only say that he has implanted in me such a mind that I cannot conceive a mountain without a valley, or an aggregate of one and two that is not three, and so on, and that such things involve a contradiction in my conception, and so on. More clearly, Part I, Letter CXV: As to the difficulty of conceiving how God, who is free and indifferent, could bring it about that it not be true that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles, or that the whole is not greater than its part, or that contradictories cannot be true at the same time, this can easily be resolved by considering that the divine power can have no limits; and further, by noting that our mind is finite, and so created that it can conceive as possible those things which God in truth willed to be possible, but not so that it can also conceive as possible those things which God could indeed have made possible, but which he nevertheless willed to make impossible. For from the former consideration it is clear that God could not have been determined or compelled to bring it about that what contradictories cannot be together should be true, and therefore that he could have decreed the contrary. Then the second consideration warns us that, although this is true, we need not labour to comprehend it, because our nature is unequal to comprehending it. Although God willed some truths to be necessary, nevertheless it does not follow that he necessarily willed them; for it is quite different to will them to be necessary than to will necessarily, or to be compelled to will this. Hence, plainly and roundly, Ibid., Letter CX: I say that it was equally free for God to make it not true that all the lines drawn from the centre of a circle to the periphery are equal, as to create the world. Lest anyone doubt Descartes's mind, I thought fit to set these words down exactly. Now I hasten straight to the examination of his principal thesis, namely, that God could have decreed that contradictories be simultaneously true.

units.la: III. Contradictoriorum possibilitas cum primæ causæ sapientia nequaquamconsistit.
units.tr: III. The possibility of contradictories is by no means consistent with the wisdom of the first cause.

units.la: Primùm quidem extra controversiæ alcam positum est, Divinam potentiam non esse vim brutam, aut merum impetum rationis moderamine destitutum. Minimè quadrat talis cogitatio in absolutam omnibus numeris primi entis perfectionem; quæ non finit id gaudere potentia, nisi absolutè perfecta, atque ideò summè rationali, quæque adeò nihil agat vel agere posset, nisi ex rationis præscripto. Evincitque abundè rerum omnium in hoc universo stupenda concatenatio, atque in suos fines directio, principium sui non minus rationale quam potens. Atquì nemo sapientem æquè agnoscere potest causam primam ac potentem, qui non fateatur, nihil à summa ratione produci posse, quod non ipsa, uti loquitur Philosophus & Poëta Christianus,
units.tr: First of all, it is beyond any controversy that divine power is not brute force, or a mere impulse lacking the guidance of reason. Such a notion fits very poorly with the absolute perfection in every respect of the first being, which does not allow it to possess power unless it is absolutely perfect, and therefore supremely rational, and which therefore acts, or could act, only according to the prescription of reason. The astonishing interconnection of all things in this universe, and their direction toward their ends, a principle no less rational than powerful, amply proves this. Now no one who is wise can recognise the first cause as equally powerful without confessing that nothing can be produced by the highest reason unless that reason itself, as the philosopher and the Christian poet puts it,

units.la: Superno Ducat ab exemplo, similique in imagine formet.
units.tr: "From the heavenly exemplar takes its lead, and forms it in a like image."

units.la: Jam verò contradictoriorum, qua talium, ideam nullam dari posse, operosâ demonstratione minimè indiget. Scilicet, quæcunque contradictoria sunt, hoc ipso contradictoria sunt, quod secundum unionem illorum prædicatorum, quorum respectu contradictoria existunt, concipi planè nequeant. Etenim, cum rei contradictio consistat in ipsa prædicatorum, ut itâ dicam, incompatibilitate, quâ per unum eorum positum alterum prorsùs evertitur, & contrà, manifestum est, rem omnem contradictoriam necessariò sui ipsius esse eversivam, quippe quæ tantum ob hoc ipsum contradictoria existit. Quumque rei conformis sit ejusdem idea, etiam, si rei contradictoriæ daretur idea, ipsa sui eversiva foret; id est, nulla omninò dari potest. Quæcunque ergò res verè contradictoria est, hoc ipso quod talis est, etiam absolutè inconceptibilis est: ut inconceptibile & contradictorium sint re verâ voces æquipollentes. Vel itaquè rerum contradictoriarum ideas Deum non habere; vel si habeat, eo ipso quia earum ideas habet, res illas contradictorias non esse, dicendum erit. Posterius contra hypothesin est. Prius aperta sequela infert, Deum res contradictorias producere non posse. Neque enim, ut jam diximus, quicquam cujus non habeat in sua mente ideam produce re is potest, qui non nisi summa cum ratione atque ex consilio sapientissimo producere potest, quodcunque producere potest.
units.tr: That there can be no idea of contradictories as such does not need a laborious demonstration. Clearly, whatever things are contradictory are contradictory for this very reason: they cannot be conceived at all in the union of those predicates in respect of which they are contradictory. For since the contradiction of a thing consists in the incompatibility, so to speak, of its predicates, by which the positing of one of them utterly overturns the other, and conversely, it is plain that every contradictory thing is necessarily destructive of itself, since it exists as contradictory only for this reason. And since the idea of a thing corresponds to the thing itself, even if an idea of a contradictory thing were given, it would destroy itself; that is, no such idea can exist at all. Therefore whatever thing is truly contradictory is, by the very fact that it is such, also absolutely inconceivable; so that "inconceivable" and "contradictory" are in fact equivalent terms. Either, then, we must say that God does not have the ideas of contradictory things, or, if he has them, that for that very reason, because he has their ideas, those things are not contradictory. The latter is against the hypothesis. The former clearly implies that God cannot produce contradictory things. For, as we have already said, no one can produce anything of which he does not have the idea in his mind, and he who can produce whatever he can produce only with supreme reason and by the wisest counsel.

units.la: Non autem hic evades (ut ab initio viam praecludamus exceptioni, quâ & hanc, & alias nostras, quas adducemus rationes, enervare nituntur) distinguendo inter id quod à nobis, atque id quod à Deo possit concipi. Posse nimirum fieri, ut rei cujuspiam, v. c. contradictoriae, idea à nobis quidem formari nequeat, quae tamen formetur à mente divina; cujus ratione incomprehensibilis sapientiae infinitus est prae nostro intellectu excessus. Verum nihil ista habent, quo quem adstrinximus nodum quicquam solvatur. Non enim hic quaeritur, quid nos concipere possimus, & an non ampliora Deus queat concipere quam nos, quae nihil ad rhombum: sed quaestio praecisè est, an quae praedicata nos in eodem conceptu unire non possumus, quia intelligimus, ex introspecta ipsa eorum intrinseca natura, omnem omninò unionem illa respuere, an, inquam, eadem haec Deus in sua mente unire, si voluisset, potuisset, consequenter & eorundem inter se unitorum ideas nobis indidisse? Ubi notandum, aliquâ specie haec dici posse, si supponeretur, mentem nostram, tantum ob sui imperfectionem & finitatem, rem quampiam contradictoriam, v. c. Circulum triangularem, concipere non posse: sic enim cogitare liceret, forsan perfectiorem intellectum, puta divinum, omninò eam concipere posse. Atqui quoties rem contradictoriam esse intelligimus, clarè distinctèque percipimus eam ideò nobis judicari contradictoriam, quia ipsa praedicatorum contradictoriorum natura propius introspecta talis deprehenditur, ut, hocipso quod talia sint, omnem mutuam unionem à parte sui respuant. Itâ quoties cogitamus, vel rei conformis est conceptus, vel non est. Si non fit, res verè contradictoria non erit, sed per errorem mentis talis tantùm nobis videbitur. Atqui Deum posse ea quae falsò contradictoria putantur, neque tamen verè talia sunt, uti indubium est, itâ ad praesentem controversiam nihil id attinet. Si verò talis conceptus rei omninò sit conformis, rogare lubet, quo pacto mens
units.tr: Nor can one escape here (so that we may cut off at the outset the objection by which they strive to weaken this and our other arguments) by distinguishing between what can be conceived by us and what can be conceived by God. It may be the case, namely, that the idea of some thing, for example a contradictory one, cannot be formed by us, yet is formed by the divine mind, whose incomprehensible wisdom surpasses our understanding infinitely. But such considerations contribute nothing toward untying the knot we have tied. For the question here is not what we are able to conceive, nor whether God can conceive more than we can; that has nothing to do with the matter. The question is precisely this: those predicates which we cannot unite in one concept, because we understand from looking into their own intrinsic nature that they reject every union whatever, could God, if he willed, unite these in his mind, and consequently implant in us the ideas of things united with each other? Here it should be noted that this could be said with some plausibility if it were supposed that our mind cannot conceive a thing that is contradictory, for example a triangular circle, only because of its own imperfection and finitude; for then one could think that a more perfect intellect, namely the divine, could conceive it altogether. But whenever we understand a thing to be contradictory, we clearly and distinctly perceive that it is judged contradictory by us for this reason: that the very nature of the contradictory predicates, when examined more closely, is found to be such that, by the very fact that they are such, they reject all mutual union on their own part. Thus, whenever we think, either the concept corresponds to the thing or it does not. If it does not, the thing will not be truly contradictory, but will seem so to us only through an error of the mind. But that God can do those things which are falsely thought to be contradictory, and yet are not truly such, is indubitable, and therefore has nothing to do with the present controversy. If, however, such a concept does wholly correspond to the thing, I ask in what way my mind

units.la: {IV} Non nostrae mentis finitudo, sed ipsa rei contradictoriae repugnantia causa existit, cur ejus idea formari nequeat. mea verè intelligat duo prædicata ob ipsam sui naturam uniri non posse, si tamen Deus ea & in sua mente unire, & unitorum idem nobis indere, & unita in eodem subjecto producere quoque quæat? Profectò, si ea conjungere possit Deus, vel mens mea prædicatorum illorum naturam non verè concipit, cum cogitat ea uniri non posse; vel eorundem naturam priusquam cum altero alterum conjungat, mutare debebit Deus. Utrumque à præsenti quæstione alienum, quandò de unione eorum disputamus, quæ verè contradictoria sunt, & talia manent. Ut absolvam, tentemus in exemplo jam allegato Circuli triangularis quid ipsa rei natura patiatur, nulla habita ratione illius quod mens nostra concipere posset, aut non possit. Posito Circulo, ponitur certè figura, in qua omnes circumferentiæ partes ab eodem centro æqualiter distant: posito Triangulo, ponitur figura, in qua omnes circumferentiæ partes ab eodem centro inæqualiter distant. Distantia hæc partium æqualis in circulo, inæqualis in triangulo, est non nostræ mentis, neque ideæ in nostra mente, sed utriusque tum circuli tum trianguli ipsius verum ac reale, quin essentiale, prædicatum, ab utroque, donec erunt circulus & triangulus, per naturam suam inseparabile. Uniantur nunc ista, si itâ lubet! Numquid unitæ figuræ partes omnes à centro distabunt æqualiter? Si distent, circulus quidem erit, sed non triangulus; si non distent, triangulus quidem erit, sed non circulus. Vides, ut utrumque, manens id quod est, cum altero, ratione prædicatorum in quibus pugnant, uniri absolutè nequeat? Ineptum itaque est quicquid pro palliando hoc absurdorum absurdissimo in medium adfertur de finitate nostri, infinitate Divini intellectûs; quæ neutra rerum naturæ quicquam vel addit vel detrahit. Atque hæc simul & semel, per omnem hanc nostram Dissertationem perpetuò deinceps observanda, monui suffecerit.
units.tr: {IV} The finitude of our mind is not the cause why the idea of a contradictory thing cannot be formed; the very repugnance of the contradictory thing is. Truly understands that two predicates cannot be united because of their own nature; yet if God could both unite them in his mind, and implant in us the idea of things united, and also produce things united in the same subject? Surely, if God could join them, either my mind does not truly conceive the nature of those predicates when it thinks they cannot be united, or God must change their nature before he joins the one with the other. Both are foreign to the present question, since we are disputing about the union of things that are truly contradictory and remain so. To make the point clear, let us try, in the example already cited of a triangular circle, to see what the very nature of the thing allows, without regard to what our mind could or could not conceive. Posit a circle, and you posit a figure in which all parts of the circumference are equally distant from the same centre; posit a triangle, and you posit a figure in which all parts of the circumference are unequally distant from the same centre. This equal distance of parts in the circle and unequal distance in the triangle is not a matter of our mind, nor an idea in our mind, but a true and real, indeed essential, predicate of both the circle and the triangle itself, which, as long as they remain a circle and a triangle, is by their nature inseparable from each. Now let these be united, if you like! Will the parts of the united figure all be equally distant from the centre? If they are equally distant, it will indeed be a circle, but not a triangle; if they are not equally distant, it will indeed be a triangle, but not a circle. Do you see how each, remaining what it is, cannot be absolutely united with the other, because of the predicates in which they conflict? It is therefore foolish to bring forward, to cloak this most absurd of absurdities, anything about the finitude of our intellect and the infinitude of the divine intellect; neither of these adds anything to, or takes anything away from, the nature of things. And let it suffice to have stated this once and for all, to be kept in mind throughout the whole of this Dissertation.

units.la: Cæterùm, non duntaxat in causæ supereminentissimæ absolutam omnibus numeris sapientiam gravissimè impingit thesis, asserens, Deum potuisse efficere, ut contradictoria sint simul; verùm & ipsam Ejus Omnipotentiam penitus evertit: tantum abest, ut infinitati illius ritè agnoscendæ ac stabiliendæ inserviat. Id facilè demonstravero, si planum fecero, eos, qui ad Omnipotentiam pertinere autumant posse contradictoria, talem Enti Omnipotenti tri-
units.tr: Moreover, the thesis that asserts that God could bring it about that contradictories are simultaneously true does not merely strike a most grievous blow against the absolute wisdom in every respect of the supreme cause; it utterly overturns his Omnipotence as well, so far is it from serving to acknowledge and establish his infinity duly. I shall easily demonstrate this if I make plain that those who maintain that contradictories belong to omnipotence ascribe to the Omnipotent Being such a Deum potuisse efficere, ut contradictoria sint simul

units.la: V. Omnipotentia Divina in veram rem æternitatem naturæ tribuere vim, quæ re verâ Potentia Nihili est : quod oppidò absurdum esse, ac Divinâ Majestate prorsus indignum, nemo negaverit, nisi nimium ab omni ratione alienus. Nimirum jam antè ostendimus, rem contradictoriam sui esse eversivam, dum prædicata involvit, quorum alterum tollit alterum ; indeque, eam ne concipi quidem posse, confecimus. Quid autem aliud Nihil est, quam quod nec est, nec concipi potest? Potentia ergò nihili est, quæ contradictoria potest. Atqui quæ potentia nihili est, nulla est revera. Omnis enim potentia, omnisque potentiæ exercitium, cum sit quid reale, realem etiam terminum, in quem terminetur, requirit. Quamobrem potentiæ alicujus terminum statuere Nihil, aliud nihil est, quam quicquid realis perfectionis in potentia quapiam continetur, reipsâ tollere & abnegare. Dic ergò Deum producere posse contradictoria, dices simul, Deum producere posse nihil : quod ut Omnipotentiam arguat tantùm abest, ut eleganter alibi & acutè concludat ex adverso Augustinus, Deum, quia nihil non potest, posse omnia. Lubet adjicere, quæ non absimilia urget, Loc. cit. Crocius, ubi inter alia disserit hunc in modum : „ Quæ combinari possunt, ea possunt habere „ rationem objecti, quod cadat sub Dei omnipotentiam. At „ contradictoria non possunt rationem objecti habere, quod sub „ Dei omnipotentiam cadat. Ratio : quia quod sub Dei omni„ potentiam cadit, id potest entis rationem habere. Est argu„ mentum Thomæ sic scribentis : Est autem considerandum, quod, „ cum unumquodque agens agat sibi simile, unicuique potentiæ activæ „ correspondet possibile, ut objectum proprium, secundum rationem „ illius actus, in quo fundatur potentia activa : sicut potentia calefa„ ctiva refertur, ut ad proprium subjectum, ad esse calefactibile. Esse „ autem Divinum, super quod ratio Divinæ potentiæ fundatur, est esse „ infinitum, non limitatum ad aliquod genus entis, sed prehabens in se „ totius esse perfectionem. Unde quicquid habere potest rationem entis, „ continetur sub possibilibus absolutis ; quorum respectu Deus dicitur „ Omnipotens. Nihil autem opponitur rationi entis, nisi non-ens. „ Hoc igitur repugnat rationi possibilis absoluti quod subditur Divinæ „ omnipotentiæ, quod implicat in se esse & non-esse simul. Hoc enim „ omnipotentia non subditur : non propter defectum Divinæ potentiæ ; „ sed quia non potest habere rationem factibilis, neque possibilis. Quacunque igitur contradictionem non implicant, sub illis possibilibus continentur, respectu quorum Deus dicitur omnipotens. Ea vero quae contradictionem implicant, sub Divina omnipotentia non continentur, quia non possunt habere possibilem rationem 1.p.q. 25. art. 3. Optimè sic, cum Thoma, Vir doctus, qui pergit ibidem sexdecim aliis rationibus impugnare dogma Weigelianum. Nos ad nostra revertimur.
units.tr: V. To ascribe to the Divine Omnipotence a power over the very nature of things, which is in truth a Potentia Nihili [power of nothing], is something that no one would deny is utterly absurd and wholly unworthy of the divine Majesty, unless he were far too alien to all reason. Indeed, we showed above that a contradictory thing destroys itself, since it involves predicates of which one cancels the other; and from this we concluded that it cannot even be conceived. But what else is Nothing, except that which neither is nor can be conceived? Therefore the power of nothing is that which can produce contradictories. But a power of nothing is in truth no power at all. For every power, and every exercise of power, since it is something real, requires a real term upon which it is directed. Hence to posit as the term of some power Nothing is nothing other than to take away and deny in fact whatever real perfection is contained in that power. Say, then, that God can produce contradictories, and you will say at the same time that God can produce nothing. This so far from proving his omnipotence that Augustine, elegantly and sharply in another place, concludes the opposite: God, because he cannot do nothing, can do all things. I am pleased to add what Crocius urges, not very different, loc. cit., where among other things he argues in this manner: "Those things which can be combined can have the character of an object falling under the omnipotence of God. But contradictories cannot have the character of an object falling under the omnipotence of God. The reason: because whatever falls under the omnipotence of God can have the character of being. This is the argument of Thomas, who writes thus: It must be considered that, since every agent acts in its own likeness, there corresponds to every active power a possible as its proper object, according to the character of that act on which the active power is founded, just as the power to heat is directed, as to its proper subject, to the capacity to be heated. But the divine being, upon which the character of divine power is founded, is infinite being, not limited to any genus of being, but containing within itself the whole perfection of being. Hence whatever can have the character of being is contained under the absolute possibles, in respect of which God is called Omnipotent. But nothing is opposed to the character of being except non-being. Therefore that which implies in itself being and non-being at once is repugnant to the character of an absolute possible, and is not subject to divine omnipotence. This is not subject to omnipotence, not because of any defect in divine power, but because it can have neither the character of something that can be made nor of something possible. Whatever, therefore, does not imply contradiction is contained under those possibles in respect of which God is called omnipotent. But those things which imply contradiction are not contained under divine omnipotence, because they cannot have the character of a possible" (Thomas, 1 p. q. 25, art. 3). A learned man has rightly argued thus with Thomas, and he goes on in the same place to attack the Weigelian dogma with sixteen other arguments. Let us return to our own.

units.la: Quod si sit admittendum, Deum statuere posse, ut contradictoria sint simul, utique nihil tam absurdum, atque ab omni ratione alienum dici poterit aut cogitari à quoquam, quod non sub Divinam potentiam cadat, ceuidoneum ejusdem objectum. Etenim, cum contradictionis ratio in hoc sita sit, quod rei cujuspiam praedicata incompatibilia existant & sese tollant, etiam in omnibus eadem illa erit atque uniformis. Itaque, admisso, Deum suâ virtute efficere posse rem contradictoriam unam, admittendum erit pariter, eundem efficere posse quamlibet. Si, V.C. itâ potuerit Deus instituere naturam, ut bis ter non sint sex, aut tres angeli trianguli rectilinei non sint æquales duobus rectis, quid ni, obsecrò, quâ ista potuit virtute etiam posset sic instituere naturam, ut Possibilia nunquam possint existere, aut, ut Homo non sit rationalis, aut, ut Materia non sit extensa, aut denique, ut Universa natura rerum talis existat qualis existit nunc, & tamen simul existat prorsus alia, quam qualis nunc existit? Hæc, similiaque sexcenta, fieri à Deo posse, numquis sibi persuadere possit, miror. Quod si quis nihilominus conetur, metuendum meritò, ne infinita hæc insania abeat tandem in purum putum Atheismum. Scilicet, si indiscriminatim quidvis possit Deus, fecit itaque (absit dicto profana cogitatio! absit blasphemia!) ut Ipse non sit Independens, adeoque non-Deus. Quid ni enim hoc possit istiusmodi potentia? Imprimis, si (quod contendunt Novatores) credendum sit itâ Deum à se esse positivè, ut ejus existentia potentiæ subjiciatur in tantum, ut hæc plane sit causa, cur Deus esse perseveret, sicque Ipse se Ipsum suâ propriâ potentiâ conservet. Quid ni quoque independentem esse faciat creaturam, eamque absolvat ab omni subjectione & reverentiâ erga sese? Et quis absurditatum finis, si quævis contradictoria Deo statuantur esse possibilia? Porrò, cum verba duntaxat signa rerum sint, nulla major absurditas est in contradictione logica, quæ notat repugnantiam in verbis, quam quæ est in contradictione metaphysica, quæ dicit repugnantiam rei, ratione prædicatorum essentialium. Imò, illa tota huic innitur, cum modus prædicandi eum qui essendi est necessario sequatur. Consequenter, qui Deus facere potest, ut contradictoria simul sint, idem ille de eadem re prædicata contradictoria enunciare quoque poterit. Quod qui absurdum non autumat, viderit, qui salvari queat, ut non omnis penitus è medio tollatur, oraculorum Divinorum indubitata Auctoritas; cujus fulcrum unicum est immutabilis illa Dei & constans veracitas, quâ in dictis & factis sibi semper similis adversari sibi nequit. Quanto rectius cum Apostolo credimus, oracula Dei esse non posse vaí xaí ú; firmiterque tenemus cum eodem, ἀδύνατον ψεύδεσθαι Θεόν: quippe qui, contradictoria revelando, non magis abnegare potest testimonii sui certitudinem, quam ἀρνήσασθαι ἑαυτὸν ἀδύνατον. Verum ista aliud imprimis spectant Novæ Scholæ mysterium (quamvis ab hoc ipso quod præ manibus est procul dubio oriundum) Deum posse fallere, si velit: quod Viris pluribus doctissimis confutatum est jam dudum. Unum addo. Frustrà, si Nostris hominibus credimus, sudarunt, quotquot unquam laborarunt Theologi maximi in conciliandis sacræ Paginæ locis in speciem repugnantibus, ac vindicandis à contradictionibus Fidei Christianæ Mysteriis. Quanto facilius nodos istos uno ictu rescidissent, si sic habuissent, Deum facere posse, ut contradictoria sint simul? At tantum non sapuerunt, quibus nondum, uti alibi loquitur profanus Philosophus S. Scripturæ Interpres, Cartesiana Philosophiæ lux affulserat. Quâ etiam destituti in tenebris palparunt haud dubiè quotquot unquam eruditi Divinam Auctoritatem derogarunt Apocryphis Christianorum, Talmudi Judæorum, Korano Muhammedanorum, hoc, inter alia, usi argumento, quod contradictiones in iis reperiantur; cujus omnis vis enervata atque tota acies vitreaest, si fletet assertio Cartesiana.
units.tr: But if it must be admitted that God can bring it about that contradictories be simultaneously true, then nothing so absurd, and so alien to all reason, could be said or thought by anyone that would not fall under the divine power as a fitting object of it. For since the nature of contradiction lies in this, that incompatible predicates of some thing exist together and cancel each other, that nature will be the same and uniform in all cases. Thus, if it is granted that God by his power can make one contradictory thing, it must equally be granted that he can make any one whatever. If, learned sir, God could have so established nature that twice three are not six, or that three angles of a rectilinear triangle are not equal to two right angles, why, I beg you, could he not by that same power also establish nature so that possibles could never exist, or that man is not rational, or that matter is not extended, or finally, that the whole nature of things exists just as it now exists, and yet at the same time exists entirely otherwise than it now exists? That God can do these things, and six hundred similar ones, I am amazed that anyone can persuade himself. But if anyone nevertheless tries, it is rightly to be feared that this endless madness may end in pure and simple atheism. Clearly, if God can do anything indiscriminately, he could also (far be such a profane thought from my words! far be such blasphemy!) bring it about that he himself is not independent, and so is not God. Why could such a power not do this? First of all, if (as the innovators contend) it must be believed that God is positively from himself, so that his existence is subject to his power to such an extent that this power is plainly the cause why God continues to be, and so he preserves himself by his own power. Why could it not also make a creature independent and release it from all subjection and reverence toward itself? And what end would there be to absurdities if any contradictories were held to be possible for God? Moreover, since words are only signs of things, there is no greater absurdity in logical contradiction, which denotes incompatibility in words, than in metaphysical contradiction, which denotes the incompatibility of a thing by reason of its essential predicates. Indeed, the former rests entirely on the latter, since the manner of predicating necessarily follows the manner of being. Consequently, he who can make contradictories simultaneously true could also state contradictory predicates of the same thing. Whoever does not judge this absurd should consider how the indubitable authority of the divine oracles can be preserved, the only prop of which is that unchanging and constant truthfulness of God, by which he, always like himself in word and deed, cannot be at odds with himself. How much more rightly do we believe with the Apostle that the oracles of God cannot be [ναὶ καὶ οὔ, yea and nay]; and we hold firmly with him that it is impossible for God to lie [ἀδύνατον ψεύδεσθαι Θεόν], since he, in revealing contradictories, can no more deny the certainty of his testimony than he can deny himself [ἀρνήσασθαι ἑαυτὸν ἀδύνατον]. But these matters concern chiefly the mystery of the New School (though undoubtedly arising from this very question before us), namely that God can deceive, if he wishes; which many most learned men have refuted long ago. I add one thing. In vain, if we believe our own people, have all the greatest theologians sweated, as many as ever laboured to reconcile passages of Holy Scripture that seem to conflict, and to vindicate the mysteries of the Christian faith from contradictions. How much more easily would they have cut these knots with one blow, had they held that God can make contradictories be simultaneously true? But they were so lacking in wisdom, as the profane philosopher and interpreter of Holy Scripture says elsewhere, that the light of Cartesian philosophy had not yet dawned upon them. Destitute of this light, they undoubtedly groped in darkness, as have all the learned men who have ever detracted from the divine authority of the Christian Apocrypha, the Jewish Talmud, and the Muslim Koran, using among other arguments the fact that contradictions are found in them. The whole force of that argument is weakened and its entire edge is glassy, if the Cartesian assertion stands.

units.la: Quin per hanc thesin simul & semel rejiciuntur atque exploduntur quotquot unquam à Theologis & Philosophis quibuscunque adducta fuerunt argumenta ab absurdo consequenti & manifesta contradictione petita. Etenim omnis iste argumentandi modus in eo fundatur & ex hoc uno robur habet, quod contradictoria nequeant simul esse vera. Facessant igitur Orthodoxi, qui passim rationibus inde desumptis Pontificiorum transsubstantiationem & Lutheranorum consubstantiationem, tanquam argumentis omnium captui manifestissimis, & cuivis rectâ ratione utenti indubiis, impugnarunt. Quam enim facile ex hac philosophatione didicerint ad illa omnia regerere, mentem suam finitam haud debere definire, num Deus ea, etsi contradictoria sint, facere possit. Habent profectò isti de quo sibi gratulentur, quod ex ipsis nostris quidam tantam dent stragem rationum bene solidarum, quibus constringebantur nimium. Certè virorum prudentium jam olim haec conjectura fuit, praecipuum Cartesio in asserenda contradictoriorum possibilitate scopum fuisse, ut viam pararet, ad se coram suae fidei hominibus liberandum facilius ab haeresEos suspicione in negotio de Missa. Quandoquidem enim secundum suae philosophiae fundamenta panem verum istic esse negare non poterat, ubi est extensio modificata omnibus modis quibus extensio panis modificari solet; contrarium tamen ejus credere juberet Romana fides, non aliud restabat effugium, quam tandem fateri, contradictoria quidem haec esse, atqui non ideò impossibilia Deo, quippe qui contradictoria quoque ut sint vera facere possit. Hac scilicet viâ incedere cum Cartesio Reformatis Doctoribus egregia laus est! Atqui, queis minus attenditur sua religio, suum saltem eis cordi esse deberet dogma. Si enim contradictoria possint esse simul, quid fiet de pulcherrimis illis Neotericorum argumentis, à contradictione petitis, quibus passim impugnare solent possibilem plurium Mundorum existentiam, duorum corporum nullo tertio interposito distantiam, Telluris quietem, &c. Omnia certè illa aliud nihil erunt quam plumbei pugiones, quibus umbonem Divinae omnipotentiae, ad contradictoria etiam se extendentis, objicere facillimum fuerit cuilibet dissentienti. Neque praesidium hic esse potest in ideis innatis, quas alias indere debuerit nobis tali in casu Deus: quid nì namque qui contradictoria potest, possit id quoque quod ideis adversatur?
units.tr: Nay, by this thesis all at once and together are rejected and exploded, as many as have ever been adduced by theologians and philosophers of whatever sort, arguments drawn from absurd consequence and manifest contradiction. For this whole mode of arguing rests on this and derives all its strength from this one thing: that contradictories cannot be simultaneously true. Let then the Orthodox desist, who everywhere have assailed the transubstantiation of the Papists and the consubstantiation of the Lutherans with arguments drawn from these, as arguments most manifest to everyone's grasp and indubitable to anyone who uses right reason. For how easily would they have learned from this philosophy to retort against all those arguments that our finite mind ought not to determine whether God can do them, even though they are contradictory! Those people truly have reason to rejoice, that some of our own men deal such a slaughter of arguments that were well founded, by which they were too much constrained. Certainly it was long ago the conjecture of prudent men that the chief aim of Descartes in asserting the possibility of contradictories was to pave a way by which he could more easily free himself, before men of his own faith, from suspicion of heresy in the matter of the Mass. For since, according to the foundations of his philosophy, he could not deny that there is true bread there, where there is extension modified in all the modes in which the extension of bread is wont to be modified, yet Roman faith bade him believe the contrary, no other escape remained than at last to confess that these are indeed contradictories, but not on that account impossible for God, who can indeed make even contradictories be true. Surely to walk this road with Descartes is an excellent distinction for Reformed teachers! And yet those to whom their religion is less a concern ought at least to hold their own doctrine dear. For if contradictories can be simultaneously true, what will become of those most beautiful arguments of the moderns, drawn from contradiction, with which they are wont everywhere to assail the possible existence of several worlds, the distance between two bodies with no third body interposed, the rest of the earth, and so on? All those will certainly be nothing but leaden daggers, which it would be very easy for any dissenter to hurl against the boss of divine omnipotence, which extends to contradictories as well. Nor can any defence be found here in innate ideas, which God would otherwise have had to implant in us in such a case: for why not? He who can do contradictories could also do what is contrary to the ideas.

units.la: Denique, absurdissimum commentum funditùs evertit scientiarum omnium principia & fundamenta, qualia sunt, Non-entis non sunt affectiones, Agere supponit esse; Totum est majus suâ parte, &c.
units.tr: Finally, this most absurd fiction utterly overthrows the principles and foundations of all the sciences, such as: "non-beings have no affections"; "acting presupposes being"; "the whole is greater than its part," and so on.
IX. Indeed, all things are overturned

units.la: X x &c. Nominatim illud primo-primum, Impossibile est idem simul esse & non esse ; cujus contrarium verissimum est, si contradictoria simul queant esse vera. Id verò si detur, mira sese offert oculis nostris rerum facies. Ineluctabilis nimirùm introducitur Scepticismus; dùm, percepto penitus omni certitudinis fundamento, nihil certi relinquitur, præter unum hoc, Contradictoria possunt simul esse vera. Atqui per hoc ipsum sic omnia alia ponuntur incerta, ut pedem nusquam figere liceat ad emergendum ex vortice, cujus centrum necessariò tandem fuerit stultissima illa persuasio, quæ quondam cujusdam Rhetorii fuisse dicitur, Bene sentire omnes, errare neminem. Quæ cogitatio cui allubescit, planè ei motum esse cerebrum oportet. Et quid, obsecrò, statuendum fuerit signatè de binis illis, quibus inædificata existit omnis Novæ sapientiæ moles, columnis, Quod clarè & distinctè percipio est verum, &c, Cogito ergò sum? Nihil certè repugnabit, falsa esse quæ clarè percipiuntur, aut, Cogitantem non exist ere, si Idem possit simul esse & non esse, sive, quod eodem redit, si contradictoria possint esse simul vera. Viderint itaque Recentiores, quantum itâ philosophantes arci suæ ipsi eripiant Palladium. Excipies forsan, etsi statuatur Deum absolutè facere potuisse, ut neque hæc principia vera forent, non tamen eum id facere voluisse. Verùm undè scis certus, non etiam voluisse, si posset? quæro ego. Justissima enim de re qualibet, etsi verissima videatur, manebit dubitandi ratio, quamdiu stat thesis, Deum facere posse ut contradictoria sint simul vera. Sed jam dudum nimius sum in convellendo absurdorum omnium absurdissimo: etenim (benè alibi Aristoteles) possibile non est, quempiam putare, Idem esse ac non esse. Plura qui cupit, præter Crocii Anti-Weigelium, conferre poterit doctissimi Hereborii Disput. Select. XL. Vol. II. Meletemat.
units.tr: &c. Especially that first-of-all principle, It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at once; the contrary of which would be most true, if contradictories could be true at the same time. If that were granted, a strange face of things would present itself to our eyes. Scepticism would indeed be unavoidably introduced: once every foundation of certainty has been utterly destroyed, nothing certain is left except this one thing, Contradictories can be true at the same time. Yet by this very thing all other things are made so uncertain that one cannot find a place to plant a foot and climb out of the whirlpool, whose centre must necessarily be that most foolish persuasion which is said once to have belonged to a certain rhetorician, All think well, no one errs. Whoever is pleased with this thought must surely have a disordered brain. And what, I ask, is to be decided about those two pillars on which the whole structure of the New Wisdom is built, What I perceive clearly and distinctly is true, etc., and I think, therefore I am? Surely nothing will prevent what is clearly perceived from being false, or the thinker from not existing, if the same thing could be and not be at once, or, which comes to the same, if contradictories could be true together. Let the Moderns see how much those who philosophise in this way snatch from their own citadel its Palladium. Perhaps you will object that, although it is granted that God could absolutely have made these principles not true, yet he did not will to do so. But how do you know for certain, I ask, that he would not have willed it too, if he could? For about any matter whatever, however true it may seem, a ground for doubt will remain as long as the thesis stands, that God can make contradictories true at the same time. But I have long been too lengthy in overthrowing the most absurd of all absurdities: for (as Aristotle well says elsewhere) it is not possible for anyone to think that the same thing is and is not. Whoever wants more, besides Crocius' Anti-Weigelius, may consult the most learned Hereborius, Select Disputations XL, Vol. II, Meletemata.

units.la: X. Potentiæ Dei cum voluntate ejusdem confusio præcipua nova assertionis basis.
units.tr: X. The confusion of God's power with his will, the chief basis of the new assertion

units.la: Præcipuum, quo nititur opinio de Contradictoriis Deo possibilibus, fundamentum est, quod ejus patroni nullam aliam possibilitatis radicem agnoscant, præter Divinam volitionem. Nempè, ajunt, liberrima hæc est, &c, utì ad alia omnia extra se, itâ quoque ad contradictoria, prorsus indifferens; adeò ut per illam oppositum ejus, quod nunc per voluntatis actum definitum est, si lubitum fuisset Deo, definiri potuisset. Sic V. G. Triangulum idcò tres angulos habere volunt duobus rectis æquales, ejusque talis idem nobis indidisse Deum, quia decreto liberrimo definiverat, triangulum tres tantùm, non plures, eosque tales & tantos, non alios, angulos habituram. At si voluisset Deus, addunt, eádem, quâ nunc hoc constituit, libertatis indifferentiâ oppositum ejus potuisset constituere; triangulum scil. habituram angulos, qui simul sumpti duobus rectis minores sint, majoresve; iis convenienter, aliam quoque menti nostræ indere trianguli idem, quam nunc indidit; alium denique de facto, quam nunc produxit, producere potuisset. Hæc omnis philosophatio quid habeat solidi, omnium optimè apparebit, ubi inquisiverimus in hypothesin, quam, ceu αρχὴν ἀνυπόθετον, præsens assertio substernit, quâque contendunt Omnipotentiam Divinam eandem omninò esse cum efficaci Numinis Voluntate. Suffodiendum paucis est hoc fundamentum, quo minori labore diruatur ei inædificata controversia thesis.
units.tr: The principal foundation on which the opinion about contradictories being possible for God rests is that its defenders acknowledge no other root of possibility besides the divine volition. Namely, they say, this volition is most free and, as it is wholly indifferent to all other things outside itself, so also to contradictories; so that by it the opposite of what has now been defined by an act of the will could have been defined, had it pleased God. Thus, for example, they hold that a triangle has its three angles equal to two right angles, and that God implanted this in us, because by a most free decree he had determined that a triangle would have only three angles, no more, and those of such and such a size, and no others. But if God had willed, they add, then by the same freedom of indifference by which he now established this, he could have established the opposite: namely, that a triangle would have angles which taken together are less or greater than two right angles. Accordingly he could have implanted in our mind another idea of a triangle than the one he now implanted, and finally could have produced in fact another triangle than the one he now produced. How solid this whole philosophising is will best appear when we examine the hypothesis which the present assertion lays down as its unhypothetical first principle [ἀρχὴν ἀνυπόθετον], and on which they contend that the divine omnipotence is altogether the same as the efficacious will of the Godhead. This foundation must be undermined in a few words, so that the controversy built upon it may more easily be overthrown.

units.la: Itaquè (ut hinc ad ista respondere ordiar) falsum est, Omnipotentiam Dei à Voluntate Ejusdem nullo pacto distingui. Si quod enim inter alia Dei Attributa existit distinctionis rationis ratiocinatæ, uti vocant, fundamentum, hoc loco certè existit. Nimirùm, non quæcunque Deus potest ea aliquando existunt. At quæcunque Deus vult efficaci Voluntate, omninò vi ejusdem aliquandò existunt. Quamobrem non frustrà Potentia à Voluntate in Deo distinguitur pro modo concipiendi nostro. Existere aliquandò omnia, quæ Deus vult voluntate efficaci, per se clarum est; neque enim efficax dici potest Voluntas, quæ non pariter sic sit efficiens, ut re ipsâ quæ vult ponantur. Quod imprimis admittendum iis, qui, cum Recentioribus, nullum operum Divinorum principium agnoscunt præter Voluntatem Dei efficacem, indèque Dei ipsam Creationem & Providentiam nihil aliud ab ea esse dicunt. Restat ergò, ut demonstremus, non ea omnia aliquandò existere, quæ Deus potest. Id manifestum evadet, si attendamus, ab una parte solius Dei prærogativam esse, ut, quemadmodum absolutissimè independens est & omnisufficiens, sic quoque perfectiones ipse possideat nullo numero nullo gradu definitas; cùm tamen ab altera parte nihil unquam creatum existat, extiterit, aut extiturum sit, quod non sit finitæ perfectionis; quandoquidem de natura rei dependentis est certis perfectionum limitibus, ex arbitrio causæ à qua pendet atque esse suum accepit, circumscriptum esse. Nunc si conferamus Dei perfectiones infinitas cum perfectionibus rei creatæ finitis, clarissimum est, nullam prorsus harum ad illas esse aut unquam esse posse proportionem. Unde sponte sua sequitur, Deum infinitum, propter ipsam persectionum suarum infinitatem, nunquam itá creaturæ finitæ has communicare posse, quin modis & gradibus infinities pluribus & majoribus eas communicare adhuc queat. Viden, nunquam existere posse, quæcunque Deus absolutè potest; posse tamen quin debere existere, quæcunque efficaciter vult? Atqui tam diversa objectorum latitudo nisi sit sufficiens & idoneum inter Potentiam Dei & Voluntatem distinguendi fundamentum, quid erit tandem?
units.tr: Therefore (so that I may begin my reply from here) it is false that the omnipotence of God is in no way distinguished from his will. For if there exists among the other attributes of God a basis for the distinction of reason reasoned, as they call it, here it certainly exists. Namely, not everything that God can do exists at some time. But whatever God wills by efficacious will certainly exists at some time, by the force of that will. Wherefore it is not in vain that in God power is distinguished from will according to our mode of conceiving. That all things God wills by efficacious will exist at some time is clear in itself; for a will cannot be called efficacious unless it is equally effective, so that the things it wills are actually placed in being. This must especially be admitted by those who, with the Moderns, acknowledge no principle of the divine works besides the efficacious will of God, and therefore say that creation and providence themselves are nothing other than that will. It remains, then, for us to demonstrate that not all the things God can do exist at some time. This will become manifest if we attend to the following. On the one hand, it is the prerogative of God alone that, just as he is absolutely independent and all-sufficient, so he possesses perfections defined by no number and no degree. On the other hand, nothing created exists, has existed, or will exist that is not of finite perfection; for it is of the nature of a dependent thing to be circumscribed within certain limits of perfection, at the discretion of the cause on which it depends and from which it received its being. Now if we compare God's infinite perfections with the finite perfections of a created thing, it is most clear that there is, and can be, no proportion between these and those at all. Whence it follows of its own accord that God, infinite on account of the very infinity of his perfections, can never communicate these to a finite creature without being able still to communicate them in ways and degrees infinitely more numerous and greater. Do you see that whatever God can absolutely do could never all exist, while whatever he efficaciously wills must exist? But if such a diversity in the range of objects is not a sufficient and suitable foundation for distinguishing between the power of God and his will, what in the end will be?

units.la: Addc, exercitium Potentiæ esse actionem transeuntem, quæ per se ponit veram rei, hactenùs merè possibilis, existentiam extra Deum; quum actio Voluntatis immanens sit, nullamque talem rei coexistentiam ex sese inferat. Ab æterno nimirùm rectè concipias Deum actuosum volendo, i. e. decernendo de futura rerum existentia: at non rectè (loquor de modo concipiendi nostro) actuosum concipis efficaci potentiâ; quippe cujus exercitium connotat actualem rei possibilis extra Deum existentiam, quam æternam concipere nec possumus nec debemus. Atque istis convenienter Theologi & Philosophi passim bene dixerunt Voluntatem Dei in rerum productione se habere ad instar principii imperantis, Potentiam ad instar exequentis. Eodemque fundamento iidem distinxerunt rectè inter Potentiam Absolutam, quâ Deus, sepositâ omni cogitatione de Decreto, attendendo duntaxat ad absolutissimam Ejusdem Sufficientiam, ea posse dicitur, quæcunque velle potest; & inter Ordinatam, quâ, æternum Decretum supponente, ea potest Deus, quę pro liberrimo beneplacito ipso facto aliquandò extitura voluit. Unde &, præcunte quoque ipsâ S. Scripturâ, plura semper iisdem habita possibilia, quam quæ Deus aut fecit unquam, aut facturus est. Neque, ut verum fatear, video, qui quent, salvis suis hypothesibus, hanc Potentiæ Divinæ divisionem, & per consequens ejus à Voluntate distinctionem, rejicere, qui tuentur, Deum potuisse statuere, ut contradictoria sint simul, non tamen id posse, posito quod has non alias nobis indere volucrit rerum ideas. Ecce ! potuit Deus absolutè , quod idem non potest, ex hypothesi quod sic voluerit, non aliter. Saltem, si Potentia Dei à Voluntate neutiquam sit distinguenda , peribit plane elegantissimus ille Cartesii conceptus, quem dictat Part. I. Epist. CXV. Mentem nostram esse finitam , atque ita creatam , ut possit concipere tanquam possibilia ea quæ Deus REVERA VOLUIT esse possibilia; sed non ita, ut possit etiam concipere tanquam possibilia, ea quæ Deus POTUISSET QUIDEM possibilia reddere , sed quæ TAMEN IPSE VOLUIT reddere impossibilia. Capiat mysterium qui potest! Sed simul absolvat, obscurò , à crassa contradictione , si nulla inter Potentiam, quâ talia potuisset quidem Deus, & Voluntatem, quâ eadem non tamen revera voluit, intercedat distinctio.
units.tr: Add that the exercise of power is a transitive action, which posits in reality the existence outside God of a thing hitherto merely possible; whereas the action of the will is immanent and does not imply any such coexistence of the thing. From eternity you may rightly conceive God as active by willing, that is, by decreeing concerning the future existence of things; but you may not rightly (I speak in our mode of conceiving) conceive him as active by efficacious power, since the exercise of that power implies the actual existence outside God of a possible thing, which we can neither conceive nor ought to conceive as eternal. In line with this, theologians and philosophers have often rightly said that the will of God, in producing things, stands as a commanding principle, and power as an executing one. On the same foundation they have rightly distinguished between absolute power, by which God, setting aside all thought of decree and attending only to his most absolute sufficiency, is said to be able to do whatever he can will; and ordained power, by which God, presupposing his eternal decree, can do those things which by his most free good pleasure he has willed to exist at some time in fact. Hence also, with Holy Scripture itself leading the way, more possibilities have always been recognised than those which God has ever done or will do. Nor, to tell the truth, do I see how those who maintain that God could have established that contradictories are true together, yet could not do so, given that he chose to give us these and not other ideas of things, can, with their hypotheses intact, reject this division of divine power, and consequently its distinction from the will. Look! God could absolutely do what he cannot do, on the hypothesis that he so willed, and not otherwise. At least, if the power of God is in no way to be distinguished from his will, that most elegant concept of Descartes will utterly perish, which he sets down in Part. I, Letter CXV: that our mind is finite and so created that it can conceive as possible those things which God REALLY WILLED to be possible; but not in such a way that it can also conceive as possible those things which God COULD INDEED HAVE MADE possible, but which HE HIMSELF WILLED to make impossible. Let him who can grasp this mystery! But let him at the same time free it, obscurely, from gross contradiction, if no distinction lies between the power by which God could indeed have made such things, and the will by which he did not truly will them.

units.la: Neque pro confundenda Divina Potentia cum Voluntate quicquam facit, quod contendant , plurimum perfectionis Voluntati Divinæ detrahi, nisi ea per se sufficiens agnoscatur ad ea producenda, quæ existere vult Deus : qualis procul dubio non agnoscitur, quandò indigere statuitur Potentiâ exequente. Speciem enim aliquam ista habere videri possent, si Voluntas in productione rerum penderet à Potentia, ut à principio quopiam revera à se distinguo. Verùm, quandoquidem omnis hæc Potentiam inter & Voluntatem distinctio, consequenter & ordo inter easdem, tantùm rationis est, & pro modo concipiendi nostro (quamvis conceptu in re fundato, respectu objectorum & effectorum, uti demonstratum dedimus) nulla utique metui hinc potest vel umbra imperfectionis ; quum aliud nihil sic indicetur , quam Deum res ipso facto extra se existentes producere , non præcisè qua Volentem, sed qua Potentem. Certè , & ipsi dissentientes non illubenter agnoscunt , res creari à Deo formaliter , non per Intellectum , sed per efficacem Voluntatem. An verò & ipsi ideò multum perfectioni Intellectûs Divini detrahere dicendi erunt, quod Deum, non qua intelligentem præcisè, sed qua volentem res producere statuant ? Nimirùm, perfectio cujusque Attributi Divini æstimanda est in suo genere; non ex collatione eorum prædicatorum quæ aliis Attributis, non huic, formaliter conveniunt. Quis v. G. Visum perfectum dici non debere autumet, si non sonos percipiat; aut Auditum, si non videat colores. Itaquè, quemadmodum perfectissimus est Intellectus Divinus , eo quod persectissimo ʃtissimo modo intelligat omnia omninò quæ intelligi possunt, etsi interim tantùm sit principium operum Divinorum dirigens, non formaliter imperans, uti est Voluntas; ità quoque Voluntas Divina perfectissima fuerit, eo quod liberrimè & independenter velit quæcunque vult, etsi rerum creatarum tantùm sit principium imperans, non exequens formaliter, quale est Potentia.
units.tr: Nor do the objectors gain anything for their claim that the Divine Will is greatly diminished in perfection unless it is recognised as sufficient in itself to produce the things God wills to exist. Clearly it is not seen as sufficient when it is said to need a power to carry it out. Such an objection might have some force if the Will in producing things depended on a Power that was really distinct from it, as from some first principle. But since this whole distinction, and the order between the two, is only one of reason, and is made according to our own manner of conceiving (though it has a basis in the thing, with respect to objects and effects, as we have shown), no shadow of imperfection can be feared from it. For nothing more is indicated than that God produces things which actually exist outside himself, not precisely as willing but as powerful. Indeed, even our opponents do not reluctantly admit that things are created by God formally, not through the Intellect but through an effective Will. Are they then to be said to take much from the perfection of the Divine Intellect because they hold that God produces things not precisely as understanding but as willing? Surely the perfection of each Divine attribute is to be measured within its own kind, and not by comparing the predicates that belong formally to other attributes and not to this one. Who, for example, would say that sight is not perfect because it does not perceive sounds, or hearing because it does not see colours? So just as the Divine Intellect is most perfect in that it understands in a most perfect manner all things that can be understood, even though it is only the principle directing the works of God and does not command formally, as the Will does, so the Divine Will is most perfect in that it wills whatever it wills most freely and independently, even though it is only the principle commanding created things and does not carry them out formally, as the Power does.

units.la: Affinc isti est aliud, quod pro tollenda inter Voluntatem & Potentiam Dei distinctione adferunt. Passim, inquiunt, quibusvis Auctoribus, Philosophis & Theologis, ipsisque imprimis Sacris Scriptoribus frequens est & solennè dicere, omnia esse & creata esse per Voluntatem Dei, sic ut Ipso jubente res existant. Unde superfluum esse concludunt, in operationibus Dei transeuntibus Potentiam concipere tanquam principium earundem proximum, à Voluntate per nos distinguendum. Sed frustrà sunt, quandò sic arguunt: neque enim ea pugnant, quæ ordinem aliquem inter se dicunt. Sunt omninò res conditæ, ut jam dixi, per Divinam Voluntatem, tanquam per principium imperans; at non id obstat, quo minus eædem creatæ sint per Potentiam, tanquam per principium exequens. Etiam in Sacris non semel Deus dicitur extendisse cælos, aut formasse terram, per Intellectum. Quid ni ergò, si ista consequentia firma sit, abundet etiam atque expungatur ipsa Voluntas. Possunt igitur creata omnia referri jure merito, & ad Intellectum Divinum, quatenus ex amussi æternarum in mente Divina idearum ea efformantur; & ad Voluntatem, quatenus operatur Deus omnia secundum immutabilis consilii seu decreti propositum; & ad Potentiam, quatenus suam sic exerit sufficientiam, ut ipso facto res existant. Quod interim res Deo jubente adesse dicantur, haud caret suâ emphasi. Non quasi justa Dei sint immediatum existentiæ rerum, nullâ intercedente ejusdem Potentiâ, principium; sed quod absque morâ res existat, itâ Volente Deo, quoniam Volitio talis comitem habet Potentiam plané irresistibilem, ac vim insuperabilem, quæ sic operatur absque omni labore & conatu, ut nihil ei obicem ponere queat, quo minus, simulac vult Deus, res existat, qualem vult: quo sensu ille inter Antiquos, Velle Dei, posse est. Cæterùm tamen non frustrà in Sacris Manus Dei cum Consilio Ejusdem conjungitur; sic ut Manu sua implere dicatur, quæ, juxta prædictiones operatur secundum consilium Voluntatis. Quæ ipsissimam nostram sententiam hac parte exprimunt. Nunc ista evincendæ distinctioni rationis ratiocinatæ inter Potentiam Dei & Voluntatem sufficiant.
units.tr: Connected with this is another argument they bring to remove the distinction between the Will and the Power of God. Everywhere, they say, among all authors, philosophers and theologians, and above all the sacred writers themselves, it is frequent and customary to say that all things are and have been created by the Will of God, so that at his command things exist. From this they conclude that it is superfluous, in God's transient operations, to conceive a Power as their proximate principle, to be distinguished by us from the Will. But they are wrong to argue thus, for those things do not conflict which say that there is some order between them. As I have already said, things are indeed created by the Divine Will as by a commanding principle; but that does not prevent them from being created by the Power as by an executing principle. In Scripture too it is said more than once that God stretched out the heavens or formed the earth by the Intellect. If that inference were sound, why should not the Will itself also be superfluous and be struck out? So all created things can rightly be referred both to the Divine Intellect, insofar as they are shaped according to the unerring standard of the eternal ideas in the Divine mind; and to the Will, insofar as God works all things according to the purpose of his unchangeable counsel or decree; and to the Power, insofar as he exercises his sufficiency in such a way that things exist by the very fact. Yet the statement that things are present at God's command is not without its emphasis. This is not because the command is the immediate principle of the existence of things with no Power intervening; rather, things exist without delay as soon as God wills, because such a volition has as its companion a Power that is altogether irresistible and an force that cannot be overcome. It works without any labour or effort, so that nothing can stand in its way to prevent a thing from existing, just as God wills it, the moment he wills it. In this sense the ancient saying was that to will is to be able for God. Moreover, it is not without purpose that in Scripture the Hand of God is joined with his Counsel, so that he is said to fill with his hand what, according to the predictions, works according to the counsel of his Will. These passages express our very own view on this point. Now let these remarks suffice to establish the distinction, made by reasoned reflection, between the Power of God and his Will.

units.la: Eâ verò admissâ, quæcunque adversâ hypothesi nituntur, morle ruunt suâ. Nominatim, quandoquidem possibilia quævis sunt possibilia, & talia denominantur, propter dependentiam à potentia alicujus causæ agentis, patet etiam quæ Deo possibilia dicuntur referenda esse ad Divinam Potentiam tanquam ad radicem suam : non autem ad Voluntatem; unde volibilia seu volita rectius dixeris, qualia sunt ea, de quorum futuritione ab æterno per decretum definitum est penes Deum. Clariora hæc evadent, si, quid per Divinam Potentiam intelligi debeat, verbo explicuerimus. Nimirum, Deus, tanquam Ens perfectissimum, omni perfectionis genere abundans, hoc ipso Omnisufficiens est. Neque sibi tantùm existit talis, sed & quibusvis quæ extra Ipsum concipi queunt alia. Attendentes igitur duntaxat ad meram hanc Dei sufficientiam, tam eam sine mensura superabundantem intelligimus, ut hinc facili viâ ducamur, ad cogitandum, ex inexhausta plenitudine entis infinitè boni scaturire profse hos istos participatæ bonitatis rivulos; juxta tritum illud, Omne bonum communicativum sui.Sic ut Potentia Divina aliud nihil sit, quam infinita ejusdem perfectio, seu sufficientia, quatenus ab ea perfectiones quædam finitæ & participatæ fluere aptæ sunt. Quæ eædem perfectiones, spectatæ ut dependentes à prima perfectione, sunt ipsa possibilia. His itaquè concipiendis nullâ opus esse de Divina Voluntate cogitatione, res ipsa monstrat; nisi indè pergas meditari, Deum, tanquam summam rationem, etiam sibi in suis perfectionibus placere; quin & placere in hoc, quod quædam suarum perfectionum, quæ antè erant merè expressibiles, ipso facto quoque aliquandò sint exprimendæ. At cùm illa voluntas approbans sit, hæc decernens, neutra ad ipsam rerum possibilitatem sese extendit. verùm utraque hanc supponit; nempe non per indifferentem Voluntatis determinationem Deus omnisufficiens est, sed ipsâ suâ naturâ. Quid ergò? Uti Deus antecedenter ad omnem suæ liberæ Voluntatis actum (loquor de modo concipiendi, quo nos ordinem inter Attributa Dei constituere solemus) Omnisufficiens est, sic & antecedenter ad eundem est Omnipotens, seque Ipsum tanquam talem re vera râ intelligit. Quumque cum Potentia immediatè atque indivisim cohæreant Possibilia, tanquam correlatum cum suo relato, luce meridianâ clarius est, etiam antecedenter ad omnem actum Divinæ Voluntatis Possibilia esse talia, & tanquam talia à Deo cognosci. Falsum igitur est, rem hanc, v.c. triangulum, esse possibilem, aliam, fume circulum triangularem, esse impossibilem, tantum quia liberrimâ volitione sic præfinivit Deus. Consequenter, non jam quæcunque Deus reddere potuit possibilia, sed ea, tanquam possibilia, producere duntaxat potest, quæ cum Omnisufficientia nexum habent indissolubilem. Tale quid non est Contradictorium; quippe quod, si detur, uti est sui eversivum, sic quoque eversivum foret sufficientiæ Divinæ, à qua fluceret, & in qua, ceu causa, contineretur. Quæ omnia tam sunt certa & manifesta, omnemque adeo hic tollunt difficultatem, ut entia citra necessitatem multiplicarem, si dictis quicquam adderem. Quid si verò liberalis quoque sim, demque, (præter ullam necessitatem, contra omnem veritatem) radicem possibilitatis esse ipsam Dei Voluntatem, ne sic quidem conficietur, etiam ad contradictoria eam extendi debere, vel posse. Certè omnis Voluntas rationalem complacentiam connotat; rationaliter autem nemo sibi placere potest in re quam non intelligit. Quare, cum voluntas tendens in rem quæ non cognoscitur etiam sapiente homine indigna fit, ipsa citra controversiam à Deo removenda est; fixumque adeo manet, nihil Deum velle, nihil velle posse, quam quod intelligat. At jam antè demonstratum dedi, rei contradictoriæ prædicata ipsâ suâ naturâ sese ita evertere, ut concipi prorsùs nequeant. Nequit ergò Deus velle contradictoria, si quod vult vult rationaliter, i.e. non nisi præviâ intellectûs perceptione.
units.tr: Once that distinction is admitted, whatever opposing hypotheses they rely on collapse by their own weight. In particular, since all possibilities are possible and are so called because of their dependence on the power of some acting cause, it is clear that those things which are said to be possible for God must be referred to the Divine Power as to their root, and not to the Will. Hence it would be more correct to call them volitional or willed, that is, those things whose future occurrence has been fixed from eternity by a definite decree in God. These points will become clearer if we explain in words what must be understood by the Divine Power. God, as the most perfect Being, abounding in every kind of perfection, is for that very reason all-sufficient. He is such not only for himself but for all the other things that can be conceived outside himself. Therefore, attending only to this mere sufficiency of God, we understand it to be so immeasurably superabundant that we are led by an easy path to think that from the inexhaustible fullness of infinitely good Being there flow forth these streams of participated goodness, according to the common saying, Good is by nature self-communicating. Thus the Divine Power is nothing other than the infinite perfection or sufficiency of God, insofar as certain finite and participated perfections are able to flow from it. These same perfections, regarded as depending on the first perfection, are the possibles themselves. That we need no thought of the Divine Will to conceive these is shown by the matter itself, unless one goes on to reflect that God, as the highest reason, is also pleased with his own perfections, and is pleased that some of his perfections, which before could be merely expressed, are at some time actually to be expressed. But since that approving will is one thing and that decreeing will is another, neither extends to the very possibility of things; rather, both presuppose it. For God is all-sufficient not by an indifferent determination of the Will but by his very nature. What follows? Just as God is all-sufficient antecedently to every act of his free Will (I speak of the way of conceiving by which we are accustomed to set up an order among the attributes of God), so he is also omnipotent antecedently to the same, and he truly understands himself as such. And since possibles cohere immediately and inseparably with the Power, as a correlative with its relative, it is clearer than noonday light that, antecedently to every act of the Divine Will, possibles are such and are known by God as such. It is therefore false that this thing, for example a triangle, is possible, while another, say a triangular circle, is impossible merely because God so determined by a most free volition. Consequently, God can produce as possible not whatever he was able to make possible, but only those things which have an indissoluble connection with his all-sufficiency. Such a thing is not a contradiction; for if it existed, it would destroy itself, as it is self-destructive, and it would equally destroy the sufficiency of God from which it would flow and in which, as in its cause, it would be contained. All these points are so certain and manifest, and so remove every difficulty here, that I would be multiplying entities without necessity if I added anything to what has been said. But even if I were generous, and granted (without any necessity and against all truth) that the root of possibility is the Will of God itself, even so it would not follow that it must or could extend to contradictories. For every will implies a rational complacency, and no one can rationally take pleasure in a thing he does not understand. Hence, since a will tending toward a thing that is not known is unworthy even of a wise man, it must undoubtedly be removed from God; and it remains fixed that God wills nothing, and can will nothing, except what he understands. But I have already shown that the predicates of a contradictory thing destroy themselves by their very nature, so that they cannot be conceived at all. Therefore God cannot will contradictories, if what he wills he wills rationally, that is, only after a prior perception by the intellect.

units.la: Nihil autem roboris objectioni accedit ex eo quod assumitur, de Actionibus Dei ad extra indifferenter liberis; quasi hinc conficiatur, indifferenti voluntate Deum definire potuisse oppositum ejus quod nunc definivit, atque ideò facere potuisse ut contradictoria fuissent possibilia, æquè ac constituit ea fore impossibilia. Notandum enim est (ne quicquid hùc pertinet adducam) receptam hanc regulam, de Deo in actionibus ad extra indifferenti, respicere illorum, quæ possibilia supponuntur, tum futuritionem, venia fit voci, atque exsistentiam, tum etiam prædicata quælibet corum eorum extra-essentialia, quæ in rem quamque plura aut pauciora conferre aut non-conferre, pro mero voluntatis placito, potuit Deus. Atqui non eo innui indifferentem esse causam primam ad quaelibet attributa, etiam contradictoria, in re qualibet ponenda, vel id satis evincit, quod dici nequaquam possit, citra divinæ perfectionis abnegationem, Deum creaturam, quam voluit producere finitam, dependentem, veram, bonam, &c. producere potuisse infinitam, independentem, falsam, malam, &c. Scilicet nulla est in ente perfectissimo cogitanda libertas, quâ indifferens existat ad ea quæ perfectissimæ suæ naturæ repugnant. Ex quibus signatè liquet, quam sit absurda illatio Cartesii, concludentis loc. cit., etiam ad contradictoria Potentiam Divinam extendi debere, quoniam liquet, Deum non potuisse determinari, seu cogi, ad faciendum, ut verum foret, quod contradictoria nequeunt esse simul; ac proinde potuisse illum statuere contrarium. Crassior profectò philosophatio, quam quæ subtilibus Viri meditamentis digna sit! Quid enim? Putandumne, Deum cogi, ut sit talis, qualis est vi suæ naturæ? An verò etiam cogitur Deus esse Immutabilis, Æternus, Bonus, Justus, Verax; ut uno verbo dicam, an cogitur esse perfectissimus, ipsequeDeus? Certè non magis congruè dici potest, cum cogi, ut sit Omnisufficiens; ex quo prædicato possibilia proximè & immediatè pendere, jam est ostensum. Necessitas aliqua, fateor, hic occurrit, quatenus Deus absolutè nequit non is esse qui est: sed non ea est coactio; quippe quæ adjunctam habet complacentiam maximè rationalem, & sic liberrima existens tantum à coactione (quæ notat vim extrinsecam majorem quæ invito infertur) distat, ut huic è diametro adversetur. Cum ergò sint multa quæ Deo vi infinitæ perfectionis conveniunt necessariò, & ad quæ neutiquam existit indifferens, quamvis interim nihil sit ad quod summa ratio ullatenus dici possit cogi, absurdè infertur, Deus non potuit ad hoc cogi, potuit ergò statuere contrarium: cum tantundem id sit, ac si dicam ego, Deus non potuit cogi ad producendam creaturam dependentem, ergò producere potuit independentem; &c. Quod si per coactionem intelligat Cartesius necessitatem ejusmodi, quæ, cum libertate consistens, indifferentiam duntaxat tollit ad oppositum, phrasi quidem utitur durâ adeò & impropriâ, ut tolerari hic hïc non debeat; rem tamen ipsam quod attinet, verissimè dicitur, Deum determinari ( non ab extrinseco, per vim & coactionem; sed ab ipsa perfectissima sua natura, concomitante spontaneâ voluntatis complacentiâ) ad faciendum ut verum sit, quod contradictoria nequeant esse simul; ac proinde, non potuisse illum statuere contrarium: quod jam fusè demonstravimus.
units.tr: Nor does the objection gain any strength from the assumption that God's external actions are indifferently free, as if it followed that by an indifferent will God could have decreed the opposite of what he has now decreed, and so could have made contradictories possible, just as he has made them impossible. For it must be noted (so that I do not bring in anything irrelevant) that this accepted rule, that God is indifferent in his external actions, concerns those things which are supposed to be possible: both their futurition (pardon the word) and their existence, and also any of their extra-essential predicates which God, by the mere pleasure of his will, could have conferred on a thing in greater or lesser number, or withheld. But that God is indifferently the first cause of any attributes whatever, even contradictory ones, in the positing of any thing, is not implied by this, and this alone sufficiently proves it: it cannot be said, without denying the divine perfection, that God could have produced an infinite, independent, false, evil creature, etc., when he willed to produce a finite, dependent, true, good one, etc. Clearly there is no freedom conceivable in the most perfect being by which he could be indifferent to those things that are repugnant to his most perfect nature. From this it is plainly evident how absurd is the inference of Descartes, who concludes in the place cited that the divine power must also extend to contradictories, since "it is clear that God could not be determined, or compelled, to make it true that contradictories cannot be simultaneously true; and therefore he could have decreed the contrary." Surely this is a cruder philosophizing than one worthy of the subtle meditations of such a man! For what? Must we think that God is compelled to be such as he is by the force of his nature? Or is God indeed compelled to be immutable, eternal, good, just, true; in a word, is he compelled to be most perfect, namely God himself? Certainly it cannot be said more fittingly that he is compelled to be all-sufficient, a predicate on which possibilities have already been shown to depend immediately and proximately. Some necessity, I admit, arises here, insofar as God absolutely cannot not be what he is; but that is not coercion, since it has attached to it a most rational complacency, and so a most free existence is as far from coercion (which denotes a greater external force inflicted on an unwilling party) as can be, and is diametrically opposed to it. Since, therefore, there are many things which belong to God necessarily by the force of infinite perfection, and for which he is in no way indifferent, although there is nothing to which supreme reason could in any way be said to be compelled, it is absurdly inferred: "God could not be compelled to this, therefore he could have decreed the contrary." This is just as if I were to say: God could not be compelled to produce a dependent creature, therefore he could have produced an independent one; and so on. But if by coercion Descartes means necessity of this kind, which, consisting together with liberty, removes only indifference to the opposite, he uses a phrase so harsh and improper that it ought not to be tolerated here; yet as to the thing itself, it is most truly said that God is determined (not from outside, by force and coercion, but by his most perfect nature itself, with a spontaneous complacency of will accompanying it) to make it true that contradictories cannot be simultaneously true; and therefore he could not have decreed the contrary, which we have already demonstrated at length.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem nostra sententia nullam ponit in Deo coactionem, ita neque inducit res possibiles à Deo independentes. Potest enim aliquid pendere ab Ente primo, etiamsi non præcisè ab indifferenti Voluntatis determinatione fluat. Quare, quamvis verum sit ex nostra hypothesi, rerum possibilitatem, pro modo concipiendi, Voluntatem Dei antecedere, non tamen idcirco ea independens habetur. Scilicet, quod & antè monuimus, Omnisufficiens est Deus, etiam citra cogitationem de ejusdem Voluntate: at cum Omnisufficientia immediatè cohærent possibilia, quatenus accuratè loquendo hæc dicunt denominationem in illa fundatam. Dependent itaque possibilia omninò à Deo, tanquam ab Omnisufficiente causa, perfectiones eorum virtualiter includentes, quanquam non formaliter tanquam ab indifferenter illa volente.
