Volente, inquam, indifferenter; Voluntatem enim quam vocant approbantem neutiquam excludimus. Nam quemadmodum Omnisufficiens existit, se id maximè volente, non tamen formaliter talis est, ideò quia se talem esse vult; itâ quoque possibilia (quæ ex Omnisufficientia Divina tanquam ex fonte proximè scaturiunt) talia sunt, Deo volente & probante, non tamen proprie idcirco talia sunt, quia Deus ea talia esse voluit. De quo pluribus §. xv. Per nostram ergo sententiam salva stat Deo sua Primitas, creaturis Possibilibus sua dependentia; quatenus denominationis istius, quâ ea possibiles dicuntur, quæque nullam includit earundem existentiam, sive præsentem, sive præteritam, sive futuram, fundamentum primum est ipsa perfectissimæ naturæ Divinæ Omnisufficientia.
units.tr: Just as our view posits no coercion in God, so neither does it make possible things independent of God. For something can depend on the first Being even if it does not flow precisely from an indifferent determination of the will. Hence, although it is true on our hypothesis that the possibility of things, in the manner of conceiving, precedes the will of God, they are not on that account regarded as independent. Indeed, as we noted before, God is all-sufficient even apart from any thought of his own will; but since possibilities cohere immediately with all-sufficiency, insofar as, strictly speaking, they denote a denomination founded in it. Therefore possibilities depend wholly on God, as on an all-sufficient cause, virtually including their perfections, though not formally as on one who wills them indifferently. Willing, I say, indifferently; for we by no means exclude the so-called approving will. For just as the all-sufficient exists, most willing it, yet is not formally such because he wills to be such, so too possibilities (which spring proximately from divine all-sufficiency as from a source) are such, God willing and approving, yet they are not properly such because God willed them to be such. Of this more at §. xv. Through our view, therefore, God's primacy stands safe, and the dependence of possible creatures stands safe; inasmuch as the denomination by which they are called possible, which includes no existence of theirs, whether present, past or future, has as its first foundation the all-sufficiency of the most perfect divine nature itself.

units.la: XVIII. Amplius ajunt: Potuisset Deus alias planè fecisse rerum naturas, quam nunc eandem fecit; atque adeò alia rebus quibusvis tribuere potuisset prædicata, etiam contradictoria eorum quæ nunc res habent: consequenter, contradictoria quoque objectum esse potentiæ divinæ, non videtur negandum. Ad quod observandum venit, potuisse omnino Deum, loco rerum nunc existentium, produxisse alias, naturæ prorsus ab his quæ nunc dantur diversæ: at tali casu, vel non has produxisset; vel, si & has & illas, non tamen ideo contradictoria prædicata produxisset unita in eodem subjecto, sed in subjectis etiam contradictorie hactenus oppositis. Neque interim & istud negandum est, potuisse res plurimas recipere, Deo itá volente, prædicata quædam contradictoria illis quæ nunc possident. v. c. Sol, qui nunc existit rotundus, produci potuisset non-rotundus, sed triangularis vel quadrangularis. Verum id accipiendum his cautionibus: Primùm, ut non eodem tempore eidem rei infuissent contradictoria prædicata; quo sensu impossibile est, Solem rotundum, existentem talem, simul esse quadratum. Deinde, ut prædicata illa, quorum ratione subjectum fuisset illi quod nunc est oppositum, talia intelligantur, quæ neque rem evertant ab una parte, neque ex essentia ejusdem necessario fluant ab altera parte: quo pacto impossibile est, ex.gr. Solem esse non-extensum, vel non-figuratum. Alterutro modo si rem quampiam prædicata contradictoria recipere posse demonstraretur, verum demum foret, Deum posse producere contradictoria.
units.tr: XVIII. They further say: God could have made entirely different natures of things than those he has now made; and so he could have attributed to things predicates contradictory to those which they now have. Consequently, it does not seem to be deniable that contradictories too are the object of divine power. To this it must be observed: God could indeed have produced, in place of the things now existing, others altogether different in nature from those which now exist; but in such a case he either would not have produced these, or, if he had produced both these and those, he would not on that account have produced contradictory predicates united in the same subject, but in subjects which are hitherto contradictorily opposed. Nor, meanwhile, must it be denied that God, by willing it, could have made very many things receive certain predicates contradictory to those they now possess. For example, the sun, which now exists round, could have been produced non-round, but triangular or quadrangular. But this must be understood with these cautions. First, that contradictory predicates should not at the same time inhere in the same thing; in this sense it is impossible that the sun, existing round, should at the same time be square. Second, that those predicates on account of which the subject would have been the opposite of what it now is must be understood as such as neither overturn the thing on the one side nor necessarily flow from its essence on the other; in which way it is impossible, for example, for the sun to be non-extended or non-figured. If it were demonstrated that some thing could receive contradictory predicates in either of these ways, then at last it would be true that God can produce contradictories.

units.la: XIX. Nulla parte immodestiæ reus est, qui contradictoria infinitæ potentiæ subducit.Sed, nos modestiæ terminos excedere vociferantur, ac nimium nostro ingeniolo tribuere, qui ausimus finito intellectu Potentiæ Divinæ infinitæ limites ponere, subducendo illi Contradictoria. Verum inanis est affectatæ modestiæ prætextus, quæsitus duntaxat pro absurda opinione pallianda. Nequicquam etenim is peccat contra modestiam, quicunque ea de Deo & attributis Divinis definit, quæ definienda esse, docet recta ratio. An verò & is violatæ modestiæ accusandus venit, qui negat Dei Intellectum intelligere posse absolutè inconceptibilia, aut Voluntatem approbare posse malasurpia, &c. Equidem, quùm Intellectus Dei & Voluntas non minus infinita sint quam Potentia, eisque nihilominus finito nostro ingenio per modestiam liceat subducere quædam, quæ infinitæ perfectioni eorundem non respondent; scire lubet, quidni pari ratione, citra ullam temeritatem aut immodestiam, liceat negare, Deum posse impossibilia, sive contradictoria? Infinitam, uti oportet, & infinitè perfectam potentiam Divinam agnoscit, qui per eam infinito operandi modo produci posse fatetur infinita possibilia. Quin contrà parum verecundè de Divina virtute sentire & loqui eos jam ostendimus, qui ad Contradictoria quoque eam extendunt; quandò sic re ipsa Divinæ potentiæ perfectionem everti, non uno modo ostendimus suo loco. Id verò mirum est, hos modestiæ patronos adeò in totum tum ejus tum sui oblivisci, quoties tam anxiè inculcant, potentiæ Divinæ subduci debere Vacuum, plures Mundos, &c. utpote contradictoria. Haud parvi interim momenti fuerit hoc loco, ante omnia modestiæ rationem habere, ac pro certissima regula menti infigere, ingenio nostro finito infinitam potentiam circumscribi non debere; quippe quæ potest supra id omne quod cogitare possumus: etsi non ideò possit, quod ipsa summa ratio cogitare absolutè nequit. Verùm quæ modestiæ regula in hoc negotio præprimis observanda veniat, in ipso hujus Disquisitionis limine jam monuimus satis.
units.tr: XIX. No one is guilty of any lack of modesty who withdraws contradictories from infinite power. But they cry out that we exceed the bounds of modesty and attribute too much to our little wit, we who have dared, with a finite understanding, to set limits to the infinite divine power by withdrawing contradictories from it. But the pretext of affected modesty is empty, sought only to gloss over an absurd opinion. For he sins against modesty in vain who defines about God and the divine attributes those things which right reason teaches must be defined. Or rather, is he to be accused of violating modesty who denies that God's understanding can understand absolutely inconceivable things, or that his will can approve wicked things, and so on? Indeed, since God's intellect and will are no less infinite than his power, and yet it is permitted to our finite wit, out of modesty, to withdraw certain things which do not correspond to their infinite perfection, I would like to know why, by the same reasoning and without any rashness or immodesty, it should not be permitted to deny that God can do impossibilities, or contradictories. He acknowledges the divine power as infinite and infinitely perfect, as it ought to be, who confesses that through it, by an infinite mode of operating, infinite possibilities can be produced. Indeed, we have already shown in its place that those who extend it even to contradictories think and speak of divine virtue with little reverence, since in this way they in fact overturn the perfection of divine power. It is truly remarkable that these patrons of modesty forget entirely both it and themselves, as often as they so anxiously insist that a void, several worlds, and so on must be withdrawn from divine power as contradictories. Meanwhile it will be of no small weight here, above all, to have regard for modesty, and to fix firmly in the mind as a most certain rule that our finite wit must not circumscribe infinite power; for it can do more than all we can think, although it is not able to do what supreme reason itself absolutely cannot conceive. But which rule of modesty is especially to be observed in this business, we have already said enough about at the very threshold of this Disquisition.

units.la: Minimè gentium autem hactenus disputatis satisfaciunt quidam, qui excipiunt & protestantur, non se affirmare, Deum contradictoria posse; sed tantum, non audere se negare, etiam ea quæ contradictionem implicant Deo esse possibilia. Verùm inane hoc effugium est. Nam audivimus Cartesium totidem verbis expresse afferere, quin & adductâ ratione probare, Deum potuisse statuere contrarium; ejus nimirum, quod contradictoria nequeant esse simul: quod totò cœlo distat ab ista judicii in hoc negotio suspensione, in qua hi se subsistere prætendunt. Adde, ut non uno argumento jam evicimus, non tantùm non vel minimam esse causam, ob quam quis merito non ausit negare, Contradictoria esse Deo possibilia; sed urgentissimas etiam ex adverso esse rationes, ob quas id negare, & possimus, & debeamus. Denique, quicunque negare non audet, ea quæ contradictionem implicant Deo possibilia esse, nihil iste ex lumine rationis de re quacunque determinare unquam poterit firmo fundamento. Quùm enim discursus nostri ac ratiocinia quævis certis quibusdam principiis sic innitantur, ut omnem suam veritatem & certitudinem ab iis mutuentur, & quidem nominatim ab illo, Impossibile est idem simul esse & non esse; manifestum est, nihil certi de re quapiam per rationis lumen unquam ab ullo definiri posse, nisi supponatur, per absolutam potentiam Divinam fieri non posse, ut quicquam simul sit & non sit: uti demonstratum dedimus, §. ix. Concludimus ex omnibus hactenus hanc in rem allatis, nihil à quopiam dici ac statui posse absurdius, quam, Deum potuisse statuere, ut contradictoria queant esse simul. Quod ipsum demonstrandum propositueramus.
units.tr: Yet those who have hitherto disputed this matter with the nations hardly give satisfaction when they except and protest that they do not affirm that God can do contradictories, but only that they do not dare to deny that even those things which involve a contradiction are possible to God. But this escape is empty. For we have heard Descartes state this in so many words, and moreover prove it by argument: that God could have brought about the contrary, namely that contradictories cannot be simultaneously true. That is utterly far from the suspension of judgement in this matter in which these men claim to stand. Add that, as we have already shown by more than one argument, there is not only not the least reason why anyone should rightly hesitate to deny that contradictories are possible to God, but on the contrary there are very urgent reasons against it, for which we both can and ought to deny it. Finally, whoever does not dare to deny that things involving a contradiction are possible to God will never be able to determine anything about any matter whatsoever from the light of reason on a firm foundation. For since our reasonings and arguments of every kind rest on certain principles in such a way that they borrow all their truth and certainty from them, and indeed chiefly from this one: "It is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be at the same time," it is evident that nothing certain about any matter can ever be defined by the light of reason, unless it is supposed that by God's absolute power it cannot be brought about that anything both is and is not at once, as we demonstrated in §. ix. We conclude from all that has hitherto been brought forward on this point that nothing more absurd can be said or asserted than that God could have brought it about that contradictories could be simultaneously true. This is exactly what we had proposed to demonstrate.

units.la: Liebet, Corollari loco, ob Quæstionis cum materia quam tractavimus affinitatem, tribus verbis expendere: An rectè dicatur Deus per immensitatem suæ Potentiæ facere quædam posse, quæ eadem facere non possit ob infinitatem suæ bonitatis? Nobis qui sic definiunt Divinæ perfectioni parùm convenienter & loqui & cogitare videntur. Quid enim id aliud est, quam Deum ipsum sibi opponere? quandoquidem in ente simplicissimo & Potentia & Bonitas unum idemque sunt; ipsa nimirum natura Divina perfectissima, quæ sibimet ipsi contraria esse nequit. Quin, sepositâ quoque Divinâ simplicitate, conceptisque Potentiæ & Bonitatis Divinæ attributis, tanquam distinctis pro modo concipiendi nostro, manet nihilominus, Potentiam Divinam cogitandam esse tanquam perfectissimam, adeòque non instar brutæ alicujus vis, sed talem, quæ comites habeat summam sapientiam, justitiam, bonitatem, veracitatem, & quæ sunt similes virtutes. Atqui has omnes à Potentia sejungere necesse habent, qui aliquid Deum posse per potentiam asserunt, quod idem nequeat efficere per bonitatem; consequenter re ipsâ concipiunt potentiam absque illis persectionibus, absque quibus cogitari à mente nequit virtus Deo digna. Crudum itaque & absonum assertum est, ac minimè Potentiæ perfectissimæ Majestati congruum, Deum fallere posse si velit; ut scilicet satis virium habeat ad fallendum, sed non sinere ejus bonitatem ut fallat. Verùm in præsens manum de hac tabula!
units.tr: By way of a corollary, on account of the affinity of this question with the matter we have treated, it is pleasing to weigh in a few words: is it rightly said that God, by the immensity of his power, can do certain things which he cannot do because of the infinity of his goodness? To us, those who define it thus seem to speak and think rather unbefittingly of the divine perfection. For what else is this than to set God against himself? Since in the most simple being power and goodness are one and the same, namely the most perfect divine nature itself, which cannot be contrary to itself. Moreover, even setting aside divine simplicity, and taking the attributes of divine power and goodness as distinct according to our manner of conceiving them, it nonetheless remains that the divine power must be thought of as most perfect, and so not as some brute force, but as one that has as its companions supreme wisdom, justice, goodness, truthfulness, and similar virtues. Yet all these must be separated from power by those who assert that God can do by power something which he cannot effect by goodness; consequently they in fact conceive a power without those perfections, without which a virtue worthy of God cannot be thought by the mind. Therefore it is a crude and absurd assertion, and by no means consistent with the majesty of most perfect power, that God could deceive if he willed, in the sense that he has enough strength to deceive, but that his goodness does not allow him to deceive. But for the present, let us lay down the pen on this topic!

units.la: . DISSERTATIO. DE SENSUUM USU IN PHILOSOPHANDO.
units.tr: . DISSERTATION. ON THE USE OF THE SENSES IN PHILOSOPHIZING.
SUMMARY

units.la: I. Difficultatis in cognoscendo vero causa est adminiculorum tum defectus tum abusus. II. Manifestum id in sensuum perceptionibus, quibus nimium adhærent, cum plebeis, Epicurei; III. Parum verò tribuunt Sceptici & Platonici: Medium inter utrofque tenent Peripatetici. IV. Illorum atque istorum errorem confutare haud operæ pretium existit. V. Cartesius hac parte Scepticismi suspicionem apud multos incurrit: VI. Dum ad innatas ideas, non sensationes, in cognitione veri, attendere jubet. VII. Ejus, quibus id inculcat, adducuntur loca: VIII. Et Claubergiana in illa paraphrasi. IX. In ea quæ mitigandæ assertionis gratiâ ab utroque admiscentur observatio. X. Status quæstionis fixus, propósito paucis Cartesianæ assertionis sensu genuino: XI. Eique oppositâ antithesi, sensus non ad vivendum tantum, etiam ad sapiendum, esse datos. XII. Impingit Cartesii assertio in legem propriam, quâ amplissima Dei opera cogitare jubet. XIII. Item in aliam, quâ de rerum naturalium fine definire quicquam prohibet. XIV. Sensus à philosophando remoti, ut major fit innatarum idearum necessitas. XV. Quoque amplior essetin fingendis vorticosi mundi elementis libertas. XVI. Ad ipsam veri cognitionem acquirendam Sensibus uti jubet Sensuum Opifex. XVII. Imò & ad confirmandam Fidei Divinæ certitudinem subjectivam. XVIII. Unde efficax, pro Sensu ultra animalis vitæ regimen extendendo, argumentum. XIX. Modus cognoscendi statum unionis consequens, Sensus ultra vitæ animalis regimen patere, evincit. XX. Maximè, cum in hoc moderando Sensationum cum cogitationibus connexio nullum habeat, juxta novam hypothesin, usum. XXI. Rerum materialium existentiam Sceptici negare coacti, tantum quod sensui nullum facerent in philosophando usum. XXII. Citra Sensuum opem de plurimis corporum adjunctis accurratè philosophari non licet. XXIII. Confirmantibus id suâ praxi ipsis dissentientibus. XXIV. Negato Sensibus usu in philosophando, etiam experientiæ nullus manet locus. XXV. Non existentia tantùm sed & natura corporum adjumento Sensuum intelligitur. XXVI. Cavendum, ne sensus sumatur adæquatum cognitionis Philosophicæ principium. XXVII. Discernendæ quoque sensationes veræ à fallacibus, ex debitæ attentionis conscientia. XXVIII. Nec non, ex explorata rectâ organorum dispositione. XXIX. Etiam, ex requisita objecti ad organum comparati proportione. XXX. Denique, ex constitutione medii legitima. XXXI. Neque difficilius hæc attenduntur, quam regulæ quibus intellectus perceptiones regruntur. XXXII. Ex sensatione repetita de bonæ sensationis requisitis facilius constat. XXXIII. Item, ex plurium sensuum de eadem re consentiente testimonio. XXXIV. Sensuum fallaciae nil obstant, quo minus eis mens utatur in cognoscendo vero: XXXV. Haud magis quam errores intellectûs hujus usum in philosophando prohibent. XXXVI. Sensuum erroribus, non minus quam intellectûs, corrigendis ad manum sunt remedia. XXXVII. Fallaciae Sensuum, si philosophationi, etiam vitae moderamini hos ineptos faciunt. XXXVIII. Innatae rerum ideae, si vel maximè dentur, absque Sensibus philosophationi non sufficiunt. XXXIX. Quamvis toti composito Sensus conveniant, non ideò tamen ad vitae usum praecisè sunt restringendi. XL. Sensus sapiendi adminicula sunt, etsi sapientes non sint qui eos semper sequuntur duces. XLI. Acumen Sensuum in brutis, eos homini ad philosophandum esse inutiles, nequaquam arguit. XLII. Cum non Deo & Angelis, homini tamen ad intelligendum cur sensu opus sit? XLIII. Quaecunque Sensui clara sunt, eadem qua talia menti existunt evidentia. XLIV. Contrà, quae nullo modo sentimus, omnium difficillimè intelligimus. XLV. Intellectûs humani à Sensu dependentis explicatio & demonstratio paucis theorematibus comprehensa.
units.tr: I. The cause of difficulty in knowing the truth is both the lack and the misuse of aids. II. This is evident in the perceptions of the senses, to which the common people, and the Epicureans, cling too closely. III. The Sceptics and the Platonists attribute too little to them; the Peripatetics hold a middle course between both. IV. It is not worth the trouble to refute the errors of these and those. V. Descartes incurs, in this respect, the suspicion of scepticism among many. VI. In that he bids us attend, in the knowledge of truth, to innate ideas and not to sensations. VII. Passages are adduced in which he urges this. VIII. And Clauberg's in that paraphrase. IX. An observation on what is mixed in by each of them in order to soften the assertion. X. The state of the question being fixed, a brief statement of the genuine sense of the Cartesian assertion. XI. And of the opposed antithesis: that the senses are given not only for living but also for knowing wisely. XII. The Cartesian assertion strikes against a law of its own, which bids us contemplate the most ample works of God. XIII. Likewise against another, which forbids us to determine anything about the final cause of natural things. XIV. The senses are removed from philosophizing, so that the necessity of innate ideas becomes greater. XV. And the freedom to devise the elements of the vortical world becomes greater. XVI. God, the Maker of the senses, bids us use the senses to acquire the very knowledge of truth. XVII. Indeed, also to confirm the subjective certainty of divine faith. XVIII. Whence the argument, effective for extending the sense beyond the governance of animal life. XIX. The mode of knowing the consequent state of union proves that the senses extend beyond the governance of animal life. XX. Especially since, in moderating this, the connection of sensations with thoughts has no use according to the new hypothesis. XXI. Sceptics, compelled to deny the existence of material things, only because they made no use of the senses in philosophizing. XXII. Without the help of the senses it is not permitted to philosophize accurately about the many accidents of bodies. XXIII. Those who dissent confirm this by their own practice. XXIV. If the use of the senses in philosophizing is denied, no room remains even for experience. XXV. Not only the existence but also the nature of bodies is understood with the aid of the senses. XXVI. Care must be taken lest sense be taken as the adequate principle of philosophical knowledge. XXVII. True sensations are also to be distinguished from false ones by the consciousness of due attention. XXVIII. Likewise by the tested right disposition of the organs. XXIX. Also by the required proportion of the object to the organ suited to it. XXX. Finally, by the lawful constitution of the medium. XXXI. These things are attended to no less difficultly than the rules by which the perceptions of the intellect are governed. XXXII. From repeated sensation the requisites of good sensation are more easily established. XXXIII. Likewise from the agreeing testimony of several senses concerning the same thing. XXXIV. The fallacies of the senses do not stand in the way of the mind's using them in knowing the truth. XXXV. No more than the errors of the intellect prohibit its use in philosophizing. XXXVI. Remedies for correcting the errors of the senses, no less than those of the intellect, are at hand. XXXVII. The fallacies of the senses, if they make these unfit for philosophizing and for the governance of life too. XXXVIII. Innate ideas of things, even if they are granted in the greatest degree, do not suffice for philosophizing without the senses. XXXIX. Although the senses belong to the whole composite, yet they are not on that account to be restricted precisely to the use of life. XL. The senses are aids to wisdom, even if those who always follow them as guides are not wise. XLI. The keenness of the senses in brutes does not at all prove that they are useless to man for philosophizing. XLII. Since God and the Angels do not need them, why does man need the senses in order to understand? XLIII. Whatever is clear to the senses is evident to the mind as such. XLIV. On the contrary, what we do not perceive by any means we understand with the greatest difficulty. XLV. An explanation and demonstration, comprised in a few theorems, of the human intellect as dependent on the senses.

units.la: I quanta humanis animis natura infinita est sciendi cupiditas, tanta quoque iisdem necessariorum ad acquirendam rerum notitiam adminiculorum copia submi-nistrata foret, simulque concessa prudentia ipsis illis, quae ad manum sunt rité utendi, nullo equidem negotio ad sapientiam grassari daretur, neque obstaret quicquam quo minus facili labore omnia, quæ hoc Universo comprehenduntur, intimè perspecta haberemus. Verum ista est mentis in hoc rerum statu imbecillitas ac conditio infelix, ut plerumque vel illi non satis opituletur hac parte natura idoneis mediis, vel si ea largita fuerit abundè, non tamen pariter addiderit peritiam eadem dextrè satis ac circumspectè applicandi ad usum. Atque indè quidem existit in mente hominis crassa ignorantia ac profunda veritatum naturalium insciitia; hinc verò multiplex ac infinitus oritur in indagando vero error. Quoties enim vel instrumentis ad sapiendum necessariò requisitis, vel genuino ac legitimo eorundem usu, destituitur intellectus scire avidus, vix potest evenire aliter, quin tanto majori impetu præceps ruat in falsitatem, quanto flagrantiori desiderio ad sciendum festinat.
units.tr: However great the infinite desire of knowing in human minds, so great also would be the abundance of the aids necessary for acquiring knowledge of things supplied to them, and, with prudence granted, the proper use of those very things that are at hand would be open to pursue wisdom with no difficulty at all; nothing would stand in the way of our having all the things comprised in this universe thoroughly understood with little labour. But such is the weakness and unhappy condition of the mind in the present state of things, that either nature does not for the most part supply it in this respect with suitable means, or, if it has bestowed them abundantly, it has not likewise added the skill to apply them rightly and carefully enough to use. Hence indeed arises in the human mind a gross ignorance and a profound unacquaintance with natural truths; hence, moreover, arises a manifold and endless error in inquiring after truth. For whenever an intellect eager to know is deprived either of the instruments necessarily required for wisdom or of their genuine and lawful use, it can hardly happen otherwise than that it rushes headlong into falsehood with the greater impetus, the more ardently it hastens to know.

units.la: Luculentum eorum quæ dixi specimen dant Sensus: quibus quo quis vel minus perfectis gaudet, vel minus prudenter novit uti, eo ferè plus reperit in veri indagine impedimenti. Atqui, quùm ut plurimùm integri satis plerisque obtingant, laborandum imprimis videtur de genuino ac recto eorundem Usu; de quo jam olim gravissimæ fuerunt agitatæ controversiæ. Speciatim (ut alia nunc taceam) disceptatum est jam olim acriter, An, & quis, Sensibus in Philosophando concedendus sit locus? Epicurei cujusvis veri & falsi judicium sic totum in Sensibus collocarunt, tantumque iis tribuerunt, ut nusquam nos per eos falli putarent; quin omnia, quæ discuntur, sensuum regulis metienda esse censerent.
units.tr: The senses give a clear example of what I have said: the less perfect the senses one has, or the less prudently one knows how to use them, the more impediments one usually finds in the search for truth. Yet since for the most part they are fairly sound in most people, the chief labour seems to lie in their genuine and correct use; and on this there were long ago very serious controversies. In particular (to pass over other matters now) it was long ago hotly disputed whether, and to what extent, the senses should be granted a place in philosophizing. The Epicureans placed the whole judgment of every truth and falsehood so entirely in the senses, and attributed so much to them, that they thought we are never deceived by them; indeed they held that everything which is learned must be measured by the rules of the senses.

units.la: Quam eorum sententiam ità exponit Lucretius: Quid referemus enim, quod nobis certius ipsis Sensibus esse queat, quo vera & falsa notentur?
units.tr: Lucretius sets out their opinion thus: For what shall we say that could be more certain than the senses themselves, by which the true and the false are marked?

units.la: Ex sensu namque omnia quae sunt credita pendent:
units.tr: For all things that are believed depend on the sense:

units.la: Cui nisi prima fides recte fundata valebit,
units.tr: And unless the first trust is rightly founded, it will have no strength,

units.la: Haud erit occultis de rebus quo referentes
units.tr: So that we could not, by reasoning from things hidden,
Confirm our minds with anything at all.

units.la: Cui opinioni eo usque indulsisse dicuntur, ut credantur hoc fundamento contendisse, solem caeterasque stellas majores non esse quam oculo apparent. Quae eadem sententia, in plerisque saltem, etiam plebeorum ferè hominum est; qui, dum usu rationis ac judicio parùm valent, vix admittunt aliud, quam quod Sensibus usurparunt, atque iis, quae sic quocunque modo percepe-runt, firmissimè onmium adhærere consueverunt. In alterum extremum abeuntes Sceptici atquè Academici, quòd aliquandò Sensus fallaces & errori obnoxios deprehendissent, eosdem, ceu testes infidos, in totum rejecerunt, omnemque omnino fidem sic iis abrogarunt, ut indè potissimum (quoniam in hoc statu unionis mens humana occasione sensationum res ferè cognoscit) natum sit ipsorum ἐποχὴν, seu assensûs de omnium rerum veritate inhibitio. Et quamvis Socrates ac Plato, ex duriorum quarundam phrasium interpretatione, fortè minus æqua, iis immerito à quibusdam accensseri videantur (majora quippe ista nomina sunt, quam ut stultæ opinioni cum aliqua veri specie prætendi possint) negandum tamen non est, ipsos justo minus Sensibus tribuisse in philosophando, iis penè neglectis, totam veri perceptionem in sola mente collocantes. Quo tendunt versus Parmenidis:
units.tr: To this opinion they are said to have yielded so far that they are believed to have contended, on this foundation, that the sun and the other stars are no larger than they appear to the eye. This same opinion is held, at least by most, almost by ordinary people as well; who, since they have little strength of reason and judgment, scarcely admit anything but what they have grasped by the senses, and are accustomed to cling most firmly to whatever they have perceived in any way at all. Going to the other extreme, the Sceptics and Academics, because they had sometimes found the senses fallacious and prone to error, rejected them altogether as untrustworthy witnesses, and so entirely withdrew all trust from them that from this above all (since in this state of union the human mind knows almost all things by occasion of sensations) arose their epochē [ἐποχὴν], that is, the suspension of assent about the truth of all things. And although Socrates and Plato, by a perhaps rather unfair interpretation of certain harsher phrases, seem to be wrongly counted among these by some (for those are names too great to be put forward for a foolish opinion with any show of truth), yet it must not be denied that they attributed too little to the senses in philosophizing, almost neglecting them, and placing the whole perception of truth in the mind alone. To this tendency belong the verses of Parmenides:

units.la: Nec tibi communis Sensus persuadeat unquamQuicquam; ut fallaces oculi, aut ut judicet auris, Aut lingua: at ratio dirimat discrimina rerum.
units.tr: Let not common sense ever persuade you of anything; nor let the eyes, which deceive, nor the ear, nor the tongue judge: but let reason decide the differences of things.

units.la: Inter istos medium tenentes Peripatetici, sic suas Menti partes in dijudicando vero & falso assignarunt, ut & Sensibus suas concesserint: afferentes, primorum quidem principiorum, aliorumque quæ nullam cum Sensibus cognationem habent, à naturali mentis lumine pendere notitiam; rerum interim singularium ac sensibilium evidentem ac certam cognitionem à Sensibus etiam petendam esse. Cui sententiæ & nos maxima ex parte subscribimus.
units.tr: Taking a middle position between these, the Peripatetics assigned the mind its own share in judging truth and falsehood, but they also granted the senses theirs. They held that knowledge of the first principles, and of other things that have no connection with the senses, depends on the natural light of the mind, while the clear and certain knowledge of particular and sensible things is to be sought from the senses as well. We agree with this view for the most part.

units.la: Opinionem quod attinet, & Epicureorum fatuissimam, & Scepticorum perniciosissimam, haud operæ pretium videtur multis eam refellere, quoniam tam manifestè illi experientia multiplex & quotidiana, huic ipsa uniuscujusque conscientia reclamat, ut quisquis evidentissimâ illâ certitudine non fuerit convictus, sperari haud debeat ullis rationibus convinci posse quantumvis validis: conscientiam enim, testem quàvis ratione efficaciorem, ejurasse atque exuisse talis censendus est. Etiam toties ista deliria absurditatis convicta sunt solidissimè à quam plurimis & doctissimis veræ ac certæ sapientiæ assertoribus ac vindicibus, ut refodiendi non videantur errores jam dudum sepulti; quandò itâ quibusvis hodiè sordent istæ ineptiæ, ut vix reperiatur, qui prorsùs cum istis Philosophis (si Philosophi appellandi sint isti omnis Philosophiæ gegenuinæ eversores ac hostes deterrimi) sentiat, saltem se sentire profiteri ausit. Quam ob causam maluerunt deinceps quidam crudam sententiam nonnihil interpolare, atque aliam illi speciem induere, si quo forte modo nova ei gratia conciliari posset.
units.tr: As for the opinion of the Epicureans, which is most foolish, and that of the Sceptics, which is most pernicious, it seems not worth the effort to refute them at length. Manifold and daily experience cries out against the one, and each person's own consciousness against the other, so plainly that anyone who has not been convinced by that most evident certainty should not be expected to be convinced by any arguments, however strong. Consciousness is a witness more effective than any argument, and whoever rejects and casts it off must be judged to have done so. Moreover, these delusions have been refuted so thoroughly and so often as absurd by very many learned defenders and champions of true and certain wisdom that the errors, long since buried, hardly seem to need digging up. Today these follies are so despised by everyone that one can scarcely find anyone who would dare to profess that he agrees, even in part, with those philosophers (if they are to be called philosophers, who are the overthrowers and most bitter enemies of all genuine philosophy). For this reason, some have preferred since then to tamper somewhat with the crude opinion and to give it another appearance, in case in some way it might thereby win new favour.

units.la: In talium, si non Scepticorum, saltem quodammodo Scepti zantium, album multi doctissimi viri non semel, ægrè licet ferentem, retulerunt jam olim Renatum Cartesium; autumantes, tam parum ejus methodum philosophandi abesse à Scepticorum castris, ut istuc per se tendere videatur, ac viam sternere, si non necessariam, facillimam saltem ac maximè pronam. Quo jure, quâ injuriâ tales censores expertus sit Nobilis Auctor? non hîc dicam; qui prudentioribus id ex sequentibus judicandum relinquere malo. Quicquid ejus sit, displicent vehementer Viri de sensibilibus omnibus (alia, quæ pari in sensu ei habentur, huc minus pertinent) dubitationes illæ, quibus in ipso philosophiæ suæ limine tantum indulget, ut facilè supponat, genium aliquem malignum summè potentem & callidum omnem industriam in eo ponere, ut ipsum fallat: sic quidem ut det, cœlum, terram, cunctaque externa nihil esse aliud quam ludificationes; seque ipsum consideret, tanquam manus non habentem, non oculos, non carnem, non aliquem sensum, sed hæc omnia se habere, falsò opinantem. Displicent, inquam, ista vel ideò, quod, si ea Sceptico largiamur, necessariò supponatur ac sequatur, Sensuum nullum esse in philosophando usum; quo asserto nimium Scepticis herbam porrigi judicamus.
units.tr: Many very learned men have long since, and more than once, counted among such people, if not Sceptics, then at least men who somewhat play the Sceptic, the reluctant Renatus Descartes, though he took it badly. They thought that his method of philosophizing was so little removed from the camp of the Sceptics that it seemed to tend that way by itself and to pave the road, if not a necessary one, at least a very easy and most inclined one. By what right, or with what injustice, such critics have assailed the noble author I will not say here; I prefer to leave that to the more prudent to judge from what follows. Whatever the case, those doubts about all sensible things (other matters, which are held in the same sense, pertain less to this) displease me greatly, the doubts in which he indulges so much at the very threshold of his philosophy that he readily supposes some malignant genius of the highest power and cunning who devotes all his effort to deceiving him, so that heaven, earth and all external things are nothing but illusions; and he considers himself as one who has no hands, no eyes, no flesh, no sense at all, but who falsely thinks that he has all these. These things displease me, I say, for this reason above all: if we grant them to the Sceptic, it must necessarily be supposed and follow that the senses have no use at all in philosophizing; and with this assertion we judge that far too much is handed to the Sceptics.

units.la: Asserit hoc nihilominus totidem verbis Cartesius. Tam est difficile medium tenere! Præconceptas ab infantia erroneas opiniones, ex fallaci Sensuum dictamine majori ex parte oriundas, feliciter philosophaturo abdicandas esse, merito inculcaverat; Sensuque omnes non semper fidos esse testes rectè demonstraverat vulgari experientia turris, cominus quadratæ, eminus conspectæ rotundæ. Si, quod indè sequebatur, conclusisset, semper & ubique in indiganda rei veritate unicè quibusvis Sensationibus standum non esse, sed adhibendam, in discernendis iis veris à fallacibus, debitam prudentiam; si, inquam, sic conclusisset, neque universam Sensuum in sapiendo fidem unâ litura delevisset, promiscuè eam omnem annumerando infantiæ præjudiciis, tam sibi feliciter cavisset à tristi Scepticismi periculo, quam ab Epicureismo totus rectè recessérat, neque adeò, quod ajunt, dum vitabat scyllam, in charybdin incidisset. Nunc verò perperam infert (ut alibi sæpius ita hic quoque Platonem nimium secutus) in philosophando sic unicè attendendum esse ad ideas omnium rerum unicuique innatas, ut Sensus habeantur insuper; quippe quorum genuinus usus non alius sit, quam in moderanda hac vita; adeò ut, si ad veritatis contemplationem Sensationes nostras extenderimus, merus sit iste futurus earundem abusus.
units.tr: Descartes nevertheless asserts this in so many words. So difficult it is to keep the middle way! He had rightly urged that the erroneous opinions conceived from infancy, arising for the most part from the deceptive judgment of the senses, must be renounced by one who is to philosophize successfully; and he had rightly shown by common experience that the senses are not always faithful witnesses, as a tower that is square when seen near at hand appears round from afar. If he had concluded from this, as it followed, that in seeking the truth of a thing one must not always and everywhere rely solely on any sensations, but must apply due prudence in distinguishing true from false ones; if, I say, he had concluded so, and had not, by one stroke, wiped out all trust in the senses in wisdom, counting them all indiscriminately among the prejudices of infancy, he would have guarded himself as happily against the sad danger of Scepticism as he had rightly withdrawn entirely from Epicureanism, and he would not, as the saying goes, have fallen into Charybdis while avoiding Scylla. But now he wrongly infers (having, as often elsewhere, followed Plato too closely here as well) that in philosophizing one must attend only to the ideas of all things innate in each person, and that the senses must be held in addition, since their genuine use is nothing but governing this life; so that if we extend our sensations to the contemplation of truth, the result will be nothing but their pure abuse.

units.la: Sed ne, quod solent, conquerantur ejus affectæ, minus rectè nos mentem ejus vel capere, vel proponere, ipsum se explicantem audiamus! Princip. Part. II. Art. III. hunc in modum disserit. „Satis erit, si advertamus, sensuum perceptiones non referri, nisi „ad istam corporis humani cum mente conjunctionem, & nobis „quidem ordinarie exhibere, quid ad illam externa corpora pro-„desse possint, aut nocere; non autem, nisi interdum & ex acci-„denti, nos docere, qualia in se ipsis existant. Ita enim sensuum „præjudicia facile deponemus, & solo intellectu, ad ideas sibi à „natura inditas diligenter attendente, hic utemur. Atque ibidem in lemmate marginali: „Sensuum perceptiones, non quid „revera sit in rebus; sed quid humano composito prosit vel obsit „docere. Hisce parallela occurrunt, Medit. VI. p. 42. „Natu„ra docet quidem ea refugere, quæ sensum doloris inferunt, & „ea prosequi quæ sensum voluptatis, & talia: sed non apparet il„lam præterea nos docere ut quicquam ex istis sensuum perceptio„nibus, sine prævio intellectus examine, de rebus extra nos positis „concludamus, quia de iis verum scire ad mentem solam, non au-„tem ad compositum videtur pertinere. Ac porrò post pauca, „Sed video me in his aliisque permultis ordinem naturæ pervertere „esse assuetum, quia nempe sensuum perceptionibus (quæ proprie „tantum à natura datæ sunt, ad menti significandum, quanam „composito, cujus pars est, commoda sint vel incommoda, & cate„nus sunt satis clarè & distinctè) utor tanquam regulis certis, ad „immediatè dignoscendum, quænam sit corporum extra nos posi-„torum essentia, de qua tamen nihil, nisi valde obscurè & consu-„sè, significant.
units.tr: But lest his followers complain, as they usually do, that we do not rightly grasp or set forth his mind, let us hear him explaining himself. In Principles, Part II, Article III, he discourses in this manner: "It will be enough if we notice that the perceptions of the senses are referred only to that union of the human body with the mind, and ordinarily show us what external bodies can benefit or harm that union; but not, except sometimes and by accident, teach us what they are like in themselves. Thus we shall easily lay aside the prejudices of the senses, and we shall use the intellect alone, attending carefully to the ideas implanted in us by nature." And in the marginal heading of the same place: "The perceptions of the senses do not teach what is really in things, but what is useful or harmful to the human composite." Parallel to these occur the words of Meditation VI, p. 42: "Nature indeed teaches us to shun those things that cause a sensation of pain and to pursue those that cause a sensation of pleasure, and so on; but it does not appear that it teaches us further to conclude anything from these perceptions of the senses, without a prior examination by the intellect, about things situated outside us, because to know the truth about them seems to pertain to the mind alone, not to the composite." And soon after: "But I see that I am accustomed to pervert the order of nature in these and very many other matters, because I use the perceptions of the senses (which are properly only given by nature to signify to the mind what is useful or harmful to the composite of which it is a part, and which are sufficiently clear and distinct in that respect) as if they were certain rules, for immediately discerning what is the essence of bodies situated outside us, of which, however, they signify nothing except very obscurely and confusedly."

units.la: Quem textum hoc modo interpretatur, qui fidus habetur præ aliis Cartesii Paraphraftes, Claubergius, Lell. ix. §. 172. „Sed non video hanc naturam nos insuper docere, ut ex istis sen-suum externorum perceptionibus, sine prævio maturæ rationis examine, de rebus extra nos constitutis certi aliquid concludamus: quoniam veri investigatio ac scientia ad solum animum nostrum, non autem ad totum hominem, quatenus animo & corpore constat, videtur pertinere. Ac porrò, §. 177. & seqq. „Sed animadverto, nos in his modo commemoratis, aliisque id genus plurimis in rebus, solere vires à Deo nobis datas in alium usum convertere, quam datas esse cognoscimus; quod est naturæ ordinem pervertere. Nam istæ sensuum perceptiones quia ad totum compositum spectant, concessæ utique nobis non fuerunt alià de causâ, quam ut indicarent animo, quænam res conveniant aut noceant toti composito, cujus ipsa pars existit. Atque in eum usum si referantur, claræ satis ac distinctæ sunt, adeo ut vitæ totius animalis regimen ab iis pendeat, &c. Hic sensuum genuinus usus cum sit, nos iis utimur tanquam puræ veritatis magistris, quasi regulas nobis certas suppeditarent, quarum beneficio, absque ulla longiore rationis deliberatione, dijudicare liceat, quæ sit rerum extra nos positarum natura atque inhærentes proprietates, de quibus tamen nihil, nisi confusè & obscurè admodum, ipsi queunt docere. Quod dum facimus, quis non videt nos naturæ ordinem sapientissimum perverrere?
units.tr: Claubergius, who is considered the most faithful of Descartes' paraphrasts, interprets this text in the following way, in Lesson IX, §172: "But I do not see that nature teaches us in addition to conclude anything certain about things existing outside us from these perceptions of the external senses without a prior examination by mature reason, since the investigation and knowledge of truth seem to pertain to the mind alone, not to the whole man, insofar as he consists of mind and body. And further, §177 and following: "But I notice that in these matters just mentioned, and in very many others of that kind, we are accustomed to turn the powers given us by God to a use other than that for which we know they were given; and this is to pervert the order of nature. For these perceptions of the senses, since they regard the whole composite, were certainly not granted to us for any other reason than to indicate to the mind what things are suitable or harmful to the whole composite of which it is itself a part. And if they are referred to that use, they are clear and distinct enough, so much so that the governing of the whole life of the animal depends on them," etc. Since this is the genuine use of the senses, we use them as though they were teachers of pure truth, as if they supplied us with certain rules, by the benefit of which it is possible to judge, without any longer deliberation of reason, what is the nature of things situated outside us and their inherent properties, about which, however, they can teach us nothing except very confusedly and obscurely. In doing this, who does not see that we pervert the most wise order of nature?

units.la: Immixta sunt, fateor, his Locis verba nonnulla, quæ emolliendæ thesi inservire primo intuitu videri possunt; qualia sunt illa, absque ulla longiore rationis deliberatione, pro quo dixerat Cartesius, sine prævio intellectus examine, sive immediatè; &c. Atqui minimè tollendæ hic difficultati ea sufficere, vel ex ipso constat Cartesio. Quis enim eorum qui posterioribus hisce seculis Philosophi esse voluerunt, asseruit unquam, sic certas regulas sapiendi nobis suppeditare Sensus, ut rationis deliberatione opus non sit? Quis extitit quin imò eorum, qui non iterùm iterùmque inculcaverit, circumspectè attendendum semper esse ad Sensus Objectum, Medium, Organum; nec quicquam de re sensibili judicandum, nisi post mentis examen plenè constet de eorundem integritate? Estne id immediatè, sine prævio intellectus examine, secundum Sensum judicare? Licet verò ista ignorare non potuerit Cartesius, carpit nihilominus omnes qui ante se extiterunt, quique fidem prorsus sensibus adhibue-runt, quod error eorum quidem emendatus fuerit aliquantulum, ubi Sensus in quamplurimis nos fallere agnoverunt (qui autem agnoverunt, nisi praevio intellectus examine?) sed radicitus sublatus non fuerit; ostendendo videlicet, non Sensibus, sed intelle-ctui soli, res distincte percipienti, rectitudinem inesse. Adeo quidem ut hoc imprimis fundamento, incredibili cum confidentia perstringere non dubitet omnes, qui ab antiqua Philosophia initium fecerunt, quod quo plus in ea desudarunt, tanto soleant ad veram percipiendam esse ineptiores. In Epist. Principiis prefixa. Ne addam, ne quidem de rebus extra nos positis, in ordine ad totum compositum cui prosint aut nocent quicquam ex Sensuum perceptionibus concludendum esse, sine praevio intellectus examine: nisi probanda sit infantium imprudens praecipitantia, ex hoc solo, quod res oculis arridet, acutum cultrum, flammam, aliaque noxia avide apprehendentium. Unde manifestum est, frustra, & tantum ad colorem obducendum regulae, de Sensibus in dignoscendo vero non fidendo, addi istud de praevio intellectus examine; vel ut Claubergius explicat, longiore rationis deliberatione.
units.tr: I admit that a few words have been slipped into these passages which might seem, at first glance, to serve to soften the thesis: phrases such as without any lengthy deliberation of reason, which Descartes rendered as without prior examination by the intellect, or immediately, and so on. But that these words are enough to remove the difficulty is clear from Descartes himself. Who among those who wished to be philosophers in these later centuries ever asserted that the senses supply us with such certain rules for judging that deliberation of reason is unnecessary? Who, indeed, has not again and again urged that one must always attend carefully to the object, the medium and the organ of sense, and that nothing should be judged about a sensible thing until the mind has examined and fully established the soundness of these? Is it to judge by the senses immediately, without prior examination by the intellect? Although Descartes cannot have been ignorant of this, he nonetheless attacks all who came before him, who placed complete faith in the senses, on the ground that their error was corrected to some extent, since they recognised that the senses deceive us in very many cases (but who recognised this, if not by prior examination by the intellect?), yet that it was not removed at the root. He shows, namely, that rectitude lies not in the senses, but in the intellect alone, which perceives things distinctly. So confidently, indeed, does he rest upon this foundation that he does not hesitate to censure all who began from ancient philosophy, saying that the more they laboured at it, the more unfit they usually became for grasping the truth. In the Epistle prefixed to the Principles. Not to add that nothing can be concluded, without prior examination by the intellect, from the perceptions of the senses about things outside us, in relation to the whole composite to which they are beneficial or harmful; unless one is to approve the rash haste of infants, who eagerly seize a sharp knife, a flame, and other harmful things merely because the thing pleases their eyes. Hence it is plain that the rule about not trusting the senses in discerning truth, and the addition of prior examination by the intellect, or, as Clauberg explains it, lengthy deliberation of reason, are vainly added, and only to colour the matter.

units.la: Ut genuina Neotericorum de Sensuum Usu sententia sit, hos non alio fine ac scopo nobis esse concessos, quam ad hoc unum, ut, cum brutis animantibus, per eos discernamus objecta quae nos tanquam prosequenda si sint utilia, tanquam evitanda si sint noci-tura, discernere ipsa naturae necessitas, ad vitae animalis conser-vationem, cogit. Tantum vero abesse, ut sensationes extendere quoque debeamus ad examinandam earum ope ipsam rerum extra nos positarum veritatem, ut potius is sit purus earundem abusus, ac sapientissimi naturae ordinis perversio, ut imprudens, ita erroris foecundissima mater. Atque istis convenienter doctorum conflictui alibi publicatam vidimus hanc thesin, uncialibus literis, nequid haereat scrupuli, sic expressam. Philosophi Scholastici &c. non tam sapius hallucinantur quam semel: neque enim Sensibus desinunt fidere, quorum natura est, NUNQUAM NON FALLERE ET SEMPER ERRARE. Nam ne oculos semel aperire, manus extendere, os diducere & contrahere, &c. quimus, quin innumerabilium errorum exercitus ac integra plaustra iis se insinuent. Ut nec dici possit, infallibilem sensum, qui nec menti imponat, nec foris circum-veniatur, veniatur, dari. Hinc intellectui cum sensibus, quos in certis tenemur jurare, lucta ἀφϑαρτὰ[?] & sempiterna est: Cujus ARBITRUM VERE SAPIENTEM, ΣΟΦΟΝ ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΟΝ, dicimus. Ipse Pyrrho, si ad nos redeat redivivus, dubito, mentem suam exprimere an possit efficacius, an ausit clarius?
units.tr: For the genuine view of the moderns on the use of the senses to be this: that they have been granted to us for no other end or purpose than this one, that, along with the brute animals, we discern through them the objects which we are compelled by nature's necessity to pursue as useful, or to avoid as harmful, for the preservation of animal life. Yet we ought so little to extend our sensations to examining, by their means, the very truth of things outside us, that this would rather be a pure abuse of them and a perversion of nature's most wise order, and, as imprudence, so the most fruitful mother of error. And in keeping with this, we have seen this thesis, in capital letters, lest any scruple should cling, set forth elsewhere in print in the conflict of the learned, thus: The Scholastic philosophers, etc., are not deceived so often as once: for they do not cease to trust the senses, whose nature is NEVER NOT TO DECEIVE AND ALWAYS TO ERR. For we cannot even open our eyes once, stretch out our hands, open and close our mouths, etc., without innumerable armies of errors and whole wagonloads of them creeping in upon us. So that it cannot be said that there is an infallible sense, which neither deceives the mind nor is cheated from outside. Hence there is an unending and everlasting struggle between the intellect and the senses, which we are bound to swear by in certain matters. We call the arbiter of this struggle truly wise, a wise philosopher [ΣΟΦΟΝ ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΟΝ]. If Pyrrho himself were to return to us from the dead, I doubt whether he could express his own mind more effectively, or dare to do so more plainly.

units.la: Has nos assertiones, aliasque his affines atque ex his ortas, prorsùs rejicimus ac in totum repudiamus, tanquam salsissimas non tantum, sed & periculosissimas, quin tales, quae per se comparatae sunt, ad omnem rerum sensibilium certam ac indubitatam notitiam omninò evertendam ac penitus exstirpandam, ac genuinam Scepticorum de sensibilibus ἐποχὴ iterùm inducendam. Non quidem negamus, salutare animalis vitae moderamen itā in solidum à Sensuum directione pendere, ut absque ea nullâ ratione consistere queat (quamobrem quoque hactenus brutis perǣquè ac hominibus eorundem usum à natura concessum esse videmus; de quo deinceps plura): non tamen istā vitae gubernatione Sensus in homine omni suo munere defungi autumamus, sed & nobiliori eos fini destinatos esse asserimus; statuimusque, cum demum rectum ac genuinum esse Sensuum in homine usum, quando mens eos legitimo modo (quis iste sit? exponemus infrà) adhibet tanquam organa à Deo sibi concessa, non tantùm ad percipienda ea, quae toti composito commoda sint aut incommoda, quà talia; sed imprimis quoque ad indagandam rerum extra nos positarum certam veritatem, cùm earum quae sub sensum directè cadunt, tum aliarum per se insensibilium, quibus cognoscendis, interveniente rationis discursu, sensationes praebent saltem occasionem. Verbo, Sensus non tantum ad vivendum, sed & ad sapiendum, nobis à Deo esse indultos.
units.tr: We utterly reject these assertions, and others akin to them and arising from them, and repudiate them entirely, as not only most absurd but also most dangerous, indeed such as, of their own nature, tend to overthrow altogether every certain and indubitable knowledge of sensible things, and to root it out completely, and to bring back once more the genuine epochē [ἐποχὴ] of the Sceptics about sensible things. We do not, indeed, deny that the wholesome guidance of animal life depends so entirely on the direction of the senses that it cannot subsist on any rational basis without them (for which reason we see that the brute animals as well as men have been granted their use by nature, of which more later). Yet we do not hold that in man the senses discharge their whole office by this guidance of life; we affirm that they are destined for a nobler end as well. And we maintain that the senses are rightly and genuinely used by man when the mind employs them in a lawful way (what this way is we shall explain below), as organs granted to it by God, not only for perceiving those things which are beneficial or harmful to the whole composite as such, but above all also for investigating the certain truth of things outside us, both of those which fall directly under the senses and of others which are in themselves insensible, and to know which the sensations provide at least the occasion, through the intervention of the reasoning of the mind. In a word, the senses have been granted to us by God not only for living but also for knowing wisely.

units.la: Miror verò vehementer (ut id praemittam, priusquam ad ipsa rationum momenta excutienda accedo) miror, inquam, qui tam confidenter ausit determinare Cartesius, Sensuum perceptiones tantum datas esse a Natura (quo nomine Deum intelligi, manifestum est) ad menti significandum, quaenam composito commoda sint vel incommoda; cùm hac assertione in utramque regulam, quam, ut rectè philosophemur, imprimis observandam inculcat, Princip. III. Art. I. II. tam incurrat directè, ut non possit magis. Prima est, Ut attendentes ad infinitam Dei potentiam & benitatem, ne vereamur nimis ampla, & pulchra, & absoluta ejus opera imaginari. At, cum Sensationum Usum tantum ad vitæ hujus regimen restringis, nonne vereris nimis ampla, & pulchra, & absoluta opera Dei imaginari? Quidni potius Sensus eorumque Usum tam amplum, pulchrum, absolutum, tibi imaginaris quam potes, ne forte minus magnificè de Creatoris potentia sentire videaris? prout hoc argumento compulsus imaginaris tibi mundum, nullos extensionis suæ fines habentem. Imprimis autem non hic limitanda videbantur opera Dei, cum non repugnet, plurima rerum corporearum attributa à Sensu nostro menti offerri prout in se sunt: unde hactenus saltem hunc idoneum esse posse, non tantum ad discernenda noxia ab utilibus, sed & ad dignoscendas ipsas quarundam rerum veritates, juxta hanc regulam, in præjudicium absolutæ divini operis amplitudinis, negandum non videtur. Frigidas quasdam allatas hùc ratiunculas quod attinet, eas suo loco diluemus.
units.tr: But I am greatly surprised (to premise this before I come to examine the arguments themselves) that Descartes should have ventured so confidently to determine that the perceptions of the senses are only given by Nature (by which name it is plain that God is meant) to signify to the mind which things are beneficial or harmful to the composite; since this assertion runs directly against both rules which he urges us above all to observe if we are to philosophise rightly, Principles III, Articles I and II, and runs against them as directly as possible. The first is: Attending to the infinite power and goodness of God, we should not fear to imagine his works as very ample, beautiful and perfect. But when you restrict the use of sensations only to the governing of this life, do you not fear to imagine the works of God as too ample, beautiful and perfect? Why not rather imagine the senses and their use as ample, beautiful and perfect as you can, lest perhaps you seem to think less magnificently of the power of the Creator? Thus, compelled by this argument, you imagine a world having no limits to its extension. Above all, the works of God did not seem to be limited here, since there is nothing contradictory in the view that very many attributes of corporeal things are presented to our mind by our sense as they are in themselves. Hence it does not seem that one can deny, to the prejudice of the absolute amplitude of the divine work, that the sense is at least thus far suited not only to discerning the harmful from the useful but also to knowing the truths of certain things themselves, according to this rule. As for the cold little arguments brought forward here, we shall refute them in their proper place.
XIII.

units.la: Alter canon, quem, ad rectè philosophandum, præscribit Auctor, est, Ut etiam caveamus, ne nimis superbè de nobis ipsis sentiamus; quod fieret maximè, si fines quos sibi Deus propositum in creando Universo, ingenii nostri vi comprehendi posse putaremus. Quodque hic de toto Mundo asserit, idem alibi extendit ad quævis hoc Universo comprehensa. Itâ enim Princip. I. Art. XXVIII. ait, Causas finales rerum non esse examinandas, quia non tantum nobis debemus arrogare, ut ejus (Dei) consiliorum participes esse putemus. Atque iterum in Respons. ad Gassendum, diserte affirmat, Par non esse, quo fine Deus quidque fecerit divinare; Considerare quem finem Deus sibi in regendo Universo propositum fuerit, in Physicis esse ineptum; Nec fingi posse, aliquos Dei fines, magis quam alios, in propatulo esse, cum omnes in imperscrutabili ejus sapientiæ abysso sint eodem modo recondit. Quam istæc omnia sint falsa, hoc loco demonstrare nil attinet. Præstitit id fusè Cartesianarum Meditationum Triumphator Gassendus, Disquisit. sue Metaphys. p. 201. & seqq. At nunc demus ea esse verissima! Si sic, quid ergò tam audes de te ipso sentire superbè, ut non divinare tantum præsumas, sed & rotundè pronunciare, Sensuum perceptiones (quæ res procul dubio physica est) à Natura tantum datas esse, hoc fine, ut significent menti, quænam homo ceu com-
units.tr: The second canon which the Author prescribes for philosophising rightly is this: that we also take care not to think too highly of ourselves; which would especially happen if we thought we could grasp with the power of our intellect the ends God proposed to himself in creating the Universe. What he asserts here of the whole world he elsewhere extends to everything contained in this Universe. Thus in Principles I, Article XXVIII, he says that the final causes of things are not to be examined, because we must not presume so much as to think ourselves sharers in his (God's) counsels. And again, in the Reply to Gassendi, he plainly affirms that it is not fitting to divine for what end God did anything; to consider what end God proposed to himself in governing the Universe is foolish in physics; nor can it be imagined that some of God's ends are more open to us than others, since all of them are hidden in the unsearchable abyss of his wisdom in the same way. That all these statements are false there is no need to show here. The Triumphator over the Cartesian Meditations, Gassendi, has done this at length, Disquisitio Metaphysica, p. 201 and following. But now let us grant that they are most true! If so, why do you dare to think so highly of yourself that you not only presume to divine, but also roundly pronounce that the perceptions of the senses (which is undoubtedly a physical matter) are given by Nature only for this purpose, that they should signify to the mind what a man, as a composite, ought to

units.la: XIII. Item in aliam, quâ de rerum naturalium fine definire quicquam prohibet. compósito incommoda refugere, ceu commoda prosequi debeat?
units.tr: XIII. Also to another [canon], which forbids us to define anything about the end of natural things, to shun the inconveniences of the composite and to pursue its conveniences?

units.la: Quod nisi nefas quoque sit inquirere in fines, ob quos, etiam contra regulas quas ipse ad rectè philosophandum praescribit, tam diligenter inculcare voluerit Cartesius, sic solius intellectûs esse verum indagare, ut nullo modo pertineat ad Sensum, operæ pretium videtur diligentius eos examinare, cum haud leve id sit allaturum ad intelligentiam sequentium momentum. Est verò ad Novæ Philosophiæ tum fundamenta tum methodum penficulatius attendenti non valdè difficile de assertionis hujus scopo divinare, conjecturâ etiam plus quam conjecturali. Nempè, ante omnia id sollicitè agendum erat, ut in tuto foret præcipuus hujus Philosophiæ thesaurus, innatæ illæ menti, à primo ejus ortu, omnium rerum ideæ. Neque enim absque earum apparatu salvari potest Nova Sapientia, imprimis Metaphysica, ubi omnis summa eorum, quæ in ea observanda præcipiuntur, huc unicè redit, ut, depositis præjudiciis, ordine attendamus ad notiones quas ipsimet habemus in nobis; ex quibus claris & distinctis facile deducemus, citra ulla alia adminicula, exîstentiam & mentis nostræ cogitantis, & Dei cæterarum rerum causæ, & propositionum æternæ veritatis, & naturæ corporeæ, & Sensuum nos assicientium. Princip. 1. Artic. penult. At verò periculum non leve imminebat istis notionibus ingenitis, tanquam supellectili otiosæ, si scientiam rerum etiam per Sensationes acquiri posse, admitteretur. Quùm ergò quantum Sensibus eorumque perceptioni in cognitione veri tribuitur, tantum decedat Cartesianis ideis, ad has, & quæ ab his pendet Novam methodum totam salvandam, necessarium erat prorsus Sensuum in Philosophando adjumentum removere, nullumque eis alium in homine relinquere Usum, quam quem habent in brutis, uti ratione, sic ideis istis, destitutis.
units.tr: But unless it is also wrong to inquire into the ends for which Descartes wished so carefully to impress upon us, even against the rules he himself prescribes for philosophising rightly, that the investigation of truth belongs to the intellect alone and in no way pertains to the senses, it seems worth examining these ends more carefully, since this will contribute no small weight to understanding what follows. Indeed, for anyone who attends closely to the foundations and the method of the New Philosophy, it is not very difficult to guess the aim of this assertion, even by more than mere conjecture. Clearly, above all, care had to be taken that the chief treasure of this Philosophy would be safe: the ideas of all things, innate in the mind from its first origin. For the New Wisdom, and above all its Metaphysics, cannot be saved without the equipment of these ideas, since the whole sum of what it prescribes to be observed comes down to this alone: that, having put aside prejudices, we attend in order to the notions which we have within ourselves; from these, clear and distinct, we will easily deduce, without any other aids, the existence of our thinking mind, of God as the cause of other things, of the propositions of eternal truth, of corporeal nature, and of the senses that affect us. Principles I, penultimate Article. But a serious danger threatened these innate notions, as if they were idle furniture, if it were admitted that knowledge of things can also be acquired through sensations. Since, therefore, as much is taken from the Cartesian ideas as is granted to the senses and their perception in the knowledge of truth, it was absolutely necessary, in order to save the whole New Method and the things that depend on these ideas, to remove the aid of the senses from philosophising, and to leave them no other use in man than that which they have in brutes, the reason being removed, and these ideas along with it.
XV.

units.la: At neque minor necessitas erat in Recentiori Physica, ob quam mens à Sensibus abducenda videbatur. Ea quippe imprimis in summo versabatur discrimine, si examini Sensuum subjecta fuisset. Scilicet, haud erat exiguum quod Cartesius moliebatur opus. Animus erat lectoribus depingere Universum, quod sit infinita ingentium ac innumerabilium vorticum compages; in qua dominentur elementa invisibilia, materia subtilis, particulæ striatæ, globuli ætherei, quæque indè fluunt id genus fexcenta. Machinam ejusmodi idealem & in mente confictam pro vero Mundi systemate difficulter obtrudi posse hominibus sanâ mente per integros sensus utentibus, facile ei erat prævidere; ut qui ignorare non poterat, defuturos nequaquam, qui, obstupescentes ad tam longam figmentorum catenam, non sine causa urgerent idem, quod quondam Leucippo objiciebat Lactantius, disputans contra Epicureos, Lib. de Ira Dei, Cap. x. Minuta illa femina, inquit, quorum concursu fortuito totum coisse mundum loquuntur, ubi aut unde sint? quæro. Quis illa vidit unquam? quis sensit? quis audivit? An solus Leucippus oculos habuit? solus mentem? qui profecto solus omnium cæcus & excors fuit, qui ea loqueretur, quæ nec æger quisquam delirare, nec dormiens posset somniare. Quatuor elementis constare omnia Philosophi veteres asserebant: ille noluit, ne alienis vestigiis videretur insistere; sed ipsorum elementorum alia voluit esse primordia, quae nec videri possint nec tangi, nec ulla corporis parte sentiri. Exauctorandi ergo erant in ipso Novae Physicae limine Sensus, eorumque in Philosophando Usus: sic enim difficultates hic moturis promptum erat os obturare, increpando eos ceu crassos ac sensuales nimium Philosophos, qui imperiti sapientissimum naturae ordinem pervertant, dum Sensationes ultra vitae regimen extendunt ad veritates etiam Philosophicas, in quibus cognoscendis solo intellectu, non Sensibus sit utendum. Nempe, facile nigrum pro albo obtrudes alicui, si semel id impetraveris, ut oculos sibi effodi patiatur: neque unquam tutius fingitur, quam cum media, quibus solis res detegi poterat, furripiuntur. Rursus nequeo praeterire literatissimum, ex quo modo quaedam allegavi, Lactantium, in casu non multum absimili, pro Socrate contra Dogmaticos, sic differentem, Lib. 11. De Falsa Sapientia, Cap. 111. Age, opinemur, quid nunc in foro geratur, quid in curia? Longum est id quoque, dicamus, interposito uno pariete quid fiat? Nemo potest id scire, nisi qui audiverit, aut viderit. Nullus nimirum audet id dicere: quia statim, non verbis, sed re ipsa praesenti refutabitur. Atqui hoc idem faciunt Philosophi, qui disputant in coelo quid agatur? Sed eo se id impune facere arbitrantur, quia nullus exstitit, qui errores eorum coarguat. Quod si existimarent defensurum esse aliquem, qui eos delirare ac mentiri doceret, ceret, nunquam quicquam de iis rebus, quas scire non possunt, disputarent. Nec tamen ideo felicior putanda est eorum impudentia & audacia, quia non redarguuntur, &c. Itaque minime horum ignarus Cartesius (absolvam haec verbis doctissimi If. Voßii, disputantis contra ipsum, de Natura Lucis) in ea praecipuè callidus fuit, quod cum a paucis postulatis & communibus valde notionibus Philosophiam suam auspicatus sit, in progressu tamen operis nemo plura assumsit, & quidem talia, quae nec ab ipso demonstrata sint, nec demonstrari a quoquam possint, etiamsi vim intellectui inferamus: quodque, cum tam plana & perspicua praemittat principia, mox tamen iis relictis alia promat, quae neque visu neque sensu percipi possunt, globulos scilicet, particulas striatas, & elementa invisibilia. Illis positis, non probatis, incipit Philosophari; Quia nempe ubi oculi & sensus deficiunt, illic fingendi incipit libertas.
units.tr: But there was no less necessity in the more recent Physics, for which the mind seemed to have to be drawn away from the senses. For that system was above all in the greatest danger if it were subjected to the examination of the senses. Certainly, what Descartes was undertaking was no small task. His purpose was to depict for his readers a Universe which is an infinite structure of countless huge vortices, in which invisible elements rule: subtle matter, striated particles, ethereal globules, and the countless other things that flow from these. It was easy for him to foresee that such an ideal machine, invented in the mind, could hardly be forced upon men who use their senses soundly as the true system of the world; since he could not be unaware that there would be no lack of those who, astonished at so long a chain of fictions, would not without reason press the same objection that Lactantius once raised against Leucippus, disputing against the Epicureans: De Ira Dei, chapter 10. Where, he says, and whence are those tiny seeds, by whose fortuitous concourse they say the whole world came together? I ask. Who ever saw them? Who felt them? Who heard them? Did Leucippus alone have eyes? Alone a mind? He was surely the only one of all men who was blind and senseless, to speak of things which no sick man could rave about, nor a sleeping man dream. The ancient philosophers asserted that all things consist of four elements; he refused, lest he seem to tread in others' footprints, but he wished the primordia of the elements themselves to be other things, which can neither be seen nor touched, nor perceived by any part of the body. The senses and their use in philosophising therefore had to be struck off right at the threshold of the New Physics: for in this way it was ready to stop the mouths of those who would raise difficulties, by scolding them as gross and excessively sensual philosophers, who, being unskilled, pervert the most wise order of nature while they extend sensations beyond the government of life to philosophical truths as well, in the knowing of which one must use the intellect alone, not the senses. Indeed, you could easily pass off black as white to someone, once you had obtained that he would allow his eyes to be put out: and nothing is ever more safely invented than when the means by which alone things could be discovered are snatched away. Again, I cannot pass over that most learned Lactantius, from whom I have quoted some of these things, who, in a case not very dissimilar, argued on behalf of Socrates against the Dogmatists in this way: On False Wisdom, Book 11, chapter 3. Come, let us suppose, what is now going on in the forum, what in the senate house? It is long to ask, let us say, what is happening behind one wall? No one can know this except one who has heard or seen. Surely no one dares to say it, because he would at once be refuted, not by words but by the present fact itself. Yet the Philosophers who dispute what is going on in heaven do the same thing. But they think they do it with impunity, because no one has arisen to convict their errors. But if they thought someone would defend the cause and teach that they rave and lie, they would never dispute about those things which they cannot know. Nor, however, should their shamelessness and audacity be thought the happier because they are not refuted, etc. And so Descartes, by no means ignorant of these things (I shall finish with the words of the most learned Is. Vossius, disputing against him, On the Nature of Light), was especially clever in this respect: that, although he began his Philosophy from a few postulates and very common notions, yet in the progress of the work no one has assumed more, and such things as have been neither demonstrated by himself nor can be demonstrated by anyone, even if we apply force to the intellect; and that, although he sets out such plain and clear principles, soon after leaving them he brings forth others which can be perceived neither by sight nor by sense, namely globules, striated particles and invisible elements. With these posited, unproved, he begins to philosophise; for, namely, where the eyes and senses fail, there the freedom of fiction begins.

units.la: Intenderit verò quodcunque Cartesius ! Nos, an rectè à cognitione veri Sensus seclusERIT, videamus ! Ac primò quidem (quod argumentum unum potest esse instar omnium) ipse de Sensuum Usu legitimo pronunciet eorundem Conditor Deus ! Aliud quid praeter discretionem commodi & incommodi in ordine ad totum hominis compositum, huic cum brutis communem, se hic intendisse tam Is inculcat disertè in Sacris, ut nequeat magis. Quid illud est, quod jubemur oculos attollere in altum, ac videre quis creaverit ista; sic ut ex sensibilium creaturarum existentia, per Sensum certò cognita, ducendi simus ad contemplandam & agnoscendam aeterni Numinis Divinitatem & potentiam? An verò & ista veritas, ope Sensûs ex sensibilibus à mente hausta, ad animalis hujus vitae regimen, ad discernenda noxia à toti composito profuturis, tantum pertinet? An verò & hic solo intellectu, contradistinctè ad Sensus, utendum? Equidem si Sensui in investigSanda scientia veritatis omnium primae ac maximè fundamentalis suus sit Usus, & quidem tam necessarius, indubitatus, acevidens; ut notitia illa Dei per Sensum ex Sensibilibus hausta etiam sufficiens sit ad Gentium m ἀπολογίαν, nescio, in qua alia veritate cognoscenda ei concedi non debeat locus? Nescio, quo colore, Sensuum perceptiones non alia de causa nobis esse concessas, quam ut indicarent animo quae sint convenientia ac nocitura toti composito, affirmetur? Quod ipsum Cartesium & Claubergium rotundè affirmantes audivimus.
units.tr: However Descartes intended, let us see whether he was right to exclude the senses from the knowledge of truth! And first of all (and this one argument can be worth all the rest), let the very Founder of the senses, God himself, pronounce on the lawful use of the senses! That he meant something other than the distinction between what is advantageous and harmful for the whole composite of man, which he shares with the brutes, Scripture teaches so plainly that it could not be plainer. What is it that we are commanded to lift up our eyes on high, and see who created these things; so that from the existence of sensible creatures, known with certainty through the senses, we are to be led to contemplate and acknowledge the divinity and power of the eternal Godhead? Or does this truth also, drawn by the mind from sensible things by means of the senses, pertain only to the government of this animal life, to distinguishing what is harmful from what will profit the whole composite? Or here too must we use the intellect alone, in contrast to the senses? Indeed, if the use of the senses in the search for the knowledge of truth is the first and most fundamental of all, and so necessary, undoubted and evident, that the knowledge of God drawn from sensible things through the senses is even sufficient for the apology [ἀπολογίαν] of the Gentiles, I do not know in what other truth to be known room should not be granted to them? I do not know with what colour it can be affirmed that sense perceptions have been granted to us for no other reason than to indicate to the mind what is suitable and what harmful to the whole composite? This is what we have heard Descartes and Clauberg affirm roundly.

units.la: Quin, parùm videbatur Spiritui S. ad veritatem naturalem & Philosophicam cognoscendam Usum Sensuum præscribere ; in ipsis etiam rebus Fide Divinâ credendis Sensu, tanquam puræ veritatis magistro, nos uti voluit ad earundem in mente nostra confirmationem.
