Hinc in fidei vacillantis sæpè nimium indubitatam obsignationem, ac certiorem gratiæ spiritualis insensibilis persuasionem, sensibilia quædam signa ac sigilla, Sacramenta puta, instituit. Hinc Servator D. Jesus ad corporis sui, crucifixi nuperac mortui, nunc redivivi, contrectationem, tanquam ad telcem, qui immediatè dignoscere docet resurrectionis veritatem, incredulum Apostolum invitavit. Hinc & ipsi Apostoli auditores suos ad fidem hortantes, plenissimam iis quæ annunciabant certitudinem conciliaturi, ad Sensus recurrunt, affirmantes se quæ persuasa esse cupiebant illis, auribus audivisse, oculis vidisse, manu contrectasse. Falsa utique, inquit gravissimus Patrum Tertullianus, disputans contra Academicos, Lib. de Anima, Cap. de Quinque Sensibus, restatio, si oculorum & aurium & manuum Sensus natura mentiuntur. Perversissima utique, dicamus nos (absit blasphemia!) sapientissimi naturæ ordinis perversio, si Sensuum perceptiones tantum à natura data sunt ad significanda in vitæ animalis regimine composito commoda & incommoda, non verò ut iis utamur tanquam pura veritatis magistris, ad aliquid certi concludendum de rebus extra nos constitutis! Ineptissima methodus demonstrandi certitudinem rei, si Sensus in certis tenemur ejurare! Quin, sallacissima fallacia! si Sensuum natura sit nunquam non fallere, & semper errare.
units.tr: Indeed, it seemed too little to the Holy Spirit to prescribe the use of the senses for knowing natural and philosophical truth. He even wished us to use the senses, as teachers of pure truth, in the very things to be believed by divine faith, to confirm them in our minds. Hence, to seal a faith that often wavers with an undoubted certainty, and to persuade us more surely of spiritual grace, which is insensible, he instituted certain sensible signs and seals, namely the Sacraments. Hence the Saviour, the Lord Jesus, invited the unbelieving Apostle to touch his body, crucified, lately dead and now restored to life, as to a witness who teaches one to recognise immediately the truth of the resurrection. Hence also the Apostles themselves, exhorting their hearers to faith and wishing to win for them the fullest certainty of what they proclaimed, have recourse to the senses, affirming that what they wished them to be persuaded of they had heard with their ears, seen with their eyes, and handled with their hands. Surely false, says the most weighty of the Fathers, Tertullian, disputing against the Academics in his book On the Soul, chapter On the Five Senses: it would be a falsehood, if the senses of the eyes and ears and hands lie by nature. Most perverse indeed, we would say (God forbid the blasphemy!), would be a perversion of the most wise order of nature, if the perceptions of the senses were given by nature only to signal the advantages and disadvantages for the governance of composite animal life, and not that we should use them as masters of pure truth, to conclude something certain about things situated outside us! A most absurd method of demonstrating the certainty of a thing, if we are bound to renounce the senses in matters of certainty! Indeed, a most deceptive deception, if the nature of the senses were never not to deceive, and always to err.

units.la: XVIII. Unde efficax, pro Sensu ultra animalis vitæ regimen extendendo, argumentum.
units.tr: XVIII. Whence an effective argument for extending the use of the senses beyond the governance of animal life.

units.la: Extra oleas nos hîc vagari & à scopo planè aberrare, regeres procul dubio cum in istis non agatur de veritate quapiam Philosophica per Sensus cognoscenda, de qua hoc loco erat controversia; sed de rebus fide divinâ recipiendis, quæ Sacra naturalibus permissenda neutiquam sunt. Verùm, præterquam quod jam assignavenrim veritatem etiam Philosophicam (naturalem scil. Dei notitiam) secundum methodum Spiritus S. ex sensibilibus beneficio Sensuum certò cognoscendam, etiam cætera firmissimum nobis suppeditant argumentum, ut vocant, à majori ad minus. Nempè, si rebus fide divinâ, omnis falsitatis ac erroris periculi prorsus expertè, firmiter credendis earumque indubitatæ certitudini firmandæ imprimis serviat Sensuum testimonium, multò magis rebus naturalibus, quarum æqua cum istis certitudo neque est, neque esse potest, certò cognoscendis idem potest esse adjumento. Unde invictâ sequelâ fluit, Sensus à natura, i.e. Deo, non tantum homini esse datos, ad discernendum quid vitæ hominis animali prosit aut noceat, sed & alium esse genuinum eorundem Usum, atque excellentiorem præ illo quem cum brutis habet communem, docere scil. etiam quid re verâ sit in rebus: neque ideò quicquam nos peccaturos, si iis utamur tanquam puræ veritatis magistris, ad judicandum secundum eos de rebus extra nos positis. Nec potuimus istud hoc loco præterire, quandoquidem nemo accuratius operum Dei finem ac usum edocere potest, quam ipse opifex, cujus hic vox argumentum est quavis ratione efficacius. Nihil vero sic committi Philosopho Christiano indignum, ostendimus alias & alibi in Exercit. de Auctoritatum in Philosophia Usu & Abusu.
units.tr: You would doubtless say here that we are wandering outside the lines and straying wholly from our aim, since in these matters the question is not about some philosophical truth to be known through the senses, which was the point of controversy here, but about things to be received by divine faith, which by no means are to be entrusted to natural things. But, besides the fact that we have already shown that even philosophical truth (namely the natural knowledge of God) is to be known with certainty from sensible things through the senses, according to the method of the Holy Spirit, the remaining argument, as they call it, from the greater to the lesser, gives us the firmest support. For if the testimony of the senses serves chiefly to firmly establish things to be firmly believed by divine faith, wholly free from any danger of falsity or error, and to confirm their undoubted certainty, then much more can it serve as an aid for knowing natural things with certainty, whose certainty is neither equal to that of the former nor can be. Hence it follows by an invincible sequence that the senses were given by nature, that is by God, not only to man to discern what benefits or harms the animal life of man, but also that there is another genuine use of them, more excellent than that which they have in common with the brutes, namely to teach also what is really the case in things. Therefore we shall not sin at all if we use them as teachers of pure truth, to judge by them of things situated outside us. Nor could we pass this over here, since no one can teach the purpose and use of God's works more accurately than the craftsman himself, whose voice here is an argument more effective in every way. That nothing so unworthy of a Christian philosopher is committed by this, we have shown elsewhere, in the Exercitation on the Use and Abuse of Authorities in Philosophy.

units.la: Et consentit cum isto Dei, de Sensuum Usu etiam latius quam ad vitæ animalis regimen extendendo, testimonio ipsa rerum natura; sive modum cognoscendi à parte mentis, sive veritatem cognoscendas à parte rei, sive denique ipsum vitæ nostræ regimen, prout id explicat nova hypothesis, spectemus. Naturam & constitutionem Animæ nostræ, quatenus in statu Unionis cum hoc corpore organico in eandem personam juncta est, si attendamus, deprehendimus inter actiones cogitativas illius & sensationes hujus nexum tam arctum & concatenationem tam insolubilem, ut vix ulla in corpore benè disposito fiat organorum Sensui inservientium motio, quin ilicò mens occultâ quadam quasi vi trahatur ad judicium ferendum de re sensibili, secundum illam Sensûs perceptionem: atque iterum vicissim vix unquam anima rationalis judicat, quin ne quidem de re quapiam cogitat, nisi conceptui formando facta fuerit per aliquam sensationem occasio. Unde & peculiaris quædam in mente nostra deprehenditur promptitudo & facilitas percipiendi res corporeas præ spiritualibus. Quæ omnia (tam evidens atque explorata exstitit hæc veritas) ipsemet Cartesius agnoscere cogitur, quando Princip. 1. Art. LXXIII. fatetur, Mentem nostram omnium difficillime ad illa attendere, quæ nec sensibus, nec quidem imaginationi præsentia sunt. Cujus rei causas ibidem investigans verissimè ait, id contingere, sive quia mens talem ex eo quod corpori conjuncta fit, habet naturam; sive quia in primis annis, cum tantum circa sensus & imaginationes occuparetur, majorem de ipsis quam de caeteris rebus cogitandi usum & facilitatem acquisivit. Accuratissimè equidem, si ratio utraque non disjuncta ab eo fuisset, sed copulata potius! Priorem enim, unionem puta, posterioris causam esse, arguit evidentissimè experientia in phreneticis, infantibus, senibus, aliisque recto rationis usu nullam aliam ob causam destitutis, quam ob denegatum integrum, per vitiata organa, Sensuum tum internorum tum externorum Usum. Accedit ipsa unionis, prout ab his Auctoribus explicatur, natura; quippe quae, si iis credimus, in nullo alio consistit, quam quod ad varias cogitationes mentis varii sequantur motus in corpore; & reciprocè ad varios corporis motus (qui illis sunt ipsae Sensationes) variae cogitationes in mente. Certè, si mens nostra talem, ex eo quod corpori conjuncta sit, habet naturam, ut difficillimè ad illa attendat, quae sensibus non sunt praesentia, adeò ut propter unionem motus corporis cum cogitationibus animae & vicissim cogitationes animae cum motibus corporis firmissimè cohaerent, utique manifestum evadit, Sensationes homini concessas esse ad usum longè ampliorem, quam tantùm ad vitae hujus regimen. Nisi quis statuere malit, ideò Deum mentem cum corpore conjungere voluisse, ut ipsa res difficillimè cognoscat, ac nunquam non erret: quod alienissimum esse à conditoris sapientia & bonitate, nemo negabit, attendens, quam Ipse voluerit, hominem, prae caeteris omnibus creaturis in ipso rationis usu, existere organum pulcherrimum divinae gloriae, atque elaboratissimum naturae opus.
units.tr: And nature itself agrees with this testimony of God, which extends the use of the senses more widely than the governance of animal life, whether we look at the mode of knowing on the side of the mind, or at the truth to be known on the side of the thing, or finally at the governance of our life itself, as the new hypothesis explains it. If we consider the nature and constitution of our soul, insofar as it is joined in the same person in a state of union with this organic body, we find between its thinking actions and the sensations of the body a connection so close and an interlinking so indissoluble that scarcely any motion of the organs serving the sense occurs in a well-disposed body without the mind being drawn, by some hidden force as it were, to pass judgement on the sensible thing according to that perception of the sense. And conversely, the rational soul hardly ever judges, nor even thinks of anything at all, unless an occasion has been given for forming the concept through some sensation. Hence also a certain peculiar readiness and facility is found in our mind for perceiving corporeal things rather than spiritual ones. All of which (so evident and established is this truth) Descartes himself is forced to acknowledge when, in Principles, Part 1, Article LXXIII, he confesses that our mind finds it most difficult to attend to those things which are present neither to the senses nor even to the imagination. Investigating the causes of this in the same place, he says most truly that it happens either because the mind has such a nature from being joined to the body, or because in its early years, when it was occupied only with the senses and the imagination, it acquired a greater practice and facility of thinking about these than about other things. Most accurately, indeed, if the two reasons had not been separated by him but rather joined together! For that the former, namely the union, is the cause of the latter is most plainly shown by experience in the frenzied, infants, the aged, and others who are deprived of the right use of reason for no other cause than that the full use of the internal and external senses is denied them through diseased organs. Add to this the nature of the union itself, as these authors explain it; for, if we believe them, it consists in nothing else than that various motions in the body follow upon various thoughts of the mind, and conversely, various thoughts in the mind follow upon various motions of the body (which for them are the sensations themselves). Certainly, if our mind, from being joined to the body, has such a nature that it attends with the greatest difficulty to those things which are not present to the senses, so that because of the union the motions of the body and the thoughts of the soul cohere most firmly with one another, it plainly follows that sensations have been granted to man for a use far wider than merely the governance of this life. Unless someone prefers to hold that God wished the mind to be joined to the body so that it might know the very thing with the greatest difficulty and never fail to err; which no one will deny is most alien to the wisdom and goodness of the Creator, if one considers how much he willed man, above all other creatures in the very use of reason, to be a most beautiful instrument of divine glory and the most elaborate work of nature.
XX.

units.la: Imprimis verò efficacissimè hoc argumento evincitur, etiam alium esse Sensuum Usum, praeterquam in vitâ hac animali moderandâ, si, secundo loco, expendamus, quid ad vitam hanc, ejusque integritatem, ex sententia Neotericorum requiratur? Ii, postquam jam dudum bruta, instar machinarum artificialium, non tam agere & movere quam agi potius & moveri statuerunt, motibus purè automaticis, per solam partium idoneam dispositionem, & spirituum animalium per nervos & musculos variam ab extrinseco solum factam versus haec & illa objecta determinationem, absque ullo principio substantiali intrinseco movente aut dirigente, idem deinceps de homine quoque affirmare coeperunt; ità quidem ut negent, vitam hominis consistere in mentis cum corpore unione, aut mortem in partis utriusque ab invicem separatione: quin contendant, vitæ nostræ animalis actiones tam parùm à mente dependere, ut etiam absque ejus præsentia & adjumento possint peragi in corpore rectè dispositó,accuratè non minus, quam cùm anima copori adest præsens. At verò, si humanum corpus, quod ad actiones animales attinet, absque ullo principio substantiali, multò magis absque mente humana, instar bruti, æquè queat discernere objecta corpori commoda ab incommodis, atque adeò vivere possit nihilo infelicius, quam cùm hæc corpori existit copulata, qua ergo de causa asseremus, Sensuum perceptiones proprie tantùm à natura datas esse, ad menti significandum, quænam compositò commoda sint vel incommoda; aut, non alia de causa easdem nobis esse concessas, quam ut indicarent animo, quænam res conveniant aut noceant toti composito; itâ ut Sensuum genuinus usus consistat in eo, ut vitæ totius animalis regimen ab iis pendeat, quod affirmare Cartesium, cum suo Paraphraste Claubergio, audivimus? Profectò, si unicus sit ac genuinus Sensuum Usus, menti indicare res in ordine ad vitæ regimen, nullus revera is tandem erit; quoniam, ex hac sententia, nudus motus, absque tali indicio per sensationem menti facto, sufficit ad vitæ regimen. Scire itaquè lubet ex Recentioribus, quamobrem (si Sensibus opus sit neque ad vitæ animalis regimen, neque ad id ut iis mediantibus mens quicquam certò cognoscat) quamobrem, inquam, Deus à sensationum motibus corporeis mentem affici voluerit, & quidem itâ, ut inter sensationes nostras in corpore & cogitationes in animâ istam voluerit esse perennem connexionem, quâ fit, ut illæ sine his, vel nunquam, vel valdè raro, habeant locum? Detur huic negotio exitus! Nos, ne sensationis cum cogitatione connexionem frustrà à Deo factam esse concederé cum adversariis cogamur, Sensibus Usum suum tribuimus utrobiquè, & in moderanda vita, & in comtemplatione rerum.
units.tr: Indeed, this point is proved most effectively, that the senses have another use besides governing this animal life, if, secondly, we consider what the moderns think is required for this life and its integrity. Having long since held that brutes, like artificial machines, do not so much act and move as are acted upon and moved, through motions that are purely automatic, through nothing but the suitable arrangement of parts and the variable direction of the animal spirits toward this or that object, which is produced from outside by the nerves and muscles, with no intrinsic substantial principle moving or directing them, they then began to affirm the same of man. They deny that the life of man consists in the union of mind with body, or his death in the separation of the one part from the other. Indeed they contend that the actions of our animal life depend so little on the mind that they can be carried on, just as accurately, in a properly disposed body even without its presence and help, as when the soul is present to the body. But if the human body, so far as its animal actions are concerned, can, without any substantial principle and much more without a human mind, like a brute's body, equally well distinguish what is useful to the body from what is harmful, and so can live no less happily than when this body is joined to a mind, then why shall we say that the perceptions of the senses are given by nature only to signify to the mind what is advantageous or harmful to the composite; or, for no other reason, that they have been granted to us except to indicate to the soul what things suit or harm the whole composite; so that the genuine use of the senses consists in this, that the regimen of the whole animal life depends on them? This is what we have heard Descartes affirm, with his paraphrast Clauberg. Certainly, if the only and genuine use of the senses is to indicate to the mind things in relation to the governing of life, then in truth there will ultimately be no such use at all; since, on this view, bare motion, without any such indication made to the mind through sensation, suffices for the governing of life. I therefore wish to learn from the more recent writers why (if there is no need for the senses either for governing animal life or for the mind to know anything certainly by their means), why, I say, God wished the mind to be affected by the bodily motions of sensations, and indeed in such a way that He willed there to be a perpetual connection between our sensations in the body and our thoughts in the soul, by which it comes about that the latter have place without the former either never, or very rarely. Let an answer be given to this matter! We, lest we be compelled with our opponents to concede that the connection of sensation with thought was made by God in vain, attribute to the senses their use on both sides, both in governing life and in contemplating things.

units.la: Quod si, tertiò, res ipsas cognoscendas spectemus, eædem plurimæ naturâ suâ tales existunt, ut absque sensationum ministerio cognosci prorsùs nequeant; quare etiam in philosophando his locum facere omninò est necessarium, nisi multarum veritatum notitiâ titiâ nostrâ culpâ ac destinato consilio carere velimus. Non jam ostendam, omnem nostram cognitionem à sensibilibus quodammodo originem primitùs ducere, sic ut animam nostram, uti ante Sensuum, itâ & Rationis, Usum, optimè Philosophus comparaverit tabulæ rasæ, cui nil est inscriptum, sed quidvis inscribi potest; asseruerit-que non immeritò, oportere intelligentem phantasmata speculari. Ista, inquam, non jam ostendam, quod sponte fluant & clarè satis innotescant ex iis quæ de naturali cogitationum nostrarum cum sensationibus connexione dicta sunt ac demonstrata, etiam ex ipso Cartefio, in præcedentibus. Iis in præsentiarum missis, solas nunc res sensibiles hìc attendi velim, quas si cognoscere desideremus, ad Sensus recurrendum est; quoniam, uti bene non-nemo, Sensibilium alius judex esse nequit, quam Sensus. Certè, nisi solo Sensuum testimonio stare velimus, de ipsa rerum materialium existentiâ quis nos unquam certò persuasos reddet? Notum, qui Sceptici, postquam de Sensuum fide dubitare cœperunt, eâdem operâ etiam res Sensibus perceptas, adeòque corporum imprimis existentiam ac veritatem dubiam & incertam dare debuerint. Neque id mirum est, quoniam de ea convinci nequimus, nisi solâ ac immediatâ Sensationis fide: quam etiam ob causam hæc veritas omni tempore habita fuit res per se ac citra ullum discursum aut ratiocinationem notissima, &, propter sensationis evidentissimam certitudinem, aliis quibusvis veritatibus maximè indubitatis annumeranda. Unde non immeritò prudentiores jam olim judicarunt, Cartefio in congressu cum Scepticis, quandò hyperbolicis suis dubitationibus tantùm indulget ut supponat nullos se sensus habere corporaque esse meras chimæras, nimiâ ac parùm circumspectâ liberalitate necessariò fuisse succumbendum: cum impossibile sit, unquam aliquem convincere de veritate, cujus cognoscendæ adminicula ipsi abjecimus. Neque Sensuum fidei denuò adstruendæ vel minimùm inservit Auctoris methodus, quâ, investigatâ primùm suæ mentis tanquam rei cogitantis, indeque adstructâ, ex clara quadam quam innatam sibi supponit Dei idea, ejusdem existentiâ, per multas demùm ambages rerum materialium certam existentiam probat: Falsas enim in hoc toto processu suppositiones multas, principii petitiones ac circulos frequentes, similiaque argumentandi vitia copiosè jam dudum in eo ostendit laudatus suprà Gassendus. Verum non jam id agebam. Si quid sensuum ope tandem de rerum materialium existentia constet, liquet, citò serò in veritatis inquisitione admittendum esse sensum ; perperam ergò hinc in totum removeri, & ad solum vitæ animalis regimen restringi: quæ est ipsa conclusio nobis probanda.
units.tr: But if, thirdly, we look at the things themselves that are to be known, many of them are by their very nature such that they cannot be known at all without the ministry of the senses; therefore it is absolutely necessary to give the senses a place also in philosophizing, unless we wish to be without knowledge of many truths through our own fault and by deliberate design. I shall not now show that all our knowledge in some way takes its origin first from sensible things, so that the Philosopher rightly compared our soul, before the use of the senses and then of reason, to a blank tablet on which nothing is written but anything can be written; and rightly asserted that the understanding must contemplate phantasms. I shall not now show these things, I say, because they follow of their own accord and are sufficiently clear from what has been said and demonstrated in the preceding pages about the natural connection of our thoughts with sensations, including from Descartes himself. Setting those aside for the present, I want only the sensible things to be considered here; if we desire to know these, we must have recourse to the senses, since, as someone has rightly said, the judge of sensible things can be none other than the sense. Certainly, unless we are willing to stand only on the testimony of the senses, who will ever persuade us with certainty of the very existence of material things? It is well known that the Sceptics, once they began to doubt the trustworthiness of the senses, had at the same time to make the things perceived by the senses, and above all the existence and truth of bodies, doubtful and uncertain. Nor is this surprising, since we cannot be convinced of it except by the sole and immediate trust in sensation. For this reason this truth has at all times been regarded as something most known in itself and without any discourse or reasoning, and, on account of the most evident certainty of sensation, it is to be counted among the most indubitable of all truths. Hence wiser men have long since judged that Descartes, in his encounter with the Sceptics, when he indulged so far in his hyperbolic doubts as to suppose that he had no senses and that bodies were mere chimeras, was necessarily compelled to yield to excessive and ill-considered generosity, since it is impossible ever to convince anyone of a truth whose means of knowing we have ourselves thrown away. Nor does the author's method serve in the least to re-establish the trustworthiness of the senses; for he first investigates his own mind as a thinking thing, and from that establishes, out of a certain clear idea of God which he supposes to be innate in him, the existence of God, and only through many long detours proves the certain existence of material things. For the aforementioned Gassendi has long since shown in detail, in his work above, the many false suppositions, petitions of principle, and frequent circles, and similar faults of argument, in this whole process. But this is not what I was undertaking. If anything about the existence of material things is at last established with the help of the senses, it is clear that the senses must be admitted in the inquiry after truth, though late and too late; it is wrongly, then, that they are removed from this altogether and restricted to the governing of animal life alone, and this is the very conclusion we have to prove.

units.la: Atque utì in rerum materialium existentiæ indubitatam notiam nemo absque Sensuum ope pervenerit ; itâ neque naturam earundem neque effecta & adjuncta ( quibus tamen indagandis universa occupatur scientia Physiologica ) quisquam concipere accuratè, aut certi quid de iis concludere poterit, nisi Sensationibus usus, tanquam pura veritatis magistris. Ad hujus rei confirmationem alio non videor indigere argumento, quam quod validissimum nobis suppeditat quotidiè frequens & obvia cuivis experientia, cum eos, qui nati sunt cæci, surdi, alteriusve Sensûs vel usu omni vel integritate privati, deprehendimus vel nullo modo, vel valdè imperfectè, obscurè, & confusè objecta intelligere, quæ eadem alii sano Sensu utentes concipiunt facillimè ac clarissimè. Quapropter de Anima nostra, dum corpori unita existit, verissimè, saltem quod ad objecta sensibilia, Palingenius, in Libra: Sunt quinque ipsius comites, fidisque ministri, Per quos cognoscit res omnes: queis sine prorsus Inscia, lethæo torpebit pressa sopore. Et post quædam: Nam contemplatur mens omnia, & omnia cauto Judicio expendit, quæcunque à Sensibus hausit. Mens igitur sol est anima, sunt sydera Sensus.
units.tr: And just as no one can attain indubitable knowledge of the existence of material things without the aid of the senses, so also no one can conceive accurately of their nature, or of their effects and accidents (which the whole science of physiology nevertheless occupies itself in investigating), nor conclude anything certain about them, unless he makes use of the senses as pure teachers of truth. To confirm this I seem to need no other argument than that which the frequent and obvious experience of everyone supplies most strongly: when we observe that those who are born blind, deaf, or deprived of another sense either entirely in its use or in its integrity, understand objects in no way, or very imperfectly, obscurely and confusedly, which others using a sound sense conceive very easily and most clearly. Therefore, concerning our soul, while it exists united to the body, Palingenius speaks most truly, at least as regards sensible objects, in his Zodiac: "There are five companions of the soul and faithful servants, through whom it knows all things; without them it would lie unaware, numbed by Lethean sleep." And after some lines: "For the mind contemplates all things, and weighs with cautious judgment whatever it has drawn from the senses. The mind, then, is the sun of the soul; the senses are the stars."

units.la: Inculces licet homini visu destituto vel millies globulorum tuorum æthereorum, secundum certam proportionem, in motu suo celeritatem ac circumvolutionem, haud tamen unquam id impetrabis, ut clarè & distinctè nobiscum concipiat colorum discrimina: nisi forte ( novo ausu, omnibusque hactenus itâ ridiculo, ut in proverbium abierit ) etiam cæco committendum sit judicium de coloribus. Idemque in aliis qualitatibus sensibilibus obtinet. Et profectò, quis nostrum plurimarum hujus mundi partium configurationem ac dispositionem; quis motuum cœlestium periodos; quis corporum mixtorum ortum & interitum ; quis admirandas plurimarum rerum vires ; quis viventium generationem ac nutritionem ; quis sexcenta ejusdem commatis alia, homini Philosopho inquirenda, concipiat clarè ac rebus convenienter, nisi Sensibus usus, tanquam purae veritatis magistris? Quisve ullus adeò existit rerum imperitus, qui, in re Anatomica & Botanica immediatam Senfationem utramque facere paginam, ac nudam <bl>'Avͅτοψίαν</bl> quibusvis rationibus potiorem habendam esse, ignoret?
units.tr: You may urge a man without sight a thousand times about the speed and rotation, in their motion according to a fixed proportion, of your ethereal globules; yet you will never bring him to conceive clearly and distinctly with us the differences of colours; unless, perhaps (by a new daring, so ridiculous to all hitherto that it has passed into a proverb), the judgment about colours must be entrusted even to a blind man. And the same holds for the other sensible qualities. Indeed, which of us would conceive clearly, and in a manner fitting to things, the configuration and arrangement of most parts of this world; the periods of the heavenly motions; the origin and decay of mixed bodies; the admirable powers of very many things; the generation and nutrition of living things; or the six hundred other matters of this kind that the philosopher must investigate, unless he makes use of the senses as pure teachers of truth? Or is there anyone so inexperienced in things that he does not know that, in anatomy and botany, immediate sensation makes both sides of the page, and that bare autopsy [αὐτοψίαν] is to be held superior to all arguments whatever?

units.la: Sed desino accumulare plura, ne nimius videar in confirmanda re tam omnibus evidente ac ingenita quasi, ut neque ipsi adversarii, hypothesium suarum quasi obliti, ad Sensum provocare metuant quoties itâ usus exigit. Idque faciunt non tantùm in rebus propinquis, ac Sensu facilè discernendis, verùm in iis quoque, de quibus, ob distantiam nimiam, aliamve ad organum ac vim perceptivam disproportionem, Sensus nihil distinctum dictare queunt. Exemplo sit globus Lunaris ! Maculas illas & lucidiores partes, quas, biduo imprimis aut triduo ante plenilunium, sole occidente, in ejus disco observamus, afferunt Recentiores, solâ oculorum tubo speculari adjutorum fide nixi, totidem esse maria, montes ac valles. Quin & eodem stantes argumento visûs, in peculiari Selenographia, tanquam in altera Geographia, omnes illas Lunæ regiones tam delineant accuratè, ut insulas & continentes, promontoria & sinus, maria & freta, certâ figurâ, magnitudine, situ, distantiâ determinata, nominibus quoque Geographicis discreta, in tabella exhibeant non solùm, sed & ulterius provecti eidem etiam, ceu Terræ habitatæ, suas tribuant plantas atque incolas, homines & feras. Fabulas si quis hæc habuerit, confictas, ne quid videatur Nova sapientia concedere Veterum, Orphei, Thaletis, Anaxagoræ, Democriti, de Luna, quæ sit Tellus habitabilis, traditionibus, ad oculorum & optici tubi fidem provocant. Egregium verò ! Scilicet, de constitutione corporis à nobis tam remoti, ut Sensum nostrum hebetem & obtusum vix afficiat nisi fallaci instrumento adjutum, aliquid certi concludendum est Philosopho ex solâ Sensûs perceptione; interim tamen, in rebus propinquis ac pluribus Sensibus obviis diiudicandis, iisdem uti tanquam veritatis magistris res erit illicita, quin sapientissimi naturæ ordinis perversio !
units.tr: But I will stop heaping up more examples, lest I seem excessive in proving a matter so evident to all and almost innate, so that even my opponents, forgetful of their own hypotheses, do not hesitate to appeal to the senses whenever the occasion requires. They do this not only in matters that are near at hand and easily discerned by the senses, but also in those things about which the senses can tell nothing distinct, because of their great distance or the disproportion between them and our organ and power of perception. Take the globe of the Moon as an example. Recent writers, relying solely on the aid of the telescope, claim that the spots and brighter parts we observe on its disc, chiefly two or three days before the full moon as the sun sets, are so many seas, mountains and valleys. Moreover, standing on the same evidence of sight, in a special Selenography, as if in a second Geography, they draw all those regions of the Moon so accurately that they display in a table not only islands and continents, promontories and bays, seas and straits, each fixed in shape, size, position and distance and distinguished by geographical names, but even, advancing further, they assign to it plants and inhabitants, men and beasts, as if it were an inhabited Earth. If anyone holds these to be fictions, lest it seem that modern wisdom yields anything to the ancients, the traditions of Orpheus, Thales, Anaxagoras and Democritus about the Moon being an habitable earth, they appeal to the testimony of the eye and the optical tube. Splendid indeed! Clearly, about the constitution of a body so remote from us that it scarcely affects our dull and blunt sense unless aided by a deceptive instrument, the philosopher is to conclude something certain from the perception of sense alone; yet meanwhile, in judging things that are near and open to several senses, to use those same senses as the teachers of truth would be unlawful, indeed a perversion of the most wise order of nature!

units.la: Denique, si in indagandis veritatibus Philosophicis solo intellectu utendum sit, nec aliquid certi ex Sensuum perceptionibus de rebus extra nos constitutis concludendum, citra eorundem abusum & naturæ ordinis perversionem, quis in Philosophia restabit Experientiæ locus? Nullus profectò; sed ipsa in totum hinc prosciribenda. Quandoquidem enim ea omnis nihil aliud est, quam crebrò repetita rei sensibilis per Sensus facta, & memoriæ ne elabatur firmiter impressa, observatio, eædem omnes rationes, quæ contra sensuum in philosophando Usum militant, eodem jure contra Experientiam militabunt. Verissimè ergò illa amplius erit magistra, non Sapientum ac Philosophorum, sed stultorum; quippe quæ, uti ipsi Sensus, non alium habebit usum, quam ut unicè inserviat stupidis hominibus ex variis vitæ ante-actæ casibus erudiendis, ut discant cautius posthac discernere ea quæ ad vitæ animalis conservationem aut destructionem faciunt; ista appetere prudentius, hæc evitare circumspectius. Mirabuntur procul dubio, quotquot hæc sedulò expendent frequentes Cartesii querelas de experimentorum defectu, in quem Physicæ suæ imperfectæ causas transfert. Quid enim attinet infinita expetere experimenta, quibus nec manus ejus nec fortuna, etiamsi millecuplo majores essent, possent sufficere? Quid necesse est, majores aut minores in natura cognitione progressus suspendere à copia ea plura aut pauciora faciendi? siquidem solo intellectu in Philosophia utendum sit; neque Sensibus, adeòque nec Experientiâ, uti liceat, tanquam veritatis magistris, ad dijudicandum quæ sit rerum extra nos positarum naturæ ac proprietates. Nec mirabuntur minus extra partes constituti promissa ingentia quorundam Neotericorum, qui jactant, se brevi per experimenta evidentissima tam clarè ad oculum comprobaturos principiorum Cartesianorum veritatem, & ad solvenda quævis phænomena sufficientiam, ut nemo sit extiturus ista capere idoneus, qui non iis sit acquieturus: unde & spem concipiunt ac gloriantur, jamjam futurum, ut quivis certatim ad disciplinam Cartesii, novi proselyt, sint transituri. Talia promittunt, qui iidem Sensibus tanquam veritatis magistris utendum non esse, sed eos in certis ejurandos, tanquam infidos testes, quorum natura sit nunquam non fallere & semper errare, vociferantur. Certè hisce quamdiu adhærent assertionibus, frustrà plane naturam rerum aperire satagunt clave non alium in finem à Deo destinata quam ad referendam earum rerum bonitatem & malitiam, quarum discretio ad vitæ animalis regimen spectat. Præstiterit itaque haud profuturo labore, igne, fumo, flatibus, ætatem non absumere; parcere præstiterit operæ, sumptibus, omnique ad experimenta capienda apparatui. Verum non hæc prosequor latius, quandò jam dudum sufficiunt adductæ rationes, ad conficiendum, tantum abesse, ut prudens Philosophus teneatur in certis Sensus ejurare, tanquam datos unicè ad vitæ animalis regimen, non ad sapiendum, ut contrà possit non solùm non uno in casu, sed & debeat, Sensuum dictamini itâ adhærere, ut eos tanquam puræ veritatis magistros, tutò sequatur in dijudicanda rerum extra nos positarum naturâ & proprietatibus, citra ullum eorundem abusum, aut sapientissimi naturæ ordinis perversionem.
units.tr: Finally, if in investigating philosophical truths one must use the intellect alone, and nothing certain is to be concluded from the perceptions of the senses about things situated outside us, without abuse of those senses and a perversion of the order of nature, what place will remain for experience in philosophy? None at all; rather, experience itself must be banished entirely. For since all experience is nothing other than an observation of a sensible thing, made through the senses again and again and firmly impressed on the memory lest it slip away, the very same arguments that militate against the use of the senses in philosophizing will militate equally against experience. Most truly, therefore, it will be a teacher not of the wise and philosophers but of fools; for it, like the senses themselves, will have no other use than to serve solely in instructing stupid men, from the various accidents of their past life, so that they may learn more cautiously hereafter to distinguish what contributes to the preservation or destruction of animal life; to seek the former more prudently, and to avoid the latter more warily. Undoubtedly all who weigh these things carefully will be amazed at the frequent complaints of Descartes about the lack of experiments, to which he attributes the causes of his imperfect physics. For what is the point of seeking infinite experiments, which neither his hand nor his fortune, even if they were a thousand times greater, could suffice for? Why is it necessary to make greater or lesser progress in the knowledge of nature depend upon the abundance of performing more or fewer of them? Provided that one must use the intellect alone in philosophy, and that one may not use the senses, and therefore not experience, as teachers of truth, for judging what the nature and properties of things situated outside us are. Nor will those placed outside the parties be less amazed at the huge promises of certain moderns, who boast that they will shortly prove, by the most evident experiments and so clearly before the eyes, the truth of the Cartesian principles and their sufficiency for resolving every phenomenon, so that no one capable of grasping these things will fail to acquiesce in them; whence they conceive hope and glory, saying that soon everyone will eagerly pass over as new proselytes to the discipline of Descartes. Those who make such promises, the same men who cry out that the senses must not be used as teachers of truth, but must be renounced in certain matters as faithless witnesses whose nature is never not to deceive and always to err, promise such things. Certainly, as long as they cling to these assertions, they labour in vain to open the nature of things with a key that God destined for no other purpose than to refer the goodness and badness of those things, the distinction of which concerns the regulation of animal life. It would therefore be better not to waste time, fire, smoke and blasts on labour that will profit nothing; it would be better to spare effort, expense, and all the apparatus for making experiments. But I do not pursue these points further, since the arguments already adduced are long sufficient to establish that a prudent philosopher is so far from being bound to renounce the senses in certain matters, as if they were given solely for the regulation of animal life and not for wisdom, that he not only can, in no single case, but must so adhere to the verdict of the senses, and so safely follow them as teachers of pure truth, in judging the nature and properties of things situated outside us, without any abuse of them or perversion of the most wise order of nature.

units.la: Minimè verò omnibus hactenus allatis satisfacit Claubergius hunc in modum differens, De Cognit. Dei & Nostri, Exercit. LXXXIII. §. 19. 20. Opponitur: Si sensus non haberemus, quomodo sciremus esse solem, &c. Resp. Non negamus, sensus nos docere, quod res sint, sive existentiam corporum (nam hoc requiritur, ut compositio prodesse aut nocere intelligantur): sed, non quid sint, sive essentiam & intimam naturam rerum, quia hoc non requiritur ad conservationem compositi, &c. Nam primùm, ineptè restringitur existentia rerum cognitio tantùm ad compositi bene-esse, cum etiam quod res sint scire debeat, quicunque ritè est philosophaturus: nisi frustrà tam anxiè tanto Meditationum & Dubitationum apparatu laboraverit Cartesius in demonstrandi rerum existentia; cui Tractatui ipse tribuere non dubitavit, titulum Primæ Philosophiæ. Verum deinceps, falsum quoque est, Sensus tantùm docere quod res sit, & non etiam quid sit. Exemplo sit cæcus, qui constanti omnium videntium consentiente testimonio persuasus esse poterit & debebit de Solis aut Lucis existentia; an autem is, absque Sensuum ope, solo intellectu indagare poterit essentiam atque intimam naturam alterutrius? Utique non poterit, si quicquam credendum sit experientiæ. Ipse Cartesius undenàm didicit lucis naturam intelligere, nisi ex hoc, quod observarit ad pressionem in oculo factam ab obvio corpore, scintillas quasi conspici? Quin hic ipse non uno textu clarè edisserit, sui quasi oblitus, Sensus etiam docere,
units.tr: Claubergius, however, by no means satisfies all that has been adduced so far, arguing in this way in De Cognitione Dei et Nostri, Exercitatio LXXXIII, §§ 19 and 20: It is objected: If we had no senses, how would we know that there is a sun, etc. Answer: We do not deny that the senses teach us that things are, that is, the existence of bodies (for this is required so that we may understand what benefits or harms the composite); but not what they are, that is, the essence and inner nature of things, because this is not required for the preservation of the composite, etc. For, first, it is foolishly restricted to the well-being of the composite alone, the knowledge of the existence of things, when anyone who is going to philosophize properly ought also to know that things are; unless Descartes laboured in vain, with such anxious apparatus of Meditations and Doubts, in demonstrating the existence of things, and to that treatise he did not hesitate to give the title First Philosophy. But further, it is also false that the senses teach only that a thing is, and not also what it is. Take as an example a blind man, who, persuaded by the constant and unanimous testimony of all who see, can and must believe in the existence of the Sun or of Light; but could he, without the aid of the senses, by the intellect alone, investigate the essence and inner nature of either? Certainly he could not, if anything is to be believed of experience. Whence did Descartes himself learn to understand the nature of light, unless from this, that he observed, on pressure made upon the eye by a body in the way, sparks as it were seen? Indeed, here he himself, in more than one passage, clearly sets out, as if forgetful of himself, that the senses also teach

units.la: XXV. Non existentia tantum sed & natura corporum adjumento Sensuum intelligitur. doccre, quid res sint & quales. Princip. 1. Artic.lxix. Quamvis enim videntes aliquod corpus, non magis certisimus illud existere, quatenus apparet figuratum, quam quatenus apparet coloratum; longè tamen evidentius agnoscimus, quid sit in eo esse figuratum, quam quid sit esse coloratum. Et, Artic. seq. Multa alia sunt, ut Magnitudo, Figura, Numerus, &c. quæ clarè percipimus non aliter à nobis sentiri vel intelligi, quam ut sunt, aut saltem esse possunt in objectis, &c. Iterùm, Princ. iii. Art. vi. Agnoscimus etiam visu ratione adjuto, Mercurium plus ducentis terræ diametris à Sole distare, &c. Rursùs, Diopt. Cap. i. Art. i. Miranda illa specilla in cœlo nova sydera detexe-re, &c. adeo ut, promota luminis acie ultra terminos, quibus imaginatio majorum sistebatur, viam simul nobis videantur aperisse ad majorem & magis absolutam naturæ cognitionem. Viderint quibus omnis Philosophiæ prora & puppis hic Auctor est, qui ista cohæreant cum iis, quæ ante audivimus asserere Cartesium, Solo intellectu utendum esse; Sensus autem datos esse ad composito commoda & incommoda indicanda; nec referri nisi ad corporis cum mente conjun- Quaecunque vero de Sensuum in philosophando usu hucusque disputavimus non sic accipienda veniunt, ac si contendamus, sensationem quamvis veritatis esse magistram, eique omni semper & ubique stare debere Philosophum. Nequaquam. Ut in re quavis alia sic & in hac sunt certi limites, quos ultra citraque rectum non consistit, quosque ideo hic assignare operae pretium fuerit, priusquam ad Objectiones descendimus; maximè cum harum solutio multo sit futura & brevior & facilior, si hac de re aliquid antè dixerimus. Summa eorum, quae observare necesse habet, quisquis Sensationes duces suae Scientiae ritè sumet, iisque judicium rebus conforme superstruet, hùc ferè redit. Caveat primo loco philosophaturus, ne Sensus assumat tanquam immediatum atque adaequatum cognitionis suae principium. Id namque si fecerit, vel infeliciter mentis suae vim nimium coarctabit, vel Sensationes ultra proprium objectum imprudenter extendet. Utroque modo errabit gravissimè. Quemadmodum enim multae veritates Philosopho occurrunt nullâ aliâ ratione indagandae quam Sensationum adjumento, sicuti ostendimus; itâ quoque inficiandum non est, res plurimas alias naturali rationis lumine cognoscendas esse,
units.tr: XXV. The nature of bodies, and not only their existence, is understood with the aid of the senses. what things are and of what kind. Principles, Part 1, Article 69: Although, when we see some body, we are no more certain that it exists insofar as it appears shaped than insofar as it appears coloured; yet we recognise far more evidently what it is to be shaped in it than what it is to be coloured. And: Article following: There are many other things, such as magnitude, figure, number, etc., which we clearly perceive are not felt or understood by us otherwise than as they are, or at least can be, in objects, etc. Again, Principles, Part 3, Article 6: We also recognise by sight, aided by reason, that Mercury is more than two hundred diameters of the earth distant from the Sun, etc. Again, Dioptrics, Chapter 1, Article 1: Those wonderful spectacles have discovered new stars in the heavens, etc., so that, the power of light having been advanced beyond the limits within which the imagination of the ancients was confined, they seem at the same time to have opened to us a way to a greater and more absolute knowledge of nature. Let those for whom this author is the beginning and end of all philosophy see how these things cohere with what we heard Descartes assert before: that one must use the intellect alone; that the senses, however, are given to indicate the benefits and harms of the composite, and refer only to the union of the body with the mind. But whatever we have so far argued about the use of the senses in philosophizing is not to be taken as if we contend that sensation is always and everywhere the teacher of truth, and that the philosopher must always and everywhere stand by it. By no means. As in any other matter, so in this there are certain limits, within which and beyond which one does not stand upright; and it will be worth while to assign them here, before we come to the objections, the more so since their solution will be much shorter and easier if we first say something on this matter. The sum of what he who rightly takes sensations as the guides of his science, and builds his judgement upon them in conformity with things, must observe, comes roughly to this. First, the philosopher must beware of taking the senses as the immediate and adequate principle of his knowledge. For if he does so, he will either unhappily restrict the power of his mind too much, or imprudently extend sensations beyond their proper object. He will err most grievously in either way. For just as many truths present themselves to the philosopher that can be investigated by no other means than with the aid of sensations, as we have shown; so too it must not be denied that many things are to be known by the natural light of reason,

units.la: XXVI. esse, quæ Sensum directè & per se vel nullo modo vel non nisi valdè debiliter afficiunt, quæque adeò ex immediata ejus perceptione simpliciter metienda nequaquam sunt. In istis uti sæpè solus Sensus sufficit, absque multa rationis indagine, itâ in his contrà sola suffecerit ratio, etiam Sensûs testimonio destituta. Putandum semper non est (verbis iterùm utar Lactantii. Instit. Lib. VII. Cap. XIII.) omnino non esse, quicquid oculis non apparet; cum mentis acies multo clarior debeat esse quam corporis, ad ea perspicienda, quorum vis ac ratio sentitur potius, quam videtur. Sensationibus qui itâ assuefacit cogitationes suas ut has ab illis nunquam divertere sinat, is parùm idoneus existit Dei rerumque Divinarum; Mentis item ejusque facultatum ac operationum; omniumque demùm veritatum spiritualium ac metaphysicarum contemplator. Ideoque (elegantèr Baco Lib. I. de Augm. Scient.) scitissimè dixit quidam Platonicus, Sensus humanos solem referre qui quidem revelat terrestrem globum, cælestem verò & stellas obsignat: Sic Sensus referant Naturalia, Divina occludunt. Atque hinc evenit, nonnullos e doctiorum manipulo in hæresin lapsos esse, quum ceratis Sensuum alis innixi, ad Divina evolare contenderent. Quid Antropomorphitis evenerit, notum. Neque alio argumento Democritus, Epicurus, Dicæarchus animam interire dixerunt, quam quia (teste Lactantio, loc. cit.) non pervidebant animæ rationem, quæ tam subtilis est, ut oculos effugiat. Confer. §. II. Non tamen hæc sic accipienda sunt, quasi iis Philosophum omni Sensationis Usu circa res Divinas & spirituales prohiberemus (nam & in iis ipsis quodammodo Sensus prodesse, jam antè §. XVI. XVII. indicatum fuit) sed id volumus, nemini itâ Sensibus adhærendum, ut in nuda eorum perceptione planè subsistat, atque altius non ascendat ratiocinando, quam quo usquè Sensus directè pertingunt.
units.tr: XXVI. ...which affect the sense directly and in themselves either not at all or only very weakly, and which therefore cannot be measured simply by its immediate perception. In such matters the sense alone often suffices, without much inquiry by reason; conversely, in these matters reason alone will suffice, even when it lacks the testimony of the senses. One must not always think (to use again the words of Lactantius, Instit. Lib. VII. Cap. XIII.) that whatever does not appear to the eyes does not exist at all; since the keenness of the mind ought to be much sharper than that of the body, for perceiving those things whose power and nature are felt rather than seen. He who so accustoms his thoughts to the senses that he never lets them turn away from them is poorly fitted to contemplate God and divine things, the mind and its faculties and operations, and finally all spiritual and metaphysical truths. Therefore (Bacon elegantly, Lib. I. de Augm. Scient.) a certain Platonist said very aptly: the human senses are like the sun, which reveals the terrestrial globe but seals up the heavenly bodies and the stars. Thus the senses reveal natural things, but shut out divine things. And from this it has happened that some of the more learned have fallen into heresy, when, relying on the waxen wings of the senses, they tried to fly up to divine things. What happened to the Anthropomorphites is well known. Democritus, Epicurus and Dicaearchus said that the soul perishes for no other reason than that (as Lactantius says, loc. cit.) they did not see the nature of the soul, which is so subtle that it escapes the eyes. Compare §. II. Yet these things should not be taken as if we forbade the philosopher every use of the senses in regard to divine and spiritual things (for it was already indicated above, §. XVI. XVII., that the senses are in some way useful even in these matters); what we mean is that no one should cling so closely to the senses as to rest entirely in their bare perception, and not rise higher by reasoning than the senses reach directly.

units.la: Deindè, id Philosopho Sensibus legitimè usuro agendum diligenter, ut cautè Sensationes veras, quas tutò in judicando sequatur, à fallacibus discernere norit. Discernet autem satis feliciter & haud difficili negotio, si in omni Sensûs operatione sedulò rationem habuerit Facultatis, Organi, Objecti, Medii. Neque enim, nisi accuratè expensis istis atque examinatis, num undequaquè bene se habeant, ex Sensûs indicio unquam judicabit prudens
units.tr: Next, the philosopher who uses the senses lawfully must take care to learn how to distinguish carefully the true sensations, which he may safely follow in judging, from the false ones. He will distinguish them quite successfully and with little difficulty, if in every operation of the senses he diligently takes account of the faculty, the organ, the object and the medium. For unless he has carefully weighed and examined these, to see whether they are altogether in good condition, the prudent person will never judge from the evidence of the senses.

units.la: XXVII. Discernenda quoque sensationes veras à fallacibus, & debita attentionis conscientia. sapientiæ studiosus. Facultatem sentiendi, sive, ut clarius dicam, ipsam suam mentem sensu quid percipientem attendet imprimis, an ea intensè satis circa oblatum objectum Sensibile fuerit actuosa, hoc unum agendo ? Si non fuerit, ipseque nihilominus negligenti Sensationi stare velit, Sensibus abutetur ; quippe qui dati sunt ad indicium veri, tunc tantùm, cùm debitâ diligentiâ & attentione vis sentiendi intenditur. Atque itâ nemo prudens, si sibi profundè meditabundo acciderit per Sensum aliqua objecti oblatio, v. c. si câmpanam aliquoties pulsari audiat, vel nummos alium numerantem videat, quicquam determinati statuet de numero pulsuum aut nummorum, etsi forte eum determinatum se observasse autumet : facilè enim animadvertit, animam suam seriò duabus diversis rebus accuratè simul observandis intentam esse minimè posse ; adeòque neque hoc in casu vim perceptivam, aliis occupatam, idoneam esse ad certò cognoscendum objectum minus attendenti oblatum.
units.tr: XXVII. The true sensations must also be distinguished from the false, and due awareness of attention. The student of wisdom must first attend to the faculty of sensing, or, to speak more clearly, to his own mind, which perceives through the sense: whether it has been sufficiently active and intent on the sensible object presented, doing this one thing alone. If it has not been, and he nevertheless wishes to rely on a careless sensation, he will be abusing the senses; for they are given as an indication of truth only when the power of sensing is exercised with due diligence and attention. And so no prudent person, if, while deep in thought, some object is presented to his sense, for instance if he hears a bell struck several times or sees someone counting coins, will state anything definite about the number of strokes or coins, even if he thinks he has observed the number exactly. For he readily notices that his mind, when seriously occupied with two different things that must both be observed accurately at once, cannot do so; and so in this case the perceptive power, being occupied with other things, is not fit to know with certainty an object presented to a mind that is not attending to it.

units.la: Organum quoque observabit, tum internum, puta, & notarum sensibilium commune receptaculum cerebrum], & carundem vehiculum spiritus animales, & meatus per quos spiritus ad cerebrum notas deferunt, nempe nervos; tum externum, unicuique Sensui proprium, oculum, aurem, &c. Id si sentiat compressum, constipatum, convulsum, distortum, disruptum, resolutum, inordinatè motum, aut alio quo modo vitiatum, Sensationi ejusmodi haud confidet; ut qui multâ experientiâ didicit, vitium organi inficere frequenter ipsam sensationem. Itâ, ex. gr. Ictericus aut Leucophlegmaticus, quamdiu talis, Visu abutetur, si eum sibi constituat ducem, ad judicandum de colorum discriminibus, dum omnia in oculo, alieno colore suffuso, pinguntur flava, aut pallida & tristiora. Sensu abutetur cbrius aut vertiginosus, si, circulatis in cerebro spiritibus animalibus, ac cum iis imaginibus impressis, pronunciet secundum cum de corporum extra se positorum motu aut quiete. Sensu abutetur strabo, si, dum, ob convulsos & distractos ex spasmo vel paralysi oculos, utramque axim visualem præcisè ad idem objecti punctum dirigere nequit, omniaque adeò apparent gemina, quid certi statuat de corporum numero, secundum visum. Sensu abutetur quicunque perplexis digitis globulum contrectans, dum, ob prae-
units.tr: He will also observe the organ, both the internal one, namely the cerebrum, the common receptacle of sensible marks, and the animal spirits, its vehicle, and the passages through which the spirits carry the marks to the brain, namely the nerves; and the external one, proper to each sense: the eye, the ear, and so on. If he perceives it to be compressed, clogged, convulsed, distorted, broken, relaxed, irregularly moved, or otherwise impaired, he will not trust such a sensation; for he has learned by much experience that a defect of the organ frequently taints the sensation itself. Thus, for example, a jaundiced or dropsical man, for as long as he is in that state, abuses his sight if he takes it as his guide in judging the differences of colours, since everything in his eye, suffused with an alien colour, is painted yellow, or pale and gloomier. A dizzy or giddy man abuses his sense if, with animal spirits circulating in his brain and images impressed on them, he pronounces on the motion or rest of bodies outside himself. A squint-eyed man abuses his sense if, because his eyes are convulsed and drawn apart by spasm or paralysis, he cannot direct both visual axes exactly to the same point of the object, so that everything appears double, and then makes some firm statement about the number of bodies according to sight. Whoever touches a globule with twisted fingers abuses his sense, when, because of the unnatural position of the nerves and the disturbed flow of spirits, he affirms that the twofold image conveyed to the sensorium by touch is one and the same, and so on.

units.la: XXVIII. Nec non, ex explorata recta organorum dispositione. præposterum nervorum situm perturbatumque spirituum fluxum gemina ejus imago ad sensorium defertur, secundum tactum, eundem esse affirmat : &c.
units.tr: XXVIII. Also, from the proven correct arrangement of the organs. ...the twofold image is conveyed to the sensorium, he asserts that it is the same by touch, etc.

units.la: A parte Objecti expendendum diligenter, an sit organo & facultati debite approportionatum, ratione distantiæ, situs, magnitudinis, motus, numeri, figuræ, aliorumque adjunctorum. Quæ si quis attendere negligat, ipse sibi erroris per Sensus exister causa, quoniam ignorare non poterat, usu edoctus, Sensum hebetiorem esse, quam ut à quovis objecto sufficienter & distincte possit affici, suamque idcirco habere activitatis sphæram, extra quam eum extendere nefas sit. Sic v. g. Sensu abutetur, quicunque de longinquo videns animal humi reptans, forte hominem, judicat esse feram; aut turrim quadrilateram esse planam vel rotundam; aut solem & stellas fixas (forte angulosas) esse præcisè orbiculares, aut non majores, quam apparent: scire enim potuisset & debuisset, nihil determinandum esse ex solo Visu de re tam procul à conspectu remota, ut radiare sufficienter nequeat, ad assiciendum satis distincte oculum per omnes & singulos sui angulos & partes. Simili modo Sensu abutetur, quicunque, visui fidens circa objecta situ suo & distantia in ordine ad oculum diversissima, autumat, series arborum secundum parallelas distantes, tandem coire; aut quadratum nec æquilaterum nec æquiangulum esse, sed rhombum aut rhomboidem; aut unum idemque triangulum, nunc orthogonium, nunc oxygonium, nunc amblygonium esse; cum cogitandum fuisset mutato situ & distantia mutari angulum visionis ac apparentem partium corporis figurationem & positu-ram. Similiter, ex non observata hac conditione à parte Objecti, Sensu abutitur, qui affirmat, titionem flammantem ocyssime circumactum integrum circulum ardentem post se relinquere: cum cogitandum sit, celerrimam circulationem ardentis puncti non permittere, ut distincta ejus per singulas spatii quod pertransit partes in oculo fiat impressio.
units.tr: On the part of the object, one must carefully consider whether it is suitably proportioned to the organ and the faculty, with regard to distance, position, size, motion, number, shape, and other accompanying circumstances. If someone neglects to attend to these, he is himself the cause of his error through the senses; for, taught by experience, he could not fail to know that the sense is too dull to be affected sufficiently and distinctly by every object, and that it therefore has its own sphere of activity, beyond which it is wrong to extend it. Thus, for example, he abuses his sense who, seeing from a distance an animal creeping on the ground, judges it perhaps to be a man, or a wild beast; or who judges a square tower to be flat or round; or who judges the sun and the fixed stars (perhaps angular) to be exactly circular, or no larger than they appear. For he could and should have known that nothing is to be determined from sight alone about a thing so remote from view that it cannot radiate enough to affect the eye sufficiently and distinctly through all its angles and parts. In the same way he abuses his sense who, trusting his sight with regard to objects whose position and distance relative to the eye are very different, asserts that a series of trees in parallel rows at a distance finally meet; or that a square that is neither equilateral nor equiangular is a rhombus or rhomboid; or that one and the same triangle is now right-angled, now acute-angled, now obtuse-angled. For he should have considered that with a change of position and distance the visual angle changes, and so does the apparent shape and arrangement of the parts of the body. Likewise, from not observing this condition on the part of the object, he abuses his sense who affirms that a burning firebrand, whirled very swiftly around, leaves behind it a complete burning circle; for one should consider that the very rapid circling of the glowing point does not allow a distinct impression of each part of the space it traverses to be made on the eye.

units.la: Medium denique, per quod species sensibilis ad organum defertur, examinandum, an non id sit varie tinctum? an non diversæ raritatis aut densitatis? an non motu irregulari agitatum? &c. Ex quibus causis non raro evenit, ut res appareant prorsus alia figura, magnitudine, loco, colore, numero, motu, &c. quam à parte te rei existunt. Quod fi ejus periculum fit, Senfationi tali fidem non plane adhibebit vir prudens, cum non una vice expertus fit, pro diversitate medii etiam diversis modis idem objectum agere in organum. Sensu itaque abutetur v g. quisquis viridi perspicillo usus res conspectas judicat esse viridis coloris, aut, quos de longinquo intuetur montes, albos re vera, esse cæruleos; quùm mutata fit, priusquam radii oculum afficiunt, per intermedii vitri aut aëris dispositionem, luminis cum umbra commixtio, quæ est præcipua colorationis causa. Sensu eâdem ratione abutetur, qui judicat, remum aquæ immissum sub fluctu esse fractum; nummum in urna, aqua superfusâ, propiorem esse oculo quam idem erat nudus; pisciculos in flumine natantes esse grandiores, quam sunt alii ejusdem magnitudinis hamo ex aqua exftracti; solem ad horizontem majorem esse quam est sub meridiano. In his enim omnibus medium diversum, majori suâ aut minori raritate, faciliorem aut difficiliorem radiis transitum præbens, eosdem etiam varie, modo à perpendiculo, modo ad perpendiculum, reflectit & refringit, consequenter angulum visionis auget vel minuit magis aut minus, pro re nata; sicque res easdem aliter atque aliter spectandas offert. Sensu similiter abutetur, qui per halitum tremulo motu ascendentem, aut per aërem crassiorem vento agitatum intuitus corpora, trepidare eadem putat; quùm non alia quam trepidans species per tremulum medium ad sensorium deferri possit: &c.
units.tr: Finally, the medium through which the sensible species is conveyed to the organ must be examined: whether it is not variously tinted; whether it is not of different rarity or density; whether it is not agitated by irregular motion, and so on. From these causes it not infrequently happens that things appear quite different in shape, size, place, colour, number, motion, and so on, from what they really are. If there is a risk of this, a prudent man will not place full trust in such a sensation, since he has not once found that the same object acts on the organ in different ways according to the diversity of the medium. Thus he abuses his sense who, using green spectacles, judges the things he sees to be of a green colour, or who judges the mountains he gazes at from afar, which are really white, to be blue, when, before the rays strike the eye, the arrangement of an intervening glass or air changes the mixture of light and shadow, which is the chief cause of colouring. He abuses his sense in the same way who judges that an oar immersed in water is broken beneath the surface; or that a coin in a jar, with water poured over it, is nearer the eye than it was when bare; or that small fish swimming in a river are larger than other fish of the same size drawn out of the water on a hook; or that the sun is larger at the horizon than it is at the meridian. For in all these cases the different medium, by its greater or lesser rarity, offering an easier or more difficult passage to the rays, also reflects and refracts them variously, now away from the perpendicular, now towards it, and consequently increases or decreases the visual angle more or less, as the case may be; and so it presents the same things to be seen differently at different times. Likewise he abuses his sense who, looking at bodies through vapour rising with a trembling motion, or through thicker air agitated by wind, thinks the bodies are trembling; since nothing but a trembling species can be conveyed to the sensorium through a trembling medium, and so on.

units.la: At fortasse omnibus hactenus allatis nihil prorsus effecisse videbimur quibusdam, qui regerent: Papæ! Tanto ad Sensibus utendum opus est apparatu! tantâ attentione! Quis demùm, istæc omnia observanda fi sint, fe quicquam rectè sentire, certus erit? Et cur non potius Sensuum Usus, in veritatibus Philosophicis inquirendis, tam iis redditur onerosus, intricatus, ac periculi plenus, ut cum vel omninò istic negligere præstiterit? Quibus suffecerit respondisse, eâdem difficultate nos absterreri posse ab ipso rationis, judicii, ac discursûs usu. Quis enim existit, cui unquam institutiones Logicæ perfectæ sunt, qui ignoret, plurimis, iisque obfervatu difficillimis regulis ac legibus ratiocinia nostra adstringi sic, ut eas non ad amussim secuti certi existere nequeamus, nos nostrâ ratione benè usos fuisse. Ne quis verò, dùm præceptorum Logicorum memini, innui tantum hìc à me putet antiquorum Philosophorum
units.tr: But perhaps some will say that everything I have adduced so far has achieved nothing at all: "Goodness! Does the use of the senses really need such apparatus, such close attention? Who, in the end, could be certain he perceives anything correctly if all these things must be observed? And why should the use of the senses, in inquiring into philosophical truths, not rather be made so burdensome, intricate and full of danger that it would be better to neglect it altogether?" It is enough to answer that we could be deterred by the same difficulty from the very use of reason, judgment and reasoning. For who has ever mastered the perfect rules of logic without knowing that our reasonings are bound by so many rules, and by such difficult ones to observe, that unless we follow them exactly we cannot be certain we have used our reason well? Lest anyone think, when I mention the precepts of logic, that I am hinting only at the logic of the ancient philosophers,

units.la: XXXI. Neque diffi-cilius hæc attendum-tur, quam regulæ qui-bus intelle-ctus perce-ptiones re-guntur.
units.tr: XXXI. Nor is this harder to attend to than the rules by which the perceptions of the intellect are governed.

units.la: rum Logicam, quam Neoterici per contemptum Vulgarem, Scholasticam, ac Pedanticam (itâ loquuntur) appellant, & totam tanquam ineptam, propterea quod innumeris inutilibus præceptis ipsorum judicio abundat, rejiciunt ac traducunt, ad ipsas Recentiorum artes dirigendi cogitationes, Tractatus de Ratiocinatione legitima, vel si quo alio exstent titulo ipsorum recte ratiocinandi regulæ, ad ipsas illas, inquam, provoco, ne excepta quidem Cartesii ipsius quatuor duntaxat canonum Logicâ, quam proponit, Differt. de Method. p. 11. 12. & quidvis ausim deponere, si intelligere ac praxi applicare præcepta in usu rationis legitimo inibi præfixa minus arduum sit, quam est observare in Sensationibus regulas modò à nobis enumeratas. Quum itaque nulla ratio reddi possit, ob quam difficilius sit Sensu in philosophando legitimè uti, quam ratione, cum utrobique cautiones, etsi difficiles satis, necessariò observandæ occurrant, hactenus non est, cur solus intellectus, non etiam Sensus, in Philosophia usurpandus præscribatur.
units.tr: which the Moderns, out of contempt, call the common, scholastic and pedantic logic (so they speak), and which they reject and disparage as worthless because, in their judgment, it abounds in countless useless precepts, I appeal to the very art of reasoning of the more recent writers to direct our thinking: their treatises on correct reasoning, or whatever other titles their rules of right reasoning bear. I appeal to those, I say, not excepting even the logic of Descartes himself with its four canons alone, which he sets out in the Discourse on Method, pp. 11, 12. And I would venture anything that understanding and applying in practice the precepts laid down there for the lawful use of reason is less arduous than observing the rules just listed concerning sensations. Since, then, no reason can be given why it should be harder to use the senses lawfully in philosophy than reason, when both require cautions that, though difficult enough, must necessarily be observed, there is so far no reason why the intellect alone, and not the senses too, should be prescribed for use in philosophy.

units.la: Interim neque adeò existit difficile notare, utrùm conditiones recensitæ adsint in nostra Senfatione, nec ne, quam fortè primâ fronte videtur, dummodò, priusquam de re sensibili ex Sensuum fide pronunciamus, hisce duobus attendendis nosmet assuefecerimus: quibus suâ sponte quasi fallax si quis fuerit nobis detegitur Sensus. Primùm, & antecfactas frequenter Senfationes revocabimus in memoriam, ac cum iis præsentes conferemus, & ipsas præsentes variis quibuscunque licuerit modis repetemus. Si contingat prorsùs alia ratione objecta Sensibus offerri, neque tamen ulla subitæ mutationis in iis deprehendatur causa; vel etiam, si recordemur in similibus circumstantiis Sensuum testimonio nos aliquandò delusos fuisse, merito suspicabimur, quin certi satis erimus, aliquid decesse Sensus perceptioni, vel à parte Facultatis, vel Organi; vel Objecti, vel Medii; nihilque adeò, vel parùm, Sensationi tali fidemus. Videat, utantè dixi, Ictericus omnia, quæ obversantur Visui, flava; non tamen, si prudens sit, flavaesse credet. Dùm enim recordatur, nuper admodum eadem illa corpora, quæ nunc uniformi colore tincta apparent, constanterac sæpissimè debita cum animi attentione se conspexisse multiplici colorum varietate interstincta, dumque simul circumstantias expendens nullam invenit à parte rei insoliti coloris causam, olfacit facilè, nisi sit extremè ineptus, non objecta, sed vel Organum, vel Medium Sentiendi, pravam aliquam subiisse mutationem, cujus vitio flava offeruntur visui, quæ talia re vera non sunt. Turrim quadratam (ut & veterem hanc contra Sensus certitudinem allatam ab Academicis objectionem verbo tollam) qui de longinquo intuetur rotundam, eam talem esse non affirmabit; quoniam, mente repetitâ objectorum remotorum quæ antehac obtigit visione, meminit, sæpius quam semel aliâ figurâ ea se ingessisse oculis, quam quâ à parte sui exstiterant: Objectum ergò hoc visui, ratione distantiæ, approportionatum non esse, per se liquet. Idemque similibus in casibus hac methodo explorare unicuique pronum est.
units.tr: Meanwhile it is not so very difficult to note whether the conditions mentioned are present in our sensation or not, as might seem at first sight, provided that, before we pronounce on a sensible thing on the strength of the senses, we have accustomed ourselves to attend to these two points, by which the sense, if it is in any way deceptive, reveals itself to us of its own accord. First, we shall often recall to mind earlier sensations, compare them with present ones, and repeat the present ones in whatever ways we can. If an object happens to be presented to the senses in a quite different way, and yet no cause of a sudden change in it is detected, or if we remember that in similar circumstances we have at some time been deceived by the testimony of the senses, we shall rightly suspect, and be sure enough, that something is lacking in the perception of the sense, whether on the side of the faculty or the organ, the object or the medium; and so we shall trust such a sensation little or not at all. Let the jaundiced man, as I said, see everything before his sight as yellow; yet if he is wise he will not believe that it is yellow. For when he recalls that these same bodies, which now appear tinted with a uniform colour, he has recently seen, and that constantly and very often with due attention, marked by a great variety of colours, and when at the same time, weighing the circumstances, he finds no cause in the thing itself for the unusual colour, he will readily perceive, unless he is extremely foolish, that it is not the object but the organ or medium of sensing that has undergone some bad change, through whose fault yellow things are presented to the sight which in truth are not so. Whoever looks from afar at a square tower and takes it to be round (let me also dispose of the old objection of the Academics against the certainty of the senses) will not affirm that it is round; for, recalling the remote objects he has seen before, he remembers that more than once they have presented themselves to his eyes in a shape other than that which they had in themselves. It is therefore plain that this object is not suited to sight at such a distance. And it is easy for anyone to test this by the same method in similar cases.

units.la: Deinde, in subsidium vocandi sunt, quantùm fieri potest, plures Sensus: quippe qui mirum in modum à natura in mutuum auxilium ordinati observantur. Itâ ut vel hinc innotescat ac firmiter concludatur, divinitùs sic constitutum esse, ut ad Sensus recurramus etiam in discernendo vero à falso. Nempè plenam fidem & indubitatam persuasionem facit duorum aut trium testium in rem eandem consensus. Jucundissimum foret, providam hanc sapientissimi Dei curam paulò plenius demonstrare in admirandâ Sensuum omnium inter se concatenatione: at ne sim in hisce prolixior justo, solùm Visum & Tactum ex cæteris obiter attendamus; quique hi sibi mutuo succurrant, ad docendum, quid verum sit quod sentitur, quid apparens, exemplo uno aut altero illustremus! Sit, cui omnia trepidare aut in gyrum agi videntur; manum si admoverit, illicò vitio turbati organi, vel tremuli medii, se errasse deprehendet. Pictum Parrhasii velum removeri jubeat imprudenter Zeuxis; at applicato digito visùs fallaciam nullo negotio castigare poterit. Multiplicet vel millies objectum superficiebus variè distinctis & inclinatis expolitum vitrum; rem unam esse ac simplicem itâ manifestè palpabit manus, ut mox appareat perspicilli fraus. Contrà, perplexis digitis pilam quis, oculis clausis, tam distinctè contrectet, ut juret geminam esse; facilìmè uno oculi nictu oriundum ex distorto organo errorem corriget visus. Quæ pauca, ex millenis aliis spectiminis ausa allata, docent abundè, quam sit facile, levi labore dignoscere, utrum Organum, Objectum, Medium, se habeant in Sensatione uti decet, nec ne?
units.tr: Second, as many senses as possible should be called in to help. For nature has marvellously arranged them to support one another. Hence it may be learned from this and firmly concluded that God has so arranged things that we should have recourse to the senses even in distinguishing truth from falsehood. Indeed, the agreement of two or three witnesses to the same matter makes full faith and an undoubted persuasion. It would be most pleasant to demonstrate this provident care of the most wise God a little more fully, in the admirable interconnection of all the senses with one another; but lest I be too long-winded here, let us briefly consider only sight and touch among the rest, and let us illustrate, by one or two examples, how these help each other to teach what is true in what is perceived and what is merely apparent. Suppose someone finds that everything seems to tremble or to turn in a circle; if he puts his hand to it, he will at once discover that he has erred through a defect of the organ or a trembling medium. Suppose Zeuxis carelessly orders the painted veil of Parrhasius to be removed; but once he applies his finger, he can easily correct the deception of sight. If a glass polished with variously shaped and inclined surfaces multiplies an object a thousand times, the hand will plainly feel that it is one simple thing, and the fraud of the spectacles will soon appear. Conversely, if someone, with eyes closed, touches a ball with crossed fingers so distinctly that he swears there are two, sight, with a single blink, will easily correct the error arising from the distorted organ. These few examples, taken from a thousand others, abundantly show how easy it is, with little labour, to discern whether the organ, the object and the medium are in the state they should be in for sensation or not.

units.la: Verùm, missis illis, ratiunculas nunc examinemus, quae contra Sensuum in philosophando usum proferuntur! Earum primaria, quam ceu formidabile Gorgonis caput objiciunt semper, petita est à fallaciis vulgò Sensibus tribui solitis. Quum enim fundamentum, cui cognitio nostra Philosophica innitetur, certum esse oporteat & erroris nequaquam obnoxium, tale verò non sit testimonium Sensuum, perperam hoc inter indubitatae scientiae principia numerari concludunt.
