Scilicet, ut alibi Cicero, ubi quis semel pejeraverit, ei credi postea, etiam si per plures Deos juret, non convenit; & secundum Juris regulam, Qui semel malus deprehenditur, semper malus praesumitur. Quae eadem ratio Epicurum movit ad statuendum, Nunquam Sensus mentiri, sed omnes veros esse, in iisque judicia rerum posita; quorum si unus semel in vita mentitus sit, sublatum esse omne judicium veri & falsi: teste Cicerone, 1. de Finib. Pari acumine ex oppositio hic infertur, Sensus interdum fallere deprehendi, ac prudentiae esse, nunquam illis plane confidere, qui nos vel semel deceperunt. Quasi & ego dicam, eâdem consequentiâ, ac totidem ferè verbis: Ideas nostras interdum fallere deprehendimus, ac prudentiae est, nunquam illis plane confidere, qui nos vel semel deceperunt. Exulent ergò jam ex Philosophia cum Sensationibus, Antiquae Philosophiae inter caetera fulcro non minimo, Ideae, Novae Sapientiae palladium! Quin exulet in inquirenda certa rei veritate omnis in universum Memoriae, Judicii ac Discursus Usus! Nemo enim mortalium tantum sibi arrogaverit, ut nunquam ab iis omnibus se deceptum fuisse affirmare ausit.
units.tr: But, leaving those aside, let us now examine the little arguments that are brought against the use of the senses in philosophy. The chief of these, which they always throw up like the dreadful head of the Gorgon, is taken from the deceptions commonly attributed to the senses. For since the foundation on which our philosophical knowledge rests ought to be certain and in no way liable to error, and the testimony of the senses is not such, they conclude that it is wrongly counted among the principles of indubitable knowledge. Clearly, as Cicero says elsewhere, when someone has once perjured himself, it is not fitting to believe him afterwards, even if he swears by several gods; and according to the rule of law, He who is once found to be bad is always presumed to be bad. The same reasoning moved Epicurus to hold: The senses never lie, but all are true, and judgments of things rest on them; if one of them has lied even once in a lifetime, all judgment of true and false is abolished, as Cicero reports in the first book On Ends. With equal acuteness the opposite is inferred here: that the senses are sometimes found to deceive, and that it is a matter of prudence never to trust completely those who have deceived us even once. As if I too were to say, by the same consequence and in almost the same words: we find that our ideas sometimes deceive us, and it is a matter of prudence never to trust completely those who have deceived us even once. Let the Ideas, then, now be banished from philosophy along with the sensations, the Ideas which, among other things, were no small prop of ancient philosophy and the palladium of the New Wisdom! Indeed, let every use of memory, judgment and reasoning in the universe be banished from the inquiry into the certain truth of things! For no mortal has ever claimed so much for himself as to dare to affirm that he has never been deceived by all of them.

units.la: Quin quanto frequentiores sunt & graviores errores Intellectus quam Sensus, tanto quoque major erit causa illi magis quam huic diffidendi in cognoscenda rerum veritate. Nempe id observandum obiter, errorem, proprie loquendo, non nisi ad mentem pertinere; quae fallitur, quoties copulat aut disjungit notiones praedicatorum, quae à parte rei copulata aut disjuncta non sunt. Sensus cum errare dicitur, denominatio duntaxat externa est; quatenus per Sensationes mentì fiunt occasiones judicium ferendi rebus Sensu perceptis difforme, adeoque erroneum. Errat quapropter Sensus nunquam sine Intellectu; imò errat re verâ solus Intellectus, imprudenti præcipitantia Sensu abutens, eumque ultra limites suos extendens. Quumque propter quod unumquodque est tale id ipsum sit magis tale, evidentissimum erit, in philosophando minus esse tribuendum Intellectui quam Sensui, siquidem verum sit, prudentiæ esse, nunquam illis planè confidere, qui nos vel semel deceperunt. Quis ergò non videat, admittendam neutiquam esse ratiocinationem, quæ, unà cum Sensuum in indagando vero ministerio, evertit alia quævis, quæ homini ad manum esse possunt, philosophandi adminicula; nihilque ei reliquum facit, quam ut in Scepticorum castra aut Fratrum ignorantiæ societatem transeat?
units.tr: Indeed, the more frequent and the more serious the errors of the intellect are compared with those of the senses, the greater will be the reason for distrusting the intellect rather than the senses in discovering the truth of things. It should be observed in passing that error, properly speaking, pertains only to the mind. The mind is deceived whenever it joins or separates the notions of predicates which, in the nature of things, are not joined or separated. When the senses are said to err, this is only an external way of speaking, since through sensations they furnish the mind with occasions for passing a judgment on things perceived by the senses that does not match them and is therefore erroneous. So the senses never err without the intellect; in truth the intellect alone errs, abusing the senses through imprudent haste and extending them beyond their limits. And since that which makes each thing what it is also makes it more so, it will be most evident that in philosophizing less should be attributed to the intellect than to the senses, if it is true that it is a mark of prudence never to trust completely those who have deceived us even once. Who then does not see that we cannot admit a line of reasoning which, along with the senses' service in searching out the truth, overthrows every other aid to philosophizing that is at hand for a man, and leaves him nothing but to go over to the camp of the Sceptics or to the fellowship of the Brethren of Ignorance?

units.la: Inquies, mentis nostræ perceptionibus tutò sæpè credimus, quia de harum veritate certò possumus exist ere persuasi; cum, si quæ in iis reperiatur falsitas, aliqua etiam nobis à Deo facultas tributa sit, ad illam emendandam. Recte equidem, & opportunè! Non minus scilicet ad manum sunt adminicula, quorum beneficio haud magis difficulter detegatur, quid veri falsive unicuique Sensationi subsit; uti manifestum est ex illis, quæ de Sensuum deceptionibus cavendis retrò disputavimus. Limitandus itaque canon, de non fidendo ei qui semel nos decepit; & res omnis salva est. Videlicet, ci qui semel decepit, iisdem in circumstantiis, quarum occasione decepit, quoties in potestate nostra non est explorare verumne testetur an falsum, fidendum planè non est. Sed nil jam ex Sensuum fallaciis conficitur amplius, quam, quemadmodum cuivis promiscuè mentis perceptioni, itâ neque omni Sensationi, semper & ubique fidendum esse; sed ci tantum, quæ adhibito tempore & cura, vera esse ac certa deprehenditur. Quibus verò indè elici queat fiduciulis, ex Sensuum perceptionibus de rebus extra nos positis nil certi concludendum esse; neque iis utendum, tanquam veritatis magistris, cum nuncupatione ordinis perversionem, quod concludendum erat, audire lubet? Alia, eaque elegantissima notat Gassendus ad hoc argumentum de Sensuum fallaciis, quæ apud ipsum vide, Instit. p. 20.
units.tr: You will object that we often trust the perceptions of our mind safely, because we can be certain of their truth, since if any falsehood is found in them, some faculty has also been given us by God to correct it. Rightly indeed, and to the point! There are no less ready aids, by whose help it is not much more difficult to detect what truth or falsehood lies under each sensation, as is clear from what we disputed above about guarding against the deceptions of the senses. The rule that one should not trust the man who has deceived us once is therefore to be limited, and the whole matter is safe. That is, one should certainly not trust the person who has deceived us once, in the same circumstances in which he deceived us, whenever it is not in our power to examine whether his testimony is true or false. But nothing more follows from the senses' deceptions than that, just as one should not trust every mental perception indiscriminately, so one should not trust every sensation always and everywhere, but only that which, with time and care applied, is found to be true and certain. But from what could a small trust be drawn, namely that nothing certain is to be concluded from sense perceptions about things outside us, and that they should not be used as teachers of truth? Is it pleasing to hear the perversion of order, with the name of order, when the conclusion was meant to be something else? Gassendus notes other and very elegant points on this argument about the deceptions of the senses; you may see them in his Institutio, p. 20.

units.la: Mirum verò, ut & hoc addam, si omnino prudentiæ sit, iis non confidere, qui vel semel deceperunt, mirum, inquam, qui imprudentiæ notam effugere queat Cartesius, quandò totius vitæ animalis malis regimini duces præficit Sensus. Certè sæpius quam semel Sensus nos decepisse, etiam in iis quæ ad res hujus vitæ pertinent, experimur quotidiè adeò multoties, ut nec difficile videatur ipse Auctor, Medit. vi. Sensus, ait, circa ea quæ ad corporis commodum spectant multo frequentius verum indicant, quam sallsum. Nec juvant quæ proximè sequuntur, de homine qui possit uti semper pluribus sensibus ad eandem rem examinandam; & insuper memoriâ, quæ præsentia cum præcedentibus conneetitur; & intellectu, qui jam omnes errandi causas perspexit; quique ideo non amplius vereri debeat, ne illa, quæ ei quotidie à Sensibus exhibentur, sint falsa. Non ista juvant, aut si juvant, etiam ab imprudentia & naturæ ordinis perversione excusant Philosophum, quandò Sensibus utitur in inquirenda rerum veritate; cum non minus hîc, quam in iis quæ ad corporis commodum spectant, ipse circa eandem rem & sensibus pluribus, & memoriâ insuper & intellectu, uti possit; quare neque hic amplius vereri debebit, si ista cura sufficit, ne illa, quæ ei quotidiè à Sensibus exhibentur cognoscenda, sint falsa. Vel ergò æquè fidus sensus est ad promovendas cogitationes philosophicas quam ad vitæ moderamen: vel, si, ob suas fallacias illis juvandis sit impar, etiam hujus imperio parum idoneus existit.
units.tr: Indeed it is remarkable, and I will add this too, that if it is truly a matter of prudence not to trust those who have deceived us even once, it is remarkable, I say, how Descartes can escape the mark of imprudence when he sets the senses as leaders over the whole bad government of animal life. Certainly we experience daily that the senses have deceived us more than once, even in those matters that pertain to the affairs of this life, and so many times that the author himself does not seem to find it difficult. In his Meditations, vi, he says: The senses, with regard to what concerns the convenience of the body, indicate the truth much more often than falsehood. Nor do the things that immediately follow help, about the man who can always use several senses to examine the same thing; and besides, memory, which connects present things with past ones; and the intellect, which has now perceived all the causes of error; and who therefore ought no longer to fear that those things which are presented to him daily by the senses are false. These things do not help; or if they help, they excuse the philosopher from imprudence and from the perversion of the order of nature only when he uses the senses in searching out the truth. For here, no less than in those things which concern the convenience of the body, he himself can use several senses about the same thing, and besides memory and intellect; wherefore he too ought no longer to fear, if this care suffices, that those things which are presented to him daily by the senses to be known are false. Either, then, the senses are equally trustworthy for advancing philosophical thought as for guiding life; or, if because of their deceptions they are unequal to helping in the one, they are also little suited to govern the other.
XXXVIII

units.la: Profligatâ sic primâ acie, quæ instrui solet ex Sensuum erroribus, satis exaggeratis, quo evincatur, eos, ceu errorum matres, atque infantilium præjudiciorum obstetrices, Philosophaturo esse ab indagine veri ceu noxios removendos, alteri nunc est occurrendum, quæ Sensuum perceptiones inutiles eidem reddere allaborat. Non minus autem hæc priore illâ terribilis est & specie & numero; itâ benè est coagmentata ex innumerabilium clarissimarum ac distinctissimarum idearum innatarum (quas fatua mens, dum in sinu circumfert, excutere tamen plerumquè ignara est) apparatu absolutissimo. Nimirùm, cum mens, quæ se ipsam novit, undiquaque circumspicit, ut cognitionem suam ulterius extendat, invenit apud se multarum rerum ideas. Princip. i. Art. xiii. Itaquè ad serio philosophandum, veritatemque omnium rerum cognoscibilium indagandam, ordine tantum attendendum ad notiones, quas ipsimet in nobis habemus. Ibid. Art. lxxv. Atque ita solo intellectu, ad ideas sibi à natura insitas diligenter attendente, hic utemur. Princip. ii. Art. iii. Nec lubet, nec opus est, hoc loco anxiè inquirere, quirere, quid ista sibi velit innatarum idearum supellex, quâ instructa mens nascatur. Eas solas (quodcunque tandem earum nomine intellectum velint) rerum cognitioni acquirendæ non sufficere, infantes & fatui abundè docent; qui, etsi non minus quam alii iis abundent, nihil tamen inde habent, ne micam quidem, intelligentiæ rerum. Nempe sensuum legitimo usu destituuntur, qui requiritur, datis etiam innatis ideis, ad excitandas saltem illas: adeò, sine sensu ideis uti nulli in hoc statu unionis est possibile. Scitè quadrat in ultos, qui ex solis ideis, remoto sensu, sapere instituunt, quod alibi, quem & sæpius citavi, Lactantius, Instit. lib. 3. Cap. 3. Scientia ab ingenio venire non potest; nec cogitatione comprehendi: quia in se ipso habere propriam scientiam, non hominis, sed Dei est. Mortalis autem natura non capit scientiam, nisi quæ venit extrinsecus. Idcirco enim oculos, & aures, & cæteros Sensus patefecit in corpore Divina solertia, ut per eos aditus scientia perveniret ad mentem.
units.tr: Once the first line of attack, which is usually drawn up from the errors of the senses (greatly exaggerated, to show that they, as the mothers of errors and the midwives of childish prejudices, must be removed as harmful from the one who is going to philosophize, in the search for truth), has been overthrown, we must now meet the second line, which labours to render the perceptions of the senses useless to the same man. Yet this line is no less terrifying than the former in appearance and in number; it is so well put together from the most complete apparatus of countless, very clear and very distinct innate ideas (which the foolish mind, while it carries them about in its bosom, is for the most part ignorant of how to shake out). Namely, when the mind, which knows itself, looks around on every side in order to extend its knowledge further, it finds within itself the ideas of many things. Principles i, art. 13. Therefore, to philosophize seriously and to search out the truth of all knowable things, we need only attend in order to the notions which we ourselves have within us. Ibid., art. 75. And so, using the intellect alone, attending diligently to the ideas implanted in it by nature, we shall proceed here. Principles ii, art. 3. It is neither pleasing nor necessary to inquire anxiously here what this stock of innate ideas, with which the mind is born equipped, means. That these alone (whatever meaning they wish to attach to the name) do not suffice for acquiring knowledge of things, infants and fools teach abundantly; for although they abound in these no less than others, they nevertheless derive from them not even a crumb of understanding of things. Clearly they lack the lawful use of the senses, which is required, even when innate ideas are given, at least to awaken those ideas; so that, in this state of union, it is impossible to use ideas without sense. Lactantius, whom I have also cited more than once, fits very aptly those fools who set out to be wise from ideas alone, with the senses removed. In his Institutes, book 3, chapter 3, he says: Knowledge cannot come from talent, nor be grasped by thought; for to have knowledge in oneself is the property not of man but of God. Mortal nature, however, does not take in knowledge except what comes from outside. For this reason the divine skill opened in the body the eyes, the ears, and the other senses, so that by these passages knowledge might reach the mind.

units.la: Quæ aliæ adferri possunt rationes, quibus sensus in philosophando inutiles demonstrentur, eas accuratè adeò congessit Claubergius, citatâ Exercitat. LXXXIII. de Cognit. Dei & Nostri, ut vix amplius quid quod alicujus sit momenti objici posse videatur: quapropter breviter examinatis quæ apud hunc occurrunt, merito finem huic Dissertationi imponemus. Postalia, quæ loc. cit. apud cum legi possunt, quæque exhibere prolixius foret, sic arguit: Quæ ratione corporis & animæ simul homini tributa sunt, illa non nisi ad compositum ipsum, qua tale, referenda. Quod cum de fame & siti, & talibus, facile quis dederit, cur non dabit de Sensibus? Resp. Nullæ actiones hominis, ne quidem rationales, v.c. judicium, discursus, &c. ita in solidum menti, dum & quatenus est in statu unionis (casus extraordinarios, qualis obtinet v. c. in ecstasi, &c. excipio) tribuendæ sunt, ut nullam sibi in iis partem vendicet corpus; suppeditando saltem occasiones, aliisve modis operationes mentis promovendo. Neque id mirum est: cum enim actiones suppositorum sint, operandique modus sequatur modum subsistendi, mens autem corpori hypostaticè exi-stat unita, omninò rationi consonum est, & experientiâ in sensibus, melancholicis, aliisque comprobatum, non sine corpore cogitare mentem, uti non sine mente movetur corpus. Igitur, cum nullæ sint actiones ho-
units.tr: The other arguments which might be brought forward to show that the senses are useless in philosophizing, Clauberg has gathered together so carefully, in the Exercitation LXXXIII, On the Knowledge of God and of Ourselves, which I have cited, that hardly anything more of any weight seems to be left to object. Therefore, having briefly examined those which occur in him, we shall rightly bring this Dissertation to an end. The other arguments, which can be read in the place cited, and which it would be too lengthy to set out, he argues thus: Whatever is attributed to man jointly from body and soul must be referred only to the composite itself, as such. Since one would easily grant this of hunger and thirst and such things, why would one not grant it of the senses? Reply: No actions of man, not even rational ones, for example judgment, discursus, and so on, are attributed so wholly to the mind, while and insofar as it is in the state of union (I except extraordinary cases, such as obtain for example in ecstasy, etc.), that the body claims for itself no part in them, supplying at least occasions or otherwise promoting the operations of the mind. Nor is this surprising: since actions belong to suppositums, and the mode of operating follows the mode of subsisting, and the mind is hypostatically united to the body, it is entirely consonant with reason, and has been proved by experience in the senses, in melancholics, and in others, that the mind does not think without the body, just as the body is not moved without the mind. Therefore, since there are no actions of man

units.la: XXXIX. Quamvis toti composito Sensus conveniant, non idè tamen ad vitæ usum pertinent, ut recte ringendi.
units.tr: XXXIX. Although the senses belong to the whole composite, they do not for that reason pertain to the use of life, so that one may rightly infer otherwise.

units.la: hominis, quæ non aliquatenus & ad mentem spectent & ad corpus, sequetur, vel omnes illas ad compositum qua tale esse referendas, nullas prorsus ad contemplationem veritatis; vel falsum esse, quod asserit Claubergius, ea quæ ratione corporis & animæ simul homini sunt tributa, non nisi ad compositum qua tale esse referenda. Facillimum foret etiam huic dubio occurere ex tribus sentiendi gradibus, quos statuit Claubergius; sed ista nunc missa facere cogor, brevitati studens. Famem quantum attinet & sitim, cum nil pro objecto habeant præter alimenta, præcisè quatenus pertinent ad nutritionem, facilè quis dederit, eas non nisi ad compositum, qua tale, esse referendas. At Sensuum disparlongè ratio est; quippe qui ad ea quoque sese extendunt, quæ cum vitæ animalis regimine nullam habent connexionem: dum viam aperiunt, ut loquar cum Cartesio ad magis absolutam naturæ cognitionem, docentes, quid sit magnitudo, numerus, figura; quantum Planetæ distent à Sole; quæ & quot sint sydera Medicæa, &c. Hisce paria cum revelaverint menti sitis & fames, nil repugno, quo minus pari loco habeantur cum Sensibus, cognitionisque humanæ instrumentis annumerentur.
units.tr: of man that do not in some way concern both the mind and the body. It would follow either that all of them are to be referred to the composite as such, and none at all to the contemplation of truth; or else that what Clauberg asserts is false, namely that those things attributed to man by reason of body and soul together are referred only to the composite as such. It would be very easy also to meet this doubt by means of the three degrees of sensing that Clauberg lays down, but I am compelled to set these aside, aiming at brevity. As far as hunger and thirst are concerned, since they have as their object nothing but food, precisely insofar as they pertain to nourishment, one may readily grant that they are to be referred only to the composite as such. But the case of the senses is quite different, for they also extend to things that have no connection with the regulation of animal life. They open the way, to use Descartes' words, to a more absolute knowledge of nature, teaching what magnitude, number and figure are, how far the planets are from the Sun, what and how many the Medicean stars are, and so on. Since thirst and hunger have revealed similar things to the mind, I have no objection to their being placed on the same footing as the senses and counted among the instruments of human knowledge.

units.la: Non semel, ait Claubergius, admiratus sui, tot ac tanta corporeis adscribi Sensibus, ut Philosophia & humanae e. uditionis omnis primi quasi magistri habeantur. Nam ita mecum ratiocinabar: Si omnis cognitio peratur à Sensibus, &c. mirum est, quod non sapientissimi, qui suos perpetuò Sensus sequuntur duces. Resp. Si verum sit, uti elt verissimum, quod alibi Aristoteles, exstimandum esse ignorasse, quicunque miratur, nil miri est, mirari hîc Claubergium; itâ se in toto hoc ratiocinio ignorare prodit, aut saltem ignorare vult videri, quæ sit mens eorum qui stant pro Sensuum veritatis magistram dixerit? Si non, quò colore infert Claubergius, sapientis fore, ex nostrâ sententiâ, Sensus perpetuò duces sequi? Sed si de isto Sensu sit sermo, qui circa proprium objectum occupatur, atque undiquaquè bene se habet (ex conditionum, quas suprà recensuimus, requisito) immò verò, qui Sensum talem circa rem sensibilem perpetuò sequitur ducem, sapientior habendus est decies & amplius eo, qui imaginarias & in mente fabricatas temerè ideas sectatur. Atque itâ meritò Aristoteles teles viii. Phyf. Ⅎtavoiaς αρρωσια laborare pronunciat cos, qui sensum dimittunt in iis, quæ Sensibus manifesta sunt, & rationes quærunt. Quicum eleganter consentit Cicero, Acad. ii. Sensuum ita clara judicia & certa sunt, ut si optio naturæ nostræ detur, & ab ea Deus aliquis requirat, contentane sit suis integris incorruptisque Sensibus: an postulet melius aliquid, non videam quid quærat amplius. Restringebam hanc sensibus haustam sapientiam ad proprium sensuum objectum. Nam & sensationum occasione de insensibilibus quomodo philosophandum sit sapienti, jam plus satis suo loco expositum. Unde quo pacto sapiens & idiota aliter & aliter sensus sequatur duces, facile intelligitur: illi sensationes sapientiæ argumentum suppeditant, huic objiciunt impedimentum.
units.tr: Not once, says Clauberg, have I wondered that so many and so great things are ascribed to the bodily senses, so that they are regarded as the first, as it were, teachers of all philosophy and human learning. For I reasoned thus with myself: If all knowledge is derived from the senses, etc., it is strange that the wisest men do not follow their senses always as their guides. Reply: If it is true, as it is most true, that Aristotle says elsewhere that whoever wonders must be judged to be ignorant, then it is no wonder that Clauberg wonders here; in this whole argument he shows that he is ignorant, or at least wishes to appear ignorant, of what the mind of those is who stand for the senses as the teacher of truth. If not, with what colour does Clauberg infer that, on our view, the wise man must always follow the senses as guides? But if the question concerns that sense which is occupied with its proper object and is in every way in good condition (by the requirement of the conditions we listed above), then indeed the one who always follows such a sense as his guide is to be regarded as wiser ten times over and more than one who rashly pursues imaginary ideas fabricated in the mind. And so Aristotle rightly declares in the eighth book of the Physics that those who abandon the senses in matters that are manifest to the senses and seek reasons are afflicted with the sickness of thought [διανοίας ἀρρωστία]. Cicero agrees with him elegantly in the second book of the Academics: The judgements of the senses are so clear and certain that if the choice were given to our nature, and some god were to ask it whether it is content with its senses whole and uncorrupted, or whether it demands something better, I do not see what more it could seek. I was restricting this wisdom drawn from the senses to the proper object of the senses. For how a wise man must philosophise about insensible things, on the occasion of sensations, has already been explained at length in its place. Hence it is easily understood how the wise man and the unlearned man follow the senses as guides in different ways: the former find in sensations a proof of wisdom, the latter find in them an obstacle.

units.la: Sed pergit mirari Claubergius. Imo mirum, quod intellectu & sapientia omni carentia animantia facultate sentiendi hominem superent; secundum versum: Nos aper audiitu, &c. Resp. Quasi in nuda Sensatione sapientia consisteret; & non potius ejus acquirendæ medium foret prudens ejusdem usus! Cujus arbitrio, mente scil. quoniam destituuntur bruta, nulla quoque, vel propter acutissimos Sensus, iis tribui potest sapientia. Liceat vero & mihi mirari! Mirum, inquam ego, si Sensus tantum dati sint ad vitæ animalis regimen, cur non illi æquè acuti concessi sint hominibus ac brutis; quasi illi minus necesse habeant commoda hujus vitæ discernere ab incommodis, quam hæc. Mihi si respondeat Claubergius (quemadmodum aliud responderi hic nequit; nisi forte dicat saginandæ v.c. Sui conducere auditus acumen) voluisse potentissimum Deum multiplicem suam manifestare sapientiam in tanta constructionis organorum varietate in variis subjectis, hoc idem sibi à me responsum putet. Quin & id mirum, si tantum ad vitæ animalis regimen dati sint sensus, cur in homine se aliter habeant quam in bruto: in illo scilicet cum cogitatione mentis conjunctæ existunt, in hoc minime. Atqui, quid ad vitæ animalis regimen cogitatio; citra quam omnem animalem vitam vivunt commodissime bruta? Sed & hac de re suo loco plura.
units.tr: But Clauberg goes on to wonder. Indeed it is strange that animals, which lack all intellect and wisdom, surpass man in the faculty of sensing; according to the verse: We are deaf to the boar's hearing, etc. Reply: As if wisdom consisted in bare sensation, and not rather in the prudent use of sensation, by which it is to be acquired! Since brutes lack mind, no wisdom can be attributed to them, not even on account of their most acute senses. But let me too be allowed to wonder! I wonder, I say, that if the senses were given only for the regulation of animal life, the most acute senses were not granted to men just as to brutes; as if men had less need to distinguish the advantages of this life from its disadvantages than brutes do. If Clauberg should answer me (as no other answer can be given here, unless perhaps he says that the keenness of hearing is useful, for example, for fattening oneself), let him think that the same answer has been given by me: that Almighty God wished to manifest his manifold wisdom in such a great variety of the construction of organs in various subjects. Moreover, it is also strange, if the senses were given only for the regulation of animal life, why they are in man otherwise than in brute beasts: in man they exist together with the thought of the mind, in brutes not at all. Yet what has thought to do with the regulation of animal life, without which brutes live most conveniently of all in their animal life? But more on this matter in its place.

units.la: Mirum, ait porro, quod qui maxime intellectu & scientia pollent, Deus & Angeli, omni Sensu corporeo distituantur. Resp. Quasi quis unquam afferere somniasset, absolutè semper & ubiquè Sensatio sationem requiri, ad quemvis intellectum & scientiam. De homine id tantùm affirmatur, in quo intellectus à Sensu dependet; sive, ut Cartesium rectè philosophari audivimus; quod mens tamen, ex eo quod corpori conjuncta sit, habet naturam, sive, quia in primis annis majorem de sensibilibus cogitandi usum & facilitatem sibi acquisivit. Hic ergò cum sermo omnis sit de cognitione spiritûs cum corpore in eandem personam uniti, qua talis, quæ insciitia est, adducere exempla suppositorum merè spiritualium, Dei, Angeli? Vin, æquam ego faciam comparationem, & mirer? Mirum, si solo intellectu utendum sit, Sensus nil nisi obscurè & confusè menti offerant, mirum, inquam, quod qui Sensuum usu destituuntur homines, quales sunt, infantes, apoplectici, &c. non maximè intellectu & scientiâ polleant, ac subtilissimi sint Philosophi.
units.tr: It is strange, he adds further, that those who especially excel in intellect and knowledge, God and the angels, are destitute of all bodily sense. Reply: As if anyone had ever dreamed of asserting that sensation is absolutely and everywhere required for every intellect and knowledge! This is affirmed only of man, in whom the intellect depends on the sense; or, as we have heard Descartes rightly philosophise, that the mind, however, because it is joined to the body, has a nature, or, because in its early years it acquired for itself a greater use and facility of thinking about sensible things. Since then all the discussion here concerns the knowledge of a spirit united with a body into one person, as such, which is the case, why bring forward examples of purely spiritual persons, God and the angels? Do you want me to make a fair comparison, and to wonder? It would be strange, if one had to use the intellect alone, and the senses offered nothing to the mind except obscurely and confusedly, that men destitute of the use of the senses, such as infants, apoplectics, and so on, do not especially excel in intellect and knowledge, and are the most subtle of philosophers. I say, it would be strange.

units.la: Mirum, addit, quod qua clarissimè sentimus, ex. gr. lucem & colorem, obscurissimè tamen intelligamus. Resp. Mirum, non occurrisse hic Auctori distinctionem, quâ ipse paulò post utitur inter rei tò ὅτι & tò διότι. Certè ut lucem clarè sentimus, ita & clarè eandem intelligimus; nempe tò ὅτι. Quòd vero tò διότι ejus tam obscurè intelligimus, non aliundè fit, quam quia ipsum tò διότι Sensum non afficit. Si enim adeò clarè visu perciperemus, quid sit lux aut color, quam quidem eo percipimus, quid sit magnitudo, figura, motus, situs, non minus etiam clarè, illa quid sint, intelligeremus, quam hæc. Atque hoc ipsum Cartesius quoque asserit, & prolixè satis prosequitur, Princip. I. Art. LXIX. LXX. Adeò ut, quod argumentum Claubergius contra Sensus militare autumat, ipsum multo magis eorundem confirmet necessitatem. Accedit hisce, nos, si quid nobis de luce aut coloribus innotesceat, quid sint, etiam id omninò sensationibus debere, quandoquidem ex earum observationibus de lucis proprietatibus & effectis hausta sunt quæ in Dioptrica de illis tradit ipse Cartesius: qui si illum tractatum scribere potuisset, nisi visu adjutus, mirum foret omnium maximum, & res solùm non prodigiosa.
units.tr: It is strange, he adds, that what we sense most clearly, for example light and colour, we understand most obscurely. Reply: It is strange that the author did not think of the distinction which he himself uses a little later between the that [τὸ ὅτι] and the why [τὸ διότι] of a thing. Certainly, as we sense light clearly, so we also understand the same clearly, namely its the that [τὸ ὅτι]. But that we understand its the why [τὸ διότι] so obscurely arises only from this, that the sense itself does not affect the the why [τὸ διότι]. For if we perceived by sight as clearly what light or colour is, as we perceive by it what magnitude, figure, motion and situation are, we would understand what those are no less clearly than these. Descartes himself also asserts this, and pursues it at sufficient length in the first part of the Principles, articles 69 and 70. So much so that the argument which Clauberg thinks makes against the senses in fact confirms their necessity much more. Besides this, if we know anything about light or colours, what they are, we owe that entirely to sensations too, since the things which Descartes himself teaches about them in the Dioptrics were drawn from observations of the properties and effects of light made through the senses. If he could have written that treatise without being aided by sight, it would be the greatest wonder of all, and a thing not merely prodigious.

units.la: Ultimum miratur Claubergius: Mirum, quod qua nullo modo sentimus, optimè tamen & facillimè intelligamus, uti cogitationes quisque suas, quas habet in animo, dum affirmat, negat, vult, nonvult, licet nullis interim verbis externis utatur, neque audeat, ut legat
units.tr: Clauberg wonders at one last thing: It is strange that what we do not sense in any way, we nonetheless understand very well and very easily, as each person understands the thoughts he has in his mind, when he affirms, denies, wills, or does not will, even though he uses no external words meanwhile, and does not dare to read

units.la: XLIII. Quæcunque Sensui clara sunt, eadem qua talia menti exi- stunt evidentia.
units.tr: XLIII. Whatever is clear to the senses is also evident to the mind as such.

units.la: XLIV. Contrà, quæ nullo modo sentimus omnium. legat quicquam. Resp. Nescio, quâ confidentiâ tam rotundè pronuncict Claubergius, optimè & facillimè intelligi cogitationes, etiam ab eo, qui nec audivit nec legit quicquam. Falsitatis hanc thesin convincunt quotquot unquam extiterunt deliri, apoplectici, lethargici, infantes, aliique, quia Sensuum, ideò & rationis usu, consequenter & suæ cogitationis intelligentiâ, destituti. Neque longùm abeamus. Mirum, si quis unquam expertus fuerit, hominem idiotam & rusticum melius & facilius intelligere, quid sint (nam de eo quod sint non est quæstio) cogitationes suæ mentis, affirmatio, negatio, volitio, nolitio, de quibus recte concipiendis ipsi inter se digladiantur eruditissimi quique, quam quid sit magnitudo, situs, aut figura corporis. Sed cum ista pertineant ad aliam controversiam, de spiritualibus utrùm ea nobis in hoc rerum statu faciliusque cognoscantur quam res corporeæ, hicsubsisto. Ostendisse nunc sufficerit, nullas fuisse Claubergio rationes, ob quas necesse habuerit mirari, tantum corporeis adscribi Sensibus, ut Philosophiæ & humanæ eruditionis magistri habeantur. Concludo tandem: Sensus non tantum datos esse ad vitæ animalis regimen, verum etiam ad dijudicandum, quæ sit rerum extra nos positarum natura, & inhærentes proprietates; per consequens: In vero indagando non solo intellectu, sed & Sensibus utendum esse, tanquam veritatis magistris, citra ullam naturæ ordinis perversionem. Quod ipsum demonstrandum erat.
units.tr: XLIV. On the contrary, there are things of which we have no sense at all. read anything. Reply: I do not know with what confidence Claubergius so flatly asserts that thoughts are understood very well and very easily, even by one who has neither heard nor read anything. The falsity of this thesis is shown by all the mad, the apoplectic, the lethargic, infants, and others who, lacking the use of the senses and therefore of reason, and consequently lacking any understanding of their own thought, have ever existed. Nor need we go far. If anyone has ever experienced it, he will find that an unlearned country man understands better and more easily what they are (for we are not asking that they are) the thoughts of his own mind, affirmation, negation, volition, and non-volition, than he understands what magnitude, position, or shape of a body is. Indeed the most learned men fight among themselves over how these are rightly conceived. But since these matters belong to another controversy, namely whether spiritual things are more easily and more readily known by us in the present state of things than corporeal things, I stop here. It will suffice to have shown now that Claubergius had no reasons for thinking it necessary to wonder that so much is ascribed to the bodily senses that they are regarded as the teachers of philosophy and of human learning. I conclude at last: The senses are given not only for the governing of animal life, but also for judging what is the nature of things placed outside us and their inherent properties; and consequently: In searching for truth we must use not only the intellect but also the senses, as teachers of truth, without any perversion of the order of nature. This was what had to be demonstrated.

units.la: Cæterùm, quandoquidem ad manum hoc loco erant positiones quædam, quibus intellectûs nostri à Sensu dependentiam breviter aliquandò explicabam, easque jam dictis confirmandis atque illustrandis conducere nonnihil judicabam, visum est hanc de Sensuum in philosophando Usu Dissertationem eisdem claudere. Atque hunc quidem in modum istic philosophabar:
units.tr: Moreover, since certain propositions were at hand here, by which I briefly explained at some point the dependence of our intellect upon the sense, and since I judged that they would contribute somewhat to confirming and illustrating what has been said, it seemed good to close this dissertation on the use of the senses in philosophizing with them. And in this manner I philosophized there:

units.la: 1. Quotquot aut explosa Platonicorum deliria, aut damnatam Epicureorum impietatem instaurare nolunt, eis certum esse debet, neque mente solâ constare hominem, neque solo corpore; sed utroque illo hypostaticâ unione in eandem personam conjuncto. Quumque actiones non partis alicujus sint, sed totius supposition, etiam non mens sola cognoscit, non corpus solum, sed homo ex utroque compositus; conferente unaquaque parte quod suum est. Quid verò, tanquam suum, quælibet pars hùc conferat? videndum est propius.
units.tr: 1. Whoever are unwilling either to revive the exploded follies of the Platonists or the condemned impiety of the Epicureans must be certain that man does not consist of mind alone, nor of body alone, but of both joined in one person by the hypostatic union. And since actions belong not to some part but to the whole supposit, it is not the mind alone that knows, nor the body alone, but man composed of both, each part contributing what is its own. But what, as its own, does each part contribute here? This must be considered more closely.
D dd 2 II. Pro-

units.la: II. Proprium intelligendi principium corpus nec esse, nec esse posse, evincit abundè illa sui quæ in omni intelligente est conscientia; cujus rem extensam atque impenetrabilem minimè esse capacem facilè est demonstrare. Imò, ex eodem fonte deducitur nullo negotio, quodcunque corporeum ex se & sua natura nullam habere cognationem aut affinitatem cum actu intelligendi spirituali.
units.tr: II. That the body is not, and cannot be, the proper principle of understanding is abundantly proved by that consciousness of self which is in every understanding being; and it is easy to demonstrate that an extended and impenetrable thing is in no way capable of it. Indeed, from the same source it is readily deduced that whatever is corporeal has, from its own nature, no kinship or affinity with the spiritual act of understanding.

units.la: III. Non itaquè ex ipsa mentis intrinseca essentia, in quantum purus spiritus est, id fluit, quod actiones ejus comitetur aliquod corporeum (uti neque in rebus merè spiritualibus, Angelis nimirùm, & Animabus separatis, tale quid obtinet) sed ex mera ordinatione primæ causæ; quæ, uti mentem in hoc statu unionis non subsistere absque corpore, itâ neque eandem sine corporis societate operari, voluit: quatenus modus operandi eum qui est subsistendi sequitur.
units.tr: III. Therefore it is not from the intrinsic essence of the mind, insofar as it is a pure spirit, that something corporeal accompanies its actions (just as nothing of the kind is found in purely spiritual beings, namely angels and separated souls). It comes rather from the mere ordinance of the first cause, which willed that the mind, as it does not subsist without a body in this state of union, so also should not operate without the company of the body, inasmuch as the mode of operating follows the mode of subsisting.

units.la: IV. Quoties ergò quicquam intelligit homo, hominis ea actio est, non solius mentis: concurrente videlicet ad eam etiam suo modo corpore. Non quòd hoc ipsas rerum notiones formet (id enim jam à corpore removimus, & mentis opus esse diximus) sed quod harum istarumve idearum formandarum idoneam saltem ansam suppeditet: idque adeò semper & ubique, ut nullam planè putemus esse in homine actualem perceptionem, cui excitandæ non aliquam; seu proximam seu remotam, sensus fecerit occasionem.
units.tr: IV. Whenever, therefore, a man understands anything, it is an act of the man, not of the mind alone: the body, in its own way, concurring with it. Not that the body forms these notions of things (for we have already removed this from the body and said that it is the work of the mind), but that it supplies at least a suitable occasion for forming these or those ideas. And this happens so always and everywhere that we think there is no actual perception in a man for whose arousing the senses have not provided some occasion, whether near or remote.

units.la: V. Dico, omnibus nostris cogitationibus per sensus aliquam saltem præberi occasionem; quatenus scilicet sensibilia rei adjuncta, causæ, effecta, opposita, similiaque, mentem cogitare faciunt de re ipsa cujus sunt affectiones. Quod diligenter notandum; ne quis istam nos insanire insaniam autumet, ut contendamus, omnes, quæ ab intellectu nostro producuntur, cogitandi formas expressa ectypa esse aliquorum phantasmatum.
units.tr: V. I say that some occasion is at least provided through the senses for all our thoughts, insofar as sensible things, whether adjuncts, causes, effects, opposites, or the like, make the mind think of the thing itself of which they are the affections. This must be carefully noted, lest anyone suppose that we are raving so far as to maintain that all the forms of thinking produced by our intellect are expressed copies of some phantasms.

units.la: VI. Remotissimum id est à mente quemadmodum nostra, sic & antiquorum Philosophorum: quippe qui eodem spiritu, &c. Nihil esse in intellectu quod non antè fuerit in sensu, dixerunt, & simul tanquam axioma celebrarunt istud, Substantia non incurrit in sensus. Neque millena esse diffitemur, quorum omni notitia mens nostra haud caret, etsi phantasmata eorum nec sint, nec esse possint. Ut qui hoc sensu Veterum sententiam impugnant cum umbra sua luctentur.
units.tr: VI. This is as far from the mind as it is from our own view, and from that of the ancient philosophers as well; for they, in the same spirit, etc., said that there is nothing in the intellect which was not first in the sense, and at the same time celebrated as an axiom this saying, Substance does not fall under the senses. Nor do we deny that there are thousands of things of which our mind has knowledge, although their phantasms neither are nor can be. Those who in this sense assail the opinion of the ancients wrestle with their own shadow.

units.la: VII. Summa ergò rei hæc est. Quemadmodum Geometra ex paucis quibusdam principiis elicit mirandam seriem demonstrationum, in principiis istis fundatarum quidem, plurimum tamen ab iisdem distantium; itâ intellectus hominis ex occasionibus quibusdam cogitandi à sensu suppeditatis, ratiocinando (scil. discurrendo, abstrahendo, &c.) notiones format omnes, etiam rerum à sensu remotissimarum. Id nùm itâ se habeat ? videamus per partes.
units.tr: VII. The sum of the matter, therefore, is this. Just as the geometer from a few principles draws out a wonderful series of demonstrations, founded indeed on those principles yet very remote from them, so the human intellect, from certain occasions of thinking supplied by the sense, by reasoning (that is, by discursion, abstraction, etc.) forms all notions, even of things most remote from the sense. Is this so? Let us examine it part by part.

units.la: VIII. Si quid à sensibus absit, absunt omnium longissimè Metaphysicæ veritates; quales sunt Deus, Anima rationalis, Principia prima, similiaque. Verùm, ne illa quidem sine sensuum auxilio actu sciri, asserimus. De quo qui dubitat, ablegandus tantùm videtur ad cunas infantium, & gyrgathos mente emotorum; quales nullam actualem habere harum rerum notitiam, ex hoc solo quod vel ipsâ sensuum activitate, vel eorundem in rectè ratiocinando legitimo usu destituuntur, clarum est.
units.tr: VIII. If anything is absent from the senses, the truths of metaphysics are absent most of all, such as God, the rational soul, the first principles, and the like. Yet we assert that even these cannot be actually known without the help of the senses. Whoever doubts this seems to be sent back only to the cradles of infants and to those dizzy-brained people whose minds have been moved out of place; that such people have no actual knowledge of these things is clear from the fact that they are deprived of the very activity of the senses, or of their lawful use in reasoning rightly.

units.la: ix. Quantum juvent in acquirenda notitia dianoëtica & existentiæ & attributorum Dei sensus nostri, ut alia sileam, omnium optimè docet Doctor Gentium Paulus, assertor ille Naturalis Theologiæ egregius, quando Ethnicos in hoc inexcusabiles pro-nunciat, quod animum non rite adjecerint ad τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, quod ipsis manifestaverat Deus. Sed quo pacto? Quatenus puta invisibilia sua, æternam potentiam ac divinitatem, conspicienda dedit & intelligenda ex creati mundi structura.
units.tr: IX. How much our senses help in acquiring the discursive knowledge both of God's existence and of his attributes, to say nothing of other things, the Teacher of the Gentiles Paul, that outstanding champion of natural theology, teaches best of all, when he pronounces the heathen inexcusable in this, that they did not duly attend to that which is known of God [τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ], which God had made manifest to them. But how? Insofar as, to be sure, he gave his invisible things, his eternal power and divinity, to be seen and understood from the structure of the created world.

units.la: x. Neque alia Animæ humanæ ratio est. Non enim ejus notitiam haberi per directum aliquem sui ipsius intuitum, evincit ipsa suæ mentis in hominibus plerisque, etiam non indoctis, ignorantia. Hanc eo magis tolli in nobis experimur, quo diligentius ad operationes attendimus quibus ipsa sese manifestat; quas inter primæ nobis observabiles sunt risus, loquela, & si quæ tales plures in sensum incurrant: hæ enim primùm de rationali principio nos cogitare faciunt.
units.tr: X. The case of the human soul is no different. That we have no direct intuition of it, as of itself, is proved by the ignorance of their own minds among most men, even the unlearned. We experience this ignorance being removed in us the more carefully we attend to the operations by which the soul manifests itself; among these the first observable to us are laughter, speech, and any others of this kind that fall under the senses, for these first make us think of a rational principle.

units.la: xi. Quod ad Principia Metaphysica, quorum nobis innata dicitur veritas, qualia sunt, v. c. Nihil nulla sunt affectiones; &c. etiam experientia dictat, nullam actualem eorum haberi intelli-tellitelligentiam à quoquam, cui non per sensus factæ fuerint occasiones res quasdam cogitandi, quibus ista principia applicantur, quorumque occursu ipsa quasi in intellectu nostro excitantur. Quæ eadem intellecta velim de veritatibus quibusvis aliis, tum Metaphysicis, tum etiam Moralibus.
units.tr: XI. As for the metaphysical principles, whose truth is said to be innate to us, such as nothing is without its affections, etc., experience also dictates that no one has an actual understanding of them unless there have been occasions, supplied by the senses, for thinking certain things to which these principles are applied, and by whose encounter they are, as it were, awakened in our intellect. I wish the same to be understood of all other truths, metaphysical as well as moral.

units.la: xii. Circa Mathematica alicui hic dubium esse posse, oppido mirum est. Etenim neminem in iis percipiendis excellere, qui non plurimum polleat viribus imaginationis, notissimum est. Et quis in triangulo rectilineo tres angulos internos duobus rectis æquales esse percipiat, cui non per sensum nota sit trianguli configuratio? Quamobrem etiam sensibus, visu imprimis, destitutis perceptu difficillimæ sunt hæ disciplinæ.
units.tr: XII. It is very strange that anyone could have doubt here about mathematics. For it is very well known that no one excels in perceiving these things who does not have great strength of imagination. And who perceives that the three interior angles of a rectilinear triangle are equal to two right angles, unless the configuration of the triangle is known to him through the senses? Therefore these disciplines, deprived of the senses, above all of sight, are very difficult to grasp.

units.la: xiii. Omnium maximè dominantur Sensus in Physica, quippe quæ objectum proprium habet res materiales, suis qualitatibus, tum etiam causis atque effectis, in sensum immediatè ut plurimum ingerentes. Addc Botanicam atque Anatomen, in quibus omne punctum fert, omnique ratione potior est, nuda autopsia. Ut mirandum merito videatur, si cui haberi queat pulchrior imago coloris, quam ex sola innata idea, scilicet! haurit cœcus, quam quæ se offert oculis alicujus bene videntis.
units.tr: xiii. Senses hold the greatest sway in physics, since it has as its proper object material things, with their qualities, and also their causes and effects, which for the most part present themselves immediately to the senses. Add botany and anatomy, in which bare autopsy carries every point and is in every way superior. So it may rightly seem remarkable if anyone can form a more beautiful picture of colour from innate idea alone, forsooth, than the one that presents itself to the eyes of someone who sees well.

units.la: xiv. Neque obstat, quod Sensus rerum existentiam & effecta tantum docere videantur, non causas, non effectorum cum causis connexionem; in quo tamen philosophica rei notitia proprie consistit. Præterquam enim quod sensibus manifestari etiam causas cum effectis connexas pluribus instantiis, à Meteoris, &c. desumptis, demonstretur facilè; etiam qui Sensuum tuentur necessitatem, hoc ipso contenti sunt, si agnoscantur tanquam requisitæ philosophandi occasiones; quales agnoscuntur, cum per oblata effecta mentem moveri, ad ratiocinandum de eorundem causis, admittitur.
units.tr: xiv. Nor is it an objection that the senses seem to teach only the existence of things and their effects, not their causes, nor the connection of effects with causes; yet philosophical knowledge of a thing properly consists in precisely this. For, apart from the fact that it can easily be shown, from many instances drawn from meteors and so on, that causes connected with effects are also made manifest to the senses, even those who defend the necessity of the senses are content with this alone: that they be recognised as the required occasions for philosophising. They are recognised as such when it is admitted that the mind is moved by the effects presented to it, so as to reason about their causes.

units.la: xv. Ipse profecto Cartesius ex principiis suis de Mundo hoc aspectabili philosophari minimè fuit ausus, nisi enarratâ primum phænomenon sensibilium historiâ. Hanc nisi normam sumsisset suarum idearum, ex hypothesibus istis suis mundum ei qui de facto datur similem cudisset nequaquam; adeò mens ejus in vortici-bus oberrans, absque sensuum auxilio determinata nunquam fuisset, ad exitum ex iis invenciendum effectibus rerum responrespondentem. Vide hæc fatentem Princip. Part. III. §. IV.
units.tr: xv. Indeed Descartes himself, working from his principles concerning this visible world, did not dare to philosophise at all, unless the history of sensible phenomena had first been set out. Had he not taken this as the norm of his ideas, he would never have fashioned a world like the one actually given, by those hypotheses of his; so much did his mind wander among the vortices that, without the aid of the senses, it would never have been determined to find the outcome of effects of things corresponding to them. See him admitting this in Princip. Part. III. §. IV.

units.la: XVI. Quandoquidem itaque eo quo explicuimus modo universa hominis cognitio in hoc nostræ mentis statu à sensibilium rerum perceptione ducit originem, verrissimè intellestum nostrum ab ortu suo similem dixit Philosophus tabulæ rasæ, cui actu inscribatur nihil, donec crescente ætate phantasmata speculando idoneas nanciscatur anima humana notiones quaslibet formandi occasiones. Quo sensu, etiam vulgò recepto, quam trita tam certa existit regula, Nihil est in intellectu quod non antè fuerit in sensu.
units.tr: XVI. Since, therefore, in the manner we have explained, all human knowledge in this state of our mind takes its origin from the perception of sensible things, the Philosopher rightly compared our intellect at birth to a blank tablet, on which nothing is actually written, until, as age advances, the human soul, by contemplating phantasms, acquires suitable occasions for forming any notions whatever. In this sense, too, the commonly received and well-worn rule holds as certainly as it is familiar: Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the senses.
EXERCITATIO
Weighing

units.la: Consectaria Ideæ, quâ absolvitur MENS HUMANA SOLA COGITATIONE.
units.tr: Corollaries of the idea by which the HUMAN MIND is completed by thought alone.
SUMMARY.

units.la: I. Nullum prudenti Philosopho recipiendum dogma novum, cujus non cautè animo prospexerit consequentias. II. Consectariorum quæ post se trahit novella idea de humana mente, quæ merá cogitatio sit, syllabus. III. Assertionis, Dei omnem essentiam in cogitatione constituentis, cum ea quæ mentem humanam solá cogitatione absolvit, demonstrata connexio: Ejusdemque paucis detecta falsitas. IV. Sententiæ, non nisi duo in Deo attributa admittentis, cum eadem hypothesi ostensus nexus:
units.tr: I. No prudent philosopher should admit a new doctrine without first carefully foreseeing its consequences. II. A synopsis of the consequences that the novel idea of the human mind as mere thought brings in its train. III. The demonstrated connection between the assertion that God constitutes all his essence in thought and the claim that the human mind is completed by thought alone, with a brief exposure of its falsity. IV. The connection shown under the same hypothesis for the opinion that admits only two attributes in God,

units.la: Ejusdemque patefacta breviter absurditas. V. Deum ratione essentiae nusquam esse, eadem hypothesis necessario infert: Dogmatis hujus addita confutatio.
units.tr: and a brief exposure of its absurdity. V. The same hypothesis necessarily implies that God is nowhere according to his essence, with an added refutation of this doctrine.

units.la: VI. Definitio Divinae Immensitatis, tantum per denominationem externam ab operatione desumptam, ex eadem hypothesi fluit: Ejus notata periculosa absurditas. VII. Utriusque Naturae in Christo unionem solâ operatione absolvere jubet eadem hypothesis: Reclamante orthodoxa Christianorum fide.
units.tr: VI. The definition of divine immensity, derived merely from an external denomination taken from operation, follows from the same hypothesis; its dangerous absurdity is noted. VII. The same hypothesis requires that the union of the two natures in Christ be effected by operation alone; this is contrary to the orthodox faith of Christians.

units.la: VIII. Angelos esse nusquam docere cogit eadem hypothesis: Dogmatis hujus Weigeliani confutatio.
units.tr: VIII. The same hypothesis compels one to teach that angels are nowhere: a refutation of this doctrine of Weigel's.

units.la: IX. Angelos de spatio in spatium non moveri, eadem hypothesis infert: Ejus assertionis offensa paucis falsitas.
units.tr: IX. The same hypothesis implies that angels do not move from space to space: a brief exposure of the falsity of this assertion.

units.la: Armen nullum edendum praecipit Poëta, quod non nonum prematur in annum, quodque non ad unguem saepius fuerit castigatum; ne scil. auctorem forte suum, si minus limatum prodeat, det in ruborem. Saluberrimi moniti ante alios probè memores esse oportet, quibus volupe est ad nova dogmata fabricanda ac divulganda animum adjicere: adeo, si quae, haec certè plena periculi res est. Etenim, quemadmodum rerum, itâ conceptuum quoque, mira longissimaque est concatenatio; cujus principium facilè finem vix reperias. Nec falsarum opinionum minor est fertilitas quam ipsarum veritatum: ut fieri non possit, quin, juxta illud πολυ-ζρύλλης Philosophi, Uno absurdo posito sequuntur plura. Hanc itaque vir prudens immotam sibi rectè figat legem, ne ullas unquam novellas admittat ideas, multo minus tanquam certas propugnet, quarum consequentias non animo prospexerit ac probè probeque secum examinaverit. Id si observatum fuisset ab omni aevo, nunquam eruditorum orbis tot laborasset controversiis; quippe quae maximâ sui parte non tam sunt destinato consilio excogitatae thesis, quam consectaria potius quarundam hypothesium, quibus tuendis dum plus justo studuerunt earundem auctores, salvandæ præconceptæ opinionis amore in istas, sæpè fortuito magis quam consulto, inciderunt. Quumque & attentissimi quique non raro sese hic deceptos deprehendant, dum primo intuitu elegantissimâ specie multi sese novi conceptus commendant, qui tamen penitius introspecti postea trahunt immanium absurdorum syrma longissimum, merito quicquid novum est, tanquam nondum satis exploratum, suspectum habetur, & jure creditur via antiqua tanto tutior, quanto est magis trita. Atque utinam nostris quoque temporibus non reperiantur, qui, ne Cartesii sui ideis vel hilum decedat, quæ ipsi horruissent ante consectaria, quandò jacta est alea, propugnant pertinacissimè, & quicquid ex iisdem nascitur monstri, quamtumvis id & horrendum & informe & ingens fuerit, ceu pulcrum sapientiæ fœtum sinu excipiunt avidissimè, fovent tenerrimè.
units.tr: The poet forbids anyone to publish a poem that has not been kept back for nine years, and not been polished to the nail many times over, lest, if it comes out less than finished, it bring its author to blush. Those who are eager to devise and spread new doctrines ought above all others to bear this most wholesome warning in mind, and this is certainly a matter full of danger. For just as there is a wonderful and very long chain of things, so there is also one of concepts, whose beginning one can scarcely find from its end. Nor is the fertility of false opinions less than that of the truths themselves, so that, as the oft-repeated saying of the Philosopher has it, once one absurdity is granted, many more follow. A prudent man should therefore fix this law firmly for himself: never to admit any novel idea, and much less to champion it as certain, until he has foreseen its consequences and examined them thoroughly and carefully with himself. If this had been observed in every age, the world of learned men would never have been troubled by so many controversies; for for the most part these are not theses devised with a fixed purpose, but rather corollaries of certain hypotheses, whose authors, while they have defended them more than was right, and out of love for saving an opinion they had already conceived, have fallen into these, often by chance rather than by design. And since even the most attentive often find themselves deceived here, while at first glance many new concepts commend themselves in a most elegant appearance, yet when examined more deeply they drag after them a very long train of monstrous absurdities, it is rightly held that whatever is new is suspect, as not yet sufficiently tested, and it is rightly believed that the old way is the safer the more it is trodden. And would that in our own times there were not those who, so that not the least jot may be yielded from their Cartesian ideas, stubbornly defend what they would have shuddered at before the consequences, now that the die has been cast, and eagerly embrace and most tenderly foster in their bosom, as a fair offspring of wisdom, whatever monster is born from these, however horrible, shapeless and huge it may be.

units.la: Ex pluribus unum idque luculentissimum hujus rei specimen exhibet nupera mentis humanæ, quæ nihil aliud sit quam mera cogitatio, idea: ex qua quæ sequuntur porismata tam latè patent, ut nullum fermè receptæ Theologiæ & Philosophiæ caput relinquant intactum; adeo utriusque per ea immutatur, etiam in rebus gravissimis, facies. Dogmatis ipsius falsitatem detectam dedimus abundè peculiari Tractatu, qui prodiit Titulo Narratoris Confutati; sive, Animadversionum in Narrationem de Controversiis nuperius in Academia Ultrajectina motis; invitante ad plenissimum rei examen Celeberrimo Antagonista. Inter cætera Tract. cit. pag. 186. 187. texebam brevem syllabum præcipuarum quarundam consequentiarum, ex nova de mente humana sententia fluentium, & præ aliis tunc temporis forte occurrentium. Nimirum: I. Essentiam Dei in cogitatione consistere. II. Duo proprie loquendo tantum dari Dei attributa interna, Intellectum & Voluntatem. III. Deum ratione essentiæ nullibi esse. IV. Omnipræsentiam ergò Ejusdem nihil aliud esse, quam denominationem extrinsecam, natam ex operatione in rebus corporeis. V. Quin & naturam divinam in Christo mediatore aliter humanæ naturæ uniri non potuisse, quam per operationes. VI. Angelos bonos aut malos ratione essentiæ nusquam esse. VII. Neque moveri de spatio in spatium. VIII. Posse nihilominus unum eorum in duobus dis-
units.tr: Among many, one most luminous example of this matter is provided by the recent idea that the human mind is nothing other than mere thought. From it follow such far-reaching corollaries that they leave almost no head of accepted theology and philosophy untouched; so much so that the face of both is changed by them, even in the most serious matters. We have amply shown the falsity of this doctrine in a separate treatise, which appeared under the title Narrator Refuted, or Animadversions on the Narrative concerning the Controversies recently stirred up in the Academy of Utrecht, inviting the most celebrated Antagonist to a full examination of the matter. Among other things, in the said treatise, pp. 186, 187, I set out a brief synopsis of certain principal consequences flowing from the new opinion about the human mind, and which then happened to occur to me before others. Namely: I. The essence of God consists in thought. II. Properly speaking, only two internal attributes of God are given, the intellect and the will. III. God is nowhere according to his essence. IV. Therefore his omnipresence is nothing other than an extrinsic denomination, arising from operation in corporeal things. V. Indeed, the divine nature in Christ the mediator could not be united with the human nature otherwise than through operations. VI. Good or evil angels are nowhere according to their essence. VII. Nor do they move from space to space. VIII. Nevertheless, one of them could produce several external operations simultaneously in two distant spaces.

units.la: II. sitis spatiis plures operationes ad extra simul producere. ix. Itá tamen ut nullam veram exerceat causalitatem, sed Deus efficiat aliquid in creaturis, ad nudám angeli voluntatem. x. Animam humanam non esse hominis formam. xi. Corpori unitam esse non ratione essentiæ, sed duntaxat ratione operationum. xii. Sic tamen ut tanquam causa proprie dicta nullas actiones transeuntes in corpore producat. xiii. Verum motus hujus ab influxu mentis non pendeant. xiv. Quin & corpus humanum vivere posse & moveri citra ejus præsentiam. xv. Animam rationalem in morte hominis non mutare suum ubi. xvi. Neque ullam post mortem ratione τῶ ubi posse illi differentiam. xvii. Sed cœlum & infernum nihil aliud notare quam mutationem cogitationum. xviii. Cæterum, Animæ actionem potentia agendi esse priorem, atque hanc ab illa fluere. xix. Habitum mentis sine actu concipi non posse. xx. Nec ullum omnino habitum dari, etiam infusum aut innatum, qui non actibus comparetur. xxi. Talem consequenter quoque esse habitum congenitæ vitiositatis; sicque hominem prius actu quam habitu peccatorem esse. xxii. Infantem ergo in matris utero actu peccare. xxiii. Ex adverso, embryonem regenitum credere fide actuali. xxiv. Quin, Spiritum S. in regeneratione nullam bonam inclinationem menti implantare posse, absque actu nostræ voluntatis. xxv. Itaque & regenitum prius actu quam habitu credentem fieri. Obtestabar istic unumquemque partem in his disputationibus nondum facientem, judicaret, tantine fieri debeat novella humanæ mentis, ceu meræ cogitationis idea, ut cum illa in orbem Reformatum intromittenda putet hæc quæ exhibuimus inaudita pleraque in hunc usque diem Ευρήματα; quæ ipsa singula suas iterum habent sequelas extendentes sese latissime. Etsi vero tum in illo nostro Tractatu tum passim in hisce Exercitationibus docuerim abunde, has omnes assertiones, & connexas esse suâ naturâ cum novo dogmate, & simul falsitatis atque periculi esse plenissimas, nequis tamen maneat calumniæ locus, preflius nonnihil agere visum fuit, hujusque rei in prioribus saltem quibusdam eo quo sequuntur se ordine breve dare experimentum. Cæterum, ex ungue Leonem! Ajebam itaque ex opinione, quæ mentis humanæ essentiam solo cogitandi actu absolvit, sequi:
units.tr: II. in distant spaces, several external operations at once, IX. provided that it exercises no true causality, but God effects something in creatures at the mere will of the angel. X. The human soul is not the form of the man. XI. It is united to the body not according to essence, but merely according to operations. XII. Yet in such a way that it produces no transeunt actions in the body as a cause properly so called. XIII. Indeed the motions of the body do not depend on the influx of the mind. XIV. Moreover, the human body can live and move without its presence. XV. The rational soul does not change its where at the death of the man. XVI. Nor after death can it have any difference in respect of the where. XVII. But heaven and hell signify nothing other than a change of thoughts. XVIII. Moreover, the power of acting is prior to the act of the soul, and the act flows from this power. XIX. A habit of the mind cannot be conceived without an act. XX. Nor is any habit at all given, even infused or innate, that is not acquired by acts. XXI. Consequently such a habit of congenital viciousness is also of this kind; and so man is a sinner in act before he is a sinner in habit. XXII. Therefore an infant in the mother's womb sins in act. XXIII. Conversely, a regenerate embryo believes by actual faith. XXIV. Indeed, the Holy Spirit cannot implant any good inclination in the mind in regeneration without an act of our will. XXV. And so the regenerate also becomes a believer in act before he is one in habit. Here I urged each party who has not yet taken a side in these disputations to judge whether the new idea of the human mind, as mere thought, must be so greatly admitted that they think these largely unheard-of inventions, which we have set forth, should be introduced into the reformed world along with it, inventions which until today have been unheard of, and each of which in turn has its own consequences extending very widely. Although indeed I have taught amply, both in that treatise of ours and throughout these Exercises, that all these assertions are connected by their very nature with the new doctrine, and at the same time are full of falsity and danger, yet, so that no place may remain for calumny, it seemed good to proceed somewhat more strictly, and to give a brief sample of this, in at least some of the first ones, in the order that follows. Moreover, "judge the lion by its claw!" So I was saying that from the opinion which completes the essence of the human mind by the mere act of thinking, the following follows:
I.

units.la: Ipsam totam Dei essentiam in hoc uno consistere, quod sit cogitatio.
units.tr: That the whole essence of God itself consists in this one thing, that it is thought.

units.la: Nimirùm, quandoquidem ex novella hypothesi conceptus cogitationis intimam naturam nostrae animae spiritualem secundum se exhibet; & quoniam illis auctoribus Deus eandem essentiam spiritualem cum mente humana habet communem (reclamante licet alibi D. Coccejo, cujus judicio spiritualitas animae & Dei non magis conveniunt, quam essentia animae & corporis, Summ. Theol. Cap. xvii. §. 12.) non potest non hac parte de Deo statui idem, quod affirmatur de humano spiritu. Disertè Poiretus, Cogit. Rat. Lib. iii. Cap. iii. §. 3. In Deo, cum ad illum attendo ex hac occasione (scil. quod completa notio rei quae cogitatione absolvitur spiritualitas dicenda sit, ob quam affero mentem meam spiritum esse, §. 1.) ita etiam cogitationem esse animadverto, ut tota ejus natura in illa sola consistat, exclusis cateris omnibus, quae praeter cogitationem possunt concipi .... Notetur idcirco, omnia quae in sequentibus Deo attribuentur, nil esse praeter meram cogitationem. Ibid. §. 4. Ex hisce facile est concipere, quid sit Dei spiritualitas, nimirum quod non tantum cogitet Deus, sed quod omnia quae in ejus natura sunt, cogitatio mera sint.
units.tr: Obviously, since by this new hypothesis the concept of thought presents the inner nature of our soul as spiritual in itself, and since, according to those authors, God has the same spiritual essence in common with the human mind (although D. Coccejus elsewhere objects, whose judgement is that the spirituality of the soul and of God agree no more than the essence of the soul and of the body, Summ. Theol. Cap. xvii. §. 12.), the same must be said of God in this respect as is affirmed of the human spirit. Poiret states it plainly: Cogit. Rat. Lib. iii. Cap. iii. §. 3. In God, when I attend to him on this occasion (namely, that the complete notion of a thing which is comprehended by thought must be called spirituality, on account of which I assert my mind to be a spirit, §. 1.), I observe in the same way that thought is his whole nature, consisting in it alone, with all others excluded which can be conceived apart from thought .... Let it therefore be noted that everything which is attributed to God in what follows is nothing but pure thought. Ibid. §. 4. From these things it is easy to grasp what the spirituality of God is, namely that God not only thinks, but that everything in his nature is pure thought.

units.la: Crudum profectò hoc dogma est non minus quam novum. Cartesius ipse, Medit. iii. contentus fuit Deum describere, Ens summè perfectum & infinitum; ut Dei nomine intelligat substantiam quandam infinitam, independentem, summè intelligentem, summè potentem, &c. Mirum certè, de cogitatione, praeter quam meram nil in Deo sit, verbum facere plané nullum; quùm illud praedicatum, quo tota Dei natura absolvitur, minimè fuerit praetereundum istic loci, ubi tanto conatu clarissimam ac distinctissimam Dei ideam urget. Sed lambendo hic foetus, uti plures, perficiendus erat paulatim. Rem ipsam quod attinet, plurima in Deo esse, quae praeter cogitationem possunt concipi, docebunt evidenter ea, quae de Æternitate, Simplicitate, &c. adferemus sequenti proximè Thesi. Nunc, quid causæ sit, scire velim, cur Deus ipse in Sacris, propius sese manifestaturus Mosi aliisque, Justitiæ quidem suæ, Longanimitatis, similiumque praedicatorum saepius meminerit, nunquam cogitationis? quam, si tota Dei natura in illa sola consistat, alto adeò silentio involvere minimè omnium convenit. Fri-volum volum est quod regerunt, præteriri cogitationem, quod supponatur ejus idea natura nota: nam etiam plurima illic recensentur passim attributa, quæ ex naturâ sunt maximè obvia, ac longè notiora quam conceptus cogitationis, in qua sola tota Dei natura consistat: quem istius temporis hominibus receptum fuisse & familiarem, miror si quis ausit asserere. Id saltem non dederit Cartesius, qui hanc sibi laudem vendicat, quod sit primus, qui cogitationem tanquam præcipuum attributum substantiæ incorporeæ (qualis quoque Deus est) consideravit. Not. ad Progr. Artic. Secund. Primus ergò quoque Cartesius erit, qui quod in Deo præcipuum est attributum ritè concipere docuerit? O pectora ante hanc lucem exortam in re tanti momenti nimiùm cœca! Et quid ni jam olim Deus ipse, si tantæ perfectionis prædicatum sit cogitatio, ut in illa sola, exclusis cæteris omnibus, tota Dei natura consistat, nomen suum memoriale, quod voluit esse יהוה, sumserit convenientius (absit blasphemia!) à cogitando, quippe quod unum, si Nostris credimus, omnia quæ in ejus natura sunt comprehendisset? Ista similiaque si cogitemus, nemini non nota esse poterit conceptus hujus absurditas. Nullum verò opinioni novæ præsidium est in Simplicitate Divina. Ea enim evincit solummodò, uti à parte rei quæcunque in Deo sunt sunt ipse Deus, itâ quoque cogitationem in sensu identico, uti loquuntur, cum Dei essentia esse eandem: haud aliter ac Justitia, Misericordia, &c. re verâ cum natura divina identificantur; etiamsi, pro nostra cogitandi ratione, primum ac radicale essentiæ divinæ prædicatum non sint. Atque hoc sensu Amesius, aliique nostri cum ipso Theologi passim docent, Actionem vitalem Dei esse ejusdem essentiam. At quemadmodum ex Simplicitate Dei non licet inferre, Ens primum nihil aliud esse in sensu formali, quam meram Justitiam, aut solam Misericordiam, &c. itâ quoque minime ex eadem conficitur, primum ac quiddITATIvum Dei conceptum notione cogitationis eo usquè absolvi, ut nihil in ipso præter eam concipi possit. Certè D. Amesius (cui cum plurimis nostris accedit ipse D. Coccejus Summ. Cap. x. §. 5.) Vitam Dei annumerat Divinis Attributis, contradistinctè ad Essentiam consideratis. Confer. §.35. cum §.19.31. Cap. iv. Lib. 1. Aledull. Tantùm verò abest, ut Attributum, in sensu formali spectatum, idem planè illi dicat cum Essentia Dei, ut expresse docet, Attri-buta huta divina Deo inesse quasi in esse secundo, quia non sunt de formali ratione essentiæ divinæ; sed ab essentia distinguuntur ratione ratiocinatâ. Ibid. §. 27. 28. Ut mirer nonnunquam hùc adduci Amesium, qui adeò è diametro novo Philosophematî adversatur. Sed de hoc, pro instituta brevitate, jam satis.
units.tr: This dogma is surely as crude as it is new. Descartes himself, in Medit. iii., was content to describe God as a most perfect and infinite being, so that by the name of God he understands a certain infinite, independent substance, most intelligent, most powerful, and so on. It is certainly strange that he says nothing at all about thought, other than which there is nothing in God, since that predicate by which the whole nature of God is comprised ought in no way to have been passed over in the place where, with such effort, he presses his most clear and distinct idea of God. But this offspring, like many others, had to be licked into shape gradually. As for the matter itself, that there are many things in God which can be conceived apart from thought, the things we shall adduce about eternity, simplicity and so on in the next thesis will clearly show. Now I should like to know the reason why God himself, in the Scriptures, when he was about to reveal himself more closely to Moses and others, often mentioned his justice, his long-suffering and similar predicates, but never his thought. If the whole nature of God consists in that alone, it is least of all fitting to wrap it in such deep silence. The objection that thought is passed over because its idea is assumed to be known by nature is trifling: for many attributes are everywhere listed there which are far more obvious from nature and much better known than the concept of thought, in which alone the whole nature of God consists; and I would be surprised if anyone dared to assert that this concept was accepted and familiar to the people of that time. Descartes at least will not yield this claim, which he vindicates for himself, that he was the first to consider thought as the principal attribute of an incorporeal substance (which God also is). Not. ad Progr. Artic. Secund. So will Descartes also be the first to teach rightly what is the principal attribute in God? O hearts too blind before this light arose in a matter of such moment! And why, if the predicate of so great a perfection is thought, so that in it alone, with all others excluded, the whole nature of God consists, did God not long ago take for his memorial name, which he willed to be Jehovah [יהוה], the more suitable one (God forbid the blasphemy!) from thinking, since, if we believe our own people, that one term would have comprehended everything that is in his nature? If we reflect on these and similar points, the absurdity of this concept will be evident to anyone. Nor is there any support for the new opinion in the Divine Simplicity. For that doctrine shows only that, with respect to the thing itself, whatever is in God is God himself; so too thought, in what is called the identical sense, is the same as the essence of God, just as justice, mercy and so on are really identified with the divine nature, even if, according to our manner of thinking, they are not the first and radical predicate of the divine essence. In this sense Amesius and other of our theologians along with him teach everywhere that the vital action of God is the same as his essence. But just as from the simplicity of God it does not follow that the first being is nothing else in the formal sense than pure justice, or mercy alone, and so on, so neither does it follow from the same that the first and quidditative concept of God is comprehended by the notion of thought to such an extent that nothing can be conceived in him apart from it. Certainly D. Amesius (with whom D. Coccejus himself agrees, along with most of our people, Summ. Cap. x. §. 5.) counts Life among the Divine Attributes, considered in contrast to the Essence. Compare §. 35 with §. 19, 31, Cap. iv. Lib. 1. Medull.
