So far is it from being the case that an attribute, regarded in the formal sense, says exactly the same thing as the Essence of God, that he expressly teaches: The divine attributes are in God as if in a secondary being, because they do not belong to the formal account of the divine essence; but they are distinguished from the essence by a reasoned distinction. Ibid. §. 27, 28. I sometimes wonder why Amesius is brought in here at all, since he so flatly opposes this new philosophical proposition. But on this matter, given the brevity I have set myself, enough has now been said.
II.

units.la: Duo proprie loquendo esse duntaxat Dei attributa, Intellectum & Voluntatem.
units.tr: Only two attributes of God are, strictly speaking, attributes: the intellect and the will.

units.la: Nempè, in Mente Humana nihil agnoscit Cartesius præter ipsam cogitationem, & varios cogitationis modos. Omnes verò cogitandi modos ad duos generales referri posse, ait: quorum unus est perceptio sive operatio intellectûs; alius vero volitio sive operatio voluntatis. Princ. I. §. 32. Quicunque ergò, uti mentis nostræ, itâ quoque Dei naturam totam in sola cogitatione consistere autumat cum Poireto, exclusis cæteris omnibus, quæ præter cogitationem possunt concipi, is necesse habet pariter, uti in mente, itâ in Deo, nihil admittere præter puræ putæ cogitationis attributa, qualia tantùm sunt Intellectus & Voluntas.
units.tr: Namely, in the human mind Descartes recognises nothing except thought itself and its various modes. He says, however, that all modes of thinking can be referred to two general ones: one of which is the perception or operation of the intellect; the other, the volition or operation of the will. Principles I, §32. Whoever therefore, as with our mind, so also maintains with Poiret that the whole nature of God consists in thought alone, all other things which can be conceived apart from thought being excluded, must likewise, as with the mind, so in God admit nothing except the attributes of pure, so-called thought, which are only the intellect and the will.

units.la: Si paulò diligentius hæc introspiciamus, deprehendemus, re verà omnia omninò Dei Attributa per hunc conceptum è medio tolli. Quandoquidem enim qui Deum nil nisi cogitationem esse volunt, cum Amesio aliisque nostris Theologis ac Philosophis, Intellectum & Voluntatem Divinam sub ratione Facultatum concipere neque volunt, neque per suas hypotheses possunt, id unum restat, ut per modum actionum ea concipiant; scilicet, tanquam cogitationis illius quæ Dei essentiam constituit certam terminationem, ut itâ loquar, in hanc vel istam rem intellectam aut volitam. Jam verò actionem quampiam nemo proprie loquendo dixerit attributum illius cujus est actio: actio enim principium respicit, attributum autem subjectum. Atque hinc nullis unquam Philosophis aut Theologis actiones Dei annumeratæ fuerunt stricte dictis Attributis. Itaque, si secundum rei naturam loqui velimus, desinunt ex hac hypothesi ipsæ quoque Intellectus & Voluntas esse attributa Dei, cujus potius sint actiones. Quumque in mera cogitatione, qualis his auctoribus Deus est, nulla alia attributa præter hæc duo iisdem sint conceptibilia, utique accuratè loquendo Dei attributa superunt penitus nulla: quod quam sit absonum, nemo non intelligit. Confirmantur haec non parum ex eo, quod solâ efficaci Dei Voluntate definiant hi Philosophi Creationem, Conservationem, Concursum, &c. Nisi forte & haec dicenda hodie sint, novâ nomenclaturâ, Attributa Dei. Quin, ut & hoc verbo moneam, quum Recentioribus spiritus tantùm agant volendo, itâ quidem ut Intellectus sit potentia passiva, non video, cur non tandem una & sola Voluntas superfit, quam Deo tanquam unicum ejus Attributum (si ullum tale restet) proprië loquendo tribuere ipsi datur possint. Ad rem ipsam ut redeam, si vel leviter attendamus ad illa quae in perfectissimo Numine concipiendo menti nostrae sese offerunt, alia certè praeter haec duo deprehendemus. Videlicet, Indepcndentia, Æternitas, Simplicitas, Immutabilitas, similiaque per se & in conceptu suo formali nullam includunt operandi actuositatem, sed simpliciter notant tantummodò modum existendi. Quumque haec non minus Deo conveniant quam duo illa de quibus lis est, manifestum existit, quaedam Dei attributa posse concipi, praecisâ etiam omni cogitatione: consequenter falsum non minus esse, duo tantum esse proprië loquendo Dei attributa, Intellectum & Voluntatem; quam, totam Dei naturam solâ cogitatione absolvi. Neque moramur, quod objicitur à Poirceto, alioqui dari in Deo respercepione destitutas, quas Deus cogitatione ab illis diversa perciperet, res brutas igitur & incogitantes; quod blasphemum esse ait, & non Deo, sed imperfecto idolo dignum conceptum. Haec enim demùm vera forent, si ista supponeremus realiter & ante mentis operam à Deo cogitante esse distincta, ac non potius abstractè à nobis duntaxat concipi. Nec stringit, si instes: Saltem ergo res brutae & incogitantes in Deo concipiuntur. Id namque ambiguè dictum est. Vel enim significat, aliquid hoc pacto à nobis in Deo concipi, quod à parte Dei brutum sit & incogitans; quod est salsissimum, cum nostrer modus concipiendi nihil omninò detrahat divinae Simplicitati, per quam, ut antè monui, in sensu identico & à parte rei, vita Dei cum omnibus ejusdem attributis identificatur. Vel notat, aliquod praedicatum in Deo à nobis concipi, quod, prout conceptu nostro substat, notionem cogitationis praecisè non includit: atque hoc ipsum verissimum est, ut jam ostendimus. Sed non rectè recte quod ita à nobis concipitur, dicetur concipi incogitans, quatenus vox hæc idem sonat quod brutum: id enim demum dixeris brutum, quod omnem cogitationem tanquam subjectum incapax negat & excludit; qualia sunt v. c. lapis, horologium, sol, &c. non id, cujus aliquod prædicatum abstractè saltem potest concipi absque expressa cogitationis idea. Omnipotentia v. c. (ut rem simili illustrem) in conceptu cujusvis Attributi divini, ex. gr. Æternitatis, aut Simplicitatis, nequaquam includitur; at non ideò qui abstractè concipit Æternitatem, non cogitando tunc temporis de Omnipotentia, concipit in Deo rem aliquam impotentem, cujus nomine blasphema dicatur hæc idea, atque idolo digna, non Deo. Quin, an non ipsis sibi hic os batuant, qui talia effutiunt, viderint. Agnoscunt enim Novatores, Voluntatem saltem Dei ab ejusdem Intellectu distinctum attributum. Dic nunc, age! qui sic illam concipiunt, an & hi formant notionem rei in Deo non-intelligentis, adeoque brutæ. Si sic, etiam conceptus adversariorum, distinguentium Intellectum inter & Voluntatem, tanquam duo proprie dicta attributa, blasphemus erit, & non Deo, sed idolo dignus. Sin minus, utique licet citra ullam in Deum injuriam, aliquid in eo concipere, quod in conceptu suo formali, quatenus is in mente est, intellectum præcisè non simul offert. Denique, cum plerique omnes ante nostram ætatem Theologi & Philosophi, ipso ne quidem excepto Cl. Coccejo, jam olim communi consensu dividant Dei attributa in primi generis, quæ sint essentiæ, atque incommunicabilia, & secundi generis, quæ sint vitæ (itâ hanc ab essentia solent distinguere) & communicabilia; quis ferat, omnem eorum cœtum ita aperte insimulari blasphemiæ, quasi, quamdiu radiis Cartesianæ Philosophiæ non fuerunt collustrati, pro Deo imperfectum idolon conceperint. Paria, si luberet, facile esset retorquere majori jure in Novatores; qui quam dignum Deo cudant conceptum, per suam cogitationem, præter quam in Deo concipi possit nihil, nunc aliis instantiis ostendere pergimus.
units.tr: If we look into these matters a little more carefully, we shall find that, in fact, all the attributes of God are altogether removed by this concept. For those who want God to be nothing but thought, together with Amesius and our other theologians and philosophers, neither wish nor are able, on their own hypotheses, to conceive the divine intellect and will under the aspect of faculties. Only one way remains: to conceive them by way of actions, that is, as a certain determination, so to speak, of that thought which constitutes the essence of God, directed to this or that thing understood or willed. Now, strictly speaking, no one would call an action an attribute of that whose action it is, for an action regards a principle, whereas an attribute regards a subject. Hence no philosophers or theologians have ever counted the actions of God among the attributes in the strict sense. So, if we wish to speak according to the nature of the matter, on this hypothesis the intellect and the will themselves cease to be attributes of God and are rather his actions. And since, in pure thought, which is what God is for these authors, no other attributes besides these two can be conceived, strictly speaking the attributes of God altogether fail to exist at all. How absurd this is, no one fails to see. This is confirmed not a little by the fact that these philosophers define creation, conservation, concurrence, and so on, by the efficacious will of God alone. Unless perhaps these too must nowadays be called attributes of God, under a new nomenclature. Indeed, to give a warning on this word as well: since for the more recent writers spirits act only by willing, so that the intellect is a passive power, I do not see why at last there should not remain one sole will, which could be properly attributed to God as his only attribute (if any such remains). But to return to the matter itself: if we attend even slightly to those things which present themselves to our mind when we conceive the most perfect Deity, we shall certainly find others besides these two. Namely, independence, eternity, simplicity, immutability, and similar things, in themselves and in their formal concept, include no activity of operating, but simply denote a mode of existing. And since these belong to God no less than those two of which there is dispute, it is clear that some attributes of God can be conceived even with all thought set aside. Consequently it is no less false that only two attributes of God are, strictly speaking, the intellect and the will, than that the whole nature of God is exhausted by thought alone. Nor do we dwell on the objection which Poiret raises: that otherwise there would be in God things destitute of perception, which God would perceive by a thought different from them, and so unthinking, brute things; he says this is a blasphemous concept, worthy not of God but of an imperfect idol. For this would indeed be true if we supposed these things to be really distinct from God thinking, and before the work of the mind, and not rather conceived by us only abstractly. Nor does it press you if you insist: "At least, then, brute and unthinking things are conceived in God." For this has been said ambiguously. Either it signifies that something is conceived by us in God which, on God's side, is brute and unthinking; and this is most false, since our manner of conceiving takes nothing at all away from the divine simplicity, through which, as I said before, in an identical sense and on the side of the thing itself, the life of God is identified with all his attributes. Or it denotes that some predicate is conceived by us in God which, as it lies within our concept, does not precisely include the notion of thought; and this itself is most true, as we have already shown. But that which is conceived by us in this way should not rightly be called "unthinking", in so far as this word means the same as "brute". For that alone is properly called brute which, as a subject incapable of thought, denies and excludes all thought, such as a stone, a clock, the sun, and so on; not that of which some predicate can be conceived at least abstractly without an express idea of thought. Omnipotence, for example (to illustrate the matter by a similar case), is by no means included in the concept of any divine attribute, such as eternity or simplicity; yet it does not follow that one who conceives eternity abstractly, without thinking at that time of omnipotence, conceives in God some impotent thing, on account of which this idea would be called blasphemous and worthy of an idol and not of God. Indeed, let them see for themselves whether they do not beat their own mouths who utter such things. For the innovators acknowledge that the will of God, at least, is an attribute distinct from his intellect. Come now, tell me! Those who conceive it thus, do they also form the notion of a thing in God that does not understand, and so is brute? If so, then the concept of our opponents, who distinguish the intellect and the will as two attributes properly so called, will also be blasphemous and worthy of an idol and not of God. But if not, then surely it is permissible, without any injury to God, to conceive in him something which, in its formal concept as it exists in the mind, does not precisely and at the same time bring the intellect to mind. Finally, since nearly all theologians and philosophers before our age, not even the distinguished Cocceius excepted, have long since by common consent divided the attributes of God into those of the first kind, which are of the essence and incommunicable, and those of the second kind, which are of life (for so they are accustomed to distinguish this from essence), and communicable; who could bear that their whole company should be so openly accused of blasphemy, as if, until they were illumined by the rays of Cartesian philosophy, they had conceived of God an imperfect idol? If we pleased, it would be easy to turn the same charge back upon the innovators with greater right. We proceed now to show by further instances what concept they forge that is worthy of God, since, by their own thought, nothing can be conceived in God except that.

units.la: III. Deum ratione essentiæ suæ planè nullibi esse.
units.tr: III. God, in respect of His essence, is nowhere at all.

units.la: Hoc necesse habent tueri, qui totam Dei essentiam sola cogitatione
units.tr: Those must maintain this who hold that the whole essence of God consists in thought alone,

units.la: V. Deum ratione essentiæ tione consistere asserunt. Etenim iisdem Cogitatio & Extensio duas constituunt rerum species sic oppositas, ut quae attributa huic tribui possunt eadem illi conveniant nulla. Jam vero aliud Ubi hi non agnoscunt, quam quod idem omnino sit cum loco physico, sive spatio corporeo quod vocant circumscriptivum; atque hoc ipsum ab extensione sive intima corporis natura nulla parte distinguunt. Quibus convenienter rei intellectuali, ab omni extensione remotae, qualis est Deus, nullum ratione essentiae, quae his est mera cogitatio, adscribi potest alicubi. Audiamus, si lubet, Clauberg[i]um, De Cognit. Dei & Nostri, Exercit. LXVI. Is ad quaestionem, An omne quod est, alicubi sit, adeo ut hoc axioma a Deo & Creatura sit abstractum? Respondet, §. 1. 2. Ut intelligatur quo sensu verum sit praescriptum effatum, quamque late se extendat, explicandum est ejus tum subjectum, tum praedicatum. Subjectum de quo dicitur quod sit alicubi, non est res intellectualis seu incorporea, sed corporea tantum sive materialis, quae in longum, latum & profundum est extensa. Adde Poiretum, Cogit. Rat. Lib. 1. Cap. VI. §. 4. Si quis quaerat, ubi sit Deus.... quaestio perabsurda est. Cum idem sit ac si quaereretur ... an spatium sit ipsa Divina essentia. Absurde quaeritur de subjecto quaestionis praedicatum toto genere diversum. Perinde quaeras de mente, in qua sit figura, vel in quo sapore?
units.tr: V. ...consist in thought, as they assert. For they make thought and extension two kinds of thing so opposed that none of the attributes which can be assigned to the one belongs to the other. Now these men recognise no "where" except what is wholly the same as physical place, or corporeal space, which they call circumscriptive; and they do not distinguish this in any respect from extension or from the inner nature of body. Accordingly, a thinking being, remote from all extension, such as God is, cannot be ascribed any "where" at all in respect of its essence, which for them is mere thought. Let us hear, if you please, Clauberg, De Cognitione Dei et Nostri, Exercitatio LXVI. On the question Whether everything that exists is somewhere, so that this axiom is abstracted from God and creature? he answers, §§ 1, 2: So that it may be understood in what sense the stated saying is true, and how widely it extends, both its subject and its predicate must be explained. The subject of which it is said that it is somewhere is not an intellectual or incorporeal thing, but only a corporeal or material thing, which is extended in length, breadth and depth. Add Poiret, Cogitationes rationales, Book 1, Chapter VI, §4: If anyone asks where God is ... the question is most absurd. It is the same as asking ... whether space is the Divine essence itself. One asks absurdly about a subject a predicate wholly of another kind. Just so you might ask of a mind what shape it has, or what flavour?

units.la: Non ero operosus in confutanda thesi, quae stare nequit, convulso jam ejus praecipuo fulcro, quod est conceptus Essentiae divinae, tanquam purae cogitationis. Sed & aliud ei subfernitur praejudicium circa conceptum Alicubi, quod extensionem praecise involvere opinantur. At perperam, quum re vera aliud nihil notet quam relationem praesentiae, sive coexistentiae, vel actualis ad rem actu existentem, vel possibilis ad rem possibilem. Ista autem praesentia vel coexistentia quod concipiatur involvere partium diffusionem, a mero infantiae praejudicio est, quo ita a teneris assueti sumus corporum duntaxat praesentiam & ubi concipere, ut mens non nisi summa cum attentione & difficillime notionem Alicubi ab idea corporis divellere queat: quod non hic tantum sed & in aliis nostrae menti in hoc unionis statu versanti accidit frequentissimum. Rem ipsam quantum attinet, quid, obsecro, vetat, essentiam corporis suo quidem modo, per partium scil. extensionem ac divisibiliter alicubi esse; Deum vero modo sibi convenien-te, te, coexistendo alicui spatio per essentiam suam indivisim & citra ullam extensionis diffusionem ? Adeò hæc sunt evidentia, ut si lubeat seponere aliquantisper disputationis fervorem, ausim hic obtestari unumquemque, an, uti rem singularem quamcunque, ità quoque Deum, ratione essentiæ concipere queat, ut non concipiat esse, uti loquuntur, & Hic & Nunc ? Experiatur quilibet, & deprehendet non magis se hic præscindere posse notionem ꟻ Alicubi, quam eam quæ est ꟻ Aliquando. Ut merito quotquot hactenus ex Cartesio philosophati non fuerunt, quemadmodum τὸ Aliquando, ità quoque τὸ Alicubi, agnoverint Entis, non qua corporei, sed qua entis, affectionem; quam & ideò admiserunt Deo non minus quam creaturis convenire. Neque melius, quo nexu indiviso ista duo cohæreant, intelligimus, quam si vel solùm attendamus, Vorstium, Socinianos, aliosque qui errarunt in conceptu Divinæ Æternitatis, errasse pariter in doctrina de Immensitate; & contrà. Uti ergò Deus negari nequit ratione essentiæ esse Aliquando, ita neque negari potest ratione essentiæ esse Alicubi. Rationes alias, easque invictissimas, hic suppeditat, & Omnipræsentia divina, & unio naturæ Divinæ hypostatica in Christo mediatore; quæ neutra orthodoxè explicari & defendi potest, si ratione essentiæ neges Deum Alicubi esse. Verum de iis mox agendum erit verbo. Nihil verò dictis obstat, quòd ab æterno Dei essentia fuerit, etiam quùm nulla essent spatia: non enim pugnat essentiam divinam relationem dixisse ad spatia possibilia, quibus, si aliquandò dentur, verè foret præsens. Neque enim ab æterno temporalia quoque spatia fuerunt; nostris nihilominus quæ jam sunt, essentia divina (modo perfectissimo licet ac se digno; videlicet absque existentiæ suæ successione aut mutatione) coëxistit præsens. Ex quibus simul liquet, per creationem ex nostra sententia Deo ratione essentiæ nihil hac parte accidisse novi; cum & ante Mundum conditum fuerit Alicubi, licet non præsens, si strictè loquaris. Plura qui cupit conferat & hic & in sequentibus Disquisitionem nostram de Nullibitate Spirituum. Fateor, errori de Deo qui ratione essentiæ nullibi sit prætexuntur quandoque magnorum Virorum nomina, sed non absque ingenti in eos injuria. Etenim quoties Deo Ubi denegant, nullo Eum contineri loco, illocalem eum esse, &c. afferunt, Ubi remo-vent, vent, non omnino penitus, sed prædicamentale duntaxat & finitum, quod circumscriptivum corporum aut definitivum spirituum creatorum vocant. Itā Augustinus Lib. vii. Confess. Cap. i. totus est in deplorando errore juventutis, quo itā conceperat Deum Alicubi, ut major pars terra majorem ejus partem haberet, & minorem minor, atque ita eo plena essent omnia, ut frustatim partibus mundi, magnis magnas, brevibus breves partes sui faceret præsentes. Merito hunc conceptum deinde damnat; at non ideo essentiam Dei alicubi esse negat. Non sic Deus dicitur complere mundum, velut aqua, velut aer, velut ipsa lux, ut minore sui parte minorem implet mundi partem & majore majorem. Novit ubique totus esse, & nullo contineri loco. Epist. iii. Occurrunt quæ hūc pertinent valdè præclara in celebri illa ad Dardanum Epistola, quæ ordine est lvii. verūm per ea jam vagari studio brevitatis non licet. Doctissimum Bisterfeldium præterire hīc nequeo, cūm is omnium clarissimè explicet, quo sensu Deus dici possit illocalis, & tamen verè alicubi existere. Sic ille Philosoph. Prim. Cap. xii. Hinc jam oritur quarta entis divisio: nempe, quod sit, vel illocale, vel locale. Illud dicitur, cujus Ubietas est Infinita; hoc, cujus est finita. Egregiè verò de Ubi Dei disserit Ibid. Reg. vi. hunc in modum. Alicubi esse, est universale omnium entium existentium attributum. Quod nusquam est non est. Hic autem, ut ubique in hac disciplina, magna vocum penuria laboramus. Itaque cogimur eas à rebus corporeis mutuari; & quasi sublimare. Quia nihil sensibus percipimus, quin id in certo loco nobis occurrat, ideo ipsimet Deo, Scripturam præeuntem imitati, locum & locorum differentias adscribimus. Secus, nec ejus præsentiam, nec efficientiam, nec eminentiam, exprimere possumus. Interim hinc claret, Deum, nec localiter moveri, nec ullo modo aliquam mutationem in se admittere posse. Alias entis infiniti ubietas foret finita. Etsi vero nos hanc Dei excellentiam ne concipere quidem queamus sine spatiis, tamen ideo Deum nulli spatio includimus. At per omnia spatia, inquis, non solum realia, sed etiam imaginaria intelligis. Omnino, sed merito: id ni faceremus, Deum, contra rectam rationem & Scripturam, huic mundo includeremus. Supra magnus fuit usus successionis imaginariæ, nunc par, si non major, est spatiorum imaginariorum. Hæc qui exagitant vel infirmam vel confusam habent imaginationem: siquidem ipsa Scriptura docet Deum nec à cælo quidem cælorum lorum capi, &c. Ecce! Illocalem Deum statuit vir doctus; quatenus nulli spatio includimus: at simul ejusdem agnoscit Ubicatem infinitam; sine qua nec ejus praesentiam, nec efficientiam, nec eminentiam exprimere possumus; quâque est Alicubi ratione spatiorum non solum realium, sed etiam imaginariorum. Neque ullus qui aliter hic sentiat alicujus notae scriptor, quantum opinor, adducetur. Ut Recentiores, qui novum hoc suum dogma suffragiis magnorum Virorum, Augustini nominatim & Bisterfeldii, stabilire laborant, hac in re prodant vel negligentiam in expendenda Auctorum mente supinissimam, vel sophisticen in citandis eorum verbis nimium crassam.
units.tr: I shall not labour to refute a thesis that cannot stand, now that its chief support, the concept of the Divine essence as pure thought, has been overthrown. But there is another prejudice underlying it, concerning the concept of Somewhere, which they think involves extension precisely. This is wrong, since in fact it signifies nothing more than a relation of presence, or coexistence, either of an actual thing to a thing actually existing, or of a possible thing to a possible thing. That this presence or coexistence should be taken to involve the diffusion of parts is a mere prejudice of infancy, by which we have been so accustomed from our youth to conceive only the presence and "where" of bodies that the mind cannot separate the notion of Somewhere from the idea of body except with the greatest attention and with the utmost difficulty; and this happens most frequently not only here but in other matters, since our mind is in this state of union. As far as the matter itself goes, I beg you, what forbids the essence of body to be somewhere in its own way, namely by the extension of its parts and divisibly, while God, in a manner fitting to Himself, coexists with a space by His essence, indivisibly and without any diffusion of extension? These things are so evident that, if you will set aside for a little the heat of dispute, I would venture to call upon anyone to consider whether he can conceive God, in respect of His essence, as he can conceive any single thing, without conceiving Him to be, as they say, Here and Now. Let anyone try, and he will find that he can no more abstract from here the notion of Somewhere than the notion of Sometime. Hence all who hitherto have not philosophised from Descartes have acknowledged that the Sometime, as well as the Somewhere, is an affection of being, not as corporeal but as being; and for this reason they have admitted that it belongs to God no less than to creatures. Nor do we understand better the indivisible bond by which these two cohere than if we merely note that Vorstius, the Socinians and others who erred concerning the concept of the Divine eternity erred likewise in the doctrine of immensity; and conversely. Therefore, just as God cannot be denied to be Sometime in respect of His essence, so neither can He be denied to be Somewhere in respect of His essence. The divine omnipresence and the hypostatic union of the Divine nature in Christ the mediator furnish other reasons here, and very unanswerable ones; and neither can be explained and defended orthodoxly if you deny that God is Somewhere in respect of His essence. But these matters must be treated shortly in words. Nor does anything said stand against the fact that the Divine essence existed from eternity, even when there were no spaces; for it does not conflict that the Divine essence should be said to be related to possible spaces, of which it would truly be present if they were ever given. For neither were temporal spaces there from eternity; nevertheless, in relation to those that now exist, the Divine essence coexists present with them (in a most perfect manner, though one that is worthy of Him, namely without any succession or change of His existence). From which it is also clear that, according to our opinion, by creation nothing new has befallen God in respect of His essence in this regard; since He was somewhere even before the world was made, though not present, if you speak strictly. Whoever desires more may consult here, and in what follows, our Disquisition on the Non-Whereness of Spirits. I admit that the names of great men are sometimes put forward as pretexts for the error that God is nowhere in respect of His essence, but not without great injury to them. For whenever they deny that God has a Where, asserting that He is contained by no place, that He is without place, and so on, they mean that the Where is removed not entirely, but only the categorical and finite Where, which they call the circumscriptive Where of bodies or the definitive Where of created spirits. Thus Augustine, Confessions, Book VII, Chapter 1, is wholly occupied with lamenting the error of his youth, by which he had so conceived God as to be Somewhere, that the greater part of the earth would hold a greater part of Him, and the lesser a lesser, and thus all things would be so full of Him that He would make parts of Himself present to parts of the world piecemeal, great parts to great, small parts to small. He rightly condemns this concept afterwards; but he does not therefore deny that the essence of God is somewhere. God is not said to fill the world as water does, or as air does, or as light itself does, so that with a smaller part of Himself He fills a smaller part of the world and with a larger part a larger. He knows how to be wholly everywhere and to be contained by no place. Epistle iii. Very excellent points pertinent to this occur in that famous Letter to Dardanus, which is numbered lvii; but for the sake of brevity I may not wander through them here. I cannot pass over here the most learned Bisterfeld, since he most clearly explains in what sense God can be called illocal and yet truly exist somewhere. Thus he, Philosophia Prima, Chapter XII: Hence arises the fourth division of being: namely that it is either illocal or local. The former is that whose Ubiety is infinite; the latter, that whose Ubiety is finite. And he discourses excellently on the Where of God in the same work, Rule VI, in this manner: To be somewhere is a universal attribute of all existing beings. That which is nowhere is not. Here, however, as everywhere in this discipline, we labour under a great scarcity of words. We are therefore compelled to borrow them from corporeal things and, as it were, to raise them up. Because we perceive nothing by the senses without its presenting itself to us in a certain place, we ourselves, imitating Scripture going before us, ascribe place and differences of place even to God Himself. Otherwise we could express neither His presence, nor His efficacy, nor His eminence. Meanwhile it is clear hence that God can neither be moved locally nor admit any change in Himself in any way. Otherwise the ubiety of an infinite being would be finite. And although we cannot even conceive this excellence of God without spaces, yet for that reason we do not include God in any space. But, you say, you understand by all spaces not only real but also imaginary ones. Certainly, but rightly so: if we did not, we would include God in this world, contrary to right reason and Scripture. Formerly the use of imaginary succession was great; now the use of imaginary spaces is equal, if not greater. Those who attack these things have either a weak or a confused imagination; for Scripture itself teaches that God is not contained even by the heaven of heavens, etc. Behold! The learned man sets up an illocal God, in so far as we include Him in no space; but at the same time he acknowledges His infinite Ubiety, without which we could express neither His presence, nor His efficacy, nor His eminence; and by which He is Somewhere in the sense of not only real but also imaginary spaces. Nor, as far as I think, will any writer of note be cited who thinks otherwise on this point. As for the more recent writers, who labour to establish this new dogma of theirs by the authority of great men, namely Augustine and Bisterfeld by name, in this matter they reveal either a most careless neglect in weighing the minds of the authors, or an excessively crude sophistry in citing their words.
IV.

units.la: Immensitatem Divinam esse nihil aliud, quam denominationem extrinsecam, natam ex operatione in rebus minationem extrinsecam, natam ex operatione in rebus corporeis.
units.tr: The Immensity of God is nothing other than an extrinsic denomination arising from his operation in corporeal things.

units.la: Eruditissimi Viri hunc in modum ex novis principiis de Dei Omnipræsentia differentis verba alibi exhibuimus. Neque aliter possunt quicunque essentiam Divinam sola cogitatione definiunt, eamque plane nullibi esse contendunt. Hoc enim posito, nihil restat quam ut omne Dei Ubi, si quod omnino ex hac sententia ei tribuendum sit, restringatur ad puram denominationem desumtam ab operationibus ejus in rebus corporeis, quæ ex nova hypothesi cum ipso Ubi sunt idem. Cartesius quidem expresse instanti Moro, Qui autem Deum positive infinitum agnoscit, i. e. ubique existentem, quod tu merito facis, &c. regerit, Epist. LXIX. Lib. I. Hoc ubique non admitto. Videris enim hic infinitatem Dei in eo ponere, quod ubique existat; cui opinioni non assentior: sed puto Deum ratione sua potentiæ ubique esse, ratione autem suæ essentiæ nullam plane habere relationem ad locum. Omnium vero, uti clarissimè, itacandidissimè secundum nova principia absolventia Divinam naturam pura cogitatione, de hisce ratiocinatur Poiretus, qui hic Cartesium recte philosophantem se sequi profitetur. Plurima notatu digna quæ hujus loci sunt occurrunt, Cogit. Rat. Lib. I. Cap. VI. Adscribam pauca ex §. 6. At quid argumento, ait, supra allato respondendum est, Cum Deus potentia sua Creaturis sit præsens, sequi & proprie essentia, quæ ipsa potentia est, præsentem eis esse dicen-dum ? dum? Negandum est, exactè dici, Deum esse creatis præsentem ratione essentialis potentiæ; sive, quod idem est, essentialem Dei potentiam in creaturis esse, &c. Adest Deus, sed effectu & operatione potentiæillius, quæ in ipso solo est, & cujus nomen si ipsis operationibus detur, ad rhetoricum tropum satius est recurrere, quam concludere, præsentiam operationis, quæ est in creatura, esse ipsam Dei potentiam, &c. Imo, quod verbo sit dictum, quacunque de pluribus modis præsentiæ divinæ dicuntur, ea in operationem ejus debent resolvi, &c. Quin pergit, §. 4. Ergo abeant dicta de præsentia Dei ratione essentiæ totius in toto mundo, & totius in qualibet parte, & similes perabsurdæ voces, &c. Credibile est homines, si quid Deus sit recte nosse, non ausuros, ne Deum dedecore afficerent, talia proponere: at illi in cognoscendo numine summo ita sunt securi & supini, ut eis nosse sufficerit ipsum esse id (ut cum Philosopho loquar) qui Latinis Deus, Gallice Dieu dicitur, & ab hominibus colitur: nil multum curantes, an quæ ejus summam deceant majestatem ipsi attribuantur.
units.tr: Learned men have already set out in this way, from the new principles, their views on God's omnipresence. Those who define the Divine essence by thought alone, and insist that it is nowhere in place, can hardly speak otherwise. For once that is granted, nothing remains but that every "where" of God, if any such term should be applied to him on this view, must be restricted to a bare denomination drawn from his operations in corporeal things, which on the new hypothesis are the same as the "where" itself. Descartes, to be sure, replied expressly to the objection of More: "But he who acknowledges God as positively infinite, that is, existing everywhere, as you rightly do, etc. I do not admit this 'everywhere'. For you seem here to place the infinity of God in his existing everywhere; I do not assent to that opinion, but I think that God is everywhere in virtue of his power, while in virtue of his essence he has no relation at all to place." But of all writers, Poiret reasons about these matters most clearly and most candidly according to the new principles, which absolve the Divine nature from mere thought. He professes to follow Descartes as a philosopher who has got things right. Many points worth noting on this passage occur in his Cogitationes rationales, book I, chapter VI. I will add a few words from §6: "But what must be answered to the argument brought forward above, namely that since God is present to creatures by his power, it follows that he is present to them properly in virtue of his essence, which is that very power? It must be denied that God is strictly said to be present to creatures in virtue of his essential power; or, what is the same thing, that the essential power of God is in creatures, etc. God is present, but by the effect and operation of his power, which is in him alone; and if the name is given to the operations themselves, it is better to have recourse to a rhetorical trope than to conclude that the presence of the operation which is in the creature is the very power of God, etc. Indeed, to put it briefly, whatever is said of the several modes of the Divine presence must be resolved into his operation, etc." He goes on, in §4: "Therefore let go the statements about God's presence in virtue of the essence being whole in the whole world and whole in every part, and similar utterly absurd expressions, etc. It is credible that men, if they really knew what God is, would not dare to put forward such things, lest they dishonour God. But they are so careless and idle in knowing the supreme Deity that it is enough for them to know that he is that which (to speak with the philosopher) is called Deus in Latin and Dieu in French, and is worshipped by men; caring little whether what befits his supreme majesty is attributed to him."

units.la: Itâ non satis erat renovare lites, jam olim orthodoxis à Vorstio & Sociis motas, de essentiali Dei Omnipræsentia, nisi quoque sententia recepta non Reformatis duntaxat, sed quibusvis Christianis, si sectæ Polonicæ fratres excipias, traducatur, tanquam Deum dedecore afficiens, nec multum curans, an quæ Dei summam decent Majestatem ipsi attribuantur. Audiat ista Christianus orbis! Audiat, inquam, & evigilet tandem! Quò non zelus pro Cartesii dogmatibus abducit hodiè viros? Ne quem autem male urat, Vorstii mentionem me fecisse hoc loco; quasi mimium id ad invidiam comparatum sit. Fateor, nec corporeum Deum, nec cœlo inclusum, cum Vorstio, statuunt Novatores; at non istis capitibus absolvitur quicquid hac parte Catholicis cum Vorstio intercessit litium. Quamvis & id nesciam, an multo tolerabilius sit, Deum planè nullibi ponere, quam cœlo cum includere. Missis autem hisce in præsens, fuit nostris cum Vorstio gravis imprimis controversia de vera Dei παντοχυσια in omnibus partibus hujus Universi: atque hanc negant Cartesiani perindè ac Vorstius; licet ex alia & alia hypothesi. Nullas quapropter causas habent querendi de injuria quæ sibi hac in parte fiat. Quin potius vel errorem agnoscant ingenuè, linguam simul cum mente corrigentes, vel prostratas dudum Vorstii copias instaurent tandem genetosè. Nobis placet istud Walæi : Omnes orthodoxi, Deum ubique per essen‐tiam, tam in cœlo quam in terra, præsentem esse, rectè contendunt; & contrariam sententiam blasphemiæ condemnant. Non est hujus loci urgere efficacissima Scripturæ loca, à Theologis nostris pro Essentiali Dei Omnipræsentia adducta, quæ novis & violentis ac plusquam Vorstianis interpretamentis eludere Novatores, conquiri‐tur Cl. Marefius, System. Noviss. Loc. II. §. 32. Lit. b. Ista sileo. Tantùm, si Immensitas sit nihil aliud, quam denominatio extrin‐seca ab operationibus transeuntibus sumta, quæ tandem restat distin‐ctio Immensitatem Divinam inter & Providentiam? quæ tamen duo distinxerunt ab omni ævo Philosophi & Theologi. Quin, si attendas, ne ullâ quidem ratione illis Deus alicubi erit, sed ejus duntaxat effecta; quæ à Deo totâ essentiâ distinctâ esse notum est. Dei enim operatio, cujus ratione ipse alicubi diceretur, vel activè spectatur à parte Dei operantis, vel passivè a parte rei productæ; tertium non datur. A parte Dei si spectetur, nihil est, si Recen‐tioribus credas, præter ipsam cogitationem, quæ essentiam Dei absolvit, quamque nullam planè relationem ad locum dicere, exer‐tim pronunciant. A parte rei productæ, est ipsa hæc res; quæ etsi alicubi sit, non ideò Deus producens alicubi est, cum toto cœlo hæc duo sint diversa. Ad metonymicam ergò locutionem claris his & distinctis Philosophis confugiendum fuit, ut ejus in‐ volucris sententiam quam profiteri pudet paliarent atque itâ orbi imponerent. Optimè hæc omnia observavit ipse Poiretus, cu‐jus & hic laudandus est candor, quandò luc. cit. ingenuè fatetur, Cartefium, Forgeum, Wittichium, cùm dixerunt, Deum‐essentiâ, essentialiter, ratione essentiæ omnibus esse præsentem, diffi‐cultatum quorundam causa, usos[uisse vocibus maximè impropriis & deceptricibus; quæ aliud ex instituto communi significant, adeoque obscuritatem conceptuum sovent; quibus, si ex ordinario usu inter‐pretentur, non significatur verum; quarumque sensus quem substi‐tuunt, ipsi verborum significationi relucietur. Egregiè! Credant vocibus deceptricibus, qui, quid monstri ex alant, ignorant. Non sibi iis imponi unquam patientur qui intelligunt, quam sit‐merito suspectum, quam veritati exitiale, quam viro bono & candido indignum, deceptricibus vocibus & non significantibus verum ludete in re adeò seria, de qua & vera dicere periculosum est. Certè nec Vorstio in eadem materia decepirices voces defuere. Terrent vestigia. Et quis obsecro, licet vel vim intellectui inferat, conceperit, Deum hìc vel istìc per essentiam operari (talis enim operandi modus, utpote absolutissimus & ente perfectissimo dignissimus, Deo est tribuendus) neque tamen per essentiam hìc vel istìc existere. Utique, si verum sit, Agere supponit esse, etiam hìc agere per essentiam, supponit (remotis vocibus omnibus impropriis & decepiricibus) hìc esse per essentiam. Ut re verâ conceptus Dei per operationem praesentis formari, quoat nullus qui non supponat conceptum Dei per essentiam praesentis. Absolvam verbis Claubergii, quae occurrunt Exercit. lxvi. §. 15. Ut unumquodque est, ita & alicubi est; sive, qualis existentia rei, talis etiam ejus est praesentia. Ratio est, quoniam per entitatem suam alicubi est, sive praesens est per suam existentiam. Sit ista major. Subsumo nunc ego: Atqui verè & proprie, remotis vocibus impropriis & decepticibus, per essentiam suam Deus est. Ergò & verè ac proprie, remotis vocibus impropriis ac decepticibus, per essentiam suam Deus alicubi est. Consequenter falsa & periculosa est Immensitatis explicatio per nihil aliud, quam denominationem externam ab operatione Dei in re corporea desumptam. Atqui hoc ipsum demonstrandum erat. Est autem refutatione indignum quod urgetur, per receptam Reformatis opinionem extensionem Dei tribui. Scilicet eum à Deo removendam esse ex Cartesio discere debebat orbis Christianus, qui jam olim cum Augustino intellexit, Deum esse magnum sine quantitate & ideò Immensum. Neque potui saepius mirari satis, totiesà Novatoribus hìc vapulasse Cel. Maresium, quòd dixerit, Omnipraesentiam Dei extendi ad omne ubi. Quicunque enim inspicere voluerit quae hac de re tradit, Syst em. Noviss. Loc. 11. §. 32. lit. a. clarè is videbit, nihil aliud contendisse Virum, quam in conceptu Omnipraesentiae divinae extensionem involvi; non à parte Dei, quam vocat extensionem subjectivam, Deoque expressè denegat; sed à parte rei cui Deus coexistit, quam vocat extensionem objectivam, quamque tribuit Deo inextensò & indivisibili. Quod totum adeò verum est & accuratum, ut ne quidem extensionis objectivae, uti vocat D. Maresius, conceptum ipsi Novatores hìc excludere queant, dùm contendunt, concipiendam esse Immensitatem per denominationem ab operatione in rebus rebus corporeis : quæ profectò absque extensione concipi non possunt.
units.tr: So it was not enough to revive the disputes, stirred long ago by Vorstius and his companions and already refuted by orthodox men, about God's essential omnipresence. The opinion commonly held, not only among the Reformed but among all Christians (except the brethren of the Polish sect), is now also to be distorted, as "dishonouring God and caring little whether what befits the supreme majesty of God is attributed to him." Let the Christian world hear these things! Let it hear them, I say, and at last wake up! To what lengths does zeal for the dogmas of Descartes lead men today? Lest anyone be offended, I mention Vorstius at this point, though it may seem that I make too much of him for the sake of odium. I admit that the innovators, with Vorstius, do not hold God to be corporeal or enclosed in heaven; but Catholics' many lawsuits with Vorstius are not settled on those heads alone. Though I do not know whether it is much more tolerable to place God nowhere at all than to enclose him in heaven. Setting these aside for the present, the most serious controversy between us and Vorstius was over the true omnipotence of God in all parts of this universe; and the Cartesians deny this just as Vorstius did, though on a different hypothesis. They therefore have no grounds for complaining of the injury done to them in this respect. Rather, let them either frankly acknowledge their error, correcting their language together with their mind, or else, at length, restore the troops of Vorstius, long since routed. I am pleased with this statement of Walaeus: "All orthodox men rightly contend that God is present everywhere by essence, in heaven as well as on earth, and they condemn the contrary opinion as blasphemy." It is not the place here to press the most effective passages of Scripture, which our theologians have adduced for God's essential omnipresence, and which, as the illustrious Maresius complains, "the innovators try to elude by new and violent interpretations, more than Vorstian ones" (System. Noviss. Loc. II, §32, lit. b). I pass over these things. But only this: if immensity is nothing other than an extrinsic denomination taken from transient operations, what distinction then remains between the Divine immensity and providence? Yet philosophers and theologians have distinguished these two from all ages. Indeed, if you look closely, God will not be anywhere in any sense on their view, but only his effects, which are known to be wholly distinct from God's essence. For the operation of God, by reason of which he would be said to be somewhere, is viewed either actively, on the side of God operating, or passively, on the side of the thing produced; there is no third. If it is viewed on God's side, it is, if you believe the more recent writers, nothing but the very thought which absolves the Divine essence, and which they loudly declare to have no relation at all to place. If it is viewed on the side of the thing produced, it is that thing itself; and although that thing is somewhere, God producing it is not thereby somewhere, since these two are wholly different. So these clear and distinct philosophers had to take refuge in a metonymical way of speaking, in order to cover up, and so impose upon the world, an opinion they are ashamed to profess. Poiret himself observed all this very well, and his candour deserves praise here, where in the passage cited he frankly confesses that Descartes, Forgeus and Wittich, when they said that God is present to all things "by essence, essentially, in virtue of his essence," used "words most improper and deceptive, which in common usage mean something else, and so foster obscurity of concepts; if these are understood in their ordinary use, the truth is not signified; and the sense they substitute is refuted by the very meaning of the words." Admirable! Let those believe in "deceptive words" who do not know what monstrous thing they feed. Those who understand will never allow themselves to be deceived by them, seeing how suspect, how destructive to truth, how unworthy of a good and candid man it is to play with "deceptive words that do not signify the truth" in a matter so serious, about which even to speak the truth is dangerous. Surely in this same matter Vorstius did not lack "deceptive words." The traces alarm us. And who, I beg you, even if he forces his intellect, could conceive that God operates here or there "through essence" (for such a mode of operating, as most absolute and most worthy of the most perfect being, is to be attributed to God), and yet does not exist here or there through essence? Surely, if it is true, "to act" presupposes "to be"; so "to act here through essence" presupposes (setting aside all "improper and deceptive" words) "to be here through essence." Indeed the concept of God acting by his presence in operation cannot be formed by anyone who does not presuppose the concept of God present by essence. I will conclude in the words of Clauberg, which occur in Exercitatio 66, §15: "As each thing is, so also it is somewhere; or, as the existence of a thing is, so also is its presence. The reason is that by its entity it is somewhere, that is, it is present by its existence." Let that be the major premise. Now I assume: but truly and properly, setting aside improper and deceptive words, God is through his essence. Therefore also truly and properly, setting aside improper and deceptive words, God is somewhere through his essence. Consequently the explanation of immensity as nothing but an external denomination drawn from God's operation in a corporeal thing is false and dangerous. Yet this very thing was to be proved. As for the objection that the Reformed opinion ascribes extension to God, it is unworthy of refutation. Surely the Christian world ought to learn from Descartes that extension must be removed from God, since long ago Augustine already understood God to be "great without quantity, and therefore immense." Nor can I wonder enough that the illustrious Maresius has been so often scourged by the innovators here for saying that the omnipresence of God "extends" to every where. For whoever cares to examine what he teaches on this matter (System. Noviss. Loc. II, §32, lit. a) will clearly see that the man contended only that the extension is involved in the concept of Divine omnipresence; not on the side of God, which he calls "subjective extension" and expressly denies to God, but on the side of the thing with which God coexists, which he calls "objective extension," and which he attributes to God as "unextended and indivisible." All this is so true and accurate that the innovators themselves cannot even exclude the concept of "objective extension," as Maresius calls it, while they insist that immensity is to be conceived through a denomination from operation "in corporeal things", which indeed cannot be conceived without extension.
V.

units.la: Naturam Divinam in Christo Mediatore naturæ humanæ uniri aliter non potuisse, quam per operationes.
units.tr: That the Divine Nature could not be united with the human nature in Christ the Mediator otherwise than through operations.

units.la: Theologici proprie fori est plena hujus propositionis discussio: quapropter, ne falcem in alienam messem mittam, duntaxat monstrabo dogma hoc revera connexum esse cum opinione asserente, uti mentis humanæ, ita Spirituum quorumvis essentiam in mera cogitatione consistere; verboque, quid de eo statuant Theologi, tantùm narrabo. Audivimus thesi præcedente exertim pronunciare Cartesium, ex hypothesi quâ Deus est nil nisi cogitatio, eundem ratione potentiæ ubique esse, ratione autem suæ essentiæ nullam planè habere relationem ad locum; id est, ad rem quampiam corpoream, quæ Cartesio cum loco eadem est. Huic consonum habuimus Poiretum profitentem, vocibus, maximè improprijs ac deceptricibus, nec significantibus verum, uti Cartesianos, qui Deum essentiâ, essentialiter, ratione essentiæ esse præsentem alicubi dixerunt. Jam verò, non aliâ ratione spiritum cum re quapiam uniri posse, quam quâ ei est præsens, per se clarissimum est. Ex quibus sponte suâ sequitur, naturam Divinam, utpote spiritualem, id est, juxta illos, meram cogitationem, cum nulla re alia, adeoque nec cum humana natura Christi Domini, aliter conjungi potuisse, quam per operationes, & ratione effectuum; omnesque, qui aliter loquuntur Cartesiani, diffi ultatum quarundam causâ, uti vocibus maximè deceptricibus & ex ordinario usu non significantibus verum. Et quamvis hactenus fere metuant, liberè profiteri genuinam hanc de re animi sententiam, non tamen abstinent ea tradere de unione personali duarum naturarum in Christo Mediatore, quæ quid sentiant, satis produnt. Hùc nimirum aurigantur quæ docent de Personalitate in divinis, quæ sit mera negatio; de hac ipsa unione, quæ tantùm sit relatio quædam conjunctionis; ut nulla sit, qualis Theologis passim traditur, sustentatio personalis; &c. Adquæ omnia jam sæpius à Clarissimis Theologis objecta vel silent, vel frigidè satis respondent. Certè in universum Poiretus; Quæcunque de pluribus modis præsentia divina dicuntur, ea in operationem ejus debent resolvi. Cogit.Rat. Lib. 1. Cap. vi. §. 6. Et speciatim de unione cujusvis mentis cum corpore, Forgæus: Oportet ergo unionem in omnibus quæ uniuntur, quærere in attributis relativis; nulla autem alia invenio, ... quam primo & in genere actionem & passionem, &c. Preterea invenio... voluntatem pro unione quæ inter mentem est & corpus, quatenus hæc voluntas extra suum subjectum procedit per suas operationes. Neque puto quemquam alia posse invenire attributa, quam hæc, quæ duas substantias simul unire possent. Tract. de Ment. Cap. xiii. §. 8.
units.tr: A full discussion of this proposition belongs properly to the theologians' domain, so, lest I put my sickle into another's harvest, I will only show that this dogma is in fact connected with the opinion that the essence of the human mind, and of every spirit, consists in pure thought, and I will simply report what the theologians have said about it. We heard the Cartesians declare plainly in the previous thesis that, on the hypothesis that God is nothing but thought, God is everywhere by reason of power, but by reason of his essence he has no relation at all to place; that is, to some corporeal thing, which for the Cartesians is the same as place. In agreement with this we have Poiret professing that the Cartesians, using words that are most improper and deceptive, and that do not signify the truth, said that God is present somewhere by essence, essentially, by reason of essence. Now, that a spirit can be united with some thing in no other way than by being present to it is perfectly clear in itself. From this it follows of its own accord that the divine nature, being spiritual, that is, according to them, mere thought, could not be joined with any other thing, and so not with the human nature of Christ the Lord, except through operations and by way of effects. And all who speak otherwise, the Cartesians say, do so for the sake of resolving certain difficulties, using words that are most deceptive and, in ordinary usage, do not signify the truth. And although hitherto they have largely feared to profess openly this genuine opinion on the matter, they nonetheless do not refrain from setting it forth concerning the personal union of the two natures in Christ the Mediator, and their views on this are sufficiently revealed. Hence come their teachings about personality in the divine being, which is a mere negation; about this very union, which is only a certain relation of conjunction; so that there is no such thing, as is commonly taught by theologians, as personal sustentation; and so on. Yet all these matters, already objected to many times by the most distinguished theologians, are either passed over in silence or answered rather coldly. Poiret says in general: Whatever is said of the divine presence in several ways, that must be resolved into his operation. Cogit. Rat. Lib. 1. Cap. vi. §. 6. And specifically concerning the union of any mind with a body, Forgeus says: It is necessary, therefore, to seek the union in all things that are united in relative attributes; but I find no others... except first and in general action and passion, etc. Moreover I find... the will to be the union that exists between mind and body, insofar as this will proceeds outside its subject through its operations. Nor do I think anyone can find other attributes than these which could unite two substances together. Tract. de Ment. Cap. xiii. §. 8.

units.la: Scholasticos passim perstringunt nostri, & merito, quòd mysteriorum profunditatem rationis acumine pervestigare laborarint, indèque tantis rebus minus opportunâ philosophatione tenebras intulerint. Quis verò neget imitari re vera eorum mores, quorum vel nomen tantopere horrent, qui in arduo negotio ex idea Dei tanquam meræ cogitationis, adeò periculosè hic sapere non verentur? Periculosè, inquam; quatenus sic omnis Ἑνωσις ὑποστατικὴ duarum naturarum in Christo Θεανθρώπῳ in ὑπάρξεως meram παράσασιν resolvitur. Quod qui sentiunt, an non, contra adverbia Ephesina ἀδιαιρέτως καὶ ἀχωρίστως, salivam Nestorii lambant? viderint Theologi. Certè, qui jam dudum ante novam sapientiam docuerunt (quorum, tanquam extra partes constitutorum, efficax imprimis est hic testimonium) contra eandem exertim pronunciant. Nestoriani veteres statuebant, has duas naturas non aliter fuisse unitas, quam quia Divina natura humanæ adsistebat in omnibus suis Operibus, & favore suo singulari eam amplecteretur. Sed hæc sententia hæretica judicata fuit in concilio Ephesino. Walæus in Enchirid. p. 177. Modus hujus unionis non explicandus est κατὰ συνάφειαν, aut simplicem inhabitationem, sicut nauta est in navi; vel κατ' ὀχέσιν, qualis est unio conjunctioque amicorum, &c. vel κατ' Αυτοξυλίαν, sive, ut alii vocant, καθ' ἀρμονίαν, respectu consensionis inter voluntatem humanam & divinam in Christo, &c. Atque hæc erant Nestorii σοφὰ Φάρμακα. Tilen. Syntagm. Part. 2. Disp. 1. Definiverat nimirùm vetus Ecclesia: Si quis dicit, secundum gratiam, vel secundum operationem; vel secundum dignitatem, vel secundum honoris æqualitatem, aut relationem, aut affectum, aut virtutem, &c. & non secundum compositionem, id est secundum subsistentiam, unitionem Verbi ad Carnem factam esse, anathema sit. Sed nos manum de hac tabula; queis sufficit observasse, quæ orthodoxorum hac parte sit sententia? quod novæ assertionis ab ea divortium? Ei an mitioribus quibusdam phraseologiis satisfiat, viderint Theologi! Sed viderint pariter, ne sibi & causæ fraus fiat vocibus deceptricibus, nec significantibus verum; quibus difficultatum quarundem causa uti suos socios in ejusdemodi rebus, aperte monentem audivimus Poiretum.
units.tr: Our men everywhere attack the Scholastics, and rightly, because they laboured to investigate the depths of the mysteries with the sharpness of reason, and thereby brought darkness upon such great matters by an ill-suited philosophizing. But who would deny that they are truly imitating the manners of those whom they so greatly abhor, when in this difficult business they do not hesitate to reason so dangerously from the idea of God as mere thought? Dangerously, I say; because in this way every hypostatic union [Ἑνωσις ὑποστατικὴ] of the two natures in the God-man [Θεανθρώπῳ] is resolved into a mere presence [παράσασιν] of existence [ὑπάρξεως]. Those who hold this, do they not, contrary to the Ephesine words inseparably and indivisibly [ἀδιαιρέτως καὶ ἀχωρίστως], lick the spittle of Nestorius? The theologians must look to it. Certainly, those who taught this long before the new wisdom (whose testimony is especially effective here, since they stood outside the parties) plainly declare the opposite. The ancient Nestorians held that these two natures were united in no other way than because the divine nature stood by the human in all its works and embraced it with its singular favour. But this opinion was judged heretical at the Council of Ephesus. Walaeus in Enchirid. p. 177. The manner of this union is not to be explained by contact [κατὰ συνάφειαν], or by simple indwelling, as a sailor is in a ship; or by carrying [κατ' ὀχέσιν], such as the union and joining of friends, etc.; or by self-wood [κατ' Αυτοξυλίαν], or, as others call it, by harmony [καθ' ἀρμονίαν], with respect to the agreement between the human and divine will in Christ, etc. And these were the wise remedies [σοφὰ Φάρμακα] of Nestorius. Tilen. Syntagm. Part. 2. Disp. 1. For the ancient Church had defined: If anyone says that the union of the Word with the flesh was made according to grace, or according to operation; or according to dignity, or according to equality of honour, or relation, or affection, or virtue, etc., and not according to composition, that is, according to subsistence, let him be anathema. But let us lay this tablet aside; it is enough for us to have observed what the orthodox opinion on this point is, and how far the new assertion departs from it. Whether it is satisfied by some milder phraseologies, the theologians must consider! But they must also consider, lest fraud be done to themselves and to the cause, by deceptive words that do not signify the truth, which we have heard Poiret openly advising, as his fellows, for the sake of resolving certain difficulties, in matters of this kind.
VI.

units.la: Angelos, sive bonos sive malos, ratione essentiæ nusquam esse.
units.tr: Angels, whether good or evil, are nowhere in respect of their essence.

units.la: Cohæret necessariò hæc assertio cum dogmate principali, unicam cogitationem agnoscente prædicatum essentiale quorumvis spirituum; adeòque Mentium Angelicarum non minus, quam humanarum. Philosophis eisdem, ut jam diximus, omne ubi sive spatium cum re corporea planè idem est. Res verò corporea eorundem judicio Spirituali non opponitur, nisi quatenus hæc cogitatio est, non illa. Ergò supererit, ut à cogitatione mera, qualis etiam eis Angelus, omne ubi longissimè removeatur. Videlicet, Omnia verò perfecta & realia (etiam mentes omnes, quæ spatio non egent) in spatiis ponere, quærere, nec ultra spaciosa omnia scandere, quasi nil praterea esset, mentis est in materia demersæ, diviniorisque mundi multum nescia. Poiret. Cogit. Rat. lib. 1. Cap. v. §. 8. Nam extra statum unionis (extra quem subsistunt Angelicæ mentes) sive corpora sint in rerum natura, sive non sint, concipi nequit subsistentiam aliquam, cujus tota essentia consistit in cogitando, esse posse in loco, sive definitive, sive circumscriptive, cogitationemque ejus posse facere, ut spatium aliquod repleat, aut situm aliquem habeat. Forgaus Tract. de Ment. Cap. xii. §. 4. Nominatim de Angelis alius haud indoctus horum mysteriorum explanator sic alibi: Angelorum tota natura consistit in cogitatione, unumquodque autem est præsens per id quod possidet, non autem per id quod non habet: cogitatione autem non potest esse præsens, nisi quando per cogitationem suam aliquid efficit. Item: Angeli in loco quandoque operantur, suntque in loco respectu illius operationis; sed quando non operantur, sed tantum cogitant intra se, opus non habent loco.
units.tr: This assertion coheres necessarily with the principal dogma, which acknowledges a single attribute of thought as the essential predicate of all spirits, and so of angelic minds no less than human ones. For these same philosophers, as we have already said, hold that space or place is wholly the same as corporeal being. Corporeal being, however, in their judgement is opposed to spiritual being only insofar as the one is thought and the other is not. It follows, then, that all place must be removed as far as possible from mere thought, such as they also take an angel to be. Namely: To seek to place all things that are perfect and real (even all minds, which need no space) in spaces, and not to climb beyond all spatial things as if there were nothing else, is the mark of a mind sunk in matter and very ignorant of the more divine world. Poiret, Cogit. Rat. book 1, chapter 5, §8. For outside the state of union (outside which angelic minds subsist), whether bodies exist in the nature of things or not, it cannot be conceived that any subsistence whose whole essence consists in thinking can be in a place, either definitively or circumscriptively, or that its thought can fill some space or have some position. Forgaus, Tract. de Ment. chapter 12, §4. Concerning angels by name, another not unlearned explainer of these mysteries says elsewhere: The whole nature of angels consists in thought; but each thing is present through what it possesses, not through what it does not have; and thought cannot make a thing present unless through its thought it effects something. Likewise: angels sometimes operate in a place and are in a place with respect to that operation; but when they do not operate, and only think within themselves, they have no need of place.

units.la: Exercitatione de Spiritum Nullibitate docebamus, hoc idem
units.tr: In the exercise On the Nowhere-ness of Spirits we taught that this same

units.la: dogma unum esse ex sublimibus sapientiæ Weigelianæ capitibus. Dedimus isthæc ipsa fanatici hominis verba, Crocio in Anti-weigelio citata, à nobis ex Germanicis latina facta. Videri inibi merentur; digna enim sunt, quæ cum exhibitis jam novorum Philosophorum verbis conferantur; adeò non ovum ovo existit magis simile. Clarissimum ea dant experimentum, quam parum, an cum Weigelio sentiant, an cum Catholicis orthodoxis, attendant, qui Cartesii ideas normam suæ sapientiæ sumserunt? Rem quod attinet, tam manifestæ veritatis est axioma, Agere supponit esse, quam est illud Neotericorum, Cogito, ergo sum. Inde, uti nemo concipiat, etsi vel sibi cerebrum excutiat, quicquam agere, nec tamen esse; itâ pariter nemo cogitet, Angelum hic agere, nec tamen hic esse. Quapropter, quemadmodum actio ordine naturæ essentiâ posterior est, sic præsentia ratione actionis naturâ suâ posterior est præsentiâ essentiæ; atque adeò hæc ad illam necessariò supponitur. Et si Angelus alicubi non sit, nisi ibidem extra se operetur, quid erit dicendum de Angelorum beatorum Cœlo, de damnatorum Inferno; quæ in Sacris tanquam propria loca eisdem passim tribuuntur? An verò Nullibisticum hoc utrumque erit, unà cum suis incolis? Sic exigit nova thesis. Imprimis, quum excogitare non detur opus quod actione transcunte istic locorum hi spiritus producant: neque enim inibi vel Ægyptiorum primogeniti suffocandi occurrunt, vel Assyriorum exercitus mactandus, vel præcipitandi in mare porci, vel corpora energumenôn exagitanda. Ubi, ubi ergò ab opere externo quiescentes exercitus cœlestes? Ubi diabolorum legiones? Nusquam; si his credimus philosophis. Quid? quod nec ipsæ actiones transeuntes ad definiendum ubi Angelorum quicquam juvare possint eos, qui nullam eis relinquunt activitatem, præter puram cogitationem: non enim illis qui in hac totam Spiritûs essentiam consistere ajunt Angelus creditur verè id agere quod extra se agere dicitur, sed ipse potius Deus. Si quæ ergò ex operatione concludenda erit præsentia, hujus cujus est actio, non illius inferri debebit. Absurdissimum verò fuerit existimare, aliquid corporeitas sibi contrahere à sua in rebus materialibus præsentia essentiali, quam nos eis asserimus, Angelicas mentes: non enim hæc magis indè metuenda contagio, quam quòd in corporeis rebus operari saltem dicantur. Quid ergò vetat concipere relationem præsentiæ Angelo competere in ordine ad spatium, etsi nihil in eo operetur? Præjudicium infantile, arbitror, quo connectere solent pueri conceptum præsentiæ cum conceptu extensionis; quia scilicet sensu observarunt corpora suis extendi spatiis, eorumque præsentiam mutuam dicere & vicinam coextensionem. Atqui eorum quæ corpori conveniunt modo corporeo, spiritui adscribi posse nihil nisi ratione prorsus eådem, quis unquam dedit probatum? Si quæ hac in re difficultas, non ea rei impossibilitatem arguit, sed mentis potius nostræ, materialia concipere à teneris nimium assuetæ, imbecillitatem.
units.tr: doctrine is one of the lofty heads of Weigelian wisdom. We gave those very words of the fanatical man, cited by Crocius in the Anti-Weigelius, translated by us from German into Latin. They deserve to be looked at there, for they are worth comparing with the words of the new philosophers now set out; so little does one egg resemble another. They give the clearest proof of how little attention those who took the ideas of Descartes as the norm of their wisdom pay to whether they agree with Weigel or with the orthodox Catholics. As to the matter, the axiom Acting presupposes being is as manifestly true as the saying of the moderns, I think, therefore I am. Hence, just as no one can conceive of acting, even if he racks his own brain, without being, so likewise no one can think that an angel acts here without being here. Therefore, just as action is by the order of nature posterior to essence, so presence, by reason of action, is by nature posterior to the essential presence, and so the latter is necessarily presupposed to the former. And if an angel is not anywhere except where he operates outside himself, what shall be said of the heaven of the blessed angels and the hell of the damned, which Scripture everywhere assigns to them as their proper places? Will this Nowhere-ist doctrine apply to both, together with their inhabitants? So the new thesis demands. First of all, since no work can be devised which these spirits produce there by transient action, for there the firstborn of the Egyptians are not found to be suffocated, nor the army of the Assyrians to be slaughtered, nor the swine to be cast into the sea, nor the bodies of the possessed to be harassed: where, then, are the heavenly armies, idle from external work? Where are the legions of devils? Nowhere, if we believe these philosophers. Moreover, not even transient actions can help to define where the angels are, for those who leave them no activity besides pure thought. For it is not believed that the angel truly does what he is said to do outside himself, since those who say that the whole essence of spirit consists in this attribute the agent is rather God himself. If, then, a presence is to be inferred from operation, it must be attributed to the one whose action it is, not to the other. It would be most absurd to suppose that anything could acquire corporeity from the essential presence of angelic minds among material things, which we ascribe to them: for this contagion is no more to be feared from that than from their being said to operate at least upon corporeal things. What, then, forbids us to conceive that a relation of presence belongs to an angel with respect to space, even if he does nothing in it? I think it is an infantile prejudice, by which children are accustomed to connect the concept of presence with the concept of extension, because they have observed by the senses that bodies extend through their spaces, and speak of their mutual presence as neighbouring co-extension. Yet who has ever proved that what belongs to a body in a bodily way can be ascribed to a spirit by no other means than the very same? If there is any difficulty in this matter, it argues not the impossibility of the thing but rather the weakness of our own mind, too much accustomed from childhood to conceive material things.
VII.

units.la: Angelos ratione essentiæ non moveri de spatio in spatium.
units.tr: Angels do not move from place to place by reason of their essence.

units.la: Ita sentire debent, qui Angelicos spiritus ratione essentiæ, quæ nihil sit nisi mera cogitatio, nusquam esse contendunt. Quæ enim res capax non est alicujus Ubi, eandem neque Ubi suum mutare posse, per se clarum atque evidens est. Et sic Cartesio non minus absurdè videtur Spiritibus tribui motus localis quam figura aut extensio. Perspicuè videmus, nullam extensionem, nec figuram, nec motum localem, nec quid simile, quod corpori sit tribuendum, ad naturam nostram (quatenus scil. mentes sumus) pertinere, sed cogitationem solam, Princip. Part. I. §. 8. Ut ergò locum, non ratione essentiæ, sed tantum respectu operationum, Angelis adscribunt, itâ quoque motum. Quam in rem disertè vir doctus: Sicut locus non competit proprie Angelis, ita nec motus; neque dici potest aliter Angelus moveri, quam quatenus ibi definit operari, hic verò operari incipit.
units.tr: Those who hold that angelic spirits, by reason of their essence, which is nothing but pure thought, are nowhere must think accordingly. For it is clear and self-evident that a thing which is not capable of any "where" cannot change its own "where." And so to Descartes it seems no less absurd to attribute local motion to spirits than figure or extension. We see clearly that no extension, nor figure, nor local motion, nor anything of the kind that must be attributed to body, pertains to our nature (that is, insofar as we are minds), but only thought, Principles of Philosophy Part I §8. Therefore, just as they ascribe place to angels not by reason of their essence but only with respect to their operations, so they ascribe motion as well. On this point a learned man has stated plainly: Just as place does not belong properly to angels, so neither does motion; nor can it be said that an angel moves otherwise than insofar as it ceases to operate here and begins to operate there.

units.la: Brevis hic ero. Neque enim ut multa congeram necesse est, ad diruendam thesin, quæ quemadmodum est dogmatis præcedentis indivisum consectarium, itâ suffossis illius fundamentis ipsa ruit suâ sponte. Notavimus jam, uniuscujusque rei actionem tam esse ejusdem conditionis cum suo principio à quo fluit, ut quæ causa ratione essentiæ nusquam est aut esse potest, eadem quoque sese tanquam actionis principium nusquam manifestare possit. Quæcunque ergò res modò in hac modò in alia mundi parte suis sese operationibus præsentem prodit, illa vel statuenda est in omnibus istis spatiis
units.tr: I will be brief. There is no need to heap up many arguments to overthrow this thesis. It is an inseparable consequence of the preceding dogma, and once its foundations are undermined it falls of its own accord. We have already noted that the action of any thing is of the same nature as the principle from which it flows, so that a cause which by reason of its essence is nowhere, or cannot be anywhere, can likewise not manifest itself as the principle of an action anywhere. Whatever thing, therefore, shows itself present by its operations now in this part of the world and now in another, must be placed in all those spaces
THE EXERCITATION ON THE OPERATIONS OF BRUTES.
SUMMARY.
