units.tr: I. The occasion of this apologetic Exercitation on the substantial principle of operations in brutes. II. The sum of the whole controversy, set out in a brief compendium. III. A prejudice about the mechanical structure of the world, the chief cause for denying brutes a substantial soul. IV. There are as many testimonies to the true cognition of brutes as there are operations of theirs that meet us. V. The necessity of admitting a substantial principle of operations in brutes, for more than one reason. VI. Descartes himself, forced to yield to this, leaves the controversy hanging in the middle. VII. Some of his followers flee to the Platonic world-soul, and others even strike out the substantial souls of men. VIII. Sacred Authority agrees with the assertion of a substantial principle of true life and cognition in brutes. IX. The thesis opposed to ours turns brutes into mere automata. X. The true cognition asserted for brutes grants them nothing of rationality: XI. since not every cognition necessarily exists of the same order and kind: XII. as the Peripatetic School teaches everywhere, and not even the Cartesian

units.la: tesiano Forgæo. XIII. Quæ brutis substantiale veræ cognitionis principium tribuit opinio, Vetus est & maximè trita.
units.tr: Forgeus. XIII. The opinion that attributes a substantial principle of true cognition to brutes is old and very much hackneyed.

units.la: Mnium ad Brutorum tum Animam tum Activitatem pertinentium justam pertractationem nec hic exspectet, monendus est in ipso limine quisquis Exercitatiunculam hanc legere parat. Latioris indaginis est hoc nobilissimum thema, quam ut paucis adeò pagellis absolvi aut debeat aut possit. In præsens brevem tantùm Apologiam dare animus est, quam parare coactus fui Thesi cuidam meæ Philosophicæ, quam olim Lugduni-Batavorum in Illustr. ac Præpotent. DD. Ordinum Hollandiæ West-Frisiæque Collegio Theologico, cujus tunc temporis eram Pro-Regens, ventilandam publicè propositui. Ita tota de verbo ad verbum itá sonat: „Datur in Brutis aliquod „substantiale vitæ, sensationis, ac veræ cognitionis principium; „sive Formæ substantialis, sive Animæ sensitivæ, sive Modi cu„jusdam substantialis, sive quocunque alio id appelletur nomine. „Atque id non itá dudum, sub nostro præsidio, ab Ornatiss. „quodam D. Defendente solidè ac benè demonstratum est ex eo, „quod istud Neotericorum ergastulum quinque modorum, Men„suræ, Quietis, Motûs, Posituræ, Figuræ, operationum „principium nec sit nec esse possit. Quum enim uti res exiistit itá „quoque eadem operetur; modi verò illi non sint, nisi beneficio „substantiæ cui insunt, etiam iidem operari non poterunt, nisi „vi alicujus principii substantialis: quod cum non sit materia, „utpote purè passiva, restat, ut sit quod aliud in corpore substan-„tiale operationum principium. Cui accedit, quod modos istos „omnes vel non-entia esse, vel tantum conditiones ad operandum „præquisitas, non autem causas, sigillatim facilè probari possit, „ac jam probatum sit. Nullo autem modo hisce adversantur au„tomata, v.c. Horologia, &c. multo minus instrumenta fabrilia, „Serra, Securis, &c. quum in iis ullam operationem, sumemo-„tum vel minimum, ab istis modis partiumque dispositione, tan„quam à principio sui, profluere, quin profluere posse, pernecgemus; atque id cuivis attendenti certissimum est; si cui non, petenti tale faciemus. Neque speciatim brutorum cognitioni obstat, quod omnis cognitio dicatur involvere cogitationem, adeoque & rationalitatem: id enim salsissimum est, neque hactenus probatum ullâ specie rationis, quæ non principium petet. Demonstrandum ergò adversariis, activam oblatæ rei sensibilis perceptionem, dirigentem ex instinctu naturæ omnes bruti operationes, inferre necessariò conscientiam, uti vocant; adeòque eam fieri debere mediantibus notionibus spiritualibus; ac porrò ponere facultatem judicandi, discurrendi, &c. Quæ omnia posteriora uti bruto denegandâ censemus, itâ & prius eidem denegabimus, simulac audiverimus vel unicum argumentum, quod ullâ ratione id evincere poterit. Quod dum fiat (fiet autem ad Kalendas Græcas) nos acquiescimus in rationibus allatis, ob quas, suffragante evidente experientiâ ac auctoritate Sacrâ, brutis & cognitionem & cognitionis principium adscribendum esse, sentimus.
units.tr: Whoever is preparing to read this little Exercitation should be warned at the very threshold that he should not expect here a full treatment of everything pertaining to the soul and activity of brutes. This most noble theme requires a wider investigation than can be either completed or contained in so few pages. At present I intend to give only a short Apology, which I was obliged to prepare for a certain Philosophical Thesis of mine, which I once put forward for public debate at Leiden before the Theological College of Their Illustrious and Most Mighty Lordships the States of Holland and West Friesland, of which I was then Pro-Regent. It reads word for word as follows: "There is in brutes some substantial principle of life, sensation, and true cognition, whether it be called the form of a substance, or a sensitive soul, or a certain substantial mode, or by whatever other name. And this was not long ago, under our presidency, soundly and well demonstrated by a certain most distinguished Defendant, from the fact that this prison-house of the moderns' five modes, Measure, Rest, Motion, Position, and Figure, is neither nor can be a principle of operations. For since a thing operates as it exists, and those modes are not except by the benefit of the substance in which they inhere, they likewise cannot operate except by the power of some substantial principle; and since matter, being purely passive, is not this, it remains that there is in the body some other substantial principle of operations. To this is added that all these modes can easily be shown, one by one, to be either non-entities or merely conditions requisite for operating, and not causes; and this has already been proved. Yet automata, for example clocks, etc., by no means oppose this, much less tools of the craftsman, a saw, an axe, etc., since in them we deny that any operation, however small, flows from those modes and the arrangement of parts as from its own principle, nor can it flow; and this is most certain to anyone who considers it, and if anyone does not, we will make such a one a demonstration upon request. Nor does it stand in the way of the cognition of brutes in particular that every cognition is said to involve thought, and so rationality; for that is most absurd, nor has it hitherto been proved by any kind of reasoning that does not beg the principle. It must therefore be demonstrated to our opponents that the active perception of a sensible object presented, directing by the instinct of nature all the operations of the brute, necessarily brings in what they call consciousness; and so this must come about through spiritual notions; and further they posit the faculty of judging, reasoning, etc. All these latter things we judge must be denied to a brute; and so we shall deny the former too, as soon as we hear a single argument which can prove it in any way. Until this is done (and it will be done at the Greek Kalends), we rest content with the reasons alleged, on account of which, with clear experience and Sacred Authority supporting, we feel that cognition and a principle of cognition must be ascribed to brutes."

units.la: Etsi verò minimè ignorarem, aliter planè hic instituere eos qui Cartesianis ideis dixerunt sacramentum, quibusque oppositta erat nostra hæc thesis, non tamen vel somniabam extiturum mortalium quemquam, cui insolens videri posset assertio, quâ per secula multa continua in medio orbe Christiano, à quo in eo viguit Peripatetica Philosophia, nulla unquam audita fuit frequentior. Præter omnem interim meam opinionem accidit, ut ejus nomine impetum in me fecerint, non unus, non alter, non tertius, verùm, inito quasi tacito contractu, omnes propemodum quotquot per ista tempora pro asserendo Cartesianismo calamum exercebant in nostra patria Viri; ubique gentium tanquam periculosè novam circumferentes à cætero corpore avulsam atque uncialibus typis expressam nostram thesin: DATUR IN BRUTIS ALIQUOD SUBSTANTIALE VITÆ, SENSATIONIS, AC VERÆ COGNITIONIS PRINCIPIUM. Itâ scilicet qui innovare hodiè sacra quælibet ac profana unicè laborant, hoc ipsum objicientes talione repercussuri, eo utuntur artificio, ut antiquissimas antiquitates novitates audacter dicere ausint. Quo agendi modo etsi facilè imponant eis qui extra Cartesium nihil sapere didicerunt, quique ut plurimùm quid vel antiquum vel novum sit æquè ignorant, detecta tectâ tamen fraude, id lucrabuntur tandem, ut eis, qui æqui existunt & idonei rerum judices, rei habeantur inexcusabilis prorsus vel imperitiæ vel calumniæ. Placuit nihilominus etiam Celeberrimo Viro publico libro, ob eandem hanc de substantiali Brutorum Anima opinionem, objicere mihi Novitatem maximam, monstrificam, periculosam, portentosam, ab omnibus retrò seculis inauditam, bonis omnibus abominabilem, execrabili denique Spinosismo proximam. Et huic quidem satisfecimus abundè Narratoris nostri Confutati §. 11. & seqq. quem locum cum cis, quæ jam hac de re in medium fumus allaturi, conferri cupio. Omnem nunc controversiam, nisi fallor, satis plenè comprehendam hac Quæstione: Num Falsa sit, aut Periculosa, aut Nova, hæc positio, Datur in brutis aliquod substantiale vitæ, sensationis, ac veræ cognitionis principium? Ad quam respondemus, Negando: siquidem hac assertione Brutis non tribuitur Anima quæ sit ordinis ac speciei ejusdem cum ea quæ hominis est, substantia nimirum rationis particeps, atque omni modo à corpore independens: sed principium duntaxat quoddam catenus huic analogum, ut sufficiat ad vendicandam Brutis suam quoque actīvitatem; neque qualemcunque, verum talem quæ dirigatur à rei oblatæ prævia perceptione, non rationali quidem (quæ notionum immaterialium formationem cum conscientia, itemque actus judicandi ac discurrendi involvit) attamen vera, in quantum non impropriè aut metaphoricè dicta est hæc cognitio, sed ea cui accuratè loquendo & ex vero generalis veræ cognitionis descriptio convenit, quæ scilicet sit actīva objecti obvii perceptio.
units.tr: Although I was by no means ignorant that those who have sworn allegiance to Cartesian ideas, and against whom this thesis of mine was directed, think otherwise, I did not even dream that any mortal would appear for whom the assertion could seem strange, since for many centuries, throughout the Christian world, where Peripatetic philosophy has flourished, none was ever heard more often. Contrary to all my expectation it happened that in its name attacks were made on me, not by one, not by another, not by a third, but, as if by a tacit agreement, nearly all the men in our country who during these times have wielded their pens in defence of Cartesianism, carrying our thesis about everywhere as something dangerously new, torn from the rest of the text and printed in capital letters: THERE IS IN BRUTES SOME SUBSTANTIAL PRINCIPLE OF LIFE, SENSATION, AND TRUE COGNITION. So, of course, those who today labour solely to make innovations in everything sacred and profane, by hurling this very charge back in retaliation, use the device of boldly calling the most ancient things novelties. And although by this method of acting they may easily deceive those who have learned to know nothing outside Descartes, and who for the most part are equally ignorant whether something is old or new, yet once the fraud is exposed they will gain this at last: that to those who are fair and fit judges of things, they will be held wholly inexcusable, whether through ignorance or through slander. Nevertheless, a most celebrated man has also chosen, in a published book, for this same opinion about the substantial soul of brutes, to object to me that it is a very great, monstrous, dangerous, portentous novelty, unheard of in all past ages, abominable to all good men, and finally close to the execrable Spinozism. And to this indeed I have replied fully in §§ 11 and following of our Confuted Narrator, a passage I wish to be compared with what I am now about to bring forward on this matter. I think I shall, unless I am mistaken, comprehend the whole controversy sufficiently fully in this question: is this proposition, There is in brutes some substantial principle of life, sensation, and true cognition, false, or dangerous, or new? To which I answer, No. For by this assertion there is not attributed to brutes a soul of the same order and kind as that of man, namely a substance partaking of reason and wholly independent of the body; but only some principle akin to it, enough to claim for brutes their own activity as well; and not just any activity, but one directed by the prior perception of the presented thing; not rational indeed (which involves the formation of immaterial notions with consciousness, and likewise the acts of judging and reasoning), yet true, inasmuch as this cognition is not spoken of improperly or metaphorically, but is that to which, speaking accurately and truly, the general description of true cognition applies, namely that it is an active perception of an object met with.

units.la: Tantam insse arbitror huic Thesi Veritatis certitudinem atque evidentiam, ut eam latere posse putem neminem, quicunque in philosophando uni Rationi & Experientiæ cedere paratus est. Conqueruntur, fateor, Cartefii nepotes, rem hanc fugere claras suas ac distinctas ideas; at id sibi imputent oportet, qui mordicus adeò adhærere amant præconceptis opinionibus, ut neque velint neque possint, valere jussis præjudiciis, quid sentire oporteat, liberâ mente ac certâ Ratione, Sensuum testimonio & sacrâ Auctoritate suffultâ, ritè expendere. Ejusmodi ingenia quid mirum, si, ut alia quæcunque in hoc Universo obvia, itâ quoque Brutorum operationes reducere nitantur ad imaginaria sua principia;
units.tr: I consider this Thesis to have such certainty and evidence of truth that I think no one can be hidden from it, whoever is willing in philosophizing to yield to reason and experience alone. The grandchildren of Descartes, I admit, complain that this matter escapes their clear and distinct ideas; but they must impute this to themselves, who cling so stubbornly to preconceived opinions that they neither wish nor are able, having put aside prejudices, to weigh properly what ought to be thought with a free mind and sure reason, supported by the testimony of the senses and by Sacred Authority. Is it any wonder, then, that such minds, as with everything else in this universe, strive also to reduce the operations of brutes to their imaginary principles,

units.la: III. Præjudicium de mechanica mundi structura animæ substantialis brutis negatæ causa præcipua. pia; secundum quæ universa rerum natura, stupendumque hoc Divinæ providentiæ sacrarium, in vilem officinam fabrilem convertitur, in qua occurrat nil præter automata quædam, omni vero propriæ actività tis principio destituta, externoque duntaxat atque ab occurrentibus forte fortuna corpusculis impresso motu impulsa. Et quid de Brutis solliciti sint, eorumque Anima, qui ne sibi quidem hic parcunt, contendentes, præeunte sic Cartesio, & ipsum hominis corpus parili modo vivere posse & moveri absque ullo Mentis præsidio; quin qui affirmant, esse majori admiratione dignum, quod mens aliqua reperiatur in unoquoque humano corpore, quam quod nulla sit in ullis brutis: Part. 1. Epist. LXVII. Minus mirabimur eos qui talia tuentur paradoxa tantum tumultuari ob nostram hanc assertionem, Datur in Brutis aliquod substantiale vitæ, sensationis ac veræ cognitionis principium: quod quale intellectum volucrim, verbis immediatè sequentibus indicabam satis: sive Forme substantialis, sive Anime sensitiva, sive Modi cujusdam substantialis, sive quocunque alio id appelletur nomine.
units.tr: III. The chief cause of denying a substantial soul to brutes is the prejudice about the mechanical structure of the world, an impious view according to which the whole of nature, and this wonderful sanctuary of divine providence, is turned into a base workshop, in which there is nothing but certain automata, wholly destitute of any principle of genuine activity and moved only by an external motion impressed on them by small bodies that happen to strike them by chance. Some who are anxious about brutes and their soul, and who spare not even themselves here, contend, following Descartes, that the human body too can live and move in the same way without any presence of the mind. Indeed, they affirm that it is more worthy of wonder that some mind is found in each human body than that none is found in any brute: Part. 1. Epist. LXVII. We shall be less surprised that those who defend such paradoxes make an uproar over our assertion: There is in brutes some substantial principle of life, sensation and true cognition. What I meant by this I indicated sufficiently in the words that immediately follow: whether it be called a substantial form, or a sensitive soul, or a certain substantial mode, or by whatever other name.

units.la: Equidem pro Veræ Cognitionis, qualem jam descripsimus, in Brutis demonstratione, nullo alio indigemus argumento, quam quod invictum suppeditant stupendæ eorundem operationes, ob hoc solum neglectæ, atque ad veritatem hanc adstruendam apud multos minus efficaces, quod sint quotidiè obviæ. At qui diligens rerum scrutator animum adjicit ad easdem penitius examinandas, istud in iis deprehendit rationis quasi vestigium & quandam ejus veluti imitationem, ut vix, imò vix, ini ipsa sensitiva cognitione acquisicere possit: adeò bestiarum actiones in miraculum usque variæ sunt, adeo ipsi humani operandi modi æmulæ. Ex millenis unum aut alterum verbo tangemus tantùm. Quanta est v. c. in prole educandâ Brutorum sollicitudo, illa etiam refundentium, proprio stomacho fraudato, quæ jam devorarunt? Quanta in cådem adversus hostem tuendâ fortitudo & industria? Conspecto illo erigunt sese, corpus interponunt, intumescunt, horrent pilis plumisque, ad terrorem arma expediunt, rostrum, dentes, ungues, cornua, calces hosti opponunt: quin &, si vis major ingruat, dolis haud raro utuntur, ad avertendum à præda vel hac ratione insidiatorem. Surreptâ verò sobole, quanta in multis comploratio, quantis aerem implent questibus, quam in-
units.tr: Indeed, for the true cognition in brutes, which we have now described, we need no other argument for its demonstration than the amazing operations of the brutes themselves. These offer an unanswerable proof, yet they are neglected for this reason alone, and are less effective in establishing this truth for many people, because they are met with every day. But the careful examiner of things, who gives his mind to studying them more deeply, finds in them a trace of reason, as it were, and a certain imitation of it, so that one can scarcely, indeed hardly, attribute it to mere sensitive cognition. So varied are the actions of beasts, to the point of wonder, and so like the human ways of acting. Of a thousand examples I shall touch on only one or two in passing. How great is the care of brutes in rearing their young, even those who regurgitate their food, having deprived their own stomach, to feed what they have already devoured? How great is their courage and diligence in defending the same young against an enemy? When they catch sight of him they raise themselves up, interpose their bodies, swell, bristle with hair or feathers, prepare their weapons for terror, and oppose to the foe beak, teeth, claws, horns and hooves. Nay, if greater force attacks them, they not seldom use tricks to turn the plunderer away from the prey. And when the offspring has been snatched away, what lamentation there is in many, how they fill the air with their cries, how unceasing their grief! How provident is the care of all in preserving themselves by strength or by cunning, in distinguishing harmful food from harmless, in seeking remedies for their diseases and wounds! Can all these things be done without true cognition? I should like to have this explained.

units.la: IV. Veræ cognitionis brutorum tot existunt testimonia, quot ferè eorundem obviæ sunt operationes. infolabilis mœror? Quam provida omnium cura in sese vel vi vel dolo conservandis, in pabulis noxiis ab innoxiis discernendis, in morborum vulnerumque suorum remediis indagandis? Istæc omnia qui absque vera cognitione fieri queant? explicari velim. Non hic seriem attexam eorum quæ narrantur de Apum industria, Formicarum disciplina, Canum sagacitate, Vulpium astutia, Cornicum solertia, Elephantis docilitate, Equi generositate, Ciconiæ pietate, &c. quæ veram cognitionem sensitivam Brutorum tam abunde evincunt, ut eâ quoque data, illorum plurima nihilominus vel subtilissimum ingenium haud parum vexare possint. Copiosam historiolarum huc pertinentium congeriem habet Rorarius, in Exercitatione Paradoxa, Quod animal a bruta ratione utan-tur melius hominē quæ sola sufficit abunde confutandis iis, quæ De Carentia Sensus & Cognitionis in Brutis, nuper scripsere quidam, non absque multa sui in re hac tractanda contradictione. Missis nunc aliis unum summamus notum atque obvium, in quo explicando vires experiantur velim quotquot Brutis veram cognitionem denegant: Cur scil. canis, cum famelicus furtim quid abstulit, clam se surripiat, & diffidenter adeo incedat ut nemini occurrenti gratuletur, sed meticulosè sibi à pœnis cavens, rostro prono & aversa suam pergat viam? En Rhodus, en saltus!
units.tr: IV. There are as many testimonies to the true cognition of brutes as there are operations of theirs that meet us. I shall not here set out the series of things that are told of the industry of bees, the discipline of ants, the sagacity of dogs, the cunning of foxes, the cleverness of crows, the docility of elephants, the spirit of horses, the affection of storks, and so on, which so abundantly prove the true sensitive cognition of brutes that, even if it be granted, many of their actions could still greatly perplex the subtlest mind. Rorarius, in his paradoxical exercise, That an animal uses brute reason better than man, has a copious heap of little stories pertaining to this, which alone suffices to refute abundantly those things which certain men have written lately On the Lack of Sense and Cognition in Brutes, not without much self-contradiction in treating this matter. Setting aside others now, let us take up one common and obvious example, in explaining which I should like all who deny true cognition to brutes to test their strength: why, namely, when a dog, being hungry, has stolen something, does he slink away secretly, and walk so timidly that he does not rejoice in meeting anyone, but, anxiously guarding himself against punishment, goes on his way with head lowered and turned aside? Here is Rhodes, here is the leap!

units.la: Quum itaque per ista constet satis de Vera Cognitione Brutorum facile inde conficitur, necessario in iis admitti debere Substantiale aliquod ejusdem Principium. Præterquam enim, quod nobiliores sint istæ operationes, quam ut à sola accidentali materiæ dispositione oriri queant, etiam sic inferebam isthoc loco, unde petitur controversa assertio. Solidè demonstrari potest, ipsum Neotericorum ergastulum quinque Modorum, Mensuræ, Quietis, Motus Positura, Figuræ, operationum principium nec esse, nec esse posse. Quum enim uti res existit, ita quoque eadem operetur; Modi vero illi non sint, nisi beneficio substantiæ cui insunt, etiam iidem operari non poterunt, nisi vi alicujus principii substantialis: quod cum non sit materia, utpote pure passiva, restat ut sit aliquod aliud in corpore substantiale operationum principium. Cui accedit, quod omnes isti modos vel non-entia esse, vel tantum conditiones ad operandum præœquisitas, non autem causas, sigillatim facile probari possit. Ad ista dum plane silent Censores, manet immota vis hujus ratiocinii. Nunc addo
units.tr: Since, therefore, it is sufficiently established from these things what the true cognition of brutes is, it is easily inferred that in them there must necessarily be admitted some substantial principle of the same. For, besides the fact that these operations are too noble to arise from the mere accidental disposition of matter, I also argued in this place, from which the disputed assertion is drawn, as follows: It can be firmly demonstrated that the modern prison of the five modes, of measure, of rest, of position, of motion and of figure, is not, and cannot be, the principle of operations. For since a thing acts in the same way as it exists, and those modes are not except by the benefit of the substance in which they inhere, they likewise cannot operate except by the power of some substantial principle. Since matter, being purely passive, is not this principle, it remains that there is some other substantial principle of operations in the body. To this must be added that all these modes can easily be proved, one by one, either to be non-entities or merely conditions prerequisite for acting, and not causes. While the critics are entirely silent about these points, the force of this reasoning remains unshaken. Now I add:

units.la: Cur obsecrò sensuum organa Brutis concessa, nostris per omnia similia, nisi corundem similis sit ei qui est nostrorum usus? Atqui instrumentorum sensationi destinatorum & inservientium nullus hic existit in nobis absque Animæ nostræ attentione & præsidio. Hoc vel indè liquet, quòd, quoties mens hærens in profunda meditatione aliud agit, nullatenus corpus afficiatur ab oblatis per organa, cæterum omni ex parte bene constituta, rebus externis, etiam maximè terribilibus ac perniciosis; sed immotum adeò manet, ac si eæ neutiquam sensorio objicerentur. Nemo est qui non id experiatur in se sæpius; fidemque ejus facit plenissimam nota cœdes Archimedis Syracusani, à milite, dum stricti gladii imago à mente, speculationibus mathematicis nimiùm immersa, non percipitur, infeliciter jugulati. Unde sequitur quam evidentissimè, ad operationes istiusmodi producendas, quales & nobis & brutis communes esse observamus, passivam receptionem externi motùs in solo corpore minimè sufficere, sed prorsùs requiri Animæ, tanquam Principii Substantialis, activam objecti perceptionem, & in spiritus per nervos mittendos imperium. Ut longè sit salsissimum quod asserit Cartesius, Part. II. Epist. VIII. Bruta tantummodo videre sic nos, dum mente alio avocata, licet objecto- rum externorum imagines in retina nostra pingantur, & forte etiam il- lorum impressiones in nervis opticis factæ ad diversos motus membra nostra determinent, nihil tamen prorsus eorum sentimus. Quin, ut & hoc addam, nisi ex effectis istis in Brutis conspicuis valeat argumentatio ad evincendam alicujus in iisdem Principii substantialis existentiam, velim equidem mihi à Cartesiano homine demonstrari, inesse re verâ Animam substantialem infantibus aliisque usu rationis destitutis hominibus; etenim in hisce aliæ nullæ obviæ sunt actiones, quam quæ eadem deprehenduntur in Brutis.
units.tr: Why, I beg you, were organs of sense given to brutes which are in every respect like ours, unless their use is like that of ours? Yet there is here in us no instrument destined and serving for sensation without the attention and presence of our soul. This is clear at once from the fact that, whenever the mind, held fast in deep meditation, is busy with something else, the body is in no way affected by the things presented through the organs, although in every other respect it is well constituted, even by external things most terrible and dangerous; rather, it remains so motionless as if those things were not presented to the sensorium at all. Everyone experiences this in himself often, and the well-known slaughter of Archimedes of Syracuse by a soldier makes it fully credible: while his mind, too deeply immersed in mathematical speculations, did not perceive the image of the drawn sword, he was unhappily cut down. Whence it follows most evidently that, to produce operations of this kind, such as we observe to be common both to us and to brutes, the passive reception of external motion in the body alone is by no means sufficient, but there is required, altogether, the active perception of the object by the soul as a substantial principle, and command over the spirits to be sent through the nerves. So very salty is what Descartes asserts, Part. II. Epist. VIII.: Brutes only see as we do when, with the mind called away elsewhere, although images of external objects are painted on our retina, and perhaps also their impressions made on the optic nerves determine our limbs to various motions, we nevertheless perceive nothing of them at all. Moreover, to add this too: unless the argument from these effects visible in brutes is valid for proving the existence of some substantial principle in them, I should indeed like to be shown by a Cartesian that a substantial soul truly is present in infants and other men destitute of the use of reason; for in these there are no other actions to be seen than those which are found in brutes.

units.la: Efficacissimum hujus ratiocinationis robur nec ipse ignoravit Cartesius, dum planè se hìc irretitum ostendit; eo usque, ut non tam difficultates illas tollere nitatur, quam urgere alias, quas ipse (licet perperam) ex oppositâ sententia fluere autumat: quem clarum & distinctum philosophandi modum minimè esse, sed ejus potius qui ad incitas est redactus, norunt quotquot ex Logicis intelligunt, quantum valeat indirecta ejusmodi responsio, scindit nimirum sic nodum, cui solvendo se quis imparem experitur.
units.tr: Descartes himself did not fail to recognise the most powerful force of this reasoning, while he shows himself here plainly entangled, to such a degree that he tries not so much to remove those difficulties as to press others, which he (though wrongly) claims follow from the opposite opinion. Whoever understands logic knows that this is not the clear and distinct mode of philosophising, but rather that of one who has been driven into a corner. How much an indirect response of this kind is worth: it cuts the knot, since a man finds himself unequal to untying it.

units.la: {Hhh 2} Sed volupe fuerit Viri, cæterùm animi confidentissimi, ac mirè crepantis ubiquè claras & distinctas ideas, hac in parte observasse hæsitationes. Sic ipse, Part. 1. Epist. lv. „Hoc ergo solum dici „possit, quod licet bruta nihil agant, quod probet illa cogitare (notandum Cogitare Cartesio idem esse quod Cognoscere; tametsi nobis ista duo distent tanquam species & genus) tamen quia corporis illorum organa à nostris valdè diversa non sunt, conjicere „licet, aliquam esse cogitationem hisce organis adjunctam, quemadmodum in nobis experimur, licet ipsorum cogitatio sit imperfectior „nostra. Ad quod nihil est quod respondeam, nisi quod si illa cogitarent, ut nos, animam etiam, ut & nos, immortalem haberent; quod non est verosimile, &c. Iterùm, Epist. lxvii. „Quamvis autem pro demonstrato habeam, probari non posse, „aliquam esse in brutis cogitationem; non ideo puto posse demonstrari nullam esse: quia mens humana eorum corda non pervadit. „Sed examinando, quidnam sit hac de re maximè probabile, nullam video rationem pro brutorum cogitatione militare, præter „hanc unam, quod cum habeant oculos, aures, linguam, & „reliqua sensuum organa sicut nos, verisimile sit, illa sentire sicut „nos; & quia in nostro sentiendi modo cogitatio includitur, similem etiam illis cogitationem tribuendam, &c. Rursùs, „Epist. cv. „Quantum ad animalia bruta, videmus quidem in „illis motus quosdam eorum similes, qui imaginationes nostras „sive sensus consequuntur; imaginationes verò aut sensus utrum illa „habeant ignoramus. E contra vero, cum isti iidem motus possint „absque imaginatione fieri, non sine causa suspicari possumus, illos in iis ita produci, quemadmodum spero me oste„furum, &c.
units.tr: But it would be amusing to observe the hesitations of this man, who was very confident in spirit and loudly boasted of clear and distinct ideas everywhere, on this point. He himself says, Part. 1, Letter lv: "So this only can be said, that although beasts do nothing that proves they think (it should be noted that for Descartes to think is the same as to know, although for us these two differ as species and genus), nevertheless, since the organs of their bodies are not very different from ours, one may conjecture that some thought is joined to these organs, just as we experience in ourselves, although their thought is more imperfect than ours. To this I have nothing to reply, except that if they did think as we do, they would also have an immortal soul as we do, which is not likely, etc." Again, Letter lxvii: "Although I hold it as proved that it cannot be shown that there is any thought in brutes, I do not think it can therefore be demonstrated that there is none, since the human mind does not penetrate their hearts. But examining what is most probable in this matter, I see no reason that supports thought in brutes except this one: since they have eyes, ears, tongue and the other organs of sense as we do, it is likely that they feel as we do; and since thought is included in our way of feeling, thought similar to ours must also be attributed to them, etc." Again, Letter cv: "As for brute animals, we indeed see in them certain motions like ours, which follow our imaginations or senses; but whether they have imaginations or senses we do not know. On the contrary, since these same motions can occur without imagination, we can reasonably suspect that they are produced in them in the way I hope I have shown, etc."

units.la: Videmus totum hic trepidantem Cartesium, nihil habentem quod respondeat, putantem, probabile dicentem, ignorantem, suspicantem; quæ quousque satisfaciant rationibus antè à nobis allatis, judicium sit penes quemvis extra partes constitutum Philosophum! Uti verò ipse dubitanti hic propior est quam quid certi determinanti, ita inter assectas ejus non desunt viri eruditi, qui quamvis cæterùm cum eo faciant, atque etiam præse ferant, explicari satis posse bestiarum actiones per solum motum partiumque dispositionem, & in hoc demonstrando multùm sint operosi, tandem
units.tr: Here we see Descartes all trembling, having nothing to reply, thinking, speaking of probability, ignorant, suspecting. How far these satisfy the arguments we have given before is a matter for any philosopher standing outside the parties to judge! But just as he is here closer to one who doubts than to one who determines anything certain, so among his followers there are not lacking learned men who, although otherwise they agree with him and even profess that the actions of beasts can be sufficiently explained by motion alone and the arrangement of parts, and labour greatly in demonstrating this, in the end

units.la: VII. Sectatorum ejus alii ad animam mundi Platonicam confugiunt, alii etiam hominum animas subjiciunt tandem tamen re omni accuratius perpensâ, adeò parum sibi in solis accidentibus & modis possunt satisfacere, ut non obscurè indicent, minimè se alienos esse, pro salvandis brutorum operationibus, ab opinione Platonica, quâ asseritur totam Universi materiam singulasque ejus partes mente instructas esse, eamque mentem pro diversitate dispositionis in materia diversimodè agere; ut sit
units.tr: VII. Some of his followers take refuge in the Platonic world-soul; others even subject the souls of men to it. Yet when they have weighed everything most carefully, they can satisfy themselves so little with accidents and modes alone that they clearly indicate they are by no means strangers, for the sake of saving the operations of brutes, to the Platonic opinion, by which it is asserted that the whole matter of the universe and each of its parts is furnished with mind, and that this mind acts in different ways according to the different arrangement of matter; so that

units.la: Inde hominum pecudumque genus animæque volantum, Et quæ marmoreo fert monstra sub æquore pontus.
units.tr: "Thence the race of men and beasts, and the souls of winged things, and the monsters that the sea bears beneath its marble surface." [Inde hominum pecudumque genus vitaeque volantum, et quae marmoreo fert monstra sub aequore pontus.]

units.la: Ex quibus elucet clarissimè vis nostræ veritatis, de Substantiali veræ cognitionis in Brutis principio, quippe quæ etiam pervicacissimos fateri,
units.tr: From these things the force of our truth shines out most clearly, concerning the substantial principle of true cognition in brutes, since even the most obstinate are compelled to confess it,

units.la: Esse apibus partem divinæ mentis, & haustus æthereos, sicque in anilia Platonis figmenta de anima mundi concedere cogit potius, quam omne substantiale cognitionis & activitatis principium bestiis denegare. Atque utinam neque hodiè existeret numerosa illorum cohors, qui ex denegata brutis substantiali anima, vitæ ac cognitionis veræ principio, occâsionem sumsissent paria philosophandi de mente humana, atque tandem in non-entium classem compingendi pariter pecudumque hominumque animas. Tales nati sunt ex hac Spina flosculi.
units.tr: "that bees have a share of the divine mind and ethereal draughts" [Esse apibus partem divinæ mentis, et haustus aethereos], and so compels them to concede the old wives' fictions of Plato about the world-soul, rather than to deny to beasts every substantial principle of cognition and activity. And would that there did not exist today a numerous band of those who, from denying a substantial soul to brutes, the principle of life and of true cognition, have taken occasion to philosophize in the same way about the human mind, and at last to rank the souls of beasts and of men alike among non-beings. Such flowerets have sprung from this thorn.
VIII.

units.la: Et ista quidem pro assertionis nostræ Veritate confirmanda, tum ex ipsa rei natura, tum ex varia adversariorum philosophatione, paucis adducta sufficiant. Per omnia nunc ire non finit instituti ratio, quæ intra brevitatis terminos hac vice nos cogit. Quamobrem neque operosus ero in urgenda Auctoritate Sacra, pluribus locis bestiis exertissimè tribuente Vitam & Cognitionem, istudque Spiraculum halitus vitæ, quod, à corpore distinctum, in morte ab eo separetur, &c. Miror autem hoc loco vehementer Censorum mearum vel ignorantiam vel impudentiam, dum inquiunt, Verbum Dei etiam sic loqui de rebus inanimatis, quibus tamen ideo substantiale principium cognitionis non convenit. Ubi verò sic loquitur Spiritus S.? Non ignoro, Vita, itemque Anime, vocabulum impropriè nonnunquam usurpari, & per catachresin, ut cum Aqua v. c. dicitur Viva; Cadaver vocatur Anima; &c. At ubi locorum rei vitâ destitutæ conjunctim tribuitur נפש חיה, רוח חיים, נשמת רוח חיים, Anima vivens, Spiritus vitæ, Flatus spiritus vitæ? vitæ? Nusquam certè. Tantum quandò vel de homine, vel de bestia sermo est, vel de utroque, promiscuè occurrunt istæ voces; claro indicio, aliquid Bestiis inesse Animæ humanæ analogum, quod idem rebus cæteris non competat. Præterea, ne prolixior sim in hisce, efficacissimas phrases, quibus brutis tribuitur Cognitio, Mors eadem cum hominibus, &c. Adquæ si sufficiat simpliciter ex Philosophiæ Cartesianæ principiis respondere, ea improprie debere accipi, viderint Theologi, an non hac ratione Philosophia reipsâ statuatur S. Scripturæ interpres? Viderint simul, ne tandem eâdem viâ enerventur Scripturæ dicta, quæ Animam humanam esse principium substantiale post fata superstes, demonstrant.
units.tr: These points, briefly set out, may suffice to confirm the truth of our assertion, both from the nature of the thing itself and from the varied philosophizing of our opponents. The plan of this work does not allow me to go through everything, since the limits of brevity compel me on this occasion. For that reason I will not labour to press the Sacred Authority, which in many places most plainly ascribes life and cognition to beasts, and calls that breath of life, which, distinct from the body, is separated from it at death, and so on. I marvel greatly, however, at this point at the ignorance or the impudence of my critics, when they say that the Word of God speaks in this way also of inanimate things, to which, nonetheless, a substantial principle of cognition does not belong for that reason. Where, then, does the Holy Spirit speak thus? I am not unaware that the words life and soul are sometimes used improperly and by catachresis, as when water, for example, is called living, and a corpse is called a soul, and so on. But where is a thing deprived of life joined with the phrases נפש חיה [nephesh chayah, living soul], רוח חיים [ruach chayim, spirit of life], נשמת רוח חיים [neshmat ruach chayim, breath of the spirit of life], living soul, spirit of life, breath of the spirit of life? Nowhere, certainly. Only when the discourse is about a human being, or a beast, or both, do these expressions occur indiscriminately. This is a clear sign that something belongs to beasts which is analogous to the human soul, and which does not likewise belong to other things. Moreover, lest I be too lengthy on these matters, there are the most forceful phrases by which cognition and a death the same as that of men are ascribed to beasts, and so on. And if it is enough simply to reply from the principles of Cartesian philosophy that these phrases must be taken improperly, let the theologians see whether philosophy is not thereby actually set up as the interpreter of Holy Scripture. Let them see, too, lest at last by the same route the sayings of Scripture be weakened, which show that the human soul survives after death as a substantial principle.
IX.

units.la: Quorsum vero, inquiunt, hujusmodi assertio abit? Eo abit, dicam, ut ne bruta convertantur in horologia & lapides, in quæ illa convertunt revera Cartesiani, quandò cognitionem eis denegant, & sensum, & vitam, & animam, & omnia. Hic autem sese prodit audacia hominum incredibilis. Quis Cartesianorum, regerunt, quando, ubi id asseruit? Nullus. Quid? Non credo ignorare viros Cartesii Tractatum de Homine, in quo totus id agit, ut ostendat, Corpus animalis instar machinæ automaticæ moveri. Sed os obstruat Viris ipse Cartesius, qui sic expresse, Part. I. Epist. LV. "Bruta per organa agunt, haud secus quam horologium, quod horam longè melius indicat, quam possumus judicio assequi. Et sine dubio, quando hirundines verno tempore adveniunt, catenus agunt horologiorum instar. Quicquid etiam agunt apes, ejusdem est naturæ, &c. Iterum, Part. II. Epist. XLIV. Quicquid in irrationalibus animalibus appetitus aut propensiones vocamus, per solas Mechanicas regulas explico. Et, Ibid. Epist. XL. "Quod ad bruta, adeo assueti sumus credere quod illa, non secus quam homines, sentiant, ut facile non fit opinionem hanc deponere. Sed, si æque assueti essemus videre automata, quæ actiones nostras omnes imitarentur, quas quidem imitari possunt, atque illa pro automatis habere, neutiquam dubitaremus quin animalia ratione destituta forent quoque automata. "Quippe inter nos & illa eandem differentiam adverteremus, quam inter nos & automata; sicuti scripsi pag. 56. methodi mex. In "mundo autem meo accuratissimè recensui quo modo organa omnia ,, omnia ad has in automatis actiones exercendas requisita in anima,, lium corporibus reperiantur. Ecce, & quando, & ubi hæc afferuerit ipse Cartesius ! Quibus convenienter non semel à Cartesianis Philosophis publicè defensum: Bruta nec cognoscunt, nec sentiunt, sed omnia automatice agunt. Item: Eodem ritu, quo artefacta suas producunt operationes, eadem producunt naturalia, cum inter hac & illa nulla nisi forte graduum sit distinctio. Atqui hæc non mutat speciem, uti scimus. Absolvam H. Mori verbis, quibus assertionis hujus nostræ scopus lepidè comprehenditur, simul & Cartesiani dogmatis absurditas facetè perstringitur. Is ad Car-tesium, Part. 1. Epist. lxvi. hac de re hunc in modum: ,, Cæte-,, rum à nulla tuarum opinionum animus meus, pro ea qua est mol-,, litie ac teneritudine, æque abhorret, ac ab internecina illa jugu,,latrice sententia, quam in Methodo tulisti, brutis omnibus vi-,, tam sensumque eripiens, dicam, an potius præripiens ? neque ,,enim vixisse unquam pateris. Hic non tam suspicio rutilantem ,, tui ingenii aciem, quam reformido, utpote de animantium fato ,, sollicitus, acumenque tuum non subtile solum agnosco, sed ,,chalybis instar rigidum ac crudele, quod uno quasi ictu univer-,, sum ferme animantium genus vita ausit sensuque spoliare, in mar-,, mora & machinas vertendo.
units.tr: But where, they say, does such an assertion lead? It leads, I answer, to this: that beasts are turned into clocks and stones, which is exactly what the Cartesians actually do when they deny beasts cognition, sensation, life, soul, and everything. Here, however, the incredible audacity of these men shows itself. Which Cartesian, they reply, ever asserted this, and when, and where? No one. What? I do not believe that they are ignorant of Descartes's Treatise on Man, in which he is wholly intent on showing that the body of an animal is moved like an automatic machine. But let Descartes himself silence these men, who state so expressly, Part I, Letter LV: "Beasts act through their organs, no differently than a clock, which indicates the hour far better than we can judge it. And undoubtedly, when swallows arrive in the spring, they act in this respect like clocks. Whatever bees do is of the same nature, etc." Again, Part II, Letter XLIV: "Whatever we call appetites or propensities in irrational animals, I explain by mechanical rules alone." And ibid., Letter XL: "As for beasts, we are so accustomed to believe that they feel just as men do, that it is not easy to put this opinion aside. But if we were equally accustomed to see automata which imitate all our actions, as far as they can be imitated, and to regard them as automata, we would by no means doubt that animals lacking reason are automata too. For we would notice between ourselves and them the same difference that we notice between ourselves and automata, as I wrote on page 56 of the Method. In my World I have also set out in detail how all the organs, all the things required in automata to perform these actions, are found in the bodies of animals." See, when and where Descartes himself asserted these things! In agreement with them, the following has been publicly defended more than once by Cartesian philosophers: Beasts neither know nor feel, but act wholly like automata. Likewise: In the same manner in which artefacts produce their operations, natural things produce theirs, since between these and those there is no distinction except perhaps of degree. Yet this does not change the species, as we know. I shall conclude with the words of H. More, in which the point of our assertion is neatly summed up, and the absurdity of the Cartesian doctrine is wittily censured. He writes to Descartes, Part I, Letter LXVI, on this matter in these words: "Moreover, my mind, given its own softness and tenderness, shrinks from none of your opinions as much as from that murderous and throat-cutting view which you put forward in the Method, stripping all beasts of life and sensation—or should I say, forestalling them? For you do not allow them ever to have lived. Here I fear not so much the gleaming edge of your wit as I am alarmed on behalf of the fate of living creatures; and I recognize your acumen not only as subtle but as rigid and cruel like steel, which with almost a single blow has dared to strip nearly the whole race of living creatures of life and sensation, turning them into marble and machines."

units.la: Itâ de assertionis nostræ Falsitate vidimus. Inquirendum restat, an non saltem Periculosa sit, aut Nova? Equidem, ex opinione Cartesiana, derogante Brutis omnem propriè dictam vitam, sensum, ac cognitionem, quæ sequuntur absurda, si cum iis con-ferantur, quæ urgeri solent à Recentioribus contra Brutorum cognitionem, adeò ista præ hisce multa & gravia deprehendentur, ut merito hæc nulla præ illis haberi debeant. Quædam eorum jam tetigi, adderemque plura; sed, quod antè monui, constitutum mihi est, non tam rem hanc omnem hic pertractare, quam excutere potius, quæ adferunt huc mei Censores. Demonstrant illi assertionis nostræ periculum. Habent ergò, inquiunt, bruta animam rationalem. Itane ! Quamobrem obsecro ? Illa enim, pergunt, unica est Substantiale Principium, fons, & fundamentum Veræ Cognitionis. En argumentum, quod aliud nihil est quam futilis petitio principii. Nempè controvertitur, An, non in homine tantùm, sed & in brutis, datur Substantiale Verae Cognitionis tionis Principium ? Negant hi; idque quia sola anima rationalis est Verae Cognitionis Principium. Atqui hoc ipsum erat τὸ κριτήριον: quod cum nullâ ratione demonstrent, satis hîc causam tradunt; imprimis cum jam dudum Adversarios ad id agendum invitaverim eo ipso in loco, unde hanc Thefin sibi exagitandam sumpsere. Dabam ibidem discrimen satis ingens & manifestum inter Cognitionem Veram Sensitivam brutorum, & Rationalem spirituum ac hominum; ut mirer, eos petere, assignari sibi essentialem differentiam, quae hominis inter brutique cognitionem intercedat. Quod si non ista sufficiant, addam quae in meis ad Physiologiam. Dan. Voet Notis sic alibi: „Ex quo videre licet longum „discrimen inter Sensationem Hominis & Bruti. Hujus animae „directò tantùm imago rei sensibilis imprimitur: illa notionem „spiritualem ipsa format. Consequenter, haec suae sensationis sibi „non est conscia: illa se sentire intelligit. Haec imagines sensibi„les conjungere ipsa non potest; multo minus per consequentiam „unam ex alia formare: illa notiones judicando copulat aut divi„dit; quin & sensatione utitur tanquam occasione proferendi per „discursum cognitionem suam etiam ad non-sensibilia. Haec ex „mero naturae instinctu ad actiones secundum sensationem insti„tuendas impellitur; illa, intercedente judicio, secundum sen„sum vivit. Facessant itaque, qui Bruta in Horologia conver„tunt, omnique sensu exuunt, inani metu, ne si sensus conce„datur iisdem, simul concedenda sit cogitatio & rationalitas. Quod si neque illa capere queant quae clarissima & distinctissima sunt, condonandum veniet animulis altùm adeò meditationibus de Deo & Mente humana sepultis, ut desuevefint jam dudùm concipere quicquam, quod non ad sublimes Cartesii speculationes de Dubitatione, de Mente quae nil sit nisi Cogitatio, de Ideis innatis claris & distinctis, &c. pertineat.
units.tr: Thus we have seen the falsity of our assertion. It remains to inquire whether it is not at least dangerous, or new. Indeed, from the Cartesian opinion, which denies to beasts all life, sensation and cognition properly so called, the absurdities that follow, if they are compared with those usually urged by recent writers against the cognition of beasts, will be found so many and so grave that they ought rightly to be regarded as nothing by comparison. I have already touched on some of them, and I could add more; but, as I said before, I have resolved not so much to treat this whole matter here as to examine what my critics bring forward. They claim that our assertion is dangerous. Therefore, they say, beasts have a rational soul. Really? And why, I ask? For that soul, they go on, is the sole substantial principle, the source and foundation of true cognition. Here is an argument which is nothing but a futile begging of the question. Obviously the point in dispute is whether a substantial principle of true cognition is given not only in man but also in beasts. These men deny it, and that because the rational soul alone is the principle of true cognition. But this very thing was the point at issue (τὸ κριτήριον); since they do not demonstrate it by any reasoning, they here furnish enough of a cause for doubt, especially since I long ago invited the opponents to undertake exactly this, in the very place from which they took up this thesis to be tested. There I drew a distinction sufficiently large and manifest between the true sensitive cognition of beasts and the rational cognition of spirits and men, so that I wonder that they seek to have assigned to them an essential difference which lies between the cognition of man and that of beasts. If these things are not enough, I will add what I have said elsewhere in my notes to Daniel Voetius's Physiology: "From this it can be seen that there is a long distance between the sensation of man and that of beast. In the soul of the latter only the image of the sensible thing is impressed directly; the former forms the spiritual notion itself. Consequently, the latter is not conscious of its own sensation; the former understands that it senses. The latter cannot join sensible images together, much less form one from another by inference; the former joins and divides notions by judgment, and indeed uses sensation as an occasion for extending its knowledge by discourse even to non-sensibles. The latter is driven by the mere instinct of nature to carry out actions in accordance with sensation; the former, with judgment intervening, lives according to sense. Let, then, those who turn beasts into clocks and strip them of all sensation go away, troubled by an empty fear that if sensation is granted to them, thought and rationality must be granted at the same time. But if they cannot grasp even what is most clear and most distinct, then allowance must be made for little souls so buried in deep meditations on God and the human mind that they have long since lost the habit of conceiving anything that does not pertain to the lofty speculations of Descartes on doubt, on the mind which is nothing but thought, on clear and distinct innate ideas, and so on."

units.la: Instant tamen, Si habeant bruta Substantiale Principium Verae Cognitionis, nec tamen animâ rationali gaudeant, etiam concludi nequit, hanc in homine dari. Quod totum concedendum est illis, quibus inter Cognitionem & Cogitationem nihil intercedit differentiae: non iis, qui alteram ab altera distinctam asserunt, ea quo explicui modo. Itaque ex mera & nuda Cognitione, per spectata, nemo unquam solidè adstruxerit animae quae in homine est rationalitatem: nihil enim rationalitatis in notione Vera Cogni-tionis involvi, jam docuimus. Meritò tamen atque efficacissimè infertur animæ humanæ rationalitas, ex hominis Cognitione; non, uti dixi, quatenus simpliciter est Vera cognitio, sed in quantum ea involvit, quibus salvandis qualiscunque Vera cognitio non sufficit, sed ea præcisè rationalis requiritur. Sic passim Philosophi Animæ Humanæ, ut Spiritualitatem & Rationalitatem, ita Immortalitatem, demonstrare solent, & rectè quidem, ex eo quòd ipsa percipiat cum conscientia, etiam res spirituales, quæque directè sensum non afficiunt; quòd judicio spirituales notiones connectat, & secundum illud omnes cæteras actiones dirigat; quòd ex cognita veritate una aliam hactenùs ignotam vel dubiam concludat, &c. Neminem verò unquam videre contigit, Cartesii assectas si excipias, qui ex qualicunque Vera Cognitione mox principii cognoscentis rationalitatem inferat; cum nihil magis tritum sit auctoribus, quam dividere Veram Cognitionem in Sensitivam & Rationalem. Adstrui igitur validè potest, animam humanam rationalem esse, etiamsi non id concludatur ex ipsa cognitione, quatenus ea simpliciter est verè talis.
units.tr: They press further: if brutes have a substantial principle of true cognition and yet do not possess a rational soul, it cannot be concluded that such a soul is given in man. All of this must be conceded to those who see no difference between cognition and cogitation, but not to those who assert that the two are distinct, in the way I have explained. Therefore no one has ever soundly established the rationality of the soul in man from bare and simple cognition alone, since we have already shown that rationality is not involved in the notion of true cognition. Yet the rationality of the human soul is rightly and most effectively inferred from man's cognition, not, as I have said, insofar as it is simply true cognition, but insofar as it involves things which cannot be accounted for by any true cognition whatever, and for which a cognition that is precisely rational is required. Thus philosophers usually prove the spirituality and rationality of the human soul, and likewise its immortality, and they do so rightly, from the fact that the soul perceives with consciousness even spiritual things, which do not directly affect the senses; that by judgement it connects spiritual notions and directs all its other actions by them; that from one truth known it concludes another hitherto unknown or doubtful, and so on. But no one has ever been found, except the followers of Descartes, who from any sort of true cognition at once infers the rationality of the knowing principle, since nothing is more commonplace among writers than to divide true cognition into sensitive and rational. Therefore it can be strongly maintained that the human soul is rational, even if this is not concluded from cognition itself, insofar as it is simply true of that kind.

units.la: Frustrà eris, si urgeas, tametsi major sit cognitio in homine, id rei essentiam minimè mutare; juxta effatum Philosophorum, Magis & minus non variant speciem. Nunquam enim quisquam eorum, quod sciam, qui Veram Cognitionem brutis tribuunt, asseruit, cognitionem bruti majorem tantùm esse eâ quæ est hominum, sic ut duntaxat per gradus, qui rei essentiam non mutant, distinguantur. Nemo certè existit vel tyro in Philosophicis, qui nesciat Peripateticis dividi Cognitionem, tanquam genus, in Sensitivam & Rationalem, ceu duas oppositas species; uti iisdem ipsum quoque Animal, Anima, Vita sic disponitur? Facultatum prima (nimirùm animæ Sensitivæ in omni animali) est Cognoscitiva, quam Sensum vocamus. COGNOSCERE vox est GENERALIS, & significat QUAMCUNQUE cujuscunque rei PERCEPTIONEM, sive fiat mediis & organis corporis, qualis est Sensus, sive fiat absque adminiculo corporis, qualis est Intellectus. Itâ hac de re disserit, ex mente Peripateticorum, Colleg. Physc. Disp. xi. §. 8. ipse Hereboordius. Pudeat homines impugnare quæ non intelligunt; traducere opiniones receptas quas ignorant! Sed Doctrinæ Peri-
units.tr: You will labour in vain if you urge that, although there is greater cognition in man, this does not in the least change the essence of the thing; according to the saying of the philosophers, greater and less do not vary the species. For no one, so far as I know, who attributes true cognition to brutes has ever asserted that the cognition of a brute is only greater than that of men, so that they are distinguished merely by degrees which do not change the essence of the thing. Surely there is no one, even a beginner in philosophy, who does not know that the Peripatetics divide cognition, as a genus, into sensitive and rational, as two opposed species; just as they arrange in the same way animal itself, soul and life. The first of the faculties (namely, of the sensitive soul in every animal) is the cognitive, which we call sense. COGNOSCERE is a GENERAL word, and signifies the PERCEPTION of WHATEVER THING, whether it takes place through the means and organs of the body, as sense does, or without the aid of the body, as the intellect does. Thus Heereboord himself discusses this matter, according to the mind of the Peripatetics, Colleg. Phys. Disp. xi. §. 8. Let men be ashamed to attack what they do not understand, and to disparage received opinions which they do not know! But the doctrine of the Peripatetics...

units.la: XII. Docente id passim Scholà Peripatetica, nec ipso differente Cartefiano Forgæo.
units.tr: XII. The Peripatetic school teaches this everywhere, and so does the Cartesian Forge himself, who does not differ from them.

units.la: Peripateticæ seu Aristotelicæ mentionem perperam coram illis facio, quibus ipsum hoc nomen vel febrim suo horrore induat. Potius amandabo ad Philosophum Cartesianum doctissimum De la Forge, longè accuratius, quam hi, hac de re hunc in modum Philosophantem, Tract. de Mente Hum. Cap. iv. „Dico, si verum sit, bruta habere aliquem Sensum, aut aliquam perceptionem interiorem, ab actione objectorum externorum super organa sensuum eorum excitatam, & si omnes „ suas actiones instituant hactenus cum animo ita faciendi; ratiocinationes hactenus allatæ, & quæ posthac adferuntur, demonstrant „ necesse esse, ut principium istius perceptionis ac propositi fit spiritale; id autem si ita esset (quod nos non credimus) [quin nec nos id credimus] minimè foret injuriosum homini: nullam enim „video necessitatem statuendi, omne id quod esset spirituale esse „EJUSDEM SPECIEI, & habere easdem perfectiones & prærogativas, quas Spiritus humanus. De cognitione quidem hæc rectè dicuntur: quæ verò de Spiritualitate admiscet, ea suo linquimus loco ac pretio. Arrigant interim ad ista Socii sui verba aures nostri isti blaterones, & discant ex iis sui hujus ratiocinii imperitiam. Si enim judice Forgæo, ne omnis quidem natura Spiritualis necessario ejusdem sit speciei & perfectionis, quanto minus omnem cognitionem ejusdem speciei & perfectionis esse existit necessarium?
units.tr: I speak of the Peripatetic or Aristotelian doctrine wrongly before those who shudder at the very name as if it were a fever. Better to send them to the most learned Cartesian philosopher De la Forge, who philosophises on this matter far more accurately than they do, in these words, Tract. de Mente Hum. Cap. iv.: "I say that, if it is true that brutes have some sense, or some inner perception, excited in them by the action of external objects upon their sense organs, and if all their actions have hitherto been performed with the purpose of acting so; then the arguments adduced so far, and those adduced hereafter, show that it is necessary that the principle of this perception and purpose be spiritual. If this were so (which we do not believe) [indeed we do not believe it], it would be by no means injurious to man: for I see no necessity for holding that everything which was spiritual must be OF THE SAME SPECIES, and have the same perfections and prerogatives, as the human spirit. What is said about cognition is rightly said; but what he mixes in about spirituality we leave to its own place and value. Meanwhile let those chatterers of ours prick up their ears at these words of their fellow, and learn from them the inexperience of his reasoning. For if, in the judgement of De la Forge, not even every spiritual nature is necessarily of the same species and perfection, how much less is it necessary that every cognition be of the same species and perfection?"

units.la: Vidimus Menti humanæ nihil imminere periculi à Vera Cognitione brutorum, ejusdemque in his Principio Substantiali. Unum superest, ut nec Novam esse hanc assertionem nostram demonstremus. Et quid multis inhæream probandæ rei quæ adeò nota, ut nulla magis? Universa schola Peripatetica Sensitivam Cognitionem (quam, uti audivimus, faciunt Veræ Cognitionis speciem, æque ac Rationalem) ut & Appetitum Sensitivum, non minus quam Facultatem Loco-motivam Brutis perindè tribuit ac hominibus. Speciatim communi omnium consensu, docet hæc eadem, Cognitionem Sensitivam non tantum Externos Sensus involvere, sed & Internos; quos numerant, præter Sensum Communem, Phantasiam, Memoriam, nominatim quoque Æstimativam. Quid verò Æstimativa his Auctoribus significet, explicantes audiamus non ex Monasteriis protra-&c.
units.tr: We have seen that no danger to the human mind arises from the true cognition of brutes, and from the substantial principle of the same in them. One thing remains: to show that this assertion of ours is not new. And why should I linger over proving a matter so well known that nothing is more so? The whole Peripatetic school attributes to brutes, no less than to men, sensitive cognition (which, as we have heard, they make a species of true cognition, just as they do the rational), as well as sensitive appetite and the faculty of locomotion. Specifically, by the common consent of all, the same school teaches that sensitive cognition involves not only the external senses but also the internal ones; and they count among the internal senses, besides the common sense, the imagination and the memory, and especially the Estimative. But what the Estimative means to these authors, let us hear them explain, not from the cloisters...

units.la: XIII. Quæ brutis subfantiale verè cognitionis principium tribuit opinio, Vetus est & maxime trita, étos Scholasticos, sed duos in orbe Reformato, ipsaque nostra patria, illustres nostri seculi Philosophos, Burgersdicium & Senguerdium seniorem, illum in inclyta Lugduno-Batava, hunc in nostra Rheno-Trajectina Academia, Philosophiae Professores Clarissimos. Ille sic, Colleg. Phys. Disp. xxvii. Thes. 6. Æstimativa munus est de rebus, quae externis sensibus percepta, aut phantasmatibus repraesentatae fuere, FORMARE NOTIONES BONI AUT MALI. Sic cum ovis videt lupum, &c. format istarum rerum primum phantasmata, & ex iis statim COLLIGIT SPECIEM MALI. Et haec Æstimatio, ait post pauca, in omnibus reperitur animantibus. Alter ita, Introduct. ad Physic. Lib. vi. Cap. v. Æstimativa munus est, æstimare, hoc est, de rebus quae externis sensibus vel phantasia percepta fuerant, FORMARE NOTIONES BONI ET MALI, JUDICARE QUASI, an objecta convenientia, an vero adversa sint, & media hac æstimatione affectus movere; &c. Hinc a nonnullis dicitur, Æstimativam ID ESSE IN BESTIIS, QUOD IN HOMINE RATIO EST. Ex dictis apparet, Æstimativam circa ea quae in sensibus externis fuerant, FORMARE etiam NOTIONES, QUAE IN EXTERNIS SENSORIIS NON FUERANT; rationes enim illae boni & mali ab Æstimativa formantur, quae sensibus externis non erant apprehensae. Ego, ut ingenuè dicam, quamvis omninò item pro Vera Cognitione Brutorum quam ante delineavi, non tamen ausim Brutis tribuere, qualem iis tribuunt hi Auctores cum omnibus fere Antiquioribus Philosophis. Verùm, quid si vel huc usque extendissem notionem vera cognitionis (quod non feci) nihil utique asseruissem, quod non in utraque Academia ante me defenderunt magni doctissimique Viri. Pudeat itaque vel ipsam calumniam, tritam assertionem, ubique ac semper receptam, Novam dicere. De Substantiali Principio non est quod laboremus. Asserunt id quotquot asserunt Formas Substantiales, quas asserere Peripateticos omnes, notum est uniculque. Absolvam verbis Doctissimi Hereboordii, qui Vol. i. Disp. xxxiv. controversiam de Formis huc redire ait, An Forma in rebus naturalibus sit SUBSTANTIA, eaque DIVERSA, AB altero rei naturalis principio, MATERIA? Atque hac DE OMNIBUS, PRÆTER RATIONALEM LEM ANIMAM, FORMIS instituitur quaestio, &c. Mox subjungit : Fateor equidem AB ALIQUOT JAM SECULIS AFFIRMANTIUM OPINIONEM INVALUISSE, atque illas egisse radices in multorum animis, ut, qui contra sentiunt, IN IPSA CENSEANTUR PHILOSOPHIÆ PRINCIPIA IMPINGERE, omnisque veritatis fundamenta subruere, &c. Lubentius Viri hujus hùc adduxi textum, tum quod in eodem Collegio Theologico, in quo ego hæc ventilanda proposui, meus fuerit in ejusdem Pro-Regimine Prædecessor, tum imprimis quod ipse hanc sententiam quam hìc proponit acerrimè impugnaverit ; ut minus suspectum esse debeat hoc testimonium. Eant nunc, qui nostram assertionem innoxiam, Datur in Brutis aliquod substantiale vitæ, sensationis, ac verae cognitionis principium, accusare audent Novitatis periculosæ ; ac nisi pudorem omnem exuerint, discant posthac intelligere prius, quæ Veteres opiniones sint quæ Novæ, quam suum de eo quod ignorant interponant judicium, uti temerarium itâ viro prudente planè indignum.
units.tr: XIII. The opinion that attributes a substantial principle of true cognition to brutes is old and very well worn, held by the Scholastics; but also by two illustrious philosophers of our century in the Reformed world, and in our own country: Burgersdijk and the elder Senguerd, the former in the famous Leiden academy, the latter in our own Utrecht academy, both most distinguished professors of philosophy. The former says thus, Colleg. Phys. Disp. xxvii. Thes. 6. The estimative faculty has the task of concerning things perceived by the external senses, or represented by images, TO FORM NOTIONS OF GOOD OR EVIL. So when a sheep sees a wolf, etc., it forms images of these things first, and from them immediately GATHERS THE SPECIES OF EVIL. And this estimation, he says a little later, is found in all animals. The other says thus: Introduct. ad Physic. Lib. vi. Cap. v. The estimative faculty has the task of estimating, that is, of concerning things which were perceived by the external senses or by the fantasy, TO FORM NOTIONS OF GOOD AND EVIL, TO JUDGE, AS IT WERE, whether objects are suitable or unsuitable, and by this estimation to move the affections; etc. Hence some say that the estimative faculty IS IN BEASTS WHAT REASON IS IN MAN. From what has been said it appears that the estimative faculty, concerning those things which were in the external senses, ALSO FORMS NOTIONS WHICH WERE NOT IN THE EXTERNAL SENSES; for those notions of good and evil which are formed by the estimative faculty were not apprehended by the external senses. To speak frankly, although I wholly agree with the true cognition of brutes which I outlined before, I would nevertheless not dare to attribute to brutes what these authors attribute to them, along with almost all the older philosophers. But what if I had extended the notion of true cognition even this far (which I did not do)? I would certainly have asserted nothing that great and most learned men in both academies have not defended before me. Let them be ashamed, then, even to call new a trite assertion, accepted everywhere and always, which is mere calumny. There is no need for us to labour over the substantial principle. All who assert substantial forms assert it, and it is known to everyone that all the Peripatetics assert substantial forms. I will end with the words of the most learned Heereboord, who in Vol. i. Disp. xxxiv. says that the controversy about forms comes down to this: Is the form in natural things a SUBSTANCE, and DISTINCT from the other principle of the natural thing, MATTER? And this question is raised about ALL FORMS EXCEPT THE RATIONAL SOUL, etc. Soon he adds: I admit indeed that for some centuries the opinion of its affirmers has prevailed, and has struck roots in the minds of many, so that those who think otherwise are considered to attack the principles of philosophy and to undermine the foundations of all truth, etc. I have cited this author's text more willingly, both because in the same Theological College, where I proposed to discuss these matters, he was my predecessor in the pro-rectorship, and especially because he himself most vehemently attacked the opinion which he here puts forward, so that this testimony ought to be the less suspect. Let those now go, who dare to accuse our harmless assertion, There is in brutes some substantial principle of life, sensation, and true cognition, of dangerous novelty; and unless they have cast off all shame, let them learn henceforth to understand which opinions are old and which new, before they interpose their judgement on what they do not know, a rash thing and wholly unworthy of a prudent man.
